shelves.title: Diabetes control by race and ethnicity in US health centers
shelves.question: In US health centers, why do diabetes control rates differ by race and ethnicity — and what closes the gap?
shelves.balance: Black patients run a few points worse than White patients in every UDS era, and the gap survives access and adherence adjustment — it is not only a clinic-door problem. Asian patients run lowest on poor control even though they are tested least, which strengthens rather than weakens the finding — but ‘Asian’ aggregates subgroups that differ, and lumping Asian with NHPI hides the NHPI gap, where published control numbers barely exist.

shelves.title: Glucose production, recycling, and gluconeogenesis (Katz & Tayek)
shelves.question: How much of the glucose your liver makes comes from new synthesis versus recycling — and what changes it in fasting, diabetes, and cancer?
shelves.balance: Across five small physiology studies, the method holds up — a single isotope plus mass isotopomer analysis measures gluconeogenesis, and the corrected production rate matches the tritium gold standard (r=0.86). The biology: after 40 hours of fasting, gluconeogenesis is 92% of glucose production; in diabetes, production runs higher (2.8 vs 1.9) because gluconeogenesis runs higher; in one cancer subgroup, gluconeogenesis supplies most of the glucose and tracks cortisol (r=0.96). The doses matter too: low-dose glucagon raises production only through glycogen breakdown, high-dose through both routes. All of it is small-n physiology — the shelf is a methods story with biological payoffs, not clinical outcomes.

cards.headline: Tayek & Katz 1996: In type 2 diabetes, the liver makes more glucose — because gluconeogenesis runs higher
cards.summary: Tracer study, 17 people after an overnight fast — glucose production 2.8 vs 1.9 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in diabetes vs controls, gluconeogenesis 1.30 vs 0.90 ; but the gluconeogenic share of production was the same (~ 47–49% ).
cards.type: Isotope tracer physiology study ([U-13C]glucose + [6-3H]glucose), Am J Physiol 1996
cards.people: 17 people after an overnight fast (8 controls, 9 with NIDDM)
cards.result: Glucose production (GP) 1.9±0.16 (range 1.3–2.5) controls vs 2.8±0.29 (1.7–4.5) mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ diabetics (P<.05); glucose–GP correlation in diabetes r=0.911 (P<.01). Recycling 8% vs 7% ; dilution by unlabeled carbon 2- vs 2.3-fold ; TCA dilution 1.5-fold (similar). Gluconeogenesis 0.90±0.08 (0.5–1.3) controls vs 1.30±0.13 (0.8–1.9) diabetics (P<.05); GNG share of GP 46.6±4.0% (26–61%) vs 48.8±5.7% (32–83%)
cards.watchOut: n=17 total; the GP difference is driven by gluconeogenesis, but the GNG share of GP is the same (~47–49%) — diabetes makes more glucose overall, not a bigger gluconeogenic fraction
cards.source: Tayek JA, Katz J. Am J Physiol. 1996;270(4 Pt 1):E709–17. PMID 8928779. DOI 10.1152/ajpendo.1996.270.4.E709
cards.search: tayek katz 1996 type 2 diabetes niddm glucose production gluconeogenesis recycling tracer u-13c 6-3h overnight fast american journal physiology pmid 8928779

cards.headline: Tayek & Katz 1997: In one group of cancer patients, gluconeogenesis supplies most of the glucose — and it tracks cortisol
cards.summary: Tracer study, 19 people after an overnight fast — glucose production similar in all groups ( 2.4±0.2 ), but gluconeogenesis 1.9 in the CAI cancer subgroup vs 0.83 in normals, and cortisol tracked the Cori cycle ( r=0.963 in normals).
cards.type: Isotope tracer physiology study ([U-13C]glucose), Am J Physiol 1997
cards.people: 19 people after an overnight fast (6 normal, 13 cancer patients — CAI/CAII)
cards.result: GP similar in all groups, 2.4±0.2 mg·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹. Recycled carbon/Cori cycle elevated in CAI: 15%/33% vs 7.8%/19% (P=0.01). Gluconeogenesis 1.9±0.1 (CAI), 1.0±0.1 (CAII), 0.83±0.11 (NL) mg·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹. NL/CAII: 20% recycling, 20% unlabeled carbon, 60% glycogenolysis; CAI: 30% recycling, 50% unlabeled, 20% glycogen. Cortisol CAI 11.2±1.2 vs CAII 7.7±1.2 µg/dL (P<.05); cortisol–Cori cycle r=0.963 (NL), r=0.771 (CA); cortisol–gluconeogenesis r²=0.967 (NL), 0.727 (CA)
cards.watchOut: n=19, and the cancer population is heterogeneous — only the CAI subgroup shows the gluconeogenic pattern; the correlations are strong but cross-sectional, not proof cortisol causes it
cards.source: Tayek JA, Katz J. Am J Physiol. 1997;272(3 Pt 1):E476–84. PMID 9124555. DOI 10.1152/ajpendo.1997.272.3.E476
cards.search: tayek katz 1997 cancer gluconeogenesis cori cycle cortisol recycling glycogenolysis tracer u-13c overnight fast american journal physiology pmid 9124555

cards.headline: Katz & Tayek 1998: After 40 hours of fasting, gluconeogenesis is 92% of glucose production
cards.summary: Tracer study, 11 healthy fasting volunteers — at 12/20/40 hours, gluconeogenesis was 41% , 71% , 92% of glucose production as glycogen ran out.
cards.type: Isotope tracer physiology study ([U-13C]glucose), Am J Physiol 1998
cards.people: 11 healthy volunteers (n=6 at 12- and 20-h fasts, n=5 at 40-h fast)
cards.result: At 12/20/40 h: blood glucose 93±2, 83±2, 71±2 mg/dL; GP 2.3, 1.8, 1.77 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; carbon recycling 8, 15, 15% ; Cori cycle 18, 35, 36% ; gluconeogenesis 41, 71, 92% of GP ( 0.96, 1.29, 1.64 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹); other sources 1.37, 0.53, 0.15 mg·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
cards.watchOut: n=11 total, healthy fasting volunteers — the cleanest demonstration on the shelf, and the smallest; the Cori-cycle share doubles as glycogen runs out
cards.source: Katz J, Tayek JA. Am J Physiol. 1998;275(3):E537–42. PMID 9725823. DOI 10.1152/ajpendo.1998.275.3.E537

cards.headline: Chhibber, Soriano & Tayek 2000: Low-dose glucagon raises glucose production one way; high-dose, two ways
cards.summary: Pituitary-pancreatic clamp study, 18 normal subjects — low-dose glucagon raised production only via nongluconeogenic release ( 8.3 vs 4.7 µmol/kg/min); high-dose raised both routes.
cards.people: 18 normal subjects (6 low-dose glucagon, 6 high-dose, 6 fasting alone)
cards.result: Low-dose glucagon ( 64±3 vs 44±7 ng/L): GP 15.5±0.5 vs baseline 13.8±0.5 (P<.05), vs fasting-alone 11.5±0.6 ; via nongluconeogenic release nearly doubling ( 8.3±0.6 vs 4.7±0.5 µmol/kg/min, P<.01). High-dose ( 125±25 ng/L): GP 15.8±0.6 vs baseline 13.5±0.5 (P<.05), vs fasting 11.5±0.6 ; via Gneo 8.5±0.5 vs 6.8±0.7 (P<.05) + nongluconeogenic 7.4±0.5 vs 4.7±0.4 (P<.05)
cards.watchOut: n=6 per arm, 4-hour infusions in healthy volunteers — a dose-response mechanism, not a clinical glucagon result
cards.source: Chhibber VL, Soriano C, Tayek JA. Metabolism. 2000;49(1):39–46. PMID 10647062. DOI 10.1016/s0026-0495(00)90638-3

cards.headline: Tayek, Bergner & Lee 1991: The single-isotope correction works: corrected production matches the tritium gold standard
cards.summary: Methods validation, 6 colon cancer patients — corrected hepatic glucose production 2.04±0.12 vs 2.05±0.15 by the (6-3H)glucose gold standard; correlation r=0.86 .

shelves.title: Cancer metabolism: glucose production, anabolism, and the liver
shelves.question: In cancer, why does the body burn glucose differently — and can feeding or hormones reverse it?
shelves.balance: Across eight small Clinical Research Center studies, cancer raises hepatic glucose production and blunts insulin action — worst in the most malnourished, where production hits 2.98 and tracks growth hormone (r=0.71) — while five days of 5-FU nudges production higher still, and the liver’s TPN injury tracks duration of feeding more than the lipid itself (though early lipid drives the AST rise). Growth hormone raises IGF-I threefold but fails to build protein overall; it works only in patients who aren’t yet severely malnourished. And the one survival signal is thin: four metabolic numbers predict survival with 59% accuracy — barely above a coin toss.

cards.headline: Tayek, Bulcavage & Chlebowski 1990: The sicker the weight loss, the higher the liver’s glucose output — and it tracks growth hormone
cards.summary: Physiology study, 44 stage D colorectal cancer patients + 7 cancer-free controls — hepatic glucose production 2.35±0.89 vs 1.75±0.16 mg/kg/min, highest ( 2.98±0.73 ) in the most malnourished, and correlated with fasting growth hormone ( r=0.71 ).
cards.people: 51 people — 44 stage D colorectal cancer patients, 7 cancer-free controls
cards.result: HGP 2.35±0.89 (cancer) vs 1.75±0.16 mg/kg/min (controls) (P<.01); most malnourished (<90% IBW) HGP 2.98±0.73 . Fasting GH 2.9±3.1 vs 0.5±0.2 ng/mL (P<.001), highest in the most malnourished. HGP correlated with fasting GH ( r=0.71 , P<.001), not with cortisol, insulin, T4, T3, or glucose
cards.watchOut: n=51, cross-sectional — the GH correlation is strong but not proof GH causes the rise; GH SD (3.1 on a mean of 2.9) shows how skewed the hormone runs in cancer
cards.source: Tayek JA, Bulcavage L, Chlebowski RT. Cancer Res. 1990;50(7):2119–22. PMID 2317802
cards.search: tayek bulcavage chlebowski 1990 colorectal cancer stage d hepatic glucose production malnutrition growth hormone weight loss cancer research pmid 2317802

cards.headline: Tayek & Katz 1997: Cancer patients make glucose differently — and cortisol tracks the difference
cards.summary: Tracer study, 19 people after an overnight fast — gluconeogenesis 1.9±0.1 in the CAI cancer subgroup vs 0.83±0.11 in normals, and cortisol tracked gluconeogenesis ( r²=0.967 in normals) and the Cori cycle ( r=0.963 ). Re-card — this card also appears on Shelf #34 and is counted once in the library total.
cards.type: Isotope tracer physiology study ([U-13C]glucose), Am J Physiol 1997
cards.people: 19 people after an overnight fast (6 normal, 13 cancer patients — CAI/CAII)
cards.result: Gluconeogenesis 1.9±0.1 (CAI) vs 0.83±0.11 (NL) mg·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹. Cortisol–gluconeogenesis r²=0.967 (NL), 0.727 (CA); cortisol–Cori cycle r=0.963 (NL)
cards.watchOut: n=19, cancer population heterogeneous — only the CAI subgroup shows the gluconeogenic pattern; correlations cross-sectional
cards.source: Tayek JA, Katz J. Am J Physiol. 1997;272(3 Pt 1):E476–84. PMID 9124555. DOI 10.1152/ajpendo.1997.272.3.E476

cards.headline: Tayek, Manglik & Abemayor 1997: Cancer cuts insulin secretion nearly in half — and the underweight make extra glucose on top
cards.summary: IVGTT study, 30 people in a 2×2 design (15 underweight, 15 normal-weight) — acute insulin response down 40–50% in cancer, glucose disposal 1.25–1.27 vs 1.81–1.82 %/min, and glucose production higher in underweight cancer patients ( 13.9±1.3 vs 10.8±0.5 µmol/kg/min).
cards.type: IVGTT physiology study (2×2: cancer × weight), Metabolism 1997
cards.people: 30 people — 15 underweight + 15 normal-weight; 10 head/neck squamous cell cancers, 20 controls
cards.result: Acute insulin response ↓ 40–50% in cancer (both weight groups, P<.05). Glucose disposal 1.25±0.29 / 1.27±0.23 %/min (cancer) vs 1.82±0.21 / 1.81±0.24 (healthy, P<.05). GP ↑ in underweight cancer vs weight-matched volunteers ( 13.9±1.3 vs 10.8±0.5 µmol/kg/min, P<.05). Insulin sensitivity ↓ 32–44% in cancer (P<.05); underweight controls had 2× the insulin sensitivity of normal-weight controls (P<.01)
cards.watchOut: n=30, and leanness itself doubles insulin sensitivity in the controls — weight and cancer pull in opposite directions, and the 2×2 design is what separates them
cards.source: Tayek JA, Manglik S, Abemayor E. Metabolism. 1997;46(2):140–5. PMID 9030818. DOI 10.1016/s0026-0495(97)90291-2
cards.search: tayek manglik abemayor 1997 head neck cancer insulin secretion ivgtt glucose disposal insulin sensitivity underweight metabolism pmid 9030818

cards.headline: Tayek 1995: Cancer’s insulin resistance starts in the muscle’s glucose storage — and low T3 travels with it
cards.summary: Euglycemic clamp study, 8 head/neck cancer patients + 8 weight-matched volunteers — insulin for half-maximal glucose utilization up 58% ( 741±124 vs 470±82 pM); non-oxidative glucose utilization down at low insulin doses, tracking T3 (r up to 0.791 ).
cards.type: Euglycemic clamp study, J Am Coll Nutr 1995
cards.people: 16 people — 8 head/neck cancer patients, 8 weight-matched volunteers
cards.result: Insulin for half-maximal glucose utilization ↑ 58% ( 741±124 vs 470±82 pM, P≤.05). Non-oxidative glucose utilization ↓ at low insulin doses ( 0.1±1.6 vs 6.4±2.1 µmol/kg/min, P≤.05; 15.1±2.0 vs 23.7±1.3 , P<.01). T3 correlated with non-oxidative utilization ( r=0.673, 0.731, 0.791 at the three insulin doses). Insulin sensitivity index 2.4±0.1 vs 4.7±0.7 (dl/min)/(µU/ml), P<.05. Fasting HGP, glucose oxidation, fat oxidation, leucine appearance similar
cards.watchOut: n=16; the T3 link is correlational and the author calls the observations preliminary — the defect appears before any abnormality in glucose production itself
cards.search: tayek 1995 insulin resistance euglycemic clamp non-oxidative glucose utilization t3 thyroid head neck cancer muscle glycogen journal american college nutrition pmid 8568110

cards.headline: Tayek & Brasel 1995: Growth hormone triples IGF-I in malnourished cancer patients — and still fails to build protein
cards.summary: 3-day growth-hormone trial, 10 cancer patients — IGF-I tripled ( 112±15 → 329±54 µg/L) and nitrogen losses fell, but leucine kinetics, glucose production, and overall nitrogen balance did not change; the anabolic signal appeared only in the 7 patients ≥90% IBW.
cards.type: Growth hormone intervention study (0.125 mg/kg/day × 3 days), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1995
cards.people: 10 malnourished cancer patients
cards.result: GH 1.6±0.4 → 15.4±3.0 µg/L; IGF-I 112±15 → 329±54 µg/L; insulin 57±11 → 184±46 pmol/L; glucose 5.4±0.1 → 6.2±0.2 mmol/L (≈97±2 → 112±4 mg/dL); urinary urea N 6.7±0.9 → 4.9±0.5 g (P<.05); total N 7.8±1.2 → 6.0±1.2 g (P<.05). But leucine appearance ( 77.3±4.0 vs 76.1±5.4 ), leucine oxidation ( 11.8±1.5 vs 9.6±1.0 ), HGP ( 13.5±0.8 vs 14.2±0.8 ), nitrogen balance ( −0.24±0.97 vs 0.85±0.75 g/day, P=0.10) NOT changed overall. Subgroup ≥90% IBW (7/10): nitrogen balance −1.46±0.99 → 0.60±1.03 g/day (P<.01); leucine oxidation 14.1±1.3 → 10.0±1.4 ; leucine appearance 81.2±3.8 → 72.9±3.3
cards.watchOut: n=10, 3-day study — the overall null is the headline; the subgroup benefit (7 patients, not severely malnourished) is where the anabolism shows, and the authors’ conclusion is conditional on it
cards.source: Tayek JA, Brasel JA. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1995;80(7):2082–7. PMID 7608259. DOI 10.1210/jcem.80.7.7608259
cards.search: tayek brasel 1995 growth hormone igf-i malnourished cancer nitrogen balance leucine anabolism journal clinical endocrinology metabolism pmid 7608259

cards.headline: Tayek & Chlebowski 1992: Five days of 5-FU pushes glucose production higher in colon cancer
cards.summary: Physiology study, 22 colon cancer patients vs matched volunteers — baseline HGP difference not significant ( 2.09±0.11 vs 1.79±0.10 , P=.10), but 5 days of continuous 5-FU raised fasting glucose ( 97±3 → 106±5 mg/dL) and HGP ( 2.09±0.11 → 2.27±0.10 ).
cards.type: Physiology study with 5-day continuous 5-FU infusion, JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr 1992
cards.people: 22 colon cancer patients vs matched normal volunteers (109±5% vs 104±4% IBW)
cards.result: GH elevated in cancer ( 3.22±0.62 vs 0.73±0.18 ng/mL, P<.05) with IGF-1 unchanged; HGP 2.09±0.11 vs 1.79±0.10 (P=.10, NS); leucine appearance 63.3±3.0 vs 57.7±4.2 (P=.25, NS). 5 days continuous 5-FU: fasting glucose 97±3 → 106±5 mg/dL (P<.05); HGP 2.09±0.11 → 2.27±0.10 (P<.05). Abstract truncated at 250 words
cards.watchOut: The baseline cancer-vs-control differences are NOT significant — the significant finding is the chemotherapy effect within patients; the abstract is truncated, so the full 5-FU results are not all visible
cards.source: Tayek JA, Chlebowski RT. JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 1992;16(6 Suppl):65S–71S. PMID 1287227. DOI 10.1177/014860719201600606

cards.headline: Tayek et al. 1995: Four metabolic numbers predict survival in colon cancer — with 59% accuracy
cards.summary: Metabolism-and-survival study, 22 colon cancer patients on 5-FU + hydrazine sulfate — half died 14±4 months after the study, half were alive 58±2 months later; survival was estimated with 59% accuracy from leucine appearance, HGP, CEA, and insulin.
cards.type: Physiology study with survival follow-up (5-FU + hydrazine sulfate), Am J Med Sci 1995
cards.people: 22 colon cancer patients
cards.result: Fasting glucose 98±2 → 94±2 mg/dL (P<.025); HGP 2.09±0.11 vs 2.03±0.13 (NS); glucose disposal 1.34±0.07 vs 1.47±0.11 %/min (P=0.15, NS); leucine appearance 63.3±3.0 → 57.1±3.9 µmol/kg/hr (P<.025); leucine oxidation unchanged ( 11.5±1.1 vs 11.2±1.1 ). Half died 14±4 months after the study; half alive 58±2 months later. Survival estimated with 59% accuracy from leucine appearance, HGP, CEA, and insulin; leucine appearance directly related to survival length; baseline HGP, CEA, insulin inversely related. Abstract truncated at 250 words
cards.watchOut: 59% accuracy is barely above a coin toss, in 22 patients, with a truncated abstract — the survival model is a suggestion, not a predictor; hydrazine sulfate is a historical therapy
cards.source: Tayek JA, Sutter L, Manglik S, Lillington LB, Grosvenor M, Chlebowski RT. Am J Med Sci. 1995;310(2):48–55. PMID 7631642. DOI 10.1097/00000441-199508000-00002
cards.search: tayek sutter manglik lillington grosvenor chlebowski 1995 survival colon cancer metabolism leucine hepatic glucose production cea insulin hydrazine sulfate american journal medical sciences pmid 7631642

cards.headline: Tayek et al. 1990: Chemical castration lowers glucose production — and the weight gained is fat
cards.summary: 12-month GnRH-agonist study, 10 men with stage C/D prostate cancer — HGP fell linearly ( 80.1±2.9 → 72.5±2.3 mg/m²/min, P<.01) while weight, triceps skinfold, cholesterol, and fat mass rose; total body water unchanged, so the weight gain was fat.
cards.type: Longitudinal intervention study (GnRH agonist buserelin, measured at 0/2/6/12 months), Metabolism 1990
cards.people: 10 men with stage C/D prostate cancer
cards.result: Baseline leucine appearance 76.2±5.4 µM/kg/h and HGP 80.1±2.9 mg/m²/min — both above normal volunteers. Therapy: testosterone/DHT/LH/cortisol ↓, T3/free T3 ↑; energy expenditure and leucine appearance unchanged; HGP fell linearly 80.1±2.9 → 79.9±2.3 → 73.7±3.4 → 72.5±2.3 (P<.01). Weight, triceps skinfold, cholesterol, fat mass ↑; total body water unchanged → weight gain was fat
cards.watchOut: n=10, no control group — the HGP fall and the fat gain are within-patient trends over a year, not a randomized comparison
cards.source: Tayek JA, Heber D, Byerley LO, Steiner B, Rajfer J, Swerdloff RS. Metabolism. 1990;39(12):1314–9. PMID 2123281. DOI 10.1016/0026-0495(90)90190-n

cards.headline: Tayek et al. 1990: On total parenteral nutrition, the liver injury tracks how long you’re fed — not the lipid
cards.summary: Prospective RCT, 25 malnourished patients on TPN ± IV lipid — liver enzymes rose in both groups; ANCOVA tied ALP and GGT to TPN duration , not lipid, while early lipid drove the AST rise (peak at day 7).
cards.type: Prospective randomized trial (TPN ± IV lipid), J Am Coll Nutr 1990
cards.people: 25 malnourished patients on TPN
cards.result: TPN ± IV lipid (200 cc 20% emulsion, 0.7 g/kg/day + ~280 mg choline/day). Early lipid: AST ↑ weeks 1–3, LDH ↑ weeks 2–3 (P<.05); ALP ↑ weeks 2–4 (lipid) and week 1 (lipid-restricted); GGT similarly elevated in both groups. ANCOVA: TPN duration (not lipid) related to ALP and GGT elevations; early lipid related to the AST rise; peak AST at day 7
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints no absolute enzyme values — only significance and timing — so the headline is the attribution (duration vs lipid), not a magnitude; abstract truncated at 250 words
cards.source: Tayek JA, Bistrian B, Sheard NF, Zeisel SH, Blackburn GL. J Am Coll Nutr. 1990;9(1):76–83. PMID 2106545. DOI 10.1080/07315724.1990.10720353

shelves.title: Diabetes drugs: sulfonylureas and the liver
shelves.question: Do sulfonylureas lower glucose by making the liver produce less — even before insulin rises?
shelves.balance: Three small studies, one thread: a very low dose of glyburide cuts fasting glucose by cutting hepatic glucose production — 16% in healthy volunteers with insulin unchanged, 19% in people with impaired fasting glucose — and a full-dose trial shows 2.5 mg of glipizide added to metformin moves A1c and fasting glucose significantly in 122 patients. The honest limit: the glipizide trial’s abstract prints p-values without effect sizes, so the card can say it worked, not by how much.

cards.headline: Tayek 1995: A whisper of glyburide cuts glucose production — without raising insulin at all
cards.summary: Physiology study, 12 healthy volunteers + 5 non-treated controls — a single very-low dose of glyburide (20 µg/kg) cut blood glucose 20±2% and hepatic glucose production 16±2% , while insulin and C-peptide did not change from baseline at all.
cards.type: Physiology study (single very-low-dose glyburide), Am J Med Sci 1995
cards.people: 17 people — 12 healthy volunteers (treated), 5 non-treated controls
cards.result: Very-low-dose glyburide 20 µg/kg orally. Blood glucose ↓ 20±2% vs 5±2% with fasting alone (P<.01). Insulin 53±9 vs 52±9 pmol/L and C-peptide 0.34±0.06 vs 0.39±0.07 ng/mL — NOT changed from baseline. Hepatic glucose production ↓ 16±2% (P<.001) vs 8±4% with fasting alone (P<.05). Abstract truncated at 250 words
cards.watchOut: n=12 treated, single dose, healthy volunteers — the carbohydrate-oxidation and leucine results are cut off by the truncated abstract; the headline is the insulin-independent liver effect, not a clinical dose
cards.search: tayek 1995 glyburide sulfonylurea hepatic glucose production insulin c-peptide healthy volunteers very low dose american journal medical sciences pmid 7879817

cards.headline: Bavirti & Tayek 2003: In impaired fasting glucose, the same low dose works harder — glucose down 29%, production down 19%
cards.summary: Physiology study, 15 nondiabetic volunteers — the same 20 µg/kg glyburide dose cut fasting glucose 29% in impaired fasting glucose vs 17% in normal fasting glucose, and glucose production 19% vs 12% , with a bigger insulin response in the IFG group.
cards.people: 15 nondiabetic volunteers — 6 with impaired fasting glucose (115±1.8 mg/dL), 9 with normal fasting glucose (94±2.3 mg/dL)
cards.result: Single very-low-dose glyburide 20 µg/kg. Fasting blood glucose ↓ 29%±2.4% (IFG) vs 17%±3.5% (NFG) (P<.05). Insulin response 17.7±3 vs 10.7±2.9 µU/mL (P<.05). Glucose production rate ↓ 19%±4% (IFG) vs 12%±3% (normals) (P<.05)
cards.watchOut: n=15, single dose — the IFG group responds more because it secretes more insulin to the drug; the paper frames this as a possible way to delay type 2 diabetes, but no one was followed to see if it did
cards.source: Bavirti S, Tayek JA. Metabolism. 2003;52(4):407–12. PMID 12701050. DOI 10.1053/meta.2003.50068
cards.search: bavirti tayek 2003 glyburide impaired fasting glucose ifg sulfonylurea glucose production insulin response metabolism pmid 12701050

cards.headline: Feinglos et al. 2005: Adding 2.5 mg of glipizide to metformin moves A1c — without weight gain
cards.summary: Multicenter double-blind RCT, 122 patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin — adding 2.5 mg/day glipizide GITS for 16 weeks improved A1c and fasting glucose significantly more than placebo (p<0.0002), with more patients reaching A1c <7.0% — and no weight gain.
cards.type: Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (16 weeks), Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2005
cards.people: 122 patients with type 2 diabetes, A1c 7–8.5%, on metformin ≥1000 mg/day for ≥3 months — 61 randomized to glipizide GITS 2.5 mg/day, 61 to placebo
cards.result: A1c and fasting plasma glucose improvements significantly greater with glipizide (p<0.0002). More patients achieved A1c<7.0% (p<0.0001) and A1c<6.5% (p<0.0033). Fasting insulin similar and unchanged. No significant or clinically relevant weight gain or BMI change; well tolerated
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints p-values WITHOUT effect sizes — no absolute A1c or FPG change is given, so the card can say it worked, not by how much. Tier 2 (randomized design) rather than Tier 1 because the magnitudes are missing from the abstract
cards.source: Feinglos M, Dailey G, Cefalu W, Osei K, Tayek J, Canovatchel W, Chaiken R, Kourides I. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2005;68(2):167–75. PMID 15860246. DOI 10.1016/j.diabres.2004.09.002
cards.search: feinglos 2005 glipizide gits metformin type 2 diabetes a1c fasting glucose randomized double blind placebo controlled weight gain diabetes research clinical practice pmid 15860246

shelves.title: Glipizide GITS: less hypoglycemia, no weight gain?
shelves.question: Does glipizide XL, through its delayed (GITS) delivery in the gut, prevent or reduce hypoglycemia and weight gain with sulfonylureas?
shelves.balance: Glipizide GITS (glipizide XL) lowers glucose without weight gain — two randomized trials in 347 patients and two combination trials found no weight change — and glipizide carries less hypoglycemia than glyburide (a 2007 meta-analysis: 83% higher risk with glyburide than with other sulfonylureas including glipizide). What is not shown: no trial compares GITS head-to-head against immediate-release glipizide on hypoglycemia, so the delayed-delivery advantage over its own immediate-release form is a mechanism — smoother levels, less between-meal insulin — not a measured outcome.

cards.headline: Two trials, 347 patients: GITS cut HbA1c by up to 1.82% with no weight gain
cards.summary: Two randomized placebo-controlled trials, 347 patients — fasting plasma glucose fell −57 to −74 mg/dL and HbA1c −1.50 to −1.82% vs placebo, with no weight gain and only 11 discontinuations for hypoglycemia across both studies.
cards.type: Two multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials
cards.people: 347 patients with NIDDM across 22 sites (age 59, BMI 29, diabetes duration 8 years), 16 weeks each
cards.result: All doses produced significant reductions vs placebo in fasting plasma glucose (range −57 to −74 mg/dL ) and HbA1c (range −1.50 to −1.82% ). Despite forced titration to a randomly assigned dose, only 11 patients in both studies discontinued therapy because of hypoglycemia. Glipizide GITS did not alter lipid levels or produce weight gain
cards.watchOut: No head-to-head comparison against immediate-release glipizide; hypoglycemia is reported as discontinuations, not an event rate
cards.source: Simonson DC et al. Diabetes Care 1997;20(4):597–606. PMID 9096986. DOI 10.2337/diacare.20.4.597
cards.search: simonson 1997 glipizide gits gastrointestinal therapeutic system extended release niddm type 2 diabetes randomized double blind placebo controlled hba1c fasting plasma glucose weight gain hypoglycemia diabetes care pmid 9096986

cards.headline: Adding 2.5 mg of glipizide GITS to metformin improved control with no weight gain
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 122 patients on metformin — adding 2.5 mg/day glipizide GITS improved A1c and fasting glucose vs placebo ( p<0.0002 ), with significantly more patients reaching A1c <7.0% — and no weight gain.
cards.people: 122 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled (A1c 7–8.5%) on metformin ≥1,000 mg/day, randomized to 2.5 mg/day glipizide GITS (n=61) or placebo (n=61) for 16 weeks, added to metformin
cards.result: Significantly greater improvements in mean A1c and fasting plasma glucose than placebo ( p<0.0002 ). Significantly more patients reached A1c <7.0% ( p<0.0001 ) and <6.5% ( p<0.0033 ). Fasting insulin concentrations were similar in both groups and unchanged by treatment. Addition of glipizide GITS to metformin did not produce any significant or clinically relevant weight gain or changes in BMI. Both regimens were well tolerated
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints p-values without effect sizes for A1c and fasting glucose, and hypoglycemia counts are not in the abstract
cards.source: Feinglos MN et al. Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2005. PMID 15860246
cards.search: feinglos 2005 glipizide gits metformin type 2 diabetes a1c fasting glucose randomized double blind placebo controlled weight gain bmi diabetes research clinical practice pmid 15860246 recard shelf 36

cards.headline: GITS or metformin, alone or combined: weight and belly fat did not change
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 91 subjects — glipizide GITS and metformin improved glycemic control comparably, alone and in combination ( P<0.0001 vs baseline); body weight and abdominal fat distribution did not change significantly in either group.
cards.people: 91 subjects, 4-week drug washout, randomized to glipizide GITS maximum 20 mg (n=46) or metformin maximum 2,550 mg (n=45), then combination therapy
cards.result: Glycemic control was markedly impaired at baseline (mean HbA1c 10.4% glipizide GITS; 10.0% metformin) but improved comparably with each agent and in combination ( P<0.0001 vs baseline). Body weight and abdominal fat distribution did not change significantly in either group. PAI-1 concentrations fell comparably with each agent and further with combination
cards.watchOut: The mechanism — a more modest rise in between-meal insulin, plus less hypoglycemia — is the authors' hypothesis, not a measured outcome
cards.source: Cefalu WT et al. Diabetes Care 2002. PMID 12453948
cards.search: cefalu 2002 glipizide gits metformin combination weight abdominal fat distribution pai-1 fibrinolytic poorly controlled type 2 diabetes randomized trial diabetes care pmid 12453948

cards.headline: Glyburide carries 83% more hypoglycemia than other sulfonylureas, including glipizide
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis — any hypoglycemic episode with glyburide vs sulfonylureas RR 1.83 (1.35–2.49) ; vs all secretagogues RR 1.52 (1.21–1.92) ; episodes per patient-year, rate ratio 1.44 (1.13–1.85) .
cards.people: Randomized trials of glyburide vs other secretagogues and insulin
cards.result: Any hypoglycemic episode — glyburide vs all secretagogues RR 1.52 (1.21–1.92) ; vs sulfonylureas RR 1.83 (1.35–2.49) ; hypoglycemic episodes per patient-year, rate ratio 1.44 (1.13–1.85) . Weight gain with glyburide vs sulfonylureas, weighted mean difference 2.49 kg (−0.48 to 5.47) , not significant
cards.watchOut: This compares glyburide against the class — it does not test GITS against immediate-release glipizide
cards.source: Gangji AS et al. Diabetes Care 2007;30(2):389–394

shelves.title: Plaque in type 2 diabetes: how common, and can icosapent ethyl regress it?
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, how common is coronary plaque, and can icosapent ethyl regress it — or is the placebo doing the work?
shelves.balance: In type 2 diabetes, plaque is common but not universal — one in five screened patients had normal coronaries. On icosapent ethyl, plaque didn't just slow, it regressed and stabilized: low-attenuation plaque down 17% while placebo rose 109%, and the lipid-rich necrotic core shrank within 9 months. The open question is the placebo arm: the published comparison says mineral oil didn't drive the progression, but that comparison is post-hoc and small — which is why the developer is asking the author directly.

cards.headline: One in five screened diabetics had normal coronaries — and they were more often women.
cards.summary: About 20% of the screened population failed screening: 14 for normal coronaries and 7 for HbA1c <7 — 108 people with type 2 diabetes screened for the STOP trial.
cards.type: Baseline/screening analysis from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
cards.people: 108 people with type 2 diabetes screened for the STOP trial (weekly subcutaneous semaglutide vs placebo, to test coronary plaque progression); 87 randomized (81%), mean age 56.4 ± 8.4 years, 62% male, documented CAD by CCTA (CAC 227.5 ± 871.5; segment involvement score 5.0 ± 3.4; total plaque score 7.0 ± 7.0; total stenosis score 7.0 ± 8.4). Enrollment required HbA1c >7 and coronary atherosclerosis on CCTA (>1 stenosis with >20% narrowing). The 14 patients with normal coronaries were younger (mean age 53.4 ± 9.0 years).
cards.result: About 20% of the screened population failed screening: 14 for normal coronaries and 7 for HbA1c <7. The 14 people with diabetes and normal coronaries (no calcification) were significantly more likely to be women.
cards.watchOut: Baseline data only — the semaglutide-vs-placebo plaque-progression results are not in this paper. Small screening sample (n=108); single center. The retrieved abstract text truncates the female comparison after "21% vs" — the direction (more often women) is as reported.
cards.source: Birudaraju D, Kinninger A, Cherukuri L, et al. J Diabetes Complications. 2021;35:107840. PMID 33419635. DOI 10.1016/j.jdiacomp.2020.107840.
cards.search: stop trial birudaraju 2021 normal coronary arteries type 2 diabetes ccta cac screening semaglutide plaque journal diabetes complications pmid 33419635 doi 10.1016/j.jdiacomp.2020.107840

cards.headline: Plaques got more stable on icosapent ethyl — and the software could tell at 9 months, patient by patient.
cards.summary: Lipid-rich necrotic core at 9 months: −2 mm³ on icosapent ethyl vs +41 mm³ on placebo (P=0.008); at 18 months, −6 mm³ vs +58 mm³ (P=0.015) — 55 EVAPORATE patients.
cards.type: Secondary imaging analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
cards.people: 55 EVAPORATE patients who completed the 18-month visit with interpretable CCTA images at all three time points; icosapent ethyl 4 g/day vs mineral-oil placebo. Plaque morphology (lipid-rich necrotic core, fibrous cap thickness, intraplaque hemorrhage) assessed with ElucidVivo software. Placebo arm (n=32): mean age 57.7 ± 11.4 years, 53% men. Icosapent ethyl arm (n=23): mean age 55.7 ± 10.3 years, 57% men.
cards.result: Lipid-rich necrotic core: at 9 months, −2 mm³ on icosapent ethyl vs +41 mm³ on placebo (P=0.008); at 18 months, −6 mm³ vs +58 mm³ (P=0.015). Wall thickness fell and cap thickness rose (not significant on a univariable basis), motivating multivariable modeling. A multivariable model of lipid-rich phenotype could assess per-patient response at 9 months (P<0.01), sustained at 18 months and generalizing to a validation cohort.
cards.watchOut: Secondary analysis of 55 of the 80 EVAPORATE patients; imaging surrogate, not clinical events; the mineral-oil question sits on Card 4.
cards.source: Buckler AJ et al. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2023;10:1204071. PMID 37600044. PMCID PMC10435977. DOI 10.3389/fcvm.2023.1204071.
cards.search: buckler 2023 evaporate icosapent ethyl plaque morphology lipid-rich necrotic core elucidvivo ccta fibrous cap intraplaque hemorrhage frontiers cardiovascular medicine pmid 37600044 pmcid pmc10435977 doi 10.3389/fcvm.2023.1204071

cards.headline: Icosapent ethyl: low-attenuation plaque −17% vs +109% on placebo over 18 months.
cards.summary: Low-attenuation plaque volume: −17% on icosapent ethyl vs +109% on placebo (P=0.0061). Total plaque −9% vs +11% (P=0.002) — 80 patients, 18 months. Re-card — this card also appears on Shelf #41 and is counted once in the library total.
cards.people: 80 patients with coronary atherosclerosis on MDCT (≥20% stenosis), on statin therapy, persistently elevated triglycerides (median 259 mg/dL); icosapent ethyl 4 g/day vs mineral-oil placebo; scans at baseline, 9 months, 18 months. Mean age 57.4 ± 8.7 years overall (icosapent ethyl 56.5 ± 8.9 years; placebo 58.3 ± 8.6 years); 54% men.
cards.result: Low-attenuation plaque volume: −17% on icosapent ethyl vs +109% on placebo (P=0.0061). Total plaque −9% vs +11% (P=0.002); fibrofatty plaque −34% vs +32% (P<0.001); fibrous plaque −20% vs +1% (P=0.003); dense calcium no significant difference (P=0.053).
cards.watchOut: The +109% placebo-arm progression is the mineral-oil question — see Card 4. Eighty patients, imaging surrogate, not clinical events. No AFib signal is reported in the published EVAPORATE results — see Shelf #41 for the AFib side.
cards.source: Budoff MJ et al. Eur Heart J. 2020;41(40):3925–3932. PMID 32860032. (Interim: Cardiovasc Res. 2021. PMID 32609331.)

cards.headline: Mineral oil vs cellulose placebo: no difference in plaque progression — but the comparison is post-hoc and small.
cards.summary: No significant differences in progression of total plaque or total non-calcified plaque volumes between the mineral-oil and cellulose placebo groups — follow-up ~10.8 months.
cards.type: Post-hoc observational comparison of placebo arms from two randomized trials.
cards.people: Mineral-oil placebo patients from EVAPORATE vs non-mineral-oil (cellulose) placebo patients from the Garlic 5 trial; plaque volumes by coronary CTA; follow-up ~10.8 months; analysis adjusted for age, sex, baseline plaque volume, baseline triglycerides, diabetes, and statin use. Mineral-oil dose ~2 g twice daily (less than a teaspoon per day). The 60 participants averaged 59 ± 9.9 years and 66% were men (Garlic 5 placebo: 58.7 ± 11.4 years, 72% men; EVAPORATE placebo: 58.6 ± 8.8 years, 59% men).
cards.result: No significant differences in progression of total plaque or total non-calcified plaque volumes between the mineral-oil and non-mineral-oil placebo groups. The authors conclude progression is not related to mineral-oil consumption in the quantities used, and that the REDUCE-IT and EVAPORATE results should not be affected by the placebo choice.
cards.watchOut: This is the published answer to the developer's mineral-oil question — but it is a post-hoc observational comparison of two trials with different inclusion criteria, small, not powered to detect differences, with residual confounding. Conflict of interest: Budoff received grant support and speakers-bureau fees from Amarin. The developer's direct question to Budoff (email pending his address) still stands.

shelves.title: Insulin, not leptin, tracks growth-hormone pulses after weight loss.
shelves.question: After weight loss, what tracks growth-hormone pulse size — insulin or leptin?
shelves.balance: The energy-balance seesaw is consistent across three decades — fasting multiplies GH production fivefold in two days (Hartman) and triples integrated GH over five (Ho); visceral fat and fasting insulin predict blunted GH in larger samples (Clasey, Makimura); and in the developer’s own weight-loss study it was insulin, not the fat hormone leptin, that tracked the pulses’ recovery. None of these small physiology studies can say whether raising GH by lowering insulin changes outcomes — they map the signal, not its clinical use.

cards.headline: After weight loss, growth-hormone pulses got nine times bigger — and insulin, not leptin, tracked them.
cards.summary: GH pulse height 11.9±4.8 vs 1.3±0.1 µg/L ; insulin inversely tracked mean GH ( r=−0.678 ) and pulse height ( r=−0.733 ); leptin tracked body fat only — 14 normal-weight volunteers.
cards.type: Physiology study, weight-loss vs no-weight-loss comparison.
cards.people: 14 normal-weight volunteers (BMI 25±1), half with diet-induced weight loss of 14%±2%; studied after 1 week of weight maintenance on a normal-calorie diet.
cards.result: In the weight-loss group, insulin was lower (3.8±0.7 vs 9.0±0.9 µU/mL, P<0.01) and C-peptide lower (0.44±0.06 vs 0.59±0.04, P<0.05); leptin was not different. GH pulse height was 11.9±4.8 vs 1.3±0.1 µg/L (P<0.05), area per pulse 57±28 vs 6±1 (P<0.05), mean GH 3.91±0.76 vs 0.85±0.16 (P<0.01). Insulin was inversely associated with mean GH (r=−0.678, P<0.01) and GH pulse height (r=−0.733, P<0.01). GHRH-stimulated GH pulse height was also higher (41.8±18.1 vs 7.1±1.6, P<0.05; AUC 161±35 vs 46±13, P<0.05), inversely correlated with insulin (r=−0.718, P<0.01). Leptin correlated with BMI (r=0.554) and body fat (r=0.744) but not with GH secretion.
cards.watchOut: n=14, young normal-weight volunteers, association not mechanism — the authors say the GH increase “may be secondary” to reduced insulin. Weight loss was 14% over 3 months, not a diet effect (both groups ate normally for 2 days before study).
cards.search: manglik 1998 growth hormone gh pulse insulin leptin weight loss pulsatility ghrh metabolism volunteers pmid 9751243 doi 10.1016/s0026-0495(98)90288-8 tayek

cards.headline: Hartman 1992: two days of fasting multiplied GH production fivefold
cards.summary: Physiology study, 9 normal men, blood sampled every 5 minutes for 24 h — 24-hour GH production 78 ± 12 → 371 ± 57 µg/Lv (P = 0.0001) on the second day of a fast: secretory bursts doubled ( 14 → 32 per 24 h) and mass per burst doubled; GH half-life and IGF-I unchanged.
cards.type: Physiology study with deconvolution analysis, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1992
cards.people: 9 normal men, blood sampled every 5 minutes for 24 hours — fed day vs second day of a fast
cards.result: 24-hour GH production rose 5-fold: 78 ± 12 → 371 ± 57 µg/L of distribution volume (P = 0.0001), from a doubling of secretory bursts ( 14 ± 2.3 → 32 ± 2.4 per 24 h, P = 0.0006) and of mass secreted per burst ( 6.3 ± 1.2 → 11 ± 1.6 µg/Lv , P = 0.002); GH half-life unchanged; IGF-I unchanged after 56 hours of fasting
cards.watchOut: Nine men, two days — an acute fasting response, not a weight-loss or treatment effect
cards.source: Hartman ML et al. Augmented growth hormone secretory burst frequency and amplitude mediate enhanced GH secretion during a two-day fast in normal men. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1992. PMID 1548337
cards.search: hartman 1992 growth hormone secretory burst two-day fast deconvolution jcem pmid 1548337 fasting gh production igf-i

cards.headline: Ho 1988: over a 5-day fast, GH pulses came nearly twice as often and integrated GH tripled
cards.summary: Physiology study, 6 normal men, fed vs days 1 and 5 of a 5-day fast — GH pulse frequency 5.8 ± 0.7 → 9.9 ± 0.7 pulses/24 h (P = 0.028); 24-hour integrated GH 2.82 ± 0.50 → 8.75 ± 0.82 µg·min/mL (P = 0.0002); maximal amplitude 5.9 → 12.3 ng/mL (P < 0.005).
cards.people: 6 normal men studied fed and on days 1 and 5 of a 5-day fast
cards.result: GH pulse frequency 5.8 ± 0.7 → 9.9 ± 0.7 pulses/24 h (P = 0.028); 24-hour integrated GH concentration 2.82 ± 0.50 → 8.75 ± 0.82 µg·min/mL (P = 0.0002); maximal pulse amplitude 5.9 ± 1.1 → 12.3 ± 1.6 ng/mL (P < 0.005)
cards.watchOut: Six men; a starvation response measured over days, not a sustainable or therapeutic state
cards.source: Ho KY et al., J Clin Invest 1988;81(4):968–975. DOI 10.1172/JCI113450

cards.headline: Clasey 2001: visceral fat and fasting insulin predict 24-hour GH — the direct corroboration of Manglik
cards.summary: Cross-sectional physiology study, 102 healthy adults, GH sampled every 10 minutes for 24 h — the model explained 65% of the variance in integrated GH; abdominal visceral fat ( P < 0.002 ) and fasting insulin ( P < 0.008 ) were consistently important predictors, independent of age, gender, and every other variable measured.
cards.type: Cross-sectional physiology study, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2001
cards.people: 102 healthy adults (40 aged 20–29, 62 aged 57–80); GH sampled every 10 minutes for 24 hours
cards.result: The regression model explained 65% of the variance in integrated 24-hour GH, and abdominal visceral fat ( P < 0.002 ) and fasting insulin ( P < 0.008 ) were consistently important predictors, independent of age, gender, and every other variable measured; IGF-I predicted GH only in the young
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional prediction, not causation — but the most direct external corroboration of the Manglik insulin finding (Reference 1)
cards.source: Clasey JL et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2001;86(8):3845–3852. PMID 11502822. DOI 10.1210/jcem.86.8.7731
cards.search: clasey 2001 abdominal visceral fat fasting insulin growth hormone predictors 24-hour integrated jcem pmid 11502822 doi 10.1210/jcem.86.8.7731

cards.headline: Makimura 2008: stimulated GH falls steeply with waist size — and waist, not BMI, survives adjustment
cards.summary: Stimulation study, 75 men given GHRH-arginine — peak GH 36.4 ± 5.4 µg/L (lean) vs 16.6 ± 2.9 (overweight) vs 7.6 ± 0.9 (obese), P < 0.001; waist ≥102 cm vs <102 cm: 7.9 ± 0.9 vs 26.9 ± 3.4 µg/L (P < 0.0001).
cards.type: Cross-sectional stimulation study (GHRH-arginine), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2008
cards.people: 75 men: 23 lean, 28 overweight, 24 obese, given GHRH-arginine stimulation
cards.result: Peak stimulated GH was 36.4 ± 5.4 µg/L in lean, 16.6 ± 2.9 in overweight, and 7.6 ± 0.9 in obese men (P < 0.001); waist circumference 102 cm or more vs less: 7.9 ± 0.9 vs 26.9 ± 3.4 µg/L (P < 0.0001); in the multivariate model waist circumference stayed independently associated (peak GH fell 1.02 µg/L per 1 cm of waist, P = 0.02) while BMI lost significance
cards.watchOut: Stimulated (pharmacologic) GH rather than spontaneous secretion; men only, cross-sectional
cards.source: Makimura H et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2008;93:4254–4260. PMID 18765508. DOI 10.1210/jc.2008-1333

shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, do SGLT2 inhibitors prevent heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular death?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Hypoglycemic Agents · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: Three large trials point the same way on the composite, but the wins differ: empagliflozin’s is mortality, dapagliflozin’s is heart-failure hospitalization with a null MACE result, and canagliflozin carries an amputation signal the others do not.

cards.headline: Empagliflozin cut cardiovascular death by more than a third in type 2 diabetes with established heart disease.
cards.summary: EMPA-REG OUTCOME — primary composite 10.5% vs 12.1% (HR 0.86); cardiovascular death 3.7% vs 5.9% (HR 0.62); death from any cause 5.7% vs 8.3% (HR 0.68) — 7,020 patients, median 3.1 years.
cards.type: Randomized placebo-controlled cardiovascular outcome trial (EMPA-REG OUTCOME)
cards.people: 7,020 patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease; median follow-up 3.1 years
cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) 10.5% on empagliflozin vs 12.1% on placebo (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74–0.99); cardiovascular death 3.7% vs 5.9% (HR 0.62); death from any cause 5.7% vs 8.3% (HR 0.68); hospitalization for heart failure 2.7% vs 4.1% (HR 0.65)
cards.watchOut: The composite win was driven by cardiovascular death — rates of MI and stroke did not differ significantly. Genital infections were more common on empagliflozin
cards.source: Zinman B, et al.; EMPA-REG OUTCOME Investigators. Empagliflozin, Cardiovascular Outcomes, and Mortality in Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2015;373:2117–2128. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1504720. PMID 26378978 · NCT01131676.

cards.headline: Canagliflozin reduced major cardiovascular events — and doubled amputations.
cards.summary: CANVAS Program — primary composite 26.9 vs 31.5 events per 1,000 patient-years (HR 0.86), but amputations 6.3 vs 3.4 per 1,000 patient-years (HR 1.97) — 10,142 patients.
cards.type: Randomized placebo-controlled outcome program (CANVAS Program, two integrated trials)
cards.people: 10,142 patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk (65.6% with established cardiovascular disease); mean follow-up 188.2 weeks
cards.result: Primary composite 26.9 vs 31.5 events per 1,000 patient-years (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75–0.97); progression of albuminuria HR 0.73; renal composite (sustained 40% eGFR reduction, renal-replacement therapy, or renal death) HR 0.60. Amputations were higher on canagliflozin: 6.3 vs 3.4 per 1,000 patient-years (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.41–2.75), mainly toe or metatarsal
cards.watchOut: Under the prespecified testing sequence the renal outcomes are not formally statistically significant. The amputation signal was not seen with the other drugs on this shelf
cards.source: Neal B, et al.; CANVAS Program Collaborative Group. Canagliflozin and Cardiovascular and Renal Events in Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2017;377:644–657. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1611925. PMID 28605608 · NCT01032629 · NCT01989754.

cards.headline: Dapagliflozin did not reduce heart attack or stroke, but cut heart-failure hospitalizations.
cards.summary: DECLARE–TIMI 58 — MACE 8.8% vs 9.4% (HR 0.93, not significant); cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization 4.9% vs 5.8% (HR 0.83), driven by heart-failure hospitalization (HR 0.73) — 17,160 patients, median 4.2 years.
cards.people: 17,160 patients (59% without established atherosclerotic disease); median follow-up 4.2 years
cards.result: MACE 8.8% vs 9.4% (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84–1.03 — not significant); cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization 4.9% vs 5.8% (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73–0.95), driven by heart-failure hospitalization (HR 0.73); cardiovascular death HR 0.98. Diabetic ketoacidosis was more common on dapagliflozin (0.3% vs 0.1%)
cards.watchOut: A null result for heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death — the benefit is heart-failure hospitalization, in the lowest-risk population of the three trials on this shelf
cards.source: Wiviott SD, et al.; DECLARE–TIMI 58 Investigators. Dapagliflozin and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2019;380:347–357. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1812389. PMID 30415602 · NCT01730534.

shelves.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and cardiovascular outcomes
shelves.question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists prevent cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Glucagon-Like Peptides · Hypoglycemic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: Three positive outcome trials, three different drivers: liraglutide’s win is cardiovascular death, semaglutide’s is nonfatal MI and stroke with a retinopathy caution attached, and dulaglutide’s is stroke in the broadest, mostly primary-prevention population.

cards.headline: Liraglutide reduced cardiovascular death in high-risk type 2 diabetes.
cards.summary: LEADER — primary composite 13.0% vs 14.9% (HR 0.87); cardiovascular death 4.7% vs 6.0% (HR 0.78); death from any cause HR 0.85 — 9,340 patients, median 3.8 years.

cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) 13.0% vs 14.9% (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78–0.97); cardiovascular death 4.7% vs 6.0% (HR 0.78); death from any cause 8.2% vs 9.6% (HR 0.85); nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and heart-failure hospitalization were nonsignificantly lower
cards.watchOut: Gastrointestinal events were the most common reason for stopping liraglutide; the individual MI and stroke differences were not significant

cards.headline: Semaglutide reduced cardiovascular events — with more retinopathy complications.
cards.summary: SUSTAIN-6 — primary composite 6.6% vs 8.9% (HR 0.74); nonfatal stroke HR 0.61 — but retinopathy complications HR 1.76 — 3,297 patients, median 2.1 years.
cards.people: 3,297 patients, 83% with established cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or both; median follow-up 2.1 years
cards.result: Primary composite 6.6% vs 8.9% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58–0.95); nonfatal stroke 1.6% vs 2.7% (HR 0.61); nonfatal MI HR 0.74 (not significant); cardiovascular death similar (HR 0.98). New or worsening nephropathy was lower (HR 0.64), but retinopathy complications were higher (HR 1.76, 95% CI 1.11–2.78)
cards.watchOut: A small, short trial for an outcomes claim (3,297 patients, 2.1 years), designed for noninferiority; the retinopathy signal — vitreous hemorrhage, blindness, or treatment-requiring disease — is part of this card’s record

cards.headline: Dulaglutide reduced cardiovascular events over five years in a mostly primary-prevention population, driven by stroke.
cards.summary: REWIND — primary composite 12.0% vs 13.4% (HR 0.88); nonfatal stroke HR 0.76; no significant differences in MI, cardiovascular death, or death from any cause — 9,901 patients, median 5.4 years.

shelves.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit: the remaining Level A trials
shelves.question: Beyond the three trials on Shelf #71, which other GLP-1 receptor agonists have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit — and which did not clear that bar?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Cardiovascular Diseases · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 · Hypoglycemic Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: Under the ADA’s own Level A wording, the GLP-1 benefit is agent-specific, not class-wide. Beyond the three trials on Shelf #71, three more agents cleared the superiority bar: albiglutide (HR 0.78, a drug no longer sold), efpeglenatide (HR 0.73, with a renal composite win), and oral semaglutide in SOUL (HR 0.86 over ~4 years). Lixisenatide and once-weekly exenatide did not clear it and are excluded from this shelf by the developer’s filter.

cards.headline: Albiglutide cut major cardiovascular events by 22% — a positive trial for a drug no longer sold.
cards.summary: Harmony Outcomes — primary composite (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke) 7.0% vs 9.0% (HR 0.78), superiority P=0.0006; NNT 50 over 1.6 years — 9,463 patients, median 1.6 years.

Acute pancreatitis 10 vs 7 patients; pancreatic cancer 6 vs 5 ; no medullary thyroid carcinoma in either group

cards.headline: Efpeglenatide cut cardiovascular events by 27% — and its renal composite by 32%.

shelves.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and the kidney
shelves.question: Do GLP-1 receptor agonists protect the kidney in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease?
shelves.balance: FLOW gives the class its dedicated kidney-outcome win — kidney failure, halved eGFR, and death in one composite, with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality benefits attached. AWARD-7 is the supporting act: against insulin in stage 3–4 CKD, dulaglutide matched glucose control, slowed eGFR decline, and caused far less hypoglycemia. Whether GLP-1 benefit adds to SGLT2 therapy is the open question FLOW could not answer.

cards.headline: Semaglutide cut major kidney events by a quarter in type 2 diabetes with CKD — 18.7% vs 23.2%.
cards.summary: FLOW — primary kidney composite 18.7% vs 23.2% (HR 0.76); cardiovascular death HR 0.71; death from any cause HR 0.80 — 3,533 patients, median 3.4 years, stopped early for efficacy.
cards.people: 3,533 patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD on RAS blockade; semaglutide 1 mg weekly vs placebo; median follow-up 3.4 years; stopped early for efficacy
cards.result: Primary composite (kidney failure, ≥50% eGFR decline, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes) 18.7% vs 23.2% (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.66–0.88); kidney-specific composite HR 0.79; cardiovascular death HR 0.71; MACE HR 0.82; death from any cause 13% vs 16% (HR 0.80); eGFR decline was 1.16 ml/min/1.73 m²/year slower. In the prespecified SGLT2-inhibitor subgroup the benefit was clear in patients not on an SGLT2 inhibitor (HR 0.73); the on-SGLT2 subgroup was small (n=550) and neutral (HR 1.07), so added value on top of SGLT2 therapy is unproven
cards.source: Perkovic V, et al.; FLOW Trial Committees and Investigators. Effects of Semaglutide on Chronic Kidney Disease in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2024;391:109–121. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2403347. PMID 38785209. SGLT2-subgroup analysis: Mann JFE, et al. Nat Med. 2024;30:2849–2856. PMID 38914124.
