cards.headline: Against insulin in stage 3–4 CKD, dulaglutide matched glucose control, slowed eGFR decline, and caused far less hypoglycemia.
cards.summary: AWARD-7 — A1c noninferior to insulin glargine; eGFR at 52 weeks 34.0 / 33.8 vs 31.3 ml/min/1.73 m²; total hypoglycemia ~50–60% vs ~75% — 577 patients with stage 3–4 CKD, 52 weeks.
cards.type: Open-label randomized trial vs insulin glargine (AWARD-7)
cards.people: 577 patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 3–4 CKD; dulaglutide 1.5 mg or 0.75 mg weekly vs titrated insulin glargine, 52 weeks
cards.result: A1c reduction was noninferior to glargine. eGFR at 52 weeks: 34.0 (dulaglutide 1.5 mg) / 33.8 (0.75 mg) vs 31.3 ml/min/1.73 m² (glargine). UACR fell in all groups with no overall between-group difference, except in the macroalbuminuria subgroup, which favored dulaglutide 1.5 mg. Total hypoglycemia ~50–60% vs ~75%; severe hypoglycemia 0% / 2.6% vs 6.7%; nausea and vomiting were more common on dulaglutide
cards.source: Tuttle KR, et al. Dulaglutide versus insulin glargine in patients with type 2 diabetes and moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease (AWARD-7): a multicentre, open-label, randomised trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2018;6:605–617. DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(18)30104-9. PMID 29910024.
cards.search: dulaglutide award-7 insulin glargine chronic kidney disease tuttle lancet diabetes endocrinology 2018 hypoglycemia egfr pmid 29910024

shelves.title: Pioglitazone and thiazolidinediones: albuminuria
shelves.question: Do thiazolidinediones lower albuminuria in diabetes — and on how much evidence?
shelves.balance: The albuminuria signal is consistent — roughly a fifth to a quarter lower — but it rests entirely on small, short trials and a surrogate endpoint. No thiazolidinedione has been tested in a kidney-outcome trial, and the class carries weight gain, fluid retention, and heart-failure baggage. This is the cluster’s thinnest shelf, and it says so.

cards.headline: Across 15 small trials, thiazolidinediones lowered albuminuria — albumin-to-creatinine ratio about 25% lower.
cards.summary: Sarafidis 2010 meta-analysis — ACR weighted mean difference −24.8% (95% CI −39.6 to −10.0) in normo-/microalbuminuria; protein excretion SMD −1.1 in overt proteinuria — 15 RCTs, 2,860 patients.
cards.people: 15 RCTs, 2,860 patients with diabetes (10 pioglitazone and 5 rosiglitazone studies), spanning normoalbuminuria to overt proteinuria
cards.result: In normo-/microalbuminuria, albumin excretion SMD −0.6 (95% CI −0.8 to −0.4) and ACR weighted mean difference −24.8% (−39.6 to −10.0); in overt proteinuria, protein excretion SMD −1.1 (−1.8 to −0.4). Heterogeneity was significant in several subgroups, and no patient-level data were available
cards.source: Sarafidis PA, Stafylas PC, Georgianos PI, Saratzis AN, Lasaridis AN. Effect of thiazolidinediones on albuminuria and proteinuria in diabetes: a meta-analysis. Am J Kidney Dis. 2010;55:835–847. DOI 10.1053/j.ajkd.2009.11.013. PMID 20110146.
cards.search: thiazolidinediones pioglitazone rosiglitazone albuminuria proteinuria meta-analysis sarafidis american journal kidney diseases 2010 pmid 20110146

cards.headline: Pioglitazone alone, across 26 studies and nearly 20,000 people, lowered albuminuria by about a fifth.
cards.summary: Zhou 2020 meta-analysis — albuminuria −18.5% (95% CI 16.0–21.1); MACE RR 0.8 in patients with established cardiovascular disease; heart-failure hospitalization RR 1.3 — 26 studies, 19,645 participants.
cards.people: 26 RCTs, 19,645 participants with or at high risk of type 2 diabetes
cards.result: Pioglitazone reduced albuminuria by 18.5% (weighted mean difference; 95% CI 16.0–21.1), with similar benefit across renal-function categories. MACE was lower (RR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7–0.9) only in patients with established cardiovascular disease; hospitalization for heart failure was higher (RR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1–1.6); all-cause mortality was unchanged (RR 1.0)
cards.source: Zhou Y, Huang Y, Ji X, Wang Y. Pioglitazone for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patients with or at high risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus: a meta-analysis. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2020;105:dgz252. PMID 31822895.
cards.search: pioglitazone meta-analysis cardiovascular renal outcomes zhou journal clinical endocrinology metabolism 2020 albuminuria 26 studies pmid 31822895

shelves.title: Methods to delay the formal diagnosis of diabetes: lifestyle
shelves.question: In people with prediabetes, can changing how they live — food, movement, weight — push back the day the diagnosis arrives, and by how long?
shelves.balance: Diabetes is progressive; nothing here cures or prevents it. What these trials show is delay, measured honestly: lifestyle pushed diagnosis back by the same ~58% on two continents (DPP, Finnish DPS), Da Qing timed the delay at about three and a half years and then watched it compound into fewer events and longer life over thirty years, and DPPOS shows the pushed-back clock keeps its lead even after the program ends. The developer’s arithmetic: roughly a pound lost, a point of glucose; ten pounds, ten points — and years. (Panel position: ADA Standards of Care — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: DPP 2002: intensive lifestyle cut new diabetes to 4.8 cases per 100 person-years vs 11.0 on placebo — a 58% slower clock.
cards.summary: Diabetes Prevention Program 2002 — diabetes incidence was 4.8 cases per 100 person-years with intensive lifestyle, 7.8 with metformin, and 11.0 with placebo over a mean 2.8 years: lifestyle cut incidence by 58% and metformin by 31% versus placebo — 3,234 adults with impaired glucose tolerance. Read on this shelf as what it was: years of diabetic-range glucose postponed, not a disease abolished.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2002
cards.people: 3,234 nondiabetic adults with elevated fasting and post-load glucose concentrations (mean age 51 years, mean body-mass index 34.0; 68% women), randomised to placebo, metformin 850 mg twice daily, or a lifestyle-modification program with goals of at least 7% weight loss and at least 150 minutes of physical activity per week. Average follow-up 2.8 years
cards.result: Diabetes incidence was 11.0 cases per 100 person-years on placebo, 7.8 on metformin, and 4.8 on lifestyle. The lifestyle intervention reduced incidence by 58% (95% CI 48–66%) and metformin by 31% (95% CI 17–43%) versus placebo, and lifestyle was significantly more effective than metformin. Over a three-year period, 6.9 people would have to take part in the lifestyle program — or 13.9 receive metformin — to hold back one case of diabetes
cards.watchOut: The trial’s own framing is a reduction in incidence, and its ten-year follow-up (Reference 4) shows the yearly rates converging once the program ends and everyone is offered lifestyle help — the honest reading, and this shelf’s, is delay: the lifestyle group crossed the diagnostic line later, on a clock pushed back. Metformin’s smaller effect on this card is the same drug whose durability anchors the medicines shelf next door (Shelf #112)
cards.source: Knowler WC, Barrett-Connor E, Fowler SE, et al; Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group. Reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes with lifestyle intervention or metformin. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(6):393–403. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa012512. PMID 11832527.
cards.search: diabetes prevention program dpp knowler lifestyle metformin incidence 100 person-years impaired glucose tolerance prediabetes nejm 2002 pmid 11832527 doi 10.1056/nejmoa012512 delay diagnosis

cards.headline: Finnish DPS 2001: the same 58% — cumulative incidence 11% vs 23% at four years, on another continent.
cards.summary: Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study 2001 — cumulative diabetes incidence after four years was 11% with individualized lifestyle counseling vs 23% in the control group, and the risk of diabetes was reduced by 58% (P<0.001) — 522 middle-aged, overweight adults with impaired glucose tolerance. The DPP result, replicated independently in Finland.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2001
cards.people: 522 middle-aged, overweight subjects (172 men and 350 women; mean age 55 years, mean body-mass index 31) with impaired glucose tolerance, randomised to an intervention group receiving individualized counseling to reduce weight and total and saturated fat intake and to increase fiber intake and physical activity, or to a control group. Oral glucose-tolerance testing annually, with the diagnosis confirmed by a second test; mean follow-up 3.2 years
cards.result: The cumulative incidence of diabetes after four years was 11% (95% CI 6–15%) in the intervention group and 23% (95% CI 17–29%) in the control group; during the trial, the risk of diabetes was reduced by 58% (P<0.001). Weight loss by the end of year 1 was 4.2 kg in the intervention group vs 0.8 kg in controls, and the reduction in diabetes incidence was directly associated with the changes in lifestyle
cards.watchOut: A counseling trial cannot be blinded, and the control group knew why its glucose was being tested every year — awareness that, if anything, biases the comparison toward the null. The endpoint is a laboratory diagnosis confirmed on a second test: what was delayed is exactly what this shelf says — the formal diagnosis, and the years of diabetic-range glucose that follow it
cards.source: Tuomilehto J, Lindström J, Eriksson JG, et al; Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study Group. Prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus by changes in lifestyle among subjects with impaired glucose tolerance. N Engl J Med. 2001;344(18):1343–1350. DOI 10.1056/NEJM200105033441801. PMID 11333990.
cards.search: finnish diabetes prevention study dps tuomilehto lifestyle impaired glucose tolerance cumulative incidence overweight nejm 2001 pmid 11333990 doi 10.1056/nejm200105033441801 delay

cards.headline: Da Qing: the trial that timed the delay — 3.6 fewer years lived with diabetes at 20 years; by 30 years, fewer cardiovascular events, fewer complications, fewer deaths.
cards.summary: Da Qing (China) — six years of lifestyle intervention in 577 adults with impaired glucose tolerance: over 20 years, cumulative diabetes incidence was 80% in the intervention groups vs 93% in controls, and intervention participants spent an average of 3.6 fewer years living with diabetes; at 30 years the median delay in diabetes onset was 3.96 years , with fewer cardiovascular disease events (HR 0.74), a lower incidence of microvascular complications (HR 0.65), and fewer cardiovascular (HR 0.67) and all-cause deaths (HR 0.74).
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial with 20- and 30-year follow-up, Lancet 2008; Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2019
cards.people: 577 adults with impaired glucose tolerance from 33 clinics in Da Qing, China, assigned by clinic in 1986 to a control group or to one of three lifestyle intervention groups (diet, exercise, or diet plus exercise); active intervention ran 6 years, to 1992, with follow-up to 20 and then 30 years
cards.result: During the active intervention period, diabetes incidence was 51% lower in the combined intervention groups (hazard rate ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.33–0.73), and 43% lower over the full 20 years (0.57, 0.41–0.81); average annual incidence was 7% vs 11%, and the 20-year cumulative incidence was 80% in the intervention groups vs 93% in the control group — intervention participants spent an average of 3.6 fewer years with diabetes . At 20 years there was no significant difference in first cardiovascular events, cardiovascular mortality, or all-cause mortality, with limited statistical power for those outcomes. By 30 years the differences had arrived: a median delay in diabetes onset of 3.96 years (95% CI 1.25–6.67), cardiovascular disease events HR 0.74 (0.59–0.92), microvascular complications HR 0.65 (0.45–0.95), cardiovascular deaths HR 0.67 (0.48–0.94), all-cause deaths HR 0.74 (0.61–0.89), and an average increase in life expectancy of 1.44 years
cards.watchOut: Randomisation was by clinic — 33 clinics — not by individual, so read the precision accordingly; and the cohort began in 1986 in a leaner China, a different world from a modern clinic panel. What transfers is the shape of the finding: years of delay, compounded over decades, became events that never happened. Note the honest sequence on outcomes: at 20 years the cardiovascular and mortality answer was “not yet”; the shelf keeps that order rather than borrowing the 30-year answer backward
cards.source: Li G, Zhang P, Wang J, et al. The long-term effect of lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes in the China Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Study: a 20-year follow-up study. Lancet. 2008;371(9626):1783–1789. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(08)60766-7. PMID 18502303. And: Gong Q, Zhang P, Wang J, et al; Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Study Group. Morbidity and mortality after lifestyle intervention for people with impaired glucose tolerance: 30-year results of the Da Qing Diabetes Prevention Outcome Study. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2019;7(6):452–461. DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(19)30093-2. PMID 31036503.
cards.search: da qing china lifestyle intervention 20-year 30-year follow-up delay onset 3.6 years cardiovascular events microvascular complications mortality life expectancy lancet 2008 2019 pmid 18502303 pmid 31036503

cards.headline: DPPOS 2009: ten years on, the pushed-back clock keeps its lead — cumulative incidence still reduced by 34% in the original lifestyle group.
cards.summary: DPP Outcomes Study 2009 — during the 10 years since DPP randomisation, diabetes incidence was reduced by 34% in the original lifestyle group and 18% in the metformin group compared with placebo; incidence rates converged during follow-up (5.9 vs 4.9 vs 5.6 cases per 100 person-years) once all groups were offered lifestyle intervention, but cumulative incidence remained lowest in the lifestyle group — 2,766 of the original participants followed.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial, Lancet 2009
cards.people: 2,766 of 3,150 eligible DPP participants (88%) enrolled for follow-up — 910 from the original lifestyle group, 924 from metformin, and 932 from placebo — for a median additional 5.7 years. All three groups were offered group-implemented lifestyle intervention; metformin was continued in the original metformin group, and the original lifestyle group was offered additional support
cards.result: Diabetes incidence during the DPP itself had been 4.8 cases per 100 person-years in the lifestyle group, 7.8 in the metformin group, and 11.0 in the placebo group. During the DPPOS follow-up, incidence rates were similar between the groups — 5.9 per 100 person-years for lifestyle, 4.9 for metformin, and 5.6 for placebo — because the former placebo and metformin groups now received lifestyle intervention too. Across the 10 years since randomisation, incidence remained reduced by 34% (95% CI 24–42%) in the lifestyle group and by 18% (7–28%) in the metformin group compared with placebo, and the cumulative incidence of diabetes remained lowest in the lifestyle group. The lifestyle group had lost weight during the DPP and partly regained it; the modest weight loss on metformin was maintained
cards.watchOut: Converging yearly rates after the trial are not the delay being “paid back” — they are what a head start looks like once everyone else starts running: the lifestyle group’s early years spent below the diagnostic line stay banked in the cumulative curve permanently. That the lead survived substantial weight regain makes the persistence more notable, not less
cards.source: Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group; Knowler WC, Fowler SE, Hamman RF, et al. 10-year follow-up of diabetes incidence and weight loss in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study. Lancet. 2009;374(9702):1677–1686. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(09)61457-4. PMID 19878986.
cards.search: dppos diabetes prevention program outcomes study 10-year follow-up incidence persistence lifestyle metformin cumulative lancet 2009 pmid 19878986 doi 10.1016/s0140-6736(09)61457-4 delay

shelves.title: Methods to delay the formal diagnosis of diabetes: medicines
shelves.question: Can a drug push back the day prediabetes becomes diabetes — and is the clock it moves the disease’s clock, or only the laboratory’s?
shelves.balance: Every glucose drug is also a clock drug. In ADOPT, rosiglitazone held monotherapy longest (15% failure at 5 years; the developer’s extrapolation reaches ~8 years to A1c 8%), canagliflozin’s slope runs to ~7, metformin’s to ~5, the DPP-4 agents and repaglinide to ~4 — a figure the developer himself questions — and glyburide, driving weight gain and insulin resistance, failed fastest: the clock can be wound forward as well as back. Durability is not destiny: rosiglitazone’s own harms are on its card. What none of these agents does is prevent diabetes — they delay its formal diagnosis, which is exactly what the developer’s decree says to call it. One caveat rides the whole shelf: a glucose-lowering drug can mask hyperglycemia rather than delay disease — hold the glucose down pharmacologically and the diagnosis is deferred whether or not the disease itself has slowed. Against pure masking stands the washout evidence: in TRIPOD (Reference 6), protection persisted eight months after the drug was stopped, which argues true delay for the thiazolidinedione class. That tension is stated here, not resolved.

cards.headline: ACT NOW 2011: pioglitazone cut conversion to 2.1% a year vs 7.6% (HR 0.28) — the strongest delay on this shelf, bought with weight and edema.
cards.summary: ACT NOW 2011 — annual incidence of type 2 diabetes was 2.1% on pioglitazone vs 7.6% on placebo, a hazard ratio for conversion of 0.28 (95% CI 0.16–0.49), over a median 2.4 years in 602 adults with impaired glucose tolerance; conversion to normal glucose tolerance occurred in 48% on pioglitazone vs 28% on placebo. The price is on the same card: weight gain 3.9 kg vs 0.77 kg, and edema 12.9% vs 6.4% .
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2011
cards.people: 602 adults with impaired glucose tolerance, randomised to pioglitazone or placebo. Median follow-up 2.4 years; fasting glucose measured quarterly and oral glucose tolerance tests performed annually, with conversion to diabetes confirmed on repeat testing
cards.result: Annual incidence rates for type 2 diabetes were 2.1% in the pioglitazone group and 7.6% in the placebo group — hazard ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.16–0.49; P<0.001), a 72% reduction in the risk of conversion. Conversion to normal glucose tolerance occurred in 48% of the pioglitazone group vs 28% on placebo (P<0.001). Pioglitazone also produced larger falls in fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose, and HbA1c, a decrease in diastolic blood pressure (2.0 mm Hg vs 0.0), and a reduced rate of carotid intima-media thickening
cards.watchOut: The delay was real and its bill was itemised in the same abstract: weight gain was greater with pioglitazone than placebo ( 3.9 kg vs 0.77 kg, P<0.001), and edema was more frequent ( 12.9% vs 6.4% , P=0.007). A median follow-up of 2.4 years also cannot say whether conversion is postponed by years or held below the line only while the drug is taken — the masking question this shelf’s balance line states openly
cards.source: DeFronzo RA, Tripathy D, Schwenke DC, et al; ACT NOW Study. Pioglitazone for diabetes prevention in impaired glucose tolerance. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(12):1104–1115. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1010949. PMID 21428766.
cards.search: act now defronzo pioglitazone impaired glucose tolerance conversion annual incidence hazard ratio weight gain edema nejm 2011 pmid 21428766 doi 10.1056/nejmoa1010949

cards.headline: DREAM 2006: rosiglitazone cut diabetes-or-death to 11.6% vs 26.0% (HR 0.40) — and its factorial partner, ramipril, did nothing (HR 0.91).
cards.summary: DREAM 2006 — in 5,269 adults with impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, the composite primary outcome of incident diabetes or death occurred in 11.6% on rosiglitazone 8 mg daily vs 26.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.40 , 95% CI 0.35–0.46) over a median 3 years, and 50.5% on rosiglitazone regressed to normoglycemia vs 30.3%. The trial’s other drug was null: ramipril’s incidence of diabetes or death was 18.1% vs 19.5% (HR 0.91, P=0.15). Heart failure developed in 14 rosiglitazone participants vs 2 on placebo.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 2-by-2 factorial, Lancet 2006 (rosiglitazone) and N Engl J Med 2006 (ramipril)
cards.people: 5,269 adults aged 30 years or more with impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, or both, and no previous cardiovascular disease, recruited from 191 sites in 21 countries and randomised to rosiglitazone (8 mg daily) or placebo and, factorially, to ramipril (up to 15 mg daily) or placebo; median follow-up 3 years
cards.result: Rosiglitazone: the composite of incident diabetes or death occurred in 306 ( 11.6% ) on rosiglitazone vs 686 ( 26.0% ) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.35–0.46; P<0.0001). Regression to normoglycemia occurred in 50.5% on rosiglitazone vs 30.3% on placebo (HR 1.71). Cardiovascular event rates were much the same in both groups, although 14 (0.5%) rosiglitazone participants and two (0.1%) on placebo developed heart failure (P=0.01). Ramipril, in the same participants, did not significantly reduce the incidence of diabetes or death: 18.1% vs 19.5% — HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.81–1.03; P=0.15) — though it did increase regression to normoglycemia (HR 1.16)
cards.watchOut: Rosiglitazone’s delay arrived with the class liability that later defined the drug — fluid retention, visible here as a heart-failure signal (14 vs 2) in people with no prior cardiovascular disease — and the shelf files DREAM as evidence about delay, not as a recommendation. The ramipril null matters to the shelf’s honesty: in the same trial, in the same people, a plausible mechanism moved nothing
cards.source: DREAM (Diabetes REduction Assessment with ramipril and rosiglitazone Medication) Trial Investigators; Gerstein HC, Yusuf S, Bosch J, et al. Effect of rosiglitazone on the frequency of diabetes in patients with impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2006;368(9541):1096–1105. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(06)69420-8. PMID 16997664. Ramipril arm: Bosch J, Yusuf S, Gerstein HC, et al; DREAM Trial Investigators. Effect of ramipril on the incidence of diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(15):1551–1562. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa065061. PMID 16980380.
cards.search: dream rosiglitazone ramipril impaired fasting glucose impaired glucose tolerance diabetes or death normoglycemia heart failure lancet nejm 2006 pmid 16997664 pmid 16980380

cards.headline: CANOE 2010: half-doses of two drugs — rosiglitazone 2 mg plus metformin 500 mg, twice daily — cut diabetes to 14% vs 39% (NNT 4).
cards.summary: CANOE 2010 — incident diabetes occurred in 14% of the low-dose combination group vs 39% on placebo over a median 3.9 years in 207 adults with impaired glucose tolerance: a relative risk reduction of 66% and an absolute risk reduction of 26%, yielding a number needed to treat of 4 . Regression to normal glucose tolerance: 80% vs 53%. The combination study the developer recalled — two partial drugs, one large delay.
cards.people: 207 patients with impaired glucose tolerance in Canadian centres, randomised to combination rosiglitazone (2 mg) and metformin (500 mg) twice daily (103) or matching placebo (104), for a median of 3.9 years; medication compliance (at least 80% of assigned medication) was 78% in the treatment group and 81% on placebo
cards.result: Incident diabetes occurred in 14 ( 14% ) of the active treatment group vs 41 ( 39% ) on placebo (P<0.0001) — relative risk reduction 66% (95% CI 41–80%), absolute risk reduction 26% (14–37), number needed to treat 4 . Seventy patients (80%) in the treatment group regressed to normal glucose tolerance vs 52 (53%) on placebo. Insulin sensitivity decreased by study end on placebo and remained unchanged on treatment, while the change in beta-cell function did not differ between groups. Diarrhoea was more frequent on treatment (16% vs 6%)
cards.watchOut: A small trial — 207 people — with a large effect is exactly where a shelf should slow down: the confidence interval on the relative risk reduction runs from 41% to 80%, the trial was not sized to weigh harms, and the rosiglitazone half of the pair carries the class watch-outs filed on Reference 2 of this shelf. CANOE shows what a low-dose combination can do to the diagnosis rate; it does not settle the price
cards.source: Zinman B, Harris SB, Neuman J, et al. Low-dose combination therapy with rosiglitazone and metformin to prevent type 2 diabetes mellitus (CANOE trial): a double-blind randomised controlled study. Lancet. 2010;376(9735):103–111. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)60746-5. PMID 20605202.
cards.search: canoe zinman low-dose rosiglitazone metformin combination impaired glucose tolerance diabetes nnt lancet 2010 pmid 20605202 doi 10.1016/s0140-6736(10)60746-5

cards.headline: STOP-NIDDM 2002: acarbose delayed conversion (32% vs 42%, relative hazard 0.75) — in a trial 31% of the drug arm left early.
cards.summary: STOP-NIDDM 2002 — diabetes developed in 32% of patients randomised to acarbose vs 42% on placebo (relative hazard 0.75 , 95% CI 0.63–0.90) in 1,429 patients with impaired glucose tolerance; 31% of the acarbose group and 19% of the placebo group discontinued treatment early — flatulence and diarrhoea were the most frequent side effects. At study end, three months back on placebo were followed by increased conversion to diabetes.
cards.people: 1,429 patients with impaired glucose tolerance — 714 allocated to acarbose 100 mg three times daily and 715 to placebo; the primary endpoint was development of diabetes on a yearly oral glucose tolerance test, analysed by intention to treat
cards.result: Diabetes developed in 221 ( 32% ) of the patients randomised to acarbose and 285 ( 42% ) randomised to placebo — relative hazard 0.75 (95% CI 0.63–0.90; P=0.0015). Acarbose also significantly increased reversion of impaired glucose tolerance to normal glucose tolerance. The trial built the masking question into its own design: at the end of the study, treatment with placebo for 3 months was associated with an increase in conversion of impaired glucose tolerance to diabetes — part of the on-treatment gap closed as soon as the drug stopped holding glucose down
cards.watchOut: Tolerability is this trial’s second result: 211 ( 31% ) of the acarbose patients and 130 (19%) on placebo discontinued treatment early, most often for gastrointestinal effects — flatulence and diarrhoea. And the shelf flags the sequel separately: a later post-hoc analysis from this trial programme claimed a cardiovascular benefit for acarbose — a claim drawn from few events, not a prespecified endpoint of this trial, and contested ever since; it is not carded here as evidence
cards.source: Chiasson JL, Josse RG, Gomis R, Hanefeld M, Karasik A, Laakso M; STOP-NIDDM Trial Research Group. Acarbose for prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus: the STOP-NIDDM randomised trial. Lancet. 2002;359(9323):2072–2077. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(02)08905-5. PMID 12086760.
cards.search: stop-niddm chiasson acarbose impaired glucose tolerance diabetes discontinuation dropout flatulence diarrhoea lancet 2002 pmid 12086760 doi 10.1016/s0140-6736(02)08905-5

cards.headline: NAVIGATOR 2010: nateglinide did NOT delay — diabetes 36% vs 34% (HR 1.07), with more hypoglycemia. The secretagogue null.
cards.summary: NAVIGATOR 2010 — among 9,306 participants with impaired glucose tolerance and cardiovascular disease or risk factors, followed a median 5.0 years, nateglinide did not reduce the cumulative incidence of diabetes: 36% vs 34% (hazard ratio 1.07 , 95% CI 1.00–1.15) — and it increased the risk of hypoglycemia. The trial’s other drug did delay, modestly: valsartan 33.1% vs 36.8% (HR 0.86), a relative reduction of 14% in diabetes incidence, with no reduction in cardiovascular events.
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial, 2-by-2 factorial, N Engl J Med 2010
cards.people: 9,306 participants with impaired glucose tolerance and either cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors, assigned to nateglinide (up to 60 mg three times daily) or placebo and, factorially, valsartan (up to 160 mg daily) or placebo, in addition to a lifestyle modification program; median follow-up 5.0 years for incident diabetes
cards.result: Nateglinide, as compared with placebo, did not significantly reduce the cumulative incidence of diabetes — 36% and 34% respectively; hazard ratio 1.07 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.15; P=0.05) — nor the core composite cardiovascular outcome (7.9% vs 8.3%; HR 0.94) or the extended composite (14.2% vs 15.2%; HR 0.93). Nateglinide did, however, increase the risk of hypoglycemia. Valsartan’s arm: cumulative diabetes incidence 33.1% vs 36.8% — HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.80–0.92; P<0.001), a relative reduction of 14% — with no significant reduction in either cardiovascular composite outcome
cards.watchOut: This card is the shelf’s control experiment for the developer’s skepticism about secretagogue delay claims: squeezing more insulin out of a beta cell under strain did not slow the diagnosis clock at all over five years — the same pattern Part B shows in ADOPT, where the sulfonylurea failed fastest. It is filed at full weight precisely because it is null
cards.source: NAVIGATOR Study Group; Holman RR, Haffner SM, McMurray JJ, et al. Effect of nateglinide on the incidence of diabetes and cardiovascular events. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(16):1463–1476. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1001122. PMID 20228402. Valsartan arm: NAVIGATOR Study Group; McMurray JJ, Holman RR, Haffner SM, et al. Effect of valsartan on the incidence of diabetes and cardiovascular events. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(16):1477–1490. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1001121. PMID 20228403.
cards.search: navigator nateglinide valsartan impaired glucose tolerance diabetes incidence hypoglycemia null secretagogue nejm 2010 pmid 20228402 pmid 20228403 doi 10.1056/nejmoa1001122

cards.headline: TRIPOD / PIPOD: troglitazone, then pioglitazone, in women with prior gestational diabetes — annual incidence 5.4% vs 12.1%, and protection that outlasted the drug.
cards.summary: TRIPOD 2002 — in high-risk Hispanic women with previous gestational diabetes, average annual diabetes incidence rates were 5.4% on troglitazone vs 12.1% on placebo over a median 30 months, and protection from diabetes persisted 8 months after study medications were stopped — the washout evidence that a glitazone’s delay is more than masking. PIPOD 2006 followed with pioglitazone in the same cohort: the decline in beta-cell function was stopped, and diabetes occurred at an average rate of 4.6% per year .
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trials (TRIPOD) and its pioglitazone follow-on (PIPOD), Diabetes 2002 and 2006
cards.people: Women with previous gestational diabetes, randomised to placebo (n=133) or troglitazone 400 mg/day (n=133); 236 women returned for at least one follow-up visit, with a median follow-up of 30 months on blinded medication, and women who did not develop diabetes returned for testing 8 months after study medications were stopped. Of 95 women not diabetic at the end of TRIPOD, 89 enrolled in PIPOD for a planned 3 years of pioglitazone treatment and 6 months of post-drug washout
cards.result: TRIPOD: average annual diabetes incidence rates were 12.1% in women assigned to placebo and 5.4% in women assigned to troglitazone (P<0.01). Protection from diabetes was closely related to the reduction in endogenous insulin requirements three months after randomisation, was associated with preservation of beta-cell compensation for insulin resistance — and persisted 8 months after study medications were stopped . PIPOD: pioglitazone stopped the decline in beta-cell function that had occurred during placebo treatment in TRIPOD and maintained the stability achieved on troglitazone; diabetes occurred at an average rate of 4.6% per year , lowest in women with the largest reduction in insulin output after one year of treatment. The authors read the two studies together as a thiazolidinedione class effect
cards.watchOut: Troglitazone was withdrawn from the market for hepatotoxicity, so this card is a class-effect and history card: the drug is gone, but the design is the shelf’s best answer to the masking question — an effect still present eight months after the drug stopped is not a drug holding a glucose value down. Read the scale honestly: a narrow, very high-risk population — Hispanic women after gestational diabetes — and small numbers next to DREAM or NAVIGATOR
cards.source: Buchanan TA, Xiang AH, Peters RK, et al. Preservation of pancreatic beta-cell function and prevention of type 2 diabetes by pharmacological treatment of insulin resistance in high-risk hispanic women. Diabetes. 2002;51(9):2796–2803. DOI 10.2337/diabetes.51.9.2796. PMID 12196473. And: Xiang AH, Peters RK, Kjos SL, et al. Effect of pioglitazone on pancreatic beta-cell function and diabetes risk in Hispanic women with prior gestational diabetes. Diabetes. 2006;55(2):517–522. DOI 10.2337/diabetes.55.02.06.db05-1066. PMID 16443789.

cards.headline: SCALE Prediabetes 2017: liraglutide 3.0 mg — diabetes in 2% vs 6% over three years (HR 0.21); time to diagnosis 2.7 times longer.
cards.summary: SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes, 3-year assessment 2017 — by week 160, diabetes had been diagnosed in 2% of the liraglutide 3.0 mg group vs 6% on placebo, and the time to onset of diabetes was 2.7 times longer with liraglutide, corresponding to a hazard ratio of 0.21 (95% CI 0.13–0.34) — 2,254 adults with prediabetes and obesity, all receiving diet and activity counseling. Weight loss at week 160: −6.1% vs −1.9%.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (3-year assessment), Lancet 2017
cards.people: 2,254 adults with prediabetes and a body-mass index of at least 30 kg/m², or at least 27 kg/m² with comorbidities, at 191 clinical research sites in 27 countries, randomised 2:1 to once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide 3.0 mg (1,505) or matched placebo (749), as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. The primary outcome was time to diabetes onset by 160 weeks
cards.result: By week 160, 26 ( 2% ) of 1,472 individuals in the liraglutide group vs 46 ( 6% ) of 738 in the placebo group were diagnosed with diabetes while on treatment. The mean time from randomisation to diagnosis was 99 weeks for those diagnosed on liraglutide vs 87 weeks on placebo; taking the different diagnosis frequencies into account, the time to onset of diabetes over 160 weeks was 2.7 times longer with liraglutide (95% CI 1.9–3.9; P<0.0001), corresponding to a hazard ratio of 0.21 (95% CI 0.13–0.34). Liraglutide produced greater weight loss at week 160 (−6.1% vs −1.9%). Serious adverse events were reported by 15% of the liraglutide group vs 13% on placebo
cards.watchOut: Half the trial walked away: only 50% of participants completed the study to week 160, after withdrawal of 47% of the liraglutide group and 55% of the placebo group, and withdrawn individuals were not followed up after discontinuation — a limitation the authors state themselves. Note also the route: liraglutide’s delay runs substantially through weight loss, which makes this card the medicines shelf’s bridge back to Shelf #111 — the drug borrows the lifestyle mechanism. What happens to the clock after the injections stop, this trial does not say
cards.source: le Roux CW, Astrup A, Fujioka K, et al; SCALE Obesity Prediabetes NN8022-1839 Study Group. 3 years of liraglutide versus placebo for type 2 diabetes risk reduction and weight management in individuals with prediabetes: a randomised, double-blind trial. Lancet. 2017;389(10077):1399–1409. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)30069-7. PMID 28237263.

cards.headline: ADOPT 2006: the durability anchor — five-year monotherapy failure 15% rosiglitazone, 21% metformin, 34% glyburide.
cards.summary: ADOPT 2006 — Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence of monotherapy failure at 5 years was 15% with rosiglitazone, 21% with metformin, and 34% with glyburide, in 4,360 patients with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes treated for a median of 4.0 years; rosiglitazone’s risk of failure was reduced by 32% vs metformin and 63% vs glyburide. Failure meant a confirmed fasting glucose above 180 mg/dL. This is the trial Part B — and the developer’s year-lines on the next card — hang on.
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2006
cards.people: 4,360 patients with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, treated with rosiglitazone, metformin, or glyburide as initial treatment for a median of 4.0 years. The primary outcome was time to monotherapy failure, defined as a confirmed fasting plasma glucose above 180 mg/dL
cards.result: Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence of monotherapy failure at 5 years: 15% with rosiglitazone, 21% with metformin, and 34% with glyburide — a risk reduction of 32% for rosiglitazone compared with metformin and 63% compared with glyburide (P<0.001 for both comparisons); the difference in durability was greater between rosiglitazone and glyburide than between rosiglitazone and metformin. Rosiglitazone was associated with more weight gain and edema than either comparator, but with fewer gastrointestinal events than metformin and less hypoglycemia than glyburide. Glyburide was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events (including congestive heart failure) than rosiglitazone
cards.watchOut: ADOPT enrolled people who already had diabetes — it is filed here as the durability engine of the delay argument, which is the developer’s construction: the drug class that holds glucose longest after diagnosis is the one whose slope best resists the diagnostic line before it. Failure was defined by fasting glucose crossing 180 mg/dL, not by A1c — so the translation to “years to A1c 8%” on the next card is an extrapolation, and is labeled one there
cards.source: Kahn SE, Haffner SM, Heise MA, et al; ADOPT Study Group. Glycemic durability of rosiglitazone, metformin, or glyburide monotherapy. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(23):2427–2443. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa066224. PMID 17145742.

cards.headline: The developer’s year-lines: years until A1c climbs back to 8% — rosiglitazone ~8, canagliflozin ~7, metformin ~5, DPP-4 agents and repaglinide ~4.
cards.summary: DEVELOPER’S ESTIMATES, labeled as such — reading the durability slopes, ADOPT’s first (Reference 8), as clocks to the A1c 8% line: rosiglitazone ~8 years (an EXTRAPOLATION from 5 years of data), canagliflozin ~7 years (developer’s estimate, from ~5 years tested; source to pin), metformin ~5 years , and DPP-4 agents and repaglinide ~4 years — this last WITH the developer’s objection printed in full: a GLP-1-pathway agent delaying less than metformin makes little mechanistic sense, and the figure is provisional.
cards.type: Developer’s synthesis — extrapolations and estimates built chiefly on ADOPT (Reference 8), labeled line by line
cards.people: No trial population of its own — a reading of the trial record, chiefly ADOPT’s 4,360 patients with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes (Reference 8)
cards.result: Rosiglitazone ~8 years: extending ADOPT’s rosiglitazone slope — the shallowest failure curve on Card 8, 15% at 5 years — to the A1c 8% line reaches roughly eight years. An EXTRAPOLATION beyond the five years of data, labeled as one. Canagliflozin ~7 years: the developer’s estimate from roughly five years of SGLT2 testing — glycosuria keeps lowering glucose while beta cells decline, the mechanism story; the pinning source for this line is still to be filed, and the line is labeled a developer’s estimate until it is. Metformin ~5 years: ADOPT’s middle curve (21% failure at 5 years); consistent with metformin’s DPP showing on Shelf #111 (−31% incidence). DPP-4 agents (linagliptin, sitagliptin) and repaglinide ~4 years: the developer’s figure — with his doubt riding on it, in Watch out
cards.watchOut: The developer’s objection, printed as given: the ~4-year line for the DPP-4 agents puzzles him — a GLP-1-pathway agent should, if anything, delay longer than metformin, not shorter; the figure makes little mechanistic sense to him and stays provisional until its source is pinned. The repaglinide line carries its own counterweight on this shelf: NAVIGATOR (Reference 5), the one large secretagogue-class delay trial, found no delay at all. Every number on this card is an estimate or an extrapolation — the trial-measured numbers are on Cards 1–8 and 10
cards.source: Developer’s estimates (John Tayek, MD, Oct 25, 2026), built on: Kahn SE, Haffner SM, Heise MA, et al; ADOPT Study Group. Glycemic durability of rosiglitazone, metformin, or glyburide monotherapy. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(23):2427–2443. PMID 17145742. The canagliflozin line’s pinning source is still to be filed; the line is labeled a developer’s estimate until it is.

cards.headline: Glyburide, the cautionary card: failed fastest in ADOPT (34% by five years) — the class that winds the diagnosis clock forward.
cards.summary: ADOPT 2006, read from the other end — glyburide’s cumulative monotherapy failure at 5 years was 34% , against 21% on metformin and 15% on rosiglitazone: the sulfonylurea exhausted itself first, and rosiglitazone’s failure risk was 63% lower than glyburide’s. The developer’s mechanism, stated as his: sulfonylureas drive weight gain and insulin resistance — the two forces that wind the diabetes clock FORWARD — so the class that treats the number can hasten the disease’s own timetable.
cards.type: Reading of a randomised trial’s glyburide arm, N Engl J Med 2006, with the developer’s mechanism stated as his
cards.people: The glyburide arm of ADOPT — patients with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes on glyburide monotherapy, within the 4,360-patient trial on Card 8
cards.result: Cumulative incidence of monotherapy failure at 5 years was 34% with glyburide, vs 21% with metformin and 15% with rosiglitazone — rosiglitazone’s risk reduction compared with glyburide was 63% (P<0.001). Glyburide was also associated with more hypoglycemia than rosiglitazone. The rhyme on this shelf is NAVIGATOR (Reference 5): the secretagogue nateglinide produced no delay at all in prediabetes (HR 1.07)
cards.watchOut: The mechanism sentence is the developer’s, labeled as his: weight gain and insulin resistance winding the clock forward is his physiological reading of the failure curve, not an ADOPT endpoint — ADOPT measured failure, weight gain, and hypoglycemia, and the failure ranking is the verified part. In fairness to the drug, ADOPT also recorded one glyburide advantage — a lower risk of cardiovascular events (including congestive heart failure) than rosiglitazone — and this shelf keeps that on the record too
cards.source: Kahn SE, Haffner SM, Heise MA, et al; ADOPT Study Group. Glycemic durability of rosiglitazone, metformin, or glyburide monotherapy. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(23):2427–2443. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa066224. PMID 17145742. Mechanism framing: developer’s comment, Oct 25, 2026.

cards.headline: D2d 2019: vitamin D3 4,000 IU a day did not significantly delay diabetes in prediabetes — HR 0.88, P = 0.12.
cards.summary: D2d 2019 — diabetes onset was 9.39 vs 10.66 per 100 person-years on vitamin D3 4,000 IU daily vs placebo (293 of 1,211 vs 323 of 1,212); hazard ratio 0.88 (0.75–1.04), P=0.12 — not significant, over a median 2.5 years in 2,423 adults with prediabetes.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 2,423 adults meeting at least two of three ADA prediabetes criteria — not chosen for vitamin D deficiency (mean starting level 28 ng/mL) — took vitamin D3 4,000 IU daily or placebo for a median 2.5 years
cards.result: Vitamin D3 4,000 IU a day did not significantly delay diabetes in prediabetes. Levels rose to 54.3 vs 28.8 ng/mL . Diabetes onset: 9.39 vs 10.66 per 100 person-years (293 of 1,211 vs 323 of 1,212); HR 0.88 (0.75–1.04), P=0.12
cards.watchOut: In a post hoc look at the 103 people starting below 12 ng/mL, HR was 0.38 (0.18–0.80) — a hypothesis, not a result
cards.source: Pittas AG, Dawson-Hughes B, Sheehan P, et al; D2d Research Group. Vitamin D supplementation and prevention of type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(6):520–530. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1900906. PMID 31173679. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01942694.

shelves.title: Time-restricted eating: the clock adds nothing
shelves.question: Does confining eating to a daily window (16:8 or similar) cause weight loss beyond what eating less already does?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose · Body Composition · Body Mass Index · Caloric Restriction · Diet Therapy · Fasting · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity · Patient Compliance · Time Factors · Weight Loss · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials asked it cleanly and got the same answer. TREAT found the fasting window produced no between-group weight difference at all — and the small loss leaned toward lean mass. Liu added time restriction on top of calorie restriction for a full year and gained nothing: the calories did all the work in both arms. Time-restricted eating is a scheduling preference some people find easier to keep; as a metabolic intervention, the trials say the clock itself contributes nothing measurable.

cards.headline: TREAT 2020: 16:8 time-restricted eating for 12 weeks — weight −0.94 kg within the group, but −0.26 kg vs control (P=0.63). No effect, and a lean-mass signal.
cards.summary: Weight fell within the time-restricted group (−0.94 kg; P=0.01) but the between-group difference — the comparison that counts — was −0.26 kg (95% CI −1.30 to 0.78; P=0.63). No significant differences in fat mass, glucose, insulin, or lipids. Appendicular lean mass index fell significantly more with time restriction (−0.16 kg/m²; P=0.005).
cards.type: Randomized trial, single center with remote follow-up
cards.people: 116 adults with overweight or obesity (mean age 46.5 years)
cards.result: Weight fell within the time-restricted group (−0.94 kg; P=0.01) but the between-group difference — the comparison that counts — was −0.26 kg (95% CI −1.30 to 0.78; P=0.63). No significant differences in fat mass, glucose, insulin, or lipids. Appendicular lean mass index fell significantly more with time restriction (−0.16 kg/m²; P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: The trial's publicity leaned on the within-group loss; the randomized comparison is null. And the lean-mass finding cuts against the usual fasting narrative: of the little weight that moved, a disproportionate share was muscle-side tissue.
cards.source: Lowe DA et al., JAMA Intern Med 2020 (PMID 32986097 · NCT03393195)

cards.headline: Liu 2022: time restriction added to calorie restriction for 12 months — −8.0 vs −6.3 kg (net −1.8 kg; P=0.11). A year long, still nothing from the clock.
cards.summary: Both groups lost substantial weight on calorie restriction; adding the 8 a.m.–4 p.m. eating window changed nothing significant — weight −8.0 kg vs −6.3 kg (net difference −1.8 kg; 95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11), with waist, body fat, blood pressure, and metabolic risk factors all consistent with the null primary result, and no difference in adverse events.
cards.people: 139 patients with obesity (118 completed 12 months)
cards.result: Both groups lost substantial weight on calorie restriction; adding the 8 a.m.–4 p.m. eating window changed nothing significant — weight −8.0 kg vs −6.3 kg (net difference −1.8 kg; 95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11), with waist, body fat, blood pressure, and metabolic risk factors all consistent with the null primary result, and no difference in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This is the strongest design the question has had — a full year, an active comparator, real weight loss in both arms — and the window's contribution is statistically indistinguishable from zero. What works is eating less; the window is one way some people manage that, not an additional mechanism.
cards.source: Liu D et al., N Engl J Med 2022 (PMID 35443107 · NCT03745612)

shelves.title: Intensive glucose control in type 2 diabetes
shelves.question: In people with long-standing type 2 diabetes, does pushing A1c toward normal with intensive therapy prevent heart attacks, strokes, and death?
shelves.balance: Three large randomized trials, 23,182 patients with long-standing diabetes: pushing A1c down to about 6.5–6.9% did not reduce heart attacks, strokes, or cardiovascular death in any of them. ACCORD — the most aggressive, targeting A1c below 6% — was stopped early because more patients died on intensive therapy (5.0% vs 4.0%). The one consistent gain was kidney protection: ADVANCE cut new or worsening nephropathy (4.1% vs 5.2%). Severe hypoglycemia rose in every trial. All three trials enrolled patients with roughly a decade of diabetes — they do not answer what early control does in the newly diagnosed.

cards.headline: Targeting A1c below 6% increased deaths — ACCORD's intensive arm was stopped early
cards.summary: A1c reached 6.4% vs 7.5% at one year. Primary composite (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, cardiovascular death): 352 vs 371 patients, HR 0.90 (0.78–1.04), P=0.16 — not significant. Deaths: 257 vs 203 (5.0% vs 4.0%), HR 1.22 (1.01–1.46), P=0.04.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (open-label targets, blinded outcome adjudication), NEJM 2008
cards.people: 10,251 patients (mean age 62.2 years; median A1c 8.1%; median diabetes duration ~10 years; 35% with a previous cardiovascular event) assigned to intensive therapy (target A1c <6.0%) or standard therapy (7.0–7.9%).
cards.result: A1c reached 6.4% vs 7.5% at one year. Primary composite (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, cardiovascular death): 352 vs 371 patients, HR 0.90 (0.78–1.04), P=0.16 — not significant. Deaths: 257 vs 203 (5.0% vs 4.0%), HR 1.22 (1.01–1.46), P=0.04. Higher mortality led to discontinuation of the intensive regimen after a mean of 3.5 years.
cards.watchOut: Hypoglycemia requiring assistance and weight gain of more than 10 kg were more frequent on intensive therapy (P<0.001 for both). The mechanism of the excess deaths was never established.
cards.source: Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes Study Group (Gerstein HC et al.). Effects of intensive glucose lowering in type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med 2008;358:2545–2559. PMID: 18539917 · NCT00000620.
cards.search: targeting a1c below 6% increased deaths — accord's intensive arm was stopped early in high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes, does intensive therapy targeting a1c below 6.0%, versus standard therapy targeting 7.0–7.9%, reduce cardiovascular events? randomized controlled trial (open-label targets, blinded outcome adjudication), nejm 2008 10,251 patients (mean age 62.2 years; median a1c 8.1%; median diabetes duration ~10 years; 35% with a previous cardiovascular event) assigned to intensive therapy (target a1c <6.0%) or standard therapy (7.0–7.9%). a1c reached 6.4% vs 7.5% at one year. primary composite (nonfatal mi, nonfatal stroke, cardiovascular death): 352 vs 371 patients, hr 0.90 (0.78–1.04), p=0.16 — not significant. deaths: 257 vs 203 (5.0% vs 4.0%), hr 1.22 (1.01–1.46), p=0.04. higher mortality led to discontinuation of the intensive regimen after a mean of 3.5 years.

cards.headline: Intensive control cut kidney disease but not heart attacks, strokes, or death
cards.summary: Mean A1c 6.5% vs 7.3%. Combined major macrovascular and microvascular events: 18.1% vs 20.0%, HR 0.90 (0.82–0.98), P=0.01 — driven by major microvascular events, primarily new or worsening nephropathy (4.1% vs 5.2%, HR 0.79 (0.66–0.93), P=0.006). Major macrovascular events: HR 0.94 (0.84–1.06), P=0.32.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (PROBE: open-label treatment, blinded endpoints), NEJM 2008
cards.people: 11,140 patients with type 2 diabetes assigned to intensive control (gliclazide modified-release plus other drugs as required, target A1c ≤6.5%) or standard control; median follow-up 5 years.
cards.result: Mean A1c 6.5% vs 7.3%. Combined major macrovascular and microvascular events: 18.1% vs 20.0%, HR 0.90 (0.82–0.98), P=0.01 — driven by major microvascular events (9.4% vs 10.9%, HR 0.86), primarily new or worsening nephropathy (4.1% vs 5.2%, HR 0.79 (0.66–0.93), P=0.006); no significant effect on retinopathy. Major macrovascular events: HR 0.94 (0.84–1.06), P=0.32. Death from cardiovascular causes: HR 0.88 (0.74–1.04). Death from any cause: HR 0.93 (0.83–1.06), P=0.28.
cards.watchOut: Severe hypoglycemia was more common on intensive control (2.7% vs 1.5%, HR 1.86 (1.42–2.40)). The significant composite rests on kidney outcomes — there was no reduction in heart attacks, strokes, or death.
cards.source: ADVANCE Collaborative Group (Patel A et al.). Intensive blood glucose control and vascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med 2008;358:2560–2572. PMID: 18539916 · NCT00145925.

cards.headline: Intensive control in veterans changed nothing — no fewer events, deaths, or complications
cards.summary: Median A1c 6.9% vs 8.4%. Primary composite: 235 vs 264 patients, HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05), P=0.14 — not significant. Death from any cause: HR 1.07 (0.81–1.42), P=0.62.
cards.people: 1,791 military veterans (mean age 60.4 years; mean 11.5 years since diagnosis; 40% with a previous cardiovascular event) who had a suboptimal response to therapy, assigned to intensive or standard glucose control; other cardiovascular risk factors treated uniformly; median follow-up 5.6 years.
cards.result: Median A1c 6.9% vs 8.4%. Primary composite (MI, stroke, cardiovascular death, congestive heart failure, surgery for vascular disease, inoperable coronary disease, amputation for ischemic gangrene): 235 vs 264 patients, HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05), P=0.14 — not significant. Death from any cause: HR 1.07 (0.81–1.42), P=0.62. No differences in microvascular complications except slower progression of albuminuria (P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Adverse events, predominantly hypoglycemia, were more frequent on intensive therapy (24.1% vs 17.6%). A 10-year post-trial follow-up suggested a delayed event reduction that was gone by 15 years — the trial itself was neutral.

shelves.title: DPP-4 inhibitors: cardiovascular safety without benefit
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, do DPP-4 inhibitors (the gliptins) prevent cardiovascular events — or at least do no cardiovascular harm?
shelves.balance: Five double-blind randomized trials, 49,564 patients: no DPP-4 inhibitor prevented cardiovascular events, and none increased the primary composite either — saxagliptin HR 1.00, alogliptin 0.96, sitagliptin 0.98, linagliptin 1.02 against placebo, and 0.98 against glimepiride. These were the FDA-era safety trials, and on ischemic events the class is acquitted. One genuine exception: saxagliptin increased hospitalization for heart failure (3.5% vs 2.8%; HR 1.27) — a signal strong enough to put a heart-failure warning on the saxagliptin and alogliptin labels, and not seen with sitagliptin (HR 1.00) or linagliptin. The glucose gains were modest throughout (A1c about 0.3 points below placebo). So the gliptins are safe, gentle glucose-lowering drugs that prevent nothing — a different species from the SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agents, which reduce events. Their clearest comparative win is against a sulfonylurea: in CAROLINA, linagliptin matched glimepiride event-for-event over 6.3 years with about a quarter of the hypoglycemia.

cards.headline: Saxagliptin: no effect on heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death — but more heart-failure hospitalizations
cards.summary: Primary composite: 613 (7.3%) vs 609 (7.2%) — HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12). Hospitalization for heart failure: 289 (3.5%) vs 228 (2.8%) — HR 1.27 (1.07–1.51).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (phase 4 safety trial)
cards.people: 16,492 patients with type 2 diabetes who had a history of, or were at risk for, cardiovascular events; median follow-up 2.1 years. Saxagliptin 5 mg daily (2.5 mg if eGFR ≤50) vs placebo, on top of usual care.
cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke): 613 (7.3%) vs 609 (7.2%) — HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12; P=0.99 for superiority; P<0.001 for noninferiority). The broader secondary composite was also neutral (12.8% vs 12.4%; HR 1.02). But hospitalization for heart failure was higher with saxagliptin: 289 (3.5%) vs 228 (2.8%) — HR 1.27 (1.07–1.51; P=0.007). Death from any cause: 4.9% vs 4.2% (HR 1.11; 0.96–1.27; P=0.15, not significant).
cards.watchOut: The heart-failure excess was a prespecified secondary endpoint — unexpected, and concentrated in patients with prior heart failure or high natriuretic-peptide levels. In 2016 the FDA added a heart-failure warning to the saxagliptin label. Pancreatitis was uncommon and similar (acute pancreatitis 0.3% vs 0.2%).

cards.headline: Right after a heart attack or unstable angina, alogliptin did not increase major cardiovascular events
cards.summary: Primary composite: 305 (11.3%) vs 316 (11.8%) — HR 0.96, upper boundary of the one-sided repeated confidence interval 1.16 (P<0.001 for noninferiority).
cards.people: 5,380 patients with type 2 diabetes and an acute myocardial infarction or unstable angina requiring hospitalization within the previous 15 to 90 days; followed for up to 40 months (median 18 months).

The FDA nonetheless added a heart-failure warning to the alogliptin label in 2016, alongside saxagliptin's.

cards.headline: Sitagliptin: no cardiovascular benefit — and, unlike saxagliptin, no heart-failure signal
cards.summary: Primary composite: 839 (11.4%) vs 851 (11.6%) — HR 0.98 (95% CI 0.88–1.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Hospitalization for heart failure: HR 1.00 (0.83–1.20).
cards.people: 14,671 patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease; median follow-up 3.0 years. Other glucose-lowering drugs could be added openly in both groups to reach glycemic targets.
cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina): 839 (11.4%; 4.06 per 100 person-years) vs 851 (11.6%; 4.17) — HR 0.98 (95% CI 0.88–1.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Hospitalization for heart failure did not differ: HR 1.00 (0.83–1.20; P=0.98). The A1c difference was small (−0.29 percentage points). Acute pancreatitis (P=0.07) and pancreatic cancer (P=0.32) did not differ significantly.

cards.headline: In diabetes with both cardiovascular and kidney risk, linagliptin was neutral for the heart — and for the kidneys
cards.summary: Primary composite: 434 of 3,494 (12.4%) vs 420 of 3,485 (12.1%) — HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.89–1.17; P<.001 for noninferiority).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial (605 sites, 27 countries)
cards.people: 6,979 patients treated (of 6,991 enrolled) with type 2 diabetes, A1c 6.5–10.0%, and high cardiovascular and renal risk: mean age 65.9 years, mean eGFR 54.6 mL/min/1.73 m², 80.1% with urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio >30 mg/g; end-stage kidney disease excluded. Median follow-up 2.2 years.
cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke): 434 of 3,494 (12.4%) vs 420 of 3,485 (12.1%) — HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.89–1.17; P<.001 for noninferiority). The kidney composite (death from kidney failure, end-stage kidney disease, or a sustained ≥40% fall in eGFR): 327 (9.4%) vs 306 (8.8%) — HR 1.04 (0.89–1.22; P=.62). Hypoglycemia was similar (at least one episode in 29.7% vs 29.4%, mostly from background drugs). Adjudicated acute pancreatitis: 9 (0.3%) vs 5 (0.1%).
cards.watchOut: Progression of albuminuria was slower with linagliptin (HR 0.86) — a surrogate gain that did not become fewer kidney failures. The trial's heart-failure analysis found no increase in heart-failure hospitalization. Linagliptin's practical niche is renal: it needs no dose adjustment as kidney function falls, and this is the trial that defends that use.

cards.headline: Head-to-head over 6.3 years: linagliptin matched glimepiride on cardiovascular events, with a fraction of the hypoglycemia
cards.summary: Primary composite: 356 of 3,023 (11.8%) with linagliptin vs 362 of 3,010 (12.0%) with glimepiride — HR 0.98 (95.47% CI 0.84–1.14). Hypoglycemia: 320 (10.6%) vs 1,132 (37.7%) — HR 0.23 (0.21–0.26).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, active-controlled noninferiority trial (607 sites, 43 countries)
cards.people: 6,042 patients randomized (6,033 treated and analyzed) with relatively early type 2 diabetes — median duration 6.3 years, mean A1c 7.2%, mean age 64.0 years, 42% with macrovascular disease; median follow-up 6.3 years, the longest on this shelf.
cards.result: Primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke): 356 of 3,023 (11.8%) with linagliptin vs 362 of 3,010 (12.0%) with glimepiride — HR 0.98 (95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; P<.001 for noninferiority; P=.76 for superiority). Hypoglycemia was far less frequent with linagliptin: at least one episode in 320 (10.6%) vs 1,132 (37.7%) — HR 0.23 (0.21–0.26). Adjudicated acute pancreatitis: 15 (0.5%) vs 16 (0.5%).
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator trial: it answers 'gliptin or sulfonylurea?' rather than 'gliptin or nothing?' — and it acquits modern glimepiride of the cardiovascular suspicion sulfonylureas have carried since the UGDP report of the 1970s. What it cannot settle is cost: glimepiride costs a few dollars a month; linagliptin, hundreds.

shelves.title: Total diet replacement programmes for type 2 diabetes remission
shelves.question: Can supervised total diet replacement followed by food reintroduction and weight-maintenance support induce remission of recent type 2 diabetes, and how durable is remission?
shelves.balance: Two independent open-label randomized trials support remission with supervised diet-replacement programmes in recent type 2 diabetes: DiRECT 46% vs 4% and DIADEM-I 61% vs 12% at 12 months. Remission tracked weight loss. DiRECT remission was 36% vs 3% at 24 months; at 5 years, 11/85 (13%) observed extension participants were in remission. That selected extension percentage is not an intention-to-treat estimate. Long-term durability is limited. DiRECT follow-up reports are the same trial, not independent replications. A small randomized feasibility trial in UK South Asian adults (STANDby) pointed the same way: remission 5/13 versus 0/12.

cards.headline: DiRECT: remission in 46% versus 4% at 12 months
cards.summary: Remission at 12 months: 68 (46%) vs 6 (4%) — OR 19.7 (95% CI 7.8–49.8), P<0.0001. Remission tracked weight loss: 31/36 (86%) of those losing ≥15 kg vs 6/89 (7%) losing 0–5 kg.
cards.people: 306 recruited; 298 in intention-to-treat analysis, 149/group, from 49 UK practices; age 20–65, diabetes ≤6 years, BMI 27–45 kg/m², no insulin.
cards.result: At 12 months, remission: 68 (46%) vs 6 (4%); OR 19.7 (95% CI 7.8–49.8), p<0.0001. Remission required HbA1c <6.5% after ≥2 months without diabetes medication. Across both groups, remission occurred in 31/36 (86%) losing ≥15 kg and 6/89 (7%) losing 0–5 kg.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, multicomponent programme. Weight-loss subgroups were not randomized. Insulin-treated patients were excluded; results do not establish lifelong remission.
cards.source: Lean MEJ et al. Lancet. 2018;391:541–551. PMID 29221645 · ISRCTN03267836

cards.headline: DIADEM-I: remission in 61% versus 12% at 12 months
cards.summary: Remission at 12 months: 61% vs 12% — OR 12.03 (95% CI 5.17–28.03), P<0.0001. Weight loss: 11.98 kg vs 3.98 kg; adjusted difference −6.08 kg.
cards.people: 158 randomized, 79/group; final analysis 147 (70 intervention, 77 control). Qatar; Middle Eastern/North African adults, age 18–50, diabetes ≤3 years, BMI ≥27 kg/m².
cards.watchOut: Open-label; remission was secondary to weight loss. The final analysis excluded 11 randomized participants. The programme included exercise and maintenance support; follow-up here is 12 months.

cards.headline: DiRECT extension: 11 of 85 observed participants in remission at five years
cards.summary: At 5 years, extension participants with data lost a mean 6.1 kg; 11/85 (13%) were in remission — an observed-case figure among 85 extension participants, not all 149 originally assigned to intervention.
cards.type: Five-year extension of a randomized trial; extension participation was not randomized
cards.people: Original DiRECT: 298 participants. Of 101 intervention participants eligible at year 2, 95 entered the extension; 85 had year-5 outcomes.

cards.headline: STANDby: remission in 5 of 13 versus 0 of 12 in South Asian adults
cards.summary: After the diet-replacement phase, remission was achieved by 5/13 versus 0/12 (P=0.039). Weight change: −7.7% in the immediate group versus −1.2% in the delayed group (P=0.005).
cards.type: Randomized proof-of-concept and feasibility trial (immediate versus delayed total diet replacement)
cards.people: 25 adults of South Asian ethnicity in the UK, age 18–65, type 2 diabetes ≤4 years, BMI 25–45 kg/m²; 13 randomized to start the diet immediately, 12 to a delayed start (usual care during the comparison period).

shelves.title: Low-carb vs low-fat for weight loss: composition is not the active ingredient
shelves.question: For weight loss, does the macronutrient composition of the diet — low-carbohydrate vs low-fat — matter?
shelves.balance: Across the large modern trials, composition barely matters: low-fat and low-carb produce near-identical weight loss, and neither genotype nor insulin secretion predicts who does better on which. Adherence is the active ingredient. The A TO Z result stands as the earlier-era outlier the two larger trials supersede. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY that no composition is meaningfully superior.

cards.headline: DIETFITS: healthy low-fat vs healthy low-carb — −5.3 kg vs −6.0 kg, a non-significant 0.7 kg apart
cards.summary: Weight loss −5.3 kg vs −6.0 kg; the 0.7 kg difference was not significant (95% CI −0.2 to 1.6). Neither genotype pattern (P=.20) nor insulin secretion (P=.47) modified the result.
cards.people: 609 adults; 12 months of healthy low-fat vs healthy low-carb eating
cards.result: Weight loss −5.3 kg vs −6.0 kg; the 0.7 kg difference was not significant (95% CI −0.2 to 1.6). Neither genotype pattern (P=.20) nor insulin secretion (P=.47) modified the result.
cards.watchOut: Both diets were 'healthy' versions of their pattern, with support in both arms — the trial tests composition under good adherence support, and composition lost.
cards.source: Gardner et al. (DIETFITS). JAMA. 2018;319:667–679. PMID 29466592 · NCT01826591.

shelves.title: Look AHEAD: intensive lifestyle in type 2 diabetes — remission without fewer heart attacks
shelves.question: In adults with established type 2 diabetes, does an intensive lifestyle intervention reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.balance: Intensive lifestyle produced large weight loss and real but modest diabetes remission — and no reduction in cardiovascular events over nearly a decade. Weight loss alone did not buy event protection in established diabetes. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — the null event result comes from a large, definitive trial.

shelves.title: Tirzepatide outcomes: heart failure, cardiovascular events, sleep apnea
shelves.question: In people with obesity-related HFpEF, type 2 diabetes with atherosclerotic disease, or obstructive sleep apnea with obesity, does tirzepatide improve clinical outcomes?
shelves.balance: Tirzepatide's outcome record is real but narrower than its weight-loss fame. In obesity-related HFpEF (SUMMIT), it cut the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure (9.9% vs 15.3%, HR 0.62) — an effect carried by fewer worsening-heart-failure events (8.0% vs 14.2%), while cardiovascular deaths were few and numerically higher on the drug (2.2% vs 1.4%, HR 1.58, 95% CI 0.52–4.83). In type 2 diabetes with established atherosclerotic disease (SURPASS-CVOT), tirzepatide was noninferior to dulaglutide for cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke (12.2% vs 13.1%, HR 0.92) — superiority was not shown (P = 0.09). In moderate-to-severe sleep apnea with obesity (SURMOUNT-OSA), it cut the apnea-hypopnea index by about 20–24 more events per hour than placebo over 52 weeks — a breathing measure, not a hard outcome. All three trials were funded by Eli Lilly.

shelves.title: Degludec vs glargine U100: hypoglycemia
shelves.question: At the same glycemic control, does basal insulin degludec cause less hypoglycemia than insulin glargine U100?
shelves.balance: At equal HbA1c — all three trials were treat-to-target — degludec causes less hypoglycemia than glargine U100 in both types of diabetes. Overall symptomatic episodes ran 11% relatively lower in type 1 (SWITCH 1, rate ratio 0.89) and 30% relatively lower in type 2 (SWITCH 2, rate ratio 0.70); nocturnal episodes ran 36–42% relatively lower (rate ratios 0.64 and 0.58). Severe hypoglycemia was clearly lower in the two larger datasets — DEVOTE: 4.9% vs 6.6% of patients (rate ratio 0.60, a prespecified superiority win) and SWITCH 1: 10.3% vs 17.1% of patients — but not significantly different in SWITCH 2 (1.6% vs 2.4%, P = 0.35), where severe events were few. Cardiovascular safety in DEVOTE: degludec noninferior to glargine for major cardiovascular events (HR 0.91, 0.78–1.06) — safety, not advantage. The comparison is against glargine U100 only; these trials say nothing about glargine U300 or once-weekly insulin. All three trials were funded by Novo Nordisk, degludec's maker.

cards.people: 7,637 patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk (3,818 degludec / 3,819 glargine U100); mean age 65.0 years; mean diabetes duration 16.4 years; mean HbA1c 8.4 ± 1.7%; 85.2% had established cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or both; 83.9% were already receiving insulin. (The abstract does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: Primary outcome (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke): 325 (8.5%) vs 356 (9.3%), HR 0.91 (0.78–1.06), P<0.001 for noninferiority (margin 1.3). HbA1c at 24 months 7.5 ± 1.2% in each group; fasting glucose lower on degludec (128 ± 56 vs 136 ± 57 mg/dL, P<0.001). Prespecified adjudicated severe hypoglycemia: 187 (4.9%) vs 252 (6.6%), absolute difference 1.7 percentage points; rate ratio 0.60 and odds ratio 0.73, both P<0.001 for superiority. shelves.title: How tight should glucose control be? Intensive control, timing, and the legacy effect
shelves.balance: Timing is the whole story. Start tight early — at diagnosis — and the payoff compounds: fewer microvascular events inside the trial, and a decade later fewer heart attacks and deaths, long after glucose levels have reconverged. Start late — older patients, a decade or more of diabetes, high cardiovascular risk — and pushing toward normal buys no cardiovascular benefit within five years, at two to three times the severe hypoglycemia; ACCORD's push below 6.0% increased mortality and was stopped for it. Glucose control is microvascular protection. In long-standing, high-risk diabetes, cardiovascular protection comes from treating the risk factors — statin, blood pressure, and the kidney- and heart-protecting diabetes medicines — not from a lower A1c.

cards.headline: UKPDS 33: intensive control at diagnosis cut microvascular complications by a quarter; heart-attack and mortality benefits were not significant within the trial itself
cards.summary: Any diabetes-related end point 12% relatively lower (95% CI 1–21; P=0.029); microvascular end points 25% relatively lower (7–40; P=0.0099); diabetes-related death and all-cause mortality not significant — 3,867 patients.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial; median 10 years of follow-up
cards.people: 3,867 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, median age 54 years (IQR 48–60), randomly assigned after 3 months of diet treatment to an intensive policy (chlorpropamide, glibenclamide, or glipizide, or insulin) or a conventional diet policy. (The abstract does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: HbA1c over 10 years was 7.0% in the intensive group compared with 7.9% in the conventional group. Any diabetes-related end point 12% relatively lower (95% CI 1–21; P=0.029); microvascular end points 25% relatively lower (7–40; P=0.0099), driven by less retinal photocoagulation. Diabetes-related death 10% relatively lower (−11 to 27; P=0.34) and all-cause mortality 6% relatively lower (−10 to 20; P=0.44) — neither significant. Major hypoglycemia per year: 0.7% conventional vs 1.0% chlorpropamide, 1.4% glibenclamide, 1.8% insulin. Weight gain was 2.9 kg more with intensive therapy (4.0 kg on insulin).
cards.watchOut: Within the trial the win was microvascular. The heart-attack and mortality gains appeared only in the decade after the trial ended (Reference 2). The drugs were 1970s–90s agents — no SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 medicines existed.
cards.source: UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) Group. Lancet 1998;352(9131):837-853. PMID 9742976 · Registry: none (pre-registration era; recruitment predates trial registries)

cards.headline: UKPDS legacy follow-up: a decade after the trial ended, heart attacks and deaths were significantly fewer in the originally intensive groups
cards.summary: Sulfonylurea-insulin group: myocardial infarction 15% relatively lower (P=0.01), death from any cause 13% relatively lower (P=0.007); metformin group: myocardial infarction 33% relatively lower (P=0.005), death 27% relatively lower (P=0.002) — 3,277 patients in post-trial monitoring.
cards.type: Post-trial monitoring of a randomized trial cohort; up to 10 years, with no attempt to maintain previously assigned therapies
cards.people: Of 5,102 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes enrolled in UKPDS, 4,209 were randomly assigned to conventional therapy (diet) or intensive therapy (sulfonylurea or insulin or, in overweight patients, metformin); 3,277 entered annual post-trial monitoring.
cards.result: Between-group differences in glycated hemoglobin levels were lost after the first year. In the sulfonylurea-insulin group, relative reductions persisted at 10 years for any diabetes-related end point (9%, P=0.04) and microvascular disease (24%, P=0.001), and reductions for myocardial infarction (15%, P=0.01) and death from any cause (13%, P=0.007) emerged over time. cards.watchOut: After the trial, care was observational — the legacy pattern is consistent across both UKPDS drug groups, but it comes from this one cohort, and it belongs to patients treated early, at diagnosis.

cards.headline: ACCORD: targeting A1c below 6.0% increased mortality and was stopped early — the harm that reset glycemic targets
cards.summary: Deaths 257 vs 203 ( 5.0% vs 4.0% ; HR 1.22 , 95% CI 1.01–1.46; P=0.04); cardiovascular death HR 1.35 (1.04–1.76); primary composite HR 0.90 (0.78–1.04), not significant — 10,251 patients.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial; the intensive arm was stopped after a mean of 3.5 years because of higher mortality
cards.people: 10,251 patients (mean age 62.2 years; 38% women; 35% with a previous cardiovascular event; median baseline A1c 8.1%). Achieved median A1c 6.4% with intensive therapy vs 7.5% with standard therapy.
cards.result: The primary composite (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) occurred in 352 intensive vs 371 standard patients (HR 0.90, 0.78–1.04; P=0.16) — not significant; nonfatal MI alone was lower (HR 0.76, 0.62–0.92). Deaths: 257 intensive vs 203 standard (HR 1.22, 1.01–1.46; P=0.04); cardiovascular deaths 135 vs 94 (HR 1.35, 1.04–1.76). Hypoglycemia requiring assistance and weight gain of more than 10 kg were more frequent in the intensive-therapy group (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The excess deaths were never explained by any single drug or by hypoglycemia alone in the trial's own analyses. The lesson is about the target and the population — near-normal A1c, pursued fast, in high-risk long-standing diabetes — not about any one agent.
