shelves.title: Anti-VEGF injections vs laser for diabetic eye disease
shelves.balance: For proliferative diabetic retinopathy, anti-VEGF injections match laser on vision and beat it on the collateral damage. At 2 years in Protocol S, ranibizumab was noninferior to panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) for visual acuity (+2.8 vs +0.2 letters) with far less peripheral visual field loss, fewer vitrectomies (4% vs 15%), and less new diabetic macular edema (9% vs 28%); CLARITY found aflibercept noninferior and superior to PRP at 1 year (+3.9 letters difference). At 5 years the vision advantage had closed — acuity was identical (about 20/25 in both groups) — but the ranibizumab group still had less visual field loss and roughly half the cumulative rate of vision-impairing macular edema (22% vs 38%). The price is burden: about 19 injections over 5 years, and injections only work while the patient keeps coming — laser, once done, does not depend on the next appointment. For diabetic macular edema itself, monthly ranibizumab in RISE and RIDE roughly tripled the chance of gaining 15 or more letters versus sham (33.6–45.7% vs 12.3–18.1% across doses and trials) and cut the need for macular laser. Anti-VEGF is first-line where follow-up is reliable; PRP remains the durable choice when it is not.

cards.headline: Protocol S at 2 years — ranibizumab noninferior to panretinal photocoagulation for vision, with less visual field loss, fewer vitrectomies, and less macular edema
cards.summary: Mean visual acuity improvement at 2 years +2.8 vs +0.2 letters (difference +2.2; 95% CI −0.5 to +5.0; P<.001 for noninferiority); peripheral visual field loss −23 vs −422 dB; vitrectomy 4% vs 15% ; diabetic macular edema 9% vs 28% — 305 adults, 394 study eyes.
cards.people: 305 adults with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (394 study eyes; both eyes enrolled for 89 participants); mean age 52 years; 44% female; 52% white. Ranibizumab 0.5 mg by intravitreous injection at baseline and as frequently as every 4 weeks based on a structured re-treatment protocol (191 eyes) vs panretinal photocoagulation completed in 1 to 3 visits (203 eyes). Eyes in both groups could receive ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema.
cards.result: Mean visual acuity letter improvement at 2 years was +2.8 in the ranibizumab group vs +0.2 in the PRP group (difference +2.2; 95% CI −0.5 to +5.0; P < .001 for noninferiority, 5-letter margin). The mean treatment group difference in visual acuity area under the curve over 2 years was +4.2 (95% CI +3.0 to +5.4; P < .001). Mean peripheral visual field sensitivity loss was worse in the PRP group (−422 vs −23 dB; difference 372 dB; 95% CI 213–531; P < .001), vitrectomy was more frequent in the PRP group (15% vs 4%; difference 9%; 95% CI 4%–15%; P < .001), and diabetic macular edema development was more frequent in the PRP group (28% vs 9%; difference 19%; 95% CI 10%–28%; P < .001). Eyes without active or regressed neovascularization at 2 years were 35% in the ranibizumab group vs 30% in the PRP group (difference 3%; 95% CI −7% to 12%; P = .58) — not significantly different. One eye in the ranibizumab group developed endophthalmitis. No significant differences between groups in rates of major cardiovascular events were identified.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority win on vision, not a superiority win at the 2-year primary end point — the advantages sit in the secondary outcomes. And the injection strategy only exists if the patient keeps returning for injections.
cards.source: Writing Committee for the Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network (Gross JG et al.). JAMA. 2015;314(20):2137-2146. PMID: 26565927 · PMCID: PMC5567801 · Registry: NCT01489189

cards.headline: Protocol S at 5 years — vision equal in both groups; the field and macular-edema advantages persist, at the price of about 19 injections
cards.summary: Mean visual acuity change at 5 years 3.1 vs 3.0 letters (adjusted difference 0.6; 95% CI −2.3 to 3.5; P=.68), mean acuity 20/25 in both groups; vision-impairing macular edema 22% vs 38% (HR 0.4 ); mean injections 19.2 vs 5.4 — 305 participants.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial, 5-year follow-up of the Protocol S cohort
cards.people: The same 305 enrolled participants (394 study eyes): mean (SD) age 52 (12) years; 135 (44%) women; 160 (52%) white. The 5-year visit was completed by 184 of 277 participants (66% excluding deaths).
cards.result: For the ranibizumab and PRP groups, the mean (SD) number of injections over 5 years was 19.2 (10.9) and 5.4 (7.9), respectively (injections in the PRP group were ranibizumab given for macular edema); the mean (SD) change in visual acuity letter score was 3.1 (14.3) and 3.0 (10.5) letters, respectively (adjusted difference 0.6; 95% CI −2.3 to 3.5; P = .68); the mean visual acuity was 20/25 (approximate Snellen equivalent) in both groups at 5 years. The mean (SD) change in cumulative visual field total point score was −330 (645) vs −527 (635) dB in the ranibizumab (n = 41) and PRP (n = 38) groups, respectively (adjusted difference 208 dB; 95% CI 9–408). Vision-impairing diabetic macular edema developed in 27 and 53 eyes in the ranibizumab and PRP groups, respectively (cumulative probabilities 22% vs 38%; hazard ratio 0.4; 95% CI 0.3–0.7). No statistically significant differences between groups in major systemic adverse event rates were identified.
cards.watchOut: Loss to follow-up was relatively high — a third of surviving participants missed the 5-year visit — so the 5-year equality of vision rests on those who completed follow-up. The trialists themselves say patient-specific factors, including anticipated visit compliance, cost, and frequency of visits, should be considered when choosing treatment.

cards.headline: CLARITY — aflibercept noninferior AND superior to panretinal photocoagulation at 1 year
cards.summary: Mean best corrected visual acuity difference 3.9 letters (95% CI 2.3–5.6; P<0.0001) favoring aflibercept — non-inferior and superior to PRP at 1 year — 232 participants.
cards.type: Multicentre, single-blinded, randomised, controlled, phase 2b, non-inferiority trial, 22 UK ophthalmic centres
cards.people: 232 participants (116 per group), adults (aged ≥18 years) with type 1 or 2 diabetes and previously untreated or post-laser treated active proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Repeated intravitreal aflibercept (2 mg at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks, then as needed from week 12) vs PRP standard care, for 52 weeks. 221 participants (112 aflibercept, 109 PRP) contributed to the modified intention-to-treat model, and 210 (104 and 106) to the per-protocol analysis. (The abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.)
cards.result: Aflibercept was non-inferior and superior to PRP in both the modified intention-to-treat population (mean best corrected visual acuity difference 3.9 letters [95% CI 2.3–5.6], P < 0.0001) and the per-protocol population (4.0 letters [2.4–5.7], P < 0.0001). The non-inferiority margin was prespecified as −5 letters, and the 95% CI adjusted difference between groups was more than that margin at both 12 weeks and 52 weeks. There were no safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: One year only, phase 2b, and single-blind — primary outcome assessors were masked, but the treating ophthalmologists and participants were not. Its role on this shelf is confirmatory: the Protocol S result is a class effect, not a ranibizumab-only one.

cards.headline: RISE and RIDE — monthly ranibizumab roughly triples the chance of gaining 15 or more letters in diabetic macular edema
cards.summary: Gained ≥15 letters at 24 months — RISE: 44.8% (0.3 mg) and 39.2% (0.5 mg) vs 18.1% sham; RIDE: 33.6% and 45.7% vs 12.3% sham — 759 patients across both trials.
cards.type: Two parallel, methodologically identical, phase III, multicenter, double-masked, sham injection-controlled, randomized studies
cards.people: Adults with vision loss from diabetic macular edema (best-corrected visual acuity 20/40–20/320 Snellen equivalent) and central subfield thickness ≥275 μm on time-domain optical coherence tomography. Monthly intravitreal ranibizumab (0.5 or 0.3 mg) or sham injections; macular laser was available per protocol-specified criteria. RISE: 377 patients randomized (127 to sham, 125 to 0.3 mg, 125 to 0.5 mg). RIDE: 382 patients randomized (130 to sham, 125 to 0.3 mg, 127 to 0.5 mg). (The abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.)
cards.result: In RISE, at 24 months, 18.1% of sham patients gained ≥15 letters versus 44.8% of 0.3-mg patients (P < 0.0001; adjusted difference 24.3%; 95% CI 13.8–34.8) and 39.2% of 0.5-mg patients (P < 0.001; adjusted difference 20.9%; 95% CI 10.7–31.1). In RIDE, 12.3% of sham patients gained ≥15 letters versus 33.6% of 0.3-mg patients (P < 0.0001; adjusted difference 20.8%; 95% CI 11.4–30.2) and 45.7% of 0.5-mg patients (P < 0.0001; adjusted difference 33.3%; 95% CI 23.8–42.8). Significant improvements in macular edema were noted on OCT, and retinopathy was less likely to worsen and more likely to improve in ranibizumab-treated patients. Ranibizumab-treated patients underwent significantly fewer macular laser procedures (mean of 1.8 and 1.6 laser procedures over 24 months in the sham groups vs 0.3–0.8 in the ranibizumab groups). Endophthalmitis occurred in 4 ranibizumab patients. The total incidence of deaths from vascular or unknown causes, nonfatal myocardial infarctions, and nonfatal cerebrovascular accidents was 4.9% to 5.5% of sham patients and 2.4% to 8.8% of ranibizumab patients.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was sham injection, not laser — these trials prove injections beat no injection for macular edema, with laser as rescue; that is why this card sits behind the two head-to-head laser trials on this shelf. The dose response was flat: 0.3 mg did about as well as 0.5 mg.

shelves.title: Metformin in pregnancy: what it buys the mother, what it costs the baby in size
shelves.question: For women with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes in pregnancy, does metformin — added to insulin, started at diagnosis, or used instead of insulin — improve outcomes for mother and baby, and what are the trade-offs versus insulin?
shelves.balance: Across all three trials the maternal side of the ledger is consistent: metformin improves or matches glucose control while using less insulin (MiTy: 1.1 vs 1.5 units/kg/day added to insulin; EMERGE: insulin initiation 38.4% vs 51.1%; MiG: noninferior to insulin as the first treatment, with insulin added in 46.3%), about 1–2 kg less weight gain, fewer caesarean births in MiTy (53% vs 63%), and women prefer the tablet (MiG: 76.6% vs 27.2% would choose the same treatment again). The baby's side is a shift, not a clear win: no trial improved its primary neonatal composite (MiTy 40% vs 40%; MiG 32.0% vs 32.2%), but babies were consistently smaller — fewer very large infants (MiTy above the 97th centile 9% vs 15%; EMERGE large-for-gestational-age 6.5% vs 14.9%) set against more small ones (MiTy small-for-gestational-age 13% vs 7%, relative risk 1.96; EMERGE 5.7% vs 2.7%, not significant), and in MiG more preterm births offset less severe neonatal hypoglycaemia. Gastrointestinal effects are the everyday price (24.3% in EMERGE; about 5% of women stopped). The practical reading: metformin is a reasonable first or add-on treatment for diabetes in pregnancy when the alternative is more insulin, provided fetal growth is watched — it trades large-baby risk for small-baby risk, and whether that trade helps or harms the child in the long term is still being followed up.

cards.headline: MiTy: adding metformin to insulin in type 2 diabetes pregnancy leaves the neonatal composite unchanged (40% vs 40%), improves maternal control on less insulin and fewer caesareans — and shifts babies smaller, with small-for-gestational-age infants doubled (13% vs 7%)
cards.summary: Primary neonatal composite 40% vs 40% (relative risk 1.02; P=0.86); insulin 1.1 vs 1.5 units/kg/day; caesarean births 53% vs 63% ; small-for-gestational-age 13% vs 7% (relative risk 1.96) — 502 women.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, international, randomised, parallel, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial; 25 centres in Canada and 4 in Australia
cards.people: 502 women with type 2 diabetes during pregnancy, all receiving insulin, with a singleton viable pregnancy, enrolled between 6 and 22 weeks plus 6 days' gestation (trial eligibility ages 18–45 years). Metformin 1000 mg twice daily (253 women) or placebo (249 women) added to insulin, with identical glucose targets in both groups (fasting <5.3 mmol/L (≈95 mg/dL), 2-h postprandial <6.7 mmol/L (≈121 mg/dL)). Complete primary-outcome data: 233 (92%) metformin, 240 (96%) placebo. (The abstract does not print a mean age.)
cards.result: The primary composite of fetal and neonatal outcomes (per the trial protocol: pregnancy loss, preterm birth, birth injury, moderate or severe respiratory distress, neonatal hypoglycaemia, or admission to intensive care for more than 24 h) occurred in 40% of the metformin group vs 40% of the placebo group (relative risk 1.02; 95% CI 0.83–1.26; P=0.86). Mothers on metformin achieved better glycaemic control (HbA1c at 34 weeks 5.90% vs 6.10%; P=0.015), required less insulin (1.1 vs 1.5 units/kg/day; difference −0.4; P<0.0001), gained less weight (7.2 vs 9.0 kg; P<0.0001), and had fewer caesarean births (125 of 234 [53%] vs 148 of 236 [63%]; relative risk 0.85; 0.73–0.99; P=0.031); hypertensive disorders were the same (23% vs 23%). Their infants weighed less (mean birthweight 3156 g vs 3375 g; difference −218 g; P=0.002) and were less fat (sum of skinfolds 16.0 vs 17.4 mm; P=0.024); fewer were above the 97th centile for birthweight (9% vs 15%; relative risk 0.58; P=0.041) or weighed 4000 g or more (12% vs 19%; relative risk 0.65; P=0.046) — but more were small for gestational age: 30 (13%) vs 15 (7%) (relative risk 1.96; 1.10–3.64; P=0.026).
cards.watchOut: The neutral composite hides the trial's real finding — a shift down the growth chart at both ends, not a change in morbidity. The near-doubling of small-for-gestational-age infants is the unresolved safety question; the trial's offspring follow-up (MiTy Kids) found no difference in BMI z-score or skinfold thickness at 24 months, but follow-up continues. Unusually for metformin, gastrointestinal events were reported equally in the two groups (38 events each).
cards.source: Feig DS et al.; MiTy Collaborative Group. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2020;8(10):834-844. PMID 32946820 · NCT01353391

cards.headline: EMERGE: early metformin at gestational diabetes diagnosis misses its primary composite (56.8% vs 63.7%, P=0.13) but cuts insulin initiation (38.4% vs 51.1%) and halves large babies; gastrointestinal effects in 1 in 4 women
cards.summary: Primary composite 56.8% vs 63.7% (P=0.13, not significant); insulin initiation 38.4% vs 51.1% ; large-for-gestational-age 6.5% vs 14.9% ; gastrointestinal effects 24.3% vs 4.1% — 510 participants, 535 pregnancies.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised clinical trial, 2 centres in Ireland
cards.people: 510 participants (535 pregnancies: 268 metformin, 267 placebo) diagnosed with gestational diabetes by WHO 2013 criteria at up to 28 weeks plus 6 days' gestation; mean age 34.3 years; a predominantly White Irish population. Metformin titrated to a maximum of 2500 mg/day (mean achieved dose 2087 mg/day) or matched placebo, in addition to usual care, from diagnosis until delivery; follow-up to 12 weeks postpartum.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (insulin initiation, or a fasting glucose level of 5.1 mmol/L (≈92 mg/dL) or greater at gestation weeks 32 or 38) occurred in 150 of 264 pregnancies (56.8%) in the metformin group vs 167 of 262 (63.7%) in the placebo group (between-group difference −6.9%; 95% CI −15.1 to 1.4; relative risk 0.89; 0.78–1.02; P=0.13) — not significant. Insulin initiation itself was lower and later: 101 of 263 (38.4%) vs 134 of 262 (51.1%) (relative risk 0.75; 0.62–0.91; P=0.004; hazard ratio for time to initiation 0.66; P=0.001). Fasting glucose was lower at week 32 (4.9 vs 5.0 mmol/L (≈88 vs 90 mg/dL); P=0.03) and week 38 (4.5 vs 4.7 mmol/L (≈81 vs 85 mg/dL); P<0.001), and women gained less weight from randomisation to delivery (0.8 vs 2.0 kg; P=0.003). Infants were smaller: mean birthweight 3393 vs 3506 g (difference −113 g; P=0.005); birthweight over 4000 g in 7.6% vs 14.8% (P=0.02); large for gestational age (over the 90th centile) in 6.5% vs 14.9% (P=0.003); small for gestational age (below the 10th centile) in 5.7% vs 2.7% (relative risk 2.1; 0.9–5.2; P=0.13, not significant). There were no differences in neonatal intensive care (15.6% vs 12.6%), respiratory support, neonatal hypoglycaemia (13.7% vs 13.0%), major congenital anomalies, or preterm birth (9.2% vs 6.5%; P=0.33); mean gestation at delivery was 39.1 weeks in both groups. Gastrointestinal adverse effects occurred in 65 women (24.3%) on metformin vs 11 (4.1%) on placebo (P<0.001), all requiring dose reduction; 13 women (4.9%) discontinued metformin because of them.
cards.watchOut: A negative primary outcome carried by positive prespecified secondaries — and the primary was a process composite (starting insulin, or one fasting value), not a baby outcome. EMERGE also started metformin at diagnosis, earlier than the usual step-up after lifestyle measures fail, in an almost entirely White Irish population; the small-for-gestational-age drift (5.7% vs 2.7%) points the same way as MiTy but is not significant here. The authors' own conclusion is that larger trials are needed.

cards.headline: MiG: metformin first (with insulin added in 46.3%) matches insulin for neonatal complications in gestational diabetes (32.0% vs 32.2%) — less severe neonatal hypoglycaemia, more preterm birth — and women preferred it 3-to-1
cards.summary: Primary composite 32.0% vs 32.2% (relative risk 0.99), inside the prespecified noninferiority margin; insulin added in 46.3% of the metformin group; would choose the same treatment again 76.6% vs 27.2% — 751 women.
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, randomised noninferiority trial, Australia and New Zealand
cards.people: 751 women with gestational diabetes mellitus at 20 to 33 weeks of gestation, randomly assigned to open treatment with metformin (363 women; 500 mg once or twice daily titrated to a maximum of 2500 mg/day, with supplemental insulin if required) or insulin (388 women, of whom 370 completed the study). (The abstract does not print a mean age.)
cards.result: The primary outcome — a composite of neonatal hypoglycaemia, respiratory distress, need for phototherapy, birth trauma, 5-minute Apgar score less than 7, or prematurity — occurred in 32.0% of infants in the metformin group vs 32.2% in the insulin group (relative risk 0.99; 95% CI 0.80–1.23, values as corrected by the journal's erratum), inside the trial's prespecified margin, which was designed to rule out a 33% relative increase (from 30% to 40%). Of the women assigned to metformin, 92.6% continued it until delivery and 46.3% received supplemental insulin. Within the composite, the components that differed moved in opposite directions, as reported in the paper: severe neonatal hypoglycaemia was less common with metformin (P=0.008) and preterm birth was more common (P=0.04); other secondary outcomes, including neonatal size measures, did not differ significantly. Maternal weight gain from enrolment to term was lower on metformin (0.4 kg vs 2.0 kg; P<0.001, as reported in the paper). More women in the metformin group than in the insulin group said they would choose the same treatment again (76.6% vs 27.2%; P<0.001). There were no serious adverse events associated with metformin.
cards.watchOut: Open-label — mothers and clinicians knew who was on tablets — and the noninferiority margin was generous: the trial could only rule out a large (one-third relative) increase in complications. It tests a metformin-first strategy rather than metformin alone, since nearly half the metformin group also received insulin. Follow-up of the children (the MiG TOFU study) found similar total body fat at 2 years but somewhat larger subcutaneous fat measures in metformin-exposed children — the long-term offspring question that hangs over this whole shelf.
cards.source: Rowan JA et al.; MiG Trial Investigators. N Engl J Med 2008;358(19):2003-2015. PMID 18463376 · ANZCTR 12605000311651

shelves.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists added to insulin in type 1 diabetes: modest gains, real hypoglycemia and ketosis costs (off-label)
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 diabetes treated with insulin, does adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist (liraglutide) improve HbA1c, body weight, and insulin dose — and at what cost in hypoglycemia and ketosis?
shelves.balance: The two phase 3 trials are mirror images and they agree. When insulin was titrated to target in both groups (ADJUNCT ONE, 52 weeks), adding liraglutide bought a small extra HbA1c reduction (estimated treatment difference −0.20% at 1.8 mg, −0.15% at 1.2 mg), about 5–8% relatively less insulin (dose ratios 0.95 and 0.92), and real weight loss (−3.6 and −4.9 kg vs placebo). When insulin was capped instead (ADJUNCT TWO, 26 weeks), the same pattern showed as a −0.33% HbA1c change at 1.8 mg against +0.01% on placebo, with −5.1 kg of weight. The safety bill was the same in both trials: symptomatic hypoglycemia rose by roughly 30% relatively at the 1.2 and 1.8 mg doses (rate ratios 1.27 and 1.31 in ADJUNCT ONE; 21.3 vs 16.6 events per patient-year at 1.2 mg in ADJUNCT TWO), and hyperglycemia with ketosis roughly doubled at 1.8 mg (rate ratio 2.22 in ADJUNCT ONE; 0.5 vs 0.1 events per patient-year in ADJUNCT TWO) — a signal that matters in people with no insulin reserve of their own. The 0.6 mg dose did little for HbA1c. Neither trial measured hard outcomes, and the trialists concluded the adverse events limit clinical use. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for type 1 diabetes, so this is off-label use. The practical reading: a niche option for selected adults with type 1 diabetes — above all those with overweight and high insulin requirements — who can check ketones and accept more hypoglycemia in exchange for less weight and slightly less insulin; not a general adjunct for the type 1 population.

cards.headline: ADJUNCT ONE: liraglutide added to treat-to-target insulin trims HbA1c a little (−0.20% at 1.8 mg vs placebo), cuts insulin dose 8% relatively and weight 4.9 kg — at the price of ~30% relatively more symptomatic hypoglycemia and twice the hyperglycemia with ketosis at the top dose
cards.summary: HbA1c estimated treatment difference −0.20% at 1.8 mg and −0.15% at 1.2 mg vs placebo; insulin dose ratio 0.92 at 1.8 mg; weight −4.9 kg ; symptomatic hypoglycemia rate ratio 1.31 ; hyperglycemia with ketosis rate ratio 2.22 at 1.8 mg — 1,398 adults.
cards.type: 52-week, phase III, multicentre, double-blind, treat-to-target randomized controlled trial (177 centres in 17 countries)
cards.people: 1,398 adults with type 1 diabetes randomized 3:1 to receive once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide (1.8, 1.2, or 0.6 mg) or placebo added to insulin, with insulin titrated to target in all groups. Mean baseline HbA1c 8.2% (66 mmol/mol). (The abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.)
cards.result: HbA1c fell 0.34–0.54% (3.7–5.9 mmol/mol) across the groups; compared with placebo the estimated treatment differences were −0.20% (95% CI −0.32; −0.07) for liraglutide 1.8 mg and −0.15% (−0.27; −0.03) for 1.2 mg, while 0.6 mg did not differ significantly (−0.09%; −0.21; 0.03). Insulin doses fell relatively more with liraglutide 1.8 and 1.2 mg (estimated treatment ratios 0.92 [0.88; 0.96] and 0.95 [0.91; 0.99]; 0.6 mg: 1.00 [0.96; 1.04]). Body weight fell significantly more in every liraglutide group (estimated treatment differences −4.9 kg [−5.7; −4.2] at 1.8 mg, −3.6 kg [−4.3; −2.8] at 1.2 mg, −2.2 kg [−2.9; −1.5] at 0.6 mg). Symptomatic hypoglycemia rates rose in all liraglutide groups (estimated rate ratios 1.31 [1.07; 1.59] at 1.8 mg, 1.27 [1.03; 1.55] at 1.2 mg, 1.17 [0.97; 1.43] at 0.6 mg), and hyperglycemia with ketosis increased significantly for liraglutide 1.8 mg only (event rate ratio 2.22 [1.13; 4.34]).
cards.watchOut: The treat-to-target design compresses the HbA1c gap — insulin was adjusted in both arms — so much of the comparison plays out in insulin dose, weight, and hypoglycemia rather than in A1c. The ketosis endpoint is hyperglycemia with ketosis as the trial reported it. The authors' own conclusion: the increased symptomatic hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia with ketosis limit clinical use in this group. Funded by Novo Nordisk, liraglutide's maker.
cards.source: Mathieu C et al.; ADJUNCT ONE Investigators. Diabetes Care 2016;39(10):1702-1710. PMID 27506222 · NCT01836523

cards.headline: ADJUNCT TWO: with insulin capped, liraglutide lowers HbA1c (−0.33% at 1.8 mg vs +0.01% on placebo) and weight (−5.1 kg), with more hypoglycemia at 1.2 mg (21.3 vs 16.6 events/patient/year) and more hyperglycemia with ketosis at 1.8 mg (0.5 vs 0.1 events/patient/year)
cards.summary: HbA1c change −0.33% at 1.8 mg vs +0.01% on placebo; weight −5.1 kg ; symptomatic hypoglycemia 21.3 vs 16.6 events/patient/year at 1.2 mg; hyperglycemia with ketosis 0.5 vs 0.1 events/patient/year at 1.8 mg — 835 subjects.
cards.type: 26-week, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group randomized controlled trial (59 centres in 12 countries)
cards.people: 835 subjects with long-standing type 1 diabetes randomized 3:1 to receive once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide (1.8, 1.2, or 0.6 mg) or placebo added to an individually capped total daily dose of insulin. Mean baseline HbA1c 8.1% (65 mmol/mol). (The abstract does not print a mean age or the sex mix.)
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell significantly more with liraglutide than placebo at week 26 (change −0.33% [3.6 mmol/mol] at 1.8 mg, −0.22% [2.4 mmol/mol] at 1.2 mg, −0.23% [2.5 mmol/mol] at 0.6 mg, vs +0.01% [0.1 mmol/mol] on placebo). Body weight fell significantly more (−5.1, −4.0, and −2.5 kg for 1.8, 1.2, and 0.6 mg) than on placebo (−0.2 kg), and daily insulin dose was significantly reduced and quality of life increased with liraglutide. Symptomatic hypoglycemia was more frequent with liraglutide 1.2 mg than placebo (21.3 vs 16.6 events/patient/year; P = 0.03), and hyperglycemia with ketosis (ketones >1.5 mmol/L) was more frequent with liraglutide 1.8 mg (0.5 vs 0.1 events/patient/year; P = 0.01).
cards.watchOut: The capped-insulin design is ADJUNCT ONE's mirror image: holding insulin doses fixed lets the A1c difference show, but fixed dosing is not how insulin is managed in practice, where doses are titrated — read the two trials together. The trial ran only 26 weeks, and its safety pattern (hypoglycemia up at 1.2 mg, hyperglycemia with ketosis up at 1.8 mg) matches ADJUNCT ONE's. Funded by Novo Nordisk, liraglutide's maker.
cards.source: Ahrén B et al.; ADJUNCT TWO Investigators. Diabetes Care 2016;39(10):1693-1701. PMID 27493132 · NCT02098395

shelves.title: Metabolic surgery for type 2 diabetes: big glycemic effects, small trials, an intention-to-treat caveat
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, does metabolic (bariatric) surgery control blood glucose better than intensive medical therapy — and how solid is that answer?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Gastric Bypass · Gastrectomy · Bariatric Surgery · Obesity · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans
shelves.balance: Across three randomized trials, metabolic surgery controls type 2 diabetes far more powerfully than intensive medical therapy — more remission (37.5% of surgical patients stayed in remission throughout 10 years in the longest trial), much larger A1c and weight falls. The fences: STAMPEDE’s intention-to-treat primary endpoint was not significant (P=0.08 and 0.17); the trials randomized 60–150 patients each; most remissions eventually relapse; and no trial shows fewer heart attacks, strokes, or deaths. The diet route to the same goal — total diet replacement (DiRECT) — lives on Shelf #201 and is not re-carded here. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: STAMPEDE at 5 years: surgery beat medical therapy among completers — the intention-to-treat primary was not significant (P=0.08 / 0.17)
cards.summary: Primary endpoint (A1c ≤6.0%) met by 5% on medical therapy vs 29% gastric bypass and 23% sleeve gastrectomy among patients with 5-year data — but in the intention-to-treat analysis the primary comparison was not significant (P=0.08 bypass, P=0.17 sleeve); A1c fell 2.1 points with surgery vs 0.3 with medical therapy — 150 patients.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (STAMPEDE), N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 150 patients with type 2 diabetes and BMI 27–43 randomized to intensive medical therapy alone or plus gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy; 134 (90%) completed 5 years. Among completers: mean age 49±8 years, 66% women, mean A1c 9.2±1.5%, mean BMI 37±3.5.
cards.result: Primary endpoint met by 2 of 38 patients (5%) on medical therapy alone vs 14 of 49 (29%) after gastric bypass and 11 of 47 (23%) after sleeve gastrectomy. The unadjusted and adjusted comparisons favored surgery, but the intention-to-treat analysis — the analysis counting everyone randomized — was not significant for either operation (P=0.08 bypass; P=0.17 sleeve), and that is printed plainly here. Mean A1c reduction was greater with surgery (2.1% vs 0.3%, P=0.003); weight change −23% (bypass), −19% (sleeve), −5% (medical); insulin use and quality-of-life measures also favored surgery. One death during follow-up; no major late surgical complications except one reoperation.
cards.watchOut: The headline 29% and 23% are completer figures; the intention-to-treat primary is the honest headline and it missed. Funded by Ethicon Endo-Surgery (a surgical-device maker) and others.
cards.source: Schauer PR et al. Bariatric Surgery versus Intensive Medical Therapy for Diabetes — 5-Year Outcomes. N Engl J Med. 2017;376:641-651. PMID 28199805 · NCT00432809.

cards.headline: Mingrone 10-year follow-up: remission durable in a minority — 50% after biliopancreatic diversion, 25% after bypass, 5.5% on medical therapy
cards.summary: At 10 years, diabetes remission was 50.0% after biliopancreatic diversion, 25.0% after gastric bypass, and 5.5% on medical therapy (P=0.0082); 58.8% of patients in remission at 2 years later relapsed — 60 patients.
cards.type: Open-label, single-centre randomized controlled trial, 10-year follow-up, Lancet 2021
cards.people: 60 patients with type 2 diabetes of more than 5 years’ duration, HbA1c >7.0%, and BMI ≥35 kg/m², randomized to medical therapy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, or biliopancreatic diversion at one Rome tertiary hospital; 57 of 60 (95.0%) followed to 10 years. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Remission at 10 years (intention-to-treat): 5.5% medical therapy, 50.0% biliopancreatic diversion (95% CI 29.9–70.1), 25.0% Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (11.2–46.9); P=0.0082. Of all surgically treated patients, 15 (37.5%) maintained remission throughout the 10 years; 20 of 34 patients (58.8%) in remission at 2 years relapsed during follow-up — but patients who relapsed still kept good control (mean HbA1c 6.7% at 10 years). Diabetes-related complications were fewer in both surgical groups (relative risk 0.07, 0.01–0.48). Serious adverse events occurred more often with biliopancreatic diversion (odds ratio 2.7 relative to medical therapy); for bypass the odds ratio was 0.7.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients at one centre, open-label — and biliopancreatic diversion, the operation with the 50% remission rate, is now rarely performed. The trial shows durability of control, not prevention of death or cardiovascular events.
cards.source: Mingrone G et al. Metabolic surgery versus conventional medical therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes: 10-year follow-up of an open-label, single-centre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2021;397:293-304. PMID 33485454 · NCT00888836.

cards.headline: Diabetes Surgery Study: adding gastric bypass to intensive medical management tripled goal control at 12 months — 49% vs 19%
cards.summary: The composite goal (HbA1c <7.0%, LDL <100 mg/dL, systolic BP <130 mm Hg) was reached by 49% with gastric bypass vs 19% with lifestyle–medical management alone (odds ratio 4.8 , 1.9–11.7); weight loss 26.1% vs 7.9% — 120 patients.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (Diabetes Surgery Study), JAMA 2013
cards.people: 120 participants at 4 teaching hospitals in the United States and Taiwan, with type 2 diabetes for at least 6 months; all received the intensive lifestyle–medical protocol, 60 were also assigned to gastric bypass. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Primary composite endpoint achieved by 28 participants (49%) in the gastric bypass group vs 11 (19%) in the lifestyle–medical group (odds ratio 4.8, 95% CI 1.9–11.7). The bypass group used 3.0 fewer medications on average (1.7 vs 4.8) and lost 26.1% vs 7.9% of initial body weight (difference 17.5%, 14.2–20.7); regression analyses attributed achieving the goal mainly to weight loss. Serious adverse events: 22 in the bypass group (including 1 cardiovascular event) vs 15 in the medical group, with 4 perioperative and 6 late postoperative complications, and more nutritional deficiency in the bypass group.
cards.watchOut: Twelve months only, unblinded, 120 patients — a proof of effect, not of durability or hard outcomes; the surgical group paid for its control with more serious adverse events.
cards.source: Ikramuddin S et al. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass vs intensive medical management for the control of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia: the Diabetes Surgery Study randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID 23736733 · NCT00641251.

shelves.title: Weekly insulin icodec: one basal injection a week instead of seven
shelves.question: In people with diabetes who need basal insulin, does once-weekly insulin icodec control blood glucose as well as once-daily basal insulin — and at what hypoglycemia cost?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Insulin, Long-Acting · Hypoglycemia · Glycated Hemoglobin · Blood Glucose · Humans
shelves.balance: One injection a week does the basal-insulin job: in insulin-naive type 2 diabetes, icodec lowered A1c slightly more than daily glargine or degludec, with hypoglycemia rates under 1 event per patient-year in both arms — somewhat higher on icodec in relative terms. In type 1 diabetes the trade was starker: equal A1c, but a 1.9 relative rate of clinically significant or severe hypoglycemia. The US approval (FDA, March 26, 2026 — Awiqli) covers type 2 diabetes only. All three trials were funded by Novo Nordisk, icodec’s maker. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: ONWARDS 1: weekly icodec beat daily glargine on A1c at 52 weeks (−1.55 vs −1.35 points)
cards.summary: A1c fell −1.55 points on weekly icodec vs −1.35 on daily glargine U100 (difference −0.19, −0.36 to −0.03; noninferior and superior); time in range 71.9% vs 66.9% ; combined clinically significant or severe hypoglycemia rate ratio 1.64 (0.98–2.75) in relative terms — 984 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3a randomized, open-label, treat-to-target trial (ONWARDS 1), N Engl J Med 2023
cards.people: 984 adults with insulin-naive type 2 diabetes (492 per group), 52-week main phase plus 26-week extension. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Mean A1c change at 52 weeks: −1.55 percentage points with icodec (8.50% → 6.93%) vs −1.35 with glargine U100 (8.44% → 7.12%); estimated difference −0.19 points (95% CI −0.36 to −0.03), confirming noninferiority (P<0.001) and superiority (P=0.02). Time in range 70–180 mg/dL in weeks 48–52: 71.9% vs 66.9% (difference 4.27 points, 1.92–6.62; P<0.001). Combined clinically significant or severe hypoglycemia: 0.30 vs 0.16 events per person-year at week 52 (estimated rate ratio 1.64, 0.98–2.75) and 0.30 vs 0.16 at week 83 (rate ratio 1.63, 1.02–2.61). No new safety signals; adverse-event incidence similar.
cards.watchOut: Open-label — patients knew whether they injected daily or weekly. The week-52 hypoglycemia rate ratio is a relative measure whose confidence interval crosses 1; by week 83 it did not. Funded by Novo Nordisk.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Weekly Icodec versus Daily Glargine U100 in Type 2 Diabetes without Previous Insulin. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:297-308. PMID 37356066 · NCT04460885.

cards.headline: ONWARDS 3: weekly icodec vs daily degludec, double-blind — A1c 7.0% vs 7.2% at 26 weeks
cards.summary: A1c fell to 7.0% on weekly icodec vs 7.2% on daily degludec (difference −0.2 points, −0.3 to −0.1; noninferior and superior); weight gain similar ( 2.8 vs 2.3 kg); combined level 2/3 hypoglycemia 0.35 vs 0.12 events per patient-year over weeks 0–26 — 588 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3a randomized, double-blind (double-dummy), treat-to-target trial (ONWARDS 3), JAMA 2023
cards.people: 588 randomized participants at 92 sites in 11 countries (294 per group); mean age 58 (SD 10) years; 219 (37%) women; 564 (96%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Mean A1c decreased from 8.6% to an estimated 7.0% on icodec vs from 8.5% to 7.2% on degludec (estimated treatment difference −0.2 points, 95% CI −0.3 to −0.1), confirming noninferiority (P<.001) and superiority (P=.002). No significant differences in fasting glucose change, final weekly insulin dose, or weight change (2.8 vs 2.3 kg; P=.17). Combined level 2 or 3 hypoglycemia: 0.31 vs 0.15 events per patient-year over weeks 0–31 (P=.11) and 0.35 vs 0.12 over weeks 0–26 (P=.01) — statistically higher on icodec, with both arms below 1 event per patient-year.
cards.watchOut: The double-dummy design (daily placebo injections in the icodec arm) makes this the programme’s most rigorous test. Funded by Novo Nordisk.
cards.source: Lingvay I et al. Once-Weekly Insulin Icodec vs Once-Daily Insulin Degludec in Adults With Insulin-Naive Type 2 Diabetes: The ONWARDS 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023;330:228-237. PMID 37354562 · NCT04795531.

cards.headline: ONWARDS 6 (type 1 diabetes): A1c noninferior — hypoglycemia rate 1.9 in relative terms on icodec
cards.summary: In type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus therapy, A1c change was −0.47 points on weekly icodec vs −0.51 on daily degludec (difference 0.05, −0.13 to 0.23; noninferior) — but combined clinically significant or severe hypoglycemia ran 19.9 vs 10.4 events per patient-year, a rate ratio of 1.9 (1.5–2.3) in relative terms — 582 patients.
cards.type: Phase 3a randomized, open-label, treat-to-target trial (ONWARDS 6), Lancet 2023
cards.people: 582 adults with type 1 diabetes (HbA1c <10.0%) at 99 sites in 12 countries, randomized to weekly icodec (n=290) or daily degludec (n=292), each with insulin aspart at meals; 26-week main phase plus 26-week safety extension. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: A1c change at week 26: −0.47 points on icodec (from 7.59%) vs −0.51 on degludec (from 7.63%); estimated difference 0.05 points (95% CI −0.13 to 0.23), confirming noninferiority (P=0.0065). Combined clinically significant or severe hypoglycemia, baseline to week 26: 19.9 vs 10.4 events per patient-year (estimated rate ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.5–2.3; P<0.0001), and the rate stayed significantly higher over 57 weeks. Serious adverse events: 39 in 24 patients (8%) on icodec vs 25 in 20 patients (7%) on degludec; one death in the icodec group, judged unlikely due to the trial product.
cards.watchOut: Type 1 diabetes sits outside icodec’s US approval (FDA approved Awiqli in March 2026 for type 2 diabetes only). Absolute hypoglycemia rates here are far higher than in the type 2 trials because basal-bolus type 1 treatment is a different risk world. Severe-episode counts are not carded: they could not be verified from the trial’s record. Funded by Novo Nordisk.
cards.source: Russell-Jones D et al. Once-weekly insulin icodec versus once-daily insulin degludec as part of a basal-bolus regimen in individuals with type 1 diabetes (ONWARDS 6). Lancet. 2023;402:1636-1647. PMID 37863084 · NCT04848480.

shelves.title: Thiazolidinedione harms: fractures, heart failure, the bladder-cancer signal
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, what harms do the thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) cause?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Thiazolidinediones · Pioglitazone · Rosiglitazone · Heart Failure · Fractures, Bone · Urinary Bladder Neoplasms · Humans
shelves.balance: Thiazolidinediones make the body hold fluid, and in randomized trials they clearly increase heart-failure admissions — RECORD: heart-failure admission or death HR 2.10 (1.35–3.27); PROactive: 5.7% vs 4.1% admitted — while neither trial showed more heart-failure or cardiovascular deaths on the drug (PROactive: heart-failure mortality did not differ; RECORD: cardiovascular death HR 0.84, 0.59–1.18). In women, rosiglitazone roughly doubles limb fractures (ADOPT: 9.3% vs 5.1% on metformin and 3.5% on glyburide over about 4 years; men unaffected) — PPAR-γ activation shifts marrow stem cells toward fat and away from bone-forming cells, and lowers insulin/IGF-1 signaling to bone. The bladder-cancer question for pioglitazone stays MAYBE (weak evidence): two large cohorts found no clear overall increase (Kaiser ever-use HR 1.2, 0.9–1.5), with weak rises after more than 2 years of use (Kaiser HR 1.4; UK rate ratio 1.83 overall, 2.54 at the highest cumulative dose) — small absolute risks, causality unproven.

cards.headline: PROactive: pioglitazone and heart failure — admissions up, heart-failure deaths not
cards.summary: Admitted to hospital with heart failure 5.7% on pioglitazone vs 4.1% on placebo; mortality rates from heart failure did not differ between groups; death/MI/stroke HR 0.84 (0.72–0.98); primary composite HR 0.90 (0.80–1.02), not significant — 5,238 patients.
cards.people: 5,238 patients with type 2 diabetes and macrovascular disease; pioglitazone (15→45 mg) vs placebo added to existing therapy; average observation 34.5 months.
cards.result: Primary composite (death, MI, stroke, ACS, coronary/leg intervention, major amputation): 514/2605 vs 572/2633, HR 0.90 (0.80–1.02), not significant. Death/MI/stroke: 301 vs 358, HR 0.84 (0.72–0.98). Admitted to hospital with heart failure: 149/2605 (5.7%) on pioglitazone vs 108/2633 (4.1%) on placebo; mortality rates from heart failure did not differ between groups (the trial's own wording).
cards.watchOut: A secondary-prevention population already prone to heart failure: the admission excess (5.7% vs 4.1%) is the harm to weigh against the death/MI/stroke gain, and the reassurance is narrow — heart-failure mortality did not differ, in the trial's own wording.
cards.source: Dormandy JA et al. Secondary prevention of macrovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes in the PROactive Study (PROspective pioglitAzone Clinical Trial In macroVascular Events): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2005;366:1279–89. PMID 16214598 · NCT00174993.

cards.headline: RECORD: rosiglitazone doubles heart-failure admissions or death, cardiovascular death not increased
cards.summary: Heart failure causing admission or death: 61 on rosiglitazone vs 29 on control — HR 2.10 (1.35–3.27); primary outcome HR 0.99 (0.85–1.16), non-inferior; cardiovascular death HR 0.84 (0.59–1.18) — 4,447 patients.
cards.people: 4,447 patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin or a sulfonylurea alone (mean HbA1c 7.9%); add-on rosiglitazone vs the metformin+sulfonylurea combination; open-label; mean follow-up 5.5 years.
cards.result: Primary outcome (cardiovascular hospitalization or cardiovascular death): 321 vs 323, HR 0.99 (0.85–1.16) — non-inferior. Cardiovascular death HR 0.84 (0.59–1.18); MI HR 1.14 (0.80–1.63); stroke HR 0.72 (0.49–1.06). Heart failure causing admission or death: 61 on rosiglitazone vs 29 on control, HR 2.10 (1.35–3.27); risk difference 2.6 per 1000 person-years. Upper and distal lower limb fracture rates were increased on rosiglitazone, mainly in women (see Card 3 for the fracture trial's own numbers).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the heart-failure endpoint is the one place the drug clearly lost: admissions or death doubled while cardiovascular death did not rise. Upper and distal lower limb fracture rates were also increased on rosiglitazone, mainly in women — Card 3 holds the fracture trial's own numbers.

cards.headline: ADOPT fracture analysis: rosiglitazone fractures in women, not men
cards.summary: Women with at least one fracture: 9.3% on rosiglitazone vs 5.1% on metformin vs 3.5% on glyburide — HR 1.81 (1.17–2.80) vs metformin and 2.13 (1.30–3.51) vs glyburide; in men, fracture rates did not differ — 4,360 patients.
cards.type: Fracture analysis of a randomized trial (ADOPT), Diabetes Care 2008
cards.people: 4,360 patients randomized to rosiglitazone, metformin, or glyburide monotherapy (analysis population 1,840 women, 2,511 men); median follow-up 4.0 years.
cards.result: Women with at least one fracture: rosiglitazone 60 (9.3%; 2.74 per 100 patient-years) vs metformin 30 (5.1%; 1.54) vs glyburide 21 (3.5%; 1.29). HR for rosiglitazone 1.81 (1.17–2.80) vs metformin and 2.13 (1.30–3.51) vs glyburide. Five-year cumulative incidence in women: 15.1% vs 7.3% vs 7.7%. Men: fracture rates did not differ between treatment groups. Fractures were predominantly in the upper and lower limbs, in pre- and postmenopausal women alike.
cards.watchOut: A fracture analysis of the ADOPT trial (parent trial: Kahn SE et al. N Engl J Med 2006;355:2427–43, PMID 17145742). The excess sits in women — pre- and postmenopausal alike — and in the upper and lower limbs; nothing in the analysis extends the signal to men.
cards.source: Kahn SE et al. Rosiglitazone-associated fractures in type 2 diabetes: an Analysis from A Diabetes Outcome Progression Trial (ADOPT). Diabetes Care. 2008;31:845–51. PMID 18223031. (Parent trial: Kahn SE et al. N Engl J Med 2006;355:2427–43, PMID 17145742.)

cards.headline: Lewis 2011 (Kaiser cohort): pioglitazone and bladder cancer — no overall increase, weak rise after 2 years
cards.summary: Ever use HR 1.2 (0.9–1.5), not significant; use for more than 24 months HR 1.4 (1.03–2.0) — 193,099 patients aged ≥40, 30,173 of them pioglitazone users; 90 bladder cancers among users vs 791 among non-users.

cards.result: Bladder cancer: 90 cases among pioglitazone users vs 791 among non-users. Ever use HR 1.2 (0.9–1.5), not significant; use for more than 24 months HR 1.4 (1.03–2.0). 95% of cancers in pioglitazone users were detected at an early stage.

shelves.title: Diabetic foot ulcers: offloading heals, adjuncts add a little
shelves.question: In people with diabetic foot ulcers, what actually heals the wound — how much comes from taking pressure off it, and what do dressings and patches add?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Foot · Foot Ulcer · Casts, Surgical · Weight-Bearing · Wound Healing · Bandages · Sucrose · Humans
shelves.balance: The ulcer heals when the pressure comes off and stays off: total contact casts and irremovable walkers beat removable devices in both offloading trials, largely because patients take removable devices off. On top of standard care, a sucrose octasulfate dressing (neuroischaemic ulcers) and the LeucoPatch (hard-to-heal ulcers) each added roughly 12–18 percentage points of healing at 20 weeks — real, modest, and adjunctive, not substitutes for offloading, debridement, vascular assessment, and infection control. Developer-approved Nov 6, 2026.

cards.headline: Armstrong 2005: making the removable walker irremovable healed 82.6% vs 51.9%
cards.summary: Healed at 12 weeks: 82.6% with the walker wrapped so it could not be removed (instant total contact cast) vs 51.9% with the same walker left removable (P=0.02); healed ulcers also closed faster, 41.6 vs 58.0 days — 50 patients.
cards.people: 50 patients with University of Texas grade 1A neuropathic diabetic foot ulcerations, randomized to a removable cast walker (RCW) or the same walker wrapped in cohesive bandage (instant total contact cast, iTCC); the paper reports mean age 65.6 years, 88% men, mean HbA1c 8.2%. Evaluated weekly for 12 weeks or until healing.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat: ulcers healed at 12 weeks in 82.6% of the iTCC group vs 51.9% of the RCW group (P=0.02; odds ratio 1.8, 95% CI 1.1–2.9, as printed in the paper). Among patients whose ulcers healed, time to healing was 41.6±18.7 days with iTCC vs 58.0±15.2 days with RCW (P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients, grade 1A ulcers only — the cleanest wound class. The intervention worked by removing a choice: identical hardware, different adherence. No trial registration exists for this 2005 trial (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Armstrong DG et al. Evaluation of removable and irremovable cast walkers in the healing of diabetic foot wounds: a randomized controlled trial. Diabetes Care. 2005;28:551-4. PMID 15735186.

cards.headline: Armstrong 2001: total contact cast healed 89.5% vs 65.0% (removable walker) vs 58.3% (half-shoe)
cards.summary: Healed by 12 weeks: 89.5% total contact cast vs 65.0% removable cast walker vs 58.3% half-shoe (cast vs the other two, P=0.026; odds ratio 5.4 , 1.1–26.1); cast patients took the fewest steps, 600 a day — 63 patients.
cards.people: 63 patients with superficial noninfected, nonischemic diabetic plantar foot ulcers, randomized to total contact cast (TCC), removable cast walker (RCW), or half-shoe; outcomes at healing or 12 weeks. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Proportion healed at 12 weeks: 89.5% TCC vs 65.0% RCW vs 58.3% half-shoe; TCC vs the two other modalities combined 89.5% vs 61.4% (P=0.026; odds ratio 5.4, 95% CI 1.1–26.1). Time-to-healing distributions also favored TCC over RCW (P=0.033) and half-shoe (P=0.012). Activity: TCC patients averaged 600.1±320.0 steps/day vs 767.6±563.3 on RCW and 1,461.8±1,452.3 on half-shoe (TCC vs half-shoe P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: Part of the cast’s advantage is enforced rest — it cannot be removed for the trip to the mailbox. Casts require trained staff and were tested here on noninfected, nonischemic ulcers only. No trial registration exists for this 2001 trial (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Armstrong DG et al. Off-loading the diabetic foot wound: a randomized clinical trial. Diabetes Care. 2001;24:1019-22. PMID 11375363.

cards.headline: Explorer: sucrose octasulfate dressing closed 48% vs 30% of neuroischaemic ulcers at 20 weeks
cards.summary: Wound closure at 20 weeks: 48% with the sucrose octasulfate dressing vs 30% with the identical dressing without it (adjusted odds ratio 2.60 , 1.43–4.73; P=0.002); target-wound infections in 20% vs 28% of patients — 240 patients.
cards.type: International, multicentre, double-blind randomized controlled trial (Explorer), Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2018
cards.people: 240 patients with diabetes and a non-infected neuroischaemic foot ulcer >1 cm² (University of Texas grade IC or IIC) at 43 specialist clinics in France, Spain, Italy, Germany, and the UK; 126 assigned to sucrose octasulfate dressing, 114 to control dressing. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix; carried as a gate item.)
cards.result: Wound closure at week 20 (intention-to-treat): 60 of 126 patients (48%) on sucrose octasulfate vs 34 of 114 (30%) on control — an 18-percentage-point difference (95% CI 5–30); adjusted odds ratio 2.60 (1.43–4.73), P=0.002. Most frequent adverse events were infections of the target wound: 25 patients (20%) in the sucrose octasulfate group vs 32 (28%) in the control group. Minor amputations not affecting the wound site: 1 vs 2 patients. Deaths: 3 vs 4, none related to treatment, procedure, wound progression, or amputation.
cards.watchOut: Funded by Laboratoires Urgo Medical, the dressing’s maker. Neuroischaemic ulcers are the hardest class — the 30% control closure rate is the context that makes 48% meaningful.
cards.source: Edmonds M et al. Sucrose octasulfate dressing versus control dressing in patients with neuroischaemic diabetic foot ulcers (Explorer): an international, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2018;6:186-196. PMID 29275068 · NCT01717183.

cards.headline: LeucoPatch: autologous leucocyte–platelet–fibrin patch healed 34% vs 22% of hard-to-heal ulcers
cards.summary: Healed within 20 weeks: 34% (45/132) with weekly LeucoPatch plus standard care vs 22% (29/134) with standard care alone (odds ratio 1.58 , 96% CI 1.04–2.40; P=0.0235); no device-related adverse events — 269 patients.
cards.type: Multicentre, international, observer-masked randomized controlled trial, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2018
cards.people: 269 participants at 32 specialist diabetic foot clinics in the UK, Denmark, and Sweden; mean age 61.9 years (SD 11.6); 217 (82%) men; 222 (83%) type 2 diabetes; 132 assigned to LeucoPatch plus standard care, 137 to standard care alone.
cards.result: Ulcers healed within 20 weeks (intention-to-treat): 45 of 132 (34%) with LeucoPatch vs 29 of 134 (22%) with standard care (odds ratio 1.58, 96% CI 1.04–2.40; P=0.0235). No difference in adverse events overall; the most common serious adverse event in both groups was diabetic foot infection (24 events in the LeucoPatch group, 20 in standard care). No device-related adverse events.

shelves.title: Testosterone in older men: cardiovascularly noninferior in TRAVERSE — with the excesses on the same card, and benefit narrower than the marketing
shelves.question: In older men with confirmed hypogonadism, is testosterone replacement safe for the heart, does it fracture bones, and which symptoms does it actually improve?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Hypogonadism · Myocardial Infarction · Stroke
shelves.balance: Split the verdict the way the evidence splits. Safety: TRAVERSE — 5,246 hypogonadal men at high cardiovascular risk — met noninferiority for major adverse cardiac events (7.0% vs 7.3%; HR 0.96), and in 2025 the FDA removed the boxed cardiovascular warning from testosterone labelling. The excesses are printed on the same card, not a different shelf: atrial fibrillation 3.5% vs 2.4%, acute kidney injury 2.3% vs 1.5%, pulmonary embolism 0.9% vs 0.5% — and the trial's own fracture study found MORE fractures on testosterone (3.50% vs 2.46%; HR 1.43) even as bone density improved. TRAVERSE and its fracture study appear as exhibits on Shelf #137 and are re-carded here, counted once at home. Benefit: the T Trials (790 men) improved sexual function and corrected anemia impressively (hemoglobin up at least 1 g/dL in 54% vs 15%), but their walking and vitality primaries were MISSED and cognition was null. Budoff's plaque substudy — more noncalcified coronary plaque growth on testosterone — stands as the caution that noninferiority on events is not the same as innocence. Tier C — developer-ruled Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: TRAVERSE (Lincoff 2023): MACE noninferior (7.0% vs 7.3%; HR 0.96) — with the AF, AKI, and PE excesses on the same card (re-card; home: Shelf #137)
cards.summary: 5,246 men with hypogonadism and high cardiovascular risk: a primary cardiac event occurred in 182 (7.0%) on testosterone vs 190 (7.3%) on placebo (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.78–1.17; P<0.001 for noninferiority). On the same card: atrial fibrillation 3.5% vs 2.4%, acute kidney injury 2.3% vs 1.5%, pulmonary embolism 0.9% vs 0.5%. (Re-card; home: Shelf #137.)
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial (TRAVERSE), New England Journal of Medicine 2023. Re-card — home: Shelf #137
cards.people: 5,246 men aged 45–80 years with hypogonadism (two low testosterone readings with symptoms) and preexisting or high risk of cardiovascular disease, randomized to testosterone gel or placebo gel. Re-card of the exhibit homed on Shelf #137; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: The primary safety end point — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke — occurred in 182 men (7.0%) on testosterone and 190 (7.3%) on placebo, meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion. Atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury, and pulmonary embolism were each more frequent on testosterone, as was erythrocytosis; the fracture excess is the next card.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is a fence, not a clean bill: the trial was designed to exclude a large excess of events, and it did — in men like these, treated like this, over a mean treatment period of about two years. The rhythm, kidney, and clot excesses were secondary safety findings — individually modest, collectively a pattern a prescriber should know before the first prescription, not after. In 2025 the FDA removed the boxed cardiovascular warning from testosterone products, a regulatory judgment that followed this trial; it does not erase the excesses printed above.
cards.source: Lincoff AM et al. Cardiovascular safety of testosterone-replacement therapy (TRAVERSE). N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID 37326322 · NCT03518034. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2215025

cards.headline: The fracture paradox (Snyder 2024): fractures ROSE on testosterone — 3.50% vs 2.46% (HR 1.43) — while bone density improved (re-card; home: Shelf #137)
cards.summary: TRAVERSE fracture study, 5,204 men, median follow-up 3.19 years: a clinical fracture occurred in 91 men on testosterone (3.50%) vs 64 on placebo (2.46%) (HR 1.43; 95% CI 1.04–1.97), with every fracture endpoint numerically higher on testosterone — despite improved bone density. (Re-card; home: Shelf #137.)
cards.type: Fracture study within a randomized trial (TRAVERSE), New England Journal of Medicine 2024. Re-card — home: Shelf #137
cards.people: 5,204 men in the TRAVERSE population with fracture follow-up (median 3.19 years). Re-card of the exhibit homed on Shelf #137; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: A clinical fracture occurred in 91 men (3.50%) in the testosterone group and 64 (2.46%) in the placebo group (HR 1.43; 95% CI 1.04–1.97). All fracture endpoints were numerically higher with testosterone, even though bone mineral density — the surrogate — improved on treatment.
cards.watchOut: The surrogate lied in the open: bone density moved one way while fractures, the outcome patients feel, moved the other. Proposed mechanisms (more physical activity and falls exposure on treatment) are speculation; the count is not. Any clinician quoting TRAVERSE for safety owes the patient this card in the same breath. All of it is one trial — the developer's one-trial caution applies, and Shelf #137 grades this strand accordingly.

cards.headline: The T Trials (Snyder 2016): sexual function improved — the walking and vitality primaries were MISSED, cognition null
cards.summary: 790 men aged 65 or older with testosterone under 275 ng/dL: testosterone restored levels to the mid-normal young-adult range and significantly increased sexual activity, desire, and erectile function. The Physical Function Trial's own primary outcome (a ≥50 m gain in 6-minute walk distance) was NOT significant within that trial, and vitality showed no significant benefit on its primary scale.
cards.type: Coordinated set of three randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (the Testosterone Trials), New England Journal of Medicine 2016
cards.people: 790 men aged 65 years or older with a serum testosterone concentration below 275 ng/dL and symptoms suggesting hypogonadism, each participating in one or more of the Sexual Function, Physical Function, and Vitality trials; testosterone gel or placebo gel for 1 year.
cards.result: Testosterone treatment was associated with significantly increased sexual activity, sexual desire, and erectile function. The percentage of men gaining at least 50 m in the 6-minute walk did not differ significantly between groups in the Physical Function Trial, but did when all three trials were pooled (20.5% vs 12.6%; P=0.003). There was no significant benefit on vitality as measured by the FACIT-Fatigue scale, though mood and depressive symptoms were slightly better on testosterone. Rates of adverse events were similar in this carefully screened population. The companion cognitive trial found no benefit.
cards.watchOut: Read the misses as carefully as the hits: three prespecified primaries — one clear win (sexual function), one miss rescued only by pooling (walking), one miss (vitality) — and a null cognitive trial beside them. This is a drug with a narrow, real symptomatic benefit in genuinely hypogonadal older men, not a rejuvenation therapy. The anemia dividend is the next card.
cards.source: Snyder PJ et al. Effects of testosterone treatment in older men. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID 26886521 · NCT00799617. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1506119

cards.headline: T Trials anemia (Roy 2017): hemoglobin rose by at least 1 g/dL in 54% vs 15% — the program's most lopsided benefit
cards.summary: In men with unexplained anemia, testosterone produced a hemoglobin increase of at least 1.0 g/dL in 54% vs 15% on placebo; in men whose anemia had a known cause, 52% vs 19%. Exploratory analyses linked the hemoglobin rise to better walking distance and vitality.
cards.type: Anemia trial within the Testosterone Trials (double-blind, placebo-controlled), JAMA Internal Medicine 2017
cards.people: 788 men aged 65 years or older with average testosterone levels below 275 ng/dL; 126 were anemic (hemoglobin ≤12.7 g/dL), of whom 62 had anemia with no recognized cause. The anemic men had a mean age of 74.8 years; testosterone gel, dose-adjusted to keep levels in the young-normal range, or placebo gel for 12 months.
cards.result: Testosterone treatment resulted in a greater percentage of men with unexplained anemia whose hemoglobin increased by 1.0 g/dL or more by month 12 (54% vs 15% on placebo), with a similar pattern in known-cause anemia (52% vs 19%). Hemoglobin rose significantly more on testosterone in anemic and non-anemic participants alike.
cards.watchOut: A real and large effect on a laboratory outcome in a defined subgroup — and still a surrogate: the trial was not powered to show fewer transfusions, hospitalizations, or deaths. It justifies testosterone as one tool for unexplained anemia in hypogonadal older men after the standard workup — not as an anemia drug for men with normal testosterone.
cards.source: Roy CN et al. Association of testosterone levels with anemia in older men: a controlled clinical trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2017. PMID 28241237 · NCT00799617. DOI 10.1001/jamainternmed.2016.9540

cards.headline: Budoff 2017: the plaque caution — noncalcified coronary plaque grew MORE on testosterone
cards.summary: 170 men in the T Trials cardiovascular substudy: over 12 months, noncalcified coronary plaque volume increased significantly more on testosterone than on placebo (estimated difference 41 mm³; 95% CI 14–67; P=0.003), as did total plaque volume (difference 47 mm³; P=0.006). Coronary artery calcium scores did not differ significantly.
cards.type: Imaging substudy of a randomized trial (Testosterone Trials), JAMA Cardiology 2017
cards.people: 170 men aged 65 years or older with low testosterone enrolled in the coronary CT angiography substudy; 138 (73 testosterone, 65 placebo) completed the study and were analyzable. Among completers, mean age was 71.2 years and 81% were white; half had severe atherosclerosis at baseline (coronary calcium score above 300).
cards.result: Noncalcified plaque volume rose from a median of 204 mm³ to 232 mm³ on testosterone vs 317 mm³ to 325 mm³ on placebo (estimated difference in change, 41 mm³; P=0.003). Total plaque volume also increased more with testosterone (estimated difference 47 mm³; P=0.006). There was no significant difference in coronary artery calcium score change.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate moving the wrong way in 138 men does not outweigh 5,246 men's event data — and this shelf does not ask it to. It is carded as what it is: the reason TRAVERSE's noninferiority should be read as 'no large excess of events detected' rather than 'proven vascular innocence,' and a standing argument against extrapolating testosterone to men unlike those TRAVERSE enrolled.
cards.source: Budoff MJ et al. Testosterone treatment and coronary artery plaque volume in older men with low testosterone. JAMA Cardiol. 2017. PMID 28241355 · NCT00799617. DOI 10.1001/jama.2016.21043

shelves.title: Treating subclinical hypothyroidism: in the older adults actually studied, levothyroxine changed nothing — symptoms, tiredness, quality of life all null
shelves.question: Should subclinical hypothyroidism — a raised TSH with normal free T4 — be treated with levothyroxine?
shelves.mesh: Hypothyroidism · Thyroxine · Thyrotropin · Quality of Life · Fatigue
shelves.balance: The trials asked the patients' own question — will I feel better? — and answered it with zeros. TRUST (737 patients, age ≥65, mean TSH 6.40): the levothyroxine-vs-placebo difference in hypothyroid symptoms was 0.0 points. The ≥80 trial (251 patients): differences of 1.3 and −0.1 points against a 9-point minimum important difference. Feller's meta-analysis of all 21 randomized trials (2,192 patients): no association with quality of life or thyroid-related symptoms. The BMJ Rapid Recommendation panel issued a strong recommendation against routine treatment. The boundaries are printed on the shelf's face, because the null has edges: TSH ≥10, genuinely symptomatic patients, younger patients, and pregnancy or trying to conceive are OUTSIDE the studied null — the trials enrolled mostly older adults with mild TSH elevations, and this shelf does not extend their answer past their populations. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: TRUST (Stott 2017): 737 patients ≥65 — symptom difference 0.0; tiredness difference 0.4; every secondary outcome null
cards.summary: 737 adults ≥65 with persisting subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.60–19.99, mean 6.40), levothyroxine vs placebo for 1 year: change in Hypothyroid Symptoms score 0.2 vs 0.2 (between-group difference 0.0 [−2.0 to 2.1]) and Tiredness score difference 0.4 [−2.1 to 2.9] — against a minimum clinically important difference of 9 points on each 0–100 scale. TSH fell as expected (to 3.63 vs 5.48) — the hormone level obeyed; the patient felt nothing.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (TRUST), New England Journal of Medicine 2017
cards.people: 737 adults at least 65 years old with persisting subclinical hypothyroidism (368 levothyroxine, 369 placebo); mean age 74.4 years; 396 (53.7%) women; mean baseline TSH 6.40 (±2.01); levothyroxine starting dose 50 µg daily (25 µg if <50 kg or coronary heart disease), titrated to TSH, median dose 50 µg.
cards.result: At 1 year, TSH had decreased to 3.63 mIU/L in the levothyroxine group vs 5.48 in the placebo group (P<0.001). There were no differences in the mean change in Hypothyroid Symptoms score (0.2±15.3 placebo vs 0.2±14.4 levothyroxine; difference 0.0 [−2.0 to 2.1]) or Tiredness score (3.2±17.7 vs 3.8±18.4; difference 0.4 [−2.1 to 2.9]). No beneficial effects were seen on any secondary-outcome measure, and there was no significant excess of prespecified serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The null is precise, not underpowered hand-waving: the confidence interval for symptoms (−2.0 to 2.1) excludes even a quarter of the 9-point minimum important difference. The fence: mean TSH was 6.40 — this trial answers for MILD subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults. It does not answer for TSH ≥10, for younger patients, or for pregnancy, and the shelf prints those boundaries rather than letting the null wander.
cards.source: Stott DJ et al.; TRUST Study Group. Thyroid Hormone Therapy for Older Adults with Subclinical Hypothyroidism. N Engl J Med. 2017;376:2534–2544. PMID 28402245 · NCT01660126 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1603825

cards.headline: The ≥80 trial (Mooijaart 2019): in 251 patients aged 80+, symptom and tiredness differences of 1.3 and −0.1 points — null at the oldest ages too
cards.summary: Prospectively planned combined analysis of 251 community-dwelling adults aged ≥80 with subclinical hypothyroidism (from TRUST and the IEMO trial): hypothyroid-symptoms score difference 1.3 [−2.7 to 5.2] (P=0.53) and tiredness difference −0.1 [−4.5 to 4.3] (P=0.96) at 1 year — both far inside the 9-point minimum clinically important difference, in the direction of no benefit. Adverse events occurred in 29.5% on levothyroxine (the record's abstract is truncated at this point; no significant excess was the trials' finding).
cards.type: Prospectively planned combined analysis of two randomized clinical trials, JAMA 2019
cards.people: 251 participants (112 levothyroxine, 139 placebo) aged 80 years and older; mean age 85 years; 118 (47%) women; 105 from the first trial and 146 from the second; 84% completed the study.
cards.result: The hypothyroid symptoms score decreased from 21.7 at baseline to 19.3 at 12 months in the levothyroxine group vs 19.8 to 17.4 in the placebo group (adjusted between-group difference 1.3 [−2.7 to 5.2]; P=0.53). The tiredness score increased in both groups (25.5→28.2 levothyroxine; 25.1→28.7 placebo; adjusted difference −0.1 [−4.5 to 4.3]; P=0.96). Both co-primary outcomes are null against a prespecified minimum clinically important difference of 9 points.
cards.watchOut: This is the oldest-old evidence: if treating subclinical hypothyroidism were going to relieve symptoms anywhere in late life, 85-year-olds with symptoms scores around 20 were the place to see it. The PubMed record for this report carries no MeSH heading list; the card's indexing terms are drawn from the shelf's other records, and the source line says what the record does and does not print. Populations outside the null (TSH ≥10, symptomatic younger patients, pregnancy) remain outside it — see the shelf balance.
cards.source: Mooijaart SP et al. Association Between Levothyroxine Treatment and Thyroid-Related Symptoms Among Adults Aged 80 Years and Older With Subclinical Hypothyroidism. JAMA. 2019;322:1977–1986. PMID 31664429 · NCT01660126 (parent trial registration). DOI 10.1001/jama.2019.17274 (the PubMed record prints no MeSH headings for this report)

cards.headline: Feller 2018: all 21 randomized trials pooled (n=2,192) — no association with quality of life or symptoms
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis, JAMA : 21 RCTs, 2,192 adults with subclinical hypothyroidism — thyroid hormone therapy normalized TSH (0.5–3.7 vs 4.6–14.7 mIU/L) but was not associated with benefit in general quality of life (standardized mean difference −0.11 [−0.25 to 0.03]) or thyroid-related symptoms (SMD 0.01 [−0.12 to 0.14]). The hormone number responds to treatment; the outcomes patients report do not.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials, JAMA 2018
cards.people: 21 trials with 2,192 adults randomized (nonpregnant adults with subclinical hypothyroidism); follow-up 3–18 months; quality-of-life analysis included 796 participants and symptom analysis 858.
cards.result: After treatment, thyroid hormone therapy was associated with lowering mean TSH into the normal range compared with placebo, but was not associated with benefit regarding general quality of life (SMD −0.11 [−0.25 to 0.03]; I²=66.7%) or thyroid-related symptoms (SMD 0.01 [−0.12 to 0.14]; I²=0.0%). Standardized mean differences of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 correspond to small, moderate, and large effects — both pooled estimates sit at or below the 'small' threshold, with intervals including zero.
cards.watchOut: Generalisability fence, printed as the review's own design: trials enrolled nonpregnant adults, predominantly older, with mostly mild TSH elevation. The pooled null inherits TRUST's boundaries — it does not test TSH ≥10 as a stratum, symptomatic younger patients, or pregnancy. Within its population, though, 21 trials pointing at zero is as settled as symptom questions get.
cards.source: Feller M et al. Association of Thyroid Hormone Therapy With Quality of Life and Thyroid-Related Symptoms in Patients With Subclinical Hypothyroidism: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA. 2018;320:1349–1359. PMID 30285179. DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.13770

cards.headline: BMJ Rapid Recommendation 2019: a strong recommendation AGAINST thyroid hormones for subclinical hypothyroidism — with its exceptions printed in the recommendation itself
cards.summary: Guideline panel (patients, clinicians, methodologists; GRADE): strong recommendation against thyroid hormones in adults with subclinical hypothyroidism — across 21 trials (n=2,192), no clinically relevant benefits for quality of life or symptoms including depression, fatigue, and BMI. The recommendation's own scope fences: it does not apply to women trying to become pregnant or to TSH >20 mIU/L, and may not apply to severely symptomatic patients or young adults (≤30 years).
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (BMJ Rapid Recommendations, GRADE), BMJ 2019
cards.people: Adults with subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal free T4) — excluding, by the panel's own scope, women trying to become pregnant and patients with TSH >20 mIU/L; applicability uncertain for severe symptoms and young adults.
cards.result: The panel issues a strong recommendation against thyroid hormones in adults with subclinical hypothyroidism, triggered by the Feller systematic review (21 trials, 2,192 participants; Card 3). For adults with SCH, thyroid hormones consistently demonstrate no clinically relevant benefits for quality of life or thyroid-related symptoms, including depressive symptoms, fatigue, and body mass index (moderate- to high-quality evidence). Thyroid hormones may have little or no effect on cardiovascular events or mortality (low-quality evidence). Other factors behind the strong recommendation: the burden of lifelong daily medication and monitoring, and uncertainty about potential harms. The panel advises monitoring for progression or resolution of the thyroid dysfunction instead.
cards.watchOut: A guideline card, labeled as such — the trials are Cards 1–3. 'Strong against' is a statement about the studied population (mostly older, mildly elevated TSH), and this card keeps the panel's own exceptions attached to the recommendation wherever it is quoted: pregnancy-seeking, TSH >20, severe symptoms, and the young sit outside it, and TSH ≥10 in particular remains the zone where many other guidelines still suggest treatment — a live disagreement the shelf reports rather than resolves.
cards.source: Bekkering GE et al. Thyroid hormones treatment for subclinical hypothyroidism: a clinical practice guideline. BMJ. 2019;365:l2006. PMID 31088853. DOI 10.1136/bmj.l2006

shelves.title: Inpatient insulin: basal-bolus beats sliding scale for glucose control — and in surgical patients cut complications, at a fivefold hypoglycemia cost printed on the same card
shelves.question: On the wards, should hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes be managed with scheduled basal-bolus insulin or with sliding-scale insulin alone?
shelves.mesh: Insulin · Insulin Glargine · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Hypoglycemic Agents · Inpatients · Postoperative Complications
shelves.balance: The glucose-control verdict is consistent across three randomized trials: scheduled basal insulin (with bolus or correction doses) controls inpatient glucose better than sliding-scale regular insulin alone, which leaves a stubborn tail of patients above 240 mg/dL. The complications claim rests mainly on one surgical trial — RABBIT 2 Surgery's composite fell from 24.3% to 8.6% — and its price is printed on the same card, as the ruling requires: hypoglycemia below 70 mg/dL in 23.1% vs 4.7%. Severe hypoglycemia (below 40) did not differ significantly in any of the three trials. The ADA's position closes the shelf: sliding-scale insulin alone is strongly discouraged (its inpatient standard carries a Grade A recommendation for scheduled basal or basal-plus regimens in noncritically ill patients), with a glucose target of 140–180 mg/dL for most hospitalized patients. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: RABBIT 2, medicine (Umpierrez 2007): basal-bolus reached target in 66% vs 38% on sliding scale; 14% on sliding scale stayed above 240 mg/dL
cards.summary: 130 insulin-naive medical inpatients with type 2 diabetes, glargine + glulisine vs sliding-scale regular insulin: a glucose target of <140 mg/dL was achieved in 66% vs 38% ; mean daily glucose ran 23–58 mg/dL lower on basal-bolus (overall difference 27 mg/dL; P<0.01). On sliding scale, 14% of patients remained above 240 mg/dL despite dose escalation. Hypoglycemia rates and length of stay did not differ.
cards.type: Prospective, multicenter, randomized trial (RABBIT 2), Diabetes Care 2007
cards.people: 130 insulin-naive patients with type 2 diabetes on general medicine wards (65 per group); mean admission glucose 229 mg/dL and A1C 8.8%. Basal-bolus starting dose 0.4 units/kg/day (glucose 140–200) or 0.5 units/kg/day (201–400), split between once-daily glargine and premeal glulisine.
cards.result: A blood glucose target of <140 mg/dL was achieved in 66% of patients on glargine and glulisine vs 38% on sliding-scale insulin. Mean daily glucose differed by 23–58 mg/dL between groups across the admission (overall difference 27 mg/dL; P<0.01). Despite increasing insulin doses, 14% of sliding-scale patients remained with glucose >240 mg/dL. There were no differences in hypoglycemia rate or hospital length of stay.
cards.watchOut: A glucose-control trial, not an outcomes trial: this card proves the regimen moves the number, in insulin-naive medical patients, against a target (<140) tighter than the 140–180 mg/dL range the ADA now recommends for most inpatients (Reference 4). Whether better ward glucose itself prevents complications is the surgical trial's question, next card — with its hypoglycemia cost attached.
