cards.headline: RABBIT 2 Surgery (Umpierrez 2011): complications 8.6% vs 24.3% — WITH hypoglycemia 23.1% vs 4.7% on the same card
cards.summary: 211 general-surgery patients with type 2 diabetes, basal-bolus (glargine + glulisine) vs sliding scale: composite of postoperative complications (wound infection, pneumonia, bacteremia, respiratory and acute renal failure) 8.6% vs 24.3% (P=0.003) — an absolute difference of 15.7 points. The cost, same card: glucose <70 mg/dL in 23.1% vs 4.7% (P<0.001). Glucose <40 mg/dL did not differ significantly (P=0.057). Mean daily glucose 145 vs 172 mg/dL.
cards.type: Randomized, multicenter trial (RABBIT 2 Surgery), Diabetes Care 2011
cards.people: 211 patients with type 2 diabetes undergoing general surgery (104 basal-bolus, 107 sliding scale). (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Mean daily glucose after day 1 was 145±32 mg/dL on basal-bolus vs 172±47 on sliding scale (P<0.01); readings <140 mg/dL occurred in 55% vs 31% (P<0.001). The composite complication outcome fell with basal-bolus (8.6% vs 24.3%; odds ratio for sliding scale vs basal-bolus 3.39 [1.50–7.65]; P=0.003). Glucose <70 mg/dL was reported in 23.1% of basal-bolus patients vs 4.7% on sliding scale (P<0.001) — roughly fivefold — but there was no significant difference in glucose <40 mg/dL (P=0.057). Benefit and harm are both this trial's results and are printed together wherever this card is quoted.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 211 patients, a composite endpoint — hence POSSIBLE for complications while control itself is LIKELY. The composite mixes wound infection with renal failure and bacteremia; the trial was not powered for any single component or for mortality. The hypoglycemia signal is mostly mild (<70, not <40), but a fivefold relative increase in any hypoglycemia is the standing price of scheduled insulin on a ward, and modern correction-dose practice (Reference 3) exists partly to pay less of it.

cards.headline: Basal Plus (Umpierrez 2013): basal insulin plus correction doses matched full basal-bolus — both beat sliding scale; hypoglycemia 13–16% vs 3%
cards.summary: 375 medical and surgical inpatients, three arms: basal-bolus vs basal-plus (once-daily glargine + correction glulisine) vs sliding scale — glucose improvement was similar between basal-bolus and basal-plus (P=0.16) and both were lower than sliding scale (P=0.04); treatment failure (>240 mg/dL) 0% vs 2% vs 19% . Glucose <70 mg/dL: 16% basal-bolus, 13% basal-plus, 3% sliding scale (P=0.02); severe hypoglycemia (<40) did not differ (P=0.76).
cards.type: Randomized, multicenter, three-arm trial (Basal Plus), Diabetes Care 2013
cards.people: 375 patients with type 2 diabetes treated with diet, oral agents, or low-dose insulin (≤0.4 units/kg/day), on general medicine and surgery wards.
cards.result: Improvement in mean daily glucose after the first day was similar between basal-bolus and basal plus (P=0.16), and both regimens resulted in lower mean daily glucose than sliding scale (P=0.04). Treatment failure occurred in 0% (basal-bolus) vs 2% (basal plus) vs 19% (sliding scale) (P<0.001). A glucose <70 mg/dL occurred in 16%, 13%, and 3% respectively (P=0.02); there was no difference in severe hypoglycemia <40 mg/dL (P=0.76). The authors' conclusion: basal plus is an effective, simpler alternative to basal-bolus in general medical and surgical patients.
cards.watchOut: The practical card: nearly one in five sliding-scale patients met the trial's failure definition, which is the operational case against sliding-scale-alone, while basal-plus buys basal-bolus-level control with fewer scheduled injections. The hypoglycemia ordering (basal regimens 13–16% vs sliding scale 3%) is the recurring trade of this whole shelf and is printed here at the same size as the efficacy result.

cards.headline: ADA Standards of Care 2025 (hospital section): sliding-scale insulin alone is strongly discouraged — scheduled basal or basal-plus, target 140–180 mg/dL
cards.summary: The American Diabetes Association's hospital standard: for noncritically ill inpatients, a scheduled basal or basal-plus-correction regimen is the preferred treatment — carrying the ADA's Grade A level of evidence support — and sliding-scale insulin alone is strongly discouraged . The recommended glucose target for most hospitalized patients is 140–180 mg/dL . This is the guideline position the three trials on this shelf built.
cards.type: Clinical practice standard (ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — 2025, Section 16: Diabetes Care in the Hospital), Diabetes Care 2025
cards.people: Hospitalized patients with diabetes, principally noncritically ill medical and surgical inpatients — the RABBIT populations of Cards 1–3; critically ill patients are addressed under separate recommendations in the same section.
cards.result: Section 16 of the ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025 states the Association's hospital recommendations: insulin is the preferred treatment for inpatient hyperglycemia; for noncritically ill patients, scheduled basal insulin or a basal-plus-correction regimen is recommended over sliding-scale (correction-only) insulin, which the Standards advise against using alone; and a target glucose range of 140–180 mg/dL is recommended for most critically ill and noncritically ill patients, with more stringent targets reserved for selected patients who can achieve them without significant hypoglycemia. Recommendation grades follow the ADA evidence system; the scheduled-insulin recommendation carries Grade A (clear evidence from well-conducted randomized trials — the RABBIT programme carded above).
cards.watchOut: A standards card, labeled as such: it summarizes and grades the trial evidence rather than adding to it, and it is revised annually — quote it with its year (2025). Note the target discipline: the ADA range (140–180) is deliberately less tight than the <140 target the 2007 RABBIT trial chased, because later ICU-era evidence priced hypoglycemia honestly. 'Strongly discouraged' applies to sliding scale as the SOLE regimen; correction doses remain a component of basal-plus care (Reference 3).

shelves.title: What happens when GLP-1 therapy stops: about two-thirds of the weight returns within a year — and no randomized tapering strategy exists
shelves.question: When semaglutide or tirzepatide treatment stops, how much of the lost weight comes back — and is there a proven way to taper off?
shelves.mesh: Semaglutide · Tirzepatide · Weight Gain · Weight Loss · Obesity · Withholding Treatment · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: Three withdrawal datasets, one direction. In the STEP 1 extension, stopping semaglutide (and the lifestyle programme with it) returned 11.6 of the 17.3 percentage points lost — about two-thirds — within one year, and the cardiometabolic improvements reverted toward baseline with it. STEP 4 randomized the question directly: switch to placebo and weight rose 6.9% over 48 weeks while continuers lost a further 7.9% — a 14.8-point gap. SURMOUNT-4 shows the same physics for tirzepatide (labeled as such — a different molecule, carded as the class's withdrawal evidence): switchers regained 14.0% while continuers lost 5.5% more, and only 16.6% of switchers kept at least 80% of their loss versus 89.5% of continuers. Printed plainly, as the shelf requires: NO randomized trial of a tapering strategy exists — no dose-reduction schedule, no drug-holiday design, nothing. Everything known says these are chronic treatments for a chronic condition; the regain figures are the reason 'stop when you reach goal' is not an evidence-based plan. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: STEP 1 extension (Wilding 2022): one year off semaglutide, 11.6 of the 17.3 points lost came back — about two-thirds regained
cards.summary: STEP 1 randomized 1,961 adults with obesity (or overweight with comorbidity), without diabetes, to 68 weeks of semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo; in the off-treatment extension subset (n=327), the semaglutide group had lost 17.3% by week 68 and regained 11.6 percentage points by week 120 — net loss 5.6% — while placebo went from −2.0% to a net −0.1%. Cardiometabolic improvements reverted toward baseline alongside the weight.
cards.type: Off-treatment extension of a randomized, double-blind trial (STEP 1 extension), Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism 2022 — analyses exploratory by design
cards.people: Extension subset of 327 participants who had completed 68 weeks of treatment — all eligible participants from sites in Canada, Germany, and the UK, plus the highest-recruiting US and Japanese sites — drawn from STEP 1's 1,961 randomized adults with BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with a weight-related comorbidity), without diabetes.
cards.result: From week 0 to week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% (SD 9.3%) with semaglutide and 2.0% (SD 6.1%) with placebo. Following treatment withdrawal — of both the drug and the lifestyle intervention — semaglutide and placebo participants regained 11.6 (SD 7.7) and 1.9 (SD 4.8) percentage points of lost weight respectively by week 120, resulting in net losses of 5.6% (SD 8.9%) and 0.1% (SD 5.8%) from week 0. Cardiometabolic improvements seen with semaglutide reverted towards baseline at week 120 for most variables. The authors' conclusion: findings confirm the chronicity of obesity and suggest ongoing treatment is required to maintain improvements.
cards.watchOut: Two reading disciplines: the extension analyses are exploratory (no hypothesis testing framework — treat the two-thirds figure as a well-measured estimate, not a tested endpoint), and the withdrawal removed lifestyle support at the same time as the drug, so the regain is the effect of stopping the whole treatment package. Neither caveat rescues a 'course of treatment' model of these drugs — STEP 4, next card, isolates the drug withdrawal itself under continued lifestyle intervention.
cards.source: Wilding JPH et al. Weight regain and cardiometabolic effects after withdrawal of semaglutide: The STEP 1 trial extension. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2022;24:1553–1564. PMID 35441470 · NCT03548935. DOI 10.1111/dom.14725

cards.headline: STEP 4 (Rubino 2021): the randomized withdrawal — switch to placebo and weight rose 6.9%; continue and it fell 7.9% more (difference −14.8 points)
cards.summary: After a 20-week semaglutide run-in (mean loss 10.6%), 803 adults were randomized 2:1 to continue semaglutide 2.4 mg or switch to placebo for 48 weeks, lifestyle intervention in both: weight change week 20→68 was −7.9% continued vs +6.9% switched (difference −14.8 points [−16.0 to −13.5]; P<0.001). Waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, and physical functioning all favored continuation. Registry verified against the record.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial (STEP 4), JAMA 2021
cards.people: 803 participants who completed the 20-week run-in and reached the 2.4 mg maintenance dose (of 902 who started run-in), randomized to continued semaglutide (n=535) or switch to placebo (n=268); mean age 46 years; 634 (79%) women; mean body weight 107.2 kg; adults with BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with a comorbidity), without diabetes, at 73 sites in 10 countries.
cards.result: With continued semaglutide, mean body weight change from week 20 to week 68 was −7.9% vs +6.9% with switch to placebo (difference −14.8 percentage points [−16.0 to −13.5]; P<0.001). Waist circumference (−9.7 cm [−10.9 to −8.5 cm]), systolic blood pressure (−3.9 mm Hg [−5.8 to −2.0]), and SF-36 physical functioning score (2.5 [1.6–3.3]) also improved with continued treatment. 98.0% completed the trial and 92.3% completed treatment.
cards.watchOut: The cleanest design on this shelf: everyone had the drug, lifestyle support continued in both arms, and only the molecule was withdrawn — so the +6.9% is the drug's absence, not the programme's. The run-in design also means the randomized population is selected for tolerating and responding to semaglutide; regain in unselected stop-everyone practice could differ in either direction. No tapering arm existed here or anywhere — see the shelf balance.
cards.source: Rubino D et al. Effect of Continued Weekly Subcutaneous Semaglutide vs Placebo on Weight Loss Maintenance in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: The STEP 4 Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: SURMOUNT-4 (Aronne 2024): tirzepatide withdrawal — switchers regained 14.0% in a year; only 16.6% kept ≥80% of their loss vs 89.5% continuing (tirzepatide — labeled as the class's withdrawal evidence)
cards.summary: After a 36-week open-label tirzepatide lead-in (mean loss 20.9%), 670 adults were randomized to continue tirzepatide or switch to placebo for 52 weeks: weight change week 36→88 was −5.5% continued vs +14.0% switched (difference −19.4 points; P<0.001). Maintaining at least 80% of the lead-in loss at week 88: 89.5% continuing vs 16.6% switched . Overall week 0→88: −25.3% vs −9.9%. Most common adverse events were mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal, more common on tirzepatide. This is TIRZEPATIDE, not semaglutide — carded here as withdrawal evidence for the incretin class, and labeled wherever it appears.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial with open-label lead-in (SURMOUNT-4), JAMA 2024 — tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, not semaglutide
cards.people: 670 participants randomized after the lead-in (335 per group) at 70 sites in 4 countries; mean age 48 years; 473 (71%) women; mean weight 107.3 kg; adults with BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with a weight-related complication), excluding diabetes. 783 entered the lead-in and received maximum tolerated tirzepatide (10 or 15 mg weekly) for 36 weeks.
cards.result: Participants completing the 36-week lead-in had a mean weight reduction of 20.9%. From week 36 to week 88, mean percent weight change was −5.5% with continued tirzepatide vs +14.0% with placebo (difference −19.4 points [−21.2 to −17.7]; P<0.001). At week 88, 300 participants (89.5%) on tirzepatide had maintained at least 80% of their lead-in weight loss, vs 16.6% on placebo (P<0.001). The overall mean weight reduction from week 0 to 88 was 25.3% (continued) vs 9.9% (switched). Registry verified against the record's own databank entry.
cards.watchOut: Molecule discipline, printed as the brief requires: SURMOUNT-4 is tirzepatide. It is on this shelf because the withdrawal question — does the weight return when incretin therapy stops? — has the same answer in both molecules' trials, and excluding the largest withdrawal dataset on a molecule technicality would hide that. It must never be quoted as a semaglutide result. Cross-molecule comparisons of regain speed (14.0% in 52 weeks here vs STEP 4's +6.9% in 48) are confounded by different lead-in losses (20.9% vs 10.6%) and are not a like-for-like race.

shelves.title: Intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes (Look AHEAD): the cardiovascular result was NULL — stopped for futility
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does intensive lifestyle intervention for weight loss prevent cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Life Style · Weight Loss · Cardiovascular Diseases · Exercise · Diet, Reducing
shelves.balance: One trial answers this shelf, and its answer is stated in its title line: Look AHEAD — 5,145 patients, nearly a decade — produced real weight loss and no reduction in cardiovascular events (HR 0.95), stopped for futility . What lifestyle intervention did do sits on Card 2 under its correct label: remission, a secondary and exploratory outcome, 11.5% vs 2.0% at year 1 and mostly partial — in this library's framing, lifestyle can DELAY and partially reverse the formal diagnosis; it did not prevent events. The post-hoc finding that participants who lost ≥10% of body weight fared better (Reference 3) is fenced as hypothesis-grade: it describes who did well, not what the intervention was proven to cause. Two of this shelf's cards are re-cards of trials whose home is Shelf #210; they are counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Look AHEAD (2013): the primary cardiovascular result was NULL — HR 0.95, stopped for futility [re-card — home Shelf #210]
cards.summary: 5,145 adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, intensive lifestyle intervention vs diabetes support and education, median follow-up 9.6 years: primary composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, hospitalization for angina) 403 vs 418 events — 1.83 vs 1.92 per 100 person-years; HR 0.95 [0.83–1.09], P=0.51 . The trial was stopped early on a futility analysis . Weight loss was real (8.6% vs 0.7% at year 1; 6.0% vs 3.5% at study end) — it simply did not convert into fewer cardiovascular events. Re-card: this trial's home is Shelf #210; it is counted once, there.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (Look AHEAD), N Engl J Med 2013 — stopped early for futility. Re-card; home Shelf #210.
cards.people: 5,145 adults aged 45–76 years with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, at 16 US centers. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 403 patients in the intervention group and 418 in the control group (1.83 and 1.92 events per 100 person-years; HR 0.95 [0.83–1.09]; P=0.51). The intervention produced greater weight loss throughout (8.6% vs 0.7% at 1 year; 6.0% vs 3.5% at study end), greater reductions in glycated hemoglobin, and greater initial improvements in fitness and all cardiovascular risk factors except LDL cholesterol. The trial was stopped early on the basis of a futility analysis at median follow-up 9.6 years.
cards.watchOut: The null is the finding, and it is stated first on this shelf by design: the largest, longest lifestyle trial in type 2 diabetes improved weight, fitness, and risk factors and did not reduce cardiovascular events. Do not let the post-hoc weight-loss analysis (Reference 3) re-write this randomized result — the randomized comparison is the one that was tested.

cards.headline: Gregg 2012: diabetes remission was a SECONDARY, exploratory outcome — 11.5% vs 2.0% at year 1, mostly partial [re-card — home Shelf #210]
cards.summary: In an ancillary analysis of 4,503 Look AHEAD participants, any remission (partial or complete — transition to prediabetes or normoglycemia off glucose-lowering medication) occurred in 11.5% vs 2.0% at year 1 and 7.3% vs 2.0% at year 4. Complete remission was rare; the authors call the absolute rates modest. This was a secondary/exploratory analysis, not the trial's primary outcome — and it sits on a shelf whose primary outcome was null. Re-card: home Shelf #210, counted once there.
cards.type: Ancillary observational analysis of a randomized trial (Look AHEAD), JAMA 2012 — exploratory by the authors' own description. Re-card; home Shelf #210.
cards.people: 4,503 US adults with BMI ≥25 and type 2 diabetes (the Look AHEAD randomized cohort with remission data). The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Intensive lifestyle participants lost more weight at year 1 (net difference −7.9%) and year 4 (−3.9%) and were more likely to experience any remission: prevalences 11.5% [10.1–12.8%] during year 1 and 7.3% [6.2–8.4%] at year 4, vs 2.0% for the control group at both time points (P<0.001 for each). Continuous sustained remission for at least 2, 3, and 4 years occurred in 9.2%, 6.4%, and 3.5% of the intervention group vs under 2% of controls. The authors' conclusion: the intervention was associated with a greater likelihood of partial remission, but absolute remission rates were modest.
cards.watchOut: Remission here is mostly partial remission — to prediabetes, not normoglycemia — and it decays: 11.5% at year 1 becomes 7.3% at year 4. It is a real secondary benefit of the intervention, carded under the developer's framing for this library: lifestyle DELAYS and can partially reverse the formal diagnosis; it did not prevent cardiovascular events (Reference 1).
cards.source: Gregg EW et al. Association of an intensive lifestyle intervention with remission of type 2 diabetes. JAMA. 2012;308:2489–2496. PMID 23288372 · NCT00017953 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1001/jama.2012.67929

cards.headline: The ≥10%-weight-loss analysis (Gregg 2016): HR 0.79 — POST HOC and hypothesis-grade only, fenced as such
cards.summary: In a post-hoc, observational re-analysis of Look AHEAD, participants who lost at least 10% of body weight in year 1 had a lower rate of the primary cardiovascular outcome than those with stable weight or gain (adjusted HR 0.79 [0.64–0.98] , P=0.034 — a relative figure; the analysis does not state arm-level absolute rates for this cut). This is not a randomized comparison : people who lose 10% differ from people who don't in ways adjustment cannot fully remove. It generates a hypothesis; it does not rescue the trial's null primary result (Reference 1).
cards.type: Post-hoc observational analysis of a randomized trial, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2016 — hypothesis-grade only.
cards.people: 4,834 Look AHEAD participants in the weight-change analysis (4,406 in the fitness-change analysis), drawn from the 5,145 randomized adults aged 45–76 with type 2 diabetes. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Over a median 10.2 years, individuals who lost at least 10% of body weight in the first year had a 21% lower relative risk of the primary outcome (adjusted HR 0.79 [0.64–0.98]; P=0.034) and a 24% lower relative risk of the secondary outcome (adjusted HR 0.76 [0.63–0.91]) compared with individuals with stable weight or weight gain. An increase of at least 2 METs in fitness was associated with the secondary outcome (HR 0.77) but not the primary (HR 0.78 [0.60–1.03]).
cards.watchOut: Post hoc means the comparison groups were created by what happened after randomization, not by the coin flip — the exact selection problem randomization exists to prevent. The shelf states this card behind a fence: it may justify trials of more potent weight-loss strategies; it may never be quoted as 'Look AHEAD showed weight loss prevents events.' The randomized answer is Card 1: it did not.
cards.source: Gregg EW et al.; Look AHEAD Research Group. Association of the magnitude of weight loss and changes in physical fitness with long-term cardiovascular disease outcomes in overweight or obese people with type 2 diabetes: a post-hoc analysis of the Look AHEAD randomised clinical trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2016;4:913–921. PMID 27595918 · NCT00017953 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S2213-8587(16)30162-0

shelves.title: Treatment protocols for diabetic macular edema: the drug matters only when vision is already poor — and sometimes the right protocol is to wait
shelves.question: In center-involved diabetic macular edema, which anti-VEGF drug, when should laser join, and when is observation the treatment?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Retinopathy · Macular Edema · Angiogenesis Inhibitors · Ranibizumab · Bevacizumab · Laser Coagulation · Watchful Waiting · Visual Acuity · Humans
shelves.balance: Four protocols, four different answers, all carded at full weight. Drug choice (Protocol T, Cards 1–2 — this shelf is Protocol T's home; Shelf #372 cross-links here): all three anti-VEGF drugs work, aflibercept's advantage is real only in eyes starting 20/50 or worse, and by 2 years it had narrowed to the bevacizumab comparison alone. Laser timing (Protocol I, Card 3): deferring laser at least 24 weeks behind ranibizumab cost no vision versus prompt laser. Threshold to treat (Protocol V, Card 4): at 20/25 or better, monitored observation with rescue treatment matched immediate injections. And the burden is carded as a cost on Card 2, not footnoted: some fifteen injections over two years in Protocol T — the visit-and-needle load is part of every protocol's real effect size. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Protocol T, year 1 (Wells 2015): all three drugs improved vision; aflibercept's edge existed ONLY in eyes starting 20/50 or worse (+18.9 vs +11.8 vs +14.2 letters)
cards.summary: 660 adults with center-involved DME (mean age 61): mean 1-year vision gain +13.3 letters aflibercept, +9.7 bevacizumab, +11.2 ranibizumab . The headline splits on baseline vision, exactly as prespecified analysis showed: in eyes starting 20/32–20/40, gains were 8.0 vs 7.5 vs 8.3 — no differences ; in eyes starting 20/50 or worse, 18.9 vs 11.8 vs 14.2 (aflibercept vs bevacizumab P<0.001; vs ranibizumab P=0.003). Serious adverse events, hospitalization, death , and major cardiovascular events did not differ among groups. This card is Protocol T's home; Shelf #372 cross-links here.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (DRCR Retina Network Protocol T), N Engl J Med 2015 — 89 sites, protocol-specified retreatment algorithm. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01627249.
cards.people: 660 adults (mean age 61±10 years) with diabetic macular edema involving the macular center: 224 aflibercept 2.0 mg, 218 bevacizumab 1.25 mg, 218 ranibizumab 0.3 mg, injected as often as every 4 weeks per protocol. The record does not state a sex split.
cards.result: From baseline to 1 year, the mean visual-acuity letter score improved by 13.3 with aflibercept, 9.7 with bevacizumab, and 11.2 with ranibizumab. Although the improvement was greater with aflibercept overall (P<0.001 vs bevacizumab; P=0.03 vs ranibizumab), the difference was driven by eyes with worse visual acuity at baseline (P<0.001 for interaction). When the initial letter score was 78–69 (≈20/32 to 20/40; 51% of participants), mean improvement was 8.0, 7.5, and 8.3 respectively (P>0.50 for each pairwise comparison). When the initial score was below 69 (≈20/50 or worse), mean improvement was 18.9, 11.8, and 14.2 (P<0.001 aflibercept vs bevacizumab; P=0.003 vs ranibizumab; P=0.21 ranibizumab vs bevacizumab). There were no significant differences in serious adverse events (P=0.40), hospitalization (P=0.51), death (P=0.72), or major cardiovascular events (P=0.56).
cards.watchOut: Protocol T is the most misquoted trial in retina care: 'aflibercept wins' is true only inside the worse-vision half of the trial, and the authors said the overall difference was not clinically meaningful for that reason. For an eye starting 20/40 or better, Protocol T gives no efficacy reason to prefer the most expensive drug — a point with large cost consequences, since bevacizumab costs a small fraction of the other two.
cards.source: Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network; Wells JA et al. Aflibercept, bevacizumab, or ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema. N Engl J Med. 2015;372:1193–1203. PMID 25692915 · NCT01627249 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1414264

cards.headline: Protocol T, year 2 (Wells 2016): the aflibercept edge narrowed — gone vs ranibizumab, kept vs bevacizumab; the bill was 15–16 injections over 2 years
cards.summary: At 2 years, mean gains were 12.8 (aflibercept), 10.0 (bevacizumab), 12.3 (ranibizumab) letters. In worse-vision eyes: 18.1 vs 13.3 vs 16.1 — aflibercept still ahead of bevacizumab (P=0.02) but no longer ahead of ranibizumab (P=0.18) ; in better-vision eyes, no differences. The burden, carded as a cost and not a footnote: a median of 15, 16, and 15 injections over 2 years , plus laser in 41%, 64%, and 52%. Vascular (APTC) events ran 5% vs 8% vs 12% (global P=0.047; P=0.09 after adjustment for potential confounders) — printed as the authors left it: warranting continued evaluation, not a verdict.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial, 2-year results (DRCR Protocol T), Ophthalmology 2016. The record carries no registry databank entry; the trial's registration (NCT01627249) is stated on the 1-year record, Card 1.
cards.people: 660 participants with visual-acuity impairment from center-involved DME, on the Protocol T regimen: injections up to monthly in year 1, visits extended to every 4 months in year 2 when stable, focal/grid laser added after 6 months if DME persisted. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Median numbers of injections were 5, 6, and 6 in year 2 and 15, 16, and 15 over 2 years in the aflibercept, bevacizumab, and ranibizumab groups (global P=0.08). Laser photocoagulation was administered in 41%, 64%, and 52% respectively. At 2 years, mean visual acuity improved by 12.8, 10.0, and 12.3 letters. With worse baseline acuity (20/50 to 20/320), mean improvement was 18.1, 13.3, and 16.1 letters (aflibercept vs bevacizumab P=0.02; aflibercept vs ranibizumab P=0.18). With better baseline acuity (20/32 to 20/40), improvement was 7.8, 6.8, and 8.6 letters (P>0.10 for pairwise comparisons). Anti-Platelet Trialists' Collaboration events occurred in 5%, 8%, and 12% (global P=0.047; global P=0.09 adjusted for potential confounders).
cards.watchOut: Two honest corrections live on this card. The efficacy correction: the 1-year 'aflibercept advantage' was partly a head start — by year 2 ranibizumab had caught up, and only the bevacizumab gap persisted. The burden correction: 'a course of injections' means roughly fifteen needle-through-the-eye procedures and years of monthly visits per patient — the real-world adherence cliff every DME protocol quietly assumes away.
cards.source: Wells JA et al. Aflibercept, bevacizumab, or ranibizumab for diabetic macular edema: two-year results from a comparative effectiveness randomized clinical trial. Ophthalmology. 2016;123:1351–1359. PMID 26935357. DOI 10.1016/j.ophtha.2016.02.022

cards.headline: Protocol I (Elman 2010): ranibizumab with DEFERRED laser matched prompt laser (+9 vs +9 letters) — the laser can wait; triamcinolone's gain came with pressure and cataract
cards.summary: 854 eyes of 691 participants with center-involved DME (vision 20/32–20/320): 1-year mean vision change was +9 letters with ranibizumab + prompt laser, +9 with ranibizumab + deferred (≥24 weeks) laser, +4 with triamcinolone + prompt laser, +3 with sham + prompt laser — both ranibizumab arms beat laser alone (P<0.001); triamcinolone did not (P=0.31). Deferring laser cost nothing in vision. The steroid's price: elevated intraocular pressure and cataract surgery were more frequent with triamcinolone; injection-related endophthalmitis occurred in 3 eyes (0.8%) across the ranibizumab groups. Two-year outcomes mirrored year 1.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (DRCR Retina Network Protocol I), Ophthalmology 2010 — multicenter. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 854 study eyes of 691 participants with visual acuity (approximate Snellen equivalent) 20/32 to 20/320 and DME involving the fovea: sham injection + prompt laser (n=293 eyes), ranibizumab + prompt laser (187), ranibizumab + deferred laser (188), triamcinolone + prompt laser (186). The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: The 1-year mean change in visual-acuity letter score was significantly greater in the ranibizumab + prompt laser group (+9±11; P<0.001) and the ranibizumab + deferred laser group (+9±12; P<0.001), but not in the triamcinolone + prompt laser group (+4±13; P=0.31), compared with the sham + prompt laser group (+3±13). Reduction in central subfield thickness with triamcinolone was similar to the ranibizumab groups, despite the weaker vision result (except in pseudophakic eyes, where triamcinolone's vision improvement appeared comparable). Three eyes (0.8%) had injection-related endophthalmitis in the ranibizumab groups, whereas elevated intraocular pressure and cataract surgery were more frequent in the triamcinolone + prompt laser group. Two-year visual-acuity outcomes were similar to 1-year outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Protocol I is the deferred-laser evidence for DME — the comparison the protocol letters sometimes mislabel elsewhere: adding laser immediately bought nothing over adding it only if still needed after 24 weeks of ranibizumab. Its second lesson is anatomical humility: triamcinolone thinned the retina as well as ranibizumab did and improved vision barely more than laser alone — thickness is not sight.
cards.source: Elman MJ et al.; Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network. Randomized trial evaluating ranibizumab plus prompt or deferred laser or triamcinolone plus prompt laser for diabetic macular edema. Ophthalmology. 2010;117:1064–1077.e35. PMID 20427088. DOI 10.1016/j.ophtha.2010.02.031

cards.headline: Protocol V (Baker 2019): at 20/25 or better, OBSERVATION matched immediate aflibercept — vision loss at 2 years 19% vs 16%, no significant difference
cards.summary: 702 adults with center-involved DME and good vision (20/25 or better): eyes losing ≥5 letters at 2 years were 19% (observation), 17% (laser), 16% (aflibercept) — aflibercept vs observation risk difference −3% [−11 to 4], relative risk 0.83 [0.55–1.27], P=0.79 . The observation strategy was not 'no treatment': aflibercept was started in 34% of observed eyes (25% of laser eyes) when vision worsened by protocol thresholds. Vascular (APTC) events: 3% observation, 5% laser, 7% aflibercept. The trial's conclusion is a protocol, not a shrug: watch closely, treat on worsening.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (DRCR Retina Network Protocol V), JAMA 2019 — 91 US and Canadian sites. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01909791.
cards.people: 702 adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes (mean age 59 years; 38% women [n=264]), each with one study eye with center-involved DME and visual acuity 20/25 or better: 226 aflibercept, 240 laser photocoagulation, 236 observation. 625 of 681 participants (92%, excluding deaths) completed the 2-year visit.
cards.result: At 2 years, the percentage of eyes with at least a 5-letter visual-acuity decrease was 16% (33/205) with aflibercept, 17% (36/212) with laser, and 19% (39/208) with observation (aflibercept vs observation risk difference −3% [−11 to 4]; relative risk 0.83 [0.55–1.27; P=0.79]). For eyes whose visual acuity decreased, aflibercept was initiated in 25% (60/240) of the laser group and 34% (80/236) of the observation group. Antiplatelet Trialists' Collaboration vascular events occurred in 15 (7%), 13 (5%), and 8 (3%) participants in the aflibercept, laser, and observation groups respectively.
cards.watchOut: Protocol V only works as a package: observation with scheduled monitoring and prespecified rescue triggers matched immediate treatment — it licenses watchful waiting inside a system that actually watches, not discharge-and-forget. Its boundary is equally plain: every eye here saw 20/25 or better at entry; nothing on this card speaks to eyes already impaired, which are Protocol T's territory (References 1–2).
cards.source: Baker CW et al.; DRCR Retina Network. shelves.title: Autonomous AI for diabetic eye screening: two pivotal trials prove the grading — outcomes untested
shelves.question: Can an autonomous AI system, with no specialist reading the images, detect diabetic retinopathy accurately enough for primary-care screening?
shelves.mesh: Artificial Intelligence · Diabetic Retinopathy · Humans · Prospective Studies · Reference Standards · Sensitivity and Specificity · Vision Screening
shelves.balance: The diagnostic question is about as well answered as diagnostic questions get: two independent preregistered pivotal trials, against reading-center reference standards, put autonomous AI sensitivity for referable diabetic retinopathy at 87.2% (IDx-DR) and 95.5% (EyeArt), with specificities of 90.7% and 85.0%. The grade stops at POSSIBLE because of what the design cannot show: no trial here randomized a screening strategy or counted referrals completed, treatment delivered, or vision saved. Accuracy is proven; benefit is inferred. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: IDx-DR pivotal trial (Abràmoff 2018, NPJ Digital Medicine): the first FDA-authorized autonomous diagnostic AI — sensitivity 87.2%, specificity 90.7% against a reading-center reference
cards.summary: 900 adults with diabetes and no prior diabetic retinopathy diagnosis, enrolled at primary care clinics; the autonomous system (IDx-DR) graded fundus photographs on site, compared with Wisconsin Fundus Photograph Reading Center grading of widefield stereoscopic photographs plus macular OCT. For more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy: sensitivity 87.2% [81.8–91.2] , specificity 90.7% [88.3–92.7] — both above the prespecified superiority endpoints — with an imageability rate of 96.1% . 198 participants (23.8% of those analyzed) had more-than-mild disease.
cards.type: Prospective, preregistered pivotal diagnostic accuracy trial, NPJ Digital Medicine 2018. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT02963441. The record carries no MeSH headings; none are printed for this card.
cards.people: 900 subjects with diabetes and no history of diabetic retinopathy, enrolled at primary care clinics. Median age 59 years (range 22–84); 47.5% male; 28.6% African American; 16.1% Hispanic.
cards.result: The AI system exceeded all prespecified superiority endpoints: sensitivity 87.2% (95% CI, 81.8–91.2%) against a superiority goal of >85%, specificity 90.7% (95% CI, 88.3–92.7%) against >82.5%, and imageability rate 96.1% (95% CI, 94.6–97.3%). On the basis of these results the FDA authorized the system — the first autonomous AI diagnostic authorized in any field of medicine — for use by health care providers to detect more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy against a reading center is not the same as sight saved: this design proves the machine grades photographs about as well as the reference standard, in patients already sitting in a clinic with a camera. It does not test whether autonomous screening gets more patients screened, referred, treated, or keeps more of them seeing — those are outcome questions no card on this shelf answers. Sensitivity of 87% also means roughly 1 in 8 cases of more-than-mild disease is missed at the visit.
cards.source: Abràmoff MD et al. Pivotal trial of an autonomous AI-based diagnostic system for detection of diabetic retinopathy in primary care offices. NPJ Digit Med. 2018;1:39. PMID 31304320 · NCT02963441. DOI 10.1038/s41746-018-0040-6

cards.headline: EyeArt pivotal evaluation (Ipp 2021, JAMA Network Open): a second autonomous system — sensitivity 95.5% for more-than-mild disease, 95.1% for vision-threatening disease, without dilation
cards.summary: 893 patients (1,786 eyes) at 15 primary care and eye care facilities; the EyeArt system read 2-field undilated fundus photographs against a reading-center ETDRS reference standard from 4 wide-field dilated images. More-than-mild diabetic retinopathy: sensitivity 95.5% [92.4–98.5] , specificity 85.0% [82.6–87.4] . Vision-threatening disease: sensitivity 95.1% [90.1–100] , specificity 89.0% [87.0–91.1] . Imageability was 87.4% undilated, rising to 97.4% when ungradable eyes were dilated per protocol.
cards.type: Prospective multicenter cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study, preregistered, JAMA Network Open 2021. The registry ID is printed in the record’s own abstract: NCT03112005.
cards.people: 942 individuals aged 18 years or older with diabetes consented at 15 US primary care and eye care facilities; 893 patients (1,786 eyes) met inclusion criteria and completed the protocol. 449 men (50.3%); mean age 53.9 years (SD 15.2); 655 White (73.3%); 206 (23.1%) had type 1 diabetes.
cards.result: Sensitivity and specificity of the AI system were high in detecting more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy (sensitivity 95.5%; 95% CI, 92.4%–98.5%; specificity 85.0%; 95% CI, 82.6%–87.4%) and vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy (sensitivity 95.1%; 95% CI, 90.1%–100%; specificity 89.0%; 95% CI, 87.0%–91.1%) without dilation. Imageability without dilation was 87.4% (95% CI, 85.2%–89.6%), improving to 97.4% (95% CI, 96.4%–98.5%) when ungradable eyes were dilated. After correction for the study’s enrichment with disease-positive patients, specificity estimates rose modestly (to 87.8% for more-than-mild disease) with sensitivity essentially unchanged.
cards.watchOut: The trade against Card 1 is visible in the numbers: EyeArt catches more disease (higher sensitivity) and flags more healthy eyes (lower specificity) — at population scale, each specificity point is thousands of extra referrals. The study population was also enriched for disease, and the authors’ enrichment correction is a modeling step; accuracy in an ordinary low-prevalence screening population will look different, mainly in how many positives are false.

cards.headline: Reading the two pivotal trials together: the grading question is answered — the screening-outcome question has not been asked in a trial
cards.summary: Two independent, preregistered, prospective pivotal studies, two different systems, the same reference-standard design — and convergent answers: an autonomous system can grade retinal photographs for referable diabetic retinopathy with sensitivity of 87–96% and specificity of 85–91% , at the point of care, with no specialist in the loop. Neither study randomized anyone, and neither measured what screening programs exist to change: completed referrals, treatment received, or vision preserved.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states the fence around their shared design.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: adults with diabetes attending primary care or eye care facilities in the United States, without known diabetic retinopathy (Reference 1) or presenting for screening (Reference 2).
cards.result: Both trials compared an autonomous AI system’s same-visit output against reading-center grading of reference-standard imaging, and both systems cleared their prespecified accuracy endpoints. The evidence therefore supports a claim about diagnostic accuracy. Claims about downstream benefit — more disease treated, less blindness — require a randomized comparison of screening strategies with those outcomes, which neither trial performed.
cards.watchOut: Do not let an accuracy shelf quietly become a benefit shelf: the history of screening is full of accurate tests whose programs did not improve outcomes, because the losses happen after the test — in referral, attendance, and treatment. This shelf grades the accuracy claim, and says so.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 31304320; PMID 34779843).

shelves.title: Hepatitis B vaccination in diabetes: the standard vaccine leaves a third unprotected — the 2-dose CpG vaccine leaves a tenth
shelves.question: In adults with diabetes, does the 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine protect more of them than the standard 3-dose vaccine?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Hepatitis B · Hepatitis B Antibodies · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens · Hepatitis B Vaccines · Humans · Immunogenicity, Vaccine · Toll-Like Receptor 9
shelves.balance: Diabetes blunts hepatitis B vaccine response so reliably that the pivotal phase 3 trial made diabetic seroprotection its primary endpoint — and the standard 3-dose alum vaccine protected only 65.1% of its diabetic participants (58.5% at ages 60–70). The 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted vaccine protected 90.0% (85.8% in the older subgroup), with one fewer visit. POSSIBLE, fenced to the endpoint: every figure here is an antibody level at week 28, and no trial has counted hepatitis B infections prevented in people with diabetes. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: HBV-23 phase 3 (Jackson 2018, Vaccine): in participants with diabetes — the trial’s primary endpoint population — seroprotection 90.0% vs 65.1%
cards.summary: 8,374 adults randomised (observer-blinded, active-controlled) to 2-dose HBsAg/CpG 1018 (Heplisav-B) at weeks 0 and 4 or 3-dose HBsAg/alum (Engerix-B) over 24 weeks. The trial’s primary immunogenicity endpoint was seroprotection in participants with type 2 diabetes (per-protocol n=961): at week 28, 90.0% on the CpG vaccine vs 65.1% on the alum vaccine — a difference of 24.9 percentage points [19.3–30.7] , meeting noninferiority and superiority. In the total per-protocol population (N=6,826) and every prespecified subpopulation, seroprotection was also significantly higher with the 2-dose vaccine.
cards.type: Phase 3, observer-blinded, randomised, active-controlled trial, Vaccine 2018. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT02117934.
cards.people: 8,374 adults aged 18–70 years, including 961 per-protocol participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus — the population in whom standard hepatitis B vaccines underperform.
cards.result: In diabetes participants, the seroprotection rate in the HBsAg-1018 group at week 28 was 90.0%, compared with 65.1% in the HBsAg-Eng group, with a difference of 24.9% (95% CI: 19.3%, 30.7%), which met the prospectively-defined criteria for noninferiority and statistical significance. In the total study per-protocol population and each pre-specified subpopulation, the seroprotection rate in the HBsAg-1018 group was statistically significantly higher than in the HBsAg-Eng group.
cards.watchOut: Seroprotection is an antibody threshold (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL), not a count of infections prevented — no hepatitis B outcomes trial exists in diabetes, and this shelf does not invent one. What the trial establishes is narrower and still clinically pointed: the standard vaccine leaves about a third of diabetic recipients below the protective threshold, and the CpG-adjuvanted vaccine leaves about a tenth. Per-protocol (not intention-to-treat) analysis is the other fence.

cards.headline: The older-diabetic subgroup (Hyer 2019, Vaccine): at ages 60–70 with diabetes, seroprotection 85.8% vs 58.5% — a post hoc analysis
cards.summary: A post hoc analysis of the same phase 3 programme, restricted to participants with type 2 diabetes aged 60–70 — the group in whom age and diabetes compound. At week 28, seroprotection was 85.8% (235/274) with the 2-dose CpG vaccine vs 58.5% (76/130) with the 3-dose alum vaccine — a difference of 27.3 percentage points [18.0–36.8] . The advantage held across sex, body-mass index and smoking subgroups. Adverse events and deaths were comparable between groups.
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a phase 3 randomised trial, Vaccine 2019. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT02117934 (the parent trial).
cards.people: Participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus aged 60–70 years in the HBV-23 trial: 327 assigned the 2-dose vaccine and 153 the 3-dose vaccine (per-protocol seroprotection denominators 274 and 130).
cards.result: The seroprotection rate at week 28 was significantly higher with HBsAg/CpG 1018 (85.8% [235/274]) than with HBsAg/alum (58.5% [76/130]) in the per-protocol analysis, for an overall difference of 27.3% (95% CI, 18.0–36.8). Seroprotection rates with HBsAg/CpG 1018 were consistently markedly higher compared with HBsAg/alum, regardless of sex, body mass index, or smoking status. Adverse events and deaths were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and per-protocol — the two standard discounts apply, and the card carries both labels. Its value is directional confirmation in the hardest-to-protect stratum: even the better vaccine leaves ~14% of older diabetic recipients unprotected, and the standard vaccine leaves ~42%. Both authors are employees of the vaccine’s maker (Dynavax), as the record’s affiliations show — a reason to want independent replication, printed here rather than discovered elsewhere.

cards.headline: Reading the hepatitis B evidence together: a better antibody answer to a real problem — with an antibody for an endpoint
cards.summary: The problem this shelf documents is genuine and quantified: diabetes (with age, obesity and smoking) blunts hepatitis B vaccine response so reliably that the phase 3 programme made diabetic seroprotection its primary endpoint — and the standard 3-dose vaccine protected only 65.1% of diabetic participants, 58.5% of those aged 60–70. The 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted vaccine protected 90.0% and 85.8% respectively, with one fewer dose and a 24-week head start. The fence is the endpoint: every number on this shelf is an antibody concentration at week 28. Hepatitis B infections, cirrhosis and liver cancers prevented in diabetic populations are the outcomes that matter, and no carded trial measures them — the shelf grades an immunogenicity claim, argued as strongly as immunogenicity can be.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 (one trial programme) together and states the endpoint fence.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: 8,374 randomised adults aged 18–70, with the diabetic per-protocol population (n=961) and its 60–70-year subgroup as the shelf’s focus.
cards.result: The evidence establishes that the 2-dose CpG-adjuvanted vaccine produces seroprotective antibody levels in substantially more diabetic recipients than the standard 3-dose alum vaccine, including at ages 60–70. It does not establish fewer hepatitis B infections or their complications in people with diabetes.
cards.watchOut: Cite this shelf for vaccine choice in a diabetic patient (an immunogenicity comparison), not for the size of the clinical problem vaccination solves — the infection-risk side of the ledger lives in epidemiology this shelf does not card.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 29289383; PMID 31431412).

shelves.title: Aerobic vs resistance vs combined training for A1c — DARE trial
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, how do aerobic training, resistance training and combined training compare for lowering hemoglobin A1c?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose · Blood Pressure · Body Composition · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Exercise Therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Lipids · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials point the same way — combined aerobic plus resistance training lowers hemoglobin A1c more than either mode alone. In DARE, combined training gave an additional -0.46 percentage point versus aerobic alone and -0.59 percentage point versus resistance alone; in HART-D only the combination group improved hemoglobin A1c versus control (-0.34%). A 47-trial meta-analysis found structured exercise overall lowered hemoglobin A1c by -0.67%, with larger falls above 150 minutes per week. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: DARE: combined aerobic and resistance training beat either mode alone for A1c
cards.summary: DARE (251 patients, 22 weeks): combined aerobic-plus-resistance training lowered HbA1c by an additional −0.46 percentage points versus aerobic alone [−0.83 to −0.09] and −0.59 versus resistance alone [−0.95 to −0.23] — the combination beat either mode by itself.
cards.people: 251 adults aged 39 to 70 years with type 2 diabetes at 8 community-based facilities; the abstract does not state sex mix or mean age.
cards.result: Exercise was performed 3 times weekly for 22 weeks. Combined exercise training resulted in an additional change in hemoglobin A1c value of -0.46 percentage point (95% CI, -0.83 to -0.09) compared with aerobic training alone and -0.59 percentage point (95% CI, -0.95 to -0.23) compared with resistance training alone. Changes in blood pressure and lipid values did not differ statistically significantly among groups, and adverse events were more common in the exercise groups. The authors conclude either aerobic or resistance training alone improves glycemic control, but improvements are greatest with combined training.
cards.watchOut: Participants were not blinded, the combined group exercised for longer in total than the single-mode groups, and generalisability to less adherent patients is uncertain. The abstract's sentence assigning the single-mode changes versus control is garbled in the record, so those two figures are not carded here — only the unambiguous combined-versus-single-mode differences are used.
cards.source: Sigal RJ et al. Effects of aerobic training, resistance training, or both on glycemic control in type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2007 Sep 18;147(6):357-69. PMID: 17876019. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00195884, as stated in the record.

cards.headline: HART-D: only combined training improved A1c versus control at 9 months
cards.summary: HART-D (262 patients, 9 months): only the combined group improved HbA1c versus control ( −0.34% [−0.64 to −0.03]); resistance alone (−0.16%) and aerobic alone (−0.24%) were not significant — the second trial pointing the same way.
cards.people: 262 sedentary men and women in Louisiana with type 2 diabetes and hemoglobin A1c 6.5% or higher; 63.0% women and 47.3% nonwhite, mean (SD) age 55.8 years (8.7 years), baseline hemoglobin A1c 7.7% (1.0%). Groups: control 41, resistance training 73, aerobic exercise 72, combined training 76.
cards.result: Compared with the control group, the absolute mean change in hemoglobin A1c in the combination training group was -0.34% (95% CI, -0.64% to -0.03%; P=.03). Mean changes were not statistically significant for resistance training alone (-0.16%; 95% CI, -0.46% to 0.15%; P=.32) or aerobic training alone (-0.24%; 95% CI, -0.55% to 0.07%; P=.14). Only the combination group improved maximum oxygen consumption versus control (mean 1.0 mL/kg per min; 95% CI, 0.5-1.5). All exercise groups reduced waist circumference by -1.9 to -2.8 cm versus control; fat mass fell by a mean of -1.4 kg in the resistance group and -1.7 kg in the combination group versus control.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre-region trial over 9 months; the single-mode A1c changes were not significant versus control in this trial, unlike in DARE, so the consistent finding is the combination advantage, not a proven effect of each mode alone.
cards.source: Church TS et al. Effects of aerobic and resistance training on hemoglobin A1c levels in patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2010 Nov 24;304(20):2253-62. PMID: 21098771. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00458133, as stated in the record's databank.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 47 trials: structured exercise lowered A1c, more so above 150 minutes a week
cards.summary: The 47-trial meta-analysis: structured exercise lowered HbA1c by −0.67% versus control [−0.84 to −0.49] — aerobic −0.73%, resistance −0.57%, combined −0.51% against control, with larger effects in programmes above 150 minutes a week.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 47 randomised controlled trials with 8,538 patients with type 2 diabetes; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Structured exercise training (23 studies) was associated with a decline in hemoglobin A1c of -0.67% (95% CI, -0.84% to -0.49%) versus control. By mode: structured aerobic exercise -0.73% (95% CI, -1.06% to -0.40%), structured resistance training -0.57% (95% CI, -1.14% to -0.01%) and both combined -0.51% (95% CI, -0.79% to -0.23%). Structured exercise of more than 150 minutes per week was associated with hemoglobin A1c reductions of 0.89%, versus 0.36% at 150 minutes or less per week. Physical activity advice alone was not associated with hemoglobin A1c changes; advice combined with dietary advice was (-0.58%; 95% CI, -0.74% to -0.43%). Heterogeneity was high (I(2) 91.3% for structured exercise overall).
cards.watchOut: Very high heterogeneity (I(2) above 90% for several pooled estimates) and the mode-specific pooled estimates do not reproduce the combined-training advantage seen in the two head-to-head trials, because they compare each mode against control across different trials.
cards.source: Umpierre D et al. Physical activity advice only or structured exercise training and association with HbA1c levels in type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2011 May 4;305(17):1790-9. PMID: 21540423. Registry ID: none in the record's databank — systematic review/meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prescribe both modes; dose above 150 minutes a week lowers A1c more
cards.summary: Two head-to-head trials and the meta-analysis converge: prescribe both modes; combined training is the best-tested prescription, and the average effect — about two-thirds of a point of HbA1c — is in the range of a glucose-lowering drug.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: two head-to-head randomised trials (251 and 262 participants) and a 47-trial meta-analysis (8,538 patients), all in type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: The two direct trials agree that combined training is best: an additional -0.46 percentage point versus aerobic alone and -0.59 percentage point versus resistance alone in DARE, and the only significant change versus control (-0.34%) in HART-D. The meta-analysis supports a real effect of structured exercise versus control (-0.67%) and a dose gradient (0.89% reduction above 150 minutes per week versus 0.36% at or below). This shelf is stamped LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: A1c is a surrogate outcome; neither head-to-head trial reports cardiovascular events or mortality, and adverse events were more common in the exercise groups in DARE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sigal RJ et al. Ann Intern Med. 2007;147(6):357-69. PMID: 17876019 (NCT00195884); Church TS et al. JAMA. 2010;304(20):2253-62. PMID: 21098771 (NCT00458133); Umpierre D et al. JAMA. 2011;305(17):1790-9. PMID: 21540423.

shelves.title: Periodontal treatment for glycemic control: meta-analyses vs the DPTT null
shelves.question: In people with type 2 diabetes and periodontitis, does nonsurgical periodontal treatment (scaling and root planing / subgingival instrumentation, with or without intensive or adjunctive therapy) lower HbA1c compared with no treatment, usual care, or supragingival cleaning alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose · Chlorhexidine · Chronic Periodontitis · Dental Scaling · Diabetes Complications · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouthwashes
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — Pooled trial evidence says periodontal treatment lowers HbA1c by a modest absolute amount (about 0.4 percentage points at 3–4 months, moderate certainty), and one intensive-treatment trial found 0.6 points at 12 months; but the largest multicentre trial, DPTT, was stopped for futility and found no effect at all. Treat periodontitis for oral health; a small glycemic benefit is plausible, not guaranteed, and no trial here was powered for diabetes complications. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: DPTT: the biggest, best-run periodontal trial in diabetes was null for HbA1c
cards.summary: DPTT (514 participants, the largest and best-run trial): at 6 months HbA1c had risen in both groups and the adjusted difference was −0.05% [−0.23 to 0.12] — null, and enrolment was stopped early for futility. The gums improved (probing depth −0.28 mm between groups); the glucose did not.
cards.people: 514 adults with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 7% to less than 9% on stable medication doses, and untreated moderate-to-advanced chronic periodontitis (257 per arm); mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At 6 months HbA1c rose 0.17% (SD 1.0) in the treatment group and 0.11% (SD 1.0) in controls — adjusted mean difference -0.05% (95% CI -0.23% to 0.12%; P = .55). Enrollment was stopped early for futility. Gum measures did improve with treatment (e.g. probing depth between-group difference 0.28 mm, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.37; P < .001), so the null was not a failure to treat the periodontitis.
cards.watchOut: Single largest trial and directly contradictory to the meta-analyses; population had HbA1c under 9% on stable doses, so results may not extend to poorly controlled diabetes or to intensive/surgical periodontal protocols.
cards.source: Engebretson SP et al. JAMA. 2013 Dec 18. PMID 24346989. Registry ID from the record: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00997178.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2022: pooled trials show a modest absolute HbA1c fall after periodontal treatment
cards.summary: Cochrane 2022 (30 studies, 2,443 analysed): periodontal treatment lowered HbA1c by an absolute 0.43% at 3–4 months [−0.59 to −0.28], moderate certainty, shrinking to 0.30% at 6 months — a real pooled signal the biggest trial does not share.
cards.people: 35 RCTs randomising 3,249 people with diabetes (type 2 in all but one study, which mixed type 1 and type 2) and periodontitis; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Moderate-certainty evidence from 30 studies (2,443 analysed) showed an absolute HbA1c reduction of 0.43% (95% CI -0.59% to -0.28%) at 3–4 months after treatment versus no treatment or usual care; 0.30% (95% CI -0.52% to -0.08%; 12 studies, 1,457 participants) at 6 months; and 0.50% (95% CI -0.55% to -0.45%) at 12 months from a single study of 264 participants. Adverse effects, where measured, were none or mild, with serious events similar between arms.
cards.watchOut: Only 2 of 35 studies were at low risk of bias (14 high, 19 unclear), most were in secondary care with 3–12 months follow-up, and the pooled estimate sits uneasily beside the DPTT null — small-study effects cannot be excluded from the abstract data.
cards.source: Simpson TC et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022 Apr 14. PMID 35420698. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — this is a Cochrane review, not a trial.

cards.headline: TASTE: intensive periodontal treatment lowered HbA1c by 0.6 points at 12 months
cards.summary: The TASTE trial (264 patients, single centre): intensive periodontal treatment — the full protocol, repeated — lowered HbA1c by 0.6 points [0.3–0.9] at 12 months versus supragingival cleaning alone. Intensity may be the difference between this and DPTT; it is one centre’s result.
cards.people: 264 patients with type 2 diabetes, moderate-to-severe periodontitis and at least 15 teeth, recruited in the UK (133 intensive treatment, 131 control); baseline mean HbA1c 8.1% (SD 1.7) in both groups; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: After adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age, sex, ethnicity, smoking, diabetes duration and BMI, HbA1c was 0.6% lower (95% CI 0.3 to 0.9; p < 0.0001) with intensive periodontal treatment than with control (supragingival scaling and polishing) at 12 months. At least one adverse event: 23% intensive vs 18% control; serious adverse events 8% in each group, including 1 death (intensive) and 3 deaths (control).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and the intervention was intensive — whole-mouth subgingival scaling plus surgery where indicated and 3-monthly support — not the plain scaling and root planing tested in DPTT; whether ordinary dental practice reproduces this is untested.
cards.source: D'Aiuto F et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2018 Dec. PMID 30472992. Registry ID from the record: ISRCTN83229304.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a small glycemic effect is plausible; the null of the largest trial caps confidence
cards.summary: A small effect is plausible (pooled ≈0.3–0.6 points) and the largest trial’s null caps confidence: supportive care alongside diabetes medication, never a substitute — and no card here reports complications, events or mortality. POSSIBLE.
cards.people: No new participants — synthesis of the three verified cards above.
cards.result: Stamp: POSSIBLE. Benefit, if real, is an absolute HbA1c fall of roughly 0.3–0.6 percentage points — supportive care alongside diabetes medication, never a substitute for it. No card on this shelf reports diabetes complications, cardiovascular events or mortality as outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Needed evidence: a multicentre replication of the intensive TASTE protocol with HbA1c and complication outcomes, designed to settle why DPTT (standard nonsurgical therapy) was null while pooled smaller trials and one intensive trial were positive.
cards.source: Closing synthesis of the verified cards on this shelf (PMIDs 24346989, 35420698, 30472992); no new data introduced.

shelves.title: Berberine for blood glucose and lipids
shelves.question: Does berberine lower glucose or lipids in type 2 diabetes or dyslipidaemia?
shelves.mesh: Berberine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cholesterol, HDL/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucose/metabolism · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Metformin/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): the carded trials report large glucose and lipid falls — HbA1c from 7.5% to 6.6% versus placebo over 3 months in Zhang 2008 (n=116) and falls comparable to metformin in Yin 2008 — but the systematic review of the same programme (Dong 2012, 14 trials, 1,068 participants) states plainly that methodological quality was generally low, sample sizes small, trials few and risks of bias unidentified, and found berberine not significantly better than oral hypoglycaemic drugs for glycaemic control when used alone. Effects of this size from trials of this quality are exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for; nothing here is placebo-controlled beyond 3 months or measures clinical outcomes.

cards.headline: Yin 2008: berberine matched metformin in newly diagnosed diabetes in a small pilot — and an uncontrolled add-on study
cards.summary: Yin 2008: berberine's within-group HbA1c fell 9.5% → 7.5% , similar to metformin — in a small pilot with an uncontrolled add-on study.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (pilot) plus a second treated cohort
cards.people: Study A: 36 adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes randomised to berberine or metformin (0.5 g three times a day) for 3 months. Study B: 48 adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes treated with added berberine for 3 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix for either study.
cards.result: In study A the hypoglycaemic effect of berberine was similar to that of metformin; in the berberine group HbA1c fell from 9.5% ± 0.5% to 7.5% ± 0.4% (P<.01), fasting blood glucose from 10.6 ± 0.9 to 6.9 ± 0.5 mmol/L (≈191 ± 16 to 124 ± 9 mg/dL) (P<.01), postprandial glucose from 19.8 ± 1.7 to 11.1 ± 0.9 mmol/L (≈356 ± 31 to 200 ± 16 mg/dL) (P<.01) and plasma triglycerides from 1.13 ± 0.13 to 0.89 ± 0.03 mmol/L (≈100 ± 12 to 79 ± 3 mg/dL) (P<.05) — within-group changes in a trial with no placebo arm. In study B, HbA1c decreased from 8.1% ± 0.2% to 7.3% ± 0.3% (P<.001), fasting insulin and HOMA insulin-resistance index fell by 28.1% and 44.7% (P<.001), and total and LDL cholesterol decreased significantly (the abstract gives no values, so none are stated here). Transient gastrointestinal adverse effects were reported in 20 patients (34.5%, as printed in the abstract); no functional liver or kidney damage was observed.
cards.watchOut: Study A compares berberine with metformin, not placebo, in 36 patients; study B as described in the abstract has no control group at all — its before-and-after falls cannot be attributed to berberine. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Zhang 2008: berberine beat placebo on glucose and lipids over 3 months in 116 patients
cards.summary: Zhang 2008 (116 patients): HbA1c 7.5% → 6.6% and fasting glucose 7.0 → 5.6 mmol/L (≈126 → 101 mg/dL) vs placebo over 3 months.
cards.people: 116 patients with type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia randomised to berberine 1.0 g daily or placebo for 3 months; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the berberine group, fasting plasma glucose fell from 7.0 ± 0.8 to 5.6 ± 0.9 mmol/L (≈126 ± 14 to 101 ± 16 mg/dL), postload glucose from 12.0 ± 2.7 to 8.9 ± 2.8 mmol/L (≈216 ± 49 to 160 ± 50 mg/dL), HbA1c from 7.5% ± 1.0% to 6.6% ± 0.7%, triglycerides from 2.51 ± 2.04 to 1.61 ± 1.10 mmol/L (≈222 ± 181 to 143 ± 97 mg/dL), total cholesterol from 5.31 ± 0.98 to 4.35 ± 0.96 mmol/L (≈205 ± 38 to 168 ± 37 mg/dL) and LDL cholesterol from 3.23 ± 0.81 to 2.55 ± 0.77 mmol/L (≈125 ± 31 to 99 ± 30 mg/dL), with all parameters differing from placebo significantly (P<0.0001 for glucose, HbA1c, total and LDL cholesterol; P=0.001 for triglycerides). Glucose disposal rate increased after berberine treatment (P=0.037) although the between-group change was not significant (P=0.063). Mild to moderate constipation was observed in five participants in the berberine group.
cards.watchOut: The strongest single card on this shelf is still one small, single-programme, 3-month trial; effects of this size in trials of this size and era are routinely larger than later, better trials find. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Dong 2012: the field's own meta-analysis warns the evidence is low quality, small and at unidentified risk of bias
cards.summary: Dong 2012: the field's own meta-analysis warns the trials are low quality, small and at unidentified risk of bias .
cards.people: 14 randomised trials involving 1,068 participants with type 2 diabetes; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with lifestyle modification with or without placebo, berberine plus lifestyle modification showed significantly hypoglycaemic and antidyslipidaemic responses, and berberine combined with the same oral hypoglycaemic drug showed better glycaemic control than the drug alone. Compared head-to-head with oral hypoglycaemics (metformin, glipizide or rosiglitazone), berberine did not demonstrate significantly better glycaemic control, though it showed a mild antidyslipidaemic effect. No serious adverse effects were reported. The authors conclude the evidence should be carefully interpreted because of low methodological quality, small sample size, the limited number of trials, and unidentified risks of bias.
cards.watchOut: This review is the ceiling-setter for the shelf: its caution applies to the Yin and Zhang results carded above, which come from the same small, mostly single-centre programme. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: Large reported falls on weak trial foundations — MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Yin 2008 (36 randomised patients plus a 48-patient treated cohort), Zhang 2008 (116 patients) and Dong 2012 (14 trials, 1,068 participants).
cards.result: The only placebo-controlled card (Zhang) reports HbA1c falling from 7.5% to 6.6% and LDL cholesterol from 3.23 to 2.55 mmol/L (≈125 to 99 mg/dL) over 3 months versus placebo, and Yin reports glucose falls comparable to metformin — but the programme's own meta-analysis rates the underlying trials as low quality, small and at unidentified risk of bias, and finds berberine alone not significantly better than oral hypoglycaemic drugs for glycaemic control. This shelf is stamped MAYBE (weak evidence): berberine may lower glucose and lipids; the carded evidence cannot say by how much, for how long, or with what outcome benefit.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial exceeds 3 months, none measures diabetes complications or cardiovascular outcomes, and the 2025 berberine ursodeoxycholate trial found in the currency sweep is a different compound and is not evidence about berberine itself.

shelves.title: Self-monitoring of blood glucose in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
shelves.question: Does routine fingerstick self-monitoring improve control or quality of life in type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring/economics/methods/psychology/standards · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/complications/prevention & control/psychology · England · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Hypoglycemia/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two randomised trials agree that routine fingerstick self-monitoring does not improve glycaemic control in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes — DiGEM found 12-month HbA1c differences of -0.14% and -0.17% versus control, neither significant, and the Monitor Trial found no significant HbA1c or quality-of-life difference at 52 weeks (-0.05% to -0.09%). DiGEM's economic analysis found self-monitoring cost more and slightly lowered quality of life, so routine monitoring in this population is unlikely to be cost-effective.

cards.headline: DiGEM: self-monitoring did not improve HbA1c at 12 months, with or without training in using the results
cards.summary: DiGEM: 12-month HbA1c differences were not significant (less intensive self-monitoring vs control −0.14% [−0.35 to 0.07]).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (main report, Health Technology Assessment)
cards.people: 453 patients with non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, aged 25 years or older with HbA1c 6.2% or higher, in 48 UK general practices (control n=152, less intensive self-monitoring n=150, more intensive self-monitoring n=151); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Differences in 12-month HbA1c between the three groups were not statistically significant (p=0.12). The difference in unadjusted mean change in HbA1c from baseline to 12 months was -0.14% (95% CI -0.35 to 0.07) for less intensive self-monitoring versus control and -0.17% (95% CI -0.37 to 0.03) for more intensive self-monitoring versus control. There was no significantly different impact in subgroups defined by duration of diabetes, therapy, complications or EQ-5D score.
cards.watchOut: Open trial; the confidence intervals exclude a large benefit but not a very small one. HbA1c is a surrogate outcome; no clinical-event outcomes are reported.
cards.source: Farmer AJ et al. Blood glucose self-monitoring in type 2 diabetes: a randomised controlled trial. Health Technol Assess. 2009 Feb;13(15):iii-iv, ix-xi, 1-50. PMID: 19254484. Registry ID: ISRCTN47464659, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DiGEM economic analysis: self-monitoring cost more and slightly lowered quality of life
cards.summary: DiGEM economics: self-monitoring cost £92/£84 more per patient — with a small initial quality-of-life decrement.
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 453 patients with non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes in UK primary care (the DiGEM trial population); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Average intervention costs were £89 for standardised usual care, £181 for less intensive self-monitoring and £173 for more intensive self-monitoring — additional costs per patient of £92 (95% CI £80 to £103) and £84 (£73 to £96). An initial negative impact of self-monitoring on quality of life averaged -0.027 (95% CI -0.069 to 0.015) in the less intensive group and -0.075 (-0.119 to -0.031) in the more intensive group. The authors conclude self-monitoring is unlikely to be cost-effective in addition to standardised usual care.
cards.watchOut: Same trial as the preceding card (DiGEM counts once as a trial); UK healthcare-perspective costs in 2005-6 prices.
cards.source: Simon J et al. Cost effectiveness of self monitoring of blood glucose in patients with non-insulin treated type 2 diabetes: DiGEM trial. BMJ. 2008 May 24;336(7654):1177-80. PMID: 18420663. Registry ID: ISRCTN47464659, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Monitor Trial: no HbA1c or quality-of-life benefit from once-daily self-monitoring at one year
cards.summary: Monitor Trial: adjusted HbA1c differences of −0.09% and −0.05% at one year (P=.74) — no benefit, no quality-of-life benefit.
cards.people: 450 patients with non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, older than 30 years, with HbA1c higher than 6.5% but lower than 9.5%, in 15 primary care practices in central North Carolina; 418 (92.9%) completed the final visit; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in HbA1c across the three groups at 52 weeks (P=.74): estimated adjusted mean difference was -0.09% (95% CI, -0.31% to 0.14%) for self-monitoring with enhanced feedback messaging versus no self-monitoring, and -0.05% (95% CI, -0.27% to 0.17%) for self-monitoring alone versus no self-monitoring. There were no significant differences in health-related quality of life, hypoglycaemia frequency, health care utilisation or insulin initiation.
cards.watchOut: Open-label pragmatic trial of once-daily testing; results do not address monitoring in insulin-treated patients or during acute illness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: routine fingerstick monitoring does not improve control in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: Routine fingerstick monitoring does not improve control in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes — LIKELY, for the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DiGEM (453 patients, UK) and the Monitor Trial (450 patients, US primary care), concordant nulls.
cards.result: Both trials found no significant HbA1c benefit from routine self-monitoring (point estimates -0.05% to -0.17%), no quality-of-life benefit, and DiGEM found higher costs with a small initial quality-of-life decrement. This shelf is stamped LIKELY for the null: two independent randomised trials in the target population agree, and the question is monitoring only — it says nothing about insulin-treated diabetes, which is covered by the CGM and pump shelves (#560, #564).
cards.watchOut: Do not extend this null to patients using insulin, to pregnancy, or to symptomatic hypoglycaemia assessment; none of those populations were studied here.
