shelves.title: Continuous glucose monitoring in type 1 diabetes on injections
shelves.question: Does CGM improve HbA1c and hypoglycaemia in adults with type 1 diabetes using multiple daily injections?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring/instrumentation/psychology/statistics & numerical data · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Hyperglycemia/blood/drug therapy · Hypoglycemia/blood/chemically induced
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections agree that CGM lowers HbA1c versus fingerstick-based care — DIAMOND by an adjusted -0.6% at 24 weeks and GOLD by -0.43% over 26-week crossover periods — with less time in hypoglycaemia in DIAMOND (median 43 vs 80 min/day below 70 mg/dL) and fewer severe hypoglycaemia events numerically in GOLD. Outcomes are glycaemic surrogates and hypoglycaemia exposure, not long-term complications.

cards.headline: DIAMOND: CGM lowered HbA1c by an adjusted 0.6% more than usual care at 24 weeks
cards.summary: DIAMOND: adjusted HbA1c difference −0.6% [−0.8 to −0.3] at 24 weeks; median time below 70 mg/dL nearly halved ( 43 vs 80 min/day ).
cards.people: 158 adults with type 1 diabetes using multiple daily insulin injections, HbA1c 7.5% to 9.9%, at 24 US endocrinology practices (CGM n=105, control n=53); mean age 48 years (SD 13), 44% women, mean baseline HbA1c 8.6% (SD 0.6%), median diabetes duration 19 years.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c reduction was 1.1% at 12 weeks and 1.0% at 24 weeks with CGM versus 0.5% and 0.4% with usual care; the adjusted treatment-group difference at 24 weeks was -0.6% (95% CI, -0.8% to -0.3%; P<.001). Median duration of hypoglycaemia below 70 mg/dL was 43 min/day (IQR 27-69) in the CGM group versus 80 min/day (IQR 36-111) in controls (P=.002). Severe hypoglycaemia events occurred in 2 participants in each group. In the CGM group, 93% used CGM 6 days/week or more in month 6.
cards.watchOut: 24-week trial with a glycaemic surrogate primary outcome; severe hypoglycaemia events were too few (2 per group) to compare reliably.
cards.source: Beck RW et al. Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes Using Insulin Injections: The DIAMOND Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017 Jan 24;317(4):371-378. PMID: 28118453. Registry ID: NCT02282397, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: GOLD: CGM lowered HbA1c by 0.43% versus conventional treatment in a crossover trial
cards.summary: GOLD (crossover): HbA1c 7.92% on CGM vs 8.35% on conventional treatment (difference −0.43%).
cards.people: 161 adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections, HbA1c at least 7.5%, at 15 Swedish diabetes clinics; mean age 43.7 years, 45.3% women, mean HbA1c 8.6%; 142 participants had follow-up data in both treatment periods.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c was 7.92% during CGM use and 8.35% during conventional treatment (mean difference -0.43% [95% CI, -0.57% to -0.29%]; P<.001). Five patients in the conventional treatment group and 1 patient in the CGM group had severe hypoglycaemia during the treatment periods; 7 patients had severe hypoglycaemia during the washout period on conventional therapy.
cards.watchOut: Crossover design with a 17-week washout; severe hypoglycaemia counts are small and were not the primary outcome. HbA1c is a surrogate outcome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: CGM improves HbA1c and reduces hypoglycaemia exposure in type 1 diabetes on injections
cards.summary: CGM improves HbA1c by roughly half a point and cuts hypoglycaemia exposure in type 1 diabetes on injections — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DIAMOND (158 adults, parallel-group) and GOLD (161 adults, crossover) — 319 randomised adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections.
cards.result: Both trials found CGM lowered HbA1c by roughly half a percentage point more than fingerstick-based care (-0.6% adjusted in DIAMOND; -0.43% in GOLD), and DIAMOND found median time below 70 mg/dL nearly halved (43 vs 80 min/day). This shelf is stamped LIKELY: two concordant randomised trials in exactly the population asked about. This shelf is monitoring only — automated delivery is #561 and pumps without automation are #564.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for severe hypoglycaemia or long-term complications; do not present the HbA1c effect as proof of reduced microvascular events.

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Randomised trials agree that automated insulin delivery improves glycaemic control in type 1 diabetes — hybrid closed-loop raised time-in-range by 10.8 percentage points versus sensor-augmented pump therapy over 12 weeks, and the iLet bionic pancreas lowered HbA1c by an adjusted -0.5% versus standard care (with CGM) at 13 weeks in both adults and youth, with time-in-range up by 11% in adults — without increasing CGM-measured hypoglycaemia. Trials are short (12-13 weeks) and outcomes are glycaemic measures, not complications.

cards.headline: Hybrid closed-loop raised time-in-range by 10.8 percentage points versus sensor-augmented pump therapy
cards.summary: Tuber 2018: time in range 65% vs 54% — a 10.8-point advantage [8.2 to 13.5] for day-and-night hybrid closed loop.
cards.people: 86 patients with type 1 diabetes aged 6 years and older, on insulin pumps with suboptimal control (HbA1c 7.5-10.0%), at 4 UK and 2 US centres (closed-loop n=46, control n=40); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Time in the target range 3.9-10.0 mmol/L (≈70-180 mg/dL) was 65% (SD 8) with closed-loop versus 54% (SD 9) with sensor-augmented pump therapy (mean difference in change 10.8 percentage points, 95% CI 8.2 to 13.5; p<0.0001). HbA1c fell to 7.4% (SD 0.6) in the closed-loop group versus 7.7% (SD 0.5) in controls after the intervention (mean difference in change 0.36%, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.53; p<0.0001). Time below 3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) and above 10.0 mmol/L (≈180 mg/dL) was shorter with closed-loop. No severe hypoglycaemia occurred; one diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in the closed-loop group due to infusion set failure.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 12-week trial after a 4-week run-in during which both groups' HbA1c already improved; outcomes are sensor measures, not clinical events.
cards.source: Tauschmann M et al. Closed-loop insulin delivery in suboptimally controlled type 1 diabetes: a multicentre, 12-week randomised trial. Lancet. 2018 Oct 13;392(10155):1321-1329. PMID: 30292578. Registry ID: NCT02523131, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: iLet bionic pancreas (adults): HbA1c down an adjusted 0.5%, time-in-range up 11% versus standard care with CGM
cards.summary: iLet bionic pancreas (adults): adjusted HbA1c difference −0.5% ; time in range up 11% (2.6 h/day) at 13 weeks.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (pivotal trial, adult report)
cards.people: 161 adults with type 1 diabetes, 18-79 years old, baseline HbA1c 5.5%-13.1% (bionic pancreas n=107, standard care n=54); before the study 32% used multiple daily injections, 27% a pump without automation, 5% a pump with predictive low-glucose suspend and 36% a hybrid closed-loop system; the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell from 7.6% to 7.1% with the bionic pancreas versus 7.6% to 7.5% with standard care (adjusted difference -0.5%, 95% CI -0.6% to -0.3%, P<0.001) at 13 weeks. Mean time-in-range 70-180 mg/dL increased by 11% (2.6 h/day) and mean CGM glucose fell by 16 mg/dL versus standard care (P<0.001). CGM-measured hypoglycaemia did not differ significantly between groups. Severe hypoglycaemic events occurred in 7 participants (6.5%) in the bionic pancreas group and 2 (1.9%) in the standard care group (P=0.40).
cards.watchOut: The comparator was standard care plus CGM, and over a third of participants were already using hybrid closed-loop before the study, so this is not a comparison against injections alone; 13-week duration.
cards.source: Kruger D et al. A Multicenter Randomized Trial Evaluating the Insulin-Only Configuration of the Bionic Pancreas in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes Technol Ther. 2022 Oct;24(10):697-711. PMID: 36173236. Registry ID: NCT04200313, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: iLet bionic pancreas (youth 6-17): HbA1c down an adjusted 0.5%, largest gains at high baseline HbA1c
cards.summary: iLet (youth 6–17): adjusted HbA1c difference −0.5% , with the largest gains at high baseline HbA1c.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (pivotal trial, youth report — same trial as the adult report)
cards.people: 165 youth with type 1 diabetes, 6-17 years old, baseline HbA1c 5.8%-12.2% (bionic pancreas n=112, standard care n=53); the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell from 8.1% to 7.5% with the bionic pancreas versus 7.8% at both baseline and 13 weeks with standard care (adjusted difference -0.5%, 95% CI -0.7% to -0.2%, P<0.001). In participants with baseline HbA1c 9.0% or higher (n=34), mean HbA1c fell from 9.7% to 7.9% with the bionic pancreas versus 9.7% to 9.8% with standard care. Mean time-in-range increased by 10% (2.4 h/day) versus standard care (P<0.001). A severe hypoglycaemia event occurred in 3 participants (2.7%) in the bionic pancreas group and 1 (1.9%) in the standard care group.
cards.watchOut: Same pivotal trial as the preceding card (NCT04200313 counts once); 13 weeks only, and the control group also used real-time CGM.

cards.headline: Synthesis: automated delivery improves time-in-range and HbA1c without more sensor-measured hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Automated delivery adds ~11 points of time-in-range and ~0.5% HbA1c without more sensor-measured hypoglycaemia — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Tauschmann hybrid closed-loop trial (86 participants, age 6+) and the iLet pivotal trial (326 participants across its adult and youth reports, one trial).
cards.result: Across both programmes, automation added roughly 11 percentage points of time-in-range and about 0.4-0.5% of HbA1c reduction over 12-13 weeks versus sensor-augmented or standard care with CGM, with no increase in CGM-measured hypoglycaemia. This shelf is stamped LIKELY: two independent randomised programmes agree on direction and size. It is distinct from #560 (monitoring only) and #564 (pumps with no automation).
cards.watchOut: All follow-up is 12-13 weeks; nothing here speaks to years-long use, device burden, or complication outcomes, and severe hypoglycaemia event counts were small and numerically higher in the iLet arm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tauschmann M et al. Lancet. 2018;392(10155):1321-1329. PMID: 30292578; Kruger D et al. Diabetes Technol Ther. 2022;24(10):697-711. PMID: 36173236; Messer LH et al. Diabetes Technol Ther. 2022;24(10):712-725. PMID: 36173237. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Metformin for antipsychotic-induced weight gain
shelves.question: Does metformin prevent or reverse weight gain caused by antipsychotic medicines?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects · Blood Glucose/drug effects · Body Mass Index · Body Weight/drug effects · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin Resistance · Metformin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Small randomised trials and a Cochrane synthesis suggest metformin blunts antipsychotic-induced weight gain — the Cochrane pooled estimate is -4.03 kg versus placebo across 4 small studies (131 participants), graded low-certainty — but the primary trials are small and short: the largest carded trial randomised 72 first-episode patients for 12 weeks, and the 24-week trial randomised only 17 participants as a feasibility pilot. The direction is consistent; the size and durability are not firmly established.

cards.headline: Metformin attenuated weight gain and insulin resistance over 12 weeks in first-episode schizophrenia
cards.summary: Wu 2008: over 12 weeks in first-episode schizophrenia, weight, BMI and insulin resistance fell on metformin and rose on placebo .
cards.people: 72 patients with first-episode schizophrenia who had gained more than 7% of their pre-drug body weight on antipsychotics; 66 (91.6%) completed treatment; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Body weight, body mass index, fasting insulin and insulin resistance index decreased significantly in the metformin group (1000 mg/day) but increased in the placebo group over 12 weeks. Significantly more patients in the metformin group lost more than 7% of their baseline weight, the trial's cutoff for clinically meaningful weight loss. The record's abstract reports the direction and significance of these changes but does not state the mean kilogram change, so no kilogram figure is printed here. Metformin was tolerated well by the majority of patients.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-programme trial of 12 weeks in first-episode patients who had already gained weight (treatment, not prevention); no registry ID appears in the record's databank fields.
cards.source: Wang M et al. Metformin for treatment of antipsychotic-induced weight gain: a randomized, placebo-controlled study. Schizophr Res. 2012 Jun;138(1):54-7. PMID: 22398127. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: 24-week pilot (n=17): weight was controlled on metformin, and the effect did not persist after stopping
cards.summary: 24-week pilot (n=17): weight was controlled on metformin — and the effect did not persist after stopping.
cards.people: 17 participants aged 16-40 with first-episode psychosis who had gained 5% or more of pre-drug weight after starting antipsychotics, in a Singapore early-psychosis programme (metformin n=8, placebo n=9).
cards.result: This was a feasibility pilot: metformin was generally well tolerated, participants in the metformin arm controlled their weight better than those on placebo over 24 weeks, and the effect did not persist after metformin was discontinued (follow-up to week 36). The record's abstract reports no kilogram figures, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Only 17 randomised participants — a feasibility study, not an efficacy estimate; it cannot carry the shelf's claim on its own. No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis: metformin may prevent weight gain by about 4 kg, on low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane: metformin may prevent weight gain by about 4 kg (−4.03 kg [−5.78 to −2.28]) — on low-certainty evidence, a few hundred patients in total.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 17 randomised trials with 1,388 participants with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like illnesses across all drug classes reviewed; the metformin weight analysis pooled 4 studies with 131 participants and the BMI analysis 5 studies with 227 participants; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Metformin may be effective in preventing weight gain (mean difference -4.03 kg, 95% CI -5.78 to -2.28; 4 studies, 131 participants; low-certainty evidence) and BMI increase (mean difference -1.63 kg/m2, 95% CI -2.96 to -0.29; 5 studies, 227 participants; low-certainty evidence). The reviewers note most included studies inadequately reported allocation concealment and blinding, and small sample sizes limited certainty.
cards.watchOut: The review's question is prevention of weight gain in people taking antipsychotics; the pooled metformin estimate rests on 131 participants and is explicitly low-certainty — it supports POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Agarwal SM et al. Pharmacological interventions for prevention of weight gain in people with schizophrenia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022 Oct 3;10(10):CD013337. PMID: 36190739. Registry ID: NCT00176449 appears in the record's databank fields (a secondary-identifier field for this review record).

cards.headline: Synthesis: metformin probably blunts antipsychotic weight gain, but the trial base is small and short
cards.summary: Metformin probably blunts antipsychotic weight gain, but the trial base is small and short — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a 72-patient 12-week trial, a 17-patient 24-week feasibility pilot, and a Cochrane synthesis whose metformin analysis pools 131-227 participants.
cards.result: Every card points the same way — less gain (or some loss) on metformin than placebo, with a pooled estimate of -4.03 kg — but total randomised numbers are a few hundred at most, follow-up is 12-24 weeks, and the Cochrane authors grade their own evidence low-certainty. This shelf is therefore stamped POSSIBLE. The pilot's loss of effect after discontinuation suggests any benefit needs continued treatment.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the -4.03 kg pooled figure without its low-certainty label and 131-participant base; prevention and treatment trials are mixed across the cards.

shelves.title: Orlistat for weight loss and diabetes delay
shelves.question: Does orlistat produce durable weight loss and delay type 2 diabetes in people with obesity?
shelves.mesh: Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus/prevention & control · Energy Intake · Glucose Tolerance Test · Lactones/therapeutic use · Life Style · Lipase/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Orlistat plus lifestyle change produced more weight loss than lifestyle alone in two large trials (XENDOS: 5.8 vs 3.0 kg at 4 years; Davidson: 8.76 vs 5.81 kg at 1 year, with less regain in year 2) — the weight effect itself is consistent. The diabetes claim is narrower: in XENDOS, cumulative diabetes incidence was 6.2% on orlistat versus 9.0% on placebo (a 37.3% relative risk reduction, 2.8 percentage points absolute), and the trial's own exploratory analysis found the delay effect explained by the subgroup with impaired glucose tolerance at baseline. Stamped POSSIBLE because the delay claim rests on one trial and one subgroup.

cards.headline: XENDOS: orlistat delayed type 2 diabetes (6.2% vs 9.0% over 4 years) and added 2.8 kg of weight loss
cards.summary: XENDOS: diabetes incidence 6.2% vs 9.0% over 4 years — a 37.3% relative reduction, 2.8 points absolute , explained by the impaired-glucose-tolerance subgroup; weight loss 5.8 vs 3.0 kg.
cards.people: 3,305 patients with BMI 30 kg/m2 or higher — 79% with normal glucose tolerance and 21% with impaired glucose tolerance — randomised to lifestyle changes plus orlistat 120 mg or placebo three times daily for 4 years; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. Treatment was completed by 52% of the orlistat group and 34% of the placebo group.
cards.result: Cumulative diabetes incidence was 6.2% with orlistat and 9.0% with placebo — a 37.3% relative risk reduction (P=0.0032), 2.8 percentage points absolute. Exploratory analyses indicated the delay effect was explained by the difference in subjects with impaired glucose tolerance. Mean weight loss at 4 years was 5.8 kg with orlistat versus 3.0 kg with placebo (P<0.001); in a baseline-carried-forward analysis, 3.6 vs 1.4 kg (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Diabetes delay was detectable only in the impaired-glucose-tolerance subgroup (21% of participants); dropout was high and unequal (52% vs 34% completed). No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields (pre-registration era). Wording follows the developer's rule: this is delay of diagnosis, stated as such.
cards.source: Torgerson JS et al. XENical in the prevention of diabetes in obese subjects (XENDOS) study. Diabetes Care. 2004 Jan;27(1):155-61. PMID: 14693982. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Two-year trial: orlistat added about 3 kg of weight loss in year 1 and halved regain in year 2
cards.summary: Two-year trial: year-1 weight loss 8.76 vs 5.81 kg , with less regain in year 2 on continued orlistat.
cards.people: 1,187 obese adults (BMI 30-43 kg/m2) entered the protocol at 18 US centres and 892 were randomised to double-blind treatment after a 4-week dietary lead-in (year-2 intention-to-treat analysis: 223 placebo, 657 orlistat); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In year 1, orlistat-treated subjects lost more weight (mean 8.76 kg, SEM 0.37) than placebo-treated subjects (5.81 kg, SEM 0.67; P<.001). Subjects kept on orlistat 120 mg three times daily in year 2 regained less weight (3.2 kg, 35.2% regain) than those rerandomised to orlistat 60 mg (4.26 kg, 51.3% regain) or placebo (5.63 kg, 63.4% regain; P<.001). Orlistat 120 mg was also associated with improvements in fasting LDL cholesterol and insulin levels.
cards.watchOut: Weight outcomes only — this trial did not test diabetes incidence. No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Davidson MH et al. Weight control and risk factor reduction in obese subjects treated for 2 years with orlistat: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 1999 Jan 20;281(3):235-42. PMID: 9918478. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: real but modest weight effect; the diabetes-delay claim belongs to the IGT subgroup of one trial
cards.summary: A real but modest weight effect; the diabetes claim is a delay shown in one trial's IGT subgroup — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: XENDOS (3,305 participants, 4 years) and the Davidson 2-year trial (892 randomised).
cards.result: Orlistat consistently added roughly 3 kg of weight loss over placebo-plus-diet at 1-4 years and reduced weight regain. Diabetes delay was shown only in XENDOS, only clearly in its impaired-glucose-tolerance subgroup, as a 37.3% relative reduction on absolute rates of 6.2% versus 9.0%. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE: LIKELY-grade consistency for weight, single-trial subgroup-dependent evidence for delay. The GLP-1 obesity shelves (#282, #356, #357) cover a different, larger-effect drug class.

shelves.title: Insulin pump (CSII) vs multiple daily injections in type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: Does pump therapy improve control or quality of life versus injections when both groups get structured education?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: When both groups receive the same structured education, the pump advantage largely disappears: REPOSE found a -0.24% HbA1c difference at 2 years favouring pumps that was not significant (95% CI -0.53 to 0.05), with both groups improving substantially from education itself, while pump users reported greater treatment satisfaction and some quality-of-life gains. A systematic review likewise found CSII and injections had similar effects on HbA1c and severe hypoglycaemia overall, with a favourable CSII effect in adults with type 1 diabetes that one study heavily influenced. These are pumps without automation — automated delivery is #561.

cards.headline: REPOSE: with equal structured education, pumps did not significantly beat injections on HbA1c at 2 years
cards.summary: REPOSE: with equal structured education, the adjusted HbA1c difference was −0.24% [−0.53 to 0.05] (P=0.10) — not significant ; satisfaction favoured pumps.
cards.type: Pragmatic multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 317 adults with type 1 diabetes willing to undertake intensive insulin treatment, with no preference for pump or injections, at 8 centres in England and Scotland (156 pump, 161 injections across 46 DAFNE course clusters); 260 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis, of whom 235 had baseline HbA1c 7.5% or higher; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean change in HbA1c at 2 years was -0.85% with pump treatment and -0.42% with multiple daily injections; adjusted for course, centre, age, sex and missing values, the difference was -0.24% in favour of pumps (95% CI -0.53 to 0.05, P=0.10) — not significant. Glycaemic control and severe hypoglycaemia rates improved in both groups. shelves.title: Replacing sugary drinks with water or diet drinks for weight control
shelves.question: Does substituting non-caloric drinks for sugar-sweetened beverages reduce weight gain in adults?
shelves.mesh: Beverages · Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Pressure · Choice Behavior · Diet · Diet, Reducing/methods · Energy Intake
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the CHOICE trial, adults replacing at least 200 kcal/day of caloric drinks with water or diet drinks lost 2.0-2.5% of body weight over 6 months, but the between-group differences versus attention control were not significant (diet drinks -2.5%, water -2.03%, control -1.76%); beverage replacement doubled the odds of reaching a 5% loss (OR 2.07). In a separate year-long trial in regular users of sweetened drinks enrolled in a weight-loss programme, the non-nutritive-sweetened group maintained a larger loss than the water group (6.21 vs 2.45 kg). Effects are modest and population-dependent. The children's substitution trials are #205, not this shelf.

cards.headline: CHOICE: replacing caloric drinks produced 2-2.5% weight loss, not significantly more than attention control
cards.summary: CHOICE: 6-month weight losses of −2.5% (diet drinks), −2.03% (water) and −1.76% (attention control) — no significant differences between groups.
cards.people: 318 overweight and obese adults (BMI 36.3, SD 5.9; 84% female; mean age 42 years, SD 10.7; 54% black) who drank at least 200 kcal/day of caloric beverages, randomised to diet beverages, water, or attention control for 6 months.
cards.result: Mean weight losses at 6 months were -2.5% (SEM 0.45) in the diet-beverage group, -2.03% (SEM 0.40) in the water group and -1.76% (SEM 0.35) in the attention-control group, with no significant differences between groups. The chance of achieving a 5% weight loss was greater in the diet-beverage group than control (OR 2.29; 95% CI 1.05 to 5.01; P=0.04); in a combined analysis, beverage-replacement participants were about twice as likely to achieve a 5% loss (OR 2.07; 95% CI 1.02 to 4.22; P=0.04). The odds ratios sit just above the 2.0 line and are responder analyses, not the primary between-group weight comparison, which was null.
cards.watchOut: The headline weight outcome is a null between-group result; the positive findings are secondary responder analyses. Six months only.
cards.source: Tate DF et al. Replacing caloric beverages with water or diet beverages for weight loss in adults: main results of the CHOICE trial. Am J Clin Nutr. 2012 Mar;95(3):555-63. PMID: 22301929. Registry ID: NCT01017783, from the record's databank fields.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CHOICE (318 adults, substitution vs attention control) and Peters 2016 (303 adults, water vs diet drinks within a programme).
cards.result: Substituting non-caloric drinks for sugary drinks is a reasonable, simple strategy with average losses around 2-2.5% over 6 months, but CHOICE's primary between-group comparison was not significant, and Peters answers a different question (which non-caloric drink, in existing diet-drink users) than substitution itself. shelves.title: Inositol for polycystic ovary syndrome
shelves.question: Do myo-inositol or D-chiro-inositol improve ovulation, hormones or metabolic measures in PCOS?
shelves.mesh: 17-alpha-Hydroxyprogesterone/blood · Androgens/blood · Blood Glucose/analysis · Inositol/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Insulin/blood · Lipids/blood · Luteinizing Hormone/blood
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The inositol evidence in PCOS is two small, short, single-centre randomised trials with striking results that have not been replicated at scale — D-chiro-inositol improved ovulation (19 of 22 women vs 6 of 22 on placebo) and lowered free testosterone in 44 obese women over 6-8 weeks, and myo-inositol raised ovulation frequency (25% vs 15% of observed weeks) in 92 women over 14 weeks. Effect sizes this large from samples this small are exactly what the MAYBE (weak evidence) label is for; no large or long trial exists.

cards.headline: D-chiro-inositol: 19 of 22 women ovulated versus 6 of 22 on placebo, in a 44-woman trial
cards.summary: D-chiro-inositol: 19 of 22 women ovulated vs 6 of 22 on placebo — in a single 44-woman trial.
cards.people: 44 obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome given D-chiro-inositol 1200 mg daily or placebo for 6-8 weeks (22 per group); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Nineteen of the 22 women given D-chiro-inositol ovulated, compared with 6 of 22 on placebo (P<0.001). Serum free testosterone fell from 1.1 (SD 0.8) to 0.5 (SD 0.5) ng/dL in the D-chiro-inositol group (P=0.006 versus the change on placebo), and plasma triglycerides fell from 184 (SD 88) to 110 (SD 61) mg/dL (P=0.002 versus placebo change). The area under the plasma insulin curve after oral glucose fell within the D-chiro-inositol group (P=0.007) but the comparison of that change against placebo was not significant (P=0.07), and glucose tolerance did not change significantly.
cards.watchOut: 44 women, 6-8 weeks, surrogate and ovulation outcomes only — no pregnancy or live-birth outcomes; results of this size from a sample this small are fragile. No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields (pre-registration era). The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Nestler JE et al. Ovulatory and metabolic effects of D-chiro-inositol in the polycystic ovary syndrome. N Engl J Med. 1999 Apr 29;340(17):1314-20. PMID: 10219066. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Myo-inositol: ovulation frequency 25% versus 15% of observed weeks over 14 weeks
cards.summary: Myo-inositol: ovulation frequency 25% vs 15% of observed weeks over 14 weeks.
cards.people: 92 women with oligomenorrhea and polycystic ovaries randomised to myo-inositol 4 g plus folic acid 400 mcg (n=45) or folic acid alone as placebo (n=47); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Ovulation frequency (luteal-phase weeks as a proportion of observation weeks) was 25% in the myo-inositol group versus 15% on placebo (P<0.01), and time to first ovulation was shorter (24.5 days, 95% CI 18 to 31, versus 40.5 days, 95% CI 27 to 54; P<0.05). More placebo patients failed to ovulate at all (P<0.05). No change in fasting glucose, fasting insulin or insulin response to glucose challenge was recorded after 14 weeks, and metabolic benefits were not observed in the subgroup with BMI above 37; efficacy was inversely related to body mass.
cards.watchOut: Ovulation is a surrogate for fertility — no pregnancy or live-birth outcomes are reported; the placebo was folic acid alone; benefit disappeared in the highest-BMI subgroup. No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: promising ovulation signals from two small trials — MAYBE (weak evidence), honestly capped
cards.summary: Promising ovulation signals from two small trials (136 women in total), with no pregnancy or live-birth outcomes — MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: 44 women (D-chiro-inositol, 6-8 weeks) and 92 women (myo-inositol, 14 weeks) — 136 randomised women in total.
cards.result: Both small trials found more ovulation on inositol than placebo, and the D-chiro trial found lower free testosterone and triglycerides; neither found a clear glucose-tolerance benefit, and neither measured pregnancy or live birth. With 136 women total, short follow-up and surrogate outcomes, this shelf is stamped MAYBE (weak evidence) and cannot go higher until a large trial exists. Prescription ovulation induction in PCOS-related infertility is #245 — a different question.
cards.watchOut: Never present the 19-of-22 ovulation figure without its 44-woman denominator; it is the kind of small-sample result that routinely shrinks on replication.

shelves.title: Teplizumab to delay clinical type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: Does a single course of teplizumab delay progression from stage 2 to clinical (stage 3) type 1 diabetes in high-risk relatives?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · CD3 Complex/antagonists & inhibitors · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/genetics/immunology/prevention & control · Disease Progression · Exanthema/chemically induced · Glucose Tolerance Test · HLA-DR3 Antigen
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single TN-10 trial, one 14-day course of teplizumab delayed clinical type 1 diabetes in high-risk relatives — median time to diagnosis 48.4 months versus 24.4 months on placebo, with diabetes diagnosed in 43% versus 72% (hazard ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.78) — but the trial randomised only 76 participants, mostly children, and there is no second trial, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. This is a delay claim, per the developer's wording rule: teplizumab delayed diagnosis by about two years at the median; it did not prevent diabetes.

cards.headline: TN-10: teplizumab delayed clinical diabetes — median 48.4 versus 24.4 months to diagnosis
cards.summary: TN-10: median time to clinical diagnosis 48.4 vs 24.4 months ; diagnosed during follow-up in 43% vs 72% (hazard ratio 0.41).
cards.people: 76 relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes who did not have diabetes but were at high risk of clinical disease (stage 2), randomised to a single 14-day course of teplizumab (n=44) or placebo (n=32); 55 participants (72%) were 18 years of age or younger; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Median time to diagnosis of clinical type 1 diabetes was 48.4 months with teplizumab and 24.4 months with placebo; diabetes was diagnosed in 19 of 44 participants (43%) on teplizumab and 23 of 32 (72%) on placebo. The hazard ratio for diagnosis was 0.41 (95% CI, 0.22 to 0.78; P=0.006), and annualised diagnosis rates were 14.9% per year versus 35.9% per year. Expected adverse events were rash and transient lymphopenia.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (76 participants) in relatives with stage 2 disease — the result delays diagnosis and does not show prevention, insulin independence, or benefit in the general population. Effects were smaller or absent in some prespecified subgroups (HLA-DR3-negative, HLA-DR4-positive, or anti-zinc-transporter-8-antibody-negative participants are reported as strata in the record).
cards.source: Herold KC et al. An Anti-CD3 Antibody, Teplizumab, in Relatives at Risk for Type 1 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2019 Aug 15;381(7):603-613. PMID: 31180194. Registry ID: NCT01030861, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real delay signal from one small trial — POSSIBLE, and always worded as delay
cards.summary: A real delay signal from one small trial of 76 at-risk relatives — POSSIBLE, and worded as delay, never prevention.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: TN-10 alone, 76 high-risk relatives, one 14-day course, follow-up by 6-monthly oral glucose tolerance tests.
cards.result: Teplizumab roughly doubled the median time to clinical diagnosis (48.4 vs 24.4 months) and reduced the proportion diagnosed during follow-up from 72% to 43%. With one trial of 76 participants there is no replication, so this shelf is stamped POSSIBLE — the single-trial ceiling. Per the developer's standing wording rule for onset material, every statement on this shelf says delay, never prevention: most treated participants who were followed long enough still progressed.
cards.watchOut: Do not describe teplizumab as preventing type 1 diabetes, and do not generalise beyond stage 2 relatives identified by autoantibody and dysglycaemia screening.

shelves.title: Testosterone to prevent or revert type 2 diabetes in high-risk men (T4DM)
shelves.question: Does testosterone treatment, added to a lifestyle programme, prevent or revert type 2 diabetes in men with impaired glucose tolerance and low-normal testosterone?
shelves.mesh: Australia · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy/pathology/prevention & control · Disease Progression · Glucose Intolerance/blood/drug therapy/pathology · Life Style · Placebos · Prediabetic State/blood/drug therapy/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single T4DM trial, testosterone undecanoate added to a lifestyle programme reduced the proportion of men meeting the diabetes threshold on oral glucose tolerance testing at 2 years (12% vs 21%; relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.80 — a relative reduction of about 41% on absolute rates of 12% versus 21%). That relative risk of 0.59 sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band the developer does not accept as solid evidence on its own, the trial is unreplicated, and the safety ledger is real (haematocrit above 54% in 22% vs 1%), so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. Testosterone for cardiovascular safety and symptoms is #344 — a different question.

cards.headline: T4DM: diabetes threshold met by 12% on testosterone versus 21% on placebo at 2 years, on top of a lifestyle programme
cards.summary: T4DM: the diabetes threshold was met by 12% vs 21% at 2 years (relative risk 0.59 [0.43 to 0.80]) on top of a lifestyle programme — with a haematocrit cost.
cards.people: 1,007 men aged 50-74 years with waist circumference 95 cm or higher, serum testosterone 14.0 nmol/L or lower without pathological hypogonadism, and impaired glucose tolerance or newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, all enrolled in a lifestyle programme (testosterone n=504, placebo n=503) at six Australian centres; primary-outcome data were available for 443 testosterone and 413 placebo participants.
cards.result: At 2 years, a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (≈200 mg/dL) or higher was reported in 55 of 443 men (12%) on testosterone and 87 of 413 (21%) on placebo (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.80; p=0.0007) — a relative reduction of about 41%, or 9 percentage points absolute. Mean change in 2-hour glucose was -1.70 mmol/L (≈-31 mg/dL) (SD 2.47) on testosterone versus -0.95 mmol/L (≈-17 mg/dL) (SD 2.78) on placebo (mean difference -0.75 mmol/L (≈-14 mg/dL), 95% CI -1.10 to -0.40; p<0.0001). The treatment effect was independent of baseline serum testosterone. A relative risk of 0.59 lies inside the 0.5-2.0 band that is not, by itself, solid evidence.
cards.watchOut: Single trial; the endpoint mixes prevention in men with impaired glucose tolerance and reversion in men with newly diagnosed diabetes, and about 15% of randomised men lacked primary-outcome data. Safety triggers: haematocrit above 54% in 106 of 491 men (22%) on testosterone versus 6 of 484 (1%) on placebo; serious adverse events in 55 of 504 (10.9%) versus 37 of 503 (7.4%).
cards.source: Wittert G et al. Testosterone treatment to prevent or revert type 2 diabetes in men enrolled in a lifestyle programme (T4DM): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 2-year, phase 3b trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2021 Jan;9(1):32-45. PMID: 33338415. cards.summary: One trial, a headline ratio inside the 0.5–2.0 not-solid band, and durability unknown — POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: The older anti-obesity drugs: phentermine–topiramate and naltrexone–bupropion
shelves.question: How much weight do the pre-GLP-1 oral agents lose versus placebo — and what did their safety programmes show (CONQUER/EQUIP; COR-I/LIGHT-era trials)?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage · Comorbidity · Drug Combinations · Fructose/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Obesity/drug therapy · Overweight/drug therapy · Phentermine/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for weight loss versus placebo; no cardiovascular-benefit claim is made): Two large double-blind phase 3 trials anchor the shelf. CONQUER (2,487 randomised) found weight change at 56 weeks of −1.2% on placebo versus −7.8% and −9.8% on the two phentermine–topiramate doses, with at least 5% loss in 21% versus 62% and 70%. COR-I (1,742 randomised) found −1.3% on placebo versus −6.1% and −5.0% on the two naltrexone–bupropion doses, with at least 5% loss in 16% versus 48% and 39%. Safety is printed on both cards. On the cardiovascular question the shelf is explicit: naltrexone–bupropion's cardiovascular-outcomes trial (LIGHT) was terminated early, so no cardiovascular benefit or safety verdict is claimed or implied here — the shelf is a weight-loss shelf, and the incretin-era agents have their own shelves in the diabetes slates.

cards.headline: CONQUER 2011: phentermine–topiramate lost 7.8% and 9.8% of bodyweight versus 1.2% on placebo at 56 weeks
cards.summary: CONQUER 2011: phentermine–topiramate lost 7.8% and 9.8% of bodyweight vs 1.2% on placebo at 56 weeks.
cards.people: 2,487 overweight or obese adults (aged 18–70 years, body-mass index 27–45 kg/m2, with at least two comorbidities such as hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes or prediabetes, or abdominal obesity) at 93 US centres, randomised to placebo (994), phentermine 7.5 mg plus topiramate 46 mg (498), or phentermine 15 mg plus topiramate 92 mg (995), once daily with diet and lifestyle modification for 56 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Change in bodyweight at 56 weeks was −1.4 kg (least-squares mean −1.2%, 95% confidence interval −1.8 to −0.7) on placebo, −8.1 kg (−7.8%, −8.5 to −7.1) on the lower dose and −10.2 kg (−9.8%, −10.4 to −9.3) on the higher dose (p<0.0001 for both). At least 5% weight loss was achieved by 204 (21%) on placebo, 303 (62%) on the lower dose (odds ratio 6.3, 4.9 to 8.0 — a relative measure) and 687 (70%) on the higher dose (odds ratio 9.0, 7.3 to 11.1); at least 10% loss by 7%, 37% and 48% respectively. The most common adverse events were dry mouth (2%, 13%, 21% across the groups), paraesthesia (2%, 14%, 21%), constipation, insomnia, dizziness and dysgeusia; depression-related adverse events occurred in 4%, 4% and 7%, and anxiety-related events in 3%, 5% and 8%.
cards.watchOut: A comorbidity-enriched population (everyone had at least two risk factors) and a combination containing a stimulant and topiramate: the adverse-event gradient (paraesthesia and dry mouth reaching one in five at the top dose) is part of the prescription decision.
cards.source: Gadde KM et al. Effects of low-dose, controlled-release, phentermine plus topiramate combination on weight and associated comorbidities in overweight and obese adults (CONQUER): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2011;377(9774):1341-52. PMID: 21481449. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00553787, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: COR-I 2010: naltrexone–bupropion lost 6.1% and 5.0% of bodyweight versus 1.3% on placebo at 56 weeks — with nausea in about three of ten treated patients
cards.summary: COR-I 2010: naltrexone–bupropion lost 6.1% and 5.0% of bodyweight vs 1.3% on placebo at 56 weeks — with nausea in about three of ten treated patients. (The LIGHT cardiovascular trial's termination is stated on the shelf; no cardiovascular claim is made.)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
cards.people: 1,742 participants (men and women aged 18–65 years, body-mass index 30–45 kg/m2, or 27–45 with dyslipidaemia or hypertension) at 34 US sites, randomised to naltrexone 32 mg plus bupropion 360 mg daily (583), naltrexone 16 mg plus bupropion 360 mg (578), or placebo (581), with a mild hypocaloric diet and exercise advice for 56 weeks; 870 (50%) completed treatment and 1,453 (83%) were included in the primary analysis. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean change in bodyweight was −1.3% (SE 0.3) on placebo, −6.1% (0.3) on naltrexone 32 mg plus bupropion and −5.0% (0.3) on the 16 mg combination (p<0.0001 versus placebo for both). A decrease in bodyweight of at least 5% was achieved by 84 (16%) on placebo, 226 (48%) on the higher dose and 186 (39%) on the lower dose. The most frequent adverse event on combination treatment was nausea (29.8% and 27.2% versus 5.3% on placebo); headache, constipation, dizziness, vomiting and dry mouth were also more frequent. A transient rise of about 1.5 mm Hg in mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure was followed by a fall of about 1 mm Hg below baseline. Combination treatment was not associated with increased depression or suicidality events compared with placebo.
cards.watchOut: Only half the participants completed 56 weeks, and the analysis is last-observation-carried-forward in a modified intention-to-treat set — the weight figures are the trial's own, read with its attrition in view. The blood-pressure blip also matters: this combination's cardiovascular-outcomes trial was terminated early (stated in the balance), so no cardiovascular safety conclusion can be drawn from COR-I.
cards.source: Greenway FL et al. Effect of naltrexone plus bupropion on weight loss in overweight and obese adults (COR-I): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9741):595-605. PMID: 20673995. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00532779, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both pre-GLP-1 combinations beat placebo by roughly 4–9 percentage points of bodyweight — LIKELY for weight loss, silent on cardiovascular outcomes
cards.summary: Both pre-GLP-1 combinations beat placebo by roughly 4–9 percentage points of bodyweight — LIKELY for weight loss, silent on cardiovascular outcomes.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CONQUER (2,487 randomised) and COR-I (1,742 randomised).
cards.result: Placebo-subtracted weight loss at 56 weeks was about 6.6 and 8.6 percentage points for the two phentermine–topiramate doses and about 4.8 and 3.7 points for the two naltrexone–bupropion doses, with 5%-responder rates two to three times placebo in both programmes. The safety profiles differ in kind — stimulant/topiramate effects (dry mouth, paraesthesia) versus opioid-antagonist/bupropion effects (nausea in ~28–30%) — and neither trial tested a hard outcome. Incretin-era agents are deliberately not compared here; they have their own shelves.
cards.watchOut: Cross-trial subtraction between CONQUER and COR-I is not a head-to-head comparison: populations, completion rates (COR-I 50%) and analyses differ.

shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibitors as add-on in type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: Does adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to insulin in type 1 diabetes improve HbA1c and weight — at what ketoacidosis cost (DEPICT-1 dapagliflozin; EASE empagliflozin)?
shelves.mesh: Benzhydryl Compounds/therapeutic use · Body Weight/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucosides/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced
shelves.balance: Split, both halves LIKELY on concordant phase 3 programmes. Benefit: DEPICT-1 (778 in the efficacy set) found HbA1c reductions versus placebo of −0.42% (5 mg) and −0.45% (10 mg) at 24 weeks with dapagliflozin; the EASE programme (1,707 participants) found placebo-subtracted HbA1c reductions of −0.28% (2.5 mg), −0.54% (10 mg) and −0.53% (25 mg) with empagliflozin, plus weight loss of 1.8 to 3.4 kg and more glucose time-in-range, without increased hypoglycaemia. Harm: adjudicated diabetic ketoacidosis in DEPICT-1 occurred in 1–2% on dapagliflozin versus 1% on placebo, and in EASE in 4.3% (10 mg) and 3.3% (25 mg) on empagliflozin versus 1.2% on placebo, while the 2.5 mg dose was comparable to placebo (0.8%). No cardiovascular-benefit claim is made on this shelf — the benefit claimed is glycaemic and weight, and the ketoacidosis cost is printed on the shelf face, as drafted.

cards.headline: DEPICT-1 2017: dapagliflozin cut HbA1c by 0.42–0.45 percentage points versus placebo at 24 weeks — definite ketoacidosis in 1–2% versus 1%
cards.summary: DEPICT-1 2017: dapagliflozin cut HbA1c by 0.42–0.45 percentage points vs placebo at 24 weeks — definite ketoacidosis in 1–2% vs 1%.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, parallel-controlled, three-arm phase 3 trial
cards.people: Adults aged 18–75 years with inadequately controlled type 1 diabetes (HbA1c at least 7.7% and at most 11.0%) on insulin for at least 12 months, at 143 sites in 17 countries: 833 patients were included in safety analyses (dapagliflozin 5 mg 277, 10 mg 296, placebo 260) and 778 randomly assigned patients in the full efficacy analysis set (259, 259, 260 — the difference reflects a randomisation error affecting 55 patients, disclosed in the report); mean baseline HbA1c was 8.53% (SD 0.67). The abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, dapagliflozin reduced HbA1c versus placebo by a mean difference of −0.42% (95% confidence interval −0.56 to −0.28) at 5 mg and −0.45% (−0.58 to −0.31) at 10 mg (both p<0.0001). Hypoglycaemia occurred in 79%, 79% and 80% of the 5 mg, 10 mg and placebo groups, with severe hypoglycaemia in 8%, 6% and 7%. Adjudicated definite diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in four patients (1%) on 5 mg, five (2%) on 10 mg and three (1%) on placebo. The most common adverse events were nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection, upper respiratory tract infection and headache, at similar rates across groups.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week glycaemic endpoint in a trial that itself flags a randomisation error (55 patients non-randomly allocated, included in safety only): the HbA1c effect is consistent with EASE, but the ketoacidosis counts are small and imprecise at this horizon.
cards.source: Dandona P et al. Efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in patients with inadequately controlled type 1 diabetes (DEPICT-1): 24 week results from a multicentre, double-blind, phase 3, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(11):864-876. PMID: 28919061. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02268214, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: EASE 2018: empagliflozin cut HbA1c by up to 0.54 points and weight by up to 3.4 kg — ketoacidosis 4.3% and 3.3% at 10/25 mg versus 1.2% on placebo
cards.summary: EASE 2018: empagliflozin cut HbA1c by up to 0.54 points and weight by up to 3.4 kg — ketoacidosis 4.3% and 3.3% at 10/25 mg vs 1.2% on placebo.
cards.type: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported together (EASE-2, 52 weeks; EASE-3, 26 weeks)
cards.people: 1,707 participants with type 1 diabetes on intensified insulin: EASE-2 randomised empagliflozin 10 mg (243), 25 mg (244) and placebo (243); EASE-3 randomised empagliflozin 2.5 mg (241), 10 mg (248), 25 mg (245) and placebo (241). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The largest mean placebo-subtracted HbA1c reductions were −0.28% (95% confidence interval −0.42 to −0.15) for 2.5 mg, −0.54% (−0.65 to −0.42) for 10 mg and −0.53% (−0.65 to −0.42) for 25 mg (all P<0.0001). Empagliflozin 2.5/10/25 mg reduced mean weight by 1.8/3.0/3.4 kg, increased glucose time-in-range by 1.0/2.9/3.1 hours per day, lowered total daily insulin dose by 6.4/13.3/12.7% and decreased systolic blood pressure by 2.1/3.9/3.7 mmHg. Genital infections occurred more frequently on empagliflozin. Adjudicated diabetic ketoacidosis occurred more with empagliflozin 10 mg (4.3%) and 25 mg (3.3%), was comparable between 2.5 mg (0.8%) and placebo (1.2%), and severe hypoglycaemia was rare and similar between groups. The authors note ketone monitoring and lower doses may help reduce the ketoacidosis risk.
cards.watchOut: The dose pattern cuts both ways: the doses with the largest HbA1c and weight effects (10/25 mg) are the doses with the clearly raised ketoacidosis rates, while the dose with placebo-like ketoacidosis (2.5 mg) had the smallest glycaemic effect (−0.28%).
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Empagliflozin as Adjunctive to Insulin Therapy in Type 1 Diabetes: The EASE Trials. Diabetes Care. 2018;41(12):2560-2569. PMID: 30287422. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02414958 and NCT02580591, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest glycaemic gain, priced in ketoacidosis at full doses — the split is the shelf
cards.summary: A real but modest glycaemic gain, priced in ketoacidosis at full doses — split LIKELY benefit / LIKELY harm.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DEPICT-1 (778 in the efficacy set) and the EASE programme (1,707 participants).
cards.result: Two drugs, two programmes, one pattern: HbA1c falls by roughly 0.3–0.5 percentage points, weight by up to about 3.4 kg, insulin dose and time-in-range improve, hypoglycaemia does not increase — and ketoacidosis rises at the type-2-diabetes doses (EASE: 4.3% and 3.3% vs 1.2% on placebo) while looking placebo-like at empagliflozin 2.5 mg (0.8%), the dose with the smallest benefit. Nothing here extends the type 2 diabetes cardiovascular story into type 1 diabetes: no cardiovascular or mortality outcome was tested in these programmes, and none is claimed.
cards.watchOut: Euglycaemic ketoacidosis is the trap this class sets in type 1 diabetes — patients can be seriously ketoacidotic without high glucose readings; the trials' own mitigation (ketone monitoring, lower doses) belongs in any clinical use of these figures.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dandona P et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017;5(11):864-876. PMID: 28919061; Rosenstock J et al. Diabetes Care. 2018;41(12):2560-2569. PMID: 30287422. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Continuous glucose monitoring in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes treated with insulin — basal insulin in primary care, or multiple daily injections — does continuous glucose monitoring improve A1c versus finger-stick monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Confidence Intervals · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,drug therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Glycemic Control/methods · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials in three insulin-treated type 2 diabetes populations point the same way. MOBILE (basal insulin, primary care) found A1c 0.4 percentage points lower with CGM at 8 months; the DIAMOND type 2 study (multiple daily injections) found 0.3 points lower at 24 weeks; and the 2026 FreeDM2 trial (basal insulin plus modern agents, UK primary and secondary care) found 0.6 points lower at 16 weeks, sustained at 32 weeks. The gains are modest and consistent, bought with a device patients must wear — the trials agree on direction and rough size, which is what carries the stamp.

cards.headline: MOBILE 2021: in basal-insulin type 2 diabetes managed in primary care, CGM lowered A1c by 0.4 points more than meter monitoring at 8 months
cards.summary: MOBILE (2021): in basal-insulin type 2 diabetes managed in primary care, CGM lowered A1c by 0.4 points more than meter monitoring at 8 months.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (2:1 allocation) in 15 US primary care centres
cards.people: 175 adults with type 2 diabetes treated with 1 or 2 daily injections of long- or intermediate-acting basal insulin without prandial insulin, randomised to CGM (116) or blood glucose meter monitoring (59); mean age 57 (SD 9) years; 88 women (50%); mean baseline HbA1c 9.1% (SD 0.9%); 165 (94%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell from 9.1% to 8.0% with CGM and from 9.0% to 8.4% with meter monitoring (adjusted difference −0.4% [95% CI, −0.8% to −0.1%]; P = .02). CGM-measured time in the target range of 70 to 180 mg/dL was 59% vs 43% (adjusted difference 15% [8% to 23%]; P < .001), time above 250 mg/dL was 11% vs 27% (adjusted difference −16% [−21% to −11%]; P < .001), and mean glucose was 179 vs 206 mg/dL (adjusted difference −26 mg/dL [−41 to −12]; P < .001). Severe hypoglycaemic events occurred in 1 participant (1%) in the CGM group and 1 (2%) in the meter group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label device trial in patients with poorly controlled diabetes (mean baseline A1c 9.1%): the absolute gain available to a better-controlled basal-insulin population is likely smaller, and the trial was not powered for hypoglycaemia or complications.
cards.source: Martens T et al. Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Treated With Basal Insulin: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021;325(22):2262-2272. PMID: 34077499. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03566693, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DIAMOND-T2D 2017: in multiple-daily-injection type 2 diabetes, CGM lowered A1c by 0.3 points more than usual care at 24 weeks
cards.summary: DIAMOND-T2D (2017): in multiple-daily-injection type 2 diabetes, CGM lowered A1c by 0.3 points more than usual care at 24 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial at 25 endocrinology practices in North America
cards.people: 158 adults with type 2 diabetes for a median of 17 years (IQR 11 to 23), receiving multiple daily insulin injections, with HbA1c 7.5% to 9.9% (mean 8.5%), randomised to CGM (79) or usual care (79); mean age 60 years (SD 10); the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c decreased to 7.7% in the CGM group and 8.0% in the control group at 24 weeks (adjusted difference in mean change, −0.3% [95% CI, −0.5% to 0.0%]; P = 0.022). The groups did not differ meaningfully in CGM-measured hypoglycaemia or quality-of-life outcomes. The CGM group averaged 6.7 days (SD 0.9) of CGM use per week.
cards.watchOut: Specialist-practice population on intensive insulin, with the confidence interval for the A1c difference reaching 0.0: a real but small average effect, in the population with the most injections to adjust.

cards.summary: CGM buys a consistent 0.3–0.6 point A1c advantage across the insulin-treated type 2 spectrum — LIKELY.

shelves.title: Oral semaglutide: the PIONEER glycaemic trials
shelves.question: Does once-daily oral semaglutide lower A1c versus sitagliptin (PIONEER 3) and versus injectable liraglutide (PIONEER 4) in type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1/agonists · Glucagon-Like Peptides/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind phase 3 trials show once-daily oral semaglutide is a real glycaemic drug, not a convenience formulation. PIONEER 3: the 7 mg and 14 mg doses beat sitagliptin on A1c at 26 weeks (−0.3 and −0.5 percentage points) with more weight loss; the 3 mg dose did not reach noninferiority. PIONEER 4: oral semaglutide 14 mg was noninferior to injectable liraglutide 1.8 mg on A1c and superior on weight. This shelf is glycaemic efficacy only — the oral semaglutide cardiovascular-outcomes evidence lives on Shelf #356 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: PIONEER 3 2019: oral semaglutide 7 mg and 14 mg beat sitagliptin on A1c and weight at 26 weeks; the 3 mg dose did not
cards.summary: PIONEER 3 (2019): oral semaglutide 7 mg and 14 mg beat sitagliptin on A1c and weight at 26 weeks; the 3 mg dose did not.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group phase 3a trial at 206 sites in 14 countries, 78 weeks
cards.people: 1864 adults with type 2 diabetes uncontrolled with metformin with or without sulfonylurea, randomised to oral semaglutide 3 mg (466), 7 mg (466) or 14 mg (465), or sitagliptin 100 mg (467); mean age 58 (SD 10) years; 879 women (47.2%); mean baseline HbA1c 8.3% (SD 0.9%); 1758 (94.3%) completed the trial.
cards.result: At week 26, semaglutide 7 mg and 14 mg reduced HbA1c significantly more than sitagliptin (differences −0.3% [95% CI, −0.4% to −0.1%] and −0.5% [−0.6% to −0.4%]; P < .001 for both) and reduced body weight more (differences −1.6 kg [−2.0 to −1.1 kg] and −2.5 kg [−3.0 to −2.0 kg]; P < .001 for both). Noninferiority of semaglutide 3 mg with respect to HbA1c was not demonstrated. At week 78, reductions in both endpoints remained significantly greater with semaglutide 14 mg than with sitagliptin. Premature treatment discontinuation was 16.7% (3 mg), 15.0% (7 mg), 19.1% (14 mg) and 13.1% (sitagliptin).
cards.watchOut: Sitagliptin is a weak comparator by modern standards: beating it establishes efficacy, not advantage over other GLP-1 agents or SGLT2 inhibitors. Discontinuation ran higher on semaglutide than on sitagliptin at every dose.

cards.headline: PIONEER 4 2019: oral semaglutide was noninferior to injectable liraglutide on A1c and superior on weight at 26 weeks
cards.summary: PIONEER 4 (2019): oral semaglutide was noninferior to injectable liraglutide on A1c and superior on weight at 26 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy phase 3a trial at 100 sites in 12 countries, 52 weeks
cards.people: 711 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–9.5%) on stable metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor, randomly assigned to oral semaglutide escalated to 14 mg (285), subcutaneous liraglutide escalated to 1.8 mg (284), or placebo (142); 341 (48%) female; mean age 56 years (SD 10).
cards.result: Mean change in HbA1c at week 26 was −1.2% (SE 0.1) with oral semaglutide, −1.1% (SE 0.1) with liraglutide and −0.2% (SE 0.1) with placebo. Oral semaglutide was non-inferior to liraglutide (estimated treatment difference −0.1%, 95% CI −0.3 to 0.0; p<0.0001) and superior to placebo (ETD −1.1%, −1.2 to −0.9; p<0.0001) on the treatment-policy estimand. Weight loss at week 26 was −4.4 kg (SE 0.2) with oral semaglutide, versus −3.1 kg (SE 0.2) with liraglutide (ETD −1.2 kg, −1.9 to −0.6; p=0.0003) and −0.5 kg (SE 0.3) with placebo (ETD −3.8 kg, −4.7 to −3.0; p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 80% on oral semaglutide, 74% on liraglutide and 67% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The liraglutide comparator dose was 1.8 mg, the diabetes dose — this trial says nothing about oral semaglutide against weekly injectable semaglutide, which is the comparison prescribers usually mean.

cards.headline: Synthesis: oral semaglutide lowers A1c like an injectable GLP-1 agent — LIKELY, on glycaemic endpoints only
cards.summary: Oral semaglutide lowers A1c like an injectable GLP-1 agent — LIKELY, on glycaemic endpoints only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PIONEER 3 (1864 adults, vs sitagliptin) and PIONEER 4 (711 adults, vs liraglutide and placebo).
cards.result: Across two double-blind trials, oral semaglutide 14 mg produced A1c reductions of about 1.2 percentage points in the trial populations, beat a DPP-4 inhibitor, matched an injectable GLP-1 agent on A1c and beat it modestly on weight (−1.2 kg difference). shelves.title: Tirzepatide versus semaglutide, head to head
shelves.question: In direct head-to-head trials, how much more do patients gain — on A1c in type 2 diabetes (SURPASS-2, vs semaglutide 1 mg) and on weight in obesity without diabetes (SURMOUNT-5, vs semaglutide 2.4 mg) — with tirzepatide than with semaglutide?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Glucagon-Like Peptides/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the only two direct head-to-head randomised trials, tirzepatide beat semaglutide in both populations tested. In type 2 diabetes (SURPASS-2, against semaglutide 1 mg weekly), tirzepatide lowered A1c by a further 0.15–0.45 percentage points across its dose range and took off 1.9–5.5 kg more weight. In obesity without diabetes (SURMOUNT-5, against semaglutide up to 2.4 mg), weight loss at 72 weeks was −20.2% versus −13.7%. Both trials were open-label — patients knew which drug they were on — and gastrointestinal adverse events were common on both drugs; neither caveat reverses differences of this size.

cards.headline: SURPASS-2 2021: tirzepatide beat semaglutide 1 mg on A1c at every dose in type 2 diabetes, and on weight by 1.9–5.5 kg
cards.summary: SURPASS-2 (2021): tirzepatide beat semaglutide 1 mg on A1c at every dose in type 2 diabetes, and on weight by 1.9–5.5 kg .
cards.people: 1879 patients with type 2 diabetes randomly assigned to tirzepatide 5 mg, 10 mg or 15 mg, or semaglutide 1 mg, once weekly for 40 weeks; at baseline the mean glycated hemoglobin level was 8.28%, mean age 56.6 years, and mean weight 93.7 kg; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Estimated mean change in glycated hemoglobin was −2.01, −2.24 and −2.30 percentage points with tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg, and −1.86 with semaglutide; estimated differences versus semaglutide were −0.15 percentage points (95% CI, −0.28 to −0.03; P = 0.02), −0.39 (−0.51 to −0.26; P<0.001) and −0.45 (−0.57 to −0.32; P<0.001). Tirzepatide at all doses was noninferior and superior to semaglutide. Weight reductions were greater with tirzepatide (least-squares mean differences −1.9 kg, −3.6 kg and −5.5 kg; P<0.001 for all). Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events (nausea 17–22% tirzepatide vs 18% semaglutide; diarrhoea 13–16% vs 12%; vomiting 6–10% vs 8%). Hypoglycaemia (glucose <54 mg/dL) was reported in 0.6%, 0.2% and 1.7% on tirzepatide doses and 0.4% on semaglutide. Serious adverse events occurred in 5–7% on tirzepatide and 3% on semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: The semaglutide comparator was 1 mg weekly — half the 2 mg dose later approved for diabetes — so this trial does not measure tirzepatide against semaglutide's maximum glycaemic dose. Open-label design.
cards.source: Frías JP et al. Tirzepatide versus Semaglutide Once Weekly in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2021;385(6):503-515. PMID: 34170647. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03987919, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SURMOUNT-5 2025: in obesity without diabetes, tirzepatide lost 20.2% of body weight versus 13.7% on semaglutide at 72 weeks
cards.summary: SURMOUNT-5 (2025): in obesity without diabetes, tirzepatide lost 20.2% of body weight versus 13.7% on semaglutide at 72 weeks.
cards.people: 751 adult participants with obesity but without type 2 diabetes, randomly assigned to the maximum tolerated dose of tirzepatide (10 mg or 15 mg) or semaglutide (1.7 mg or 2.4 mg) once weekly for 72 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.

shelves.title: Insulin glargine 300 U/mL versus glargine 100 U/mL (EDITION 1 and 2)
shelves.question: Does the more concentrated glargine 300 U/mL control glucose as well as glargine 100 U/mL with less hypoglycaemia — in type 2 diabetes on basal-plus-mealtime insulin (EDITION 1) and on basal insulin with oral agents (EDITION 2)?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced,epidemiology · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — equal glycaemic control · POSSIBLE — less nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Two large open-label trials (EDITION 1, basal-plus-mealtime insulin; EDITION 2, basal insulin with oral agents) found glargine 300 U/mL and glargine 100 U/mL lowered HbA1c identically (differences −0.00% and −0.01%). Both also found fewer participants with nocturnal confirmed or severe hypoglycaemia on the 300 U/mL formulation (36% vs 46% and a relative risk of 0.77) — but relative risks of 0.79 and 0.77 sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid on their own, so the hypoglycaemia advantage is stamped POSSIBLE even though two trials agree on it.

cards.headline: EDITION 1 2014: glargine 300 U/mL matched glargine 100 U/mL on A1c, with fewer participants having nocturnal hypoglycaemia (36% vs 46%)
cards.summary: EDITION 1 (2014): glargine 300 U/mL matched glargine 100 U/mL on A1c, with fewer participants having nocturnal hypoglycaemia ( 36% vs 46% ).
cards.type: 6-month, multinational, open-label, parallel-group randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 807 people with type 2 diabetes on basal insulin (≥42 units/day) plus mealtime insulin, randomised to glargine 300 U/mL or glargine 100 U/mL once daily for 6 months; mean age 60 years, diabetes duration 16 years, BMI 36.6 kg/m2, HbA1c 8.15%; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: HbA1c reduction was equivalent between regimens: least squares mean difference −0.00% (95% CI −0.11 to 0.11). Fewer participants reported one or more confirmed (≤3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL)) or severe nocturnal hypoglycaemic events between week 9 and month 6 with glargine 300 (36% vs 46% with glargine 100; relative risk 0.79 [95% CI 0.67–0.93]; P < 0.005 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it above); nocturnal hypoglycaemia incidence and event rates were also lower in the first 8 weeks. No between-treatment differences in tolerability or safety were identified.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the hypoglycaemia relative risk of 0.79 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band: the absolute gap (36% vs 46% of participants over ~4 months) is the honest way to state the advantage.
cards.source: Riddle MC et al. cards.summary: EDITION 2 (2014): on basal insulin with oral agents, glargine 300 U/mL again matched A1c and lowered nocturnal hypoglycaemia (relative risk 0.77 ).

cards.people: 811 people with type 2 diabetes using basal insulin (≥42 units/day) plus oral antihyperglycaemic drugs, randomised to glargine 300 U/mL or glargine 100 U/mL once daily for 6 months; mean (SD) HbA1c 8.24% (0.82) and BMI 34.8 kg/m2 (6.4); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.

shelves.title: Nasal glucagon for severe hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: Does glucagon given as a nasal powder rescue insulin-induced hypoglycaemia as reliably as intramuscular glucagon — in adults, and in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Cohort Studies · Cross-Over Studies · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised crossover trial in adults found nasal glucagon 3 mg non-inferior to intramuscular glucagon 1 mg for reversing insulin-induced hypoglycaemia — every participant in the efficacy analysis succeeded on both routes. A small phase 1 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study in children and adolescents aged 4 to <17 years found the same glucose rise with nasal powder. That is one pivotal efficacy trial plus one small dose-finding study, in induced (not spontaneous) hypoglycaemia with study staff giving the dose — enough for POSSIBLE that the nose rescues as reliably as the muscle, not yet LIKELY.

cards.headline: Suico 2020: nasal glucagon 3 mg was non-inferior to intramuscular glucagon — 100% treatment success on both routes in adults
cards.summary: Nasal glucagon trial (2020): nasal glucagon 3 mg was non-inferior to intramuscular glucagon — 100% treatment success on both routes in adults.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, two-period crossover trial at two clinical sites
cards.people: 66 adults with type 1 diabetes included in the primary efficacy analysis, each receiving both nasal glucagon 3 mg and intramuscular glucagon 1 mg in a two-period crossover during insulin-induced hypoglycaemia (plasma glucose target <3.3 mmol/L [60 mg/dL]), with glucagon given by study staff; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: All 66 participants (100%) achieved treatment success — plasma glucose rising to ≥3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) or by ≥1.1 mmol/L (20 mg/dL) from nadir within 30 minutes — on both routes, demonstrating non-inferiority of nasal to intramuscular glucagon. All participants achieved success within 25 minutes; mean time to success was 11.4 minutes (nasal) and 9.9 minutes (intramuscular). No serious adverse events occurred. Treatment-emergent adverse events numbered 48 after nasal and 51 after intramuscular glucagon, mostly mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: Hypoglycaemia was induced in a clinic and the dose was given by study staff: the trial proves the drug works by the nasal route, not that a frightened family member will deliver it as fast at home — which is the real-world bet the formulation makes.
cards.source: Suico JG et al. Glucagon Administration by Nasal and Intramuscular Routes in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes During Insulin-Induced Hypoglycaemia: A Randomised, Open-Label, Crossover Study. Diabetes Ther. 2020;11(7):1591-1603. PMID: 32514794. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03339453, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Sherr 2016: in youth aged 4 to <17 years, nasal glucagon powder raised glucose as reliably as intramuscular glucagon
cards.summary: Nasal glucagon in youth (2016): raised glucose as reliably as intramuscular glucagon (58 of 59 intranasal doses met the rise criterion).
cards.type: Phase 1 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic randomised study at seven clinical centres
cards.people: 48 youth with type 1 diabetes at seven clinical centres: the two youngest cohorts (4 to <8 and 8 to <12 years) were randomly assigned to 2 or 3 mg intranasal glucagon in two sessions or a single weight-based intramuscular dose; participants aged 12 to <17 years received 1 mg intramuscular glucagon in one session and 3 mg intranasal in the other. Glucose was lowered to <80 mg/dL (mean nadir 67–75 mg/dL).
cards.result: All 24 intramuscular and 58 of 59 intranasal doses produced a ≥25 mg/dL rise in glucose from nadir within 20 minutes of dosing. Times to peak plasma glucose and glucagon levels were similar for both routes. Transient nausea occurred in 67% of intramuscular sessions versus 42% of intranasal sessions (P = 0.05). The 2 mg and 3 mg intranasal doses performed similarly in the youngest cohorts, supporting a single 3 mg intranasal dose across ages 4 to <17 years.
cards.watchOut: A phase 1 dose-finding study, not a powered efficacy trial: it supports the adult noninferiority result in children but cannot carry the shelf on its own.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the nose works as well as the muscle in induced hypoglycaemia — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: The nose works as well as the muscle in induced hypoglycaemia — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Suico 2020 (66 adults, crossover, induced hypoglycaemia) and Sherr 2016 (48 youth, phase 1 pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study).
cards.result: In adults, nasal glucagon matched intramuscular glucagon exactly on the success endpoint (66 of 66 on both routes), at the cost of about 1.5 minutes' slower mean time to success (11.4 vs 9.9 minutes). In youth, 58 of 59 intranasal doses produced the target glucose rise within 20 minutes. One pivotal trial plus one small supporting study, both in experimentally induced hypoglycaemia with staff administration, caps this shelf at POSSIBLE under the library's single-pivotal-trial rule.

shelves.title: Closed-loop insulin delivery for type 2 diabetes: hospital and home
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does fully closed-loop insulin delivery keep glucose in range better than conventional insulin therapy — in hospital inpatients on general wards, and in outpatients at home?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,drug therapy · Hospitalization · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Infusions, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage · Insulin Infusion Systems/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In hospital, one open-label randomised trial (Bally 2018, 136 inpatients on general wards) found fully closed-loop delivery put sensor glucose in range 65.8% of the time versus 41.5% on conventional subcutaneous therapy, with no difference in hypoglycaemia exposure. Out of hospital, one small single-centre crossover trial (Daly 2023, 28 randomised adults) found the same direction, much larger: 66.3% versus 32.3% time in range over 8-week periods. Each setting rests on a single trial — the inpatient one moderately sized, the outpatient one small — so the shelf is POSSIBLE in both settings, with the direction consistent.

cards.headline: Bally 2018: on general wards, closed-loop delivery kept glucose in range 65.8% of the time versus 41.5% on conventional insulin therapy
cards.summary: Closed-loop delivery on general wards (2018): kept glucose in range 65.8% of the time versus 41.5% on conventional insulin therapy.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial on general wards in two tertiary hospitals
cards.people: 136 adults with type 2 diabetes requiring subcutaneous insulin therapy on general wards in two tertiary hospitals (UK and Switzerland), assigned to closed-loop insulin delivery (70) or conventional subcutaneous insulin therapy (66), for up to 15 days or until discharge; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The mean percentage of time sensor glucose was in the target range of 100 to 180 mg/dL was 65.8% (SD 16.8) in the closed-loop group and 41.5% (SD 16.9) in the control group — a difference of 24.3 percentage points (95% CI, 18.6 to 30.0; P<0.001). Time above range was 23.6% versus 49.5% (difference 25.9 points [19.2 to 32.7]; P<0.001), and mean glucose was 154 vs 188 mg/dL (P<0.001). There was no significant difference in the duration of hypoglycaemia (sensor glucose <54 mg/dL; P=0.80) or in insulin delivered (median 44.4 U vs 40.2 U; P=0.50). No episode of severe hypoglycaemia or clinically significant hyperglycaemia with ketonaemia occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: A glucose-control (surrogate) endpoint over at most 15 days in two tertiary centres with research support: the trial does not show fewer infections, shorter stays, or any clinical outcome benefit, and ward staffing in the trial is not ward staffing in general.
cards.source: Bally L et al. Closed-Loop Insulin Delivery for Glycemic Control in Noncritical Care. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(6):547-556. PMID: 29940126. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01774565, from the record's databank fields.
