cards.headline: Daly 2023: at home, fully closed-loop delivery doubled time in range versus standard insulin therapy in a small crossover trial (66.3% vs 32.3%)
cards.summary: Closed-loop at home (2023): doubled time in range versus standard insulin therapy in a small crossover trial ( 66.3% vs 32.3% ).
cards.people: 26 adults with type 2 diabetes analysed (30 recruited, 28 randomised) — 7 women and 19 men among those described; mean age 59 years (SD 11); baseline HbA1c 9.0% (SD 1.4%) — each undergoing two 8-week periods of fully closed-loop delivery (CamAPS HX, no meal bolusing) and standard insulin therapy with a masked sensor, in random order.
cards.result: Time in the target range (3.9–10.0 mmol/L (≈70–180 mg/dL)) was 66.3% (SD 14.9) with closed-loop versus 32.3% (SD 24.7) with control (mean difference 35.3 percentage points [95% CI, 28.0–42.6]; P < 0.001). Mean glucose was 9.2 (SD 1.2) vs 12.6 (SD 3.0) mmol/L (≈166 vs 227 mg/dL) (difference −3.6 mmol/L (≈-65 mg/dL) [−4.6 to −2.5]; P < 0.001), and HbA1c was lower after closed-loop (7.3% [SD 0.8]) than after control (8.7% [SD 1.2]; difference −1.4% [−1.0 to −1.8]; P < 0.001). Time below 3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) was similar (median 0.44% vs 0.08%; P = 0.43). No severe hypoglycaemia occurred in either period; one treatment-related serious adverse event occurred during closed-loop.
cards.watchOut: Pinned at build as the topic file's 'outpatient confirmatory trial': it confirms direction, but with 28 randomised participants at one expert centre and a poorly controlled study population (baseline HbA1c 9.0%), its effect size should not be quoted as the expected real-world gain.

cards.headline: Synthesis: closed-loop beats conventional insulin delivery on time in range in both settings — POSSIBLE, one trial per setting
cards.summary: Closed-loop beats conventional insulin delivery on time in range in both settings — POSSIBLE, one trial per setting.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bally 2018 (136 hospital inpatients) and Daly 2023 (28 randomised outpatients, crossover).
cards.result: Both randomised comparisons favour fully closed-loop delivery by wide margins on time in range (+24.3 points inpatient, +35.3 points outpatient) with no increase in hypoglycaemia time in either. shelves.title: Dual-release hydrocortisone for adrenal insufficiency
shelves.question: Does once-daily dual-release hydrocortisone give a more physiological cortisol profile and better metabolic and quality-of-life outcomes than conventional thrice-daily hydrocortisone in adrenal insufficiency?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Insufficiency/blood,drug therapy,metabolism · Area Under Curve · Chemistry, Pharmaceutical · Cross-Over Studies · Delayed-Action Preparations · Hydrocortisone/administration & dosage,blood,metabolism,pharmacokinetics · Metabolome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A single randomised crossover programme supports once-daily dual-release hydrocortisone. Johannsson 2012 (64 adults with primary adrenal insufficiency) found the dual-release tablet gave a more circadian cortisol profile than the same daily dose split three times daily, with small metabolic gains at 12 weeks: weight −0.7 kg, systolic blood pressure −5.5 mm Hg, glycated hemoglobin −0.1% overall and −0.6% in the subgroup with diabetes. The programme's 5-year open-label extension (71 patients) found no safety signal, at the price of rising fasting glucose over the years. One randomised trial, small surrogate gains: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Johannsson 2012: dual-release hydrocortisone gave a more physiological cortisol profile and small metabolic gains versus thrice-daily tablets
cards.summary: Dual-release hydrocortisone trial (2012): gave a more physiological cortisol profile and small metabolic gains versus thrice-daily tablets.
cards.type: Open, randomised, two-period, 12-week crossover multicentre trial with a 24-week extension
cards.people: 64 adults with primary adrenal insufficiency (11 with concomitant diabetes mellitus), in an open, randomised, two-period 12-week crossover trial at five university hospital centres, receiving the same daily hydrocortisone dose as once-daily dual-release or conventional thrice-daily tablets, with a 24-week extension; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with thrice-daily dosing, once-daily dual-release provided a sustained serum cortisol profile 0–4 hours after the morning dose and reduced late-afternoon and 24-hour cortisol exposure. At 12 weeks, mean weight (difference −0.7 kg, P = 0.005), systolic blood pressure (difference −5.5 mm Hg, P = 0.0001), diastolic blood pressure (difference −2.3 mm Hg, P = 0.03) and glycated hemoglobin (absolute difference −0.1%, P = 0.0006) were all reduced on once-daily versus thrice-daily treatment. In patients with concomitant diabetes, glycated hemoglobin fell by 0.6% on once-daily treatment (P = 0.004).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 64 patients, 12-week periods, surrogate endpoints: the average glycated-hemoglobin gain (−0.1%) is clinically trivial outside the small diabetes subgroup (n = 11), where the −0.6% figure is a subgroup result in eleven people.
cards.source: Johannsson G et al. Improved cortisol exposure-time profile and outcome in patients with adrenal insufficiency: a prospective randomized trial of a novel hydrocortisone dual-release formulation. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2012;97(2):473-481. PMID: 22112807. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the record's abstract prints no registration number.

cards.headline: Nilsson 2017: five years of dual-release hydrocortisone showed no safety concern — and a slow rise in fasting glucose
cards.summary: Five-year extension (2017): no safety concern — and a slow rise in fasting glucose.
cards.people: 71 adult patients with primary adrenal insufficiency on stable glucocorticoid replacement, recruited at five Swedish university clinics into a prospective, open-label, 5-year extension study of once-daily dual-release hydrocortisone (total exposure 328 patient-treatment years); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Seventy patients reported 1060 adverse events (323 per 100 patient-years); 85% were considered unrelated to dual-release hydrocortisone. The most common were nasopharyngitis (70%), fatigue (52%) and gastroenteritis (48%). Of 65 serious adverse events in 32 patients (20 per 100 patient-years), four were considered possibly related: acute adrenal insufficiency (2), gastritis (1) and syncope (1). Two deaths were reported (fall from height and subarachnoid haemorrhage), both considered unrelated. Intercurrent illness episodes were relatively stable over 5 years (mean 2.6–5.4 per patient per year); fasting plasma glucose rose by 0.7 mmol/L (≈13 mg/dL) (P < 0.0001) and HDL cholesterol by 0.2 mmol/L (≈8 mg/dL) (P < 0.0001); quality-of-life total scores were unchanged, but physical functioning worsened (P = 0.008).
cards.watchOut: Pinned at build as the topic file's 'long-term safety follow-up of the same programme'. An extension study has no comparator: it can show a treatment is tolerated for five years, not that it beats the thrice-daily regimen it replaced — and its fasting glucose rose over the period.
cards.source: Nilsson AG et al. Long-term safety of once-daily, dual-release hydrocortisone in patients with adrenal insufficiency: a phase 3b, open-label, extension study. Eur J Endocrinol. 2017;176(6):715-725. PMID: 28292927. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is an open-label extension study and its record carries no databank registration field.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a more physiological profile and small metabolic gains, from one small crossover programme — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: A more physiological profile and small metabolic gains, from one small crossover programme — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Johannsson 2012 (64 adults, randomised crossover) and Nilsson 2017 (71 adults, 5-year open-label extension of the same programme).
cards.result: The randomised evidence is one 64-patient crossover trial: better cortisol timing, −0.7 kg, −5.5 mm Hg systolic, and a glycated-hemoglobin effect that matters only in the 11-patient diabetes subgroup. The extension adds five years of tolerability without a comparator. That is a reasonable basis for offering the formulation, and a thin basis for claiming outcome benefit — hence POSSIBLE. shelves.title: Oral octreotide capsules for acromegaly
shelves.question: In patients with acromegaly controlled on injectable somatostatin-receptor ligands, does switching to oral octreotide capsules maintain biochemical control versus placebo (OPTIMAL) and versus staying on injections (MPOWERED)?
shelves.mesh: Acromegaly/blood,diagnosis,drug therapy · Administration, Oral · Drug Substitution/adverse effects,methods · Human Growth Hormone/blood · Injections/adverse effects · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/analysis · Octreotide/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In patients already controlled on injectable somatostatin-receptor ligands, oral octreotide capsules maintain biochemical control. The double-blind OPTIMAL trial (56 patients) found IGF-1 normalisation maintained in 58.2% on oral octreotide versus 19.4% on placebo over 36 weeks. The open-label MPOWERED trial found oral octreotide noninferior to staying on injections — in the selected patients who had already responded during an oral-octreotide run-in (91% vs 100% maintaining response). Both trials enrol proven responders, and only one is blinded: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: OPTIMAL 2020: switching controlled patients to oral octreotide maintained IGF-1 control in 58.2% versus 19.4% on placebo
cards.summary: OPTIMAL (2020): switching controlled patients to oral octreotide maintained IGF-1 control in 58.2% versus 19.4% on placebo.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (CHIASMA OPTIMAL), 36 weeks
cards.people: 56 patients with acromegaly who had previously demonstrated biochemical control on injectable somatostatin-receptor ligands, stratified by prior ligand dose and randomly assigned 1:1 to oral octreotide capsules or placebo for 36 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean IGF-1 was 0.80 and 0.97 × the upper limit of normal (ULN) at baseline and end of treatment on oral octreotide, versus 0.84 and 1.69 × ULN on placebo. IGF-1 normalisation (≤1.0 × ULN) was maintained in 58.2% on oral octreotide versus 19.4% on placebo (P = .008); growth hormone was maintained (<2.5 ng/mL) in 77.7% versus 30.4% (P = .0007). Median time to loss of response on placebo was 16 weeks and was not reached on oral octreotide (P < .0001). 75% of the oral-octreotide group completed the trial on oral therapy. The safety profile was consistent with previous somatostatin-ligand experience.
cards.watchOut: Only 56 patients, all pre-selected for having achieved control on injections: the trial measures maintenance in responders, not the capsule's power to gain control in uncontrolled disease — and 42% of even these responders lost IGF-1 normalisation on the capsule.

cards.headline: MPOWERED 2022: oral octreotide was noninferior to injectable ligands for maintaining response — in patients who had already responded to the capsule in a run-in
cards.summary: MPOWERED (2022): oral octreotide was noninferior to injectable ligands for maintaining response — in patients who had already responded to the capsules.
cards.type: Open-label, randomised controlled phase 3 trial with a 26-week oral-octreotide run-in (MPOWERED)
cards.people: 92 participants randomly assigned (oral octreotide 55; injectable somatostatin-receptor ligands 37), drawn from 146 enrolled adults with acromegaly on injectable ligands for at least 6 months who entered a 26-week oral-octreotide run-in and completed it as biochemical responders (IGF-I <1.3 × ULN and mean integrated growth hormone <2.5 ng/mL); randomised phase conducted at 29 sites in 10 countries.
cards.result: Biochemical response was maintained throughout the randomised phase in 50 (91%) of 55 participants on oral octreotide and 37 (100%) of 37 on injectable ligands. The lower bound of the 95% CI for the adjusted difference (−19.9 to 0.5 percentage points) met the prespecified noninferiority criterion of −20 percentage points. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 19 (35%) of 55 on oral octreotide and 15 (41%) of 37 on injectables, most commonly gastrointestinal in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Pinned at build as the topic file's second phase 3 report. The noninferiority margin was a wide −20 percentage points, the point estimate favoured injections (91% vs 100%), and the randomised population had already proven it could respond to the capsule — 30 of 146 run-in entrants discontinued before randomisation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: oral octreotide maintains control in selected responders — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Oral octreotide maintains control in selected responders — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OPTIMAL (56 patients, double-blind, versus placebo) and MPOWERED (92 randomised patients, open-label, versus continued injections, after a responder run-in).
cards.result: The two trials answer complementary maintenance questions: against placebo, the capsule clearly holds control more often (58.2% vs 19.4% maintaining IGF-1 normalisation); against staying on injections, it is noninferior within a generous margin in run-in responders (91% vs 100%). Both populations were controlled on injections before switching, so the shelf supports switching stable patients who prefer capsules — not starting the capsule in uncontrolled disease. cards.watchOut: Quote the OPTIMAL maintenance rate whole: 58.2% maintained normalisation means roughly two in five switched responders lost it within 36 weeks and needed their injections back.

shelves.title: Structured education at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (DESMOND)
shelves.question: Does a single structured group education programme for people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (DESMOND) improve biomedical outcomes, illness beliefs, and lifestyle at one year — and do the effects persist at three years?
shelves.mesh: Attitude to Health · Body Weight · Cluster Analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/prevention & control · Diabetic Angiopathies/prevention & control · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — no A1c benefit (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE — short-term weight, smoking and illness-belief gains. DESMOND, a single six-hour structured group education course for people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, was tested in one large cluster trial (824 adults, 207 practices) with a three-year follow-up. It did not improve HbA1c at 12 months (adjusted difference 0.05%, CI spanning zero) or at three years (−0.02), and by three years the groups did not differ on any biomedical or lifestyle outcome. At 12 months the education group had lost more weight (−2.98 vs −1.86 kg), had higher odds of not smoking, and held better illness beliefs — beliefs that were still better at three years. A large, well-run null on the biomedical primary carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference); the secondary gains are POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: DESMOND 2008: a six-hour education course did not improve HbA1c at 12 months, but patients lost more weight and understood their diabetes better
cards.summary: DESMOND (2008): a six-hour education course did not improve HbA1c at 12 months, but patients lost more weight and understood their diabetes better.
cards.type: Multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial in primary care, 12 months
cards.people: 824 adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (55% men, mean age 59.5 years) in 207 general practices in 13 UK primary care sites, cluster-randomised by practice to a six-hour structured group education programme delivered by two trained educators, or usual care.
cards.result: HbA1c at 12 months had decreased by 1.49% in the intervention group and 1.21% in the control group; after adjustment for baseline and clustering, the difference was not significant: 0.05% (95% confidence interval −0.10% to 0.20%). Weight loss was greater in the intervention group: −2.98 kg (−3.54 to −2.41) versus −1.86 kg (−2.44 to −1.28), P=0.027 at 12 months. The odds of not smoking were 3.56 (1.11 to 11.45), P=0.033, higher in the intervention group — a relative odds figure with a wide interval, resting on few smokers. Illness-belief scores improved significantly more in the intervention group (P=0.001), and the depression score was lower (mean difference −0.50 [−0.96 to −0.04]; P=0.032).
cards.watchOut: Both groups' HbA1c fell by more than a point after diagnosis — usual care at diagnosis is itself powerful, which is exactly what a single education course must beat and did not. The smoking odds ratio of 3.56 sits outside solid-evidence territory on its interval width alone and is a secondary outcome.

cards.headline: DESMOND 2012: at three years, no biomedical or lifestyle benefit remained — only the illness-belief gains persisted
cards.summary: DESMOND at three years (2012): no biomedical or lifestyle benefit remained — only the illness-belief gains persisted.
cards.type: Three-year follow-up of a multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial in primary care
cards.people: 731 of the 824 original participants eligible for the three-year follow-up of the same cluster trial (biomedical data on 604 [82.6%], questionnaire data on 513 [70.1%]), in the same 207 UK general practices.
cards.result: HbA1c at three years had decreased in both groups; after adjustment for baseline and clustering the difference was not significant (difference −0.02, 95% confidence interval −0.22 to 0.17). The groups did not differ for the other biomedical and lifestyle outcomes or for drug use. shelves.title: Continuous glucose monitoring in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes (CONCEPTT)
shelves.question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring improve glycaemic control and neonatal outcomes versus capillary monitoring alone (CONCEPTT)?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/diagnosis,drug therapy · Insulin/administration & dosage · Internationality · Monitoring, Physiologic/methods · Observer Variation · Odds Ratio
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large multicentre randomised trial (CONCEPTT, 325 women) found CGM in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes produced a small HbA1c advantage (−0.19 percentage points at 34 weeks) and better neonatal outcomes: fewer large-for-gestational-age babies (odds ratio 0.51), fewer neonatal intensive care admissions over 24 hours (0.48), fewer neonatal hypoglycaemia episodes (0.45), and one day shorter neonatal hospital stay — with comparable severe hypoglycaemia in mothers. Those odds ratios sit at or inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's edge, and a single trial caps this shelf at POSSIBLE, however welcome the direction. No benefit was found in women planning pregnancy.

cards.headline: CONCEPTT 2017: CGM in pregnancy improved neonatal outcomes — fewer large babies, fewer NICU admissions, less neonatal hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: CONCEPTT (2017): CGM in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes improved neonatal outcomes — fewer large babies, fewer NICU admissions, less neonatal hypoglycaemia — on a small maternal A1c gain (−0.19%).
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial (two parallel trials: pregnant and planning pregnancy)
cards.people: 325 women aged 18–40 years with type 1 diabetes for at least 12 months on intensive insulin therapy — 215 pregnant (≤13 weeks 6 days) and 110 planning pregnancy — randomised at 31 hospitals in Canada, England, Scotland, Spain, Italy, Ireland and the USA to CGM plus capillary monitoring (108 pregnant, 53 planning) or capillary monitoring alone (107 pregnant, 57 planning).
cards.result: In pregnant women, HbA1c differed by −0.19% (95% CI −0.34 to −0.03; p=0.0207) favouring CGM at 34 weeks; CGM users spent more time in target (68% vs 61%; p=0.0034) and less time hyperglycaemic (27% vs 32%; p=0.0279), with comparable severe hypoglycaemia episodes (18 CGM vs 21 control) and time spent hypoglycaemic (3% vs 4%; p=0.10). Neonatal outcomes improved: large for gestational age (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.90; p=0.0210), neonatal intensive care admissions lasting more than 24 h (0.48; 0.26 to 0.86; p=0.0157), neonatal hypoglycaemia (0.45; 0.22 to 0.89; p=0.0250) — all relative odds figures; the abstract does not print the absolute event rates for these outcomes — and length of hospital stay was 1 day shorter (p=0.0091). No apparent benefit of CGM was found in women planning pregnancy. Skin reactions were the most common adverse events (49 [48%] of 103 CGM participants vs 8 [8%] of 104 controls during pregnancy).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and its neonatal odds ratios (0.51, 0.48, 0.45) sit at or inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band — individually they would not count as solid evidence; the pattern across outcomes plus the glycaemic mechanism is what supports the shelf, and the stamp stays POSSIBLE. The planning-pregnancy half of the programme found no benefit, and that null belongs with the headline.

shelves.title: Retatrutide, the triple-hormone agonist: phase 2 in obesity and in type 2 diabetes
shelves.question: Does once-weekly retatrutide (GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist) produce weight loss in adults with obesity (phase 2) — and glycaemic control and weight loss in type 2 diabetes against dulaglutide and placebo (phase 2) — at what gastrointestinal price, ahead of any outcomes trial?
shelves.mesh: Body Mass Index · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1/agonists · Obesity/complications,drug therapy · Weight Loss/drug effects · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/agonists · Receptors, Glucagon/agonists · Injections, Subcutaneous
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The phase 2 signal has been confirmed at phase 3 scale for weight. TRIUMPH-1 (2,339 adults with obesity without diabetes) found −25.0% body weight at 80 weeks on 12 mg versus −3.9% on placebo, extending the phase 2 obesity result (−24.2% at 48 weeks; Jastreboff 2023). In type 2 diabetes, the phase 2 trial (Rosenstock 2023: HbA1c −2.02% on 12 mg at 24 weeks versus −0.01% on placebo and −1.41% on dulaglutide 1.5 mg) is backed by two phase 3 reports fenced in the synthesis (TRIUMPH-2 and TRANSCEND-T2D-1). Randomised blinded trials at both stages earn LIKELY for the weight and glycaemic claims. There is still no cardiovascular-outcomes trial, the gastrointestinal price and the dose-dependent heart-rate signal from phase 2 stand, and no event claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: Jastreboff 2023: retatrutide produced dose-dependent weight loss up to −24.2% at 48 weeks versus −2.1% on placebo (phase 2, obesity)
cards.summary: Jastreboff (2023, phase 2): retatrutide produced dose-dependent weight loss up to −24.2% at 48 weeks vs −2.1% on placebo in obesity.
cards.people: 338 adults with a body-mass index of 30 or higher, or 27 to less than 30 plus at least one weight-related condition, randomised to subcutaneous retatrutide (1 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg or 12 mg, with varying starting doses) or placebo once weekly for 48 weeks; 51.8% were men. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The least-squares mean percentage change in body weight at 24 weeks (primary end point) was −7.2% (1 mg), −12.9% (combined 4 mg), −17.3% (combined 8 mg) and −17.5% (12 mg), versus −1.6% with placebo. At 48 weeks the changes were −8.7%, −17.1%, −22.8% and −24.2%, versus −2.1% with placebo. At 48 weeks, a weight reduction of 5% or more, 10% or more, and 15% or more had occurred in 100%, 93% and 83% of the 12-mg group, versus 27%, 9% and 2% of the placebo group. The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, dose-related, mostly mild to moderate, and partially mitigated by a lower (2 mg) starting dose; dose-dependent increases in heart rate peaked at 24 weeks and declined thereafter.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 dose-finding with 338 participants and no outcomes trial: the 48-week weight figures are the programme's best case at its highest dose, and neither cardiovascular safety nor durability after stopping is known.

cards.headline: Rosenstock 2023: in type 2 diabetes, retatrutide lowered HbA1c by up to −2.02% at 24 weeks, more than dulaglutide 1.5 mg (−1.41%) or placebo (−0.01%)
cards.summary: Rosenstock (2023): in type 2 diabetes, retatrutide lowered HbA1c by up to −2.02% at 24 weeks, more than dulaglutide (−1.41%).
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled and active comparator-controlled trial
cards.people: 281 adults aged 18–75 years with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.5%), BMI 25–50 kg/m2, treated with diet and exercise alone or stable metformin, at 42 US centres; mean age 56.2 years (SD 9.7), 156 (56%) female, 235 (84%) White; randomised to placebo, dulaglutide 1.5 mg, or retatrutide maintenance doses of 0.5–12 mg once weekly; 275 were included in the efficacy analyses and 237 (84%) completed the study.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, least-squares mean HbA1c changes with retatrutide were −0.43% (0.5 mg), −1.39% and −1.30% (4 mg groups), −1.99% and −1.88% (8 mg groups) and −2.02% (12 mg), versus −0.01% with placebo and −1.41% with dulaglutide 1.5 mg; reductions were significantly greater than placebo in all but the 0.5 mg group (p<0.0001). Secondary end points included change in HbA1c and bodyweight at 36 weeks, assessed in the same trial.

shelves.question: Does daily oral orforglipron — a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist needing no food or water restrictions — produce weight loss in obesity (phase 2) and A1c and weight reductions in type 2 diabetes (phase 2 dose-response)?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glucagon-Like Peptides · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Obesity/complications,drug therapy,chemically induced · Weight Loss/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: A daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonist, taken with no food or water restrictions, now has concordant randomised evidence at both stages — phase 2 in obesity (Wharton 2023, 272 adults: −9.4% to −14.7% at 36 weeks versus −2.3% on placebo) and in type 2 diabetes (Frias 2023, 383 adults: HbA1c up to −2.10% at 26 weeks versus −0.43% on placebo), and phase 3 in obesity (ATTAIN-1, 3,127 patients: −11.2% at the 36 mg dose versus −2.1% at 72 weeks). cards.headline: Wharton 2023: daily oral orforglipron lowered body weight by −9.4% to −14.7% at 36 weeks versus −2.3% on placebo (phase 2, obesity)
cards.summary: Wharton (2023, phase 2): daily oral orforglipron lowered body weight by −9.4% to −14.7% at 36 weeks vs −2.3% on placebo.
cards.people: 272 adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related coexisting condition, and without diabetes, randomised to orforglipron (12, 24, 36 or 45 mg) or placebo once daily for 36 weeks; mean body weight at baseline was 108.7 kg and mean body-mass index 37.9. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At week 26 (primary end point) the mean change in body weight ranged from −8.6% to −12.6% across the orforglipron dose cohorts and was −2.0% in the placebo group; at week 36 the changes were −9.4% to −14.7% with orforglipron and −2.3% with placebo. A weight reduction of at least 10% by week 36 occurred in 46 to 75% of orforglipron participants versus 9% on placebo, and all prespecified weight-related and cardiometabolic measures improved. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common, mild to moderate, mainly during dose escalation, and led to discontinuation in 10 to 17% of participants across dose cohorts.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 with 272 participants: the dose cohorts are small, discontinuation for gastrointestinal events reached 17% in some cohorts, and there is no outcomes trial.

cards.headline: Frias 2023: in type 2 diabetes, orforglipron lowered HbA1c by up to −2.10% at 26 weeks versus −0.43% on placebo and −1.10% on dulaglutide
cards.summary: Frias (2023): in type 2 diabetes, orforglipron lowered HbA1c by up to −2.10% at 26 weeks vs −0.43% on placebo and −1.10% on dulaglutide.
cards.type: Phase 2, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, dose-response trial
cards.people: 383 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.5%, BMI 23 kg/m2 or more) treated with diet and exercise, with or without metformin, at 45 centres in the USA, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia, randomised to placebo, dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly, or orforglipron 3–45 mg daily under two escalation regimens; mean age 58.9 years, mean HbA1c 8.1%, mean BMI 35.2 kg/m2, 226 (59%) men and 157 (41%) women; 352 (92%) completed the study.
cards.result: At week 26, mean HbA1c change with orforglipron was up to −2.10% (−1.67% placebo adjusted), versus −0.43% with placebo and −1.10% with dulaglutide; the reduction was statistically superior to placebo (estimated treatment difference −0.8% to −1.7%). Mean bodyweight change was up to −10.1 kg (95% CI −11.5 to −8.7; 7.9 kg placebo adjusted) versus −2.2 kg with placebo and −3.9 kg with dulaglutide. cards.headline: ATTAIN-1 (Wharton 2025): phase 3 — orforglipron lowered body weight by −11.2% (36 mg) versus −2.1% on placebo at 72 weeks in obesity
cards.summary: ATTAIN-1 (2025, phase 3): −11.2% (36 mg) vs −2.1% on placebo at 72 weeks in obesity.
cards.type: Phase 3, multinational, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (treatment-regimen estimand)
cards.people: 3,127 patients with obesity without diabetes, randomised 3:3:3:4 to orforglipron 6, 12 or 36 mg once daily or placebo, as an adjunct to healthy diet and physical activity, for 72 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The mean change in body weight at week 72 was −7.5% (95% CI −8.2 to −6.8) on 6 mg, −8.4% (−9.1 to −7.7) on 12 mg and −11.2% (−12.0 to −10.4) on 36 mg, versus −2.1% (−2.8 to −1.4) on placebo (P<0.001 for all comparisons). On 36 mg, 54.6% of patients lost at least 10% of body weight, 36.0% at least 15% and 18.4% at least 20%, versus 12.9%, 5.9% and 2.8% on placebo; waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, triglyceride levels and non-HDL cholesterol all improved significantly versus placebo. Adverse events led to discontinuation in 5.3 to 10.3% of orforglipron patients versus 2.7% on placebo; the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, mostly mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: The phase 3 top-dose effect (−11.2%) sits at the lower end of the phase 2 range (−9.4% to −14.7% in smaller cohorts): the honest reading is a solid daily oral option, not a result that outclasses the injectables.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a daily GLP-1 pill with no food or water rules — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: a daily GLP-1 pill with no food or water rules, consistent from phase 2 to phase 3 — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Wharton 2023 (272 adults with obesity, phase 2), Frias 2023 (383 adults with type 2 diabetes, phase 2) and ATTAIN-1 (3,127 patients with obesity, phase 3).
cards.result: The evidence now runs phase 2 to phase 3 in one direction: roughly −10 to −15% body weight in obesity and up to −2.10% HbA1c in diabetes at the higher doses in phase 2, and −11.2% at the top dose in the 3,127-patient phase 3 obesity trial. The molecule's claim to attention is the formulation — a small molecule taken once daily with no food or water restrictions — not a new mechanism. The phase 3 diabetes programme (ACHIEVE, including ACHIEVE-3 against oral semaglutide, PMID 41765029; ACHIEVE-5 added to insulin glargine, PMID 42251769; and the cardiovascular-safety trial ACHIEVE-4, PMID 42815506, whose titles were verified in this shelf's currency sweep) is fenced here by name rather than carded. Oral semaglutide is a different molecule with its own evidence, home on the GLP-1 shelves, and is not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Cagrilintide plus semaglutide (CagriSema): the REDEFINE phase 3 pair
shelves.question: Does co-administered once-weekly cagrilintide (amylin analogue) with semaglutide beat either component's expected effect on weight — in obesity without diabetes (REDEFINE 1) and in type 2 diabetes (REDEFINE 2)?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Body Mass Index · Obesity/complications,drug therapy,physiopathology · Overweight/drug therapy,physiopathology · Weight Loss/drug effects,physiology · Islet Amyloid Polypeptide/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials of the same combination — REDEFINE 1 (3,417 adults without diabetes: −20.4% body weight at 68 weeks versus −3.0% on placebo) and REDEFINE 2 (1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes: −13.7% versus −3.4%, with 73.5% versus 15.9% reaching an HbA1c of 6.5% or less) — agree that co-administered cagrilintide plus semaglutide produces weight loss beyond either component's established effect, at a gastrointestinal price paid by roughly three quarters of treated participants (79.6% and 72.5%, versus 39.9% and 34.4% on placebo). Two large blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the weight and glycaemic outcomes; there is no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of the combination, and no event claim is made.

cards.headline: REDEFINE 1 (Garvey 2025): CagriSema lowered body weight by −20.4% at 68 weeks versus −3.0% on placebo in adults without diabetes

cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, one answer — the amylin combination deepens weight loss, at the class's gastrointestinal price
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, one answer — the amylin combination deepens weight loss, at the class's gastrointestinal price — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: REDEFINE 1 (3,417 adults without diabetes) and REDEFINE 2 (1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes).
cards.result: Across the diabetes divide the combination's effect is consistent: −20.4% body weight without diabetes and −13.7% with diabetes at 68 weeks, against −3.0% and −3.4% on placebo. The programme's earlier phase 2 combination report in type 2 diabetes is background to this shelf and is not carded as a third trial. Semaglutide's own weight and outcomes evidence is home on Shelves #71, #72 and #952 and is not re-carded here. In diabetes care the standing order applies to any use of this combination: an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 agent come first, with metformin a reasonable third. The programme's next reports — REIMAGINE 2 (CagriSema versus its components in type 2 diabetes, PMID 42251859) and REIMAGINE 3 (as add-on to basal insulin, PMID 42251856), both title-verified in this shelf's currency sweep — are fenced here by name: they extend the combination into diabetes treatment sequences the REDEFINE pair did not test, and are not carded on this weight-focused shelf.
cards.watchOut: No cardiovascular-outcomes trial of the combination exists: the −20.4% headline is a weight result, and semaglutide's event data cannot be transferred to the combination by assumption.

shelves.title: Setmelanotide for melanocortin-4-receptor pathway obesity: POMC/LEPR deficiency and Bardet–Biedl syndrome
shelves.question: Does the MC4R agonist setmelanotide produce weight loss and hunger reduction in severe obesity due to POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency (single-arm phase 3 trials, judged against a pre-set responder bar) — and in Bardet–Biedl and Alström syndromes, where a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trial exists?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Insufficiency/complications · Anti-Obesity Agents/therapeutic use · Obesity/complications,drug therapy,etiology,pathology · Pro-Opiomelanocortin/deficiency · Prognosis · Receptor, Melanocortin, Type 4/agonists · Receptors, Leptin/deficiency
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — POMC/LEPR deficiency · POSSIBLE — Bardet–Biedl syndrome (Alström inconclusive). In ultra-rare MC4R-pathway disease the evidence cannot take the usual shape: the POMC/LEPR programme (Clément 2020) is two single-arm, open-label phase 3 trials in 21 people, judged against a prespecified responder bar — 8 of 10 (80%) with POMC deficiency and 5 of 11 (45%) with LEPR deficiency reached at least 10% weight loss at about one year, with hunger scores falling 27.1% and 43.7%. The Bardet–Biedl programme (Haqq 2022) has the randomised design — 38 patients, 14 weeks blinded then open-label — with 32.3% of patients aged 12 or older with Bardet–Biedl syndrome reaching at least 10% weight loss after 52 weeks of setmelanotide; the Alström results were inconclusive. Dramatic responses in diseases with no alternative therapy earn POSSIBLE on both halves, not more: there is no blinded placebo-controlled weight comparison in either programme.

cards.headline: Clément 2020: in single-arm phase 3 trials, 80% of POMC-deficiency and 45% of LEPR-deficiency participants lost at least 10% of body weight on setmelanotide
cards.summary: Clément (2020): in single-arm phase 3 trials, 80% of POMC-deficiency and 45% of LEPR-deficiency participants lost at least 10% of body weight.
cards.type: Two single-arm, open-label, multicentre phase 3 trials with a placebo-controlled withdrawal sequence
cards.people: Ten participants in the POMC trial and 11 in the LEPR trial, aged 6 years or older with severe obesity due to POMC or LEPR deficiency, at ten hospitals across Canada, the USA, Belgium, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the UK; all received open-label setmelanotide for 12 weeks, responders entering an 8-week placebo-controlled withdrawal sequence then 32 further weeks open-label. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Eight (80%) participants in the POMC trial and five (45%) in the LEPR trial achieved at least 10% weight loss at approximately 1 year (the primary end point, against the trials' prespecified responder threshold). The mean percentage change in the most hunger score was −27.1% (n=7; 90% CI −40.6 to −15.0; p=0.0005) in the POMC trial and −43.7% (n=7; −54.8 to −29.1; p<0.0001) in the LEPR trial. Injection-site reaction and hyperpigmentation were reported in all ten POMC participants, with nausea in five and vomiting in three; in the LEPR trial, injection-site reaction occurred in all 11, skin disorders in five and nausea in four. No serious treatment-related adverse events occurred in either trial.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm trials in 10 and 11 people: the '80%' is eight people. The responder bar was prespecified and the withdrawal sequence supports causality, but there is no parallel placebo group for the weight end point.
cards.source: Clément K et al. Efficacy and safety of setmelanotide, an MC4R agonist, in individuals with severe obesity due to LEPR or POMC deficiency: single-arm, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trials. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2020;8(12):960-970. PMID: 33137293. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03287960 and NCT02896192, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Haqq 2022: in Bardet–Biedl syndrome, 32.3% of patients aged 12 or older reached at least 10% weight loss after 52 weeks of setmelanotide; Alström inconclusive
cards.summary: Haqq (2022): in Bardet–Biedl syndrome, 32.3% of patients ≥12 years reached at least 10% weight loss at 52 weeks; the Alström cohort was inconclusive.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with an open-label period
cards.people: 38 patients aged 6 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of Bardet–Biedl syndrome or Alström syndrome and obesity (16 with Bardet–Biedl and three with Alström in each arm), randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous setmelanotide (up to 3.0 mg daily) or placebo for a 14-week double-blind period, followed by 52 weeks of open-label setmelanotide, at 12 sites in the USA, Canada, the UK, France and Spain. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: In terms of the primary end point, 32.3% (95% CI 16.7 to 51.4; p=0.0006) of patients aged 12 years or older with Bardet–Biedl syndrome reached at least a 10% reduction in bodyweight after 52 weeks of setmelanotide treatment; the authors state the results were inconclusive in Alström syndrome (three patients per arm). The most commonly reported treatment-emergent adverse events were skin hyperpigmentation (23 [61%] of 38) and injection-site erythema (18 [48%]). Two patients had four serious adverse events (blindness, anaphylactic reaction, and suicidal ideation); none were considered related to setmelanotide.
cards.watchOut: The primary end point is measured after the open-label period, so it is not a blinded placebo comparison; the Alström subgroup (six patients in total) can support no conclusion either way.
cards.source: Haqq AM et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a targeted drug for pathway-defined obesity — real responses, rare-disease evidence shape
cards.summary: Synthesis: a targeted drug for pathway-defined obesity — real responses, rare-disease evidence shape — split POSSIBLE / POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Clément 2020 (21 participants with POMC or LEPR deficiency) and Haqq 2022 (38 patients with Bardet–Biedl or Alström syndrome).
cards.result: Setmelanotide is the library's clearest case of mechanism-matched therapy: where the MC4R pathway itself is broken, replacing its signal produces weight loss and hunger reduction that no lifestyle programme in these diseases has matched — 80% and 45% responder rates in the single-arm POMC and LEPR trials, 32.3% in Bardet–Biedl. The evidence shape (tiny samples, one blinded period of 14 weeks, an open-label primary end point in the randomised trial) is why both halves of the stamp sit at POSSIBLE despite the dramatic numerators. Nothing on this shelf generalises to common obesity: the general obesity drug shelves (#71, #72, #282 and the incretin shelves) are different questions and are not re-carded here. A 2026 trial of setmelanotide in acquired hypothalamic obesity (PMID 42418774, title verified in this shelf's currency sweep) is fenced here by name: an acquired pathway injury is a neighbouring question, not the genetic diseases this shelf covers.
cards.watchOut: Hyperpigmentation (in 61% of the randomised trial) and injection-site reactions are near-universal prices; families should hear the responder rates as 'of 10' and 'of 11', not as population percentages.

shelves.title: Survodutide, the glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, for obesity
shelves.question: Does once-weekly survodutide (glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist) produce dose-dependent weight loss in adults with obesity in its phase 2 dose-finding trial — and how do its gastrointestinal discontinuation rates read against the class?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Glucagon · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1/therapeutic use · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Obesity/drug therapy · Peptides · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: LIKELY (weight loss in obesity) — with the MASH claim at phase 2 only. The obesity question now has two randomised, double-blind trials at two stages: phase 2 dose-finding (le Roux 2024, 386 treated: −14.9% at the 4.8 mg dose versus −2.8% on placebo at 46 weeks) and phase 3 (SYNCHRONIZE-1, 725 adults: −13.0% at 6.0 mg versus −5.4% on placebo at 76 weeks). The liver claim rests on a single phase 2 biopsy trial (Sanyal 2024: histologic improvement in 47–62% across doses versus 14% on placebo) and is fenced at that strength in the synthesis. Across all three trials the price is gastrointestinal — events in 75% of treated participants in the phase 2 obesity trial and up to 89.7% in phase 3.

cards.headline: le Roux 2024: survodutide lowered body weight dose-dependently, −14.9% at 46 weeks on 4.8 mg versus −2.8% on placebo (phase 2)
cards.summary: le Roux (2024, phase 2): survodutide lowered body weight dose-dependently, −14.9% at 46 weeks on 4.8 mg vs −2.8% on placebo.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding phase 2 trial
cards.people: 387 participants aged 18–75 years with BMI of 27 kg/m2 or more and without diabetes, at 43 centres in 12 countries, randomised to subcutaneous survodutide (0.6, 2.4, 3.6 or 4.8 mg) or placebo once weekly for 46 weeks; 386 were treated and 233 (60.4%) completed the 46-week treatment period. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix (randomisation was stratified by sex).
cards.result: By planned treatment, mean changes in bodyweight from baseline to week 46 were −6.2% (0.6 mg), −12.5% (2.4 mg), −13.2% (3.6 mg) and −14.9% (4.8 mg), versus −2.8% with placebo. Adverse events occurred in 281 (91%) of 309 survodutide recipients and 58 (75%) of 77 placebo recipients, and were primarily gastrointestinal in 232 (75%) of 309 survodutide recipients and 32 (42%) of 77 placebo recipients.
cards.watchOut: Dose-finding phase 2 with 39.6% of participants not completing treatment: the planned-treatment analysis carries substantial missing data, and the glucagon component's long-term hepatic and cardiac profile is untested at scale.
cards.source: le Roux CW et al. Glucagon and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist survodutide for obesity: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding phase 2 trial. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2024;12(3):162-173. PMID: 38330987. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04667377 and EudraCT 2020-002479-37, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Sanyal 2024: in MASH with fibrosis, survodutide improved liver histology versus placebo (47–62% versus 14%) in its phase 2 trial
cards.summary: Sanyal (2024): in MASH with fibrosis, survodutide improved liver histology vs placebo ( 47–62% vs 14% ) in phase 2.
cards.type: Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with biopsy end points
cards.people: 293 adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and fibrosis stage F1 through F3, randomly assigned to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide (2.4, 4.8 or 6.0 mg) or placebo for 48 weeks (24 weeks rapid dose escalation, then 24 weeks maintenance) who received at least one dose. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Improvement in MASH with no worsening of fibrosis (primary end point) occurred in 47% of the 2.4-mg group, 62% of the 4.8-mg group and 43% of the 6.0-mg group, versus 14% with placebo (P<0.001 for the quadratic dose-response curve). A decrease in liver fat content of at least 30% occurred in 63%, 67% and 57% versus 14%, and improvement in fibrosis by at least one stage in 34%, 36% and 34% versus 22%. Adverse events more frequent with survodutide included nausea (66% vs 23%), diarrhoea (49% vs 23%) and vomiting (41% vs 4%); serious adverse events occurred in 8% with survodutide and 7% with placebo.
cards.watchOut: Histology is a surrogate: the dose-response was non-monotonic (the 6.0 mg dose did worse than 4.8 mg on the primary end point), and no liver-outcome data exist. This card is the molecule's companion programme, carded here because the record was verified free of any other shelf; the library's MASH drug shelf is #323, whose resmetirom, semaglutide and tirzepatide trials are not re-carded here.
cards.source: Sanyal AJ et al. A Phase 2 Randomized Trial of Survodutide in MASH and Fibrosis. N Engl J Med. 2024;391(4):311-319. PMID: 38847460. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04771273 and EudraCT 2020-002723-11, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SYNCHRONIZE-1 (le Roux 2026): phase 3 — survodutide lowered body weight by −13.0% (6.0 mg) versus −5.4% on placebo at 76 weeks
cards.summary: SYNCHRONIZE-1 (2026, phase 3): −13.0% (6.0 mg) vs −5.4% on placebo at 76 weeks.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (treatment-regimen estimand)
cards.people: 725 adults with a body-mass index of 30 or higher, or 27 or higher with at least one obesity-related complication (excluding diabetes), randomised 1:1:1 to survodutide titrated to 3.6 mg (241), survodutide 6.0 mg (242) or placebo (242), once weekly plus lifestyle counselling; mean age 47.1 years, 294 (40.6%) men, mean BMI 37.9, mean body weight 108.8 kg.
cards.result: At week 76, the mean change in body weight was −12.2% (95% CI −13.6 to −10.8) on 3.6 mg, −13.0% (−14.4 to −11.6) on 6.0 mg and −5.4% (−6.9 to −4.0) on placebo; a weight reduction of at least 5% occurred in 72.6%, 71.9% and 46.3% respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). Gastrointestinal symptoms (typically mild to moderate) occurred in 80.9% of the 3.6-mg group, 89.7% of the 6.0-mg group and 47.9% of the placebo group. No deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group lost 5.4% under trial lifestyle counselling, so the drug-attributable margin is roughly 7 to 8 percentage points — and gastrointestinal events in up to 89.7% of treated participants remain the heaviest toll in the incretin-adjacent class.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the dual glucagon/GLP-1 agonist has delivered at phase 3 scale for weight, with the class's heaviest gastrointestinal toll so far — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: le Roux 2024 (387 participants with obesity, phase 2), Sanyal 2024 (293 participants with MASH and fibrosis, phase 2) and SYNCHRONIZE-1 (725 adults with obesity, phase 3).

shelves.title: Bimagrumab in type 2 diabetes with obesity: fat mass down, lean mass up?
shelves.question: Does the activin type II receptor antibody bimagrumab reduce body fat mass while preserving or increasing lean mass versus placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity (phase 2) — the body-composition claim no incretin drug makes?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Body Composition/drug effects · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Infusions, Intravenous · Obesity/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Bimagrumab makes the body-composition claim no incretin drug makes — fat mass down, lean mass up — and two phase 2 randomised, double-blind trials support its direction: in type 2 diabetes with obesity (Heymsfield 2021, 75 patients), fat mass fell 20.5% while lean mass rose 3.6% over 48 weeks against placebo's −0.5% and −0.8%; in obesity without diabetes (Heymsfield 2026, 507 adults), high-dose bimagrumab alone lowered body weight by 9.3 kg and its combination with semaglutide 2.4 mg by 17.8 kg versus 3.3 kg on placebo at 48 weeks. The stamp is POSSIBLE: the diabetes trial randomised only 75 patients and analysed completers, the obesity trial's primary end point is weight rather than composition, and neither trial measures function, strength outcomes or clinical events.

cards.headline: Heymsfield 2021: bimagrumab cut body fat mass by 20.5% and raised lean mass by 3.6% over 48 weeks in type 2 diabetes with obesity (phase 2)
cards.summary: Heymsfield (2021): bimagrumab cut body fat mass by 20.5% and raised lean mass by 3.6% over 48 weeks in type 2 diabetes with obesity (phase 2).
cards.type: Double-masked, placebo-controlled, 48-week, phase 2 randomised clinical trial
cards.people: 75 adults with type 2 diabetes, BMI between 28 and 40 and HbA1c 6.5–10.0%, at 9 US and UK sites, randomised to intravenous bimagrumab (10 mg/kg up to 1200 mg every 4 weeks; 37 patients, 23 [62.2%] women) or placebo (38 patients, 12 [31.6%] women), both with diet and exercise counselling; mean age 60.4 (SD 7.7) years, mean BMI 32.9, mean body weight 93.6 kg, mean fat mass 35.4 kg, mean HbA1c 7.8%; 58 (77.3%) completed the 48-week study and only completers were analysed.
cards.result: At week 48, changes for bimagrumab versus placebo were: total body fat mass −20.5% (−7.5 kg [80% CI, −8.3 to −6.6]) versus −0.5% (−0.18 kg [80% CI, −0.99 to 0.63]) (P<.001); lean mass +3.6% (1.70 kg [80% CI, 1.1 to 2.3]) versus −0.8% (−0.4 kg) (P<.001); waist circumference −9.0 cm versus +0.5 cm (P<.001); HbA1c −0.76 percentage points versus −0.04 (P=.005); and body weight −6.5% (−5.9 kg) versus −0.8% (−0.8 kg) (P<.001). The safety and tolerability profile was consistent with prior studies.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-five patients, completers-only analysis, and 80% confidence intervals (a phase 2 convention) rather than 95%: the composition effects are large but the trial is small, and no strength or functional end point is reported in the abstract.
cards.source: Heymsfield SB et al. Effect of Bimagrumab vs Placebo on Body Fat Mass Among Adults With Type 2 Diabetes and Obesity: A Phase 2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2021;4(1):e2033457. PMID: 33439265. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03005288, from the record's databank fields.

cards.result: The least-squares mean absolute changes in body weight at week 48 (primary end point) were −9.3 kg (bimagrumab 30 mg/kg), −14.2 kg (semaglutide 2.4 mg) and −17.8 kg (high-dose bimagrumab 30 mg/kg plus semaglutide 2.4 mg), versus −3.3 kg with placebo (all P<0.001 versus placebo), with continued improvements through week 72. Common adverse events for bimagrumab included muscle spasms, diarrhoea and acne; semaglutide was associated with nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and fatigue.
cards.watchOut: Nine arms across 507 participants means each arm is small; the abstract reports weight, not the fat-versus-lean split that is the drug's rationale, and the comparison that matters clinically — combination versus semaglutide alone on composition — is not quantified in the abstract.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Heymsfield 2021 (75 patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity) and Heymsfield 2026 (507 adults with obesity without diabetes).
cards.result: The two trials are consistent on direction and complementary on question: the small diabetes trial proves the composition effect (fat mass −20.5%, lean mass +3.6% at 48 weeks), and the larger obesity trial proves weight efficacy, alone (−9.3 kg) and added to semaglutide (−17.8 kg for the high-dose combination versus −14.2 kg for semaglutide 2.4 mg alone and −3.3 kg for placebo). shelves.title: Verapamil to preserve beta-cell function in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does daily oral verapamil preserve stimulated C-peptide at 52 weeks versus placebo — the randomised test of the thioredoxin-interacting-protein (TXNIP) hypothesis?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · C-Peptide/metabolism,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Verapamil/adverse effects · Insulin-Secreting Cells/drug effects · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy,pathology,physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised, double-blind trials at two ages point the same way on the same surrogate: in children and adolescents (Forlenza 2023, 88 participants), verapamil held stimulated C-peptide essentially flat over 52 weeks (0.66 to 0.65 pmol/mL) while placebo fell (0.60 to 0.44 pmol/mL; adjusted difference 0.14 pmol/mL, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.27) — a 30% higher C-peptide level at one year; in adults (Ovalle 2018), the trial reports improved mixed-meal-stimulated C-peptide at 3 and 12 months with lower insulin requirements and fewer hypoglycaemic events, though its abstract prints no figures. The stamp is POSSIBLE: C-peptide is a surrogate for beta-cell function, both trials are small, and neither shows durability beyond a year or a clinical-outcome benefit. This is preservation after diagnosis, not delay of onset — teplizumab's delay question is home on Shelf #567 and is not re-opened here.

cards.headline: Forlenza 2023: verapamil partially preserved stimulated C-peptide at 52 weeks in newly diagnosed paediatric type 1 diabetes (0.65 vs 0.44 pmol/mL trajectory)
cards.summary: Forlenza (2023): verapamil partially preserved stimulated C-peptide at 52 weeks in newly diagnosed paediatric type 1 diabetes ( 0.65 vs 0.44 pmol/mL).
cards.people: 88 children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes weighing 30 kg or more, at 6 US centres, randomised 1:1 to once-daily oral verapamil (47) or placebo (41) within a factorial design also assigning intensive versus standard diabetes management; mean age 12.7 (SD 2.4) years, 36 (41%) female, mean time from diagnosis to randomisation 24 (SD 4) days; 83 (94%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Mean C-peptide area under the curve was 0.66 pmol/mL at baseline and 0.65 pmol/mL at 52 weeks in the verapamil group, versus 0.60 and 0.44 pmol/mL in the placebo group (adjusted between-group difference 0.14 pmol/mL [95% CI 0.01 to 0.27]; P=.04) — a 30% higher C-peptide level at 52 weeks with verapamil. A 52-week peak C-peptide of 0.2 pmol/mL or greater was present in 95% (41 of 43) on verapamil versus 71% (27 of 38) on placebo. HbA1c at 52 weeks was 6.6% versus 6.9% (adjusted difference −0.3% [95% CI −1.0% to 0.4%]). Eight participants (17%) in each group had a nonserious adverse event considered related to treatment (8 of 47 verapamil; 8 of 41, 20%, placebo).
cards.watchOut: The primary result is a surrogate (stimulated C-peptide AUC) with a confidence interval reaching 0.01 pmol/mL, in a factorial trial whose other factor was management intensity; no outcome beyond 52 weeks is known.
cards.source: Forlenza GP et al. Effect of Verapamil on Pancreatic Beta Cell Function in Newly Diagnosed Pediatric Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023;329(12):990-999. PMID: 36826844. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04233034, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Ovalle (2018): in adults with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, a year of verapamil improved stimulated C-peptide and reduced insulin requirements (the record's abstract is qualitative — the card says so).
cards.people: Adults with recent-onset type 1 diabetes receiving a standard insulin regimen, randomised to oral verapamil daily or placebo for 12 months. cards.result: The record's abstract reports that verapamil, compared with placebo, was well tolerated and was associated with an improved mixed-meal-stimulated C-peptide area under the curve (the prespecified primary end point) at 3 and 12 months, as well as a lower increase in insulin requirements, fewer hypoglycaemic events and on-target glycaemic control (secondary end points). cards.headline: Synthesis: an old, cheap calcium-channel blocker slows early beta-cell loss in two age groups — on a surrogate, for a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: an old, cheap calcium-channel blocker slows early beta-cell loss in two age groups — on a surrogate, for a year — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Forlenza 2023 (88 children and adolescents) and Ovalle 2018 (adults; number not stated in the abstract).
cards.result: Read together, the TXNIP hypothesis has survived its first two randomised human tests: stimulated C-peptide at one year is higher on verapamil in both children (adjusted difference 0.14 pmol/mL) and adults (reported improvement, unquantified in the abstract). The shelf's limits are equally clear: one-year horizons, small samples, and a surrogate end point — preserved C-peptide is associated with better long-term outcomes in type 1 diabetes, but no trial here shows fewer complications. Established type 1 diabetes drug questions are different questions: GLP-1 agonists added to insulin in established disease are home on Shelf #287, and teplizumab to delay clinical onset is home on Shelf #567; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Verapamil is a cardiac drug with its own contraindications (heart block, hypotension, constipation, drug interactions): a positive surrogate trial is not a prescribing recommendation for every newly diagnosed patient.
cards.source: Synthesis of Forlenza GP et al. JAMA. 2023;329(12):990-999. PMID: 36826844; Ovalle F et al. Nat Med. 2018;24(8):1108-1112. PMID: 29988125. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Dorzagliatin, the glucokinase activator: the SEED and DAWN phase 3 pair
shelves.question: Does the dual-acting glucokinase activator dorzagliatin lower A1c in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes (SEED) and as add-on to metformin (DAWN) versus placebo — the first phase 3 programme of a class three decades in development?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucokinase · Glucose · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis,therapeutic use · Hypoglycemic Agents
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, double-blind trials in the same journal issue — SEED (463 drug-naïve patients: HbA1c −1.07% on dorzagliatin versus −0.50% on placebo at 24 weeks; estimated treatment difference −0.57%) and DAWN (767 patients on metformin: −1.02% versus −0.36%; difference −0.66%) — agree that the first glucokinase activator lowers HbA1c by a modest, consistent margin, with adverse-event rates similar to placebo and no severe hypoglycaemia or drug-related serious adverse events in either trial. Two concordant blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the glycaemic claim. The caveats are scope, not consistency: a single-country (China) programme, 24 weeks of controlled treatment, and no cardiovascular-outcomes data for a class whose predecessors failed on durability and hypoglycaemia.

cards.headline: SEED (Zhu 2022): dorzagliatin lowered HbA1c by −1.07% versus −0.50% on placebo at 24 weeks in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes (phase 3)
cards.summary: SEED (2022): dorzagliatin lowered HbA1c by −1.07% vs −0.50% on placebo at 24 weeks in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes (phase 3).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with an open-label extension
cards.people: 463 drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes, randomly assigned 2:1 to dorzagliatin or placebo for 24 weeks of double-blind treatment, followed by 28 weeks of open-label dorzagliatin for all patients. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, the least-squares mean change in HbA1c from baseline was −1.07% (95% CI −1.19 to −0.95) in the dorzagliatin group and −0.50% (−0.68 to −0.32) in the placebo group (estimated treatment difference −0.57%; 95% CI −0.79 to −0.36; P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events was similar between the two groups, and there were no severe hypoglycaemia events or drug-related serious adverse events in the dorzagliatin group.
cards.watchOut: A single-country programme with 24 weeks of blinded treatment: glucokinase activators as a class have a history of waning effect and lipid signals that only longer, broader trials can exclude.
cards.source: Zhu D et al. Dorzagliatin in drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Nat Med. 2022;28(5):965-973. PMID: 35551294. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DAWN (Yang 2022): as add-on to metformin, dorzagliatin lowered HbA1c by −1.02% versus −0.36% on placebo at 24 weeks (phase 3)
cards.summary: DAWN (2022): as add-on to metformin, −1.02% vs −0.36% at 24 weeks (phase 3).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with an open-label extension
cards.people: 767 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin alone, randomly assigned 1:1 to dorzagliatin or placebo as add-on to metformin 1,500 mg per day for 24 weeks of double-blind treatment, followed by 28 weeks of open-label dorzagliatin for all patients. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, the least-squares mean HbA1c change was −1.02% (95% CI −1.11 to −0.93) in the dorzagliatin group and −0.36% (−0.45 to −0.26) in the placebo group (estimated treatment difference −0.66%; 95% CI −0.79 to −0.53; P<0.0001). cards.headline: Synthesis: a new mechanism with an old-fashioned, modest glycaemic effect — proven for HbA1c, unproven for everything else
cards.summary: Synthesis: a new mechanism with an old-fashioned, modest glycaemic effect — proven for HbA1c, unproven for everything else — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SEED (463 drug-naïve patients) and DAWN (767 patients on metformin).
cards.result: The pair is internally consistent: placebo-adjusted HbA1c reductions of −0.57% (monotherapy) and −0.66% (add-on to metformin) at 24 weeks, with clean short-term tolerability in both. That is a real but mid-sized glycaemic effect, in the range of several established oral classes, from a programme run in one country with no outcomes trial. Under the standing drug-order rule, dorzagliatin enters behind the agents with cardiovascular benefit: an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 agent first, metformin a reasonable third — this shelf establishes that the drug lowers glucose, not where it belongs in sequence.
cards.watchOut: Both trials switch everyone to open-label dorzagliatin after week 24, so controlled evidence ends at six months; durability claims beyond that are extension-phase observations.

shelves.title: Imeglimin in type 2 diabetes: the TIMES programme
shelves.question: Does imeglimin — the first glimin, targeting mitochondrial bioenergetics — lower A1c as add-on to insulin (TIMES 3) and across its Japanese dose-ranging phase 2b trial, in a development programme run almost entirely in one country?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/chemically induced,drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Insulin/adverse effects · Japan · Triazines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The TIMES programme shows a consistent, modest glycaemic effect in Japanese patients — TIMES 3 (215 patients on insulin: placebo-adjusted HbA1c difference −0.60% at 16 weeks, sustained to 52 weeks in open-label extension) and the phase 2b dose-ranging trial (299 patients: placebo-adjusted differences of −0.52%, −0.94% and −1.00% across the 500, 1000 and 1500 mg twice-daily doses at 24 weeks) — with hypoglycaemia balanced against placebo in both. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because the entire controlled programme was run in one country (Japan), the phase 3 primary period is 16 weeks, and there are no data in other populations or on any outcome beyond HbA1c.

cards.headline: TIMES 3 (Reilhac 2022): imeglimin added to insulin lowered HbA1c by a placebo-adjusted −0.60% at 16 weeks in Japanese patients (phase 3)
cards.summary: TIMES 3 (2022): imeglimin added to insulin lowered HbA1c by a placebo-adjusted −0.60% at 16 weeks in Japanese patients (phase 3).
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with a 36-week open-label extension
cards.people: 215 Japanese patients aged 20 years or older with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on insulin, at 35 sites in Japan, randomly assigned to imeglimin 1000 mg twice daily (108) or matched placebo (107) with insulin for 16 weeks, followed by a 36-week open-label extension in which all patients received imeglimin. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, the adjusted mean difference in HbA1c change at week 16 (primary end point) was −0.60% (95% CI −0.80 to −0.40; P<0.0001), and the decrease was sustained to 52 weeks (mean decrease −0.64% [95% CI −0.82 to −0.46] versus baseline, in the extension). The incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events was similar between groups; the number of patients experiencing hypoglycaemia was similar, all imeglimin-group events were mild, and no episode required assistance.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks of controlled treatment in one country: TIMES 2, the programme's long-term report, is open-label with no control group and is fenced as background, not carded as evidence on this shelf.
cards.source: Reilhac C et al. Efficacy and safety of imeglimin add-on to insulin monotherapy in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes (TIMES 3): A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with a 36-week open-label extension period. cards.headline: Dubourg 2021: imeglimin monotherapy lowered HbA1c dose-dependently — placebo-adjusted −0.94% at the 1000 mg twice-daily dose (phase 2b)
cards.summary: Dubourg (2021): imeglimin monotherapy lowered HbA1c dose-dependently — placebo-adjusted −0.94% at 1000 mg twice daily (phase 2b).
cards.type: 24-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging phase 2b trial
cards.people: 299 Japanese adults aged 20 years or older with type 2 diabetes, treatment-naïve or previously treated with one oral agent, randomly assigned 1:1:1:1 to imeglimin 500, 1000 or 1500 mg twice daily or placebo for 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a first-in-class mitochondrial drug with a metformin-sized glycaemic effect, proven only in Japan
cards.summary: Synthesis: a first-in-class mitochondrial drug with a metformin-sized glycaemic effect, proven only in Japan — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TIMES 3 (215 patients on insulin) and Dubourg 2021 (299 patients, monotherapy dose-ranging).
cards.result: Dose-ranging and add-on-to-insulin trials agree on a placebo-adjusted HbA1c effect of roughly −0.6 to −1.0%, with no hypoglycaemia penalty — a profile closest to the older oral classes, not to the incretin or SGLT2 era. The single-country programme is the shelf's binding limit: every controlled patient was Japanese, so transportability is assumed, not shown. Under the standing drug-order rule, imeglimin sits behind the agents with outcome data in any sequencing discussion: an SGLT2 inhibitor and a GLP-1 agent first, metformin a reasonable third.

shelves.title: Tesamorelin for HIV-associated visceral adiposity
shelves.question: In people with HIV and excess abdominal fat on antiretroviral therapy, does the growth-hormone-releasing-factor analogue tesamorelin reduce visceral adipose tissue versus placebo — and what does it do to glucose, the metabolic price of pushing the GH axis?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue/drug effects · Anti-Retroviral Agents/adverse effects · Body Composition/drug effects · Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,pharmacology,therapeutic use · HIV Infections/complications,drug therapy,metabolism · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/metabolism · Lipids/blood
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled trials agree that daily tesamorelin selectively shrinks visceral fat in people with HIV and abdominal fat accumulation on antiretroviral therapy — Falutz 2007 (412 patients: visceral adipose tissue −15.2% versus +5.0% on placebo at 26 weeks) and Falutz 2010 (404 patients: −10.9% versus −0.6% at 6 months, deepening to about −18% in those continuing to 12 months and rapidly lost in those switched to placebo) — with triglyceride and cholesterol-ratio improvements in both and, on the shelf's key safety question, no significant differences in glycaemic measures in either trial. Two concordant blinded phase 3 trials earn LIKELY for the visceral-fat claim. The outcome is imaging-measured fat, not cardiovascular events: the metabolic rationale is plausible, the event benefit unproven.

cards.headline: Falutz 2007: tesamorelin reduced visceral adipose tissue by 15.2% while placebo gained 5.0% over 26 weeks in HIV-associated abdominal fat accumulation
cards.summary: Falutz (2007): tesamorelin reduced visceral adipose tissue by 15.2% while placebo gained 5.0% over 26 weeks in HIV-associated abdominal fat accumulation.
cards.people: 412 patients with HIV (86% men) who had an accumulation of abdominal fat on antiretroviral therapy, randomly assigned to daily subcutaneous tesamorelin 2 mg or placebo for 26 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Visceral adipose tissue on computed tomography (primary end point) decreased by 15.2% in the tesamorelin group and increased by 5.0% in the placebo group; triglycerides decreased by 50 mg per deciliter versus an increase of 9 mg per deciliter, and the total-cholesterol to HDL-cholesterol ratio decreased by 0.31 versus an increase of 0.21 (P<0.001 for all comparisons). IGF-I levels increased by 81.0% versus a 5.0% decrease (P<0.001). Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups, but more tesamorelin patients withdrew because of an adverse event. No significant differences were observed in glycaemic measures.
cards.watchOut: A 26-week imaging end point in a selected trial population: visceral fat is a surrogate, and the trial shows the fat returns when treatment stops (see the companion trial) — this is a chronic-therapy claim, not a course of treatment.
cards.source: Falutz J et al. Metabolic effects of a growth hormone-releasing factor in patients with HIV. N Engl J Med. 2007;357(23):2359-2370. PMID: 18057338. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00123253, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Falutz 2010: the confirmatory phase 3 trial replicated the visceral-fat effect (−10.9% vs −0.6% at 6 months), maintained at 12 months only while treatment continued
cards.summary: Falutz (2010): the confirmatory phase 3 trial replicated the effect ( −10.9% vs −0.6% at 6 months), maintained at 12 months only with continued treatment.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with a blinded safety extension
cards.people: 404 HIV-infected patients with excess abdominal fat in the context of antiretroviral therapy, randomly assigned 2:1 to tesamorelin 2 mg subcutaneously daily or placebo for the 6-month efficacy phase; in the extension phase, tesamorelin patients were re-randomised to continue tesamorelin or switch to placebo, and placebo patients switched to tesamorelin; patients and investigators were blinded throughout. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Visceral adipose tissue decreased by −10.9% (−21 cm2) in the tesamorelin group versus −0.6% (−1 cm2) in the placebo group at 6 months (P<0.0001). Trunk fat (P<0.001), waist circumference (P=0.02) and waist-to-hip ratio (P=0.001) improved, with no change in limb or abdominal subcutaneous fat. IGF-I increased (P<0.001), but no change in glucose parameters was observed. Visceral fat was reduced by approximately 18% (P<0.001) in patients continuing tesamorelin for 12 months, and the initial improvements were rapidly lost in those switching to placebo. Patient rating of belly appearance distress and physician rating of belly profile were significantly improved (P=0.02 for both).
cards.watchOut: The 12-month figures come from a re-randomised extension; the pooled analysis of this trial with Falutz 2007 (PMID 20554713) also exists in the literature and is deliberately NOT carded here — a pooling of the two trials is not a third trial.

shelves.title: Screening for type 2 diabetes, then treating hard: ADDITION-Europe and the Danish screening comparison
shelves.question: In people whose diabetes is found by screening, does early intensive multifactorial treatment reduce cardiovascular events versus routine care — and does the screening invitation itself change population mortality?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Analysis · Denmark/epidemiology · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/diagnosis,drug therapy,mortality,therapy · Diabetic Angiopathies/mortality,prevention & control · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Mass Screening
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — Tier C, developer’s personal verdict (the treatment trial’s primary composite includes cardiovascular death and the screening question is a mortality question): ADDITION-Europe (3,055 screen-detected patients, cluster-randomised) found first cardiovascular events in 7.2% versus 8.5% with intensive versus routine treatment (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.05 — a relative figure whose interval includes no effect) and all-cause mortality of 6.2% versus 6.7% (hazard ratio 0.91). The Danish population comparison (1,912,392 adults) found screening invitation associated with no reduction in mortality (hazard ratio 0.99) or cardiovascular events (0.99). This shelf is about screen-detected diabetes and earlier treatment; it makes no claim about delaying diabetes onset, and the word for onset is not used here. Delaying the formal diagnosis in prediabetes lives on Shelves #111/#112 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: ADDITION-Europe (Griffin 2011): cardiovascular events 7.2% versus 8.5% (relative hazard ratio 0.83, CI includes 1); mortality 6.2% versus 6.7% (0.91)
cards.summary: ADDITION-Europe (2011): cardiovascular events 7.2% vs 8.5% (HR 0.83 relative, CI includes 1); mortality 6.2% vs 6.9% — not significant.
cards.type: Pragmatic, cluster-randomised, parallel-group trial (343 general practices in Denmark, the Netherlands and the UK)
cards.people: 3,057 patients aged 40–69 years with diabetes detected by screening (primary endpoint data for 3,055), whose practices were assigned to screening followed by intensive multifactorial treatment or screening followed by routine care; mean age 60.3 (SD 6.9) years; mean follow-up 5.3 (SD 1.6) years. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Risk-factor improvements (HbA1c, cholesterol, blood pressure) were slightly but significantly better with intensive treatment. First cardiovascular event (cardiovascular mortality and morbidity, revascularisation, non-traumatic amputation): 7.2% (13.5 per 1000 person-years) intensive versus 8.5% (15.9 per 1000) routine (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.05 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). All-cause mortality: 6.2% versus 6.7% (hazard ratio 0.91, 0.69 to 1.21); mortality is printed beside the cardiovascular figures throughout this shelf, as the library requires. The authors describe a small, non-significant reduction in cardiovascular events and death.
cards.watchOut: Five years may be too short for a legacy effect of earlier control, and routine care in these health systems was already good — the trial tests 'earlier and harder' against a strong comparator, not against neglect. The 0.83 hazard ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Tier C proposed.
cards.source: Griffin SJ et al. Effect of early intensive multifactorial therapy on 5-year cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes detected by screening (ADDITION-Europe): a cluster-randomised trial. Lancet. 2011;378(9786):156-67. PMID: 21705063. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00237549.
