cards.headline: ADDITION-Denmark screening comparison (Simmons 2017): inviting a population to screening changed neither mortality (hazard ratio 0.99) nor cardiovascular events (0.99)
cards.summary: ADDITION-Denmark screening comparison (2017): inviting a population to screening changed neither mortality (HR 0.99) nor events.
cards.type: Register-based, non-randomised, controlled trial (post hoc population analysis, intention-to-screen)
cards.people: 1,912,392 Danish adults aged 40–69 years without known diabetes: 153,107 registered with 181 ADDITION-Denmark practices who were sent a diabetes risk-score questionnaire (screening group), versus 1,759,285 registered with all other Danish practices (retrospectively constructed no-screening group); median follow-up 9.5 years. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Of the screening group, 27,177 (18%) attended for assessment and 1,533 were diagnosed with diabetes. Deaths numbered 11,826 in the screening group and 141,719 in the no-screening group (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.02; p=0.66); cardiovascular events numbered 17,941 and 208,476 (hazard ratio 0.99, 0.96 to 1.02; p=0.49) — relative figures; the abstract reports event counts rather than group rates, and no rates are printed here. The authors conclude the stepwise screening programme was not associated with reduced mortality or cardiovascular events between 2001 and 2012.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised with a retrospectively built control group — confounding by practice and region cannot be excluded, which is why this card supports, and cannot lead, the shelf's null. Only 18% of the invited group attended, diluting any screening effect toward null. No registry ID in the record's databank fields (register-based controlled trial). Tier C proposed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: find it earlier, treat it harder — events did not significantly fall, and invitations changed nothing — POSSIBLE the null, Tier C proposed
cards.summary: Synthesis: find it earlier, treat it harder — events did not significantly fall, and invitations changed nothing — POSSIBLE the null (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ADDITION-Europe (3,055 screen-detected patients) and the Danish population comparison (1,912,392 adults).
cards.result: The screening story has two links, and both were tested: invitation to screening did not move population mortality or events (hazard ratios 0.99 and 0.99), and among the screen-detected, intensive treatment produced better numbers but not significantly fewer events at 5 years (0.83, CI 0.65 to 1.05) with mortality flat beside it (0.91). cards.watchOut: A non-significant 0.83 is not proof of no benefit — it is absence of demonstrated benefit at 5 years in one trial; quote it as such, never as 'screening harms' or 'screening works'.

shelves.title: Crinecerfont in classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia: adult and paediatric phase 3 trials
shelves.question: Does crinecerfont, a CRF type 1 receptor antagonist that lowers ACTH drive, let patients with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia cut their glucocorticoid dose while keeping androgens controlled, in adults and in children?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Hyperplasia, Congenital/blood,complications,drug therapy · Androstenedione/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Hydrocortisone/blood · Amines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Thiazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel phase 3 trials in the two age populations agree: in adults, crinecerfont reduced the glucocorticoid dose by -27.3% vs -10.3% on placebo at week 24 while androstenedione control was maintained, with 63% vs 18% reaching a physiologic dose; in children, androstenedione fell at week 4 (-197 vs +71 ng/dL) and the glucocorticoid dose fell by -18.0% vs +5.6% at week 28 with control maintained. Hormone and dose-reduction outcomes only; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Auchus 2024 (adults): crinecerfont cut the glucocorticoid dose further than placebo (-27.3% vs -10.3%) while keeping androstenedione controlled; 63% vs 18% reached a physiologic dose
cards.summary: Auchus (2024, adults): crinecerfont cut the glucocorticoid dose further than placebo ( −27.3% vs −10.3% ) while keeping androstenedione controlled.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (24 weeks; glucocorticoid reduction phase after week 4)
cards.people: 182 adults with classic 21-hydroxylase-deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia randomised 2:1 to crinecerfont (122) or placebo (60); 97% remained at week 24. Mean baseline glucocorticoid dose 17.6 mg/m2/day in hydrocortisone equivalents; mean androstenedione elevated at 620 ng/dL. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At week 24, the change in daily glucocorticoid dose with androstenedione control was -27.3% with crinecerfont vs -10.3% with placebo (least-squares mean difference -17.0 percentage points; P<0.001). A physiologic glucocorticoid dose with control was reported in 63% vs 18% (P<0.001). At week 4, androstenedione changed by -299 ng/dL on crinecerfont vs +45.5 on placebo (difference -345; P<0.001). Fatigue and headache were the most common adverse events in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is dose reduction under maintained biochemical control over 24 weeks: whether years of lower glucocorticoid exposure translate into less obesity, bone loss or cardiovascular risk is the rationale, not a trial result.
cards.source: Auchus RJ et al. Phase 3 Trial of Crinecerfont in Adult Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia. The New England journal of medicine. 2024;391(6):504-514. PMID: 38828955. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04490915, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Sarafoglou 2024 (children): crinecerfont lowered androstenedione at week 4 (-197 vs +71 ng/dL) and cut the glucocorticoid dose by week 28 (-18.0% vs +5.6%) with control kept
cards.summary: Sarafoglou (2024, children): crinecerfont lowered androstenedione at week 4 ( −197 vs +71 ng/dL ) and cut the glucocorticoid dose by week 28.
cards.type: Phase 3, multinational, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (28 weeks)
cards.people: 103 paediatric participants with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia randomised 2:1 to crinecerfont (69) or placebo (34); 100 (97%) remained at week 28. shelves.title: Baricitinib to preserve beta cells in new-onset type 1 diabetes (BANDIT)
shelves.question: Does daily baricitinib preserve stimulated C-peptide over 48 weeks in children and young adults with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Australia · Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · C-Peptide/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood,drug therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Insulin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One phase 2 trial (BANDIT, 91 patients diagnosed within the previous 100 days) found higher mixed-meal-stimulated C-peptide at week 48 on baricitinib than placebo (median 0.65 vs 0.43 nmol/litre/min, P=0.001) and a lower daily insulin dose (0.41 vs 0.52 U/kg/day), with similar glycaemic levels. A C-peptide-surrogate trial; no claim about insulin independence or complications is made. BANDIT is post-diagnosis preservation — this library says DELAY, never prevention, for diabetes onset, and teplizumab's pre-diagnosis delay is home on Shelf #567.

cards.headline: BANDIT 2023: baricitinib preserved stimulated C-peptide at 48 weeks (median 0.65 vs 0.43 nmol/litre/min, P=0.001) in new-onset type 1 diabetes
cards.summary: BANDIT (2023): baricitinib preserved stimulated C-peptide at 48 weeks (median 0.65 vs 0.43 nmol/L/min; P=0.001) in new-onset type 1 diabetes.
cards.type: Phase 2, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (48 weeks)
cards.people: 91 patients with type 1 diabetes diagnosed during the previous 100 days, assigned to baricitinib 4 mg once daily (60) or placebo (31). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — median mixed-meal-stimulated mean C-peptide at week 48 — was 0.65 nmol per litre per minute (IQR 0.31 to 0.82) on baricitinib vs 0.43 (0.13 to 0.63) on placebo (P=0.001). Mean daily insulin dose at week 48 was 0.41 U/kg/day (95% CI 0.35 to 0.48) vs 0.52 (0.44 to 0.60). Glycated haemoglobin levels were similar between groups, while the mean coefficient of variation of glucose on continuous monitoring was 29.6% (27.8 to 31.3) on baricitinib vs 33.8% (31.5 to 36.2) on placebo. Adverse-event frequency and severity were similar, and no serious adverse events were attributed to baricitinib or placebo.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-one patients, 48 weeks, a surrogate endpoint: preserved C-peptide is a validated marker of residual beta-cell function, but whether it converts into fewer complications or durable insulin sparing needs longer, larger trials.

shelves.title: Oxygen under pressure for the diabetic foot: DAMO2CLES and Löndahl
shelves.question: Does hyperbaric oxygen therapy heal ischaemic diabetic foot ulcers and save legs — DAMO2CLES, which did not significantly improve its primary limb outcomes, against Löndahl, where healing improved?
shelves.mesh: Amputation, Surgical · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/therapy · Hyperbaric Oxygenation · Ischemia/therapy · Limb Salvage · Sample Size
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — healing · MAYBE (weak evidence) — limb salvage — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: major amputation and amputation-free survival sit inside DAMO2CLES's outcome frame). The two randomised trials disagree in a way that tracks their populations. DAMO2CLES (120 patients with diabetes and ischaemic ulcers, intention-to-treat) found no significant benefit on limb salvage (risk difference 10%, 95% CI −4 to 23), healing (RD 3%, −14 to 21) or amputation-free survival (RD 13%, −2 to 28); its better outcomes in the 65% who completed the chamber protocol are a completer analysis, not randomised evidence. Löndahl (94 patients with chronic ulcers >3 months, double-blind against hyperbaric air) found healing of 52% versus 29% at 1 year (P=0.03). Healing in selected chronic ulcers: POSSIBLE. Limb salvage: only the null DAMO2CLES answers it directly, its intervals are wide, and the completer signal is exactly the bias randomisation exists to remove — MAYBE (weak evidence). No mortality benefit is claimed anywhere on this shelf: DAMO2CLES reports amputation-free survival, printed on its card with its interval, and Löndahl's abstract reports no mortality figures. Offloading and dressings for diabetic foot ulcers are Shelf #291, fenced, not re-carded.

cards.headline: DAMO2CLES 2018: hyperbaric oxygen did not significantly improve limb salvage, healing or amputation-free survival at 12 months
cards.summary: DAMO2CLES (2018): hyperbaric oxygen did not significantly improve limb salvage, healing or amputation-free survival at 12 months.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (standard care with versus without hyperbaric oxygen), intention-to-treat
cards.people: 120 patients with diabetes and an ischaemic lower-extremity wound (60 standard care, 60 standard care plus hyperbaric oxygen). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix. In the hyperbaric group, 21 patients (35%) were unable to complete the protocol as planned.
cards.result: Limb salvage at 12 months: 47 patients (standard care) versus 53 (plus HBOT) — risk difference 10% (95% CI −4 to 23). Index wounds healed: 28 versus 30 — RD 3% (−14 to 21). Amputation-free survival: 41 versus 49 patients — RD 13% (−2 to 28). None is statistically significant. Among the subgroup completing HBOT as planned, major amputations were significantly fewer and amputation-free survival higher (RD for AFS 26%, 10 to 38) — a completer subgroup, printed here as the authors report it and weighted as such in the balance. Mortality is reported only inside the amputation-free-survival composite; the abstract gives no standalone mortality rates, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: The completer analysis is the shelf's trap: patients who tolerate 40 chamber sessions differ from those who cannot, so the 26% completer figure cannot be read as the treatment effect — the randomised comparison is the null intention-to-treat result above it.
cards.source: Santema KTB, Stoekenbroek RM, Koelemay MJW et al. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy in the Treatment of Ischemic Lower- Extremity Ulcers in Patients With Diabetes: Results of the DAMO2CLES Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial. Diabetes Care. 2018;41(1):112-119. PMID: 29074815. Registry ID: NTR3944 (Netherlands Trial Register), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Löndahl 2010 (HODFU): hyperbaric oxygen healed 52% of chronic diabetic foot ulcers versus 29% on hyperbaric air at 1 year
cards.summary: Löndahl (2010, HODFU): hyperbaric oxygen healed 52% of chronic diabetic foot ulcers vs 29% on hyperbaric air at 1 year.
cards.type: Randomised, single-centre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (hyperbaric air comparator)
cards.people: 94 patients with diabetes and Wagner grade 2, 3 or 4 ulcers present for >3 months, treated in a multiplace chamber 85 minutes daily, 5 days a week for 8 weeks (40 sessions), as outpatients; intention-to-treat analysis included 48 in the HBOT group and 42 in the placebo group at 1-year follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Complete healing of the index ulcer at 1 year: 25 of 48 (52%) on hyperbaric oxygen versus 12 of 42 (29%) on hyperbaric air (P=0.03). In those completing >35 sessions, healing was 23 of 38 (61%) versus 10 of 37 (27%) (P=0.009) — again a completer analysis, labelled as such. Adverse events were infrequent. The abstract reports no amputation or mortality rates, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, 94 patients, and a chronic-ulcer population selected for >3 months of non-healing: it is the best blinded evidence for HBOT and it is still one small trial — its healing result and DAMO2CLES's ischaemic-population null may both be true, for different feet.
cards.source: Löndahl M, Katzman P, Nilsson A et al. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy facilitates healing of chronic foot ulcers in patients with diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2010;33(5):998-1003. PMID: 20427683. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00953186, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: which patient belongs in the chamber is unresolved — POSSIBLE for healing, MAYBE (weak evidence) for limb salvage, Tier C proposed
cards.summary: Synthesis: which patient belongs in the chamber is unresolved — POSSIBLE for healing, MAYBE (weak evidence) for limb salvage (Tier C; the sweep's two DAMO2CLES-companion records are fenced, not carded).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DAMO2CLES 2018 (120 ischaemic ulcers, multicentre, unblinded) and Löndahl 2010 (94 chronic ulcers, single-centre, double-blind).
cards.result: The discordance is the finding: the blinded trial in chronic non-ischaemic-selected ulcers shows a 23-percentage-point healing advantage; the larger pragmatic trial in frankly ischaemic ulcers shows nothing significant on any primary outcome, with 35% unable to complete the protocol. A 2025-26 sweep addition — a small single-centre RCT (94 patients; amputation 4.6% vs 11.7%, no significance stated in its abstract; PMID 41498373) — is fenced here as consistent-but-underpowered, not carded. The DAMO2CLES economic analysis (PMID 39675733) is a companion report of the carded trial and likewise fenced, not re-carded. Chamber therapy for the diabetic foot stays a selected-patient, shared-decision intervention on this evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote completer analyses from either trial as efficacy: both trials' randomised comparisons are the figures on their cards, and DAMO2CLES's are null.

shelves.title: Suction on the open wound: negative-pressure therapy for open fractures (WOLLF) and after diabetic foot amputation (Armstrong)
shelves.question: Does negative-pressure wound therapy on the open wound itself help — in severe open fractures of the lower limb (WOLLF), and after partial diabetic foot amputation (Armstrong)?
shelves.mesh: Disability Evaluation · Persons with Disabilities/classification · Fractures, Open/surgery,therapy · Injury Severity Score · Lower Extremity/injuries · Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy · Air Pressure
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — open fractures · POSSIBLE — post-amputation diabetic foot wounds. WOLLF (460 patients, multicentre) is a large, well-powered null: disability at 12 months did not improve with negative-pressure therapy (Disability Rating Index 45.5 vs 42.4; difference −3.9, 95% CI −8.9 to 1.2, against a minimal important difference of 8), nor did deep infection (7.1% vs 8.1%) or quality of life — a single very large null trial may carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), and this one does. Armstrong (162 patients, multicentre) found more post-amputation diabetic foot wounds healed on NPWT (56% vs 39%; P=0.040) and healed faster — a single positive trial, capped at POSSIBLE. Same suction, different wounds: the split is the shelf. Incisional NPWT over CLOSED incisions is Shelf #651 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: WOLLF 2018: negative-pressure therapy did not improve 12-month disability in severe open fractures (45.5 vs 42.4 points)
cards.summary: WOLLF (2018): negative-pressure therapy did not improve 12-month disability in severe open fractures (45.5 vs 42.4 points).
cards.people: 460 patients aged 16 or older with a severe open fracture of the lower limb, recruited across the UK Major Trauma Network (2012-2015), randomised to NPWT (226) or standard dressings (234) after first surgical debridement; mean age 45.3 years; 74% men; 88% of available participants completed the trial.
cards.result: Disability Rating Index at 12 months (0 = no disability, 100 = completely disabled; minimal clinically important difference 8 points): mean 45.5 on NPWT versus 42.4 on standard dressings — mean difference −3.9 as printed (95% CI −8.9 to 1.2; P=0.13), not significant and not in NPWT's favour on the point estimate. Deep surgical-site infection: 16 (7.1%) versus 19 (8.1%) (difference 1.0%, −4.2 to 6.3; P=0.64). Quality-of-life differences were likewise null (EQ-5D difference 0.02, −0.05 to 0.08). The authors conclude the findings do not support NPWT for severe open fractures.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (a dressing cannot be blinded) with a self-rated primary outcome: bias would be expected to favour the device, which makes the null more, not less, credible — but the result covers severe lower-limb open fractures after debridement, not every open wound.
cards.source: Costa ML, Achten J, Bruce J et al. Effect of Negative Pressure Wound Therapy vs Standard Wound Management on 12-Month Disability Among Adults With Severe Open Fracture of the Lower Limb: The WOLLF Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018;319(22):2280-2288. PMID: 29896626. Registry ID: ISRCTN33756652, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Armstrong 2005: after partial foot amputation in diabetes, NPWT healed 56% versus 39% on moist wound care
cards.summary: Armstrong (2005): after partial foot amputation in diabetes, NPWT healed 56% vs 39% on moist wound care.
cards.people: 162 patients with diabetes and partial foot amputation wounds up to the transmetatarsal level with adequate perfusion, in the USA, randomised to NPWT via the Vacuum Assisted Closure system with dressing changes every 48 hours (77) or standard moist wound care (85), treated until healing or 112 days; analysis by intention to treat. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: More patients healed on NPWT than control (43 [56%] vs 33 [39%]; P=0.040). Time to complete closure was faster on NPWT (P=0.005), as was time to 76-100% granulation tissue formation (P=0.002). The frequency and severity of adverse events — most commonly wound infection — were similar in both groups. The authors note NPWT could potentially lead to fewer re-amputations, a possibility their abstract does not report as a measured significant result, and it is not claimed here.
cards.watchOut: A 2005 device trial from the technology's early era, unblinded, with healing judged in an industry-defining study: a single positive trial of 162 patients caps at POSSIBLE, and its control (moist wound care of that era) is not today's offloading-centred standard (Shelf #291).

cards.headline: Synthesis: the wound, not the device, decides — LIKELY null in open fractures, POSSIBLE benefit after diabetic foot amputation
cards.summary: Synthesis: the wound, not the device, decides — LIKELY the null in open fractures, POSSIBLE benefit after diabetic foot amputation.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: WOLLF 2018 (460 open-fracture patients) and Armstrong 2005 (162 post-amputation diabetic foot wounds).
cards.result: Both trials are multicentre randomised tests of the same therapy on open wounds, and they split cleanly by wound type: a large null where the wound is traumatic and the outcome is the patient's disability at a year, and a moderate positive where the wound is a surgical amputation bed and the outcome is closure. Nothing here supports extrapolating Armstrong's closure benefit to trauma wounds, or WOLLF's null to amputation beds. Closed-incision NPWT (Shelf #651) is a third, separate question with its own home.
cards.watchOut: Armstrong's healing percentages (56% vs 39%) sit beside a P of 0.040 — one or two events moving arms would erase significance; treat the size of the benefit as provisional even within its own wound type.

shelves.title: Manufactured healing for the diabetic foot: Dermagraft, and becaplermin gel
shelves.question: Do manufactured biological adjuncts — Dermagraft living dermal substitute and becaplermin growth-factor gel — close chronic diabetic foot ulcers that standard care has not, and does the modern comparative trial (DOLCE) still find a benefit?
shelves.mesh: Cryopreservation · Diabetic Foot/therapy · Fibroblasts/cytology · Patient Selection · Safety · Shoes · Skin, Artificial/adverse effects,standards
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The two registration-era trials were positive but modest against good standard care: Dermagraft closed 30.0% of ulcers by 12 weeks versus 18.3% on conventional therapy (Marston 2003), and becaplermin 100 µg/g closed 50% versus 35% on placebo gel (a 43% relative increase, with the absolute rates beside it on the card; Wieman 1998). But the modern head-to-head trial, DOLCE 2025, found no difference at all between cellular matrix (Dermagraft), acellular matrix and standard care alone (healing by 12 weeks 49% vs 69% vs 57%; P=0.16 — with standard care matching the products). Two older positives against a null modern comparative trial, all in pre-modern-offloading eras for the positives: POSSIBLE, and falling. Shelf #291 (offloading, dressings, LeucoPatch) is the diabetic-foot home for standard care and is fenced, not re-carded; the Integra dermal template was excluded at drafting as a non-randomised postapproval report and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Marston 2003: Dermagraft closed 30.0% of chronic diabetic foot ulcers by 12 weeks versus 18.3% on conventional therapy
cards.summary: Marston (2003): Dermagraft closed 30.0% of chronic diabetic foot ulcers by 12 weeks vs 18.3% on conventional therapy.
cards.people: 314 patients with chronic diabetic foot ulcers enrolled at 35 US centres, randomised to Dermagraft (human fibroblast-derived dermal substitute) plus conventional therapy or conventional therapy alone, all receiving pressure-reducing footwear and remaining ambulatory; complete closure by 12 weeks was assessed in 130 Dermagraft and 115 control patients with ulcers of >6 weeks' duration. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Complete wound closure by week 12: 30.0% (39 of 130) on Dermagraft versus 18.3% (21 of 115) on control (P=0.023) — an absolute gain of about 12 percentage points. Overall adverse-event incidence was similar between groups, but the Dermagraft group had significantly fewer ulcer-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Closure assessed in a subset (245 of 314 enrolled) defined by ulcer duration, in a trial of the product's own era: the 12-point absolute gain is real on its terms, but the control arm's 18.3% closure reflects 2003 conventional care without modern offloading standards.
cards.source: Marston WA, Hanft J, Norwood P et al. The efficacy and safety of Dermagraft in improving the healing of chronic diabetic foot ulcers: results of a prospective randomized trial. Diabetes Care. 2003;26(6):1701-5. PMID: 12766097. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Wieman 1998: becaplermin gel 100 µg/g closed 50% of ulcers versus 35% on placebo gel — a 43% relative increase (absolute rates on this card)
cards.summary: Wieman (1998): becaplermin gel 100 µg/g closed 50% of ulcers vs 35% on placebo gel — a 43% relative increase, absolute rates printed beside it.
cards.type: Phase III, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study
cards.people: 382 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and chronic neuropathic lower-extremity ulcers of at least 8 weeks' duration, randomised after sharp debridement to becaplermin gel 30 µg/g, becaplermin gel 100 µg/g or placebo gel, each with a standardised good-wound-care regimen, until closure or 20 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Becaplermin 100 µg/g increased complete wound closure by 43% relative to placebo gel — in absolute terms, 50% versus 35% closed (P=0.007). Time to complete closure fell by 32% relative (86 vs 127 days; estimated 35th percentile; P=0.013). Adverse events during treatment and 3-month follow-up were similar in nature and incidence across groups. The 30 µg/g dose's closure result is not given in the abstract, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: The headline '43% increase' is a relative figure for a 15-percentage-point absolute gain (50% vs 35%) — the library's wording rule applies, and both numbers travel together. The gel was an adjunct to debridement and good wound care, not a replacement for them.
cards.source: Wieman TJ, Smiell JM, Su Y et al. Efficacy and safety of a topical gel formulation of recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor-BB (becaplermin) in patients with chronic neuropathic diabetic ulcers. cards.headline: DOLCE 2025: in a modern three-arm trial, Dermagraft (cellular) healed 49%, acellular matrix 69% and standard care alone 57% — no significant difference
cards.summary: DOLCE (2025): in a modern three-arm trial, Dermagraft (cellular) healed 49%, acellular matrix 69% and standard care alone 57% — no significant difference (carded from the currency sweep).
cards.people: 117 patients aged 18 or older with a full-thickness non-healing diabetic foot ulcer (of 138 enrolled, 169 eligible), randomised to standard care alone (28), cellular matrix — Dermagraft (41) or acellular matrix (48) for 12 weeks; 21 withdrew, 7 of them after reaching the first primary endpoint. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Complete re-epithelialisation by 12 weeks occurred in 59% of all participants: 49% cellular matrix, 69% acellular matrix and 57% standard care (P=0.16 by chi-square — no significant difference). At 28 weeks, healing was 61% (cellular), 56% (acellular) and 64% (standard care) (P=0.78). Wound recurrence and adverse events did not differ between groups. The authors conclude standard care alone can reduce the economic burden of diabetic foot ulcer treatment.
cards.watchOut: Small arms (28-48) and 21 withdrawals limit precision — DOLCE cannot exclude a modest product benefit — but its standard-care healing rate (57%) dwarfs the 2003 trial's control rate (18.3%), which is itself the lesson: as standard care improved, the adjuncts' margin disappeared.

cards.headline: Synthesis: real gains over 1998-2003 standard care, no gain over 2025 standard care — POSSIBLE, and the standard-care arm is the story

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Marston 2003 (314 enrolled), Wieman 1998 (382) and DOLCE 2025 (117 randomised).

Dermagraft and becaplermin each beat the standard care of their day by 12-15 percentage points; neither has beaten the standard care of 2025 in a randomised test. Offloading and the other adjuncts home on Shelf #291 stay there.

shelves.title: Three versus six weeks of antibiotics after debridement for diabetic foot osteomyelitis
shelves.question: In patients with diabetic foot osteomyelitis treated with surgical debridement, is 3 weeks of antibiotic therapy non-inferior to 6 weeks for remission?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Diabetes Mellitus · Diabetic Foot · Female · Humans · Male · Osteomyelitis · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised pilot trial, and the pilot status matters. In the Gariani trial (93 patients with diabetic foot osteomyelitis after surgical debridement), remission in the intention-to-treat population was 84% (37 of 44) with 3 weeks of antibiotics versus 73% (36 of 49) with 6 weeks (P=0.21), and per-protocol results were similar (33 of 39 vs 32 of 43); adverse events were similar (17 of 44 vs 16 of 49). The authors declared noninferiority against a 25% margin — a wide margin that a 93-patient pilot cannot narrow. Note for the developer: the drafting note describes this anchor as a full trial backed by 'a supportive randomised pilot'; the record shows the anchor itself is the pilot (its own title says so), and the companion pilot from the same programme (Pham 2022) asked a different question — 10 versus 20 days for soft-tissue diabetic foot infection without osteomyelitis — so it is fenced in the synthesis, not carded as support. Direction reassuring, precision low: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Gariani 2021 (pilot): 3 weeks after debridement gave remission rates at least as high as 6 weeks (84% vs 73% intention-to-treat), within a wide 25% noninferiority margin
cards.summary: Gariani 2021 (pilot): 3 weeks after debridement gave remission rates at least as high as 6 weeks (84% vs 73% intention-to-treat), within a wide 25% noninferiority margin
cards.people: 93 patients with diabetic foot osteomyelitis who had undergone surgical debridement (18% women; median age 65 years), randomised to 3 weeks (44 patients) or 6 weeks (49) of systemic antibiotic therapy; the median number of debridements was 1. Minimum follow-up after end of therapy was 2 months.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat population, remission occurred in 37 of 44 patients (84%) in the 3-week arm versus 36 of 49 (73%) in the 6-week arm (P=0.21). Per-protocol remission was 33 of 39 versus 32 of 43 (P=0.26). Adverse events were similar (17 of 44 vs 16 of 49; P=0.51). On multivariate analysis, the shorter course was not significantly associated with remission (intention-to-treat hazard ratio 1.1; 95% CI 0.6 to 1.7; per-protocol HR 0.8; 95% CI 0.5 to 1.4). The authors concluded the 3-week course was statistically noninferior under the trial's 25% noninferiority margin (80% power).
cards.watchOut: Three cautions. The 25% margin is generous: 'noninferior' here means 'not worse by more than a quarter', which many clinicians would not accept as equivalence. All patients had surgical debridement — the result does not address medically managed osteomyelitis without surgery. And the point estimates actually favour the shorter course, a pattern more consistent with noise in a 93-patient pilot than with shorter being better.
cards.source: Gariani K et al. Three Weeks Versus Six Weeks of Antibiotic Therapy for Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis: A Prospective, Randomized, Noninferiority Pilot Trial. shelves.title: DHEA replacement in adrenal insufficiency
shelves.question: In adults with adrenal insufficiency, does dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) replacement improve psychological well-being and sexual function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Insufficiency/blood/drug therapy/psychology · Adult · Affect/drug effects · Androgens/blood · Anxiety/drug therapy/etiology · Cross-Over Studies · Dehydroepiandrosterone/adverse effects/deficiency/therapeutic use · Depression/drug therapy/etiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lipids/blood · Mental Health · Middle Aged · Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin/analysis · Sexuality/drug effects · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two crossover trials agree on well-being and disagree, by population, on sexuality. Arlt 1999 (24 WOMEN with adrenal insufficiency): DHEA 50 mg/day improved overall well-being (global severity index change −0.18 vs +0.03 on placebo; P=0.02), depression and anxiety scores, and sexual thoughts, interest and satisfaction (P=0.002 to 0.02) — the topic draft's question said 'adults', but this record is women only, and the shelf is scoped accordingly. Hunt 2000 (39 patients with Addison's disease, both sexes): DHEA improved self-esteem, mood and fatigue, but had NO effect on sexual function. So: POSSIBLE for psychological well-being and mood (two small trials, same direction); the sexuality claim rests on one 24-woman trial and was not reproduced in the mixed-sex trial — it is not confirmed. Scope boundary: DHEA supplementation in older adults without adrenal insufficiency is a different question, homed on its own shelf.

cards.headline: Arlt 1999: DHEA improved well-being and sexuality in 24 women with adrenal insufficiency
cards.summary: Arlt 1999: DHEA improved well-being and sexuality in 24 women with adrenal insufficiency
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled crossover trial (4 months per period, 1-month washout)
cards.people: 24 women with adrenal insufficiency received DHEA 50 mg orally each morning and placebo in random order. (Women only — the record's population, narrower than the draft question's 'adults'.)
cards.result: DHEA restored initially low DHEA, DHEA sulfate, androstenedione and testosterone concentrations into the normal range; sex hormone-binding globulin, total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol fell significantly. Overall well-being improved: the global severity index changed by −0.18 ± 0.29 after DHEA versus +0.03 ± 0.29 after placebo (P=0.02), with significant improvements in depression and anxiety scores. Versus placebo, DHEA increased frequency of sexual thoughts (P=0.006), sexual interest (P=0.002), and satisfaction with the mental (P=0.009) and physical (P=0.02) aspects of sexuality.
cards.watchOut: 24 women, crossover design, questionnaire outcomes, and a 1999 pre-registration-era record (no registry ID). The sexuality findings come from this trial alone and were not reproduced in the mixed-sex trial carded next.
cards.source: Arlt W et al. Dehydroepiandrosterone replacement in women with adrenal insufficiency. N Engl J Med. 1999. PMID: 10502590. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Hunt 2000: DHEA improved mood, self-esteem and fatigue in Addison's disease — but not sexual function
cards.summary: Hunt 2000: DHEA improved mood, self-esteem and fatigue in Addison's disease — but not sexual function
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (12 weeks per period, 4-week washout)
cards.people: 39 patients with Addison's disease (both sexes) received DHEA 50 mg/day or placebo in crossover order. The abstract does not print the sex split or mean age.
cards.result: DHEA raised DHEAS and androstenedione to the physiological range. Psychological assessment showed significant enhancement of self-esteem, a tendency to improved overall well-being, and significant improvement in mood and fatigue (benefit most evident in the evenings). There were NO effects on cognitive or sexual function, body composition, lipids, or bone mineral density, and no significant adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The null sexual-function result in a mixed-sex Addison's population is the counterweight to Arlt's women-only positive finding; the two trials should not be averaged into a general sexuality claim. Small crossover trial; pre-registration era (no registry ID in the record).

shelves.title: Growth hormone replacement in adult growth hormone deficiency
shelves.question: In adults with growth hormone deficiency, does GH replacement improve body composition and quality of life versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Basal Metabolism/drug effects · Body Composition/drug effects · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Energy Metabolism/drug effects · Female · Glucose/metabolism · Growth Hormone/deficiency/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Humans · Lipid Metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Proteins/metabolism · Recombinant Proteins/pharmacology/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the body-composition claim is supported by the trial that actually measured it; the topic draft's pinned anchor did not. The draft anchored this shelf on PMID 8231841 (Fowelin 1993) described as a body-composition trial; that record is a 9-patient clamp study of insulin sensitivity with no body-composition results, so it is demoted to a second card and the shelf is re-anchored on Salomon 1989 (n=24): lean body mass rose 5.5 kg and fat mass fell 5.7 kg on GH over 6 months (both P<0.0001), with no weight change. Two gaps are stated plainly: neither carded trial measures quality of life with any instrument, so the QoL half of the question is unanswered by the verified record; and the trials are small and old (1989, 1993), from the pre-registration era. Fowelin's metabolic angle is worth keeping on the shelf: GH transiently reduced insulin action at 6 weeks, a difference gone by 26 weeks.

cards.headline: Salomon 1989: GH replacement increased lean body mass by 5.5 kg and reduced fat mass by 5.7 kg over 6 months
cards.summary: Salomon 1989: GH replacement increased lean body mass by 5.5 kg and reduced fat mass by 5.7 kg over 6 months
cards.people: 24 adults with growth hormone deficiency (most adult-onset, after treatment for pituitary tumours), all on appropriate thyroid, adrenal and gonadal replacement; recombinant human GH 0.07 U/kg/day subcutaneously at bedtime versus placebo. The abstract does not print the arm sizes, mean age, or the sex split.
cards.result: Lean body mass increased by 5.5 ± 1.1 kg (P<0.0001) and fat mass decreased by 5.7 ± 0.9 kg (P<0.0001) in the GH group, with neither changing significantly on placebo; body weight did not change. Basal metabolic rate rose significantly, IGF-I rose from 0.41 ± 0.05 to 1.53 ± 0.16 U/litre, and fasting cholesterol was lower on GH (P<0.05) with triglycerides similar.
cards.watchOut: 24 patients from 1989, body-composition surrogates, and no quality-of-life measurement — the trial answers the composition half of this shelf's question only. Pre-registration era: no registry ID in the record.
cards.source: Salomon F et al. The effects of treatment with recombinant human growth hormone on body composition and metabolism in adults with growth hormone deficiency. N Engl J Med. 1989. PMID: 2687691. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Fowelin 1993: GH transiently reduced insulin action at 6 weeks, with no significant difference by 26 weeks (9-patient clamp study)
cards.summary: Fowelin 1993: GH transiently reduced insulin action at 6 weeks, with no significant difference by 26 weeks (9-patient clamp study)
cards.type: Double-blind, crossover, placebo-controlled trial (26 weeks; euglycaemic clamp)
cards.people: 9 patients with adult-onset growth hormone deficiency received recombinant human GH or placebo in crossover, with glucose production and utilisation measured by labelled-glucose infusion during euglycaemic clamps.
cards.result: After 6 weeks of GH, the glucose infusion rate during the clamp was lower than on placebo (2.6 ± 0.4 vs 4.1 ± 0.7 mg/kg/min) — reduced insulin action, driven by less insulin-stimulated glucose utilisation; fasting glucose and insulin were also higher at 6 weeks. After 26 weeks there was no significant difference in glucose infusion rates or in glucose and insulin concentrations. The authors state it is unclear whether the early change represents new insulin resistance or restoration toward normal, as no healthy control group was included.
cards.watchOut: This record was the topic draft's pinned anchor for the body-composition question, but it reports no body-composition outcomes at all — it is carded second, for its distinct metabolic-safety angle, with the mismatch disclosed. Nine patients; pre-registration era (no registry ID).

shelves.title: Levoketoconazole in Cushing's syndrome (LOGICS randomised withdrawal)
shelves.question: In patients with Cushing's syndrome responding to levoketoconazole, does continuing the drug maintain urinary free cortisol normalisation versus switching to placebo (randomised withdrawal)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cushing Syndrome/drug therapy · Hydrocortisone/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Adrenal Insufficiency · Logic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a clean randomised-withdrawal result in an enriched population. LOGICS randomised 44 patients who had already responded to and tolerated levoketoconazole: 95.5% of those switched to placebo lost urinary free cortisol response within ~8 weeks versus 40.9% of those continuing the drug (difference −54.5%, 95% CI −75.7 to −27.4; P=0.0002), and cortisol normalisation at the end of withdrawal was 50.0% versus 4.5% (P=0.0015). The design proves the drug's specific effect — it does not estimate efficacy in untreated patients. Scope note: the topic draft asked about 'Cushing's disease'; the record's population is endogenous Cushing's syndrome, and the question above follows the record. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single (withdrawal) trial; the open-label SONICS study is its non-randomised companion and is not carded.

cards.headline: LOGICS: withdrawing levoketoconazole lost cortisol control in 95.5% versus 40.9% who continued (P=0.0002)
cards.summary: LOGICS: withdrawing levoketoconazole lost cortisol control in 95.5% versus 40.9% who continued (P=0.0002)
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised-withdrawal trial (~8-week withdrawal phase)
cards.people: 79 patients with endogenous Cushing's syndrome received levoketoconazole in an open-label titration-maintenance phase; 44 proceeded to randomisation (39 who were stable on dose, plus 5 completers of the SONICS study): 22 continued levoketoconazole and 22 switched to placebo. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — loss of mean urinary free cortisol (mUFC) response — occurred in 21 of 22 patients withdrawn to placebo (95.5%) versus 9 of 22 continuing levoketoconazole (40.9%); treatment difference −54.5% (95% CI −75.7 to −27.4; P=0.0002). At the end of withdrawal, mUFC normalisation was present in 11 of 22 (50.0%) on drug versus 1 of 22 (4.5%) on placebo (difference 45.5%, 19.2 to 67.9; P=0.0015). Restoration of levoketoconazole reversed the loss of control in most patients. Adverse events across all treatment phases (89% of patients) were most commonly nausea (29%) and hypokalaemia (26%); prespecified events of special interest were liver-related (10.7%), QT interval prolongation (10.7%) and adrenal insufficiency (9.5%).
cards.watchOut: Enriched design: everyone randomised had already normalised on the drug and tolerated it, so the trial cannot say how often levoketoconazole works in a treatment-naive patient, and the harm rates come from a pre-selected tolerant population. No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields or abstract text.
cards.source: Pivonello R et al. Levoketoconazole in the treatment of patients with endogenous Cushing's syndrome: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized withdrawal study (LOGICS). cards.headline: Synthesis: withdrawal proves drug-specific cortisol control in responders — POSSIBLE, exception candidate
cards.summary: Synthesis: withdrawal proves drug-specific cortisol control in responders — POSSIBLE, exception candidate

shelves.title: Relacorilant in endogenous Cushing's syndrome (GRACE)
shelves.question: In patients with endogenous Cushing's syndrome and diabetes or hypertension, does the glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist relacorilant improve glycaemic and blood-pressure control versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cushing Syndrome/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Middle Aged · Male · Adult · Aged · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Hypertension/drug therapy · Aged, 80 and over · Imidazoles/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Pyridines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — for blood-pressure control only, on this record; with a flagged gap on the glycaemic half of the question. GRACE is a randomised-withdrawal trial: 62 responders to open-label relacorilant were randomised to continue the drug or switch to placebo, and loss of hypertension response was significantly more frequent on placebo (proportion difference 34%; OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.77; p=0.022 — a relative measure, printed beside the proportion difference). The record's abstract prints NO glycaemic outcome figures, so the draft question's glycaemic claim cannot be carded and is flagged rather than filled. The withdrawal design in enriched responders proves maintenance of effect, not efficacy in untreated patients. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial.

cards.headline: GRACE: continuing relacorilant maintained hypertension control better than switching to placebo (OR 0.17 for losing response; p=0.022)
cards.summary: GRACE: continuing relacorilant maintained hypertension control better than switching to placebo (OR 0.17 for losing response; p=0.022)
cards.type: Multicentre, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised-withdrawal trial (12-week withdrawal phase)
cards.people: 152 adults with endogenous hypercortisolism and hypertension, hyperglycaemia, or both were enrolled across 77 centres in 11 countries and received open-label relacorilant (100 mg escalating to 400 mg daily) for 22 weeks; 62 who met response criteria were randomised — 30 to continue relacorilant and 32 to placebo — of whom 21 and 22 respectively had met hypertension response criteria. In the randomised groups, mean age was 46.6 years (SD 11.0) on relacorilant and 48.8 (14.4) on placebo; 73% and 81% were female.
cards.result: The primary outcome — loss of hypertension response during the 12-week randomised-withdrawal phase — occurred significantly more often on placebo: proportion difference 34%, odds ratio 0.17 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.77), p=0.022 (the odds ratio is a relative measure; the proportion difference is printed beside it). Adverse events in the withdrawal phase were similar between groups (back pain 17% vs 19%; headache 10% vs 13%; acne 10% vs 0); no cases of adrenal insufficiency, drug-induced hypokalaemia, or QT prolongation were reported. The abstract prints no glycaemic outcome results, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Only patients who had already responded to and tolerated 22 weeks of open-label drug were randomised — an enriched population; and the glycaemic outcomes the trial enrolled for (hyperglycaemia was an entry criterion for many) are absent from this record's abstract, an absence flagged here rather than repaired from any other source.

shelves.title: Adrenalectomy for subclinical Cushing's syndrome (Toniato)
shelves.question: In patients with adrenal incidentaloma and subclinical Cushing's syndrome, does adrenalectomy improve metabolic abnormalities (diabetes, hypertension, obesity) versus conservative management?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Gland Neoplasms/complications/therapy · Adrenalectomy · Aged · Cushing Syndrome/etiology/surgery/therapy · Female · Humans · Incidental Findings · Laparoscopy · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one small randomised surgical trial with very long follow-up and very small denominators. In 45 patients followed for a mean of 7.7 years, adrenalectomy normalised or improved diabetes in 5 of 8 affected patients (62.5%), hypertension in 12 of 18 (67%), hyperlipidaemia in 3 of 8 (37.5%) and obesity in 3 of 6 (50%), while the conservative arm is described only as showing 'some worsening' — the record prints no figures or P values for the conservative arm's outcomes, so no comparative effect size can be carded. Direction favours surgery in patients meeting the trial's selection criteria; precision is minimal. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single small trial; it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: Toniato 2009: adrenalectomy normalised or improved diabetes in 62.5% and hypertension in 67% of affected patients over ~7.7 years
cards.summary: Toniato 2009: adrenalectomy normalised or improved diabetes in 62.5% and hypertension in 67% of affected patients over ~7.7 years
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, single-centre trial (mean follow-up 7.7 years, range 2–17)
cards.people: 45 patients with subclinical Cushing's syndrome due to an adrenal incidentaloma: 23 randomised to laparoscopic adrenalectomy (all performed by the same surgeon) and 22 to conservative management; 3 patients assigned to conservative management crossed over to surgery because the adrenal mass grew beyond 3.5 cm. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: In the surgical group, diabetes mellitus normalised or improved in 62.5% of patients (5 of 8), hypertension in 67% (12 of 18), hyperlipidaemia in 37.5% (3 of 8), and obesity in 50% (3 of 6); bone parameters did not change in patients with osteoporosis. For the conservatively managed group, the record states only that 'some worsening' of diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia was noted — it prints no counts, percentages, or P values for that arm, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: The denominators behind the headline percentages are 8, 18, 8 and 6 patients; a change in one or two patients moves each figure by double digits. Single centre, single surgeon, crossovers, and an asymmetrically reported control arm cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. The registry number (ANZCTR12608000567325) appears in the abstract text only.

shelves.title: Flash glucose monitoring in type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections (IMPACT)
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections, does flash glucose monitoring reduce time in hypoglycaemia versus self-monitoring of blood glucose?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemia/prevention & control · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin/therapeutic use · Inventions · Monitoring, Physiologic/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY — one large multicentre trial, carded in its primary report and in the pre-specified MDI subgroup report that answers this shelf's question (counted once: they are the same trial). In IMPACT (n=241, well-controlled type 1 diabetes, HbA1c ≤7.5%), flash monitoring cut time in hypoglycaemia by 1.24 h/day versus SMBG overall (P<0.0001; a 38% relative reduction), and by 1.65 h/day (95% CI −2.21 to −1.09; P<0.0001) in the MDI subgroup of 163 patients — without deterioration in HbA1c. The population was well controlled at baseline, so the result addresses hypoglycaemia avoidance in people already at target, not glucose lowering in poorly controlled diabetes. Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form), but a large, consistent, precisely estimated one. Scope boundary: flash (intermittently scanned) monitoring is a distinct device class from the real-time CGM questions homed on Shelves #560/#561 and from the older-adult CGM question on Shelf #1762.

cards.headline: IMPACT (primary report): flash monitoring cut time in hypoglycaemia by 1.24 h/day versus SMBG in well-controlled type 1 diabetes
cards.summary: IMPACT (primary report): flash monitoring cut time in hypoglycaemia by 1.24 h/day versus SMBG in well-controlled type 1 diabetes
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, non-masked, randomised controlled trial (6 months) — primary report
cards.people: 241 adults with well-controlled type 1 diabetes (HbA1c ≤58 mmol/mol [7.5%]) at 23 European centres were randomised (120 flash glucose monitoring, 121 self-monitoring of blood glucose; outcomes evaluated in 239); both MDI and pump users were included, with randomisation stratified by type of insulin administration. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Mean time in hypoglycaemia (<3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL)) changed from 3.38 h/day at baseline to 2.03 h/day at 6 months on flash monitoring (adjusted change −1.39) versus 3.44 to 3.27 h/day on SMBG (−0.14): a between-group difference of −1.24 h/day (SE 0.239; P<0.0001), equating to a 38% relative reduction. No device-related hypoglycaemia or safety issues were reported; 13 sensor-related adverse events occurred in ten participants (including allergy and insertion-site symptoms).
cards.watchOut: Non-masked by design, in patients already well controlled — the trial shows hypoglycaemia can be trimmed without losing control; it does not show flash monitoring improves HbA1c, and its authors call for studies in less well-controlled and younger patients. The MDI-specific estimate is the subgroup report carded next.

cards.headline: IMPACT MDI subgroup (pre-specified): time in hypoglycaemia fell by 1.65 h/day versus SMBG in injection users
cards.summary: IMPACT MDI subgroup (pre-specified): time in hypoglycaemia fell by 1.65 h/day versus SMBG in injection users
cards.type: Pre-specified subgroup analysis of the IMPACT randomised trial (MDI users, 6 months)
cards.people: 163 IMPACT participants using multiple daily injections were randomised (82 flash monitoring, 81 SMBG); the full analysis set included 161 after one pregnancy exclusion in each group. Participants had type 1 diabetes for ≥5 years, HbA1c ≤7.5%, and had self-monitored ≥3 times daily before entry.
cards.result: Mean time in hypoglycaemia fell by 46.0% in the intervention group (3.44 to 1.86 h/day; adjusted change −1.65 h/day) and was unchanged in controls (3.73 to 3.66 h/day; change 0.00): between-group difference −1.65 h/day (95% CI −2.21 to −1.09; P<0.0001). HbA1c did not deteriorate, treatment satisfaction and hypo/hyperglycaemia perception improved, and scanning averaged ~15 times daily while fingerstick testing fell from 5.5 to 0.5 tests/day. Four intervention participants withdrew because of sensor insertion/wear adverse events; no device-related hypoglycaemia or safety issues were reported.

shelves.title: Flash glucose monitoring in type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin (REPLACE)
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin therapy, does flash glucose monitoring improve HbA1c and reduce hypoglycaemia versus self-monitoring of blood glucose?
shelves.mesh: No MeSH terms in the record
shelves.balance: SPLIT — REPLACE's randomised phase separates the two halves of the question cleanly. HbA1c at 6 months: no difference (−0.29% flash versus −0.31% SMBG; p=0.8222) — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the HbA1c claim overall, with a nominally positive under-65 subgroup (p=0.0301) disclosed as a subgroup finding, not the trial's answer. Hypoglycaemia: time below 3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL) fell by 0.47 h/day versus control (P=0.0006; 43% relative) — POSSIBLE. The trial's 12-month report is demoted to a second card with its status disclosed: after month 6 the control group disappears into an open-access phase, so its 12-month figures are within-group changes against baseline, not randomised evidence. Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf.

cards.headline: REPLACE (6-month primary report): HbA1c unchanged (−0.29% vs −0.31%; p=0.8222), time in hypoglycaemia reduced by 0.47 h/day
cards.summary: REPLACE (6-month primary report): HbA1c unchanged (−0.29% vs −0.31%; p=0.8222), time in hypoglycaemia reduced by 0.47 h/day
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial (6-month randomised phase) — primary report
cards.people: 224 adults with type 2 diabetes on intensive insulin therapy at 26 European centres, randomised 2:1 (149 flash glucose monitoring, 75 self-monitoring of blood glucose). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split, and the record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: The primary outcome — HbA1c change at 6 months — did not differ: −0.29 ± 0.07% on flash versus −0.31 ± 0.09% on SMBG (p=0.8222). Time in hypoglycaemia (<3.9 mmol/L (≈70 mg/dL)) fell by 0.47 ± 0.13 h/day versus control (P=0.0006), a 43% relative reduction; time below 3.1 mmol/L (≈56 mg/dL) fell by 0.22 ± 0.07 h/day (P=0.0014), 53% relative. A prespecified age analysis found an HbA1c difference only in participants under 65 (−0.53% vs −0.20%; p=0.0301) — a subgroup result, disclosed as such. Treatment satisfaction was higher with flash (DTSQ 13.1 vs 9.0; P<0.0001); no serious adverse events or severe hypoglycaemic events were related to sensor use.
cards.watchOut: Open-label. The under-65 HbA1c finding must not be promoted over the null primary outcome; and the hypoglycaemia benefit, while randomised and significant, is a single trial's secondary outcome — hence POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY for that half of the split.

shelves.balance: LIKELY — one well-designed multicentre trial directly in the population the question names, with the hypoglycaemia benefit visible in both continuous and event terms: median time below 70 mg/dl fell from 5.1% at baseline to 2.7% during follow-up on CGM versus 4.7% to 4.9% on BGM (adjusted difference −1.9% of the day, 95% CI −2.8% to −1.1%; P<0.001), and severe hypoglycaemic events numbered 1 on CGM versus 10 on BGM — the last being the more clinically important signal, though with counts too small for a rate ratio. HbA1c fell slightly more on CGM (adjusted difference −0.3%, P<0.001). Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form). Scope boundary: this is real-time CGM in older adults with type 1 diabetes; flash monitoring in younger MDI users is Shelf #1760, and hybrid closed loop is shelf #561.

cards.headline: WISDM: CGM halved time below 70 mg/dl in adults ≥60 with type 1 diabetes, with 1 versus 10 severe hypoglycaemic events
cards.summary: WISDM: CGM halved time below 70 mg/dl in adults ≥60 with type 1 diabetes, with 1 versus 10 severe hypoglycaemic events
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre trial (6 months; 22 US centres)
cards.people: 203 adults aged 60 years or older with type 1 diabetes (median age 68 years [IQR 65–71]; 52% female; median diabetes duration 36 years [IQR 25–48]; 53% using insulin pumps; mean HbA1c 7.5% [SD 0.9]) were randomised at 22 US endocrinology practices to continuous glucose monitoring (n=103) or standard blood glucose monitoring (n=100).
cards.result: Median time with glucose below 70 mg/dl was 5.1% (73 minutes/day) at baseline and 2.7% (39 minutes/day) during follow-up on CGM, versus 4.7% (68 minutes/day) at baseline and 4.9% (70 minutes/day) during follow-up on BGM — an adjusted treatment difference of −1.9% (−27 minutes/day; 95% CI −2.8% to −1.1%; P<0.001). Mean HbA1c fell more on CGM (adjusted difference −0.3%; 95% CI −0.4% to −0.1%; P<0.001), and 83% of the CGM group used CGM at least 6 days per week during month 6. The most commonly reported adverse events, CGM versus BGM respectively, were severe hypoglycaemia (1 and 10), fractures (5 and 1), falls (4 and 3), and emergency department visits (6 and 8).
cards.watchOut: A population of whom about half used insulin pumps at entry (53%) — the absolute hypoglycaemia reduction may differ in MDI-treated older adults. The severe-event contrast (1 vs 10) is a count, not a powered endpoint; the powered evidence is the time-below-range result.
cards.source: Pratley RE et al.; Wireless Innovation for Seniors With Diabetes Mellitus (WISDM) Study Group. Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Hypoglycemia in Older Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 32543682. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03240432, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Insulin pump (CSII) versus multiple daily injections in type 2 diabetes failing MDI (OpT2mise)
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes poorly controlled on high-dose multiple daily injections, does continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion improve HbA1c versus continuing MDI?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Insulin Infusion Systems · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a large multicentre randomised trial in exactly the population the question names: patients selected for failure on high-dose MDI. At 6 months HbA1c fell by 1.1% on pump versus 0.4% on continued MDI (between-group difference −0.7%, 95% CI −0.9 to −0.4; p<0.0001), with total daily insulin dose ending lower on pump (97 versus 122 units; p<0.0001) and no significant difference in bodyweight change between groups. Screening context matters: 590 patients were screened and 331 randomised, so the result applies to the subset meeting the trial's run-in criteria, not to all MDI-failing patients. Single trial, stated on the face of the shelf (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form).

cards.headline: OpT2mise: pump therapy lowered HbA1c by 0.7% more than continuing MDI in type 2 diabetes failing injections
cards.summary: OpT2mise: pump therapy lowered HbA1c by 0.7% more than continuing MDI in type 2 diabetes failing injections
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, parallel-group, open-label trial (6 months)
cards.people: 331 adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes on multiple daily injections were randomised (168 pump, 163 MDI) from 590 screened (495 entered the run-in), after a 2-month dose-optimisation run-in; mean baseline HbA1c was 9.0% in both groups. The abstract does not print mean age, diabetes duration, or the sex split.
cards.result: At 6 months HbA1c had fallen by 1.1% (SD 1.2) on pump versus 0.4% (SD 1.1) on MDI — a between-group difference of −0.7% (95% CI −0.9 to −0.4; p<0.0001). Mean total daily insulin dose at study end was lower on pump (97 units [SD 56] versus 122 units [SD 68]; p<0.0001), with no significant difference in bodyweight change (1.5 kg [SD 3.5] versus 1.1 kg [SD 3.6]; p=0.322). Two diabetes-related serious adverse events (hyperglycaemia or ketosis without acidosis) requiring hospital admission occurred on pump versus one on MDI; no ketoacidosis occurred in either group, and one episode of severe hypoglycaemia occurred in the MDI group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a run-in that selected patients able and willing to engage with intensified monitoring — do not generalise the 0.7% advantage to all-comers failing MDI. Industry-era device trial; 6-month horizon; no hard outcomes.
cards.source: Reznik Y et al.; OpT2mise Study Group. Insulin pump treatment compared with multiple daily injections for treatment of type 2 diabetes (OpT2mise): a randomised open-label controlled trial. Lancet. 2014. PMID: 24998009. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01182493, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Open-source automated insulin delivery versus sensor-augmented pump in type 1 diabetes (CREATE)
shelves.question: In children and adults with type 1 diabetes, does open-source automated insulin delivery increase time in range versus sensor-augmented pump therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Australia · Blood Glucose/analysis · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Infusion Pumps · Insulin/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a clean randomised result for a community-built system: time in range (3.9–10.0 mmol/L (≈70–180 mg/dL)) during the final 2 weeks was 71.2% on open-source AID versus 54.5% on sensor-augmented pump, an adjusted between-group difference of 14 percentage points (95% CI 9.2 to 18.8; P<0.001), with no severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis in either group over 24 weeks. Caveats on the face: 97 patients, an open-label trial of a highly motivated population willing to run open-source software, and a 24-week horizon — safety beyond that rests on community experience, not randomised data. Single trial (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form). Scope boundary: commercial hybrid closed-loop systems are Shelf #561; CREATE is specifically the open-source question.

cards.headline: CREATE: open-source AID raised time in range by 14 points versus sensor-augmented pump (71.2% vs 54.5%)
cards.summary: CREATE: open-source AID raised time in range by 14 points versus sensor-augmented pump (71.2% vs 54.5%)
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, randomised controlled trial (24 weeks)
cards.people: 97 patients with type 1 diabetes in New Zealand — 48 children (aged 7–15 years) and 49 adults (16–70 years) — were randomised to open-source AID (n=44) or sensor-augmented pump therapy (n=53). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: During the final 2 weeks (days 155–168), mean time in range (glucose 3.9–10.0 mmol/L [70–180 mg/dl]) rose from 61.2% (SD 12.3) at baseline to 71.2% (12.1) on open-source AID and fell from 57.7% (14.3) to 54.5% (16.0) on sensor-augmented pump — an adjusted difference of 14.0 percentage points (95% CI 9.2 to 18.8; P<0.001), equivalent to 3 hours 21 minutes more per day in range. There was no difference in treatment effect by age group (P=0.56). No severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in either group; two AID patients withdrew because of connectivity issues.
cards.watchOut: Open-source means unregulated, community-supported software run on compatible hardware — participants who volunteer for such a trial are not a random sample of pump users, and the 24-week window cannot exclude rare safety events. The trial is registered as ACTRN12620000034932 (the record’s databank fields).
cards.source: Burnside MJ et al.; CREATE Trial Team. Open-Source Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 36069869. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12620000034932, from the record’s databank fields. shelves.title: Suspend-before-low and threshold-suspend insulin pumps in type 1 diabetes (PROLOG, ASPIRE)
shelves.question: In patients with type 1 diabetes at risk of hypoglycaemia, do automated insulin-suspension pump features reduce hypoglycaemic events versus sensor-augmented pump therapy without suspension?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Algorithms · Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring/methods · Child · Cross-Over Studies · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy · Drug Delivery Systems · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemia/blood/chemically induced/prevention & control · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Insulin/administration & dosage · Insulin Infusion Systems · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Ambulatory · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials of successive generations of the same idea agree. PROLOG (predictive low-glucose suspend, n=103, 6 weeks): median sensor time below 70 mg/dl was 2.6% with suspend-before-low versus 3.2% on sensor-augmented pump (difference −0.8 percentage points; P<0.001), a 31% relative reduction in mean time below range, with no increase in mean glucose. ASPIRE (threshold suspend, n=247, 3 months): the area-under-curve rate of nocturnal hypoglycaemic events was 37.5% lower (a relative measure; P<0.001), the event rate was 31.8% lower (also relative), with nocturnal events at 1.5 versus 2.2 per patient-week — the absolute rates are printed beside the relative ones. PROLOG recorded one severe hypoglycaemic event, in the sensor-augmented-pump period; ASPIRE recorded four patients with severe events, all in the control group, and no DKA in either. Mean glucose did not rise in PROLOG and HbA1c did not differ in ASPIRE — suspension is a hypoglycaemia-safety feature, not a glucose-lowering one. Generation boundary stated: threshold-suspend reacts at a threshold; suspend-before-low predicts; full hybrid closed loop is Shelf #560/#561 territory and is not claimed here.

cards.headline: PROLOG: predictive low-glucose suspend cut median time below 70 mg/dl to 2.6% versus 3.2% on sensor-augmented pump
cards.summary: PROLOG: predictive low-glucose suspend cut median time below 70 mg/dl to 2.6% versus 3.2% on sensor-augmented pump
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised crossover trial (6 weeks; two 3-week periods)
cards.people: 103 people with type 1 diabetes (age 6–72 years; mean HbA1c 7.3%) took part in a randomised crossover comparison of the predictive low-glucose suspend system (t:slim X2 with Basal-IQ) versus sensor-augmented pump therapy; 99% completed both study periods. The abstract does not print the sex split.
cards.result: Median time below 70 mg/dl fell from 3.6% at baseline to 2.6% in the PLGS period versus 3.2% in the SAP period (difference −0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −1.1 to −0.5; P<0.001); the corresponding mean values (4.4% at baseline, 3.1% PLGS, 4.5% SAP) represent a 31% relative reduction. Mean sensor glucose did not increase (159 vs 159 mg/dl; P=0.40), nor did time above 180 mg/dl (32% vs 33%; P=0.12). One severe hypoglycaemic event occurred in the SAP period and none in the PLGS period. Mean pump suspension time was 104 minutes/day.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is short (two 3-week crossover periods), and a crossover of device features cannot blind participants. The 31% figure is the relative reduction in mean time below 70 mg/dl; the absolute median difference was 0.8 percentage points — the carded primary result.
cards.source: Forlenza GP et al. Predictive Low-Glucose Suspend Reduces Hypoglycemia in Adults, Adolescents, and Children With Type 1 Diabetes in an At-Home Randomized Crossover Study: Results From the PROLOG Trial. Diabetes Care. 2018. PMID: 30089663. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03195140, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ASPIRE: threshold-suspend reduced nocturnal hypoglycaemic event exposure by 37.5% (relative), with events at 1.5 versus 2.2 per patient-week
cards.summary: ASPIRE: threshold-suspend reduced nocturnal hypoglycaemic event exposure by 37.5% (relative), with events at 1.5 versus 2.2 per patient-week
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised controlled trial (3 months; nocturnal hypoglycaemia phase)
cards.people: 247 patients with type 1 diabetes and documented nocturnal hypoglycaemia (121 threshold-suspend, 126 sensor-augmented pump control). The abstract does not print mean age, diabetes duration, HbA1c, or the sex split.
cards.result: The co-primary outcome of nocturnal hypoglycaemic-event area under the curve was 980 ± 1200 versus 1568 ± 1995 mg/dl × minutes on control — 37.5% lower (a relative measure; P<0.001). Nocturnal hypoglycaemic events occurred 31.8% less frequently (relative): 1.5 ± 1.0 versus 2.2 ± 1.3 events per patient-week (P<0.001). The percentages of nocturnal sensor values below 50, 50 to <60, and 60 to <70 mg/dl were each significantly reduced (P<0.001 for each range; the record prints no percentages). HbA1c changes were similar in the two groups (the record prints no figures). Four patients, all in the control group, had a severe hypoglycaemic event; no patient had diabetic ketoacidosis.
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are relative reductions in event exposure; the absolute night-level rates (1.5 vs 2.2 events per patient-week) are the scale of benefit a patient experiences. Threshold-suspend is the older, reactive generation of the feature — carded alongside PROLOG's predictive version with the generational distinction stated, not merged.
cards.source: Bergenstal RM et al. Threshold-based insulin-pump interruption for reduction of hypoglycemia. N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID: 23789889. cards.headline: Synthesis: automatic suspension prevents hypoglycaemia without improving HbA1c — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: automatic suspension prevents hypoglycaemia without improving HbA1c — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PROLOG (Forlenza 2018), 103 patients, and ASPIRE (Bergenstal 2013), 247 patients — two trials, two technology generations.

shelves.title: Community health workers plus peer leaders in diabetes self-management (Latino adults)
shelves.question: In Latino adults with type 2 diabetes, does a diabetes self-management programme combining community health workers and peer leaders improve HbA1c versus enhanced usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Community Health Workers/organization & administration · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/ethnology/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Health Education/methods/organization & administration · Hispanic or Latino · Humans · Leadership · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Participation/methods · Peer Group · Self Care/methods · Self-Management/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single two-stage randomised trial in Latino adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. A CHW-led 6-month self-management programme lowered HbA1c more than enhanced usual care at 6 months (between-group difference −0.45%; 95% CI −0.87 to −0.03; P<0.05), and participants stepped into a peer-leader maintenance phase maintained their HbA1c improvements at 12 and 18 months on the record’s reporting, while CHW-only telephone follow-up maintained diabetes-distress improvements. One trial, 222 randomised patients, single programme; the peer-leader companion literature (Heisler 2010, reciprocal peer support by telephone) is a different design and is fenced rather than carded. Nothing here supports claims for non-Latino populations.

cards.headline: Spencer 2018: CHW-led self-management lowered HbA1c 0.45% more than enhanced usual care at 6 months; peer-leader maintenance sustained gains to 18 months
cards.summary: Spencer 2018: CHW-led self-management lowered HbA1c 0.45% more than enhanced usual care at 6 months; peer-leader maintenance sustained gains to 18 months
cards.type: Two-stage randomised controlled trial (6-month intervention; maintenance randomisation to 18 months)
cards.people: 222 Latino adults with type 2 diabetes and poor glycaemic control, recruited from a federally qualified health centre, were randomised to a community-health-worker-led 6-month diabetes self-management education programme or to enhanced usual care (EUC). After the 6-month programme, participants in the CHW arm were re-randomised to 12 months of CHW-delivered monthly telephone outreach (CHW-only) or weekly peer-leader group sessions with telephone outreach for those unable to attend (CHW+PL). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.

shelves.title: Structured self-monitoring of blood glucose in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes (STeP)
shelves.question: In patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin, does structured self-monitoring of blood glucose improve HbA1c versus active usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose/drug effects · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring/methods · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/diagnosis/drug therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Patient Participation · Primary Health Care · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the STeP trial is positive but modest, and its two reports must not be confused. The primary report (carded first) randomised 483 patients: structured SMBG lowered HbA1c by 0.3% more than an active control at 12 months (−1.2% vs −0.9%; P=0.04) in the intention-to-treat analysis. The primary report’s per-protocol difference was larger (−0.5%; P<0.003), and the companion report — the record pinned in the topic draft — found the benefit concentrated in patients who received treatment-change recommendations (−1.2% versus −0.8% among those with at least one recommendation; P<0.03): a physician-behaviour analysis, not the trial’s answer, and it is demoted to a second card with that status stated. Scope boundary within the library: the DiGEM trial of SMBG strategies in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes is carded on Shelf #559 (a different, largely null trial of monitoring intensity without STeP's structured-profile protocol); STeP's distinct angle — a defined 7-point-profile structure reviewed at each visit — is what this shelf answers, and DiGEM is fenced here rather than re-carded.

cards.headline: STeP (primary report): structured SMBG lowered HbA1c by 0.3% more than active control at 12 months (P=0.04)
cards.summary: STeP (primary report): structured SMBG lowered HbA1c by 0.3% more than active control at 12 months (P=0.04)
cards.type: Prospective, cluster-randomised, multicentre trial (12 months) — primary report
cards.people: 483 patients at 34 US primary care practices with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin were randomised by practice cluster to the structured testing group (STG) or an active control group (ACG) receiving enhanced usual care (intention-to-treat analysis: 256 STG, 227 ACG). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat: mean HbA1c fell by 1.2% in the STG versus 0.9% in the ACG — a 0.3% greater reduction with structured SMBG (P=0.04). In the per-protocol population the difference was 0.5% (P<0.003). Significantly more STG patients received a treatment-change recommendation at the month-1 visit (179 [75.5%] versus 61 [28.0%]; P<0.0001), and general well-being improved significantly in both groups (P<0.0001 in each).
cards.watchOut: An active control (enhanced usual care) makes this a fair test, and the effect is correspondingly small; cluster randomisation by practice. The structured protocol — quarterly 7-point profiles reviewed with the clinician — is the intervention, not fingerstick testing in general.

cards.headline: STeP companion report: the larger A1c advantage appeared only when physicians acted on the profile — a physician-behaviour analysis, not the trial's primary answer
cards.summary: STeP companion report: the larger A1c advantage appeared only when physicians acted on the profile — a physician-behaviour analysis, not the trial's primary answer
cards.type: Companion analysis of the STeP randomised trial — secondary report of the same trial
cards.people: The companion analysis examined the same 483-patient trial by physician behaviour: structured-group and control patients who received treatment-change recommendations (TMRs) were compared, as were structured-group patients with and without a TMR at the month-1 visit — comparisons by physician behaviour, not by randomisation. cards.result: More STG than ACG patients received a TMR at each study visit (P<0.0001). Among patients who received at least one TMR, HbA1c fell more in the STG than the ACG (−1.2% versus −0.8%; P<0.03). Patients with baseline HbA1c ≥8.5% who received a TMR at the month-1 visit had greater HbA1c reductions than those without an initial TMR (P=0.002).
