cards.watchOut: Demoted to second card with its status stated: physicians who act on data may differ from those who do not in ways randomisation cannot protect against here, so this report explains a plausible mechanism for the primary result — it does not enlarge it. This was the record pinned in the topic draft; the draft's framing matches this companion, not the primary report.

shelves.title: Pharmacist prescribing for cardiovascular risk in chronic kidney disease (RxEACH-CKD)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease at high cardiovascular risk, does pharmacist-led assessment and prescribing reduce estimated cardiovascular risk versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alberta · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Community Pharmacy Services/statistics & numerical data · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/diagnosis/epidemiology · Male · Middle Aged · Pharmacists · Professional Role · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/epidemiology · Risk Assessment/methods/statistics & numerical data · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a positive secondary analysis of a parent trial, on an estimated-risk endpoint, stated as such. RxEACH-CKD (n=290, CKD patients at high cardiovascular risk) found the estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk fell by 20% more in relative terms with pharmacist assessment, prescribing and follow-up than with usual care (difference in change in estimated risk, P<0.001), with significant improvements in systolic blood pressure (P<0.001), A1c (P<0.001), LDL cholesterol (P=0.004) and smoking cessation (P=0.04). The '20%' is a relative difference in the change of a risk estimate — not a reduction in events; the parent RxEACH trial (Al Hamarneh 2017), which randomised diabetics broadly and is carded on Shelf #1009, found the same direction of effect. This shelf's distinct angle is the CKD population; it is NOT Tier C: the primary endpoint is estimated risk, and no mortality or event claim is made or supported.

cards.headline: RxEACH-CKD: pharmacist prescribing cut estimated cardiovascular risk change by a relative 20% versus usual care (P<0.001)
cards.summary: RxEACH-CKD: pharmacist prescribing cut estimated cardiovascular risk change by a relative 20% versus usual care (P<0.001)
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised controlled trial (RxEACH; 3 months)
cards.people: 290 patients with chronic kidney disease at high cardiovascular risk, randomised to pharmacist-led assessment, prescribing and follow-up or to usual care, in Alberta, Canada. The abstract does not print the arm sizes, mean age, or the sex split.
cards.result: After adjustment for baseline values, the difference between groups in the change in estimated cardiovascular risk was 20% (P<0.001) — a relative difference in the change of an estimated risk score, as printed in the record, and not a measure of actual events. Comparing intervention with control, the changes were 0.2 mmol/L (≈8 mg/dL) in LDL cholesterol (P=0.004), 10.5 mmHg in systolic blood pressure (P<0.001), 0.7% in HbA1c (P<0.001), and 19.6% in smoking cessation (P=0.04). The reduction in estimated risk was larger in rural than in urban participants.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions belong on the face of this shelf. First, the endpoint is a computed risk estimate over 3 months — risk-factor arithmetic, not observed myocardial infarctions or deaths. Second, this is a secondary analysis of the RxEACH trial population's CKD subset; the parent trial (Shelf #1009) is the primary home of the RxEACH evidence, and this shelf exists for the CKD-specific angle only.
cards.source: Al Hamarneh YN et al.; RxEACH Investigators. Effectiveness of Pharmacist Interventions on Cardiovascular Risk in Patients With CKD: A Subgroup Analysis of the Randomized Controlled R(x)EACH Trial. Am J Kidney Dis. 2018. PMID: 28912054. shelves.title: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin for uncomplicated diabetic ketoacidosis
shelves.question: In patients with uncomplicated diabetic ketoacidosis, does subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin achieve resolution comparable to intravenous insulin infusion?
shelves.mesh: 3-Hydroxybutyric Acid/blood · Adult · Bicarbonates/blood · Blood Glucose/drug effects/metabolism · Critical Care/economics/methods · Diabetic Ketoacidosis/drug therapy/economics/metabolism · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hospital Charges/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/economics/pharmacology · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives/economics/pharmacology · Insulin Lispro · Ketones/blood · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two small single-centre randomised trials of two different analogues point the same way. Umpierrez 2004 (insulin lispro hourly subcutaneously, n=40): time to resolution of ketoacidosis (10 vs 11 h) and of hyperglycaemia (7 vs 7 h) did not differ significantly from IV regular insulin; hospital stay did not differ; no deaths occurred. Umpierrez 2004 (insulin aspart every 1–2 h, n=45): time to hyperglycaemia correction (6.9 and 6.1 h for hourly and 2-hourly aspart versus 7.1 h) and to DKA resolution (10 and 10.7 versus 11 h) were comparable; length of stay did not differ; there were no deaths in any group — mortality is printed beside the resolution outcomes, as required, and shows only that these small uncomplicated-DKA cohorts had no signal either way. Both trials are small (40 and 45 patients) and explicitly excluded complicated DKA (severe acidosis, altered mentation, hypotension and comorbidity exclusions vary slightly between them) — the shelf's claim does not extend to severe or complicated DKA, children, or pregnancy.

cards.headline: Umpierrez 2004 (lispro): hourly subcutaneous lispro resolved uncomplicated DKA as fast as IV insulin (10 vs 11 h)
cards.summary: Umpierrez 2004 (lispro): hourly subcutaneous lispro resolved uncomplicated DKA as fast as IV insulin (10 vs 11 h)
cards.people: 40 consecutive patients with uncomplicated diabetic ketoacidosis were randomised to subcutaneous insulin lispro (n=20; managed in regular medicine wards [n=10] or an intermediate care unit [n=10]) or intravenous regular insulin infusion (n=20; managed in the intensive care unit). Admission values were similar between groups (lispro: glucose 674 ± 154 mg/dl, bicarbonate 9.2 ± 4 mEq/l, pH 7.17 ± 0.10; IV: glucose 611 ± 264 mg/dl, bicarbonate 10.6 ± 4 mEq/l, pH 7.19 ± 0.08).
cards.result: The duration of treatment until correction of hyperglycaemia was 7 ± 3 h on lispro versus 7 ± 2 h on IV insulin, and until resolution of ketoacidosis 10 ± 3 versus 11 ± 4 h; neither difference was significant. There were no deaths in either group, and no differences in length of hospital stay, insulin amount until resolution, or hypoglycaemia rate. ICU care was associated with 39% higher hospitalisation charges than lispro treatment in a non-ICU setting ($14,429 ± $5,243 versus $8,801 ± $5,549; P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: 'Uncomplicated' is the operative word — patients with persistent hypotension, severe comorbidities, or pregnancy were excluded, and treatment took place in a monitored step-down unit. Twenty patients per arm: the trial shows feasibility, not powered non-inferiority.
cards.source: Umpierrez GE et al. Efficacy of subcutaneous insulin lispro versus continuous intravenous regular insulin for the management of patients with diabetic ketoacidosis. Am J Med. 2004. PMID: 15336577. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era for this literature). shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single DKA-specific randomised comparison, a secondary (subgroup) analysis of two companion cluster trials, answers the DKA question directly. In the Self 2020 analysis of the SALT-ED and SMART trials (n=172 DKA patients), balanced crystalloids shortened median time to DKA resolution (13.0 vs 16.9 h; adjusted HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.38; P=.004) and time to insulin-infusion discontinuation (9.8 vs 13.4 h; aHR 1.45, 1.03 to 2.03) versus saline — the hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute medians they summarise. The parent fluid shelves answer the general critical-care question (Shelf #123, SALT-ED/SMART-era evidence in acutely ill adults); this shelf's distinct angle is the DKA population and its resolution endpoint, and the parent trials are not re-carded here. One trial subgroup (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form); the SCOPE-DKA randomised trial is the in-flight confirmatory test named on the closing card.

cards.headline: Self 2020 (SALT-ED/SMART DKA subgroup): balanced crystalloids resolved DKA in 13.0 versus 16.9 hours versus saline
cards.summary: Self 2020 (SALT-ED/SMART DKA subgroup): balanced crystalloids resolved DKA in 13.0 versus 16.9 hours versus saline
cards.type: Secondary (subgroup) analysis of two companion cluster-randomised, multiple-crossover trials (SALT-ED and SMART)
cards.people: 172 adults who presented to the emergency department with diabetic ketoacidosis (94 balanced crystalloids [lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte A], 78 saline) in a single US academic centre; median age 29 years (IQR 24–45) overall, and 90 of 172 (52.3%) were women. Median isotonic fluid volume administered in the ED and ICU was 4,478 ml (IQR 3,000–6,372).
cards.result: Median time to DKA resolution (American Diabetes Association criteria) was 13.0 h (IQR 9.5–18.8) on balanced crystalloids versus 16.9 h (11.9–34.5) on saline — adjusted hazard ratio 1.68 (95% CI 1.18 to 2.38; P=.004), a relative measure printed beside the absolute medians. Median time to discontinuation of continuous insulin infusion was 9.8 h (IQR 5.1–17.0) versus 13.4 h (11.0–17.9); aHR 1.45 (95% CI 1.03 to 2.03; P=.03).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of two cluster-crossover trials, unblinded, single-centre: the parent trials' randomisation unit was the site-period, not the patient, and fluids were given by the crossover schedule in ED and ICU. Resolution time depends on the trial's biochemical criteria; harder outcomes (mortality, length of stay) are not the DKA subgroup's reported endpoints here.
cards.source: Self WH et al. Clinical Effects of Balanced Crystalloids vs Saline in Adults With Diabetic Ketoacidosis: A Subgroup Analysis of Cluster Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA Netw Open. 2020. PMID: 33196806. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02614040 (SALT-ED) and NCT02444988 (SMART), printed in the record's trial-registration statement. shelves.title: Liraglutide versus sulfonylurea during Ramadan fasting in type 2 diabetes (LIRA-Ramadan)
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes who fast during Ramadan, does liraglutide maintain glycaemic control as well as sulfonylurea, with less weight gain and hypoglycaemia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Drug Substitution/methods · Drug Therapy, Combination · Fasting/metabolism · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Islam · Liraglutide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Metformin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Sulfonylurea Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one open-label randomised trial in a specific and clinically distinct setting: patients switched from metformin plus sulfonylurea to metformin plus liraglutide before Ramadan, then compared through the fast. The primary outcome — change in fructosamine during Ramadan — was similar between groups (estimated treatment difference +3.51 µmol/L, 95% CI −5.26 to 12.28; p=0.43): sulfonylurea's within-Ramadan fall was slightly larger, but the liraglutide arm entered Ramadan with lower fructosamine because the switch had already improved control, and HbA1c fell more on liraglutide overall (ETD −0.59%; p<0.0001) — a design feature disclosed on the card, since the comparison bundles the switch with the drug. Body weight decreased more on liraglutide during Ramadan (ETD −0.54 kg; p=0.0091), and documented symptomatic hypoglycaemic episodes were reported by 2% of liraglutide patients (3 subjects) versus 11% on sulfonylurea (18 subjects), with no severe episodes in either arm. Single trial, open-label (two-trial-gate exception candidate in form), in adults with HbA1c 7–10% who intended to fast — the result does not extend to patients advised not to fast, or to insulin-treated patients.

cards.headline: LIRA-Ramadan: liraglutide maintained control through Ramadan with greater weight reduction and fewer documented hypoglycaemic episodes than sulfonylurea
cards.summary: LIRA-Ramadan: liraglutide maintained control through Ramadan with greater weight reduction and fewer documented hypoglycaemic episodes than sulfonylurea
cards.type: Open-label, randomised, active-controlled, parallel-group, multinational trial (up to 33 weeks; switch ≥10 weeks before Ramadan, then Ramadan and follow-up)
cards.people: Adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7–10%) treated with metformin plus a sulfonylurea who intended to fast during Ramadan were randomised to switch to metformin plus liraglutide (up to 1.8 mg daily) or to continue metformin plus sulfonylurea. The abstract does not print the total sample size or the arm sizes, nor mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in fructosamine during Ramadan — was similar between groups: liraglutide −12.8 µmol/L, sulfonylurea −16.4 µmol/L; estimated treatment difference +3.51 µmol/L (95% CI −5.26 to 12.28; p=0.43), with fructosamine already lower in the liraglutide group at the start of Ramadan. Documented symptomatic hypoglycaemic episodes during Ramadan were reported by 2% of liraglutide-treated patients (three subjects) versus 11% on sulfonylurea (18 subjects); no severe hypoglycaemic episodes were reported by either group. Body weight decreased more during Ramadan with liraglutide (ETD −0.54 kg; 95% CI −0.94 to −0.14; p=0.0091). HbA1c reduction was greater on liraglutide over the trial (ETD −0.59%, 95% CI −0.79 to −0.38; p<0.0001). The proportion of patients reporting adverse events was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparison bundles two things: starting liraglutide (with titration time before the fast) versus staying on sulfonylurea — the HbA1c and start-of-Ramadan fructosamine advantages accrued partly before the fast began. The fructosamine primary outcome was met as 'similar', not superior. Total N is not printed in the record's abstract and is not invented here.
cards.source: Azar ST et al. Efficacy and safety of liraglutide compared to sulphonylurea during Ramadan in patients with type 2 diabetes (LIRA-Ramadan): a randomized trial. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2016. PMID: 27376711. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01917656, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Collaborative care for depression with diabetes and/or coronary disease (TEAMcare)
shelves.question: In adults with depression and poorly controlled diabetes, coronary heart disease, or both, does nurse-led collaborative care improve depression scores and cardiometabolic control (HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure) versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Chronic Disease · Cooperative Behavior · Coronary Disease/blood/physiopathology/psychology/therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/complications/nursing/physiopathology/therapy · Diabetes Mellitus/blood/physiopathology/psychology/therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Patient Care Team · Patient-Centered Care/methods · Primary Health Care · Risk Factors · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial, so this shelf is a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer. TEAMcare (n=214) randomised patients with depression and poorly controlled diabetes, coronary heart disease, or both — the topic file's question said diabetes alone; the question is re-scoped to the record, which enrolled the mixed population and cannot be read as a diabetes-only result. The intervention improved all four modelled outcomes together at 12 months (between-group differences: HbA1c 0.58%, LDL cholesterol 6.9 mg/dL, systolic blood pressure 5.1 mm Hg, depression score 0.40 points; combined primary model P<0.001), with more medication adjustment in the intervention arm. The abstract does not print P values for the individual outcomes, only for the combined model, and none are supplied here. Distinct angle: Shelf #533 cards this same trial for depression outcomes in primary care; this shelf asks the disease-control question (glycaemic, lipid and blood-pressure control), and the two shelves should not be merged or double-counted. If the developer rejects the single-trial exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or folded into #533.

cards.headline: TEAMcare: collaborative care improved HbA1c, LDL, systolic pressure and depression together at 12 months (combined model P<0.001)
cards.summary: TEAMcare: collaborative care improved HbA1c, LDL, systolic pressure and depression together at 12 months (combined model P<0.001)
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled trial (14 primary care clinics, integrated health system, Washington State)
cards.people: 214 participants with poorly controlled diabetes, coronary heart disease, or both, with coexisting depression. A medically supervised nurse, working with each patient's primary care physician, delivered guideline-based collaborative care management aimed simultaneously at depression and cardiometabolic risk factors. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: At 12 months the intervention group had greater overall improvement across the four modelled outcomes than usual care: glycated haemoglobin differed by 0.58%, LDL cholesterol by 6.9 mg/dL (0.2 mmol/L), systolic blood pressure by 5.1 mm Hg, and SCL-20 depression score by 0.40 points (combined primary model P<0.001; the abstract prints no P values for the individual outcomes). Intervention patients were more likely to have one or more adjustments of insulin (P=0.006), antihypertensive medication (P<0.001) and antidepressant medication (P<0.001), and reported better quality of life and satisfaction with care (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: One trial, single-blind, in one integrated US health system; the gains ride on intensified medication adjustment, so the trial tests a care-management package, not a drug. Because enrolment mixed diabetes-only, heart-disease-only and combined patients, no diabetes-specific effect can be extracted from this record.
cards.source: Katon WJ et al. Collaborative care for patients with depression and chronic illnesses. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 21190455. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00468676, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Sitagliptin-based therapy for inpatient hyperglycaemia
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with type 2 diabetes on general medicine and surgery wards, does sitagliptin alone or combined with basal insulin achieve glycaemic control similar to basal-bolus insulin?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Hyperglycemia/drug therapy · Hypoglycemia/drug therapy,etiology · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Inpatients · Insulin/therapeutic use · Insulin Glargine · Insulin Lispro/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Insulin, Long-Acting/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Sitagliptin Phosphate · Triazoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — a single 90-patient open-label pilot trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file asked whether sitagliptin is 'non-inferior' to basal-bolus insulin; the record is a pilot randomised study with no non-inferiority design or margin, so the question is re-scoped to the similarity the pilot actually observed, and the correction is disclosed here. Mean daily glucose, readings in target, readings above 200 mg/dL, treatment failures, length of stay and hypoglycaemic events did not differ between sitagliptin alone, sitagliptin plus glargine, and basal-bolus insulin, while total insulin dose and injection count were significantly lower in the sitagliptin arms. The abstract prints P values without the groups' absolute glucose values, so no absolute control figures are carded. The authors' conclusion that sitagliptin is 'safe and effective' overstates what a 90-patient open-label pilot can establish; the card records the data, not the claim. If the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

cards.headline: Umpierrez 2013 pilot: sitagliptin-based inpatient therapy matched basal-bolus glucose control with far less insulin — in 90 patients
cards.summary: Umpierrez 2013 pilot: sitagliptin-based inpatient therapy matched basal-bolus glucose control with far less insulin — in 90 patients
cards.people: 90 hospitalised patients with type 2 diabetes treated before admission with diet, oral agents, or low-dose insulin (≤0.4 units/kg/day), on general medicine and surgery wards, randomised to sitagliptin alone, sitagliptin plus glargine, or basal-bolus insulin (glargine plus lispro with correction doses). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Glycaemic control improved similarly in all groups. There were no differences in mean daily blood glucose after the first treatment day (P=0.23), readings within the 70–140 mg/dL target (P=0.53), readings above 200 mg/dL (P=0.23), or treatment failures — defined as three or more consecutive readings above 240 mg/dL or a mean daily glucose above 240 mg/dL (P>0.99). Total daily insulin dose and number of insulin injections were significantly lower in the sitagliptin groups than with basal-bolus (both P<0.001). Length of stay (P=0.78) and hypoglycaemic events (P=0.86) did not differ. The abstract reports P values without printing the absolute glucose values, and none are supplied here.
cards.watchOut: A pilot, not a non-inferiority trial: 90 patients, open-label, and powered for feasibility. 'No difference detected' in a pilot is not demonstrated equivalence, and the authors' 'safe and effective' phrasing goes beyond the design; hypoglycaemia safety in particular rests on very few events.
cards.source: Umpierrez GE et al. Safety and efficacy of sitagliptin therapy for the inpatient management of general medicine and surgery patients with type 2 diabetes: a pilot, randomized, controlled study. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 23877988. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Abatacept in new-onset type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does co-stimulation blockade with abatacept preserve stimulated C-peptide versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abatacept · Adolescent · Adult · Autoimmunity · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy/immunology/physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunoconjugates/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Insulin-Secreting Cells/physiology · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · T-Lymphocytes/immunology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial with a surrogate endpoint, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. In 112 patients aged 6–45 with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, two years of abatacept left stimulated C-peptide AUC 59% higher in relative terms (95% CI 6.1–112) than placebo — absolute values 0.378 versus 0.238 nmol/L (P=0.0029) — an estimated 9.6-month delay in C-peptide decline. The trial's own interpretation notes that after month 6 the decline ran parallel to placebo despite continued infusions, so the drug bought time rather than changing the trajectory's slope. C-peptide preservation is a surrogate: this record shows no clinical-outcome benefit (no hypoglycaemia, HbA1c or complication outcomes are claimed), and no mortality claim is made or supported. If the developer rejects the single-trial exception, this shelf should be withdrawn.

cards.headline: Orban 2011: abatacept kept C-peptide 59% higher (relative) than placebo at 2 years — an estimated 9.6-month delay in decline
cards.summary: Orban 2011: abatacept kept C-peptide 59% higher (relative) than placebo at 2 years — an estimated 9.6-month delay in decline
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (2 years, 27 infusions)
cards.people: 112 patients aged 6–45 years with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes were randomised 2:1 to abatacept 10 mg/kg (maximum 1000 mg) (77 patients) or placebo (35); the primary analysis included 73 and 30 patients with outcome data. The abstract does not print the sex split.
cards.result: Baseline-adjusted geometric mean 2-hour C-peptide AUC at 2 years was 59% higher in relative terms (95% CI 6.1–112) with abatacept than placebo — absolute values 0.378 versus 0.238 nmol/L (P=0.0029) — corresponding to an estimated 9.6 months' delay (95% CI 3.47–15.6) in C-peptide reduction. Infusion reactions occurred in 22% of abatacept patients versus 17% on placebo; infections were similar (42% versus 43%), as was neutropenia (9% versus 14%).
cards.watchOut: Surrogate endpoint in a single trial: preserved C-peptide is not itself a clinical outcome, and the authors note the C-peptide decline became parallel to placebo after 6 months despite continued treatment — a delay, not a halt. Whether the effect persists after infusions stop was unresolved in this record.

shelves.title: Dasiglucagon for severe hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In people with type 1 diabetes and insulin-induced severe hypoglycaemia, does ready-to-use dasiglucagon restore plasma glucose faster than placebo, and how does its speed compare with reconstituted glucagon?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Glucagon/analogs & derivatives · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced/drug therapy · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Insulin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — three randomised double-blind phase 3 trials (two adult, one paediatric) agree. A correction to the topic file is disclosed here: the file pinned the paediatric trial (PMID 33934456) as the anchor and quoted '10 versus 12 minutes' against reconstituted glucagon; those figures are from the adult trial (Pieber 2021), and the adult trial's primary comparison was against placebo, with reconstituted glucagon as a reference arm — no formal non-inferiority test is printed in the record. In adults, dasiglucagon restored glucose in a median 10 minutes versus 40 minutes on placebo (P<0.001), essentially matching reconstituted glucagon's 12 minutes while removing the reconstitution step; an autoinjector trial and the paediatric trial (ages 6–17) show the same 10-minute median. Recovery within 15 minutes: 99% of adults on dasiglucagon versus 2% on placebo. Nausea and vomiting were the common adverse effects, as expected for glucagon-class drugs.

cards.headline: Pieber 2021 (adults): dasiglucagon restored glucose in a median 10 minutes versus 40 on placebo; reconstituted glucagon took 12
cards.summary: Pieber 2021 (adults): dasiglucagon restored glucose in a median 10 minutes versus 40 on placebo; reconstituted glucagon took 12
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind trial (single dose during controlled insulin-induced hypoglycaemia)
cards.people: 170 adults with type 1 diabetes randomised 2:1:1 to a single subcutaneous dose of dasiglucagon 0.6 mg, placebo, or reconstituted glucagon 1 mg. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Median time to plasma glucose recovery (rise of ≥20 mg/dL without rescue intravenous glucose) was 10 minutes (95% CI 10–10) with dasiglucagon versus 40 minutes (30–40) with placebo (P<0.001); reconstituted glucagon took 12 minutes (10–12). Recovery within 15 minutes was achieved by 99% on dasiglucagon, 2% on placebo (P<0.001) and 95% on reconstituted glucagon. The most frequent adverse effects were nausea and vomiting.
cards.watchOut: The trial's primary comparison is against placebo; glucagon was a reference arm, so 'as fast as glucagon' is a descriptive match of medians (10 versus 12 minutes), not a tested non-inferiority claim. Hypoglycaemia was insulin-induced under controlled conditions, not spontaneous real-world episodes. (The record's MeSH list includes a type 2 diabetes term although the enrolled population had type 1 diabetes; the MeSH is copied as printed.)

shelves.title: Metformin in type 1 diabetes (REMOVAL)
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 diabetes aged 40 and over with cardiovascular risk factors, does metformin slow carotid intima-media thickness progression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Atherosclerosis/complications/drug therapy · Carotid Intima-Media Thickness · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/complications/metabolism/physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one large trial, stated on the face of the shelf. REMOVAL (428 patients, 3 years) missed its primary outcome: progression of mean carotid intima-media thickness was −0.005 mm/year on metformin (95% CI −0.012 to 0.002; P=0.1664), not significant. A prespecified tertiary outcome (maximal cIMT) did fall significantly (−0.013 mm/year; P=0.0093), and metformin produced small sustained reductions in weight (−1.17 kg) and LDL cholesterol (−0.13 mmol/L (≈-5 mg/dL)) with a rise in eGFR (+4.0 mL/min/1.73m²); the average HbA1c reduction (−0.13%) was driven by a 3-month effect that was not sustained. Gastrointestinal intolerance drove discontinuation in 27% versus 12%. Tier C is ruled NOT applicable, with the deviation logic stated explicitly: the topic file said no, and the record agrees — the primary outcome is a surrogate, and the five versus two deaths were a safety count judged unrelated to study medication; no cardiovascular-event or mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf. Single trial: if the developer wants a second randomised test before any stamp, this shelf should be held rather than upgraded.

cards.headline: REMOVAL: metformin did not significantly slow mean carotid IMT progression over 3 years in type 1 diabetes (P=0.1664)
cards.summary: REMOVAL: metformin did not significantly slow mean carotid IMT progression over 3 years in type 1 diabetes (P=0.1664)
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (23 clinics, five countries; 3 years)
cards.people: 428 adults aged 40 or over with type 1 diabetes of at least 5 years' duration and at least three of ten cardiovascular risk factors were randomised to metformin 1000 mg twice daily (219) or placebo (209), on top of titrated insulin. Baseline HbA1c was 8.1% (metformin) and 8.0% (placebo).
cards.result: The primary outcome — progression of averaged mean far-wall carotid intima-media thickness — was not significantly reduced: −0.005 mm/year (95% CI −0.012 to 0.002; P=0.1664). The prespecified tertiary outcome, maximal cIMT, was reduced (−0.013 mm/year; P=0.0093). Over 3 years, HbA1c fell by −0.13% on average, accounted for by a −0.24% reduction at 3 months that was not sustained; bodyweight fell by −1.17 kg and LDL cholesterol by −0.13 mmol/L (≈-5 mg/dL), eGFR rose by 4.0 mL/min/1.73m², and insulin requirement was not reduced on average. There was no effect on endothelial function or retinopathy. Discontinuation was 27% on metformin versus 12% on placebo (P=0.0002), mainly gastrointestinal. Five deaths occurred on metformin and two on placebo, none judged related to study medication.
cards.watchOut: cIMT is a surrogate: even the significant maximal-cIMT result does not show fewer cardiovascular events, and the trial was not powered for events. The HbA1c pattern (early fall, not sustained) undercuts any claim that metformin improves glycaemic control in long-standing type 1 diabetes — the authors say so themselves.

Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017. PMID: 28615149. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01483560, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Pramlintide as adjunct insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 diabetes, does adjunctive pramlintide improve HbA1c and body weight versus insulin alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amyloid/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Body Weight/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/epidemiology · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Incidence · Insulin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Islet Amyloid Polypeptide · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Placebos
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two randomised double-blind trials, with an honest inconsistency between them on HbA1c. In the 52-week trial (Whitehouse 2002, n=480), pramlintide cut HbA1c by −0.67% versus −0.16% on placebo at week 13 (P<0.0001), the placebo-corrected difference was sustained through week 52 (P=0.0071, magnitude not printed in the abstract), and patients lost weight rather than gaining, without an increase in overall severe hypoglycaemia. In the 29-week trial run with proactive mealtime-insulin reduction and re-optimisation (Edelman 2006, n=296), HbA1c fell identically in both groups (−0.5%), while postprandial excursions and weight clearly favoured pramlintide (weight −1.3 kg versus +1.2 kg; P<0.0001) and the severe hypoglycaemia rate was higher on pramlintide (0.57 versus 0.30 events/patient-year; P<0.05). Read together: the weight and postprandial effects are consistent; the HbA1c advantage depends on how insulin is managed around it; nausea is frequent (63% versus 36% in Edelman). POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because the headline glycaemic claim is design-dependent.

cards.headline: Whitehouse 2002: pramlintide lowered HbA1c (−0.67% vs −0.16% at week 13) with weight loss rather than gain over 52 weeks
cards.summary: Whitehouse 2002: pramlintide lowered HbA1c (−0.67% vs −0.16% at week 13) with weight loss rather than gain over 52 weeks
cards.type: 52-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre randomised trial, with a 1-year open-label extension (extension fenced — see watch-out)
cards.people: 480 patients with type 1 diabetes were randomised to preprandial placebo or pramlintide 30 µg four times daily added to existing insulin; at week 20, pramlintide patients with less than 1% HbA1c reduction were re-randomised to 30 or 60 µg. 342 patients completed the 52-week study. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by 0.67% on pramlintide versus 0.16% on placebo at week 13 (P<0.0001), and a significant placebo-corrected difference was sustained through week 52 (P=0.0071; the abstract does not print the week-52 magnitude, and none is supplied here). The HbA1c reduction came with average weight loss rather than the gain typical of insulin intensification (no weight figures are printed in the abstract). There was no increase in the overall event rate of severe hypoglycaemia. The most common adverse events were mild nausea and anorexia, early and dissipating.
cards.watchOut: The 1-year open-label extension (236 of the 342 completers) is not randomised evidence and is not carded as such; it is mentioned only to fence it. This trial added pramlintide to unchanged insulin regimens; the Edelman trial below, which cut mealtime insulin first, got a different HbA1c answer.

cards.headline: Edelman 2006: with insulin re-optimised, HbA1c fell equally in both groups — but weight (−1.3 vs +1.2 kg) and postprandial glucose favoured pramlintide
cards.summary: Edelman 2006: with insulin re-optimised, HbA1c fell equally in both groups — but weight (−1.3 vs +1.2 kg) and postprandial glucose favoured pramlintide
cards.type: 29-week double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (dose escalation with proactive mealtime insulin reduction)
cards.people: 296 patients with type 1 diabetes (baseline HbA1c 8.1% in both groups) randomised to pramlintide (escalated 15 to 60 µg per meal, with 30–50% mealtime insulin reductions at initiation) or placebo, followed by insulin re-optimisation. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: HbA1c at week 29 had fallen by −0.5% in both groups (pramlintide 95% CI −0.61 to −0.33; placebo −0.63 to −0.35). Postprandial glucose excursions were substantially smaller on pramlintide (incremental AUC −175 ± 40 versus −64 ± 38 mg·h/dL; P<0.0005), weight diverged (−1.3 ± 0.30 kg versus +1.2 ± 0.30 kg; P<0.0001), and insulin dose fell 28% on pramlintide versus 4% on placebo. Nausea was reported by 63% versus 36% (P<0.01). Severe hypoglycaemia rates were low in both groups but higher on pramlintide (0.57 ± 0.09 versus 0.30 ± 0.06 events/patient-year; P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: The severe-hypoglycaemia signal here runs opposite to Whitehouse's 'no increase' — plausibly a consequence of the insulin-reduction protocol and dose escalation, but it is on the record and belongs on the card. When insulin is actively re-titrated in both arms, pramlintide's HbA1c edge disappears; its durable contributions are postprandial flattening and weight.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent weight and postprandial benefit; HbA1c benefit depends on insulin handling — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent weight and postprandial benefit; HbA1c benefit depends on insulin handling — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Whitehouse 2002 (480 patients, 52 weeks) and Edelman 2006 (296 patients, 29 weeks) — two independent randomised trials, 776 patients.
cards.result: Pramlintide reliably flattens postprandial glucose and produces weight loss instead of insulin-associated gain in type 1 diabetes. Its HbA1c advantage (~0.5% placebo-corrected) appears when added to fixed insulin, and vanishes when insulin is re-optimised in both arms — so the honest claim is a postprandial/weight drug with a conditional glycaemic bonus, at the cost of frequent early nausea.
cards.watchOut: The two trials disagree on severe hypoglycaemia (no increase in one, a small significant increase in the other); quote both or neither. Four-times-daily (later three-times-daily) injections bound real-world uptake, which these efficacy records do not measure.

shelves.title: 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation for painful diabetic neuropathy (SENZA-PDN): large relief in an open-label trial
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy refractory to gabapentinoids and at least one other analgesic class, does adding 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation to conventional medical management produce ≥50% pain relief without neurological worsening, compared with medical management alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Diabetic Neuropathies · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Spinal Cord Stimulation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A dramatic result from an unblinded trial. In SENZA-PDN, 216 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy refractory to gabapentinoids and at least one other analgesic class were randomised to conventional medical management alone or with an implanted 10-kHz spinal cord stimulator. At 3 months, 79% of the stimulation group had at least 50% pain relief without neurological worsening, versus 5% on medical management alone; mean pain scores at 6 months were 1.7 versus 6.9 on a 10-cm scale. The catch is structural: patients knew whether they had an implant (open-label, no sham), pain is the most expectation-sensitive endpoint there is, and the 24-month durability figures come from follow-up after most controls crossed over to the device, so there is no long-term comparator. Real relief, quite possibly large — but the design cannot separate device effect from expectation effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C: no.

cards.headline: SENZA-PDN (Petersen 2021): ≥50% pain relief in 79% with stimulation vs 5% with medical management alone at 3 months
cards.summary: SENZA-PDN (Petersen 2021): ≥50% pain relief in 79% with stimulation vs 5% with medical management alone at 3 months
cards.people: 216 patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy for at least a year, refractory to gabapentinoids and at least one other analgesic class, lower-limb pain at least 5 cm on a 10-cm visual analogue scale, HbA1c no more than 10%, recruited across US academic and community pain clinics. Randomised open-label to conventional medical management (CMM) alone or 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation plus CMM; 187 evaluated at 6 months, with optional crossover at 6 months.
cards.result: The prespecified primary endpoint — at least 50% pain relief without worsening of baseline neurological deficits at 3 months — was met by 75 of 95 patients (79%) in the stimulation group versus 5 of 94 (5%) on CMM alone (difference 73.6 percentage points, 95% CI 64.2 to 83.0, P<.001). Mean pain VAS at 6 months: 1.7 cm (from 7.6 at baseline) with stimulation versus 6.9 cm (from 7.0) on CMM. Neurological examination improvement at 6 months in 62% (52/84) versus 3% (3/92). Infections requiring device explant occurred in 2 patients (2%) in the stimulation group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: every patient knew whether a device was implanted and switched on, and the endpoint is self-reported pain — the combination most vulnerable to expectation and reporting effects. There was no sham-stimulation arm, so the trial measures the whole implant experience against tablets, not the electrical effect alone. Cross-point: Shelf #996 covers spinal cord stimulation for chronic back and leg pain, a different population and question.

cards.summary: SENZA-PDN 24-month follow-up: relief persisted in device patients — but the comparison group had crossed over
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of the same randomised trial (post-crossover, uncontrolled)
cards.people: 142 patients with an implanted 10-kHz system followed to 24 months — 84 originally randomised to stimulation and 58 who crossed over from medical management after 6 months of insufficient relief. Same trial (NCT03228420), long-term report.
cards.result: At 24 months, mean pain reduction from baseline was 79.9%, with 90.1% of participants reporting at least 50% pain relief; health-related quality of life and sleep improved, and 65.7% showed clinically meaningful neurological improvement on investigator assessment. shelves.title: Mirogabalin for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain: small, replicated pain-score gains in Asian trials
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, does mirogabalin (a gabapentinoid licensed in parts of Asia) reduce average daily pain scores compared with placebo over 14 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analgesics · Bridged Bicyclo Compounds · Diabetic Neuropathies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Neuralgia · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A real but small effect, replicated in the same direction. Mirogabalin, a gabapentinoid licensed in parts of Asia, beat placebo on average daily pain scores in a Chinese phase 3 trial (difference −0.39 points on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.04) and in the pooled Japanese pivotal programme (−0.31 and −0.63 points at the two twice-daily doses) — statistically significant, consistently, and clinically modest: fractions of one point on a ten-point scale, over 14 weeks, against a large placebo response. Somnolence and dizziness rise steeply with dose (up to 19% and 13%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the drug works a little, in Asian populations, over three months; durability and comparative value against pregabalin or duloxetine are not established by these records.

cards.headline: Guo 2024 (China phase 3): pain score fell 0.39 points more on mirogabalin than placebo at week 14
cards.summary: Guo 2024 (China phase 3): pain score fell 0.39 points more on mirogabalin than placebo at week 14
cards.people: 393 Chinese patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain in a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Mirogabalin was given at 5 mg twice daily for one week, then titrated to 15 mg twice daily, for 14 weeks total (196 mirogabalin, 197 placebo). Primary endpoint: change from baseline in weekly average daily pain score (ADPS) at week 14.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference in ADPS change versus placebo was −0.39 (95% CI −0.74 to −0.04, p=0.0301) in favour of mirogabalin. Patient global impression, sleep interference, and quality-of-life measures also favoured mirogabalin. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 75.0% on mirogabalin and 75.1% on placebo; discontinuation for adverse events was 2.6% versus 1.5%. The authors note the effect size was reduced by a large placebo effect.
cards.watchOut: A 0.39-point average advantage on a 0–10 pain scale is small for an individual patient, and 14 weeks says nothing about the years-long course of diabetic neuropathic pain. Chinese population only in this trial.
cards.source: Guo X et al. A Phase 3, Multicenter, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled 14-Week Study of Mirogabalin in Chinese Patients with Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathic Pain. Pain and Therapy. 2024. PMID: 38896199. Registry ID: NCT04094662, from the record. MeSH: none — the record carries no MeSH headings; none have been invented.

cards.summary: Kato 2021 (pooled Japanese pivotal programme): twice-daily doses beat placebo by 0.31–0.63 points; somnolence up to 19%
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised double-blind trials
cards.people: Pooled analysis of the two pivotal 14-week double-blind phase 3 trials of mirogabalin at about 350 sites across Asia: 1,587 patients in total — 824 with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain and 763 with post-herpetic neuralgia — randomised to placebo (633) or mirogabalin 15 mg once daily, 10 mg twice daily, or 15 mg twice daily (954).
cards.result: At week 14, average daily pain score improved versus placebo by −0.31 (95% CI −0.55 to −0.08) for 10 mg twice daily and −0.63 (−0.86 to −0.40) for 15 mg twice daily; the once-daily dose did not separate significantly. Somnolence rose with dose: 3.8% on placebo, 10.8%, 14.5%, and 19.1% across the ascending dose groups; dizziness 2.7%, 5.7%, 9.1%, and 13.1%. Discontinuations for adverse events were uncommon (≤1.9% per group).
cards.watchOut: The pool is not a pure diabetic-neuropathy population: nearly half the patients had post-herpetic neuralgia. The diabetic phase 3 trial inside the pool is genuine replication of direction, but this shelf cannot quote a diabetes-only effect size from the pooled record — the diabetes-specific trial numbers are Guo 2024's.

shelves.title: Home foot temperature monitoring to prevent ulcer recurrence: early win, larger trial missed its primary endpoint
shelves.question: In people with diabetes at high risk of foot ulceration (previous ulcer or amputation), does daily home infrared temperature monitoring of the feet, with activity reduction and nurse contact when a hot spot appears, prevent ulcer recurrence compared with standard preventive care?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Foot · Humans · Incidence · Recurrence · Skin Temperature · Diabetes Mellitus · Secondary Prevention
shelves.balance: The first trial said yes clearly; the bigger, later trial could not confirm it on its own primary endpoint. Armstrong 2007 (225 patients, physician-blinded): ulceration 4.7% with home thermometry versus 12.2% with standard therapy over 18 months. DIATEMP (304 patients, multicentre, assessor-blinded): recurrence at the measured sites 29.1% versus 37.3% — relative risk 0.78, confidence interval crossing 1, p=0.133 — though recurrence at any foot site was significantly lower (relative risk 0.76), and the benefit concentrated in patients who actually reduced activity when a hotspot appeared. The intervention is really a behaviour loop — measure, spot asymmetry, rest the foot — and it works only when the loop is completed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: promising, cheap, harmless, and not yet proven at the standard the largest trial set.

cards.headline: Armstrong 2007: ulceration 4.7% with home thermometry vs 12.2% with standard therapy over 18 months
cards.summary: Armstrong 2007: ulceration 4.7% with home thermometry vs 12.2% with standard therapy over 18 months
cards.people: 225 patients with diabetes at high risk of foot ulceration, in an 18-month physician-blinded randomised trial. Both groups received therapeutic footwear, foot education, regular foot care, and daily structured foot inspection; the thermometry group additionally measured skin temperature at 6 sites on each foot twice daily with an infrared thermometer, and were told to contact the study nurse and reduce activity if corresponding sites differed by more than 4°F.
cards.result: Overall 8.4% (19 patients) ulcerated. Ulceration occurred in 4.7% of the thermometry group versus 12.2% of the standard therapy group (odds ratio 3.0 for standard therapy versus thermometry, 95% CI 1.0 to 8.5, P=.038); the absolute difference is 7.5 percentage points. Time to ulceration was significantly longer with thermometry in adjusted analysis (P=.04). In the week before ulceration, the temperature difference at the ulcer site was 4.8 times greater than in non-ulcerating patients — the physiological premise of the intervention, verified in the same trial.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre-era result with a wide confidence interval (odds ratio 1.0 to 8.5), from a highly supported trial population with nurse contact built in — the monitoring came with a care structure around it.

cards.headline: DIATEMP 2021: primary endpoint missed — recurrence 29.1% vs 37.3% (relative risk 0.78, p=0.133); any-site recurrence significantly lower
cards.summary: DIATEMP 2021: primary endpoint missed — recurrence 29.1% vs 37.3% (relative risk 0.78, p=0.133); any-site recurrence significantly lower
cards.people: 304 people with diabetes, neuropathy, and a foot ulcer in the previous 4 years (295) or Charcot neuro-arthropathy (9), in a multicentre outcome-assessor-blinded randomised trial (7 hospitals, 4 podiatry practices). Usual care versus usual care plus daily measurement of skin temperature at 6–8 plantar sites per foot; a left–right difference above 2.2°C on two consecutive days triggered instructions to reduce activity until the hotspot disappeared and contact the podiatrist.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat: ulcer recurrence at a primary-outcome site in 44 of 151 (29.1%) on enhanced therapy versus 57 of 153 (37.3%) on usual care — relative risk 0.782 (95% CI 0.566 to 1.080), p=0.133, not significant. Recurrence at any foot site was significantly lower: relative risk 0.760 (0.579 to 0.997), p=0.046. Among the 83 enhanced-therapy participants who measured a hotspot, the 24 who then reduced activity had significantly fewer recurrences than usual care (relative risk 0.336, 0.114 to 0.986, p=0.017) — a post-randomisation subgroup, not a randomised comparison.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest and most rigorous trial of the three and it missed its prespecified primary endpoint. Its positive findings are a secondary endpoint and a subgroup defined by what patients did after randomisation — hypothesis-supporting, not confirmatory. Most participants who found a hotspot did not reduce their activity, which is the intervention's weak joint.

cards.headline: Van Netten 2024 (DIATEMP cost analysis): fewer recurrences and lower costs, slightly fewer QALYs — 'at best equally cost-effective'
cards.summary: Van Netten 2024 (DIATEMP cost analysis): fewer recurrences and lower costs, slightly fewer QALYs — 'at best equally cost-effective'
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis within the DIATEMP randomised trial
cards.people: The same 304 DIATEMP participants, followed for 18 months with foot-care costs (prevention and ulcer treatment, including hospitalisation and amputation) and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) compared between monitoring plus usual care and usual care alone.
cards.result: Fewer participants in the monitoring group had ulcer recurrence over 18 months (36% vs 47%, p=0.045). Foot-care costs were lower with monitoring (€6,067 vs €7,376, p=0.45, not significant), but QALYs were also slightly lower (1.09 vs 1.12, p=0.35, not significant), especially in participants without recurrence. The intervention had a 45% probability of being cost-effective at a willingness-to-accept of €50,000 per QALY lost; the authors conclude it is at best equally cost-effective, with savings from prevented ulcers offset by a possible quality-of-life cost of the daily self-monitoring burden.
cards.watchOut: A companion analysis, not independent replication: it re-reads DIATEMP's data through costs and quality of life, and both of its headline differences (costs, QALYs) are themselves non-significant.

shelves.title: Bilayered living skin equivalent (Graftskin/Apligraf) for diabetic foot ulcers (Veves): faster, fuller closure in a single pivotal trial
shelves.question: In noninfected, non-ischaemic chronic plantar diabetic foot ulcers, does a bilayered living skin equivalent added to debridement and off-loading achieve complete wound closure by 12 weeks more often than saline-moistened gauze with the same adjunctive care?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Foot · Diabetic Neuropathies · Humans · Skin, Artificial · Skin Transplantation · Treatment Outcome · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: One pivotal trial, a clean result, and no replication on this shelf. In 208 patients with noninfected, non-ischaemic chronic plantar diabetic foot ulcers, adding the bilayered living skin equivalent Graftskin (Apligraf) — up to five weekly applications — to debridement and off-loading produced complete healing at 12 weeks in 56% versus 38% with saline-moistened gauze (odds ratio 2.14 relative), and cut median time to closure from 90 to 65 days. Osteomyelitis and amputations were also less frequent in the treatment group, though the record gives no figures for those. An 18-percentage-point absolute gain in closure from a single 2001 manufacturer-era trial, unblinded by necessity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Veves 2001: complete healing 56% with Graftskin vs 38% with gauze at 12 weeks; closure 25 days faster
cards.summary: Veves 2001: complete healing 56% with Graftskin vs 38% with gauze at 12 weeks; closure 25 days faster
cards.people: 208 patients with noninfected, non-ischaemic chronic plantar diabetic foot ulcers at 24 US centres, randomised to Graftskin (112) or saline-moistened gauze (96). Both groups received extensive surgical debridement and adequate off-loading. Graftskin was applied at the start and weekly for up to 4 weeks (maximum five applications), or until healing. Primary assessment: complete wound healing by intention to treat at the 12-week visit.
cards.result: Complete healing at 12 weeks: 63 of 112 (56%) with Graftskin versus 36 of 96 (38%) with control (P=0.0042) — an absolute difference of 18 percentage points; the odds ratio for complete healing was 2.14 (95% CI 1.23 to 3.74, a relative odds measure). Kaplan–Meier median time to complete closure: 65 days versus 90 days (P=0.0026). Adverse reaction rates were similar overall, with osteomyelitis and lower-limb amputations both less frequent in the Graftskin group (the record reports the direction, not the counts).
cards.watchOut: Single trial from 2001, sponsored era of the product's launch, and impossible to blind — healing was assessed in patients whose treatment was visible. Both arms received strong standard care (debridement plus off-loading), so the 38% control healing rate is part of the message: the adjunct added to good care, it did not replace it.

shelves.title: Autologous platelet-rich plasma gel for diabetic foot ulcers: consistent direction, fragile anchor trial
shelves.question: In nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers, does autologous platelet-rich plasma gel added to standard care increase complete healing over 12 weeks compared with standard care with a saline gel dressing?
shelves.mesh: Blood Platelets · Diabetic Foot · Double-Blind Method · Gels · Humans · Plasma · Transplantation, Autologous · Treatment Outcome · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: The direction is consistent and the foundations are shaky. The named pivotal trial (Driver 2006) found significance only after an independent audit excluded 32 of its 72 randomised patients from the per-protocol analysis and five wound-size outliers were set aside: 81.3% versus 42.1% healed in the adjusted per-protocol set. A 2024 systematic review pooling 8 small randomised trials (598 patients) found healing improved overall (relative risk 1.32 relative) and healing time shortened by about 17 days. Many small trials, varying preparations, one fragile anchor: the sum is a probable benefit of uncertain size on top of good standard care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Driver 2006: healing advantage appears only in the per-protocol, outlier-adjusted analysis (81.3% vs 42.1%)
cards.summary: Driver 2006: healing advantage appears only in the per-protocol, outlier-adjusted analysis (81.3% vs 42.1%)
cards.people: 72 patients with nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers who completed screening at multiple centres, randomised double-blind to autologous platelet-rich plasma gel plus standard care or control saline gel, treated for 12 weeks or until healing, with healing confirmed one week after closure. An independent audit excluded 32 of the 72 randomised patients from the final per-protocol analysis for protocol violations and incomplete treatment.
cards.result: In the per-protocol set, 13 of 19 (68.4%) PRP-gel wounds healed versus 9 of 21 (42.9%) control wounds. After adjustment for wound-size outliers (5 patients removed), 13 of 16 (81.3%) versus 8 of 19 (42.1%) healed (P=0.036); time to healing also differed significantly (log-rank P=0.0177). No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported, and the bovine thrombin used in preparation caused no factor V inhibition.
cards.watchOut: Read the denominators: nearly half the randomised patients vanished from the headline analysis, and statistical significance arrived only after outlier adjustment. An intention-to-treat result is not reported in the record. This card is the caution, not the proof.
cards.source: Driver VR et al. A prospective, randomized, controlled trial of autologous platelet-rich plasma gel for the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers. Ostomy/Wound Management. 2006. PMID: 16799184. Registry ID: none in record. cards.headline: Platini 2024 (systematic review, 8 RCTs): healing relative risk 1.32, healing about 17 days faster
cards.summary: Platini 2024 (systematic review, 8 RCTs): healing relative risk 1.32, healing about 17 days faster
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled trials with 598 patients, examining autologous platelet-rich plasma gel versus standard or conventional treatment for diabetic foot ulcers in older adults.
cards.result: Pooled results favoured PRP gel: wound healing relative risk 1.32 (95% CI 1.22 to 1.57, a relative measure, p<0.0001); healing time shorter by a mean of 16.97 days (−32.64 to −1.29); hospital stay shorter by 20.11 days (−38.02 to −2.20); and a lower amputation rate (effect estimate 0.36, 0.16 to 0.84, as reported in the record).

shelves.title: Alendronate for acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy: the placebo-controlled trial's record carries no abstract
shelves.question: In acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy of the foot in diabetes, does six months of alendronate, added to off-loading, reduce disease activity (foot temperature, pain, bone-turnover markers) compared with off-loading alone?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Alendronate · Arthropathy, Neurogenic · Bone Resorption · Diabetic Neuropathies · Humans · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The honest answer is that the abstract-bearing record cannot settle this question. A randomised controlled trial of six months of alendronate in acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy exists (Pitocco 2005) — but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so under this library's rule no figures may be carded from it, and the drug-versus-off-loading effect cannot be verified from the record. The one comparative trial with an abstract (Bharath 2013) randomised patients between zoledronic acid and weekly alendronate, both with total contact casting: 75% reached complete clinical resolution in about 122 days on average, with no significant difference between the two drugs — but there was no cast-only arm, so it cannot show that either drug beats casting alone. Bisphosphonate treatment of acute Charcot remains a practice resting on an unverifiable-here trial and clinical habit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Bharath 2013: zoledronic acid and weekly alendronate resolved acute Charcot at the same speed — both with casting, no cast-only arm
cards.summary: Bharath 2013: zoledronic acid and weekly alendronate resolved acute Charcot at the same speed — both with casting, no cast-only arm
cards.type: Randomised comparative trial (drug versus drug, both with casting)
cards.people: 45 patients with diabetes and acute Charcot arthropathy of the foot at an Indian endocrinology and podiatry clinic, randomised to intravenous zoledronic acid plus total contact cast, or oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly plus total contact cast; 40 completed the study. Primary endpoint: complete clinical resolution, defined as a temperature difference between the affected and normal foot of less than 1°F.
cards.result: 30 of 40 patients (75%) reached complete clinical resolution. The mean time to complete resolution was approximately 122 days from treatment initiation, with no significant difference between the zoledronic acid and alendronate groups. Bone-scan activity fell substantially in both groups (visual score down by more than 50%; skeletal-phase target-to-non-target ratio down about 40%). Alendronate was the more cost-effective of the two.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers 'which bisphosphonate?' — equally fast — not 'bisphosphonate or not?'. Every patient received a drug and a cast; resolution rates without a drug are not measured here.

shelves.title: Relamorelin for diabetic gastroparesis: composite symptoms improved in phase 2 — vomiting did not beat placebo
shelves.question: In diabetic patients with moderate-to-severe gastroparesis symptoms and objectively delayed gastric emptying, does the ghrelin agonist relamorelin improve cardinal symptoms and accelerate gastric emptying compared with placebo over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/complications,diagnosis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications,diagnosis · Gastric Emptying/drug effects · Gastrointestinal Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Gastroparesis/diagnosis,drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Humans · Oligopeptides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/etiology
shelves.balance: A phase 2 trial with a split personality. Relamorelin, a ghrelin agonist, significantly reduced the composite of cardinal gastroparesis symptoms (nausea, abdominal pain, postprandial fullness, bloating) versus placebo across all three doses over 12 weeks, and accelerated gastric emptying by about 12% — but vomiting, the symptom patients rank worst and the one most improved from baseline (down 75%), was NOT significantly better than placebo. It also worsened glycaemic control in 14.5% of patients who received it — a serious asterisk in a diabetes drug. The phase 3 programme was never completed and the drug remains unapproved. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a genuine symptom signal in a single phase 2 trial of a drug that does not exist on the market.

cards.headline: Camilleri 2017 (phase 2B): composite symptoms significantly improved; vomiting was not significantly better than placebo
cards.summary: Camilleri 2017 (phase 2B): composite symptoms significantly improved; vomiting was not significantly better than placebo
cards.people: 393 patients with diabetes and moderate-to-severe gastroparesis — objectively delayed gastric emptying on a breath test, recent vomiting, and a cardinal symptom score of at least 2.6 — randomised after a 2-week single-blind placebo run-in to placebo (104) or relamorelin 10 µg (98), 30 µg (109), or 100 µg (82) twice daily for 12 weeks. Symptoms were recorded in daily electronic diaries.
cards.result: Vomiting frequency fell by 75% from baseline on relamorelin but the difference versus placebo was not significant. The composite diabetic gastroparesis symptom score and each of the four individual symptoms (nausea, abdominal pain, postprandial fullness, bloating) were significantly reduced versus placebo in all three dose groups over the 12 weeks (all P<.05, longitudinal analysis). Gastric emptying accelerated significantly versus placebo (by 12%, P<.05 at 10 µg and 30 µg; P=.051 at 100 µg). Dose-related worsening of glycaemic control occurred in 14.5% of relamorelin-treated patients, some requiring insulin or other drug dose adjustments.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint pattern matters: the headline symptom (vomiting) missed significance while the composite hit it — the reverse of the order patients care about. The placebo run-in period may also have enriched the randomised population for placebo non-responders, flattering the drug's contrast.
cards.source: Camilleri M et al. Efficacy and Safety of Relamorelin in Diabetics With Symptoms of Gastroparesis: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study. Gastroenterology. 2017. PMID: 28760384. shelves.title: Metformin causes vitamin B12 deficiency (HOME substudy): a 4.3-year placebo-controlled trial
shelves.question: In insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, does long-term metformin treatment cause vitamin B12 deficiency — the trial basis for monitoring B12 in metformin users?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Folic Acid · Homocysteine · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Metformin · Risk Factors · Vitamin B 12 · Vitamin B 12 Deficiency
shelves.balance: Settled by a proper trial: yes, metformin causes vitamin B12 deficiency, gradually and measurably. In 390 insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes randomised to metformin or placebo for 4.3 years (the HOME trial's B12 substudy), B12 concentrations fell 19% on metformin relative to placebo, and the absolute risk of frank deficiency (<150 pmol/L) was 7.2 percentage points higher — one extra case of deficiency for roughly every 14 patients treated for 4.3 years. The trial measured blood levels, not clinical outcomes like anaemia or neuropathy, but deficiency of this size is exactly what monitoring exists to catch, and it is preventable and treatable once seen. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — a harm claim on a biochemical endpoint, supported by one long, clean, placebo-controlled trial.

cards.headline: de Jager 2010: B12 fell 19% on metformin; absolute deficiency risk 7.2 points higher over 4.3 years (NNH ≈ 14)
cards.summary: de Jager 2010: B12 fell 19% on metformin; absolute deficiency risk 7.2 points higher over 4.3 years (NNH ≈ 14)
cards.people: 390 patients with type 2 diabetes receiving insulin at three Dutch hospitals, randomised to metformin 850 mg three times daily or placebo for 4.3 years. Outcomes: percentage change in vitamin B12, folate, and homocysteine, and the incidence of B12 deficiency (<150 pmol/L) and low B12 (150–220 pmol/L).
cards.result: Versus placebo, metformin lowered B12 concentration by a mean of 19% (95% CI −24% to −14%; P<0.001; a relative change) and folate by 5% (−10% to −0.4%; P=0.033 — an effect that lost significance after adjustment for BMI and smoking), and raised homocysteine by 5% (−1% to 11%; P=0.091). The absolute risk of B12 deficiency at study end was 7.2 percentage points higher on metformin (2.3 to 12.1; P=0.004), a number needed to harm of 13.8 per 4.3 years; the absolute risk of low B12 was 11.2 points higher (4.6 to 17.9; P=0.001), NNH 8.9. Patients ending deficient had mean homocysteine 23.7 µmol/L versus 14.9 µmol/L in those with normal B12.
cards.watchOut: The endpoints are biochemical: the trial shows deficiency developing, not patients becoming anaemic or neuropathic within 4.3 years. The population was insulin-treated and Dutch; the effect is a class property of metformin exposure, but absolute rates will vary with diet, dose, and duration. Cross-point: Shelf #198 covers how to replace B12 (pills versus injections) once deficiency is found.
cards.source: de Jager J et al. Long term treatment with metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes and risk of vitamin B-12 deficiency: randomised placebo controlled trial. BMJ. 2010. PMID: 20488910. Registry ID: NCT00375388, from the record. shelves.title: Starting finerenone and empagliflozin together lowers albuminuria more than either alone (CONFIDENCE)
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with CKD and albuminuria on a renin-angiotensin inhibitor, does simultaneous initiation of finerenone plus empagliflozin lower albuminuria more than starting either drug alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albuminuria · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Benzhydryl Compounds · Creatinine · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Glucosides · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Naphthyridines · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Serum Albumin, Human · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors
shelves.balance: A clean answer to a narrow, practical question — on a surrogate endpoint, over six months. In CONFIDENCE, patients with type 2 diabetes, CKD and albuminuria, all on a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, were randomised to finerenone alone, empagliflozin alone, or both started together. At 180 days the combination reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 29% more in relative terms than finerenone alone and 32% more in relative terms than empagliflozin alone, with no unexpected adverse events; symptomatic hypotension, acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia leading to discontinuation were uncommon. Albuminuria is a well-worn surrogate, not kidney failure or death, and 180 days cannot show whether starting both together changes hard outcomes or simply reaches the same place faster. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a real, additive effect on albuminuria from one well-run trial; whether it converts into fewer kidney failures is not yet shown (THIN: surrogate endpoint, 6 months).

cards.headline: Agarwal 2025 (CONFIDENCE): combination cut UACR 29% more than finerenone alone and 32% more than empagliflozin alone at 180 days (relative differences)
cards.summary: Agarwal 2025 (CONFIDENCE): combination cut UACR 29% more than finerenone alone and 32% more than empagliflozin alone at 180 days (relative differences)
cards.people: Participants with CKD (eGFR 30 to 90 ml/min/1.73 m2), albuminuria (UACR 100 to 5000 mg/g) and type 2 diabetes, already taking a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, randomised 1:1:1 to finerenone 10 or 20 mg daily (with empagliflozin-matching placebo), empagliflozin 10 mg daily (with finerenone-matching placebo), or the combination. Baseline median UACR was 579 (IQR 292 to 1092) among those with data (265 combination, 258 finerenone, 261 empagliflozin). Primary outcome: relative change in log-transformed mean UACR from baseline to day 180.
cards.result: At day 180, the reduction in UACR with combination therapy was 29% greater in relative terms than with finerenone alone (least-squares mean ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.82; P<0.001) and 32% greater in relative terms than with empagliflozin alone (least-squares mean ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.79; P<0.001). Neither agent, alone or in combination, led to unexpected adverse events; symptomatic hypotension, acute kidney injury, and hyperkalaemia leading to drug discontinuation were uncommon.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is albuminuria, a surrogate: the trial ran 180 days and was not designed or powered to show fewer kidney failures, cardiovascular events or deaths. It also does not test starting both against a sequenced start months apart — only against each drug alone.

shelves.title: Second-line drugs on metformin compared head-to-head (GRADE): glargine and liraglutide held A1c best
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes of under 10 years' duration on metformin with A1c 6.8-8.5%, which added drug — insulin glargine, glimepiride, liraglutide, or sitagliptin — best maintains A1c below 7.0% over years of follow-up, and at what hypoglycaemia and weight cost?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dipeptidyl-Peptidase IV Inhibitors · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin Glargine · Liraglutide · Metformin · Sitagliptin Phosphate · Sulfonylurea Compounds · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The fairest comparison the field has: one large, publicly funded, five-year head-to-head trial of the four commonest second-line choices added to metformin. All four lowered A1c, but insulin glargine and liraglutide held the A1c target modestly better — confirmed A1c at or above 7.0% occurred at 26.5 and 26.1 per 100 participant-years respectively, against 30.4 for glimepiride and 38.1 for sitagliptin. Severe hypoglycaemia was uncommon but most frequent with glimepiride (2.2% of participants, versus 1.3% glargine, 1.0% liraglutide, 0.7% sitagliptin), and liraglutide caused more gastrointestinal side effects and the most weight loss. The companion GRADE outcomes paper found no material differences between the four groups in microvascular complications or death over the same five years, so the ranking is about durability of glucose control, not about preventing complications. PROPOSED LIKELY — one pivotal-grade comparative-effectiveness trial, internally consistent across its glycaemic and outcomes papers.

cards.headline: GRADE 2022 (glycaemic outcomes): A1c failure rates 26.1-26.5 per 100 participant-years on liraglutide/glargine vs 30.4 glimepiride and 38.1 sitagliptin; severe hypoglycaemia most frequent with glimepiride (2.2%)
cards.summary: GRADE 2022 (glycaemic outcomes): A1c failure rates 26.1-26.5 per 100 participant-years on liraglutide/glargine vs 30.4 glimepiride and 38.1 sitagliptin; severe hypoglycaemia most frequent with glimepiride (2.2%)
cards.people: 5,047 participants with type 2 diabetes of less than 10 years' duration, receiving metformin, with glycated haemoglobin 6.8 to 8.5%, randomised to insulin glargine U-100, glimepiride, liraglutide, or sitagliptin added to metformin; followed for a mean of 5.0 years. Primary metabolic outcome: confirmed glycated haemoglobin of 7.0% or higher.
cards.result: The cumulative incidence of the primary outcome differed significantly among the four groups (P<0.001 for the global test): rates with glargine (26.5 per 100 participant-years) and liraglutide (26.1) were similar and lower than with glimepiride (30.4) and sitagliptin (38.1). Differences for the secondary outcome (confirmed A1c above 7.5%) paralleled the primary outcome. Severe hypoglycaemia was rare but significantly more frequent with glimepiride (2.2% of participants) than glargine (1.3%), liraglutide (1.0%), or sitagliptin (0.7%). Participants on liraglutide reported more gastrointestinal side effects and lost more weight than those in the other groups.
cards.watchOut: GRADE compared these four older classes only — SGLT2 inhibitors and newer GLP-1 drugs were not randomised arms, so the trial cannot rank today's commonest choices. The advantage of glargine and liraglutide was real but modest, and maintenance of target A1c was difficult in every group.
