shelves.title: Acarbose in coronary disease with impaired glucose tolerance (ACE): no cardiovascular benefit; diabetes onset delayed
shelves.question: In patients with established coronary heart disease and impaired glucose tolerance, does acarbose reduce cardiovascular events — and does it delay the onset of type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Acarbose · Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Disease · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucose Intolerance · Glycoside Hydrolase Inhibitors · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A split result, and the stamp is split to match. On the question the trial was built to answer — cardiovascular events — acarbose did nothing: the five-point composite occurred in 14% on acarbose versus 15% on placebo in absolute terms over a median 5.0 years (HR 0.98; p=0.73), with no difference in the three-point composite, death, or any component. On the secondary question, diabetes onset was delayed: diabetes developed in 13% on acarbose versus 16% on placebo in absolute terms (rate ratio 0.82, an 18% lower relative rate; p=0.005) — delay, not prevention: acarbose lowers post-meal glucose while it is taken, which postpones crossing the diagnostic threshold. Gastrointestinal disorders were the commonest reason for discontinuation or dose change (7% vs 5%). The population was entirely Chinese patients with coronary disease, which bounds how far the result travels. PROPOSED SPLIT — (the treatment made no difference) for cardiovascular events; POSSIBLE for delaying diabetes onset (Tier C).

cards.headline: Holman 2017 (ACE): five-point CV composite 14% vs 15% (HR 0.98, p=0.73); diabetes developed in 13% vs 16% (rate ratio 0.82, p=0.005)
cards.summary: Holman 2017 (ACE): five-point CV composite 14% vs 15% (HR 0.98, p=0.73); diabetes developed in 13% vs 16% (rate ratio 0.82, p=0.005)
cards.people: 6,522 Chinese patients with coronary heart disease and impaired glucose tolerance, recruited from 176 hospital outpatient clinics in China, randomised to oral acarbose 50 mg three times daily (n=3,272) or matched placebo (n=3,250) added to standardised cardiovascular secondary prevention therapy; median follow-up 5.0 years. Primary outcome: five-point composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, hospital admission for unstable angina, and hospital admission for heart failure.
cards.result: The primary composite occurred in 470 (14%; 3.33 per 100 person-years) on acarbose and 479 (15%; 3.41 per 100 person-years) on placebo (HR 0.98; 95% CI 0.86-1.11; p=0.73). No significant differences were seen for the secondary three-point composite, death from any cause, cardiovascular death, fatal or non-fatal MI or stroke, hospital admission for unstable angina or heart failure, or impaired renal function. Diabetes developed less frequently on acarbose (436 [13%] of 3,272; 3.17 per 100 person-years) than placebo (513 [16%] of 3,250; 3.84 per 100 person-years; rate ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.71-0.94; p=0.005) — an 18% lower relative rate of onset. Gastrointestinal disorders leading to discontinuation or dose change: 215 (7%) on acarbose vs 150 (5%) on placebo (p=0.0007).
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) population with established coronary disease — the cardiovascular null may not transfer exactly to other populations, and the diabetes-onset effect is a delay measured while on treatment, not prevention of diabetes. Diabetes onset was a secondary endpoint.

shelves.title: Intensive insulin after myocardial infarction in diabetes (DIGAMI 1 and 2): the two trials disagree
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes (DIGAMI 1: diabetes broadly) after acute myocardial infarction, does an insulin-glucose infusion followed by long-term multidose insulin reduce mortality compared with conventional glucose management?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Diabetes Complications · Diabetes Mellitus · Female · Glucose · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin · Male · Myocardial Infarction · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: The two trials of the same strategy point in opposite directions, so the stamp is split. DIGAMI 1 (620 patients, 1995) found that an insulin-glucose infusion followed by at least 3 months of multidose insulin cut 1-year mortality to 18.6% versus 26.1% on conventional care in absolute terms — a 29% lower relative mortality (p=0.027), with the largest absolute gain in the low-risk, previously insulin-naive subgroup (8.6% vs 18.0%). DIGAMI 2 (1,253 patients, 2005), designed to confirm it, found no mortality difference at all: 23.4% with infusion plus long-term insulin-based control versus 22.6% with infusion plus standard control (HR 1.03), and 19.3% with routine management. DIGAMI 2 never achieved the glucose separation it planned (HbA1c converged to about 6.8% in all groups), which its authors note as a caveat — but a strategy that cannot be separated in practice cannot claim the benefit either. PROPOSED SPLIT — DIGAMI 1 alone would merit POSSIBLE; DIGAMI 2 showed (the treatment made no difference); taken together the claim rests at MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C).

cards.headline: Malmberg 1995 (DIGAMI 1): 1-year mortality 18.6% vs 26.1% (29% lower in relative terms, p=0.027); low-risk insulin-naive subgroup 8.6% vs 18.0%
cards.summary: Malmberg 1995 (DIGAMI 1): 1-year mortality 18.6% vs 26.1% (29% lower in relative terms, p=0.027); low-risk insulin-naive subgroup 8.6% vs 18.0%
cards.people: 620 patients with diabetes and suspected acute myocardial infarction randomised to an insulin-glucose infusion for at least 24 hours followed by subcutaneous multidose insulin for at least 3 months (n=306) or to conventional treatment (n=314), in the pre-statin, pre-primary-PCI era of coronary care.
cards.result: Total mortality at 1 year was 18.6% (57 deaths) in the infusion group versus 26.1% (82) in the control group — a 29% lower relative mortality (p=0.027), an absolute difference of 7.5 percentage points. The effect was most pronounced in a prespecified low-risk subgroup of patients not previously on insulin: 1-year mortality 8.6% versus 18.0%, a 52% lower relative mortality (p=0.020).
cards.watchOut: A 1995 trial: background coronary care has changed completely since (primary PCI, potent antiplatelets, high-intensity statins), so the absolute benefit cannot be assumed today. This is precisely the result DIGAMI 2 was mounted to confirm — and did not.

cards.headline: Malmberg 2005 (DIGAMI 2): mortality 23.4% vs 22.6% vs 19.3% across the three strategies — no difference (HR 1.03 for the primary comparison)
cards.summary: Malmberg 2005 (DIGAMI 2): mortality 23.4% vs 22.6% vs 19.3% across the three strategies — no difference (HR 1.03 for the primary comparison)
cards.people: 1,253 patients (mean age 68 years, 67% men) with type 2 diabetes and suspected acute myocardial infarction randomised to group 1, insulin-glucose infusion followed by long-term insulin-based control (n=474); group 2, insulin-glucose infusion followed by standard control (n=473); or group 3, routine metabolic management (n=306). Median study duration 2.1 years. Primary endpoint: all-cause mortality, groups 1 vs 2.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ between group 1 (23.4%) and group 2 (22.6%) (HR 1.03; 95% CI 0.79-1.34; P=0.831), nor between group 2 (22.6%) and group 3 (19.3%) (HR 1.23; 95% CI 0.89-1.69; P=0.203); overall mortality was 18.4%. There were no significant differences in non-fatal reinfarction or stroke. Blood glucose fell more at 24 hours in the infusion groups (9.1 and 9.1 vs 10.0 mmol/L (≈164 and 164 vs 180 mg/dL)), but by the end of follow-up HbA1c did not differ among groups (about 6.8% in all), and the group 1 fasting glucose target of 5-7 mmol/L (≈90-126 mg/dL) was never reached.
cards.watchOut: DIGAMI 2's failure to separate glucose control between groups is the standing excuse for its null result — but it is also the practical finding: in real coronary care the intensive strategy did not achieve different control, and outcomes were the same.

shelves.title: Intensive glucose control after coronary bypass surgery (GLUCO-CABG): no fewer complications in patients with diabetes
shelves.question: In patients with hyperglycaemia after coronary artery bypass graft surgery, does an intensive insulin target of 100-140 mg/dL reduce perioperative complications compared with a conservative target of 141-180 mg/dL — in patients with and without diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Glucose · Coronary Artery Bypass · Diabetes Mellitus · Female · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Insulin · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One randomised trial, and for patients with diabetes — the population this library serves — the answer is plainly no difference. In GLUCO-CABG, 302 patients with hyperglycaemia after coronary bypass surgery (152 with diabetes, 150 without) were randomised to intensive insulin targeting 100-140 mg/dL or conservative targeting 141-180 mg/dL; achieved ICU glucose was 132 vs 154 mg/dL. Overall, the composite of complications was 42% vs 52% in absolute terms (P=0.08, not significant). Split by diabetes status, there was heterogeneity: among patients with diabetes, complications were identical (49% vs 48%; P=0.87), while the apparent benefit was confined to patients without diabetes (34% vs 55%; P=0.008) — a subgroup finding in the group this shelf is not about. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for patients with diabetes after CABG (THIN: single trial; the diabetes answer rests on its diabetes stratum).

cards.headline: Umpierrez 2015 (GLUCO-CABG): composite complications 42% vs 52% overall (P=0.08); in patients with diabetes 49% vs 48% (P=0.87) — no difference
cards.summary: Umpierrez 2015 (GLUCO-CABG): composite complications 42% vs 52% overall (P=0.08); in patients with diabetes 49% vs 48% (P=0.87) — no difference
cards.people: 302 patients with hyperglycaemia after coronary artery bypass graft surgery — 152 with diabetes and 150 without — randomised to intensive insulin targeting 100-140 mg/dL (n=151) or conservative targeting 141-180 mg/dL (n=151) in the ICU, followed by a single treatment regimen on the ward and 90 days post-discharge. Primary outcome: composite of mortality, wound infection, pneumonia, bacteraemia, respiratory failure, acute kidney injury, and major cardiovascular events.
cards.result: Mean ICU glucose was 132 ± 14 mg/dL on intensive versus 154 ± 17 mg/dL on conservative treatment (P<0.001). The composite of complications did not differ significantly overall (42% vs 52%; P=0.08). There was heterogeneity by diabetes status: among patients with diabetes there was no difference in complications between intensive and conservative regimens (49% vs 48%; P=0.87), whereas patients without diabetes had fewer complications on intensive treatment (34% vs 55%; P=0.008).
cards.watchOut: The overall trend (42% vs 52%) is driven by patients without diabetes. Quoting it for a patient with diabetes would misstate the trial: in the diabetes stratum the event rates were 49% and 48%. Single trial, modest size.
cards.source: Umpierrez G et al. Randomized Controlled Trial of Intensive Versus Conservative Glucose Control in Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery: GLUCO-CABG Trial. Diabetes Care. 2015. PMID: 26180108. No registry ID on the record. shelves.title: Paricalcitol for albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease (VITAL): a near-miss on its primary endpoint
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with albuminuria already treated with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, does adding the vitamin D analogue paricalcitol reduce albuminuria?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Albuminuria · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Double-Blind Method · Ergocalciferols · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Receptors, Calcitriol · Renin-Angiotensin System
shelves.balance: A well-run trial that missed its own finish line. In VITAL, 281 patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria on ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy received placebo or paricalcitol 1 or 2 micrograms daily for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint — percentage change in urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio for the combined paricalcitol groups versus placebo — came out at a between-group difference of −15% in relative terms (95% CI −28 to 1; p=0.071): not statistically significant. The 2-microgram dose alone gave −18% (−32 to 0; p=0.053), and a longitudinal look at that dose showed sustained reductions of −18% to −28% (p=0.014 vs placebo in that analysis) — suggestive, but secondary. Hypercalcaemia and adverse events were similar across groups. A surrogate endpoint, six months, and a primary result on the wrong side of significance cannot carry more than a maybe. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (THIN: surrogate endpoint, primary endpoint formally non-significant).

cards.headline: de Zeeuw 2010 (VITAL): combined paricalcitol vs placebo UACR difference −15% (95% CI −28 to 1; p=0.071) — primary endpoint not significant; 2 µg dose −18% (p=0.053)
cards.summary: de Zeeuw 2010 (VITAL): combined paricalcitol vs placebo UACR difference −15% (95% CI −28 to 1; p=0.071) — primary endpoint not significant; 2 µg dose −18% (p=0.053)
cards.people: 281 patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria receiving ACE inhibitors or ARBs, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo (n=93), paricalcitol 1 µg/day (n=93), or paricalcitol 2 µg/day (n=95) for 24 weeks. Primary endpoint: percentage change in geometric mean urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) from baseline to last measurement on treatment, combined paricalcitol groups vs placebo, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: UACR changed by −3% on placebo and −16% in the combined paricalcitol groups, a between-group difference of −15% in relative terms (95% CI −28 to 1; p=0.071). By dose: 1 µg gave a difference of −11% (−27 to 8; p=0.23); 2 µg gave −18% (−32 to 0; p=0.053). Patients on 2 µg paricalcitol showed a nearly sustained UACR reduction ranging from −18% to −28% over time (p=0.014 vs placebo in that analysis). Incidence of hypercalcaemia, adverse events, and serious adverse events was similar between paricalcitol and placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own interpretation ('safely lowers residual albuminuria') leans on the 2 µg dose and a secondary time-course analysis; the prespecified primary comparison missed significance. Albuminuria is a surrogate — no kidney failure or mortality data here.
cards.source: de Zeeuw D et al. Selective vitamin D receptor activation with paricalcitol for reduction of albuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes (VITAL study): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 21055801. Registry ID: NCT00421733, from the record. shelves.title: Dietary protein restriction in type 1 diabetic nephropathy (Hansen): GFR decline unchanged, fewer reached ESRD or death
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes with progressive diabetic nephropathy, does a low-protein diet (0.6 g/kg/day prescribed) slow GFR decline or reduce end-stage renal disease or death compared with a usual-protein diet?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Diabetic Nephropathies · Diet, Protein-Restricted · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Status · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Regression Analysis · Renal Dialysis
shelves.balance: Two answers in one small trial, and they do not agree — so the stamp is split. On the direct measure of kidney function, protein restriction did nothing: GFR declined at 3.8 ml/min/year on the low-protein diet versus 3.9 on usual protein, identical over four years, and the achieved separation in intake was modest (0.89 vs 1.02 g/kg/day against a 0.6 g/kg/day prescription). On the clinical endpoint, end-stage renal disease or death occurred in 10% on low protein versus 27% on usual protein in absolute terms (log-rank P=0.042; adjusted relative risk 0.23, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.72) — but in 82 patients that is roughly 4 versus 11 events, a handful of events carrying a large claim, with blood pressure and glycaemic control comparable between groups. PROPOSED SPLIT — (the treatment made no difference) for rate of GFR decline; MAYBE (weak evidence) for fewer ESRD or death events (THIN: 82 patients, few events, incomplete dietary separation).

cards.headline: Hansen 2002: GFR decline identical (3.8 vs 3.9 ml/min/year); ESRD or death 10% vs 27% (log-rank P=0.042; adjusted RR 0.23)
cards.summary: Hansen 2002: GFR decline identical (3.8 vs 3.9 ml/min/year); ESRD or death 10% vs 27% (log-rank P=0.042; adjusted RR 0.23)
cards.people: 82 patients with type 1 diabetes and progressive diabetic nephropathy (pre-study mean GFR decline 7.1 ml/min/year) in a four-year prospective trial with concealed randomisation, comparing a low-protein diet (0.6 g/kg/day prescribed) with a usual-protein diet, on top of antihypertensive treatment. Main outcomes: decline in GFR and development of ESRD or death.
cards.result: Achieved protein intake was 0.89 g/kg/day (95% CI 0.83 to 0.95) on the low-protein diet versus 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10) on usual protein (P=0.005) — well short of the 0.6 g/kg/day prescribed. Mean GFR decline was 3.8 ml/min/year (2.8 to 4.8) on low protein versus 3.9 (2.7 to 5.2) on usual protein — no difference. ESRD or death occurred in 10% of patients on the low-protein diet versus 27% on usual protein (log-rank P=0.042); the relative risk of ESRD or death was 0.23 (0.07 to 0.72) after adjustment for baseline cardiovascular disease (P=0.01). Blood pressure and glycaemic control were comparable in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The hard-endpoint signal rests on roughly 15 events total in 82 patients, and the GFR data — the more sensitive measure — show no effect at all. The diet as actually eaten differed by only about 0.13 g/kg/day between groups.
cards.source: Hansen HP et al. Effect of dietary protein restriction on prognosis in patients with diabetic nephropathy. Kidney Int. 2002. PMID: 12081581. No registry ID (pre-registration era; none on the record). shelves.title: Pirfenidone for diabetic nephropathy (Sharma): eGFR rose at the lower dose in one small trial
shelves.question: In diabetic nephropathy with reduced eGFR and albuminuria, does the antifibrotic pirfenidone (1200 or 2400 mg/day) improve the one-year change in eGFR compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Albuminuria · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Biomarkers · Creatinine · Diabetic Nephropathies · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibrosis · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Kidney · Male · Middle Aged · Pyridones · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One small, fragile trial. In 77 patients with diabetic nephropathy, eGFR 20-75 and albuminuria, one year of pirfenidone 1200 mg/day was followed by a mean eGFR rise of +3.3 ml/min/1.73 m2 versus a fall of −2.2 on placebo (P=0.026) among the 52 patients who completed the study. The higher dose showed no such effect (−1.9, not significantly different from placebo) and lost 11 of its 25 patients to dropout — so the dose-response runs the wrong way, and the positive arm is the one with tolerability on its side rather than a stronger pharmacological push. Dialysis initiation (4 on placebo, 1 on 2400 mg, 0 on 1200 mg) did not differ significantly (P=0.25). Pirfenidone is named here as the specific tested antifibrotic product under study for this use. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (THIN: 77 randomised, 52 completers, inverted dose-response, surrogate endpoint).

cards.headline: Sharma 2011: 1-year eGFR change +3.3 on pirfenidone 1200 mg vs −2.2 on placebo (P=0.026); 2400 mg no better than placebo, with 11 of 25 dropping out
cards.summary: Sharma 2011: 1-year eGFR change +3.3 on pirfenidone 1200 mg vs −2.2 on placebo (P=0.026); 2400 mg no better than placebo, with 11 of 25 dropping out
cards.people: 77 subjects with diabetic nephropathy, elevated albuminuria and eGFR 20 to 75 ml/min/1.73 m2, randomised to placebo (n=26), pirfenidone 1200 mg/day (n=26), or pirfenidone 2400 mg/day (n=25); 52 subjects completed the study. Prespecified primary outcome: change in eGFR after 1 year of therapy.
cards.result: Mean eGFR increased in the pirfenidone 1200 mg group (+3.3 ± 8.5 ml/min/1.73 m2) and decreased on placebo (−2.2 ± 4.8; P=0.026 for the 1200 mg comparison). The change on 2400 mg (−1.9 ± 6.7) was not significantly different from placebo, and the dropout rate in that group was high (11 of 25). Of the 77 subjects, 4 initiated haemodialysis on placebo, 1 on pirfenidone 2400 mg, and none on 1200 mg (P=0.25). Baseline plasma biomarkers of inflammation and fibrosis correlated with baseline eGFR but did not predict response to therapy.
cards.watchOut: Only 52 of 77 patients completed, the higher dose failed where the lower dose 'worked', and the standard deviations (±8.5 ml/min) dwarf the mean difference. This is a hypothesis-generating result, not a basis for treatment.
cards.source: Sharma K et al. Pirfenidone for diabetic nephropathy. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2011. PMID: 21511828. No registry ID on the record. shelves.title: Faster-acting insulin aspart (onset 1 programme): noninferior A1c, better post-meal glucose in type 1 diabetes
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus therapy, does fast-acting insulin aspart (faster aspart) control HbA1c and postprandial glucose at least as well as conventional insulin aspart, at 26 and 52 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Insulin Aspart · Insulin Detemir · Male · Meals · Middle Aged · Postprandial Period
shelves.balance: One large phase 3 trial programme (the onset 1 trial, reported at 26 and 52 weeks) gives a consistent answer: faster aspart is noninferior to conventional insulin aspart for HbA1c and slightly better, with clearly better post-meal glucose. At 26 weeks, mealtime faster aspart beat aspart on HbA1c by an estimated −0.15 percentage points (statistically superior, P=0.0003, on top of confirmed noninferiority), and postmeal dosing was also noninferior (+0.04 points) — so the faster formulation can be given after the meal without losing control. At 52 weeks the HbA1c advantage persisted (−0.10 points; P=0.0424) and the 1-hour postprandial glucose increment remained lower (−0.91 mmol/L (≈-16 mg/dL); P=0.0002), with no difference in severe or blood-glucose-confirmed hypoglycaemia. The gains are real but small — fractions of a percent of A1c and better meal spikes, not a step change. PROPOSED LIKELY for noninferiority with modest postprandial superiority.

cards.headline: Russell-Jones 2017 (onset 1, 26 weeks): HbA1c difference −0.15 points for mealtime faster aspart vs aspart (P=0.0003); postmeal dosing noninferior; 1-hour post-meal glucose increment −1.18 mmol/L (≈-21 mg/dL)
cards.summary: Russell-Jones 2017 (onset 1, 26 weeks): HbA1c difference −0.15 points for mealtime faster aspart vs aspart (P=0.0003); postmeal dosing noninferior; 1-hour post-meal glucose increment −1.18 mmol/L (≈-21 mg/dL)
cards.people: 1,143 adults with type 1 diabetes randomised after an 8-week run-in to double-blind mealtime fast-acting insulin aspart (n=381), conventional insulin aspart (n=380), or open-label postmeal faster aspart (n=382), each with insulin detemir, in a treat-to-target design. Primary endpoint: change in HbA1c after 26 weeks.
cards.result: Noninferiority to insulin aspart was confirmed for both mealtime faster aspart (estimated treatment difference −0.15%; 95% CI −0.23 to −0.07) and postmeal faster aspart (+0.04%; −0.04 to 0.12); mealtime faster aspart was statistically significantly superior on HbA1c (P=0.0003). Postprandial glucose increments were significantly lower with mealtime faster aspart at 1 hour (ETD −1.18 mmol/L (≈-21 mg/dL); P<0.0001) and 2 hours (−0.67 mmol/L (≈-12 mg/dL); P=0.0375). The overall rate of severe or blood-glucose-confirmed hypoglycaemic episodes and safety profiles were similar between treatments.
cards.watchOut: Treat-to-target trials are engineered to equalise HbA1c; the −0.15 point difference, though significant, is small. The postmeal arm was open-label.

cards.headline: Mathieu 2018 (onset 1, 52 weeks): HbA1c change −0.08% vs +0.01% (ETD −0.10; P=0.0424); 1-hour post-meal glucose ETD −0.91 mmol/L (≈-16 mg/dL) (P=0.0002); hypoglycaemia no different
cards.summary: Mathieu 2018 (onset 1, 52 weeks): HbA1c change −0.08% vs +0.01% (ETD −0.10; P=0.0424); 1-hour post-meal glucose ETD −0.91 mmol/L (≈-16 mg/dL) (P=0.0002); hypoglycaemia no different
cards.people: The same onset 1 cohort followed to 52 weeks: 381 participants on double-blind mealtime faster aspart and 380 on insulin aspart, each with once- or twice-daily insulin detemir, at 165 sites in 9 countries. This report covers the full 52-week period of the onset 1 trial.
cards.result: After 52 weeks, estimated mean HbA1c change was −0.08% on faster aspart versus +0.01% on insulin aspart (estimated treatment difference −0.10%; 95% CI −0.19 to −0.00; P=0.0424). The 1-hour postprandial glucose increment favoured faster aspart (ETD −0.91 mmol/L (≈-16 mg/dL); 95% CI −1.40 to −0.43; P=0.0002). There was no difference in overall severe or blood-glucose-confirmed hypoglycaemic episodes or treatment-emergent adverse events between treatments.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial as the 26-week card, reported later — the two cards are two reports of one randomised trial, not two independent trials. Durability is shown; superiority remains a tenth of a percent of A1c.

shelves.title: Inhaled technosphere insulin for type 1 diabetes: noninferior A1c, less hypoglycaemia, much more cough
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes on basal insulin, does prandial inhaled technosphere insulin control HbA1c as well as injected rapid-acting insulin analogues (aspart, lispro), and how do hypoglycaemia, weight and cough compare?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin Aspart · Insulin, Regular, Human · Male · Microspheres · Middle Aged · Powders · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two independent randomised trials agree that inhaled technosphere insulin — the specific tested inhaled insulin product — lowers HbA1c about as much as injected mealtime analogues, with less hypoglycaemia, less weight gain, and a lot more cough. In the larger trial (345 patients, 24 weeks, open-label), HbA1c fell −0.21% on inhaled insulin versus −0.40% on insulin aspart — a between-group difference of 0.19 points that met the 0.4-point noninferiority margin, though fewer inhaled-insulin patients reached HbA1c below 7.0% (18.3% vs 30.7%); hypoglycaemia was lower (9.8 vs 14.0 events per patient-month) and weight fell slightly (−0.4 kg vs +0.9 kg), but cough affected 31.6% versus 2.3% and drove 5.7% to stop treatment. The second trial (138 patients, stopped early against a planned 230) likewise found comparable HbA1c against insulin lispro, lower early post-meal glucose, and fewer mild-to-moderate hypoglycaemic events (5.97 vs 8.01; P=0.0269), with cough again the commonest adverse event. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — consistent noninferiority across two trials, but open-label, marginal, and with the second trial under-enrolled (THIN elements).

cards.headline: Bode 2015 (Affinity 1): HbA1c −0.21% inhaled vs −0.40% aspart (difference 0.19, noninferior); target reached 18.3% vs 30.7%; hypoglycaemia 9.8 vs 14.0 events/patient-month; cough 31.6% vs 2.3%
cards.summary: Bode 2015 (Affinity 1): HbA1c −0.21% inhaled vs −0.40% aspart (difference 0.19, noninferior); target reached 18.3% vs 30.7%; hypoglycaemia 9.8 vs 14.0 events/patient-month; cough 31.6% vs 2.3%
cards.people: Patients with type 1 diabetes and HbA1c 7.5-10.0% randomised in an open-label noninferiority trial to prandial technosphere insulin (n=174) or subcutaneous insulin aspart (n=171), both with basal insulin, for 24 weeks. Primary comparison: change in HbA1c from baseline to week 24 (noninferiority margin 0.4%).
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change was −0.21% on technosphere insulin (from 7.94%) versus −0.40% on aspart (from 7.92%); the between-group difference of 0.19% (95% CI 0.02 to 0.36) satisfied the 0.4% noninferiority margin. However, more aspart patients achieved HbA1c below 7.0% (30.7% vs 18.3%). Technosphere insulin patients lost a little weight (−0.4 kg) versus a gain on aspart (+0.9 kg; P=0.0102) and had a lower hypoglycaemia event rate (9.8 vs 14.0 events per patient-month; P<0.0001). Cough (generally mild) was the most frequent adverse event (31.6% vs 2.3%), leading to discontinuation in 5.7%; the small mean difference in FEV1 change (40 mL) disappeared after technosphere insulin was stopped.
cards.watchOut: Noninferior on mean HbA1c change but clearly worse on the proportion reaching target — the two framings coexist in the same trial. Open-label, and nearly one in three inhaled-insulin patients coughed.
cards.source: Bode BW et al. Inhaled Technosphere Insulin Compared With Injected Prandial Insulin in Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized 24-Week Trial. Diabetes Care. 2015. PMID: 26180109. Registry ID: NCT01445951, from the record. cards.headline: McGill 2021: HbA1c unchanged and comparable vs lispro (7.7% vs 7.6% at endpoint); post-meal glucose lower in the first 90 minutes; mild/moderate hypoglycaemia 5.97 vs 8.01 (P=0.0269)
cards.summary: McGill 2021: HbA1c unchanged and comparable vs lispro (7.7% vs 7.6% at endpoint); post-meal glucose lower in the first 90 minutes; mild/moderate hypoglycaemia 5.97 vs 8.01 (P=0.0269)
cards.people: Adults with type 1 diabetes in a 16-week phase 3 randomised trial of technosphere insulin versus insulin lispro; planned enrolment was 230 but only 138 were enrolled because the study was discontinued prematurely. Primary efficacy endpoint: HbA1c noninferiority at a 0.4% margin.
cards.result: HbA1c was similar in the two groups at baseline (7.8% technosphere insulin, 7.6% lispro) and at endpoint (7.7% and 7.6%), with similar least-squares mean changes. Glucose after a standard meal was significantly lower with technosphere insulin in the first 90 minutes. Mild or moderate hypoglycaemia event rates were significantly lower with technosphere insulin (5.97 vs 8.01; P=0.0269). Cough was the most commonly reported adverse event with technosphere insulin; FEV1 did not differ between groups at baseline, 16 weeks, or 4 weeks off study drug.
cards.watchOut: The trial stopped at 138 of a planned 230 participants, so its noninferiority conclusion is underpowered relative to plan. Directionally it matches Bode 2015, which is why the pair is carded together.
cards.source: McGill JB et al. Understanding inhaled Technosphere Insulin: Results of an early randomized trial in type 1 diabetes mellitus. J Diabetes. 2021. PMID: 32737923. shelves.title: Quick-release bromocriptine safety (Cycloset Safety Trial): serious adverse events no higher; a small cardiovascular signal
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes on usual therapy, is quick-release bromocriptine safe overall — serious adverse events and cardiovascular events — compared with placebo over 52 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bromocriptine · Cardiovascular Diseases · Comorbidity · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dopamine Agonists · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Risk Factors · Risk Reduction Behavior · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One large safety trial. The Cycloset Safety Trial randomised 3,095 patients with type 2 diabetes 2:1 to quick-release bromocriptine or placebo on top of usual therapy for 52 weeks. It met its purpose: serious adverse events occurred in 8.6% on bromocriptine versus 9.6% on placebo in absolute terms (HR 1.02, with the upper bound of the 96% one-sided CI at 1.27, inside the prespecified 1.5 noninferiority margin). A prespecified cardiovascular composite (MI, stroke, revascularisation, hospitalisation for angina or heart failure) occurred less often on bromocriptine — 1.8% versus 3.2% in absolute terms (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.96) — but that is 37 versus 32 events in a trial designed and powered for safety, not efficacy, so it is a signal to test, not a benefit shown. Nausea was the commonest adverse event. Note on sources: the trial's design paper (Scranton 2007) describes this same trial and registry number; it is not a second trial, so this shelf honestly rests on one randomised trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — safety established to the trial's standard; the cardiovascular signal is hypothesis-grade (Tier C).

cards.headline: Gaziano 2010 (Cycloset Safety Trial): serious adverse events 8.6% vs 9.6% (HR 1.02, noninferior); prespecified CV composite 1.8% vs 3.2% (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.35-0.96)

cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled safety trial (Cycloset Safety Trial)
cards.people: 3,095 patients with type 2 diabetes randomised 2:1 to quick-release bromocriptine or placebo in conjunction with usual diabetes therapy (diet alone or up to two antidiabetes medications, including insulin), treated for 52 weeks. Primary safety endpoint: any serious adverse event, with a hazard-ratio noninferiority margin of 1.5; a prespecified analysis examined a cardiovascular composite of MI, stroke, coronary revascularisation, and hospitalisation for angina or congestive heart failure.
cards.result: Serious adverse events were reported by 176 patients (8.6%) on bromocriptine-QR versus 98 (9.6%) on placebo (HR 1.02; 96% one-sided CI upper bound 1.27), meeting noninferiority against the 1.5 margin. Fewer patients on bromocriptine-QR reported a cardiovascular endpoint (37 [1.8%] vs 32 [3.2%]; HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.35-0.96). Nausea was the most commonly reported adverse event in the bromocriptine-QR group.
cards.watchOut: The cardiovascular composite was a prespecified analysis inside a safety trial: 69 events total and a confidence interval reaching 0.96. It cannot support a claim that bromocriptine prevents cardiovascular events — only that no safety excess appeared and a benefit signal is worth testing.

shelves.title: Colesevelam added to insulin or sulfonylurea therapy: A1c down about half a point, LDL down too
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on insulin-based or sulfonylurea-based therapy, does adding the bile acid sequestrant colesevelam improve HbA1c and LDL cholesterol compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Allylamine · Anticholesteremic Agents · Blood Glucose · Cholesterol, LDL · Colesevelam Hydrochloride · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypercholesterolemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Male · Mexico · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: Two modest, consistent, industry-era trials from the drug's diabetes development programme. Added to insulin-based therapy (Goldberg 2008, 287 patients, 16 weeks), colesevelam lowered A1c by a treatment difference of −0.50 percentage points versus placebo (−0.41% vs +0.09%; P<0.001) and lowered LDL cholesterol by 12.8% relative to placebo. Added to sulfonylurea-based therapy (Fonseca 2008, 461 patients, 26 weeks), the A1c difference was −0.54 points (−0.32% vs +0.23%; P<0.001) and the LDL difference was −16.7% in relative terms. The effect is real but small, the endpoints are surrogates, the trials ran 16-26 weeks, and the drug's pill burden and gastrointestinal effects sit outside these abstracts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (THIN: small, short trials; surrogate endpoints; a half-point A1c effect).

cards.people: 461 adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycaemic control (A1C 7.5-9.5%) on sulfonylurea monotherapy or sulfonylurea-based combination therapy, randomised to colesevelam 3.75 g/day (n=230) or placebo (n=231) for 26 weeks. cards.result: Least-squares mean A1C change was −0.32% on colesevelam versus +0.23% on placebo, a treatment difference of −0.54 percentage points (P<0.001). shelves.title: Once-weekly insulin efsitora (QWINT programme): noninferior A1c to daily basal insulin in three settings
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes — insulin-naive, on basal insulin, or on basal-bolus therapy — does once-weekly insulin efsitora control HbA1c noninferiorly to once-daily basal insulin (glargine or degludec), and how does hypoglycaemia compare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin Glargine · Insulin, Long-Acting · Insulins · Male · Middle Aged · Recombinant Fusion Proteins · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Three large phase 3 trials, one in each starting situation, all open-label treat-to-target, and all telling the same story: once-weekly efsitora is noninferior to daily basal insulin for HbA1c. In insulin-naive patients (QWINT-1, 795 patients, vs daily glargine) the A1c difference was −0.03 points, and clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia was actually less frequent on the weekly insulin (0.50 vs 0.88 events per participant-year; rate ratio 0.57). In patients switching from daily basal insulin (QWINT-3, 986 patients, vs degludec) the difference was −0.09 points with similar hypoglycaemia (0.84 vs 0.74 events per patient-year). In basal-bolus patients (QWINT-4, 730 patients, vs glargine, both with mealtime lispro) A1c fell −1.01 vs −1.00 points, hypoglycaemia 6.6 vs 5.9 events per patient-year. What weekly dosing buys is convenience — 52 injections a year instead of 365, and in QWINT-1 a median of 2 dose adjustments versus 8 — not better glucose control. PROPOSED LIKELY for noninferiority across the programme (DOUBLE-A: three independent trials).

cards.headline: Rosenstock 2025 (QWINT-1): A1c difference −0.03 points vs daily glargine in insulin-naive patients (noninferior); level 2/3 hypoglycaemia 0.50 vs 0.88 events per participant-year (rate ratio 0.57)
cards.summary: Rosenstock 2025 (QWINT-1): A1c difference −0.03 points vs daily glargine in insulin-naive patients (noninferior); level 2/3 hypoglycaemia 0.50 vs 0.88 events per participant-year (rate ratio 0.57)
cards.people: 795 adults with type 2 diabetes and no previous insulin therapy, randomised 1:1 to once-weekly efsitora (fixed-dose regimen: start 100 U weekly, adjusted every 4 weeks in fixed steps of 150, 250 and 400 U) or once-daily insulin glargine U100 (adjusted weekly or more often), both targeting fasting glucose 80-130 mg/dL, for 52 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in HbA1c at 52 weeks, noninferiority margin 0.4 points.
cards.result: HbA1c fell from 8.20% to 7.05% on efsitora (least-squares mean change −1.19 points) and from 8.28% to 7.08% on glargine (−1.16); the estimated difference of −0.03 points (95% CI −0.18 to 0.12) confirmed noninferiority; superiority was not shown (P=0.68). Combined clinically significant (level 2) or severe (level 3) hypoglycaemia was less frequent on efsitora (0.50 vs 0.88 events per participant-year; estimated rate ratio 0.57; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.84). Mean total weekly insulin dose at week 52 was 289.1 U on efsitora versus 332.8 U on glargine, and the median number of dose adjustments was 2 versus 8.
cards.watchOut: The efsitora arm used a deliberately simple fixed-dose algorithm adjusted only every 4 weeks, against glargine titrated weekly — the comparison is of two treatment strategies, not molecule against molecule at equal titration intensity. Open-label.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Weekly Fixed-Dose Insulin Efsitora in Type 2 Diabetes without Previous Insulin Therapy. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 40548694. cards.headline: Philis-Tsimikas 2025 (QWINT-3): switching from daily basal insulin — A1c difference −0.09 points vs degludec (noninferior); hypoglycaemia 0.84 vs 0.74 per patient-year (rate ratio 1.14, NS)

cards.people: 986 adults with type 2 diabetes currently treated with basal insulin (A1c 6.5-10.0%, up to three non-insulin glucose-lowering drugs, no prandial insulin) randomised 2:1 to once-weekly efsitora (n=655) or once-daily insulin degludec (n=331) at 127 sites in nine countries, in a 78-week open-label treat-to-target trial. Primary endpoint: change in HbA1c from baseline to week 26, noninferiority margin 0.4 points.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change to week 26 was −0.81 points on efsitora versus −0.72 on degludec (estimated treatment difference −0.09; 95% CI −0.19 to 0.01), indicating noninferiority. Combined level 2 or level 3 hypoglycaemia to week 78 occurred at a similar rate (0.84 vs 0.74 events per patient-year; estimated rate ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.83-1.56; p=0.43). Serious adverse events occurred in 16% on efsitora versus 11% on degludec; nine deaths occurred (seven efsitora, two degludec), none related to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: Serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on efsitora (16% vs 11%) without a treatment-related pattern identified by the authors; the trial was not powered to resolve that difference. Open-label.
cards.source: Philis-Tsimikas A et al. Once-weekly insulin efsitora alfa versus once-daily insulin degludec in adults with type 2 diabetes currently treated with basal insulin (QWINT-3): a phase 3, randomised, non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40562047. Registry ID: NCT05275400, from the record. cards.headline: Blevins 2025 (QWINT-4): in basal-bolus therapy, A1c −1.01 vs −1.00 points vs glargine (noninferior); hypoglycaemia 6.6 vs 5.9 events per patient-year (rate ratio 1.11, NS)
cards.summary: Blevins 2025 (QWINT-4): in basal-bolus therapy, A1c −1.01 vs −1.00 points vs glargine (noninferior); hypoglycaemia 6.6 vs 5.9 events per patient-year (rate ratio 1.11, NS)
cards.people: 730 adults with type 2 diabetes (A1c 7.0-10.0%) treated with basal and prandial insulin randomised 1:1 to once-weekly efsitora (n=365) or once-daily insulin glargine U100 (n=365), both with prandial insulin lispro, for 26 weeks in an open-label treat-to-target trial. Primary endpoint: HbA1c change to week 26, noninferiority margin 0.4 points.
cards.result: HbA1c change was −1.01 points on efsitora versus −1.00 on glargine (week-26 values 7.17% vs 7.18%), indicating noninferiority. Level 2 or level 3 hypoglycaemia rates were similar (6.6 vs 5.9 events per patient-year; estimated rate ratio 1.11; 95% CI 0.85-1.44; p=0.44); nocturnal rates were 0.67 vs 1.00 (rate ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.44-1.01; p=0.058). Serious adverse events were reported by 7% on efsitora and 6% on glargine.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six weeks only, open-label, and the mealtime insulin in both arms remained daily — the injection saving applies to the basal component only.

cards.headline: Synthesis: weekly efsitora matches daily basal insulin on A1c in all three settings — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: weekly efsitora matches daily basal insulin on A1c in all three settings — LIKELY
cards.people: 795 insulin-naive patients (QWINT-1), 986 patients switching from basal insulin (QWINT-3), and 730 patients on basal-bolus therapy (QWINT-4), all with type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: A1c differences of −0.03, −0.09 and −0.01 points against daily basal insulin — noninferior in every trial; hypoglycaemia lower in QWINT-1 and similar in QWINT-3 and QWINT-4. PROPOSED LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is the whole claim: weekly dosing trades daily injections for a long-acting insulin that cannot be withdrawn quickly once given. All three trials were open-label and sponsor-run.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rosenstock J et al. N Engl J Med. 2025 (PMID: 40548694), Philis-Tsimikas A et al. Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 40562047) and Blevins T et al. Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 40562048). Registry IDs as on the trial cards.

shelves.title: Early vildagliptin plus metformin in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (VERIFY): treatment failure halved over five years
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, does starting vildagliptin plus metformin together from diagnosis delay initial treatment failure (confirmed HbA1c at or above 7.0%) compared with the standard stepwise approach of starting metformin alone?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Vildagliptin
shelves.balance: One large, long, double-blind trial with a striking result on a process endpoint. In VERIFY, 2,001 people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes were randomised to start vildagliptin plus metformin immediately or to start metformin alone, with vildagliptin added only after confirmed failure — the standard stepwise strategy. Over five years, initial treatment failure occurred in 43.6% on early combination versus 62.1% on the stepwise approach in absolute terms (HR 0.51, a 49% lower relative hazard; p<0.0001); median time to failure was 36.1 months on monotherapy and beyond the study's 61.9 months on combination. Both approaches were safe and well tolerated, with no treatment-related deaths. Two cautions cap the stamp: this is a single trial, and 'treatment failure' is crossing an A1c threshold — a durability-of-control endpoint, not a complication, event or mortality endpoint; whether starting two drugs at diagnosis changes what happens to eyes, kidneys or hearts is not shown here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (THIN: single trial, glycaemic process endpoint).

cards.headline: Matthews 2019 (VERIFY): initial treatment failure 43.6% early combination vs 62.1% stepwise (HR 0.51; p<0.0001); median time to failure 36.1 months vs beyond 61.9 months
cards.summary: Matthews 2019 (VERIFY): initial treatment failure 43.6% early combination vs 62.1% stepwise (HR 0.51; p<0.0001); median time to failure 36.1 months vs beyond 61.9 months
cards.people: 2,001 patients aged 18-70 with type 2 diabetes diagnosed within 2 years and HbA1c 6.5-7.5%, at 254 centres in 34 countries, randomised after a metformin run-in to early combination therapy (metformin plus vildagliptin 50 mg twice daily; n=998) or initial metformin monotherapy with placebo (n=1,003), in which vildagliptin replaced placebo once failure was confirmed. Primary endpoint: time from randomisation to initial treatment failure, defined as HbA1c at least 7.0% at two consecutive scheduled visits 13 weeks apart. 1,598 patients (79.9%) completed the 5-year study.
cards.result: Initial treatment failure occurred in 429 patients (43.6%) in the combination group versus 614 (62.1%) in the monotherapy group. The hazard ratio for time to initial treatment failure was 0.51 (95% CI 0.45-0.58; p<0.0001) — a 49% lower relative hazard. Median time to treatment failure was 36.1 months on monotherapy, versus an estimated beyond 61.9 months (past the study duration) on early combination. Both approaches were safe and well tolerated, with no unexpected findings and no deaths related to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: The comparison builds in its own logic: the stepwise arm could only 'fail' onto the very drug the other arm started on, and failure means crossing A1c 7.0% twice — not a complication. The trial cannot say whether early combination prevents a single microvascular or cardiovascular event.
cards.source: Matthews DR et al. Glycaemic durability of an early combination therapy with vildagliptin and metformin versus sequential metformin monotherapy in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (VERIFY): a 5-year, multicentre, randomised, double-blind trial. Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31542292. Registry ID: NCT01528254, from the record. shelves.title: Fixed-ratio insulin/GLP-1 combinations beat their own components (DUAL I and LixiLan-O)
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral therapy, does a once-daily fixed-ratio combination of basal insulin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist lower HbA1c more than either component given alone?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Combinations · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin, Long-Acting · Liraglutide · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two independent development programmes, testing two different fixed-ratio products, asked the same question against the same comparators — each combination against its own two components — and got the same answer. In DUAL I (1,663 insulin-naive patients), insulin degludec/liraglutide lowered A1c by −1.9% versus −1.4% on degludec alone and −1.3% on liraglutide alone (differences −0.47 and −0.64 points, both p<0.0001), with nausea in 8.8% (versus 19.7% on liraglutide alone) and confirmed hypoglycaemia at 1.8 events per patient-year (versus 2.6 on degludec, 0.2 on liraglutide). In LixiLan-O (1,170 patients), insulin glargine/lixisenatide lowered A1c by −1.6% versus −1.3% on glargine and −0.9% on lixisenatide (both P<0.0001), with 74% reaching A1c below 7% versus 59% and 33%, weight essentially neutral (−0.3 kg versus +1.1 kg on glargine), and nausea 9.6% versus 24% on lixisenatide alone. The combination predictably sits between its components on both gastrointestinal effects and hypoglycaemia, and above both on A1c. PROPOSED LIKELY (DOUBLE-A: two independent randomised programmes).

cards.headline: Gough 2014 (DUAL I): A1c −1.9% on insulin degludec/liraglutide vs −1.4% degludec and −1.3% liraglutide (differences −0.47 and −0.64; p<0.0001); nausea 8.8% vs 19.7% on liraglutide
cards.summary: Gough 2014 (DUAL I): A1c −1.9% on insulin degludec/liraglutide vs −1.4% degludec and −1.3% liraglutide (differences −0.47 and −0.64; p<0.0001); nausea 8.8% vs 19.7% on liraglutide
cards.people: 1,663 insulin-naive adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7-10%) on metformin with or without pioglitazone, randomised 2:1:1 to daily fixed-ratio insulin degludec/liraglutide (n=834), insulin degludec (n=414), or liraglutide 1.8 mg (n=415) for 26 weeks in an open-label treat-to-target trial; 825, 412 and 412 patients were analysed. Primary endpoint: change in HbA1c at 26 weeks (noninferiority vs degludec; superiority vs liraglutide).
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell by 1.9% to 6.4% on the combination, by 1.4% to 6.9% on degludec, and by 1.3% to 7.0% on liraglutide. The combination was noninferior to degludec (estimated treatment difference −0.47%; 95% CI −0.58 to −0.36; p<0.0001) and superior to liraglutide (−0.64%; −0.75 to −0.53; p<0.0001). Nausea was reported by 8.8% on the combination, 19.7% on liraglutide and 3.6% on degludec. Confirmed hypoglycaemic events were 1.8 per patient-year on the combination, 2.6 on degludec and 0.2 on liraglutide. Serious adverse events occurred in 2%, 2% and 3% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 26 weeks, and the fixed ratio caps how far each component can be titrated independently — the design trades dosing flexibility for simplicity. Hypoglycaemia on the combination is an insulin-class effect (1.8 events per patient-year), far above liraglutide alone.
cards.source: Gough SCL et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2014. PMID: 25190523. Registry ID: NCT01336023, from the record. cards.headline: Rosenstock 2016 (LixiLan-O): A1c −1.6% on insulin glargine/lixisenatide vs −1.3% glargine and −0.9% lixisenatide (both P<0.0001); target reached 74% vs 59% vs 33%; nausea 9.6% vs 24%
cards.summary: Rosenstock 2016 (LixiLan-O): A1c −1.6% on insulin glargine/lixisenatide vs −1.3% glargine and −0.9% lixisenatide (both P<0.0001); target reached 74% vs 59% vs 33%; nausea 9.6% vs 24%
cards.people: 1,170 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin with or without a second oral agent (mean diabetes duration about 8.8 years, baseline A1c 8.1%), randomised after a metformin-optimisation run-in to open-label once-daily fixed-ratio insulin glargine/lixisenatide, insulin glargine alone, or lixisenatide 20 µg alone, for 30 weeks. Primary outcome: HbA1c change at 30 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by −1.6% on the combination (to 6.5%), −1.3% on glargine (to 6.8%) and −0.9% on lixisenatide (to 7.3%), both comparisons P<0.0001. More patients reached HbA1c below 7% on the combination (74%) than on glargine (59%) or lixisenatide (33%). Mean body weight fell on the combination (−0.3 kg) and lixisenatide (−2.3 kg) and rose on glargine (+1.1 kg). Documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia was similar on the combination and glargine (1.4 and 1.2 events per patient-year) and lower on lixisenatide (0.3). Nausea occurred in 9.6% on the combination versus 24% on lixisenatide; vomiting 3.2% versus 6.4%.
cards.watchOut: A different product from DUAL I (glargine/lixisenatide rather than degludec/liraglutide) — the two trials support the fixed-ratio concept as a class, not either pen specifically. Open-label; insulin dose capped at 60 units/day by design.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. shelves.title: Concentrated U-500 insulin for severe insulin resistance: twice- or thrice-daily dosing equivalent; pump delivery slightly better
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes requiring more than 200 units of insulin a day, how should concentrated regular U-500 insulin be given — twice-daily versus thrice-daily injections, and pump (CSII) versus multiple daily injections?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Insulin Resistance · Insulin, Regular, Human · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two open-label strategy trials in the small, highly insulin-resistant population that needs U-500 regular insulin (500 units/mL) — named here as the specific concentrated product these trials tested. On scheduling, Hood 2015 randomised 325 patients previously on a mean 287.5 units/day of U-100 insulin to thrice-daily or twice-daily U-500: A1c fell −1.12% and −1.22% respectively, a difference of −0.10 points (95% CI −0.33 to 0.12) meeting the 0.4-point clinical-equivalence margin, with documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia less frequent on thrice-daily dosing and weight gain similar (5.4 vs 4.9 kg). On delivery method, the VIVID study randomised 420 patients to U-500 by pump or by injections: the pump group achieved a larger A1c fall (−1.27% vs −0.85%; difference −0.42; P<0.001) with almost no dose increase (+2.8 U vs +51.3 U), at the cost of a higher rate of nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Both trials are open-label dosing-strategy studies over 24 weeks with glycaemic endpoints — enough for practical guidance, not for hard outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (DOUBLE-A: two independent randomised trials; THIN: open-label, strategy comparisons).

cards.headline: Hood 2015: U-500 thrice-daily vs twice-daily — A1c −1.12% vs −1.22%, difference −0.10 (clinically equivalent); symptomatic hypoglycaemia lower with thrice-daily
cards.summary: Hood 2015: U-500 thrice-daily vs twice-daily — A1c −1.12% vs −1.22%, difference −0.10 (clinically equivalent); symptomatic hypoglycaemia lower with thrice-daily
cards.people: 325 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on high-dose U-100 insulin (mean dose 287.5 units/day in a median of 5 injections; mean baseline A1c 8.7%, BMI 41.9 kg/m2), randomised after a 4-week lead-in to thrice-daily (n=162) or twice-daily (n=163) regular U-500 insulin for 24 weeks in an open-label titration-to-target trial. Primary outcome: HbA1c change from baseline (noninferiority margin 0.4%).
cards.result: Both regimens significantly reduced HbA1c (thrice-daily −1.12%; twice-daily −1.22%; both P<0.001), with a difference of −0.10% (95% CI −0.33 to 0.12) demonstrating clinical equivalence. Total daily U-500 dose rose comparably (242.7 to 343.1 units thrice-daily; 249.0 to 335.0 twice-daily). Incidence and rate of documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia (at or below 70 mg/dL) were lower with thrice-daily dosing (P=0.003 and P=0.02); severe hypoglycaemia was similar. Weight gain was similar (5.4 kg thrice-daily; 4.9 kg twice-daily).
cards.watchOut: There is no U-100 control arm: the trial compares two ways of giving U-500, not U-500 against staying on high-volume U-100. Both groups gained about 5 kg, and total doses rose by roughly 100 units a day.
cards.source: Hood RC et al. cards.headline: Grunberger 2020 (VIVID): U-500 by pump vs injections — A1c −1.27% vs −0.85% (difference −0.42; P<0.001); dose change +2.8 U vs +51.3 U; more nocturnal hypoglycaemia with pump

cards.people: 420 adults with type 2 diabetes (A1c 7.5-12.0%, total daily insulin dose above 200 and up to 600 units/day) randomised to regular U-500 insulin by continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion via a pump designed for U-500 (n=209) or by multiple daily injections (n=211), after a two-week transition to thrice-daily U-500 injections; 365 completed 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change was −1.27% with pump delivery versus −0.85% with injections (difference −0.42%; P<0.001). Fasting plasma glucose changed by −33.9 mg/dL versus +1.7 mg/dL (difference −35.6 mg/dL; P<0.001), and total daily dose changed by +2.8 units versus +51.3 units (P<0.001). shelves.title: Switching to biosimilar insulin glargine LY2963016 (ELEMENT 1 and 2): same control, same safety as originator glargine
shelves.question: In type 1 and type 2 diabetes already treated with insulin glargine, does switching to the biosimilar insulin glargine LY2963016 at the same dose maintain glycaemic control and safety compared with staying on originator insulin glargine?
shelves.mesh: Biosimilar Pharmaceuticals · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin Glargine
shelves.balance: For a biosimilar, 'no difference' is the success criterion, and that is what the randomised evidence shows. The carded report pools the prespecified subgroups of patients in the two ELEMENT trials who were already on originator insulin glargine before randomisation — 452 with type 1 diabetes in the 52-week open-label ELEMENT-1 and 299 with type 2 diabetes in the 24-week double-blind ELEMENT-2 — and who switched at equivalent doses either to the biosimilar LY2963016 insulin glargine (the specific tested product, named because identifying the exact biosimilar is the question) or stayed on originator glargine. No statistically significant treatment differences were found in efficacy or safety outcomes, apart from three isolated findings — weight change in type 1 diabetes, overall incidence of detectable insulin antibodies in type 2 diabetes, and serious adverse events in type 2 diabetes — which were not consistent across both studies or in the total populations and were judged not clinically meaningful. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — read here as demonstrated similarity, the intended result for a biosimilar switch (DOUBLE-A: the anchor report covers both randomised trials).

cards.headline: Hadjiyianni 2016 (ELEMENT-1 and ELEMENT-2 subgroups): no significant efficacy or safety differences between LY2963016 glargine and originator glargine after switching at equal doses
cards.summary: Hadjiyianni 2016 (ELEMENT-1 and ELEMENT-2 subgroups): no significant efficacy or safety differences between LY2963016 glargine and originator glargine after switching at equal doses
cards.type: Randomised controlled trials — combined subgroup report (ELEMENT-1 and ELEMENT-2)
cards.people: Subgroups of patients reporting prestudy originator insulin glargine treatment in two randomised trials: ELEMENT-1, a 52-week open-label study in type 1 diabetes (subgroup n=452; full trial 535), and ELEMENT-2, a 24-week double-blind study in type 2 diabetes (subgroup n=299; full trial 756). At randomisation, patients transitioned from prestudy glargine to equivalent doses of LY2963016 insulin glargine or originator insulin glargine. Primary efficacy: change in HbA1c from baseline to 24 weeks.
cards.result: No statistically significant treatment differences were identified for efficacy and safety outcomes except for weight change (type 1 diabetes), overall incidence of detectable insulin antibodies (type 2 diabetes), and serious adverse events (type 2 diabetes). These differences were neither consistently observed across both studies nor observed in the total study populations, and their magnitude suggests they were not clinically meaningful. The authors conclude that LY2963016 insulin glargine and originator insulin glargine show similar efficacy and safety profiles in patients reporting prestudy glargine treatment.
cards.watchOut: This card reports the prestudy-glargine subgroups of the two trials rather than the full trial populations, and its abstract reports the similarity conclusion without arm-level HbA1c numbers — the claim carried is 'no significant differences found', not a precise equivalence margin. ELEMENT-1 was open-label.
cards.source: Hadjiyianni I et al. Efficacy and safety of LY2963016 insulin glargine in patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes previously treated with insulin glargine. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2016. shelves.title: Cabergoline versus bromocriptine in hyperprolactinaemia: more effective and better tolerated
shelves.question: In women with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea (mostly microprolactinoma or idiopathic), is cabergoline more effective and better tolerated than bromocriptine for restoring normoprolactinaemia and ovulatory cycles?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Amenorrhea · Bromocriptine · Cabergoline · Dopamine Agents · Double-Blind Method · Ergolines · Female · Humans · Hyperprolactinemia · Middle Aged · Prolactin
shelves.balance: One landmark double-blind trial settled the comparison for women with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea. In 459 women (Webster 1994; 279 with microprolactinomas, 167 with idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia), stable normoprolactinaemia was achieved in 83% on cabergoline (0.5–1.0 mg twice weekly) versus 59% on bromocriptine (2.5–5.0 mg twice daily) — a 24-percentage-point absolute advantage (P<0.001). Ovulatory cycles or pregnancy occurred in 72% versus 52%, amenorrhoea persisted in 7% versus 16%, adverse effects were recorded in 68% versus 78% (P=0.03), and discontinuation for intolerance was 3% versus 12% (P<0.001), with gastrointestinal symptoms less frequent, less severe, and shorter-lived on cabergoline. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single large trial, but double-blind for its first phase, with large concordant advantages on efficacy and tolerability; only the first 8 weeks were double-blind, the following 16 weeks open with dose adjustment.

cards.headline: Webster 1994: normoprolactinaemia in 83% on cabergoline vs 59% on bromocriptine; intolerance dropouts 3% vs 12%
cards.summary: Webster 1994: normoprolactinaemia in 83% on cabergoline vs 59% on bromocriptine; intolerance dropouts 3% vs 12%
cards.type: Randomised comparative trial (8 weeks double-blind, then 16 weeks open)
cards.people: 459 women with hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea — 279 with microprolactinomas, 3 with macroprolactinomas, 1 with a craniopharyngioma, 167 with idiopathic hyperprolactinemia, and the remainder with an empty sella — treated with cabergoline 0.5–1.0 mg twice weekly (n=223) or bromocriptine 2.5–5.0 mg twice daily (n=236), double-blind for 8 weeks then open for 16 weeks with dose adjustment, over 6 months total.
cards.result: Stable normoprolactinemia was achieved in 186 of 223 women on cabergoline (83%) versus 138 of 236 on bromocriptine (59%) (P<0.001). Ovulatory cycles or pregnancy occurred in 72% versus 52% (P<0.001); amenorrhea persisted in 7% versus 16%. Adverse effects were recorded in 68% versus 78% (P=0.03), and 3% discontinued cabergoline versus 12% bromocriptine because of intolerance (P<0.001); gastrointestinal symptoms were significantly less frequent, less severe, and shorter-lived with cabergoline. The authors conclude cabergoline is more effective and better tolerated than bromocriptine in hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea.
cards.watchOut: Women only, and mostly microprolactinoma or idiopathic disease — macroprolactinoma (n=3 here) and men are outside this trial's evidence. The open second phase allows dose adjustment and expectation effects into the later results. Long-term issues that emerged later for dopamine agonists (for example valvulopathy at high Parkinson's-disease doses) are not addressed by a 6-month trial at prolactin doses.
cards.source: Webster J et al. (Cabergoline Comparative Study Group). A comparison of cabergoline and bromocriptine in the treatment of hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea. N Engl J Med. 1994. shelves.title: Withdrawing cabergoline in prolactinoma: about two-thirds stay in remission; an MRI remnant predicts relapse
shelves.question: In nontumoral hyperprolactinaemia, microprolactinoma, and macroprolactinoma with normalised prolactin and major tumour shrinkage on long-term cabergoline, what happens after withdrawal — recurrence rates, tumour regrowth, and predictors?
shelves.mesh: Cabergoline · Dopamine Agonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Hyperprolactinemia/drug therapy · Prolactinoma/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: This shelf is observational by design — a prospective withdrawal cohort, not a randomised trial — and is stamped accordingly. In 200 carefully selected patients whose prolactin had normalised on long-term cabergoline and whose MRI showed no tumour or at least 50% shrinkage (Colao 2003), hyperprolactinaemia recurred within 2–5 years of withdrawal in 24% of nontumoral cases, 31% of microprolactinomas, and 36% of macroprolactinomas — so roughly two in three stayed in remission. No patient had renewed tumour growth, though gonadal dysfunction redeveloped in 22% of women and 39% of men whose hyperprolactinaemia recurred. A visible tumour remnant on MRI at withdrawal predicted recurrence: estimated 5-year recurrence was 78% versus 33% in macroprolactinomas with versus without a remnant, and 42% versus 26% in microprolactinomas. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — large, prospective, and directly on-question, but a single selected cohort with no randomised continue-versus-stop comparison; the rates apply only to patients meeting the study's strict withdrawal criteria.

cards.headline: Colao 2003: recurrence after cabergoline withdrawal in 24% (nontumoral), 31% (micro), 36% (macro); no tumour regrowth in anyone
cards.summary: Colao 2003: recurrence after cabergoline withdrawal in 24% (nontumoral), 31% (micro), 36% (macro); no tumour regrowth in anyone
cards.people: 200 patients in an observational, prospective withdrawal study — 25 with nontumoral hyperprolactinemia, 105 with microprolactinomas, and 70 with macroprolactinomas. Withdrawal was considered only if prolactin levels were normal, MRI showed no tumour (or ≥50% reduction, >5 mm from the optic chiasm, without cavernous sinus invasion), and at least 24 months of follow-up was possible.
cards.result: Recurrence rates 2–5 years after withdrawal were 24% in nontumoral hyperprolactinemia, 31% in microprolactinomas, and 36% in macroprolactinomas. Renewed tumour growth occurred in no patient; gonadal dysfunction redeveloped in 10 women (22%) and 7 men (39%) with recurrent hyperprolactinemia, and prolactin at recurrence was significantly lower than at diagnosis in all groups (P<0.001). Kaplan-Meier estimated 5-year recurrence was higher with a visible remnant tumour at withdrawal: macroprolactinomas 78% versus 33% (P=0.001) and microprolactinomas 42% versus 26% (P=0.02). The authors conclude cabergoline can be safely withdrawn when prolactin is normalised and no tumour is evident, with close monitoring — especially for macroprolactinomas.
cards.watchOut: Selection is the whole story: these patients had already normalised prolactin and shrunk their tumours on treatment, so the recurrence rates do not apply to unselected patients stopping early or with uncontrolled prolactin. Follow-up of 2–5 years cannot exclude later tumour regrowth, as the authors themselves state. There is no randomised comparison against continuing treatment.
cards.source: Colao A et al. Withdrawal of long-term cabergoline therapy for tumoral and nontumoral hyperprolactinemia. N Engl J Med. 2003. PMID: 14627787. shelves.title: Liraglutide before IVF in PCOS: a large pregnancy-rate signal in a 28-woman pilot
shelves.question: In obese women with PCOS and poor response to first-line reproductive treatment, does preconception liraglutide added to metformin improve IVF pregnancy rates and weight compared with metformin alone?
shelves.mesh: Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fertilization in Vitro · Humans · Liraglutide/therapeutic use · Metformin/therapeutic use · Polycystic Ovary Syndrome/therapy · Pregnancy Rate
shelves.balance: A striking result in a trial far too small to trust at face value. In a pilot randomised open-label study of just 28 infertile obese women with PCOS who had responded poorly to first-line reproductive treatment (Salamun 2018), 12 weeks of liraglutide 1.2 mg daily added to metformin — followed by a 4-week medication-free period before IVF — gave a pregnancy rate per embryo transfer of 85.7% versus 28.6% on metformin alone (P=0.03), and a 12-month cumulative pregnancy rate of 69.2% versus 35.7%, despite nearly identical weight loss (7.5 kg vs 7.0 kg). With 28 patients, a handful of pregnancies moving between groups would erase the difference, there was no blinding, and live birth was not the endpoint. A second small randomised study from the same centre (Jensterle 2016, 44 women) supports only the weight part of the story: metformin plus low-dose liraglutide lost 6.2 kg versus 3.8 kg on liraglutide alone over 12 weeks — it tested weight, not pregnancy, and its comparison differs. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — pilot-size, open-label, single-centre evidence for a large claimed fertility effect that needs a proper confirmatory trial.

cards.headline: Salamun 2018: IVF pregnancy rate per transfer 85.7% with liraglutide + metformin vs 28.6% on metformin alone — in 28 women
cards.summary: Salamun 2018: IVF pregnancy rate per transfer 85.7% with liraglutide + metformin vs 28.6% on metformin alone — in 28 women
cards.people: 28 infertile obese women with PCOS (mean age 31.07 ± 4.75 years; BMI 36.7 ± 3.5 kg/m²) with poor response to first-line reproductive treatments, in a prospective randomised open-label study: metformin 1000 mg twice daily (MET) or metformin plus liraglutide 1.2 mg daily subcutaneously (COMBI) for 12 weeks, with ovarian stimulation started after a 4-week medication-free period. Pregnancy rate was clinical pregnancies (fetal cardiac activity on ultrasound) per cycle or embryo transfer; spontaneous pregnancies were followed for 12 months.
cards.result: Weight loss did not differ significantly between groups: 7.0 ± 6.0 kg on MET (P=0.001 within group) versus 7.5 ± 3.9 kg on COMBI (P<0.001), between-group P=0.246. Pregnancy rate per embryo transfer was significantly higher on COMBI (85.7%) than MET (28.6%) (P=0.03) — an absolute difference of 57.1 percentage points in 28 patients. The 12-month cumulative pregnancy rate was 69.2% (COMBI) versus 35.7% (MET). The authors conclude preconception low-dose liraglutide added to metformin is superior for pregnancy rates despite comparable weight loss, and call for further exploration of GLP-1 effects on the reproductive system.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-eight patients: the headline percentages rest on very small numerators and denominators, the study was open-label, and pregnancy (not live birth) was the endpoint. Effects this large in pilots this small usually shrink in confirmatory trials. Liraglutide was stopped 4 weeks before stimulation in this protocol — the trial does not support taking GLP-1 drugs during IVF stimulation or pregnancy.
cards.source: Salamun V et al. Liraglutide increases IVF pregnancy rates in obese PCOS women with poor response to first-line reproductive treatments: a pilot randomized study. Eur J Endocrinol. 2018. PMID: 29703793. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jensterle 2016: metformin added to low-dose liraglutide increased weight loss (6.2 kg vs 3.8 kg) — a weight trial, not a fertility trial
cards.summary: Jensterle 2016: metformin added to low-dose liraglutide increased weight loss (6.2 kg vs 3.8 kg) — a weight trial, not a fertility trial
cards.people: 44 obese women with PCOS randomised to combined metformin 1000 mg twice daily plus liraglutide 1.2 mg daily (COMBO) or liraglutide 1.2 mg daily alone for 12 weeks; 43 completed (mean age 30.3 ± 4.4 years; BMI 37.2 ± 4.5 kg/m²). Primary outcome: change in obesity measures (weight/BMI).
cards.result: COMBO lost 6.2 ± 2.4 kg versus 3.8 ± 3.5 kg on liraglutide alone (P=0.024); BMI fell 2.2 ± 0.8 versus 1.4 ± 1.2 kg/m² (P=0.024). A ≥5% weight reduction was achieved by 59.1% (COMBO) versus 42.9% (liraglutide alone). Glucose reductions after oral glucose tolerance testing and androstenedione reductions were also greater with COMBO; side effects were mild and transient in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Carded for what it is: evidence that the liraglutide–metformin combination moves weight in obese PCOS — the background plausibility for the Salamun fertility question. It does NOT test pregnancy, its comparison (combination vs liraglutide alone) is the reverse of Salamun's (combination vs metformin alone), and it comes from the same Ljubljana centre, so it is not independent replication of the fertility claim.

shelves.title: Modified-release hydrocortisone in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Chronocort): the phase 3 primary endpoint failed
shelves.question: In adults with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, does modified-release hydrocortisone (designed to mimic the circadian cortisol profile) control androgen excess better than standard glucocorticoid therapy without increasing total exposure?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Hyperplasia, Congenital/drug therapy · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Humans · Hydrocortisone/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: The trial's own primary endpoint failed, and the honest shelf is that failure plus what was found underneath it. In the 6-month randomised phase 3 trial of the specific tested modified-release hydrocortisone programme (Chronocort; 122 adults with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia), the primary outcome — change in 24-hour 17-hydroxyprogesterone SD score — was not met at 6 months. Secondary measures favoured modified-release hydrocortisone: lower 17OHP SDS at 4 weeks (P=.007) and 12 weeks (P=.019) and between 07:00 and 15:00 at 6 months (P=.044), with controlled 09:00 17OHP in 91% versus 71% on standard therapy (P=.002); in the single-arm extension, control was 80% at 18 months and the median daily hydrocortisone dose fell from 25 mg at baseline to 20 mg. Patient-reported benefits included menses restoration in 8 patients (1 on standard therapy) and 3 patient and 4 partner pregnancies (none on standard therapy); three adrenal crises occurred in phase 3, none on modified-release hydrocortisone, and 4 in the extension. SPLIT: (the treatment made no difference) on the prespecified primary outcome; POSSIBLE for better morning biochemical control — secondary and extension-phase findings that a failed-primary trial cannot promote to proven benefit.

cards.headline: Merke 2021: phase 3 trial FAILED its primary 24-hour 17OHP endpoint; morning control and dose findings come from secondary measures and the extension
cards.summary: Merke 2021: phase 3 trial FAILED its primary 24-hour 17OHP endpoint; morning control and dose findings come from secondary measures and the extension
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial with single-arm extension
cards.people: 122 adults with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 6-month randomised phase 3 study of modified-release hydrocortisone (MR-HC, the Chronocort programme) versus standard glucocorticoid therapy, followed by a single-arm MR-HC extension study. Primary outcome (phase 3): change in 24-hour SD score (SDS) of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17OHP).
cards.result: The study failed its primary outcome at 6 months. Evidence of better biochemical control on MR-HC included lower 17OHP SDS at 4 weeks (P=.007) and 12 weeks (P=.019), and between 07:00h and 15:00h at 6 months (P=.044). Controlled 09:00h serum 17OHP (<1200 ng/dL) rose from 52% at baseline to 91% on MR-HC versus 71% on standard therapy at 6 months (P=.002), and was 80% on MR-HC at 18 months in the extension. Median daily hydrocortisone dose was 25 mg at baseline; at 6 months, 31 mg (standard) and 30 mg (MR-HC); after 18 months, 20 mg (MR-HC). Three adrenal crises occurred in phase 3, none on MR-HC, and 4 occurred in the extension. Menses were restored in 8 patients (1 on standard therapy), with 3 patient and 4 partner pregnancies (none on standard therapy).
cards.watchOut: A failed primary endpoint disciplines everything else on this card: the positive findings are secondary timepoints, a single time-of-day control measure, and an uncontrolled extension in which dose fell — designs that cannot exclude regression to the mean, titration effects, or selection of continuers. Several authors are employees of the product's developer (Diurnal Ltd). Adrenal crises still occurred, including on extension treatment — circadian release does not remove crisis risk or sick-day rules.
cards.source: Merke DP et al. Modified-Release Hydrocortisone in Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2021. PMID: 33527139. Registry ID: NCT02716818 and NCT03062280, from the record. at 6 months, 31 mg (standard) and 30 mg (mr-hc); after 18 months, 20 mg (mr-hc). three adrenal crises occurred in phase 3, none on mr-hc, and 4 occurred in the extension. menses were restored in 8 patients (1 on standard therapy), with 3 patient and 4 partner pregnancies (none on standard therapy). a failed primary endpoint disciplines everything else on this card: the positive findings are secondary timepoints, a single time-of-day control measure, and an uncontrolled extension in which dose fell — designs that cannot exclude regression to the mean, titration effects, or selection of continuers. several authors are employees of the product's developer (diurnal ltd). adrenal crises still occurred, including on extension treatment — circadian release does not remove crisis risk or sick-day rules. merke dp et al. modified-release hydrocortisone in congenital adrenal hyperplasia. j clin endocrinol metab. 2021. pmid: 33527139. registry id: nct02716818 and nct03062280, from the record. mesh: adrenal hyperplasia, congenital/drug therapy · adrenal hyperplasia, congenital/metabolism · adrenal hyperplasia, congenital/pathology · adult · aged · anti-inflammatory agents/administration & dosage · anti-inflammatory agents/chemistry · anti-inflammatory agents/metabolism · female · follow-up studies · humans · hydrocortisone/administration & dosage · hydrocortisone/chemistry · hydrocortisone/metabolism · male · middle aged · prognosis · young adult
