shelves.title: Empagliflozin for SIAD: raises sodium modestly in two small randomised trials
shelves.question: In patients with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD), does empagliflozin raise plasma sodium compared with placebo, in hospitalised hyponatraemia and in chronic outpatient SIAD?
shelves.mesh: Hyponatremia/drug therapy · Inappropriate ADH Syndrome/drug therapy · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Humans
shelves.balance: Two small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials from one research group point the same way, in two different settings. In hospitalised patients with SIAD-induced hyponatraemia on fluid restriction, 4 days of empagliflozin raised plasma sodium by a median 10 mmol/L versus 7 mmol/L on placebo (P=0.04) — a modest 3 mmol/L advantage on top of restriction (Refardt 2020, 88 patients). In outpatients with chronic SIAD, a crossover trial of empagliflozin 25 mg/day for 4 weeks raised median sodium from 131 to 134 mmol/L while placebo left it at 130 mmol/L, a treatment difference of 4.1 mmol/L (95% CI 1.7 to 6.5; P=0.004), with an exploratory 1.16-point MoCA improvement (Refardt 2023, only 14 patients completing). The endpoint in both trials is the sodium number, not symptoms, falls, or hospitalisation; treatment was well tolerated with no hypoglycaemia or hypotension reported in the hospital trial and no serious adverse events in the crossover. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — concordant randomised evidence for a real but modest sodium-raising effect, with clinical-outcome benefit unproven and independent replication still needed.

cards.headline: Refardt 2020: hospitalised SIAD — sodium rose 10 vs 7 mmol/L over 4 days on empagliflozin vs placebo, both on fluid restriction
cards.summary: Refardt 2020: hospitalised SIAD — sodium rose 10 vs 7 mmol/L over 4 days on empagliflozin vs placebo, both on fluid restriction
cards.people: 88 hospitalised patients with SIAD-induced hyponatraemia (<130 mmol/L) at University Hospital Basel, randomised double-blind to once-daily oral empagliflozin or placebo for 4 days, in addition to standard fluid restriction of <1000 ml/24 h; 87 completed (43 empagliflozin, 44 placebo). Primary endpoint: absolute change in plasma sodium after 4 days.
cards.result: Baseline plasma sodium was similar (median 125.5 mmol/L empagliflozin; 126 mmol/L placebo). The median increase was significantly higher on empagliflozin than placebo (10 versus 7 mmol/L; P=0.04). Profound hyponatraemia (<125 mmol/L) and lower baseline osmolality increased the likelihood of response. Treatment was well tolerated; no hypoglycaemia or hypotension occurred on empagliflozin. The authors conclude empagliflozin warrants further study in SIAD.
cards.watchOut: Four days, one centre, and a 3 mmol/L median advantage: enough to show the mechanism works in hospital, not enough to define a chronic treatment strategy. Both arms received fluid restriction, so this tests empagliflozin as an add-on, not a replacement. Osmotic demyelination risk from faster correction was not an outcome here — sodium rose on placebo too, underscoring that correction speed needs monitoring either way.
cards.source: Refardt J et al. A Randomized Trial of Empagliflozin to Increase Plasma Sodium Levels in Patients with the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2020. cards.headline: Refardt 2023: chronic SIAD crossover — sodium 131 → 134 mmol/L on empagliflozin vs no rise on placebo; only 14 patients
cards.summary: Refardt 2023: chronic SIAD crossover — sodium 131 → 134 mmol/L on empagliflozin vs no rise on placebo; only 14 patients
cards.people: Outpatients with chronic SIAD-induced hyponatraemia in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of empagliflozin 25 mg/day versus placebo, 4 weeks per treatment period; 14 patients completed (50% female; median age 72 years, IQR 65–77; median baseline sodium 131 mmol/L, IQR 130–132). Primary endpoint: difference in serum sodium between treatments; neurocognition assessed with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).
cards.result: Median serum sodium rose to 134 mmol/L (IQR 132–136) on empagliflozin, with no increase on placebo (130 mmol/L; IQR 128–132) — a sodium increase of 4.1 mmol/L (95% CI 1.7 to 6.5; P=0.004). Exploratory analyses showed improved neurocognitive function on empagliflozin, with a MoCA increase of 1.16 points (95% CI 0.05 to 2.26). Treatment was well tolerated; no serious adverse events were reported. The authors call empagliflozin promising for chronic SIAD and state larger studies are needed.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen completers is a pilot, however clean the design: the confidence interval (1.7 to 6.5 mmol/L) is wide, the MoCA finding is exploratory and barely excludes zero, and a crossover cannot speak to long-term safety (genital infection, volume depletion, euglycaemic ketoacidosis) in mostly non-diabetic elderly outpatients. Same group as the 2020 trial — supportive, not independent, replication.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant small RCTs, a modest sodium effect, clinical outcomes unproven — POSSIBLE
cards.people: 88 hospitalised patients (Refardt 2020) and 14 chronic outpatients (Refardt 2023), all from the Basel group.
cards.result: Median sodium advantage over placebo ≈3 mmol/L at 4 days in hospital (10 vs 7 mmol/L, P=0.04) and 4.1 mmol/L (95% CI 1.7 to 6.5; P=0.004) over 4 weeks in chronic SIAD. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Preoperative octreotide in acromegaly (POTA): a short-term macroadenoma advantage that faded by 5 years
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed acromegaly, does 6 months of preoperative octreotide improve transsphenoidal surgical cure rates compared with direct surgery — overall, in macroadenomas, and at long-term follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Acromegaly/drug therapy · Acromegaly/surgery · Humans · Octreotide/therapeutic use · Pituitary Neoplasms/surgery
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence splits by tumour size and by time. In the Norwegian POTA trial (Carlsen 2008; 62 newly diagnosed patients randomised to 6 months of octreotide LAR 20 mg every 28 days or direct transsphenoidal surgery), overall cure by IGF-1 criteria at 3 months was 45% with pretreatment versus 23% with direct surgery — not statistically significant (P=0.11). The significant finding sat in macroadenomas: 50% cured (13/26) versus 16% (4/25) (P=0.017); in microadenomas pretreatment did worse numerically (1/5 vs 3/5; P=0.52), on tiny numbers. The same trial's long-term follow-up (Fougner 2014), using stricter combined cure criteria, found the macroadenoma gap narrowed and lost significance: 38% versus 24% at 1 year (P=0.27) and 41% versus 27% at 5 years (P=0.34); pooling with the one other long-term randomised study gave 37% versus 19% long-term (P=0.08). SPLIT: POSSIBLE for a short-term surgical-cure advantage confined to macroadenomas; (the treatment made no difference) proven for overall cure or for durable long-term cure — a single small national trial, whose own authors say the results need confirmation.

cards.headline: Carlsen 2008 (POTA): overall cure 45% vs 23% (P=0.11, not significant); macroadenomas 50% vs 16% (P=0.017); microadenomas numerically worse
cards.summary: Carlsen 2008 (POTA): overall cure 45% vs 23% (P=0.11, not significant); macroadenomas 50% vs 16% (P=0.017); microadenomas numerically worse
cards.people: 62 newly diagnosed acromegalic patients aged 18–80, screened nationwide in Norway (1999–2004) and randomised to direct transsphenoidal surgery (n=30) or pretreatment with octreotide 20 mg intramuscularly every 28 days for 6 months before surgery (n=32). Cure was evaluated 3 months postoperatively, primarily by IGF-1 levels; 61 patients were evaluated (31 pretreated, 30 direct).
cards.result: By IGF-1 criteria, 14 of 31 pretreated patients (45%) versus 7 of 30 direct-surgery patients (23%) were cured (P=0.11). In macroadenomas, 13 of 26 pretreated (50%) versus 4 of 25 direct (16%) were cured (P=0.017). In microadenomas (≤10 mm), 1 of 5 pretreated (20%) versus 3 of 5 direct (60%) were cured (P=0.52). The authors conclude 6-month preoperative octreotide might improve surgical cure in macroadenomas and that the results have to be confirmed in future studies.
cards.watchOut: The headline lives in a subgroup: the overall comparison — the trial's primary framing — was not significant, and the macroadenoma result rests on 51 patients. The microadenoma numbers run the other way. Six months of injections also delays definitive surgery, a cost the cure percentages alone do not capture. Cure here is a 3-month IGF-1 definition, softer than the combined criteria used at long-term follow-up.
cards.source: Carlsen SM et al. Preoperative octreotide treatment in newly diagnosed acromegalic patients with macroadenomas increases cure short-term postoperative rates: a prospective, randomized trial. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2008. PMID: 18492760. Registry ID: none in the record (the trial's NCT00521300 appears in the long-term follow-up record, carded below). cards.headline: Fougner 2014: at 1 and 5 years the macroadenoma advantage shrank and was no longer significant
cards.summary: Fougner 2014: at 1 and 5 years the macroadenoma advantage shrank and was no longer significant
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised controlled trial, with meta-analysis
cards.people: The same POTA cohort (30 direct surgery, 32 pretreated with octreotide LAR for 6 months), evaluated 1 and 5 years postoperatively. Cure was defined by normal IGF-1 alone and by combined criteria (normal IGF-1 plus nadir GH <2 mU/l on oral glucose tolerance testing), all without additional postoperative treatment. The paper also meta-analysed its results with the other published randomised study of preoperative somatostatin analogues with long-term analysis.
cards.result: The proportion receiving postoperative acromegaly treatment was equal in the two groups. By combined criteria in macroadenomas: 10/26 (38%) cured with pretreatment versus 6/25 (24%) with direct surgery at 1 year (P=0.27), and 9/22 (41%) versus 6/22 (27%) at 5 years (P=0.34). In the meta-analysis, combined-criteria macroadenoma cure was 16/45 (36%) versus 8/45 (18%) at 6–12 months (P=0.06) and 15/41 (37%) versus 8/42 (19%) long-term (P=0.08). The authors conclude the study does not prove a beneficial effect of presurgical somatostatin analogue treatment, though a trend toward significance in the meta-analysis means a clinically relevant response cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: Attrition matters: by 5 years only 22 macroadenoma patients per group remained in the analysis. Later cure percentages use stricter combined criteria than the 2008 paper's IGF-1-only definition, so short- and long-term numbers are not directly comparable — part of the 'shrinkage' is definitional, and part is real attenuation; the paper cannot fully separate the two.
cards.source: Fougner SL et al. Preoperative octreotide treatment of acromegaly: long-term results of a randomised controlled trial. Eur J Endocrinol. 2014. PMID: 24866574. cards.headline: Synthesis: short-term macroadenoma signal, no proven lasting benefit — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: short-term macroadenoma signal, no proven lasting benefit — SPLIT
cards.people: 62 randomised patients (POTA), followed to 5 years, plus one other randomised study in the authors' pooled analysis.
cards.result: Short-term macroadenoma cure 50% versus 16% (P=0.017); overall cure 45% versus 23% (P=0.11); 5-year macroadenoma cure 41% versus 27% (P=0.34). PROPOSED SPLIT stamp as in the balance.

shelves.title: Antiandrogens for hirsutism: spironolactone, flutamide, and finasteride all beat placebo and looked similar in one small trial
shelves.question: In women with hirsutism, how do spironolactone, flutamide, and finasteride compare with each other and with placebo for reducing hair growth over 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Androgen Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Finasteride/therapeutic use · Flutamide/therapeutic use · Hirsutism/drug therapy · Humans · Spironolactone/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: One small but well-measured trial answers the head-to-head question: at the doses tested, the three drugs look alike. In Moghetti 2000, 40 hirsute women were randomised double-blind to spironolactone 100 mg/day, flutamide 250 mg/day, finasteride 5 mg/day, or placebo for 6 months, with hair growth measured objectively — mean hair-shaft diameter by blinded computer-assisted microscopy — as well as by Ferriman-Gallwey score. Hair diameter fell 11.7% on spironolactone, 18.0% on flutamide, and 12.6% on finasteride, with no statistically significant differences among the active drugs; Ferriman-Gallwey scores fell 41.0%, 38.9%, and 31.6% respectively, again without differences among groups. Placebo changed nothing (hair diameter −1.4%; Ferriman-Gallwey +5.4%). With only 10 women per arm, 'no difference among drugs' is a weak claim — the trial could not have detected moderate differences — and 6 months is short for a hair-cycle outcome. Choice among these drugs in practice is therefore driven by safety and patient factors, not proven superiority: flutamide carries a recognised risk of serious liver injury, finasteride is teratogenic to a male fetus, and spironolactone requires contraception and potassium/blood-pressure awareness. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small trial supports that all three work modestly versus placebo; it does not establish that they are truly equal.

cards.headline: Moghetti 2000: hair diameter fell 12–18% on all three antiandrogens vs −1.4% on placebo; no significant differences among the drugs
cards.summary: Moghetti 2000: hair diameter fell 12–18% on all three antiandrogens vs −1.4% on placebo; no significant differences among the drugs
cards.people: 40 hirsute women randomised double-blind to spironolactone 100 mg/day, flutamide 250 mg/day, finasteride 5 mg/day, or placebo for 6 months. Hirsutism was measured quantitatively by computer-assisted light microscopy of the largest diameter of 5 hairs plucked from the linea alba (averaged as mean hair-shaft diameter), assessed by an investigator blinded to time and treatment, plus a modified Ferriman-Gallwey (F-G) score by a single investigator. Groups were similar at baseline.
cards.result: After 6 months, all active-drug groups reduced hair diameter, without statistically significant differences among groups (mean change ± SEM: spironolactone −11.7 ± 5.6%; flutamide −18.0 ± 6.1%; finasteride −12.6 ± 6.7%). F-G scores were significantly reduced on antiandrogens, again without differences among groups (spironolactone −41.0 ± 5.5%; flutamide −38.9 ± 7.2%; finasteride −31.6 ± 3.7%). The placebo group showed no significant change in hair diameter (−1.4 ± 5.2%) or F-G score (+5.4 ± 3.7%). The authors conclude all three drugs are effective in hirsutism and that, at these doses over 6 months, their clinical efficacies are similar.
cards.watchOut: Ten women per arm: the trial was powered to see drug-versus-placebo effects, not to rank the drugs — absence of a significant difference is not proof of equivalence. The abstract reports no systematic safety outcomes; in particular, flutamide's known hepatotoxicity (the reason it is now rarely used for hirsutism despite the largest point estimate here) comes from outside this trial, and none of these drugs should be used in women who could be pregnant without reliable contraception. Results are for abdominal (linea alba) hair and F-G score over 6 months.
cards.source: Moghetti P et al. Comparison of spironolactone, flutamide, and finasteride efficacy in the treatment of hirsutism: a randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled trial. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2000. PMID: 10634370. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). shelves.title: Diabetes with retinopathy: intensive LDL lowering to below 70 mg/dL did not significantly cut cardiovascular events (EMPATHY)
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and diabetic retinopathy but no prior cardiovascular disease, does intensive lipid lowering targeting LDL cholesterol below 70 mg/dL reduce cardiovascular events versus standard targeting of 100 to under 120 mg/dL?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Retinopathy · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Cholesterol, LDL · Humans
shelves.balance: THIN — one large Japanese trial that missed its target separation and its primary endpoint. EMPATHY randomised 5,144 patients with type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and diabetic retinopathy, without prior cardiovascular disease, to intensive therapy targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL or standard therapy targeting 100 to under 120 mg/dL. The primary endpoint of cardiovascular events or cardiovascular death gave a hazard ratio of 0.84 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.07; P=0.15) — not significant. The achieved LDL gap was small (about 28 mg/dL), and fewer than half of either group reached their target, so the trial tested a strategy that was only weakly delivered; a retinopathy substudy (157 patients with fundus photographs) likewise found no significant difference in retinopathy progression. One correction to this shelf's originating draft: the standard-care target was 100 to under 120 mg/dL, not 70–100, and the trial's primary endpoint was cardiovascular, not eye progression. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — intensive targeting may help, but this trial does not show it.

cards.headline: EMPATHY 2018: primary endpoint HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.67–1.07; P=0.15); targets reached by under half of patients
cards.summary: EMPATHY 2018: primary endpoint HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.67–1.07; P=0.15); targets reached by under half of patients
cards.people: 5,144 patients with type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and diabetic retinopathy, without a history of cardiovascular disease, randomised in a multicentre prospective open-label blinded-endpoint trial in Japan to intensive lipid lowering (target LDL-C below 70 mg/dL) or standard therapy (target LDL-C 100 to under 120 mg/dL). Primary endpoint: cardiovascular events or death from cardiovascular causes.
cards.result: The primary endpoint did not differ significantly between groups (hazard ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.07; P=0.15). The targets were achieved by less than 50% of patients in either group, and the between-group difference in achieved LDL-C was only 0.72 mmol/L (27.7 mg/dL). In the retinopathy substudy of 157 patients with serial fundus photographs, two-step progression of retinopathy severity did not differ significantly between groups (P=0.4380).
cards.watchOut: THIN: a single trial with a diluted contrast — a strategy trial in which the strategy was delivered to fewer than half — cannot exclude the 16% relative benefit its point estimate suggests; equally, it provides no positive proof. The retinopathy substudy (n=157) is far too small to judge eye outcomes.
cards.source: Itoh H et al. Intensive Treat-to-Target Statin Therapy in High-Risk Japanese Patients With Hypercholesterolemia and Diabetic Retinopathy: Report of a Randomized Study (EMPATHY). Diabetes Care. 2018. PMID: 29626074. Registry ID: UMIN000003486 (UMIN registry, as cited for the trial). Main-trial effect estimates as reported for the trial programme; retinopathy substudy figures from the trial's retinopathy report.

shelves.title: Metformin added to insulin in type 1 diabetes: no sustained HbA1c benefit and no slowing of carotid thickening (REMOVAL) — weight and insulin dose moved, stomachs objected
shelves.question: In people with type 1 diabetes, does adding metformin to insulin improve glycaemic control, weight, or atherosclerosis progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Atherosclerosis/complications, drug therapy · Carotid Intima-Media Thickness · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/complications, metabolism, physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Metformin is often added to insulin in type 1 diabetes to fight weight gain and insulin resistance, and two randomised trials bound what it actually does. REMOVAL (428 adults aged 40+ with type 1 diabetes and cardiovascular risk factors, 3 years) found no significant slowing of carotid intima-media thickness progression, its primary outcome (−0.005 mm/year; p=0.1664); HbA1c fell by an average 0.13%, an effect carried by the first 3 months and not sustained, while weight (−1.17 kg) and LDL cholesterol (−0.13 mmol/L (≈-5 mg/dL)) did improve and 27% stopped metformin versus 12% on placebo, mainly for gastrointestinal effects. In adolescents (140 overweight teenagers), an early HbA1c advantage at 13 weeks (−0.3%) had vanished by 26 weeks (0.0%), though insulin dose and adiposity measures favoured metformin and gastrointestinal events were far commoner. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for glycaemic control and atherosclerosis; the modest weight effect is real and is recorded as such, not upgraded into the stamp.

cards.headline: REMOVAL: metformin did not significantly slow carotid IMT progression over 3 years (p=0.1664); HbA1c −0.13% unsustained; weight −1.17 kg; 27% discontinued
cards.summary: REMOVAL: metformin did not significantly slow carotid IMT progression over 3 years (p=0.1664); HbA1c −0.13% unsustained; weight −1.17 kg; 27% discontinued
cards.people: 428 adults aged ≥40 with type 1 diabetes of ≥5 years and at least three cardiovascular risk factors, at 23 clinics in five countries, randomised to metformin 1,000 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 years on top of titrated insulin; primary outcome progression of mean carotid intima-media thickness.
cards.result: Mean cIMT progression: −0.005 mm/year on metformin (95% CI −0.012 to 0.002; p=0.1664 — not significant); a prespecified tertiary measure (maximal cIMT) did fall significantly (−0.013 mm/year; p=0.0093). HbA1c averaged −0.13% vs placebo (p=0.0060) but only via a 3-month fall (−0.24%) that was not sustained. Weight −1.17 kg (p<0.0001), LDL −0.13 mmol/L (≈-5 mg/dL) (p=0.0117), eGFR +4.0 mL/min/1.73 m². Insulin dose was not reduced on average. Discontinuation 27% vs 12% (p=0.0002), mainly gastrointestinal; no excess hypoglycaemia; five deaths on metformin vs two on placebo, none judged drug-related.
cards.watchOut: Carotid IMT is a surrogate; the trial was not powered for cardiovascular events, so 'no difference' here means no demonstrated effect on the marker or on sustained glycaemia — not proof of no vascular effect in any form.
cards.source: Petrie JR et al.. Cardiovascular and metabolic effects of metformin in patients with type 1 diabetes (REMOVAL): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28615149. Registry ID: NCT01483560. shelves.title: Cinnamon for blood sugar: small trials, mixed answers, one flagged paper
shelves.question: In people with type 2 diabetes, does cinnamon (powder or extract) lower fasting glucose or HbA1c compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Cinnamomum zeylanicum · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Lipids · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts · Triglycerides · Humans
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Four small placebo-controlled trials give mixed answers. Khan 2003 reported large falls — fasting glucose −18–29%, triglycerides −23–30%, LDL cholesterol −7–27% and total cholesterol −12–26% after 1, 3 or 6 g per day for 40 days, with no changes on placebo — but in 2025 the American Diabetes Association issued an Expression of Concern about that paper, so its numbers cannot be taken at face value. Mang 2006 found fasting glucose fell more on an aqueous extract (−10.3% versus −3.4%, P = .046) with no significant HbA1c or lipid effect. Akilen 2010 found a small HbA1c fall (8.22% to 7.86% on cinnamon versus 8.55% to 8.68% on placebo, p < .005). Lu 2012 reported significant HbA1c and fasting-glucose reductions in both extract arms but published no effect sizes in its abstract. The preparations — powder and different extracts, at doses from 120 mg to 6 g per day — are not interchangeable, and none of the trials names a retail brand. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): small, inconsistent trials of differing preparations, with the largest reported effects in a paper now under an Expression of Concern.

cards.headline: Mang 2006: fasting glucose fell 10.3% versus 3.4% on placebo (P = .046), but HbA1c and lipids did not change significantly
cards.summary: Mang 2006: fasting glucose fell 10.3% versus 3.4% on placebo (P = .046), but HbA1c and lipids did not change significantly
cards.people: 79 patients with type 2 diabetes not on insulin therapy but treated with oral antidiabetics or diet, randomly assigned in a double-blind study to a cinnamon extract or placebo capsule three times a day for 4 months; the aqueous cinnamon extract corresponded to 3 g of cinnamon powder per day.
cards.result: There was a significantly higher reduction in fasting plasma glucose in the cinnamon group (10.3%) than in the placebo group (3.4%) (P = .046). No significant intragroup or intergroup differences were observed regarding HbA1c or lipid profiles. The decrease in plasma glucose correlated significantly with baseline concentrations, indicating that subjects with a higher initial level may benefit more. No adverse effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: Fasting glucose moved without a significant HbA1c change — an internal inconsistency that tempers the finding. An aqueous extract equivalent to 3 g per day is not the same preparation as cinnamon powder, and no retail brand is named in the record. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Mang B et al.. Effects of a cinnamon extract on plasma glucose, HbA, and serum lipids in diabetes mellitus type 2. European Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2006. PMID: 16634838. cards.headline: Akilen 2010: HbA1c fell from 8.22% to 7.86% on 2 g per day while placebo rose — lipids unchanged
cards.summary: Akilen 2010: HbA1c fell from 8.22% to 7.86% on 2 g per day while placebo rose — lipids unchanged
cards.people: 58 type 2 diabetic patients in the UK (25 males and 33 females, aged 54.9 ± 9.8 years), treated only with hypoglycaemic agents and with an HbA1c over 7%, randomly assigned to 2 g of cinnamon or placebo daily for 12 weeks in a double-blind trial.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c decreased significantly in the cinnamon group (8.22% to 7.86%) compared with the placebo group (8.55% to 8.68%) (P < 0.005). Systolic blood pressure fell from 132.6 to 129.2 mmHg and diastolic from 85.2 to 80.2 mmHg in the cinnamon group, versus 134.5 to 134.9 mmHg and 86.8 to 86.1 mmHg on placebo (P < 0.001 for both). Fasting plasma glucose, waist circumference and BMI fell at week 12 compared with baseline in the cinnamon group, but those changes were not significant compared with placebo, and there were no significant differences in lipid profiles.
cards.watchOut: Small single trial, and baseline HbA1c differed between groups (8.22% versus 8.55%). The blood-pressure falls are secondary findings. The preparation was 2 g per day of cinnamon and no retail brand is named in the record. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Lu 2012: significant HbA1c and fasting-glucose reductions at both extract doses — but the abstract reports no effect sizes
cards.summary: Lu 2012: significant HbA1c and fasting-glucose reductions at both extract doses — but the abstract reports no effect sizes
cards.people: 66 Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes, randomly divided in a double-blinded study into three groups — placebo, low-dose cinnamon extract 120 mg per day, or high-dose 360 mg per day for 3 months; patients in all three groups took gliclazide during the entire study.
cards.result: Both HbA1c and fasting blood glucose levels were significantly reduced in the low-dose and high-dose groups, whereas they were not changed in the placebo group. Blood triglyceride levels were also significantly reduced in the low-dose group. Total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and liver transaminases remained unchanged in the three groups. The abstract reports significance but no effect sizes, so the size of any benefit cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: No numbers in the abstract — a 'significant' result of unknown size, in 66 patients all on background gliclazide. Extract doses of 120–360 mg per day are not comparable with the gram doses of powder in the other cards, and no retail brand is named in the record. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one flagged paper with very large effects, three small trials with modest or unquantified ones — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one flagged paper with very large effects, three small trials with modest or unquantified ones — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: 263 people with type 2 diabetes across the four randomised trials above: Khan 2003 (60), Mang 2006 (79), Akilen 2010 (58) and Lu 2012 (66).
cards.result: Outside the flagged Khan 2003 paper, the pattern is a modest fasting-glucose fall without an HbA1c change (Mang), a small HbA1c fall (Akilen), and significant but unquantified reductions (Lu), with lipids essentially unchanged outside Khan. The preparations differ in species preparation, form and dose — powder, aqueous extract and other extracts, from 120 mg to 6 g per day — so the trials do not test one single intervention. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Cinnamon as a food spice is not the question here; as a treatment, no preparation, dose or brand has been established by these trials, and none names a retail brand a reader could buy. Cinnamon should not displace glucose-lowering medicines with proven outcome benefits.
cards.source: Synthesis of Khan A et al. Diabetes Care. 2003 (PMID: 14633804); Mang B et al. European Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2006 (PMID: 16634838); Akilen R et al. Diabetic Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20854384); Lu T et al. Nutrition Research. 2012 (PMID: 22749176).

shelves.title: Apple cider vinegar: small trials, small effects — a real post-meal glucose blunting, no proven weight-loss drug
shelves.question: Does apple cider vinegar (or vinegar generally) lower blood sugar or help with weight loss?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Fat · Acetic Acid · Adipose Tissue · Adult · Asian People · Blood Pressure · Body Weight · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity · Placebo Effect · Time Factors · Triglycerides
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one 12-week double-blind trial found vinegar drinks reduced weight, visceral fat and triglycerides versus placebo (its abstract reports no effect sizes), one 11-person crossover found vinegar increased muscle glucose uptake and blunted post-meal glucose, and one 10-person pilot found the same gastric-slowing that blunts glucose made gastroparesis worse. Small, short, surrogate outcomes throughout — and the large weight-loss claims circulating online rest on evidence far weaker than these.

cards.headline: Vinegar drinks for 12 weeks reduced weight, visceral fat and triglycerides vs placebo in obese Japanese adults
cards.summary: Vinegar drinks for 12 weeks reduced weight, visceral fat and triglycerides vs placebo in obese Japanese adults
cards.people: Obese Japanese subjects in a double-blind trial, randomised to 500 mL daily of a beverage containing 15 mL vinegar (750 mg acetic acid), 30 mL vinegar (1,500 mg acetic acid), or no vinegar, for 12 weeks
cards.result: Body weight, BMI, visceral fat area, waist circumference and serum triglyceride levels were significantly lower in both vinegar groups than in the placebo group at 12 weeks. The abstract reports no effect sizes, so the size of the benefit cannot be stated from the record.
cards.watchOut: The tested intervention was a vinegar beverage (not necessarily apple cider vinegar), the trial was short, and with no numbers in the abstract this card cannot support the dramatic weight-loss figures used in marketing. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: In 11 people with type 2 diabetes, vinegar before a meal increased muscle glucose uptake and lowered glucose, insulin and triglycerides
cards.summary: In 11 people with type 2 diabetes, vinegar before a meal increased muscle glucose uptake and lowered glucose, insulin and triglycerides
cards.people: 11 subjects with type 2 diabetes in a randomised crossover study; vinegar or placebo before a mixed meal on two days a week apart, with forearm muscle glucose uptake measured directly
cards.result: Compared with placebo, vinegar increased forearm glucose uptake (P = 0.0357) and decreased plasma glucose (P = 0.0279), insulin (P = 0.0457) and triglycerides (P = 0.0439), without changing fat breakdown markers. Registry ID: NCT02309424 (stated in the record).
cards.watchOut: Eleven people and a single meal — a mechanism demonstration, not evidence that vinegar improves long-term glucose control (no A1c outcome). The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: The catch: in type 1 diabetes with gastroparesis, apple cider vinegar slowed stomach emptying further (27% to 17%)
cards.summary: The catch: in type 1 diabetes with gastroparesis, apple cider vinegar slowed stomach emptying further (27% to 17%)
cards.people: 10 patients with type 1 diabetes and diabetic gastroparesis in an investigator-blinded crossover trial; 30 mL apple cider vinegar in water daily for two weeks vs water alone, gastric emptying measured by ultrasound after rice pudding
cards.result: Median gastric emptying rate was 27% without vinegar and 17% with vinegar (P < 0.05) — vinegar significantly slowed emptying that was already pathologically slow, which the authors note might disadvantage glycaemic control in these patients. Registry ID: ISRCTN33841495 (stated in the record).
cards.watchOut: Delayed gastric emptying is part of how vinegar blunts post-meal glucose in everyone — helpful in a normal stomach, a liability in gastroparesis. Anyone with gastroparesis should not use vinegar this way. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Hlebowicz J et al.. Effect of apple cider vinegar on delayed gastric emptying in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus: a pilot study. BMC Gastroenterol. 2007. PMID: 18093343. cards.headline: Synthesis: a condiment with a measurable metabolic nudge — not a treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: a condiment with a measurable metabolic nudge — not a treatment
cards.people: Three small trials: 12 weeks in obese adults, a single-meal crossover in 11 people with type 2 diabetes, and 10 patients with gastroparesis
cards.result: Vinegar before or with food modestly blunts the glucose rise and may trim weight and triglycerides slightly over 12 weeks; the evidence is too small and short for any stronger claim, and no trial measured A1c change or clinical outcomes. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Undiluted vinegar can injure teeth and oesophagus, and it can lower potassium and interact with insulin and diuretics — none of which these small trials were sized to detect. Diabetes medicines should never be adjusted around vinegar without the prescriber.

shelves.title: Green tea for weight loss: pooled trials outside Japan show −0.04 kg — the positive trials are all Japanese and can't be pooled
shelves.question: Do green tea extracts or catechin drinks cause meaningful weight loss?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Weight · Camellia sinensis · Humans · Japan · Obesity · Overweight · Phytotherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tea · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the Cochrane pooling of trials outside Japan found a mean weight difference of −0.04 kg (P = 0.88): nothing. Japanese trials (mostly of high-catechin beverages) report losses up to 3.5 kg but could not be pooled and differ in population, product and diet context. If green tea extract helps weight at all, the effect is too small and too inconsistent to matter clinically — the Cochrane authors' own conclusion.

cards.headline: Cochrane: outside Japan, green tea's weight effect was −0.04 kg (95% CI −0.5 to 0.4) — statistically and clinically nothing
cards.summary: Cochrane: outside Japan, green tea's weight effect was −0.04 kg (95% CI −0.5 to 0.4) — statistically and clinically nothing
cards.people: Randomised trials of at least 12 weeks of green tea preparations vs control in overweight or obese adults; six non-Japanese studies (532 participants) pooled for weight; eight Japanese studies (1,030 participants) too heterogeneous to pool
cards.result: Weight: mean difference −0.04 kg (95% CI −0.5 to 0.4; P = 0.88) outside Japan. BMI: −0.2 kg/m² (−0.5 to 0.1; P = 0.21). Waist circumference: −0.2 cm (−1.4 to 0.9). Japanese studies reported weight differences from −0.2 to −3.5 kg in favour of green tea but could not be combined. Weight maintenance after loss: no significant effect. Adverse events were mostly mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: The Japan/non-Japan split is the story of this shelf: something differs between the two literatures — product dose, diet, genetics or publication patterns — and the pooled, more generalisable answer is null.
cards.source: Jurgens TM et al.. Green tea for weight loss and weight maintenance in overweight or obese adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012. PMID: 23235664. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The best Japanese trial: high-catechin green tea (583 mg/day) beat a low-catechin control on fat measures in 240 adults
cards.summary: The best Japanese trial: high-catechin green tea (583 mg/day) beat a low-catechin control on fat measures in 240 adults
cards.people: 240 Japanese adults with visceral-fat-type obesity analysed per protocol (123 catechin, 117 control); green tea containing 583 mg catechins vs 96 mg catechins daily for 12 weeks, double-blind, usual diet and activity maintained
cards.result: Decreases in body weight, BMI, body fat ratio and mass, waist and hip circumference, and visceral and subcutaneous fat area were all greater in the catechin group. Systolic pressure fell more in the catechin group among those starting at 130 mmHg or above, and LDL cholesterol decreased more. The abstract reports no kilogram figures, so the size of the weight effect cannot be stated from the record.
cards.watchOut: The 'control' tea still contained 96 mg of catechins, participants were Japanese adults eating a Japanese diet, and the analysis was per-protocol — all reasons the result may not travel. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Nagao T et al.. A green tea extract high in catechins reduces body fat and cardiovascular risks in humans. Obesity. 2007. PMID: 17557985. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: In type 2 diabetes, a catechin drink shrank waists more than control — but A1c did not differ overall
cards.summary: In type 2 diabetes, a catechin drink shrank waists more than control — but A1c did not differ overall
cards.people: 43 patients with type 2 diabetes not on insulin; green tea with 582.8 mg catechins (n = 23) vs 96.3 mg catechins (n = 20) daily for 12 weeks, double-blind
cards.result: Waist circumference fell significantly more in the catechin group, and adiponectin rose only in that group. Overall there was no apparent difference between groups in glucose or haemoglobin A1c; in the subgroup taking insulinotropic agents, insulin rose more and A1c fell more with catechins.
cards.watchOut: 43 patients and a subgroup-driven A1c signal — hypothesis-generating only, and no support for using green tea to treat diabetes. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Nagao T et al.. A catechin-rich beverage improves obesity and blood glucose control in patients with type 2 diabetes. Obesity. 2009. PMID: 19008868. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: drink it if you like it — not as a weight-loss treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: drink it if you like it — not as a weight-loss treatment
cards.people: Over 1,500 adults across the Cochrane pooling and the two Japanese trials carded
cards.result: Pooled non-Japanese trials show no weight effect; Japanese high-catechin beverage trials show small favourable changes that have never been reproduced in a poolable way elsewhere. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for weight loss as generally claimed.
cards.watchOut: Concentrated green tea extracts (not the drink) have a separate safety literature, including rare liver injury at high catechin doses — a harm question this shelf does not cover; brewed green tea as a beverage is not the exposure studied here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jurgens TM et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012 (PMID: 23235664); Nagao T et al. Obesity. 2007 (PMID: 17557985); Nagao T et al. Obesity. 2009 (PMID: 19008868).

shelves.title: Non-sugar sweeteners: swapping them for sugar trims about a kilogram in trials; against water the advantage is unproven; the harm signals come from cohort studies that cannot separate the sweetener from the reasons people choose it
shelves.question: Do non-sugar sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, stevia and similar) help with weight and metabolic health when they replace sugar — and is there evidence they cause harm?
shelves.mesh: Animals · *Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Energy Intake/*drug effects · Evidence-Based Medicine · Humans · Models, Animal · Non-Nutritive Sweeteners/*pharmacology · Obesity/*prevention & control · Observational Studies as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reproducibility of Results · Sweetening Agents/pharmacology · *Weight Gain
shelves.balance: The answer depends entirely on the comparison, and the literature's three big syntheses disagree mainly because they weight the comparisons differently. Against sugar, the randomised evidence is consistent and modest: Rogers 2016 (PMID: 26365102) pooled the sustained intervention trials and found low-energy sweeteners reduced body weight by 1.35 kg relative to sugar (95% CI −2.28 to −0.42), with short-term energy intake 94 kcal lower than after sugar and no different from water (−2 kcal). Against nothing in particular, the Cochrane-methodology review for the WHO (Toews 2019, PMID: 30602577) found the cupboard nearly bare: a small BMI advantage in adults (−0.6, from two studies totalling 174 people, low certainty), a smaller BMI z-score rise in children versus sugar (−0.15, moderate certainty), and no detectable effect on any other outcome — including no effect in adults or children actively trying to lose weight. The one head-to-head trial inside a weight-loss programme cuts the other way on water: Peters 2014 (PMID: 24862170) randomised 303 adults to sweetened beverages or water and the sweetener group lost more at 12 weeks (5.95 vs 4.09 kg). The harm story is observational: Azad 2017 (PMID: 28716847) found the randomised trials null on BMI (mean difference −0.37, 95% CI −1.10 to 0.36) while 30 cohort studies linked routine sweetener use to higher weight, waist circumference, obesity, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular events — associations fully compatible with reverse causation, since people gaining weight or developing diabetes are exactly the people who switch to sweeteners. The individual beverage-substitution trials in children and adults are homed at shelves #205 and #565; this shelf judges the sweeteners themselves. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (small benefit when replacing sugar).

cards.headline: Rogers 2016: in sustained randomised trials, low-energy sweeteners versus sugar reduced body weight by 1.35 kg; versus water the pooled difference was 1.24 kg from only three comparisons
cards.summary: Rogers 2016: in sustained randomised trials, low-energy sweeteners versus sugar reduced body weight by 1.35 kg; versus water the pooled difference was 1.24 kg from only three comparisons
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analyses of human and animal studies of low-energy sweeteners consumed with ad libitum access to food: 129 short-term randomised comparisons of energy intake, the sustained intervention randomised trials (4 weeks to 40 months), and 12 prospective cohort studies in humans.
cards.result: Short-term trials: energy intake was 94 kcal lower with sweeteners than with sugar-sweetened food or drink before an ad libitum meal (95% CI −122 to −66), and no different from water (−2 kcal; −30 to 26). Sustained intervention trials: sweetener consumption versus sugar led to relatively reduced body weight (nine comparisons; −1.35 kg; 95% CI −2.28 to −0.42), and a similar relative reduction versus water (three comparisons; −1.24 kg; −2.22 to −0.26). The 12 human cohort studies were inconsistent (−0.002 kg/m² per year in BMI; 95% CI −0.009 to 0.005). The authors conclude the preponderance of randomised evidence is that sweeteners do not increase energy intake or body weight, and that use in place of sugar reduces both.
cards.watchOut: The versus-water estimate — the comparison that matters for someone choosing between a diet drink and water — rests on three comparisons, and the review pools all sweetener types and delivery formats as one exposure. Its authors also flag the reverse-causation problem in the cohort literature themselves; the randomised pool is the part of this review to quote.
cards.source: Rogers PJ et al. Does low-energy sweetener consumption affect energy intake and body weight? A systematic review, including meta-analyses, of the evidence from human and animal studies. International Journal of Obesity. 2016. PMID: 26365102. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Toews 2019: the Cochrane-methodology review behind the WHO guideline found mostly absence of evidence — a small adult BMI effect from two tiny studies, no effect in people actively trying to lose weight
cards.summary: Toews 2019: the Cochrane-methodology review behind the WHO guideline found mostly absence of evidence — a small adult BMI effect from two tiny studies, no effect in people actively trying to lose weight
cards.people: Systematic review (Cochrane methodology) of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials and observational studies of named non-sugar sweeteners within acceptable daily intakes, intervention duration at least 7 days, in generally healthy or overweight/obese adults and children: 56 studies, of which 35 were observational.
cards.result: In adults, low-to-very-low-certainty evidence from a few small studies indicated a small beneficial effect on BMI (mean difference −0.6; 95% CI −1.19 to −0.01; two studies, n=174) and fasting blood glucose (−0.16 mmol/L (≈-3 mg/dL); −0.26 to −0.06; two studies, n=52). For all other outcomes — including glycaemic control beyond that, cancer, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, mood and adverse effects — no differences were detected between sweetener use and non-use or between doses. There was no evidence of any effect in overweight or obese adults or children actively trying to lose weight. In children, BMI z score rose less with sweeteners than with sugar (−0.15; −0.17 to −0.12; two studies, n=528, moderate certainty), without a significant body-weight difference (−0.60 kg; −1.33 to 0.14).
cards.watchOut: This is substantially a review of missing evidence: most outcomes rest on one or two small, short studies, which is why the WHO's 2023 recommendation against using sweeteners for weight control is a conditional recommendation built on low-certainty data. 'No difference detected' in this review usually means 'barely studied', not 'studied and exonerated' — in either direction.
cards.source: Toews I et al. Association between intake of non-sugar sweeteners and health outcomes: systematic review and meta-analyses of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials and observational studies. BMJ. 2019. PMID: 30602577. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42017047668. cards.headline: Azad 2017: randomised trials showed no significant BMI effect (−0.37, CI −1.10 to 0.36), while cohort studies associated routine sweetener use with higher BMI, obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular events
cards.summary: Azad 2017: randomised trials showed no significant BMI effect (−0.37, CI −1.10 to 0.36), while cohort studies associated routine sweetener use with higher BMI, obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular events
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs and cohort studies (Azad 2017)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (1,003 participants, median follow-up 6 months) and 30 prospective cohort studies (405,907 participants, median follow-up 10 years) of nonnutritive sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, stevioside and others) in adults and adolescents.
cards.result: In the trials, nonnutritive sweeteners had no significant effect on BMI (mean difference −0.37 kg/m²; 95% CI −1.10 to 0.36) and no consistent effects on other body-composition measures. In the cohort studies, sweetener consumption was associated with a modest increase in BMI (mean correlation 0.05; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.06) and with increases in weight and waist circumference and higher incidence of obesity, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular events; publication bias was indicated for the diabetes outcome. The authors conclude the trials do not clearly support the intended benefits for weight management and that the observational associations warrant further research.
cards.watchOut: The cohort associations are the shelf's harm signal and its weakest evidence: people at rising cardiometabolic risk selectively switch to sweeteners, and no adjustment fully removes that reverse causation — the same dataset's randomised half shows no harm and no clear benefit. Quoting the cohort half without the trial half (or vice versa) misrepresents this paper.
cards.source: Azad MB et al. Nonnutritive sweeteners and cardiometabolic health: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies. CMAJ. 2017. PMID: 28716847. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42015019749. cards.headline: Peters 2014: inside a behavioural weight-loss programme, adults assigned non-nutritive sweetened beverages lost more weight at 12 weeks than those assigned water (5.95 vs 4.09 kg)
cards.summary: Peters 2014: inside a behavioural weight-loss programme, adults assigned non-nutritive sweetened beverages lost more weight at 12 weeks than those assigned water (5.95 vs 4.09 kg)
cards.people: Randomised equivalence trial in 303 men and women enrolled in a 12-week behavioural weight-loss treatment programme ('The Colorado Diet'), assigned to drink non-nutritive sweetened beverages or water as the main study factor; the report covers the weight-loss phase of a 1-year trial.
cards.result: The two treatments were not equivalent: the sweetened-beverage group lost significantly more weight than the water group at 12 weeks (5.95 kg versus 4.09 kg; P<0.0001), and reported significantly greater reductions in subjective feelings of hunger. The authors conclude water was not superior to sweetened beverages for weight loss during a comprehensive behavioural programme.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, inside an intensive programme whose support dwarfs the beverage assignment, and participants could not be blinded to what they were drinking — expectancy and adherence effects are plausible explanations for a 1.9 kg gap that the pooled trial literature (Rogers: three comparisons versus water) cannot confirm at this size. It proves sweetened drinks did not sabotage a diet programme; it does not prove they outperform water in ordinary life.
cards.source: Peters JC et al. The effects of water and non-nutritive sweetened beverages on weight loss during a 12-week weight loss treatment program. Obesity. 2014. PMID: 24862170. Registry ID: NCT01766700. randomised controlled trial (peters 2014) randomised equivalence trial in 303 men and women enrolled in a 12-week behavioural weight-loss treatment programme ('the colorado diet'), assigned to drink non-nutritive sweetened beverages or water as the main study factor; the report covers the weight-loss phase of a 1-year trial. the two treatments were not equivalent: the sweetened-beverage group lost significantly more weight than the water group at 12 weeks (5.95 kg versus 4.09 kg; p<0.0001), and reported significantly greater reductions in subjective feelings of hunger. the authors conclude water was not superior to sweetened beverages for weight loss during a comprehensive behavioural programme. twelve weeks, inside an intensive programme whose support dwarfs the beverage assignment, and participants could not be blinded to what they were drinking — expectancy and adherence effects are plausible explanations for a 1.9 kg gap that the pooled trial literature (rogers: three comparisons versus water) cannot confirm at this size. it proves sweetened drinks did not sabotage a diet programme; it does not prove they outperform water in ordinary life. peters jc et al. the effects of water and non-nutritive sweetened beverages on weight loss during a 12-week weight loss treatment program. obesity. 2014. pmid: 24862170. registry id: nct01766700. mesh: adult · aged · *beverages · body mass index · drinking water/*administration & dosage · energy intake · female · follow-up studies · humans · male · middle aged · motor activity · non-nutritive sweeteners/*administration & dosage · prospective studies · sedentary behavior · *weight loss · *weight reduction programs · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: a small, real benefit when sweeteners displace sugar; no proven benefit over water; harm unproven — POSSIBLE (small benefit when replacing sugar)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small, real benefit when sweeteners displace sugar; no proven benefit over water; harm unproven — POSSIBLE (small benefit when replacing sugar)
cards.people: Three systematic reviews (Rogers 2016; Azad 2017 — 7 RCTs and 30 cohorts; Toews 2019 — 56 studies) and one head-to-head randomised trial against water within a weight-loss programme (n=303).
cards.result: Versus sugar, randomised evidence converges on roughly 1–1.4 kg less weight gain/loss advantage and ~94 kcal lower short-term energy intake. Versus water, the pooled estimate (−1.24 kg) rests on three comparisons and one unblinded 12-week trial found a 1.86 kg advantage; the honest verdict is unproven either way. Cohort associations with obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular events are consistent but confounded by reverse causation, and the trial literature shows no harm signal. The large beverage-substitution trials themselves are carded at #205 (children) and #565 (adults).
cards.watchOut: Almost every trial is short (weeks to months), industry-adjacent questions about specific sweeteners (aspartame vs sucralose vs stevia vs sugar alcohols such as erythritol) are pooled away, and long-term randomised data on diabetes or cardiovascular endpoints do not exist. The shelf answers the weight question with moderate confidence and every harder question with 'not established'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rogers PJ et al. International Journal of Obesity. 2016 (PMID: 26365102); Azad MB et al. CMAJ. 2017 (PMID: 28716847); Toews I et al. BMJ. 2019 (PMID: 30602577); Peters JC et al. Obesity. 2014 (PMID: 24862170).

shelves.title: Inhaled insulin (Exubera): glucose control matched injected insulin in both types of diabetes — the lungs lost a little FEV1 early, reversibly, and a third of patients coughed
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, does inhaled insulin control glucose as well as injected mealtime insulin, and what does it do to the lungs?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Follow-Up Studies · Forced Expiratory Volume · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Safety · Time Factors
shelves.balance: The Exubera programme answered both halves of the question in randomised trials. For glucose: in type 2 diabetes, inhaled insulin matched injected insulin at 6 months (HbA1c −0.7% vs −0.6%; adjusted difference −0.07%, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.17; Hollander 2004, PMID: 15451900) with more patients reaching HbA1c <7% (46.9% vs 31.7%); in type 1 diabetes over 2 years it ran slightly behind (adjusted HbA1c difference 0.25% favouring injections; Skyler 2007, PMID: 17327324), while causing fewer severe hypoglycaemic events (risk ratio 0.67) and about 1.3 kg less weight gain in both types. For the lungs: FEV1 fell a little faster on inhaled insulin — in type 1, an extra −0.017 L/year averaged over 2 years — but the gap opened in the first 3 months and did not widen from month 3 to 24 in either type (Rosenstock 2008, PMID: 18535196, difference 0.000 L/year over months 3–24), diffusing capacity never differed, and the type 1 extension showed the difference vanishing on a 6-month washout and returning at the same size on restarting (Skyler 2008, PMID: 18824271) — a reversible functional effect, not progressive damage. The everyday cost was cough (37.6% vs 13.1% initially in type 1). All trials excluded smokers and people with lung disease, and all tested the one product, Exubera, since withdrawn from the market; the technosphere inhaled insulin record in type 1 diabetes is homed separately at shelf #2051. PROPOSED LIKELY (not Tier C: three randomised programmes, consistent results; the stamp carries the lung and cough qualifications on its face).

cards.headline: Skyler 2007: in type 1 diabetes over 2 years, inhaled insulin held HbA1c close to injected insulin (adjusted difference 0.25% favouring injections) — and produced a small early fall in FEV1 that did not progress after month 3
cards.summary: Skyler 2007: in type 1 diabetes over 2 years, inhaled insulin held HbA1c close to injected insulin (adjusted difference 0.25% favouring injections) — and produced a small early fall in FEV1 that did not progress after month 3
cards.people: Randomised trial in 580 adults with type 1 diabetes (290 inhaled human insulin [Exubera], 290 subcutaneous insulin), each plus basal intermediate- or long-acting insulin, followed for 2 years. The primary endpoint was pulmonary: the annual rate of decline in FEV1 and carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (DLCO).
cards.result: Glycaemic control was sustained in both groups; the adjusted mean treatment difference in HbA1c change at month 24 was 0.25% (95% CI 0.13 to 0.37) in favour of subcutaneous insulin. FEV1 fell faster on inhaled insulin over months 0–24 (annual change −0.051 vs −0.034 L/year; difference −0.017 L/year, 90% CI −0.028 to −0.005), but the difference developed in the first 3 months and was not progressive thereafter (months 3–24 difference −0.011 L/year, not significant); the DLCO difference was not significant. Overall hypoglycaemia was comparable (4.0 vs 3.8 events per subject-month) but severe hypoglycaemia was lower on inhaled insulin (2.8 vs 4.1 events per 100 subject-months; risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.79). Cough was far commoner on inhaled insulin (37.6% vs 13.1%), usually mild, and fell to 1.3% by month 24. Weight rose less on inhaled insulin (adjusted difference −1.25 kg).
cards.watchOut: Open-label by necessity — patients knew whether they were inhaling or injecting, which matters for the subjective outcomes (cough reporting, satisfaction) though not for FEV1 or HbA1c. The 0.25% HbA1c gap favouring injections is small but real, and it is the largest, longest type 1 test: 'comparable' here means close, not identical.
cards.source: Skyler JS et al. Two-year safety and efficacy of inhaled human insulin (Exubera) in adult patients with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2007. PMID: 17327324. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hollander 2004: in type 2 diabetes, 6 months of inhaled insulin matched injected insulin for HbA1c (−0.7% vs −0.6%), and more patients reached HbA1c below 7% (46.9% vs 31.7%)
cards.summary: Hollander 2004: in type 2 diabetes, 6 months of inhaled insulin matched injected insulin for HbA1c (−0.7% vs −0.6%), and more patients reached HbA1c below 7% (46.9% vs 31.7%)
cards.people: Randomised 6-month comparative trial in 299 patients with type 2 diabetes previously on at least two daily insulin injections: premeal inhaled insulin (Exubera) plus a bedtime injection of long-acting insulin (n = 149) versus at least two daily subcutaneous injections of mixed regular/NPH insulin (n = 150). Primary endpoint: change in HbA1c.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by 0.7% on inhaled insulin and 0.6% on subcutaneous insulin (adjusted difference −0.07%, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.17). More inhaled-insulin patients reached HbA1c <7.0% (46.9% vs 31.7%; odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.24 to 4.14). Overall hypoglycaemia was slightly lower on inhaled insulin (1.4 vs 1.6 events per subject-month; risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.97) with no difference in severe events. Pulmonary function testing showed no difference at 6 months; cough was commoner on inhaled insulin, insulin antibody binding rose more, and treatment satisfaction was greater.
cards.watchOut: Six months is too short to judge the lungs — the pulmonary question needs the 2-year trials (Skyler 2007; Rosenstock 2008). The comparator (twice-daily mixed insulin) was a modest regimen by modern standards, and the trial predates analogue-based basal–bolus care; the satisfaction advantage is real but was measured unblinded.
cards.source: Hollander PA et al. Efficacy and safety of inhaled insulin (exubera) compared with subcutaneous insulin therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes: results of a 6-month, randomized, comparative trial. Diabetes Care. 2004. PMID: 15451900. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rosenstock 2008: the dedicated 2-year pulmonary trial in type 2 diabetes — a small FEV1 difference favouring injections in the first 3 months, none thereafter, and no DLCO difference
cards.summary: Rosenstock 2008: the dedicated 2-year pulmonary trial in type 2 diabetes — a small FEV1 difference favouring injections in the first 3 months, none thereafter, and no DLCO difference
cards.people: Randomised trial in 635 nonsmoking adults with type 2 diabetes assigned to prandial inhaled insulin (Exubera) or subcutaneous regular/short-acting insulin, each plus basal insulin, for 2 years. Primary endpoints: annual rate of decline in FEV1 and DLCO.
cards.result: The adjusted treatment difference in FEV1 annual rate of change was −0.007 L/year (90% CI −0.021 to 0.006) over months 0–24 and 0.000 L/year (−0.016 to 0.016) over months 3–24 — the small early difference did not progress. DLCO differences were not significant. HbA1c fell similarly by month 24 (7.7% to 7.3% on inhaled insulin; 7.8% to 7.3% on subcutaneous), fasting glucose fell more on inhaled insulin (adjusted difference −12.4 mg/dL, 90% CI −19.7 to −5.0), hypoglycaemia incidence was comparable, and weight rose less on inhaled insulin (−1.3 kg, 95% CI −1.9 to −0.7). Mild cough and dyspnoea were commoner on inhaled insulin.
cards.watchOut: Nonsmokers only — the population most likely to be offered an inhaled insulin today (and the one in whom any lung effect matters most, smokers and people with asthma or COPD) was excluded from every Exubera trial. Two years is also short against a therapy intended for decades.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Two-year pulmonary safety and efficacy of inhaled human insulin (Exubera) in adult patients with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2008. PMID: 18535196. Registry ID: NCT00136916. cards.headline: Skyler 2008: stop inhaled insulin and the lung-function difference disappears; restart it and the same small difference returns — a reversible, non-progressive effect (3-year extension report of the Skyler 2007 trial)
cards.summary: Skyler 2008: stop inhaled insulin and the lung-function difference disappears; restart it and the same small difference returns — a reversible, non-progressive effect (3-year extension report of the Skyler 2007 trial)
cards.type: Randomised trial extension report (Skyler 2008; same trial as Skyler 2007)
cards.people: Extension report of the same 580-patient type 1 trial as Skyler 2007 (not a separate trial): after the 2-year comparative phase, all patients switched to subcutaneous insulin for 6 months (washout), then back to their original therapy for 6 months, with standardised lung-function testing throughout.
cards.result: The small treatment-group differences in FEV1 and DLCO that favoured subcutaneous insulin occurred early and were non-progressive; they resolved during the 6-month washout and recurred at the same magnitude on readministration. Glycaemic control was maintained and hypoglycaemia rates were similar throughout. Insulin antibody levels plateaued at 12 months, fell to near baseline during washout, and rose again on readministration without exceeding the levels seen in the comparative phase. The authors conclude the lung effect is reversible, non-progressive and non-pathological.
cards.watchOut: This is the same cohort as the first card on this shelf, reported again — it adds the reversibility evidence, not independent confirmation. Reversibility over 6 months of washout does not prove that decades of inhalation would remain harmless; it proves the early FEV1 dip is a functional, not a destructive, change.
cards.source: Skyler JS et al. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2008. PMID: 18824271. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: inhaled insulin controlled glucose about as well as injected mealtime insulin in both types of diabetes; the lungs paid a small, early, non-progressive and reversible FEV1 toll, and cough was the everyday price
cards.summary: Synthesis: inhaled insulin controlled glucose about as well as injected mealtime insulin in both types of diabetes; the lungs paid a small, early, non-progressive and reversible FEV1 toll, and cough was the everyday price
cards.people: Four reports from three randomised programmes: Skyler 2007 with its 2008 extension (type 1, n = 580, up to 3 years), Hollander 2004 (type 2, n = 299, 6 months) and Rosenstock 2008 (type 2, n = 635, 2 years, pulmonary endpoints primary).
cards.result: HbA1c differences versus injected insulin were −0.07% (type 2, 6 months) and +0.25% favouring injections (type 1, 24 months); in type 2, more patients reached HbA1c <7% on inhaled insulin (46.9% vs 31.7%). FEV1 declined slightly faster on inhaled insulin in the first 3 months (type 1 difference −0.017 L/year over 2 years) with no progression from month 3 to 24 in either type and no DLCO signal; the difference reversed on stopping and recurred on restarting. Cough affected over a third of type 1 patients initially (37.6% vs 13.1%). Weight gain was consistently ~1.3 kg less, and severe hypoglycaemia was lower in the type 1 trial (risk ratio 0.67).
cards.watchOut: Every trial tested the same product — Exubera, the dry-powder inhaled human insulin, since withdrawn from the market — in nonsmokers without lung disease. The newer technosphere inhaled insulin is a different formulation with its own record, homed at shelf #2051 for type 1 diabetes; this shelf answers the class question the Exubera programme was built to test, and its lung data should not be transferred uncritically to other inhaled insulins.
cards.source: Synthesis of Skyler JS et al. Diabetes Care. 2007 (PMID: 17327324); Hollander PA et al. Diabetes Care. 2004 (PMID: 15451900); Rosenstock J et al. Diabetes Care. 2008 (PMID: 18535196); Skyler JS et al. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2008 (PMID: 18824271).

shelves.title: Preventing the next diabetic foot ulcer: pressure-designed insoles and custom footwear work in high-risk patients who wear them — ordinary therapeutic shoes, and unworn prescriptions, do not
shelves.question: In people with diabetes and a healed foot ulcer, do therapeutic shoes and custom insoles prevent ulcer recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Foot/epidemiology/physiopathology/rehabilitation · Disease Progression · Equipment Design · Follow-Up Studies · Foot/physiopathology · Humans · Incidence · Netherlands/epidemiology · Pressure · Recurrence · Retrospective Studies · *Shoes · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials divide cleanly by risk and by whether the device was actually pressure-targeted and worn. In high-risk neuropathic patients with a prior ulcer, insoles designed from foot shape and barefoot plantar pressure cut submetatarsal ulcer recurrence (hazard ratio 3.4, 95% CI 1.3 to 8.7, for standard insoles versus pressure-based; Ulbrecht 2014, PMID: 24760263), and custom footwear with improved offloading cut recurrence from 47.8% to 25.7% in the patients who wore it for at least 80% of steps (Bus 2013, PMID: 24130357). But the same trial's intention-to-treat result was null (38.8% vs 44.2%; odds ratio 0.80, 0.44 to 1.47) because fewer than half the patients wore the footwear enough, and in lower-risk patients who did not need custom shoes, therapeutic shoes with either cork or prefabricated inserts showed no benefit at all over 2 years (15% and 14% vs 17%; Reiber 2002, PMID: 12020336). The honest summary: the prescription that prevents recurrence is pressure measurement plus custom manufacture plus adherence — footwear dispensed generically, or dispensed and not worn, has no demonstrated effect. Healing of active ulcers and offloading during treatment are a different question, homed at shelf #291. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: three randomised trials; the benefit is real but conditional, which the stamp grade reflects).

cards.headline: Bus 2013 (DIAFOS): pressure-improved custom footwear did not significantly cut ulcer recurrence overall (38.8% vs 44.2%) — but in patients who actually wore it for at least 80% of steps, recurrence fell from 47.8% to 25.7%
cards.summary: Bus 2013 (DIAFOS): pressure-improved custom footwear did not significantly cut ulcer recurrence overall (38.8% vs 44.2%) — but in patients who actually wore it for at least 80% of steps, recurrence fell from 47.8% to 25.7%
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial in 171 neuropathic diabetic patients with a recently healed plantar foot ulcer, assigned to custom-made footwear with improved, preserved offloading (about 20% peak-pressure relief achieved by modifying the footwear) or to usual custom-made footwear without improvement. Primary outcome: plantar ulcer recurrence within 18 months; adherence was measured objectively.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat, recurrence was 38.8% (33 of 85) with improved footwear versus 44.2% (38 of 86) with usual care — odds ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.47), P = 0.48, not significant; ulcer-free survival did not differ (P = 0.40). In the 79 patients (46%) with measured adherence of at least 80% of steps, recurrence was 25.7% (9 of 35) versus 47.8% (21 of 44) — odds ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.99), P = 0.045.
cards.watchOut: The headline is an adherence story, not a footwear story: fewer than half the patients wore the shoes for 80% of their steps, and the significant result lives in that subgroup — a per-protocol-flavoured analysis in which adherent patients may differ in other protective ways. The intention-to-treat answer, the one a prescribing service actually buys, is null.
cards.source: Bus SA et al. Effect of custom-made footwear on foot ulcer recurrence in diabetes: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 24130357. cards.headline: Ulbrecht 2014 (CareFUL): insoles designed from each patient's foot shape and barefoot plantar pressure cut submetatarsal ulcer recurrence — control patients had 3.4 times the ulcer hazard
cards.summary: Ulbrecht 2014 (CareFUL): insoles designed from each patient's foot shape and barefoot plantar pressure cut submetatarsal ulcer recurrence — control patients had 3.4 times the ulcer hazard
cards.people: Single-blinded multicentre randomised trial in 130 people with diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and a previous submetatarsal plantar ulcer: shape- and pressure-based in-shoe orthoses (n = 66) versus standard-of-care A5513 orthoses (n = 64), followed for 15 months. Endpoints: forefoot plantar ulcer, or the composite of ulcer plus non-ulcerative plantar lesions.
cards.result: The composite endpoint showed only a trend favouring the experimental orthoses (P = 0.13), driven entirely by ulcers: ulcer occurrence differed significantly (P = 0.007) while non-ulcerative lesions did not (P = 0.76). The hazard ratio for a submetatarsal head plantar ulcer in the control versus experimental arm was 3.4 (95% CI 1.3 to 8.7) over the study; the ulcer-prevention effect was already significant at 180 days (P = 0.003), as was the composite at that point (P = 0.042).
cards.watchOut: A narrowly defined population (prior submetatarsal ulcer, neuropathy) and a narrowly defined outcome (ulcer at that site) — the trial does not speak to first ulcers, other sites, or patients without neuropathy. The composite primary endpoint missed significance; the ulcer-only result, though strong, is the secondary reading.
cards.source: Ulbrecht JS et al. Prevention of recurrent foot ulcers with plantar pressure-based in-shoe orthoses: the CareFUL prevention multicenter randomized controlled trial. Diabetes Care. 2014. PMID: 24760263. Registry ID: NCT00803608. cards.headline: Reiber 2002: in 400 patients with a previous ulcer but no deformity needing custom shoes, therapeutic shoes with cork or polyurethane inserts did not reduce reulceration at all (15% and 14% vs 17% on usual footwear)
cards.summary: Reiber 2002: in 400 patients with a previous ulcer but no deformity needing custom shoes, therapeutic shoes with cork or polyurethane inserts did not reduce reulceration at all (15% and 14% vs 17% on usual footwear)
cards.people: Randomised trial in 400 patients with diabetes and a history of foot ulcer at two Washington State health care organisations, who did not require custom shoes for foot deformity: three pairs of therapeutic shoes with customised cork inserts (n = 121), the same shoes with prefabricated polyurethane inserts (n = 119), or usual footwear (n = 160), followed for 2 years.
cards.result: Two-year cumulative reulceration was 15% with cork inserts, 14% with prefabricated inserts and 17% in controls. Risk ratios versus control were 0.88 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.52) for cork and 0.85 (0.48 to 1.48) for prefabricated inserts — neither significant. The authors conclude the study does not support widespread dispensing of therapeutic shoes and inserts to patients like these, while noting it does not exclude benefit in severe foot deformity or where professional foot care is less attentive; nearly all ulcers occurred in patients with foot insensitivity.
cards.watchOut: The null here is informative, not contradictory: Reiber's patients had lower baseline risk (17% recurrence over 2 years, versus ~40% over 18 months in DIAFOS) and were explicitly those who did NOT need custom shoes. Generic therapeutic footwear for unselected post-ulcer patients is the intervention that failed; pressure-targeted devices in high-risk patients are a different intervention.
cards.source: Reiber GE et al. Effect of therapeutic footwear on foot reulceration in patients with diabetes: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002. PMID: 12020336. cards.headline: Synthesis: pressure-targeted footwear and insoles prevent recurrence in high-risk neuropathic patients — when worn; ordinary therapeutic shoes in lower-risk patients show nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: pressure-targeted footwear and insoles prevent recurrence in high-risk neuropathic patients — when worn; ordinary therapeutic shoes in lower-risk patients show nothing
cards.people: Three randomised trials spanning the risk spectrum: Reiber 2002 (n = 400, no custom-shoe need, 2 years), Bus 2013 (n = 171, recently healed plantar ulcer, 18 months) and Ulbrecht 2014 (n = 130, prior submetatarsal ulcer, 15 months).
cards.result: Where the device was built from the patient's own plantar pressures and the patients were high-risk, ulcers fell: hazard ratio 3.4 (1.3 to 8.7) against standard insoles (Ulbrecht), and 25.7% vs 47.8% recurrence in DIAFOS patients wearing improved footwear for at least 80% of steps. Where either condition was missing — DIAFOS intention-to-treat (odds ratio 0.80, CI 0.44 to 1.47) or Reiber's off-the-shelf therapeutic shoes (risk ratios 0.88 and 0.85, both non-significant) — there was no demonstrated benefit. The intervention that works is a system: pressure measurement, custom manufacture, and adherence.
cards.watchOut: None of these trials tests footwear for a first ulcer, and none separates the device from the specialist service that fitted and reviewed it. Adherence in DIAFOS was measured by temperature/pressure sensors in a research setting; in routine care the worn-as-prescribed subgroup — the only one with proven benefit — may be smaller still.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bus SA et al. Diabetes Care. 2013 (PMID: 24130357); Ulbrecht JS et al. Diabetes Care. 2014 (PMID: 24760263); Reiber GE et al. JAMA. 2002 (PMID: 12020336).
