shelves.title: Closed loop in type 1 diabetes pregnancy (AiDAPT): time in the pregnancy target range rose by about 10 points and HbA1c fell — from one trial, on glucose endpoints
shelves.question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does automated insulin delivery (hybrid closed loop) improve glucose control versus standard pump or injection therapy with continuous glucose monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Pregnancy · *Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · *Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/complications/drug therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · *Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · *Insulin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · *Insulin Infusion Systems/adverse effects · *Pregnancy in Diabetics/blood/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One randomised programme answers the glucose question convincingly. In AiDAPT, 124 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes using the CamAPS FX hybrid closed-loop system spent 68.2% of time in the pregnancy target range (63–140 mg/dL) versus 55.6% with standard insulin therapy — an adjusted difference of 10.5 percentage points (95% CI 7.0 to 14.0) — with HbA1c 0.31 points lower and no excess of severe hypoglycaemia or ketoacidosis, both groups using CGM throughout (Lee 2023, PMID: 37796241). The prespecified postpartum extension found the advantage held for 6 months after delivery (time in range 72% vs 54%; Lee 2025, PMID: 39884300). What the evidence does not show is equally important: the trial was powered for glucose metrics, not for pre-eclampsia, caesarean delivery or neonatal outcomes, and it tested one system in UK clinics. CGM in pregnancy is homed at shelf #959 (CONCEPTT) and closed-loop therapy outside pregnancy at shelf #561; this shelf is the pregnancy-specific automated-delivery question. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: a single trial programme — one randomised trial plus its extension — however clean the result).

cards.headline: Lee 2023 (AiDAPT): hybrid closed loop in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes raised time in the pregnancy target range from 55.6% to 68.2% — an adjusted gain of 10.5 percentage points — and lowered HbA1c by 0.31 points
cards.summary: Lee 2023 (AiDAPT): hybrid closed loop in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes raised time in the pregnancy target range from 55.6% to 68.2% — an adjusted gain of 10.5 percentage points — and lowered HbA1c by 0.31 points
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial at nine UK sites: 124 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes and HbA1c at least 6.5% (mean age 31.1 years, mean baseline HbA1c 7.7%) assigned to hybrid closed-loop therapy (CamAPS FX) or standard insulin therapy (pump or injections), both groups using continuous glucose monitoring. Primary outcome: percentage of time in the pregnancy-specific glucose target range (63–140 mg/dL) from 16 weeks' gestation to delivery.
cards.result: Time in target range was 68.2% ± 10.5% on closed loop versus 55.6% ± 12.5% on standard care (mean adjusted difference 10.5 percentage points, 95% CI 7.0 to 14.0; P < 0.001). Closed-loop participants spent less time hyperglycaemic (difference −10.2 points, 95% CI −13.8 to −6.6), had more overnight time in range (difference 12.3 points, 8.3 to 16.2) and lower HbA1c (difference −0.31 points, −0.50 to −0.12), with little time in hypoglycaemia in either group. Safety: severe hypoglycaemia 6 versus 5 instances, diabetic ketoacidosis 1 in each group, and 12 device-related adverse events in the closed-loop group (7 related to the therapy).
cards.watchOut: Glucose outcomes, not baby outcomes: with 124 women the trial was powered for time in range, and it does not establish fewer pre-eclampsias, caesareans or neonatal admissions. Participants had to be willing and able to use the system from early pregnancy, and the comparator already included CGM for everyone — the gain is the algorithm's, on top of sensor use.
cards.source: Lee TTM et al. Automated Insulin Delivery in Women with Pregnancy Complicated by Type 1 Diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 37796241. Registry ID: ISRCTN56898625. cards.headline: Lee 2025 (AiDAPT postpartum extension): the advantage persisted into the first 6 months after delivery — time in range 72% versus 54%, an adjusted difference of 15 points (same trial, prespecified extension)
cards.summary: Lee 2025 (AiDAPT postpartum extension): the advantage persisted into the first 6 months after delivery — time in range 72% versus 54%, an adjusted difference of 15 points (same trial, prespecified extension)
cards.type: Prespecified extension report of a randomised trial (Lee 2025, AiDAPT)
cards.people: Prespecified extension of the AiDAPT trial: of the 124 randomised women, 57 who remained eligible and consented continued their assigned treatment (hybrid closed loop with CamAPS FX, or standard insulin therapy with CGM) for the first 6 months postpartum. Primary outcome: percentage of time in the standard glucose range (70–180 mg/dL) over 6 months postpartum.
cards.result: Time in range was 72% ± 12% on closed loop versus 54% ± 17% on standard care (adjusted treatment difference 15 percentage points, 95% CI 7 to 22). Time hyperglycaemic was lower (−14 points, 95% CI −23 to −6) and mean CGM glucose lower (−1.3 mmol/L (≈-23 mg/dL), −2.3 to −0.3) on closed loop; hypoglycaemia time was low and similar (2.4% vs 2.6%), the effect did not vary between months 0–3 and 3–6, and there were no unanticipated safety problems.
cards.watchOut: An extension of the same 124-woman trial, in the 57 women who continued — not independent confirmation, and the continuation group is self-selected from a trial population already able to use the technology. It answers 'should women who used closed loop in pregnancy stop at delivery?' (no) rather than the pregnancy question itself.
cards.source: Lee TTM et al. Automated insulin delivery during the first 6 months postpartum (AiDAPT): a prespecified extension study. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2025. PMID: 39884300. Registry ID: ISRCTN56898625 (the AiDAPT trial registration, as stated in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial programme shows closed loop clearly improves glucose control in type 1 diabetes pregnancy and after delivery — neonatal and maternal outcome benefits remain unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial programme shows closed loop clearly improves glucose control in type 1 diabetes pregnancy and after delivery — neonatal and maternal outcome benefits remain unproven
cards.people: The AiDAPT randomised trial (124 women, nine UK sites) and its prespecified 6-month postpartum extension (57 women), both using the CamAPS FX hybrid closed-loop system against standard insulin therapy with CGM in both arms.
cards.result: Pregnancy: time in the pregnancy target range 68.2% versus 55.6% (adjusted difference 10.5 points, 95% CI 7.0 to 14.0), HbA1c 0.31 points lower, no excess severe hypoglycaemia (6 vs 5 events) or ketoacidosis (1 vs 1). Postpartum: time in range 72% versus 54% (adjusted difference 15 points, 7 to 22), hypoglycaemia unchanged. The effect sizes are large for a diabetes technology trial and internally consistent across pregnancy and postpartum, but they rest on a single trial programme, a single system, and glycaemic endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Whether 10 extra points of time in range in pregnancy translates into fewer complicated deliveries or healthier babies is the question that matters most and the one this evidence cannot yet answer; the CONCEPTT trial (shelf #959) showed CGM itself improves some neonatal outcomes, which supports — but does not prove — the same for closed loop. Generalisability beyond motivated, technology-using UK clinic populations is untested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lee TTM et al. N Engl J Med. 2023 (PMID: 37796241); Lee TTM et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2025 (PMID: 39884300).
cards.search: synthesis: one well-run trial programme shows closed loop clearly improves glucose control in type 1 diabetes pregnancy and after delivery — neonatal and maternal outcome benefits remain unproven synthesis: one well-run trial programme shows closed loop clearly improves glucose control in type 1 diabetes pregnancy and after delivery — neonatal and maternal outcome benefits remain unproven in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does automated insulin delivery (hybrid closed loop) improve glucose control versus standard pump or injection therapy with continuous glucose monitoring? synthesis the aidapt randomised trial (124 women, nine uk sites) and its prespecified 6-month postpartum extension (57 women), both using the camaps fx hybrid closed-loop system against standard insulin therapy with cgm in both arms. pregnancy: time in the pregnancy target range 68.2% versus 55.6% (adjusted difference 10.5 points, 95% ci 7.0 to 14.0), hba1c 0.31 points lower, no excess severe hypoglycaemia (6 vs 5 events) or ketoacidosis (1 vs 1). postpartum: time in range 72% versus 54% (adjusted difference 15 points, 7 to 22), hypoglycaemia unchanged. the effect sizes are large for a diabetes technology trial and internally consistent across pregnancy and postpartum, but they rest on a single trial programme, a single system, and glycaemic endpoints. whether 10 extra points of time in range in pregnancy translates into fewer complicated deliveries or healthier babies is the question that matters most and the one this evidence cannot yet answer; the conceptt trial (shelf #959) showed cgm itself improves some neonatal outcomes, which supports — but does not prove — the same for closed loop. generalisability beyond motivated, technology-using uk clinic populations is untested. synthesis of lee ttm et al. n engl j med. 2023 (pmid: 37796241); lee ttm et al. lancet diabetes endocrinol. 2025 (pmid: 39884300).

shelves.title: CPAP for sleep apnoea in type 2 diabetes: sleepiness improves, HbA1c does not — the pooled trial difference is −0.10 points with a confidence interval that excludes a useful effect
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with obstructive sleep apnoea, does CPAP improve HbA1c?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Comorbidity · *Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/epidemiology/therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · *Insulin Resistance · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/epidemiology/therapy
shelves.balance: The pooled randomised record is a clean null. Across six trials with 581 patients, CPAP changed HbA1c by −0.10 percentage points (95% CI −0.25 to 0.04) at 12–24 weeks, moderate-certainty evidence, with no effect in either adherence stratum (Labarca 2018, PMID: 30073792). The best-designed individual trial agrees: double-blind therapeutic versus sham CPAP for 3 months moved HbA1c by −0.02% versus +0.1% (P = 0.7), even as sleepiness and wakefulness improved significantly — proof the treatment was working on the apnoea while doing nothing for glucose (West 2007, PMID: 17557769). The one positive trial (Martínez-Cerón 2016, PMID: 26910598) was small (n = 50), open-label and reports no HbA1c effect size in its abstract; it does not outweigh the sham-controlled and pooled results. CPAP should be prescribed for the apnoea — symptoms and sleep — not as a diabetes treatment, and an HbA1c that fails to fall on CPAP is the expected result, not non-adherence. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (not Tier C: a meta-analysis of six randomised trials plus a sham-controlled trial, consistently null).

cards.headline: Martínez-Cerón 2016: the one positive trial — 6 months of CPAP improved HbA1c versus no CPAP in 50 patients with type 2 diabetes and sleep apnoea, in an open-label study whose abstract reports no size for the HbA1c difference
cards.summary: Martínez-Cerón 2016: the one positive trial — 6 months of CPAP improved HbA1c versus no CPAP in 50 patients with type 2 diabetes and sleep apnoea, in an open-label study whose abstract reports no size for the HbA1c difference
cards.people: Open-label randomised trial in 50 patients with obstructive sleep apnoea and suboptimally controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c at least 6.5% on two measurements), assigned to CPAP (n = 26) or no CPAP (n = 24) for 6 months with diabetes medication held unchanged. Outcomes included HbA1c, insulin resistance and sensitivity indices, biomarkers and quality of life.
cards.result: After 6 months the CPAP group achieved a greater decrease in HbA1c than the control group (the abstract reports the direction and significance but no point estimate for the HbA1c difference). Insulin resistance and sensitivity measures in non-insulin users, and serum IL-1β, IL-6 and adiponectin, also improved on CPAP. In the CPAP group, mean nocturnal oxygen saturation and baseline IL-1β independently predicted the 6-month HbA1c change (r² = 0.510, P = 0.002).
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 50), single-centre and open-label — patients knew whether they had CPAP, and there was no sham comparator, so behaviour change (including in diabetes self-care) cannot be separated from the airway effect. It is the outlier against the sham-controlled trial and the pooled estimate on this shelf, and its abstract does not state how large the HbA1c fall was.
cards.source: Martínez-Cerón E et al. Effect of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure on Glycemic Control in Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Type 2 Diabetes. A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: West 2007: the sham-controlled test — therapeutic CPAP versus placebo CPAP for 3 months changed HbA1c by −0.02% versus +0.1% (P = 0.7), while sleepiness and wakefulness clearly improved
cards.summary: West 2007: the sham-controlled test — therapeutic CPAP versus placebo CPAP for 3 months changed HbA1c by −0.02% versus +0.1% (P = 0.7), while sleepiness and wakefulness clearly improved
cards.people: Double-blind randomised trial in 42 men with type 2 diabetes and newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea (more than 10 oxygen-desaturation dips per hour), assigned to therapeutic (n = 20) or placebo (subtherapeutic) CPAP (n = 22) for 3 months. Outcomes: HbA1c, euglycaemic-clamp and HOMA insulin sensitivity, adiponectin, sleepiness and maintenance of wakefulness.
cards.result: Glycaemic control and insulin resistance did not change in either group: HbA1c −0.02% (SD 1.5) on therapeutic CPAP versus +0.1% (0.7) on placebo (P = 0.7; 95% CI for the difference −0.6% to +0.9%); clamp, HOMA and adiponectin were likewise unchanged, with no correlation between hours of CPAP use and any glycaemic measure. Sleep outcomes separated clearly: Epworth sleepiness improved more on therapeutic CPAP (−6.6 vs −2.6, P = 0.01) and maintenance of wakefulness improved (+10.6 vs −4.7 minutes, P = 0.001). Mean use was 3.6 hours per night.
cards.watchOut: Men only, 3 months, and modest adherence (3.6 hours per night) — a fair critic can say the dose was low and the trial small (n = 42). Its value is the design: it is the trial that separates the machine's metabolic effect from the experience of being treated, and on that test the metabolic effect was zero while the sleep effect was obvious.
cards.source: West SD et al. Effect of CPAP on insulin resistance and HbA1c in men with obstructive sleep apnoea and type 2 diabetes. Thorax. 2007. PMID: 17557769. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Labarca 2018: pooling all six randomised trials (581 patients), CPAP changed HbA1c by −0.10 percentage points (95% CI −0.25 to 0.04) — no significant effect, at moderate-certainty evidence, whatever the adherence
cards.summary: Labarca 2018: pooling all six randomised trials (581 patients), CPAP changed HbA1c by −0.10 percentage points (95% CI −0.25 to 0.04) — no significant effect, at moderate-certainty evidence, whatever the adherence
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of CPAP in patients with obstructive sleep apnoea and type 2 diabetes: 6 RCTs, 581 participants, with GRADE evidence assessment and a prespecified subgroup analysis by CPAP adherence (more or less than 4 hours per night).
cards.result: CPAP showed no effectiveness for HbA1c at 12 or 24 weeks: pooled mean difference −0.10 percentage points (95% CI −0.25 to 0.04), graded moderate certainty. The adherence subgroup analysis confirmed the null in both higher- and lower-adherence strata, and fasting glucose was also similar between CPAP and control. The reviewers conclude CPAP does not improve glycaemic control as measured by HbA1c.
cards.watchOut: A pooled null across small, short trials: the confidence interval excludes an HbA1c benefit larger than about a quarter of a point, which is below what would change management, but the trials ran only 12–24 weeks and enrolled patients whose diabetes treatment was otherwise static. The meta-analysis answers 'does CPAP lower HbA1c?' — it says nothing against CPAP for the apnoea itself.
cards.source: Labarca G et al. CPAP in patients with obstructive sleep apnea and type 2 diabetes mellitus: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Respir J. 2018. PMID: 30073792. cards.headline: Synthesis: treated sleep apnoea, untreated HbA1c — the pooled randomised evidence excludes a clinically useful glucose effect of CPAP in type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: Synthesis: treated sleep apnoea, untreated HbA1c — the pooled randomised evidence excludes a clinically useful glucose effect of CPAP in type 2 diabetes
cards.people: Six randomised trials pooled (581 patients), the largest sham-controlled trial (West 2007, n = 42 men, double-blind) and the one positive open-label trial (Martínez-Cerón 2016, n = 50).
cards.result: Pooled HbA1c effect: −0.10 percentage points (95% CI −0.25 to 0.04), moderate-certainty, null in both adherence strata. The double-blind trial found −0.02% versus +0.1% (P = 0.7) alongside clear improvements in sleepiness and wakefulness. The single positive trial was small, open-label and reported no effect size in its abstract. If CPAP lowered HbA1c by an amount worth prescribing for, this record would very likely have shown it.
cards.watchOut: This shelf judges CPAP only as a glucose treatment. CPAP remains the treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea itself — symptoms, sleepiness and the apnoea's own risks — and nothing here argues against using it for those reasons in a patient who also has diabetes. It argues against expecting the HbA1c to fall because the apnoea is treated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Labarca G et al. Clin Respir J. 2018 (PMID: 30073792); West SD et al. Thorax. 2007 (PMID: 17557769); Martínez-Cerón E et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2016 (PMID: 26910598).

shelves.title: Preserving beta cells in new-onset type 1 diabetes: alefacept and low-dose ATG each slowed C-peptide decline for two years — in phase 2 trials of 49 and 89 patients
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, do alefacept or low-dose anti-thymocyte globulin preserve beta-cell function?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Alefacept · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy/immunology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Delivery Systems/methods · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Immunologic Memory/drug effects/immunology · Male · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/administration & dosage · T-Lymphocytes/drug effects/immunology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two small randomised programmes, testing different immune strategies in patients within 100 days of diagnosis, converge on the same answer: beta-cell decline can be slowed, not stopped. Alefacept (T1DAL, 49 patients) missed its 12-month primary endpoint (2-hour C-peptide, P = 0.065) but preserved 4-hour C-peptide (P = 0.019), cut insulin use and roughly halved hypoglycaemic events; by 24 months both C-peptide measures were significantly preserved (Rigby 2013, PMID: 24622414; Rigby 2015, PMID: 26193635). Low-dose ATG (TrialNet, 89 patients) preserved C-peptide at 1 year (AUC 0.646 vs 0.406 nmol/L, P = 0.0003) and at 2 years (P = 0.00005), with lower HbA1c; adding G-CSF never improved on ATG alone (Haller 2018, PMID: 30012675; Haller 2019, PMID: 30967424). The qualifications are structural: phase 2 sample sizes, a surrogate primary endpoint, and neither agent available as routine treatment — alefacept was withdrawn from its psoriasis market, and ATG is unapproved for diabetes. Abatacept's new-onset record is homed at shelf #1776. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: two small single-programme phase 2 records resting on a surrogate endpoint).

cards.headline: Rigby 2013 (T1DAL): alefacept missed its primary endpoint at 12 months (2-hour C-peptide, P = 0.065) but met the key secondaries — 4-hour C-peptide preserved (P = 0.019), less insulin, and far fewer hypoglycaemic events (10.9 vs 17.3 per person-year)
cards.summary: Rigby 2013 (T1DAL): alefacept missed its primary endpoint at 12 months (2-hour C-peptide, P = 0.065) but met the key secondaries — 4-hour C-peptide preserved (P = 0.019), less insulin, and far fewer hypoglycaemic events (10.9 vs 17.3 per person-year)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Rigby 2013, T1DAL)
cards.people: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled trial at 14 US sites: 49 patients aged 12–35 with type 1 diabetes within 100 days of diagnosis, randomised 2:1 to alefacept (two 12-week courses of 15 mg intramuscularly weekly, separated by a 12-week pause; n = 33) or placebo (n = 16). Primary endpoint: change in 2-hour C-peptide AUC at 12 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: 2-hour C-peptide AUC changed by +0.015 nmol/L on alefacept versus −0.115 nmol/L on placebo (P = 0.065). Key secondary endpoints were met: 4-hour C-peptide AUC was significantly higher on alefacept (+0.015 vs −0.156 nmol/L; P = 0.019), daily insulin use was lower (0.36 vs 0.48 units/kg/day; P = 0.02) and hypoglycaemic events fewer (10.9 vs 17.3 events per person per year; P < 0.0001). HbA1c did not differ (P = 0.75). No serious adverse events were reported in this report; grade 3–4 events occurred in 42% of the alefacept group.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint with positive secondaries is a hypothesis strengthened, not a question settled — the 2-hour mixed-meal test was the prespecified measure and it did not reach significance at 12 months. The trial was small (49 patients, only 16 on placebo), and C-peptide preservation is a surrogate: the clinical dividends (less insulin, fewer hypos) are encouraging but were secondary outcomes.
cards.source: Rigby MR et al. Targeting of memory T cells with alefacept in new-onset type 1 diabetes (T1DAL study): 12 month results of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial. cards.headline: Rigby 2015: at 24 months — 15 months after the last alefacept dose — both C-peptide measures were significantly preserved, insulin needs were lower and major hypoglycaemia was about halved (follow-up report of the same T1DAL trial)
cards.summary: Rigby 2015: at 24 months — 15 months after the last alefacept dose — both C-peptide measures were significantly preserved, insulin needs were lower and major hypoglycaemia was about halved (follow-up report of the same T1DAL trial)
cards.type: Randomised trial follow-up report (Rigby 2015; same trial as T1DAL 2013)
cards.people: The 24-month report of the T1DAL trial (same 49 patients as Rigby 2013; not a separate trial): endpoints were meal-stimulated C-peptide AUC, insulin use, hypoglycaemic events and immunological responses, assessed 15 months after the final alefacept dose.
cards.result: At 24 months the 4-hour and 2-hour C-peptide AUCs were both significantly greater on alefacept than placebo (P = 0.002 and P = 0.015). Exogenous insulin requirements were lower (P = 0.002) and rates of major hypoglycaemic events were about 50% lower (P < 0.001). There was no between-group difference in glycaemic control or adverse events. Immunologically, alefacept depleted CD4+ and CD8+ central and effector memory T cells, preserved regulatory T cells, and increased Treg-to-memory ratios and PD-1+ memory T cells (all P < 0.01).
cards.watchOut: Same patients, later timepoint: this report converts the 12-month 'promising secondaries' into a more coherent 24-month picture, but it cannot add statistical independence — the whole alefacept evidence base in type 1 diabetes is these 49 patients. Alefacept was withdrawn from its psoriasis market by its manufacturer and is not available as a diabetes treatment; the finding is mechanistic proof of concept for memory-T-cell targeting.
cards.source: Rigby MR et al. Alefacept provides sustained clinical and immunological effects in new-onset type 1 diabetes patients. J Clin Invest. 2015. PMID: 26193635. Registry ID: NCT00965458. randomised trial follow-up report (rigby 2015; same trial as t1dal 2013) the 24-month report of the t1dal trial (same 49 patients as rigby 2013; not a separate trial): endpoints were meal-stimulated c-peptide auc, insulin use, hypoglycaemic events and immunological responses, assessed 15 months after the final alefacept dose. at 24 months the 4-hour and 2-hour c-peptide aucs were both significantly greater on alefacept than placebo (p = 0.002 and p = 0.015). exogenous insulin requirements were lower (p = 0.002) and rates of major hypoglycaemic events were about 50% lower (p < 0.001). there was no between-group difference in glycaemic control or adverse events. immunologically, alefacept depleted cd4+ and cd8+ central and effector memory t cells, preserved regulatory t cells, and increased treg-to-memory ratios and pd-1+ memory t cells (all p < 0.01). same patients, later timepoint: this report converts the 12-month 'promising secondaries' into a more coherent 24-month picture, but it cannot add statistical independence — the whole alefacept evidence base in type 1 diabetes is these 49 patients. alefacept was withdrawn from its psoriasis market by its manufacturer and is not available as a diabetes treatment; the finding is mechanistic proof of concept for memory-t-cell targeting. rigby mr et al. alefacept provides sustained clinical and immunological effects in new-onset type 1 diabetes patients. j clin invest. 2015. pmid: 26193635. registry id: nct00965458. mesh: adolescent · adult · alefacept · c-peptide/blood · cd4 lymphocyte count · *cd4-positive t-lymphocytes/immunology/metabolism · *cd8-positive t-lymphocytes/immunology/metabolism · child · dermatologic agents/administration & dosage · *diabetes mellitus, type 1/blood/drug therapy/immunology · double-blind method · female · humans · immunologic memory/drug effects · male · recombinant fusion proteins/administration & dosage · time factors

cards.headline: Haller 2018 (TrialNet): low-dose ATG alone preserved C-peptide at 1 year (AUC 0.646 vs 0.406 nmol/L, P = 0.0003) and lowered HbA1c — adding G-CSF did not help (P = 0.031 against a 0.025 threshold)
cards.summary: Haller 2018 (TrialNet): low-dose ATG alone preserved C-peptide at 1 year (AUC 0.646 vs 0.406 nmol/L, P = 0.0003) and lowered HbA1c — adding G-CSF did not help (P = 0.031 against a 0.025 threshold)
cards.people: Three-arm randomised double-masked placebo-controlled TrialNet trial in 89 patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes (duration under 100 days): low-dose anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG, 2.5 mg/kg intravenously) plus pegylated G-CSF (n = 29), ATG alone (n = 29), or placebo (n = 31). Primary endpoint: 2-hour mixed-meal C-peptide AUC at 1 year; significance defined as one-sided P < 0.025.
cards.result: One-year C-peptide AUC was significantly higher on ATG alone than placebo (0.646 vs 0.406 nmol/L; P = 0.0003) but not on ATG/G-CSF (0.528 nmol/L; P = 0.031, short of the prespecified threshold). HbA1c was significantly reduced at 1 year in both active arms (ATG P = 0.002; ATG/G-CSF P = 0.011). The authors conclude low-dose ATG slowed beta-cell decline and that G-CSF added nothing to it.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 scale (89 patients across three arms) with a surrogate primary endpoint, and a one-sided significance convention that flatters borderline results — note the ATG/G-CSF arm is 'negative' only against that stricter threshold. ATG is a potent immunosuppressant with infusion and serum-sickness risks; the trial's safety experience in 58 exposed patients cannot exclude uncommon harms.

cards.headline: Haller 2019: the ATG advantage persisted at 2 years (C-peptide P = 0.00005 versus placebo; HbA1c still lower) — two-year report of the same TrialNet trial
cards.summary: Haller 2019: the ATG advantage persisted at 2 years (C-peptide P = 0.00005 versus placebo; HbA1c still lower) — two-year report of the same TrialNet trial
cards.type: Randomised trial two-year report (Haller 2019; same trial as Haller 2018)
cards.people: Two-year report of the TrialNet ATG trial (same 89 randomised patients as Haller 2018; 82 analysed for the C-peptide endpoint): prespecified secondary endpoints were 2-year C-peptide AUC and HbA1c, with immunological correlates by flow cytometry.
cards.result: At 2 years, C-peptide AUC remained significantly higher on ATG alone than placebo (P = 0.00005, ANCOVA adjusted for baseline C-peptide, age and sex) but not on ATG/G-CSF (P = 0.032, against the one-sided 0.025 threshold). HbA1c was significantly reduced at 2 years in both active arms (ATG P = 0.011; ATG/G-CSF P = 0.022). Flow cytometry showed reduced CD4:CD8 ratios, increased regulatory-to-conventional T-cell ratios and increased PD-1+ CD4+ T cells after ATG-containing therapy.
cards.watchOut: Durability to 2 years is genuinely informative — many immunotherapies' C-peptide effects fade — but this remains one 89-patient trial, and 'preserved C-peptide' has not been tied in this programme to the outcomes patients feel (severe hypoglycaemia rates and long-term complications were not endpoints). Whether ATG prevents or delays diabetes when given earlier is a separate, untested question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two different immune strategies — memory-T-cell depletion (alefacept) and low-dose ATG — each slowed C-peptide decline for about 2 years in small phase 2 trials; neither is a treatment patients can be offered
cards.summary: Synthesis: two different immune strategies — memory-T-cell depletion (alefacept) and low-dose ATG — each slowed C-peptide decline for about 2 years in small phase 2 trials; neither is a treatment patients can be offered
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled programmes in new-onset type 1 diabetes (within 100 days of diagnosis): T1DAL (alefacept, 49 patients, reports at 12 and 24 months) and TrialNet ATG (89 patients, reports at 1 and 2 years), with abatacept's separate record homed at shelf #1776.
cards.result: Alefacept: primary endpoint missed at 12 months (P = 0.065) but C-peptide significantly preserved at 24 months (P = 0.002–0.015), with lower insulin use and roughly half the major hypoglycaemic events. ATG alone: C-peptide AUC 0.646 vs 0.406 nmol/L at 1 year (P = 0.0003), still significant at 2 years (P = 0.00005), with lower HbA1c at both timepoints; adding G-CSF never helped. Both programmes point the same way — early immune intervention can slow beta-cell loss — and both rest on surrogate endpoints in fewer than 140 randomised patients combined.
cards.watchOut: C-peptide AUC is a laboratory surrogate: the field accepts it because it predicts later hypoglycaemia and complications in cohort data, but neither trial was powered for those outcomes. Alefacept is commercially unavailable and ATG is unapproved for this indication — the shelf records what the biology allows, and its practical use today is in counselling families who read about these trials, and in trial referral.

shelves.title: Islet transplantation for type 1 diabetes with dangerous hypoglycaemia: severe episodes are abolished in most recipients and awareness returns — insulin independence usually lasts about 15 months, and immunosuppression is forever
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia and impaired awareness, does islet transplantation restore awareness and prevent severe episodes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/metabolism · C-Peptide/metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/complications/metabolism/surgery · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/metabolism/prevention & control · Immunosuppression Therapy/methods · Islets of Langerhans Transplantation/methods · Male · Middle Aged · North America · Young Adult
shelves.balance: No randomised trial exists in this population, and the observational record is unusually coherent. In the single-arm phase 3 CIT-07 study, 48 adults whose severe hypoglycaemia persisted despite expert care met the composite endpoint (HbA1c <7.0% and no severe hypoglycaemic events) at a rate of 87.5% at 1 year and 71% at 2 years, with median HbA1c 5.6% and awareness restored (Hering 2016, PMID: 27208344). The registry's 677 recipients show steady improvement by era — 3-year insulin independence 27% rising to 44% — with enduring resolution of severe hypoglycaemia (Barton 2012, PMID: 22723582). The Edmonton 5-year view supplies the necessary cold water: about 80% still secreted C-peptide at 5 years but only about 10% stayed insulin-free, and median insulin independence was 15 months (Ryan 2005, PMID: 15983207). The price is procedural (bleeding requiring transfusion in about 1 in 10) and permanent (immunosuppression, with measurably falling GFR). Judged against its actual indication — abolishing life-threatening hypoglycaemia in the few who fail everything else — the benefit is real; judged as a cure for diabetes, it is not one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: single-arm and registry evidence only, by the nature of the question).

cards.headline: Hering 2016 (CIT-07): in 48 adults whose severe hypoglycaemia persisted despite expert care, islet transplantation met its primary endpoint in 87.5% at 1 year — HbA1c below 7% with no severe hypoglycaemic events — and 71% at 2 years
cards.summary: Hering 2016 (CIT-07): in 48 adults whose severe hypoglycaemia persisted despite expert care, islet transplantation met its primary endpoint in 87.5% at 1 year — HbA1c below 7% with no severe hypoglycaemic events — and 71% at 2 years
cards.people: Multicentre single-arm phase 3 study at eight North American centres: 48 adults with type 1 diabetes for more than 5 years, absent stimulated C-peptide, and documented impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia with severe hypoglycaemic events despite expert care. Each received immunosuppression and one or more transplants of a standardised purified human islet product. Primary endpoint: HbA1c <7.0% at day 365 plus freedom from severe hypoglycaemic events from day 28 to day 365.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met by 87.5% of subjects at 1 year and 71% at 2 years. Median HbA1c was 5.6% at both 1 and 2 years. Hypoglycaemia awareness was restored, with highly significant improvements in Clarke and HYPO scores (the abstract prints 'P > 0.0001', evidently a misprint for <0.0001). There were no study-related deaths or disabilities. Harms: 5 of 48 enrollees (10.4%) had bleeds requiring transfusion (5 of 75 procedures), 2 (4.1%) had infections attributed to immunosuppression, glomerular filtration rate fell significantly on immunosuppression, and donor-specific antibodies developed in 2 patients.
cards.watchOut: No control group — ethically difficult in this population, but it means the comparison is against these patients' own documented history of severe events despite expert care. The endpoint is a composite that most recipients met while still taking insulin: this is a hypoglycaemia treatment, not a cure, and it is bought with lifelong immunosuppression whose renal cost is already visible at 2 years.
cards.source: Hering BJ et al. Phase 3 Trial of Transplantation of Human Islets in Type 1 Diabetes Complicated by Severe Hypoglycemia. Diabetes Care. 2016. PMID: 27208344. Registry ID: NCT00434811. cards.headline: Barton 2012 (CITR): across 677 registry recipients, outcomes improved era by era — insulin independence at 3 years rose from 27% (1999–2002) to 44% (2007–2010), with fewer infusions and fewer adverse events
cards.summary: Barton 2012 (CITR): across 677 registry recipients, outcomes improved era by era — insulin independence at 3 years rose from 27% (1999–2002) to 44% (2007–2010), with fewer infusions and fewer adverse events
cards.type: Registry cohort analysis (Barton 2012, Collaborative Islet Transplant Registry)
cards.people: Collaborative Islet Transplant Registry analysis of 677 islet-transplant-alone or islet-after-kidney recipients with type 1 diabetes and severe hypoglycaemia, transplanted 1999–2010, compared across three eras with follow-up to 5 years. Outcomes: insulin independence, C-peptide graft function, HbA1c, severe hypoglycaemia resolution, fasting glucose and safety.
cards.result: Insulin independence at 3 years improved from 27% in the early era (1999–2002, n = 214) to 37% in the mid era (2003–2006, n = 255) and 44% in the recent era (2007–2010, n = 208; P = 0.01 for era). C-peptide at or above 0.3 ng/mL (graft function) was retained longer in the recent era (P < 0.001); HbA1c reduction and resolution of severe hypoglycaemia showed enduring long-term effects; fasting glucose stabilised better. Reinfusion by 1 year fell from 60–65% in 1999–2006 to 48% in 2007–2010 (P < 0.01), and adverse events modestly declined. Recipients who ever achieved insulin independence kept graft function longer (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: A registry, not a trial: era comparisons entangle better technique with changing patient selection and immunosuppression, and centres reporting to a registry are the experienced ones. The registry's own framing is improvement over time — the 44% three-year insulin independence of the best era is simultaneously the ceiling this record offers.
cards.source: Barton FB et al. Improvement in outcomes of clinical islet transplantation: 1999-2010. Diabetes Care. 2012. PMID: 22723582. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ryan 2005 (Edmonton): at 5 years about 80% of recipients still made C-peptide but only about 10% remained insulin-free — median insulin independence lasted 15 months, while hypoglycaemia protection endured
cards.summary: Ryan 2005 (Edmonton): at 5 years about 80% of recipients still made C-peptide but only about 10% remained insulin-free — median insulin independence lasted 15 months, while hypoglycaemia protection endured
cards.people: Five-year follow-up of the Edmonton cohort: 65 patients (mean age 42.9 years, mean diabetes duration 27.1 years, 57% women) who received islet transplants, mainly for problematic hypoglycaemia; 44 completed transplantation as defined by achieving insulin independence. Outcomes at 5 years: C-peptide persistence, insulin independence, HbA1c, hypoglycaemia scores, and procedural and immunosuppression complications across 128 procedures.
cards.result: At 5 years roughly 80% of completed patients had detectable C-peptide but only about 10% maintained insulin independence; median duration of insulin independence was 15 months (interquartile range 6.2–25.5). HbA1c was 6.4% in those off insulin, 6.7% in those back on insulin but C-peptide positive, and 9.0% in those who lost graft function (P < 0.05); those back on insulin needed about half their pre-transplant dose. Hypoglycaemia score and lability index improved significantly and durably. Complications: bleeding in 15 of 128 procedures and branch portal vein thrombosis in 5; immunosuppression effects included mouth ulcers, diarrhoea, anaemia and ovarian cysts; antihypertensive use rose from 6% to 42% of patients.
cards.watchOut: The pioneering cohort, with the earliest protocol and the longest view: its 5-year numbers are the floor, not the current expectation (CITR shows later eras doing better). Even so, its central lesson has not been overturned — graft function (C-peptide, hypoglycaemia protection) is durable, while complete insulin independence usually is not.
cards.source: Ryan EA et al. Five-year follow-up after clinical islet transplantation. Diabetes. 2005. PMID: 15983207. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. median duration of insulin independence was 15 months (interquartile range 6.2–25.5). hba1c was 6.4% in those off insulin, 6.7% in those back on insulin but c-peptide positive, and 9.0% in those who lost graft function (p < 0.05); those back on insulin needed about half their pre-transplant dose. hypoglycaemia score and lability index improved significantly and durably. complications: bleeding in 15 of 128 procedures and branch portal vein thrombosis in 5; immunosuppression effects included mouth ulcers, diarrhoea, anaemia and ovarian cysts; antihypertensive use rose from 6% to 42% of patients. the pioneering cohort, with the earliest protocol and the longest view: its 5-year numbers are the floor, not the current expectation (citr shows later eras doing better). even so, its central lesson has not been overturned — graft function (c-peptide, hypoglycaemia protection) is durable, while complete insulin independence usually is not. ryan ea et al. five-year follow-up after clinical islet transplantation. diabetes. 2005. pmid: 15983207. registry id: none — pre-registration era. mesh: adult · blood glucose/metabolism · c-peptide/blood · diabetes mellitus, type 1/blood/surgery · female · follow-up studies · humans · hypoglycemia/epidemiology · insulin/therapeutic use · islets of langerhans transplantation/methods/mortality/physiology · male · postoperative complications · survival analysis · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: for the narrow group with type 1 diabetes, lost hypoglycaemia awareness and severe events despite expert care, islet transplantation reliably restores awareness and abolishes severe hypoglycaemia while the graft works — durable insulin freedom is the exception
cards.summary: Synthesis: for the narrow group with type 1 diabetes, lost hypoglycaemia awareness and severe events despite expert care, islet transplantation reliably restores awareness and abolishes severe hypoglycaemia while the graft works — durable insulin freedom is the exception
cards.people: One single-arm phase 3 study (48 patients), the international registry (677 recipients, 1999–2010) and the Edmonton 5-year cohort (65 patients) — no randomised trial exists or is likely to in this population.
cards.result: Protection from severe hypoglycaemia: primary endpoint (HbA1c <7% and no severe events) met by 87.5% at 1 year and 71% at 2 years in CIT-07, with median HbA1c 5.6%; registry data show severe-hypoglycaemia resolution enduring to 5 years. Insulin independence: 44% at 3 years in the best registry era, about 10% at 5 years in Edmonton, median duration 15 months. Costs: transfusion-requiring bleeding in about 1 in 10 recipients, procedural thrombosis, falling GFR and the full burden of lifelong immunosuppression.
cards.watchOut: Every number here comes from patients selected for the most dangerous form of type 1 diabetes — recurrent severe hypoglycaemia with impaired awareness despite specialist care. Nothing on this shelf supports transplantation for ordinary glycaemic control, and the comparison that matters for eligible patients is against their own event history, not against insulin therapy in general. Technology (sensors, closed loop) has since claimed part of this population; the residual candidates are those in whom technology has also failed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hering BJ et al. Diabetes Care. 2016 (PMID: 27208344); Barton FB et al. Diabetes Care. 2012 (PMID: 22723582); Ryan EA et al. Diabetes. 2005 (PMID: 15983207).

shelves.title: Glyburide for gestational diabetes: glucose control equals insulin, but babies are heavier, with more macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia — and perinatal noninferiority was never proven
shelves.question: In gestational diabetes needing drug treatment, is glyburide as safe and effective as insulin or metformin?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Congenital Abnormalities/epidemiology · Diabetes, Gestational/drug therapy · Female · Fetal Blood/chemistry · Fetal Macrosomia/epidemiology · Glyburide/blood/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemia/epidemiology · Hypoglycemic Agents/blood/therapeutic use · Infant, Newborn · Insulin/blood/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome
shelves.balance: Split the question in two. Effective? Yes: the founding randomised trial found glyburide and insulin indistinguishable for glucose control (mean glucose 105 vs 105 mg/dL; 4% of the glyburide group needed insulin added; Langer 2000, PMID: 11036118). As safe? The record says no. Pooling 15 randomised comparisons, glyburide versus insulin produced heavier babies (+109 g), more macrosomia (risk ratio 2.62, 95% CI 1.35 to 5.08) and more neonatal hypoglycaemia (risk ratio 2.04, 1.30 to 3.20) — the reviewers' verdict was 'clearly inferior' (Balsells 2015, PMID: 25609400; glyburide and glibenclamide are the same drug). And the large French INDAO trial, designed specifically to prove perinatal noninferiority within a 7% margin, failed to do so: composite complications 27.6% versus 23.4%, with the confidence interval reaching +10.5% (Sénat 2018, PMID: 29715355). Where metformin is an option it beat glyburide on the same outcomes; the metformin-in-pregnancy record is homed at shelf #286. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) (not Tier C: multiple randomised trials plus a meta-analysis; graded POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the harm rests on pooled small trials and a failed noninferiority test rather than a single decisive harm trial).

cards.headline: Langer 2000: the founding trial — glyburide controlled glucose exactly as well as insulin in 404 women (mean glucose 105 vs 105 mg/dL), with no significant difference in large babies, macrosomia or neonatal hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Langer 2000: the founding trial — glyburide controlled glucose exactly as well as insulin in 404 women (mean glucose 105 vs 105 mg/dL), with no significant difference in large babies, macrosomia or neonatal hypoglycaemia
cards.people: Randomised trial in 404 women with singleton pregnancies and gestational diabetes requiring treatment, assigned between 11 and 33 weeks' gestation to glyburide or insulin under an intensified protocol. Primary endpoint: achievement of target glycaemic control; secondary endpoints: maternal and neonatal complications.
cards.result: Mean glucose during treatment was identical (105 ± 16 vs 105 ± 18 mg/dL; P = 0.99), and only 8 women (4%) on glyburide needed insulin added. No significant differences: large for gestational age 12% vs 13%; macrosomia (birth weight at least 4000 g) 7% vs 4%; neonatal lung complications 8% vs 6%; neonatal hypoglycaemia 9% vs 6%; neonatal intensive care admission 6% vs 7%; fetal anomalies 2% vs 2%. Glyburide was not detected in the cord serum of any infant in the glyburide group.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 404 women cannot exclude moderate harm: the macrosomia (7% vs 4%) and neonatal hypoglycaemia (9% vs 6%) point estimates both leaned the wrong way, non-significantly, in exactly the direction the later pooled analysis confirmed. 'Not detected in cord serum' reflected the assay of the time; later pharmacology showed glyburide does cross the placenta.
cards.source: Langer O et al. A comparison of glyburide and insulin in women with gestational diabetes mellitus. N Engl J Med. 2000. PMID: 11036118. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Balsells 2015: pooling 15 randomised comparisons (2,509 women), glyburide versus insulin meant heavier babies (+109 g), 2.6 times the macrosomia and twice the neonatal hypoglycaemia — the authors call glibenclamide 'clearly inferior'
cards.summary: Balsells 2015: pooling 15 randomised comparisons (2,509 women), glyburide versus insulin meant heavier babies (+109 g), 2.6 times the macrosomia and twice the neonatal hypoglycaemia — the authors call glibenclamide 'clearly inferior'
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in gestational diabetes requiring drug treatment, comparing glibenclamide (glyburide) with insulin, metformin with insulin, and metformin with glibenclamide: 15 articles, 2,509 women, with 14 primary maternal and fetal outcomes.
cards.result: Glibenclamide versus insulin: birth weight was higher by a mean of 109 g (95% CI 35.9 to 181), macrosomia risk ratio 2.62 (1.35 to 5.08) and neonatal hypoglycaemia risk ratio 2.04 (1.30 to 3.20). Metformin versus glibenclamide also favoured metformin (birth weight −209 g; macrosomia risk ratio 0.33, 0.13 to 0.81; large for gestational age 0.44, 0.21 to 0.92), though treatment failure was commoner on metformin. The authors conclude that glibenclamide is clearly inferior to both insulin and metformin in the short term and should not be used for gestational diabetes if insulin or metformin is available.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are mostly small and of variable quality, and several predate modern glyburide dosing; pooling cannot manufacture precision the trials lack. But the direction is consistent across three separate outcomes, and it is the direction Langer's own point estimates hinted at — this is confirmation, not contradiction, of the early signal.
cards.source: Balsells M et al. Glibenclamide, metformin, and insulin for the treatment of gestational diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2015. PMID: 25609400. Registry ID: NCT01998113 (the review's own registration). cards.headline: Sénat 2018 (INDAO): the trial designed to prove glyburide's perinatal safety failed to — complications were 27.6% on glyburide versus 23.4% on insulin, and the confidence interval (up to +10.5%) crossed the 7% noninferiority margin
cards.summary: Sénat 2018 (INDAO): the trial designed to prove glyburide's perinatal safety failed to — complications were 27.6% on glyburide versus 23.4% on insulin, and the confidence interval (up to +10.5%) crossed the 7% noninferiority margin
cards.people: Multicentre noninferiority randomised trial (INDAO) in 13 French tertiary hospitals: 914 women with singleton pregnancies and gestational diabetes diagnosed at 24–34 weeks who needed drug treatment after 10 days of dietary therapy, assigned to oral glyburide (n = 460, titrated to a maximum of 20 mg/day) or subcutaneous insulin (n = 454). Primary outcome: a composite of macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia; noninferiority margin 7%.
cards.result: In the per-protocol analysis (367 glyburide and 442 insulin mother–infant pairs), the primary outcome occurred in 27.6% on glyburide versus 23.4% on insulin — a difference of 4.2% with a one-sided 97.5% confidence interval extending to 10.5% (P = 0.19 for noninferiority). Because the interval crossed the 7% margin, noninferiority was not demonstrated. The authors conclude the findings do not justify glyburide as a first-line treatment for gestational diabetes.
cards.watchOut: Failing to prove noninferiority is not proof of inferiority — the point estimate (4.2% more complications) sits inside the margin while the interval does not. The per-protocol population also shrank asymmetrically (367 of 460 analysed on glyburide versus 442 of 454 on insulin), largely through treatment failure and switching, which is itself informative about glyburide's practical limits.
cards.source: Sénat MV et al. Effect of Glyburide vs Subcutaneous Insulin on Perinatal Complications Among Women With Gestational Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29715355. Registry ID: NCT01731431. cards.headline: Synthesis: glyburide lowers glucose as well as insulin — that was never the problem; on the baby's outcomes the record tilts against it, and the one trial built to prove perinatal noninferiority could not
cards.summary: Synthesis: glyburide lowers glucose as well as insulin — that was never the problem; on the baby's outcomes the record tilts against it, and the one trial built to prove perinatal noninferiority could not
cards.people: One founding RCT (Langer 2000, n = 404), one meta-analysis of 15 randomised comparisons (Balsells 2015, 2,509 women) and one large noninferiority trial (Sénat 2018, n = 914). Glyburide and glibenclamide are the same drug (US and international names).
cards.result: Glycaemic control: identical mean glucose in Langer (105 vs 105 mg/dL), with 4% needing added insulin. Neonatal outcomes: macrosomia risk ratio 2.62 (1.35 to 5.08), neonatal hypoglycaemia 2.04 (1.30 to 3.20) and birth weight +109 g for glyburide versus insulin in the pooled record; INDAO's composite of perinatal complications was 27.6% versus 23.4%, difference 4.2%, with the confidence interval crossing the prespecified 7% noninferiority margin. Metformin, where compared, beat glyburide on the same outcomes (shelf #286 homes the metformin-in-pregnancy record).
cards.watchOut: All outcomes here are short-term and perinatal; no trial follows the children for the metabolic outcomes that motivate treating gestational diabetes in the first place. The practical question is rarely glyburide versus insulin in the abstract — it is glyburide versus a woman's refusal or inability to inject — and none of these trials enrolled women on that basis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Langer O et al. N Engl J Med. 2000 (PMID: 11036118); Balsells M et al. BMJ. 2015 (PMID: 25609400); Sénat MV et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29715355).

shelves.title: DAFNE education in type 1 diabetes: quality of life and dietary freedom improve durably, HbA1c improves modestly and fades — one 5-day course, no extra severe hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes, does dose-adjustment education (DAFNE) improve quality of life and glycaemic control versus standard education?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/therapy · *Diet · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Insulin/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: The trial evidence supports both halves of the claim, with different durability. In the DAFNE randomised trial (169 adults with type 1 diabetes and suboptimal control), a 5-day course in flexible intensive insulin management produced HbA1c of 8.4% versus 9.4% on the waiting-list control at 6 months, with significant improvements in dietary freedom, overall quality-of-life impact, wellbeing and treatment satisfaction — and no change in severe hypoglycaemia, weight or lipids (DAFNE Study Group 2002, PMID: 12364302). At a mean of 44 months, the quality-of-life gains were fully maintained, but the HbA1c advantage over baseline had shrunk to 0.36 points and was decaying (Speight 2010, PMID: 20399523). The REPOSE trial (homed at shelf #564) later delivered DAFNE-style education to both arms and found pumps added nothing to injections — evidence that the education itself is the active ingredient. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: one randomised trial with a waiting-list control, plus an uncontrolled cohort follow-up; the quality-of-life outcomes are unblindable by design).

cards.headline: DAFNE Study Group 2002: a 5-day course in flexible intensive insulin management cut HbA1c from 9.4% to 8.4% at 6 months versus waiting-list control — and improved quality of life and dietary freedom without more severe hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: DAFNE Study Group 2002: a 5-day course in flexible intensive insulin management cut HbA1c from 9.4% to 8.4% at 6 months versus waiting-list control — and improved quality of life and dietary freedom without more severe hypoglycaemia
cards.people: Randomised trial in three English health districts: 169 adults with type 1 diabetes and moderate or poor glycaemic control assigned to attend the DAFNE course (Dose Adjustment For Normal Eating — training in flexible intensive insulin therapy with dietary freedom) immediately, or after a 6-month waiting-list delay. Outcomes: HbA1c, severe hypoglycaemia, and the impact of diabetes on quality of life (ADDQoL).
cards.result: At 6 months HbA1c was 8.4% in the immediate-DAFNE group versus 9.4% in the delayed group (P < 0.0001). The negative impact of diabetes on dietary freedom improved significantly (P < 0.0001), as did its impact on overall quality of life (P < 0.01); general wellbeing and treatment satisfaction also improved, and the improvement in present quality of life became significant by 1 year. Severe hypoglycaemia, weight and lipids were unchanged.
cards.watchOut: A waiting-list control cannot blind anyone: participants knew they had been trained, and quality-of-life outcomes are exactly the kind that expectation and attention can move. The HbA1c gap at 6 months (a full point) is larger than education alone usually delivers and partly reflects the control group's stagnation; the follow-up cohort (Speight 2010) shows how much of it survived.
cards.source: DAFNE Study Group. Training in flexible, intensive insulin management to enable dietary freedom in people with type 1 diabetes: dose adjustment for normal eating (DAFNE) randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2002. cards.summary: Speight 2010: four years on, the quality-of-life gains were fully maintained but the HbA1c gain had shrunk to 0.36 points (9.32% to 8.96%) — one course, durable confidence, decaying glucose effect
cards.type: Cohort follow-up of a randomised trial (Speight 2010)
cards.people: Cohort follow-up of the original DAFNE trial participants in the same three English districts, at a mean of 44 months (range 37–51) after the course: 104 participants (74%) provided biomedical data and 88 (63%) completed questionnaires including the ADDQoL quality-of-life measure.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c improved by 0.36 percentage points from baseline (9.32% ± 1.1% to 8.96% ± 1.2%; P < 0.01) — still significant at 44 months but significantly decayed from the 12-month value (P < 0.05). The quality-of-life improvements seen at 12 months were sustained at 44 months (for example, the impact of diabetes on dietary freedom: −1.78 ± 2.33 at 44 months versus −4.27 ± 2.94 at baseline; P < 0.0001). Results were similar with last-observation-carried-forward analysis. The authors conclude further intervention would be needed to reach recommended HbA1c targets.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up cohort, not a comparison: by 44 months there was no control group left (the waiting-list group had been trained), so the sustained quality-of-life scores are before-and-after observations in the 63–74% who responded — the people who stayed engaged with a programme they valued. Attrition and goodwill both push these numbers up.
cards.source: Speight J et al. Long-term biomedical and psychosocial outcomes following DAFNE (Dose Adjustment For Normal Eating) structured education to promote intensive insulin therapy in adults with sub-optimally controlled Type 1 diabetes. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2010. PMID: 20399523. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: DAFNE-style education durably improves how life with type 1 diabetes feels and modestly improves HbA1c, fading over years — with no hypoglycaemia penalty
cards.summary: Synthesis: DAFNE-style education durably improves how life with type 1 diabetes feels and modestly improves HbA1c, fading over years — with no hypoglycaemia penalty
cards.people: One randomised trial (169 adults, waiting-list control, 6–12 months) and its 44-month cohort follow-up, with the REPOSE trial's education-in-both-arms design homed at shelf #564 as supporting context.
cards.result: HbA1c: 8.4% versus 9.4% at 6 months in the trial; +0.36 points better than baseline at 44 months in the cohort, significantly decayed from the 1-year value. Quality of life and dietary freedom: significantly improved in the trial and fully maintained at 44 months. Severe hypoglycaemia: unchanged in the trial. The REPOSE trial later gave DAFNE-style education to both its pump and injection arms and found the delivery device made no difference — consistent with the education, not the hardware, being the active ingredient.
cards.watchOut: DAFNE was tested in adults with suboptimal control willing to attend a 5-day course in 1999–2002, before sensors and pumps were routine; how much it adds on top of modern CGM-based care is not what these studies measured. The glycaemic effect's decay argues for structured refreshers — which the follow-up data support only by implication, not by test.
cards.source: Synthesis of DAFNE Study Group. BMJ. 2002 (PMID: 12364302); Speight J et al. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2010 (PMID: 20399523). REPOSE trial (REPOSE Study Group, BMJ 2017, PMID: 28360027) homed at shelf #564.

shelves.title: Diabetes distress in type 2 diabetes (REDEEM): distress falls with any structured support — the distress-specific programme adds value only in the most distressed — and HbA1c does not move
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and high diabetes distress, does a distress-focused self-management intervention improve distress and HbA1c?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/psychology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Self Care/methods · Young Adult
shelves.balance: REDEEM randomised 392 adults with type 2 diabetes and elevated distress to computer-assisted self-management, the same plus distress-specific problem-solving (CAPS), or minimal computer support. Distress fell significantly and clinically meaningfully in all three arms (P < 0.001) with no overall between-group difference; the distress-specific content earned its keep only in the subgroup with high baseline regimen distress (interaction P < 0.02). Self-management behaviours — eating, activity, medication adherence — improved alongside distress. HbA1c did not change in any arm (Fisher 2013, PMID: 23735726). So the intervention family does what its name promises for distress, non-specifically, and does nothing measurable for glucose; the trial had no untreated control, so some of the universal improvement may be time and regression to the mean in a group recruited at peak distress. Treating depression in diabetes is a different question with a different record. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for reducing diabetes distress / no improvement in HbA1c (Tier C: a single pragmatic trial, no untreated comparator).

cards.headline: Fisher 2013 (REDEEM): in 392 adults with type 2 diabetes and raised distress, all three programmes — including minimal computer support — reduced distress significantly; the distress-specific programme won only in the most distressed, and HbA1c did not change in any arm
cards.summary: Fisher 2013 (REDEEM): in 392 adults with type 2 diabetes and raised distress, all three programmes — including minimal computer support — reduced distress significantly; the distress-specific programme won only in the most distressed, and HbA1c did not change in any arm
cards.people: Pragmatic randomised trial (REDEEM) in 392 non-clinically depressed adults with type 2 diabetes and diabetes distress, assigned to computer-assisted self-management (CASM), CASM plus distress-specific problem-solving therapy (CAPS), or a computer-administered minimal supportive intervention. Primary outcomes: Diabetes Distress Scale (DDS) total and its Emotional Burden and Regimen Distress subscales, plus diet, exercise and medication adherence.
cards.result: Significant, clinically meaningful reductions in distress (DDS total, Emotional Burden and Regimen Distress) and improvements in self-management behaviours occurred in all three conditions (P < 0.001), with no significant between-group differences overall. A group-by-baseline-distress interaction (P < 0.02) showed that patients with high baseline Regimen Distress did significantly better in the distress-specific CAPS arm than in the other two. Regimen Distress was both the largest source of distress and the most responsive to intervention. Distress reductions were accompanied by significant improvements in healthy eating, physical activity and medication adherence — but not by any change in HbA1c.
cards.watchOut: There is no untreated control: the 'minimal' arm was itself an intervention, so the trial shows distress falls with structured attention of any of these kinds — it cannot show how much of the fall is the programmes versus time, regression to the mean in people recruited at high distress, or trial participation itself. And the outcome patients and payers ultimately care about, HbA1c, did not move.
cards.source: Fisher L et al. REDEEM: a pragmatic trial to reduce diabetes distress. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 23735726. Registry ID: NCT00714441. MeSH: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/psychology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Self Care/methods · Young Adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: diabetes distress in type 2 diabetes is genuinely malleable — structured self-management support of almost any kind reduces it — but distress-specific content adds measurable value only for the most distressed, and none of it lowers HbA1c
cards.summary: Synthesis: diabetes distress in type 2 diabetes is genuinely malleable — structured self-management support of almost any kind reduces it — but distress-specific content adds measurable value only for the most distressed, and none of it lowers HbA1c
cards.people: One pragmatic randomised trial (REDEEM, 392 adults with type 2 diabetes and elevated distress, three active arms, no untreated control). The companion trial in type 1 diabetes (T1-REDEEM) answers a different population's question and is not carded here.
cards.result: Distress: significant reductions in total distress, emotional burden and regimen distress in all three arms (P < 0.001), no overall between-group difference; the distress-specific arm (CAPS) separated from the others only among patients with high baseline regimen distress (interaction P < 0.02). Behaviour: healthy eating, physical activity and medication adherence all improved alongside distress. HbA1c: unchanged in every arm. The defensible claim is narrower than the hope: support reduces distress and improves self-management behaviour; it does not follow that glucose improves.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, from the research group that defined the distress construct and built the measuring scale — independent replication in type 2 diabetes is thin, and the type 1 diabetes counterpart trial (T1-REDEEM, 2018) found a similar pattern in a different population. Distress and depression are different constructs; this shelf is about distress in people who are not clinically depressed, and says nothing about treating depression in diabetes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fisher L et al. Diabetes Care. 2013 (PMID: 23735726).

shelves.title: Starting insulin in type 2 diabetes (4T): begin with basal — control converges by 3 years, hypoglycaemia and weight gain stay lowest, and a premixed start reaches target least often
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes starting insulin on top of oral therapy, which initiation strategy — basal alone, premixed (biphasic), or prandial — controls glucose best with least hypoglycaemia?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Data Interpretation, Statistical · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Insulin/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Insulin Aspart · Insulin Detemir · Insulin, Long-Acting · Metformin/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Probability · Sulfonylurea Compounds/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: The 4T trial (708 patients on metformin plus a sulfonylurea) is the one direct randomised comparison of the three ways to start insulin, and its two reports must be read together. At 1 year, meal-covering regimens looked better (HbA1c 7.3% biphasic, 7.2% prandial, 7.6% basal) — but that compared one insulin against two meal-covering regimens, and the basal arm paid far less for its result: 2.3 hypoglycaemic events per patient-year versus 5.7 and 12.0, and 1.9 kg weight gain versus 4.7 and 5.7 kg (Holman 2007, PMID: 17890232). By 3 years, once a second insulin was added when needed (as happened in 68–82% of patients), HbA1c converged (medians 7.1%, 6.8%, 6.9%; P = 0.28), the basal start kept the least hypoglycaemia (1.7 vs 3.0 and 5.7 events/year) and the biphasic start reached HbA1c at most 6.5% least often (31.9% vs 44.7% and 43.2%) (Holman 2009, PMID: 19850703). Strategy verdict: start basal, intensify by adding prandial insulin when required, and do not start with a premixed insulin. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: a single trial — two reports of one experiment — however large and well conducted).

cards.headline: Holman 2007 (4T, year 1): adding biphasic or prandial insulin lowered HbA1c more than basal insulin alone (7.3% and 7.2% vs 7.6%) — at 5.7 and 12.0 hypoglycaemic events per patient-year against 2.3, and roughly triple the weight gain
cards.summary: Holman 2007 (4T, year 1): adding biphasic or prandial insulin lowered HbA1c more than basal insulin alone (7.3% and 7.2% vs 7.6%) — at 5.7 and 12.0 hypoglycaemic events per patient-year against 2.3, and roughly triple the weight gain
cards.people: Open-label multicentre randomised trial (Treating to Target in Type 2 Diabetes, 4T): 708 patients with HbA1c 7.0–10.0% on maximally tolerated metformin and sulfonylurea, assigned to biphasic insulin aspart twice daily, prandial insulin aspart three times daily, or basal insulin detemir once (twice if required) daily. Outcomes at 1 year: HbA1c, proportion reaching HbA1c at most 6.5%, hypoglycaemia rates and weight gain.
cards.result: At 1 year, mean HbA1c was 7.3% on biphasic, 7.2% on prandial and 7.6% on basal insulin (basal higher than both, P < 0.001). The proportions reaching HbA1c at most 6.5% were 17.0%, 23.9% and 8.1% respectively. Hypoglycaemic events per patient per year were 5.7 (biphasic), 12.0 (prandial) and 2.3 (basal); mean weight gains were 4.7 kg, 5.7 kg and 1.9 kg. Overall adverse event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: The 1-year comparison is structurally unfair to the basal arm: a single basal insulin, titrated once or twice daily, against regimens already covering meals. The protocol's own design anticipated this — a second insulin type was added in later years when control fell short — so year 1 answers 'which single insulin works fastest?', not 'which starting strategy is best?'. That is the 3-year report's question.
cards.source: Holman RR et al. Addition of biphasic, prandial, or basal insulin to oral therapy in type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2007. PMID: 17890232. Registry ID: ISRCTN51125379. cards.headline: Holman 2009 (4T, year 3): with a second insulin added when needed, HbA1c converged (medians 7.1%, 6.8%, 6.9%) — but the biphasic-start group reached target least often (31.9% vs 44.7% and 43.2%), and basal start kept the least hypoglycaemia (1.7 events/year) and least weight gain
cards.summary: Holman 2009 (4T, year 3): with a second insulin added when needed, HbA1c converged (medians 7.1%, 6.8%, 6.9%) — but the biphasic-start group reached target least often (31.9% vs 44.7% and 43.2%), and basal start kept the least hypoglycaemia (1.7 events/year) and least weight gain
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Holman 2009, 4T — 3-year report of the same trial as Holman 2007)
cards.people: Three-year report of the same 4T trial (708 patients; not a separate trial). During years 2–3, sulfonylurea was replaced by a second type of insulin if hyperglycaemia became unacceptable or HbA1c exceeded 6.5% — by 3 years 67.7% (biphasic-start), 73.6% (prandial-start) and 81.6% (basal-start) were taking a second insulin. Outcomes: HbA1c, proportion at most 6.5%, hypoglycaemia, weight.
cards.result: Median HbA1c at 3 years was similar across strategies (biphasic 7.1%, prandial 6.8%, basal 6.9%; P = 0.28). Fewer biphasic-start patients reached HbA1c at most 6.5% (31.9%) than prandial-start (44.7%; P = 0.006) or basal-start (43.2%; P = 0.03). Median hypoglycaemia rates per patient per year were lowest on basal-start (1.7), higher on biphasic (3.0) and highest on prandial (5.7; P < 0.001). Mean weight gain was higher in the prandial group than in either other group; other adverse event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: By year 3 most patients in every arm were on two insulin types, so the trial compares starting strategies within one intensification philosophy, not three pure regimens. It used detemir and aspart in a metformin-plus-sulfonylurea era — before GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors rewrote what 'starting insulin' competes with — and glycaemic targets (6.5%) were tighter than many services now aim for.
cards.source: Holman RR et al. Three-year efficacy of complex insulin regimens in type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19850703. Registry ID: ISRCTN51125379. cards.headline: Synthesis: start basal — by 3 years all three strategies reached the same HbA1c once intensification was allowed, and the basal start paid the least for it in hypoglycaemia and weight; a biphasic start was the weakest of the three
cards.summary: Synthesis: start basal — by 3 years all three strategies reached the same HbA1c once intensification was allowed, and the basal start paid the least for it in hypoglycaemia and weight; a biphasic start was the weakest of the three
cards.people: One randomised trial (4T, 708 patients on metformin plus sulfonylurea), reported at 1 year (Holman 2007) and 3 years (Holman 2009) — two reports, one experiment, carded separately because each answers a different half of the question.
cards.result: Year 1 (single-insulin phase): HbA1c 7.3% biphasic, 7.2% prandial, 7.6% basal; hypoglycaemia 5.7, 12.0 and 2.3 events per patient-year; weight gain 4.7, 5.7 and 1.9 kg. Year 3 (intensification allowed; 68–82% on a second insulin): median HbA1c 7.1%, 6.8% and 6.9% (P = 0.28); reaching at most 6.5%: 31.9%, 44.7% and 43.2%; hypoglycaemia 3.0, 5.7 and 1.7 events per year. The early basal 'deficit' was an artefact of comparing one insulin against meal-covering regimens; the durable differences are the biphasic start's weaker target attainment and the prandial start's hypoglycaemia and weight costs.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, however well run, anchors this shelf — and its clinical world (sulfonylurea background, no GLP-1 or SGLT2 agents, detemir as the basal insulin) has moved on. The strategy lesson (basal first, add prandial when needed, avoid premixed starts) is consistent with how practice evolved, but the modern version of this question — basal insulin versus adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist — is a different shelf's question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Holman RR et al. N Engl J Med. 2007 (PMID: 17890232); Holman RR et al. N Engl J Med. 2009 (PMID: 19850703).
