shelves.title: Stepwise prandial insulin in type 2 diabetes: one injection at the largest meal matched three on average HbA1c in both randomised tests — with less hypoglycaemia, but fewer patients reaching target
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes not at target on basal insulin, does adding prandial insulin stepwise — starting with one daily injection at the largest meal — achieve glycaemic control comparable to immediate full basal-bolus (three daily injections), and with what hypoglycaemia and burden trade-offs?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · *Algorithms · Blood Glucose/drug effects/metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/*drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Insulin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*analogs & derivatives/*therapeutic use · Insulin, Long-Acting · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Failure · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials have tested the stepwise idea directly, and they agree. In Davidson 2011 (PMID: 21324825), 631 adults with type 2 diabetes and A1C of 8.0% or more on oral agents entered a 14-week insulin glargine run-in; the 343 (54%) still above 7.0% were randomised to insulin glulisine once, twice, or three times daily for 24 weeks. A1C reductions with one or two injections were noninferior to three (95% CIs for the differences −0.39 to 0.36 and −0.30 to 0.43) — but the share reaching A1C below 7.0% was lower with fewer injections (30% with one, 33% with two, 46% with three), while severe hypoglycaemia ran the other way (7%, 8%, and 16% respectively; the differences were not statistically significant). In FullSTEP (Rodbard 2014, PMID: 24622667), 401 patients uncontrolled on basal insulin were randomised to stepwise addition of insulin aspart — one bolus at the largest meal, with further mealtime doses added at weeks 11 and 22 only if HbA1c remained at or above 7% — or to full basal-bolus from the start: HbA1c fell 0.98% versus 1.12% over 32 weeks (difference 0.14%, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.30; noninferior), and hypoglycaemic episodes were significantly fewer with the stepwise approach (rate ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.75 — a relative rate). So on average glucose control, starting with one prandial injection at the largest meal and adding more only if needed gives up nothing measurable against routine three-injection basal-bolus; what it buys is fewer injections, fewer glucose checks, and less hypoglycaemia. What it may cost is the top end: in Davidson, more patients crossed below 7.0% when all three meals were covered from the outset. A third randomised comparison, Riddle 2014 (PMID: 24118931), which initiated and advanced insulin over one year, found the same shape — basal plus a single prandial injection noninferior to premixed insulin, with full basal-bolus only slightly ahead on target attainment — and is cross-referenced here rather than carded, because its question spans initiation (shelf #2640's home). Initiation strategy itself is shelf #2640; the self-monitoring burden each extra injection drags with it is shelves #559 and #1768; adding a GLP-1 agonist instead of prandial insulin is shelf #2653.

cards.headline: Davidson 2011: after a glargine run-in, one or two daily glulisine injections were noninferior to three for A1C reduction — but target attainment was 30% and 33% versus 46%, and severe hypoglycaemia 7% and 8% versus 16%
cards.summary: Davidson 2011: after a glargine run-in, one or two daily glulisine injections were noninferior to three for A1C reduction — but target attainment was 30% and 33% versus 46%, and severe hypoglycaemia 7% and 8% versus 16%
cards.people: 631 adults with type 2 diabetes on oral antidiabetic drugs with A1C of 8.0% or more entered a 14-week insulin glargine run-in; 343 (54%) still had A1C above 7.0% and were randomised 1:1:1 to insulin glulisine once, twice, or three times daily — given before the meals of greatest glycaemic impact — for 24 weeks. Open-label, parallel-group.
cards.result: A1C reductions with glulisine once daily and twice daily were noninferior to three times daily (95% CIs for the between-arm differences: −0.39 to 0.36 and −0.30 to 0.43; P > .5 for both; the abstract reports these noninferiority intervals rather than per-arm point reductions). More patients reached A1C below 7.0% with three injections (46%) than with two (33%) or one (30%). Severe hypoglycaemia occurred in 16% of patients on three injections versus 8% on two and 7% on one — twice as many, but the differences did not reach statistical significance. The authors conclude that initiating prandial insulin in a simplified stepwise approach is an effective alternative to the routine three-injection basal-bolus approach.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on the mean is not equality at the target: the trial's own numbers show roughly three in ten reaching goal on one injection versus nearly one in two on three. And the randomised 343 are a selected minority — 46% of the run-in cohort was never randomised, having reached target on glargine alone or left the study — so these results describe true basal failure, not all basal starters. Doses were placed before the meals of 'greatest glycemic impact', a selection step real clinics may not reproduce.
cards.source: Davidson MB et al. A stepwise approach to insulin therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and basal insulin treatment failure. Endocrine Practice. 2011. PMID: 21324825. cards.headline: FullSTEP 2014: stepwise aspart addition (extra mealtime doses only if still above target) matched full basal-bolus on HbA1c (−0.98% vs −1.12%) with significantly fewer hypoglycaemic episodes (rate ratio 0.58)
cards.summary: FullSTEP 2014: stepwise aspart addition (extra mealtime doses only if still above target) matched full basal-bolus on HbA1c (−0.98% vs −1.12%) with significantly fewer hypoglycaemic episodes (rate ratio 0.58)
cards.type: Randomised open-label treat-to-target noninferiority trial (FullSTEP; Rodbard 2014)
cards.people: 401 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on basal insulin plus oral agents (mean age 59.8 years, HbA1c 7.9%, mean diabetes duration 12.6 years), block-randomised at 150 sites in seven countries to stepwise bolus addition or full basal-bolus for 32 weeks. In the stepwise arm, one insulin aspart dose was given with the largest meal; additional doses before the next largest meals were added at weeks 11 and 22 only if HbA1c remained at or above 7%.
cards.result: HbA1c change at 32 weeks was −0.98% (95% CI −1.09 to −0.87) in the stepwise group and −1.12% (−1.23 to −1.00) in the basal-bolus group; mean treatment difference 0.14% (−0.02 to 0.30), meeting the prespecified 0.4% noninferiority margin (P = 0.0876 for the difference). Fewer hypoglycaemic episodes occurred in the stepwise group (rate ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.75 — a relative rate; P < 0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events did not differ between arms; the authors also report better patient satisfaction with the stepwise approach.
cards.watchOut: The stepwise arm is a strategy, not a fixed low dose: by design, patients still above target at weeks 11 and 22 received second and third boluses, so the trial shows that deferring extra injections until they are proven necessary loses nothing — not that one injection suffices for everyone. Funded by Novo Nordisk, the maker of insulin aspart; 32 weeks is short for a lifelong regimen.

cards.headline: Synthesis: stepwise prandial cover matches basal-bolus on average control in both randomised trials, with less hypoglycaemia — the trade is fewer patients at target — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: stepwise prandial cover matches basal-bolus on average control in both randomised trials, with less hypoglycaemia — the trade is fewer patients at target — LIKELY
cards.people: Two randomised noninferiority trials in basal-insulin failure: Davidson 2011 (343 randomised after a glargine run-in) and FullSTEP 2014 (401 patients); a third comparison, Riddle 2014 (588 patients initiating and advancing insulin over one year), is cross-referenced in the balance rather than carded.
cards.result: Average HbA1c reduction: noninferior for stepwise in both trials (Davidson 95% CIs −0.39 to 0.36 for one injection and −0.30 to 0.43 for two, versus three; FullSTEP difference 0.14%, −0.02 to 0.30). Hypoglycaemia: significantly fewer episodes with stepwise in FullSTEP (rate ratio 0.58, 0.45–0.75); severe hypoglycaemia numerically doubled on three injections in Davidson (16% vs 7–8%, not significant). Target attainment favoured more injections in Davidson (46% below 7.0% on three injections versus 30% on one). The burden difference — one daily injection and its monitoring instead of three — is the intervention’s other active ingredient.
cards.watchOut: Both trials were open-label and industry-funded, and both enrolled patients already failing basal insulin — they say nothing about patients who could instead add a non-insulin agent (shelf #2653) or simplify an existing basal-bolus regimen (shelf #2652). Noninferiority margins of 0.4% mean a small true disadvantage of stepwise cannot be excluded; the Davidson target-attainment gap is its visible part.
cards.source: Synthesis of Davidson MB et al. Endocrine Practice. 2011 (PMID: 21324825) and Rodbard HW et al. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. 2014 (PMID: 24622667); Riddle MC et al. Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism. 2014 (PMID: 24118931) cross-referenced, not carded.

shelves.title: De-intensifying basal-bolus insulin: three randomised trials kept HbA1c level when mealtime insulin was swapped for a GLP-1 agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor — on a fraction of the insulin dose and with less hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes already on a basal-bolus regimen, does de-intensification — dropping the prandial doses for basal insulin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist (or fixed-ratio combination) or an SGLT2 inhibitor — maintain glycaemic control with less hypoglycaemia, weight gain, and injection burden?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · *Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Feasibility Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · *Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials have now tested deliberate de-intensification of basal-bolus insulin, and in all three glycaemic control held. In BEYOND (Giugliano 2021, PMID: 33883195), 305 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on basal-bolus (mean HbA1c 8.6%) were randomised to intensifying the basal-bolus regimen, switching to a once-daily fixed-ratio basal insulin/GLP-1 receptor agonist combination, or switching to basal insulin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor. At 6 months HbA1c had fallen equally (−0.6%, −0.6%, and −0.7%; noninferiority P < 0.001), but total insulin dose moved in opposite directions — up to 62 units/day on intensified basal-bolus versus down to 27 and 21 units/day in the switch arms — and hypoglycaemia was less frequent after switching (17.8% of patients versus 7.8% and 5.9%; P = 0.015). In the IDEAL trial (Novodvorský 2026, PMID: 41395661), 90 patients on multiple daily injections (HbA1c at most 9%, total dose at most 0.8 IU/kg, preserved fasting C-peptide) were randomised to once-daily iGlarLixi or continued injections: the HbA1c difference was −0.12% (95% CI −0.48 to 0.23), with weight 4.19 kg lower and insulin dose 28.6 IU/day lower on the simplified regimen. In a smaller Japanese trial (Ando 2021, PMID: 33650779), 40 patients well controlled on multiple daily injections had all bolus insulin replaced by canagliflozin or liraglutide: HbA1c and glucose variability were maintained for 24 weeks, insulin dose fell, quality-of-life scores rose, and there was no severe hypoglycaemia. The consistent picture: in patients with residual beta-cell function, much of the prandial insulin in a basal-bolus regimen is replaceable — control is kept while injections, dose, hypoglycaemia, and, where measured, weight all fall. The limits are equally consistent: every trial is open-label, none exceeds 6 months, the two smaller trials enrolled selected patients (well controlled, or dose-capped with measurable C-peptide), and BEYOND's switch arms lost 9–12 patients to dropout against none on continued basal-bolus — de-intensification suits many, not all. A 4-year follow-up of the BEYOND cohort has been reported (PMID: 40877579); its PubMed record carries no abstract data, so no figures are taken from it here. The mirror-image question — whether prandial insulin should be added stepwise in the first place — is shelf #2651; adding a GLP-1 agonist instead of prandial insulin when basal alone fails is shelf #2653.

cards.headline: BEYOND 2021: switching basal-bolus patients to a fixed-ratio basal/GLP-1 combination or basal insulin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor matched intensified basal-bolus on HbA1c (−0.6 to −0.7%) — at 21–27 units of insulin a day instead of 62, with hypoglycaemia in 6–8% versus 18% of patients
cards.summary: BEYOND 2021: switching basal-bolus patients to a fixed-ratio basal/GLP-1 combination or basal insulin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor matched intensified basal-bolus on HbA1c (−0.6 to −0.7%) — at 21–27 units of insulin a day instead of 62, with hypoglycaemia in 6–8% versus 18% of patients
cards.people: 305 participants with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycaemic control on a full basal-bolus insulin regimen (mean HbA1c 8.6%), randomised 1:1:1 to intensification of the basal-bolus regimen (n = 101), a fixed ratio of basal insulin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist (n = 102), or basal insulin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor (n = 102), followed for 6 months. Pragmatic and open-label; the primary outcome was change in HbA1c.
cards.result: HbA1c change at 6 months was −0.6 ± 0.8% on intensified basal-bolus, −0.6 ± 0.8% on the fixed combination, and −0.7 ± 0.9% on the SGLT2 combination (noninferiority P < 0.001 versus basal-bolus); the proportions reaching HbA1c of 7.5% or less were similar (34%, 28%, and 27%; P = 0.489). Total insulin dose increased to 62 units/day on basal-bolus and decreased to 27 units/day (fixed combination) and 21 units/day (SGLT2 combination) (P < 0.01). The proportion of patients with hypoglycaemia was 17.8% versus 7.8% and 5.9% (P = 0.015). Dropouts numbered 12 in the fixed-combination arm and 9 in the SGLT2 arm, against none on basal-bolus.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own framing is 'feasibility': open-label, single-country, six months. The asymmetric dropout — 21 patients left the switch arms and none left basal-bolus — cuts against switching in a way a noninferiority headline can hide: some patients cannot or will not simplify. Durability beyond six months is unproven in the randomised data; a 4-year follow-up report exists but its PubMed record carries no abstract figures (PMID: 40877579).
cards.source: Giugliano D et al. Feasibility of simplification from a basal-bolus insulin regimen to a fixed-ratio formulation of basal insulin plus a GLP-1RA or to basal insulin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor: BEYOND, a randomized, pragmatic trial. Diabetes Care. 2021. PMID: 33883195. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04196231. cards.headline: IDEAL 2026: multiple daily injections swapped for once-daily iGlarLixi — HbA1c difference −0.12% (95% CI −0.48 to 0.23), with 4.19 kg less weight and 28.6 fewer units of insulin a day
cards.summary: IDEAL 2026: multiple daily injections swapped for once-daily iGlarLixi — HbA1c difference −0.12% (95% CI −0.48 to 0.23), with 4.19 kg less weight and 28.6 fewer units of insulin a day
cards.people: 90 people with type 2 diabetes at five centres (mean age 66.2 years, HbA1c 7.9%, diabetes duration 17.5 years, BMI 33.6 kg/m²) on multiple daily injections, eligible only with HbA1c of 9% or less, total daily insulin of 0.8 IU/kg or less, and fasting C-peptide above the lower limit of normal; randomised 1:1 to once-daily iGlarLixi (fixed-ratio glargine/lixisenatide) or continuation of the multiple-injection regimen for 24 weeks.
cards.result: The between-group difference in HbA1c change at 24 weeks was −0.12% (95% CI −0.48 to 0.23), indicating comparable glycaemic control. Significant differences favouring iGlarLixi: body weight −4.19 kg (−5.95 to −2.43), BMI −1.49 kg/m² (−2.11 to −0.86), total daily insulin dose −28.57 IU (−34.89 to −22.24), time spent in level 2 hyperglycaemia −4.9 percentage points (−9.4 to −0.34), and glycaemia risk index −13.6 (−25.1 to −2.1).
cards.watchOut: Eligibility did the selecting: a dose cap (0.8 IU/kg or less), an HbA1c ceiling (9%), and required residual C-peptide define exactly the patients in whom prandial insulin is most likely redundant — the trial cannot speak for high-dose or C-peptide-negative patients. Small (90 patients), open-label, 24 weeks. (The abstract’s denominators are internally inconsistent — 90 randomised, one percentage computed on 91 — so no figure depending on that denominator is used here.)
cards.source: Novodvorský P et al. Insulin therapy DE-intensificAtion with iGlarLixi: a phase 4, open-label, parallel-group randomised controlled trial. Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism. 2026. PMID: 41395661. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ando 2021: in 40 patients well controlled on multiple daily injections, replacing all bolus insulin with canagliflozin or liraglutide held HbA1c and glucose variability for 24 weeks, cut insulin dose, and improved quality of life
cards.summary: Ando 2021: in 40 patients well controlled on multiple daily injections, replacing all bolus insulin with canagliflozin or liraglutide held HbA1c and glucose variability for 24 weeks, cut insulin dose, and improved quality of life
cards.people: 40 patients with type 2 diabetes controlled to HbA1c below 7.5% on multiple daily insulin injections; all bolus insulin was randomly switched to canagliflozin 100 mg/day or liraglutide 0.3–0.9 mg/day for 24 weeks, with basal insulin continued and adjusted by a predefined algorithm. Endpoints included HbA1c change, continuous-glucose-monitoring variability, body mass index, insulin dose, quality of life, and safety.
cards.result: The change in HbA1c was comparable between the two switch treatments; both maintained HbA1c at baseline levels with stable glucose variability and no severe hypoglycaemia over 24 weeks. Both decreased total insulin dose and significantly increased quality-of-life scores, and the change in quality of life was significantly associated with injection frequency. (The abstract reports these outcomes without arm-level point values for HbA1c.)
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, all already well controlled — this is de-intensification in success, not rescue in failure — and the comparison is between two switch drugs, not against staying on basal-bolus, so the trial shows a switch can hold control rather than that it beats continuation. Liraglutide doses (0.3–0.9 mg/day) are the Japanese range, below the 1.8 mg used elsewhere.
cards.source: Ando Y et al. Simplification of complex insulin regimens using canagliflozin or liraglutide in patients with well-controlled type 2 diabetes: a 24-week randomized controlled trial. Journal of Diabetes Investigation. 2021. PMID: 33650779. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: control held in all three randomised de-intensification trials while insulin dose, injections, and hypoglycaemia fell — POSSIBLE, on small, short, open-label evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: control held in all three randomised de-intensification trials while insulin dose, injections, and hypoglycaemia fell — POSSIBLE, on small, short, open-label evidence
cards.people: Three randomised trials, 435 patients in total: BEYOND (n = 305, inadequately controlled on basal-bolus), IDEAL (n = 90, dose-capped with preserved C-peptide), and Ando (n = 40, well controlled on multiple daily injections).
cards.result: HbA1c after switching: noninferior in BEYOND (−0.6 to −0.7% in all three arms); between-group difference −0.12% (−0.48 to 0.23) in IDEAL; maintained at baseline in Ando. Insulin dose: down to 21–27 units/day in the switch arms versus 62 on intensified basal-bolus (BEYOND); −28.6 IU/day versus continued injections (IDEAL). Hypoglycaemia: 5.9–7.8% of switch patients versus 17.8% on basal-bolus (BEYOND); no severe hypoglycaemia in Ando. Weight: −4.19 kg on iGlarLixi versus continued injections (IDEAL). Burden: one daily injection replaces three or four in the fixed-ratio strategies, and quality of life tracked injection frequency (Ando).
cards.watchOut: All three trials are open-label and six months or shorter, and none enrolled the high-dose, long-duration, low-C-peptide patients in whom basal-bolus is hardest to unwind; BEYOND’s switch arms also carried all the dropouts. Observational simplification series in older and frailer patients point the same way but are not carded here — the randomised floor under this shelf is these 435 patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Giugliano D et al. Diabetes Care. 2021 (PMID: 33883195); Novodvorský P et al. Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism. 2026 (PMID: 41395661); Ando Y et al. Journal of Diabetes Investigation. 2021 (PMID: 33650779).

shelves.title: Adding a GLP-1 agonist versus adding mealtime insulin to basal insulin: equal HbA1c in the head-to-head trial and across 13 pooled trials — with about half the hypoglycaemia, weight loss instead of gain, and 30 fewer units of insulin a day
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on basal insulin, does adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist control glucose as well as adding prandial insulin — and how do hypoglycaemia, weight, and insulin dose compare?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/*drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Endpoint Determination · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor/metabolism · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemia/prevention & control · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Insulin Glargine/*administration & dosage · Male · Meals · Metformin/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Overweight/complications · Peptides/*administration & dosage · Postprandial Period · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Glucagon-Like Peptide-2 Receptor
shelves.balance: The direct head-to-head exists. In GetGoal Duo-2 (Rosenstock 2016, PMID: 27222510), patients whose HbA1c remained 7–9% after a 12-week glargine optimisation run-in were randomised to add lixisenatide once daily, insulin glulisine once daily, or glulisine three times daily: HbA1c ended at 7.2%, 7.2%, and 7.0% respectively — lixisenatide met its noninferiority endpoints against both prandial strategies — while symptomatic hypoglycaemia and body weight were lower with lixisenatide, at the price of more gastrointestinal events. A propensity-matched pooling of five randomised trials (Raccah 2014, PMID: 24246441) found basal insulin plus lixisenatide about twice as likely as basal insulin plus once-daily rapid-acting insulin to reach HbA1c below 7% without symptomatic hypoglycaemia (odds ratio 1.90, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.55 — a relative, odds-based measure) and without weight gain (OR 2.58, 1.23 to 5.40). Across the class, a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (Castellana 2019, PMID: 30270567) found GLP-1 agonist/insulin combinations and basal-plus/basal-bolus statistically indistinguishable on HbA1c (difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.02), with 3.72 kg greater weight loss, roughly half the risk of hypoglycaemic events (relative risk 0.46, 0.38 to 0.55), and 30.3 IU/day less insulin. So for the average patient failing basal insulin, the prandial effect does not require prandial insulin: a GLP-1 agonist buys the same average control with less hypoglycaemia, no mealtime injections, and weight moving the other way. The caveats: the direct trial evidence rests largely on one short-acting agent (lixisenatide) over 26 weeks; gastrointestinal intolerance is the GLP-1 class's own burden; and patients with very high HbA1c, catabolic symptoms, or little residual beta-cell function were not these trials' population — prandial insulin keeps that territory. Fixed-ratio combinations as an initiation strategy are shelf #2056; switching an established basal-bolus regimen down to basal insulin plus a GLP-1 agonist is shelf #2652; adding prandial insulin stepwise is shelf #2651.

cards.headline: GetGoal Duo-2 2016: lixisenatide added to glargine matched glulisine once daily and three times daily on HbA1c (final values 7.2%, 7.2%, 7.0%) — with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia and lower body weight, and more gastrointestinal events
cards.summary: GetGoal Duo-2 2016: lixisenatide added to glargine matched glulisine once daily and three times daily on HbA1c (final values 7.2%, 7.2%, 7.0%) — with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia and lower body weight, and more gastrointestinal events
cards.type: Randomised open-label three-arm trial (GetGoal Duo-2; Rosenstock 2016)
cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on basal insulin glargine with or without oral agents whose HbA1c remained between 7% and 9% after a 12-week glargine optimisation run-in (oral agents other than metformin were stopped at the start of optimisation); the abstract reports n = 298 with baseline characteristics similar between arms (mean diabetes duration 12.2 years, basal insulin duration 3.2 years, BMI 32.2 kg/m²). Randomised to lixisenatide once daily, insulin glulisine once daily, or glulisine three times daily for 26 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c improved from 8.5% to 7.9% during the glargine optimisation run-in and then to 7.2% with lixisenatide, 7.2% with glulisine once daily, and 7.0% with glulisine three times daily at 26 weeks; all coprimary endpoints were met — noninferiority of lixisenatide versus glulisine once daily and versus glulisine three times daily on HbA1c (noninferiority margin 0.4%), with the body-weight superiority comparison against thrice-daily glulisine also addressed. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia and body weight were lower in lixisenatide than in glulisine patients; gastrointestinal events occurred more often with lixisenatide. (The abstract reports directions, not point values, for hypoglycaemia and weight.)
cards.watchOut: One agent carries the direct class claim: lixisenatide is short-acting and prandial-focused, and the result should not be read across uncritically to every GLP-1 agonist — nor to patients unlike the run-in survivors, whose HbA1c was capped at 9% after optimisation. Twenty-six weeks, open-label, and funded by the maker of both glargine and lixisenatide.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Prandial options to advance basal insulin glargine therapy: testing lixisenatide plus basal insulin versus insulin glulisine either as basal-plus or basal-bolus in type 2 diabetes: the GetGoal Duo-2 trial. Diabetes Care. 2016. PMID: 27222510. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01768559. cards.headline: Raccah 2014: across five trials, basal insulin plus lixisenatide was about twice as likely as basal insulin plus once-daily rapid-acting insulin to reach HbA1c below 7% without symptomatic hypoglycaemia (OR 1.90) and without weight gain (OR 2.58)
cards.summary: Raccah 2014: across five trials, basal insulin plus lixisenatide was about twice as likely as basal insulin plus once-daily rapid-acting insulin to reach HbA1c below 7% without symptomatic hypoglycaemia (OR 1.90) and without weight gain (OR 2.58)
cards.type: Propensity-matched pooled analysis of five RCTs (Raccah 2014)
cards.people: Patient-level data from five randomised controlled trials of basal insulin plus insulin glulisine (three trials) or basal insulin plus lixisenatide (two trials) in type 2 diabetes insufficiently controlled on basal insulin; patients in the lixisenatide cohort were matched to patients in the rapid-acting-insulin cohort by propensity score. A matched secondary analysis of trial data — not itself a randomised head-to-head.
cards.result: In the matched population, basal insulin plus lixisenatide versus basal insulin plus once-daily rapid-acting insulin: odds ratio 1.90 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.55; P = 0.0455) for the composite of HbA1c below 7% with no symptomatic hypoglycaemia; OR 1.97 (1.06 to 3.66; P = 0.0311) for HbA1c below 7% with no severe hypoglycaemia; and OR 2.58 (1.23 to 5.40; P = 0.0119) for HbA1c below 7% with no weight gain and no symptomatic hypoglycaemia. These odds ratios are relative measures; the abstract does not report the underlying absolute attainment rates.
cards.watchOut: Matching is not randomisation: patients were never assigned between the two strategies within a single trial, so residual confounding survives the propensity score, and two of the three confidence intervals only just clear 1.0. Read this card as corroboration of GetGoal Duo-2's randomised result, not as independent proof.
cards.source: Raccah D et al. Once-daily prandial lixisenatide versus once-daily rapid-acting insulin in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus insufficiently controlled with basal insulin: analysis of data from five randomized, controlled trials. Journal of Diabetes and its Complications. 2014. PMID: 24246441. Registry ID: none in the record (pooled analysis of five trials). cards.headline: Castellana 2019: across 13 randomised trials, GLP-1 agonist plus insulin versus basal-plus/basal-bolus — HbA1c difference −0.06%, weight −3.72 kg, hypoglycaemia relative risk 0.46, insulin dose −30.3 IU/day
cards.summary: Castellana 2019: across 13 randomised trials, GLP-1 agonist plus insulin versus basal-plus/basal-bolus — HbA1c difference −0.06%, weight −3.72 kg, hypoglycaemia relative risk 0.46, insulin dose −30.3 IU/day
cards.people: 13 randomised controlled trials (from 1,885 records screened to July 2018) comparing GLP-1 receptor agonist/insulin combinations with basal-plus or basal-bolus insulin regimens in type 2 diabetes not at target on basal insulin; outcomes were HbA1c, body weight, daily insulin dose, hypoglycaemic events, and discontinuation due to lack of efficacy. The review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42017079547).
cards.result: HbA1c reduction was similar between strategies (difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.14 to 0.02; P = 0.13; I² = 52%). Body weight favoured the GLP-1 combinations by −3.72 kg (−4.49 to −2.95; P < 0.001; I² = 89%). Hypoglycaemic events were fewer with GLP-1 combinations (relative risk 0.46, 0.38 to 0.55 — a relative measure; P < 0.001; I² = 99%). Daily insulin dose was 30.3 IU/day lower with GLP-1 combinations (−41.2 to −19.3; P < 0.001; I² = 94%). There was no difference in discontinuation due to lack of efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The pooled hypoglycaemia, weight, and dose advantages carry I² values of 89–99% — the averages conceal wide variation between trials and agents — and the search closed in July 2018, before later agents and trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: same HbA1c, about half the hypoglycaemia, weight down instead of up, 30 fewer units of insulin a day — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: same HbA1c, about half the hypoglycaemia, weight down instead of up, 30 fewer units of insulin a day — LIKELY
cards.people: One direct three-arm randomised trial (GetGoal Duo-2; n = 298 reported per arm), one propensity-matched pooling of five randomised trials, and one meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials — all in basal-insulin failure.
cards.result: HbA1c: final values 7.2% (lixisenatide) versus 7.2% (glulisine once daily) and 7.0% (glulisine three times daily) in the direct trial; pooled difference −0.06% (−0.14 to 0.02) across 13 trials. Hypoglycaemia: pooled relative risk 0.46 (0.38–0.55); less symptomatic hypoglycaemia in the direct trial. Weight: −3.72 kg pooled advantage; composite of target without weight gain or hypoglycaemia OR 2.58 in the matched analysis. Insulin dose: −30.3 IU/day pooled. Counterweight: more gastrointestinal events with the GLP-1 strategy in the direct trial.
cards.watchOut: Lixisenatide dominates the direct evidence and is no longer marketed in some countries; longer-acting GLP-1 agonists are usually substituted on this class evidence — an extrapolation the trials themselves do not test head-to-head against prandial insulin. Nothing here addresses the patient with HbA1c far above 9%, osmotic symptoms, or insulin deficiency: prandial insulin keeps that territory.

shelves.title: Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia in hospital: the randomised record is scarce and mostly negative — the one strategy that helped was adding NPH insulin to a basal-bolus regimen
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia, does scheduled insulin (basal or basal-bolus regimens adapted to the steroid dose) control glucose better than correction-only or oral-agent strategies, and at what hypoglycaemia cost?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects · Hyperglycemia*/chemically induced · Hyperglycemia*/therapy · Dexamethasone/adverse effects · Steroids/adverse effects · COVID-19 Drug Treatment*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest summary of this shelf is how little randomised evidence exists for a problem every hospital ward meets daily. The systematic review (Brooks D et al., PMID: 35940469) screened 1,230 references on non-COVID glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia and included 33 articles, plus 7 studies of dexamethasone-associated hyperglycaemia in COVID-19, and found the randomised trials scarce, inconsistent in their definitions of hyperglycaemia, varied in strategy and endpoint, and generally not effective — the single exception being neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin added to basal-bolus regimens. That means the common contest — scheduled basal or basal-bolus insulin versus correction-only sliding scale or oral agents — has never been settled by an adequate trial, and the review establishes no pooled hypoglycaemia price for any strategy. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): scheduled insulin for steroid-induced hyperglycaemia rests on physiology and practice habit rather than trial proof; the one randomised signal favours adding NPH insulin to a basal-bolus regimen, and the hypoglycaemia cost of any approach remains unquantified in the trial record.

cards.headline: Brooks 2022 (systematic review): 33 non-COVID articles and 7 COVID-19 dexamethasone studies — randomised trials scarce and generally ineffective, except NPH insulin added to basal-bolus regimens
cards.summary: Brooks 2022 (systematic review): 33 non-COVID articles and 7 COVID-19 dexamethasone studies — randomised trials scarce and generally ineffective, except NPH insulin added to basal-bolus regimens
cards.people: A systematic review of glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia management searching PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, Embase and Web of Science for 2011 to January 2022. The non-COVID search identified 1,230 references, of which 33 articles were included; the COVID-19 dexamethasone search identified 63 references, of which 7 were included. Randomised controlled trials were included for the management review; COVID-19 studies were included regardless of quality.
cards.result: The reviewers found that randomised trials of management strategies were scarce, did not use standard definitions for hyperglycaemia, evaluated a variety of treatment strategies with varying primary endpoints, and were generally not found to be effective — except for neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin added to basal-bolus regimens. No pooled glucose-control or hypoglycaemia estimate for scheduled basal or basal-bolus insulin versus correction-only or oral-agent strategies is reported. The authors conclude that few randomised trials are available evaluating glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycaemia management and that further studies are needed to support clinical guidelines, especially given the widespread use of dexamethasone during the COVID-19 pandemic.
cards.watchOut: This is a descriptive systematic review, not a meta-analysis: heterogeneity of definitions, strategies and endpoints prevented pooling, so the shelf cannot quote an effect size or a hypoglycaemia rate for any regimen. 'Generally not effective' describes a small, inconsistent trial set — absence of proof rather than proof that scheduled insulin fails — and the one positive signal (added NPH) comes from within that same thin record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a ubiquitous inpatient problem with almost no randomised footing — one positive signal (added NPH), no measured hypoglycaemia price
cards.summary: Synthesis: a ubiquitous inpatient problem with almost no randomised footing — one positive signal (added NPH), no measured hypoglycaemia price
cards.people: The full randomised record as assembled by Brooks 2022: 33 included non-COVID articles and 7 COVID-19 dexamethasone studies drawn from 1,230 and 63 screened references respectively.
cards.result: Glucose control: no strategy class — basal, basal-bolus, correction-only or oral — carries a pooled randomised benefit; the exception is NPH insulin added to basal-bolus regimens. Hypoglycaemia: not quantifiably reported for any strategy in the review. Definitions and endpoints: non-standard across trials, which is itself part of why the question remains open. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as evidence against treating steroid hyperglycaemia — untreated inpatient hyperglycaemia has its own observational harms literature, which is a different claim. What the trials have not done is rank the insulin strategies against each other or price their hypoglycaemia. A steroid-dose-adapted randomised trial with standard glucose and hypoglycaemia definitions is the missing study.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brooks D et al. Endocrine Practice. 2022 (PMID: 35940469).

shelves.title: Insulin for early cystic fibrosis diabetes: weight loss reversed in the one purpose-built trial, lungs unchanged — and the Cochrane pool still calls it unproven
shelves.question: In cystic fibrosis-related diabetes without fasting hyperglycaemia, does insulin therapy improve body mass index and lung function compared with an oral hypoglycaemic agent or no therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Mass Index* · Cystic Fibrosis/complications · Diabetes Mellitus/drug therapy · Diabetes Mellitus/etiology · Female · Humans · Hyperglycemia/complications · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin/adverse effects · Insulin/therapeutic use · Male
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the one multicentre randomised trial built for this question (Moran A et al., PMID: 19592632; 100 adults, 81 completing) found that a year of premeal insulin reversed the pre-treatment slide in body mass index in cystic fibrosis-related diabetes without fasting hyperglycaemia — from losing 0.30 BMI units in the year before therapy to gaining 0.39 units on therapy (P = 0.02) — while repaglinide's early gain (0.53 units, P = 0.01) was not sustained to 12 months and placebo changed nothing. No group differed in lung-function decline or hospitalisations. The Cochrane review (Onady GM et al., PMID: 33075159) is more guarded: across its included comparisons it found no conclusive between-group differences in blood glucose, lung function or nutritional status, on low to very low quality evidence, and no mortality data anywhere. So insulin's weight benefit rests on one trial's within-patient reversal pattern rather than a robust pooled between-group effect, and a lung benefit is unproven. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): insulin probably helps weight in CFRD without fasting hyperglycaemia; whether it protects the lungs is unknown.

cards.headline: Moran 2009 (CFRDT Trial): premeal insulin reversed chronic BMI decline in CFRD without fasting hyperglycaemia (−0.30 units/year before therapy to +0.39 on therapy, P = 0.02); repaglinide's gain faded by 12 months; lung function unchanged in every arm
cards.summary: Moran 2009 (CFRDT Trial): premeal insulin reversed chronic BMI decline in CFRD without fasting hyperglycaemia (−0.30 units/year before therapy to +0.39 on therapy, P = 0.02); repaglinide's gain faded by 12 months; lung function unchanged in every arm
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 3 arms (Moran 2009, CFRDT Trial)
cards.people: A three-arm multicentre randomised trial comparing 1 year of premeal insulin aspart, repaglinide, or oral placebo in 100 adults with cystic fibrosis and abnormal glucose tolerance; 81 completed the study, including 61 with cystic fibrosis-related diabetes without fasting hyperglycaemia (CFRD FH−) and 20 with severely impaired glucose tolerance. Body mass index had declined in all groups during the year before therapy.
cards.result: Among patients with CFRD FH−, insulin-treated patients lost 0.30 ± 0.21 BMI units in the year before therapy; after 1 year of insulin this reversed to a gain of 0.39 BMI units (P = 0.02). Placebo-treated patients showed no significant change in the rate of BMI decline (P = 0.45). Repaglinide-treated patients gained 0.53 ± 0.19 BMI units initially (P = 0.01) but the effect was not sustained — after 6 months they lost weight, so by 12 months the rate of BMI change did not differ from the pre-therapy year (P = 0.33). In the impaired-glucose-tolerance subgroup, neither insulin nor repaglinide affected the rate of BMI decline. No significant differences were seen in the rate of lung function decline or the number of hospitalisations in any group. The authors conclude insulin therapy safely reversed chronic weight loss in CFRD FH−.
cards.watchOut: The headline analysis compares each group's on-treatment BMI trajectory with its own pre-treatment year rather than resting on a large between-group difference at 12 months, and 19 of 100 enrolled patients did not complete the study. The trial was powered for weight, not lungs: the null lung-function and hospitalisation results are 'not shown', in a population where decline is slow, rather than proof of no pulmonary effect.

cards.headline: Onady 2020 (Cochrane): across four trials, no conclusive advantage for insulin or repaglinide on glucose, lung function or nutrition — evidence low to very low quality, mortality never reported
cards.summary: Onady 2020 (Cochrane): across four trials, no conclusive advantage for insulin or repaglinide on glucose, lung function or nutrition — evidence low to very low quality, mortality never reported
cards.type: Systematic review, 4 RCTs with results (Onady 2020, Cochrane)
cards.people: A Cochrane review of randomised trials of pharmacological diabetes therapy in cystic fibrosis-related diabetes. Searches identified 29 trials (45 references); four trials provided results, including a 7-adult cross-over trial, the long-term multicentre trials of insulin versus repaglinide versus placebo (61 and 67 adults), and a 12-week cross-over of insulin glargine versus NPH insulin (20 adults).
cards.result: For insulin versus placebo (39 participants in the extractable trial), there was no difference in blood glucose levels (very low-quality evidence), lung function (low-quality) or nutritional status (low-quality), nor in hypoglycaemic episodes, secondary infections or quality of life; the 7-participant trial mirrored this narratively. Repaglinide versus placebo (38 participants) likewise showed no differences on any primary or secondary outcome. Across three trials comparing insulin with repaglinide (119 participants), one trial (n = 67) found no difference in blood glucose at 12 or 24 months (high-quality evidence for that outcome), two trials (112 participants) found no difference in lung function or nutritional status (moderate-quality), and one small trial (7 participants) reported a benefit of insulin over repaglinide. Mortality was not reported by any trial. The reviewers conclude there is no conclusive evidence that any agent has a distinct advantage over another in CFRD.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane between-group extractions and Moran's trajectory analysis answer slightly different statistical questions, which is why this shelf can honestly carry both a positive trial and an inconclusive review. Downgrading was driven by allocation-concealment and selective-reporting concerns, small samples and low event rates; doses of insulin and repaglinide may also not have been comparable across trials.
cards.source: Onady GM et al. Drug treatments for managing cystic fibrosis-related diabetes. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 33075159. Registry ID: NCT00662714. cards.headline: Synthesis: insulin reverses weight loss in the one purpose-built trial; the review-level verdict is 'unproven', and lungs are untouched in both
cards.summary: Synthesis: insulin reverses weight loss in the one purpose-built trial; the review-level verdict is 'unproven', and lungs are untouched in both
cards.people: One multicentre three-arm RCT (100 enrolled, 81 completing; Moran 2009) plus a Cochrane review of four result-bearing trials (Onady 2020) covering insulin, repaglinide, placebo and basal-insulin comparisons in CFRD.
cards.result: Weight/BMI: insulin reversed a −0.30 unit/year decline to a +0.39 unit gain (P = 0.02) in Moran; Cochrane between-group nutritional-status comparisons were null on low-quality evidence. Repaglinide: early BMI gain (+0.53, P = 0.01) not sustained at 12 months (P = 0.33). Lung function and hospitalisations: no difference in any arm of any trial. Hypoglycaemia: no between-group difference in the review. Mortality: never reported. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: CFRD without fasting hyperglycaemia carries no microvascular or macrovascular complication risk in the trial's framing, so the case for treatment stands or falls on weight and lungs — and only weight moved, in one trial. Treatment burden in cystic fibrosis is already heavy; that is why the Cochrane authors keep oral therapy on the table despite the insulin signal. Tier C is set because the positive finding is a single trial's trajectory analysis against a null pooled between-group record.

shelves.title: Botox into the pylorus for gastroparesis: two controlled trials, no win over saline — the placebo injection did just as well
shelves.question: In diabetic gastroparesis with delayed gastric emptying, does intrapyloric botulinum toxin injection improve gastric emptying and symptoms compared with placebo injection?
shelves.mesh: Botulinum Toxins, Type A/pharmacology · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastric Emptying/drug effects · Gastroparesis/drug therapy · Humans · Injections · Male · Middle Aged · Neuromuscular Agents/pharmacology · Neuromuscular Agents/therapeutic use · Pylorus
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the open-label literature promised a great deal for intrapyloric botulinum toxin, and the two controlled trials delivered none of it. In the placebo-controlled trial (Friedenberg FK et al., PMID: 18070232; 32 patients with idiopathic or diabetic gastroparesis), the response rate at one month was actually lower with botulinum toxin than with saline placebo — 37.5% versus 56.3% achieving the study's improvement definition — and although gastric emptying improved within the toxin group, it was not superior to placebo. The double-blind cross-over trial (Arts J et al., PMID: 17944739; 23 patients, 19 of them idiopathic) found the same pattern: symptoms and emptying improved after the first injection whichever fluid it was, with no significant difference between toxin and saline on solid or liquid emptying half-times, meal-related symptoms or the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): intrapyloric botulinum toxin has not beaten placebo on symptoms or emptying in controlled trials; the apparent benefits in uncontrolled series are what a strong placebo and procedure effect looks like. Diabetic-specific controlled data are thinner still — most cross-over participants were idiopathic.

cards.headline: Friedenberg 2008: 32 patients — response at 1 month was 37.5% with botulinum toxin versus 56.3% with placebo; emptying improved but not beyond placebo
cards.summary: Friedenberg 2008: 32 patients — response at 1 month was 37.5% with botulinum toxin versus 56.3% with placebo; emptying improved but not beyond placebo
cards.people: A single-institution, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 32 patients with delayed gastric emptying (idiopathic and diabetic gastroparesis) and a Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index score of at least 27, randomised to intrapyloric botulinum toxin A 200 units or saline placebo injection, with symptom reassessment and repeat gastric emptying scan at 1 month.
cards.result: At 1-month follow-up, 37.5% of patients randomised to botulinum toxin and 56.3% randomised to placebo achieved improvement as defined by the study. There were no identifiable clinical predictors of response. The botulinum toxin group demonstrated improvement in gastric emptying; however, this was not superior to placebo. No serious adverse events were attributable to botulinum toxin. The authors conclude they are unable to recommend botulinum toxin therapy for widespread use in the treatment of delayed gastric emptying until more data are available.
cards.watchOut: Small (16 per arm) and short (1 month), with a mixed idiopathic-and-diabetic population, so the diabetic subgroup cannot be read separately from this record. The numerically higher placebo response is a reminder that endoscopy, sedation and expectation move gastroparesis symptoms a long way — the very effect uncontrolled series had credited to the toxin.
cards.source: Friedenberg FK et al. Botulinum toxin A for the treatment of delayed gastric emptying. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2008. PMID: 18070232. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arts 2007 (cross-over): 23 patients — symptoms and emptying improved after the first injection regardless of content; toxin not superior to saline on any measure
cards.summary: Arts 2007 (cross-over): 23 patients — symptoms and emptying improved after the first injection regardless of content; toxin not superior to saline on any measure
cards.people: A randomised, double-blind, controlled cross-over study in 23 gastroparesis patients (5 men, mean age 45 ± 3 years, 19 idiopathic) who underwent two upper endoscopies 4 weeks apart, receiving saline or botulinum toxin (4 × 25 units) in randomised order, with solid and liquid gastric emptying breath tests, meal-related symptom scores and the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index before the study and 4 weeks after each treatment.
cards.result: Twelve patients received botulinum toxin first and 11 saline first. Significant improvement in emptying and in the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index was seen after the initial injection of saline or botulinum toxin; no further improvement occurred after the second injection. Pooled data showed no significant difference in improvements of solid emptying half-time (3.4 ± 7.4 versus 16.3 ± 8.3, not significant), liquid half-time (8.2 ± 13.7 versus 22.5 ± 7.7, not significant), meal-related symptom scores, or Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index (6.1 ± 1.5 versus 3.8 ± 1.5, not significant). The authors conclude botulinum toxin is not superior to placebo in improving symptoms or the rate of gastric emptying.
cards.watchOut: Predominantly idiopathic gastroparesis (19 of 23), so its directness for diabetic gastroparesis is limited, and a 100-unit total dose is half the Friedenberg dose — dose inadequacy is a possible, if unproven, explanation for the null. Cross-over designs in a fluctuating symptom condition also invite period effects, which the 'first injection helps, second does not' pattern displays.
cards.source: Arts J et al. Clinical trial: a randomized-controlled crossover study of intrapyloric injection of botulinum toxin in gastroparesis. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2007. cards.headline: Synthesis: two controlled trials, zero wins over placebo — the uncontrolled enthusiasm was a procedure effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: two controlled trials, zero wins over placebo — the uncontrolled enthusiasm was a procedure effect
cards.people: The controlled record: one parallel placebo-controlled trial (32 patients, mixed idiopathic/diabetic) and one double-blind cross-over trial (23 patients, mostly idiopathic) of intrapyloric botulinum toxin in gastroparesis.
cards.result: Symptoms: response 37.5% (toxin) versus 56.3% (placebo) in Friedenberg; no significant Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index difference in Arts. Gastric emptying: improved within groups in both trials, superior to placebo in neither. Safety: no serious adverse events attributable to toxin in Friedenberg. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — of no demonstrated benefit over placebo.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small and short, and neither isolates a purely diabetic population at the higher 200-unit dose with longer follow-up — so the correct claim is 'not shown to work', not 'proven never to work in anyone'. But the burden of proof sits with the intervention: after two null controlled trials, routine intrapyloric injection for diabetic gastroparesis is a procedure in search of its first positive trial. Tier C is set because the total controlled sample is 55 patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Friedenberg FK et al. The American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2008 (PMID: 18070232); Arts J et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2007 (PMID: 17944739).

shelves.title: Setmelanotide for hypothalamic obesity: 89% lost at least 5% of BMI in 16 open-label weeks — a dramatic signal awaiting a randomised trial
shelves.question: In acquired hypothalamic obesity, does setmelanotide reduce body mass index and hunger compared with baseline in an open-label trial, ahead of any randomised outcomes data?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Adult · Adolescent · Obesity*/drug therapy · Young Adult · Hypothalamic Diseases*/drug therapy · Child · alpha-MSH*/analogs & derivatives · alpha-MSH*/therapeutic use · alpha-MSH*/administration & dosage · Receptor, Melanocortin, Type 4/agonists · Treatment Outcome · Body Mass Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the effect size in this small open-label trial is far beyond what placebo or natural history produces in hypothalamic obesity, but the design still caps the stamp. In the phase 2 trial (Roth CL et al., PMID: 38697184), 16 of 18 patients (89%) met the primary endpoint of at least a 5% body mass index reduction at 16 weeks, against a prespecified historic control rate of under 5% (p<0.0001); mean BMI fell 15% (SD 10), and patients aged 12 or older reported a mean 45% reduction in hunger score. Twelve of 14 patients who rolled into the long-term extension and completed at least 12 months had a mean BMI change of −26% (SD 12) from index-trial baseline. The price was tolerability: nausea in 61%, vomiting in 33%, skin hyperpigmentation in 33% and diarrhoea in 22%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): setmelanotide produces large, durable BMI reductions in acquired hypothalamic obesity in open-label treatment; a randomised trial is still owed before the stamp can rise, and nausea and pigmentation are part of the deal.

cards.headline: Roth 2024 (phase 2, open-label): 16 of 18 patients (89%) cut BMI by at least 5% in 16 weeks versus a historic control rate under 5% (p<0.0001); mean BMI −15%, hunger score −45% in those 12 and older
cards.summary: Roth 2024 (phase 2, open-label): 16 of 18 patients (89%) cut BMI by at least 5% in 16 weeks versus a historic control rate under 5% (p<0.0001); mean BMI −15%, hunger score −45% in those 12 and older
cards.people: A phase 2, open-label, multicentre trial at five US centres in 18 patients aged 6 to 40 years (mean age 15.0 years, SD 5.3; 61% male; mean BMI 38.0 kg/m2, SD 6.5) with obesity after hypothalamic injury or a treated non-malignant hypothalamic tumour (surgery, chemotherapy or radiation). Setmelanotide was titrated to 3.0 mg subcutaneously once daily for 16 weeks; the primary endpoint was the proportion achieving at least a 5% BMI reduction, compared with a historic control rate of less than 5%.
cards.result: Of 19 patients screened, 18 were enrolled and dosed, and 16 (89%) completed the study and met the primary endpoint (p<0.0001). Mean BMI reduction across all patients was 15% (SD 10). A composite clinically-meaningful-change proportion of 89% (90% CI 69 to 98; p<0.0001) comprised a BMI Z-score reduction of at least 0.2 points in patients under 18 (92%, 68 to 100) and at least 5% bodyweight reduction in those 18 or older (80%, 34 to 99). Patients aged 12 or older had a mean 45% reduction in hunger score. Frequent adverse events were nausea (61%), vomiting (33%), skin hyperpigmentation (33%) and diarrhoea (22%). Of 14 patients continuing into a long-term extension study, 12 completed at least 12 months and had a mean BMI change of −26% (SD 12) from index-trial baseline.
cards.watchOut: No concurrent control group: the comparator is a prespecified historic rate, in a condition where families and clinicians enrol at peak weight, so regression to the mean and trial participation effects cannot be excluded — only discounted by the size of the effect. Eighteen patients, mostly adolescents, at five US centres; the extension figures describe the 12 of 14 who stayed on treatment, a completer picture. Industry-funded (Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, per the record).
cards.source: Roth CL et al. Setmelanotide for the treatment of acquired hypothalamic obesity: a phase 2, open-label, multicentre trial. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. 2024. PMID: 38697184. Registry ID: NCT04725240. cards.headline: Synthesis: a very large open-label effect against a near-zero historic benchmark — strong enough for POSSIBLE, not yet randomised enough for more
cards.summary: Synthesis: a very large open-label effect against a near-zero historic benchmark — strong enough for POSSIBLE, not yet randomised enough for more
cards.people: One phase 2 open-label trial (18 patients, 16 weeks) with a long-term extension subset (12 completers at 12 months or more) in acquired hypothalamic obesity.
cards.result: Primary endpoint: 89% achieved at least 5% BMI reduction versus a historic control expectation under 5% (p<0.0001). Mean BMI: −15% (SD 10) at 16 weeks; −26% (SD 12) at 12+ months in extension completers. Hunger: mean score −45% in patients 12 or older. Adverse events: nausea 61%, vomiting 33%, skin hyperpigmentation 33%, diarrhoea 22%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf descends from 18 uncontrolled patients. Hypothalamic obesity after tumour treatment is a condition with essentially no effective drug therapy and a flat natural history, which is why a historic-control design was acceptable to regulators — but weight outcomes are exactly where open-label trials flatter most, and the randomised trial, when it reports, is the document that will move this stamp. Tier C is set for the single small uncontrolled study.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roth CL et al. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. 2024 (PMID: 38697184).

shelves.title: Metreleptin in lipodystrophy: insulin sensitivity swings 32–41% within two weeks of starting or stopping — with food intake held constant
shelves.question: In generalised and partial lipodystrophy, does metreleptin improve insulin sensitivity, triglycerides and glycaemic control in open-label long-term treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Eating/drug effects · Female · Humans · Insulin Resistance* · Leptin/administration & dosage · Leptin/analogs & derivatives · Lipodystrophy/blood · Lipodystrophy/drug therapy · Lipodystrophy/pathology · Liver/metabolism · Liver/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Triglycerides/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — lipodystrophy is the human model of leptin deficiency, and the mechanistic trial on this shelf isolates the drug's effect from its appetite effect: with food intake held constant on a metabolic ward (Brown RJ et al., PMID: 29723161), stopping metreleptin for 14 days cut peripheral insulin sensitivity by 41%, while starting it raised sensitivity by 32% in 14 days; in the initiation cohort fasting glucose fell 11%, triglycerides fell 41%, hepatic insulin sensitivity rose and liver fat fell from 21.8% to 18.7%. After 6 months of open treatment, lipolysis fell 30–35%. The systematic review of genotype-stratified treatment in monogenic insulin resistance (Semple RK et al., PMID: 37794082) concurs at lower resolution: metreleptin is associated with lower triglycerides and HbA1c across generalised and partial lipodystrophy (n = 111), while rating every included study at moderate or serious risk of bias. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metreleptin genuinely improves insulin sensitivity, triglycerides and glycaemia in lipodystrophy — an open-label, small-numbers certainty, in a rare disease where randomised trials are barely feasible.

cards.headline: Brown 2018: with food intake held constant, stopping metreleptin cut insulin sensitivity 41% in 14 days and starting it raised sensitivity 32% — triglycerides −41% and liver fat 21.8% to 18.7% on initiation
cards.summary: Brown 2018: with food intake held constant, stopping metreleptin cut insulin sensitivity 41% in 14 days and starting it raised sensitivity 32% — triglycerides −41% and liver fat 21.8% to 18.7% on initiation
cards.people: Patients with generalised and partial lipodystrophy hospitalised for 19 days on a controlled diet in an inpatient metabolic ward, in a non-randomised cross-over design: a withdrawal cohort of 8 patients previously treated with metreleptin (continued 5 days, then stopped for 14 days) and an initiation cohort of 14 metreleptin-naive patients (studied off, then on treatment, and re-evaluated after 6 months of treatment on an ad libitum diet). Insulin sensitivity was measured by hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, lipolysis by isotopic tracers and liver fat by magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
cards.result: With food intake constant, peripheral insulin sensitivity decreased by 41% after stopping metreleptin for 14 days (withdrawal cohort) and increased by 32% after 14 days of metreleptin (initiation cohort). In the initiation cohort only, metreleptin decreased fasting glucose by 11% and triglycerides by 41% and increased hepatic insulin sensitivity; liver fat decreased from 21.8% to 18.7%. Changes in lipolysis were not independent of food intake in the short study, but after 6 months of treatment on an ad libitum diet lipolysis decreased by 30% (palmitate turnover) to 35% (glycerol turnover). The authors conclude metreleptin improves insulin sensitivity and decreases hepatic and circulating triglycerides independent of its effects on food intake.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two patients in total, no randomisation and no blinding — the design's strength is physiological (clamp-measured sensitivity with intake clamped by the ward diet), not statistical. Percent changes are within-patient metabolic measures, not clinical outcomes: no diabetes-complication, pancreatitis or survival endpoint is tested here, and 14 days of withdrawal cannot speak to long-term safety.
cards.source: Brown RJ et al. Metreleptin-mediated improvements in insulin sensitivity are independent of food intake in humans with lipodystrophy. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2018. PMID: 29723161. Registry ID: NCT01778556. cards.headline: Semple 2023 (systematic review): metreleptin associated with lower triglycerides and HbA1c across all lipodystrophy (n = 111) — but every included study rated moderate or serious risk of bias
cards.summary: Semple 2023 (systematic review): metreleptin associated with lower triglycerides and HbA1c across all lipodystrophy (n = 111) — but every included study rated moderate or serious risk of bias
cards.people: A systematic review of pharmacological and surgical interventions in monogenic insulin resistance (lipodystrophy and insulin-signalling disorders), searching PubMed, MEDLINE and Embase from 1987 to June 2021 and extracting individual-level data: 10 non-randomised experimental studies, 8 case series and 23 case reports met inclusion, all rated moderate or serious risk of bias.
cards.result: Metreleptin use is associated with lowering of triglycerides and HbA1c in all lipodystrophy (n = 111), partial lipodystrophy (n = 71) and generalised lipodystrophy (n = 41), and in the LMNA, PPARG, AGPAT2 and BSCL2 genetic subgroups (n = 72, 13, 21 and 21 respectively). Body mass index is lowered in partial and generalised lipodystrophy and in LMNA and BSCL2 subgroups, but not in PPARG or AGPAT2 subgroups. The reviewers rate the evidence guiding genotype-specific treatment of monogenic insulin resistance as low to very low quality, and conclude metreleptin appears to improve metabolic markers in lipodystrophy.
cards.watchOut: This review reports directions of association, not pooled effect sizes, and its underlying material is case series and reports — publication bias toward dramatic responders is built in. It corroborates the metabolic-ward study's direction; it cannot add precision to it. The record carries no MeSH terms, so none are quoted.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a coherent physiological story — leptin replacement moves clamp-measured insulin sensitivity within days, and the case literature points the same way
cards.summary: Synthesis: a coherent physiological story — leptin replacement moves clamp-measured insulin sensitivity within days, and the case literature points the same way
cards.people: One controlled-feeding cross-over study (22 patients; Brown 2018) plus a systematic review of the monogenic insulin resistance literature (111 metreleptin-treated lipodystrophy patients; Semple 2023).
cards.result: Peripheral insulin sensitivity: −41% on 14-day withdrawal, +32% on 14-day initiation, food intake held constant. Fasting glucose: −11% and triglycerides: −41% on initiation; liver fat 21.8% to 18.7%. Review level: triglycerides and HbA1c lower on metreleptin in generalised (n = 41) and partial (n = 71) lipodystrophy. Clinical endpoints (complications, pancreatitis, mortality): untested in either source. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Rare-disease evidence rules apply: the absence of randomised trials reflects a worldwide patient pool in the hundreds, not investigator laziness — but it still means effect sizes come from selected, closely monitored patients. Long-term questions (antibody formation, durability, hard outcomes) sit outside both sources. Tier C is set for the small, non-randomised evidence base.

shelves.title: Growth hormone in Prader–Willi infants: lean mass up, fat down, motor gains doubled in six months — and the 36-study pool agrees
shelves.question: In infants and young children with Prader–Willi syndrome, does growth hormone treatment improve body composition and motor development compared with no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Anthropometry · Body Composition/drug effects · Child Development/drug effects · Child, Preschool · Chromosomes · Female · Growth/drug effects · Human Growth Hormone/adverse effects · Human Growth Hormone/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Male · Motor Activity/drug effects · Phenotype · Prader-Willi Syndrome/drug therapy · Prader-Willi Syndrome/genetics · Prader-Willi Syndrome/physiopathology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the infant randomised trial (Whitman B et al., PMID: 15198290; 25 infants, mean age 15.5 months), six months of growth hormone significantly increased lean body mass (6.4 ± 2.4 kg to 8.9 ± 2.7 kg) and decreased body fat (27.6 ± 9.9% to 22.4 ± 10.3%), and age-equivalent motor scores improved by 4 months in the treated group against 2 months in controls (p < 0.01). The systematic review and meta-analysis across infancy, childhood and adolescence (Passone CGB et al., PMID: 32411831; 16 randomised and 20 non-randomised controlled trials) points the same way at larger scale: height improved by 1.67 standard deviation scores (95% CI 1.54 to 1.81), body mass index z-score fell 0.67 SD (−0.87 to −0.47) and fat mass proportion fell 6.5% (−8.46 to −4.54) versus controls, on evidence the reviewers call high quality for those outcomes; cognition data could not be aggregated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): growth hormone in Prader–Willi syndrome improves body composition and stature and, started in infancy, motor development — the open questions are cognitive benefit and very long-term outcomes, not whether the body-composition effect is real.

cards.headline: Whitman 2004: 25 infants — six months of growth hormone raised lean mass (6.4 to 8.9 kg), cut body fat (27.6% to 22.4%), and doubled motor-score gains versus controls (4 versus 2 months, p < 0.01)
cards.summary: Whitman 2004: 25 infants — six months of growth hormone raised lean mass (6.4 to 8.9 kg), cut body fat (27.6% to 22.4%), and doubled motor-score gains versus controls (4 versus 2 months, p < 0.01)
cards.people: Twenty-five infants with Prader–Willi syndrome (mean age 15.5 months) who underwent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry assessment of body composition and motor assessment with the Toddler Infant Motor Evaluation (TIME), then were randomised to growth hormone treatment (the Genotropin preparation, 1 mg/m2/day) or control, with reassessment at 6 months.
cards.result: Growth hormone treatment significantly increased lean body mass (6.4 ± 2.4 kg to 8.9 ± 2.7 kg) and decreased body fat (27.6 ± 9.9% to 22.4 ± 10.3%). Age-equivalent motor scores improved 4 months in the treated group versus 2 months in controls (p < 0.01). The authors conclude infants with Prader–Willi syndrome show significant body composition and motor development improvement following 6 months of growth hormone therapy, and note they are investigating whether this leads to long-term reductions in obesity.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five infants and six months: the trial proves short-term body-composition and motor change, not adult obesity, diabetes or lifespan outcomes, and the abstract reports within-group body-composition changes for the treated arm. Untreated Prader–Willi infants are hypotonic and developmentally delayed at baseline, so motor trajectories need the control comparison — which the trial does provide for the motor score, its most decision-relevant number.

cards.headline: Passone 2020 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 16 RCTs and 20 non-randomised trials): height +1.67 SD scores, BMI z-score −0.67, fat mass −6.5% versus controls on growth hormone
cards.summary: Passone 2020 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 16 RCTs and 20 non-randomised trials): height +1.67 SD scores, BMI z-score −0.67, fat mass −6.5% versus controls on growth hormone
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of recombinant human growth hormone in Prader–Willi syndrome across infancy, childhood and adolescence, including all genetic subtypes with or without growth hormone deficiency, drawing on MEDLINE, Embase and Cochrane Central: 16 randomised controlled trials and 20 non-randomised controlled trials (cohort and before-and-after studies).
cards.result: Compared with controls, the treated group improved in height (1.67 standard deviation scores, 95% CI 1.54 to 1.81), body mass index z-score (−0.67 SDS, −0.87 to −0.47) and fat mass proportion (−6.5%, −8.46 to −4.54). Data on cognition could not be aggregated. The reviewers conclude, on high quality evidence, that growth hormone treatment favoured improvement of stature, body composition and body mass index, modifying the disease's natural history, and may also be implicated in improved cognition and motor development at a young age.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimates mix randomised with non-randomised and before-and-after designs, and mix ages from infancy to adolescence — the infant-specific question leans on Whitman, with this review supplying breadth rather than infant precision. Cognition, the outcome families may care about most, could not be pooled at all. The record carries no MeSH terms, so none are quoted.

cards.headline: Synthesis: body composition and stature benefits are consistent from a 25-infant trial to a 36-study pool; cognition and adult outcomes remain the gaps
cards.summary: Synthesis: body composition and stature benefits are consistent from a 25-infant trial to a 36-study pool; cognition and adult outcomes remain the gaps
cards.people: One infant RCT (25 infants, 6 months; Whitman 2004) and one systematic review/meta-analysis of 36 controlled studies across childhood (Passone 2020) of growth hormone in Prader–Willi syndrome.
cards.result: Body composition: lean mass 6.4 to 8.9 kg and body fat 27.6% to 22.4% in the infant trial; fat mass −6.5% and BMI z-score −0.67 pooled. Motor development: age-equivalent gain 4 versus 2 months (p < 0.01) in infants. Height: +1.67 SD scores pooled. Cognition: not aggregable in the review. Long-term obesity and metabolic outcomes: under investigation, not yet reported in either source. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Starting growth hormone in infancy is now standard practice in many centres, which makes future placebo-controlled infant trials unlikely — the evidence will stay at this grade. Safety surveillance (sleep apnoea and sudden death reports in Prader–Willi syndrome) sits outside both carded sources and should not be read into this shelf either way. Tier C follows the miner's flag for the small infant-specific randomised base.

shelves.title: Meglitinides for type 2 diabetes: HbA1c lowering on par with metformin — paid for in weight gain and mild hypos, with zero outcomes trials
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, do meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide) improve HbA1c compared with placebo or other oral agents, and how does hypoglycaemia compare?
shelves.mesh: Benzamides/therapeutic use · Carbamates/adverse effects · Carbamates/therapeutic use · Cyclohexanes/adverse effects · Cyclohexanes/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Metformin/therapeutic use · Nateglinide · Phenylalanine/adverse effects · Phenylalanine/analogs & derivatives · Phenylalanine/therapeutic use · Piperidines/adverse effects · Piperidines/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Cochrane review (Black C et al., PMID: 17443551; 15 trials, 3,781 participants) finds meglitinides genuinely lower HbA1c: against placebo, reductions ran 0.1% to 2.1% for repaglinide and 0.2% to 0.6% for nateglinide, and in head-to-head data repaglinide matched metformin's glucose-lowering (three trials, 248 participants) while nateglinide was similar or slightly weaker than metformin (one study, 355 participants); in the two trials comparing the two meglitinides directly (342 participants), repaglinide reduced HbA1c more. The costs: weight gain was generally greater than with metformin (up to 3 kg in three months), diarrhoea was less frequent, and hypoglycaemia was more frequent though rarely severe enough to require assistance. No study reported mortality or morbidity outcomes at all. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): meglitinides are a metformin-strength glucose-lowering option — reasonable where metformin is intolerable or contraindicated — bought with more weight and more, usually mild, hypoglycaemia, and with long-term outcome benefit entirely unproven.

cards.headline: Black 2007 (Cochrane, 15 trials, 3,781 participants): repaglinide cut HbA1c 0.1–2.1% and nateglinide 0.2–0.6% versus placebo; repaglinide matched metformin; hypoglycaemia more frequent but rarely severe; weight up to 3 kg more than metformin
cards.summary: Black 2007 (Cochrane, 15 trials, 3,781 participants): repaglinide cut HbA1c 0.1–2.1% and nateglinide 0.2–0.6% versus placebo; repaglinide matched metformin; hypoglycaemia more frequent but rarely severe; weight up to 3 kg more than metformin
cards.people: A Cochrane review of randomised parallel or cross-over trials of at least 10 weeks comparing meglitinide analogues (repaglinide, nateglinide) with placebo, with each other, with metformin, or in combination with insulin, in type 2 diabetes: 15 trials involving 3,781 participants, 11 of them placebo-controlled.
cards.result: No studies reported the effect of meglitinides on mortality or morbidity. In the 11 placebo comparisons, both drugs reduced HbA1c — by 0.1% to 2.1% for repaglinide and 0.2% to 0.6% for nateglinide. Two trials (342 participants) compared repaglinide with nateglinide, with greater HbA1c reduction on repaglinide. Repaglinide (248 participants in three trials) reduced HbA1c to a similar degree as metformin; nateglinide had a similar or slightly less marked effect than metformin (one study, 355 participants). Weight gain was generally greater with meglitinides than metformin (up to 3 kg in three months). Diarrhoea occurred less frequently and hypoglycaemia occurred more frequently, but rarely severely enough to require assistance. The reviewers conclude meglitinides may offer an alternative of similar potency to metformin where metformin is intolerable or contraindicated, with no evidence on long-term outcomes, particularly mortality.
cards.watchOut: The repaglinide placebo range (0.1% to 2.1%) is very wide — dose, baseline HbA1c and trial length varied, and the review reports ranges rather than a single pooled estimate, so no precise class effect can be quoted. The evidence is also old (search to 2007) and entirely surrogate: not one trial reported a clinical endpoint, so this class's value proposition is purely glycaemic.

cards.headline: Synthesis: metformin-strength glucose lowering from a mealtime secretagogue — with weight gain and mild hypoglycaemia as the price, and no outcomes data
cards.summary: Synthesis: metformin-strength glucose lowering from a mealtime secretagogue — with weight gain and mild hypoglycaemia as the price, and no outcomes data
cards.people: One Cochrane review: 15 randomised trials, 3,781 participants, comparing repaglinide and nateglinide with placebo, each other, metformin and insulin combinations in type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: HbA1c versus placebo: repaglinide −0.1% to −2.1%, nateglinide −0.2% to −0.6%. Versus metformin: repaglinide equivalent; nateglinide similar or slightly less. Head-to-head: repaglinide stronger than nateglinide (342 participants). Weight: up to 3 kg more gain than metformin in three months. Hypoglycaemia: more frequent than comparators, rarely requiring assistance. Mortality and morbidity: reported by no trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: A 2007 review cannot see the modern treatment landscape — meglitinides now compete with drug classes that carry cardiovascular and kidney outcome data, which meglitinides entirely lack. The shelf answers the glycaemic question asked; it should not be read as a reason to prefer this class over outcome-proven alternatives where those are available and tolerated.
