shelves.title: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: HbA1c down 0.8 points on acarbose — a real effect with a hard dose ceiling and a gastrointestinal bill
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, do alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol, voglibose) improve HbA1c compared with placebo, and what gastrointestinal price do patients pay?
shelves.mesh: 1-Deoxynojirimycin/analogs & derivatives · Acarbose/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Glucosamine/analogs & derivatives · Glucosamine/therapeutic use · Glycoside Hydrolase Inhibitors* · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Imino Pyranoses · Inositol/analogs & derivatives · Inositol/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Cochrane meta-analysis (Van de Laar FA et al., PMID: 15846673; 41 trials, 8,130 participants) gives acarbose a clear, quantified glycaemic effect against placebo: HbA1c −0.8% (95% CI −0.9 to −0.7), fasting glucose −1.1 mmol/L (≈-20 mg/dL) (−1.4 to −0.9) and post-load glucose −2.3 mmol/L (≈-41 mg/dL) (−2.7 to −1.9), with a dose ceiling — above 50 mg three times daily there was no additional HbA1c effect, only more adverse effects. The gastrointestinal price is the class's signature: adverse effects were mostly gastrointestinal in origin and dose-dependent, and against sulfonylureas acarbose caused more adverse effects while delivering inferior glycaemic control, though it lowered fasting and post-load insulin levels. There were no clinically relevant effects on lipids or body weight, and the reviewers found only few data on mortality, morbidity and quality of life — whether the class changes any hard outcome remains unclear. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): alpha-glucosidase inhibitors lower HbA1c by about 0.8 percentage points, a real but modest gain that patients pay for in dose-dependent gut symptoms.

cards.headline: Van de Laar 2005 (Cochrane, 41 trials, 8,130 participants): acarbose lowered HbA1c 0.8% versus placebo (95% CI 0.7 to 0.9) — with dose-dependent gastrointestinal adverse effects and no mortality or morbidity data to speak of
cards.summary: Van de Laar 2005 (Cochrane, 41 trials, 8,130 participants): acarbose lowered HbA1c 0.8% versus placebo (95% CI 0.7 to 0.9) — with dose-dependent gastrointestinal adverse effects and no mortality or morbidity data to speak of
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 41 RCTs (Van de Laar 2005, Cochrane)
cards.people: A Cochrane review of randomised trials of at least 12 weeks of alpha-glucosidase inhibitor monotherapy in type 2 diabetes: 41 trials with 8,130 participants — 30 of acarbose, 7 of miglitol, 1 of voglibose and 3 comparing different agents. Study duration was 24 weeks in most cases; only two studies lasted amply longer than one year.
cards.result: Acarbose had a clear effect on glycaemic control versus placebo: glycated haemoglobin −0.8% (95% confidence interval −0.9 to −0.7), fasting blood glucose −1.1 mmol/L (≈-20 mg/dL) (−1.4 to −0.9) and post-load blood glucose −2.3 mmol/L (≈-41 mg/dL) (−2.7 to −1.9). The HbA1c effect was not dose-dependent, and dosages above 50 mg three times daily offered no additional HbA1c effect but more adverse effects. Post-load insulin fell; there were no clinically relevant effects on lipids or body weight. Adverse effects were mostly gastrointestinal and dose-dependent. Compared with sulfonylurea, acarbose decreased fasting insulin by −24.8 pmol/L (−43.3 to −6.3) and post-load insulin by −133.2 pmol/L (−184.5 to −81.8), caused more adverse effects, and had an inferior glycaemic profile. Only few data existed on mortality, morbidity and quality of life, and whether the class influences them remains unclear.
cards.watchOut: Most trials ran about 24 weeks and the reviewers warn the glycaemic effects are less sure with longer use — durability is the weak point behind the tidy −0.8%. The evidence is acarbose-heavy (30 of 41 trials), so miglitol and voglibose borrow the class stamp on thin data of their own. Searches closed in 2003, and the near-absence of mortality, morbidity and quality-of-life data in 8,130 randomised patients is itself the finding on outcomes.

shelves.title: Liraglutide on dialysis: blood levels run 49% higher, glucose still improves — one 12-week trial says start low and titrate slowly
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with end-stage kidney disease on dialysis, does liraglutide achieve glycaemic control safely compared with placebo, given altered drug exposure in uraemia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose/drug effects · Body Weight/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/drug effects · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Hypoglycemic Agents/pharmacokinetics · Insulin/therapeutic use · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications · Kidney Failure, Chronic/physiopathology · Liraglutide/administration & dosage · Liraglutide/adverse effects · Liraglutide/pharmacokinetics · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/drug therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this shelf rests on a single small investigator-initiated trial (Idorn T et al., PMID: 26283739): 24 patients with type 2 diabetes and dialysis-dependent end-stage kidney disease plus 23 diabetic controls with normal kidney function, of whom 20 and 20 completed 12 weeks. Its primary outcome was pharmacokinetic, and it answered that question clearly: dose-corrected plasma trough liraglutide concentration was 49% higher (95% CI 6 to 109; P = 0.02) in the kidney-disease group — exposure really does rise in uraemia. Glycaemic control tended to improve in both liraglutide groups on daily glucose measurements (P < 0.01) with parallel reductions in baseline insulin dose (P < 0.04), and weight fell in both (−2.4 ± 0.8 kg in the kidney group, not significant at P = 0.22; −2.9 ± 1.0 kg in controls, P = 0.03). The cost was gastrointestinal: initial, temporary nausea and vomiting occurred more frequently in liraglutide-treated patients with kidney failure than in controls (P < 0.04). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): liraglutide can be used in dialysis patients with glycaemic effect, but exposure is roughly half again as high, so the trialists advise reduced doses and slower titration — a dosing caution, on 20 completing patients, not a settled safety profile.

cards.headline: Idorn 2016: liraglutide exposure 49% higher in dialysis patients (95% CI 6 to 109) — glucose tended to improve and insulin dose fell, but nausea and vomiting were more frequent than in diabetic controls
cards.summary: Idorn 2016: liraglutide exposure 49% higher in dialysis patients (95% CI 6 to 109) — glucose tended to improve and insulin dose fell, but nausea and vomiting were more frequent than in diabetic controls
cards.people: An investigator-initiated, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group randomised trial: 24 patients with type 2 diabetes and dialysis-dependent end-stage renal disease and 23 control subjects with type 2 diabetes and normal kidney function, allocated 1:1 to 12 weeks of liraglutide (titrated to a maximum of 1.8 mg) or placebo as add-on to ongoing antidiabetic treatment; 20 patients in each population completed. The primary outcome was dose-corrected plasma trough liraglutide concentration at the final visit.
cards.result: Dose-corrected plasma trough liraglutide concentration at the final visit was increased by 49% (95% CI 6 to 109, P = 0.02) in the end-stage renal disease group compared with controls. Initial and temporary nausea and vomiting occurred more frequently among liraglutide-treated patients with renal disease than among control subjects (P < 0.04). Glycaemic control tended to improve during the study in both liraglutide-treated groups on daily blood glucose measurements (P < 0.01), and baseline insulin dose was reduced in parallel (P < 0.04). Body weight fell in both liraglutide groups: −2.4 ± 0.8 kg (mean ± SE) in the renal group (P = 0.22) and −2.9 ± 1.0 kg in controls (P = 0.03). The authors advise that reduced treatment doses and a prolonged titration period may be advisable in this population.
cards.watchOut: Ten liraglutide-treated dialysis patients completing is the entire direct safety base: the trial can detect a pharmacokinetic shift and common gut effects, nothing rarer, and 12 weeks cannot judge hypoglycaemia burden, nutrition or cardiovascular safety in a dialysis population. The glycaemic findings are reported as tendencies on daily measurements rather than a definitive HbA1c treatment difference — in dialysis, where HbA1c itself is distorted, that caution is appropriate but limits the efficacy claim.
cards.source: Idorn T et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: exposure up by half, glucose trending down, gut effects up — a usable drug in dialysis, dosed gently, on very small numbers
cards.summary: Synthesis: exposure up by half, glucose trending down, gut effects up — a usable drug in dialysis, dosed gently, on very small numbers
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial: 24 patients with type 2 diabetes on dialysis and 23 diabetic controls with normal kidney function; 20 completers in each population over 12 weeks (Idorn 2016).
cards.result: Pharmacokinetics: dose-corrected trough liraglutide +49% (95% CI 6 to 109) in end-stage renal disease. Glycaemia: tendency to improve in both liraglutide groups (P < 0.01) with reduced insulin doses (P < 0.04). Weight: −2.4 kg in the renal group (P = 0.22), −2.9 kg in controls (P = 0.03). Tolerability: nausea and vomiting more frequent in renal patients on liraglutide (P < 0.04). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here generalises automatically to other agents of the class, to peritoneal dialysis, or to non-dialysis advanced kidney disease — each has its own exposure story. The practical output of this shelf is narrow and useful: in haemodialysis patients liraglutide accumulates measurably, works glycaemically, and should be started low and titrated slowly, with the evidence grade honestly labelled as one small trial. Tier C is set accordingly.

shelves.title: Glargine alongside the DKA insulin drip: resolution about four hours faster in the pooled small trials — stay and hypoglycaemia unchanged
shelves.question: In diabetic ketoacidosis, does adding subcutaneous insulin glargine to intravenous insulin infusion shorten time to resolution and hospital stay compared with intravenous insulin alone?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Ketoacidosis/drug therapy · Humans · Hyperglycemia/prevention & control · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin Glargine/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the meta-analysis (Andrade-Castellanos CA et al., PMID: 27861474) pooled just four randomised trials and 135 patients, and on low-quality evidence found that subcutaneous insulin glargine co-administered with standard intravenous insulin shortened time to resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis by a mean of 4.19 hours (95% CI −7.81 to 0.57 as printed in the record; p = 0.02), with neutral differences in length of hospital stay and hypoglycaemic episodes. Four hours faster biochemical resolution, if real, is clinically convenient — less infusion time, earlier step-down — but the evidence carrying it is thin: three of the four trials contributed to the resolution estimate, the printed confidence interval crosses zero despite the reported p-value, and no effect on stay or any harder outcome was shown. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): adding glargine early in DKA may shave about four hours off time to resolution without extra hypoglycaemia, but the pooled base is 135 patients and the finding needs a properly sized trial before it changes protocol by itself.

cards.headline: Andrade-Castellanos 2016 (meta-analysis, 4 trials, 135 patients): glargine added to IV insulin cut time to DKA resolution by 4.19 hours on low-quality evidence; hospital stay and hypoglycaemia unchanged
cards.summary: Andrade-Castellanos 2016 (meta-analysis, 4 trials, 135 patients): glargine added to IV insulin cut time to DKA resolution by 4.19 hours on low-quality evidence; hospital stay and hypoglycaemia unchanged
cards.people: A systematic review with meta-analysis searching MEDLINE, EMBASE and CENTRAL for randomised controlled trials comparing co-administration of subcutaneous insulin glargine plus standard intravenous insulin treatment versus standard treatment alone in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis, with efficacy and clinically important outcomes required for eligibility; two reviewers extracted data, assessed risk of bias and graded strength of evidence with GRADE. Four studies with 135 participants during hospital follow-up were included.
cards.result: Low-quality evidence from three trials suggested that subcutaneously administered insulin glargine, in addition to standard treatment, significantly reduces the time to resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis (mean difference −4.19 hours; 95% CI −7.81 to 0.57; p = 0.02, as printed in the record). There was a neutral difference between the groups regarding length of hospital stay and hypoglycaemic episodes. The authors conclude that glargine co-administration reduces time to resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis with neutral effects on hypoglycaemic episodes.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval as printed in the abstract (−7.81 to 0.57) includes zero while the reported p-value is 0.02 — an internal inconsistency in the record that, alongside the authors' own low-quality GRADE rating and 135 total patients, argues for treating the 4.19-hour figure as provisional. Resolution time is also a definition-sensitive endpoint (which biochemical threshold, checked how often) that varied across the small contributing trials.
cards.source: Andrade-Castellanos CA et al. Systematic review with meta-analysis: Subcutaneous insulin glargine coadministration for diabetic ketoacidosis. Gaceta Medica de Mexico. 2016. cards.headline: Synthesis: a plausible four-hour gain in resolution time, neutral on stay and hypoglycaemia — resting on 135 randomised patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: a plausible four-hour gain in resolution time, neutral on stay and hypoglycaemia — resting on 135 randomised patients
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomised trials (135 participants) of early subcutaneous glargine added to intravenous insulin in diabetic ketoacidosis (Andrade-Castellanos 2016).
cards.result: Time to resolution: mean difference −4.19 hours favouring glargine co-administration (low-quality evidence, three trials). Length of hospital stay: no difference. Hypoglycaemic episodes: no difference. Harder outcomes (mortality, cerebral complications, ICU stay): not established in the pooled record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is strictly the adjunct question — whether adding basal insulin early helps once intravenous insulin is running. The separate questions of subcutaneous-versus-intravenous insulin regimens and fluid choice in DKA live on their own shelves (#1770 and #1771). A single adequately powered trial with a standard resolution definition would either confirm a genuinely useful shortcut or retire it; until then the intervention is cheap and plausible but unproven at scale.
cards.source: Synthesis of Andrade-Castellanos CA et al. Gaceta Medica de Mexico. 2016 (PMID: 27861474).

shelves.title: HypoAware for lost hypo awareness: impaired-awareness odds significantly lower (OR 0.38), distress down, severe events leaning lower — at €2,233 per event prevented
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes with impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, does the HypoAware psychoeducational programme restore awareness and reduce severe hypoglycaemia compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Awareness · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Hypoglycemia/diagnosis · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin/adverse effects · Insulin/therapeutic use · Internet · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic* · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the cluster-randomised trial (Rondags SM et al., PMID: 27797931; 137 participants with type 1 or insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and problematic hypoglycaemia, eight Dutch clinics, 6 months) found HypoAware significantly reduced the odds of impaired hypoglycaemia awareness (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.95; P = 0.038) and hypo-distress (relative risk 0.70, 0.56 to 0.88; P = 0.002 — a 30% relative reduction), with median severe hypoglycaemic events of 1 (IQR 0–6.5) in the HypoAware group versus 2.5 (IQR 1–10) on usual care over 6 months (P = 0.030); the adjusted episode-rate estimate, a 33% relative reduction (relative risk 0.67, 0.39 to 1.16), was not significant (P = 0.150), and HbA1c did not change. The economic evaluation (de Wit M et al., PMID: 29150861) puts the proportion with at least one severe event 0.22 lower and impaired awareness 0.16 lower on HypoAware, at €2,233 per severe event prevented and €708 higher mean societal costs, concluding the programme was not cost-effective on quality-adjusted life-years (€119,360 per QALY). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HypoAware restores awareness and cuts distress and severe-event burden modestly — a clinical benefit whose cost-effectiveness, on QALY terms, its own evaluators dispute.

cards.headline: Rondags 2016 (cluster RCT, 137 participants): HypoAware cut the odds of impaired awareness (OR 0.38) and hypo-distress (RR 0.70); median severe events 1 versus 2.5 over 6 months; adjusted severe-episode rate (RR 0.67) not significant
cards.summary: Rondags 2016 (cluster RCT, 137 participants): HypoAware cut the odds of impaired awareness (OR 0.38) and hypo-distress (RR 0.70); median severe events 1 versus 2.5 over 6 months; adjusted severe-episode rate (RR 0.67) not significant
cards.people: A two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial in eight Dutch clinics enrolling 137 adults with type 1 or insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and problematic hypoglycaemia, comparing HypoAware — a brief, partly web-based group psychoeducational intervention based on Blood Glucose Awareness Training — with care as usual. Outcomes (self-reported severe hypoglycaemia, impaired awareness by Gold score, worries and distress) were assessed at baseline and at 2, 4 and 6 months, analysed intention-to-treat with generalised estimating equations.
cards.result: Adjusted analyses over the four time points showed 33% fewer severe hypoglycaemic episodes in relative terms in the HypoAware group (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.16; P = 0.150 — not significant), significantly reduced odds of impaired awareness (odds ratio 0.38, 0.15 to 0.95; P = 0.038), a trend to 20% fewer worries about hypoglycaemia in relative terms (relative risk 0.80, 0.64 to 1.01; P = 0.059), and significantly 30% less hypo-distress in relative terms (relative risk 0.70, 0.56 to 0.88; P = 0.002). Over the 6 months, median severe hypoglycaemic events were 1 (IQR 0–6.5) in the HypoAware group versus 2.5 (IQR 1–10) in controls (P = 0.030). There was no significant change in HbA1c within or between groups.
cards.watchOut: The trial's most quoted number cuts both ways: the unadjusted median-event comparison is significant while the adjusted episode-rate model is not, and severe events are self-reported in an unblinded education trial — expectation can move reporting as well as events. Eight clinics is a small number of clusters, and the population was Dutch clinic patients already engaged with services; awareness gains at 6 months say nothing about durability at 2 years.

cards.headline: de Wit 2018 (economic evaluation of the same trial): severe-event proportion 0.22 lower and impaired awareness 0.16 lower on HypoAware; €2,233 per severe event prevented — but not cost-effective per QALY (€119,360/QALY)
cards.summary: de Wit 2018 (economic evaluation of the same trial): severe-event proportion 0.22 lower and impaired awareness 0.16 lower on HypoAware; €2,233 per severe event prevented — but not cost-effective per QALY (€119,360/QALY)
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of a cluster RCT (de Wit 2018)
cards.people: An economic evaluation from societal and healthcare perspectives using data from the 6-month multicentre cluster-randomised HypoAware trial (n = 137) in people with type 1 and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes at high risk of severe hypoglycaemia, comparing HypoAware with usual care.
cards.result: The proportion of people with at least one severe hypoglycaemic event per 6 months was 0.22 lower (95% CI −0.39 to −0.06) and the proportion with impaired hypoglycaemia awareness was 0.16 lower (95% CI −0.34 to 0.02) in the HypoAware group. There was no difference in quality-adjusted life-years (0.0; 95% CI −0.05 to 0.05). Mean total societal costs were €708 higher on HypoAware (95% CI −951 to 2298). The mean incremental cost per severe hypoglycaemic event prevented was €2,233; at a willingness-to-pay threshold of €20,000 per event prevented, the probability of cost-effectiveness was 54% (societal) and 55% (healthcare). For quality-adjusted life-years the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was €119,360 per QALY gained, with low probability of cost-effectiveness at all ceiling ratios. The authors conclude HypoAware is not cost-effective compared with usual care, and call for research in less well-resourced settings and more severely affected patients.
cards.watchOut: The QALY verdict and the clinical verdict diverge because severe hypoglycaemia prevention barely registers in generic quality-of-life instruments over 6 months — a measurement limitation the authors acknowledge by reporting the per-event-prevented ratio alongside. Costs and thresholds are Dutch and dated; transfer to other health systems is indicative only. Note the awareness difference here (−0.16) has a confidence interval crossing zero, unlike the trial's own adjusted odds ratio.
cards.source: de Wit M et al. Diabetic Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29150861. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: awareness and distress improve significantly, severe events fall on the simpler comparisons — and the economists still say the QALY maths fails
cards.summary: Synthesis: awareness and distress improve significantly, severe events fall on the simpler comparisons — and the economists still say the QALY maths fails
cards.people: One cluster-randomised trial (137 participants, 8 clinics, 6 months; Rondags 2016) and its companion economic evaluation (de Wit 2018) of the HypoAware blended group-and-online programme in insulin-treated diabetes with problematic hypoglycaemia.
cards.result: Impaired awareness: odds ratio 0.38 (0.15 to 0.95) in the trial; proportion 0.16 lower in the economic analysis. Severe hypoglycaemia: median 1 versus 2.5 events over 6 months (P = 0.030); adjusted relative rate 0.67 (0.39 to 1.16, not significant); proportion with at least one event 0.22 lower. Distress: relative risk 0.70 (0.56 to 0.88). HbA1c and QALYs: unchanged. Cost: €2,233 per severe event prevented; €119,360 per QALY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Awareness restoration is a surrogate with a strong face claim — people who feel hypos again can act on them — but the trial's own adjusted severe-event endpoint missed significance, so the shelf should not be quoted as proving fewer severe hypos. What is proven is improved awareness scores and less fear and distress, with event counts leaning the right way. Tier C is set for the single small cluster trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rondags SM et al. Diabetes Care. 2016 (PMID: 27797931); de Wit M et al. Diabetic Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29150861).

shelves.title: Diabetes-specific tube feeds: fasting glucose and HbA1c lower than standard formula in the pooled trials — lipids essentially unmoved
shelves.question: In patients with diabetes receiving enteral nutrition, does a diabetes-specific formula improve glycaemic and cardiometabolic measures compared with a standard formula?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers/blood · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/diagnosis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/diet therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/epidemiology · Diet, Diabetic*/adverse effects · Energy Metabolism* · Enteral Nutrition*/adverse effects · Female · Food, Formulated*/adverse effects · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Glycemic Index · Humans · Lipids/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Nutritional Status · Nutritive Value* · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the systematic review and meta-analysis (Ojo O et al., PMID: 31443185; 14 studies reviewed, 5 pooled) found every included study reporting lower blood glucose parameters on diabetes-specific formula than on standard formula, and the pooled analysis confirmed significantly lower fasting blood glucose (mean difference −1.15, 95% CI −2.07 to −0.23; p = 0.01) and significantly lower glycated haemoglobin (p = 0.005 after sensitivity analysis). The lipid story is thinner: no significant differences in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol or triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol was higher by a mean of 0.09 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.18; p = 0.04) — a result the authors note was not consistent on sensitivity analysis, as the fasting-glucose result also lost significance when some studies were removed. The formulas differ from standard feeds in several ways at once (low-glycaemic-index carbohydrate, less carbohydrate, more protein, monounsaturated fats, different fibre), so no single ingredient can take the credit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): diabetes-specific enteral formula improves fasting glucose and HbA1c modestly in type 2 diabetes; claims beyond glycaemia — lipids, outcomes — are not supported by the pooled record.

cards.headline: Ojo 2019 (meta-analysis, 5 of 14 studies pooled): diabetes-specific formula lowered fasting glucose by 1.15 (95% CI 0.23 to 2.07) and HbA1c significantly; lipids unchanged except a small, fragile HDL rise
cards.summary: Ojo 2019 (meta-analysis, 5 of 14 studies pooled): diabetes-specific formula lowered fasting glucose by 1.15 (95% CI 0.23 to 2.07) and HbA1c significantly; lipids unchanged except a small, fragile HDL rise
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Ojo 2019)
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of diabetes-specific enteral nutrition formula versus standard formula in patients with type 2 diabetes (a population that includes patients fed enterally after conditions such as stroke affecting swallowing), searching PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO and Google Scholar to 2 January 2019: 14 articles in the systematic review, 5 selected for meta-analysis.
cards.result: All 14 studies in the systematic review showed diabetes-specific formula effective in lowering blood glucose parameters compared with standard formula. In the meta-analysis, fasting blood glucose was significantly lower on diabetes-specific formula (p = 0.01), with a mean difference of −1.15 (95% CI −2.07 to −0.23), and glycated haemoglobin was significantly lower (p = 0.005) following meta-analysis and sensitivity analysis; however, the fasting-glucose difference was not significant in sensitivity analyses removing some studies. For lipids, no significant differences (p > 0.05) were found for total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol or triglycerides; HDL cholesterol was significantly higher on diabetes-specific formula (p = 0.04), mean difference 0.09 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.18), though this was not consistent on sensitivity analysis. The authors attribute the differences to the formulas' low-glycaemic-index carbohydrate, lower carbohydrate and higher protein content, monounsaturated fatty acids and fibre profile, and state confidence would be increased by further studies.
cards.watchOut: Only 5 of 14 studies were poolable, the record does not state the total pooled participant count, and two of the three positive findings (fasting glucose, HDL) wobble under sensitivity analysis — the HbA1c result is the sturdiest and even it is reported without a pooled mean difference in the abstract. 'Diabetes-specific formula' is a family of commercial recipes, not one product, so the pooled effect is a class average across differing compositions.
cards.source: Ojo O et al. The Effect of Diabetes-Specific Enteral Nutrition Formula on Cardiometabolic Parameters in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials. Nutrients. 2019. PMID: 31443185. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: glycaemia better on diabetes-specific feeds in every reviewed study and in the pool — lipids and harder outcomes not carried
cards.summary: Synthesis: glycaemia better on diabetes-specific feeds in every reviewed study and in the pool — lipids and harder outcomes not carried
cards.people: One systematic review (14 randomised studies) with a 5-study meta-analysis of diabetes-specific versus standard enteral formula in type 2 diabetes (Ojo 2019).
cards.result: Fasting glucose: mean difference −1.15 (−2.07 to −0.23), p = 0.01, but not robust to all sensitivity analyses. HbA1c: significantly lower, p = 0.005 after sensitivity analysis. HDL cholesterol: +0.09 (0.00 to 0.18), p = 0.04, inconsistent on sensitivity analysis. Total cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides: no significant difference. Clinical outcomes (infections, stay, mortality): not established in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tube-fed patients are usually acutely ill, and glucose in that setting is also driven by illness, steroids and insulin protocols that varied across the small trials — the formula is one lever among several. The shelf supports choosing a diabetes-specific feed for glycaemic reasons; it does not support paying a premium for lipid or outcome claims the pooled data do not show.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ojo O et al. Nutrients. 2019 (PMID: 31443185).

shelves.title: Insulin for TPN: in-the-bag regular insulin and half-and-half glargine tie during the infusion — glargine wins the two days after, with more mild hypos
shelves.question: In non-critically ill hospitalised patients with diabetes receiving total parenteral nutrition, does subcutaneous glargine control glucose as well as regular insulin added to the nutrition bag, and with how much hypoglycaemia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/therapeutic use · Insulin Glargine/administration & dosage · Insulin Glargine/therapeutic use · Male · Parenteral Nutrition, Total/methods · Prospective Studies · Spain · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the one randomised trial built for this question (Olveira G et al., PMID: 30930133; INSUPAR, 161 non-critically ill inpatients with type 2 diabetes on total parenteral nutrition) found the two strategies glycaemically equivalent during the infusion: mean capillary glucose 165.3 ± 35.4 mg/dL with 100% regular insulin in the bag versus 172.5 ± 43.6 mg/dL with half the regular insulin in the bag and half as subcutaneous glargine (p = 0.25), on similar total insulin doses, with similar proportions of readings above 180 mg/dL and no differences in length of stay, infectious complications or hospital mortality. The split comes at the edges: in the two days after parenteral nutrition stopped, glucose ran significantly lower on the glargine strategy (141.7 ± 43.8 versus 160.3 ± 45.1 mg/dL; p = 0.024) — but the glargine group also had significantly more capillary readings at or below 70 mg/dL, more hypoglycaemic episodes per 100 days of nutrition, and more patients with non-severe hypoglycaemia, though no severe hypoglycaemia occurred in either arm. The systematic review of glucose management on parenteral and enteral nutrition (Laesser CI et al., PMID: 31261760; 15 studies, 1,170 patients) found the underlying study base generally of limited quality and no consensus regimen. PROPOSED SPLIT: on the nutrition bag the routes tie; glargine buys better post-infusion control at the price of more non-severe hypoglycaemia.

cards.headline: Olveira 2020 (INSUPAR, 161 patients): glucose on TPN statistically identical either way (165.3 versus 172.5 mg/dL, p = 0.25) — glargine better after TPN stopped (141.7 versus 160.3, p = 0.024) but with significantly more non-severe hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Olveira 2020 (INSUPAR, 161 patients): glucose on TPN statistically identical either way (165.3 versus 172.5 mg/dL, p = 0.25) — glargine better after TPN stopped (141.7 versus 160.3, p = 0.024) but with significantly more non-severe hypoglycaemia
cards.people: A prospective, open-label, multicentre randomised trial (INSUPAR) in 161 adult non-critically ill inpatients with type 2 diabetes receiving total parenteral nutrition in Spain: 81 patients received 100% of their regular insulin added to the nutrition bag, and 80 received 50% of regular insulin in the bag plus 50% as subcutaneous insulin glargine. Analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.result: No differences were observed in average total daily insulin dose (programmed or correction) or in capillary mean blood glucose during TPN infusion: 165.3 ± 35.4 mg/dL on regular-insulin-in-bag versus 172.5 ± 43.6 mg/dL on the glargine regimen (p = 0.25). The percentage of capillary glucose readings above 180 mg/dL was similar in both groups. Mean capillary glucose was significantly lower in the glargine group in the two days after TPN interruption (141.7 ± 43.8 versus 160.3 ± 45.1 mg/dL; p = 0.024). However, the rate of capillary glucose at or below 70 mg/dL, the number of hypoglycaemic episodes per 100 days of TPN, and the percentage of patients with non-severe hypoglycaemia were all significantly higher in the glargine group. No severe hypoglycaemia was detected in either group, and there were no differences in length of stay, infectious complications or hospital mortality.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparison is not pure route-versus-route: the glargine arm still had half its regular insulin in the bag, so the trial tests a hybrid strategy, not glargine alone. The abstract reports the hypoglycaemia differences as significant without giving the absolute episode rates, so the size of the excess cannot be stated from this record — only its direction and that no episode was severe. Capillary means around 165–173 mg/dL in both arms also show neither regimen achieved tight control.
cards.source: Olveira G et al. Regular insulin added to total parenteral nutrition vs subcutaneous glargine in non-critically ill diabetic inpatients, a multicenter randomized clinical trial: INSUPAR trial. cards.headline: Laesser 2019 (systematic review, 15 studies, 1,170 patients): no consensus regimen for glucose on parenteral or enteral nutrition — studies generally of limited quality
cards.summary: Laesser 2019 (systematic review, 15 studies, 1,170 patients): no consensus regimen for glucose on parenteral or enteral nutrition — studies generally of limited quality
cards.people: A systematic review of strategies to manage glucose control in non-critically ill hospitalised adults receiving parenteral and/or enteral nutrition, searching PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central and ClinicalTrials.gov for records from April 1999 to April 2019: 15 completed studies comprising 1,170 patients, of which 11 were clinical trials and 4 observational studies.
cards.result: Four studies adapted the nutritional regimen itself; the remainder assessed different insulin regimens and administration routes. Diabetes-specific nutritional regimens that reduced glycaemic excursions, and algorithm-driven insulin delivery approaches allowing flexible glucose-responsive dosing, were both effective in improving glycaemic control. However, the assessed studies were in general of limited quality, and the reviewers state there is no consensus on best practice and a clear need for future rigorous studies to establish standards of care for hyperglycaemia during nutrition support.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative review without pooled effect sizes, spanning both parenteral and enteral nutrition — it frames how unsettled the field is rather than adjudicating the glargine question, which is why INSUPAR carries this shelf. The record carries no MeSH terms, so none are quoted.
cards.source: Laesser CI et al. Management of Glucose Control in Noncritically Ill, Hospitalized Patients Receiving Parenteral and/or Enteral Nutrition: A Systematic Review. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31261760. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a dead heat during infusion, a glargine edge after it stops, and a hypoglycaemia bill for that edge — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: a dead heat during infusion, a glargine edge after it stops, and a hypoglycaemia bill for that edge — SPLIT
cards.people: One multicentre open-label RCT (161 patients; INSUPAR) set against a 15-study, 1,170-patient systematic review showing no established standard regimen for insulin during parenteral nutrition.
cards.result: During TPN: mean glucose 165.3 versus 172.5 mg/dL (p = 0.25); readings above 180 mg/dL similar; insulin doses similar. After TPN: mean glucose 141.7 (glargine strategy) versus 160.3 mg/dL (p = 0.024). Hypoglycaemia: significantly more readings ≤70 mg/dL, more episodes per 100 TPN days and more affected patients on glargine; severe hypoglycaemia zero in both arms. Stay, infections, mortality: no difference. PROPOSED SPLIT — equivalent control on the bag; glargine better after cessation, with more non-severe hypoglycaemia.
cards.watchOut: The practical reading is about transitions, not superiority: basal insulin already on board when the bag stops smooths the handover to ordinary feeding or fasting, and that same persistence is what produces the extra lows if intake falters. Critically ill patients were excluded from INSUPAR — nothing here transfers to intensive care parenteral nutrition. Tier C is set for the single open-label trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Olveira G et al. Clinical Nutrition. 2020 (PMID: 30930133); Laesser CI et al. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31261760).

shelves.title: Metformin in kidney disease: lactic acidosis at 3–10 per 100,000 person-years, no different from background — a reassurance built entirely without randomised trials
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease, does continuing metformin increase the risk of lactic acidosis or other serious adverse events compared with other glucose-lowering therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis, Lactic/chemically induced · Contraindications · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Metformin/adverse effects · Metformin/therapeutic use · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications · Risk
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this is a harm question answered without a single randomised trial: the systematic review (Inzucchi SE et al., PMID: 25536258) assembled 65 articles — pharmacokinetic studies, large case series, retrospective studies, meta-analyses and one clinical trial — and found that in mild to moderate chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2) metformin levels generally remain within the therapeutic range and lactate concentrations are not substantially increased. The overall incidence of lactic acidosis in metformin users across studies ran from approximately 3 to 10 per 100,000 person-years and was generally indistinguishable from the background rate in the overall diabetes population; data suggesting increased risk in kidney disease were limited, and population studies found metformin prescribed against prevailing renal guidelines in up to 1 in 4 patients with type 2 diabetes without, in most reports, increased lactic acidosis rates. The reviewers support cautious expansion of metformin use in mild to moderate kidney disease with dose reduction and kidney-function monitoring — while being explicit that no randomised trial has tested safety in significantly impaired kidney function. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): continuing metformin at eGFR 30–60 has not been shown to raise lactic acidosis above background rates, but the reassurance is observational, and below that range the record is silent rather than reassuring.

cards.headline: Inzucchi 2014 (JAMA systematic review, 65 articles): lactic acidosis on metformin ran 3–10 per 100,000 person-years — indistinguishable from background diabetes rates — with no randomised safety trial in kidney disease
cards.summary: Inzucchi 2014 (JAMA systematic review, 65 articles): lactic acidosis on metformin ran 3–10 per 100,000 person-years — indistinguishable from background diabetes rates — with no randomised safety trial in kidney disease
cards.people: A systematic review searching MEDLINE and the Cochrane databases in July 2014 for English-language articles on metformin, kidney disease and lactic acidosis in humans from 1950 to June 2014: of 818 articles screened, 65 were included — pharmacokinetic and metabolic studies, large case series, retrospective studies, meta-analyses and a clinical trial. Reviews, letters, editorials, case reports and small case series were excluded.
cards.result: Although metformin is renally cleared, drug levels generally remain within the therapeutic range and lactate concentrations are not substantially increased when the drug is used in mild to moderate chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate 30–60 mL/min per 1.73 m2). The overall incidence of lactic acidosis in metformin users varies across studies from approximately 3 per 100,000 person-years to 10 per 100,000 person-years and is generally indistinguishable from the background rate in the overall population with diabetes. Data suggesting an increased risk of lactic acidosis in metformin-treated patients with chronic kidney disease are limited, and no randomised controlled trials have been conducted to test the safety of metformin in patients with significantly impaired kidney function. Population-based studies show metformin may be prescribed counter to prevailing guidelines in up to 1 in 4 patients with type 2 diabetes, use which in most reports has not been associated with increased rates of lactic acidosis. Observational studies also suggest a potential benefit of metformin on macrovascular outcomes even in patients with prevalent renal contraindications. The authors conclude the evidence supports cautious expansion of metformin use in mild to moderate chronic kidney disease, with appropriate dosage reductions and careful follow-up of kidney function.
cards.watchOut: Lactic acidosis at 3–10 per 100,000 person-years is rare enough that observational comparisons can miss a real but small excess, and confounding by indication runs both ways — clinicians stop metformin in the sickest patients, which can make continued users look spuriously safe. The review's reassurance is explicitly bounded at eGFR 30–60; it offers no evidence for more advanced kidney disease, and acute illness (sepsis, hypoxia, acute kidney injury) is a separate risk setting this chronic-use review does not settle.
cards.source: Inzucchi SE et al. Metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease: a systematic review. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25536258. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: at eGFR 30–60 the feared harm is unmeasurably rare in the assembled record — but the record is observational from top to bottom
cards.summary: Synthesis: at eGFR 30–60 the feared harm is unmeasurably rare in the assembled record — but the record is observational from top to bottom
cards.people: One JAMA systematic review of 65 included articles (818 screened) on metformin in type 2 diabetes with kidney disease (Inzucchi 2014): pharmacokinetic studies, case series, retrospective studies, meta-analyses and one clinical trial; no randomised safety trial in impaired kidney function.
cards.result: Lactic acidosis incidence on metformin: approximately 3 to 10 per 100,000 person-years, generally indistinguishable from background rates in diabetes. Drug levels: within therapeutic range, and lactate not substantially increased, at eGFR 30–60. Off-guideline use: up to 1 in 4 patients in population studies, mostly without increased lactic acidosis rates. Randomised evidence in significantly impaired kidney function: none. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: 'No shown increase' is not 'proven safe': for a harm this rare, the honest statement is that any excess risk in mild-to-moderate kidney disease is too small to see in the available data, set against a real glycaemic benefit and possible macrovascular benefit in the same observational record. Dose reduction and monitoring as kidney function falls — the review's own conditions — are part of the intervention being judged, not optional extras. Tier C is set because the entire safety case is non-randomised.
cards.source: Synthesis of Inzucchi SE et al. JAMA. 2014 (PMID: 25536258).

shelves.title: Gliclazide MR versus glimepiride: same HbA1c, fewer lows — 3.7% versus 8.9% confirmed hypoglycaemia in the one large head-to-head trial
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does once-daily gliclazide modified-release cause less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride at equivalent glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gliclazide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/prevention & control · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Sulfonylurea Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head randomised record points one way. In GUIDE (Schernthaner G et al., PMID: 15305887), 845 patients achieved identical control on both drugs (HbA1c 7.2% in both arms; final difference −0.06%, noninferiority P < 0.0001), yet confirmed hypoglycaemia below 3 mmol/L (≈54 mg/dL) occurred in 3.7% on gliclazide modified-release versus 8.9% on glimepiride (P = 0.003) — an absolute difference of 5.2 percentage points — and no episode in either arm required external assistance. A network meta-analysis of sulfonylureas added to metformin (Andersen SE et al., PMID: 27426428) ranked gliclazide lowest for hypoglycaemia, with an odds ratio of 0.40 versus glimepiride, although its 95% credible interval (0.13 to 1.27) crosses 1, so the pooled estimate alone is not conclusive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): at equal glycaemic control, gliclazide modified-release probably causes less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride, on one large direct trial backed by a consistent but imprecise network estimate.

cards.headline: GUIDE 2004: identical HbA1c (7.2% both arms) but confirmed hypoglycaemia in 3.7% on gliclazide MR versus 8.9% on glimepiride (P = 0.003)
cards.summary: GUIDE 2004: identical HbA1c (7.2% both arms) but confirmed hypoglycaemia in 3.7% on gliclazide MR versus 8.9% on glimepiride (P = 0.003)
cards.people: 845 adults with type 2 diabetes randomised double-blind for 27 weeks to once-daily gliclazide modified-release 30–120 mg or glimepiride 1–6 mg, as monotherapy or added to existing metformin or an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, under everyday clinical practice conditions.
cards.result: HbA1c fell from 8.4% to 7.2% on gliclazide MR and from 8.2% to 7.2% on glimepiride; the mean between-group difference in final HbA1c was −0.06% (noninferiority P < 0.0001). About 50% of patients reached HbA1c below 7% and 25% below 6.5%. No hypoglycaemia requiring external assistance occurred. Hypoglycaemia with blood glucose below 3 mmol/L (≈54 mg/dL) occurred in 3.7% of patients on gliclazide MR versus 8.9% on glimepiride (P = 0.003), described by the authors as approximately 50% fewer confirmed episodes; dose distributions were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A single 27-week trial from the sponsor era of both drugs, with hypoglycaemia counted by the European Agency definition of the time and no severe episodes in either arm — so the comparison is about mild-to-moderate lows, not about the rare severe events that drive harm. Background therapy was mixed (monotherapy or add-on), which mirrors practice but blurs any single-regimen reading.
cards.source: Schernthaner et al. GUIDE study: double-blind comparison of once-daily gliclazide MR and glimepiride in type 2 diabetic patients. European journal of clinical investigation. 2004. cards.headline: Andersen 2016 network meta-analysis: gliclazide ranked lowest for hypoglycaemia among newer sulfonylureas on metformin — OR 0.40 versus glimepiride, but the credible interval crosses 1
cards.summary: Andersen 2016 network meta-analysis: gliclazide ranked lowest for hypoglycaemia among newer sulfonylureas on metformin — OR 0.40 versus glimepiride, but the credible interval crosses 1
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials of 12–52 weeks adding a sulfonylurea to metformin (at least 1000 mg/day) in type 2 diabetes: 13 sulfonylurea trials and 14 trials of other oral agents, 16,260 patients in total, using indirect as well as direct comparisons.
cards.result: All agents produced comparable HbA1c reductions (−0.66% to −0.84%). The risk of hypoglycaemia of any severity was lowest with gliclazide: odds ratio 0.22 versus glipizide (95% credible interval 0.05 to 0.96), 0.40 versus glimepiride (0.13 to 1.27) and 0.21 versus glibenclamide (0.03 to 1.48). The authors conclude that when added to metformin, gliclazide was associated with the lowest hypoglycaemia risk among the newer-generation sulfonylureas.
cards.watchOut: Most comparisons are indirect, hypoglycaemia was reported only as an adverse event with varying definitions across trials, and the key gliclazide-versus-glimepiride interval (0.13 to 1.27) includes no difference — the ranking is suggestive, not proven, and it is the direct GUIDE trial that carries the weight on this shelf.
cards.source: Andersen et al. Hypoglycaemia when adding sulphonylurea to metformin: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. British journal of clinical pharmacology. 2016. PMID: 27426428. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal control, fewer lows on gliclazide MR — one large direct trial plus a consistent network ranking
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal control, fewer lows on gliclazide MR — one large direct trial plus a consistent network ranking
cards.people: One 845-patient double-blind head-to-head trial (GUIDE) and one network meta-analysis of 27 trials (16,260 patients) of sulfonylureas added to metformin.
cards.result: Glycaemic control: identical in GUIDE (final HbA1c 7.2% both arms, difference −0.06%). shelves.title: Glycated albumin in dialysis diabetes: it predicts death (HR 1.02 per unit across 25,932 patients) where A1C is distorted — but no trial shows managing to it helps
shelves.question: In diabetes treated with dialysis, does glycated albumin reflect glycaemic control and predict mortality better than HbA1c, which is distorted by anaemia and uraemia?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/mortality · Glycation End Products, Advanced · Humans · Kidney Failure, Chronic/mortality · Renal Dialysis · Serum Albumin/metabolism · Glycated Serum Albumin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as a prognostic marker, not as proven better day-to-day control guidance. The anchor record (Freedman BI, PMID: 22723586) is a point-counterpoint narrative, not a cohort study: it argues that HbA1c is distorted in end-stage kidney disease — where dialysis mortality is about 20% per year and both high and low A1C levels have been associated with mortality in large diabetic dialysis cohorts — and proposes glycated albumin as the preferred marker, a position the paired counterpoint disputes. The pooled data come from a meta-analysis of 12 studies and 25,932 dialysis patients with diabetes (Copur S et al., PMID: 32862262): higher glycated albumin was associated with all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.02 per unit, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.03; P < 0.001) irrespective of dialysis type, but not significantly with cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.06) or cardiovascular events (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.09). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glycated albumin carries real prognostic signal in diabetic dialysis patients where HbA1c is distorted, but the per-unit effect is small and no trial shows that managing to glycated albumin improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Freedman 2012 point-counterpoint: A1C is distorted in dialysis and both its high and low levels track with death — glycated albumin proposed instead, and disputed in the same article
cards.summary: Freedman 2012 point-counterpoint: A1C is distorted in dialysis and both its high and low levels track with death — glycated albumin proposed instead, and disputed in the same article
cards.people: A two-part point-counterpoint narrative on glycaemic markers in advanced nephropathy and end-stage kidney disease, in a dialysis population of whom about half are diabetic and who experience mortality of about 20% per year; Freedman argues the case for glycated albumin and Kalantar-Zadeh defends A1C in the paired counterpoint.
cards.result: The record reports no primary data. Its factual claims are that A1C is the unquestioned gold standard outside dialysis; that in large cohorts of diabetic dialysis patients A1C at both higher and lower levels was associated with mortality; and that the metabolic dysregulation of dialysis creates a critical need for accurate glycaemic assays that relate to cardiovascular endpoints. Freedman concludes glycated albumin may be the preferred glycaemic marker in dialysis subjects; the counterpoint maintains A1C as the gold standard for glycaemic management in dialysis.
cards.watchOut: This is an argued position piece with an opposing counterpoint, carded because it is the named anchor for the question — it must never be cited as outcome data. It contains no glycated albumin measurements, no hazard ratios and no head-to-head accuracy comparison; every number on this shelf that quantifies prediction comes from the meta-analysis card.

cards.headline: Copur 2021 meta-analysis (25,932 dialysis patients): higher glycated albumin predicted all-cause mortality (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.03) but not cardiovascular mortality or events
cards.summary: Copur 2021 meta-analysis (25,932 dialysis patients): higher glycated albumin predicted all-cause mortality (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.03) but not cardiovascular mortality or events
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies including 25,932 dialysis patients with diabetes mellitus, with maximum follow-up of 11 years, searched to February 2020; glycated albumin reflects glycaemic status over the preceding 2–3 weeks.
cards.result: Higher glycated albumin levels were associated with all-cause mortality in dialysis patients with diabetes (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.03; P < 0.001), irrespective of the type of dialysis. Higher glycated albumin was not significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.06; P = 0.15) or with fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.09; P = 0.31), although both estimates trended in the same direction.
cards.watchOut: A hazard ratio of 1.02 is per unit of glycated albumin as modelled in the source studies — statistically robust across 25,932 patients but small per unit, and the analysis does not show glycated albumin outperforming HbA1c in a direct discrimination comparison, nor that acting on it changes outcomes. Observational cohorts throughout: confounding by nutrition, inflammation and albumin turnover (which itself alters glycated albumin) cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Copur et al. Serum glycated albumin predicts all-cause mortality in dialysis patients with diabetes mellitus: meta-analysis and systematic review of a predictive biomarker. cards.headline: Synthesis: glycated albumin predicts death in diabetic dialysis patients where A1C misleads — a prognostic signal, not yet a management strategy
cards.summary: Synthesis: glycated albumin predicts death in diabetic dialysis patients where A1C misleads — a prognostic signal, not yet a management strategy
cards.people: One point-counterpoint narrative (Freedman 2012) framing the A1C problem in dialysis, and one meta-analysis of 12 cohort studies (25,932 patients) quantifying glycated albumin and mortality.
cards.result: All-cause mortality: HR 1.02 per unit higher glycated albumin (95% CI 1.01 to 1.03). Cardiovascular mortality: HR 1.03 (0.99 to 1.06), not significant. Cardiovascular events: HR 1.03 (0.97 to 1.09), not significant. Direct evidence that glycated albumin reflects control better than A1C, or that targeting it improves outcomes: none in these records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) as a prognostic marker only.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf as showing glycated albumin is a better measure of glycaemic control than HbA1c — neither card performs that head-to-head accuracy test; the meta-analysis shows mortality prediction only, and the narrative shows the question is contested. Tier C is set because the anchor is a narrative and the quantitative evidence is observational.

shelves.title: SURPASS-4: tirzepatide beat insulin glargine on HbA1c by about 1 percentage point in high-cardiovascular-risk type 2 diabetes — with less hypoglycaemia and no excess of cardiovascular events, in an open-label trial
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes on background metformin-based therapy, does once-weekly tirzepatide lower HbA1c and weight more than once-daily insulin glargine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose · Body Weight/drug effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Female · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin Glargine/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Tirzepatide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large open-label phase 3 trial. In 1,995 treated patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or high risk, inadequately controlled on oral agents (Del Prato S et al., PMID: 34672967), HbA1c at 52 weeks fell by 2.43% on tirzepatide 10 mg and 2.58% on 15 mg versus 1.44% on titrated insulin glargine (estimated differences −0.99% and −1.14%). Hypoglycaemia (glucose <54 mg/dL or severe) occurred in 6–9% on tirzepatide versus 19% on glargine. Adjudicated MACE-4 events were not increased on tirzepatide (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.08), with 25 deaths (3%) on tirzepatide versus 35 (4%) on glargine — reassuring on safety, but the confidence interval is too wide to claim cardiovascular benefit, and this library does not stamp one from it. Gastrointestinal effects were the price: nausea 12–23%, diarrhoea 13–22% and vomiting 5–9% on tirzepatide versus 2%, 4% and 2% on glargine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clearly better glycaemic control than basal insulin with less hypoglycaemia in a single open-label trial; a cardiovascular-outcome benefit is not shown by this record.

cards.headline: SURPASS-4 (Del Prato 2021): HbA1c −2.43% and −2.58% on tirzepatide 10/15 mg versus −1.44% on glargine; hypoglycaemia 6–9% versus 19%
cards.summary: SURPASS-4 (Del Prato 2021): HbA1c −2.43% and −2.58% on tirzepatide 10/15 mg versus −1.44% on glargine; hypoglycaemia 6–9% versus 19%
cards.people: 2,002 randomised (1,995 treated) adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, sulfonylurea and/or SGLT2 inhibitor, baseline HbA1c 7.5–10.5%, BMI at least 25 kg/m², and established cardiovascular disease or high cardiovascular risk, at 187 sites in 14 countries; once-weekly tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg versus once-daily insulin glargine titrated to fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL, for at least 52 weeks (up to 104) with adjudication of major adverse cardiovascular events.
cards.result: At 52 weeks mean HbA1c change was −2.43% on tirzepatide 10 mg and −2.58% on 15 mg versus −1.44% on glargine (estimated treatment differences −0.99% [97.5% CI −1.13 to −0.86] and −1.14% [−1.28 to −1.00]); the 0.3% non-inferiority margin was met for both doses. Hypoglycaemia (glucose <54 mg/dL or severe) occurred in 6–9% on tirzepatide versus 19% on glargine — and in 1–3% versus 16% among participants not on sulfonylureas. Adjudicated MACE-4 occurred in 109 participants and was not increased on tirzepatide (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.08); deaths were 25 (3%) on tirzepatide and 35 (4%) on glargine. Nausea (12–23%), diarrhoea (13–22%), decreased appetite (9–11%) and vomiting (5–9%) were more frequent on tirzepatide than glargine (2%, 4%, under 1% and 2%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label design (injections versus titrated insulin cannot be blinded easily), a glycaemic primary endpoint, and a MACE analysis powered for safety rather than benefit — the 0.74 point estimate must not be read as proven event reduction. Glargine titration to a fasting target below 100 mg/dL is a real-world-reasonable comparator, which makes the glycaemic gap more credible, not less.
cards.source: Del Prato S et al. Tirzepatide versus insulin glargine in type 2 diabetes and increased cardiovascular risk (SURPASS-4): a randomised, open-label, parallel-group, multicentre, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34672967. Registry ID: NCT03730662. shelves.title: SURPASS-1: tirzepatide alone lowered HbA1c by 1.87–2.07% versus +0.04% on placebo in drug-naive type 2 diabetes — and 31–52% reached an HbA1c below 5.7%
shelves.question: In drug-naive type 2 diabetes, does once-weekly tirzepatide monotherapy lower HbA1c and weight versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Body Weight/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · India · Japan · Male · Middle Aged · North America · Treatment Outcome · Tirzepatide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind placebo trial in early, mild diabetes. In 478 adults whose type 2 diabetes was managed by diet and exercise alone (mean baseline HbA1c 7.9%, mean duration 4.7 years; Rosenstock J et al., PMID: 34186022), 40 weeks of once-weekly tirzepatide lowered HbA1c by 1.87% (5 mg), 1.89% (10 mg) and 2.07% (15 mg) versus a 0.04% rise on placebo (treatment differences −1.91% to −2.11%, all p<0.0001); 87–92% reached HbA1c below 7.0% versus 20%, and 31–52% reached below 5.7% versus 1%. Weight fell dose-dependently by 7.0 to 9.5 kg. Gastrointestinal events were the main cost (nausea 12–18% versus 6%, diarrhoea 12–14% versus 8%), with no clinically significant or severe hypoglycaemia reported on tirzepatide. These are large effects in the easiest population to treat — short-duration diabetes on no medicines — and say nothing about durability beyond 40 weeks or about outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): potent monotherapy glycaemic and weight effects in a single placebo trial in early diabetes.

cards.headline: SURPASS-1 (Rosenstock 2021): HbA1c −1.87% to −2.07% across doses versus +0.04% on placebo; below-5.7% target reached by 31–52% versus 1%
cards.summary: SURPASS-1 (Rosenstock 2021): HbA1c −1.87% to −2.07% across doses versus +0.04% on placebo; below-5.7% target reached by 31–52% versus 1%
cards.people: 478 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise alone and naive to injectable therapy (mean HbA1c 7.9%, age 54.1 years, diabetes duration 4.7 years, BMI 31.9 kg/m²), at 52 centres in India, Japan, Mexico and the USA, randomised double-blind to once-weekly tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg or placebo for 40 weeks.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell by 1.87% (5 mg), 1.89% (10 mg) and 2.07% (15 mg) versus a rise of 0.04% on placebo (estimated treatment differences −1.91%, −1.93% and −2.11%; all p<0.0001). HbA1c below 7.0% was reached by 87–92% on tirzepatide versus 20% on placebo; below 6.5% by 81–86% versus 10%; and below 5.7% by 31–52% versus 1%. Bodyweight fell dose-dependently by 7.0 to 9.5 kg. Nausea occurred in 12–18% versus 6%, diarrhoea in 12–14% versus 8% and vomiting in 2–6% versus 2%; no clinically significant (<54 mg/dL) or severe hypoglycaemia was reported with tirzepatide. One death occurred in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparator in patients on no background therapy maximises the visible effect; baseline HbA1c of 7.9% and 4.7-year duration are far milder than typical clinic populations, 14% discontinued study drug, and 40 weeks cannot speak to durability, complications, or what happens on stopping.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Efficacy and safety of a novel dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist tirzepatide in patients with type 2 diabetes (SURPASS-1): a double-blind, randomised, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34186022. shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Female · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/administration & dosage · Glycated Hemoglobin/drug effects · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin, Long-Acting/therapeutic use · Internationality · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Tirzepatide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large open-label trial against a modern basal insulin. In 1,437 insulin-naive patients on metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor (Ludvik B et al., PMID: 34370970), HbA1c at 52 weeks fell by 1.93% (tirzepatide 5 mg), 2.20% (10 mg) and 2.37% (15 mg) versus 1.34% on titrated insulin degludec (treatment differences −0.59% to −1.04%, p<0.0001 for all doses), and HbA1c below 7.0% was reached by 82–93% versus 61%. The weight contrast was stark: −7.5 kg to −12.9 kg on tirzepatide versus +2.3 kg on degludec. Hypoglycaemia (<54 mg/dL or severe) occurred in 1–2% on tirzepatide versus 7% on degludec. The trade was gastrointestinal: nausea 12–24%, diarrhoea 15–17% and vomiting 6–10% on tirzepatide versus 2%, 4% and 1% on degludec, and treatment discontinuation for adverse events was more common on tirzepatide. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): better glycaemia, large weight advantage and less hypoglycaemia than degludec in a single open-label trial, paid for in gastrointestinal tolerability.

cards.headline: SURPASS-3 (Ludvik 2021): HbA1c −1.93% to −2.37% versus −1.34%; weight −7.5 to −12.9 kg versus +2.3 kg on degludec
cards.summary: SURPASS-3 (Ludvik 2021): HbA1c −1.93% to −2.37% versus −1.34%; weight −7.5 to −12.9 kg versus +2.3 kg on degludec
cards.people: 1,437 treated insulin-naive adults with type 2 diabetes (baseline HbA1c 7.0–10.5%, mean 8.17%; BMI at least 25 kg/m²) on metformin alone or with an SGLT2 inhibitor for at least 3 months, at 122 sites in 13 countries, randomised open-label to once-weekly tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg or once-daily insulin degludec titrated weekly to fasting glucose below 5.0 mmol/L (90 mg/dL) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c reductions at week 52 were 1.93% (5 mg), 2.20% (10 mg) and 2.37% (15 mg) versus 1.34% on degludec (estimated treatment differences −0.59% to −1.04%; p<0.0001 for all doses; the 0.3% non-inferiority margin was met). HbA1c below 7.0% was achieved by 82–93% on tirzepatide versus 61% on degludec. From a baseline of 94.3 kg, weight fell by 7.5 to 12.9 kg on tirzepatide and rose by 2.3 kg on degludec (differences −9.8 to −15.2 kg; p<0.0001). Hypoglycaemia (<54 mg/dL or severe) was reported in 1%, 1% and 2% on tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg versus 7% on degludec. Nausea (12–24%), diarrhoea (15–17%), decreased appetite (6–12%) and vomiting (6–10%) were more frequent on tirzepatide than degludec (2%, 4%, 1% and 1%); discontinuation for adverse events was more common on tirzepatide.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a treat-to-target insulin comparator whose dose depends on titration behaviour; the glycaemic and weight endpoints are surrogates, follow-up is 52 weeks, and the gastrointestinal discontinuation excess is the honest counterweight to the efficacy gap.
cards.source: Ludvik B et al. Once-weekly tirzepatide versus once-daily insulin degludec as add-on to metformin with or without SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with type 2 diabetes (SURPASS-3): a randomised, open-label, parallel-group, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34370970. Registry ID: NCT03882970. shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes already on insulin glargine, does adding once-weekly tirzepatide improve HbA1c and weight versus glargine titration alone?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Glycemic Control/methods · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin Glargine/administration & dosage · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Weight Loss/drug effects · Tirzepatide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one placebo-controlled add-on trial. In 475 adults inadequately controlled on insulin glargine with or without metformin (mean HbA1c 8.31%; Dahl D et al., PMID: 35133415), adding once-weekly tirzepatide for 40 weeks lowered HbA1c by 2.11% (5 mg), 2.40% (10 mg) and 2.34% (15 mg) versus 0.86% on placebo added to titrated glargine (differences −1.24% to −1.53%, P<0.001), and 85–90% reached HbA1c below 7% versus 34%. Weight moved the 'wrong' way for insulin therapy — in the patient's favour: −5.4 to −8.8 kg on tirzepatide versus +1.6 kg on placebo (differences −7.1 to −10.5 kg). The costs were gastrointestinal (diarrhoea 12–21% versus 10%; nausea 13–18% versus 3%) and persistence: premature discontinuation was 10%, 12% and 18% across the tirzepatide doses versus 3% on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large add-on glycaemic and weight effect in a single trial, with tolerability — not efficacy — as the limiting factor.

cards.headline: SURPASS-5 (Dahl 2022): HbA1c −2.40% on tirzepatide 10 mg versus −0.86% on placebo; weight −7.5 kg versus +1.6 kg
cards.summary: SURPASS-5 (Dahl 2022): HbA1c −2.40% on tirzepatide 10 mg versus −0.86% on placebo; weight −7.5 kg versus +1.6 kg
cards.people: 475 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on once-daily insulin glargine with or without metformin (mean age 60.6 years, mean HbA1c 8.31%), at 45 centres in 8 countries, randomised double-blind to once-weekly tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg or volume-matched placebo added to titrated glargine for 40 weeks; 451 (94.9%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change at week 40 was −2.11% (5 mg), −2.40% (10 mg) and −2.34% (15 mg) versus −0.86% on placebo (differences −1.24% [95% CI −1.48 to −1.01], −1.53% [97.5% CI −1.80 to −1.27] and −1.47% [−1.75 to −1.20]; P<0.001 for all). HbA1c below 7% was achieved by 85–90% on tirzepatide versus 34% on placebo. Weight changed by −5.4, −7.5 and −8.8 kg versus +1.6 kg (differences −7.1 to −10.5 kg; P<0.001). Diarrhoea occurred in 12–21% versus 10% and nausea in 13–18% versus 3%. Treatment was discontinued prematurely by 10%, 12% and 18% on tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg versus 3% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Forty weeks, surrogate endpoints, and a discontinuation gradient that rises with dose — the trial's own numbers say a substantial minority cannot stay on the drug, so intention-to-treat averages flatter real-world persistence. Glargine continued to be titrated in both arms, which is the right comparator for the add-on question.
cards.source: Dahl D et al. shelves.title: SUSTAIN 7: semaglutide beat dulaglutide head-to-head at both dose pairs — HbA1c by an extra 0.40–0.41 points and weight by an extra 2.3–3.6 kg, with gastrointestinal events in 43–44%
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, how do once-weekly semaglutide and dulaglutide compare head-to-head on HbA1c and weight?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Body Weight · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptides/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/therapeutic use · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one open-label head-to-head trial, consistent across both dose pairs. In 1,201 patients on metformin alone (Pratley RE et al., PMID: 29397376), at 40 weeks semaglutide 0.5 mg lowered HbA1c by 1.5 points versus 1.1 on dulaglutide 0.75 mg (difference −0.40 points, p<0.0001), and semaglutide 1.0 mg by 1.8 versus 1.4 on dulaglutide 1.5 mg (difference −0.41, p<0.0001). Weight showed the same pattern: −4.6 versus −2.3 kg at the low doses (difference −2.26 kg) and −6.5 versus −3.0 kg at the high doses (difference −3.55 kg), both p<0.0001. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequent adverse events, occurring in 43–44% of patients on semaglutide. The comparison is between the doses as marketed at the time — dulaglutide has since been tested at 3.0 and 4.5 mg (AWARD-11, on its own shelf) — so this shelf settles semaglutide versus dulaglutide 0.75/1.5 mg, not versus today's higher dulaglutide doses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): semaglutide the stronger drug at the compared doses, in a single open-label trial.

cards.headline: SUSTAIN 7 (Pratley 2018): HbA1c −1.5 versus −1.1 (low doses) and −1.8 versus −1.4 (high doses); weight −4.6 versus −2.3 kg and −6.5 versus −3.0 kg
cards.summary: SUSTAIN 7 (Pratley 2018): HbA1c −1.5 versus −1.1 (low doses) and −1.8 versus −1.4 (high doses); weight −4.6 versus −2.3 kg and −6.5 versus −3.0 kg
cards.people: 1,201 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.5%) on metformin monotherapy, at 194 sites in 16 countries, randomised open-label to once-weekly semaglutide 0.5 mg, dulaglutide 0.75 mg, semaglutide 1.0 mg or dulaglutide 1.5 mg for 40 weeks; the trial was powered for HbA1c non-inferiority (margin 0.4%) and weight superiority; 72 patients (6%) withdrew.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c fell by 1.5 points on semaglutide 0.5 mg versus 1.1 on dulaglutide 0.75 mg (estimated difference −0.40 points [95% CI −0.55 to −0.25]; p<0.0001) and by 1.8 on semaglutide 1.0 mg versus 1.4 on dulaglutide 1.5 mg (difference −0.41 [−0.57 to −0.25]; p<0.0001). Weight fell by 4.6 versus 2.3 kg (difference −2.26 kg [−3.02 to −1.51]) and by 6.5 versus 3.0 kg (difference −3.55 kg [−4.32 to −2.78]), both p<0.0001. Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequently reported adverse events, in 129 (43%) of 301 patients on semaglutide 0.5 mg and 133 (44%) of 300 on semaglutide 1.0 mg.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 40 weeks, surrogate endpoints — and a moving comparator: dulaglutide 1.5 mg was its top dose then, but 3.0/4.5 mg doses now exist, so the verdict is dose-pair-specific. The record's abstract is truncated on dulaglutide-arm gastrointestinal rates, so no comparative tolerability claim is made on this shelf.
cards.source: Pratley RE et al. Semaglutide versus dulaglutide once weekly in patients with type 2 diabetes (SUSTAIN 7): a randomised, open-label, phase 3b trial. Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. 2018. PMID: 29397376. Registry ID: NCT02648204. randomised phase 3b trial (pratley 2018, sustain 7) 1,201 adults with type 2 diabetes (hba1c 7.0–10.5%) on metformin monotherapy, at 194 sites in 16 countries, randomised open-label to once-weekly semaglutide 0.5 mg, dulaglutide 0.75 mg, semaglutide 1.0 mg or dulaglutide 1.5 mg for 40 weeks; the trial was powered for hba1c non-inferiority (margin 0.4%) and weight superiority; 72 patients (6%) withdrew. mean hba1c fell by 1.5 points on semaglutide 0.5 mg versus 1.1 on dulaglutide 0.75 mg (estimated difference −0.40 points [95% ci −0.55 to −0.25]; p<0.0001) and by 1.8 on semaglutide 1.0 mg versus 1.4 on dulaglutide 1.5 mg (difference −0.41 [−0.57 to −0.25]; p<0.0001). weight fell by 4.6 versus 2.3 kg (difference −2.26 kg [−3.02 to −1.51]) and by 6.5 versus 3.0 kg (difference −3.55 kg [−4.32 to −2.78]), both p<0.0001. gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequently reported adverse events, in 129 (43%) of 301 patients on semaglutide 0.5 mg and 133 (44%) of 300 on semaglutide 1.0 mg. open-label, 40 weeks, surrogate endpoints — and a moving comparator: dulaglutide 1.5 mg was its top dose then, but 3.0/4.5 mg doses now exist, so the verdict is dose-pair-specific. the record's abstract is truncated on dulaglutide-arm gastrointestinal rates, so no comparative tolerability claim is made on this shelf. pratley re et al. semaglutide versus dulaglutide once weekly in patients with type 2 diabetes (sustain 7): a randomised, open-label, phase 3b trial. lancet diabetes & endocrinology. 2018. pmid: 29397376. registry id: nct02648204. mesh: blood glucose/analysis · body weight · diabetes mellitus, type 2/drug therapy · female · glucagon-like peptides/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · humans · hypoglycemic agents/therapeutic use · immunoglobulin fc fragments/therapeutic use · male · middle aged · prognosis · recombinant fusion proteins/therapeutic use · semaglutide
