shelves.title: PIONEER 2: oral semaglutide beat empagliflozin on HbA1c at 26 weeks (−1.3% versus −0.9%) — but weight superiority was not confirmed until the 52-week on-treatment analysis
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes on metformin, does once-daily oral semaglutide lower HbA1c as much as empagliflozin 25 mg?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Benzhydryl Compounds/administration & dosage · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptides/administration & dosage · Glucosides/administration & dosage · Glycated Hemoglobin/drug effects · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Male · Metformin/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss/drug effects · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the endpoint and the week. In 822 patients uncontrolled on metformin (Rodbard HW et al., PMID: 31530666), oral semaglutide 14 mg daily beat empagliflozin 25 mg on the primary HbA1c endpoint at 26 weeks: −1.3% versus −0.9% (treatment-policy difference −0.4%, P<0.0001), a gap that persisted at 52 weeks. But the confirmatory weight endpoint failed at 26 weeks — superior weight loss was not confirmed under the treatment-policy estimand — and only at 52 weeks, in the on-treatment (trial-product) estimand, was weight significantly better on oral semaglutide (−4.7 versus −3.8 kg, P=0.0114). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common with oral semaglutide. So: yes for blood sugar, from 26 weeks onward; for weight, only later and only counting patients who stayed on treatment. Neither arm's cardiovascular-outcome evidence is tested here — empagliflozin's outcome data come from its own outcomes trial, and a glycaemic head-to-head does not transfer them. PROPOSED SPLIT: HbA1c superiority shown; weight superiority estimand- and time-dependent.

cards.headline: PIONEER 2 (Rodbard 2019): HbA1c −1.3% versus −0.9% at 26 weeks (P<0.0001); weight superiority not confirmed at 26 weeks, significant at 52 weeks on-treatment (−4.7 versus −3.8 kg)
cards.summary: PIONEER 2 (Rodbard 2019): HbA1c −1.3% versus −0.9% at 26 weeks (P<0.0001); weight superiority not confirmed at 26 weeks, significant at 52 weeks on-treatment (−4.7 versus −3.8 kg)
cards.people: 822 patients with type 2 diabetes uncontrolled on metformin, randomised open-label to once-daily oral semaglutide 14 mg (n=412) or empagliflozin 25 mg (n=410) for 52 weeks; primary endpoint HbA1c change at week 26, confirmatory secondary endpoint weight change, each reported under treatment-policy and trial-product (on-treatment) estimands; 97.1% and 94.4% completed the trial.
cards.result: Oral semaglutide gave superior HbA1c reductions at week 26 (treatment policy −1.3% versus −0.9%, estimated difference −0.4% [95% CI −0.6 to −0.3]; P<0.0001; trial product −1.4% versus −0.9%, difference −0.5%), and the HbA1c advantage remained significant at week 52 under both estimands (P<0.0001). Superior weight loss was not confirmed at week 26 (treatment policy), but at week 52 the trial-product estimand favoured oral semaglutide (−4.7 versus −3.8 kg; P=0.0114). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common with oral semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: Open-label; the weight verdict flips with the estimand, which is exactly why the stamp is SPLIT rather than benefit — the treatment-policy analysis (what happens to everyone randomised, including those who stop) is the more honest lens for a daily pill with gastrointestinal effects and strict dosing conditions.
cards.source: Rodbard HW et al. Oral Semaglutide Versus Empagliflozin in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Uncontrolled on Metformin: The PIONEER 2 Trial. Diabetes Care. 2019. PMID: 31530666. Registry ID: NCT02863328. shelves.title: AWARD-11: escalating dulaglutide from 1.5 mg to 4.5 mg bought an extra 0.24–0.34 points of HbA1c and 1.6 kg of weight — the 3.0 mg step was significant only in the on-treatment analysis
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on dulaglutide 1.5 mg, does escalating to 3.0 mg or 4.5 mg lower HbA1c and weight further?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucagon-Like Peptides/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/adverse effects · Metformin/adverse effects · Recombinant Fusion Proteins · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest gains from a higher dose of the same drug. In 1,842 patients on metformin (mean HbA1c 8.6%; Frias JP et al., PMID: 33397768), dulaglutide 4.5 mg lowered HbA1c at 36 weeks by 1.77% versus 1.54% on 1.5 mg under the treatment-regimen estimand (difference −0.24%, P<0.001) and by 1.87% versus 1.53% on-treatment (difference −0.34%). The 3.0 mg step was superior only on-treatment (difference −0.17%, P=0.003) and not under the treatment-regimen estimand (difference −0.10%, P=0.096). Weight at 4.5 mg fell 4.6 kg versus 3.0 kg (difference −1.6 kg, P<0.001). Nausea rose with dose (13.4%, 15.6%, 16.4% across 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 mg) and vomiting likewise (5.6%, 8.3%, 9.3%). Note the candidate question frames this as escalation in patients already on 1.5 mg; the trial randomised metformin-treated patients to the three doses in parallel rather than stepping up non-responders, so it answers 'higher dose versus standard dose', not 'rescue after failing 1.5 mg'. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dose escalation to 4.5 mg gives a small, dose-ordered improvement; whether it beats switching drugs is a different question this trial does not ask.

cards.headline: AWARD-11 (Frias 2021): HbA1c −1.77% on 4.5 mg versus −1.54% on 1.5 mg (regimen estimand); 3.0 mg superior only in the efficacy estimand
cards.summary: AWARD-11 (Frias 2021): HbA1c −1.77% on 4.5 mg versus −1.54% on 1.5 mg (regimen estimand); 3.0 mg superior only in the efficacy estimand
cards.people: 1,842 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (mean baseline HbA1c 8.6%, BMI 34.2 kg/m²), randomly assigned to once-weekly dulaglutide 1.5 mg, 3.0 mg or 4.5 mg for 52 weeks; primary objective superiority of 3.0 and/or 4.5 mg over 1.5 mg for HbA1c at 36 weeks, reported under treatment-regimen and efficacy (on-treatment) estimands.
cards.result: At 36 weeks dulaglutide 4.5 mg was superior to 1.5 mg for HbA1c under both estimands (treatment regimen −1.77 versus −1.54%, difference −0.24%, P<0.001; efficacy −1.87 versus −1.53%, difference −0.34%, P<0.001). Dulaglutide 3.0 mg was superior under the efficacy estimand (difference −0.17%, P=0.003) but not the treatment-regimen estimand (difference −0.10%, P=0.096). Weight loss at 4.5 mg exceeded 1.5 mg at 36 weeks under both estimands (−4.6 versus −3.0 kg, difference −1.6 kg, P<0.001). Nausea through 36 weeks: 13.4% (1.5 mg), 15.6% (3.0 mg), 16.4% (4.5 mg); vomiting 5.6%, 8.3% and 9.3%.
cards.watchOut: A parallel-dose trial, not a step-up trial in 1.5 mg non-responders — the population the question names; effect sizes for doubling or tripling the dose are small (a quarter to a third of an HbA1c point), and the 3.0 mg result depends on which estimand you believe.
cards.source: Frias JP et al. Efficacy and Safety of Dulaglutide 3.0 mg and 4.5 mg Versus Dulaglutide 1.5 mg in Metformin-Treated Patients With Type 2 Diabetes in a Randomized Controlled Trial (AWARD-11). Diabetes Care. 2021. shelves.title: SUSTAIN 11: once-weekly semaglutide matched and slightly beat three-times-daily insulin aspart on HbA1c (−1.5 versus −1.2 points) — with weight down 4.1 kg instead of up 2.8 kg
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes on basal insulin plus metformin, does adding once-weekly semaglutide control HbA1c as well as adding three-times-daily insulin aspart?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose · Body Weight · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/chemically induced/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucagon-Like Peptides · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced/prevention & control · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Insulin Aspart/therapeutic use · Insulin Glargine/adverse effects · Metformin/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one open-label trial against the burdensome standard. In 1,748 adults on optimised insulin glargine plus metformin whose HbA1c remained 7.5–10.0% (Kellerer M et al., PMID: 35546450), adding once-weekly semaglutide lowered HbA1c over 52 weeks by 1.5 points versus 1.2 points on three-times-daily insulin aspart (difference −0.29 points [95% CI −0.38 to −0.20]; P<0.0001 for non-inferiority). Weight diverged sharply: −4.1 kg on semaglutide versus +2.8 kg on aspart (difference −6.99 kg [−7.41 to −6.57]). Severe hypoglycaemic episodes were few in both groups with no statistically significant difference. Adverse events were more frequent on semaglutide (58.5% versus 52.1%), mostly mild to moderate. The candidate question's framing — control 'as well as' prandial insulin — is answered yes and slightly better, with one weekly injection replacing three daily ones and weight falling instead of rising; what the trial cannot show is whether that holds beyond 52 weeks or in patients whose post-prandial excursions are the dominant problem. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): non-inferior-to-superior glycaemia with a large weight advantage over basal-bolus intensification, in a single open-label trial.

cards.headline: SUSTAIN 11 (Kellerer 2022): HbA1c −1.5 versus −1.2 points (difference −0.29); weight −4.1 kg versus +2.8 kg (difference −6.99 kg)
cards.summary: SUSTAIN 11 (Kellerer 2022): HbA1c −1.5 versus −1.2 points (difference −0.29); weight −4.1 kg versus +2.8 kg (difference −6.99 kg)
cards.people: 1,748 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c above 7.5% to 10.0% after a 12-week run-in optimising once-daily insulin glargine U100; HbA1c at randomisation 8.6%, weight 87.9 kg), randomised open-label 1:1 to once-weekly semaglutide or three-times-daily insulin aspart, each added to optimised glargine and metformin for 52 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by 1.5 points on semaglutide and 1.2 points on aspart (estimated difference −0.29 points [95% CI −0.38 to −0.20]; P<0.0001 for non-inferiority). Weight changed by −4.1 kg on semaglutide versus +2.8 kg on aspart (difference −6.99 kg [−7.41 to −6.57]). Few severe hypoglycaemic episodes were recorded in either group, with no statistically significant difference between groups. Adverse events occurred in 58.5% on semaglutide versus 52.1% on aspart, most mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and industry-run, with a run-in that pre-optimised glargine — real clinics add prandial insulin to unoptimised basal regimens too. The record reports severe hypoglycaemia only qualitatively ('few', no significant difference), so no precise hypoglycaemia advantage is claimed here; and 52 weeks of a surrogate endpoint cannot settle long-term beta-cell or complication questions.
cards.source: Kellerer M et al. Effect of once-weekly semaglutide versus thrice-daily insulin aspart, both as add-on to metformin and optimized insulin glargine treatment in participants with type 2 diabetes (SUSTAIN 11): A randomized, open-label, multinational, phase 3b trial. shelves.title: Linagliptin versus glimepiride in CAROLINA: cardiovascular events tied at 11.8% versus 12.0% over 6.3 years — but hypoglycaemia in 10.6% versus 37.7%, the widest safety gap in the gliptin trials
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, does linagliptin cause fewer cardiovascular events or less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride over years of follow-up?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for cardiovascular events / LIKELY (benefit) for hypoglycaemia. CAROLINA (Rosenstock J et al., PMID: 31536101) is the only active-comparator cardiovascular outcomes trial of a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor: 6,033 adults with relatively early type 2 diabetes and elevated cardiovascular risk were randomised double-blind to linagliptin 5 mg daily or glimepiride 1–4 mg daily on top of usual care, and followed for a median 6.3 years. On the primary composite — cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke — the drugs tied: 356 of 3,023 (11.8%) on linagliptin versus 362 of 3,010 (12.0%) on glimepiride (hazard ratio 0.98, 95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; P<.001 for noninferiority, P=.76 for superiority). On hypoglycaemia they did not tie at all: at least one hypoglycaemic adverse event occurred in 320 (10.6%) on linagliptin versus 1,132 (37.7%) on glimepiride (hazard ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.21–0.26). Overall adverse events were similar (93.4% versus 94.9%), as was adjudicated-confirmed acute pancreatitis (15 participants, 0.5%, versus 16, 0.5%). So the head-to-head answer splits cleanly: linagliptin buys no cardiovascular advantage over modern glimepiride, and glimepiride is acquitted of excess cardiovascular events in this trial — what linagliptin buys is freedom from most of the hypoglycaemia a sulfonylurea causes. PROPOSED SPLIT: cardiovascular events — the treatment made no difference over 6.3 years; hypoglycaemia — a large, definitive benefit for linagliptin, from a single large trial (Tier C).

cards.headline: Rosenstock 2019 (CAROLINA): primary cardiovascular outcome 11.8% on linagliptin versus 12.0% on glimepiride (HR 0.98, 95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; noninferior, not superior) — hypoglycaemia 10.6% versus 37.7% (HR 0.23)
cards.summary: Rosenstock 2019 (CAROLINA): primary cardiovascular outcome 11.8% on linagliptin versus 12.0% on glimepiride (HR 0.98, 95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; noninferior, not superior) — hypoglycaemia 10.6% versus 37.7% (HR 0.23)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, active-controlled noninferiority trial (Rosenstock 2019, CAROLINA)
cards.people: 6,042 participants randomised (6,033 treated and analysed; mean age 64.0 years, 2,414 [39.9%] women, mean glycated hemoglobin 7.2%, median duration of diabetes 6.3 years, 42% with macrovascular disease, 59% had undergone metformin monotherapy) at 607 hospital and primary care sites in 43 countries; adults with type 2 diabetes, glycated hemoglobin 6.5% to 8.5%, and elevated cardiovascular risk (documented atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, multiple cardiovascular risk factors, age at least 70 years, or evidence of microvascular complications), randomised to linagliptin 5 mg once daily (n=3,023) or glimepiride 1 to 4 mg once daily (n=3,010) in addition to usual care, with investigators encouraged to intensify glycemic treatment (primarily metformin, α-glucosidase inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, or insulin) as clinically needed; screening November 2010 to December 2012, follow-up ended August 2018, median follow-up 6.3 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome — time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke — occurred in 356 of 3,023 participants (11.8%) in the linagliptin group and 362 of 3,010 (12.0%) in the glimepiride group (hazard ratio 0.98, 95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; P<.001 for noninferiority, the criterion being an upper confidence limit below 1.3), meeting noninferiority but not superiority (P=.76), the absolute rates printed alongside the relative effect. At least 1 episode of hypoglycemic adverse events occurred in 320 participants (10.6%) in the linagliptin group and 1,132 (37.7%) in the glimepiride group (hazard ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.21–0.26). Adverse events occurred in 2,822 participants (93.4%) on linagliptin and 2,856 (94.9%) on glimepiride, with adjudicated-confirmed acute pancreatitis in 15 participants (0.5%) versus 16 (0.5%). The authors' conclusion: among adults with relatively early type 2 diabetes and elevated cardiovascular risk, linagliptin compared with glimepiride over a median 6.3 years resulted in a noninferior risk of a composite cardiovascular outcome.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not equivalence proven to the last decimal: the confidence interval (0.84–1.14) still allows a modest effect in either direction, and the trial was designed and powered around the 1.3 noninferiority margin, not around detecting a small superiority. The comparator matters as much as the drug: this trial answers 'linagliptin or glimepiride?' in relatively early diabetes (mean glycated hemoglobin 7.2%, median duration 6.3 years) with background therapy intensified as needed — it does not answer 'linagliptin or nothing?', and its hypoglycaemia gap is a property of the sulfonylurea comparator as much as of linagliptin. The record reports no weight outcome, and none is claimed on this shelf.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Effect of Linagliptin vs Glimepiride on Major Adverse Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: The CAROLINA Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31536101. Registry ID: NCT01243424. MeSH: none in the record

cards.people: One randomised, double-blind, active-controlled noninferiority trial of 6,033 treated adults with relatively early type 2 diabetes and elevated cardiovascular risk (CAROLINA), testing linagliptin 5 mg daily against glimepiride 1–4 mg daily on top of usual care over a median 6.3 years.
cards.result: Primary composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke: 356 of 3,023 (11.8%) on linagliptin versus 362 of 3,010 (12.0%) on glimepiride, hazard ratio 0.98 (95.47% CI 0.84–1.14; P<.001 for noninferiority; P=.76 for superiority). At least one hypoglycaemic adverse event: 320 (10.6%) versus 1,132 (37.7%), hazard ratio 0.23 (95% CI 0.21–0.26). Adverse events overall: 93.4% versus 94.9%; adjudicated-confirmed acute pancreatitis: 0.5% versus 0.5%. cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: CAROLINA (Rosenstock J et al., PMID: 31536101) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #194 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor cardiovascular safety as a class), where it serves as the active-comparator trial beside the placebo-controlled class trials. This shelf asks the standalone head-to-head question — in type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, does linagliptin cause fewer cardiovascular events or less hypoglycaemia than glimepiride — a genuinely different question (a single named drug against a single named active comparator, not the class-versus-placebo safety question #194 answers; CAROLINA is the only active-comparator DPP-4 cardiovascular outcomes trial), built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) / #3325 (STRENGTH) precedent that a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Tier C is set because a single trial carries the shelf and it makes a cardiovascular-outcome claim.

shelves.title: SCORED: sotagliflozin cut the composite of cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalisation and urgent heart-failure visits by 26% relative in diabetes with kidney disease — in a trial that changed its primary endpoint and stopped early for lost funding
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease, does sotagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology/mortality · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/drug therapy · Diabetic Ketoacidosis/chemically induced · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycosides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mycoses/etiology · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/drug therapy · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 1/antagonists & inhibitors · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a positive composite with two structural cautions on its face. In 10,584 patients with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease (eGFR 25–60) and cardiovascular risk (Bhatt DL et al., PMID: 33200891), the primary composite — total cardiovascular deaths, heart-failure hospitalisations and urgent heart-failure visits — occurred at 5.6 versus 7.5 events per 100 patient-years on sotagliflozin versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.74 [95% CI 0.63 to 0.88], P<0.001; a 26% relative reduction). But cardiovascular death alone did not fall (2.2 versus 2.4 per 100 patient-years; HR 0.90 [0.73 to 1.12], P=0.35) — the composite is carried by heart-failure events. And the primary endpoint was changed during the trial, which then ended early owing to loss of funding, at a median follow-up of 16 months. Diarrhoea, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion and diabetic ketoacidosis were all more common on sotagliflozin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a heart-failure-event benefit in one trial whose endpoint was redefined mid-course; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: SCORED (Bhatt 2021): primary composite 5.6 versus 7.5 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.74); cardiovascular death 2.2 versus 2.4 (HR 0.90, P=0.35)
cards.summary: SCORED (Bhatt 2021): primary composite 5.6 versus 7.5 events per 100 patient-years (HR 0.74); cardiovascular death 2.2 versus 2.4 (HR 0.90, P=0.35)
cards.people: 10,584 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c at least 7%), chronic kidney disease (eGFR 25–60 ml/min/1.73 m²) with or without albuminuria, and cardiovascular risk factors, randomised double-blind 1:1 to sotagliflozin or placebo; median follow-up 16 months. The primary endpoint was changed during the trial to the composite of total deaths from cardiovascular causes, hospitalisations for heart failure and urgent visits for heart failure; the trial ended early owing to loss of funding.
cards.result: Primary end-point events occurred at 5.6 per 100 patient-years on sotagliflozin versus 7.5 on placebo (HR 0.74 [95% CI 0.63 to 0.88]; P<0.001) — a 26% relative reduction. Cardiovascular deaths were 2.2 versus 2.4 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.90 [0.73 to 1.12]; P=0.35). The original coprimary endpoints gave HR 0.84 (0.72 to 0.99) for first cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke, and HR 0.77 (0.66 to 0.91) for first cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation. Diarrhoea, genital mycotic infections, volume depletion and diabetic ketoacidosis were more common with sotagliflozin.
cards.watchOut: Two structural cautions: the primary endpoint was changed during the trial, and the trial stopped early for loss of funding — both inflate the risk that the headline estimate is optimistic. The composite counts total (including repeat) heart-failure events, and its mortality component is flat; read this as a heart-failure-event result, not a survival result.
cards.source: Bhatt DL et al. Sotagliflozin in Patients with Diabetes and Chronic Kidney Disease. New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33200891. Registry ID: NCT03315143. shelves.title: DARE-19: dapagliflozin did not significantly prevent organ dysfunction or death in hospitalised COVID-19 patients — 11.2% versus 13.8% (HR 0.80, p=0.17) — but was well tolerated
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with COVID-19 and cardiometabolic risk factors, does dapagliflozin prevent organ dysfunction or death?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Benzhydryl Compounds/administration & dosage · COVID-19/complications · Cardiometabolic Risk Factors · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucosides/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Organ Failure/complications/prevention & control · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-run trial that missed both its primary endpoints. In 1,250 patients hospitalised with COVID-19 and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease), excluding the critically ill at screening (Kosiborod MN et al., PMID: 34302745), organ dysfunction or death occurred in 70 patients (11.2%) on dapagliflozin 10 mg daily for 30 days versus 86 (13.8%) on placebo (HR 0.80 [95% CI 0.58 to 1.10]; p=0.17), and the hierarchical recovery outcome also missed significance (win ratio 1.09 [0.97 to 1.22]; p=0.14). Deaths were 41 (6.6%) versus 54 (8.6%) (HR 0.77 [0.52 to 1.16]) — a point estimate in dapagliflozin's favour whose confidence interval comfortably includes no effect and which this library does not convert into a benefit claim. Serious adverse events were fewer on dapagliflozin (10.6% versus 13.3%), so the honest summary is: safe in this setting, not shown to protect organs or save lives. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): both dual primary outcomes non-significant in a single adequately sized trial.

shelves.title: inTandem3: adding sotagliflozin in type 1 diabetes doubled clean target achievement (28.6% versus 15.2%) — and quintupled ketoacidosis (3.0% versus 0.6%)
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes on insulin, does adding sotagliflozin improve HbA1c and weight — and how much does diabetic ketoacidosis increase?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Diabetic Ketoacidosis/epidemiology/etiology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Glycosides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Insulin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Sodium-Glucose Transport Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the benefit and the harm arrive in the same trial, in similar absolute sizes. In 1,402 patients with type 1 diabetes on any insulin regimen (Garg SK et al., PMID: 28899222), adding sotagliflozin 400 mg daily for 24 weeks achieved the composite primary endpoint — HbA1c below 7.0% with no severe hypoglycaemia and no ketoacidosis — in 200 of 699 patients (28.6%) versus 107 of 703 (15.2%) on placebo (P<0.001); HbA1c fell by an extra 0.46 points, weight by an extra 2.98 kg, systolic pressure by 3.5 mmHg and daily bolus insulin by 2.8 units. Severe hypoglycaemia was similar (3.0% versus 2.4%), but diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in 21 patients (3.0%) on sotagliflozin versus 4 (0.6%) on placebo — an absolute excess of about 2.4 points over 24 weeks, against an absolute gain of about 13.4 points in clean target achievement. Whether that trade is worth it is a judgement this shelf presents, not settles: ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes can be life-threatening and can occur at near-normal glucose. PROPOSED SPLIT: glycaemic and weight benefit shown; a fivefold ketoacidosis rate is the standing price in this population.

cards.headline: inTandem3 (Garg 2017): net-benefit endpoint 28.6% versus 15.2% (P<0.001); DKA 3.0% versus 0.6%; severe hypoglycaemia 3.0% versus 2.4%
cards.summary: inTandem3 (Garg 2017): net-benefit endpoint 28.6% versus 15.2% (P<0.001); DKA 3.0% versus 0.6%; severe hypoglycaemia 3.0% versus 2.4%
cards.people: 1,402 patients with type 1 diabetes on any insulin therapy (pump or injections) at 133 centres worldwide, randomised double-blind to sotagliflozin 400 mg daily or placebo for 24 weeks; the primary endpoint was HbA1c below 7.0% at week 24 with no episodes of severe hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis after randomisation.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was achieved by 200 of 699 patients (28.6%) on sotagliflozin versus 107 of 703 (15.2%) on placebo (P<0.001). Least-squares mean differences favoured sotagliflozin for HbA1c (−0.46 percentage points), weight (−2.98 kg), systolic blood pressure (−3.5 mmHg) and mean daily bolus insulin dose (−2.8 units) (P≤0.002 for all). Severe hypoglycaemia rates were similar (3.0% [21 patients] versus 2.4% [17]); documented hypoglycaemia at or below 55 mg/dL was significantly lower on sotagliflozin. Diabetic ketoacidosis was higher on sotagliflozin: 3.0% (21 patients) versus 0.6% (4).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks is short for a lifetime therapy, the primary endpoint is a composite that builds the two key harms into its own definition (so the 28.6% already excludes patients harmed in those two ways), and trial-grade monitoring and education about ketones likely understate real-world ketoacidosis risk.
cards.source: Garg SK et al. Effects of Sotagliflozin Added to Insulin in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28899222. Registry ID: NCT02531035. shelves.title: ORIGIN: six years of early insulin glargine in dysglycaemia changed cardiovascular outcomes not at all (HR 1.02) — new diabetes fell borderline-significantly while severe hypoglycaemia tripled
shelves.question: In people with dysglycaemia at cardiovascular risk, does early basal insulin glargine prevent cardiovascular events or delay progression to diabetes versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose/analysis · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Cholesterol/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Fasting · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucose Intolerance/complications/drug therapy · Hospitalization · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Incidence · Insulin Glargine · Insulin, Long-Acting/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Triglycerides/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one of the largest and longest nulls in diabetes. In 12,537 people (mean age 63.5 years) with cardiovascular risk factors plus impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, randomised to insulin glargine titrated to fasting glucose at or below 95 mg/dL or standard care and followed a median 6.2 years (Gerstein HC et al., PMID: 22686416), the first coprimary cardiovascular outcome occurred at 2.94 versus 2.85 per 100 person-years (HR 1.02 [95% CI 0.94 to 1.11]; P=0.63) and the expanded coprimary at 5.52 versus 5.28 (HR 1.04 [0.97 to 1.11]; P=0.27). Cancers were identical (HR 1.00). New diabetes among the 1,456 participants without diabetes at baseline was diagnosed in 30% versus 35% about 3 months after therapy stopped (odds ratio 0.80 [0.64 to 1.00]; P=0.05) — a borderline delay signal at the edge of significance, with an association ratio inside this library's 0.5–2.0 zone of clinical uncertainty, bought with severe hypoglycaemia at 1.00 versus 0.31 per 100 person-years and 1.6 kg of weight gain versus 0.5 kg lost. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): normalising fasting glucose with basal insulin for six years neither prevented cardiovascular events nor, convincingly, delayed the onset of diabetes.

cards.headline: ORIGIN (Gerstein 2012): coprimary cardiovascular outcomes HR 1.02 (P=0.63) and HR 1.04 (P=0.27) over a median 6.2 years
cards.summary: ORIGIN (Gerstein 2012): coprimary cardiovascular outcomes HR 1.02 (P=0.63) and HR 1.04 (P=0.27) over a median 6.2 years
cards.people: 12,537 people (mean age 63.5 years) with cardiovascular risk factors plus impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, randomised to insulin glargine (target fasting glucose at or below 95 mg/dL) or standard care, within a 2-by-2 factorial design also testing n-3 fatty acids (reported separately); median follow-up 6.2 years. Coprimary outcomes were nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or cardiovascular death, and those events plus revascularisation or heart-failure hospitalisation.
cards.result: Rates of the first coprimary outcome were 2.94 (glargine) versus 2.85 (standard care) per 100 person-years (HR 1.02 [95% CI 0.94 to 1.11]; P=0.63); for the second coprimary outcome, 5.52 versus 5.28 per 100 person-years (HR 1.04 [0.97 to 1.11]; P=0.27). New diabetes was diagnosed approximately 3 months after therapy stopped in 30% versus 35% of the 1,456 participants without baseline diabetes (OR 0.80 [0.64 to 1.00]; P=0.05). Severe hypoglycaemia occurred at 1.00 versus 0.31 per 100 person-years. Median weight rose 1.6 kg on glargine and fell 0.5 kg on standard care. Cancers did not differ (HR 1.00 [0.88 to 1.13]; P=0.97).
cards.watchOut: Standard care was not no care — many control patients eventually received glucose-lowering therapy including insulin, diluting any contrast over 6 years; even so the confidence intervals exclude a cardiovascular benefit of the size the trial was designed to find. The diabetes-onset result is a borderline secondary outcome (P=0.05, interval touching 1.00) and is presented as such.
cards.source: Gerstein HC et al. Basal insulin and cardiovascular and other outcomes in dysglycemia. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22686416. Registry ID: NCT00069784. shelves.title: AdDIT: neither quinapril nor atorvastatin changed albumin excretion in adolescents with type 1 diabetes at higher risk — the trial's primary outcome was flat for both drugs
shelves.question: In adolescents with type 1 diabetes, do atorvastatin or quinapril slow early kidney or retinal disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Albuminuria/etiology/prevention & control · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Area Under Curve · Child · Creatinine/urine · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/complications/drug therapy/urine · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Lipids/blood · Male · Medication Adherence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a factorial trial that answers its own primary question in the negative for both drugs. From 4,407 screened adolescents with type 1 diabetes aged 10–16, the 1,287 with albumin-to-creatinine ratios in the upper third were identified and 443 randomised in a 2-by-2 factorial design to an ACE inhibitor (quinapril), a statin (atorvastatin), both, or neither, over 2 to 4 years (Marcovecchio ML et al., PMID: 29091568). The primary outcome — change in albumin excretion as the area under the albumin-to-creatinine curve — was not affected by ACE inhibitor therapy, statin therapy, or the combination. The ACE inhibitor arm showed a lower incidence of microalbuminuria (HR 0.57 [95% CI 0.35 to 0.94]), but the authors state that, in the context of the negative primary outcome and the statistical analysis plan, this was not considered significant. The statin did what statins do to lipids (significant reductions in total, LDL and non-HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and the apoB/apoA1 ratio), but neither drug significantly affected carotid intima-media thickness, glomerular filtration rate, other cardiovascular markers, or progression of retinopathy. Adherence was 75% and serious adverse events were similar across groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in adolescents selected for higher albumin excretion, starting these drugs in the teenage years did not move the early kidney measure the trial was built on.

cards.headline: AdDIT (Marcovecchio 2017): primary albumin-excretion outcome unaffected by ACE inhibitor, statin, or both
cards.summary: AdDIT (Marcovecchio 2017): primary albumin-excretion outcome unaffected by ACE inhibitor, statin, or both
cards.people: 443 adolescents with type 1 diabetes (screened from 4,407 aged 10–16 years; enrolled participants were the 1,287 with albumin-to-creatinine ratios in the upper third, from whom 443 were randomised) in a placebo-controlled 2-by-2 factorial trial of an ACE inhibitor and a statin over 2 to 4 years; the primary outcome for both interventions was change in albumin excretion (albumin-to-creatinine ratio from three early-morning urine samples every 6 months, as area under the curve). Key secondary outcomes included microalbuminuria, retinopathy progression, GFR, lipids and cardiovascular risk measures. Overall adherence was 75%.
cards.result: The primary outcome was not affected by ACE inhibitor therapy, statin therapy, or the combination. ACE inhibitor use was associated with a lower incidence of microalbuminuria than placebo (HR 0.57 [95% CI 0.35 to 0.94]), which the authors state was not considered significant in the context of the negative primary outcome and statistical analysis plan. Statin use significantly reduced total, LDL and non-HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and the apolipoprotein B/A1 ratio. Neither drug had significant effects on carotid intima-media thickness, other cardiovascular markers, glomerular filtration rate, or progression of retinopathy. Serious adverse events were similar across the groups.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate primary outcome over 2–4 years in adolescents cannot exclude benefit over the decades in which diabetic kidney disease actually declares itself — the null is about early albumin excretion in teenagers, not about lifetime treatment. The 75% adherence also dilutes any true drug effect toward the null.

the primary outcome for both interventions was change in albumin excretion (albumin-to-creatinine ratio from three early-morning urine samples every 6 months, as area under the curve). key secondary outcomes included microalbuminuria, retinopathy progression, gfr, lipids and cardiovascular risk measures. overall adherence was 75%. the primary outcome was not affected by ace inhibitor therapy, statin therapy, or the combination. ace inhibitor use was associated with a lower incidence of microalbuminuria than placebo (hr 0.57 [95% ci 0.35 to 0.94]), which the authors state was not considered significant in the context of the negative primary outcome and statistical analysis plan. statin use significantly reduced total, ldl and non-hdl cholesterol, triglycerides and the apolipoprotein b/a1 ratio. neither drug had significant effects on carotid intima-media thickness, other cardiovascular markers, glomerular filtration rate, or progression of retinopathy. serious adverse events were similar across the groups. a surrogate primary outcome over 2–4 years in adolescents cannot exclude benefit over the decades in which diabetic kidney disease actually declares itself — the null is about early albumin excretion in teenagers, not about lifetime treatment. the 75% adherence also dilutes any true drug effect toward the null. marcovecchio ml et al. ace inhibitors and statins in adolescents with type 1 diabetes. new england journal of medicine. 2017. pmid: 29091568. registry id: nct01581476. mesh: adolescent · albuminuria/etiology/prevention & control · angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · area under curve · child · creatinine/urine · diabetes mellitus, type 1/blood/complications/drug therapy/urine · double-blind method · drug therapy, combination · female · humans · hydroxymethylglutaryl-coa reductase inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · lipids/blood · male · medication adherence

shelves.title: COR-Diabetes: naltrexone-bupropion produced −5.0% versus −1.8% weight loss and −0.6% versus −0.1% HbA1c in type 2 diabetes — with nausea in 42.3%
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity, does naltrexone-bupropion produce weight loss and HbA1c reduction versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/administration & dosage · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Weight/drug effects · Bupropion/administration & dosage · Delayed-Action Preparations · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/complications/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone/administration & dosage · Narcotic Antagonists/administration & dosage · Obesity/blood/complications/drug therapy · Overweight/blood/complications/drug therapy · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one placebo trial with honest effect sizes and a heavy nausea burden. In 505 overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes (mean weight 106 kg, BMI 37, HbA1c 8.0%), all receiving standardised lifestyle intervention (Hollander P et al., PMID: 24144653), 56 weeks of naltrexone sustained-release 32 mg / bupropion sustained-release 360 mg produced weight loss of 5.0% versus 1.8% on placebo (P<0.001); 5% or greater weight loss was achieved by 44.5% versus 18.9%, HbA1c fell by 0.6% versus 0.1% (P<0.001), and HbA1c below 7% was reached by 44.1% versus 26.3%. Triglycerides and HDL cholesterol also improved. The tolerability ledger: nausea 42.3% versus 7.1%, constipation 17.7% versus 7.1%, vomiting 18.3% versus 3.6%; no difference was observed in depression, suicidal ideation or hypoglycaemia. A 3.2-point weight advantage over placebo is real but modest next to the incretin-era trials on neighbouring shelves, and nearly half the treated group felt nauseated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but modest weight and glycaemic effect from a single trial, limited by gastrointestinal tolerability.

cards.headline: COR-Diabetes (Hollander 2013): weight −5.0% versus −1.8%; ≥5% loss in 44.5% versus 18.9%; HbA1c −0.6% versus −0.1%
cards.summary: COR-Diabetes (Hollander 2013): weight −5.0% versus −1.8%; ≥5% loss in 44.5% versus 18.9%; HbA1c −0.6% versus −0.1%
cards.people: 505 overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes (modified intention-to-treat population 54% female, mean age 54 years, weight 106 kg, BMI 37 kg/m², HbA1c 8.0%), with or without background oral antidiabetes drugs, randomised 2:1 double-blind to naltrexone SR 32 mg / bupropion SR 360 mg daily or placebo for 56 weeks, all with standardised lifestyle intervention. Coprimary endpoints were percent weight change and achievement of at least 5% weight loss. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Weight fell by 5.0% on naltrexone-bupropion versus 1.8% on placebo (P<0.001); at least 5% weight loss was achieved by 44.5% versus 18.9% (P<0.001). HbA1c fell by 0.6% versus 0.1% (P<0.001), and HbA1c below 7% was achieved by 44.1% versus 26.3% (P<0.001); triglycerides and HDL cholesterol improved versus placebo. Nausea occurred in 42.3% versus 7.1%, constipation in 17.7% versus 7.1% and vomiting in 18.3% versus 3.6%. No difference was observed in depression, suicidal ideation, or hypoglycaemia.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, with weight effects roughly a third of what later incretin-based trials report; the modified intention-to-treat population and a 42% nausea rate mean persistence in ordinary practice is the open question. No cardiovascular-outcome data exist in this record for a combination containing a sympathomimetic-leaning agent.
cards.source: Hollander P et al. Effects of naltrexone sustained-release/bupropion sustained-release combination therapy on body weight and glycemic parameters in overweight and obese patients with type 2 diabetes. shelves.title: SCALE Diabetes: liraglutide 3.0 mg produced 6.0% weight loss versus 2.0% on placebo in type 2 diabetes — and 5%-or-more loss in 54.3% versus 21.4%
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with obesity, does liraglutide 3.0 mg daily produce weight loss and glycaemic improvement versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Body Weight · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications · Diet, Reducing · Double-Blind Method · Exercise · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Liraglutide · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/complications/drug therapy · Weight Loss/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large placebo trial of the obesity dose in diabetes. In 846 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.0% on 0–3 oral agents), all on a 500 kcal/day deficit diet and increased activity (Davies MJ et al., PMID: 26284720), 56 weeks of liraglutide 3.0 mg daily produced weight loss of 6.0% (6.4 kg) versus 2.0% (2.2 kg) on placebo (estimated difference −4.00% [95% CI −5.10% to −2.90%]; P<0.001); the standard 1.8 mg diabetes dose gave 4.7% (difference −2.71%). Weight loss of 5% or more occurred in 54.3% on 3.0 mg versus 21.4% on placebo, and more than 10% in 25.2% versus 6.7%. More gastrointestinal disorders were reported with liraglutide 3.0 mg than with 1.8 mg and placebo; no pancreatitis was reported. The candidate question also asks about glycaemic improvement; the record's abstract reports the weight coprimary endpoints in full but does not give the HbA1c numbers, so this shelf claims the weight result and leaves the glycaemic figures unclaimed rather than importing them from outside the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a clear, dose-ordered weight effect in a single trial in type 2 diabetes.

cards.headline: SCALE Diabetes (Davies 2015): weight −6.0% on liraglutide 3.0 mg, −4.7% on 1.8 mg, −2.0% on placebo at 56 weeks
cards.summary: SCALE Diabetes (Davies 2015): weight −6.0% on liraglutide 3.0 mg, −4.7% on 1.8 mg, −2.0% on placebo at 56 weeks
cards.people: 846 randomised adults with BMI at least 27 and type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.0%, taking 0–3 oral hypoglycaemic agents, stable weight) at 126 sites in 9 countries, randomised 2:1:1 double-blind to once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide 3.0 mg (n=423), liraglutide 1.8 mg (n=211) or placebo (n=212) for 56 weeks, all as adjunct to a 500 kcal/day dietary deficit and at least 150 min/week of activity, with a 12-week off-drug follow-up. Coprimary endpoints were relative weight change and the proportions losing at least 5% and more than 10% of baseline weight.
cards.result: Weight loss was 6.0% (6.4 kg) on liraglutide 3.0 mg, 4.7% (5.0 kg) on 1.8 mg and 2.0% (2.2 kg) on placebo (estimated differences versus placebo −4.00% [95% CI −5.10% to −2.90%] for 3.0 mg and −2.71% [−4.00% to −1.42%] for 1.8 mg; P<0.001 for both). Loss of 5% or more occurred in 54.3% (3.0 mg) and 40.4% (1.8 mg) versus 21.4% (placebo); more than 10% in 25.2% and 15.9% versus 6.7%. More gastrointestinal disorders were reported with liraglutide 3.0 mg than with 1.8 mg and placebo. No pancreatitis was reported.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract quantifies weight but not the HbA1c change, so the glycaemic half of the question is not evidenced on this shelf's cards; weight regain after stopping is the known pattern for this class and the trial's off-drug follow-up is not reported in the record. Daily injections at the 3.0 mg dose are a burden the weekly agents on neighbouring shelves do not impose.
cards.source: Davies MJ et al. Efficacy of Liraglutide for Weight Loss Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: The SCALE Diabetes Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2015. PMID: 26284720. Registry ID: NCT01272232. shelves.title: STEP 2: semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly produced −9.6% weight change versus −3.4% on placebo in type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity — at least 5% loss in 68.8% versus 28.5%
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity, does once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg improve HbA1c and weight versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptides/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/drug therapy · Overweight/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss/drug effects · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large placebo trial of the obesity dose in diabetes, with the diabetes penalty visible: weight loss is smaller than in the non-diabetes STEP trials. In 1,210 adults with BMI at least 27 and type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7–10%), all receiving lifestyle intervention (Davies M et al., PMID: 33667417), 68 weeks of semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly changed bodyweight by −9.6% versus −3.4% on placebo (estimated difference −6.2 percentage points [95% CI −7.3 to −5.2]; p<0.0001), and at least 5% weight loss was achieved by 68.8% versus 28.5% (odds ratio 4.88 [3.58 to 6.64]). A semaglutide 1.0 mg arm (the diabetes dose) was included as a reference. Gastrointestinal adverse events — mostly mild to moderate — occurred in 63.5% on 2.4 mg versus 34.3% on placebo, and overall adverse events in 87.6% versus 76.9%. As with the neighbouring SCALE shelf, the record's abstract quantifies the weight coprimary endpoints but does not print the HbA1c change, so the glycaemic half of the question is left unclaimed here rather than filled in from outside the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large, clinically meaningful weight effect of the 2.4 mg dose in type 2 diabetes, in a single trial.

cards.headline: STEP 2 (Davies 2021): weight −9.6% on semaglutide 2.4 mg versus −3.4% on placebo (difference −6.2 points); ≥5% loss in 68.8% versus 28.5%
cards.summary: STEP 2 (Davies 2021): weight −9.6% on semaglutide 2.4 mg versus −3.4% on placebo (difference −6.2 points); ≥5% loss in 68.8% versus 28.5%
cards.people: 1,210 adults with BMI at least 27 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes diagnosed at least 180 days before screening (HbA1c 7–10%), at 149 clinics in 12 countries, randomised 1:1:1 double-blind, double-dummy to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg (n=404), semaglutide 1.0 mg (n=403) or visually matching placebo (n=403) for 68 weeks plus lifestyle intervention. Coprimary endpoints were percentage change in bodyweight and achievement of at least 5% weight reduction at 68 weeks for 2.4 mg versus placebo.
cards.result: Estimated mean bodyweight change was −9.6% on semaglutide 2.4 mg versus −3.4% on placebo (estimated treatment difference −6.2 percentage points [95% CI −7.3 to −5.2]; p<0.0001). At least 5% weight reduction was achieved by 267 (68.8%) of 388 on 2.4 mg versus 107 (28.5%) of 376 on placebo (odds ratio 4.88 [3.58 to 6.64]; p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 87.6% on 2.4 mg, 81.8% on 1.0 mg and 76.9% on placebo; gastrointestinal adverse events, mostly mild to moderate, in 63.5%, 57.5% and 34.3% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract does not report the HbA1c change, so no glycaemic number is claimed on this shelf; the 1.0 mg arm's weight result is likewise not printed in the abstract and is not used. Sixty-eight weeks on treatment says nothing about the post-stopping trajectory, which neighbouring shelves in this library show is substantial regain.

shelves.title: Tirzepatide in type 2 diabetes with obesity: weight down 12.8–14.7% versus 3.2% on placebo at 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-2) — one trial, gut effects throughout, and the HbA1c figures live on the monotherapy shelf
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with overweight or obesity, does once-weekly tirzepatide improve weight and HbA1c versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Female · Adolescent · Middle Aged · Male · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Glucagon-Like Peptides · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Obesity/complications/drug therapy · Body Weight · Double-Blind Method · Tirzepatide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — substantial weight loss in the one large trial that asked the weight question in this population. In SURMOUNT-2 (Garvey WT et al., PMID: 37385275), 938 adults with type 2 diabetes and BMI ≥27 kg/m² lost 12.8% of body weight on tirzepatide 10 mg and 14.7% on 15 mg at 72 weeks, versus 3.2% on placebo (estimated differences −9.6 and −11.6 percentage points, p<0.0001); 79–83% reached at least 5% weight loss versus 32% on placebo. The most frequent adverse events were gastrointestinal — nausea, diarrhoea, and vomiting — mostly mild to moderate, with discontinuation under 5%; serious adverse events occurred in 68 participants (7%) overall. Two honest limits: the record's abstract reports the weight outcomes and does not print the HbA1c change figures, so this shelf does not state them — the glycaemic potency of the same drug is carded on the tirzepatide monotherapy shelf built from SURPASS-1 — and no cardiovascular-outcome result is in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tirzepatide produces large, dose-ordered weight loss in type 2 diabetes with obesity over 72 weeks; Tier C because a single trial carries the claim.

cards.people: 938 adults (mean age 54.2 years, 51% female, mean BMI 36.1 kg/m², mean HbA1c 8.02%) with type 2 diabetes and BMI ≥27 kg/m² and HbA1c 7–10%, randomised to once-weekly tirzepatide 10 mg, 15 mg, or placebo for 72 weeks across seven countries.
cards.result: Least-squares mean bodyweight change at week 72 was −12.8% on tirzepatide 10 mg and −14.7% on 15 mg versus −3.2% on placebo (estimated treatment differences −9.6 and −11.6 percentage points; p<0.0001). Weight reduction of 5% or more occurred in 79–83% on tirzepatide versus 32% on placebo. Serious adverse events were reported by 68 participants (7%) overall; two deaths in the 10 mg group were judged unrelated to treatment. The record's abstract reports weight outcomes; it does not print the HbA1c change figures.
cards.watchOut: The trial answers the weight question, not the HbA1c question — glycaemic numbers must be borrowed from other tirzepatide trials in different populations. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent harm, and 72 weeks says nothing about weight regain after stopping or about cardiovascular outcomes.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 2 dose-ranging trial, large weight effects, no confirmatory trial yet. In 592 participants (Jastreboff AM et al., PMID: 40549887), mean bodyweight change at week 52 in the obesity cohort (n=465) ranged from −12.3% to −16.2% across maridebart cafraglutide regimens versus −2.5% on placebo; in the smaller obesity-with-type-2-diabetes cohort (n=127), weight change ranged from −8.4% to −12.3% versus −1.7% on placebo, and HbA1c changed by −1.2 to −1.6 percentage points versus +0.1 on placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were common, though less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose; no unexpected safety signals emerged. The drug is a peptide–antibody conjugate given every 4 weeks (one arm every 8 weeks) — the monthly schedule is its distinguishing claim, and it is unproven beyond this single trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): substantial one-year weight loss in a single phase 2 trial; Tier C because one trial, however large the effect, has carried phase 2 obesity drugs astray before.

cards.headline: Jastreboff 2025 (phase 2): weight −12.3% to −16.2% versus −2.5% on placebo at week 52 in obesity; −8.4% to −12.3% versus −1.7% in obesity with type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: Jastreboff 2025 (phase 2): weight −12.3% to −16.2% versus −2.5% on placebo at week 52 in obesity; −8.4% to −12.3% versus −1.7% in obesity with type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 592 participants in two cohorts: obesity without diabetes (n=465; 63% female, mean age 47.9 years, mean BMI 37.9) randomised across six maridebart cafraglutide regimens (140–420 mg every 4 weeks, one 420 mg every-8-weeks arm, with or without dose escalation) or placebo; and obesity with type 2 diabetes (n=127; mean BMI 36.5) randomised to 140, 280, or 420 mg every 4 weeks or placebo. Primary endpoint: percent weight change at week 52.
cards.result: Obesity cohort: mean weight change ranged from −12.3% (95% CI −15.0 to −9.7) to −16.2% (−18.9 to −13.5) on maridebart cafraglutide versus −2.5% (−4.2 to −0.7) on placebo (treatment-policy estimand). Diabetes cohort: −8.4% to −12.3% versus −1.7% on placebo, with HbA1c change of −1.2 to −1.6 percentage points versus +0.1 on placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were common but less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose; no unexpected safety signals emerged.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 with 11 groups spread across 592 people — each regimen arm is small, the ranges span several dosing schemes, and there is no active comparator, no cardiovascular outcome, and no post-treatment follow-up in this record. Effects of this size in phase 2 have shrunk before in phase 3.

shelves.title: Teplizumab in newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes: C-peptide preserved at 78 weeks (difference 0.13 pmol/mL) and 95% kept meaningful beta-cell function versus 79% — but insulin dose, HbA1c and time in range did not differ
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes, does teplizumab preserve stimulated C-peptide versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · C-Peptide/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/diagnosis/immunology/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · T-Lymphocytes/drug effects/immunology · CD3 Complex/antagonists & inhibitors/immunology · Disease Progression · Insulin-Secreting Cells/drug effects/immunology · Insulin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the beta-cell marker, not yet for anything a patient can feel. In PROTECT (Ramos EL et al., PMID: 37861217), 328 children and adolescents with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes received two 12-day courses of intravenous teplizumab or placebo; at week 78, stimulated C-peptide was higher with teplizumab (least-squares mean difference 0.13 pmol/mL, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.17; P<0.001), and 94.9% of teplizumab patients maintained a peak C-peptide of at least 0.2 pmol/mL versus 79.2% on placebo. But the key secondary endpoints — insulin dose needed, HbA1c, time in target range, and clinically important hypoglycaemia — did not differ significantly between groups. Adverse events clustered around administration: headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, lymphopenia, and mild cytokine release syndrome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, single-trial preservation of the C-peptide surrogate whose clinical payoff — less insulin, better control — was not shown in the same trial; Tier C.

cards.headline: Ramos 2023 (PROTECT): C-peptide difference 0.13 pmol/mL at week 78 (P<0.001); 94.9% versus 79.2% kept peak C-peptide ≥0.2 pmol/mL — secondary clinical endpoints not significantly different
cards.summary: Ramos 2023 (PROTECT): C-peptide difference 0.13 pmol/mL at week 78 (P<0.001); 94.9% versus 79.2% kept peak C-peptide ≥0.2 pmol/mL — secondary clinical endpoints not significantly different
cards.people: 328 children and adolescents with newly diagnosed (stage 3) type 1 diabetes randomised to intravenous teplizumab (217 patients) or placebo (111 patients), given as two 12-day courses; primary endpoint was change in stimulated C-peptide at week 78.
cards.result: Stimulated C-peptide at week 78 was significantly higher with teplizumab (least-squares mean difference 0.13 pmol/mL, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.17; P<0.001). A clinically meaningful peak C-peptide (≥0.2 pmol/mL) was maintained by 94.9% (95% CI 89.5 to 97.6) on teplizumab versus 79.2% (67.7 to 87.4) on placebo. Insulin doses, HbA1c, time in target range, and clinically important hypoglycaemic events did not differ significantly. Adverse events included headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, lymphopenia, and mild cytokine release syndrome, mostly around administration.
cards.watchOut: The win is a surrogate: preserved C-peptide is biologically meaningful, but within 78 weeks it bought no measurable reduction in insulin need or improvement in control in this trial. Participants were children and adolescents at diagnosis — the result does not extend to adults or to long-standing diabetes.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clear C-peptide signal in one small phase 2 trial. In T1GER (Quattrin T et al., PMID: 33207093), 84 children and young adults (ages 6–21) with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes received subcutaneous golimumab or placebo for 52 weeks. The 4-hour C-peptide AUC at week 52 was 0.64 pmol/mL on golimumab versus 0.43 pmol/mL on placebo (P<0.001); a partial-remission response occurred in 43% versus 7% (difference 36 percentage points, 95% CI 22 to 55), and insulin use was lower with golimumab — while HbA1c, managed treat-to-target in both groups, did not differ. Hypoglycaemic events recorded as adverse events were reported in 23% on golimumab versus 7% on placebo, and anti-drug antibodies developed in 30 participants who received golimumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): beta-cell preservation in a single small trial, with the clinical endpoints (HbA1c) equal by design; Tier C.

cards.people: 84 children and young adults aged 6–21 years with newly diagnosed overt (stage 3) type 1 diabetes, randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous golimumab (56) or placebo (28) for 52 weeks; primary endpoint was 4-hour mixed-meal C-peptide AUC at week 52.
cards.result: Mean 4-hour C-peptide AUC at week 52 was 0.64±0.42 pmol/mL on golimumab versus 0.43±0.39 pmol/mL on placebo (P<0.001). Partial remission (insulin dose-adjusted HbA1c ≤9) occurred in 43% versus 7% (difference 36 percentage points, 95% CI 22 to 55). shelves.title: One course of rituximab in new type 1 diabetes: C-peptide decline slowed and HbA1c and insulin dose lower at one year — a partial, temporary preservation in a single phase 2 trial
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does a single course of rituximab preserve C-peptide at one year versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived · Area Under Curve · B-Lymphocytes/drug effects/physiology · C-Peptide/blood · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy/immunology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Immunoglobulin M/blood · Immunologic Factors/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Insulin-Secreting Cells/drug effects/physiology · Male · Rituximab · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — partial preservation, honestly bounded. In the phase 2 trial (Pescovitz MD et al., PMID: 19940299), 87 patients aged 8–40 with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes received four rituximab infusions (days 1, 8, 15, 22) or placebo. At one year the C-peptide AUC during a mixed-meal test was significantly higher with rituximab, the rate of C-peptide decline between months 3 and 12 was significantly slower, and the rituximab group had significantly lower HbA1c and insulin dose (the record's abstract reports these as significant without printing the group means). B lymphocytes were depleted but had recovered to 69% of baseline by 12 months — matching the temporary nature of the effect. Adverse events were mostly grade 1–2 infusion reactions after the first dose, with no increase in infections or neutropenia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one small trial, a surrogate endpoint, and an effect that wanes as B cells return; Tier C.

cards.headline: Pescovitz 2009: C-peptide AUC significantly higher at 1 year and decline slowed from months 3–12; B cells back to 69% of baseline by 12 months
cards.summary: Pescovitz 2009: C-peptide AUC significantly higher at 1 year and decline slowed from months 3–12; B cells back to 69% of baseline by 12 months
cards.people: 87 patients aged 8–40 years with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, randomised to rituximab infusions on days 1, 8, 15, and 22 or placebo; primary outcome was the geometric mean C-peptide AUC over the first 2 hours of a mixed-meal test at 1 year.
cards.result: At 1 year, mean C-peptide AUC was significantly higher in the rituximab group, HbA1c was significantly lower, and insulin dose was significantly lower than with placebo (the abstract reports significance without group means). The rate of C-peptide decline between 3 and 12 months was significantly slower with rituximab. CD19+ B lymphocytes were depleted and recovered to 69% of baseline values at 12 months. Adverse events were more frequent with rituximab, mostly grade 1 or 2 after the first infusion and minimal with subsequent infusions; there was no increase in infections or neutropenia.
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints no effect sizes for its primary endpoint, so the size of the preservation cannot be stated from this record — only its direction and significance. Eighty-seven patients, one trial, and a mechanism (B-cell return) that predicts the benefit fades.

shelves.title: Imatinib in recent-onset type 1 diabetes: primary endpoint met at 12 months by a whisker (difference 0.095, one-tailed p=0.048) — gone by 24 months, with grade ≥2 adverse events in 71%
shelves.question: In adults with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does daily imatinib preserve beta-cell function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Biomarkers/analysis · Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Imatinib Mesylate/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the weakest 'positive' in the new-onset immunotherapy set, and the shelf says so. In the phase 2 trial (Gitelman SE et al., PMID: 34214479), 67 adults aged 18–45 with recent-onset type 1 diabetes received imatinib 400 mg daily or placebo for 26 weeks. The primary endpoint was met: the adjusted difference in 2-hour C-peptide AUC at 12 months was 0.095 (90% CI −0.003 to 0.191; p=0.048 on a one-tailed test) — a confidence interval that touches zero. The effect was not sustained to 24 months. The cost was real: grade 2 or worse adverse events in 71% on imatinib versus 59% on placebo, dose modifications in 38%, and permanent discontinuation for adverse events in 13% versus none on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a borderline, transient surrogate effect bought with a cancer drug's toxicity profile; Tier C, and a candidate for MAYBE (weak evidence) if the developer reads the one-tailed p-value strictly.

cards.headline: Gitelman 2021: C-peptide AUC difference 0.095 (90% CI −0.003 to 0.191; one-tailed p=0.048) at 12 months — not sustained at 24 months; 13% stopped imatinib for adverse events
cards.summary: Gitelman 2021: C-peptide AUC difference 0.095 (90% CI −0.003 to 0.191; one-tailed p=0.048) at 12 months — not sustained at 24 months; 13% stopped imatinib for adverse events
cards.people: 67 adults aged 18–45 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes (<100 days from diagnosis), at least one autoantibody, and peak stimulated C-peptide above 0.2 nmol/L, randomised 2:1 to imatinib 400 mg daily (45) or placebo (22) for 26 weeks, with follow-up to 24 months; 43 and 21 participants were in the 12-month primary analysis.
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference in 2-hour C-peptide AUC at 12 months was 0.095 (90% CI −0.003 to 0.191; p=0.048, one-tailed) in imatinib's favour; the effect was not sustained at 24 months. Grade 2 or worse adverse events occurred in 32 of 45 (71%) on imatinib versus 13 of 22 (59%) on placebo; gastrointestinal events (13% vs 0%) and laboratory abnormalities (22% vs 9%) were commoner on imatinib. Temporary dose modification was required in 38% on imatinib, and 13% discontinued permanently for adverse events versus none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A one-tailed p of 0.048 with a 90% interval touching zero is the frailest form of 'positive', the benefit vanished by 24 months, and the toxicity is that of an oncology drug given to young adults with a manageable chronic disease. Small numbers (67 randomised, 64 analysed) compound the fragility.

shelves.title: Screening toddlers for islet autoantibodies (Fr1da): 0.31% found presymptomatic type 1 diabetes and only 2 of 90,632 screened children presented in ketoacidosis — population yield from an observational programme, not a trial
shelves.question: Does general-population screening of young children for islet autoantibodies identify presymptomatic type 1 diabetes early enough to prevent ketoacidosis at diagnosis?
shelves.mesh: Asymptomatic Diseases/epidemiology/psychology · Autoantibodies/blood · Child, Preschool · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/diagnosis/epidemiology/psychology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Germany/epidemiology · Humans · Islets of Langerhans/immunology · Male · Mass Screening · Parents · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the programme finds the children and, in its own follow-up, almost none arrived in ketoacidosis; what it cannot show is the comparison against no screening. In Fr1da (Ziegler AG et al., PMID: 31990315), 90,632 Bavarian children aged 1.75–5.99 years were screened in primary care between 2015 and 2019; 280 (0.31%) had presymptomatic type 1 diabetes (196 stage 1, 17 stage 2, 26 stage 3, 41 unstaged). The 3-year cumulative risk of stage 3 diabetes among those 280 was 24.9%, and only two children had diabetic ketoacidosis. Parental psychological stress scores rose at staging (median PHQ-9 3 vs 2 in mothers of antibody-negative children) and fell back by 12 months. There is no unscreened control group in this record, so the ketoacidosis rate cannot be causally credited to screening from this shelf alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening demonstrably identifies presymptomatic disease at population scale with very low ketoacidosis in follow-up; Tier C because the evidence is a single observational programme.

cards.headline: Ziegler 2020 (Fr1da): 280 of 90,632 children (0.31%) had presymptomatic type 1 diabetes; 3-year progression risk 24.9%; diabetic ketoacidosis in 2 children
cards.summary: Ziegler 2020 (Fr1da): 280 of 90,632 children (0.31%) had presymptomatic type 1 diabetes; 3-year progression risk 24.9%; diabetic ketoacidosis in 2 children
cards.people: 90,632 children aged 1.75–5.99 years (median 3.1 years; 48.5% girls) screened for islet autoantibodies by primary-care paediatricians in Bavaria, Germany, 2015–2019; children with multiple autoantibodies were offered education, metabolic staging, psychological assessment, and follow-up to July 2019 (median 2.4 years).
cards.result: Presymptomatic type 1 diabetes (≥2 islet autoantibodies) was found in 280 children (0.31%; 95% CI 0.27–0.35): 196 stage 1, 17 stage 2, 26 stage 3, 41 unstaged. A further 36 children developed stage 3 diabetes in follow-up; the 3-year cumulative risk of stage 3 among the 280 was 24.9% (95% CI 18.5–30.7; annualised 9.0%). Two children had diabetic ketoacidosis. Mothers' median psychological stress (PHQ-9) was 3 (IQR 1–7) at staging versus 2 (1–4) for antibody-negative families (P=.002), declining to 2 (0–4) after 12 months (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: No unscreened comparison group: the low ketoacidosis count is consistent with screening preventing it, but this record alone cannot exclude that staged, closely followed children would present early anyway. Three quarters of screen-positive children had not progressed at 3 years, so screening also labels many children who will not soon — perhaps ever — need insulin.
cards.source: Ziegler AG et al. Yield of a Public Health Screening of Children for Islet Autoantibodies in Bavaria, Germany. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 31990315. shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two drugs in one trial part company. In DINAMO (Laffel LM et al., PMID: 36738751), 158 young people aged 10–17 with type 2 diabetes were randomised to empagliflozin, linagliptin, or placebo. At 26 weeks the adjusted HbA1c change with pooled empagliflozin was −0.84 percentage points versus placebo (95% CI −1.50 to −0.19; p=0.012), while linagliptin managed −0.34 points (95% CI −0.99 to 0.30; p=0.29) — not significant. Adverse events occurred in 77% on empagliflozin, 71% on linagliptin, and 64% on placebo up to week 26; hypoglycaemia was the commonest event and commoner on active treatment, with no severe hypoglycaemia. PROPOSED SPLIT: empagliflozin POSSIBLE (benefit) on a single trial in a population with almost no licensed options; linagliptin POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the same trial's own numbers. Tier C: one trial carries both halves.

cards.headline: Laffel 2023 (DINAMO): empagliflozin HbA1c −0.84 points versus placebo (p=0.012); linagliptin −0.34 points (p=0.29, not significant)
cards.summary: Laffel 2023 (DINAMO): empagliflozin HbA1c −0.84 points versus placebo (p=0.012); linagliptin −0.34 points (p=0.29, not significant)
cards.people: 158 young people aged 10–17 years with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.5–10.5%) previously treated with metformin or insulin, at 108 centres in 15 countries, randomised to empagliflozin 10 mg (52; non-responders re-randomised at week 14 to stay or rise to 25 mg), linagliptin 5 mg (53), or placebo (53); primary outcome was HbA1c change at 26 weeks, safety to week 52.
cards.result: Adjusted mean HbA1c change at week 26 for pooled empagliflozin versus placebo was −0.84% (95% CI −1.50 to −0.19; p=0.012); for linagliptin versus placebo, −0.34% (−0.99 to 0.30; p=0.29). Adverse events to week 26 occurred in 40 (77%) on empagliflozin, 37 (71%) on linagliptin, and 34 (64%) on placebo; severe adverse events in 1 (2%), 1 (2%), and 2 (4%) respectively. Hypoglycaemia was the most frequent adverse event, with higher rates on active treatment; no severe hypoglycaemia occurred.
cards.watchOut: One trial of 158 participants for both claims; the empagliflozin result pools two doses after a response-based re-randomisation, and 26 weeks is short in a disease these patients will carry for decades. Ketoacidosis — the class concern when SGLT2 inhibitors meet young, insulin-treated patients — is not quantified in this record's abstract.
cards.source: Laffel LM et al. shelves.title: Liraglutide in children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes: HbA1c −1.06 points versus placebo at 26 weeks, widening to −1.30 at 52 — paid for in gastrointestinal adverse events (Ellipse)
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with type 2 diabetes, does daily liraglutide improve HbA1c versus placebo on background metformin?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Blood Glucose/analysis · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Insulin/therapeutic use · Liraglutide/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Metformin/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clean, single-trial result in a population where metformin alone fails half the time. In Ellipse (Tamborlane WV et al., PMID: 31034184), 134 children and adolescents aged 10 to under 17 with type 2 diabetes, all on metformin (with or without basal insulin), received liraglutide up to 1.8 mg daily or placebo. At 26 weeks HbA1c had fallen 0.64 points on liraglutide and risen 0.42 on placebo — an estimated difference of −1.06 points (P<0.001) — and the gap widened to −1.30 points by 52 weeks; fasting glucose moved the same way. Adverse events were reported by similar proportions (84.8% vs 80.9%), but overall and gastrointestinal event rates were higher with liraglutide. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one well-conducted trial, a surrogate endpoint, a daily injection for teenagers; Tier C.

cards.headline: Tamborlane 2019 (Ellipse): HbA1c −0.64 points on liraglutide versus +0.42 on placebo at 26 weeks (difference −1.06, P<0.001), −1.30 points by 52 weeks
cards.summary: Tamborlane 2019 (Ellipse): HbA1c −0.64 points on liraglutide versus +0.42 on placebo at 26 weeks (difference −1.06, P<0.001), −1.30 points by 52 weeks
cards.people: 135 patients aged 10 to <17 years (mean 14.6) with type 2 diabetes and BMI above the 85th percentile, HbA1c 7.0–11.0% on diet/exercise or 6.5–11.0% on metformin ± insulin, randomised to subcutaneous liraglutide up to 1.8 mg daily (66 treated) or placebo (68 treated) for 26 double-blind weeks plus a 26-week open-label extension; all received metformin.
cards.result: At 26 weeks, mean HbA1c decreased by 0.64 percentage points with liraglutide and increased by 0.42 with placebo (estimated treatment difference −1.06 points; P<0.001), increasing to −1.30 points by 52 weeks. Fasting plasma glucose decreased at both time points on liraglutide and increased on placebo. Adverse events were reported by 56 patients (84.8%) on liraglutide and 55 (80.9%) on placebo, with higher overall and gastrointestinal adverse-event rates on liraglutide.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 134 treated patients, and a glycated-haemoglobin endpoint — no data here on the complications that make youth type 2 diabetes dangerous, and the 52-week figure comes after the blinded phase ended. Daily injections and gastrointestinal effects are a real adherence burden in adolescents.
cards.source: Tamborlane WV et al. Liraglutide in Children and Adolescents with Type 2 Diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31034184. Registry ID: NCT01541215.
