shelves.title: Youth type 2 diabetes (TODAY): metformin alone failed in 51.7% within four years — adding rosiglitazone cut failure to 38.6%, adding lifestyle did not significantly help
shelves.question: In youth-onset type 2 diabetes, how do metformin alone, metformin plus rosiglitazone, and metformin plus lifestyle compare on durable glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Mass Index · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy/therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Life Style · Male · Metformin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Rosiglitazone · Survival Analysis · Thiazolidinediones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Failure · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the combination over metformin alone, inside a trial whose headline is how badly youth type 2 diabetes behaves. In TODAY (Zeitler P et al., PMID: 22540912), 699 young people aged 10–17 with recent-onset type 2 diabetes were randomised to metformin alone, metformin plus rosiglitazone, or metformin plus an intensive lifestyle programme, and followed for a mean of 3.86 years. Loss of glycaemic control (HbA1c ≥8% for 6 months or decompensation needing insulin) struck 51.7% on metformin alone, 38.6% on metformin plus rosiglitazone (superior to metformin alone, P=0.006), and 46.6% on metformin plus lifestyle — intermediate and not significantly different from either. Serious adverse events were reported in 19.2% of participants. Rosiglitazone is now little used, so the practical residue is the prognosis: roughly half of youth lose control on metformin within a few years, and lifestyle added to metformin did not significantly change that. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin plus rosiglitazone beat metformin alone on durability in the only large trial of its kind; Tier C.

cards.headline: Zeitler 2012 (TODAY): loss of glycaemic control in 51.7% (metformin), 38.6% (metformin + rosiglitazone, P=0.006 vs metformin), 46.6% (metformin + lifestyle, not significant)
cards.summary: Zeitler 2012 (TODAY): loss of glycaemic control in 51.7% (metformin), 38.6% (metformin + rosiglitazone, P=0.006 vs metformin), 46.6% (metformin + lifestyle, not significant)
cards.people: 699 children and adolescents aged 10–17 years with type 2 diabetes of mean duration 7.8 months, first run-in on metformin 1000 mg twice daily to reach HbA1c below 8%, then randomised to metformin alone (232), metformin plus rosiglitazone 4 mg twice daily (233), or metformin plus a weight-loss lifestyle programme (234); primary outcome was loss of glycaemic control over mean follow-up of 3.86 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 319 participants (45.6%): failure rates were 51.7% (120/232) on metformin alone, 38.6% (90/233) on metformin plus rosiglitazone, and 46.6% (109/234) on metformin plus lifestyle. Metformin plus rosiglitazone was superior to metformin alone (P=0.006); the lifestyle combination was intermediate and not significantly different from either other arm. Metformin alone was least effective in non-Hispanic Black participants, and the rosiglitazone combination most effective in girls. Serious adverse events were reported in 19.2% of participants.
cards.watchOut: The winning drug is the story's problem: rosiglitazone fell from routine use over cardiovascular concerns in adults, so the trial's durable-control winner is rarely prescribed to youth today. The trial predates GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors in this age group — it defines the natural history those newer drugs must beat, not the current best treatment.
cards.source: Zeitler P et al. A clinical trial to maintain glycemic control in youth with type 2 diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22540912. Registry ID: NCT00081328. shelves.title: Preserving beta cells in early dysglycaemia (RISE): glargine, liraglutide and metformin all improved beta-cell function on treatment — and none of it survived three months off treatment
shelves.question: In adults with impaired glucose tolerance or early type 2 diabetes, can glargine-metformin, liraglutide-metformin, or sitagliptin-metformin preserve beta-cell function after treatment withdrawal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Arginine · B-Lymphocytes/metabolism · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Weight · C-Peptide/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Fasting/blood · Female · Glucose Intolerance/blood/drug therapy · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Insulin Glargine/administration & dosage · Insulin Resistance/physiology · Liraglutide/administration & dosage · Male · Metformin/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — after withdrawal, which is the only version of the question that matters for 'preservation'. In the RISE Adult Medication Study (RISE Consortium, PMID: 31178434), 267 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (74%) or type 2 diabetes diagnosed within 12 months received 12 months of metformin alone, insulin glargine for 3 months followed by metformin, liraglutide plus metformin, or placebo. On treatment, all three active arms improved HbA1c, weight, and clamp-measured beta-cell responses — most with liraglutide plus metformin. Three months after everything stopped, no treatment group showed any sustained improvement in beta-cell function versus baseline. (The candidate question also names a sitagliptin-metformin arm; that comparison belongs to the RISE paediatric study, not this adult record, and the shelf is built on the adult arms the record reports.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): drug-induced beta-cell improvement in early dysglycaemia is a rental, not a purchase — it lasts only while treatment continues; Tier C, single consortium trial.

cards.headline: RISE Consortium 2019: on-treatment beta-cell gains in all three active arms — zero sustained improvement in any arm 3 months after withdrawal
cards.summary: RISE Consortium 2019: on-treatment beta-cell gains in all three active arms — zero sustained improvement in any arm 3 months after withdrawal
cards.type: Randomised trial (RISE Consortium 2019, RISE Adult Medication Study)
cards.people: 267 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (n=197, 74%) or treatment-naive type 2 diabetes of <12 months' duration (n=70, 26%), randomised to 12 months of metformin alone, 3 months of insulin glargine (target fasting glucose <5 mmol/L (≈90 mg/dL)) followed by 9 months of metformin, liraglutide plus metformin for 12 months, or placebo; beta-cell function was measured by hyperglycaemic clamp at baseline, 12 months (on treatment), and 15 months (3 months off treatment).
cards.result: All three active treatments reduced weight and HbA1c versus placebo on treatment, most with liraglutide plus metformin; glucose-stimulated C-peptide responses improved at 12 months in all three active groups (arginine-stimulated incremental C-peptide response fell in the liraglutide plus metformin group). At 15 months — 3 months after withdrawal — there were no sustained improvements in beta-cell function in any treatment group. The authors conclude continued intervention may be required to alter progressive beta-cell dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports directions, not effect sizes, for the clamp outcomes, so the size of the on-treatment gain cannot be stated from this record. The population mixes impaired glucose tolerance with very early diabetes, and three months off treatment is a short test of 'durability' — but it is the test the preservation claim has to pass, and every arm failed it.
cards.source: RISE Consortium et al. Lack of Durable Improvements in β-Cell Function Following Withdrawal of Pharmacological Interventions in Adults With Impaired Glucose Tolerance or Recently Diagnosed Type 2 Diabetes. shelves.title: Insulin detemir versus NPH in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes: A1C noninferior at 36 weeks (6.27% vs 6.33%), fasting glucose lower, perinatal outcomes alike — one trial, two reports
shelves.question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does insulin detemir achieve glycaemic control and perinatal outcomes comparable to NPH insulin?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Insulin Aspart/therapeutic use · Insulin Detemir · Insulin, Isophane/therapeutic use · Insulin, Long-Acting/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy in Diabetics/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — which, for a noninferiority question, is the finding the trial was built to deliver. In the randomised trial (Mathiesen ER et al., PMID: 22851598), 310 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (or planning pregnancy) received insulin detemir or NPH, both with prandial aspart. A1C at 36 gestational weeks was 6.27% on detemir versus 6.33% on NPH (difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.08), meeting the 0.4% noninferiority margin; fasting glucose was significantly lower with detemir at 24 weeks (96.8 vs 113.8 mg/dL, P=0.012) and 36 weeks (85.7 vs 97.4 mg/dL, P=0.017), with similar hypoglycaemia rates. The companion perinatal report (Hod M et al., PMID: 23617228) found 128 versus 136 live births, perinatal deaths of two versus one, and malformations in 5.6% versus 5.5% — no perinatal safety signal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): detemir is a comparable basal insulin in pregnancy on this single trial, with a fasting-glucose edge; Tier C because one trial carries both reports.

cards.headline: Mathiesen 2012: A1C at 36 weeks 6.27% (detemir) versus 6.33% (NPH) — noninferior; fasting glucose lower with detemir at 24 and 36 weeks; hypoglycaemia similar
cards.summary: Mathiesen 2012: A1C at 36 weeks 6.27% (detemir) versus 6.33% (NPH) — noninferior; fasting glucose lower with detemir at 24 and 36 weeks; hypoglycaemia similar
cards.people: 310 women with type 1 diabetes randomised and exposed to insulin detemir (152) or NPH insulin (158), both with prandial insulin aspart, starting up to 12 months before pregnancy (48%) or at 8–12 weeks' gestation (52%); primary analysis was A1C at 36 gestational weeks against a 0.4% noninferiority margin.
cards.result: Estimated A1C at 36 weeks was 6.27% with detemir and 6.33% with NPH (full analysis set difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.08; per protocol −0.15%, −0.34 to 0.04) — noninferiority declared. Fasting plasma glucose was significantly lower with detemir at 24 weeks (96.8 vs 113.8 mg/dL, P=0.012) and 36 weeks (85.7 vs 97.4 mg/dL, P=0.017). Major and minor hypoglycaemia rates during pregnancy were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: An open-label noninferiority trial: 'no difference' here means 'not worse by more than 0.4 A1C points', and the fasting-glucose advantage, while significant, did not translate into an A1C advantage. Half the women started before conception, which is not how most basal-insulin switches in pregnancy happen.
cards.source: Mathiesen ER et al. Maternal efficacy and safety outcomes in a randomized, controlled trial comparing insulin detemir with NPH insulin in 310 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes. cards.headline: Hod 2014 (same trial, perinatal report): live births 128 versus 136, perinatal deaths 2 versus 1, malformations 5.6% versus 5.5% — no perinatal safety difference
cards.summary: Hod 2014 (same trial, perinatal report): live births 128 versus 136, perinatal deaths 2 versus 1, malformations 5.6% versus 5.5% — no perinatal safety difference
cards.people: The same 310 women with type 1 diabetes randomised to insulin detemir (152) or NPH (158) with insulin aspart, reported here for perinatal and obstetric outcomes.
cards.result: Live births numbered 128 with detemir and 136 with NPH; early fetal losses 11 versus 9; perinatal deaths two versus one. Gestational age at delivery was greater with detemir (treatment difference 0.49 weeks, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.88; p=0.012). Sixteen children had a malformation: 8 of 142 (5.6%) with detemir and 8 of 145 (5.5%) with NPH. Adverse-event incidence was similar between treatments, and the authors identified no perinatal safety issue.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same single trial, not independent confirmation — and with ~145 births per arm it cannot exclude differences in rare outcomes such as specific malformations. It answers 'no signal seen', not 'proven equally safe'.
cards.source: Hod M et al. A randomized trial comparing perinatal outcomes using insulin detemir or neutral protamine Hagedorn in type 1 diabetes. Journal of Maternal-Fetal & Neonatal Medicine. 2014. shelves.title: After gestational diabetes, lifestyle and metformin each cut progression to diabetes by about half over the DPP years — and metformin worked in these women as well as lifestyle, unlike in women without prior GDM
shelves.question: In women with prior gestational diabetes, do intensive lifestyle or metformin prevent diabetes over ten years compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiovascular Diseases/prevention & control · Diabetes Mellitus/prevention & control · Diabetes, Gestational/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucose Intolerance/complications/prevention & control · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Life Style · Metformin/therapeutic use · Motor Activity · Pregnancy · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a prespecified subgroup of a landmark trial, with the ten-year frame softened to what this record shows (the DPP treatment period; the decade-long follow-up is a separate report). Among 350 women with a history of gestational diabetes in the Diabetes Prevention Program (Ratner RE et al., PMID: 18826999), diabetes incidence on placebo ran 71% higher than in parous women without prior GDM at the same glucose levels — this is a genuinely high-risk group. Both intensive lifestyle and metformin reduced incidence by approximately 50% versus placebo in the prior-GDM women; in parous women without GDM the reductions were 49% for lifestyle but only 14% for metformin. So in women after gestational diabetes, metformin performed like lifestyle — the reverse of the pattern in other women. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lifestyle and metformin each roughly halve progression after GDM on this analysis; Tier C because the shelf rests on a subgroup analysis of one trial, however prespecified and plausible.

cards.headline: Ratner 2008 (DPP, prior-GDM analysis): diabetes incidence ~50% lower with both lifestyle and metformin versus placebo in 350 women with prior gestational diabetes
cards.summary: Ratner 2008 (DPP, prior-GDM analysis): diabetes incidence ~50% lower with both lifestyle and metformin versus placebo in 350 women with prior gestational diabetes
cards.type: Randomised trial subgroup analysis (Ratner 2008, Diabetes Prevention Program)
cards.people: 350 women with a reported history of gestational diabetes among 2,190 women randomised in the Diabetes Prevention Program (impaired glucose tolerance; 27 US centres) to standard lifestyle plus placebo, metformin, or intensive lifestyle intervention; compared with 1,416 parous women without a GDM history. Primary outcome was time to diabetes by semiannual fasting glucose and annual oral glucose tolerance testing.
cards.result: Women with prior GDM randomised to placebo had a crude diabetes incidence rate 71% higher than parous women without GDM, despite similar glucose levels at entry. Among prior-GDM women, both intensive lifestyle and metformin reduced diabetes incidence by approximately 50% compared with placebo; among parous women without GDM, the reductions were 49% (lifestyle) and 14% (metformin). The authors conclude metformin may be more effective in women with a GDM history than in those without.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup analysis — 350 women — of a trial whose headline result lives on the live delay-diagnosis shelves; the record reports relative reductions ('approximately 50%') without printing the absolute incidence rates for this subgroup, and it covers the DPP treatment period, not the ten years of the candidate question (the long-term DPP Outcomes Study report is a different record). Self-reported GDM history is another soft edge.
cards.source: Ratner RE et al. Prevention of diabetes in women with a history of gestational diabetes: effects of metformin and lifestyle interventions. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism. 2008. PMID: 18826999. shelves.title: Intensive insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes (DCCT): retinopathy risk cut 76% in prevention and progression slowed 54%, microalbuminuria cut 39% and neuropathy 60% — at two-to-three times the severe hypoglycaemia, with a cardiovascular dividend 17 years later
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes, does intensive insulin therapy prevent or slow retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy versus conventional therapy over the long term?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Confidence Intervals · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/complications/drug therapy · Diabetic Nephropathies/prevention & control · Diabetic Neuropathies/prevention & control · Diabetic Retinopathy/prevention & control · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Insulin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Insulin Infusion Systems · Male · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the foundational trial of diabetes care, with its harm printed in the same breath. In the DCCT (Diabetes Control and Complications Trial Research Group, PMID: 8366922), 1,441 patients with type 1 diabetes were randomised to intensive therapy (pump or ≥3 daily injections, frequent monitoring) or conventional therapy (1–2 injections) for a mean of 6.5 years. Intensive therapy reduced the adjusted mean risk of developing retinopathy by 76% (95% CI 62 to 85) in the primary-prevention cohort, slowed retinopathy progression by 54% (39 to 66) in the secondary cohort, and reduced microalbuminuria by 39%, albuminuria by 54%, and clinical neuropathy by 60% — all relative reductions, from a trial where the chief adverse event was a two-to-threefold increase in severe hypoglycaemia. The long echo came from EDIC follow-up (Nathan DM et al., PMID: 16371630): over 17 years, prior intensive treatment reduced any cardiovascular event by 42% and the composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death by 57%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): concordant microvascular benefits in the trial itself plus a cardiovascular legacy in follow-up; Tier C is set because the shelf claims a cardiovascular-event benefit, which the developer reviews personally.

cards.headline: DCCT Research Group 1993: retinopathy development −76% (relative), progression −54%, microalbuminuria −39%, albuminuria −54%, neuropathy −60% — severe hypoglycaemia 2–3× more frequent
cards.summary: DCCT Research Group 1993: retinopathy development −76% (relative), progression −54%, microalbuminuria −39%, albuminuria −54%, neuropathy −60% — severe hypoglycaemia 2–3× more frequent
cards.type: Randomised trial (Diabetes Control and Complications Trial Research Group 1993, DCCT)
cards.people: 1,441 patients with insulin-dependent (type 1) diabetes — 726 with no retinopathy at baseline (primary-prevention cohort) and 715 with mild retinopathy (secondary-intervention cohort) — randomised to intensive therapy (external pump or ≥3 daily injections guided by frequent glucose monitoring) or conventional therapy (1–2 daily injections), followed for a mean of 6.5 years.
cards.result: Intensive therapy reduced the adjusted mean risk of developing retinopathy by 76% (95% CI 62 to 85) in the primary-prevention cohort; in the secondary cohort it slowed retinopathy progression by 54% (39 to 66) and reduced proliferative or severe nonproliferative retinopathy by 47% (14 to 67). Combined cohorts: microalbuminuria reduced by 39% (21 to 52), albuminuria by 54% (19 to 74), and clinical neuropathy by 60% (38 to 74) — all relative reductions. The chief adverse event was a two-to-threefold increase in severe hypoglycaemia with intensive therapy.
cards.watchOut: A 1983–1993 trial: 'conventional therapy' (1–2 injections, no analogue insulins, no continuous glucose monitoring) is not modern standard care, so the absolute gains available from intensifying today are smaller than these relative figures suggest. The hypoglycaemia cost was measured in an era before CGM alarms.
cards.source: Diabetes Control and Complications Trial Research Group et al. cards.headline: Nathan 2005 (DCCT/EDIC): 17 years on, prior intensive therapy had cut any cardiovascular event by 42% (relative) and MI, stroke or cardiovascular death by 57%
cards.summary: Nathan 2005 (DCCT/EDIC): 17 years on, prior intensive therapy had cut any cardiovascular event by 42% (relative) and MI, stroke or cardiovascular death by 57%
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (Nathan 2005, EDIC)
cards.people: The DCCT cohort (1,441 patients with type 1 diabetes), 93% followed observationally in the EDIC study to February 2005 — a mean of 17 years from DCCT randomisation — comparing cardiovascular outcomes by original treatment assignment.
cards.result: During 17 years, 46 cardiovascular disease events occurred in 31 patients originally assigned to intensive treatment versus 98 events in 52 patients assigned to conventional treatment. Intensive treatment reduced the risk of any cardiovascular disease event by 42% (95% CI 9 to 63; P=0.02) and of nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular disease by 57% (12 to 79; P=0.02) — relative reductions. The DCCT-era HbA1c difference was significantly associated with most of the benefit; group differences survived adjustment for albuminuria.
cards.watchOut: EDIC is observational follow-up of a randomised contrast that ended in 1993 — after the DCCT, both groups were taught intensive therapy, so this is a legacy ('metabolic memory') effect of an early 6.5-year difference, with few events (46 vs 98) behind the percentages.

long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (nathan 2005, edic) the dcct cohort (1,441 patients with type 1 diabetes), 93% followed observationally in the edic study to february 2005 — a mean of 17 years from dcct randomisation — comparing cardiovascular outcomes by original treatment assignment. during 17 years, 46 cardiovascular disease events occurred in 31 patients originally assigned to intensive treatment versus 98 events in 52 patients assigned to conventional treatment. intensive treatment reduced the risk of any cardiovascular disease event by 42% (95% ci 9 to 63; p=0.02) and of nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular disease by 57% (12 to 79; p=0.02) — relative reductions. the dcct-era hba1c difference was significantly associated with most of the benefit; group differences survived adjustment for albuminuria. edic is observational follow-up of a randomised contrast that ended in 1993 — after the dcct, both groups were taught intensive therapy, so this is a legacy ('metabolic memory') effect of an early 6.5-year difference, with few events (46 vs 98) behind the percentages. nathan dm et al. intensive diabetes treatment and cardiovascular disease in patients with type 1 diabetes. new england journal of medicine. 2005. pmid: 16371630. mesh: adolescent · adult · cardiovascular diseases/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · diabetes mellitus, type 1/blood/complications/drug therapy · female · follow-up studies · glycated hemoglobin/analysis · humans · hypoglycemic agents/administration & dosage · insulin/administration & dosage · male · middle aged · proportional hazards models · risk · treatment outcome

cards.summary: Synthesis: intensify early, gain for decades — the trial that set the HbA1c era, hypoglycaemia included

shelves.title: Steno-2: intensive multifactorial treatment in type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria halved cardiovascular events (HR 0.47) — and at 13 years, deaths were 24 versus 40 (HR 0.54) in a single 160-patient trial
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria, does intensive multifactorial intervention (glucose, blood pressure, lipids, aspirin) reduce cardiovascular events and mortality versus conventional care?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — striking hazard ratios from one small, open, single-centre trial; the size of the effect is exactly why it needs the caution. In Steno-2 (Gaede P et al., PMID: 12556541), 160 patients with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria received target-driven intensive multifactorial therapy or conventional guideline care for a mean of 7.8 years. Intensive therapy lowered the cardiovascular composite (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.73) and the risks of nephropathy (HR 0.39), retinopathy (HR 0.42), and autonomic neuropathy (HR 0.37) — relative effects the authors summarise as 'about 50%'. In the follow-up report (Gaede P et al., PMID: 18256393), at 13.3 years 24 intensive-group patients had died versus 40 on conventional therapy (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.89), with cardiovascular death HR 0.43 and cardiovascular events HR 0.41; progression to end-stage renal disease occurred in 1 versus 6 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a mortality claim from a single 160-patient trial is Tier C by rule, and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE until a larger trial speaks.

cards.headline: Gaede 2003 (Steno-2): cardiovascular composite HR 0.47, nephropathy HR 0.39, retinopathy HR 0.42, autonomic neuropathy HR 0.37 over 7.8 years
cards.summary: Gaede 2003 (Steno-2): cardiovascular composite HR 0.47, nephropathy HR 0.39, retinopathy HR 0.42, autonomic neuropathy HR 0.37 over 7.8 years
cards.people: 160 patients with type 2 diabetes and persistent microalbuminuria (mean age 55.1 years) randomised to conventional treatment per national guidelines (80) or intensive target-driven multifactorial therapy (80) — stepwise behaviour change and drugs targeting hyperglycaemia, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and microalbuminuria, plus aspirin — for a mean of 7.8 years; open, parallel design.
cards.result: Declines in HbA1c, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, cholesterol, triglycerides, and urinary albumin excretion were all significantly greater with intensive therapy. Intensive therapy lowered the primary cardiovascular composite (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, revascularisation, amputation) with hazard ratio 0.47 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.73), nephropathy HR 0.39 (0.17 to 0.87), retinopathy HR 0.42 (0.21 to 0.86), and autonomic neuropathy HR 0.37 (0.18 to 0.79) — relative effects of roughly one half.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 160 patients, open treatment, and a bundle of a dozen simultaneous changes — the trial can credit the package, never any component. Event counts behind the hazard ratios are small, and 'conventional care' was year-2000 Danish guideline care, a softer comparator than today's.
cards.source: Gaede P et al. Multifactorial intervention and cardiovascular disease in patients with type 2 diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine. 2003. PMID: 12556541. cards.headline: Gaede 2008 (Steno-2 follow-up): deaths 24 versus 40 at 13.3 years (HR 0.54); cardiovascular death HR 0.43; end-stage renal disease 1 versus 6 patients
cards.summary: Gaede 2008 (Steno-2 follow-up): deaths 24 versus 40 at 13.3 years (HR 0.54); cardiovascular death HR 0.43; end-stage renal disease 1 versus 6 patients
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (Gaede 2008, Steno-2)
cards.people: The same 160 patients, treated for a mean of 7.8 years and then followed observationally for a further mean of 5.5 years (to 13.3 years from randomisation); primary endpoint was time to death from any cause.
cards.result: Twenty-four patients in the intensive group died versus 40 in the conventional group (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.89; P=0.02). Death from cardiovascular causes: HR 0.43 (0.19 to 0.94; P=0.04); cardiovascular events: HR 0.41 (0.25 to 0.67; P<0.001). Progression to end-stage renal disease occurred in 1 intensive-group patient versus 6 conventional (P=0.04), and fewer intensive patients required retinal photocoagulation (relative risk 0.45, 0.23 to 0.86). Few major side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: The mortality result rests on 64 deaths in total from a single small trial — the confidence interval (0.32 to 0.89) is wide, and no second multifactorial trial of this design has replicated it. It is the best evidence for the strategy and simultaneously fragile evidence.
cards.source: Gaede P et al. Effect of a multifactorial intervention on mortality in type 2 diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine. 2008. PMID: 18256393. Registry ID: NCT00320008. shelves.title: Painful diabetic neuropathy (OPTION-DM): all three first-line pathways cut pain from 6.6 to 3.3 and none beat the others — adding the second drug beat staying on one (extra 1.0 versus 0.2 points)
shelves.question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, which first-line pathway — amitriptyline, duloxetine, or pregabalin, alone or combined — gives the best pain relief?
shelves.mesh: Amitriptyline · Analgesics · Cross-Over Studies · Diabetes Mellitus · Diabetic Neuropathies · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Humans · Neuralgia · Pregabalin · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between pathways; the trial's actionable finding is about combining, not choosing. In OPTION-DM (Tesfaye S et al., PMID: 36007534), 130 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (mean daily pain ≥4/10) rotated through three 16-week pathways — amitriptyline supplemented with pregabalin, pregabalin supplemented with amitriptyline, and duloxetine supplemented with pregabalin — with the second drug added at week 6 only if pain remained above 3. Pain fell from a mean 6.6 at baseline to 3.3 at week 16 in all three pathways, with between-pathway differences of −0.1, −0.1, and 0.0 points — none significant. Patients who went on to combination therapy gained a further mean 1.0-point reduction versus 0.2 in those who stayed on monotherapy. Adverse events were the familiar ones, split by pathway: more dizziness with pregabalin-first, nausea with duloxetine-first, dry mouth with amitriptyline-first. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) between the three pathways: start with any first-line drug, and add a second when one is not enough; Tier C, single trial.

cards.headline: Tesfaye 2022 (OPTION-DM): week-16 pain 3.3 on every pathway from 6.6 at baseline; pathway differences −0.1 to 0.0 (not significant); combination added −1.0 versus −0.2 for monotherapy
cards.summary: Tesfaye 2022 (OPTION-DM): week-16 pain 3.3 on every pathway from 6.6 at baseline; pathway differences −0.1 to 0.0 (not significant); combination added −1.0 versus −0.2 for monotherapy
cards.people: 140 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (mean daily pain NRS ≥4 of 10) at 13 UK centres, randomised to one of six sequences of three 16-week pathways — amitriptyline→pregabalin (A-P), pregabalin→amitriptyline (P-A), duloxetine→pregabalin (D-P) — with monotherapy for 6 weeks, then the second drug added if pain remained >3; 130 started a pathway and 84 completed at least two. Doses titrated to maximum tolerated (amitriptyline 75 mg, duloxetine 120 mg, pregabalin 600 mg daily).
cards.result: The 7-day average pain score fell from mean 6.6 (SD 1.5) at baseline to 3.3 (1.8) at week 16 in all three pathways. Mean differences were −0.1 (98.3% CI −0.5 to 0.3) for D-P versus A-P, −0.1 (−0.5 to 0.3) for P-A versus A-P, and 0.0 (−0.4 to 0.4) for P-A versus D-P — none significant. Pain reduction on combination therapy exceeded that on continued monotherapy (mean 1.0 [SD 1.3] vs 0.2 [1.5]). Adverse events were predictable: significantly more dizziness in the P-A pathway, nausea in D-P, and dry mouth in A-P.
cards.watchOut: A crossover in 130 starters with 84 completing two or more pathways — attrition and period effects soften the comparison, and the combination-versus-monotherapy contrast is not a randomised comparison (patients combined because monotherapy had already failed them, inviting regression to the mean). Pain is a symptom score, not a hard outcome.
cards.source: Tesfaye S et al. Comparison of amitriptyline supplemented with pregabalin, pregabalin supplemented with amitriptyline, and duloxetine supplemented with pregabalin for the treatment of diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (OPTION-DM): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised crossover trial. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 36007534. Registry ID: ISRCTN17545443. shelves.title: After standard-dose failure in diabetic neuropathic pain (COMBO-DN): combining duloxetine with pregabalin was not significantly better than pushing either drug to its maximum dose (pain −2.35 vs −2.16, p=0.370)
shelves.question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy inadequately controlled on monotherapy, does combining duloxetine with pregabalin beat high-dose monotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analgesics/administration & dosage · Diabetic Neuropathies/diagnosis/drug therapy/epidemiology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Female · Humans · Internationality · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/diagnosis/drug therapy/epidemiology · Pregabalin · Thiophenes/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the primary endpoint, with every secondary signal leaning the combination's way and none reaching significance. In COMBO-DN (Tesfaye S et al., PMID: 23732189), patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain who had not responded to 8 weeks of standard-dose duloxetine (60 mg) or pregabalin (300 mg) were randomised to the combination (duloxetine 60 mg + pregabalin 300 mg) or to high-dose monotherapy (duloxetine 120 mg or pregabalin 600 mg). Among 339 patients in the combination/high-dose phase, mean 24-hour pain change was −2.35 on combination versus −2.16 on high-dose monotherapy (P=0.370); 50% response rates were 52.1% versus 39.3% (P=0.068). Both strategies were well tolerated. An exploratory analysis of the initial phase found standard-dose duloxetine superior to standard-dose pregabalin (P<0.001, uncorrected). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): combination and dose-escalation are both reasonable next steps after standard-dose failure; this trial does not crown either; Tier C, single trial.

cards.headline: Tesfaye 2013 (COMBO-DN): pain change −2.35 (combination) versus −2.16 (high-dose monotherapy), P=0.370; 50% response 52.1% versus 39.3%, P=0.068
cards.summary: Tesfaye 2013 (COMBO-DN): pain change −2.35 (combination) versus −2.16 (high-dose monotherapy), P=0.370; 50% response 52.1% versus 39.3%, P=0.068
cards.people: 804 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain entered 8 weeks of initial therapy with duloxetine 60 mg/day or pregabalin 300 mg/day; 339 non-responders entered the 8-week randomised phase: combination therapy (duloxetine 60 mg + pregabalin 300 mg) versus high-dose monotherapy (duloxetine 120 mg or pregabalin 600 mg). Primary outcome: change in Brief Pain Inventory 24-hour average pain after the combination/high-dose phase.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between combination and high-dose monotherapy on the primary outcome (mean pain change −2.35 vs −2.16; P=0.370), and most secondary endpoints, though consistently favouring combination, were also non-significant. Fifty-percent response rates were 52.1% for combination and 39.3% for high-dose monotherapy (P=0.068). In exploratory, multiplicity-uncorrected analyses of the initial 8 weeks, duloxetine 60 mg was superior to pregabalin 300 mg (P<0.001). Both drugs and their combination were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The trial randomised only non-responders from its own run-in, pooled two different high-dose monotherapies into one comparator, and ran the decisive phase for just 8 weeks. A 12.8-point response-rate gap that misses significance (P=0.068) is 'unproven', not 'disproven' — the honest stamp is no demonstrated difference, not equivalence.
cards.source: Tesfaye S et al. Duloxetine and pregabalin: high-dose monotherapy or their combination? randomised trial (tesfaye 2013, combo-dn) 804 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain entered 8 weeks of initial therapy with duloxetine 60 mg/day or pregabalin 300 mg/day; 339 non-responders entered the 8-week randomised phase: combination therapy (duloxetine 60 mg + pregabalin 300 mg) versus high-dose monotherapy (duloxetine 120 mg or pregabalin 600 mg). primary outcome: change in brief pain inventory 24-hour average pain after the combination/high-dose phase. there was no significant difference between combination and high-dose monotherapy on the primary outcome (mean pain change −2.35 vs −2.16; p=0.370), and most secondary endpoints, though consistently favouring combination, were also non-significant. fifty-percent response rates were 52.1% for combination and 39.3% for high-dose monotherapy (p=0.068). in exploratory, multiplicity-uncorrected analyses of the initial 8 weeks, duloxetine 60 mg was superior to pregabalin 300 mg (p<0.001). both drugs and their combination were well tolerated. the trial randomised only non-responders from its own run-in, pooled two different high-dose monotherapies into one comparator, and ran the decisive phase for just 8 weeks. a 12.8-point response-rate gap that misses significance (p=0.068) is 'unproven', not 'disproven' — the honest stamp is no demonstrated difference, not equivalence. tesfaye s et al. duloxetine and pregabalin: high-dose monotherapy or their combination? shelves.title: Small-particle diet for diabetic gastroparesis: nausea, fullness and bloating all improved significantly in the only randomised diet trial — 56 patients, 20 weeks, symptoms only
shelves.question: In diabetic gastroparesis, does a diet of small-particle food improve cardinal symptoms versus a standard diabetic diet?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anxiety Disorders · Depressive Disorder · Diabetes Complications · Diet, Diabetic · Feeding Behavior · Female · Gastroparesis · Humans · Insulin · Male · Middle Aged · Particle Size · Quality of Life · Radionuclide Imaging · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Upper Gastrointestinal Tract
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms, on one small randomised trial plus a mechanistic meal study. In the only randomised trial of diet in diabetic gastroparesis (Olausson EA et al., PMID: 24419482), 56 insulin-treated patients randomised to a small-particle diet or the standard recommended diabetic diet for 20 weeks had significantly greater reductions in nausea/vomiting (P=0.01), postprandial fullness (P=0.02), bloating (P=0.006) and regurgitation/heartburn (P=0.02), but not abdominal pain, with no difference in body weight or HbA1c. The mechanism is supported by a randomised crossover meal study in 7 patients with type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis (Olausson EA et al., PMID: 18237818): a small-particle solid meal emptied faster (significantly less radioactivity remaining in the stomach at 120 minutes) and produced a smaller, shorter postprandial glucose dip than an identical large-particle meal. Anxiety also fell on the intervention diet, but depression and quality of life did not change in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): grinding food to small particle size is a low-risk dietary change with randomised evidence for the cardinal upper-gut symptoms — but the trial base is one 56-patient, 20-week study, so this is Tier C.

cards.headline: Olausson 2014: small-particle diet beat standard diabetic diet on nausea/vomiting (P=0.01), fullness (P=0.02) and bloating (P=0.006) over 20 weeks — abdominal pain unmoved
cards.summary: Olausson 2014: small-particle diet beat standard diabetic diet on nausea/vomiting (P=0.01), fullness (P=0.02) and bloating (P=0.006) over 20 weeks — abdominal pain unmoved
cards.people: 56 subjects with insulin-treated diabetes and gastroparesis, randomised to a diet of small particle size or the recommended diabetic diet (control), with dietitian advice on 7 occasions over 20 weeks; GI symptom severity, nutrient intake and glycaemic control measured before and after.
cards.result: A significantly greater reduction in severity of the key gastroparetic symptoms — nausea/vomiting (P=0.01), postprandial fullness (P=0.02) and bloating (P=0.006) — was seen on the intervention diet versus control, as for regurgitation/heartburn (P=0.02), but not for abdominal pain. Anxiety was reduced after the intervention diet but not after the control diet; no effect on depression or quality of life in either group. Fat intake was higher in the intervention group, but there were no differences in body weight, HbA1c or other nutrient intake.
cards.watchOut: The record reports P values for symptom-score changes rather than absolute score differences, the trial is small (56 patients) and unblinded by necessity (patients can see their food), and 20 weeks says nothing about durability or about hard outcomes such as hospitalisation for vomiting.
cards.source: Olausson EA et al. A small particle size diet reduces upper gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with diabetic gastroparesis: a randomized controlled trial. The American journal of gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 24419482. Registry ID: NCT01557296. cards.headline: Olausson 2008 meal study: an identical small-particle meal emptied faster and blunted the postprandial glucose dip in 7 patients with type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis
cards.summary: Olausson 2008 meal study: an identical small-particle meal emptied faster and blunted the postprandial glucose dip in 7 patients with type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis
cards.people: 7 subjects with type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis and 7 healthy subjects; two solid meals of identical composition but different particle size, labelled with technetium-99m, ingested in randomised order; gastric emptying by gamma camera and blood glucose/insulin over 180 minutes.
cards.result: In the diabetic subjects the lag phase was significantly shorter and the radioactivity remaining in the stomach after 120 minutes significantly less after the small-particle meal than the large-particle meal, and the postprandial blood glucose dip was smaller and of shorter duration. After a small-particle meal, gastric emptying did not differ significantly between diabetic and healthy subjects.
cards.watchOut: Seven patients and a single test meal: this is mechanism, not treatment evidence — it shows why the diet might work, and its glucose finding (less late postprandial dipping) is a surrogate measured over 3 hours.
cards.source: Olausson EA et al. Small particle size of a solid meal increases gastric emptying and late postprandial glycaemic response in diabetic subjects with gastroparesis. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small randomised diet trial, concordant mechanism, symptom benefit only
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small randomised diet trial, concordant mechanism, symptom benefit only
cards.people: One randomised controlled trial of 56 insulin-treated patients with diabetic gastroparesis over 20 weeks, plus a 7-patient randomised crossover scintigraphy meal study.
cards.result: Symptoms: nausea/vomiting, postprandial fullness, bloating and regurgitation/heartburn all improved significantly more on the small-particle diet (P=0.006–0.02); abdominal pain did not. Glycaemia and weight: no HbA1c or weight difference in the trial; the meal study showed faster emptying and a smaller postprandial glucose dip. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single small trial carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Dietary advice is the standard first step in gastroparesis yet rested, until this trial, on no randomised evidence at all; the effect sizes are reported as significance levels rather than absolute symptom-score changes, so the size of the benefit a patient should expect is genuinely uncertain.

shelves.title: Ultra-rapid lispro in type 1 diabetes: HbA1c non-inferior to lispro, 1-hour post-meal excursions 1.55 mmol/L (≈28 mg/dL) lower — at the price of ~14× the injection-site reactions
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes, does ultra-rapid lispro (Lyumjev) improve postprandial glucose and HbA1c versus conventional lispro?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin Glargine · Insulin Lispro · Postprandial Period
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for postprandial glucose, not for HbA1c. In PRONTO-T1D (Klaff L et al., PMID: 32488923), 1,222 adults with type 1 diabetes were randomised to mealtime ultra-rapid lispro (URLi), conventional lispro, or open-label post-meal URLi for 26 weeks. HbA1c change was non-inferior for both URLi arms (treatment difference −0.08% for mealtime, +0.13% for post-meal, versus lispro), but mealtime URLi was superior on the meal-test excursions: −1.55 mmol/L (≈-28 mg/dL) at 1 hour and −1.73 mmol/L (≈-31 mg/dL) at 2 hours (both P<0.001). Hypoglycaemia rates were similar overall, with a 37% lower rate more than 4 hours after meals on mealtime URLi (P=0.013); injection-site reactions were reported by 2.9% on mealtime URLi versus 0.2% on lispro. The 52-week extension (Bue-Valleskey J et al., PMID: 33458803) showed the pattern held: HbA1c 7.47% versus 7.54%, 1-hour post-meal glucose 9.23 versus 10.14 mmol/L (≈166 versus 183 mg/dL) (P<0.001), injection-site reactions 3.3% versus 0.9%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but narrow win — flatter post-meal curves at equal HbA1c, from a single trial programme, so Tier C.

cards.headline: PRONTO-T1D (Klaff 2020): HbA1c non-inferior (−0.08% mealtime difference), meal-test excursions −1.55 mmol/L (≈-28 mg/dL) at 1 h and −1.73 mmol/L (≈-31 mg/dL) at 2 h versus lispro (both P<0.001)
cards.summary: PRONTO-T1D (Klaff 2020): HbA1c non-inferior (−0.08% mealtime difference), meal-test excursions −1.55 mmol/L (≈-28 mg/dL) at 1 h and −1.73 mmol/L (≈-31 mg/dL) at 2 h versus lispro (both P<0.001)
cards.people: Adults with type 1 diabetes after an 8-week lead-in optimising basal glargine or degludec, randomised to double-blind mealtime ultra-rapid lispro (n=451) or lispro (n=442), or open-label post-meal ultra-rapid lispro (n=329), for 26 weeks; primary endpoint HbA1c change (non-inferiority margin 0.4%).
cards.result: Both mealtime and post-meal ultra-rapid lispro were non-inferior to lispro for HbA1c: estimated treatment difference −0.08% (95% CI −0.16 to 0.00) for mealtime and +0.13% (95% CI 0.04 to 0.22) for post-meal dosing, with endpoint HbA1c significantly higher for post-meal dosing (P=0.003). Mealtime ultra-rapid lispro was superior for postprandial excursions after a meal test: −1.55 mmol/L (≈-28 mg/dL) (95% CI −1.96 to −1.14) at 1 hour and −1.73 mmol/L (≈-31 mg/dL) (95% CI −2.28 to −1.18) at 2 hours, both P<0.001. Severe, documented and postprandial hypoglycaemia rates were similar, but the rate more than 4 hours after meals was 37% lower on mealtime ultra-rapid lispro (P=0.013) — a relative rate reduction. Injection-site reactions: 2.9% mealtime ultra-rapid lispro, 2.4% post-meal, 0.2% lispro.
cards.watchOut: The headline benefit is a meal-test excursion, a short-term surrogate; HbA1c — the outcome that tracks complications — was merely non-inferior, and dosing after the meal actually ended with a higher HbA1c. The trial was industry-run and treat-to-target, which compresses HbA1c differences by design.
cards.source: Klaff L et al. Ultra rapid lispro improves postprandial glucose control compared with lispro in patients with type 1 diabetes: Results from the 26-week PRONTO-T1D study. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. PMID: 32488923. cards.headline: PRONTO-T1D extension (Bue-Valleskey 2021): at 52 weeks HbA1c 7.47% versus 7.54%, post-meal glucose advantage maintained, injection-site reactions 3.3% versus 0.9%
cards.summary: PRONTO-T1D extension (Bue-Valleskey 2021): at 52 weeks HbA1c 7.47% versus 7.54%, post-meal glucose advantage maintained, injection-site reactions 3.3% versus 0.9%
cards.people: The double-blind mealtime ultra-rapid lispro (n=451) and lispro (n=442) groups from PRONTO-T1D continued for a further 26 weeks (total 52) on basal degludec or glargine, to assess long-term efficacy and safety.
cards.result: HbA1c rose marginally in both groups during weeks 26–52, to 7.47% (ultra-rapid lispro) and 7.54% (lispro); the week-52 treatment difference in HbA1c change was −0.06% (95% CI −0.16 to 0.03). HbA1c <7% was reached by 26.8% versus 24.5%. Self-monitored 1-hour (9.23 versus 10.14 mmol/L (≈166 versus 183 mg/dL)) and 2-hour (8.40 versus 9.53 mmol/L (≈151 versus 172 mg/dL)) post-meal glucose remained significantly lower on ultra-rapid lispro (P<0.001). Hypoglycaemia rates were similar, with a 31% lower rate more than 4 hours after meals (P=0.023) — a relative rate reduction. Injection-site reactions: 3.3% versus 0.9%.
cards.watchOut: An extension of the same trial, not an independent replication: the patients, sites and sponsor are PRONTO-T1D's, and only the double-blind mealtime comparison continued, so the post-meal dosing question is unanswered beyond 26 weeks.
cards.source: Bue-Valleskey J et al. Long-Term Efficacy and Safety of Ultra Rapid Lispro (URLi) in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes: The PRONTO-T1D Extension. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial programme — equal HbA1c, flatter post-meal curves, more injection-site reactions
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial programme — equal HbA1c, flatter post-meal curves, more injection-site reactions
cards.people: One phase 3 trial programme (PRONTO-T1D, 1,222 adults with type 1 diabetes) with a 52-week extension of its double-blind arms.
cards.result: HbA1c: non-inferior at 26 weeks (−0.08% mealtime difference) and essentially identical at 52 weeks (7.47% versus 7.54%). Postprandial glucose: superior at 1 and 2 hours at both time points (−1.55 and −1.73 mmol/L (≈-28 and -31 mg/dL) on the 26-week meal test). Hypoglycaemia: similar overall, with a lower late post-meal rate. Harm on the face: injection-site reactions roughly 3% versus under 1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial programme carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: No second randomised trial compares ultra-rapid with conventional lispro, and no trial is powered for severe hypoglycaemia or long-term complications; the case for switching rests on excursion curves and convenience, not on outcomes.

shelves.title: Patient self-titration of basal insulin (AT.LANTUS): HbA1c fell 1.22% versus 1.08% with physician-led titration in 4,961 patients — severe hypoglycaemia 1.1% versus 0.9%
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes starting basal insulin, does a simple patient self-titration algorithm achieve control as safely as physician-led titration?
shelves.mesh: Algorithms · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Insulin Glargine · Insulin, Long-Acting · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Selection · Safety · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — patients titrating their own glargine did at least as well as physicians, in one very large pragmatic trial. AT.LANTUS (Davies M et al., PMID: 15920040) randomised 4,961 people with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (72% already on insulin, mean duration 12.3 years) to investigator-led titration or a simple subject-administered algorithm for 24 weeks. HbA1c fell from 8.9% to 7.8% overall, with a significantly greater decrease on self-titration (−1.22% versus −1.08%, P<0.001) and a greater fasting glucose fall (−62 versus −57 mg/dL, P<0.001); self-titrators also ended on a higher mean dose increase (21.6 versus 18.7 IU, P<0.003). Severe hypoglycaemia was uncommon and not significantly different: 1.1% self-titration versus 0.9% investigator-led. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a simple self-titration algorithm is safe and marginally more effective than physician-led titration — a single (though very large) open-label trial, so Tier C.

cards.headline: AT.LANTUS (Davies 2005): self-titration −1.22% HbA1c versus −1.08% physician-led (P<0.001); severe hypoglycaemia 1.1% versus 0.9% in 4,961 patients
cards.summary: AT.LANTUS (Davies 2005): self-titration −1.22% HbA1c versus −1.08% physician-led (P<0.001); severe hypoglycaemia 1.1% versus 0.9% in 4,961 patients
cards.people: 4,961 subjects with suboptimally controlled type 2 diabetes (mean duration 12.3 years, 72% pretreated with insulin, baseline HbA1c 8.9%) at 611 centres in 59 countries, randomised to insulin glargine initiation and titration by algorithm 1 (investigator-led, n=2,493) or algorithm 2 (performed by the study subjects, n=2,468) for 24 weeks, open-label.
cards.result: HbA1c fell from 8.9 ± 1.3% to 7.8 ± 1.2%, with a greater decrease on self-titration (−1.22%) than investigator-led titration (−1.08%, P<0.001). Fasting blood glucose fell from 170 to 110 mg/dL, again more with self-titration (−62 versus −57 mg/dL, P<0.001). Mean basal dose rose from 22.9 ± 15.5 to 43.0 ± 25.5 IU, with a larger increase in the self-titration group (21.6 versus 18.7 IU, P<0.003). Severe hypoglycaemia incidence did not differ significantly: 0.9% (investigator-led) versus 1.1% (self-titration).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and industry-era (2005, glargine U100): the self-titration advantage is small in absolute terms (0.14% HbA1c) and partly explained by patients simply taking more insulin (a 2.9 IU larger dose increase) — the algorithm works by removing physician caution, which is also its risk in less-selected real-world patients.
cards.source: Davies M et al. Improvement of glycemic control in subjects with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes: comparison of two treatment algorithms using insulin glargine. Diabetes care. 2005. PMID: 15920040. shelves.title: Liraglutide for antipsychotic-associated prediabetes: normal glucose tolerance in 63.8% versus 16.0% at 16 weeks — but glucose back to baseline a year after stopping
shelves.question: In people with prediabetes and glucose intolerance treated with antipsychotics, does liraglutide reverse prediabetes and reduce weight versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antipsychotic Agents · Blood Glucose · Body Weight · Clozapine · Denmark · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucose Tolerance Test · Humans · Liraglutide · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity · Olanzapine · Overweight · Prediabetic State · Schizophrenia · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — while the drug is taken. In the Larsen trial (Larsen JR et al., PMID: 28601891), 103 patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders on clozapine or olanzapine, overweight or obese with prediabetes, were randomised to liraglutide or placebo for 16 weeks. Glucose tolerance improved significantly more on liraglutide (P<0.001): 63.8% of liraglutide-treated participants developed normal glucose tolerance versus 16.0% on placebo (P<0.001; number needed to treat 2), and body weight fell by 5.3 kg more than placebo (−5.3 kg; 95% CI −7.0 to −3.7). The 1-year follow-up after treatment stopped (Svensson CK et al., PMID: 30374965) is the catch: fasting glucose, HbA1c, C-peptide and lipids had all returned to baseline, though a placebo-subtracted weight loss of −3.8 kg (95% CI −7.3 to −0.2, P=0.04) persisted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): liraglutide reverses antipsychotic-associated prediabetes in about two-thirds of patients during treatment — a single small trial, and the glycaemic benefit does not survive stopping, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Larsen 2017: normal glucose tolerance restored in 63.8% on liraglutide versus 16.0% on placebo (NNT 2); weight −5.3 kg versus placebo at 16 weeks
cards.summary: Larsen 2017: normal glucose tolerance restored in 63.8% on liraglutide versus 16.0% on placebo (NNT 2); weight −5.3 kg versus placebo at 16 weeks
cards.people: 103 randomised patients (97 in the efficacy analysis; mean age 42.5 years, mean BMI 33.8) with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders on stable clozapine or olanzapine, overweight or obese, with prediabetes, at two Danish sites; once-daily liraglutide or placebo for 16 weeks, titrated over the first 2 weeks; 96 participants (93.2%) completed the trial.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — change in glucose tolerance on a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test — improved in the liraglutide group compared with placebo (P<0.001). Altogether 30 liraglutide-treated participants (63.8%) developed normal glucose tolerance compared with 8 placebo-treated participants (16.0%) (P<0.001; number needed to treat, 2). Body weight decreased with liraglutide compared with placebo (−5.3 kg; 95% CI −7.0 to −3.7 kg), as did waist circumference (−4.1 cm; 95% CI −6.0 to −2.3).
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks, 103 patients, and a surrogate primary endpoint (glucose tolerance on an OGTT) — no diabetes-incidence or cardiovascular outcome data. Participants were selected for prediabetes on the two highest-metabolic-risk antipsychotics, so the size of the win may not transfer to other agents or to normoglycaemic patients.
cards.source: Larsen JR et al. Effect of Liraglutide Treatment on Prediabetes and Overweight or Obesity in Clozapine- or Olanzapine-Treated Patients With Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Svensson 2019 follow-up: one year after stopping, glucose, HbA1c and lipids back to baseline — weight loss partly held (−3.8 kg versus placebo, P=0.04)
cards.summary: Svensson 2019 follow-up: one year after stopping, glucose, HbA1c and lipids back to baseline — weight loss partly held (−3.8 kg versus placebo, P=0.04)
cards.type: Follow-up study of a randomised trial (Svensson 2019)
cards.people: Participants of the Larsen 16-week liraglutide-versus-placebo trial, re-examined 1 year after the intervention ended; changes in weight, fasting glucose, HbA1c, C-peptide and lipids compared with end-of-treatment and baseline levels.
cards.result: From end of treatment to the 1-year follow-up, body weight increased in the liraglutide-treated group; however, compared with baseline, the placebo-subtracted weight loss remained significantly reduced (−3.8 kg, 95% CI −7.3 to −0.2, P=0.04). Fasting glucose, HbA1c, C-peptide and lipids had each returned to baseline levels 1 year after stopping liraglutide.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of a stopped intervention, not a maintenance trial: it cannot distinguish 'benefit requires continued treatment' (the pattern with all GLP-1 therapy) from any rebound, and numbers followed up are smaller than the 103 randomised.
cards.source: Svensson CK et al. One-year follow-up on liraglutide treatment for prediabetes and overweight/obesity in clozapine- or olanzapine-treated patients. Acta psychiatrica Scandinavica. 2019. cards.result: On treatment: normal glucose tolerance 63.8% versus 16.0% (NNT 2); weight −5.3 kg versus placebo. One year after stopping: glycaemic measures back to baseline; weight −3.8 kg versus placebo retained. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single small trial carries the shelf.

shelves.title: KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes: 90% came off insulin onto sulfonylurea tablets, HbA1c 8.1% to 6.4% — and 93% were still tablet-only a decade later
shelves.question: In permanent neonatal diabetes due to KCNJ11 mutations, can patients transfer from insulin to oral sulfonylureas with better control?
shelves.mesh: ATP-Binding Cassette Transporters · Cohort Studies · Diabetes Mellitus · Female · Glyburide · Glycated Hemoglobin · Heterozygote · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Insulin · Insulin-Secreting Cells · Male · Mutation · Potassium Channels · Potassium Channels, Inwardly Rectifying · Receptors, Drug · Sulfonylurea Compounds · Sulfonylurea Receptors · Tolbutamide · Kcnj11 Channel
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one of the clearest pharmacogenetic wins in medicine, though never randomised. In the transfer series (Pearson ER et al., PMID: 16885550), 44 of 49 consecutive patients (90%) with diabetes due to KCNJ11 (Kir6.2) mutations successfully discontinued insulin after switching to sulfonylureas, and glycated haemoglobin improved in every patient who switched, from 8.1% before treatment to 6.4% after 12 weeks (P<0.001), sustained at one year. The 10-year international cohort (Bowman P et al., PMID: 29880308) shows the win lasts: of 81 patients followed a median 10.2 years, 75 (93%) remained on sulfonylurea therapy alone, median HbA1c was 6.4% at most recent follow-up versus 8.1% before transfer, and no severe hypoglycaemia was recorded in 809 patient-years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent, large, mechanism-anchored cohort evidence — but it is observational, so Tier C, and it applies only to genetically confirmed KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes.

cards.headline: Pearson 2006: 44 of 49 patients (90%) came off insulin entirely on sulfonylureas; HbA1c 8.1% → 6.4% at 12 weeks (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Pearson 2006: 44 of 49 patients (90%) came off insulin entirely on sulfonylureas; HbA1c 8.1% → 6.4% at 12 weeks (P<0.001)
cards.people: 49 consecutive patients with diabetes due to heterozygous activating KCNJ11 (Kir6.2) mutations — the cause of 30–58% of diabetes diagnosed under 6 months of age — switched from insulin to appropriate-dose sulfonylureas, with insulin-secretory substudies in smaller subgroups.
cards.result: A total of 44 patients (90%) successfully discontinued insulin after receiving sulfonylureas. Glycated haemoglobin improved in all patients who switched (from 8.1% before treatment to 6.4% after 12 weeks, P<0.001), and improved control was sustained at one year. Sulfonylurea treatment increased insulin secretion, stimulated more by oral glucose or a mixed meal than by intravenous glucose; the in-vitro tolbutamide blockade of mutant channels reflected the clinical response.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised — no ethics committee would randomise these infants back to insulin once the mechanism was shown — and 5 of 49 patients could not switch, so genetic confirmation and a supervised transfer are essential; the result says nothing about sulfonylureas in ordinary type 1 or type 2 diabetes.
cards.source: Pearson ER et al. Switching from insulin to oral sulfonylureas in patients with diabetes due to Kir6.2 mutations. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16885550. Registry ID: NCT00334711. cards.headline: Bowman 2018: at a median 10.2 years, 93% still on sulfonylurea alone, HbA1c 6.4%, zero severe hypoglycaemia in 809 patient-years
cards.summary: Bowman 2018: at a median 10.2 years, 93% still on sulfonylurea alone, HbA1c 6.4%, zero severe hypoglycaemia in 809 patient-years
cards.people: 81 patients with KCNJ11 permanent neonatal diabetes from five international laboratories (Exeter, Rome, Bergen, Paris, Krakow) who had transferred from insulin to sulfonylureas before November 2006, followed a median 10.2 years (IQR 9.3–10.8) with annual clinical data.
cards.result: At most recent follow-up, 75 (93%) of 81 participants remained on sulfonylurea therapy alone. In the 64 patients with paired data, median HbA1c was 8.1% before transfer, 5.9% at 1 year and 6.4% at most recent follow-up (median 10.3 years; P<0.0001 versus pre-transfer). Median sulfonylurea dose fell from 0.30 mg/kg/day at 1 year to 0.23 mg/kg/day at follow-up (P=0.03). No severe hypoglycaemia was recorded in 809 patient-years; 11 patients (14%) reported mild, transient side-effects that did not require stopping treatment.
cards.watchOut: Cohort follow-up of successful transferrers identified through genetics laboratories — patients who failed transfer early or were never genotyped are under-counted, and neurological outcomes (a major feature of KCNJ11 disease) are reported separately from the glycaemic headline.
cards.source: Bowman P et al. Effectiveness and safety of long-term treatment with sulfonylureas in patients with neonatal diabetes due to KCNJ11 mutations: an international cohort study. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018. PMID: 29880308. Registry ID: NCT02624817. international cohort study (bowman 2018) 81 patients with kcnj11 permanent neonatal diabetes from five international laboratories (exeter, rome, bergen, paris, krakow) who had transferred from insulin to sulfonylureas before november 2006, followed a median 10.2 years (iqr 9.3–10.8) with annual clinical data. at most recent follow-up, 75 (93%) of 81 participants remained on sulfonylurea therapy alone. in the 64 patients with paired data, median hba1c was 8.1% before transfer, 5.9% at 1 year and 6.4% at most recent follow-up (median 10.3 years; p<0.0001 versus pre-transfer). median sulfonylurea dose fell from 0.30 mg/kg/day at 1 year to 0.23 mg/kg/day at follow-up (p=0.03). no severe hypoglycaemia was recorded in 809 patient-years; 11 patients (14%) reported mild, transient side-effects that did not require stopping treatment. cohort follow-up of successful transferrers identified through genetics laboratories — patients who failed transfer early or were never genotyped are under-counted, and neurological outcomes (a major feature of kcnj11 disease) are reported separately from the glycaemic headline. bowman p et al. effectiveness and safety of long-term treatment with sulfonylureas in patients with neonatal diabetes due to kcnj11 mutations: an international cohort study. the lancet. diabetes & endocrinology. 2018. pmid: 29880308. registry id: nct02624817. mesh: adolescent · adult · blood glucose · child · child, preschool · diabetes mellitus · female · follow-up studies · glycated hemoglobin · humans · hypoglycemic agents · infant · infant, newborn · insulin · male · mutation · potassium channels, inwardly rectifying · sulfonylurea compounds · treatment outcome · young adult · kcnj11 channel

cards.headline: Synthesis: 90% transfer success, HbA1c ~6.4% sustained a decade, no severe hypoglycaemia — observational but overwhelming
cards.summary: Synthesis: 90% transfer success, HbA1c ~6.4% sustained a decade, no severe hypoglycaemia — observational but overwhelming
cards.people: 49 consecutive genotyped patients in the original transfer series and 81 patients in the 10-year international cohort, all with KCNJ11 permanent neonatal diabetes.
cards.result: Transfer success 90% (44/49); HbA1c 8.1% → 6.4% at 12 weeks and 6.4% at ~10 years; 93% still on sulfonylurea alone at 10 years; severe hypoglycaemia 0 events in 809 patient-years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: the evidence is cohort-only, which is why this is LIKELY and personal-review, despite an effect size few randomised trials match.
cards.watchOut: The stamp is strong because the counterfactual is visible in the same patients (insulin-treated before, tablet-treated after, for a decade) and the mechanism is proven in vitro — not because the design is randomised. Extrapolation beyond KCNJ11 (and the related ABCC8) neonatal diabetes is not licensed by this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pearson ER et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16885550); Bowman P et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2018 (PMID: 29880308).

shelves.title: Inpatient CGM: time in range not significantly better in either randomised trial (54.5% versus 48.6%, P=0.14) — hypoglycaemia events and recurrence clearly down
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with diabetes, does real-time continuous glucose monitoring improve time in range versus point-of-care fingerstick testing?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glucose · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Insulin, Regular, Human
shelves.balance: SPLIT — no significant time-in-range gain in either inpatient trial, but hypoglycaemia burden fell. In Spanakis EK et al. (PMID: 35984478), 185 general medicine and surgery patients on basal-bolus insulin were randomised to insulin adjustment guided by real-time CGM or by point-of-care (POC) fingerstick testing: time in range 70–180 mg/dL did not differ significantly (54.51% versus 48.64%, P=0.14), nor did mean daily glucose (183.2 versus 186.8 mg/dL, P=0.36); among patients who had a hypoglycaemic event, CGM guidance cut recurrence (1.80 versus 2.94 events/patient, P=0.03) and time below 70 mg/dL (1.89% versus 5.47%, P=0.02). In Singh LG et al. (PMID: 32759361), 72 high-risk insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes on general wards randomised to real-time CGM with glucose telemetry or POC testing had fewer hypoglycaemic events per patient (0.67 versus 1.69, P=0.024) and fewer events below 54 mg/dL (0.08 versus 0.75, P=0.003), with time below 70 mg/dL 0.40% versus 1.88% (P=0.002) — but again no difference in time in range. PROPOSED SPLIT: CGM in hospital is a hypoglycaemia-safety intervention, not a proven time-in-range intervention, on current randomised evidence.

cards.headline: Spanakis 2022: time in range 54.5% versus 48.6% (P=0.14, not significant) — but recurrent hypoglycaemia cut in patients who had an event (1.80 versus 2.94 events, P=0.03)
cards.summary: Spanakis 2022: time in range 54.5% versus 48.6% (P=0.14, not significant) — but recurrent hypoglycaemia cut in patients who had an event (1.80 versus 2.94 events, P=0.03)
cards.people: 185 general medicine and surgery patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes on a basal-bolus insulin regimen; all wore a Dexcom G6 and had POC testing before meals and bedtime, randomised to insulin adjustment based on the daily CGM profile or on POC results (blinded CGM), with time in range 70–180 mg/dL and hypoglycaemia as primary endpoints.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in time in range (54.51% ± 27.72 versus 48.64% ± 24.25; P=0.14), mean daily glucose (183.2 ± 40 versus 186.8 ± 39 mg/dL; P=0.36), or the percentage of patients with CGM values <70 mg/dL (36% versus 39%; P=0.68) or <54 mg/dL (14% versus 24%; P=0.12). Among patients with one or more hypoglycaemic events, the CGM group had significantly fewer recurrences (1.80 ± 1.54 versus 2.94 ± 2.76 events/patient; P=0.03), less time below 70 mg/dL (1.89% ± 3.27 versus 5.47% ± 8.49; P=0.02), and lower incidence rate ratios below 70 mg/dL (0.53; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.92) and below 54 mg/dL (0.37; 95% CI 0.17 to 0.83) — relative rate reductions.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own primary framing — time in range — was null; the hypoglycaemia wins are concentrated in the subgroup who already had an event, and both arms wore CGM (the control arm's was blinded), so this tests CGM-guided dosing, not CGM versus no monitoring in any broader sense.
cards.source: Spanakis EK et al. Continuous Glucose Monitoring-Guided Insulin Administration in Hospitalized Patients With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Diabetes care. 2022. PMID: 35984478. Registry ID: NCT03877068. cards.headline: Singh 2020 (Glucose Telemetry): hypoglycaemic events 0.67 versus 1.69 per patient (P=0.024), events <54 mg/dL 0.08 versus 0.75 (P=0.003) — time in range again not different
cards.summary: Singh 2020 (Glucose Telemetry): hypoglycaemic events 0.67 versus 1.69 per patient (P=0.024), events <54 mg/dL 0.08 versus 0.75 (P=0.003) — time in range again not different
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Singh 2020, Glucose Telemetry System)
cards.people: 72 insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes at high risk of hypoglycaemia on general wards (interim analysis), randomised to real-time CGM with the glucose telemetry system (remote monitoring, n=36) or point-of-care blood glucose testing (n=36).
cards.result: The CGM/telemetry group had fewer hypoglycaemic events (<70 mg/dL) per patient (0.67 [95% CI 0.34–1.30] versus 1.69 [1.11–2.58], P=0.024) and fewer clinically significant events (<54 mg/dL) per patient (0.08 [0.03–0.26] versus 0.75 [0.51–1.09], P=0.003), with less time below 70 mg/dL (0.40% versus 1.88%, P=0.002) and below 54 mg/dL (0.05% versus 0.82%, P=0.017). There were no differences in nocturnal hypoglycaemia, time in range 70–180 mg/dL, or time above range. The CGM group had no prolonged hypoglycaemia, versus 0.20 episodes <54 mg/dL and 0.40 episodes <70 mg/dL per patient in the POC group.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis of 72 patients at a single centre, in patients pre-selected as high risk for hypoglycaemia — the population most likely to benefit; the telemetry model (staff watching a central feed) is a staffing intervention as much as a sensor intervention, and neither trial measures length of stay or mortality.
cards.source: Singh LG et al. Reducing Inpatient Hypoglycemia in the General Wards Using Real-time Continuous Glucose Monitoring: The Glucose Telemetry System, a Randomized Clinical Trial. Diabetes care. 2020. PMID: 32759361. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: split verdict — hypoglycaemia down in both trials, time in range not significantly improved in either
cards.summary: Synthesis: split verdict — hypoglycaemia down in both trials, time in range not significantly improved in either
cards.people: Two randomised trials of real-time CGM-guided care versus point-of-care testing in hospital inpatients on insulin (185 and 72 patients).
cards.result: Time in range 70–180 mg/dL: 54.5% versus 48.6% (P=0.14) in Spanakis; no difference in Singh. Hypoglycaemia: events per patient 0.67 versus 1.69 (Singh) and recurrence 1.80 versus 2.94 events among affected patients (Spanakis); time below range roughly halved or better in both. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit for hypoglycaemia avoidance, the treatment made no difference to time in range; Tier C is not set, as two concordant randomised trials carry each half of the split.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small, single-country, and enrol insulin-treated patients; ICU patients, where the monitoring argument is strongest, are not the population studied here, and cost/workflow outcomes are absent from both records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Spanakis EK et al. Diabetes care. 2022 (PMID: 35984478); Singh LG et al. Diabetes care. 2020 (PMID: 32759361).

shelves.title: Metformin XR versus IR: pooled trials show no gut advantage except dyspepsia (RR 0.58) — and HbA1c a shade worse on XR (0.09%)
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does extended-release metformin cause fewer gastrointestinal side effects than immediate-release at equal HbA1c?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Metformin · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the widely repeated claim that extended-release metformin is much gentler on the gut does not survive meta-analysis. Abrilla AA et al. (PMID: 33887354) pooled 9 randomised trials (2,609 adults) comparing equal daily doses of extended-release (MXR) and immediate-release (MIR) metformin: immediate-release was statistically associated with slightly better HbA1c lowering (mean difference 0.09%; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.17), extended-release reduced only dyspepsia among the gastrointestinal symptoms (risk ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.34 to 0.98 — a relative reduction), and the cumulative incidence of abdominal discomfort or pain, diarrhoea, and nausea and vomiting was similar with both formulations. A small single-centre randomised trial (Hameed M et al., PMID: 28718236) pointed the other way on tolerability — diarrhoea, dyspepsia and flatulence in 40% on immediate-release 1,000 mg twice daily versus less than half that rate on the same dose of extended-release — with no statistical difference in HbA1c reduction at 3 months (1.0% versus 0.7%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): at equal doses the formulations are glycaemically near-identical and, dyspepsia aside, gastrointestinal tolerability is similar in the pooled randomised evidence.

cards.headline: Abrilla 2021 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (2,609 adults): only dyspepsia reduced on XR (RR 0.58); diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal pain similar; HbA1c marginally better on IR (MD 0.09%)
cards.summary: Abrilla 2021 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (2,609 adults): only dyspepsia reduced on XR (RR 0.58); diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal pain similar; HbA1c marginally better on IR (MD 0.09%)
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials randomising 2,609 adults with type 2 diabetes to equal daily doses of metformin extended-release or immediate-release, pooled in a random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42019148008); primary outcomes HbA1c change and key gastrointestinal symptoms.
cards.result: Immediate-release was statistically associated with better HbA1c lowering (mean difference 0.09% [95% CI 0.01% to 0.17%]). Extended-release only reduced dyspepsia (risk ratio 0.58 [95% CI 0.34 to 0.98] — a relative reduction), and both formulations were associated with a similar cumulative incidence of the other key gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal discomfort or pain, diarrhoea, and nausea and vomiting). The authors concluded extended-release was associated with statistically worse but likely clinically similar HbA1c lowering and minimal improvement in gastrointestinal intolerance.
cards.watchOut: Trials comparing formulations at equal doses in patients who can tolerate metformin cannot answer the clinically common question — whether a patient already intolerant of immediate-release will tolerate extended-release — because such patients are typically excluded or switched outside randomised comparisons.
cards.source: Abrilla AA et al. Metformin extended-release versus metformin immediate-release for adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Hameed 2017: GI side effects 40% on IR 1,000 mg twice daily versus less than half on XR at the same dose — HbA1c falls 1.0% versus 0.7%, not significantly different
cards.summary: Hameed 2017: GI side effects 40% on IR 1,000 mg twice daily versus less than half on XR at the same dose — HbA1c falls 1.0% versus 0.7%, not significantly different
cards.people: 90 patients with type 2 diabetes at a Lahore hospital outpatient clinic, randomised to metformin immediate-release 1,000 mg twice daily, extended-release 1,000 mg twice daily, or extended-release 500 mg twice daily for 3 months; HbA1c at baseline and 3 months, with weekly fasting and random glucose.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by 1.0% on immediate-release 1,000 mg twice daily, 0.7% on extended-release at the same dose and 0.4% on extended-release 500 mg twice daily, with no statistical difference in HbA1c reduction among groups at 3 months and all groups equally effective on fasting and random glucose. Side effects (diarrhoea, dyspepsia and flatulence) were greatest with immediate-release (40%), less than half that rate with extended-release at the equivalent dose, and negligible at half the dose.
cards.watchOut: Ninety patients, non-probability purposive sampling into a 'randomized control trial', unblinded side-effect reporting, and a composite side-effect rate with no per-symptom breakdown — this small trial's tolerability gap is exactly what the larger pooled analysis failed to confirm, except for dyspepsia.
