cards.headline: Synthesis: dyspepsia aside, XR and IR are interchangeable at equal doses — the gut advantage is mostly a myth in pooled data
cards.summary: Synthesis: dyspepsia aside, XR and IR are interchangeable at equal doses — the gut advantage is mostly a myth in pooled data
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (2,609 adults) plus one small 90-patient single-centre trial, all at equal (or stated) daily doses in type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: HbA1c: mean difference 0.09% favouring immediate-release (meta-analysis); 1.0% versus 0.7% falls in the small trial, not significant. Gastrointestinal symptoms: only dyspepsia significantly reduced on extended-release in pooled data (RR 0.58); diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting and abdominal pain similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C is not set: a 9-trial meta-analysis carries the shelf, and the small discordant trial is shown on its face.
cards.watchOut: The honest clinical residue: switching an intolerant patient to extended-release remains a reasonable individual experiment (and dyspepsia may genuinely improve), but patients should not be promised the broad gastrointestinal advantage that marketing implies and the pooled trials do not show.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abrilla AA et al. Diabetes research and clinical practice. 2021 (PMID: 33887354); Hameed M et al. Journal of Ayub Medical College, Abbottabad : JAMC. 2017 (PMID: 28718236).

shelves.title: Ustekinumab in new type 1 diabetes: C-peptide 49% higher at 12 months in a 72-adolescent phase 2 trial — a surrogate signal awaiting a larger trial
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does ustekinumab preserve stimulated C-peptide versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Adolescent · Double-Blind Method · Child · Female · Male · Ustekinumab · C-Peptide · Interleukin-17 · Th17 Cells · Insulin-Secreting Cells · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a phase 2 signal in adolescents, nothing more yet. In the UST1D trial (Tatovic D et al., PMID: 39079992), 72 adolescents aged 12–18 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes were randomised double-blind to ustekinumab or control: treatment was well tolerated with no increase in adverse events, and at 12 months stimulated C-peptide was 49% higher in the intervention group (P=0.02) — a relative difference — meeting the prespecified primary outcome. C-peptide preservation correlated with reductions in IL-17A/interferon-γ co-secreting TH17.1 cells. The earlier phase 1b dose-finding study in 20 young adults (Marwaha AK et al., PMID: 35072168) had found ustekinumab safe at psoriasis doses, with the 90 mg maintenance cohort showing the smallest mean C-peptide decline at 1 year (0.1 pmol/ml). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): IL-12/23 blockade preserved measurably more C-peptide at 12 months in one small phase 2 trial — Tier C, and C-peptide is a surrogate for the outcomes that matter (insulin dose, hypoglycaemia, complications).

cards.people: 20 adults with recent-onset type 1 diabetes (<100 days from diagnosis) at the University of British Columbia, sequentially enrolled open-label into four subcutaneous dosing cohorts (45 mg or 90 mg, loading or maintenance schedules); primary endpoint safety, with mixed-meal C-peptide, insulin use and HbA1c also measured (NCT02117765).
cards.result: Only two adverse events (bacterial vaginosis and hallucinations) were judged possibly related to the drug, and the data and safety monitoring board deemed ustekinumab safe to progress to efficacy studies. At 1 year, the 90 mg maintenance cohort had the smallest mean decline in C-peptide AUC (0.1 pmol/ml). cards.watchOut: Open-label, 20 patients, no control group: this study can support safety and dose choice only — its C-peptide comparisons are between tiny dose cohorts, not against placebo, and it must not be read as efficacy evidence.

shelves.title: Flash CGM on tablets only (IMMEDIATE): time in range up 9.9 points (2.4 h/day) and HbA1c down 0.3% in 16 weeks — one open-label trial of 116 patients
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes treated only with oral agents, does intermittently scanned or real-time CGM improve HbA1c versus fingerstick monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Middle Aged · Hypoglycemic Agents · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Blood Glucose · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Glycated Hemoglobin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one trial aimed exactly at this population. IMMEDIATE (Aronson R et al., PMID: 36546594) randomised 116 adults with type 2 diabetes on non-insulin therapy only (at least one oral agent, HbA1c ≥7.5%, mean 8.6%) to intermittently scanned CGM plus diabetes self-management education, or education alone, for 16 weeks. Time in range in the final 2 weeks was greater by 9.9 percentage points (2.4 hours/day) with the sensor (P<0.01), time above range was less by 8.1 percentage points (1.9 hours/day, P=0.037), and HbA1c fell by 0.3% more than control (P=0.048). Time below range was low and not significantly different, hypoglycaemic events were few in both groups, and glucose-monitoring satisfaction was higher among sensor users. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest glycaemic gain from scanning in oral-agent-only type 2 diabetes — one open-label 16-week trial, so Tier C.

cards.headline: IMMEDIATE (Aronson 2023): time in range +9.9 points (2.4 h/day, P<0.01) and HbA1c −0.3% versus education alone at 16 weeks in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: IMMEDIATE (Aronson 2023): time in range +9.9 points (2.4 h/day, P<0.01) and HbA1c −0.3% versus education alone at 16 weeks in non-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 116 adults with type 2 diabetes using at least one non-insulin therapy and HbA1c ≥7.5% (mean age 58 years, diabetes duration 10 years, mean HbA1c 8.6%), randomised 1:1 at multiple sites to intermittently scanned CGM plus diabetes self-management education or education alone; primary outcome time in range in the final 2 weeks, measured by blinded CGM.
cards.result: At 16 weeks the sensor-plus-education arm had significantly greater mean time in range by 9.9% (2.4 hours/day; P<0.01), significantly less time above range by 8.1% (1.9 hours/day; P=0.037), and a greater reduction in mean HbA1c by 0.3% (P=0.048) versus education alone. Time below range was low and not significantly different between groups, hypoglycaemic events were few in both groups, and glucose monitoring satisfaction was higher among sensor users (adjusted difference −0.5, P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 116 patients, 16 weeks: the intervention bundles the sensor with education and with the attention of wearing a device, the HbA1c difference (0.3%) sits at the edge of significance (P=0.048), and there are no data on durability, medication changes, costs, or any clinical event.

shelves.title: Stem cells for diabetic foot ulcers: complete healing up in pooled trials (RR 1.63) but only for ulcers under 5 cm² — amputation and recurrence unmoved
shelves.question: In non-healing diabetic foot ulcers, does cellular (stem-cell-based) therapy increase complete healing versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetic Foot · Mesenchymal Stem Cell Transplantation · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Wound Healing · Treatment Outcome · Amputation, Surgical
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for complete healing of smaller ulcers; not for amputation or recurrence. The meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mei XH et al., PMID: 40530428) pooled 6 RCTs of mesenchymal stem cell therapy for diabetic foot ulcers: complete healing rates were significantly higher with cell therapy (risk ratio 1.63; 95% CI 1.23 to 2.16; P=0.0007 — a relative effect), driven by small ulcers under 5 cm² (RR 1.71; 95% CI 1.11 to 2.63; P=0.02), with no efficacy for large ulcers (RR 1.18; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.86; P=0.46) and no significant differences in amputation risk (P=0.16), serious adverse events (P=0.38) or recurrence (P=0.33). The largest single trial, of placenta-derived cells PDA-002 (Pollak R et al., PMID: 41077558; the tested product is PDA-002, human placenta-derived cells — Celularity), randomised 159 patients with chronic ulcers with and without peripheral artery disease to one of three intramuscular doses or placebo: the best result was in the peripheral-artery-disease subgroup at the lowest dose (complete closure 38.5% versus 22.6% on placebo, sustained 4 weeks), and no treatment-related serious adverse events occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cell therapy probably helps some chronic ulcers close — heterogeneous small trials, a subgroup-driven largest trial, and no amputation benefit, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Mei 2025 meta-analysis of 6 RCTs: complete healing RR 1.63 (1.23–2.16) with mesenchymal stem cells — benefit confined to ulcers <5 cm² (RR 1.71); amputation and recurrence unchanged
cards.summary: Mei 2025 meta-analysis of 6 RCTs: complete healing RR 1.63 (1.23–2.16) with mesenchymal stem cells — benefit confined to ulcers <5 cm² (RR 1.71); amputation and recurrence unchanged
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials of mesenchymal stem cell-based therapy versus control in patients with diabetic foot ulcers, pooled with random-/fixed-effects models; primary endpoints complete healing (100% epithelialisation), amputation, serious adverse events and recurrence.
cards.result: Mesenchymal stem cell therapy significantly improved overall complete healing rates (risk ratio 1.63, 95% CI 1.23–2.16; P=0.0007 — a relative effect), particularly in small ulcers (<5 cm²; RR 1.71, 95% CI 1.11–2.63, P=0.02), but showed no efficacy for large ulcers (≥5 cm²; RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.75–1.86, P=0.46). No significant differences emerged in amputation risk (P=0.16), serious adverse events (P=0.38) or recurrence (P=0.33). Low heterogeneity and no publication bias were observed.
cards.watchOut: Six small RCTs of differing cell sources, doses and delivery routes pooled under one label ('mesenchymal stem cells'), with healing expressed only as a relative ratio — the record gives no pooled absolute healing rates, so how many extra ulcers close per 100 treated cannot be stated from this source.

cards.headline: PDA-002 phase 2 (Pollak 2025): in the artery-disease subgroup, closure 38.5% versus 22.6% on placebo at the lowest cell dose; no treatment-related serious adverse events
cards.summary: PDA-002 phase 2 (Pollak 2025): in the artery-disease subgroup, closure 38.5% versus 22.6% on placebo at the lowest cell dose; no treatment-related serious adverse events
cards.people: 159 adults with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, stratified by peripheral artery disease status, randomised double-blind to intramuscular PDA-002 (human placenta-derived cells, Celularity) at 3×10⁶, 10×10⁶ or 30×10⁶ cells, or placebo; primary endpoint complete wound closure within 3 months sustained for a further 4 weeks (NCT02264288).
cards.result: PDA-002 was well tolerated, with no treatment-related serious adverse events. The highest efficacy was at the 3×10⁶-cell dose within the peripheral artery disease subgroup (38.5% versus 22.6% for placebo) on the stringent 4-week durability endpoint. The record's abstract does not report a significant overall-population primary-endpoint result across all doses.
cards.watchOut: The headline number is a subgroup (peripheral artery disease) at one of three doses — the classic pattern of a phase 2 trial that has not yet shown its effect in the whole randomised population; 'shows promise' is the authors' own framing, and a phase 3 confirmation does not yet exist in this record.

shelves.title: Glargine versus NPH (Treat-to-Target): identical HbA1c, 6.96% versus 6.97% — the difference is nocturnal hypoglycaemia, 33.2% versus 26.7% reaching target without it
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does insulin glargine titrated to fasting glucose achieve HbA1c comparable to NPH insulin with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Algorithms · Blood Glucose · Body Weight · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Insulin Glargine · Insulin, Isophane · Insulin, Long-Acting · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — equal control, less nocturnal hypoglycaemia. In the Treat-to-Target trial (Riddle MC et al., PMID: 14578243), 756 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral agents were randomised to bedtime glargine or NPH, both titrated to fasting glucose ≤100 mg/dL for 24 weeks: endpoint fasting glucose (117 versus 120 mg/dL) and HbA1c (6.96% versus 6.97%) were essentially identical, and about 60% on each insulin reached HbA1c ≤7% — but 25% more patients reached target without documented nocturnal hypoglycaemia on glargine (33.2% versus 26.7%, P<0.05), and rates of other symptomatic hypoglycaemia categories were 21–48% lower (relative reductions). The Cochrane review (Semlitsch T et al., PMID: 33166419) pooling 16 glargine-versus-NPH trials found HbA1c changes comparable, with glargine reducing confirmed and confirmed nocturnal hypoglycaemia; the severe-hypoglycaemia risk ratio was 0.68 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.01; P=0.06; absolute risk reduction −1.2%), on very low-certainty evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glargine's advantage over NPH is hypoglycaemia — chiefly nocturnal — not glycaemic potency.

cards.headline: Treat-to-Target (Riddle 2003): HbA1c 6.96% versus 6.97% — but target without nocturnal hypoglycaemia in 33.2% versus 26.7% (P<0.05)
cards.summary: Treat-to-Target (Riddle 2003): HbA1c 6.96% versus 6.97% — but target without nocturnal hypoglycaemia in 33.2% versus 26.7% (P<0.05)
cards.people: 756 overweight men and women with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c >7.5% on one or two oral agents, randomised open-label to bedtime insulin glargine or human NPH once daily for 24 weeks, both titrated with a simple algorithm to fasting plasma glucose ≤100 mg/dL, continuing prestudy oral agents.
cards.result: Mean endpoint fasting plasma glucose was similar (117 versus 120 mg/dL), as was HbA1c (6.96% versus 6.97%); approximately 60% of patients on each insulin attained HbA1c ≤7%. However, nearly 25% more patients attained this without documented nocturnal hypoglycaemia (≤72 mg/dL) with glargine (33.2% versus 26.7%, P<0.05) — a relative difference — and rates of other categories of symptomatic hypoglycaemia were 21–48% lower with glargine (relative reductions).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 24 weeks, and a treat-to-target design that forces HbA1c equality by titration — the trial was built to compare hypoglycaemia at matched control, so 'no difference in HbA1c' is a design feature, not a finding; weight and cost outcomes are not in this record's headline results.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020 (Semlitsch): across 16 glargine–NPH trials HbA1c was comparable; severe hypoglycaemia RR 0.68 (0.46–1.01), confirmed nocturnal hypoglycaemia reduced — very low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020 (Semlitsch): across 16 glargine–NPH trials HbA1c was comparable; severe hypoglycaemia RR 0.68 (0.46–1.01), confirmed nocturnal hypoglycaemia reduced — very low-certainty evidence
cards.people: Cochrane review of 24 randomised trials of (ultra-)long-acting insulin analogues versus NPH in adults with type 2 diabetes (16 trials of glargine versus NPH: 3,419 randomised to glargine; 8 of detemir versus NPH), trial durations 24 weeks to 5 years, all with unclear or high risk of bias in several domains.
cards.result: Changes in HbA1c were comparable for long-acting analogues and NPH. For glargine versus NPH, the risk ratio for severe hypoglycaemia was 0.68 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.01; P=0.06; absolute risk reduction −1.2%, 95% CI −2.0 to 0; 14 trials, 6,164 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and for serious hypoglycaemia 0.75 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.09; low-certainty evidence); glargine reduced confirmed hypoglycaemia and confirmed nocturnal hypoglycaemia. There was no clear difference in weight gain, adverse-event incidence was comparable, and data on death, complications and quality of life were insufficient or lacking in almost all trials.
cards.watchOut: The pooled severe-hypoglycaemia advantage does not reach conventional significance (P=0.06) and rests on very low-certainty evidence from trials at risk of bias; the robust, consistent finding is narrower — fewer confirmed (especially nocturnal) episodes — which is a patient-comfort and safety outcome, not a complications outcome.

shelves.title: Insulin plus metformin (HOME): weight gain prevented (−3.07 kg) and insulin dose cut by ~20 units/day over 4.3 years — primary vascular endpoint null, macrovascular signal secondary
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does combining insulin with metformin improve control and reduce weight gain and hypoglycaemia versus insulin alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Pressure · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Diabetic Angiopathies · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Lipids · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — continuing metformin after starting insulin prevents weight gain, improves control and cuts insulin dose; the hard-outcome win is a secondary endpoint. In the HOME trial (Kooy A et al., PMID: 19307526), 390 insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes were randomised to metformin 850 mg (1–3 times daily) or placebo added to insulin for 4.3 years. The primary endpoint — an aggregate of microvascular and macrovascular morbidity and mortality — was not improved. But metformin prevented weight gain (mean difference −3.07 kg; P<0.001), improved glycaemic control (HbA1c 0.4 percentage points lower; P<0.001) despite the aim of similar control in both groups, and reduced insulin requirements by 19.63 IU/day (P<0.001). The secondary macrovascular endpoint favoured metformin (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.94; P=0.02; number needed to treat 16.1), partly explained by the weight difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the metabolic benefits are primary-analysis-grade; the macrovascular claim is a secondary endpoint in a single trial, and because it is a cardiovascular-event benefit claim this shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: HOME (Kooy 2009): primary composite not improved — but weight −3.07 kg, HbA1c −0.4 points, insulin dose −19.6 IU/day, and macrovascular HR 0.61 (secondary) over 4.3 years

cards.people: 390 patients with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin at three Dutch hospital outpatient clinics, randomised double-blind to metformin hydrochloride 850 mg one to three times daily or placebo added to insulin, followed 4.3 years; primary endpoint an aggregate of microvascular and macrovascular morbidity and mortality (NCT00375388).
cards.result: Metformin was not associated with an improvement in the primary endpoint. It prevented weight gain (mean weight gain difference −3.07 kg [range −3.85 to −2.28 kg]; P<0.001), improved glycaemic control (mean HbA1c reduction 0.4 percentage points [95% CI 0.25 to 0.55]; P<0.001) despite the aim of similar control in both groups, and reduced insulin requirements (mean reduction 19.63 IU/day [95% CI 14.36 to 24.91]; P<0.001). The secondary macrovascular endpoint improved (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.94; P=0.02), partly explained by the weight difference; the number needed to treat to prevent one macrovascular endpoint was 16.1 (95% CI 9.2 to 66.6).
cards.watchOut: The macrovascular result — the number most likely to be quoted — is a secondary endpoint in a 390-patient trial whose primary endpoint was null, and the authors note it is partly explained by weight; hypoglycaemia outcomes for the combination are not in this record's headline results, and the trial predates SGLT2/GLP-1 outcome therapy.

shelves.title: Acarbose versus metformin first-line (MARCH): HbA1c −1.11% versus −1.12% at 48 weeks in 784 newly diagnosed Chinese patients — a dead heat
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in Chinese patients, is acarbose as effective initial therapy as metformin for HbA1c?
shelves.mesh: Acarbose · Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · China · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — acarbose matched metformin almost exactly as initial therapy in Chinese patients. In the MARCH trial (Yang W et al., PMID: 24622668), 784 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (mean HbA1c 7.5%) at 11 Chinese sites were randomised open-label to acarbose or metformin monotherapy for 24 weeks, followed by 24 weeks in which add-on therapy was allowed if targets were missed. HbA1c reduction at week 24 was −1.17% on acarbose and −1.19% on metformin; at week 48 it was −1.11% versus −1.12% (difference 0.01%; 95% CI −0.12 to 0.14; P=0.8999), inside the 0.3% non-inferiority margin. Serious adverse events occurred in 2% of each group and hypoglycaemic episodes in 1% of each. The BMI-stratified analysis (Wang G et al., PMID: 25148570) found the similarity held in normal-weight, overweight and obese strata: HbA1c reductions and the proportion reaching HbA1c ≤6.5% were similar, though metformin lowered fasting glucose more in the overweight stratum (−1.73 versus −1.37 mmol/L (≈-31 versus -25 mg/dL), P<0.05) and acarbose lowered 2-hour post-challenge glucose more (−3.34 versus −2.35 mmol/L (≈-60 versus -42 mg/dL), P<0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a genuine non-inferiority result — from a single open-label trial programme in one population, so Tier C.

cards.summary: MARCH (Yang 2014): HbA1c −1.11% on acarbose versus −1.12% on metformin at 48 weeks (difference 0.01%, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.14) — non-inferior
cards.people: 788 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (mean HbA1c 7.5%) at 11 sites in China, randomised after a 4-week lifestyle run-in to 24 weeks of acarbose or metformin monotherapy, then a 24-week phase with add-on therapy if prespecified targets were not achieved; 784 started the assigned drug; non-inferiority margin 0.3% (ChiCTR-TRC-08000231).
cards.result: HbA1c reduction at week 24 was −1.17% in the acarbose group and −1.19% in the metformin group. At week 48 the reduction was −1.11% (acarbose) and −1.12% (metformin), difference 0.01% (95% CI −0.12 to 0.14, P=0.8999). Six (2%) patients in the acarbose group and seven (2%) in the metformin group had serious adverse events, and two (1%) and four (1%) had hypoglycaemic episodes.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and industry-funded (Bayer Healthcare China and Double Crane Pharma), in newly diagnosed Chinese patients with a mean HbA1c of only 7.5% and a high-carbohydrate dietary pattern in which an α-glucosidase inhibitor is pharmacologically favoured; the second 24 weeks allowed add-on therapy, so week-48 equality is equality of treatment strategies, not of monotherapy alone.

cards.headline: MARCH2 (Wang 2014): similarity held across BMI strata — metformin better on fasting glucose in the overweight, acarbose better on post-challenge glucose
cards.summary: MARCH2 (Wang 2014): similarity held across BMI strata — metformin better on fasting glucose in the overweight, acarbose better on post-challenge glucose
cards.type: Stratified analysis of a randomised trial (Wang 2014, MARCH2)
cards.people: All 784 MARCH participants, divided into normal-weight (BMI <24), overweight (BMI 24–28) and obese (BMI ≥28) groups, comparing 48 weeks of acarbose versus metformin within each stratum.
cards.result: The reduction in HbA1c and the proportion of patients reaching HbA1c ≤6.5% were similar between acarbose and metformin in all three BMI groups. In the overweight group, fasting glucose fell more on metformin at 48 weeks (−1.73 [95% CI −1.99 to −1.46] versus −1.37 [−1.61 to −1.12] mmol/L (≈-31 versus -25 mg/dL), P<0.05), while 2-hour post-challenge glucose fell more on acarbose (−3.34 [−3.83 to −2.84] versus −2.35 [−2.85 to −1.85] mmol/L (≈-60 versus -42 mg/dL), P<0.01). Both treatments significantly decreased waist circumference, hip circumference, weight and BMI in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: A secondary, BMI-stratified re-analysis of the same single trial — it adds texture (which glucose each drug moves) but no independent confirmation, and its between-stratum comparisons were not the trial's randomised question.

cards.watchOut: Metformin's first-line status rests on far more than HbA1c (UKPDS outcomes, cost, weight, decades of safety data), none of which MARCH measured; acarbose's case here is glycaemic equivalence in a Chinese dietary context, and its gastrointestinal tolerability is not quantified in these records' headline results.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yang W et al. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2014 (PMID: 24622668); Wang G et al. PloS one. 2014 (PMID: 25148570).

shelves.title: Exenatide weekly versus liraglutide daily (DURATION-6): HbA1c −1.28% versus −1.48% — liraglutide wins on glucose, exenatide on nausea (9% versus 21%)
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, how does once-weekly exenatide compare with daily liraglutide on HbA1c and weight?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Administration Schedule · Exenatide · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Liraglutide · Male · Middle Aged · Peptides · Treatment Outcome · Venoms
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for liraglutide on HbA1c, and for exenatide on tolerability; the head-to-head splits. In DURATION-6 (Buse JB et al., PMID: 23141817), 911 patients with type 2 diabetes on oral agents were randomised open-label to liraglutide 1.8 mg once daily or exenatide 2 mg once weekly for 26 weeks. HbA1c fell more on liraglutide (−1.48%) than on exenatide (−1.28%); the treatment difference of 0.21% (95% CI 0.08 to 0.33) failed the predefined non-inferiority criterion for exenatide (upper confidence limit <0.25%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were commoner on liraglutide: nausea 21% versus 9%, diarrhoea 13% versus 6%, vomiting 11% versus 4% — falling in frequency over time in both groups — and discontinuation for adverse events was 5% versus 3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily liraglutide lowers HbA1c by about 0.2% more than weekly exenatide, at roughly double the gastrointestinal side-effect rates — a single open-label trial, so Tier C. The candidate question asks how the two compare; the stamp direction is liraglutide's glycaemic edge, with exenatide's tolerability and weekly dosing on the face of the shelf.

cards.headline: DURATION-6 (Buse 2013): HbA1c −1.48% on liraglutide versus −1.28% on exenatide weekly — difference 0.21% (0.08–0.33), exenatide non-inferiority not met; nausea 21% versus 9%
cards.summary: DURATION-6 (Buse 2013): HbA1c −1.48% on liraglutide versus −1.28% on exenatide weekly — difference 0.21% (0.08–0.33), exenatide non-inferiority not met; nausea 21% versus 9%
cards.people: 912 patients aged 18 or older with type 2 diabetes treated with lifestyle modification and oral antihyperglycaemic drugs, at 105 sites in 19 countries, randomised open-label to liraglutide 1.8 mg once daily (n=450 in the intention-to-treat analysis) or exenatide 2 mg once weekly (n=461) for 26 weeks; primary endpoint change in HbA1c (NCT01029886).
cards.result: The least-squares mean change in HbA1c was greater on liraglutide (−1.48%, SE 0.05) than on exenatide (−1.28%, SE 0.05), with the treatment difference (0.21%, 95% CI 0.08–0.33) not meeting the predefined non-inferiority criteria (upper limit of CI <0.25%). The most common adverse events were nausea (21% liraglutide versus 9% exenatide), diarrhoea (13% versus 6%) and vomiting (11% versus 4%), occurring less frequently with exenatide and with decreasing incidence over time in both groups. Discontinuation because of adverse events: 5% (liraglutide) versus 3% (exenatide).
cards.watchOut: Open-label (patients knew whether they injected daily or weekly, which colours both adherence and nausea reporting), 26 weeks, and funded by the exenatide manufacturers; weight outcomes are not in this record's headline results, and both drugs have since been overtaken in potency by later GLP-1 agents — the shelf answers the historical head-to-head as asked.
cards.source: Buse JB et al. Exenatide once weekly versus liraglutide once daily in patients with type 2 diabetes (DURATION-6): a randomised, open-label study. Lancet (London, England). 2013. cards.summary: Synthesis: a 0.2% HbA1c edge for daily liraglutide, bought with about double the gastrointestinal adverse events
cards.people: One open-label randomised trial of 911 patients with type 2 diabetes on oral agents, 26 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c: −1.48% (liraglutide daily) versus −1.28% (exenatide weekly). Nausea 21% versus 9%; diarrhoea 13% versus 6%; vomiting 11% versus 4%; discontinuation for adverse events 5% versus 3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for liraglutide's glycaemic effect, Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf, and the benefit direction depends on whether the reader weights HbA1c or tolerability.

shelves.title: Exenatide plus dapagliflozin (DURATION-8): HbA1c −2.0% for the pair versus −1.6% and −1.4% for each drug alone — superior on every secondary endpoint
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes on metformin, does combining once-weekly exenatide with dapagliflozin lower HbA1c more than either drug alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Benzhydryl Compounds · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Exenatide · Female · Glucosides · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Peptides · Treatment Failure · Venoms
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the combination beat each drug alone on every efficacy measure in its one large double-blind trial. In DURATION-8 (Frías JP et al., PMID: 27651331), 685 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (mean HbA1c 9.3%) were randomised to exenatide once weekly plus dapagliflozin daily, exenatide plus placebo, or dapagliflozin plus placebo for 28 weeks. HbA1c fell −2.0% on the combination versus −1.6% on exenatide alone and −1.4% on dapagliflozin alone (combination versus exenatide −0.4%; 95% CI −0.6 to −0.1; P=0.004; versus dapagliflozin −0.6%; 95% CI −0.8 to −0.3; P<0.001). The combination was significantly superior to either drug alone for all secondary efficacy endpoints — fasting and postprandial glucose, the proportion reaching HbA1c <7.0%, weight loss, the proportion losing ≥5% of weight, and systolic blood pressure (all P≤0.025). Adverse events were recorded in 57% (combination), 54% (exenatide) and 52% (dapagliflozin), with no episodes of major or minor hypoglycaemia reported. A mechanistic substudy (Ferrannini E et al., PMID: 31469220) showed the combination abolished the dapagliflozin-induced rise in β-hydroxybutyrate while maintaining glycosuria. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a large, double-blind, internally consistent trial — held at LIKELY rather than higher because it remains a single trial programme, and flagged Tier C on that basis.

cards.headline: DURATION-8 (Frías 2016): HbA1c −2.0% on exenatide+dapagliflozin versus −1.6% and −1.4% on each drug alone (P=0.004 and P<0.001); superior on every secondary endpoint; no hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: DURATION-8 (Frías 2016): HbA1c −2.0% on exenatide+dapagliflozin versus −1.6% and −1.4% on each drug alone (P=0.004 and P<0.001); superior on every secondary endpoint; no hypoglycaemia
cards.people: 695 patients randomised (685 in the intention-to-treat population; mean HbA1c 9.3%) with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on stable metformin ≥1,500 mg/day, at 109 sites in six countries, to exenatide 2 mg once weekly plus dapagliflozin 10 mg daily (n=231), exenatide plus oral placebo (n=231), or dapagliflozin plus placebo injection (n=233), double-blind for 28 weeks (NCT02229396).
cards.result: HbA1c change at week 28 was −2.0% (95% CI −2.1 to −1.8) on the combination, −1.6% (−1.8 to −1.4) on exenatide alone and −1.4% (−1.6 to −1.2) on dapagliflozin alone; the combination beat exenatide by −0.4% (95% CI −0.6 to −0.1; P=0.004) and dapagliflozin by −0.6% (95% CI −0.8 to −0.3; P<0.001). The combination was significantly superior to either drug alone for all secondary efficacy endpoints (fasting and postprandial glucose, HbA1c <7.0% attainment, weight loss, ≥5% weight loss, systolic blood pressure; all P≤0.025). Adverse events: 57% (combination), 54% (exenatide), 52% (dapagliflozin); the commonest were diarrhoea, injection-site nodules, nausea and urinary tract infections. No episodes of major or minor hypoglycaemia were reported.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-eight weeks and surrogate endpoints throughout: no cardiovascular, kidney or mortality outcomes, in a population starting at HbA1c 9.3% where large falls are easiest; the trial was funded by AstraZeneca (the dapagliflozin manufacturer), and absolute weight and blood-pressure changes are reported in the record only as superiority statements, not numbers.
cards.source: Frías JP et al. cards.headline: DURATION-8 mechanistic substudy (Ferrannini 2020): the combination abolished dapagliflozin's ketone rise while keeping glycosuria — a plausible safety complement
cards.summary: DURATION-8 mechanistic substudy (Ferrannini 2020): the combination abolished dapagliflozin's ketone rise while keeping glycosuria — a plausible safety complement
cards.type: Mechanistic substudy of a randomised trial (Ferrannini 2020, DURATION-8)
cards.people: 678 DURATION-8 participants with fasting and post-mixed-meal insulin, glucagon, free fatty acids and β-hydroxybutyrate measured, comparing exenatide+dapagliflozin with each drug alone at weeks 28 and 52.
cards.result: β-hydroxybutyrate, free fatty acids and glycerol rose most with dapagliflozin alone, fell with exenatide alone, and changed intermediately with the combination; the combination abolished the dapagliflozin-induced rise in β-hydroxybutyrate, reduced the exenatide-induced increase in the insulin-to-glucagon ratio, maintained glycosuria, and increased haematocrit. Patients in the top quartile of β-hydroxybutyrate change were more often on dapagliflozin alone and had higher urine glucose-to-creatinine ratios.
cards.watchOut: A biomarker substudy of the same trial, not independent evidence: ketone concentrations in a trial that excluded high-risk patients cannot establish protection against clinical ketoacidosis, which is rare and was not an outcome here.
cards.source: Ferrannini E et al. Hormone-substrate changes with exenatide plus dapagliflozin versus each drug alone: The randomized, active-controlled DURATION-8 study. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. PMID: 31469220. cards.headline: Synthesis: combination wins on HbA1c by 0.4–0.6% over its components, with a clean short-term safety record
cards.summary: Synthesis: combination wins on HbA1c by 0.4–0.6% over its components, with a clean short-term safety record
cards.people: One double-blind phase 3 trial (685 patients on metformin, 28 weeks) plus its mechanistic substudy.
cards.result: HbA1c: −2.0% combination versus −1.6% exenatide and −1.4% dapagliflozin. All secondary efficacy endpoints favoured the combination (P≤0.025). Adverse events 57% versus 54% and 52%; no major or minor hypoglycaemia reported. shelves.title: Empagliflozin plus metformin from day one: HbA1c −1.9% to −2.1% versus −1.4% and −1.2% to −1.8% for the single drugs in 1,364 drug-naïve patients
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does starting empagliflozin and metformin together beat starting either component alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Benzhydryl Compounds · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucosides · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — starting both drugs together beat starting either alone in one large double-blind trial. Hadjadj S et al. (PMID: 27493136) randomised 1,364 drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >7.5% to ≤12%; mean baseline 8.6–8.9%) to twice-daily empagliflozin+metformin combinations at two dose levels of each drug, empagliflozin once daily (10 or 25 mg), or metformin twice daily (500 or 1,000 mg), for 24 weeks. HbA1c fell −1.9% to −2.1% on the twice-daily combination regimens, −1.4% on both empagliflozin once-daily regimens, and −1.2% to −1.8% on metformin twice daily; the combination reductions were significantly greater than with empagliflozin once daily (P<0.001) and with metformin twice daily (P<0.01). Weight fell significantly more on the combinations (−2.8 to −3.8 kg) than on metformin (−0.5 to −1.3 kg; P<0.001 for all). Adverse-event rates were similar across groups (56.7–66.3%), and no hypoglycaemic events required assistance. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a big, clean, double-blind win on HbA1c and weight — a single 24-week trial with surrogate endpoints, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Hadjadj 2016: HbA1c −1.9% to −2.1% on empagliflozin+metformin twice daily versus −1.4% on empagliflozin alone and −1.2% to −1.8% on metformin alone; weight −2.8 to −3.8 kg versus −0.5 to −1.3 kg
cards.summary: Hadjadj 2016: HbA1c −1.9% to −2.1% on empagliflozin+metformin twice daily versus −1.4% on empagliflozin alone and −1.2% to −1.8% on metformin alone; weight −2.8 to −3.8 kg versus −0.5 to −1.3 kg
cards.people: 1,364 drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >7.5% to ≤12%) randomised double-blind for 24 weeks to empagliflozin 12.5 mg twice daily + metformin 1,000 or 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 5 mg twice daily + metformin 1,000 or 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 25 or 10 mg once daily, or metformin 1,000 or 500 mg twice daily; primary endpoint HbA1c change at week 24 (NCT01719003).
cards.result: Reductions in HbA1c (mean baseline 8.6–8.9%) were −1.9% to −2.1% with the empagliflozin+metformin twice-daily regimens, −1.4% with both empagliflozin once-daily regimens, and −1.2% to −1.8% with metformin twice-daily regimens — significantly greater for the combinations than for empagliflozin once daily (P<0.001) and metformin twice daily (P<0.01). Weight reductions were significantly greater with the combinations (−2.8 to −3.8 kg) than with metformin (−0.5 to −1.3 kg) (P<0.001 for all). Adverse-event rates were similar across groups (56.7–66.3%). No hypoglycaemic adverse events required assistance.
cards.watchOut: The winning regimens are twice-daily combinations (empagliflozin split across the day, not the marketed once-daily dose), the trial lasts 24 weeks in drug-naïve patients starting near HbA1c 8.7% — the easiest population in which to show large falls — and there are no outcome, durability or cost data; twice-daily dosing also doubles the pill burden the combination was meant to simplify.

randomised double-blind trial (hadjadj 2016) 1,364 drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes (hba1c >7.5% to ≤12%) randomised double-blind for 24 weeks to empagliflozin 12.5 mg twice daily + metformin 1,000 or 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 5 mg twice daily + metformin 1,000 or 500 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 25 or 10 mg once daily, or metformin 1,000 or 500 mg twice daily; primary endpoint hba1c change at week 24 (nct01719003). reductions in hba1c (mean baseline 8.6–8.9%) were −1.9% to −2.1% with the empagliflozin+metformin twice-daily regimens, −1.4% with both empagliflozin once-daily regimens, and −1.2% to −1.8% with metformin twice-daily regimens — significantly greater for the combinations than for empagliflozin once daily (p<0.001) and metformin twice daily (p<0.01). weight reductions were significantly greater with the combinations (−2.8 to −3.8 kg) than with metformin (−0.5 to −1.3 kg) (p<0.001 for all). adverse-event rates were similar across groups (56.7–66.3%). no hypoglycaemic adverse events required assistance. the winning regimens are twice-daily combinations (empagliflozin split across the day, not the marketed once-daily dose), the trial lasts 24 weeks in drug-naïve patients starting near hba1c 8.7% — the easiest population in which to show large falls — and there are no outcome, durability or cost data; twice-daily dosing also doubles the pill burden the combination was meant to simplify. hadjadj s et al. initial combination of empagliflozin and metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes. diabetes care. 2016. pmid: 27493136. registry id: nct01719003. mesh: adult · benzhydryl compounds · blood glucose · diabetes mellitus, type 2 · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · drug therapy, combination · female · glucosides · glycated hemoglobin · humans · hypoglycemic agents · male · metformin · middle aged · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: initial combination beats either starter drug on HbA1c and weight, at 24 weeks, in drug-naïve patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: initial combination beats either starter drug on HbA1c and weight, at 24 weeks, in drug-naïve patients
cards.people: One double-blind randomised trial of 1,364 drug-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes, eight dose-regimen arms, 24 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c: −1.9% to −2.1% (combinations) versus −1.4% (empagliflozin once daily) and −1.2% to −1.8% (metformin). Weight: −2.8 to −3.8 kg versus −0.5 to −1.3 kg against metformin. Adverse events similar (56.7–66.3%); no assisted hypoglycaemia. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: The comparison cannot distinguish 'combination is better' from 'two drugs lower glucose more than one' — a pharmacological near-certainty; the clinically live questions (does early combination change long-term trajectory, complications, or treatment burden versus stepwise addition?) are exactly the ones a 24-week HbA1c trial cannot answer.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hadjadj S et al. Diabetes care. 2016 (PMID: 27493136).

shelves.title: Pioglitazone and the death/MI/stroke composite: 4.4% versus 5.7% across 19 trials (hazard ratio 0.82) — with serious heart failure raised from 1.8% to 2.3%
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes with established macrovascular disease, does pioglitazone reduce the composite of death, myocardial infarction, and stroke versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Myocardial Ischemia/epidemiology · Pioglitazone · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk · Thiazolidinediones/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for ischaemic events, with a heart-failure price printed on the same card. The PROactive trial record itself (Dormandy et al., PMID: 16214598) is already carded on the live thiazolidinedione-harms shelf, so this shelf is built on the patient-level meta-analysis of 19 randomised pioglitazone trials (16,390 patients): death, myocardial infarction or stroke occurred in 375 of 8,554 patients (4.4%) on pioglitazone versus 450 of 7,836 (5.7%) on control (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.94, P=.005), an 18% relative reduction. Serious heart failure went the other way: 200 (2.3%) versus 139 (1.8%) (hazard ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.14–1.76, P=.002), without an associated increase in mortality. In the PROactive prior-stroke subgroup (984 patients), pioglitazone reduced fatal or nonfatal stroke from 10.2% to 5.6% (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.34–0.85, P=0.0085), while the main secondary composite in that subgroup (15.6% versus 19.7%; hazard ratio 0.78) did not reach significance. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): pioglitazone lowers the death/MI/stroke composite by about a fifth relative, at the cost of more serious heart failure. Tier C is set because this is a mortality/cardiovascular-event benefit claim.

cards.headline: Lincoff 2007: death, MI or stroke in 4.4% on pioglitazone versus 5.7% on control (HR 0.82) — serious heart failure 2.3% versus 1.8% (HR 1.41)
cards.summary: Lincoff 2007: death, MI or stroke in 4.4% on pioglitazone versus 5.7% on control (HR 0.82) — serious heart failure 2.3% versus 1.8% (HR 1.41)
cards.people: 19 randomised, double-blind trials enrolling 16,390 patients with type 2 diabetes (8,554 pioglitazone, 7,836 control — placebo or active comparator); treatment duration 4 months to 3.5 years; individual patient-level time-to-event data supplied by the manufacturer for independent analysis.
cards.result: Death, myocardial infarction or stroke: 375/8,554 (4.4%) on pioglitazone versus 450/7,836 (5.7%) on control (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.94, P=.005) — an 18% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed alongside. Component hazard ratios ranged from 0.80 to 0.92. Serious heart failure: 200 (2.3%) versus 139 (1.8%) (hazard ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.14–1.76, P=.002), with no associated increase in mortality and no heterogeneity across trials (I²=0% for both endpoints).
cards.watchOut: A manufacturer-supplied database analysed independently is not the same as 19 published outcome trials: most component trials were glycaemic trials in which cardiovascular events were collected as safety data, and only PROactive was powered for macrovascular outcomes — and PROactive's own primary composite was not significant, its death/MI/stroke composite being the main secondary endpoint.
cards.source: Lincoff AM et al. Pioglitazone and risk of cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a meta-analysis of randomized trials. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 17848652. cards.headline: Wilcox 2007 (PROactive stroke subgroup): recurrent fatal or nonfatal stroke 5.6% versus 10.2% (HR 0.53) in patients with a previous stroke — no effect on first stroke in those without
cards.summary: Wilcox 2007 (PROactive stroke subgroup): recurrent fatal or nonfatal stroke 5.6% versus 10.2% (HR 0.53) in patients with a previous stroke — no effect on first stroke in those without
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (Wilcox 2007, PROactive 04)
cards.people: 5,238 patients with type 2 diabetes and macrovascular disease randomised to pioglitazone (titrated to 45 mg) or placebo on top of existing therapy for a mean 34.5 months; this analysis covers the 984 patients with a previous stroke (486 pioglitazone, 498 placebo) and the 4,254 without.
cards.result: In patients with previous stroke, fatal or nonfatal stroke occurred in 5.6% on pioglitazone versus 10.2% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.34–0.85, P=0.0085), and cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke in 13.0% versus 17.7% (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.52–1.00, P=0.0467); the main secondary composite of death/MI/stroke was 15.6% versus 19.7% (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.58–1.06, P=0.1095, not significant). In patients without previous stroke, no treatment effect on first stroke was observed.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of a trial whose primary endpoint was neutral: the recurrent-stroke finding is hypothesis-strengthening, not proof, and it applies only to the highest-risk stratum (prior stroke), not to pioglitazone for primary stroke prevention.
cards.source: Wilcox R et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: a real ischaemic-event reduction of about a fifth relative, bought with heart failure — the trade, not either number alone, is the shelf
cards.people: 19 randomised trials (16,390 patients) pooled at patient level, plus the PROactive prior-stroke subgroup (984 patients) — spanning glycaemic trials and the one dedicated macrovascular-outcome trial in type 2 diabetes with established macrovascular disease.
cards.result: Death/MI/stroke: 4.4% versus 5.7% (hazard ratio 0.82). Serious heart failure: 2.3% versus 1.8% (hazard ratio 1.41), without excess mortality. Recurrent stroke after a previous stroke: 5.6% versus 10.2% (hazard ratio 0.53). shelves.title: Linagliptin and kidney progression in CARMELINA: no difference in renal death, end-stage kidney disease or sustained ≥40% eGFR fall (HR 1.04) at any level of kidney function — albuminuria progression fell, events did not
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does linagliptin increase kidney disease progression versus placebo over long follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Cardiovascular System/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy/epidemiology · Diabetic Nephropathies/drug therapy/epidemiology · Dipeptidyl-Peptidase IV Inhibitors/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Incidence · Kidney/drug effects · Kidney Failure, Chronic/complications/epidemiology/physiopathology/prevention & control · Linagliptin/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Prognosis · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications/drug therapy/epidemiology/physiopathology · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — linagliptin neither increased nor decreased hard kidney progression in CARMELINA. The trial's main JAMA record (Rosenstock et al., PMID: 30418475) is already carded on the live DPP-4 cardiovascular-safety shelf, so this shelf is built on the trial's kidney-focused secondary analyses. Across 6,979 participants followed for a median 2.2 years, the secondary kidney outcome (renal death, end-stage kidney disease, or sustained ≥40% decrease in eGFR) had a hazard ratio of 1.04 (95% CI 0.89–1.22) for linagliptin versus placebo, consistent across all baseline eGFR categories; progression of albuminuria was reduced and HbA1c fell without more hypoglycaemia. In the 646 participants with nephrotic-range proteinuria, the kidney composite likewise showed no clear benefit (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.63–1.01 for the ≥40% eGFR-decline definition, with significant heterogeneity against the non-nephrotic subgroup), and renal death or end-stage kidney disease did not differ (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): over 2.2 years linagliptin is kidney-neutral on hard outcomes — it does not increase progression, and it does not prevent it either.

cards.headline: Perkovic 2020 (CARMELINA by kidney function): kidney composite HR 1.04 (0.89–1.22) and 3-point MACE HR 1.02 — no effect at any eGFR level; albuminuria progression reduced
cards.summary: Perkovic 2020 (CARMELINA by kidney function): kidney composite HR 1.04 (0.89–1.22) and 3-point MACE HR 1.02 — no effect at any eGFR level; albuminuria progression reduced
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised outcome trial (Perkovic 2020, CARMELINA)
cards.people: 6,979 participants with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease and/or chronic kidney disease (mean age 65.9 years, mean eGFR 54.6 mL/min/1.73 m², 80.1% with albuminuria) randomised to linagliptin 5 mg or placebo and followed for a median 2.2 years; analyses stratified by baseline eGFR (≥60, 45–<60, 30–<45, <30 mL/min/1.73 m²).
cards.result: Linagliptin did not affect the secondary kidney outcome of renal death, end-stage kidney disease, or sustained ≥40% decrease in eGFR (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.89–1.22), nor the primary cardiovascular composite (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.89–1.17), with no interaction by eGFR category (P>0.05). Albuminuria progression was reduced with linagliptin, as was HbA1c, without increased hypoglycaemia; adverse events were balanced overall and across eGFR categories.
cards.watchOut: Median follow-up of 2.2 years is short for kidney progression, and the kidney composite was a secondary outcome of a cardiovascular trial; the albuminuria effect is a surrogate that did not convert into fewer hard kidney events within the trial's horizon.
cards.source: Perkovic V et al. Effects of Linagliptin on Cardiovascular and Kidney Outcomes in People With Normal and Reduced Kidney Function: Secondary Analysis of the CARMELINA Randomized Trial. Diabetes care. 2020. PMID: 32444457. Registry ID: NCT01897532. cards.headline: Wanner 2021 (CARMELINA, nephrotic-range proteinuria): kidney events 12–14 times more frequent with nephrotic-range proteinuria, but linagliptin still neutral on renal death and end-stage kidney disease (HR 0.88)
cards.summary: Wanner 2021 (CARMELINA, nephrotic-range proteinuria): kidney events 12–14 times more frequent with nephrotic-range proteinuria, but linagliptin still neutral on renal death and end-stage kidney disease (HR 0.88)
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a randomised outcome trial (Wanner 2021, CARMELINA)
cards.people: The 646 of 6,979 CARMELINA participants (9.3%; 317 linagliptin, 329 placebo) with nephrotic-range proteinuria at baseline (urinary albumin:creatinine ratio ≥2200 mg/g; median 3486 mg/g, mean eGFR 39.9 mL/min/1.73 m²), followed for a median 2.2 years.
cards.result: The kidney composite (renal death, end-stage kidney disease, or ≥40% eGFR decline) occurred at a 12.3-fold higher rate in the nephrotic-range group; the linagliptin hazard ratio in that subgroup was 0.80 (95% CI 0.63–1.01) versus 1.25 (1.02–1.54) without nephrotic-range proteinuria (P-interaction 0.005), but for renal death or end-stage kidney disease alone there was no heterogeneity and no benefit (0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21). Regression to normoalbuminuria (hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 1.07–1.34) and ≥50% albuminuria reduction (1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.25) were more frequent on linagliptin regardless of proteinuria status.
cards.watchOut: A 646-patient subgroup with a significant interaction on one composite definition but not on the harder renal-death/end-stage definition is a signal to note, not a benefit to claim; the honest headline remains neutrality on hard kidney outcomes even in the highest-risk stratum.
cards.source: Wanner C et al. Effect of linagliptin versus placebo on cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in nephrotic-range proteinuria and type 2 diabetes: the CARMELINA randomized controlled trial. Clinical kidney journal. 2021. PMID: 33564423. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: kidney-neutral on events, albuminuria-favourable on paper — safety reassurance, not kidney protection
cards.summary: Synthesis: kidney-neutral on events, albuminuria-favourable on paper — safety reassurance, not kidney protection
cards.people: One large cardiorenal outcome trial (CARMELINA, 6,979 participants, median 2.2 years) examined through its two kidney-focused secondary analyses, including the 646 participants with nephrotic-range proteinuria.
cards.result: Kidney composite (renal death, end-stage kidney disease, sustained ≥40% eGFR fall): hazard ratio 1.04 (95% CI 0.89–1.22). Renal death or end-stage kidney disease in nephrotic-range proteinuria: hazard ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.64–1.21). Albuminuria progression reduced; HbA1c reduced; hypoglycaemia not increased. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The main CARMELINA record (PMID: 30418475) is carded on live shelf #194 under the cardiovascular-safety question, so per the one-home rule it is not re-carded here; this shelf rests on the trial's kidney secondary analyses — a swap the coordinator should note. A 2.2-year horizon cannot exclude slower divergence in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Perkovic V et al. Diabetes Care. 2020 (PMID: 32444457); Wanner C et al. Clinical Kidney Journal. 2021 (PMID: 33564423).

shelves.title: Text-message support for type 2 diabetes: HbA1c fell about 0.4 points more than usual care — in one tailored-programme trial and across an 11-trial meta-analysis
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does a text-messaging support programme improve HbA1c versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Health Promotion · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · New Zealand · Program Evaluation · Quality of Life · Self-Management/methods · Text Messaging · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest, consistent, and small. In the SMS4BG randomised trial (366 adults with poorly controlled type 1 or type 2 diabetes, HbA1c ≥8%), nine months of individually tailored text-message support reduced HbA1c by 8.85 mmol/mol versus 3.96 mmol/mol with usual care (adjusted mean difference −4.23 mmol/mol, 95% CI −7.30 to −1.15, P=0.007) — roughly 0.4 percentage points. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials in type 2 diabetes (1,710 participants) found a closely similar pooled HbA1c reduction of 0.38% (95% CI −0.53 to −0.23, P<0.001), with five of the eleven trials individually significant. Only 4 of 21 secondary outcomes in SMS4BG improved significantly, and the trialists themselves note the clinical significance of a 0.4-point fall is unclear. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): text-message support lowers HbA1c by about 0.4 percentage points on average — a real but small effect from a cheap intervention.

cards.headline: Dobson 2018 (SMS4BG): HbA1c fell 8.85 versus 3.96 mmol/mol at 9 months (adjusted difference −4.23 mmol/mol, P=0.007); 95% of users called it useful
cards.summary: Dobson 2018 (SMS4BG): HbA1c fell 8.85 versus 3.96 mmol/mol at 9 months (adjusted difference −4.23 mmol/mol, P=0.007); 95% of users called it useful
cards.people: 366 participants aged 16 years and over in New Zealand primary and secondary care with poorly controlled type 1 or type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≥65 mmol/mol or 8%), randomised to a tailored text-message self-management package for up to 9 months plus usual care (n=183) or usual care alone (n=183).
cards.result: HbA1c reduction at 9 months was −8.85 mmol/mol (SD 14.84) in the intervention group versus −3.96 mmol/mol (17.02) in controls (adjusted mean difference −4.23, 95% CI −7.30 to −1.15, P=0.007). Of 21 secondary outcomes only four improved significantly, including foot-care behaviour (adjusted difference 0.85, P<0.001) and health status on the EQ-5D visual analogue scale (4.38, P=0.03); 161 of 169 respondents (95%) found the programme useful and 164 (97%) would recommend it.
cards.watchOut: The trial mixed type 1 and type 2 diabetes (the shelf question is type 2), follow-up was 9 months, and a −4.23 mmol/mol average difference is below what most clinicians would call a meaningful drug-sized effect — the authors state its clinical significance is unclear.
cards.source: Dobson R et al. Effectiveness of text message based, diabetes self management support programme (SMS4BG): two arm, parallel randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2018. PMID: 29773539. Registry ID: ACTRN12614001232628. cards.headline: Haider 2019: across 11 text-messaging trials in type 2 diabetes (1,710 patients), pooled HbA1c fell 0.38% (95% CI −0.53 to −0.23)
cards.summary: Haider 2019: across 11 text-messaging trials in type 2 diabetes (1,710 patients), pooled HbA1c fell 0.38% (95% CI −0.53 to −0.23)
cards.people: 11 randomised controlled trials (1,710 participants) of text-messaging interventions of at least 4 weeks in type 2 diabetes, identified from 208 screened papers; unidirectional educational/motivational messaging (bidirectional messaging and type 1, pre-diabetes and gestational diabetes trials excluded).
cards.result: Five of the eleven trials showed a significant HbA1c improvement and the remainder trended favourable; the meta-analysis of nine trials found an overall HbA1c reduction of 0.38% (95% CI −0.53 to −0.23, P<0.001) with lifestyle-focused text messaging versus control.
cards.watchOut: Small, short, heterogeneous trials of varying message content and intensity; publication bias toward positive small trials is a standing concern in mHealth literature, and no trial in this set measured complications or admissions.
cards.source: Haider R et al. Mobile phone text messaging in improving glycaemic control for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Diabetes research and clinical practice. 2019. PMID: 30822496. cards.headline: Synthesis: two independent reads of the evidence land on the same number — about 0.4 HbA1c points
cards.summary: Synthesis: two independent reads of the evidence land on the same number — about 0.4 HbA1c points
cards.people: One 366-patient tailored-programme trial (9 months, mixed type 1/type 2, poorly controlled diabetes) and an 11-trial type 2 diabetes meta-analysis (1,710 participants).
cards.result: SMS4BG adjusted HbA1c difference: −4.23 mmol/mol (≈0.4 percentage points, P=0.007). Meta-analysis pooled difference: −0.38% (95% CI −0.53 to −0.23, P<0.001). No hard-outcome data in either record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The effect is an average over programmes that differ widely; a generic reminder service should not expect the tailored programme's result. Tier C is not set: a randomised trial plus a concordant meta-analysis of randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dobson R et al. BMJ. 2018 (PMID: 29773539); Haider R et al. Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice. 2019 (PMID: 30822496).

shelves.title: Degludec versus detemir in children with type 1 diabetes: equal HbA1c at one year (7.9% versus 7.8%), a 30% lower basal dose — and significantly fewer hyperglycaemia-with-ketosis episodes (rate ratio 0.41)
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes, does insulin degludec achieve control comparable to insulin detemir with lower rates of ketosis?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Diabetic Ketoacidosis · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Infant · Insulin Aspart/administration & dosage · Insulin Detemir/administration & dosage · Insulin, Long-Acting/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ketosis, on top of equal glucose control. In the BEGIN Young trial (350 children aged 1–17 years), degludec once daily was non-inferior to detemir (once or twice daily) for HbA1c at 26 weeks (estimated treatment difference 0.15%, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.32), and at 52 weeks HbA1c was 7.9% versus 7.8% with fasting glucose significantly lower on degludec (treatment difference −1.62 mmol/L (≈-29 mg/dL), P=0.0090) at a lower basal dose (0.38 versus 0.55 units/kg). Hypoglycaemia rates did not differ significantly, but hyperglycaemia with ketosis was significantly less frequent on degludec (0.7 versus 1.1 events per patient-year; treatment ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22–0.78, P=0.0066). A pooled analysis of the two paediatric degludec trials confirmed lower ketosis rates with degludec-based treatment despite similar hyperglycaemia rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): degludec matches detemir for control in children and cuts ketosis episodes by more than half relative.

cards.headline: Thalange 2015 (BEGIN Young): HbA1c non-inferior at 26 weeks and 7.9% versus 7.8% at 52 weeks; ketosis 0.7 versus 1.1 per patient-year (ratio 0.41, P=0.0066)
cards.summary: Thalange 2015 (BEGIN Young): HbA1c non-inferior at 26 weeks and 7.9% versus 7.8% at 52 weeks; ketosis 0.7 versus 1.1 per patient-year (ratio 0.41, P=0.0066)
cards.people: 350 children and adolescents aged 1–17 years with type 1 diabetes (85 aged 1–5, 138 aged 6–11, 127 aged 12–17) randomised to insulin degludec once daily or insulin detemir once/twice daily, each with bolus insulin aspart, for 26 weeks plus a 26-week extension (280 participants).
cards.result: Non-inferiority for HbA1c at 26 weeks was confirmed (estimated treatment difference 0.15%, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.32). At 52 weeks HbA1c was 7.9% (degludec) versus 7.8% (detemir); fasting plasma glucose change favoured degludec (−1.29 versus +1.10 mmol/L (≈20 mg/dL); difference −1.62, 95% CI −2.84 to −0.41, P=0.0090) and basal dose was 0.38 versus 0.55 units/kg, with 64% of detemir patients needing twice-daily dosing. Confirmed hypoglycaemia (57.7 versus 54.1 per patient-year) and severe hypoglycaemia (0.51 versus 0.33) did not differ significantly; hyperglycaemia with ketosis was significantly lower on degludec (0.7 versus 1.1 per patient-year; treatment ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.22–0.78, P=0.0066).
cards.watchOut: Open-label design with treat-to-target titration; the ketosis advantage comes from a secondary safety endpoint, and severe hypoglycaemia was numerically (not significantly) more frequent on degludec — the trade is fewer ketosis episodes, not fewer hypos.
cards.source: Thalange N et al. Insulin degludec in combination with bolus insulin aspart is safe and effective in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes. Pediatric diabetes. 2015. PMID: 25683037. Registry ID: NCT01513473. cards.headline: Thalange 2019: pooled across both paediatric degludec trials, hyperglycaemia rates were similar but ketosis rates were lower with degludec-based treatment
cards.summary: Thalange 2019: pooled across both paediatric degludec trials, hyperglycaemia rates were similar but ketosis rates were lower with degludec-based treatment
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised trials (Thalange 2019)
cards.people: Children and adolescents aged 1–17 years with type 1 diabetes from two phase 3b trials: degludec versus detemir over 26+26 weeks (Study 1) and degludec/aspart co-formulation versus detemir over 16 weeks (Study 2), both with mealtime aspart; post hoc analysis applying a uniform hyperglycaemia threshold of 14.0 mmol/L (≈252 mg/dL).
cards.result: Despite similar rates of hyperglycaemia with degludec-based treatment compared with detemir, the rates of ketosis were lower with degludec/degludec-aspart in both trials — the first systematic collection of ketosis data in paediatric type 1 diabetes trials, supporting a reduced risk of metabolic decompensation.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and descriptive: the record reports the direction and consistency of the ketosis difference across the two trials rather than a single pooled effect estimate, and one of the two trials tested a co-formulation rather than degludec alone.
cards.source: Thalange N et al. shelves.title: Teplizumab as treatment for new-onset type 1 diabetes: C-peptide decline slowed at 2 years in two randomised programmes — a 75% smaller decline in AbATE, preservation concentrated in early, younger, better-controlled patients
shelves.question: In recent-onset type 1 diabetes, does teplizumab treatment (as distinct from prevention) delay C-peptide decline over two years?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · C-Peptide/metabolism · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for beta-cell function as measured by C-peptide, a surrogate, over two years. In the AbATE trial (52 patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes given two 2-week courses of teplizumab, at diagnosis and after 1 year), the decline in C-peptide at 2 years was −0.28 nmol/L on teplizumab versus −0.46 nmol/L in controls (P=0.002), described by the authors as a 75% improvement in the decline. In the larger phase 3 Protégé trial (516 randomised patients), the 14-day full-dose regimen reduced the loss of C-peptide area under the curve at 2 years versus placebo — a prespecified secondary endpoint, the primary composite endpoint having been missed in the trial's first-year report — with preservation concentrated in patients treated within 6 weeks of diagnosis, aged 8–17, with HbA1c below 7.5% and lower insulin use. The common adverse events were rash, transient upper respiratory infections, headache and nausea; antidrug antibodies developed in some Protégé patients without apparent loss of effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two courses of teplizumab slow the loss of endogenous insulin secretion for at least two years in a responder subgroup — this shelf is about treatment after diagnosis, not the separate prevention question (stage 2 disease) shelved elsewhere.

cards.headline: Herold 2013 (AbATE): C-peptide decline at 2 years −0.28 versus −0.46 nmol/L (P=0.002) after two courses of teplizumab
cards.summary: Herold 2013 (AbATE): C-peptide decline at 2 years −0.28 versus −0.46 nmol/L (P=0.002) after two courses of teplizumab
cards.people: 52 patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes treated with teplizumab for 2 weeks at diagnosis and again after 1 year, versus control, with C-peptide followed for 2 years after disease onset; responder characterisation was post hoc.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis of the primary endpoint, the decline in C-peptide at 2 years was −0.28 nmol/L (95% CI −0.36 to −0.20) with teplizumab versus −0.46 nmol/L (95% CI −0.57 to −0.35) in controls (P=0.002), a 75% improvement in the decline as the authors express it. The most common adverse events were rash, transient upper respiratory infections, headache, and nausea. Baseline metabolic and immunologic features distinguished clinical responders from non-responders in post hoc analysis.
cards.watchOut: Small (52 patients) and open-label, with the responder definition constructed after the data were seen; C-peptide preservation is a surrogate — the record does not show fewer hypoglycaemic events or complications.

cards.headline: Hagopian 2013 (Protégé, 2 years): full-dose teplizumab reduced C-peptide loss versus placebo, with the largest preservation in patients randomised within 6 weeks of diagnosis
cards.summary: Hagopian 2013 (Protégé, 2 years): full-dose teplizumab reduced C-peptide loss versus placebo, with the largest preservation in patients randomised within 6 weeks of diagnosis
cards.people: 516 patients with new-onset type 1 diabetes randomised to one of three intravenous teplizumab regimens (14 days at baseline and again after 26 weeks) or placebo; 513 treated and 462 completed 2 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Teplizumab (14-day full dose) reduced the loss of C-peptide mean area under the curve, a prespecified secondary endpoint, at 2 years versus placebo. Greater preservation was seen in prespecified and post hoc subsets: US residents, baseline C-peptide mean AUC above 0.2 nmol/L, randomisation within 6 weeks of diagnosis, HbA1c below 7.5% (58 mmol/mol), insulin use below 0.4 units/kg/day, and age 8–17 years. Exogenous insulin needs tended to be reduced versus placebo; antidrug antibodies developed in some patients without apparent change in efficacy, and no new safety issues emerged in year 2.
cards.watchOut: The trial's primary composite endpoint was not met in its first-year analysis, so the 2-year C-peptide result is a secondary-endpoint success inside a formally negative trial; the subset pattern, though partly prespecified, invites responder-selection optimism.
cards.source: Hagopian W et al. Teplizumab preserves C-peptide in recent-onset type 1 diabetes: two-year results from the randomized, placebo-controlled Protégé trial. Diabetes. 2013. PMID: 23801579. shelves.title: GAD65 vaccine for new-onset type 1 diabetes: a promising small trial missed its primary endpoint, and the 334-patient phase 3 trial showed no preservation of C-peptide at all (P=0.10)
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, does GAD65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) vaccine preserve beta-cell function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Analysis of Variance · Autoantibodies/blood · C-Peptide/blood · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/immunology/metabolism/therapy · Female · Glutamate Decarboxylase/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Immunotherapy · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage/metabolism/therapeutic use · Insulin Secretion · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — at the dose and schedule tested in the definitive trial. The first randomised trial (70 patients aged 10–18, GAD-alum on days 1 and 30) missed its primary endpoint: no significant effect on the change in fasting C-peptide at 15 months, though over 30 months fasting C-peptide declined less on GAD-alum (−0.21 versus −0.27 nmol/L, P=0.045) and stimulated secretion likewise (P=0.04), with no effect in patients treated 6 months or more after diagnosis. The phase 3 trial (334 patients aged 10–20, treated within 3 months of diagnosis) then found the stimulated C-peptide level declined to a similar degree in all groups, with no significant difference between the combined active groups and placebo at 15 months (P=0.10), and no effect on insulin dose, HbA1c, or hypoglycaemia rate; adverse events were infrequent and mild in both programmes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): GAD-alum as tested does not preserve beta-cell function — the small trial's late secondary signals were not confirmed when the question was asked properly at scale.

cards.headline: Ludvigsson 2008: primary endpoint missed at 15 months; fasting C-peptide decline over 30 months −0.21 versus −0.27 nmol/L (P=0.045)
cards.summary: Ludvigsson 2008: primary endpoint missed at 15 months; fasting C-peptide decline over 30 months −0.21 versus −0.27 nmol/L (P=0.045)
cards.people: 70 patients aged 10–18 years with type 1 diabetes diagnosed within 18 months, fasting C-peptide above 0.1 nmol/L and GAD autoantibodies present, randomised to subcutaneous GAD-alum 20 µg (n=35) or placebo (alum alone, n=35) on days 1 and 30, with mixed-meal tolerance tests to 30 months.
cards.result: The treatment had no significant effect on the change in fasting C-peptide at 15 months (the primary endpoint). Over 30 months, fasting C-peptide declined less with GAD-alum than placebo (−0.21 versus −0.27 nmol/L, P=0.045), as did stimulated C-peptide area under the curve (−0.72 versus −1.02 nmol/L per 2 hours, P=0.04); no protective effect was seen in patients treated 6 months or more after diagnosis, and insulin requirement did not change. Adverse events were mild and similar between groups; a GAD-specific immune response was induced.
cards.watchOut: The positive numbers are secondary timepoints in a 70-patient trial whose prespecified primary endpoint was negative — exactly the pattern that larger trials exist to test, and the phase 3 trial below is that test.
cards.source: Ludvigsson J et al. GAD treatment and insulin secretion in recent-onset type 1 diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 18843118. Registry ID: NCT00435981. cards.headline: Ludvigsson 2012 (phase 3): stimulated C-peptide fell equally in all groups at 15 months (P=0.10) — no effect on insulin dose, HbA1c or hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Ludvigsson 2012 (phase 3): stimulated C-peptide fell equally in all groups at 15 months (P=0.10) — no effect on insulin dose, HbA1c or hypoglycaemia
cards.people: 334 patients aged 10–20 years with type 1 diabetes diagnosed within 3 months, fasting C-peptide above 0.1 nmol/L (0.3 ng/mL) and detectable GAD65 autoantibodies, randomised to four doses of GAD-alum, two doses of GAD-alum followed by two of placebo, or four doses of placebo; primary outcome the change in stimulated C-peptide at 15 months.
cards.result: The stimulated C-peptide level declined to a similar degree in all study groups, and the primary outcome at 15 months did not differ significantly between the combined active-drug groups and the placebo group (P=0.10). GAD-alum did not affect insulin dose, glycated haemoglobin level, or hypoglycaemia rate. Adverse events were infrequent and mild in the three groups, with no significant differences.
cards.watchOut: The trial tested subcutaneous GAD-alum at these doses in recent-onset disease; it does not exclude other routes (such as intralymphatic administration, studied later) — but for the vaccine as originally proposed and tested at scale, the answer is no.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the small trial's whisper was not confirmed by the large trial's answer — no preservation
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials of GAD-alum in recent-onset type 1 diabetes in young people: 70 patients (ages 10–18) followed to 30 months, and 334 patients (ages 10–20) followed to 15 months.
cards.result: Primary endpoints: not significant in either trial (15-month fasting C-peptide change; 15-month stimulated C-peptide change, P=0.10). Secondary 30-month signals in the small trial (−0.21 versus −0.27 nmol/L fasting decline) were not reproduced. Clinical outcomes (insulin dose, HbA1c, hypoglycaemia): no effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: A null verdict on a well-tested formulation, not on the antigen concept in every possible delivery system; later intralymphatic studies answer a different delivery question. Tier C is not set: the base is two randomised trials with the larger one definitive.
