shelves.title: Low-dose interleukin-2 in type 1 diabetes: regulatory T cells rose dose-dependently (up to +4.8 percentage points versus +0.5 on placebo) with no deterioration in glucose control — in two small early-phase studies
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes, does low-dose interleukin-2 expand regulatory T cells safely without worsening glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/diagnosis/drug therapy/immunology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Interleukin-2/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · T-Lymphocytes, Regulatory/drug effects/immunology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the immunological aim was met in tiny early-phase studies; no clinical benefit has been tested. In the randomised phase 1/2 trial (24 adults with established type 1 diabetes), a 5-day course of interleukin-2 at 0.33, 1 or 3 million IU/day increased the proportion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) as a percentage of CD4+ cells by 2.8, 3.9 and 4.8 percentage points respectively, versus 0.5 on placebo (P=0.0039 at each dose), with no serious adverse events and no deleterious changes in glucose-metabolism variables; non-serious events (injection-site reactions, influenza-like syndrome) rose with dose. In the DILT1D adaptive dose-finding study (40 adults, single subcutaneous doses of aldesleukin), the doses estimated to raise Treg frequency by 10% and 20% were 0.101×10⁶ and 0.497×10⁶ IU/m², though even the lowest doses transiently pushed plasma IL-2 above the in-vitro Treg-specific window and caused an early dose-dependent dip in circulating Tregs before the rebound. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): low-dose IL-2 reliably expands Tregs over days and did not worsen glucose control in these small studies — whether that translates into preserved beta-cell function is unanswered by either record. Tier C is set: early-phase, small, surrogate-endpoint evidence.

cards.headline: Hartemann 2013: Tregs rose 2.8–4.8 percentage points across IL-2 doses versus 0.5 on placebo (P=0.0039); no serious adverse events, no glucose harm
cards.summary: Hartemann 2013: Tregs rose 2.8–4.8 percentage points across IL-2 doses versus 0.5 on placebo (P=0.0039); no serious adverse events, no glucose harm
cards.people: 24 adults aged 18–55 years with established insulin-dependent type 1 diabetes and at least one diabetes autoantibody, randomised (6 per group) to placebo or interleukin-2 at 0.33, 1, or 3 million IU/day for a 5-day course, followed for 60 days; participants and investigators masked.
cards.result: Interleukin-2 induced a dose-dependent increase in Tregs as a percentage of CD4+ T cells from day 1 to day 60: placebo +0.5% (SD 0.4); 0.33 MIU +2.8% (1.2), 1 MIU +3.9% (1.8), 3 MIU +4.8% (1.9) (P=0.0039 for each dose versus placebo). No serious adverse events occurred; non-serious events during the 5-day phase rose with dose (1 patient on placebo, 3 on 0.33 MIU, 5 on 1 MIU, 6 on 3 MIU), chiefly injection-site reactions and influenza-like syndrome. IL-2 did not induce deleterious changes in glucose-metabolism variables.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four patients, 60 days, and a flow-cytometry endpoint: the trial was designed to find a dose, not to test whether Treg expansion preserves C-peptide or changes any outcome a patient would feel.
cards.source: Hartemann A et al. Low-dose interleukin 2 in patients with type 1 diabetes: a phase 1/2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2013. cards.headline: Todd 2016 (DILT1D): single-dose aldesleukin dose-response mapped — 0.497×10⁶ IU/m² estimated for a 20% Treg rise, with an early transient Treg dip and receptor desensitisation
cards.summary: Todd 2016 (DILT1D): single-dose aldesleukin dose-response mapped — 0.497×10⁶ IU/m² estimated for a 20% Treg rise, with an early transient Treg dip and receptor desensitisation
cards.type: Adaptive dose-finding trial, non-randomised open-label (Todd 2016, DILT1D)
cards.people: 40 adults with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes at a single centre, given single subcutaneous doses of aldesleukin from 0.04×10⁶ to 1.5×10⁶ IU/m² in an adaptive design (39 evaluable); primary endpoint the maximum percentage increase in Tregs over 7 days.
cards.result: The estimated optimal doses to induce 10% and 20% increases in Treg frequency were 0.101×10⁶ IU/m² (95% CI −0.052 to 0.254) and 0.497×10⁶ IU/m² (95% CI 0.316 to 0.678). Circulating Treg frequency first fell dose-dependently at 90 minutes and day 1 (mean decrease 11.6%), then rebounded above baseline by day 7; effector T cells, natural killer cells and eosinophils responded similarly, and the IL-2 receptor beta chain (CD122) was down-modulated on Tregs by a mean 58.0%. Plasma IL-2 at 90 minutes exceeded the hypothetical Treg-specific window (0.015–0.24 IU/mL) even at the lowest doses.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised, single-dose, blood-only measurements in adults: DILT1D defines the pharmacology and its complications (trafficking, desensitisation) rather than any treatment effect, and its findings argue that repeat-dose regimens, not single doses, are the real question.
cards.source: Todd JA et al. Regulatory T Cell Responses in Participants with Type 1 Diabetes after a Single Dose of Interleukin-2: A Non-Randomised, Open Label, Adaptive Dose-Finding Trial. PLoS medicine. 2016. PMID: 27727279. Registry ID: NCT01827735. adaptive dose-finding trial, non-randomised open-label (todd 2016, dilt1d) 40 adults with recently diagnosed type 1 diabetes at a single centre, given single subcutaneous doses of aldesleukin from 0.04×10⁶ to 1.5×10⁶ iu/m² in an adaptive design (39 evaluable); primary endpoint the maximum percentage increase in tregs over 7 days. the estimated optimal doses to induce 10% and 20% increases in treg frequency were 0.101×10⁶ iu/m² (95% ci −0.052 to 0.254) and 0.497×10⁶ iu/m² (95% ci 0.316 to 0.678). circulating treg frequency first fell dose-dependently at 90 minutes and day 1 (mean decrease 11.6%), then rebounded above baseline by day 7; effector t cells, natural killer cells and eosinophils responded similarly, and the il-2 receptor beta chain (cd122) was down-modulated on tregs by a mean 58.0%. plasma il-2 at 90 minutes exceeded the hypothetical treg-specific window (0.015–0.24 iu/ml) even at the lowest doses. non-randomised, single-dose, blood-only measurements in adults: dilt1d defines the pharmacology and its complications (trafficking, desensitisation) rather than any treatment effect, and its findings argue that repeat-dose regimens, not single doses, are the real question. todd ja et al. regulatory t cell responses in participants with type 1 diabetes after a single dose of interleukin-2: a non-randomised, open label, adaptive dose-finding trial. plos medicine. 2016. pmid: 27727279. registry id: nct01827735. mesh: adolescent · adult · biomarkers · chemokines/biosynthesis · diabetes mellitus, type 1/prevention & control · dose-response relationship, drug · eosinophils/drug effects · female · humans · immunophenotyping · inflammation mediators/metabolism · interleukin-2/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/pharmacology · killer cells, natural/drug effects/immunology · lymphocyte count · male · middle aged · recombinant proteins/adverse effects/pharmacology · t-lymphocytes, regulatory/drug effects · young adult

cards.summary: Synthesis: the Treg target is hittable and glucose was not harmed — everything beyond that is still unproven
cards.people: Two early-phase studies in adults with type 1 diabetes: a 24-patient randomised 5-day dose-ranging trial (60-day follow-up) and a 40-patient single-dose adaptive pharmacology study (7-day primary endpoint).
cards.result: Treg proportion change: +2.8 to +4.8 percentage points on IL-2 versus +0.5 on placebo (P=0.0039). Serious adverse events: none. Glucose-metabolism variables: no deleterious change. Clinical outcomes (C-peptide, HbA1c, hypoglycaemia): not tested in either record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Both records answer the question as asked — Treg expansion and short-term safety — and neither touches efficacy; the stamp must not be read as evidence that low-dose IL-2 treats diabetes. Tier C is set for small, early-phase, surrogate-endpoint evidence.

shelves.title: Zimislecel stem-cell islets in type 1 diabetes with severe hypoglycaemia: all 12 full-dose patients were free of severe hypoglycaemic events at a year and 10 of 12 were insulin-independent — in an uncontrolled 14-patient study, with neutropenia and two deaths
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes with recurrent severe hypoglycaemia, do stem-cell-derived islet cells (zimislecel) restore endogenous insulin and eliminate severe hypoglycaemic events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · C-Peptide/blood · Cell Differentiation · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy/surgery · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Hypoglycemia/blood/diagnosis/etiology · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Infusions, Intravenous · Insulin/therapeutic use · Islets of Langerhans/cytology · Islets of Langerhans Transplantation/adverse effects/methods · Transplantation, Homologous
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — striking results in a very small, uncontrolled, interim study, bought with full immunosuppression. In the phase 1–2 FORWARD study, 14 patients with type 1 diabetes and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness (C-peptide undetectable at baseline in all) received zimislecel — allogeneic stem-cell-derived fully differentiated islets, a product of Vertex Pharmaceuticals — by portal-vein infusion with glucocorticoid-free immunosuppression; 2 received a half dose and 12 a full dose. All 14 had engraftment with detectable C-peptide after infusion. Among the 12 full-dose patients, all were free of severe hypoglycaemic events from day 90 to 365 and had HbA1c below 7% (the part C primary endpoint), spent more than 70% of time in the 70–180 mg/dL range, and 10 of 12 (83%) were insulin-independent at day 365. Neutropenia was the most common serious adverse event (3 participants), and two deaths occurred — one from cryptococcal meningitis and one from progression of preexisting neurocognitive impairment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): zimislecel restored endogenous insulin and abolished severe hypoglycaemia for a year in this first small cohort — Tier C, because a single uncontrolled 14-patient interim analysis, however dramatic, is not yet a proven therapy.

cards.headline: Reichman 2025 (FORWARD): C-peptide restored in 14/14; severe hypoglycaemic events eliminated and HbA1c <7% in 12/12 full-dose patients; 10/12 insulin-independent at day 365
cards.summary: Reichman 2025 (FORWARD): C-peptide restored in 14/14; severe hypoglycaemic events eliminated and HbA1c <7% in 12/12 full-dose patients; 10/12 insulin-independent at day 365
cards.people: 14 patients with type 1 diabetes (2 in part A receiving a half dose of 0.4×10⁹ cells, 12 in parts B/C receiving a full dose of 0.8×10⁹ cells) given a single portal-vein infusion of zimislecel plus glucocorticoid-free immunosuppressive therapy, all with undetectable baseline C-peptide, completing at least 12 months of follow-up; analyses were interim and not prespecified.
cards.result: All 14 participants had engraftment and islet function (detectable C-peptide on mixed-meal testing). All 12 full-dose participants met the part C primary endpoint: freedom from severe hypoglycaemic events during days 90–365 with HbA1c below 7% or a fall of at least 1 percentage point; they spent more than 70% of time in the 70–180 mg/dL range, and 10 of 12 (83%) were insulin-independent between days 180 and 365. Neutropenia was the most common serious adverse event (3 participants); two deaths occurred, one caused by cryptococcal meningitis and one by severe dementia with agitation from progression of preexisting neurocognitive impairment.
cards.watchOut: No control group, 14 patients, interim non-prespecified analyses, and a selected population (recurrent severe hypoglycaemia with absent C-peptide) willing to take lifelong immunosuppression — the infection death is part of the intervention's price, not background noise. Durability beyond a year is unknown.
cards.source: Reichman TW et al. Stem Cell-Derived, Fully Differentiated Islets for Type 1 Diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40544428. Registry ID: NCT04786262. shelves.title: Tighter glucose targets in gestational diabetes: large-for-gestational-age unchanged (14.7% versus 15.1%), serious infant outcomes fewer (1.3% versus 2.6%) but serious maternal outcomes more (5.9% versus 3.0%) — and no benefit visible 4.5 years later
shelves.question: In gestational diabetes, do tighter glycaemic targets improve perinatal outcomes versus less-tight targets?
shelves.mesh: Australia · Blood Glucose · Cesarean Section · Diabetes, Gestational/drug therapy/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Infant · Morbidity · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the primary outcome was null and the secondary outcomes point in opposite directions for baby and mother. In the TARGET stepped-wedge cluster trial (1,100 women with gestational diabetes in 10 New Zealand hospitals), tighter targets (fasting ≤5.0, 1-hour ≤7.4, 2-hour ≤6.7 mmol/L — ≈90, 133 and 121 mg/dL) versus less-tight targets did not reduce large-for-gestational-age infants (88/599, 14.7% versus 76/502, 15.1%; adjusted relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66–1.40, P=0.839). The composite of serious infant outcomes (perinatal death, birth trauma, shoulder dystocia) was lower with tighter targets (8/599, 1.3% versus 13/505, 2.6%; adjusted relative risk 0.23, 95% CI 0.06–0.88, P=0.032), but the composite of serious maternal outcomes was higher (35/595, 5.9% versus 15/501, 3.0%; adjusted relative risk 2.29, 95% CI 1.14–4.59, P=0.020), and more women on tighter targets needed pharmacological treatment (67.9% versus 58.5%). At 4.5-year follow-up, maternal HbA1c and child BMI z-score did not differ, and several child motor and behavioural measures favoured the less-tight group. PROPOSED SPLIT: tighter targets did not deliver their primary aim and traded a possible infant gain against a maternal cost, with no long-term advantage — whether to tighten is a values-weighted decision, not an evidence mandate.

cards.headline: Crowther 2022 (TARGET): LGA 14.7% versus 15.1% (aRR 0.96, P=0.839); serious infant composite 1.3% versus 2.6% (aRR 0.23) against serious maternal composite 5.9% versus 3.0% (aRR 2.29)
cards.summary: Crowther 2022 (TARGET): LGA 14.7% versus 15.1% (aRR 0.96, P=0.839); serious infant composite 1.3% versus 2.6% (aRR 0.23) against serious maternal composite 5.9% versus 3.0% (aRR 2.29)
cards.people: 1,100 women with gestational diabetes (1,108 infants) at 10 New Zealand hospitals, all starting on less-tight targets (fasting <5.5, 1-hour <8.0, 2-hour <7.0 mmol/L — ≈99, 144 and 126 mg/dL) with two hospitals crossing every 4 months to tighter targets (fasting ≤5.0, 1-hour ≤7.4, 2-hour ≤6.7 mmol/L — ≈90, 133 and 121 mg/dL); 598 women (602 infants) in tighter periods and 502 (506 infants) in less-tight periods; women blinded to the targets in use.
cards.result: Large for gestational age: 88/599 (14.7%) tighter versus 76/502 (15.1%) less tight (adjusted relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66–1.40, P=0.839). Serious infant composite (perinatal death, birth trauma, shoulder dystocia): 8/599 (1.3%) versus 13/505 (2.6%) (adjusted relative risk 0.23, 95% CI 0.06–0.88, P=0.032). Serious maternal composite (major haemorrhage, coagulopathy, embolism, obstetric complications): 35/595 (5.9%) versus 15/501 (3.0%) (adjusted relative risk 2.29, 95% CI 1.14–4.59, P=0.020). No differences in pre-eclampsia, induction, or caesarean birth; pharmacological treatment was more frequent with tighter targets (404/595, 67.9% versus 293/501, 58.5%; adjusted relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 1.00–1.44, P=0.047).
cards.watchOut: A cluster design comparing hospital-era target policies, not individually randomised treatment: the dramatic infant-composite relative risk rests on 8 versus 13 events, and the maternal composite moves the other way — both secondary signals are fragile, and the prespecified primary outcome was plainly null.
cards.source: Crowther CA et al. Tighter or less tight glycaemic targets for women with gestational diabetes mellitus for reducing maternal and perinatal morbidity: A stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. PLoS medicine. 2022. cards.headline: Douglas 2026 (TARGET 4.5-year follow-up): maternal HbA1c and child BMI no different; coordination difficulties and total difficulties scores worse in the tighter-target children
cards.summary: Douglas 2026 (TARGET 4.5-year follow-up): maternal HbA1c and child BMI no different; coordination difficulties and total difficulties scores worse in the tighter-target children
cards.type: Post-hoc follow-up of a randomised trial (Douglas 2026, TARGET follow-up)
cards.people: 315 of 427 eligible mothers (74%) and 313 of their children (73%) assessed 4.5 years after the TARGET trial, comparing those managed under tight versus less-tight glycaemic targets during pregnancy; outcomes from questionnaires and health records.
cards.result: Maternal HbA1c was similar (40 mmol/mol (SD 12.6) tight versus 38 (8.8) less tight; adjusted mean difference 2.17, 95% CI −0.26 to 4.60, P=0.080), as was child BMI z-score (0.83 (1.72) versus 0.75 (1.48); adjusted difference 0.12, 95% CI −0.24 to 0.48, P=0.498). Children in the tight group were taller (adjusted difference 1.83 cm, P=0.004) but had more coordination difficulties (31/109, 28.4% versus 21/118, 17.8%; adjusted relative risk 1.66, 95% CI 1.01–2.73, P=0.044), more likely autism-spectrum-range behaviour scores (10/108, 9.3% versus 3/117, 2.6%; adjusted relative risk 3.67, 95% CI 1.02–13.23, P=0.047), and higher total difficulties scores (adjusted difference 1.75, P=0.006).
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, questionnaire-based, with 26–27% loss to follow-up and many comparisons: the adverse child signals are hypothesis-generating at most — but they remove any presumption that tighter targets bought long-term benefit to set against the maternal cost seen in the main trial.
cards.source: Douglas LJ et al. Mother and child health 4.5 years after gestational diabetes mellitus managed using tight or less tight targets for glycaemic control: Post-hoc follow-up study of the TARGET trial. PLoS medicine. 2026. PMID: 41632754. shelves.title: Duodenal mucosal resurfacing in type 2 diabetes: the sham-controlled REVITA-2 trial missed its primary endpoint overall (P=0.147) — the HbA1c signal lived in the European subgroup and in patients with high fasting glucose
shelves.question: In type 2 diabetes, does duodenal mucosal resurfacing improve HbA1c versus a sham endoscopic procedure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Catheter Ablation · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Duodenum/surgery · Endoscopic Mucosal Resection · Feasibility Studies · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hyperthermia, Induced · Intestinal Mucosa/surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a negative primary endpoint with subgroup signals, preceded by an encouraging open-label study. REVITA-2 (108 patients in Europe and Brazil) found median HbA1c change at 24 weeks of −10.4 mmol/mol with duodenal mucosal resurfacing (DMR, using the Revita system as named in the publication) versus −7.1 mmol/mol with sham (P=0.147, not significant), and liver-fat change at 12 weeks of −5.4% versus −2.9% (P=0.096). Marked heterogeneity between regions (interaction P=0.063) led to stratified reporting: in the European cohort HbA1c fell −6.6 versus −3.3 mmol/mol (P=0.033) and liver fat −5.4% versus −2.2% (P=0.035), while Brazil showed a large sham effect; in the per-protocol population, patients with baseline fasting glucose ≥10 mmol/L (≈180 mg/dL) had significantly greater HbA1c reductions with DMR (P=0.002). The earlier open-label first-in-human programme (36 patients analysed) saw HbA1c fall 0.9% at 24 weeks and remain improved at 12 months, with 52% of patients having a procedure-related adverse event, 81% of them mild. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): DMR may lower HbA1c modestly in selected patients, but its only sham-controlled trial did not prove it overall. Tier C is set: the benefit claim rests on subgroups of a single sham-controlled trial.

cards.headline: Mingrone 2022 (REVITA-2): HbA1c −10.4 versus −7.1 mmol/mol at 24 weeks (P=0.147, NS); European subgroup −6.6 versus −3.3 (P=0.033)
cards.summary: Mingrone 2022 (REVITA-2): HbA1c −10.4 versus −7.1 mmol/mol at 24 weeks (P=0.147, NS); European subgroup −6.6 versus −3.3 (P=0.033)
cards.people: 108 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 59–86 mmol/mol, BMI 24–40, fasting insulin above 48.6 pmol/L, on at least one oral agent) in Europe (DMR 39, sham 37) and Brazil (DMR 17, sham 16), randomised to hydrothermal duodenal mucosal resurfacing with the single-catheter Revita system or a sham endoscopic procedure; primary endpoints safety, HbA1c change at 24 weeks, and liver MRI fat fraction at 12 weeks.
cards.result: Overall modified intention-to-treat (DMR n=56, sham n=52): median HbA1c change −10.4 (IQR 18.6) mmol/mol with DMR versus −7.1 (16.4) with sham (P=0.147); in patients with baseline liver fat above 5%, fat change was −5.4 (5.6)% versus −2.9 (6.2)% (P=0.096). Regional heterogeneity (interaction P=0.063) prompted stratification: in Europe, HbA1c change was −6.6 versus −3.3 mmol/mol (P=0.033) and liver-fat change −5.4% versus −2.2% (P=0.035); Brazilian results trended to DMR benefit on HbA1c amid a large sham effect. In the overall per-protocol population, baseline fasting glucose ≥10 mmol/L (≈180 mg/dL) predicted significantly greater HbA1c reduction with DMR (P=0.002). Most adverse events were mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own primary comparison is negative; everything favourable comes from a region-stratified analysis undertaken after heterogeneity was seen, plus a per-protocol subgroup — the classic anatomy of a result that needs a confirmatory trial, not adoption.

cards.headline: van Baar 2020 (first international DMR study): HbA1c −0.9% at 24 weeks, sustained at 12 months — open-label, no sham, 52% with a procedure-related adverse event
cards.summary: van Baar 2020 (first international DMR study): HbA1c −0.9% at 24 weeks, sustained at 12 months — open-label, no sham, 52% with a procedure-related adverse event
cards.people: 46 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.5–10.0%, BMI 24–40) on stable oral glucose-lowering medication undergoing duodenal mucosal resurfacing at international centres; 37 (80%) received complete DMR and 36 were analysed, with medication held stable for at least 24 weeks.
cards.result: At 24 weeks HbA1c fell by 10±2 mmol/mol (0.9%±0.2%, P<0.001), fasting glucose by 1.7±0.5 mmol/L (≈31±9 mg/dL) (P<0.001) and HOMA-IR by 2.9±1.1 (P<0.001), with modest weight loss (2.5±0.6 kg, P<0.001); effects were sustained at 12 months and HbA1c change did not correlate with weight loss. Twenty-four patients (52%) had at least one DMR-related adverse event, 81% of them mild, with one serious adverse event and no unanticipated events.
cards.watchOut: No control group: regression to the mean, trial participation effects and the substantial sham response later seen in REVITA-2 (HbA1c −7.1 mmol/mol on sham) can each account for much of an open-label 0.9% fall.

shelves.title: Oral semaglutide alone in drug-naive type 2 diabetes: HbA1c fell 1.1–1.4 points more than placebo at the 14 mg dose over 26 weeks, with 2.3–2.6 kg more weight loss
shelves.question: In drug-naive type 2 diabetes, does oral semaglutide monotherapy lower HbA1c and weight versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy · Diet · Double-Blind Method · Exercise · Female · Glucagon-Like Peptides/administration & dosage · Glycated Hemoglobin/drug effects · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Weight Loss/drug effects · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as monotherapy against placebo, the cleanest comparison in the PIONEER programme. In PIONEER 1 (703 patients with type 2 diabetes managed by diet and exercise alone, mean baseline HbA1c 8.0%), 26 weeks of once-daily oral semaglutide reduced HbA1c versus placebo by 0.6% (3 mg), 0.9% (7 mg) and 1.1% (14 mg) on the treatment-policy estimand, and by 0.7%, 1.2% and 1.4% on the trial-product estimand (P<0.001 for all doses); body weight fell by an additional 2.3 kg (treatment policy) to 2.6 kg (trial product) at 14 mg (P<0.001). Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events, mild-to-moderate and transient, with discontinuations in 2.3–7.4% on semaglutide versus 2.2% on placebo. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 oral-semaglutide trials (8,536 patients) confirms the pattern against placebo and active comparators alike: lower HbA1c, weight and fasting glucose, more patients reaching HbA1c below 7.0%, and more nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, without increased hypoglycaemia or pancreatitis. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): oral semaglutide monotherapy lowers HbA1c by about 1–1.4 points versus placebo at the top dose — this shelf covers monotherapy versus placebo only; comparisons with sitagliptin and liraglutide live on the PIONEER glycaemic-trials shelf.

cards.headline: Aroda 2019 (PIONEER 1): HbA1c −1.1% versus placebo at 14 mg (treatment policy; −1.4% trial product), weight −2.3 kg; all doses P<0.001
cards.summary: Aroda 2019 (PIONEER 1): HbA1c −1.1% versus placebo at 14 mg (treatment policy; −1.4% trial product), weight −2.3 kg; all doses P<0.001
cards.people: 703 adults with type 2 diabetes insufficiently controlled by diet and exercise alone (mean age 55 years, 50.8% male, mean baseline HbA1c 8.0%) at 93 sites in nine countries, randomised to once-daily oral semaglutide 3 mg, 7 mg, 14 mg, or placebo for 26 weeks, analysed under treatment-policy and trial-product estimands.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted HbA1c reductions at week 26 (treatment policy): −0.6% (3 mg), −0.9% (7 mg), −1.1% (14 mg); (trial product): −0.7%, −1.2%, −1.4% (P<0.001 for all). Body-weight differences at 14 mg: −2.3 kg (treatment policy, P<0.001) and −2.6 kg (trial product, P<0.001); the 7 mg weight effect was −0.9 to −1.0 kg. Mild-to-moderate transient gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events; trial-product discontinuation occurred in 2.3–7.4% on oral semaglutide versus 2.2% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six weeks in diet-and-exercise-only patients with a mean HbA1c of 8.0%: the trial says nothing about durability beyond 6 months, about patients already on other drugs, or about cardiovascular outcomes (covered by other shelves in the semaglutide family).

cards.headline: Li 2021: across 10 oral-semaglutide trials (8,536 patients), HbA1c, weight and fasting glucose all fell versus placebo — nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting rose, hypoglycaemia did not
cards.summary: Li 2021: across 10 oral-semaglutide trials (8,536 patients), HbA1c, weight and fasting glucose all fell versus placebo — nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting rose, hypoglycaemia did not
cards.people: 10 randomised trials involving 8,536 patients with type 2 diabetes comparing oral semaglutide with placebo or other antihyperglycaemic agents, identified from PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library and ClinicalTrials.gov.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, oral semaglutide significantly reduced HbA1c, body weight, fasting plasma glucose and self-measured glucose, significantly increased the proportion achieving HbA1c below 7.0%, and was associated with fewer serious adverse events and deaths in the pooled placebo comparisons. Compared with active comparators it also reduced HbA1c, weight and self-measured glucose. It did not increase overall adverse events, hypoglycaemia (severe or confirmed symptomatic), myocardial infarction, heart-failure hospitalisation, stroke or acute pancreatitis, but did increase nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools monotherapy and add-on trials against mixed comparators, so it corroborates the class effect rather than the specific monotherapy-versus-placebo estimate, which comes from PIONEER 1 alone; pooled mortality differences from short glycaemic trials should not be read as an outcomes benefit.
cards.source: Li J et al. Efficacy and safety of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist oral semaglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Diabetes research and clinical practice. 2021. PMID: 33434602. shelves.title: Glargine 300 versus glargine 100 in type 1 diabetes: identical HbA1c control (difference 0.04%), fewer severe hypoglycaemic events in pooled trials (6.2% versus 9.3% of patients), and less weight gain
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes, does insulin glargine 300 U/mL achieve control comparable to glargine 100 U/mL with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Insulin Glargine/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — equal control with a hypoglycaemia edge that is clearest early and for severe events. In EDITION 4 (549 adults with long-duration type 1 diabetes), glargine 300 U/mL was non-inferior to glargine 100 U/mL for HbA1c change at 6 months (difference 0.04%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.19, from a baseline of 8.1%); overall hypoglycaemia did not differ, except in the first 8 weeks, when nocturnal confirmed or severe hypoglycaemia was lower with glargine 300 (rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.53–0.91), and weight gain was lower. A pooled meta-analysis of the three 6-month phase 3 trials in type 1 diabetes (EDITION 4, EDITION JP 1, EDITION JUNIOR; 1,255 patients) found fewer patients with at least one severe hypoglycaemic event on glargine 300 (6.2% versus 9.3%) and a lower risk of a first severe event (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.44–0.98, P=0.038), with similar HbA1c reductions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in type 1 diabetes glargine 300 matches glargine 100 for control and buys a modest reduction in severe and early nocturnal hypoglycaemia — the type 2 diabetes EDITION comparisons live on their own shelf.

cards.headline: Home 2015 (EDITION 4): HbA1c difference 0.04% (non-inferior); nocturnal hypoglycaemia lower only in the first 8 weeks (rate ratio 0.69); less weight gain
cards.summary: Home 2015 (EDITION 4): HbA1c difference 0.04% (non-inferior); nocturnal hypoglycaemia lower only in the first 8 weeks (rate ratio 0.69); less weight gain
cards.people: 549 adults with type 1 diabetes (mean age 47 years, mean diabetes duration 21 years, BMI 27.6 kg/m², baseline HbA1c 8.1%) on basal-bolus therapy, randomised to glargine 300 U/mL or glargine 100 U/mL (each with morning or evening injection strata) for 6 months, continuing mealtime analogue insulin.
cards.result: HbA1c change was equivalent (difference 0.04%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.19; 0.4 mmol/mol), meeting non-inferiority, with similar pre-breakfast self-measured glucose and 8-point profiles. Hypoglycaemia overall did not differ, except during the first 8 weeks, when nocturnal confirmed or severe hypoglycaemia was lower with glargine 300 (rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.53–0.91). The basal insulin dose was somewhat higher at 6 months with glargine 300; adverse events did not differ, and weight gain was lower with glargine 300.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 6 months, and the nocturnal advantage is confined to the titration window — over the full 6 months the headline hypoglycaemia comparison is neutral, so the benefit claim must stay as narrow as the data.

cards.headline: Danne 2020: pooled across three type 1 trials (1,255 patients), severe hypoglycaemia occurred in 6.2% on glargine 300 versus 9.3% on glargine 100 (first-event HR 0.65, P=0.038)
cards.summary: Danne 2020: pooled across three type 1 trials (1,255 patients), severe hypoglycaemia occurred in 6.2% on glargine 300 versus 9.3% on glargine 100 (first-event HR 0.65, P=0.038)
cards.people: Pooled post hoc meta-analysis of three similarly designed 6-month phase 3 trials in type 1 diabetes — EDITION 4, EDITION JP 1 and EDITION JUNIOR — with 629 patients randomised to glargine 300 U/mL and 626 to glargine 100 U/mL, including a paediatric trial (EDITION JUNIOR).
cards.result: HbA1c reductions were similar between groups. Fewer participants experienced at least one severe hypoglycaemic event with glargine 300 (6.2%) than with glargine 100 (9.3%); the risk of a first severe event from baseline to month 6 was lower with glargine 300 (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.44–0.98, P=0.038). Severe-event rates were numerically lower with glargine 300 (relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.49–1.29, P=0.356), as were rates in the first 8 weeks (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.37–1.44, P=0.369).
cards.watchOut: Post hoc pooling by the manufacturer's trial programme, and the significant result is for time-to-first-event while the event-rate comparison itself is not significant — supportive, concordant evidence rather than an independent replication.
cards.source: Danne T et al. shelves.title: Enalapril or losartan in normotensive type 1 diabetes: five years of renin–angiotensin blockade did not slow kidney structural progression — but cut the odds of retinopathy progression by about two-thirds
shelves.question: In normotensive type 1 diabetes, do enalapril or losartan prevent progression of nephropathy or retinopathy versus placebo over five years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Albuminuria · Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor Blockers/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy/pathology/physiopathology · Diabetic Nephropathies/prevention & control · Diabetic Retinopathy/prevention & control · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Enalapril/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate/drug effects · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Glomerulus/drug effects/pathology · Logistic Models · Losartan/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Male · Mesangial Cells/drug effects/pathology · Renin-Angiotensin System/drug effects · Retina/drug effects/pathology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the kidney answer is no, the eye answer is yes, from the same five-year trial. In the Renin-Angiotensin System Study (285 normotensive, normoalbuminuric patients with type 1 diabetes randomised to losartan 100 mg, enalapril 20 mg, or placebo for 5 years, with kidney biopsies), the primary renal endpoint — change in mesangial fractional volume — did not differ between placebo (0.016 units) and enalapril (0.005, P=0.38) or losartan (0.026, P=0.26), and no other biopsy-assessed structural variable favoured treatment. Microalbuminuria developed in 6% on placebo, 4% on enalapril (P=0.96) — and 17% on losartan (P=0.01), a paradoxical harm signal for the ARB. Retinopathy told the opposite story: the odds of progression by two or more steps were reduced by 65% with enalapril (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.14–0.85) and by 70% with losartan (odds ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.12–0.73), independently of blood-pressure changes. Chronic cough occurred in 12 patients on enalapril, 6 on losartan and 4 on placebo; three biopsy-related serious adverse events resolved completely. PROPOSED SPLIT: early renin–angiotensin blockade in normotensive type 1 diabetes does not prevent nephropathy — and losartan may hasten microalbuminuria — while both drugs slowed retinopathy progression in this single trial. Tier C is set: the benefit and the harm signals each rest on one trial.

cards.headline: Mauer 2009 (RASS): mesangial fractional volume change 0.016 (placebo) versus 0.005 (enalapril, P=0.38) and 0.026 (losartan, P=0.26); retinopathy progression OR 0.35 and 0.30
cards.summary: Mauer 2009 (RASS): mesangial fractional volume change 0.016 (placebo) versus 0.005 (enalapril, P=0.38) and 0.026 (losartan, P=0.26); retinopathy progression OR 0.35 and 0.30
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Mauer 2009, Renin-Angiotensin System Study)
cards.people: 285 normotensive patients with type 1 diabetes and normoalbuminuria at multiple centres, randomised to losartan 100 mg daily, enalapril 20 mg daily, or placebo for 5 years; 90% had complete renal-biopsy data and 82% complete retinopathy data; primary endpoint the change in the fraction of glomerular volume occupied by mesangium on biopsy.
cards.result: Change in mesangial fractional volume over 5 years did not differ significantly between placebo (0.016 units) and enalapril (0.005, P=0.38) or losartan (0.026, P=0.26), nor did other biopsy-assessed renal structural variables favour treatment. The 5-year cumulative incidence of microalbuminuria was 6% on placebo, 4% on enalapril (P=0.96) and 17% on losartan (P=0.01 by log-rank). The odds of retinopathy progression by two or more steps were reduced by 65% with enalapril (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.14–0.85) and by 70% with losartan (odds ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.12–0.73), independently of blood-pressure changes. Three biopsy-related serious adverse events resolved completely; chronic cough occurred in 12 patients on enalapril, 6 on losartan, and 4 on placebo.
cards.watchOut: One trial carrying opposite verdicts for two organs: the retinopathy benefit is a secondary endpoint in a trial designed and powered around kidney histology, and the losartan–microalbuminuria signal (17% versus 6%) is unexplained — both findings need the single-trial caution this shelf's Tier C flag records.
cards.source: Mauer M et al. Renal and retinal effects of enalapril and losartan in type 1 diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2009. PMID: 19571282. Registry ID: NCT00143949. cards.headline: Synthesis: five years, three arms, two organs, two opposite answers
cards.summary: Synthesis: five years, three arms, two organs, two opposite answers
cards.people: One multicentre 5-year randomised trial (285 normotensive, normoalbuminuric patients with type 1 diabetes) with paired kidney biopsies and graded retinal photographs — losartan 100 mg, enalapril 20 mg, or placebo.
cards.result: Kidney structure (primary endpoint): no benefit from either drug. Microalbuminuria at 5 years: 6% placebo, 4% enalapril, 17% losartan. Retinopathy progression (≥2 steps): odds ratio 0.35 with enalapril and 0.30 with losartan versus placebo. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: These were normotensive patients without albuminuria — the result does not argue against ACE inhibitors or ARBs where they are indicated for hypertension or established albuminuria. Tier C is set: single trial, with both a benefit claim (retinopathy) and a harm signal (losartan and microalbuminuria).
cards.source: Synthesis of Mauer M et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19571282).

shelves.title: Continuous glucose monitoring in young people with type 1 diabetes: in the JDRF trial the HbA1c benefit was confined to adults 25 and older (−0.53%) — ages 8–14 (−0.13%) and 15–24 (+0.08) showed no significant gain, and teenagers wore the sensor least
shelves.question: In children, adolescents, and young adults with type 1 diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring improve HbA1c versus fingerstick monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring/instrumentation/methods · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage · Insulin Infusion Systems · Male · Monitoring, Ambulatory/instrumentation/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the age groups this question asks about, in the trial that defined the field. The JDRF Continuous Glucose Monitoring trial (322 children and adults on intensive therapy, HbA1c 7.0–10.0%) found the HbA1c effect varied markedly by age (P=0.003 for interaction): among patients 25 years and older, CGM improved HbA1c change by −0.53% (95% CI −0.71 to −0.35, P<0.001), but among 15–24-year-olds the difference was +0.08 (95% CI −0.17 to 0.33, P=0.52) and among 8–14-year-olds −0.13 (95% CI −0.38 to 0.11, P=0.29) — neither significant. Use tracked the result: sensor wear of 6.0 or more days per week was achieved by 83% of adults 25 and older, 50% of 8–14-year-olds, and only 30% of 15–24-year-olds. Severe hypoglycaemia rates were low and did not differ. In the 6-month extension, the 83 adults who continued CGM sustained their benefit (A1C −0.4±0.6% at 12 months in those starting at or above 7.0%), confirming the adult effect without adding paediatric evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for children, adolescents and young adults as studied in 2008-era devices, CGM did not significantly improve HbA1c — the proven benefit belonged to the adults, and adherence, not sensor accuracy, was the binding constraint.

cards.headline: Tamborlane 2008 (JDRF CGM): age interaction P=0.003 — HbA1c benefit significant only at age ≥25 (−0.53%); 8–14 years −0.13% (P=0.29), 15–24 years +0.08 (P=0.52)
cards.summary: Tamborlane 2008 (JDRF CGM): age interaction P=0.003 — HbA1c benefit significant only at age ≥25 (−0.53%); 8–14 years −0.13% (P=0.29), 15–24 years +0.08 (P=0.52)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Tamborlane 2008, JDRF Continuous Glucose Monitoring Study)
cards.people: 322 adults and children with type 1 diabetes already receiving intensive therapy, with HbA1c 7.0–10.0%, randomised to continuous glucose monitoring or home blood-glucose-meter monitoring, stratified into three age groups (8–14, 15–24, ≥25 years); primary outcome the change in HbA1c at 26 weeks.
cards.result: The between-group difference in HbA1c change varied by age (P=0.003): −0.53% favouring CGM at age 25 and older (95% CI −0.71 to −0.35, P<0.001); +0.08 at ages 15–24 (95% CI −0.17 to 0.33, P=0.52); and −0.13 at ages 8–14 (95% CI −0.38 to 0.11, P=0.29). Sensor use of 6.0 or more days per week was reported by 83% of the oldest group, 50% of the youngest, and 30% of the middle group. The rate of severe hypoglycaemia was low and did not differ between groups, though the trial was not powered for that outcome.
cards.watchOut: Devices and sensors of 2006–2008, worn without the alarms, sharing and closed-loop integration of later systems: the trial answers what CGM did for young people then, and its adherence gradient (30% adequate wear at 15–24) is the mechanism it actually demonstrates. Adult CGM evidence is shelved separately (#560) and is not re-argued here.
cards.source: Tamborlane WV et al. Continuous glucose monitoring and intensive treatment of type 1 diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 18779236. Registry ID: NCT00406133. cards.headline: Bode 2009 (JDRF extension, adults): 12-month CGM use held at 6.8 days/week and A1C stayed down (−0.4±0.6%) — durability shown in adults only
cards.summary: Bode 2009 (JDRF extension, adults): 12-month CGM use held at 6.8 days/week and A1C stayed down (−0.4±0.6%) — durability shown in adults only
cards.type: Extension study of a randomised trial (Bode 2009)
cards.people: 83 of the 86 participants aged 25 years and older from the JDRF trial's CGM group who continued into a 6-month extension after the 6-month randomised phase (12 months of CGM in total).
cards.result: Median CGM use at 12 months was 6.8 days per week. In participants with baseline A1C at or above 7.0%, the mean change in A1C from baseline to 12 months was −0.4±0.6% (P<0.001); A1C remained stable at 6.4% in those starting below 7.0%. The severe hypoglycaemia incidence rate fell from 21.8 events per 100 person-years in the first 6 months to 7.1 in the last 6 months, and time per day in the 71–180 mg/dL range increased significantly (P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled extension in the one age stratum that had already responded — it supports durability in adults and says nothing about children or adolescents, the population this shelf is asked about.

cards.people: One 322-patient age-stratified randomised trial (26 weeks) plus its adult-only 6-month extension (83 participants).
cards.result: HbA1c differences versus fingerstick monitoring: −0.13% (ages 8–14, P=0.29), +0.08 (ages 15–24, P=0.52), −0.53% (age ≥25, P<0.001). Adequate sensor wear (≥6 days/week): 50%, 30% and 83% in the same strata. Severe hypoglycaemia: no difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the asked population.

shelves.title: Sensor-augmented pump versus injections in type 1 diabetes: HbA1c 7.5% versus 8.1% at one year in STAR 3 — in adults and children alike, with no difference in severe hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes with suboptimal control, does sensor-augmented pump therapy lower HbA1c more than multiple daily injections with fingerstick monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Diabetic Ketoacidosis/etiology · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced/prevention & control · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Insulin Infusion Systems · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Ambulatory · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-run trial, unblinded by necessity. In STAR 3 (485 patients — 329 adults and 156 children — with inadequately controlled type 1 diabetes, baseline HbA1c 8.3% in both groups), sensor-augmented pump therapy brought HbA1c to 7.5% at 1 year versus 8.1% with multiple daily injections plus fingerstick monitoring (P<0.001), and a greater proportion of both adults and children reached the below-7% target on the pump. Severe hypoglycaemia did not differ (13.31 versus 13.48 events per 100 person-years, P=0.58), and neither group gained significant weight. A post hoc analysis of the North American cohort found the incremental pump benefit similar in the United States (−0.93% versus −0.31% A1C change, pump versus injections) and Canada (−1.14% versus −0.67%), alongside higher sensor use in Canada (79% versus 68% of the time). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sensor-augmented pump therapy lowers HbA1c by about 0.6 points more than injections over a year. Tier C is set because the benefit rests on a single trial programme — its post hoc analyses are the same patients, not independent confirmation.

cards.people: 485 patients with inadequately controlled type 1 diabetes (329 adults, 156 children; baseline mean HbA1c 8.3% in both groups) at multiple centres, randomised to sensor-augmented pump therapy or multiple daily injections with fingerstick monitoring for 1 year, all using recombinant insulin analogues under expert clinical teams.
cards.result: At 1 year, mean HbA1c was 7.5% in the pump-therapy group versus 8.1% in the injection-therapy group (P<0.001), and a significantly greater proportion of both adults and children in the pump group reached the HbA1c target of below 7%. The rate of severe hypoglycaemia did not differ significantly (13.31 versus 13.48 cases per 100 person-years, P=0.58), and there was no significant weight gain in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label technology trial run by expert teams with structured support: the comparison bundles the sensor, the pump and the attention together, and usual-care clinics should not expect the full 0.6-point advantage without the same support. One trial, however large, is one trial.

cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised trial (Perkins 2015, STAR 3)
cards.people: The 329 adults of STAR 3 treated at 26 US sites (n=271) and 4 Canadian sites (n=58), randomised to sensor-augmented pump or glargine-based multiple daily injections, comparing baseline to 1-year A1C change by country.
cards.result: Canadian participants had greater A1C reductions overall (P=0.02), but the incremental benefit of sensor-augmented pump therapy was similar in the US (pump −0.93%±0.73% versus injections −0.31%±0.81%, P<0.001) and in Canada (−1.14%±0.72% versus −0.67%±0.71%, P<0.001). shelves.title: Mini-dose glucagon in sick children with type 1 diabetes: glucose rose from 3.44 to 8.11 mmol/L (≈62 to 146 mg/dL) within 30 minutes in 33 episodes — from one uncontrolled case series, with no comparator
shelves.question: In children with type 1 diabetes and impending hypoglycaemia during exercise or fasting, does mini-dose glucagon avert hypoglycaemia without rebound hyperglycaemia?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Blood Glucose/drug effects/metabolism · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Child · Child, Preschool · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/complications/drug therapy · Gastroenteritis/complications/physiopathology · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Glucagon/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemia/drug therapy/etiology · Injections, Subcutaneous · Insulin/adverse effects · Parents/education
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a physiologically coherent rescue that has only ever been described, never tested against a comparator. The single study behind this shelf reports 33 episodes of impending or mild hypoglycaemia in 28 children with type 1 diabetes (mean age about 6.6 years) during gastroenteritis or poor oral intake, treated at home with small subcutaneous glucagon doses measured in insulin-syringe units (20 µg for children aged 2 years or under; 1 unit per year of age up to 150 µg above that age). Blood glucose rose from 3.44±0.15 mmol/L (≈62±3 mg/dL) before treatment to 8.11±0.72 mmol/L (≈146±13 mg/dL) at 30 minutes; in 14 children hypoglycaemia recurred and responded to a doubled repeat dose (3.48±0.18 to 6.94±0.72 mmol/L (≈63±3 to 125±13 mg/dL)), and four children needed a third dose. In 28 of the 33 episodes the children stayed home and recovered fully; five were taken to hospital for dehydration or fever concerns, none for hypoglycaemia. The authors do not report rebound hyperglycaemia as a problem, but with no control group there is no way to know how many episodes would have resolved with oral carbohydrate or time alone. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): mini-dose glucagon appears to avert hypoglycaemia in sick children who cannot keep carbohydrate down — a practice supported by one small case series and two decades of clinical use, not by a trial. Tier C is set: uncontrolled observational evidence.

cards.headline: Haymond 2001: 33 episodes in 28 children — glucose 3.44±0.15 to 8.11±0.72 mmol/L (≈62±3 to 146±13 mg/dL) at 30 minutes; 28 of 33 episodes managed fully at home
cards.summary: Haymond 2001: 33 episodes in 28 children — glucose 3.44±0.15 to 8.11±0.72 mmol/L (≈62±3 to 146±13 mg/dL) at 30 minutes; 28 of 33 episodes managed fully at home
cards.people: 28 children with type 1 diabetes (ages 6.6±0.7 years as reported) experiencing 33 episodes of impending or mild hypoglycaemia during gastroenteritis or poor carbohydrate intake, treated by parents at home with subcutaneous mini-dose glucagon dosed by age in insulin-syringe units (20 µg if aged 2 years or under; 1 unit per year of age to a maximum of 15 units/150 µg), with a doubled repeat dose at 30 minutes if glucose had not risen, and frequent telephone contact with the diabetes team.
cards.result: Blood glucose was 3.44±0.15 mmol/L (≈62±3 mg/dL) before glucagon and 8.11±0.72 mmol/L (≈146±13 mg/dL) 30 minutes after. In 14 children relative hypoglycaemia recurred and responded to retreatment (3.48±0.18 rising to 6.94±0.72 mmol/L (≈125±13 mg/dL)); four children required a third dose. The glucagon was well tolerated. In 28 of the 33 episodes the children remained at home and fully recovered; five were taken to their local hospital because of concerns about dehydration or fever, but none for hypoglycaemia.
cards.watchOut: No control group, no randomisation, and episodes selected precisely because oral carbohydrate was failing or impossible: spontaneous recovery and concurrent care cannot be separated from the drug's effect, and the candidate question's exercise setting is not the studied one — these were illness/fasting episodes at home. Full-dose glucagon rescue for severe hypoglycaemia is a different intervention with its own shelves (#954, #1777).

shelves.title: Insulin aspart versus human insulin in pregnant type 1 diabetes: equal HbA1c in the second and third trimesters, smaller postprandial glucose rises, and a non-significant halving of major nocturnal hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In pregnant women with type 1 diabetes, does insulin aspart control postprandial glucose and HbA1c as well as human regular insulin without worse perinatal outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Europe · Female · Gestational Age · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemia/epidemiology · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Insulin/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Insulin Aspart · Insulin, Isophane/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/blood/drug therapy · Pregnancy Outcome · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for postprandial control, on a base of equal HbA1c and comparable safety in one open-label trial. In the randomised trial of 322 pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (aspart versus regular human insulin as the mealtime insulin, both with NPH basal), HbA1c was comparable in the second trimester (difference −0.04, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.11) and third trimester (−0.08, 95% CI −0.23 to 0.06), with 80% of participants reaching HbA1c at or below 6.5%. Average postprandial plasma glucose increments were significantly lower with aspart at the end of the first and third trimesters (P=0.003 and P=0.044), as was mean glucose 90 minutes after breakfast (P=0.044 and P=0.001). Major hypoglycaemia occurred at 1.4 versus 2.1 episodes per year of exposure (relative risk 0.720, 95% CI 0.36–1.46), and the risk of major or major nocturnal hypoglycaemia was 52% lower in relative terms with aspart (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.20–1.143) without reaching significance. Maternal safety profiles and pregnancy outcomes were similar between treatments, per the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aspart matches human insulin for HbA1c in pregnancy and improves the postprandial profile it was designed to improve. Tier C is set: a single trial carries the shelf. The candidate anchor (Hod et al. 2008) is a perinatal-outcomes report of this same trial programme; the shelf is built on the trial's primary randomised report — a swap declared for the coordinator.

Average postprandial plasma glucose increments were significantly lower with aspart at the end of the first (P=0.003) and third (P=0.044) trimesters, as were mean plasma glucose levels 90 minutes after breakfast (P=0.044 and P=0.001). Major hypoglycaemia occurred at 1.4 versus 2.1 episodes per year of exposure (relative risk 0.720, 95% CI 0.36–1.46); the risk of major/major nocturnal hypoglycaemia was lower in relative terms with aspart (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.20–1.143, not significant). shelves.title: Lidocaine 5% plaster for painful diabetic neuropathy: response matched pregabalin in an open-label trial (66.7% versus 69.1% responders in the diabetic subgroup) — with far fewer drug-related adverse events (5.8% versus 41.2%)
shelves.question: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the lidocaine 5% medicated plaster relieve pain versus placebo or pregabalin?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Algorithms · Analgesics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Casts, Surgical/adverse effects · Diabetic Neuropathies/complications/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Lidocaine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/chemistry · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia, Postherpetic/complications/drug therapy · Osmolar Concentration · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Pregabalin · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — comparable pain response to pregabalin in one open-label non-inferiority programme, with no placebo arm to prove the plaster beats nothing. In the two-stage adaptive trial (204 patients with painful diabetic polyneuropathy and 96 with postherpetic neuralgia), 4-week responder rates (a fall of at least 2 points, or a score of 4 or less, on the 11-point pain scale) were 66.4% on the lidocaine 5% medicated plaster versus 61.5% on pregabalin overall; within the diabetic polyneuropathy subgroup the per-protocol responder rates were 66.7% (plaster) versus 69.1% (pregabalin). Tolerability clearly favoured the plaster: any adverse event in 18.7% versus 46.4% of patients, drug-related adverse events in 5.8% versus 41.2%, with fewer treatment-related discontinuations. In the 8-week second phase, patients who had responded inadequately to either monotherapy gained additional clinically relevant pain reduction when the two were combined. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the plaster relieves diabetic neuropathic pain about as well as pregabalin in head-to-head open-label data and is much better tolerated — but without a placebo comparison in this population, the size of its true drug effect is unknown. Tier C is set: open-label, mixed-indication, single-programme evidence.

cards.headline: Baron 2009 (comparative phase): responders 66.4% on lidocaine plaster versus 61.5% on pregabalin overall; in diabetic polyneuropathy 66.7% versus 69.1% (per protocol); drug-related adverse events 5.8% versus 41.2%
cards.summary: Baron 2009 (comparative phase): responders 66.4% on lidocaine plaster versus 61.5% on pregabalin overall; in diabetic polyneuropathy 66.7% versus 69.1% (per protocol); drug-related adverse events 5.8% versus 41.2%
cards.people: Adults with postherpetic neuralgia (n=96) or painful diabetic polyneuropathy (n=204) in a two-stage adaptive multicentre study; the 4-week comparative phase randomised patients to lidocaine 5% medicated plaster applied to the most painful area or twice-daily pregabalin capsules titrated per its product information; primary endpoint the responder rate (≥2-point fall, or absolute score ≤4, on the 11-point Numerical Rating Scale averaged over the last 3 days).
cards.result: Overall responder rates were 66.4% with the plaster and 61.5% with pregabalin (per protocol: 65.3% versus 62.0%). In postherpetic neuralgia the plaster did better (per protocol 62.2% versus 46.5%); in painful diabetic polyneuropathy response was comparable (per protocol 66.7% versus 69.1%). Reductions of 30% and 50% in pain scores were greater with the plaster, and both treatments reduced allodynia severity. Adverse events occurred in 18.7% (plaster) versus 46.4% (pregabalin) of patients, drug-related adverse events in 5.8% versus 41.2%, with fewer related discontinuations on the plaster; quality-of-life (EQ-5D) improvements favoured the plaster in both indications.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a subjective endpoint and no placebo arm: expectation effects can move a pain score by the margins seen here, and the diabetic subgroup is two-thirds of a mixed-indication trial analysed as a subgroup. Non-inferiority to pregabalin is not proof of efficacy against no treatment.
cards.source: Baron R et al. 5% lidocaine medicated plaster versus pregabalin in post-herpetic neuralgia and diabetic polyneuropathy: an open-label, non-inferiority two-stage RCT study. Current medical research and opinion. 2009. PMID: 19485723. cards.headline: Baron 2009 (combination phase): adding the plaster to pregabalin, or pregabalin to the plaster, gave further clinically relevant pain falls in monotherapy non-responders over 8 weeks
cards.summary: Baron 2009 (combination phase): adding the plaster to pregabalin, or pregabalin to the plaster, gave further clinically relevant pain falls in monotherapy non-responders over 8 weeks
cards.type: Second phase of a randomised programme (Baron 2009, combination phase)
cards.people: 229 patients (68 postherpetic neuralgia, 161 diabetic polyneuropathy, per-protocol set) completing 4 weeks of monotherapy: adequate responders continued their treatment (71 plaster, 57 pregabalin), while insufficient responders received combination therapy (57 had pregabalin added to the plaster; 44 had the plaster added to pregabalin) for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Patients continuing monotherapy showed additional decreases in pain scores. Patients receiving combination therapy achieved clinically relevant further reductions in pain scores beyond the improvement of the 4-week monotherapy phase, similar in the two combination groups, with considerable improvements in treatment satisfaction; adverse-event incidences were in line with previous reports for the two treatments and combination therapy was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: An uncontrolled add-on phase in selected non-responders: regression to the mean and continued natural history are fully confounded with any combination effect, so this phase supports tolerability of the combination, not its efficacy.
cards.source: Baron R et al. Efficacy and safety of combination therapy with 5% lidocaine medicated plaster and pregabalin in post-herpetic neuralgia and diabetic polyneuropathy. shelves.title: Voglibose in impaired glucose tolerance: diabetes onset delayed — 50 cases versus 106 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.595) in a trial stopped early at its interim analysis after a mean of only 48 weeks
shelves.question: In impaired glucose tolerance, does voglibose delay progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Analysis of Variance · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucose Intolerance/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Glycoside Hydrolase Inhibitors · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Incidence · Inositol/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Japan/epidemiology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Life Style · Male · Middle Aged · Prevalence · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Assessment · Risk Reduction Behavior · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial, stopped early, in a single population; in line with this library's standing language for prediabetes, the effect is a delay in the formal diagnosis, not prevention of the disease. In the Japanese trial (1,780 people with impaired glucose tolerance, all on standard diet and exercise advice), voglibose 0.2 mg three times daily reduced progression to type 2 diabetes versus placebo (50 of 897 versus 106 of 881 patients; hazard ratio 0.595, 95% CI 0.433–0.818, P=0.0014) — a 40% relative reduction — and more patients achieved normoglycaemia on voglibose (599 of 897 versus 454 of 881; hazard ratio 1.539, 95% CI 1.357–1.746, P<0.0001). But the trial was stopped at a pre-planned interim analysis after a mean treatment duration of only 48.1 weeks, although the protocol envisaged a minimum of 3 years, and early stopping is known to inflate effect estimates. Adverse events were reported by 90% of the voglibose group versus 85% on placebo. The Cochrane review of alpha-glucosidase inhibitors for delaying type 2 diabetes rated the voglibose-versus-placebo evidence (this single trial) as low certainty (risk ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.34–0.64), with the class's firmer data coming from acarbose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): voglibose delays the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in Japanese adults with impaired glucose tolerance over about a year of treatment — Tier C, a single early-stopped trial.

cards.headline: Kawamori 2009: progression to diabetes 50/897 on voglibose versus 106/881 on placebo (HR 0.595, P=0.0014); normoglycaemia 599 versus 454 patients (HR 1.539)
cards.summary: Kawamori 2009: progression to diabetes 50/897 on voglibose versus 106/881 on placebo (HR 0.595, P=0.0014); normoglycaemia 599 versus 454 patients (HR 1.539)
cards.people: 1,780 Japanese adults with impaired glucose tolerance on a standard diet and regular exercise, randomised to oral voglibose 0.2 mg three times daily (n=897) or placebo (n=883) at multiple centres; treatment was to continue until diabetes developed, normoglycaemia was reached, or for a minimum of 3 years, subject to interim analysis; registered with the UMIN registry (UMIN 000001109) as reported in the record.
cards.result: At the interim analysis (mean treatment duration 48.1 weeks, SD 36.3), voglibose was superior to placebo (P=0.0026) and the trial was stopped. Progression to type 2 diabetes occurred in 50 of 897 patients on voglibose versus 106 of 881 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.595, 95% CI 0.433–0.818, P=0.0014) — a 40% relative reduction, with the absolute rates printed alongside. Normoglycaemia was achieved by 599 of 897 versus 454 of 881 (hazard ratio 1.539, 95% CI 1.357–1.746, P<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 810 (90%) of the voglibose group versus 750 (85%) on placebo; serious adverse events were single cases in each group.
cards.watchOut: A trial stopped early for benefit after a mean of 48 weeks against a planned minimum of 3 years: early-stopped trials systematically overestimate effects, and nothing here shows what happens to diabetes incidence after voglibose is withdrawn, or in non-Japanese populations.
cards.source: Kawamori R et al. Voglibose for prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus: a randomised, double-blind trial in Japanese individuals with impaired glucose tolerance. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19395079. Registry ID: UMIN 000001109. cards.headline: Moelands 2018 (Cochrane): voglibose versus placebo reduced diabetes incidence (risk ratio 0.46) on low-certainty evidence from this one trial; the class case rests mainly on acarbose
cards.summary: Moelands 2018 (Cochrane): voglibose versus placebo reduced diabetes incidence (risk ratio 0.46) on low-certainty evidence from this one trial; the class case rests mainly on acarbose
cards.people: Cochrane review of 10 randomised trials (11,814 participants) of alpha-glucosidase inhibitors for at least 1 year in people with impaired glucose tolerance, impaired fasting glucose, moderately raised HbA1c, or combinations — eight trials of acarbose and two of voglibose (one against placebo, one against diet and exercise).
cards.result: Voglibose compared with placebo reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes: 50 of 897 participants (5.6%) developed diabetes versus 106 of 881 (12%) on placebo (risk ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.34–0.64, P<0.0001; 1 trial, 1,778 participants; low-certainty evidence), with no clear differences on other outcomes. For acarbose versus placebo, diabetes incidence was 16.7% versus 20.3% (risk ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.75–0.89; 3 trials, 8,008 participants; moderate-certainty evidence); no firm evidence showed benefit on cardiovascular mortality or events for the class.
cards.watchOut: The review's voglibose estimate is the same single early-stopped trial re-expressed — it adds a certainty rating (low), not new data; and per this library's founder's rule for prediabetes material, delayed diagnosis must not be read as diabetes prevented.
cards.source: Moelands SV et al. shelves.title: Canagliflozin and amputation: the pooled patient-level analysis could not explain why CANVAS showed an increase and CREDENCE did not (heterogeneity P=0.02) — and the class-wide trial meta-analysis finds no significant increase (risk ratio 1.24, 95% CI 0.96–1.60)
shelves.question: Does canagliflozin increase amputation risk compared with other SGLT2 inhibitors or placebo when CANVAS and CREDENCE are pooled?
shelves.mesh: Amputation, Surgical · Canagliflozin/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy/epidemiology · Humans · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/adverse effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by trial, and the pooled analysis says so itself. In the patient-level pooled analysis of CANVAS (10,142 participants, median follow-up 2.4 years; 187 amputations, 1.8% annual event rate) and CREDENCE (4,401 participants, median 2.5 years; 133 amputations, 3.0% annual rate), the effect of canagliflozin on amputation risk differed significantly between the two trials (P for heterogeneity 0.02, I²=82%): increased in CANVAS, null in CREDENCE, with no explanation found in participant or trial differences and no evidence that the foot-care protocols introduced during CREDENCE accounted for it; a previous amputation was the strongest predictor of a future one in both trials. The authors conclude the CANVAS finding may have been the result of chance. The trial-level meta-analysis of all SGLT2-inhibitor cardiovascular outcome trials (6 trials, 51,713 participants, 858 amputations) found amputation rates of 2.0% on SGLT2 inhibitors versus 1.3% on control and a pooled risk ratio of 1.24 (95% CI 0.96–1.60) that was not statistically significant, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=67.5%) and no significant increase in any subgroup, including patients with peripheral artery disease. PROPOSED SPLIT: a canagliflozin-specific amputation signal exists in CANVAS and nowhere else — neither the same drug's kidney trial nor the class-wide evidence confirms it. Tier C is set: a harm claim resting on discordant trial data.

cards.headline: Arnott 2020: CANVAS and CREDENCE pooled (14,543 patients) — canagliflozin's amputation effect differed significantly between the two trials (P-heterogeneity 0.02, I²=82%), unexplained by patient or trial differences
cards.summary: Arnott 2020: CANVAS and CREDENCE pooled (14,543 patients) — canagliflozin's amputation effect differed significantly between the two trials (P-heterogeneity 0.02, I²=82%), unexplained by patient or trial differences
cards.type: Pooled patient-level analysis of two randomised trials (Arnott 2020)
cards.people: Participants in the CANVAS Program (n=10,142; median follow-up 2.4 years; 66% with cardiovascular disease, 17.5% with nephropathy; 2.3% with previous amputation) and the CREDENCE trial (n=4,401; median 2.5 years; 100% with nephropathy, 50% with cardiovascular disease; 5.3% with previous amputation), both comparing canagliflozin with placebo in type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: There were 187 amputations in CANVAS (1.8% annual event rate) and 133 in CREDENCE (3.0% annual rate); prior amputation was the strongest predictor of future amputation in both. The effects of canagliflozin on amputation risk were significantly different between trials (P-heterogeneity 0.02, I²=82%), and this was not explained by participant or trial differences; there was no evidence that foot-disease management protocols instituted during CREDENCE ameliorated amputation risk. The authors conclude that, in the context of null effects in CREDENCE and all other large trials, the CANVAS finding may have been the result of chance.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis whose honest output is heterogeneity, not a pooled estimate: quoting a single combined hazard ratio for canagliflozin and amputation would misrepresent this record. Baseline amputation history and kidney disease differed sharply between the trials, and neither was designed around amputation as a primary outcome.
cards.source: Arnott C et al. The effect of canagliflozin on amputation risk in the CANVAS program and the CREDENCE trial. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. PMID: 32436638. cards.headline: Huang 2020: across 6 SGLT2-inhibitor outcome trials (51,713 patients, 858 amputations), pooled risk ratio 1.24 (95% CI 0.96–1.60) — not significant, including in peripheral artery disease
cards.summary: Huang 2020: across 6 SGLT2-inhibitor outcome trials (51,713 patients, 858 amputations), pooled risk ratio 1.24 (95% CI 0.96–1.60) — not significant, including in peripheral artery disease
cards.people: Six randomised placebo-controlled cardiovascular outcome trials of SGLT2 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes (51,713 participants): empagliflozin (EMPA-REG OUTCOME), canagliflozin (CANVAS Program and CREDENCE), dapagliflozin (DECLARE-TIMI 58 and DAPA-HF) and ertugliflozin (VERTIS CV); 858 participants required amputation.
cards.result: Amputation event rates were 2.0% (535/26,778) in the SGLT2-inhibitor groups and 1.3% (323/24,927) in control groups; the random-effects pooled risk ratio was 1.24 (95% CI 0.96–1.60), not statistically significant, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=67.5%). The neutral effect was consistent across subgroups, including patients with and without established peripheral artery disease; amputation events arose primarily from critical limb ischaemia and infection rather than acute limb ischaemia.
cards.watchOut: Trial-level (not patient-level) pooling dominated by the CANVAS signal in one drug: the confidence interval (0.96–1.60) cannot exclude a real class increase of up to about 60% relative, so 'not significant' must not be paraphrased as 'proven safe'.
cards.source: Huang CY et al. Sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors and major adverse limb events: A trial-level meta-analysis including 51 713 individuals. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. shelves.title: Switching mealtime insulin to inhaled insulin in type 1 diabetes: HbA1c non-inferior to usual care at 17 weeks (adjusted difference 0.11%) — with smaller post-meal excursions, more patients worsening by >0.5%, and cough the commonest side effect
shelves.question: In type 1 and type 2 diabetes, does switching mealtime insulin to inhaled insulin maintain HbA1c versus usual care over 17 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/drug therapy/blood · Adult · Female · Male · Administration, Inhalation · Insulin, Long-Acting/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Insulin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Blood Glucose/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior HbA1c maintenance over 17 weeks in type 1 diabetes, with a postprandial advantage and a wider spread of individual responses. In INHALE-3 (123 adults with type 1 diabetes, mostly previously on automated insulin delivery or multiple daily injections), a regimen of inhaled Technosphere insulin plus insulin degludec was non-inferior to usual care for HbA1c at 17 weeks (7.62%±1.06% versus 7.54%±0.77% from baselines of 7.57% and 7.59%; adjusted difference 0.11%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.33, P for non-inferiority=0.01). More patients improved by over 0.5% on inhaled insulin (12 of 62, 21% versus 3, 5%) — but more also worsened by over 0.5% (15, 26% versus 2, 3%). The commonest side effect was a brief cough, and eight participants discontinued inhaled insulin because of side effects. In the trial's meal-challenge study (122 adults), the glucose area above 180 mg/dL over 2 hours after a meal was smaller with inhaled insulin than with rapid-acting analogue (adjusted difference −12 mg/dL, 95% CI −22 to −2, P=0.02), with a lower peak reached sooner; in the 30-week extension, patients continuing inhaled insulin plus degludec held HbA1c at 7.4%±1.0% with time in range 54%±20%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): inhaled insulin maintains HbA1c as well as usual care over 17 weeks in type 1 diabetes and flattens the post-meal rise — noting that the trial enrolled type 1 diabetes only, although the candidate question also names type 2. Tier C is set: a single trial programme.

cards.headline: Hirsch 2025 (INHALE-3): HbA1c 7.62% on inhaled insulin plus degludec versus 7.54% on usual care at 17 weeks (adjusted difference 0.11%, non-inferior); >0.5% worsening in 26% versus 3%
cards.summary: Hirsch 2025 (INHALE-3): HbA1c 7.62% on inhaled insulin plus degludec versus 7.54% on usual care at 17 weeks (adjusted difference 0.11%, non-inferior); >0.5% worsening in 26% versus 3%
cards.people: 123 adults with type 1 diabetes at 19 sites, previously using automated insulin delivery (48%) or multiple daily injections (45%) with continuous glucose monitoring, randomised to inhaled Technosphere insulin (Afrezza, as named in the trial reports) plus insulin degludec (n=62) or continuation of their prestudy usual-care delivery method (n=61) for 17 weeks; mean baseline HbA1c 7.57%±0.97% and 7.59%±0.80%.
cards.result: HbA1c at 17 weeks was 7.62%±1.06% in the inhaled-insulin group and 7.54%±0.77% in the usual-care group (adjusted difference 0.11%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.33; P value for non-inferiority=0.01). HbA1c improved by more than 0.5% in 12 participants (21%) on inhaled insulin versus 3 (5%) on usual care, but worsened by more than 0.5% in 15 (26%) versus 2 (3%). The most common side effect of inhaled insulin was a brief cough; eight participants discontinued it because of side effects.
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority is an average: the inhaled regimen produced both more improvers and far more worseners than usual care, which in this trial usually meant an automated delivery system doing the work — switching a well-controlled AID user is a different bet from switching an injection user. Seventeen weeks is short, and the population is type 1 only.
cards.source: Hirsch IB et al. A Randomized Trial Comparing Inhaled Insulin Plus Basal Insulin Versus Usual Care in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes. Diabetes care. 2025. PMID: 39641970. cards.headline: Hirsch 2024 (INHALE-3 meal challenge): post-meal glucose area above 180 mg/dL lower with inhaled insulin (adjusted difference −12 mg/dL, P=0.02); peak lower and earlier
cards.summary: Hirsch 2024 (INHALE-3 meal challenge): post-meal glucose area above 180 mg/dL lower with inhaled insulin (adjusted difference −12 mg/dL, P=0.02); peak lower and earlier
cards.type: Randomised meal-challenge study within a trial programme (Hirsch 2024, INHALE-3)
cards.people: 122 adults with type 1 diabetes using multiple daily injections, a non-automated pump, or automated insulin delivery, randomised to bolus with inhaled Technosphere insulin (n=61) or their usual subcutaneous rapid-acting analogue insulin (n=61) for a standardised meal challenge.
cards.result: The primary outcome — the treatment difference in area under the curve for glucose above 180 mg/dL over 2 hours — favoured inhaled insulin (adjusted difference −12 mg/dL, 95% CI −22 to −2, P=0.02). The glucose excursion was smaller (P=0.01), the peak glucose lower (P=0.01), and the time to peak shorter (P=0.006) with inhaled insulin. Blood glucose below 70 mg/dL occurred in one participant in each group.
cards.watchOut: A single supervised meal challenge demonstrates pharmacodynamics, not daily life: it cannot capture dosing errors, missed inhalations, or pulmonary effects over months of use.
cards.source: Hirsch IB et al.
