cards.headline: Beck 2025 (INHALE-3 extension): at 30 weeks on inhaled insulin plus degludec, HbA1c 7.4%±1.0% and time in range 54%±20% — in the self-selected continuers
cards.summary: Beck 2025 (INHALE-3 extension): at 30 weeks on inhaled insulin plus degludec, HbA1c 7.4%±1.0% and time in range 54%±20% — in the self-selected continuers
cards.type: Extension study of a randomised trial (Beck 2025, INHALE-3 extension)
cards.people: 45 of the 62 participants randomised to inhaled Technosphere insulin plus insulin degludec who continued the regimen for a further 13 weeks after the 17-week randomised phase (30 weeks total), with no scheduled visits before the final visit, approximating real-world care.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c was 7.6%±1.0% at baseline, 7.6%±1.0% at 17 weeks and 7.4%±1.0% at 30 weeks (change from 17 to 30 weeks −0.21%, 95% CI −0.33 to −0.09, P<0.001); HbA1c below 7.0% was present in 21% at baseline, 30% at 17 weeks and 42% at 30 weeks. Mean time in range (70–180 mg/dL) was 52%±18%, 53%±20% and 54%±20% at the same points, and time below 54 mg/dL was 0.4%±0.6%, 0.4%±0.8% and 0.6%±1.0%. The mean total daily inhaled-insulin dose at 30 weeks was 53±31 units, about twice the pre-study rapid-acting analogue dose of 24±12 units.
cards.watchOut: Only 45 of 62 randomised patients continued — the extension describes people who chose to stay on inhaled insulin, so its stability figures are a best-case, self-selected read of durability.
cards.source: Beck RW et al. Inhaled Technosphere Insulin Plus Insulin Degludec for Adults with Type 1 Diabetes: The INHALE-3 Extension Study. Diabetes technology & therapeutics. 2025. PMID: 40098468. cards.summary: Synthesis: HbA1c held, meals flattened, responses polarised — a genuine option for selected type 1 patients, not a like-for-like swap for everyone

shelves.question: In people with diabetes who have no symptoms of coronary artery disease, does routine screening for silent coronary disease — by stress myocardial perfusion imaging or by CT coronary angiography — reduce cardiac death, myocardial infarction and related events?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised screening trials, two imaging technologies, one answer. In DIAD (1,123 asymptomatic patients with type 2 diabetes), cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction over 4.8 years occurred in 2.7% of the screened group and 3.0% of the unscreened group (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.88); overall event rates were low (2.9% cumulative), and even moderate-to-large perfusion defects had a positive predictive value of only 12%. In FACTOR-64 (900 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes), CT-angiography screening gave a primary outcome (death, nonfatal infarction, or unstable-angina hospitalisation) in 6.2% versus 7.6% on standard care (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32), and the ischaemic composite was numerically worse with screening (4.4% versus 3.8%; hazard ratio 1.15). Finding silent disease did not translate into preventing events, largely because background preventive therapy rose equally in both arms. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine imaging screening for coronary disease in asymptomatic diabetes does not reduce cardiac events.

cards.headline: DIAD (Young 2009): cardiac death or nonfatal infarction in 2.7% of the screened group versus 3.0% unscreened (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.88) over 4.8 years
cards.summary: DIAD (Young 2009): cardiac death or nonfatal infarction in 2.7% of the screened group versus 3.0% unscreened (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.88) over 4.8 years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (DIAD — Detection of Ischemia in Asymptomatic Diabetics)
cards.people: 1,123 participants with type 2 diabetes and no symptoms of coronary artery disease, recruited from diabetes clinics and practices, randomised to screening with adenosine-stress radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging or to no screening, and followed for a mean of 4.8 years; the primary outcome was cardiac death or nonfatal myocardial infarction.
cards.result: The cumulative cardiac event rate was 2.9% over 4.8 years (0.6% per year). Seven nonfatal infarctions and 8 cardiac deaths (2.7%) occurred in the screened group and 10 nonfatal infarctions and 7 cardiac deaths (3.0%) in the unscreened group (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.44 to 1.88; P = .73). Among screened patients, moderate or large perfusion defects predicted events (2.4% per year versus 0.4% per year with normal or small defects; hazard ratio 6.3) but the positive predictive value of a moderate or large defect was only 12%. Coronary revascularisation was infrequent in both groups (5.5% screened versus 7.8% unscreened), and primary medical prevention intensified significantly and equally in both groups during the study.
cards.watchOut: Event rates were far lower than expected when the trial was designed, limiting power for small effects; the trial tests a screening strategy in type 2 diabetes, not the diagnostic use of imaging in symptomatic patients.
cards.source: Young et al. Cardiac outcomes after screening for asymptomatic coronary artery disease in patients with type 2 diabetes: the DIAD study: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2009. PMID: 19366774. Registry ID: NCT00769275. cards.headline: FACTOR-64 (Muhlestein 2014): primary outcome in 6.2% with CT-angiography screening versus 7.6% on standard care (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32; P = .38)
cards.summary: FACTOR-64 (Muhlestein 2014): primary outcome in 6.2% with CT-angiography screening versus 7.6% on standard care (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32; P = .38)
cards.people: 900 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and no symptoms of coronary artery disease, randomised to screening with coronary CT angiography (452 patients), with guideline-directed care recommended from the findings, or to standard national-guideline-based care (448); mean follow-up 4.0 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome (all-cause mortality, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unstable angina requiring hospitalisation) occurred in 6.2% (28 events) in the CT-angiography group and 7.6% (34 events) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.80; 95% CI 0.49 to 1.32; P = .38). The secondary ischaemic composite (coronary death, nonfatal infarction, or unstable angina) occurred in 4.4% (20 events) versus 3.8% (17 events) (hazard ratio 1.15; 95% CI 0.60 to 2.19; P = .68). The authors concluded the findings do not support CT-angiography screening in this population.
cards.watchOut: A single health-system trial with modest event counts; screening triggered more downstream testing and therapy by design, which is part of the strategy being judged — and it still did not reduce events.
cards.source: Muhlestein et al. Effect of screening for coronary artery disease using CT angiography on mortality and cardiac events in high-risk patients with diabetes: the FACTOR-64 randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25402757. Registry ID: NCT00488033. cards.headline: Synthesis: in asymptomatic diabetes, looking harder for coronary disease did not prevent it from declaring itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: in asymptomatic diabetes, looking harder for coronary disease did not prevent it from declaring itself
cards.people: People with diabetes and no cardiac symptoms, in whom routine coronary screening is proposed.
cards.result: DIAD (hazard ratio 0.88 for cardiac death or infarction) and FACTOR-64 (hazard ratio 0.80 for its primary composite, 1.15 for the ischaemic composite) agree across imaging modalities: screening finds risk markers but does not reduce events, because effective preventive therapy is — and should be — given on the basis of diabetes itself.
cards.watchOut: Coronary artery calcium scoring as a risk-refinement tool, and imaging for symptoms or pre-operative assessment, are different questions not graded by these trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of DIAD (PMID: 19366774) and FACTOR-64 (PMID: 25402757).

shelves.title: Salsalate in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c about 0.4 percentage points lower over 48 weeks in TINSAL-T2D — a real glycaemic effect, with rising urine albumin and no outcome data
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes, does salsalate — a salicylate prodrug with anti-inflammatory action — improve glycaemic control compared with placebo, and what safety signals accompany it?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Albuminuria/chemically induced · Blood Glucose/*metabolism · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/*blood/*drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Lipids/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Prodrugs/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Salicylates/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Tinnitus/chemically induced · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the blood test only: two stages of one research programme show a consistent, modest HbA1c reduction and a renal signal to watch. In the 14-week dose-ranging trial (108 patients), HbA1c fell by 0.36, 0.34 and 0.49 percentage points more than placebo at salsalate doses of 3.0, 3.5 and 4.0 g/day. In the 48-week TINSAL-T2D trial (286 patients), mean HbA1c was 0.37 percentage points lower on salsalate 3.5 g/day than on placebo (95% CI -0.53 to -0.21; P < 0.001), achieved despite more reductions in other diabetes medications in the salsalate group; triglycerides and adiponectin improved, but weight and LDL cholesterol rose, and urinary albumin increased (reversing on discontinuation, with estimated GFR unchanged). No trial measured cardiovascular or renal outcomes. As a single-programme surrogate benefit, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): salsalate probably lowers HbA1c by roughly 0.4 percentage points in type 2 diabetes; whether that helps or harms patients over years is unknown.

cards.headline: Dose-ranging trial (Goldfine 2010): HbA1c changes of -0.36%, -0.34% and -0.49% versus placebo at salsalate 3.0, 3.5 and 4.0 g/day over 14 weeks
cards.summary: Dose-ranging trial (Goldfine 2010): HbA1c changes of -0.36%, -0.34% and -0.49% versus placebo at salsalate 3.0, 3.5 and 4.0 g/day over 14 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (TINSAL-T2D programme, stage 1)
cards.people: 108 patients aged 18 to 75 years with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0% to 9.5%, fasting glucose 12.5 mmol/L (≈225 mg/dL) or less) on stable diet, exercise and oral medication, randomised to placebo or salsalate 3.0, 3.5 or 4.0 g/day (27 patients per group) for 14 weeks at US practices and universities.
cards.result: Higher proportions of patients in all three salsalate groups achieved HbA1c decreases of at least 0.5% (P = 0.009). Mean HbA1c changes versus placebo were -0.36% at 3.0 g/day (P = 0.02), -0.34% at 3.5 g/day (P = 0.02) and -0.49% at 4.0 g/day (P = 0.001). Other glycaemic markers, triglycerides and adiponectin also improved. Mild hypoglycaemia was more common with salsalate (only in patients taking sulfonylureas), and urine albumin concentrations increased in all salsalate groups versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Small and short — the authors themselves said the numbers and duration were insufficient to recommend salsalate for type 2 diabetes; tinnitus is a recognised salicylate effect at these doses (it appears in the record's indexed adverse-effect terms).
cards.source: Goldfine et al. The effects of salsalate on glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2010. PMID: 20231565. Registry ID: NCT00392678. cards.headline: TINSAL-T2D (Goldfine 2013): HbA1c 0.37 percentage points lower on salsalate over 48 weeks (95% CI -0.53 to -0.21; P < 0.001); urine albumin rose, weight and LDL cholesterol rose
cards.summary: TINSAL-T2D (Goldfine 2013): HbA1c 0.37 percentage points lower on salsalate over 48 weeks (95% CI -0.53 to -0.21; P < 0.001); urine albumin rose, weight and LDL cholesterol rose
cards.people: 286 patients aged 18 to 75 years with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0% to 9.5%) randomised to salsalate 3.5 g/day (146 patients) or placebo (140) in addition to current therapy for 48 weeks at US academic centres and practices; 283 were analysed.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c over 48 weeks was 0.37 percentage points lower in the salsalate group than the placebo group (95% CI -0.53 to -0.21; P < 0.001), and glycaemia improved despite more reductions in concomitant diabetes medications among salsalate recipients. Circulating leukocyte, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts fell (the anti-inflammatory signature), and adiponectin rose while fasting glucose, uric acid and triglycerides fell; however, weight and LDL cholesterol increased, and urinary albumin levels increased on salsalate — reversing after discontinuation, with estimated glomerular filtration rates unchanged.
cards.watchOut: The albuminuria signal, though reversible in this trial, is exactly the wrong direction in diabetes and was unresolved at publication; 48 weeks and 286 patients cannot settle long-term cardiorenal safety or benefit.
cards.source: Goldfine et al. Salicylate (salsalate) in patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2013. PMID: 23817699. Registry ID: NCT00799643. cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine but small glucose-lowering effect, bought with high gram doses and an open renal question
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine but small glucose-lowering effect, bought with high gram doses and an open renal question
cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes in whom an inexpensive anti-inflammatory glucose-lowering drug is attractive.
cards.result: Two randomised stages agree on size: about 0.4 percentage points of HbA1c (dose-ranging -0.34 to -0.49; 48-week -0.37). Against that stand increased urine albumin in both trials, weight and LDL increases in the longer trial, and a complete absence of cardiovascular or kidney outcome data — enough for POSSIBLE on glycaemia, nothing more.
cards.watchOut: Salsalate is not an approved diabetes treatment; this shelf grades the trial evidence, not a recommendation, and says nothing about salicylates for cardiovascular prevention, where aspirin has its own shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of the salsalate dose-ranging trial (PMID: 20231565) and TINSAL-T2D (PMID: 23817699).

shelves.title: Oral insulin to delay type 1 diabetes in autoantibody-positive relatives (TrialNet): diabetes in 28.5% versus 33% — no significant delay overall, with a signal in one small secondary stratum
shelves.question: In autoantibody-positive relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes who still have normal glucose tolerance, does daily oral insulin delay the onset of clinical type 1 diabetes compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Autoantibodies/blood · Child · Child, Preschool · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/genetics/*prevention & control · Family · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucose Tolerance Test · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Insulin/adverse effects/immunology/*therapeutic use · Male · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the prespecified main analysis was null; one small subgroup keeps the hypothesis alive but cannot carry it. In the TrialNet oral insulin trial, the main study group comprised 389 autoantibody-positive relatives with preserved first-phase insulin release: over a median of 2.7 years, diabetes was diagnosed in 28.5% on oral insulin versus 33% on placebo, and time to diabetes did not differ significantly (hazard ratio 0.87; 1-sided 95% CI reported as 0 to 1.2; P = .21). In secondary stratum 1 — just 55 participants with lower first-phase insulin release — diabetes developed in 48.1% versus 70.3%, with a significantly longer time to diabetes on oral insulin (hazard ratio 0.45; P = .006); the other secondary strata combined showed nothing (hazard ratio 1.03). A 55-person subgroup inside a null 560-person trial is a reason to run another trial, not to treat. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): oral insulin has not been shown to delay type 1 diabetes in at-risk relatives overall; the low-insulin-release subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating only.

cards.headline: TrialNet oral insulin trial (Krischer 2017): in the main group, diabetes in 58 participants (28.5%) on oral insulin versus 62 (33%) on placebo; time to diabetes hazard ratio 0.87 (P = .21) — not significant
cards.summary: TrialNet oral insulin trial (Krischer 2017): in the main group, diabetes in 58 participants (28.5%) on oral insulin versus 62 (33%) on placebo; time to diabetes hazard ratio 0.87 (P = .21) — not significant
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet Oral Insulin Study)
cards.people: 560 autoantibody-positive relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes (at least two autoantibodies including insulin autoantibodies, with normal glucose tolerance), enrolled across nine countries between 2007 and 2015 and randomised to oral insulin 7.5 mg daily (283 participants) or placebo (277). The main study group (389 participants; median age 8.4 years) had first-phase insulin release above the prespecified threshold on intravenous glucose tolerance testing; secondary stratum 1 (55) had the same antibody profile with lower first-phase release, and secondary strata 2 and 3 (117) had different antibody/threshold combinations.
cards.result: During a median follow-up of 2.7 years in the main study group, diabetes was diagnosed in 58 participants (28.5%) in the oral insulin group and 62 (33%) in the placebo group; time to diabetes was not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.87; 1-sided 95% CI 0 to 1.2; P = .21, against a 1-sided significance threshold of .05). In secondary stratum 1, diabetes was diagnosed in 13 participants (48.1%) on oral insulin versus 19 (70.3%) on placebo, with significantly longer time to diabetes (hazard ratio 0.45; P = .006). In the remaining secondary strata combined (116 participants), the hazard ratio was 1.03 (P = .53).
cards.watchOut: The positive stratum was small (55 participants), secondary, and one of several strata examined — its P value is not adjusted for the multiplicity of subgroup looks; the trial's own primary conclusion was that oral insulin did not delay onset in the main group.
cards.source: Krischer et al. Effect of Oral Insulin on Prevention of Diabetes in Relatives of Patients With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 29164254. Registry ID: NCT00419562. p = .006). in the remaining secondary strata combined (116 participants), the hazard ratio was 1.03 (p = .53). the positive stratum was small (55 participants), secondary, and one of several strata examined — its p value is not adjusted for the multiplicity of subgroup looks; the trial's own primary conclusion was that oral insulin did not delay onset in the main group. krischer et al. effect of oral insulin on prevention of diabetes in relatives of patients with type 1 diabetes: a randomized clinical trial. jama. 2017. pmid: 29164254. registry id: nct00419562. mesh: administration, oral · adolescent · autoantibodies/blood · child · child, preschool · diabetes mellitus, type 1/blood/genetics/*prevention & control · family · female · follow-up studies · glucose tolerance test · humans · hypoglycemic agents/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · insulin/adverse effects/immunology/*therapeutic use · male · treatment failure

cards.summary: Synthesis: an elegant tolerance idea, a null main result, and one subgroup that needs its own trial

shelves.title: Short intensive insulin therapy at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes: 1-year drug-free remission in 51% (pump) and 45% (multiple injections) versus 27% on oral agents in the Weng trial
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, does a short course of intensive insulin therapy (continuous subcutaneous infusion or multiple daily injections), stopped once normoglycaemia is achieved, produce higher drug-free remission rates at 1 year than initial treatment with oral hypoglycaemic agents?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/*drug therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/drug effects · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacology/*therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Intravenous · Insulin/administration & dosage/pharmacology/*therapeutic use · Insulin-Secreting Cells/*drug effects/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Remission Induction
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial with a striking remission difference, supported by a meta-analysis whose underlying studies are mostly non-randomised. In the Weng trial (382 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in China), target glycaemic control was reached by 97.1% on pump therapy and 95.2% on multiple daily injections versus 83.5% on oral agents, and faster (4.0 and 5.6 days versus 9.3 days); after treatment stopped and patients were followed on diet and exercise alone, 1-year remission rates were 51.1% (pump), 44.9% (injections) and 26.7% (oral agents; P = 0.0012). A systematic review of short-term intensive insulin studies (7 studies, 839 participants) found drug-free remission in about 46.3% at 12 months and 42.1% at 24 months, with beta-cell function improved (HOMA-B pooled increase 1.13) — but five of its seven studies were non-randomised. Because the benefit claim (remission, a surrogate for disease modification) rests substantially on one randomised trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a short intensive insulin course at diagnosis probably induces drug-free remission in roughly half of newly diagnosed patients at 1 year — about double the rate with oral agents — though durability beyond 2 years and hard outcomes are unproven.

cards.headline: Weng 2008: remission at 1 year in 51.1% (insulin pump) and 44.9% (multiple injections) versus 26.7% on oral hypoglycaemic agents (P = 0.0012) in 382 newly diagnosed patients
cards.summary: Weng 2008: remission at 1 year in 51.1% (insulin pump) and 44.9% (multiple injections) versus 26.7% on oral hypoglycaemic agents (P = 0.0012) in 382 newly diagnosed patients
cards.people: 382 patients aged 25 to 70 years with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (fasting plasma glucose 7.0 to 16.7 mmol/L (≈126 to 301 mg/dL)) at nine centres in China, randomised to continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (137 patients), multiple daily insulin injections (124), or oral hypoglycaemic agents (121); treatment in all groups was stopped after normoglycaemia had been maintained for 2 weeks, and patients were then followed on diet and exercise alone.
cards.result: Target glycaemic control was achieved by 97.1% of the pump group and 95.2% of the injection group versus 83.5% of the oral-agent group, in less time (4.0 days [SD 2.5] and 5.6 days [SD 3.8] versus 9.3 days [SD 5.3]). Remission rates after 1 year were 51.1% with pump therapy and 44.9% with injections versus 26.7% with oral agents (P = 0.0012). Beta-cell function (HOMA-B and acute insulin response) improved significantly after the intensive interventions, and the increase in acute insulin response was sustained at 1 year in the insulin groups but declined in the oral-agent group among patients in remission.
cards.watchOut: Analysis was per protocol rather than intention-to-treat, the trial was unblinded, and all participants were Chinese patients treated at diagnosis with high presenting glucose — remission here means drug-free normoglycaemia at 1 year, not cure, and relapse beyond the first year was common in the wider literature.
cards.source: Weng et al. Effect of intensive insulin therapy on beta-cell function and glycaemic control in patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a multicentre randomised parallel-group trial. Lancet (London, England). 2008. PMID: 18502299. Registry ID: NCT00147836. cards.headline: Systematic review (Kramer 2013): drug-free remission in about 66% at 3 months, 59% at 6 months, 46% at 12 months and 42% at 24 months after short intensive insulin — across seven mostly non-randomised studies
cards.summary: Systematic review (Kramer 2013): drug-free remission in about 66% at 3 months, 59% at 6 months, 46% at 12 months and 42% at 24 months after short intensive insulin — across seven mostly non-randomised studies
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of interventional studies
cards.people: Seven studies (839 participants) of short-term intensive insulin therapy (2 to 3 weeks) in adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, published 1950 to 2012; five of the seven were non-randomised. Four studies (559 participants) reported drug-free glycaemic remission.
cards.result: Pooled analysis showed an increase in HOMA beta-cell function after intensive insulin therapy (1.13; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.25) and a decrease in HOMA insulin resistance (-0.57; -0.84 to -0.29). The proportion in drug-free remission was about 66.2% (292 of 441 patients) at 3 months, 58.9% (222 of 377) at 6 months, 46.3% (229 of 495) at 12 months and 42.1% (53 of 126) at 24 months. Patients achieving remission had higher baseline body mass index (by 1.06 kg/m²) and lower fasting glucose (by 0.59 mmol/L (≈11 mg/dL)) than those who did not.
cards.watchOut: Mostly non-randomised, single-arm evidence — the remission proportions describe what happens after the therapy, not what the therapy adds versus a comparator; the Weng trial supplies the randomised comparison, and this review mainly shows the effect is seen consistently and wanes over time.
cards.source: Kramer et al. Short-term intensive insulin therapy in type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2013. PMID: 24622264. cards.headline: Synthesis: remission is achievable in about half of newly diagnosed patients — the randomised margin over oral agents is the finding
cards.summary: Synthesis: remission is achievable in about half of newly diagnosed patients — the randomised margin over oral agents is the finding
cards.people: Patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, particularly with high presenting glucose, offered a short intensive insulin course.
cards.result: The randomised comparison (51.1% and 44.9% versus 26.7% in remission at 1 year) shows the insulin-first strategy roughly doubles drug-free remission versus starting with oral agents, and the review's pooled time course (about 46% at 12 months, 42% at 24 months) shows remission is common but erodes. No trial reports cardiovascular or microvascular outcome benefits from the strategy.
cards.watchOut: Intensive insulin at diagnosis means injections or a pump, hypoglycaemia risk during titration, and close supervision; the evidence does not address patients diagnosed with milder hyperglycaemia or long-standing diabetes.
cards.source: Synthesis of the Weng trial (PMID: 18502299) and the Kramer systematic review (PMID: 24622264).

shelves.title: Testosterone in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance and HbA1c improve in two trials — a clamp study finds no glycaemic effect at all
shelves.question: In men with hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes, does testosterone improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Body Composition/drug effects · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/pathology/physiopathology · Humans · Hypogonadism/drug therapy · Insulin Resistance · Male · Metabolic Syndrome/pathology/physiopathology · Middle Aged · Testosterone/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the glycaemic signal depends on which trial and which endpoint you read. In TIMES-2 (220 hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes and/or metabolic syndrome), transdermal testosterone cut insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) by 15.2% at 6 months (P = 0.018) and 16.4% at 12 months (P = 0.006), and in the diabetic subgroup HbA1c was better than placebo at month 9 (treatment difference −0.446%, P = 0.035) — but not at the earlier timepoints the trial emphasised. In BLAST (211 men with type 2 diabetes), long-acting testosterone undecanoate significantly reduced HbA1c at 6 and 18 weeks, most markedly in men with baseline HbA1c above 7.5%, where the reduction was 0.41% within 6 weeks. Against both, the small clamp study (Magnussen 2016, 39 men on metformin alone) found no change at all in clamp-measured insulin sensitivity (p = 0.18), HbA1c, or glucose production — while body composition improved (lean mass +1.9 kg, p = 0.001). No trial tests diabetes outcomes, only surrogates, and none runs beyond a year of blinded treatment. PROPOSED SPLIT: glycaemic improvement in the two larger trials (HbA1c about 0.4% in the subgroups and timepoints that reached significance), no glycaemic effect in the small mechanistic trial; body-composition effects consistent across all three.

cards.headline: TIMES-2 (Jones 2011): HOMA-IR down 15.2% at 6 months (P = 0.018); HbA1c better than placebo only at month 9 in the diabetic subgroup (−0.446%, P = 0.035)
cards.summary: TIMES-2 (Jones 2011): HOMA-IR down 15.2% at 6 months (P = 0.018); HbA1c better than placebo only at month 9 in the diabetic subgroup (−0.446%, P = 0.035)
cards.people: 220 hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes and/or metabolic syndrome in a multicentre trial of a transdermal 2% testosterone gel versus placebo over 12 months; the primary outcome was change in HOMA-IR, with efficacy focused on months 0–6 (no medication changes allowed) and medication changes permitted in months 6–12.
cards.result: Testosterone reduced HOMA-IR in the overall population by 15.2% at 6 months (P = 0.018) and 16.4% at 12 months (P = 0.006) relative to placebo. In men with type 2 diabetes, glycaemic control was significantly better on testosterone at month 9 (HbA1c treatment difference −0.446%, P = 0.035). Improvements in total and LDL cholesterol, lipoprotein(a), body composition, libido and sexual function occurred in selected groups. Adverse and serious adverse event frequencies did not differ significantly between groups; more than 95% of adverse events were mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: The headline endpoint is a surrogate (HOMA-IR), the population mixes diabetes with metabolic syndrome, and the HbA1c separation appears at one timepoint (month 9) inside the phase where diabetes medications could change — exactly the window in which confounding by medication adjustment is possible. TIMES-2 cannot say whether testosterone changes any outcome a patient feels or any diabetes complication.
cards.source: Jones TH et al. Testosterone replacement in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes and/or metabolic syndrome (the TIMES2 study). Diabetes Care. 2011. PMID: 21386088. cards.headline: BLAST (Hackett 2014): testosterone undecanoate cut HbA1c significantly at 6 and 18 weeks — by 0.41% in men starting above 7.5% — with no benefit in men with depression
cards.summary: BLAST (Hackett 2014): testosterone undecanoate cut HbA1c significantly at 6 and 18 weeks — by 0.41% in men starting above 7.5% — with no benefit in men with depression
cards.people: 211 men with type 2 diabetes identified from the registers of seven UK general practices, randomised to long-acting testosterone undecanoate 1,000 mg or placebo for 30 weeks of double-blind treatment, followed by 52 weeks of open-label testosterone for all.
cards.result: Testosterone undecanoate produced a statistically significant reduction in HbA1c at 6 and 18 weeks; the effect was most marked in poorly controlled men with baseline HbA1c above 7.5%, where the reduction was 0.41% within 6 weeks, with a further 0.46% reduction after 52 weeks of open-label treatment. Waist circumference, weight and body mass index fell significantly in men without depression, and response depended on achieving adequate serum testosterone levels; metabolic improvements were not seen in men with coexisting depression. There were no significant safety issues.
cards.watchOut: The quantified HbA1c figures in the record are subgroup figures (baseline HbA1c above 7.5%, and the non-depressed), and the 52-week extension is open-label with no comparator — the further 0.46% cannot be attributed to the drug. Thirty weeks of blinded treatment in 211 men is a surrogate-endpoint evidence base, and the depression interaction means the average effect overstates what a depressed patient should expect.
cards.source: Hackett G et al. Testosterone replacement therapy improves metabolic parameters in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes but not in men with coexisting depression: the BLAST study. cards.headline: Magnussen 2016: clamp-measured insulin sensitivity unchanged (p = 0.18) and HbA1c unaltered — while lean mass rose 1.9 kg (p = 0.001) in 39 men
cards.summary: Magnussen 2016: clamp-measured insulin sensitivity unchanged (p = 0.18) and HbA1c unaltered — while lean mass rose 1.9 kg (p = 0.001) in 39 men
cards.people: 39 men aged 50 to 70 years with type 2 diabetes controlled on metformin monotherapy and bioavailable testosterone below 7.3 nmol/L, randomised to testosterone gel (20) or placebo (19) for 24 weeks, with insulin sensitivity measured by euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp with glucose tracer and body composition by DXA.
cards.result: Insulin-stimulated glucose disposal did not change on testosterone versus placebo (p = 0.18), and glycated haemoglobin and basal and insulin-stimulated endogenous glucose production and substrate oxidation were unaltered. Body composition did change: lean body mass increased (β = 1.9 kg, p = 0.001), total fat mass fell (β = −1.3 kg, p = 0.009), and HDL cholesterol fell (β = −0.11 mmol/L (≈4.3 mg/dL), p = 0.009). The authors conclude testosterone is not supported as a treatment for glycaemic control in this population.
cards.watchOut: The most rigorous glycaemic measurement in the set (the clamp) is also the smallest trial — 39 men for 24 weeks can miss a modest HbA1c effect, and its men were already metformin-controlled, leaving less room to improve. Its null result disciplines the larger trials' surrogate claims rather than refuting them outright; the split is the finding.
cards.source: Magnussen LV et al. Effect of testosterone on insulin sensitivity, oxidative metabolism and body composition in aging men with type 2 diabetes on metformin monotherapy. Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2016. PMID: 27265844. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (magnussen 2016) 39 men aged 50 to 70 years with type 2 diabetes controlled on metformin monotherapy and bioavailable testosterone below 7.3 nmol/l, randomised to testosterone gel (20) or placebo (19) for 24 weeks, with insulin sensitivity measured by euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp with glucose tracer and body composition by dxa. insulin-stimulated glucose disposal did not change on testosterone versus placebo (p = 0.18), and glycated haemoglobin and basal and insulin-stimulated endogenous glucose production and substrate oxidation were unaltered. body composition did change: lean body mass increased (β = 1.9 kg, p = 0.001), total fat mass fell (β = −1.3 kg, p = 0.009), and hdl cholesterol fell (β = −0.11 mmol/l (≈4.3 mg/dl), p = 0.009). the authors conclude testosterone is not supported as a treatment for glycaemic control in this population. the most rigorous glycaemic measurement in the set (the clamp) is also the smallest trial — 39 men for 24 weeks can miss a modest hba1c effect, and its men were already metformin-controlled, leaving less room to improve. its null result disciplines the larger trials' surrogate claims rather than refuting them outright; the split is the finding. magnussen lv et al. effect of testosterone on insulin sensitivity, oxidative metabolism and body composition in aging men with type 2 diabetes on metformin monotherapy. diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2016. pmid: 27265844. mesh: adult · aged · aging/blood/drug effects/physiology · blood glucose/drug effects/metabolism · body composition/drug effects · diabetes mellitus, type 2/complications/drug therapy/metabolism · double-blind method · eunuchism/complications/drug therapy/metabolism · hormone replacement therapy/adverse effects · humans · insulin/metabolism · insulin resistance · male · metformin/therapeutic use · middle aged · oxidation-reduction/drug effects · placebos · testosterone/pharmacology/therapeutic use · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: two positive surrogate trials, one rigorous null — testosterone is not a diabetes drug on this record
cards.summary: Synthesis: two positive surrogate trials, one rigorous null — testosterone is not a diabetes drug on this record
cards.people: Three randomised double-blind trials in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes: TIMES-2 (220 men, testosterone gel, 12 months, diabetes and/or metabolic syndrome), BLAST (211 men, testosterone undecanoate, 30 weeks blinded), and Magnussen 2016 (39 men on metformin, testosterone gel, 24 weeks, clamp-measured).
cards.result: HOMA-IR: −15.2% at 6 months and −16.4% at 12 months in TIMES-2 (P = 0.018 and P = 0.006). HbA1c: −0.446% versus placebo at month 9 in TIMES-2's diabetic subgroup (P = 0.035); significant reductions at 6 and 18 weeks in BLAST, 0.41% within 6 weeks in men starting above 7.5%. Clamp insulin sensitivity and HbA1c: unchanged in Magnussen 2016 (p = 0.18). Body composition improved in all three. PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible small glycaemic benefit that the most mechanistic trial does not confirm, on surrogate endpoints only.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is the diabetes-subpopulation boundary of the testosterone literature: the T Trials and TRAVERSE shelves (older hypogonadal men generally, and cardiovascular safety) are homed elsewhere, as is T4DM (testosterone to prevent or revert diabetes in men with impaired glucose tolerance, live #568) — none of those answers the glycaemic-control question in established type 2 diabetes, which is the only question carded here. Tier C: SPLIT stamp on surrogate endpoints.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jones TH et al. Diabetes Care. 2011 (PMID: 21386088); Hackett G et al. The Journal of Sexual Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24308723); Magnussen LV et al. Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2016 (PMID: 27265844).

shelves.title: Side effects of GLP-1 drugs: nausea affects about 1 in 5 users in trials (relative risk 2.90 versus placebo), vomiting about 1 in 11 — and the rare serious signals (gastroparesis, thyroid cancer) come with conflicting answers
shelves.question: What are the side effects of GLP-1 drugs? In people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide, dulaglutide or tirzepatide for diabetes or weight loss, how common are gut side effects, and what is the evidence on gastroparesis, bowel obstruction, pancreatitis, thyroid cancer, and retained stomach contents at endoscopy or surgery?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Exenatide/adverse effects · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Gastrointestinal Diseases/epidemiology · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Glucagon-Like Peptides/adverse effects · Glucagon-Like Peptides/analogs & derivatives · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects · Immunoglobulin Fc Fragments/adverse effects · Liraglutide/adverse effects · Nausea/chemically induced · Pancreatitis/chemically induced · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recombinant Fusion Proteins · Semaglutide · Tirzepatide · Vomiting/chemically induced
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The common side effects are not in doubt: across 101 randomised trials (Joy 2026), nausea (22.8% of users; relative risk 2.90 versus placebo), vomiting (9.12%; RR 3.60), diarrhoea (13%; RR 1.97), constipation (7.39%; RR 2.41) and decreased appetite (2.61%; RR 3.51) are class effects, and the same analysis found pancreatitis at 1.07% incidence with a relative risk of 2.24. The rarer, more serious signals rest on observational data and conflict. A US claims study (Sodhi 2023) found higher rates of gastroparesis, bowel obstruction and pancreatitis than with bupropion-naltrexone, but on only 613 semaglutide users and with very wide confidence intervals. For thyroid cancer, a French case-control study found an association after 1–3 years of use (adjusted HR 1.58), while a Scandinavian active-comparator cohort of 437,077 starters found none (HR 0.93; upper confidence limit consistent with no more than a 31% relative increase). Around procedures, GLP-1 users much more often have retained stomach contents at endoscopy (OR 6.30) and more aborted procedures (OR 5.50), but aspiration itself was not significantly increased (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.86–1.87).

cards.headline: Joy 2026 (meta-analysis of 101 randomised trials, 57,684 patients): nausea in 22.8% on a GLP-1 drug (relative risk 2.90 versus placebo), vomiting 9.12% (3.60), diarrhoea 13% (1.97), constipation 7.39% (2.41), pancreatitis 1.07% (2.24)
cards.summary: Joy 2026 (meta-analysis of 101 randomised trials, 57,684 patients): nausea in 22.8% on a GLP-1 drug (relative risk 2.90 versus placebo), vomiting 9.12% (3.60), diarrhoea 13% (1.97), constipation 7.39% (2.41), pancreatitis 1.07% (2.24)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Joy 2026)
cards.people: 57,684 patients in 101 randomised trials of five GLP-1 receptor agonists used for type 2 diabetes and weight management; 41,443 received a GLP-1 drug (liraglutide in 37 studies, semaglutide 28, exenatide 25, dulaglutide 18, tirzepatide 8).
cards.result: All six gastrointestinal adverse effects were significantly more common than on placebo (all P<0.00001). Relative risks (relative measures) with the pooled incidence on drug: nausea RR 2.90, incidence 22.8%; vomiting RR 3.60, 9.12%; diarrhoea RR 1.97, 13%; constipation RR 2.41, 7.39%; decreased appetite RR 3.51, 2.61%; pancreatitis RR 2.24, 1.07%. In head-to-head comparisons, tirzepatide carried the highest risk ratios for nausea and diarrhoea, while semaglutide carried the highest for vomiting and constipation.
cards.watchOut: Incidences are pooled across doses, titration schedules and indications, so any one patient's chance depends on the drug and how fast the dose rises. The pancreatitis relative risk of 2.24 rests on an incidence of about 1% and few events. The abstract does not print the placebo-group rates, so absolute excesses cannot be computed from it.
cards.source: Joy B, Ramsamooj A, Ibrahim S, Wen J, Hsu N, Frezza E. Exploring the rates of Gastrointestinal adverse effects among five GLP-1 receptor agonists: A systematic review and Meta-Analysis of randomized controlled trials. Endocrine. 2026. PMID: 41489846. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Sodhi 2023 (US insurance-claims study): gastroparesis adjusted HR 3.67, bowel obstruction 4.22, pancreatitis 9.09 versus bupropion-naltrexone — but the semaglutide group was only 613 people and the intervals are very wide
cards.summary: Sodhi 2023 (US insurance-claims study): gastroparesis adjusted HR 3.67, bowel obstruction 4.22, pancreatitis 9.09 versus bupropion-naltrexone — but the semaglutide group was only 613 people and the intervals are very wide
cards.type: Observational cohort study of insurance claims, published as a research letter (Sodhi 2023)
cards.people: People in a random sample of about 16 million US insurance patients (PharMetrics Plus, 2006–2020) who used medicines for weight loss: 613 used semaglutide, 4,144 used liraglutide and 654 used the comparator bupropion-naltrexone.
cards.result: Incidence per 1,000 person-years on semaglutide, liraglutide and bupropion-naltrexone respectively: gastroparesis 9.1, 7.3 and 3.1; pancreatitis 4.6, 7.9 and 1.0; biliary disease 11.7, 18.6 and 12.6. Adjusted hazard ratios (relative measures) for GLP-1 users versus bupropion-naltrexone: pancreatitis 9.09 (95% CI 1.25–66.00), bowel obstruction 4.22 (1.02–17.40), gastroparesis 3.67 (1.15–11.90); biliary disease 1.50 (0.89–2.53) was not significant.
cards.watchOut: Claims data: diagnoses come from billing codes rather than examinations, events were few (hence intervals like 1.25–66.00), and people prescribed GLP-1 drugs for weight loss differ from people prescribed bupropion-naltrexone in ways claims cannot fully capture. PubMed carries no abstract for this research letter; the numbers are taken from the letter itself.
cards.source: Sodhi M, Rezaeianzadeh R, Kezouh A, Etminan M. Risk of Gastrointestinal Adverse Events Associated With Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists for Weight Loss. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37796527. Registry ID: none in the record (observational claims study). cards.headline: Bezin 2023 (French national data, 2,562 thyroid cancers): 1–3 years of GLP-1 use — adjusted HR 1.58 for all thyroid cancer and 1.78 for medullary thyroid cancer
cards.summary: Bezin 2023 (French national data, 2,562 thyroid cancers): 1–3 years of GLP-1 use — adjusted HR 1.58 for all thyroid cancer and 1.78 for medullary thyroid cancer
cards.people: Adults with type 2 diabetes in the French national health insurance database (SNDS) treated with second-line antidiabetes drugs between 2006 and 2018: 2,562 case subjects with thyroid cancer, matched with 45,184 control subjects.
cards.result: Use of a GLP-1 receptor agonist for 1 to 3 years was associated with an increased risk of all thyroid cancer (adjusted hazard ratio 1.58, 95% CI 1.27–1.95) and of medullary thyroid cancer (adjusted HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.04–3.05). The abstract reports the association for the 1–3 year cumulative-duration band.
cards.watchOut: Observational: people prescribed GLP-1 drugs may have their thyroids examined more often (detection bias), and medullary thyroid cancer is rare, so the 1.78 estimate rests on few cases (CI 1.04–3.05). This result conflicts with the Scandinavian cohort carded next — the two should be read together.
cards.source: Bezin J, Gouverneur A, Pénichon M, Mathieu C, Garrel R, Hillaire-Buys D, Pariente A, Faillie JL. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and the Risk of Thyroid Cancer. Diabetes Care. 2023. PMID: 36356111. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Pasternak 2024 (Scandinavian registries, 437,077 starters): thyroid cancer 1.33 versus 1.46 per 10,000 person-years on GLP-1 versus DPP-4 drugs — HR 0.93, no increase found
cards.summary: Pasternak 2024 (Scandinavian registries, 437,077 starters): thyroid cancer 1.33 versus 1.46 per 10,000 person-years on GLP-1 versus DPP-4 drugs — HR 0.93, no increase found
cards.people: 145,410 patients in Denmark, Norway and Sweden who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist (2007–2021), compared with 291,667 who started a DPP-4 inhibitor; mean follow-up 3.9 years (SD 3.5) in the GLP-1 group and 5.4 years (SD 3.5) in the DPP-4 group.
cards.result: Thyroid cancer developed in 76 of 145,410 GLP-1 starters (incidence 1.33 per 10,000 person-years) and 184 of 291,667 DPP-4 starters (1.46 per 10,000 person-years): hazard ratio 0.93 (95% CI 0.66–1.31), rate difference −0.13 (−0.61 to 0.36) per 10,000 person-years. For medullary thyroid cancer the HR was 1.19 (0.37–3.86); in the additional comparison with SGLT2 inhibitor starters the HR was 1.16 (0.65–2.05). The authors note the upper confidence limit in the main analysis is consistent with no more than a 31% relative increase.
cards.watchOut: Mean follow-up of 3.9 years may be short for cancer latency, and medullary cases were few (CI 0.37–3.86), so a small risk in that rare subtype cannot be excluded. But the design — new users compared against another diabetes drug class in nationwide registers — is the strongest observational design on this shelf, and it contradicts the French case-control result.
cards.source: Pasternak B, Wintzell V, Hviid A, Eliasson B, Gudbjörnsdottir S, Jonasson C, Hveem K, Svanström H, Melbye M, Ueda P. Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist use and risk of thyroid cancer: Scandinavian cohort study. BMJ. 2024. PMID: 38683947. Registry ID: none in the record (cohort study). cards.headline: Tarar 2025 (meta-analysis, 105,515 endoscopy patients): retained stomach contents far more common on GLP-1 drugs (OR 6.30) and more procedures aborted (OR 5.50) — but aspiration itself was not significantly increased (OR 1.26; 0.73% versus 0.35%)
cards.summary: Tarar 2025 (meta-analysis, 105,515 endoscopy patients): retained stomach contents far more common on GLP-1 drugs (OR 6.30) and more procedures aborted (OR 5.50) — but aspiration itself was not significantly increased (OR 1.26; 0.73% versus 0.35%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of endoscopy outcomes (Tarar 2025)
cards.people: 105,515 patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy across 12 studies: 32,144 taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist and 73,273 in the control group.
cards.result: Aspiration events: 234 (0.73%) in GLP-1 users versus 257 (0.35%) in controls — odds ratio 1.26 (95% CI 0.86–1.87, I²=34%), not significant. Retained gastric content was much more common on GLP-1 drugs (OR 6.30, 95% CI 5.30–7.49, I²=0%), as were aborted procedures (OR 5.50, 3.25–9.32) and repeated procedures (OR 2.19, 1.42–3.38). Retained contents were most frequent with tirzepatide (18.9% of users) and least with exenatide (6.2%); undergoing concomitant colonoscopy was associated with lower odds of retained contents (OR 0.26, 0.04–0.48).
cards.watchOut: Mostly observational endoscopy series rather than randomised fasting trials: they show the stomach is often not empty on these drugs, yet the feared outcome — aspiration — was not significantly more frequent, though at under 1% in both groups the power to detect a difference is limited. The authors note that simple measures such as a clear liquid diet for 24 hours, routine for colonoscopy, may reduce retained residue.
cards.source: Tarar ZI, Farooq U, Chaudhry A, Gandhi M, El Alayli A, Ayoub M, Singh B, Daglilar E, Thosani N. Evidence Report on the Safety of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy in Patients on Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Diagnostics. 2025. PMID: 40150111. cards.headline: Synthesis: expect gut symptoms; the serious-harm questions are open, and the thyroid evidence points both ways
cards.summary: Synthesis: expect gut symptoms; the serious-harm questions are open, and the thyroid evidence points both ways
cards.people: People taking GLP-1 receptor agonists for diabetes or weight loss, and clinicians counselling them or planning procedures.
cards.result: Established: nausea (~23%), vomiting (~9%), diarrhoea (~13%) and constipation (~7%) are common class effects in randomised trials, with relative risks of roughly 2–3.6 versus placebo, and pancreatitis appears at about 1% incidence with a relative risk of 2.24 in the same trial pool. Contested: gastroparesis and bowel obstruction signals come from one claims study with wide intervals; thyroid cancer has one positive French case-control study (HR 1.58) against one null Scandinavian cohort (HR 0.93) an order of magnitude larger. Practical: before endoscopy, retained stomach contents are common (OR 6.30) and procedures are more often aborted, but measured aspiration was not significantly increased.
cards.watchOut: Harms shelves age fast: these drugs are recent, doses and indications keep shifting, and the observational harm signals may shrink or grow as larger active-comparator studies report. The randomised-trial incidences describe trial populations on trial titration schedules, not every real-world user.

shelves.title: Metformin and heart attacks: UKPDS 34's overweight substudy showed 32–42% relative reductions in diabetes endpoints and death — but the abstract prints no absolute rates, the pooled trial record is non-significant, and the 10-year legacy result lives on Shelf #284
shelves.question: Does metformin prevent heart attacks? In people with type 2 diabetes — particularly the overweight patients studied in UKPDS 34 — does taking metformin reduce myocardial infarction and cardiovascular death compared with diet alone, other glucose-lowering drugs, or no metformin?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a famous claim resting on a narrow base. The claim comes from one substudy: UKPDS 34 (PMID: 9742977), in which 342 overweight patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes allocated intensive control with metformin, versus 411 allocated a conventional diet-first policy, had relative risk reductions of 32% (95% CI 13–47; P=0.002) for any diabetes-related endpoint, 42% for diabetes-related death (9–63; P=0.017) and 36% for all-cause mortality (9–55; P=0.011) over a median 10.7 years, at HbA1c 7.4% versus 8.0%. Every one of those numbers is a RELATIVE reduction: the abstract prints no absolute event rates, so no honest absolute benefit can be quoted from this record — a gap this shelf states rather than fills. The same paper contains the counter-signal: in its supplementary randomised trial, early addition of metformin to sulphonylurea-treated patients was associated with a 96% relative INCREASE in diabetes-related death (95% CI 2–275; P=0.039) versus continuing sulphonylurea alone — although the paper's own combined analysis (19% relative reduction in diabetes-related endpoints, P=0.033) and its epidemiological assessment in 4,416 patients (5% relative reduction, P=0.78) did not confirm the harm. The one other randomised test, SPREAD-DIMCAD (Hong 2013, PMID: 23230096; 304 patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease), found fewer composite cardiovascular events on metformin than glipizide (adjusted HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30–0.90 — relative; P=0.026) over a median 5.0 years, but it is a single small trial against an active comparator, not placebo. When Griffin (2017, PMID: 28770324) pooled the 13 randomised trials that isolate metformin against diet, lifestyle or placebo (2,079 people allocated metformin), NO outcome reached significance — all-cause mortality RR 0.96 (0.84–1.09), cardiovascular death 0.97 (0.80–1.16), myocardial infarction 0.89 (0.75–1.06), stroke 1.04 (0.73–1.48) — and UKPDS itself supplied 52.3% to 70.5% of the weight, so the pool is not independent corroboration. The 10-year post-trial legacy follow-up, in which the metformin group showed myocardial infarction 33% relatively lower (P=0.005) and death 27% relatively lower (P=0.002), is homed on Shelf #284 (how tight should glucose control be) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded, under the one-home rule. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin probably reduces cardiovascular events when started early in overweight type 2 diabetes, but the direct evidence is one positive substudy plus one small active-comparator trial, the pooled isolated-effect estimate is non-significant, and the absolute size of any heart-attack benefit has never been printed in the landmark abstract.

cards.headline: UKPDS 34 (1998): in overweight, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, metformin beat a diet-first policy by 32% relative on any diabetes-related endpoint, 42% relative on diabetes-related death and 36% relative on all-cause mortality — relative figures only; the abstract prints no absolute event rates
cards.summary: UKPDS 34 (1998): in overweight, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, metformin beat a diet-first policy by 32% relative on any diabetes-related endpoint, 42% relative on diabetes-related death and 36% relative on all-cause mortality — relative figures only; the abstract prints no absolute event rates
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — the metformin substudy of UKPDS (UKPDS 34, 1998)
cards.people: Of 4,075 patients recruited to UKPDS in 15 centres, 1,704 overweight (>120% ideal bodyweight) patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, mean age 53 years, with raised fasting plasma glucose (6.1–15.0 mmol/L [≈110–270 mg/dL]) after 3 months of diet, entered the programme; 753 were included in the randomised controlled comparison at the heart of this card — conventional policy, primarily diet alone (n=411), versus intensive blood-glucose control with metformin aiming for fasting plasma glucose below 6 mmol/L (≈108 mg/dL) (n=342) — followed for a median of 10.7 years. A secondary analysis compared the 342 metformin patients with 951 overweight patients allocated intensive control with chlorpropamide (n=265), glibenclamide (n=277) or insulin (n=409).
cards.result: Median HbA1c was 7.4% in the metformin group versus 8.0% in the conventional group. Patients allocated metformin, compared with the conventional group, had risk reductions of 32% (95% CI 13–47; P=0.002) for any diabetes-related endpoint, 42% for diabetes-related death (95% CI 9–63; P=0.017), and 36% for all-cause mortality (95% CI 9–55; P=0.011) — all RELATIVE reductions; the abstract does not print the groups' absolute event rates. Among patients allocated intensive blood-glucose control, metformin showed a greater effect than chlorpropamide, glibenclamide or insulin for any diabetes-related endpoint (P=0.0034), all-cause mortality (P=0.021) and stroke (P=0.032). The authors concluded that intensive glucose control with metformin appears to decrease diabetes-related endpoints in overweight diabetic patients, with less weight gain and fewer hypoglycaemic attacks than insulin or sulphonylureas, and may be the first-line pharmacological therapy of choice in these patients.
cards.watchOut: Three disciplines on this card. First, the population: overweight patients at diagnosis in the 1970s–90s, before statins, modern blood-pressure treatment, SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 drugs — the comparison is metformin against a diet-first policy, not against today's background care. Second, the endpoints are aggregates ('any diabetes-related endpoint' mixes microvascular and macrovascular events); the abstract does not print a myocardial-infarction-specific result, so the popular 'metformin prevents heart attacks by X%' cannot be sourced to this abstract — the heart-attack-specific legacy figure lives on Shelf #284. Third, every benefit number here is relative, and the abstract's silence on absolute rates means the absolute benefit — the number a patient actually feels — is not documented in this record.
cards.source: UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) Group. Effect of intensive blood-glucose control with metformin on complications in overweight patients with type 2 diabetes (UKPDS 34). Lancet. 1998. PMID: 9742977. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: UKPDS 34's own supplementary trial (1998): early addition of metformin to sulphonylurea was associated with a 96% relative increase in diabetes-related death (P=0.039) — a signal the same paper's combined and epidemiological analyses did not confirm
cards.summary: UKPDS 34's own supplementary trial (1998): early addition of metformin to sulphonylurea was associated with a 96% relative increase in diabetes-related death (P=0.039) — a signal the same paper's combined and epidemiological analyses did not confirm
cards.type: Supplementary randomised controlled trial and combined/epidemiological analyses within UKPDS 34 (1998)
cards.people: A supplementary randomised controlled trial within the same UKPDS 34 publication: 537 non-overweight and overweight patients, mean age 59 years, already on maximum sulphonylurea therapy with raised fasting plasma glucose (6.1–15.0 mmol/L [≈110–270 mg/dL]), allocated to continuing sulphonylurea alone (n=269) or addition of metformin (n=268). The paper also reports a combined analysis of the main and supplementary studies and an epidemiological assessment in 4,416 patients of diabetes-related death by concurrent therapy.
cards.result: Early addition of metformin in sulphonylurea-treated patients was associated with an increased risk of diabetes-related death — a 96% relative increase (95% CI 2–275; P=0.039) — compared with continued sulphonylurea alone. However, the combined analysis of the main and supplementary studies showed fewer metformin-allocated patients having diabetes-related endpoints (relative risk reduction 19%, 95% CI 2–33; P=0.033), and the epidemiological assessment did not show an increased risk of diabetes-related death in patients treated with a combination of sulphonylurea and metformin (relative risk reduction 5%, 95% CI −33 to 32; P=0.78).
cards.watchOut: This card exists because honest shelving cannot print the main trial's benefit and bury its own paper's harm signal. Read both ways with care: the 96% figure is a relative increase on a small supplementary trial (537 patients) with a very wide confidence interval (2–275), and the two larger analyses in the same paper point the other way — but 'not confirmed' is not 'refuted', and this substudy is part of why the shelf's stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. The combination question (metformin added to a sulphonylurea) is also a different clinical act from starting metformin first-line, which is what the main trial tested.

Lancet. 1998. PMID: 9742977. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial; supplementary randomised comparison reported in the same publication). cards.headline: SPREAD-DIMCAD (Hong 2013): in type 2 diabetes with coronary artery disease, metformin beat glipizide on the composite cardiovascular endpoint — adjusted HR 0.54 (relative) over a median 5 years — in a single 304-patient trial
cards.summary: SPREAD-DIMCAD (Hong 2013): in type 2 diabetes with coronary artery disease, metformin beat glipizide on the composite cardiovascular endpoint — adjusted HR 0.54 (relative) over a median 5 years — in a single 304-patient trial
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind trial, metformin versus glipizide (SPREAD-DIMCAD, Hong 2013)
cards.people: 304 patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of coronary artery disease, mean age 63.3 years (range 36–80), at multiple centres in China, randomised double-blind to glipizide 30 mg daily or metformin 1.5 g daily for 3 years, with a median follow-up of 5.0 years. The primary endpoint was the time to a composite of recurrent cardiovascular events: cardiovascular death, death from any cause, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or arterial revascularisation.
cards.result: At the end of study-drug administration both groups had similar HbA1c (7.1% glipizide, 7.0% metformin). At a median follow-up of 5.0 years, 91 participants had developed 103 primary endpoints. Intention-to-treat analysis showed an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.54 (95% CI 0.30–0.90; P=0.026) for the composite of cardiovascular events with metformin compared with glipizide — a relative measure; the abstract prints no per-group absolute event rates. Secondary endpoints and adverse events were not significantly different between the groups. The authors concluded that 3 years of metformin substantially reduced major cardiovascular events over a median 5.0 years compared with glipizide, indicating a potential benefit of metformin on cardiovascular outcomes in high-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator result cannot separate 'metformin protects' from 'glipizide harms' — sulphonylureas carry their own cardiovascular suspicions, and this trial has no placebo or diet arm. It is also small (304 patients, 103 endpoints), single-country, and its composite includes revascularisation, a clinician-driven endpoint. It corroborates UKPDS 34's direction; it does not independently establish a heart-attack effect, and under this library's rules a single small trial caps a claim at POSSIBLE.

Effects of metformin versus glipizide on cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 23230096. Registry ID: NCT00513630. cards.headline: Griffin 2017 (meta-analysis of the isolated metformin effect): across 13 randomised trials, no cardiovascular outcome reached significance — mortality RR 0.96, myocardial infarction RR 0.89, stroke RR 1.04 — and UKPDS supplied most of the weight
cards.summary: Griffin 2017 (meta-analysis of the isolated metformin effect): across 13 randomised trials, no cardiovascular outcome reached significance — mortality RR 0.96, myocardial infarction RR 0.89, stroke RR 1.04 — and UKPDS supplied most of the weight
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials isolating the metformin effect (Griffin 2017)
cards.people: Ten articles reporting 13 randomised trials in adults with type 2 diabetes comparing oral metformin with no intervention, placebo or a lifestyle intervention and reporting mortality or a cardiovascular outcome; 2,079 individuals were allocated to metformin, with a similar number to comparison groups. Only four trials compared metformin with placebo and collected cardiovascular outcome data. The summary estimates rested on 416 myocardial infarction/ischaemic heart disease events in seven studies and 111 strokes in four studies.
cards.result: All outcomes except stroke favoured metformin, with limited heterogeneity, but none achieved statistical significance: all-cause mortality RR 0.96 (95% CI 0.84–1.09); cardiovascular death RR 0.97 (0.80–1.16); myocardial infarction RR 0.89 (0.75–1.06); stroke RR 1.04 (0.73–1.48); peripheral vascular disease RR 0.81 (0.50–1.31) — all relative measures. The UK Prospective Diabetes Study contributed the majority of the data, with weights from 52.3% for myocardial infarction to 70.5% for stroke. The authors concluded there remains uncertainty about whether metformin reduces cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes, mainly from absence of evidence, and that a definitive placebo-controlled cardiovascular endpoint trial is unlikely to be forthcoming.
cards.watchOut: Do not misread this card in either direction. It does not show metformin has no cardiovascular effect — its confidence intervals include worthwhile benefit (the myocardial infarction interval runs to a 25% relative reduction) — it shows the non-UKPDS randomised record is too small and too short to settle the question, and that pooling cannot manufacture independence when one substudy supplies most of the weight. Most included trials were glycaemic-control trials with few events, not cardiovascular outcome trials.
cards.source: Griffin SJ, Leaver JK, Irving GJ. Impact of metformin on cardiovascular disease: a meta-analysis of randomised trials among people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetologia. 2017. PMID: 28770324. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive overweight substudy (relative reductions only), one small active-comparator win, one internal harm signal never confirmed, and a pooled estimate that is non-significant — the heart claim is probable, not proven
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive overweight substudy (relative reductions only), one small active-comparator win, one internal harm signal never confirmed, and a pooled estimate that is non-significant — the heart claim is probable, not proven
cards.people: UKPDS 34 main randomised comparison (342 metformin versus 411 conventional policy, median 10.7 years) and its supplementary trial (268 versus 269) with combined and epidemiological analyses in the same publication; SPREAD-DIMCAD (304 patients, NCT00513630); and the Griffin 2017 meta-analysis (13 trials, 2,079 allocated metformin). The UKPDS 10-year post-trial legacy follow-up is homed on Shelf #284 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Within-trial, overweight newly diagnosed patients: any diabetes-related endpoint 32% relatively lower, diabetes-related death 42% relatively lower, all-cause mortality 36% relatively lower on metformin versus diet-first policy (UKPDS 34) — relative measures, with no absolute rates in the abstract. Against glipizide in established coronary disease: composite cardiovascular events HR 0.54 (relative) (SPREAD-DIMCAD). Against the claim's certainty: early metformin addition to sulphonylurea carried a 96% relative increase in diabetes-related death in the supplementary trial, unconfirmed by the same paper's larger analyses; and pooling every trial that isolates metformin gives non-significant estimates throughout (mortality RR 0.96; myocardial infarction RR 0.89; stroke RR 1.04), dominated by UKPDS weight (Griffin 2017). The legacy follow-up on Shelf #284 adds the metformin group's later myocardial infarction (33% relatively lower) and mortality (27% relatively lower) figures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Boundary: this shelf answers the cardiovascular question for metformin started in type 2 diabetes. It does not cover metformin for glycaemic control itself, metformin in type 1 diabetes (Shelf #1778), pregnancy (Shelves #286, #1333), antipsychotic weight gain (Shelf #562), or cancer adjuvant use (Shelf #2022). No modern cardiovascular outcome trial of metformin against placebo exists; every number here predates contemporary background therapy, so the absolute benefit a patient today would gain — never printed in the landmark abstract — cannot be stated from this record.

shelves.title: Blood sugar 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) at bedtime but 165 mg/dL (≈9.2 mmol/L) in the morning: the dawn phenomenon typically adds only about 16–22 mg/dL (≈0.9–1.2 mmol/L) overnight and about 0.4% to HbA1c, no oral drug eliminated it, and acarbose blunted it in one small trial analysis (n=50)
shelves.question: 'My blood sugar is 94 at bedtime but 165 in the morning — how can I lower it?' — 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) at bedtime, 165 mg/dL (≈9.2 mmol/L) before breakfast: how big is the dawn phenomenon in type 2 diabetes, how much does it contribute to HbA1c, and what has been shown to blunt the overnight rise?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Circadian Rhythm · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/therapy · Diet · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors
shelves.balance: The dawn phenomenon is real, common, and modest in size — which is the first thing to set against this person's numbers. In 248 non-insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes wearing continuous glucose monitors, the median overnight rise from the nocturnal low to the pre-breakfast value was 16.0 mg/dL (≈0.9 mmol/L), and its average impact was 4.3 ± 1.3 mmol/mol (0.39 ± 0.12%) on HbA1c and 12.4 ± 2.4 mg/dL (≈0.7 mmol/L) on 24-hour mean glucose; crucially, the impact was not eliminated by any available oral agent class (Monnier 2013, PMID: 24170753). An age-stratified study found dawn increments of 18.0–22.0 mg/dL (≈1.0–1.2 mmol/L) across age groups, present (a rise over 10 mg/dL, ≈0.6 mmol/L) in 52–70% of patients (Monnier 2012, PMID: 22991448). The gap in the question — 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) at bedtime to 165 mg/dL (≈9.2 mmol/L) in the morning, a 71 mg/dL (≈3.9 mmol/L) difference — is three to four times the typical dawn increment, and the studies measure from the overnight low, not from a bedtime reading, so either this rise is unusually large or something beyond the classic dawn effect contributes. On blunting it, the fetched record is thin: in a post-hoc analysis of a randomised trial in 50 patients on metformin, adding acarbose reduced the dawn magnitude from 35.9 ± 15.7 to 28.3 ± 16.5 mg/dL (≈2.0 to ≈1.6 mmol/L; p=0.037) while glibenclamide did not (Wang 2021, PMID: 34394904) — one small secondary analysis, not a treatment trial. No fetched record carded a bedtime snack or insulin-timing intervention, so this shelf makes no claim for them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the dawn rise itself is well documented; proven ways to blunt it are not.

cards.headline: Monnier 2013: the dawn phenomenon's median size was 16.0 mg/dL (≈0.9 mmol/L), it added about 0.39% to HbA1c — and no oral drug class eliminated it
cards.summary: Monnier 2013: the dawn phenomenon's median size was 16.0 mg/dL (≈0.9 mmol/L), it added about 0.39% to HbA1c — and no oral drug class eliminated it
cards.type: Observational continuous-glucose-monitoring study of dawn phenomenon magnitude and HbA1c impact (Monnier 2013)
cards.people: 248 patients with type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin, assessed by continuous glucose monitoring: 53 managed by diet alone, 82 on insulin sensitisers (metformin and/or thiazolidinediones), and 113 on insulin secretagogues alone or combined with sensitisers.
cards.result: The median dawn increment (rise from the nocturnal glucose nadir to the pre-breakfast value) was 16.0 mg/dL (≈0.9 mmol/L), with an interquartile range of 0–31.5 mg/dL (≈0–1.8 mmol/L), and did not differ significantly between treatment groups. The phenomenon's mean impact was 4.3 ± 1.3 mmol/mol (0.39 ± 0.12%) on HbA1c and 12.4 ± 2.4 mg/dL (≈0.7 mmol/L) on 24-hour mean glucose. The authors concluded that the dawn phenomenon has a real but modest impact of about 0.4% on HbA1c, is of genuine concern for overall glucose exposure, and is not eliminated by any of the currently available oral agent classes.
cards.watchOut: An observational measurement study, not an intervention trial — it sizes the problem rather than solving it. The increment is measured from the overnight low point, which fingerstick pairs (bedtime and waking) do not capture: a bedtime reading of 94 mg/dL (≈5.2 mmol/L) is not the nadir, so the bedtime-to-morning gap overstates the dawn increment as these studies define it. Patients were not on insulin, so nothing here speaks to insulin timing.
cards.source: Monnier L, Colette C, Dejager S, Owens D. Magnitude of the dawn phenomenon and its impact on the overall glucose exposure in type 2 diabetes: is this of concern? Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 24170753. Registry ID: none in the record (observational continuous-glucose-monitoring study). cards.headline: Monnier 2012: the dawn rise was 18.0–22.0 mg/dL (≈1.0–1.2 mmol/L) in every age group and present in 52–70% of patients — it does not fade with age
cards.summary: Monnier 2012: the dawn rise was 18.0–22.0 mg/dL (≈1.0–1.2 mmol/L) in every age group and present in 52–70% of patients — it does not fade with age
cards.type: Observational continuous-glucose-monitoring study of dawn phenomenon frequency and severity by age (Monnier 2012)
cards.people: 81 patients with type 2 diabetes not using insulin, in three age groups of 27 (70 years and over, 60–69 years, and 59 years and under), matched for HbA1c and assessed by ambulatory continuous glucose monitoring.
cards.result: The dawn glucose increment was 22.0 ± 4.7 mg/dL (≈1.2 mmol/L) in patients aged 70 and over, 21.3 ± 3.6 mg/dL (≈1.2 mmol/L) at 60–69 years, and 18.0 ± 3.6 mg/dL (≈1.0 mmol/L) at 59 years and under — slightly but significantly higher in the oldest group. The prevalence of the phenomenon (an increment over 10 mg/dL, ≈0.6 mmol/L) was 52%, 70% and 59% in the three groups respectively. Most people with type 2 diabetes have a measurable dawn rise, of roughly 20 mg/dL (≈1.1 mmol/L), at every age.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (27 per age band) from a single research programme, in patients selected for stable HbA1c-matched comparison — prevalence figures describe clinic patients like these, not everyone with type 2 diabetes. Like its companion study, it measures the phenomenon; it tests no remedy, and its increments are again nadir-to-breakfast, not bedtime-to-breakfast.
cards.source: Monnier L, Colette C, Sardinoux M, Baptista G, Regnier-Zerbib A, Owens D. Frequency and severity of the dawn phenomenon in type 2 diabetes: relationship to age. Diabetes Care. 2012. PMID: 22991448. Registry ID: none in the record (observational continuous-glucose-monitoring study). cards.headline: Wang 2021: adding acarbose to metformin blunted the dawn rise (35.9 to 28.3 mg/dL; ≈2.0 to ≈1.6 mmol/L) while glibenclamide did not — one small post-hoc analysis, n=50 printed on the face
cards.summary: Wang 2021: adding acarbose to metformin blunted the dawn rise (35.9 to 28.3 mg/dL; ≈2.0 to ≈1.6 mmol/L) while glibenclamide did not — one small post-hoc analysis, n=50 printed on the face
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a randomised add-on therapy trial, n=50 (Wang 2021)
cards.people: 50 patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin monotherapy (mean age 53.5 ± 8.2 years, HbA1c 8.4 ± 1.2%), randomised in the parent trial to add-on acarbose (n=27) or glibenclamide (n=23) for 16 weeks, with continuous glucose monitoring; this report is a post-hoc analysis of that trial (n=50).
cards.result: The magnitude of the dawn phenomenon fell significantly only in the acarbose group: from 35.9 ± 15.7 to 28.3 ± 16.5 mg/dL (≈2.0 to ≈1.6 mmol/L; p=0.037). In the glibenclamide group it was essentially unchanged: 35.9 ± 20.6 to 34.6 ± 17.0 mg/dL (≈2.0 to ≈1.9 mmol/L; p=0.776). HbA1c improved significantly in both groups over the 16 weeks — so the dawn-specific effect and the overall glucose effect came apart: both drugs lowered average glucose, only acarbose measurably shrank the overnight rise, and even then only by about 8 mg/dL (≈0.4 mmol/L).
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and small: the dawn phenomenon was not the parent trial's primary endpoint, 50 patients split two ways leaves wide uncertainty, and a p of 0.037 on a secondary analysis is fragile. The baseline dawn magnitude in these patients (35.9 mg/dL, ≈2.0 mmol/L) was larger than in the Monnier cohorts — these were patients with HbA1c 8.4% on metformin alone, not a general type 2 population. This card shows a drug can blunt the rise modestly; it does not establish acarbose as a dawn-phenomenon treatment.
cards.source: Wang JS et al. The dawn phenomenon in type 2 diabetes: its association with glucose excursions and changes after oral glucose-lowering drugs. Therapeutic Advances in Chronic Disease. 2021. PMID: 34394904. Registry ID: NCT00417729. MeSH: not captured from the record this session
