cards.headline: Synthesis: the dawn rise is typically ~16–22 mg/dL (≈0.9–1.2 mmol/L) and worth ~0.4% of HbA1c — a 71 mg/dL (≈3.9 mmol/L) bedtime-to-morning gap is far bigger, and proven blunting strategies are lacking
cards.summary: Synthesis: the dawn rise is typically ~16–22 mg/dL (≈0.9–1.2 mmol/L) and worth ~0.4% of HbA1c — a 71 mg/dL (≈3.9 mmol/L) bedtime-to-morning gap is far bigger, and proven blunting strategies are lacking
cards.people: The fetched record: two observational continuous-glucose-monitoring cohorts from one research programme (Monnier 2013 — 248 patients; Monnier 2012 — 81 patients) and one small post-hoc trial analysis (Wang 2021 — 50 patients). No fetched record tested a bedtime snack, insulin timing or type, or any intervention with the dawn phenomenon as its primary endpoint.
cards.result: Size: median dawn increment 16.0 mg/dL (≈0.9 mmol/L) (Monnier 2013) and age-group means of 18.0–22.0 mg/dL (≈1.0–1.2 mmol/L) with prevalence 52–70% (Monnier 2012). Cost: about 0.39% of HbA1c and 12.4 mg/dL (≈0.7 mmol/L) of 24-hour mean glucose (Monnier 2013). Remedies: no oral agent class eliminated the phenomenon (Monnier 2013); acarbose blunted it by about 8 mg/dL (≈0.4 mmol/L) in one small post-hoc analysis while glibenclamide did not (Wang 2021). Applied to the question: the bedtime-to-morning difference of 71 mg/dL (≈3.9 mmol/L) is three to four times the typical measured dawn increment — and bedtime is not the overnight nadir these studies measure from — so the classic dawn phenomenon alone probably does not explain a rise of this size; waning medication effect, evening food, or an unusually strong dawn response would each need separate assessment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the phenomenon is well measured but barely treatable on current evidence; the practical yield of this shelf is calibration — know the expected size (~20 mg/dL, ≈1.1 mmol/L), and investigate gaps much larger than that rather than chasing the dawn effect itself.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. The stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) because the treatment half of the question rests on a single small post-hoc analysis, and the measurement half comes from one research group's cohorts of non-insulin-treated patients. Nothing on this shelf addresses insulin-treated diabetes (where basal insulin timing and type are the usual levers), type 1 diabetes, or the Somogyi effect; a bedtime-snack literature exists but no cardable record for it was fetched this session, so no claim — for or against — is made.
cards.source: Synthesis of Monnier L et al. Diabetes Care. 2013 (PMID: 24170753); Monnier L et al. Diabetes Care. 2012 (PMID: 22991448); Wang JS et al. Therapeutic Advances in Chronic Disease. 2021 (PMID: 34394904).

shelves.title: Insulin-only bionic pancreas (iLet) in type 1 diabetes: one pivotal programme (NCT04200313) — HbA1c fell 0.5 percentage points and time in range rose 12–14% versus standard care with CGM over 13 weeks, with no increase in measured hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In type 1 diabetes, does the insulin-only bionic pancreas (iLet) improve HbA1c and time in range versus standard care with CGM?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Bionics · Blood Glucose · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Insulin Aspart · Insulin Infusion Systems · Insulin Lispro · Middle Aged · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme (the Insulin-Only Bionic Pancreas Pivotal Trial, NCT04200313), so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite consistent results. In the 13-week randomised trial (326 participants aged 6–79), HbA1c fell from 7.9% to 7.3% on the bionic pancreas and was unchanged at 7.7% on standard care with CGM (adjusted difference −0.5 percentage points), with time below 54 mg/dL non-inferior and no diabetic ketoacidosis in either group (Russell 2022, PMID: 36170500). The adult fast-acting-insulin-aspart report of the same programme found the same −0.5% HbA1c difference and 14% more time in range (3.4 h/day) versus standard care (Beck 2022, PMID: 36173235), and the single-arm extension, in which the former standard-care group crossed to the device, reproduced the improvement (HbA1c 7.7% to 7.1%; time in range 53% to 65%; Lynch 2022, PMID: 36173238). Severe hypoglycaemia rates did not differ significantly. The youth-specific pivotal report of this programme is homed at live shelf #561 (closed-loop umbrella) and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.

cards.headline: Russell 2022 (NEJM pivotal trial): the insulin-only bionic pancreas cut HbA1c by 0.5 percentage points versus standard care with CGM at 13 weeks (7.9%→7.3% vs 7.7%→7.7%), with hypoglycaemia time non-inferior
cards.summary: Russell 2022 (NEJM pivotal trial): the insulin-only bionic pancreas cut HbA1c by 0.5 percentage points versus standard care with CGM at 13 weeks (7.9%→7.3% vs 7.7%→7.7%), with hypoglycaemia time non-inferior
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial — iLet pivotal programme (Russell 2022)
cards.people: 326 participants aged 6 to 79 years with type 1 diabetes, randomised 2:1 to the insulin-only bionic pancreas (iLet) with insulin aspart or lispro (n = 219) or standard care — any insulin-delivery method with unblinded real-time CGM (n = 107) — for 13 weeks at multiple centres; the device is initialised on body weight alone, with meal announcements but no carbohydrate counting.
cards.result: Glycated haemoglobin fell from 7.9% to 7.3% in the bionic-pancreas group and did not change (7.7% at both time points) in the standard-care group (mean adjusted difference −0.5 percentage points; 95% CI −0.6 to −0.3; P < 0.001). Time with glucose below 54 mg/dL did not differ significantly (adjusted difference 0.0 percentage points; 95% CI −0.1 to 0.04; P < 0.001 for non-inferiority against a 1-percentage-point limit). Severe hypoglycaemia rates were 17.7 versus 10.8 events per 100 participant-years (P = 0.39), and no diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in either group. Time in range is not reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen weeks only, and the comparator already included real-time CGM for everyone — the gain is over monitored standard care, but durability, and performance outside a trial with device support, are not shown here.
cards.source: Russell SJ et al. Multicenter, Randomized Trial of a Bionic Pancreas in Type 1 Diabetes. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36170500. Registry ID: NCT04200313. cards.headline: Beck 2022: in 275 adults, the bionic pancreas with fast-acting insulin aspart matched the HbA1c gain (−0.5%) and added 14% time in range (3.4 h/day) versus standard care — but was no better than the device running standard aspart/lispro
cards.summary: Beck 2022: in 275 adults, the bionic pancreas with fast-acting insulin aspart matched the HbA1c gain (−0.5%) and added 14% time in range (3.4 h/day) versus standard care — but was no better than the device running standard aspart/lispro
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial — iLet pivotal programme, adult aspart report (Beck 2022)
cards.people: 275 adults with type 1 diabetes (18–83 years, baseline HbA1c 5.3%–14.9%), randomised 2:2:1 to the bionic pancreas with fast-acting insulin aspart (n = 114), the bionic pancreas with aspart or lispro (n = 107), or standard care plus real-time CGM (n = 54), for 13 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell from 7.8% to 7.1% with fast-acting aspart in the device versus 7.6% to 7.5% with standard care (adjusted difference −0.5%; 95% CI −0.7 to −0.3; P < 0.001). Time in range 70–180 mg/dL increased by 14% (3.4 h/day) and mean CGM glucose fell by 18 mg/dL versus standard care (P < 0.001), with time below 54 mg/dL non-inferior. Against the device using standard aspart/lispro there was no HbA1c difference (adjusted difference −0.0%; 95% CI −0.2 to 0.1). Severe hypoglycaemia rates did not differ among the three groups.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same pivotal programme (same registry number), not an independent replication — and its internal comparison shows the faster insulin added nothing, so the benefit belongs to the device algorithm, not the insulin choice.

cards.headline: Lynch 2022 (extension): when 90 former standard-care participants crossed to the bionic pancreas for 13 weeks, HbA1c fell 7.7%→7.1% and time in range rose 53%→65% — the same size of gain as the randomised phase
cards.summary: Lynch 2022 (extension): when 90 former standard-care participants crossed to the bionic pancreas for 13 weeks, HbA1c fell 7.7%→7.1% and time in range rose 53%→65% — the same size of gain as the randomised phase
cards.type: Single-arm extension study — iLet pivotal programme (Lynch 2022)
cards.people: 90 adults and children (age 6–71 years; 42 adults, 48 paediatric participants) from the pivotal trial's standard-care arm who, after completing the randomised phase, used the insulin-only bionic pancreas (iLet) for 13 weeks in a single-arm extension.
cards.result: On the device, mean HbA1c fell from 7.7% to 7.1% (mean change −0.55%; P < 0.001), time in range 70–180 mg/dL rose from 53% to 65% (+12.0%; P < 0.001), and mean glucose fell from 182 to 164 mg/dL (−18 mg/dL; P < 0.001); gains were larger at higher baseline HbA1c and similar in adults and children. Time below 70 mg/dL fell by 0.50% (P = 0.02) and time below 54 mg/dL was unchanged. Two severe hypoglycaemia events (in the same participant) and one diabetic ketoacidosis event occurred.
cards.watchOut: No concurrent control group: everyone knew they were on the new device, and only 90 of 107 standard-care participants took part — expectation and selection effects can inflate a before–after gain, which is why this card supports, but cannot substitute for, the randomised result.

cards.summary: Synthesis: within one pivotal programme, the iLet bionic pancreas reproducibly improved HbA1c by about half a percentage point and time in range by 12–14% over 13 weeks versus CGM-supported standard care, without more measured hypoglycaemia
cards.people: The carded evidence is one trial programme (NCT04200313): the 326-participant randomised trial, its 275-adult fast-acting-aspart randomised report, and its 90-participant single-arm extension. The programme's youth-specific report is homed at live shelf #561 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: HbA1c: −0.5 percentage points versus standard care in both randomised reports (Russell 2022; Beck 2022), and −0.55% after crossover in the extension (Lynch 2022). Time in range: +14% (3.4 h/day) versus standard care in adults (Beck 2022) and +12% on crossover (Lynch 2022); the NEJM record does not report time in range. Time below 54 mg/dL was non-inferior in both randomised reports, severe hypoglycaemia did not differ significantly, and diabetic ketoacidosis was absent in the randomised phase but occurred once in the extension. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single trial programme.
cards.watchOut: Every card shares one registry number and one sponsor programme: consistency across its own reports is not independent confirmation, and 13 weeks says nothing about years of real-world device use.

shelves.title: Aspirin in pregestational diabetes to prevent preeclampsia: unproven — the dedicated IRELAnD trial (134 women, 150 mg from the first trimester) found no difference in placental-dysfunction outcomes, and the pooled diabetes-specific estimate is non-significant
shelves.question: In pregestational diabetes, does low-dose aspirin started in pregnancy prevent preterm preeclampsia versus placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Humans · Aspirin · Pregnancy · Female · Double-Blind Method · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Adult · Pregnancy in Diabetics · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Pre-Eclampsia · Ireland · Premature Birth · Pregnancy Outcome · Infant, Newborn · Fetal Growth Retardation · Insulin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — the diabetes-specific evidence does not demonstrate prevention, and the record for the one dedicated trial does not report preterm preeclampsia separately. The IRELAnD randomised trial (134 women with pregestational diabetes; aspirin 150 mg from 11–14 weeks to 36 weeks versus placebo) found no difference in its composite of placental dysfunction — 25% on aspirin versus 21% on placebo (P = .796; the treatment made no difference) — in a trial stopped far short of its planned 566 participants (Finnegan 2024, PMID: 38461094). The diabetes-specific systematic review found an individual-patient meta-analysis of 930 women with diabetes gave a non-significant odds ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.20–1.71) for preeclampsia (Zen 2022, PMID: 34806161), and a secondary analysis of the older Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units high-risk trial — which included insulin-treated pregestational diabetes among its risk groups, at 60 mg — found no preeclampsia reduction in any subgroup, with diabetes-specific results not reported separately (Tolcher 2020, PMID: 33345910). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven — underpowered and null so far; a larger diabetes-specific trial is still needed.

cards.headline: Finnegan 2024 (IRELAnD): aspirin 150 mg from the first trimester did not reduce placental-dysfunction outcomes in pregestational diabetes — composite 25% vs 21% on placebo (P = .796) — in a trial that enrolled 134 of a planned 566 women
cards.summary: Finnegan 2024 (IRELAnD): aspirin 150 mg from the first trimester did not reduce placental-dysfunction outcomes in pregestational diabetes — composite 25% vs 21% on placebo (P = .796) — in a trial that enrolled 134 of a planned 566 women
cards.people: 134 women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes of at least 6 months' duration (67 aspirin, 67 placebo) at 6 Irish university perinatology centres; women with chronic hypertension or nephropathy were excluded. Aspirin 150 mg daily or placebo ran from 11–14 weeks' gestation until 36 weeks; 101 participants (80%) had type 1 and 25 (20%) type 2 diabetes as printed in the record, compliance was 97% versus 94%, and retrospective power was 64% after COVID-19 limited recruitment.
cards.result: The primary composite of placental dysfunction (preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth before 34 weeks, or perinatal mortality) did not differ between groups: 25% on aspirin versus 21% on placebo (P = .796) — the treatment made no difference to the composite. The record does not report preeclampsia, or preterm preeclampsia, as a separate outcome. Insulin requirements rose less on aspirin (average within-patient increase 83% versus 181% by 36 weeks; P = .002), and serial HbA1c was lower on aspirin without reaching significance.
cards.watchOut: Severely underpowered for its own question: 134 women against a planned 566, and the highest-risk women (chronic hypertension, nephropathy) were excluded — a null here does not exclude a real effect in the women clinicians most worry about.
cards.source: Finnegan C et al. The IRELAnD study-investigating the role of early low-dose aspirin in diabetes mellitus: a double-blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized trial. American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM. 2024. PMID: 38461094. Registry ID: NCT03574909. cards.headline: Zen 2022: in women with pre-existing diabetes, the pooled randomised evidence for aspirin was a non-significant odds ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.20–1.71) for preeclampsia — 930 women, too little data to meta-analyse the trials properly
cards.summary: Zen 2022: in women with pre-existing diabetes, the pooled randomised evidence for aspirin was a non-significant odds ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.20–1.71) for preeclampsia — 930 women, too little data to meta-analyse the trials properly
cards.people: Systematic review (searched to February 2021) of randomised trials of aspirin versus placebo for preeclampsia prophylaxis: 40 trials identified, 11 including a confirmed subset of women with diabetes; the quantitative result comes from an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 930 women with diabetes plus unpublished data from one trial.
cards.result: The individual-patient meta-analysis showed a non-significant difference in preeclampsia between aspirin and placebo in women with diabetes (odds ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.20–1.71; P = 0.33). Data from the 11 diabetes-including trials were insufficient for a conventional meta-analysis. The authors conclude any risk reduction in women with pre-existing diabetes may be similar to that in women without diabetes, but the randomised data are insufficient and further studies in this high-risk group are warranted.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.20–1.71) spans everything from a large benefit to harm: 'non-significant' here means uninformative, not disproven — and the pooled trials used varying, mostly lower, aspirin doses and later starts than modern practice.
cards.source: Zen M et al. Aspirin for the prevention of pre-eclampsia in women with pre-existing diabetes: Systematic review. cards.headline: Tolcher 2020: in the older high-risk aspirin trial (2,539 women, including insulin-treated pregestational diabetes, 60 mg aspirin), no ethnic subgroup showed a preeclampsia reduction — and diabetes-specific results were not reported separately
cards.summary: Tolcher 2020: in the older high-risk aspirin trial (2,539 women, including insulin-treated pregestational diabetes, 60 mg aspirin), no ethnic subgroup showed a preeclampsia reduction — and diabetes-specific results were not reported separately
cards.type: Secondary analysis of two randomised controlled trials (Tolcher 2020)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of two Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network randomised trials of 60 mg aspirin versus placebo started at 13–26 weeks: a low-risk trial (3,135 normotensive nulliparous women) and a high-risk trial (2,539 women with pregestational insulin-treated diabetes, chronic hypertension, multiple gestation, or previous preeclampsia).
cards.result: In the high-risk trial, stratifying by ethnicity and race revealed no decreased incidence of preeclampsia for any subgroup (all P > .05), and no significant differences in preterm delivery, placental abruption, small-for-gestational-age, stillbirth, or neonatal death; the record does not report the diabetes subgroup's results separately. In the low-risk trial, preeclampsia was reduced only in non-Hispanic white women (relative risk 0.19; 95% CI 0.06–0.63), while placental abruption was increased overall on aspirin (P = .025) and stillbirth was increased in non-Hispanic black women on aspirin (P = .048).
cards.watchOut: Diabetes is bundled with three other high-risk conditions and never separated in this record, and the dose was 60 mg started as late as 26 weeks — this card bounds what the older evidence shows; it cannot answer the modern 150 mg first-trimester question.
cards.source: Tolcher MC et al. Low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention: efficacy by ethnicity and race. American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM. 2020. PMID: 33345910. cards.headline: Synthesis: for pregestational diabetes specifically, aspirin prophylaxis remains unproven — the one dedicated trial was null and underpowered, the pooled diabetes data are non-significant, and preterm preeclampsia is not separately reported
cards.summary: Synthesis: for pregestational diabetes specifically, aspirin prophylaxis remains unproven — the one dedicated trial was null and underpowered, the pooled diabetes data are non-significant, and preterm preeclampsia is not separately reported
cards.people: The carded evidence: one dedicated double-blind randomised trial in pregestational diabetes (134 women), one diabetes-specific systematic review with individual-patient data (930 women), and one secondary analysis of older trials in which diabetes was one of several high-risk entry conditions (2,539 high-risk women).
cards.result: IRELAnD found no difference in its placental-dysfunction composite (25% vs 21%; the treatment made no difference) and does not report preeclampsia or preterm preeclampsia separately (Finnegan 2024). The diabetes-specific pooled estimate was OR 0.58 with a confidence interval crossing both benefit and harm (Zen 2022). The older high-risk trial showed no subgroup benefit at 60 mg (Tolcher 2020). None of this proves aspirin does not work in pregestational diabetes — the trials are too small and, in IRELAnD, excluded the highest-risk women — but prevention is not demonstrated by the evidence carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) unproven.
cards.watchOut: Absence of demonstrated benefit is not demonstrated absence of benefit: guideline recommendations for aspirin in pregestational diabetes rest largely on extrapolation from non-diabetes high-risk trials, which are homed elsewhere and not carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Finnegan C et al. American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM. 2024 (PMID: 38461094); Zen M et al. shelves.title: Diabetic foot ulcers — non-removable beats removable: a walker made irremovable healed 80% versus 74% for a total contact cast (41 patients), and syntheses favour non-removable offloading (pooled RR 1.43; OR 2.64 in randomised trials), though one synthesis found the removable-walker contrast alone non-significant
shelves.question: In diabetic foot ulcers, does a non-removable total contact cast heal ulcers faster than a removable cast walker?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Adult · Aged · Casts, Surgical · Diabetic Foot/therapy · Diabetic Neuropathies/therapy · Equipment Design · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Perception · Tibial Neuropathy/therapy · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vibration · Weight-Bearing
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — making the device non-removable, not the cast brand, is what the evidence supports. The head-to-head trial of the two non-removable forms found them equivalent: in 41 patients, ulcers healed within 12 weeks in 80% on a removable walker rendered irremovable (iTCC) versus 74% on a standard total contact cast (Katz 2005, PMID: 15735187). The removable-versus-non-removable contrast is where the difference sits: a 2013 meta-analysis found non-removable devices healed more ulcers than removable devices overall (pooled RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.84), although its removable-cast-walker subgroup contrast alone was not statistically significant (Morona 2013, PMID: 23303652); a 2016 meta-analysis of 1,605 patients found improved healing with total contact casting over a removable cast walker (Elraiyah 2016, PMID: 26804369); and a 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials found total contact cast or a non-removable knee-high walker healed more ulcers than other offloading devices (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 1.43 to 4.89) (Gauna 2024, PMID: 38489054). The slate anchor trial, Armstrong 2005 (PMID: 15735186), is already carded on live shelf #291 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for a non-removable total contact cast over a removable cast walker.

cards.headline: Katz 2005: a removable walker made irremovable healed 80% of ulcers in 12 weeks versus 74% for a standard total contact cast — the two non-removable forms were equivalent, and the irremovable walker was faster to apply and cheaper
cards.summary: Katz 2005: a removable walker made irremovable healed 80% of ulcers in 12 weeks versus 74% for a standard total contact cast — the two non-removable forms were equivalent, and the irremovable walker was faster to apply and cheaper
cards.people: 41 consecutive diabetic patients with chronic, non-ischaemic, neuropathic plantar foot ulcers, randomised to a removable cast walker rendered irremovable by wrapping it in a single layer of fibreglass (iTCC) or to a standard total contact cast (TCC); primary outcomes were the proportion healed at 12 weeks or less, healing rates, complications, cast placement/removal times and costs.
cards.result: Ulcers healed within 12 weeks in 80% of the iTCC group and 74% of the TCC group (94% and 93% respectively when patients lost to follow-up were excluded). Survival analysis of healing rates was statistically equivalent in the two groups, as were complication rates, with a trend toward benefit in the iTCC group. The iTCC took significantly less time to place and remove (39% and 36% reductions) and cost less overall. The authors conclude the iTCC may be equally efficacious, faster to place, easier to use and less expensive than the TCC.
cards.watchOut: A small single trial (N = 41) comparing two non-removable devices — it shows the irremovable form is what matters, but it does not itself compare either device against a walker the patient can take off.
cards.source: Katz IA et al. A randomized trial of two irremovable off-loading devices in the management of plantar neuropathic diabetic foot ulcers. Diabetes Care. 2005. PMID: 15735187. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Morona 2013: non-removable offloading healed more ulcers than removable devices overall (pooled RR 1.43) — but against removable cast walkers specifically, the advantage was not statistically significant
cards.summary: Morona 2013: non-removable offloading healed more ulcers than removable devices overall (pooled RR 1.43) — but against removable cast walkers specifically, the advantage was not statistically significant
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of systematic reviews and controlled studies comparing off-loading devices for neuropathic diabetic foot ulcers, searched January 1966 to May 2012; the non-removable versus removable pooling included 10 studies (k = 10).
cards.result: Compared with removable devices, non-removable off-loading devices were on average more effective at promoting healing (pooled RR 1.43; 95% CI 1.11 to 1.84; I² = 66.9%; p = 0.001; k = 10). Stratified by removable device type, no statistically significant difference was detected between non-removable devices and removable cast walkers, while non-removable devices performed better than therapeutic shoes (pooled RR 1.68; 95% CI 1.09 to 2.58; k = 6). The two non-removable types — total contact casts and instant total contact casts (a removable walker secured irremovable) — were equally effective (pooled RR 1.06; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.27; k = 2). The authors attribute the non-removable advantage to facilitated patient compliance with off-loading.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 66.9%) and the contrast that matters most for this shelf's question — non-removable versus removable cast walkers — did not reach significance in this pooling, so the headline RR 1.43 is driven partly by comparisons against shoes and other removable devices.
cards.source: Morona JK et al. cards.headline: Elraiyah 2016: across 19 studies and 1,605 patients, total contact casting improved healing over a removable cast walker, therapeutic shoes and conventional therapy — on evidence the authors rate as low quality
cards.summary: Elraiyah 2016: across 19 studies and 1,605 patients, total contact casting improved healing over a removable cast walker, therapeutic shoes and conventional therapy — on evidence the authors rate as low quality
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 interventional studies (13 randomised controlled trials) including data from 1,605 patients with diabetic foot ulcers using an off-loading method, searched through October 2011; predefined outcomes were complete wound healing, time to healing, amputation, infection and relapse.
cards.result: The analysis demonstrated improved wound healing with total contact casting over removable cast walker, therapeutic shoes and conventional therapy, and no advantage of irremovable cast walkers over total contact casting. A half-shoe improved healing compared with conventional wound care, and therapeutic shoes and insoles reduced relapse rate compared with regular footwear. Data were sparse for other off-loading methods, the risk of bias in included studies was moderate, and the authors state the benefits rest on low-quality evidence warranting lower certainty. The record reports no pooled effect size for the total-contact-cast versus removable-walker contrast.
cards.watchOut: No pooled effect size for the key contrast appears in the record, and the authors themselves grade the underlying evidence as low quality — direction is consistent with the other syntheses, precision is not available from this record.
cards.source: Elraiyah T et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of off-loading methods for diabetic foot ulcers. Journal of Vascular Surgery. 2016. PMID: 26804369. cards.headline: Gauna 2024: in a meta-analysis of randomised trials, total contact cast or a non-removable knee-high walker healed more ulcers than other offloading devices (OR 2.64)
cards.summary: Gauna 2024: in a meta-analysis of randomised trials, total contact cast or a non-removable knee-high walker healed more ulcers than other offloading devices (OR 2.64)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled studies of duration over 12 weeks in patients with diabetes and non-infected neuropathic foot ulcer, comparing offloading devices against no device or conventional footwear, removable versus non-removable devices, and surgical versus device offloading; 184 studies were identified and 18 were eligible; the primary endpoint was ulcer healing.
cards.result: Any plantar offloading, compared with no offloading device, was associated with higher ulcer healing (MH-OR 3.13; 95% CI 1.08 to 9.11; p = 0.04; I² = 0%). Total contact cast or a non-removable knee-high walker, compared with other offloading devices, had a higher ulcer healing rate (MH-OR 2.64; 95% CI 1.43 to 4.89; p = 0.002; I² = 51%). Surgical offloading for active ulcers combined with post-surgery offloading achieved a higher healing rate than offloading devices alone (MH-OR 6.77; 95% CI 1.64 to 27.93). The authors conclude a total contact cast or non-removable knee-high walker is preferable, while calling for larger studies with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The 'other offloading devices' comparator mixes removable walkers, shoes and lesser devices, so OR 2.64 is not a pure total-contact-cast versus removable-walker estimate; heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 51%).
cards.source: Gauna C et al. Offloading systems for the treatment of neuropathic foot ulcers in patients with diabetes mellitus: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials for the development of the Italian guidelines for the treatment of diabetic foot syndrome. Acta Diabetologica. 2024. PMID: 38489054. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: non-removable offloading heals more diabetic foot ulcers than removable devices in most syntheses — the advantage tracks with the device staying on, not with the total contact cast itself
cards.summary: Synthesis: non-removable offloading heals more diabetic foot ulcers than removable devices in most syntheses — the advantage tracks with the device staying on, not with the total contact cast itself
cards.people: The carded evidence: one head-to-head randomised trial of two non-removable devices (41 patients) and three systematic reviews/meta-analyses (10-study pooling; 19 studies, 1,605 patients; 18 randomised trials). The slate anchor trial (Armstrong 2005, PMID: 15735186) is not carded here — it is homed on live shelf #291 and cross-pointed.
cards.result: A removable walker rendered irremovable healed ulcers as well as a standard total contact cast (80% versus 74% healed within 12 weeks; Katz 2005). Non-removable devices beat removable devices overall (pooled RR 1.43; Morona 2013) and a total contact cast or non-removable walker beat other devices in randomised trials (OR 2.64; Gauna 2024), with total contact casting also favoured over a removable cast walker by Elraiyah 2016 — though Morona's removable-cast-walker subgroup contrast alone was not statistically significant, and Elraiyah graded the evidence low quality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for a non-removable total contact cast over a removable cast walker.
cards.watchOut: Every synthesis pools overlapping trials, including the Armstrong 2005 trial homed on live shelf #291 — the syntheses are carded here as distinct publications answering this narrower head-to-head question, but their trial bases are not independent of one another.
cards.source: Synthesis of Katz IA et al. Diabetes Care. 2005 (PMID: 15735187); Morona JK et al. Diabetes/Metabolism Research and Reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23303652); Elraiyah T et al. Journal of Vascular Surgery. 2016 (PMID: 26804369); Gauna C et al. Acta Diabetologica. 2024 (PMID: 38489054).

shelves.title: Erythromycin for diabetic gastroparesis flares (weak evidence for symptoms): gastric emptying normalises acutely, but only 43% of patients reported symptom improvement in the small trials reviewed
shelves.question: Is erythromycin effective for acute gastroparesis flares in adults with diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Diabetic Neuropathies · Erythromycin · Female · Gastric Emptying · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Paralysis · Stomach · Stomach Diseases
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — erythromycin reliably speeds gastric emptying in the short term, but symptom relief, which is what a flare means to the patient, is unproven in the carded evidence. Janssens 1990 (PMID: 2320062, N = 10, double-blind crossover) found intravenous erythromycin 200 mg normalised emptying: solid retention at 120 minutes was 4% ± 1% on erythromycin versus 63% ± 9% on placebo. Desautels 1995 (PMID: 7821102, N = 10, double-blind) found a single oral 250 mg dose cut solid half-emptying time from 151 ± 40 minutes on placebo to 58 ± 10 minutes. But the systematic review of oral erythromycin for symptoms (Maganti 2003, PMID: 12591038) found improvement in only 26 of 60 patients (43%) across five weak trials, none of which used symptoms as a primary endpoint, all with 13 or fewer subjects and 4 or fewer weeks of treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a potent short-term prokinetic for emptying; effectiveness for flare symptoms rests on small, short, mostly open-label studies.

cards.headline: Janssens 1990: intravenous erythromycin normalised gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis — solid retention at 120 minutes was 4% on erythromycin versus 63% on placebo (N = 10, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Janssens 1990: intravenous erythromycin normalised gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis — solid retention at 120 minutes was 4% on erythromycin versus 63% on placebo (N = 10, printed on the face)
cards.people: 10 patients with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and gastroparesis, studied in a double-blind crossover design with a double-isotope technique: emptying of liquids and solids measured after intravenous erythromycin 200 mg or placebo on separate days; 10 healthy subjects provided reference values. Study N = 10.
cards.result: Erythromycin shortened the prolonged gastric-emptying times for both liquids and solids to normal. For solids, mean (± SE) retention 120 minutes after the meal was 63% ± 9% with placebo and 4% ± 1% with erythromycin, compared with 9% ± 3% in healthy subjects; for liquids the values were 32% ± 4%, 9% ± 3% and 4% ± 1% respectively. Gastric emptying also improved, but to a lesser degree, after 4 weeks of oral erythromycin 250 mg three times a day. The record reports emptying measures only — no symptom scores — so no symptom effect is printed here.
cards.watchOut: A preliminary study of 10 patients measuring a scan, not symptoms: normalising emptying for a test meal after an intravenous dose does not by itself prove a flare feels better or resolves faster.
cards.source: Janssens J et al. Improvement of gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis by erythromycin. Preliminary studies. N Engl J Med. 1990. PMID: 2320062. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Desautels 1995: a single oral erythromycin dose cut solid half-emptying time from 151 minutes on placebo to 58 minutes at 250 mg and 40 minutes at 1000 mg — with no dose-dependence shown (N = 10, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Desautels 1995: a single oral erythromycin dose cut solid half-emptying time from 151 minutes on placebo to 58 minutes at 250 mg and 40 minutes at 1000 mg — with no dose-dependence shown (N = 10, printed on the face)
cards.people: 10 insulin-requiring diabetic patients with gastroparesis. Gastric emptying was measured after oral erythromycin 250 mg, erythromycin 1000 mg, or placebo, given in randomised double-blind fashion 30 minutes before a radiolabelled meal (labelled beef stew and orange juice), with gamma-camera imaging for 3 hours. Study N = 10.
cards.result: Both doses of oral erythromycin significantly improved solid-phase gastric emptying: mean half-emptying time fell from 151 ± 40 minutes with placebo to 58 ± 10 minutes with 250 mg and 40 ± 9 minutes with 1000 mg. A dose-dependent relationship was not demonstrated between the two doses. The authors suggest a single 250 mg dose will significantly improve gastric emptying for most patients. The record reports emptying times only — no symptom outcomes — so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Single doses in 10 patients: this is an acute pharmacology result. It says nothing about repeated dosing over a flare, where tolerance and adverse effects decide usefulness.
cards.source: Desautels SG et al. Gastric emptying response to variable oral erythromycin dosing in diabetic gastroparesis. Dig Dis Sci. 1995. PMID: 7821102. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Maganti 2003: for symptoms — the outcome that matters in a flare — only 26 of 60 patients (43%) improved on oral erythromycin across five weak trials, and no trial used symptoms as its primary endpoint
cards.summary: Maganti 2003: for symptoms — the outcome that matters in a flare — only 26 of 60 patients (43%) improved on oral erythromycin across five weak trials, and no trial used symptoms as its primary endpoint
cards.people: Systematic review of clinical trials of erythromycin in gastroparesis identified by MEDLINE search 1966–2001: 35 trials identified, 5 met inclusion criteria (symptom assessment as an endpoint). Three evaluated diabetic or idiopathic gastroparesis; one each involved post-surgical and systemic-sclerosis gastroparesis. Sixty patients contributed to the symptom tally.
cards.result: Improvement was reported in 26 of 60 patients (43%); among the 23 subjects with individual symptom scores available, 11 (48%) improved. One open-label crossover study comparing erythromycin with metoclopramide found no difference between the agents (the treatment made no difference in that comparison). All studies were methodologically weak: four of five were open-label, every sample size was 13 subjects or fewer, and treatment duration was 4 weeks or less in all studies. The authors conclude well-designed trials of symptom relief are needed.
cards.watchOut: The review's 60 patients come from the same small early literature the other cards sample, so the tallies overlap rather than add independent patients; and uncontrolled improvement rates in gastroparesis are inflated by placebo response and natural fluctuation.
cards.source: Maganti K et al. Oral erythromycin and symptomatic relief of gastroparesis: a systematic review. Am J Gastroenterol. 2003. PMID: 12591038. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: erythromycin is a proven short-term accelerator of gastric emptying and an unproven treatment for flare symptoms — the two halves of the question have opposite evidence quality
cards.summary: Synthesis: erythromycin is a proven short-term accelerator of gastric emptying and an unproven treatment for flare symptoms — the two halves of the question have opposite evidence quality
cards.people: The carded evidence: two double-blind emptying studies of 10 patients each (intravenous and single-dose oral erythromycin) and one systematic review of symptom outcomes (60 patients across five trials). Unique-patient totals cannot be cleanly summed because the review covers the same early literature; each primary study's N = 10 is printed on its face.
cards.result: On emptying, the effects are large and immediate: solid retention 4% versus 63% at 120 minutes intravenously (Janssens 1990) and half-emptying 58 versus 151 minutes after a single 250 mg oral dose (Desautels 1995). On symptoms, 43% improved across weak, short, mostly open-label trials with no symptom-primary-endpoint study (Maganti 2003). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for effectiveness against acute flares: reasonable to expect faster emptying, not established that patients' flare symptoms improve.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is the endpoint swap the literature itself makes: nearly everything rigorous is about scintigraphy, and nearly everything about how patients feel is small and uncontrolled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Janssens J et al. N Engl J Med. 1990 (PMID: 2320062); Desautels SG et al. Dig Dis Sci. 1995 (PMID: 7821102); Maganti K et al. Am J Gastroenterol. 2003 (PMID: 12591038).

shelves.title: Screening for prediabetes and offering lifestyle intervention: the intervention delays progression (4% vs 10% at one year in pooled trials), but the screening tests miss and misclassify many people
shelves.question: Does screening for prediabetes and offering lifestyle intervention delay progression to diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glucose Tolerance Test · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Life Style · Mass Screening · Metformin · Prediabetic State · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for delaying progression in people found to have prediabetes, with a screening-accuracy caveat printed on the face. The definitive trials themselves (the Diabetes Prevention Program, PMID: 11832527, and the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study, PMID: 11333990) are already homed on live shelf #111 and are NOT re-carded here; this shelf answers the screening-framed question from the screen-and-treat evidence. Barry 2017 (PMID: 28052845), a systematic review of 49 screening-test studies and 50 intervention trials in people identified through screening, found lifestyle intervention associated with a 36% relative reduction in progression to type 2 diabetes over six months to six years, attenuating to 20% relative after the trials ended — but also found the screening tests themselves inaccurate (HbA1c sensitivity 0.49; fasting glucose sensitivity 0.25), so many people are misclassified in both directions. Glechner 2018 (PMID: 30076075), pooling 16 randomised trials, found progression of 4% versus 10% at one year (RR 0.46) and 14% versus 23% at three years (RR 0.64) with lifestyle intervention versus usual care. Roberts 2017 (PMID: 29146638) found screening-plus-intervention programmes cost-effective in modelling, though intervention-only programmes were generally more cost-effective than programmes that also included screening, and population impact on incident cases was small (0.1%–1.6% reduction). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): offering lifestyle intervention to people identified with prediabetes delays diabetes for the individual; the weakness is the screening step, not the intervention.

cards.headline: Barry 2017: in people identified through screening, lifestyle intervention was associated with a 36% relative reduction in progression to diabetes — but the screening tests themselves were inaccurate (HbA1c sensitivity 0.49, fasting glucose 0.25)
cards.summary: Barry 2017: in people identified through screening, lifestyle intervention was associated with a 36% relative reduction in progression to diabetes — but the screening tests themselves were inaccurate (HbA1c sensitivity 0.49, fasting glucose 0.25)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of screening tests and interventions (Barry 2017)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 studies of screening tests (five of them prevalence studies) and 50 intervention trials in people with pre-diabetes identified through screening; 2,874 titles were scanned and 148 papers (138 studies) reviewed in full. No language restrictions.
cards.result: HbA1c had a mean sensitivity of 0.49 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.58) and specificity of 0.79 (0.73 to 0.84) for identification of pre-diabetes against the oral glucose tolerance test; fasting plasma glucose had a mean sensitivity of 0.25 (0.19 to 0.32) and specificity of 0.94 (0.92 to 0.96), and different measures identified different subpopulations (47% of people with abnormal HbA1c had no other glycaemic abnormality). Lifestyle interventions were associated with a 36% (28% to 43%) reduction in relative risk of type 2 diabetes over six months to six years, attenuating to 20% (8% to 31%) at follow-up after the trials. The authors conclude that interventions in screen-classified pre-diabetes have some efficacy, but that as screening is inaccurate, 'screen and treat' policies alone are unlikely to have substantial impact on the diabetes epidemic.
cards.watchOut: The intervention trials pooled here are the familiar diabetes-delay trials re-framed by screening identification; the novel and cautionary finding is test inaccuracy — a positive screen is often wrong and a negative screen often falsely reassuring, which caps the population benefit of any screen-and-treat policy.
cards.source: Barry E et al. Efficacy and effectiveness of screen and treat policies in prevention of type 2 diabetes: systematic review and meta-analysis of screening tests and interventions. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2017. PMID: 28052845. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glechner 2018: pooling 16 randomised trials, lifestyle intervention cut progression to diabetes from 10% to 4% at one year (RR 0.46) and from 23% to 14% at three years (RR 0.64)
cards.summary: Glechner 2018: pooling 16 randomised trials, lifestyle intervention cut progression to diabetes from 10% to 4% at one year (RR 0.46) and from 23% to 14% at three years (RR 0.64)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Glechner 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of lifestyle intervention versus treatment as usual in people with prediabetes as defined by the American Diabetes Association (older studies used the 1985 World Health Organization definition); literature searched from January 1980 through November 2015 with an update search on April 26, 2017; certainty of evidence rated with GRADE.
cards.result: Pooled results of 16 randomised controlled trials showed that people with prediabetes who received lifestyle intervention had a lower rate of progression to type 2 diabetes after one year (4% vs. 10%, RR 0.46 [CI 0.32, 0.66]) and after three years of follow-up (14% vs. 23%, RR 0.64 [95% CI 0.53, 0.77]) — relative reductions of 54% and 36% respectively, with absolute differences of 6 and 9 percentage points. The majority of studies also showed greater weight loss in lifestyle intervention participants, with great variation between studies. Costs per quality-adjusted life-year were lower when benefits were analysed over a lifelong horizon than over only the intervention period. The authors conclude lifestyle intervention is an efficacious, safe, and cost-effective measure to reduce progression in people diagnosed with prediabetes.
cards.watchOut: These trials enrolled people already identified as having prediabetes — they prove the intervention works once people are found; they do not by themselves prove that a screening programme finds the right people, which is Barry 2017's caution on the companion card.
cards.source: Glechner A et al. Effects of lifestyle changes on adults with prediabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Primary care diabetes. 2018. PMID: 30076075. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Roberts 2017: screening-plus-lifestyle programmes appeared cost-effective in economic models, but intervention-only programmes were generally more cost-effective than programmes that also included screening, and modelled population impact was small
cards.summary: Roberts 2017: screening-plus-lifestyle programmes appeared cost-effective in economic models, but intervention-only programmes were generally more cost-effective than programmes that also included screening, and modelled population impact was small
cards.people: Systematic review of economic evaluations of lifestyle interventions and metformin in people at high risk of developing diabetes, alone and in combination with a screening programme to identify high-risk individuals; 27 studies were included, all evaluating lifestyle interventions and 12 also evaluating metformin.
cards.result: Lifestyle programmes and metformin appeared to be cost effective in delaying diabetes in high-risk individuals (median incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of £7490/quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) and £8428/QALY, respectively), but economic estimates varied widely between studies. Intervention-only programmes were in general more cost effective than programmes that also included a screening component. The longer the period evaluated, the more cost-effective interventions appeared. Budget impact of these programmes was moderate (0.13%-0.2% of total healthcare budget), financial payoffs were delayed (by 9-14 years) and impact on incident cases of diabetes was limited (0.1%-1.6% reduction). There was insufficient evidence to say whether lifestyle programmes are more cost effective than metformin, or whether low-intensity programmes are more cost effective than the intensive programmes tested in trials.
cards.watchOut: These are modelled cost-effectiveness estimates built on heterogeneous definitions of pre-diabetes and programme intensity — they support offering the intervention, but the screening component is exactly where the added value is least clear.
cards.source: Roberts S et al. Preventing type 2 diabetes: systematic review of studies of cost-effectiveness of lifestyle programmes and metformin, with and without screening, for pre-diabetes. BMJ open. 2017. PMID: 29146638. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: lifestyle intervention offered to people identified with prediabetes delays diabetes (4% vs 10% at one year; 14% vs 23% at three years in pooled trials) — the weak link is screening accuracy, not the intervention
cards.summary: Synthesis: lifestyle intervention offered to people identified with prediabetes delays diabetes (4% vs 10% at one year; 14% vs 23% at three years in pooled trials) — the weak link is screening accuracy, not the intervention
cards.people: The carded evidence: one screen-and-treat systematic review covering 50 intervention trials and 49 screening-test studies (Barry 2017), one meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials in prediabetes (Glechner 2018), and one systematic review of 27 economic evaluations with and without screening (Roberts 2017). The underlying definitive trials (Diabetes Prevention Program, Finnish DPS, Da Qing) are homed on live shelf #111 and were not re-carded. The pooled trial populations number in the tens of thousands, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Lifestyle intervention in screen-identified pre-diabetes was associated with a 36% relative reduction in progression over six months to six years (Barry 2017) and with absolute progression rates of 4% versus 10% at one year and 14% versus 23% at three years (Glechner 2018). Screening tests are the limitation: HbA1c sensitivity 0.49 and fasting glucose sensitivity 0.25 mean many cases are missed and many positives misclassified, and economic modelling finds the screening component adds cost without clear added value over intervening in already-identified high-risk people (Roberts 2017). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for delaying progression in identified prediabetes, with the screening-accuracy caveat on the face.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as proof that population screening programmes reduce diabetes incidence at scale: the carded reviews themselves put the modelled population impact at 0.1%-1.6% of incident cases, because the tests misclassify so many people.
cards.source: Synthesis of Barry E et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2017 (PMID: 28052845); Glechner A et al. Primary care diabetes. 2018 (PMID: 30076075); Roberts S et al. BMJ open. 2017 (PMID: 29146638).

shelves.title: Relaxing the A1C target in frail older adults (SPLIT): tighter targets cause severe hypoglycaemia in trials, but the A1C number itself does not predict hypoglycaemia in older adults — the drug regimen does, and the head-to-head target trial has not been done
shelves.question: In older adults with type 2 diabetes and frailty, does relaxing the A1C target to below 8.5% reduce hypoglycemia versus a target below 7.5%?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cause of Death · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hyperglycemia · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT (trial evidence: tighter targets cause more severe hypoglycaemia; older-adult evidence: the A1C number itself does not predict hypoglycaemia — drug burden does) — and the direct trial this question names does not exist in the records fetched: no study randomised frail older adults to an A1C target under 8.5% versus under 7.5% and counted hypoglycaemia. What the evidence does show pulls in two directions. Randomised target trials prove the direction of harm: intensive targets more than doubled severe hypoglycaemia (relative risk 2.18, relative; Hemmingsen 2013). But in older adults themselves, hypoglycaemia duration on glucose monitoring did not differ across A1C groups from under 7% to over 9%, before or after de-intensification (Munshi 2017), and in 201,705 adults the A1C association was U-shaped and small beside regimen associations of 7- to 28-fold for sulfonylureas and insulin (McCoy 2020); modelled US data attribute roughly 9,578 hypoglycaemia hospital events over 2 years to intensive treatment, concentrated in clinically complex adults (Mahoney 2019). So relaxing the printed target without changing the prescription is unproven to reduce hypoglycaemia; the benefit, where it exists, runs through de-intensifying hypoglycaemia-causing drugs, which a relaxed target permits but does not itself accomplish. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stated above.

cards.headline: Hemmingsen 2013 (Cochrane): targeting intensive glycaemic control more than doubled severe hypoglycaemia (relative risk 2.18, relative; 28,794 participants) across 28 trials — the trial proof that tighter targets cost hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Hemmingsen 2013 (Cochrane): targeting intensive glycaemic control more than doubled severe hypoglycaemia (relative risk 2.18, relative; 28,794 participants) across 28 trials — the trial proof that tighter targets cost hypoglycaemia
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Hemmingsen 2013)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials that prespecified intensive versus conventional glycaemic-control targets in adults with type 2 diabetes: 28 trials with 34,912 participants (18,717 intensive versus 16,195 conventional); intervention duration ranged from 3 days to 12.5 years and only two trials had low risk of bias on all domains. The trials were not restricted to older or frail patients.
cards.result: Targeting intensive control significantly increased severe hypoglycaemia (relative risk 2.18 [95% CI 1.53 to 3.11], a relative measure; 28,794 participants, 12 trials), with trial sequential analysis confirming firm evidence for at least a 30% relative increase, and also increased mild hypoglycaemia (the record reports the increase as significant with substantial heterogeneity and gives no single pooled relative risk, printed here plainly) and serious adverse events (relative risk 1.06 [95% CI 1.02 to 1.10]). All-cause mortality (relative risk 1.00 [95% CI 0.92 to 1.08]) and cardiovascular mortality (relative risk 1.06 [95% CI 0.94 to 1.21]) did not differ — the treatment made no difference to mortality.
cards.watchOut: These trials compared target strategies in mostly middle-aged, non-frail populations and bundled many drug regimens: they prove direction (tighter target, more severe hypoglycaemia) but cannot price the exchange for a frail patient choosing between an A1C under 8.5% and under 7.5%.
cards.source: Hemmingsen B et al. Targeting intensive glycaemic control versus targeting conventional glycaemic control for type 2 diabetes mellitus. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 24214280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Munshi 2017: in 65 older insulin-treated adults wearing glucose monitors, hypoglycaemia duration did not differ between A1C groups — under 7%, 7.1–8%, 8.1–9% or over 9% — before or after de-intensification (N = 65, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Munshi 2017: in 65 older insulin-treated adults wearing glucose monitors, hypoglycaemia duration did not differ between A1C groups — under 7%, 7.1–8%, 8.1–9% or over 9% — before or after de-intensification (N = 65, printed on the face)
cards.people: Prospective continuous-glucose-monitoring study at a Boston centre: 65 older adults with type 2 diabetes on insulin (mean age 76 ± 6 years; on average 3.7 ± 1.3 insulin injections per day). Hypoglycaemia duration and A1C were measured at baseline on multiple daily injections and again after de-intensification to once-daily basal insulin with non-insulin agents. At baseline 26% had A1C under 7%, 42% 7.1–8%, 21% 8.1–9% and 11% over 9%.
cards.result: The duration of hypoglycaemia (below 70 mg/dL, below 60 mg/dL and below 50 mg/dL) was not different between the A1C groups, regardless of treatment intensity (multiple insulin injections or once-daily basal insulin with non-insulin agents) — the treatment target made no difference to measured hypoglycaemia in this study. The authors conclude that A1C levels are not associated with hypoglycaemia risk in the older population with type 2 diabetes on insulin therapy, and that higher A1C goals do not protect against hypoglycaemia. The record reports no effect size for the group comparisons, printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-five highly selected insulin users at one centre, with hypoglycaemia measured over monitoring windows rather than severe events over years: it can refute a simple 'higher A1C = safer' rule for insulin-treated patients, but it cannot estimate severe-hypoglycaemia rates at the two target levels this shelf compares.
cards.source: Munshi MN et al. Liberating A1C goals in older adults may not protect against the risk of hypoglycemia. Journal of diabetes and its complications. 2017. PMID: 28343792. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McCoy 2020: in 201,705 adults with diabetes, hypoglycaemia hospital care was U-shaped in A1C — raised at A1C 5.6% or below (incidence rate ratio 1.45, relative) and at 10% or above (1.24) — while insulin and sulfonylurea regimens multiplied risk 7- to 28-fold (relative)
cards.summary: McCoy 2020: in 201,705 adults with diabetes, hypoglycaemia hospital care was U-shaped in A1C — raised at A1C 5.6% or below (incidence rate ratio 1.45, relative) and at 10% or above (1.24) — while insulin and sulfonylurea regimens multiplied risk 7- to 28-fold (relative)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study of US claims and laboratory data (OptumLabs): 201,705 adults with diabetes (mean age 65.8 years; mean index HbA1c 7.2%) with an HbA1c result in 2015, followed for hypoglycaemia-related emergency-department visits and hospitalisations over the following year.
cards.result: Overall there were 9.06 (95% CI 8.64–9.47) hypoglycaemia-related emergency visits and hospitalisations per 1,000 persons per year. Against a reference HbA1c of 6.5%–6.9%, risk was increased at HbA1c 5.6% or below (incidence rate ratio 1.45 [95% CI 1.12–1.87], a relative measure) and at HbA1c 10% or above (incidence rate ratio 1.24 [95% CI 1.02–1.50]). The dominant associations were treatment and frailty markers: sulfonylurea use (incidence rate ratio 6.73), basal insulin (12.53), basal plus bolus insulin (27.65), 8 or more comorbidities (4.12), prior hypoglycaemia care (6.60) and age 75 or older (1.56) — all relative measures. The authors conclude the highest risk sits with type 1 diabetes, multiple comorbidities, prior severe hypoglycaemia and sulfonylurea and/or insulin use.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confounded by indication — low A1C in this cohort often marks intensive insulin treatment or illness rather than a chosen target — but its central message is hard to escape: within the range this shelf compares, the regimen predicts hypoglycaemia far more strongly than the A1C number does.
cards.source: McCoy RG et al. cards.headline: Mahoney 2019: modelling of US survey data estimated about 9,578 hypoglycaemia hospitalisations and emergency visits over 2 years were attributable to intensive treatment — which was just as common in clinically complex adults as in others
cards.summary: Mahoney 2019: modelling of US survey data estimated about 9,578 hypoglycaemia hospitalisations and emergency visits over 2 years were attributable to intensive treatment — which was just as common in clinically complex adults as in others
cards.people: Population-based modelling study using the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011–2014: US adults with diabetes and HbA1c under 7.0%. 'Clinically complex' meant age 75 or older, 2 or more limitations in activities of daily living, end-stage renal disease, or 3 or more chronic conditions. Intensive treatment was defined by very low achieved HbA1c on glucose-lowering medication (5.6% or below on any regimen, or 5.7%–6.4% on 2 or more drugs). Attributable events were modelled from published event-risk data.
cards.result: Almost half (48.8%, representing 10.7 million US adults) had HbA1c under 7.0%; of them 32.3% were clinically complex and 21.6% were intensively treated, with no difference in intensive treatment by clinical complexity. Over a 2-year period the authors estimated 31,511 hospitalisations and 30,954 emergency visits for hypoglycaemia in this population, of which 4,774 hospitalisations (95% CI 954–9,714) and 4,804 emergency visits (95% CI 862–9,851) were attributable to intensive treatment — about 9,578 events in total. The authors conclude patients at risk may benefit from treatment de-intensification.
cards.watchOut: Modelled, not observed: the attributable counts inherit every assumption of the published risk estimates they were built from, and 'intensive treatment' here is an achieved-A1C-plus-drugs definition, not a randomised target — it sizes the problem rather than testing the remedy.
cards.source: Mahoney GK et al. Severe Hypoglycemia Attributable to Intensive Glucose-Lowering Therapy Among US Adults With Diabetes: Population-Based Modeling Study, 2011-2014. Mayo Clinic proceedings. 2019. PMID: 31422897. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the exchange this question assumes — relax the target, buy less hypoglycaemia — is only half-supported: tighter targets demonstrably cause severe hypoglycaemia in trials, yet in older adults the A1C level itself barely predicts hypoglycaemia; the drug regimen does
cards.summary: Synthesis: the exchange this question assumes — relax the target, buy less hypoglycaemia — is only half-supported: tighter targets demonstrably cause severe hypoglycaemia in trials, yet in older adults the A1C level itself barely predicts hypoglycaemia; the drug regimen does
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane pool of 28 target trials (34,912 participants, mostly not frail or elderly-specific), a 65-person prospective glucose-monitoring study in older insulin users (N printed on its face), a 201,705-person cohort, and a national modelling study. No carded study randomised frail older adults to an A1C target under 8.5% versus under 7.5% — that direct trial does not appear in the records fetched, and the shelf says so rather than dressing indirect evidence as direct.
cards.result: Intensive targets increased severe hypoglycaemia (relative risk 2.18, relative; Hemmingsen 2013). But hypoglycaemia duration did not differ across A1C groups in older insulin users, even after de-intensification (Munshi 2017), and in the large cohort the A1C association was U-shaped and small (incidence rate ratio 1.45 at 5.6% or below, relative) beside regimen associations of 6.73–27.65 (McCoy 2020); modelled US harm concentrates in intensively treated, clinically complex adults (Mahoney 2019). PROPOSED SPLIT: relaxing the target number alone is unproven to reduce hypoglycaemia; reducing hypoglycaemia-causing drug burden is where the carded evidence points.
cards.watchOut: Clinicians reading only the trial card would over-promise what a target change buys; reading only the cohort cards would understate that target-driven intensification is how patients end up on the high-risk regimens in the first place. The two halves correct each other.

shelves.title: Phentermine-topiramate beats phentermine alone head-to-head (EQUATE): the combination lost 8.5–9.2% of body weight at 28 weeks versus 46.2% reaching 5% loss on phentermine 15 mg — one direct components trial, cross-pointed to the placebo-controlled shelf #746
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, does phentermine-topiramate produce more weight loss than phentermine alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage · Delayed-Action Preparations · Drug Combinations · Female · Fructose/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/drug therapy · Phentermine/administration & dosage · Placebos · Topiramate · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single direct head-to-head trial, printed on the face. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #746 already covers phentermine-topiramate versus placebo (the EQUIP/CONQUER programme); the uncovered slice carded here is the head-to-head against phentermine alone. Only one trial has ever randomised that comparison directly: EQUATE (Aronne 2013), a 28-week, seven-arm components trial in which both combination doses beat their respective monotherapies on percentage weight loss (P < 0.05) and on the share reaching at least 5% loss (62.1% and 66.0% for the combinations versus 43.3% and 46.2% for phentermine 7.5 mg and 15 mg). The two network meta-analyses carded here frame but do not replace that comparison: the American College of Physicians living review (Damen 2026) includes phentermine and phentermine-topiramate as separate network interventions across 69 studies and 112,511 participants yet states plainly that direct head-to-head comparisons were limited and prints no pairwise estimate for this pairing in its record; the BMJ network meta-analysis (Nong 2026; 262 trials, 99,791 participants) puts phentermine-topiramate's one-year effect versus lifestyle modification at a mean difference of −8.1% (95% CI −9.7 to −6.5), again without a printed phentermine-alone contrast. One earlier network meta-analysis considered for this shelf (Shi 2022) was NOT carded because its PubMed record is flagged as a retracted publication. The direct evidence is therefore a single 28-week trial programme, which caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): phentermine-topiramate produces more weight loss than phentermine alone, on one direct randomised components trial; longer and replicated head-to-head evidence does not exist in the records fetched this session.

cards.headline: EQUATE (Aronne 2013): the only direct head-to-head trial — phentermine-topiramate ER lost 8.5% (7.5/46 mg) and 9.2% (15/92 mg) of body weight at 28 weeks, greater than placebo (−1.7%) and greater than the respective monotherapies (P < 0.05 for the monotherapy comparisons)
cards.summary: EQUATE (Aronne 2013): the only direct head-to-head trial — phentermine-topiramate ER lost 8.5% (7.5/46 mg) and 9.2% (15/92 mg) of body weight at 28 weeks, greater than placebo (−1.7%) and greater than the respective monotherapies (P < 0.05 for the monotherapy comparisons)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — components (head-to-head) trial (Aronne 2013, EQUATE)
cards.people: Adults with obesity randomised to one of seven arms for 28 weeks: placebo, phentermine 7.5 mg, phentermine 15 mg, topiramate extended-release 46 mg, topiramate extended-release 92 mg, phentermine-topiramate ER 7.5/46 mg, or phentermine-topiramate ER 15/92 mg; all participants received lifestyle intervention counselling. The total randomised N is not stated in the record fetched this session and is printed here as not documented in the record.
cards.result: Primary endpoints were percent weight loss and achievement of at least 5% weight loss. At week 28, phentermine-topiramate ER 7.5/46 (−8.5%) and 15/92 (−9.2%) achieved greater percentage weight loss versus placebo (−1.7%; P < 0.0001) and versus their respective monotherapies (P < 0.05). The percentage achieving at least 5% weight loss was 15.5% for placebo, 43.3% for phentermine 7.5 mg, 46.2% for phentermine 15 mg, 39.2% for topiramate ER 46 mg, 48.6% for topiramate ER 92 mg, 62.1% for phentermine-topiramate ER 7.5/46, and 66.0% for phentermine-topiramate ER 15/92. The combination was generally well tolerated; formal cognitive testing showed impairment only in the attention domain.
cards.watchOut: This is one 28-week trial with seven arms, so each pairwise contrast rests on a fraction of the total sample, and the record does not print the per-arm percentage weight loss for the phentermine-alone arms — only the responder proportions and the significance of the combination-versus-monotherapy comparisons. Nothing carded here runs beyond 28 weeks for this comparison.
cards.source: Aronne LJ et al. Evaluation of phentermine and topiramate versus phentermine/topiramate extended-release in obese adults. Obesity (Silver Spring, Md.). 2013. PMID: 24136928. cards.summary: Damen 2026: the ACP living network meta-analysis includes phentermine and phentermine-topiramate as separate interventions (69 studies, 112,511 participants) — but states that direct head-to-head comparisons were limited and prints no pairwise estimate for this pairing
cards.type: Living systematic review and network meta-analysis (Damen 2026, for the American College of Physicians)
cards.people: Adults with overweight or obesity (body mass index 25 kg/m2 or above) in randomised trials of weight-management drugs, including phentermine and phentermine-topiramate among the listed interventions, with or without lifestyle intervention; 69 studies with a total of 112,511 participants, 37 at low risk of bias.
cards.result: Nearly all studied interventions were more effective than placebo and/or lifestyle intervention in reducing weight, with more discontinuations due to adverse events; semaglutide and tirzepatide led the network. For this shelf's question the operative sentence is the limitation: the authors state that direct head-to-head comparisons of different treatments were limited, and the record prints no phentermine-topiramate-versus-phentermine effect estimate — that absence is printed plainly rather than filled in.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis can rank both drugs against common comparators without any trial having compared them directly; the only direct evidence for this shelf's exact comparison remains the EQUATE card above.

cards.headline: Nong 2026 (BMJ): across 262 trials (99,791 participants), phentermine-topiramate produced a one-year mean weight difference of −8.1% versus lifestyle modification (95% CI −9.7 to −6.5) — network context, not a phentermine-alone contrast
cards.summary: Nong 2026 (BMJ): across 262 trials (99,791 participants), phentermine-topiramate produced a one-year mean weight difference of −8.1% versus lifestyle modification (95% CI −9.7 to −6.5) — network context, not a phentermine-alone contrast
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis (Nong 2026, BMJ)
cards.people: Adults with overweight or obesity in randomised trials of at least 12 weeks comparing one or more drugs with lifestyle modification, placebo, or another drug; 262 trials, 99,791 participants, 19 drugs, follow-up 12 to 172 weeks.
cards.result: Compared with lifestyle modification alone at one year, moderate-to-high certainty evidence showed phentermine-topiramate among the agents with substantial weight loss (mean difference −8.1%, 95% CI −9.7 to −6.5). Discontinuation because of adverse events was highest for a group of agents including phentermine-topiramate (risk ratios 1.9 to 4.2 across that group, as printed in the record). The record does not print a phentermine-alone arm or a direct combination-versus-phentermine estimate.
cards.watchOut: The −8.1% figure is measured against lifestyle modification, not against phentermine; quoting it as the head-to-head margin would overstate what this record shows. It is carded as corroborating context for the size of the combination's effect.
cards.source: Nong K et al. Comparative effects of drugs for adults with overweight or obesity: systematic review and network meta-analysis. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2026. PMID: 42419792. cards.summary: Synthesis: one direct trial answers the question — the combination beat phentermine alone at 28 weeks; the networks corroborate the combination's size of effect but add no second direct comparison
cards.people: The carded evidence: one seven-arm randomised components trial (EQUATE, 28 weeks; total N not documented in its record), one living network meta-analysis carrying both drugs as separate nodes (69 studies, 112,511 participants), and one BMJ network meta-analysis (262 trials, 99,791 participants).
cards.result: In EQUATE, phentermine-topiramate ER 7.5/46 and 15/92 produced −8.5% and −9.2% weight loss, significantly greater than their respective monotherapies (P < 0.05), with at least 5% weight loss in 62.1% and 66.0% versus 43.3% (phentermine 7.5 mg) and 46.2% (phentermine 15 mg). shelves.title: Naltrexone-bupropion beats placebo on top of lifestyle intervention in general obesity (COR programme): −6.4% versus −1.2% at 56 weeks in COR-II and −9.3% versus −5.1% added to intensive behaviour modification in COR-BMOD
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, does naltrexone-bupropion produce more weight loss than placebo when combined with lifestyle intervention?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3498 already covers naltrexone-bupropion in type 2 diabetes with obesity (the COR-Diabetes trial); the uncovered slice carded here is obesity generally — the rest of the COR programme, in which every participant received lifestyle intervention alongside drug or placebo. COR-II (Apovian 2013; 1,496 participants) found −6.5% versus −1.9% at week 28 and −6.4% versus −1.2% at week 56, with at least 5% weight loss in 55.6% versus 17.5% at week 28 and 50.5% versus 17.1% at week 56. COR-BMOD (Wadden 2011; 793 participants) layered the drug on intensive behaviour modification — 28 group sessions and an energy-reduced diet in both arms — and still found an added drug effect: −9.3% versus −5.1% at week 56. The pooled programme analysis (Fujioka 2016; 2,043 on drug, 1,319 on placebo across the four phase 3 trials) adds the responder rule: patients reaching at least 5% loss by week 16 went on to average 11.7% loss at week 56. The programme's first trial, COR-I (Greenway 2010), is already carded in the live library and is therefore cross-pointed here in prose rather than re-carded; its direction and size (−6.1% versus −1.3% at 56 weeks for the 32 mg dose) match the trials carded on this shelf. Nausea was the most common adverse event in every trial. Two large concordant phase 3 trials plus a pooled programme analysis support the stamp. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): naltrexone-bupropion produces more weight loss than placebo when combined with lifestyle intervention in adults with obesity.

cards.headline: COR-II (Apovian 2013): naltrexone-bupropion lost −6.4% versus −1.2% on placebo at 56 weeks in 1,496 adults with obesity or overweight with dyslipidaemia/hypertension; at least 5% loss in 50.5% versus 17.1%
cards.summary: COR-II (Apovian 2013): naltrexone-bupropion lost −6.4% versus −1.2% on placebo at 56 weeks in 1,496 adults with obesity or overweight with dyslipidaemia/hypertension; at least 5% loss in 50.5% versus 17.1%
cards.people: 1,496 participants with obesity (body mass index 30–45 kg/m2) or overweight (27–45 kg/m2 with dyslipidaemia and/or hypertension), randomised 2:1 to naltrexone sustained-release 32 mg/day plus bupropion sustained-release 360 mg/day or placebo for up to 56 weeks, in a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study.
cards.result: Weight loss was significantly greater with the combination than placebo at week 28 (−6.5% vs −1.9%; P < 0.001) and week 56 (−6.4% vs −1.2%). More combination-treated participants achieved at least 5% weight loss at week 28 (55.6% vs 17.5%; P < 0.001) and week 56 (50.5% vs 17.1%). The combination also produced greater improvements in cardiometabolic risk markers, weight-related quality of life, and control of eating. The most common adverse event was nausea, generally mild to moderate and transient; the combination was not associated with increased depression or suicidality versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: The record does not print the background lifestyle programme's content in detail, and week-56 placebo loss of only −1.2% shows the comparison is drug-plus-lifestyle against a lightly responding placebo-plus-lifestyle arm — the margin is the drug's added effect, not its effect against no care.
cards.source: Apovian CM et al. A randomized, phase 3 trial of naltrexone SR/bupropion SR on weight and obesity-related risk factors (COR-II). Obesity (Silver Spring, Md.). 2013. PMID: 23408728.
