cards.headline: COR-BMOD (Wadden 2011): added to intensive behaviour modification in both arms, naltrexone-bupropion still won — −9.3% versus −5.1% at 56 weeks in 793 participants
cards.summary: COR-BMOD (Wadden 2011): added to intensive behaviour modification in both arms, naltrexone-bupropion still won — −9.3% versus −5.1% at 56 weeks in 793 participants
cards.people: 793 participants (mean body mass index 36.5 ± 4.2 kg/m2) randomised 1:3 to placebo plus behaviour modification (n = 202) or naltrexone sustained-release 32 mg/day plus bupropion sustained-release 360 mg/day plus behaviour modification (n = 591) for 56 weeks; both groups were prescribed an energy-reduced diet and 28 group behaviour-modification sessions. Efficacy analyses used a modified intention-to-treat population (193 and 482 participants).
cards.result: At week 56, weight loss was 5.1 ± 0.6% with placebo plus behaviour modification versus 9.3 ± 0.4% with the combination plus behaviour modification (P < 0.001); a completers analysis gave 7.3 ± 0.9% versus 11.5 ± 0.6%, and an all-randomised analysis 4.9 ± 0.6 versus 7.8 ± 0.4% (both P < 0.001). Significantly more combination-treated participants lost at least 5% and at least 10% of initial weight, with greater improvements in cardiometabolic risk markers. Nausea was reported more often with the combination.
cards.watchOut: The placebo arm here lost 5.1% — far more than in COR-II — because the lifestyle intervention was intensive; the drug's added margin (about 4 percentage points) is the figure to carry, not the headline 9.3%.
cards.source: Wadden TA et al. Weight loss with naltrexone SR/bupropion SR combination therapy as an adjunct to behavior modification: the COR-BMOD trial. Obesity (Silver Spring, Md.). 2011. PMID: 20559296. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fujioka 2016 (pooled COR programme): patients reaching at least 5% weight loss by week 16 on naltrexone-bupropion went on to average 11.7% loss at week 56 — the programme's early-response rule
cards.summary: Fujioka 2016 (pooled COR programme): patients reaching at least 5% weight loss by week 16 on naltrexone-bupropion went on to average 11.7% loss at week 56 — the programme's early-response rule
cards.type: Pooled analysis of the four phase 3 COR trials (Fujioka 2016)
cards.people: Pooled modified intention-to-treat data from the four phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled, 56-week trials of naltrexone-bupropion 32/360 mg (drug n = 2,043; placebo n = 1,319); the week-56 completers population was 1,310 on drug and 763 on placebo.
cards.result: Among drug-treated participants who completed 1 year, those with at least 5% weight loss at week 16 (n = 873) had a least-squares mean weight loss of 11.7% at week 56, and 85% of them maintained at least 5% loss at week 56. The week-16 at-least-5% threshold correctly identified 80% (95% CI 78–82%) of participants who would and would not achieve at least 5% loss at week 56. Safety and tolerability were similar to the previously published trial reports.
cards.watchOut: This is an exploratory pooled analysis of response prediction, not a fifth trial: it re-uses the same programme's patients (including the COR-I and COR-Diabetes populations homed elsewhere) and its completer framing flatters the drug, since non-responders who dropped out are out of the denominator.
cards.source: Fujioka K et al. The relationship between early weight loss and weight loss at 1 year with naltrexone ER/bupropion ER combination therapy. International Journal of Obesity (2005). 2016. cards.headline: Synthesis: in general obesity, naltrexone-bupropion added roughly 4–5 percentage points of weight loss over placebo on top of lifestyle intervention, consistently across the COR programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: in general obesity, naltrexone-bupropion added roughly 4–5 percentage points of weight loss over placebo on top of lifestyle intervention, consistently across the COR programme
cards.people: The carded evidence: COR-II (1,496 randomised), COR-BMOD (793 randomised), and the pooled four-trial programme analysis (2,043 drug, 1,319 placebo, modified intention-to-treat). The COR-I trial is cross-pointed in the balance, not re-carded, and the diabetes-specific COR-Diabetes trial homes on live shelf #3498.
cards.result: COR-II: −6.4% versus −1.2% at 56 weeks, at least 5% loss in 50.5% versus 17.1%. COR-BMOD, with intensive behaviour modification in both arms: −9.3% versus −5.1%. Pooled: week-16 responders averaged 11.7% at week 56. Nausea was the most common adverse event throughout. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: All carded trials are 56 weeks, industry-programme trials with lifestyle co-intervention in both arms; the shelf answers drug-versus-placebo on top of lifestyle help, not drug versus lifestyle alone, and says nothing about weight maintenance after stopping.

shelves.title: Pasireotide in acromegaly inadequately controlled on first-generation analogs: the PAOLA trial (homed on #745) showed control in 15–20% versus 0% on continued octreotide/lanreotide; switch and real-world reports carded here put IGF-1 control at 14.6% in a single-arm switch study and 57.9% pooled in practice
shelves.question: In adults with acromegaly, is pasireotide more effective than octreotide for biochemical control in people inadequately controlled on first-generation somatostatin analogs?
shelves.mesh: Acromegaly/drug therapy · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers/blood · Blood Glucose · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Human Growth Hormone/blood · Humans · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein 2/blood · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein 3/blood · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Octreotide/therapeutic use · Peptides, Cyclic/therapeutic use · Retreatment · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #745 frames pasireotide versus octreotide in medically untreated acromegaly, and the head-to-head trial for this shelf's population — PAOLA (Gadelha 2014), whose primary record is already carded in the live library — is cross-pointed here in prose rather than re-carded. In PAOLA, 198 patients inadequately controlled after at least 6 months of high-dose octreotide or lanreotide were randomised to pasireotide 40 mg, pasireotide 60 mg, or continued first-generation treatment: biochemical control at 24 weeks was 15% and 20% versus 0% on continued treatment (absolute differences 15.4 and 20.0 percentage points), with hyperglycaemia in 33%/31% versus 14%. The free reports carded here fill out that population without re-carding PAOLA's primary record: its planned biomarker analysis (Schmid 2016) shows responders started with lower growth hormone and IGF-1 and that 47% of pasireotide-treated patients never needed antidiabetic medication; a single-arm phase IIIb switch study (Gadelha 2019; 123 patients) found full biochemical control in 14.6% at week 36 after switching; and a real-world meta-analysis (Biagetti 2025; 12 studies, 409 patients resistant to first-generation ligands) pooled IGF-1 control at 57.9% with tumour shrinkage in 33.3%, alongside worsened glucose measures. The direction is consistent — pasireotide controls some patients whom octreotide/lanreotide cannot — but the carded slice evidence is a biomarker substudy, an uncontrolled switch study, and observational practice data, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE even though the underlying randomised result is positive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Schmid 2016 (PAOLA biomarker analysis): pasireotide responders in inadequately controlled acromegaly started with lower GH (5.1 vs 7.9 ng/mL) and IGF-1 (519 vs 672 ng/mL) than non-responders; 47% of pasireotide patients never needed antidiabetic medication
cards.summary: Schmid 2016 (PAOLA biomarker analysis): pasireotide responders in inadequately controlled acromegaly started with lower GH (5.1 vs 7.9 ng/mL) and IGF-1 (519 vs 672 ng/mL) than non-responders; 47% of pasireotide patients never needed antidiabetic medication
cards.type: Randomised trial biomarker analysis — planned exploratory objective of the PAOLA study (Schmid 2016)
cards.people: Patients who completed the PAOLA study — a 24-week, phase III, randomised, three-arm trial of pasireotide long-acting release 40 mg and 60 mg versus octreotide long-acting repeatable 30 mg or lanreotide Autogel 120 mg in patients with inadequately controlled acromegaly. The biomarker-analysis population size is not stated separately in the record fetched this session.
cards.result: Responders to pasireotide (mean growth hormone under 2.5 µg/L and normal IGF-1 at 24 weeks) had lower baseline growth hormone (5.1 ng/mL) and IGF-1 (519 ng/mL) than non-responders (7.9 and 672 ng/mL). The frequency of hyperglycaemia after pasireotide was similar in responders and non-responders and depended more on baseline fasting plasma glucose. Overall, 47% of patients treated with pasireotide 40 or 60 mg did not receive antidiabetic medication at any time during the study, and the authors conclude a large subset of patients does not experience major disturbances in glucose homeostasis on pasireotide.
cards.watchOut: This is a biomarker and predictor analysis of the PAOLA population, not a second efficacy trial: it identifies who responds (lower starting GH/IGF-1) and who develops hyperglycaemia (higher starting glucose), and must not be counted as independent confirmation of PAOLA's control rates, which are cross-pointed in the balance.
cards.source: Schmid HA et al. Effect of pasireotide on glucose- and growth hormone-related biomarkers in patients with inadequately controlled acromegaly. Endocrine. 2016. PMID: 26906713. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gadelha 2019: switching 123 patients uncontrolled on maximal first-generation analogs to pasireotide gave full biochemical control in 14.6% at week 36 — with hyperglycaemia reported in 41.5%
cards.summary: Gadelha 2019: switching 123 patients uncontrolled on maximal first-generation analogs to pasireotide gave full biochemical control in 14.6% at week 36 — with hyperglycaemia reported in 41.5%
cards.people: 123 adults with uncontrolled acromegaly (mean growth hormone at least 1 µg/L and IGF-1 over 1.3 times the upper limit of normal) despite at least 3 months on maximal approved doses of long-acting octreotide or lanreotide, switched to open-label long-acting pasireotide 40 mg every 28 days (titratable to 60 mg); 88 continued into a 36-week extension.
cards.result: At week 36, 18 patients (14.6%, 95% CI 8.9–22.1) achieved the primary endpoint of mean growth hormone under 1 µg/L with IGF-1 below the upper limit of normal; control was achieved in 42.9% of patients whose screening mean growth hormone was 1.0–2.5 µg/L but only 6.4% of those above 2.5 µg/L. Among extension patients, control rates at weeks 36–72 stayed between 11.4% and 14.8%. The most frequent drug-related adverse events were hyperglycaemia (41.5%), diabetes mellitus (23.6%), and diarrhoea (11.4%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and open-label: with no continued-octreotide control group, the 14.6% cannot by itself prove superiority — its value is showing the switch yield in exactly this shelf's population, closely matching the randomised PAOLA margin cross-pointed in the balance.
cards.source: Gadelha M et al. Evaluation of the Efficacy and Safety of Switching to Pasireotide in Patients With Acromegaly Inadequately Controlled With First-Generation Somatostatin Analogs. cards.headline: Biagetti 2025: in real-world practice (12 studies, 409 patients resistant to first-generation ligands), pooled IGF-1 control on pasireotide was 57.9% and tumour shrinkage 33.3% — with glucose metabolism worsening
cards.summary: Biagetti 2025: in real-world practice (12 studies, 409 patients resistant to first-generation ligands), pooled IGF-1 control on pasireotide was 57.9% and tumour shrinkage 33.3% — with glucose metabolism worsening
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of real-world studies (Biagetti 2025)
cards.people: 409 patients with acromegaly resistant to first-generation somatostatin receptor ligands treated with pasireotide long-acting release in 12 real-world studies published 2014–2023.
cards.result: The pooled rate of IGF-1 control was 57.9% (95% CI 48.4–66.8) and 33.3% (95% CI 19.7–50.4) of patients had tumour shrinkage; growth hormone and IGF-1 levels fell significantly. Glucose metabolism worsened, as the record prints it: fasting glucose standardised mean difference −0.8 mg/dL (95% CI −1.0 to −0.5), glycated haemoglobin −0.5%, and type 2 diabetes prevalence −11.5% in the authors' signed convention for deterioration. The authors note real-world IGF-1 control (over 60% in their summary) exceeded the roughly 30% seen in clinical trials, with high heterogeneity across studies.
cards.watchOut: Real-world series select who gets switched and who stays on treatment, so the 57.9% pooled control rate is not comparable with trial rates; the record's glucose figures are printed in the authors' own signed standardised-mean-difference convention and are reproduced here as printed, with the direction (worsening) stated by the authors.
cards.source: Biagetti B et al. Real-world evidence of effectiveness and safety of pasireotide in the treatment of acromegaly: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Reviews in Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders. 2025. PMID: 39527181. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Cabergoline beats bromocriptine in prolactinoma: meta-analysis of the randomised trials favours cabergoline for prolactin normalization, and a 498-patient comparison found normalization in 87.4% versus 41.4% with tumour shrinkage of 79.8% versus 54.1%
shelves.question: In adults with prolactinoma, is cabergoline more effective than bromocriptine for normalizing prolactin and shrinking tumor?
shelves.mesh: Bromocriptine/therapeutic use · Cabergoline · Dopamine Agonists/therapeutic use · Ergolines/therapeutic use · Humans · Hyperprolactinemia/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2070 covers this comparison in women with hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea (the Webster 1994 trial population); the uncovered slice carded here is prolactinoma in adults generally, including men and macroprolactinoma, with tumour shrinkage as an outcome. The meta-analysis of the randomised trials (dos Santos Nunes 2011; four randomised trials in prolactinoma and idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia) found a significant difference in favour of cabergoline for normalization of serum prolactin (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.80, as printed in the record) and for restoration of ovulatory cycles (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.83), with more adverse effects on bromocriptine (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.98). A small randomised trial enrolling mostly prolactinoma patients (Sabuncu 2001; 34 patients, 22 with micro- or macroprolactinoma) found greater prolactin reduction on cabergoline (−93% vs −87.5%; P < 0.05) and normalization in 82% versus 59%. The largest comparison, a retrospective single-centre series (Arduc 2015; 498 patients), found prolactin normalization in 87.4% on cabergoline versus 41.4% on bromocriptine and mean tumour-volume shrinkage of 79.8% versus 54.1%, with side effects in 5.3% versus 29.1%. The randomised-trial meta-analysis pools the home shelf's Webster trial among its four trials; it is carded here as a distinct publication answering the broader prolactinoma question, and Webster's own record is not re-carded. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): cabergoline is more effective than bromocriptine for normalizing prolactin and shrinking prolactinoma, and is better tolerated.

cards.headline: dos Santos Nunes 2011: meta-analysis of the four randomised cabergoline-versus-bromocriptine trials (prolactinomas and idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia) favoured cabergoline for prolactin normalization (RR 0.67) with fewer adverse effects
cards.summary: dos Santos Nunes 2011: meta-analysis of the four randomised cabergoline-versus-bromocriptine trials (prolactinomas and idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia) favoured cabergoline for prolactin normalization (RR 0.67) with fewer adverse effects
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (dos Santos Nunes 2011)
cards.people: Patients with idiopathic hyperprolactinaemia and prolactinomas in four randomised controlled trials comparing cabergoline with bromocriptine, selected from 418 references screened; the record does not print the pooled participant total.
cards.result: The meta-analysis of normalization of serum prolactin levels showed a significant difference in favour of the cabergoline group (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.80), as did restoration of menstruation with return of ovulatory cycles (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.83). The number of adverse effects was significantly higher in the bromocriptine group than the cabergoline group (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.98). The authors conclude the meta-analysis shows new evidence favouring cabergoline over bromocriptine for the treatment of prolactinomas and idiopathic hyperprolactinemia.
cards.watchOut: Only four randomised trials survived the review's exclusions, the pooled N is not printed in the record, and the printed risk ratios are reproduced exactly as the record gives them with the authors' stated direction (in favour of cabergoline); one of the four pooled trials is the home shelf #2070 trial in hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea, so this card overlaps the home population while extending it to prolactinoma generally.

cards.headline: Sabuncu 2001 (N = 34): in patients mostly with prolactinoma, cabergoline reduced prolactin more than bromocriptine (−93% vs −87.5%) and normalized it in 82% versus 59%, with adverse events in 12% versus 53%
cards.summary: Sabuncu 2001 (N = 34): in patients mostly with prolactinoma, cabergoline reduced prolactin more than bromocriptine (−93% vs −87.5%) and normalized it in 82% versus 59%, with adverse events in 12% versus 53%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Sabuncu 2001) — small N printed on the face
cards.people: 34 hyperprolactinaemic patients treated for 12 weeks: 17 given bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily (5 mg for macroprolactinomas) — 7 microprolactinoma, 4 macroprolactinoma, 6 idiopathic — and 17 given cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly — 8 microprolactinoma, 4 macroprolactinoma, 5 idiopathic. Total N = 34, printed on the face.
cards.result: Prolactin reduction was significantly greater with cabergoline than bromocriptine (−93% vs −87.5%; P < 0.05). Normalization of prolactin was achieved in 14 of 17 cabergoline patients (82%) and 10 of 17 bromocriptine patients (59%) (P = 0.13). Among macroprolactinoma patients, normalization occurred in 3 of 4 (75%) on cabergoline and 2 of 4 (50%) on bromocriptine. Adverse events were noted in 53% of bromocriptine patients and 12% of cabergoline patients (P < 0.01). The record reports no tumour-size outcome.
cards.watchOut: A 34-patient, 12-week trial: the normalization difference (82% vs 59%) is not statistically significant at this size (P = 0.13), the macroprolactinoma subgroups are four patients per arm, and tumour shrinkage — half of this shelf's question — is not reported in this record at all.
cards.source: Sabuncu T et al. Comparison of the effects of cabergoline and bromocriptine on prolactin levels in hyperprolactinemic patients. Internal Medicine (Tokyo, Japan). 2001. PMID: 11579944. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arduc 2015: in 498 patients, prolactin normalization was 87.4% on cabergoline versus 41.4% on bromocriptine, and tumour volume shrinkage 79.8% versus 54.1%
cards.summary: Arduc 2015: in 498 patients, prolactin normalization was 87.4% on cabergoline versus 41.4% on bromocriptine, and tumour volume shrinkage 79.8% versus 54.1%
cards.people: 498 patients with hyperprolactinaemia at a single centre (mean age 33.3 years; 450 women, 48 men) treated with cabergoline (n = 450; mean dose 1.5 mg/week) or bromocriptine (n = 48; mean dose 3.8 mg/day) for a mean of about 18 months; baseline tumour volume was higher in the cabergoline group, while baseline prolactin and symptom frequencies were similar.
cards.result: The prolactin normalization rate (87.4% vs 41.4%; P = 0.029) and tumour volume shrinkage (79.8 ± 39.1% vs 54.1 ± 55.3%; P = 0.015) were significantly higher in cabergoline-treated patients, while tumour cure rates were similar. Symptom relief was higher with cabergoline, and more side effects were recorded with bromocriptine (29.1% vs 5.3%; P < 0.001). The authors conclude cabergoline was more effective for controlling symptoms, normalizing prolactin, and shrinking prolactinomas.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and severely unbalanced (450 versus 48 patients): bromocriptine patients are a small, likely selected minority (intolerance, era, or cost), so the 46-percentage-point normalization gap almost certainly overstates the true drug difference — the randomised evidence above is the anchor, and this card supplies the tumour-shrinkage outcome the trials report thinly.
cards.source: Arduc A et al. Retrospective comparison of cabergoline and bromocriptine effects in hyperprolactinemia: a single center experience. Journal of Endocrinological Investigation. 2015. cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis of four randomised trials (pooled N not documented in the record), a 34-patient randomised trial (22 with prolactinoma), and a 498-patient retrospective comparison. Total carded participants with documented N exceed 530, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the small trial's N is printed on its face.

Trial: normalization 82% versus 59%, prolactin reduction −93% versus −87.5%. Practice comparison: normalization 87.4% versus 41.4%, tumour shrinkage 79.8% versus 54.1%, side effects 5.3% versus 29.1%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tumour shrinkage rests mainly on the retrospective card; the randomised evidence is strongest for prolactin normalization and tolerability. The women-with-amenorrhoea trial population homes on live shelf #2070 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded.

shelves.title: Oral desmopressin maintains control in central diabetes insipidus after switching from intranasal (small old studies only): stable antidiuresis over 1 year on oral therapy in 10 adults, at roughly a 16–17-fold higher microgram dose
shelves.question: In adults with central diabetes insipidus, is oral desmopressin as effective as intranasal desmopressin for controlling symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Administration, Oral · Adult · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics · Diabetes Insipidus/drug therapy,metabolism · Diuresis/drug effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Osmolar Concentration · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — equivalence in practice, on small old studies, printed on the face). This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2906 covers how long desmopressin's antidiuretic action lasts by formulation and dose; the uncovered slice carded here is the direct oral-versus-intranasal efficacy comparison in adults with central diabetes insipidus. The evidence is three small switch studies from the intranasal era. Lam 1996 compared the routes head-to-head in 10 adults previously controlled on intranasal desmopressin: oral dosing produced dose-dependent antidiuresis peaking at 4 hours, the bioequivalent intranasal-to-oral ratio was 1:16, and over a 1-year prospective phase oral desmopressin 300–600 µg/day maintained stable, satisfactory antidiuresis comparable with previous intranasal therapy, with no side effect warranting withdrawal. Carraro 1991 switched 13 patients to tablets (150–600 µg/day) for 4 weeks with daily urine volume and osmolarity compared against their intranasal period and very good compliance. Murakami 2014 retrospectively studied 15 Japanese patients switched from intranasal desmopressin to the orally disintegrating tablet and found it safe and effective at a mean oral-to-nasal dose ratio of 17.0. No study randomised patients to oral versus intranasal treatment or tested formal equivalence, and all three predate modern formulations — so 'as effective' rests on maintained control after switching in 38 patients total. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: oral desmopressin is as effective as intranasal for controlling central diabetes insipidus in adults who switch, provided the dose is re-titrated at roughly 16–17 times the intranasal microgram dose.

cards.headline: Lam 1996 (N = 10): oral desmopressin produced dose-dependent antidiuresis (bioequivalent intranasal:oral ratio 1:16), and 1 year of oral therapy maintained antidiuresis comparable with previous intranasal treatment
cards.summary: Lam 1996 (N = 10): oral desmopressin produced dose-dependent antidiuresis (bioequivalent intranasal:oral ratio 1:16), and 1 year of oral therapy maintained antidiuresis comparable with previous intranasal treatment
cards.type: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic crossover comparison with 1-year prospective oral follow-up (Lam 1996) — small N printed on the face
cards.people: 10 Chinese adults with central diabetes insipidus previously controlled on intranasal desmopressin, in a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic comparison of intranasal and oral desmopressin, followed by acute testing of 100, 200 and 400 µg oral tablets and a 1-year prospective evaluation of oral treatment. N = 10, printed on the face.
cards.result: After 20 µg intranasal and 200 µg oral dosing, plasma desmopressin peaked at 45.6 and 93.3 minutes with terminal half-lives of 2.2 and 2.0 hours; the bioequivalent intranasal/oral ratio by area under the curve was 1:16. Antidiuretic activity rose during the second hour and peaked at 4 hours by either route; antidiuresis duration and magnitude correlated with oral dose, and increasing from 200 to 400 µg did not significantly increase maximal activity. During 1 year on oral desmopressin 300–600 µg/day in two to three doses, stable and satisfactory antidiuresis comparable with that on previous intranasal therapy was maintained, tablets were well tolerated, and no side effect warranted withdrawal.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients, one centre, 1996 tablet formulations: 'comparable antidiuresis' is the authors' clinical judgement in a switch cohort, not a randomised equivalence test, and the 1:16 ratio is a population average around which individual titration varied (300–600 µg/day).
cards.source: Lam KS et al. Pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, long-term efficacy and safety of oral 1-deamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin in adult patients with central diabetes insipidus. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 1996. PMID: 8877030. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Carraro 1991 (N = 13): switching from intranasal to oral desmopressin tablets (150–600 µg/day) maintained urine volume and osmolarity control over 4 weeks, with very good compliance
cards.summary: Carraro 1991 (N = 13): switching from intranasal to oral desmopressin tablets (150–600 µg/day) maintained urine volume and osmolarity control over 4 weeks, with very good compliance
cards.type: Controlled clinical (switch) study (Carraro 1991) — small N printed on the face
cards.people: 13 patients with central diabetes insipidus previously treated with intranasal desmopressin, switched to desmopressin tablets for 4 weeks, with daily urinary volume and osmolarity compared between the peroral and intranasal treatment periods. N = 13, printed on the face.
cards.result: The effective tablet dosage was between 150 and 600 µg/day, and patients showed very good compliance during the 4 weeks of treatment with desmopressin tablets. The record reports the comparison of urinary volume and osmolarity between routes qualitatively — it prints no numerical between-route difference or effect size, and that absence is stated plainly here rather than filled in.
cards.watchOut: A 1991 Italian-language switch report with an English abstract: four weeks is short, there is no parallel control group, and the record gives no numbers for the route comparison — it corroborates feasibility of switching, nothing stronger.

cards.headline: Murakami 2014 (N = 15): switching from intranasal desmopressin to the orally disintegrating tablet was safe and effective, at a mean oral-to-nasal dose ratio of 17.0
cards.summary: Murakami 2014 (N = 15): switching from intranasal desmopressin to the orally disintegrating tablet was safe and effective, at a mean oral-to-nasal dose ratio of 17.0
cards.type: Retrospective switch study (Murakami 2014) — small N printed on the face
cards.people: 15 Japanese patients with central diabetes insipidus at a single centre, switched retrospectively from intranasal desmopressin (spray or drops) to the desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet. N = 15, printed on the face.
cards.result: The daily mean dose of the orally disintegrating tablet was 104 ± 46.3 µg and the mean ratio of oral to nasal desmopressin dose was 17.0 ± 7.6 — considerably smaller doses than a previous dose-titration study had predicted. The nasal spray group needed significantly smaller switching ratios than the nasal drop group (11.7 ± 6.5 vs 21.0 ± 5.5; P = 0.02), and the required ratio correlated inversely with the previous nasal dose. The authors conclude the orally disintegrating tablet was safe and effective after switching from intranasal desmopressin.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, 15 patients, and a different oral formulation (orally disintegrating tablet) from the 1990s tablets: its lower absolute doses (mean 104 µg/day) show the switching ratio depends on both formulations, so neither this ratio nor Lam's 1:16 should be applied mechanically to an individual switch.
cards.source: Murakami T et al. Desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet in Japanese patients with central diabetes insipidus: a retrospective study of switching from intranasal desmopressin. cards.headline: Synthesis: in 38 adults across three switch studies, oral desmopressin maintained the control previously achieved intranasally — at roughly 16–17 times the microgram dose, individually titrated
cards.summary: Synthesis: in 38 adults across three switch studies, oral desmopressin maintained the control previously achieved intranasally — at roughly 16–17 times the microgram dose, individually titrated
cards.people: The carded evidence totals 38 adults: a 10-patient crossover pharmacodynamic study with 1-year oral follow-up, a 13-patient 4-week switch comparison, and a 15-patient retrospective switch to the orally disintegrating tablet. No randomised oral-versus-intranasal trial is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.result: Oral desmopressin produced dose-dependent antidiuresis with a bioequivalent intranasal:oral ratio of 1:16 and maintained stable antidiuresis over 1 year (Lam 1996); tablets at 150–600 µg/day maintained urine volume/osmolarity control over 4 weeks with very good compliance (Carraro 1991); switching to the orally disintegrating tablet was safe and effective at a mean dose ratio of 17.0 (Murakami 2014). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — equivalence in practice).
cards.watchOut: Every carded study switched stable patients rather than randomising routes, so the shelf supports 'oral can replace intranasal with re-titration', not proven equivalence in new patients; desmopressin duration-of-action by formulation homes on live shelf #2906.

shelves.title: Metformin versus lifestyle over 60 in prediabetes (SPLIT): lifestyle intervention was most effective in the oldest DPP group while metformin's effect faded with age — a partial completion of shelf #3519
shelves.question: In adults with prediabetes, does metformin delay progression to diabetes in people over 60 versus lifestyle intervention?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glucose · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Incidence · Life Style · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3519, which covers metformin and lifestyle after gestational diabetes; this shelf homes the over-60 prediabetes comparison, and the DPP primary report and the DPP Outcomes Study follow-up carded elsewhere in the library are cross-pointed, not re-carded. The DPP's own predefined age analysis (Crandall 2006) answers the question directly: intensive lifestyle intervention (ILS) grew more effective with age — incidence 3.3 cases per 100 person-years at age 60–85, its best result in any age group — while metformin grew less effective with age, with incidence rising to 9.3 cases per 100 person-years at 60–85 and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.63 for age 60–85 versus 25–44 within the metformin arm. Long-term DPPOS data show metformin itself was safe and durably weight-reducing over 10 years (Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group 2012), so the issue in older adults is comparative efficacy, not tolerability. A 2023 head-to-head meta-analysis of five trials found no significant overall difference between metformin and lifestyle (relative risk 1.14, not significant) — an average that conceals the age gradient the DPP analysis documents. PROPOSED SPLIT (lifestyle: strong benefit over 60; metformin: effect faded with age) — in people over 60, lifestyle intervention is the effective treatment for delaying diabetes and metformin should not be presented as its equal: its delaying effect was weakest, and trended to absent, in the oldest group.

cards.headline: Crandall 2006 (DPP age analysis): lifestyle intervention was most effective in the oldest group (3.3 cases per 100 person-years at age 60–85) while metformin was least effective there (9.3 per 100 person-years), with diabetes risk rising with age on metformin (hazard ratio 1.63 for age 60–85 vs. 25–44)
cards.summary: Crandall 2006 (DPP age analysis): lifestyle intervention was most effective in the oldest group (3.3 cases per 100 person-years at age 60–85) while metformin was least effective there (9.3 per 100 person-years), with diabetes risk rising with age on metformin (hazard ratio 1.63 for age 60–85 vs. 25–44)
cards.type: Predefined age-subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (Crandall 2006, DPP)
cards.people: Participants in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomised trial of intensive lifestyle intervention (ILS), metformin and placebo in adults at high risk of type 2 diabetes; this report is the DPP's predefined secondary analysis of whether treatment effects varied by age, comparing the 25–44, 45–59 and 60–85 year age groups. At baseline the 60–85 group was leaner, with the best insulin sensitivity and lowest insulin secretion. The total DPP enrolment is not stated in this record.
cards.result: Diabetes incidence rates did not differ by age in the placebo group, but ILS was more effective with increasing age (6.3, 4.9, and 3.3 cases per 100 person-years in the 25–44, 45–59, and 60–85 year age groups, respectively; p(trend) = .007). Participants aged 60–85 had the most weight loss and the most metabolic-equivalent hours of physical activity. The metformin group showed a trend toward higher diabetes incidence among older participants (6.7, 7.7, and 9.3 cases per 100 person-years across the same age groups; p(trend) = .07), and diabetes risk increased with age on metformin (hazard ratio [age 60–85 vs. 25–44] 1.63, p = .02) after adjusting for the greater weight loss in the 60–85 group. The authors conclude lifestyle modification was exceptionally effective in older individuals and recommend it for older people at high risk, while metformin's limited effectiveness in older persons may reflect age-related differences in insulin action and secretion.
cards.watchOut: This is a subgroup analysis of one trial, and the record gives incidence rates by age and treatment without the placebo rate for the 60–85 group specifically — so the exact absolute benefit of either treatment over placebo in the oldest group cannot be computed from this record alone; the within-arm age gradients are the finding.
cards.source: Crandall J et al. The influence of age on the effects of lifestyle modification and metformin in prevention of diabetes. The Journals of Gerontology. cards.headline: DPPOS 2012: metformin taken to delay diabetes was safe and well tolerated over the long term, with durable weight loss (2.0% vs. 0.2% on placebo through follow-up) — tolerability is not the reason to prefer lifestyle in older adults; comparative efficacy is
cards.summary: DPPOS 2012: metformin taken to delay diabetes was safe and well tolerated over the long term, with durable weight loss (2.0% vs. 0.2% on placebo through follow-up) — tolerability is not the reason to prefer lifestyle in older adults; comparative efficacy is
cards.type: Long-term safety and weight analysis of a randomised trial programme (DPPOS 2012)
cards.people: Participants in the randomised, double-blind Diabetes Prevention Program (metformin or placebo) followed by a 7–8 year open-label extension in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study (DPPOS), examining long-term metformin safety, tolerability, weight and waist circumference, including adverse events and the effect of adherence. The record does not report results separately for participants over 60.
cards.result: No significant safety issues were identified. Gastrointestinal symptoms were more common on metformin than placebo and declined over time; average haemoglobin and haematocrit were slightly lower on metformin, with the decreases occurring in the first year and no further change thereafter. During the DPP, metformin participants lost more weight and waist circumference than placebo (weight −2.06 ± 5.65% vs. 0.02 ± 5.52%, P < 0.001; waist −2.13 ± 7.06 cm vs. −0.79 ± 6.54 cm, P < 0.001), weight loss was directly related to adherence (P < 0.001), and through the unblinded follow-up weight loss remained significantly greater on metformin (2.0 vs. 0.2%, P < 0.001). The authors conclude metformin used to delay diabetes is safe, well tolerated, and produces durable weight loss for at least 10 years.
cards.watchOut: Safety and weight are not diabetes delay: this card shows an older adult can take metformin safely for years, not that it delays diabetes at their age — and because it pools all ages, it cannot rescue metformin's weak over-60 efficacy signal on the Crandall card.
cards.source: Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group. Long-term safety, tolerability, and weight loss associated with metformin in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study. Diabetes Care. 2012. PMID: 22442396. Registry ID: NCT00004992 and NCT00038727. cards.headline: Vajje 2023: pooled head-to-head across five trials, metformin versus lifestyle showed no significant difference in diabetes risk (relative risk 1.14; and 1.31 in the direct comparison, also not significant) — an all-ages average that hides the age gradient
cards.summary: Vajje 2023: pooled head-to-head across five trials, metformin versus lifestyle showed no significant difference in diabetes risk (relative risk 1.14; and 1.31 in the direct comparison, also not significant) — an all-ages average that hides the age gradient
cards.people: Five eligible randomised studies comparing metformin with lifestyle interventions for delaying diabetes in individuals with prediabetes, pooled in a meta-analysis following PRISMA guidelines (databases searched to 1 September 2023). The record does not report the pooled population's age structure or any age subgroup.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the risk of developing diabetes between the metformin and lifestyle intervention groups (relative risk: 1.14, 95% confidence interval: 0.77–1.68 — the treatment made no significant difference). In the direct metformin-versus-lifestyle comparison the risk was slightly higher with metformin but not statistically significant (relative risk: 1.31, 95% confidence interval: 0.93–1.86). Metformin plus lifestyle versus lifestyle alone also showed no significant difference (relative risk: 0.88, 95% confidence interval: 0.74–1.04). The authors conclude the incidence was slightly higher on metformin alone than with lifestyle, without reaching significance, and call for further trials.
cards.watchOut: An all-ages pooled null is exactly what a real age interaction looks like after averaging: the DPP — the largest contributing programme — found lifestyle pulling ahead precisely in the over-60s, so this card must be read as context for the overall comparison, never as evidence about people over 60 specifically.
cards.source: Vajje J et al. Comparison of the Efficacy of Metformin and Lifestyle Modification for the Primary Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: over 60, the DPP's own age analysis makes lifestyle the clear winner — its best incidence rate was in the oldest group — while metformin's delaying effect faded with age; metformin's long-term safety is not in question
cards.summary: Synthesis: over 60, the DPP's own age analysis makes lifestyle the clear winner — its best incidence rate was in the oldest group — while metformin's delaying effect faded with age; metformin's long-term safety is not in question
cards.people: The carded evidence: the DPP's predefined age analysis (age groups 25–44, 45–59, 60–85), the DPP/DPPOS long-term metformin safety and weight analysis (randomised phase plus 7–8 year extension), and a five-trial head-to-head meta-analysis with no age reporting. The DPP primary report and DPPOS incidence follow-up are carded elsewhere in the library and are cross-pointed from live shelf #3519's programme, not re-carded here.
cards.result: At age 60–85, diabetes incidence was 3.3 cases per 100 person-years on intensive lifestyle versus 9.3 on metformin, with metformin risk rising with age (hazard ratio 1.63, oldest vs. youngest) and lifestyle effectiveness rising with age (p(trend) = .007) (Crandall 2006). Metformin remained safe and weight-reducing over at least 10 years (DPPOS 2012). Pooled all-ages head-to-head data show no significant metformin–lifestyle difference (relative risk 1.14) (Vajje 2023). PROPOSED SPLIT (lifestyle: strong benefit over 60; metformin: effect faded with age).
cards.watchOut: The over-60 answer rests on one trial programme's subgroup analysis — predefined and biologically coherent (older participants lost the most weight and were most active), but a subgroup nonetheless; no second trial has randomised an over-60 prediabetes cohort to metformin versus lifestyle.

shelves.title: Metformin versus lifestyle in younger adults with obesity (SPLIT): near-equal in younger cohorts and strongest in the more obese, but pooled head-to-head data still favour lifestyle — a partial completion of shelf #3519
shelves.question: In adults with prediabetes, is metformin as effective as intensive lifestyle intervention for delaying diabetes in younger adults with obesity?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Metformin · Prediabetic State
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3519, which covers metformin and lifestyle in women with prior gestational diabetes; this shelf homes the younger, obese general-prediabetes comparison, and the DPP primary report carded elsewhere is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The fairest summary is 'close, but not equal — and closest exactly in the young and heavy'. The DPP/DPPOS metformin review (Aroda 2017) records that metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% relative versus placebo overall, with a greater effect in those who were more obese, had higher fasting glucose, or had a history of gestational diabetes — the younger-heavier profile. The Indian Diabetes Prevention Programme (Ramachandran 2006), in a younger cohort (mean age 45.9 years), found lifestyle and metformin almost identical: 3-year cumulative incidence 39.3% on lifestyle and 40.5% on metformin versus 55.0% on control (relative risk reductions 28.5% and 26.4%). But the pooled head-to-head meta-analysis (Mousavi 2023; mean age 50, mean BMI 35.5) still favours lifestyle: diabetes incidence was 25.3% relatively lower with lifestyle modification than with metformin (relative risk 0.747, p = 0.007). PROPOSED SPLIT (lifestyle modestly ahead overall; metformin essentially as effective in younger, more obese cohorts) — metformin is a reasonable near-equal where lifestyle programmes are not feasible in younger adults with obesity, but the pooled direct comparison does not support calling the two equal.

cards.headline: Aroda 2017 (DPP/DPPOS review): metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% relative versus placebo, with a greater effect in participants who were more obese, had higher fasting glucose, or had prior gestational diabetes — the profile of the younger adult with obesity
cards.summary: Aroda 2017 (DPP/DPPOS review): metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% relative versus placebo, with a greater effect in participants who were more obese, had higher fasting glucose, or had prior gestational diabetes — the profile of the younger adult with obesity
cards.type: Review of a randomised trial programme (Aroda 2017, DPP/DPPOS)
cards.people: The Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomised trial of 3,234 adults at high risk of diabetes assigned to masked placebo (n = 1,082), metformin 850 mg twice daily (n = 1,073) or intensive lifestyle intervention (n = 1,079), with primary outcome at 2.8 years; 88% (n = 2,776) of surviving participants continued into the DPP Outcomes Study, with over 15 years of follow-up at the time of this review. This card reports the programme's metformin findings as summarised in the review; the DPP primary report itself is carded elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: After an average follow-up of 2.8 years, metformin reduced the incidence of diabetes by 31% relative compared with placebo, with a greater effect in those who were more obese, had a higher fasting glucose or a history of gestational diabetes. The review summarises the programme's long-term glycaemic, cardiometabolic, health-economic and safety findings for metformin in people at high risk of diabetes; it reports no single head-to-head metformin-versus-lifestyle effect size, and no absolute incidence rates in the portion of the record fetched.
cards.watchOut: A programme review, not a new trial: its 'greater effect in the more obese' is a subgroup pattern from the DPP, and because the review gives the 31% figure as a relative reduction versus placebo only, it cannot by itself rank metformin against lifestyle in younger adults — the other two cards carry that comparison.

cards.headline: Ramachandran 2006 (IDPP-1): in younger Asian Indian adults with impaired glucose tolerance (mean age 45.9 years), lifestyle and metformin were nearly identical — 3-year diabetes incidence 39.3% vs. 40.5%, against 55.0% on control (relative risk reductions 28.5% and 26.4%)
cards.summary: Ramachandran 2006 (IDPP-1): in younger Asian Indian adults with impaired glucose tolerance (mean age 45.9 years), lifestyle and metformin were nearly identical — 3-year diabetes incidence 39.3% vs. 40.5%, against 55.0% on control (relative risk reductions 28.5% and 26.4%)
cards.people: 531 native Asian Indian subjects with impaired glucose tolerance (421 men, 110 women; mean age 45.9 ± 5.7 years, BMI 25.8 ± 3.5 kg/m2 — younger and leaner than the DPP cohort, as the authors state) randomised to four groups: control, lifestyle modification advice, metformin, or lifestyle plus metformin. Median follow-up 30 months; primary outcome was type 2 diabetes by World Health Organization criteria.
cards.result: The 3-year cumulative incidences of diabetes were 55.0% (control), 39.3% (lifestyle), 40.5% (metformin) and 39.5% (lifestyle plus metformin). The relative risk reduction was 28.5% with lifestyle (95% confidence interval 20.5–37.3, p = 0.018), 26.4% with metformin (95% confidence interval 19.1–35.1, p = 0.029) and 28.2% with the combination (95% confidence interval 20.3–37.0, p = 0.022), each versus control; there was no added benefit from combining them. The number needed to treat to delay one case was 6.4 for lifestyle, 6.9 for metformin and 6.5 for the combination.
cards.watchOut: This cohort was younger but lean (mean BMI 25.8), so it supports metformin's near-equality in younger adults, not specifically in younger adults with obesity; its lifestyle arm was advice-based rather than the DPP's intensive programme, which may flatter metformin in the comparison.

cards.headline: Mousavi 2023: pooled head-to-head, lifestyle modification beat metformin — diabetes incidence was 25.3% relatively lower with lifestyle (relative risk 0.747, p = 0.007) — in a pooled population of mean age 50 years and mean BMI 35.5
cards.summary: Mousavi 2023: pooled head-to-head, lifestyle modification beat metformin — diabetes incidence was 25.3% relatively lower with lifestyle (relative risk 0.747, p = 0.007) — in a pooled population of mean age 50 years and mean BMI 35.5
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mousavi 2023)
cards.people: Five randomised trials including both lifestyle modification and metformin interventions in adults over 18 without diabetes, with intervention of at least 6 months; the pooled population had a mean age of 50 years, mean BMI 35.5 and mean fasting blood sugar 104.7 mg/dL, with 2–3 years of follow-up for diabetes onset (mean 2.8 years).
cards.result: Lifestyle modification decreased the probability of type 2 diabetes incidence by 25.3% relative compared with the metformin intervention (relative risk: 0.747, 95% confidence interval, 0.6–0.92; p-value = 0.007). The authors conclude lifestyle modification is more efficacious than metformin in diminishing type 2 diabetes incidence and can be a therapeutic strategy especially in high-risk individuals. The record reports the relative comparison only; no pooled absolute incidence rates are given.
cards.watchOut: Five trials pooled across different populations and lifestyle intensities; the pooled mean age of 50 sits between 'younger' and the DPP's older groups, so this card supports a modest overall lifestyle edge rather than a precise estimate for any single age band.
cards.source: Mousavi SS et al. Comparing the effectiveness of metformin with lifestyle modification for the primary prevention of type II diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Endocrine Disorders. 2023. PMID: 37723440. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in younger adults with obesity, metformin comes closest to lifestyle of any subgroup — near-identical in the younger IDPP cohort and strongest in the DPP's more obese participants — but the pooled direct comparison still favours lifestyle by about a quarter relative
cards.summary: Synthesis: in younger adults with obesity, metformin comes closest to lifestyle of any subgroup — near-identical in the younger IDPP cohort and strongest in the DPP's more obese participants — but the pooled direct comparison still favours lifestyle by about a quarter relative
cards.people: The carded evidence: the DPP/DPPOS programme review (3,234 randomised adults), the IDPP-1 randomised trial (531 younger adults with impaired glucose tolerance), and a five-trial head-to-head meta-analysis (pooled mean age 50 years, mean BMI 35.5). The gestational-diabetes population is homed on live shelf #3519 and the DPP primary report is carded elsewhere; neither is re-carded here.
cards.result: Metformin reduced diabetes incidence by 31% relative versus placebo in the DPP, with greater effect in the more obese (Aroda 2017). In IDPP-1, 3-year incidence was 39.3% on lifestyle and 40.5% on metformin versus 55.0% on control — a near-tie (Ramachandran 2006). Pooled head-to-head, lifestyle was 25.3% relatively better than metformin (relative risk 0.747) (Mousavi 2023). PROPOSED SPLIT (lifestyle modestly ahead overall; metformin essentially as effective in younger, more obese cohorts).
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised younger adults with obesity alone to metformin versus an intensive DPP-style lifestyle programme and reported that subgroup head-to-head; the shelf's answer is assembled from a programme subgroup pattern, a younger-but-lean trial, and an all-comers pooled comparison, and it says so.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aroda VR et al. Diabetologia. 2017 (PMID: 28770322); Ramachandran A et al. Diabetologia. 2006 (PMID: 16391903); Mousavi SS et al. BMC Endocrine Disorders. 2023 (PMID: 37723440).

shelves.title: Linagliptin in stage 4 CKD: safe and effective against placebo at full dose — but never randomised against dose-adjusted sitagliptin or vildagliptin, which show near-identical placebo-adjusted HbA1c effects in parallel trials
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 4, is linagliptin safe and effective versus other DPP-4 inhibitors requiring dose adjustment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Kidney · Linagliptin · Male · Middle Aged · Purines · Quinazolines · Renal Insufficiency · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3552, which covers linagliptin's cardiovascular and kidney outcomes versus placebo (CARMELINA); this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, the stage-4 head-to-head comparison against dose-adjusted DPP-4 rivals, and none of #3552's carded records is re-carded here. The honest headline is that the direct trial does not exist in the records fetched: the Cochrane CKD review (Lo 2018) found only one DPP-4-versus-DPP-4 study in the entire CKD literature (vildagliptin versus sitagliptin) and no linagliptin head-to-head. What exists is parallel placebo-controlled evidence at stage-4-range kidney function: full-dose linagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.72 points more than placebo at 1 year in severe impairment with three severe hypoglycaemia cases per group (McGill 2013, N = 133); dose-adjusted vildagliptin (50 mg daily) lowered it by 0.7 points more than placebo in severe impairment with a placebo-like safety profile (Kothny 2012); and dose-adjusted sitagliptin (25 mg daily in severe insufficiency) matched glipizide with symptomatic hypoglycaemia in 6.2% versus 17.0% (Arjona Ferreira 2013). Each agent is individually safe and effective at low eGFR; which is best has never been randomised. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): linagliptin's no-adjustment convenience is real and its stage-4 efficacy and safety are trial-proven against placebo, but superiority or equivalence versus dose-adjusted rivals is unproven — the comparison is indirect only.

cards.headline: McGill 2013: in severe renal impairment (eGFR under 30), full-dose linagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.60 percentage points more than placebo at 12 weeks and 0.72 points more at 1 year, with three severe hypoglycaemia cases in each group (N = 133 on the face)
cards.summary: McGill 2013: in severe renal impairment (eGFR under 30), full-dose linagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.60 percentage points more than placebo at 12 weeks and 0.72 points more at 1 year, with three severe hypoglycaemia cases in each group (N = 133 on the face)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial in severe renal impairment (McGill 2013)
cards.people: 133 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.0%) and severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²) randomised to linagliptin 5 mg once daily (n = 68, no dose adjustment) or placebo (n = 65), added to existing background therapy, for 1 year.
cards.result: Adjusted mean HbA1c change at week 12 was −0.76% with linagliptin and −0.15% with placebo (treatment difference −0.60%; 95% CI −0.89 to −0.31; P < 0.0001); at 1 year the changes were −0.71% versus +0.01% (difference −0.72%, −1.03 to −0.41; P < 0.0001). Mean insulin doses fell by 6.2 units with linagliptin and 0.3 units with placebo. Overall adverse events were similar (94.1% vs 92.3%); severe hypoglycaemia occurred in three patients per group; median eGFR change was −0.8 versus −2.2 mL/min/1.73 m² and no drug-related renal failure occurred.
cards.watchOut: This is linagliptin against placebo, not against another DPP-4 inhibitor: it proves the unadjusted dose works and is tolerated in stage 4–5-range kidneys, but says nothing directly about whether it beats a dose-adjusted rival.
cards.source: McGill JB et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of linagliptin in patients with type 2 diabetes and severe renal impairment: a 1-year, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 23033241. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arjona Ferreira 2013: dose-adjusted sitagliptin (50 mg daily in moderate, 25 mg daily in severe renal insufficiency) was noninferior to glipizide for HbA1c at 54 weeks, with symptomatic hypoglycaemia in 6.2% versus 17.0% (N = 426)
cards.summary: Arjona Ferreira 2013: dose-adjusted sitagliptin (50 mg daily in moderate, 25 mg daily in severe renal insufficiency) was noninferior to glipizide for HbA1c at 54 weeks, with symptomatic hypoglycaemia in 6.2% versus 17.0% (N = 426)
cards.type: Randomised active-comparator trial of dose-adjusted sitagliptin (Arjona Ferreira 2013)
cards.people: 426 patients with type 2 diabetes and moderate-to-severe chronic renal insufficiency with inadequate glycaemic control, randomised 1:1 to dose-adjusted sitagliptin or glipizide (2.5 mg daily titrated to a maximum of 10 mg twice daily), stratified by renal status, cardiovascular disease and heart failure history.
cards.result: At week 54 HbA1c change was −0.8% with sitagliptin versus −0.6% with glipizide (between-group difference −0.11%; 95% CI −0.29 to 0.06), meeting the prespecified 0.4% noninferiority margin. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia occurred in 6.2% versus 17.0% (P = 0.001), and weight changed by −0.6 kg versus +1.2 kg (difference −1.8 kg; P < 0.001). Gastrointestinal adverse-event incidence was low with both treatments in the record.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a sulfonylurea, not linagliptin, and moderate and severe renal insufficiency are pooled — the record does not report the stage-4 subgroup separately, so this card shows a dose-adjusted DPP-4 inhibitor can be used safely at low eGFR, not how it compares with linagliptin.

cards.headline: Kothny 2012: dose-adjusted vildagliptin (50 mg once daily) lowered HbA1c by 0.7 points more than placebo at 1 year in severe renal impairment, with adverse events 85% versus 88% and deaths 3% versus 2% (N = 369)
cards.summary: Kothny 2012: dose-adjusted vildagliptin (50 mg once daily) lowered HbA1c by 0.7 points more than placebo at 1 year in severe renal impairment, with adverse events 85% versus 88% and deaths 3% versus 2% (N = 369)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial of dose-adjusted vildagliptin (Kothny 2012)
cards.people: 369 patients with type 2 diabetes and moderate (GFR 30 to <50 mL/min/1.73 m²; 211 patients) or severe (GFR <30; 158 patients) renal impairment randomised to vildagliptin 50 mg once daily (n = 216) or placebo (n = 153) added to stable background therapy for 52 weeks; most patients (72% moderate, 82% severe) were receiving insulin.
cards.result: Between-treatment HbA1c differences at 1 year were −0.4 ± 0.2% in moderate impairment (p = 0.005) and −0.7 ± 0.2% in severe impairment (p < 0.0001). In severe impairment, any adverse event occurred in 85% (vildagliptin) versus 88% (placebo), serious adverse events in 25% versus 25%, discontinuation for adverse events in 10% versus 6%, and death in 3% versus 2% — a safety profile the record describes as similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Again a placebo comparison: vildagliptin's adjusted dose is effective and tolerated in severe impairment, but no patient in this trial received linagliptin, so any linagliptin-versus-vildagliptin ranking is an indirect inference across trials with different background therapy.

cards.headline: Lo 2018 (Cochrane): across 44 studies in diabetes with CKD, DPP-4 inhibitors lowered HbA1c by 0.62 points versus placebo — but the only DPP-4-versus-DPP-4 comparison in the whole review was a single vildagliptin-versus-sitagliptin study, and no linagliptin head-to-head existed
cards.summary: Lo 2018 (Cochrane): across 44 studies in diabetes with CKD, DPP-4 inhibitors lowered HbA1c by 0.62 points versus placebo — but the only DPP-4-versus-DPP-4 comparison in the whole review was a single vildagliptin-versus-sitagliptin study, and no linagliptin head-to-head existed
cards.people: Cochrane review of 44 randomised studies (13,036 participants) of glucose-lowering therapy in people with diabetes and CKD (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²), including 13 studies of DPP-4 inhibitors versus placebo and a small set of head-to-head comparisons.
cards.result: Versus placebo, DPP-4 inhibitors may reduce HbA1c (7 studies, 867 participants: mean difference −0.62%, 95% CI −0.85 to −0.39; low-certainty evidence) and probably have little or no effect on cardiovascular death (2 studies, 5,897 participants: relative risk 0.93, 0.77 to 1.11) or weight. The review's head-to-head list contains one study each of vildagliptin versus sitagliptin and linagliptin versus voglibose (not a DPP-4 inhibitor), and its authors state that for head-to-head comparisons only individual studies were available so no conclusions could be made. Versus glipizide, sitagliptin probably reduces hypoglycaemia (2 studies, 551 participants: relative risk 0.40, 0.23 to 0.69).
cards.watchOut: A 2018 evidence map cannot exclude a later head-to-head trial, and its CKD population spans eGFR under 60 rather than stage 4 alone; it is carded because it documents, systematically, that the direct comparison this shelf asks for was not in the trial literature it searched.
cards.source: Lo C et al. Insulin and glucose-lowering agents for treating people with diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 30246878. cards.headline: Synthesis: each drug works against placebo at low eGFR — linagliptin at full dose, sitagliptin and vildagliptin at reduced doses — but no carded trial has ever randomised linagliptin against a dose-adjusted DPP-4 rival in stage 4 CKD, so the head-to-head question is unanswered rather than answered in linagliptin's favour
cards.summary: Synthesis: each drug works against placebo at low eGFR — linagliptin at full dose, sitagliptin and vildagliptin at reduced doses — but no carded trial has ever randomised linagliptin against a dose-adjusted DPP-4 rival in stage 4 CKD, so the head-to-head question is unanswered rather than answered in linagliptin's favour
cards.people: The carded evidence: one placebo-controlled trial of linagliptin in severe renal impairment (N = 133), one active-comparator trial of dose-adjusted sitagliptin versus glipizide in moderate-to-severe insufficiency (N = 426), one placebo-controlled trial of dose-adjusted vildagliptin spanning moderate and severe impairment (N = 369), and one Cochrane review of 44 studies (13,036 participants) mapping the comparisons that exist. Unique participants in the three trials total 928, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted 1-year HbA1c effects were −0.72 points for linagliptin in severe impairment (McGill 2013) and −0.7 points for vildagliptin in severe impairment (Kothny 2012); dose-adjusted sitagliptin matched glipizide with less hypoglycaemia (6.2% vs 17.0%; Arjona Ferreira 2013). Safety profiles against placebo were similar for linagliptin and vildagliptin. The Cochrane review found no linagliptin-versus-DPP-4 trial to analyse. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): linagliptin is safe and effective in stage 4-range CKD, but its standing versus dose-adjusted rivals rests on indirect cross-trial comparison only.
cards.watchOut: Cross-trial HbA1c differences (−0.72 vs −0.7 points) look identical, but the trials differ in background insulin use, baseline HbA1c and era — treating that as proof of equivalence would be exactly the indirect leap this shelf refuses to make.
cards.source: Synthesis of McGill JB et al. Diabetes Care. 2013 (PMID: 23033241); Arjona Ferreira JC et al. Diabetes Care. 2013 (PMID: 23248197); Kothny W et al. Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2012 (PMID: 22690943); Lo C et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 30246878).

shelves.title: Automated insulin delivery in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes outpatients (PARTIAL completion of live #955 and #561): HbA1c 0.6 points better than usual delivery with CGM in the one randomised trial
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections, does automated insulin delivery improve glucose control compared with injections plus continuous glucose monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Insulin Infusion Systems · Continuous Glucose Monitoring · Young Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #955 already homes fully closed-loop delivery in type 2 diabetes in hospital inpatients and in one small outpatient crossover trial (Daly 2023, 28 randomised adults, not re-carded here), and live shelf #561 homes closed-loop therapy predominantly in type 1 diabetes. This shelf answers the uncovered slice — modern outpatient automated insulin delivery (AID) systems in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, most participants previously on multiple daily injections, against continued usual insulin delivery with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). The one randomised trial (Kudva 2025, 319 adults, 13 weeks) found HbA1c fell 0.6 percentage points more with AID than with continued pretrial insulin delivery plus CGM (adjusted difference −0.6, 95% CI −0.8 to −0.4), with time in range 14 percentage points higher. Two single-arm studies point the same way: in 305 adults (73% previously on multiple daily injections) HbA1c fell 0.8 points after switching to AID (Pasquel 2025), and in a 24-person feasibility study switching from injections HbA1c fell 1.3 points (Davis 2023). Hypoglycaemia stayed low in all three reports. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the randomised evidence is a single 13-week trial, and the supporting studies have no concurrent control group, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite the consistent direction.

cards.headline: Kudva 2025 (2IQP): in 319 adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, automated insulin delivery cut HbA1c by 0.6 percentage points more than continued usual insulin delivery with CGM over 13 weeks
cards.summary: Kudva 2025 (2IQP): in 319 adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, automated insulin delivery cut HbA1c by 0.6 percentage points more than continued usual insulin delivery with CGM over 13 weeks
cards.people: 319 adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes randomised 2:1 at multiple centres to an automated insulin delivery system or to continue their pretrial insulin-delivery method (control); both groups used continuous glucose monitoring. Primary outcome was HbA1c at 13 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by 0.9 percentage points in the AID group (8.2% to 7.3%) and by 0.3 points in the control group (8.1% to 7.7%) — mean adjusted difference −0.6 percentage points (95% CI −0.8 to −0.4; P<0.001). Time in the target range 70–180 mg/dL rose from 48% to 64% with AID and from 51% to 52% in controls (mean difference 14 percentage points, 95% CI 11 to 17). CGM-measured hypoglycaemia was infrequent in both groups; one severe hypoglycaemia event occurred in the AID group.
cards.watchOut: The control group continued whatever insulin delivery it was already using — mostly injections, but not exclusively multiple daily injections — and 13 weeks is short; the trial shows a glucose-control advantage, not effects on complications, weight or durability beyond one quarter.
cards.source: Kudva YC et al. A Randomized Trial of Automated Insulin Delivery in Type 2 Diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40105270. Registry ID: NCT05785832. cards.headline: Pasquel 2025: in 305 adults with type 2 diabetes (73% on multiple daily injections), switching to automated insulin delivery lowered HbA1c from 8.2% to 7.4% over 13 weeks — single-arm, no randomised comparator
cards.summary: Pasquel 2025: in 305 adults with type 2 diabetes (73% on multiple daily injections), switching to automated insulin delivery lowered HbA1c from 8.2% to 7.4% over 13 weeks — single-arm, no randomised comparator
cards.people: 305 adults aged 18–75 with type 2 diabetes using insulin for at least 3 months at 21 US centres (73% on multiple daily injections, 21% basal insulin only, 6% already on a pump; 62% already using CGM), studied in a single-arm prospective trial: 14 days of standard therapy, then 13 weeks on the Omnipod 5 automated insulin delivery system (named as tested in the publication).
cards.result: HbA1c fell from 8.2% at baseline to 7.4% at 13 weeks (mean difference −0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −1.0 to −0.7; P<0.001 for superiority against baseline), and time in range 70–180 mg/dL rose from 45% to 66% (difference 20 points, 95% CI 18 to 22). Time below 54 mg/dL and below 70 mg/dL was non-inferior to standard therapy. There was 1 episode of severe hypoglycaemia and no diabetic ketoacidosis.
cards.watchOut: With no concurrent control group, some of this improvement may reflect trial participation, CGM initiation in the 38% not previously using it, and regression to the mean — it corroborates the randomised trial's direction but cannot size the effect on its own.
cards.source: Pasquel FJ et al. Automated Insulin Delivery in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2025. PMID: 39951268. Registry ID: NCT05815342. cards.headline: Davis 2023: in 24 adults with type 2 diabetes switching from injections, 8 weeks of automated insulin delivery lowered HbA1c by 1.3 percentage points and raised time in range by 21.9 points
cards.summary: Davis 2023: in 24 adults with type 2 diabetes switching from injections, 8 weeks of automated insulin delivery lowered HbA1c by 1.3 percentage points and raised time in range by 21.9 points
cards.people: 24 adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 61 years, baseline HbA1c 9.4%, diabetes duration 19 years) previously using basal-only or basal-bolus insulin injections, with or without CGM, in a multicentre outpatient feasibility trial: 2 weeks of standard therapy with CGM, then 8 weeks on the Omnipod 5 automated insulin delivery system (named as tested in the publication).
cards.result: HbA1c fell by 1.3% ± 0.7% (P<0.0001) and time in target range rose by 21.9% ± 15.2% (P<0.0001) on AID versus standard therapy, with no significant change in total daily insulin dose or BMI. Time at or above 250 mg/dL fell by 16.9% ± 16.2%, while time below 54 mg/dL stayed near zero in both phases (median 0.0% vs 0.00%; P=0.45).
cards.watchOut: Only 24 participants, 8 weeks of device use, and a before–after design in people selected for HbA1c of at least 8% — a proof-of-feasibility result whose size should not be quoted as the expected effect; the randomised trial above is the anchor.
cards.source: Davis GM et al. Safety and Efficacy of the Omnipod 5 Automated Insulin Delivery System in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: From Injections to Hybrid Closed-Loop Therapy. cards.headline: Synthesis: outpatient automated insulin delivery improves glucose control in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes — one randomised trial, supported by two single-arm switch studies
cards.summary: Synthesis: outpatient automated insulin delivery improves glucose control in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes — one randomised trial, supported by two single-arm switch studies
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 13-week randomised trial (319 adults), one large single-arm switch trial (305 adults) and one small feasibility study (24 adults) — 648 participants in total, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: The randomised comparison against continued usual insulin delivery with CGM showed an HbA1c advantage of −0.6 percentage points and 14 points more time in range for AID (Kudva 2025). Both uncontrolled switch studies found improvements of similar or larger size (HbA1c −0.8 and −1.3 points), and hypoglycaemia remained low throughout. The hospital and fully closed-loop evidence is homed on live shelf #955 and type 1 evidence on live shelf #561; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single randomised trial programme caps the stamp, however consistent the direction.
cards.watchOut: All carded follow-up is 13 weeks or less and every endpoint is a glucose metric; nothing here speaks to long-term complications, cost, or who among injection-treated patients benefits most.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kudva YC et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40105270); Pasquel FJ et al. JAMA network open. 2025 (PMID: 39951268); Davis GM et al. Diabetes care. 2023 (PMID: 36787903).

shelves.title: SGLT2 inhibitors and new-onset atrial fibrillation (GAP-E, secondary-analysis evidence): about a fifth fewer reported AF events across the outcome trials, no dedicated prevention trial
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce new-onset atrial fibrillation compared with placebo or other glucose-lowering drugs?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Benzhydryl Compounds · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glucosides · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: GAP-E with care, as the slate directs: no trial has ever randomised patients to test atrial fibrillation (AF) prevention as its primary question. Everything carded here is secondary-analysis evidence — AF events collected as adverse-event reports inside cardiovascular outcome trials, plus meta-analyses pooling them. Within that limit the direction is consistent: the prespecified DECLARE-TIMI 58 analysis found dapagliflozin reduced first AF/atrial flutter events by 19% relative (hazard ratio 0.81) in 17,160 patients with type 2 diabetes, and two meta-analyses of the randomised trials found relative risks of 0.76 and an odds ratio of 0.82 for incident AF. Because AF was captured from adverse-event reporting rather than systematic rhythm monitoring, silent AF is undercounted in every source, and the finding is hypothesis-supporting rather than proof. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), labelled as secondary-analysis evidence: SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with fewer reported new AF events in trial populations with type 2 diabetes.

cards.headline: Zelniker 2020 (DECLARE-TIMI 58 analysis): dapagliflozin reduced reported atrial fibrillation/flutter events by 19% relative — 7.8 versus 9.6 events per 1,000 patient-years
cards.summary: Zelniker 2020 (DECLARE-TIMI 58 analysis): dapagliflozin reduced reported atrial fibrillation/flutter events by 19% relative — 7.8 versus 9.6 events per 1,000 patient-years
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised cardiovascular outcome trial (DECLARE-TIMI 58, Zelniker 2020)
cards.people: 17,160 patients with type 2 diabetes and either multiple cardiovascular risk factors (n=10,186) or established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (n=6,974) in the DECLARE-TIMI 58 cardiovascular outcome trial of dapagliflozin versus placebo; this analysis examined first and total AF/atrial flutter events identified from the trial safety database, in patients with and without prevalent AF at baseline.
cards.result: Dapagliflozin reduced the risk of a first AF/atrial flutter event by 19% relative (264 versus 325 events; 7.8 versus 9.6 events per 1,000 patient-years; hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.95; P=0.009), and reduced the total (first plus recurrent) event count as well (incidence rate ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.92). The relative reduction was consistent in patients with and without previous AF, atherosclerotic disease, or heart failure (all interaction P values non-significant).
cards.watchOut: AF was not a prespecified efficacy outcome of DECLARE and events came from adverse-event reporting, not scheduled ECGs or rhythm monitoring — asymptomatic AF is systematically missed, so this measures reported clinical AF, and the analysis is hypothesis-generating by its authors' own framing.
cards.source: Zelniker TA et al. Effect of Dapagliflozin on Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Insights From the DECLARE-TIMI 58 Trial. Circulation. 2020. PMID: 31983236. cards.headline: Li 2020 meta-analysis: across 16 randomised trials in type 2 diabetes (38,335 patients), SGLT2 inhibitors reduced AF/atrial flutter — relative risk 0.76
cards.summary: Li 2020 meta-analysis: across 16 randomised trials in type 2 diabetes (38,335 patients), SGLT2 inhibitors reduced AF/atrial flutter — relative risk 0.76
cards.people: 16 randomised controlled trials comprising 38,335 patients with type 2 diabetes comparing an SGLT2 inhibitor with placebo, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis of AF/atrial flutter outcomes reported within the trials.
cards.result: SGLT2 inhibitors reduced AF/atrial flutter events compared with placebo (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.90; p=0.001). The reduction was not modified by baseline age, body weight, HbA1c or systolic blood pressure. The same pooling found lower all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.91) and fewer heart failure events (relative risk 0.73) on SGLT2 inhibitors; cerebrovascular events and myocardial infarction did not increase. The record reports relative risks without the pooled absolute event rates for the AF comparison.
cards.watchOut: Every pooled trial captured AF as an adverse event rather than a monitored endpoint, and most were not designed or powered for AF — the pooled relative effect is consistent but rests on incompletely ascertained events.
cards.source: Li WJ et al. SGLT2 inhibitors and atrial fibrillation in type 2 diabetes: a systematic review with meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials. Cardiovascular diabetology. 2020. cards.headline: Zheng 2022 meta-analysis: across 20 randomised trials (63,604 patients), SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with less incident AF (odds ratio 0.82) and no difference in stroke
cards.summary: Zheng 2022 meta-analysis: across 20 randomised trials (63,604 patients), SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with less incident AF (odds ratio 0.82) and no difference in stroke
cards.people: 20 randomised controlled trials involving 63,604 patients with type 2 diabetes, heart failure or chronic kidney disease, comparing dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, empagliflozin or ertugliflozin with control treatment, with follow-up from 24 to 202 weeks.
cards.result: Incident AF was significantly less frequent on SGLT2 inhibitors than on control (odds ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.93; P=0.002). Stroke did not differ between groups (odds ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.15; P=0.908) — so the AF signal has not been shown to translate into fewer strokes within these trials. The record reports odds ratios without pooled absolute event rates for this comparison.
cards.watchOut: This pooling mixes populations with and without diabetes and overlaps substantially with the trials in the Li 2020 card — the two meta-analyses are corroboration of one underlying trial dataset, not two independent bodies of evidence.
