cards.summary: Synthesis: secondary analyses consistently associate SGLT2 inhibitors with about a fifth fewer reported new AF events — but no dedicated AF-prevention trial exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large outcome-trial secondary analysis (17,160 patients) and two meta-analyses of the randomised trial programme (16 trials / 38,335 patients and 20 trials / 63,604 patients, overlapping).
cards.result: Dapagliflozin reduced first AF/atrial flutter events in DECLARE-TIMI 58 (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.95; absolute rates 7.8 versus 9.6 per 1,000 patient-years), and trial-level pooling gives a relative risk of 0.76 (Li 2020) and an odds ratio of 0.82 (Zheng 2022) for incident AF, with no accompanying stroke reduction shown. shelves.title: Dexamethasone suppression test accuracy in adrenal incidentaloma (GAP-E): sensitive at 50 nmol/L, specificity limited and threshold-dependent — positives need verification
shelves.question: In adults with an adrenal incidentaloma, how accurate is the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test for autonomous cortisol secretion?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Adolescent · Adrenal Gland Neoplasms · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Case-Control Studies · Chromatography, Liquid · Cortisone · Cushing Syndrome · Dexamethasone · Female · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Incidental Findings · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Saliva · Tandem Mass Spectrometry · Young Adult
shelves.balance: GAP-E test-accuracy shelf. The honest headline is that accuracy here is threshold-dependent and partly circular: autonomous cortisol secretion (ACS) is itself defined by the post-dexamethasone cortisol value in the ESE/ENSAT guideline framework, so there is no independent gold standard against which the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) can be validated — the carded studies instead measure what the test does at the standard 50 nmol/L (about 1.8 µg/dL) cortisol cutoff. At that cutoff the test is sensitive but poorly specific: in a 165-patient incidentaloma cohort the overnight test performed no better than longer suppression protocols and the companion tests (late-night salivary cortisol, urinary free cortisol, DHEAS) discriminated poorly (Ueland 2020). Measuring the dexamethasone level itself reclassified about a fifth of false positives and improved specificity (Ueland 2017), and a suppressed ACTH after the test helps verify true non-suppression (sensitivity 75–81%, specificity 78–85% for inadequate suppression; Puvaneswaralingam 2021). Live shelf #1758 covers adrenalectomy for this condition, not test accuracy, and is not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence): the 1 mg overnight DST at 50 nmol/L is a reasonable rule-out screen whose positive results are frequently false or borderline and need confirmatory context — assay, dexamethasone level, ACTH and repeat testing — before ACS is diagnosed.

cards.headline: Ueland 2020: in 165 incidentaloma patients, no companion test discriminated autonomous cortisol secretion well, and the 2-day suppression test added nothing over the 1 mg overnight test
cards.summary: Ueland 2020: in 165 incidentaloma patients, no companion test discriminated autonomous cortisol secretion well, and the 2-day suppression test added nothing over the 1 mg overnight test
cards.people: 165 patients with adrenal incidentalomas evaluated retrospectively with morning ACTH, late-night salivary cortisol, DHEAS, 24-hour urinary free cortisol and dexamethasone suppression testing, and classified by current European guideline criteria as non-functioning incidentaloma (n=82) or autonomous cortisol secretion (n=83).
cards.result: Late-night salivary cortisol discriminated poorly between non-functioning incidentalomas and ACS, with 23 of 63 false-positive and 38 of 69 false-negative results. The conventional low-dose (2-day) dexamethasone suppression test did not improve diagnostic specificity compared with the 1 mg overnight DST. DHEAS performed modestly (area under the ROC curve 0.76; sensitivity 58% and specificity 80% at the 1.04 µmol/L (40 µg/dL) cutoff). The authors conclude that none of the companion tests usefully separates non-functioning incidentalomas from ACS and that alternative biomarkers are needed.
cards.watchOut: The reference classification (ACS versus non-functioning) was itself built from the same family of cortisol tests, so this study measures agreement and discrimination within the guideline framework — it cannot supply an independent sensitivity/specificity for the DST against a separate gold standard, because none exists.
cards.source: Ueland GÅ et al. Diagnostic testing of autonomous cortisol secretion in adrenal incidentalomas. Endocrine connections. 2020. PMID: 33032259. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Ueland 2017: at the 50 nmol/L cutoff the overnight DST over-called autonomous cortisol secretion — measuring the dexamethasone level removed about 20% of false positives
cards.summary: Ueland 2017: at the 50 nmol/L cutoff the overnight DST over-called autonomous cortisol secretion — measuring the dexamethasone level removed about 20% of false positives
cards.people: 302 subjects who underwent an overnight dexamethasone suppression test with simultaneous serum cortisol, cortisone and dexamethasone measured by LC-MS/MS: 49 patients with suspected Cushing's syndrome, 152 with adrenal incidentaloma and 101 healthy controls, with a replication cohort of 58.
cards.result: Serum cortisol was at or above 50 nmol/L (about 1.8 µg/dL) after dexamethasone in 83 subjects, of whom 11 had Cushing's syndrome and 27 had autonomous cortisol secretion. Nine patients combined a low serum dexamethasone with a positive DST, and three of them had been misdiagnosed as having ACS — their 'non-suppression' reflected inadequate dexamethasone exposure, not cortisol autonomy. Simultaneous dexamethasone measurement reduced false-positive DSTs by 20% and improved specificity; a serum dexamethasone above 3.3 nmol/L was sufficient for cortisol suppression below 50 nmol/L. DST results were highly reproducible and confirmed in the replication cohort.
cards.watchOut: Part of the DST's apparent inaccuracy is pharmacokinetic — variable dexamethasone absorption and metabolism — not biology; laboratories that do not measure the dexamethasone level cannot make this correction, so real-world specificity is worse than in this LC-MS/MS study.
cards.source: Ueland GÅ et al. Simultaneous assay of cortisol and dexamethasone improved diagnostic accuracy of the dexamethasone suppression test. European journal of endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28298353. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Puvaneswaralingam 2021: a post-test ACTH verifies true non-suppression — sensitivity 75–81% and specificity 78–85% for detecting inadequate suppression behind a positive DST
cards.summary: Puvaneswaralingam 2021: a post-test ACTH verifies true non-suppression — sensitivity 75–81% and specificity 78–85% for detecting inadequate suppression behind a positive DST
cards.people: 373 patients with adrenal incidentalomas and basal ACTH of at least 2.0 pmol/L who underwent a 1 mg overnight DST in a cross-sectional study; post-DST cortisol of at least 50 nmol/L (about 1.8 µg/dL) was found in 140 patients, and post-DST ACTH measures were tested against adequate versus inadequate suppression (the latter defined by the fall in cortisol on a 2-day suppression test, n=16).
cards.result: The best cutoffs for flagging a genuinely non-suppressed result were post-DST ACTH of at least 0.6 pmol/L (sensitivity 75%, specificity 78% for inadequate suppression) and an ACTH ratio of at least 18% of basal (sensitivity 81%, specificity 85%). The authors propose that a post-DST cortisol of at least 50 nmol/L together with a suppressed ACTH (below 0.6 pmol/L, or ACTH ratio below 18%) should raise suspicion of true autonomous cortisol secretion — i.e., the cortisol number alone over-diagnoses, and the ACTH pattern separates assay/absorption artefact from autonomy.
cards.watchOut: The 'inadequate suppression' reference group numbered only 16 patients, so the sensitivity and specificity estimates carry wide uncertainty; this is a verification strategy for positive results, not a replacement screening test.
cards.source: Puvaneswaralingam S et al. ACTH following overnight dexamethasone suppression can be used in the verification of autonomous cortisol secretion in patients with adrenal incidentalomas. Clinical endocrinology. 2021. PMID: 33108675. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the 1 mg overnight DST is a sensitive screen with threshold-dependent, often poor specificity — a positive result is the start of verification, not a diagnosis
cards.summary: Synthesis: the 1 mg overnight DST is a sensitive screen with threshold-dependent, often poor specificity — a positive result is the start of verification, not a diagnosis
cards.people: The carded evidence: three diagnostic-accuracy studies in incidentaloma populations (165, 302 and 373 patients). Total carded participants exceed 800, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: At the standard cutoff (post-DST cortisol 50 nmol/L, about 1.8 µg/dL), longer suppression protocols added nothing (Ueland 2020), about a fifth of false positives were explained by low dexamethasone exposure and removable by measuring the drug level (Ueland 2017), and a non-suppressed ACTH pattern verified true autonomy with sensitivity 75–81% and specificity 78–85% (Puvaneswaralingam 2021). Because ACS is defined through these same tests, no study can quote a gold-standard sensitivity/specificity — accuracy must be presented as threshold- and assay-dependent, as this shelf does. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (test-accuracy, observational evidence).
cards.watchOut: Quoting any single sensitivity/specificity pair for this test without its cutoff, assay and verification step would misstate the evidence — the ESE/ENSAT categories (possible versus definite ACS by cortisol band) exist precisely because one number cannot carry the diagnosis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ueland GÅ et al. Endocrine connections. 2020 (PMID: 33032259); Ueland GÅ et al. European journal of endocrinology. 2017 (PMID: 28298353); Puvaneswaralingam S et al. Clinical endocrinology. 2021 (PMID: 33108675).

shelves.title: What drives aldosterone: potassium's hair-trigger, angiotensin II's sodium-set gain, and ACTH's fading third place — human dose-response evidence
shelves.question: In humans, what determines aldosterone secretion — the relative potency of potassium, angiotensin II and ACTH?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aldosterone · Angiotensin II · Blood · Female · Glucose · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Infusions, Parenteral · Kinetics · Male · Potassium · Renin · Sodium
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology). The textbooks rank the regulators of aldosterone: potassium is the most sensitive direct stimulus — the zona glomerulosa responds to changes within the physiological range too small to matter for any other hormone; angiotensin II is the second major stimulus, with adrenal sensitivity itself set by sodium balance; ACTH stimulates aldosterone only transiently, its chronic effect being permissive at most. The carded human dose-response studies are unusually exact matches to that ranking. Graded potassium infusions raised aldosterone by 46% in response to a plasma potassium increment of only 0.2 mEq/L (5%), with renin and angiotensin II unchanged — a direct adrenal effect operating across the 0.1–0.5 mEq/L band (Himathongkam 1975). Graded angiotensin II infusions showed the aldosterone dose-response slope steepening on a low-sodium diet, an adrenal sensitisation that persisted when captopril normalised the circulating angiotensin level — sodium status sets the gain (Dawson-Hughes 1981). And ACTH behaved exactly as the textbooks say: continuous cosyntropin drove aldosterone back to pre-infusion levels by 72 hours despite sustained cortisol stimulation, while pulsatile ACTH maintained it (Seely 1989). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: potassium first (direct, exquisitely sensitive), angiotensin II second (gain set by sodium balance), ACTH third and transient.

cards.headline: Himathongkam 1975: in 8 normal subjects, a 0.2 mEq/L rise in plasma potassium raised aldosterone 46% — with renin and angiotensin II unchanged (N = 8, below 10)
cards.summary: Himathongkam 1975: in 8 normal subjects, a 0.2 mEq/L rise in plasma potassium raised aldosterone 46% — with renin and angiotensin II unchanged (N = 8, below 10)
cards.type: Human physiology study (graded potassium infusion dose-response, Himathongkam 1975) — N = 8
cards.people: 8 normal subjects on a fixed intake (10 mEq sodium, 100 mEq potassium) given graded constant potassium chloride infusions over 2 hours (0.17, 0.33 and 0.5 mEq/min), with frequent sampling of aldosterone, renin activity, angiotensin II, cortisol, potassium and sodium; a glucose-ingestion sub-study was performed in 6 normal subjects. N = 8 (and 6) — small classic studies, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires. Potassium in mEq/L is numerically identical to mmol/L.
cards.result: During the lowest infusion rate (0.17 mEq/min), plasma potassium did not rise significantly until 120 minutes, yet plasma aldosterone rose significantly by 30–60 minutes: the mean increment above control was 0.2 mEq/L (5%) for potassium against 13 ng/100 ml (46%) for aldosterone. There were stepwise increments in both as the infusion rate rose, with the most sensitive region of the dose-response curve at potassium increments of 0.1–0.5 mEq/L. Plasma sodium, renin activity and angiotensin II did not change significantly. In the glucose sub-study, a mean maximal potassium fall of 0.3 mEq/L (8%) coincided with a 46% fall in aldosterone — the relationship ran in both directions.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 and N = 6, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the numbers on the face. Subjects were sodium-restricted (10 mEq/day), which sensitises the whole axis; the qualitative point — aldosterone answering potassium changes inside the normal range, independently of renin — is the finding, not the exact percentage at other sodium intakes.
cards.source: Himathongkam T et al. Potassim-aldosterone-renin interrelationships. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1975. PMID: 1167307. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dawson-Hughes 1981: sodium restriction steepened the aldosterone response to infused angiotensin II in normal man — and captopril did not unsteepen it
cards.summary: Dawson-Hughes 1981: sodium restriction steepened the aldosterone response to infused angiotensin II in normal man — and captopril did not unsteepen it
cards.type: Human physiology study (graded angiotensin II infusion across sodium states, Dawson-Hughes 1981)
cards.people: Normal volunteer subjects who received graded infusions of angiotensin II in three states: high sodium intake, low sodium intake, and low sodium intake after captopril pretreatment to lower the plasma angiotensin II level to the sodium-loaded range; the record does not print the number of subjects (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: The slope of the aldosterone–angiotensin II regression line during infusion was significantly steeper on low sodium intake than on high sodium intake — the adrenal becomes more responsive to angiotensin II when sodium is restricted. Adding captopril did not decrease that slope, indicating the endogenous angiotensin II concentration is not what maintains the heightened adrenal sensitivity. (For vascular responses the pattern reversed: the blood-pressure slope was steeper on high sodium, and captopril partly restored vascular responsiveness — tissue-specific regulation.)
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, and the readout is a regression slope rather than a single threshold dose — the card supports 'angiotensin II is a major stimulus whose adrenal gain is set by sodium balance', not any fixed potency ratio against potassium, which no carded study measures head-to-head.
cards.source: Dawson-Hughes BF et al. Plasma angiotensin II concentration regulates vascular but not adrenal responsiveness to restriction of sodium intake in normal man. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 1981. PMID: 7026131. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Seely 1989: continuous ACTH let aldosterone fall back to baseline by 72 hours despite sustained stimulation, while pulsatile ACTH maintained it — in 8 normal men (N = 8, below 10)
cards.summary: Seely 1989: continuous ACTH let aldosterone fall back to baseline by 72 hours despite sustained stimulation, while pulsatile ACTH maintained it — in 8 normal men (N = 8, below 10)
cards.type: Human physiology study (continuous versus pulsatile ACTH infusion, Seely 1989) — N = 8
cards.people: 8 normal male subjects on a 10-mEq sodium, 100-mEq potassium diet who received both continuous and pulsatile (0.33 U per pulse over 15 minutes, every 2 hours) infusions of cosyntropin (ACTH 1-24), 4 U per 24 hours, for 48 hours (n = 4) or 72 hours (n = 4), with aldosterone and cortisol sampled every 6 hours. N = 8 — printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Continuous infusion stimulated aldosterone, which then progressively declined to pre-infusion levels by 72 hours (pre-infusion 29 ± 5 ng/dL; 72 hours 38 ± 10 ng/dL; P = 0.40) even though cortisol stimulation was sustained. Pulsatile infusion maintained the aldosterone stimulation to 72 hours (33 ± 7 to 85 ± 13 ng/dL; P < 0.05). Regression from the 18-hour peak showed a significant decline over time for continuous infusion (r = 0.63, P = 0.001) and none for pulsatile (r = 0.02, P = 0.85), with no differences in sodium, potassium, renin, angiotensin II or cortisol to explain the divergence.
cards.watchOut: N = 8, below the usual 10-human floor — carded under the physiology labelling rule with the number on the face. The experiment isolates ACTH's time course, not its peak potency: a single ACTH bolus does raise aldosterone acutely; the finding is that the effect cannot be sustained by continuous ACTH, unlike potassium's or angiotensin II's.
cards.source: Seely EW et al. Adrenocorticotropin stimulation of aldosterone: prolonged continuous versus pulsatile infusion. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1989. PMID: 2551915. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: potassium is the fine tuner, angiotensin II the volume-linked driver with sodium-set gain, ACTH a transient third
cards.summary: Synthesis: potassium is the fine tuner, angiotensin II the volume-linked driver with sodium-set gain, ACTH a transient third
cards.people: The carded evidence: graded potassium infusions in 8 normal subjects (Himathongkam 1975, N on the face), graded angiotensin II infusions across sodium states (Dawson-Hughes 1981, N not documented in the record), and continuous versus pulsatile ACTH in 8 normal men (Seely 1989, N on the face).
cards.result: Aldosterone rose 46% for a 0.2 mEq/L potassium increment with renin and angiotensin II unmoved, and fell 46% when glucose ingestion lowered potassium by 0.3 mEq/L; the aldosterone response to infused angiotensin II steepened under sodium restriction independently of the circulating angiotensin level; and continuous ACTH's aldosterone effect extinguished by 72 hours (29 to 38 ng/dL, P = 0.40) while its cortisol effect persisted. That ordering — potassium most sensitive and direct, angiotensin II potent with state-dependent gain, ACTH transient — is precisely the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: No carded study infuses all three stimuli in the same subjects, so the ranking is a triangulation across studies plus the textbook account — stated as such; the individual dose-response behaviours, which are what the cards actually prove, are not in doubt.
cards.source: Synthesis of Himathongkam T et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1975 (PMID: 1167307); Dawson-Hughes BF et al. Clinical science (London, England : 1979). 1981 (PMID: 7026131); Seely EW et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1989 (PMID: 2551915). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: GLP-1 weight loss and lean mass — an evidence question: about one quarter of the weight lost is lean mass in the DXA substudy and the pooled trial analyses; no carded trial measured frailty or function outcomes in older adults
shelves.question: In older adults treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists, how much of the weight lost is lean mass, and does it worsen frailty or function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Absorptiometry, Photon · Anti-Obesity Agents/therapeutic use · Body Composition/drug effects · Body Mass Index · Obesity/drug therapy · Overweight/drug therapy · Tirzepatide · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss/drug effects
shelves.balance: EVIDENCE QUESTION — this shelf reports what is measured, it does not stamp a benefit or harm claim. What is measured: in the SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy (Look 2025; 160 participants with baseline and week-72 scans), tirzepatide reduced body weight by 21.3%, fat mass by 33.9% and lean mass by 10.9% (placebo: 5.3%, 8.2% and 2.6%; p < 0.001 for all), and of the weight lost approximately 75% was fat mass and 25% was lean mass in both the tirzepatide and placebo groups, consistently across sex, age (including 65 years and over) and weight-loss tertiles. Across 22 randomised trials (2,258 participants), the network meta-analysis (Karakasis 2025) found GLP-1-based agents reduced weight by a mean 3.55 kg, fat mass by 2.95 kg and lean mass by 0.86 kg versus comparators — again with lean mass loss comprising approximately 25% of total weight loss, while relative lean mass (percentage of body weight) was unaffected; tirzepatide 15 mg weekly and semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly lost the most weight and were among the least lean-preserving. The frailty half of the question has no direct trial answer in the fetched records: the Metabolism review (Stefanakis 2024) states that over 25% of weight lost from pharmacotherapy or surgery typically comes from fat-free mass, and that muscle and bone loss can compromise physical function especially in older adults — a mechanistic and clinical concern, with candidate selection (advanced age, prefrailty) flagged as a judgement call, not a measured trial outcome. Premise correction: the STEP 1 body-composition substudy exists as a conference-abstract report, not a full journal article in the fetched PubMed records, so semaglutide's composition numbers are carried here by the pooled network analysis rather than by a carded STEP 1 substudy paper. PROPOSED: an evidence-question shelf — the lean-mass fraction is quantified and concordant (about one quarter); the frailty/function consequence in older adults is unmeasured, and the stamp says so.

cards.headline: Look 2025 (SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy, n = 160): tirzepatide cut weight 21.3%, fat mass 33.9% and lean mass 10.9% at 72 weeks; about 75% of weight lost was fat and 25% lean in both arms
cards.summary: Look 2025 (SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy, n = 160): tirzepatide cut weight 21.3%, fat mass 33.9% and lean mass 10.9% at 72 weeks; about 75% of weight lost was fat and 25% lean in both arms
cards.people: 160 participants from the SURMOUNT-1 trial of adults with obesity or overweight (of 2,539 in the main trial) who had dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry at baseline and week 72 (pooled tirzepatide doses n = 124, placebo n = 36; 73% women; mean weight 102.5 kg, mean BMI 38.0 kg/m2), with post-hoc subgroups by sex, age (under 50, 50 to under 65, 65 and over) and weight-loss tertile.
cards.result: Change from baseline to week 72 was −21.3% for body weight, −33.9% for fat mass and −10.9% for lean mass with tirzepatide, versus −5.3%, −8.2% and −2.6% with placebo (p < 0.001 for all comparisons). Of the body weight lost, approximately 75% was fat mass and 25% was lean mass for both tirzepatide and placebo, and these proportions remained consistent across most subgroup analyses including the age subgroups. No frailty or physical-function outcome is reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: A 160-participant substudy of a trial whose participants were mostly middle-aged (73% women); DXA lean mass includes water and organ mass, not muscle alone, and the same 75/25 fat-to-lean split on placebo shows the proportion is a property of weight loss, not unique to the drug.
cards.source: Look M et al. Body composition changes during weight reduction with tirzepatide in the SURMOUNT-1 study of adults with obesity or overweight. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2025. PMID: 39996356. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Karakasis 2025 (network meta-analysis, 22 trials, 2,258 participants): GLP-1-based agents reduced lean mass by a mean 0.86 kg — about 25% of the 3.55 kg total weight lost — while relative lean mass was unaffected
cards.summary: Karakasis 2025 (network meta-analysis, 22 trials, 2,258 participants): GLP-1-based agents reduced lean mass by a mean 0.86 kg — about 25% of the 3.55 kg total weight lost — while relative lean mass was unaffected
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and pairwise plus network meta-analyses of 22 randomised controlled trials (2,258 participants) of GLP-1 receptor agonists and GLP-1/GIP dual agonists in adults with diabetes and/or overweight or obesity, searched to 12 November 2024.
cards.result: GLP-1-based agents significantly reduced total body weight (mean difference −3.55 kg, 95% CI −4.81 to −2.29), fat mass (−2.95 kg, −4.11 to −1.79) and lean mass (−0.86 kg, −1.30 to −0.42) versus comparators, with lean mass loss comprising approximately 25% of total weight loss; relative lean mass (percentage change from baseline) was unaffected. Liraglutide was the only agent with significant weight reduction without significant lean-mass reduction; tirzepatide 15 mg weekly and semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly were the most effective for weight and fat loss but among the least effective at preserving lean mass. No frailty or function endpoint is pooled in this record.
cards.watchOut: Pooled across drugs, doses, populations (diabetes and non-diabetes) and mostly non-elderly trial populations; it quantifies composition, and its lean-mass figures cannot by themselves answer what happens to strength, gait or frailty in a 75-year-old.
cards.source: Karakasis P et al. Effect of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and co-agonists on body composition: Systematic review and network meta-analysis. Metabolism: clinical and experimental. 2025. PMID: 39719170. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stefanakis 2024 (review): over 25% of weight lost with pharmacotherapy or surgery typically comes from fat-free mass, and the authors flag older, prefrail patients as the group in whom this matters most — a concern, not a trial result
cards.summary: Stefanakis 2024 (review): over 25% of weight lost with pharmacotherapy or surgery typically comes from fat-free mass, and the authors flag older, prefrail patients as the group in whom this matters most — a concern, not a trial result
cards.people: Narrative/mechanistic review of weight loss, fat-free mass, muscle, bone and haematopoiesis in the era of incretin-based pharmacotherapy achieving 15–25% weight loss, with attention to older adults and to the myostatin–activin pathway and lean-preserving compounds in development.
cards.result: The review states that over 25% of total weight lost from both surgery and pharmacotherapy typically comes from fat-free mass including skeletal muscle, that loss of muscle and bone can compromise physical function, metabolic rate and overall health especially in older adults, and that for the time being advanced age and prefrailty may affect the choice of suitable candidates for anti-obesity medications because of the associated sarcopenia risk. It reports no new trial data and no measured frailty or function outcome in older adults on GLP-1 therapy.
cards.watchOut: A review, carded for the frailty framing of an evidence question, not as outcome evidence: its 25% figure is a cross-therapy generalisation and its older-adult caution is expert reasoning, not a measured effect.
cards.source: Stefanakis K et al. The impact of weight loss on fat-free mass, muscle, bone and hematopoiesis health: Implications for emerging pharmacotherapies aiming at fat reduction and lean mass preservation. Metabolism: clinical and experimental. 2024. PMID: 39481534. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the lean-mass fraction is measured and concordant (about one quarter of weight lost); the frailty consequence in older adults is unmeasured — an evidence question, not an efficacy claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: the lean-mass fraction is measured and concordant (about one quarter of weight lost); the frailty consequence in older adults is unmeasured — an evidence question, not an efficacy claim
cards.people: Direct composition data: a 160-participant DXA substudy and 22 pooled trials with 2,258 participants, predominantly middle-aged adults with obesity, with or without diabetes; older-adult-specific and frailty-endpoint data: none in the carded records.
cards.result: Two independent data types agree that roughly 25% of the weight lost on potent GLP-1-based therapy is lean mass (75% fat), that the proportion resembles ordinary weight loss (the SURMOUNT-1 placebo arm split the same way), and that relative lean mass as a share of body weight is preserved. What no carded record measures is the clinical half of the question — incident frailty, strength, gait speed or function in older adults. PROPOSED STAMP: EVIDENCE QUESTION, worded to carry both halves and to claim neither benefit nor harm on frailty.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert '25% of weight lost is lean' into 'GLP-1 drugs cause frailty': absolute lean-mass loss, preserved relative lean mass, and unmeasured function point in different directions, and resistance-exercise or protein co-interventions were not tested in the carded records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Look M et al. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2025 (PMID: 39996356); Karakasis P et al. Metabolism: clinical and experimental. 2025 (PMID: 39719170); Stefanakis K et al. Metabolism: clinical and experimental. 2024 (PMID: 39481534). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: The glucose-threshold hierarchy: hormones at 66–69 mg/dL, symptoms at 53 mg/dL, cognition below that — the Schwartz, Cryer and Fanelli clamp measurements
shelves.question: In humans, at what falling blood-glucose levels do counter-regulatory hormones switch on, symptoms appear, and cognition fail (the glucose-threshold hierarchy)?
shelves.mesh: 3-Hydroxybutyric Acid · Adult · Blood Glucose/metabolism · C-Peptide/blood · Epinephrine/blood · Fatty Acids, Nonesterified/blood · Female · Glucagon/blood · Growth Hormone/blood · Humans · Hydrocortisone/blood · Hydroxybutyrates/blood · Hypoglycemia/physiopathology · Insulin/blood · Lactates/blood · Lactic Acid · Male · Norepinephrine/blood
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep (textbook framing, not evidence). Schwartz & Cryer 1987 (N=10) measured the ladder in a single stepped clamp: epinephrine 69 ± 2 mg/dL, glucagon 68 ± 2, growth hormone 66 ± 2, cortisol 58 ± 3, symptoms 53 ± 2 mg/dL. The Fanelli programme placed cognitive failure below the symptom threshold (deterioration across the descent to 40 mg/dL) and showed the thresholds are plastic — antecedent hypoglycemia shifts hormone and symptom responses down (Heller & Cryer 1991), and in type 1 diabetes shifts the cognitive threshold too (Fanelli 1998). Every mmol/L value in this pack carries its mg/dL equivalent. This is threshold physiology; the library's hypoglycaemia shelves are treatment shelves and do not home this question.

cards.headline: Schwartz & Cryer 1987: the hierarchy measured in one stepped clamp — counter-regulatory hormones switch on at 66–69 mg/dL, symptoms only at 53 mg/dL
cards.summary: Schwartz & Cryer 1987: the hierarchy measured in one stepped clamp — counter-regulatory hormones switch on at 66–69 mg/dL, symptoms only at 53 mg/dL
cards.people: 10 normal humans studied during stepped reductions in plasma glucose (six 10-mg/dL hourly steps, from 90 to 40 mg/dL) under hyperinsulinemic clamp conditions, compared with the same measurements during maintained euglycemia (90 mg/dL) over 6 hours. Glucose values are arterialized venous plasma glucose, in mg/dL as printed in the record (multiply by 0.0555 for mmol/L: 69 mg/dL ≈ 3.8 mmol/L).
cards.result: Glycemic thresholds were 69 ± 2 mg/dL for epinephrine secretion, 68 ± 2 mg/dL for glucagon, 66 ± 2 mg/dL for growth hormone and 58 ± 3 mg/dL for cortisol. The threshold for symptoms was 53 ± 2 mg/dL — significantly lower than the thresholds for epinephrine (P<0.001), glucagon (P<0.001) and growth hormone (P<0.01). The authors conclude the counter-regulatory systems switch on within or just below the physiological glucose range, substantially before symptoms — they serve prevention as well as correction of hypoglycemia.
cards.watchOut: Stepped clamp in 10 normal humans under hyperinsulinemia — thresholds under insulin-driven descent may differ from spontaneous or insulin-treated falls, and arterialized venous values were used.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (stepped hypoglycemic clamp) | Schwartz NS et al. Glycemic thresholds for activation of glucose counterregulatory systems are higher than the threshold for symptoms. J Clin Invest. 1987. PMID: 3546378. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era physiology). cards.headline: Heller & Cryer 1991: one episode of hypoglycemia shifts the whole hierarchy down — the next day's hormone and symptom responses to the same low glucose are blunted
cards.summary: Heller & Cryer 1991: one episode of hypoglycemia shifts the whole hierarchy down — the next day's hormone and symptom responses to the same low glucose are blunted
cards.people: Nine nondiabetic humans studied during clamped hypoglycemia (2.8 mmol/L ≈ 50 mg/dL) on consecutive mornings on two occasions, with interval afternoon hypoglycemia (3.0 mmol/L ≈ 54 mg/dL) on one occasion and interval afternoon euglycemia (5.0 mmol/L ≈ 90 mg/dL) on the other.
cards.result: Interval euglycemia reduced none of the measured responses. After interval afternoon hypoglycemia, the next morning's plasma epinephrine (P<0.005), glucagon (P<0.005), pancreatic polypeptide (P<0.01) and cortisol (P<0.02) responses, and total (P<0.001), neurogenic (P<0.001) and neuroglycopenic (P<0.05) symptom responses to the same hypoglycemia were all reduced. The thresholds of the hierarchy are therefore not fixed constants: a single antecedent episode moves the defences to lower glucose levels — the mechanism the authors link to iatrogenic hypoglycemia in insulin-treated diabetes.
cards.watchOut: Threshold plasticity shown in nondiabetic humans after a single afternoon episode; the size and duration of the shift after repeated episodes in diabetes is a separate, larger literature not carded here.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (clamp, crossover) | Heller SR, Cryer PE. Reduced neuroendocrine and symptomatic responses to subsequent hypoglycemia after 1 episode of hypoglycemia in nondiabetic humans. Diabetes. 1991. PMID: 1991573. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era physiology). cards.headline: Fanelli programme 1996: cognition fails as glucose descends through the stepped clamp (85 down to 40 mg/dL) — and, unlike the hormone thresholds, the cognitive threshold barely shifts after antecedent hypoglycemia in nondiabetic humans
cards.summary: Fanelli programme 1996: cognition fails as glucose descends through the stepped clamp (85 down to 40 mg/dL) — and, unlike the hormone thresholds, the cognitive threshold barely shifts after antecedent hypoglycemia in nondiabetic humans
cards.people: 16 healthy young adults (7 women, 9 men) studied on two occasions in random sequence — once after afternoon hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (2.6 ± 0.1 mmol/L, 47 ± 1 mg/dL) and once after afternoon euglycemia (4.8 ± 0.1 mmol/L, 86 ± 5 mg/dL) — with neuroendocrine, symptom and cognitive responses measured the next morning during stepped hypoglycemic clamps (4.7, 4.2, 3.6, 3.0, 2.8, 2.5 and 2.2 mmol/L; 85, 75, 65, 55, 50, 45 and 40 mg/dL). Cognitive tests: Serial Addition, Stroop Arrow Word, Delayed Non-Match to Sample and Paragraph Recall.
cards.result: Performance on the cognitive tests deteriorated during the stepped hypoglycemic clamps (P<0.0001) — that is, cognition failed progressively as glucose descended through the steps below the symptom threshold region. As expected, glucagon (P=0.0094), epinephrine (P=0.0063) and pancreatic polypeptide (P=0.0046) responses were significantly reduced after afternoon hypoglycemia, but there were no significant overall effects of antecedent hypoglycemia on hypoglycemic cognitive dysfunction (small task-specific differences at the 2.8 mmol/L (50 mg/dL) to 2.5 mmol/L (45 mg/dL) steps on two of four tasks only). The authors conclude glycemic thresholds for cognitive dysfunction, unlike those for hormone responses and symptoms, do not shift substantially after recent antecedent hypoglycemia in nondiabetic humans.
cards.watchOut: Cognitive thresholds are task-dependent (four different tests behaved differently); 'cognition fails' is a gradient across tasks, not a single glucose number.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (stepped clamp, randomised crossover) | Hvidberg A, Fanelli CG et al. Impact of recent antecedent hypoglycemia on hypoglycemic cognitive dysfunction in nondiabetic humans. Diabetes. 1996. PMID: 8690148. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era physiology). cards.headline: Fanelli 1998 (type 1 diabetes): after nocturnal hypoglycemia, cognitive deterioration during the morning clamp was less overall — in diabetes the cognitive threshold does shift down, unlike in nondiabetic humans
cards.summary: Fanelli 1998 (type 1 diabetes): after nocturnal hypoglycemia, cognitive deterioration during the morning clamp was less overall — in diabetes the cognitive threshold does shift down, unlike in nondiabetic humans
cards.people: 15 patients with type 1 diabetes studied on two occasions in random sequence: cognitive function during morning stepped hypoglycemic clamps (85, 75, 65, 55 and 45 mg/dL steps) after nocturnal (2330–0300) hypoglycemia (48 ± 2 mg/dL) versus after nocturnal euglycemia (109 ± 1 mg/dL); compared with 12 nondiabetic control subjects.
cards.result: Patients had absent glucagon (P=0.0009) and reduced epinephrine (P=0.0010), norepinephrine (P=0.0001) and neurogenic symptom (P=0.0480) responses to hypoglycemia, reduced further after nocturnal hypoglycemia. After nocturnal hypoglycemia there was less deterioration of cognitive function overall during the clamp (P=0.0065), with relative preservation of pattern recognition/memory (P=0.0371) and attention (P=0.0395) but not information processing or declarative memory. The authors conclude that in type 1 diabetes, glycemic thresholds for cognitive dysfunction, like those for autonomic and symptomatic responses, shift to lower glucose concentrations after recent antecedent hypoglycemia — contrasting with the nondiabetic finding on the previous card.
cards.watchOut: The type 1 diabetes finding (thresholds shift) and the nondiabetic finding on the previous card (cognitive threshold largely unshifted) genuinely differ — the contrast is kept on the faces rather than averaged away.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (stepped clamp, randomised crossover) | Fanelli CG et al. Impact of nocturnal hypoglycemia on hypoglycemic cognitive dysfunction in type 1 diabetes. Diabetes. 1998. PMID: 9836525. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era physiology). cards.headline: Synthesis: the glucose-threshold hierarchy — hormones at about 65–70 mg/dL, symptoms at about 53 mg/dL, cognition failing below that — and the whole ladder slides down after recent hypoglycemia
cards.summary: Synthesis: the glucose-threshold hierarchy — hormones at about 65–70 mg/dL, symptoms at about 53 mg/dL, cognition failing below that — and the whole ladder slides down after recent hypoglycemia
cards.people: Synthesis of Schwartz 1987, Heller & Cryer 1991 and the Fanelli programme (1996, 1998), framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not evidence cards). Hypoglycemia treatment shelves elsewhere in the library are different questions; this shelf is the threshold physiology only.
cards.result: Measured in stepped clamps, the defences engage in a fixed order as glucose falls: glucagon and epinephrine at 68–69 mg/dL (≈3.8 mmol/L), growth hormone at 66 mg/dL, cortisol at 58 mg/dL, symptoms at 53 mg/dL (≈2.9 mmol/L), and measurable cognitive failure as glucose descends below the symptom region through the 50–40 mg/dL steps (Fanelli programme). The hierarchy is plastic: one antecedent episode of hypoglycemia blunts the next day's hormone and symptom responses at the same glucose (Heller & Cryer), and in type 1 diabetes the cognitive threshold also shifts down after nocturnal hypoglycemia (Fanelli 1998) — the physiological basis of hypoglycemia-associated autonomic failure, as the textbook account frames it.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: thresholds are population- and history-dependent; the hierarchy's order is the established finding, the exact mg/dL values are the carded studies' values in clamp conditions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schwartz NS et al. J Clin Invest. 1987 (PMID: 3546378); Heller SR, Cryer PE. Diabetes. 1991 (PMID: 1991573); Hvidberg A, Fanelli CG et al. Diabetes. 1996 (PMID: 8690148); Fanelli CG et al. Diabetes. 1998 (PMID: 9836525). Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: The first three days of fasting: glucose and insulin fall steadily, counter-regulatory hormones and free fatty acids rise, ketones climb, and urinary nitrogen loss continues — the whole-body fuel switch, distinct from the liver's glucose-production fractions
shelves.question: In humans fasted for 24–72 hours, how do glucose, insulin, ketones and nitrogen loss change over time?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · B-Lymphocytes/chemistry · Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · C-Peptide/blood · Chemistry, Clinical/standards · Epinephrine/blood · Fasting/physiology · Fatty Acids, Nonesterified/blood · Female · Glucagon/blood · Human Growth Hormone/blood · Humans · Hydrocortisone/blood · Hyperinsulinism/blood,diagnosis · Hypoglycemia/blood,diagnosis · Insulin/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/blood · Peptides/analysis · Proinsulin/blood · Reference Values · Serum Albumin · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for a deliberately narrow slice. Live shelf #34 already homes hepatic glucose production and its gluconeogenesis/recycling fractions during fasting (the Katz & Tayek tracer programme); this shelf does not re-card any of that work and asks the uncovered whole-body question: what happens to circulating glucose, insulin, ketones and nitrogen loss across 24–72 hours. The carded human studies agree: glucose, insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin all fall progressively through a 72-hour fast in 33 healthy subjects (Højlund 2001, the reference-interval study); counter-regulatory hormones and free fatty acids rise; and in non-obese subjects fasted 3–7 days, blood ketones rose progressively, glucose and alanine fell, insulin and triiodothyronine fell, urea nitrogen excretion fell while total urinary nitrogen did not change significantly (Garty 1985). Sherwin's ketone-infusion experiments supply the mechanism the time course implies: raising blood ketones itself lowers alanine and urinary nitrogen, part of how the fast becomes protein-sparing as ketones climb. The fuller Cahill/Owen account — respiratory quotient falling toward fat oxidation and nitrogen loss declining over weeks — is presented in the Synthesis as the Guyton & Hall textbook framing where the 24–72-hour carded records do not themselves print those numbers.

cards.headline: Højlund 2001: across a 72-hour fast in 33 healthy subjects, glucose, insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin all decreased while glucagon and free fatty acids rose linearly
cards.summary: Højlund 2001: across a 72-hour fast in 33 healthy subjects, glucose, insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin all decreased while glucagon and free fatty acids rose linearly
cards.type: Human physiological study (supervised 72-hour fast, reference intervals), Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2001
cards.people: Thirty-three healthy subjects (16 men, 17 women) studied through a supervised 72-hour fast to establish reference intervals for beta-cell and counter-regulatory responses to prolonged fasting.
cards.result: Glucose, insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin levels decreased through the fast (P < 0.001), and counter-regulatory factors increased (P < 0.05): glucagon and free fatty acids with a linear rise across the 72 hours, and epinephrine, norepinephrine and cortisol rising with a circadian rhythm underneath. Growth hormone secretion increased from day 1 to day 3 overall but decreased from day 2 to day 3. Men kept higher glucose and glucagon and lower free fatty acids than women; higher body mass index meant higher insulin and C-peptide throughout. This is the cleanest modern description of the hormonal half of the 24–72-hour window.
cards.watchOut: The record reports directions and significance, not a table of absolute glucose or insulin values at each time point, so no invented day-by-day numbers are printed; ketones were not among this study's reported analytes — the ketone time course is carried by the Garty card.
cards.source: Højlund K et al. Reference intervals for glucose, beta-cell polypeptides, and counterregulatory factors during prolonged fasting. Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab. 2001. PMID: 11120658. cards.headline: Garty 1985: in 8 non-obese subjects fasted 3–7 days, ketones rose progressively, glucose and insulin fell, urea nitrogen excretion fell — but total urinary nitrogen did not change significantly
cards.summary: Garty 1985: in 8 non-obese subjects fasted 3–7 days, ketones rose progressively, glucose and insulin fell, urea nitrogen excretion fell — but total urinary nitrogen did not change significantly
cards.type: Human physiological study (3–7-day fasts with urinary nitrogen fractions), Isr J Med Sci 1985
cards.people: Eight non-obese subjects fasted for periods ranging from 3 to 7 days, with serial blood metabolites, hormones and urinary nitrogen fractions. N = 8 — a small classic fasting study, printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Blood ketones rose progressively as the fast lengthened (the record prints the day-range value with an apparent unit misprint, so the rise is reported qualitatively rather than as a number). Glucose and alanine concentrations decreased significantly; serum insulin and triiodothyronine decreased; urinary 17-hydroxycorticosteroid excretion doubled. Urea nitrogen excretion decreased in those who fasted 5–7 days, while total urinary nitrogen excretion did not change significantly — and 3-methylhistidine excretion (a muscle-protein breakdown marker) rose, in some subjects more than doubling, a discrepancy the authors read as a high rate of nitrogen recycling.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 and the fasts extend beyond the 72-hour window (3–7 days), so this card bounds the window's far edge rather than describing its interior; the ketone concentration in the record carries an apparent unit misprint and is not reproduced as a number.
cards.source: Garty R et al. Excretion of 3-methylhistidine in nonobese fasting subjects. Isr J Med Sci. 1985. PMID: 3908395. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Sherwin 1975: infusing ketones to fasting-range levels cut plasma alanine 21% in 3 hours and urinary nitrogen 30% — hyperketonaemia itself drives the nitrogen-sparing of the fast
cards.summary: Sherwin 1975: infusing ketones to fasting-range levels cut plasma alanine 21% in 3 hours and urinary nitrogen 30% — hyperketonaemia itself drives the nitrogen-sparing of the fast
cards.type: Human physiological study (ketone infusion across fasting states), J Clin Invest 1975
cards.people: Non-obese and obese subjects studied postabsorptively, after 3 days of starvation, and after 3–5.5 weeks of starvation, receiving primed continuous infusions of sodium DL-beta-hydroxybutyrate for 3–6 hours (one obese group received 12-hour infusions on 2 consecutive days after 5–10 weeks of fasting). The record does not print a total participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Ketone infusion in the postabsorptive state raised total blood ketones to 1.1–1.2 mmol/L (about 11–12 mg/dL as beta-hydroxybutyrate equivalents), lowered plasma glucose by 5–15 mg/100 mL (5–15 mg/dL), and cut plasma alanine by 21% within 3 hours (P < 0.001) and 37% by 6 hours, while other amino acids moved less than 10%; saline and bicarbonate controls did not reproduce this. In prolonged-fasted subjects, repeated 12-hour infusions cut urinary nitrogen excretion by 30%, returning to baseline when infusions stopped. Fasted subjects showed two- to fourfold greater ketone increments from the same infusion — the ketone signal both marks and mediates the shift to protein sparing.
cards.watchOut: An infusion experiment, not a fasting time course: it isolates ketones' causal contribution to alanine and nitrogen changes but does not itself chart the 24–72-hour trajectory. Glucose fall is printed in the record's mg/100 mL, which equals mg/dL. N not documented in the record, printed on the face.
cards.source: Sherwin RS et al. Effect of ketone infusions on amino acid and nitrogen metabolism in man. J Clin Invest. 1975. PMID: 1133179. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Synthesis: by 72 hours the fast has switched fuels — glucose and insulin down, fatty acids and glucagon up, ketones climbing, nitrogen still being lost but increasingly spared as ketones rise
cards.summary: Synthesis: by 72 hours the fast has switched fuels — glucose and insulin down, fatty acids and glucagon up, ketones climbing, nitrogen still being lost but increasingly spared as ketones rise
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Højlund 2001; Garty 1985; Sherwin 1975), framed by Guyton & Hall's account of the Cahill/Owen starvation programme as textbook framing.
cards.result: Within the carded window the pattern is concordant: insulin secretion (insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin) falls progressively and glucose settles lower (Højlund); glucagon and free fatty acids rise roughly linearly; ketones rise progressively across days 3–7 (Garty) and, once raised, themselves suppress alanine release and urinary nitrogen (Sherwin) — the beginnings of protein sparing, though total urinary nitrogen has not yet fallen significantly by day 3–7 and urea nitrogen falls first. The textbook account (Guyton & Hall, presenting the Cahill/Owen programme) extends the curve beyond the carded window: respiratory quotient falls toward ~0.7 as fat becomes the dominant fuel and daily nitrogen loss declines over subsequent weeks as the brain adapts to ketones — presented as the textbook's account, since no carded 24–72-hour record prints respiratory-quotient values. What this shelf does not do is re-derive the liver's glucose-production fractions: those live on shelf #34 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The three cards measure different slices (hormones over 72 hours; metabolites and nitrogen over 3–7 days; ketone infusions across fasting states), so the time course is a composite, and absolute day-by-day glucose and ketone values vary with sex, adiposity and prior diet — the Højlund record itself shows sex and BMI effects. One card is N = 8 and one record prints no N; both are labelled on their faces.
cards.source: Synthesis of Højlund K et al., Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2001 (PMID: 11120658); Garty R et al., Isr J Med Sci 1985 (PMID: 3908395); Sherwin RS et al., J Clin Invest 1975 (PMID: 1133179). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Mazdutide (Innovent, China only) for obesity and type 2 diabetes: phase 3 trials show 10-17% weight loss and HbA1c falls up to 2.15% - a single Chinese programme, capped at POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In adults with obesity (with or without type 2 diabetes), does the dual glucagon/GLP-1 receptor agonist mazdutide, compared with placebo or standard care, produce clinically important weight loss and glycaemic improvement?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Body Mass Index · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Obesity/drug therapy · Overweight/drug therapy · Receptors, Glucagon/agonists · Weight Loss/drug effects · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Treatment Outcome · Peptides · East Asian People
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme cap. Mazdutide is a once-weekly dual glucagon receptor / GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by Innovent Biologics (the tested product is named here under the clarification exception: it is not FDA-approved and was approved only in China as of 2025). PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate question called mazdutide a 'dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist'; every fetched record describes a glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist, and the pack question is worded accordingly. In obesity without diabetes (GLORY-1, 610 adults), weight fell 10.09% on 4 mg and 12.55% on 6 mg at week 32 against +0.45% on placebo; in more severe obesity (GLORY-2, 9 mg), weight fell 16.65% against 1.50% at week 60. In type 2 diabetes, mazdutide monotherapy lowered HbA1c by 1.57-2.15% against 0.14% on placebo (DREAMS-1), and beat dulaglutide 1.5 mg on both HbA1c (differences -0.24% and -0.30%) and weight (differences -3.78% and -5.76%) (DREAMS-2). Gastrointestinal adverse events are frequent (vomiting in 53.1% on the 9 mg dose in GLORY-2) but mostly mild to moderate, with low discontinuation rates. All four trials are Innovent's Chinese phase 3 programme: the effects are large and internally consistent, but generalisability beyond Chinese populations and long-term cardiovascular safety are untested, which is why the stamp stops at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: GLORY-1 (2025): mazdutide 4 mg and 6 mg produced weight loss of -10.09% and -12.55% at week 32 against +0.45% on placebo in 610 Chinese adults with overweight or obesity
cards.summary: GLORY-1 (2025): mazdutide 4 mg and 6 mg produced weight loss of -10.09% and -12.55% at week 32 against +0.45% on placebo in 610 Chinese adults with overweight or obesity
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GLORY-1) - 610 participants
cards.people: 610 Chinese adults aged 18-75 with a body-mass index of at least 28, or 24 to under 28 plus at least one weight-related coexisting condition (mean body weight 87.2 kg, mean BMI 31.1), randomised 1:1:1 to once-weekly mazdutide 4 mg, mazdutide 6 mg, or placebo for 48 weeks. The tested product was Innovent Biologics mazdutide; the trial was funded by Innovent Biologics.
cards.result: At week 32 the mean percentage change in body weight was -10.09% (95% CI -11.15 to -9.04) on 4 mg, -12.55% (95% CI -13.64 to -11.45) on 6 mg, and +0.45% (95% CI -0.61 to 1.52) on placebo; a weight reduction of at least 5% was achieved by 73.9%, 82.0% and 10.5% respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). At week 48, weight change was -11.00%, -14.01% and +0.30%, and at least 15% loss was achieved by 35.7%, 49.5% and 2.0%. Beneficial effects on all prespecified cardiometabolic measures were seen. The most frequent adverse events were gastrointestinal and mostly mild to moderate; discontinuation for adverse events was 1.5% (4 mg), 0.5% (6 mg) and 1.0% (placebo).
cards.watchOut: A single-country (China), single-sponsor phase 3 trial in people without diabetes as the primary population; the week-32 primary estimand counts effects regardless of discontinuation or rescue therapy. Weight loss of this size is in the range of other dual agonists, but no non-Chinese population has been randomised to mazdutide.
cards.source: Ji L et al. Once-Weekly Mazdutide in Chinese Adults with Obesity or Overweight. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40421736. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05607680, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: GLORY-2 (2026): mazdutide 9 mg produced weight loss of -16.65% against -1.50% on placebo at week 60 in Chinese adults with obesity (BMI at least 30)
cards.summary: GLORY-2 (2026): mazdutide 9 mg produced weight loss of -16.65% against -1.50% on placebo at week 60 in Chinese adults with obesity (BMI at least 30)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GLORY-2) - 461 participants treated
cards.people: Chinese adults with obesity (BMI at least 30), with or without type 2 diabetes, at 27 hospitals: 461 participants received study treatment (307 mazdutide 9 mg once weekly, 154 placebo) as an adjunct to reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for 60 weeks; 64.0% were women, 16.1% had type 2 diabetes, mean age was 33.9 years, mean body weight 94.0 kg and mean BMI 34.3. The tested product was Innovent Biologics mazdutide.
cards.result: At week 60, mean percentage weight change was -16.65% (95% CI -18.19% to -15.12%) on mazdutide against -1.50% (95% CI -3.43% to 0.43%) on placebo (between-group difference -15.15%, 95% CI -17.22% to -13.09%; P<.001). A reduction of at least 5% was achieved by 84.3% against 33.1% (difference 51.6%, 95% CI 43.0% to 60.1%; P<.001). Adverse events leading to discontinuation were reported in 2.9% on mazdutide against 0% on placebo; the most common adverse events were vomiting (53.1% vs 1.3%), nausea (46.9% vs 3.2%) and diarrhoea (39.4% vs 6.5%), mostly mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: The 9 mg dose carries a heavy gastrointestinal burden - over half of treated participants vomited - even though few stopped treatment. Participants were young (mean age 33.9) and Chinese; tolerability and effect in older or non-Chinese populations are unknown.
cards.source: Gao L et al. Treatment With 9-mg Mazdutide for Weight Reduction in Chinese Adults With Obesity: The GLORY-2 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 42251595. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06164873, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: DREAMS-1 (2026): mazdutide monotherapy lowered HbA1c by -1.57% (4 mg) and -2.15% (6 mg) against -0.14% on placebo at week 24 in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes on diet and exercise alone
cards.summary: DREAMS-1 (2026): mazdutide monotherapy lowered HbA1c by -1.57% (4 mg) and -2.15% (6 mg) against -0.14% on placebo at week 24 in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes on diet and exercise alone
cards.people: 320 Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with diet and exercise alone (mean HbA1c 8.24%, mean BMI 28.2 kg/m2, mean diabetes duration 1.9 years), randomised 1:1:1 to once-weekly mazdutide 4 mg, mazdutide 6 mg, or placebo for 24 weeks, followed by a 24-week extended mazdutide treatment period. The tested product was Innovent Biologics mazdutide.
cards.result: At week 24, HbA1c fell by -1.57% on 4 mg and -2.15% on 6 mg against -0.14% on placebo (treatment differences -1.43% and -2.02%; both P<0.0001). Weight fell by -5.61% (4 mg) and -7.81% (6 mg) against -1.26% on placebo (both P<0.0001). More participants on mazdutide achieved HbA1c under 7.0%, weight loss of at least 5%, and the composite of both. The most common adverse events were diarrhoea, decreased appetite and nausea, consistent with GLP-1 receptor agonists.
cards.watchOut: A monotherapy trial in early, diet-treated diabetes (mean duration 1.9 years) - the glycaemic falls are larger than would be expected in longer-standing diabetes on background drugs. The record carries no registry identifier, and the population is again exclusively Chinese.
cards.source: Zhu D et al. Mazdutide versus placebo in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes. Nature. 2026. PMID: 41407859. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: DREAMS-2 (2026): mazdutide 4 mg and 6 mg were superior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg for HbA1c (differences -0.24% and -0.30%) and weight (differences -3.78% and -5.76%) at week 28 in type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: DREAMS-2 (2026): mazdutide 4 mg and 6 mg were superior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg for HbA1c (differences -0.24% and -0.30%) and weight (differences -3.78% and -5.76%) at week 28 in type 2 diabetes
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind comparative trial (DREAMS-2) - 731 participants
cards.people: 731 Chinese participants with type 2 diabetes on background oral antidiabetic drugs, randomised 1:1:1 to mazdutide 4 mg, mazdutide 6 mg, or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly for 28 weeks. The tested product was Innovent Biologics mazdutide.
cards.result: Both mazdutide doses showed non-inferiority and superiority to dulaglutide 1.5 mg for change in HbA1c at week 28: least-squares mean treatment differences of -0.24% (P=0.0032) for 4 mg and -0.30% (P=0.0003) for 6 mg. Weight reductions were significantly greater with mazdutide (differences -3.78% for 4 mg and -5.76% for 6 mg; both P<0.0001), and significantly more mazdutide participants reached the composite of HbA1c under 7.0% with at least 5% weight loss. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, with a higher incidence of gastrointestinal events on mazdutide than dulaglutide.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is dulaglutide at its 1.5 mg dose, not the higher dulaglutide doses or semaglutide/tirzepatide; superiority over this one comparator does not rank mazdutide within the incretin class. Gastrointestinal tolerability was worse than the comparator.
cards.source: Guo L et al. Mazdutide versus dulaglutide in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes. Nature. 2026. PMID: 41407860. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - one sponsor's Chinese phase 3 programme shows large, consistent weight and HbA1c effects; nothing outside that programme yet tests the drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit) - one sponsor's Chinese phase 3 programme shows large, consistent weight and HbA1c effects; nothing outside that programme yet tests the drug
cards.people: The carded evidence is the complete Innovent phase 3 programme as published: GLORY-1 (610 adults with overweight/obesity), GLORY-2 (461 treated adults with obesity, 9 mg dose), DREAMS-1 (320 adults with early type 2 diabetes, monotherapy) and DREAMS-2 (731 adults with type 2 diabetes versus dulaglutide). No trial outside China, and no cardiovascular-outcome trial, exists in the fetched records.
cards.result: Weight: -10.09% to -12.55% at week 32 (GLORY-1, 4-6 mg), -16.65% at week 60 on 9 mg (GLORY-2), each against minimal placebo change. Glycaemia: HbA1c -1.57% to -2.15% as monotherapy (DREAMS-1) and superiority over dulaglutide 1.5 mg on HbA1c and weight (DREAMS-2). Harms are dominated by gastrointestinal events, frequent at the 9 mg dose (vomiting 53.1%) but with discontinuation rates under 3%. The balance favours real, clinically important efficacy within the tested populations; the unknowns are generalisability, long-term safety, and cardiovascular outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Single-programme cap: all four trials share one sponsor, one country and short horizons (24-60 weeks). The stamp must not be read as class-level proof, and the product's regulatory status (approved only in China as of 2025) means availability and manufacturing oversight differ from FDA-approved dual agonists.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ji L et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40421736, NCT05607680); Gao L et al. JAMA. 2026 (PMID: 42251595, NCT06164873); Zhu D et al. shelves.title: Macimorelin stimulation test for adult GH deficiency (test accuracy): sensitivity 87% and specificity 96% at the 2.8 ng/mL cut-off against the insulin tolerance test; 92% and 96% at 5.1 ng/mL
shelves.question: In adults being evaluated for growth hormone deficiency, how accurately does the oral macimorelin stimulation test, compared with the insulin tolerance test, diagnose adult GH deficiency?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Age of Onset · Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Diagnostic Tests, Routine/adverse effects,methods · Female · Human Growth Hormone/deficiency · Humans · Hypopituitarism/blood,diagnosis,epidemiology · Indoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Pituitary Function Tests/adverse effects,methods · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity · Tryptophan/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Test-accuracy question - stamped as such. The phase 3 crossover validation trial (Garcia 2018; NCT02558829) compared single-dose oral macimorelin with the insulin tolerance test (ITT) in people at high, intermediate and low likelihood of adult GH deficiency plus matched controls. At the prespecified cut-offs (2.8 ng/mL for macimorelin, 5.1 ng/mL for ITT), sensitivity was 87% and specificity 96%, with negative agreement 95.38% and positive agreement 74.32%; 99% of macimorelin tests were evaluable against 82% of ITTs, test-retest reproducibility was 97%, and no serious adverse events occurred. Post hoc analyses in the same trial, confirmed by the 2021 reanalysis, found that a 5.1 ng/mL macimorelin cut-off raises sensitivity to 92% while holding specificity at 96%. The earlier 2013 validation study (against arginine+GHRH, not the ITT) found sensitivity 82% and specificity 92% at a 2.7 ng/mL cut point. The evidence is one development programme with spectrum-enriched samples (known likelihood strata plus healthy controls), which tends to flatter accuracy; that is why the accuracy verdict is POSSIBLE rather than stronger.

cards.headline: Garcia 2018 (phase 3 validation vs the insulin tolerance test): at a 2.8 ng/mL cut-off, macimorelin sensitivity was 87% and specificity 96%; 99% of macimorelin tests were evaluable against 82% of ITTs
cards.summary: Garcia 2018 (phase 3 validation vs the insulin tolerance test): at a 2.8 ng/mL cut-off, macimorelin sensitivity was 87% and specificity 96%; 99% of macimorelin tests were evaluable against 82% of ITTs
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre, open-label, randomised two-way crossover diagnostic validation trial (Garcia 2018) - 139 subjects in the efficacy analysis
cards.people: Subjects with high (n=38), intermediate (n=37) and low (n=39) likelihood of adult GH deficiency and healthy matched controls (n=25) in the efficacy analysis of a multicentre, open-label, randomised two-way crossover trial; each subject underwent both single-dose oral macimorelin and the insulin tolerance test (ITT).
cards.result: After the first test, 99% of macimorelin tests and 82% of ITTs were evaluable. Using GH cut-offs of 2.8 ng/mL for macimorelin and 5.1 ng/mL for the ITT, negative agreement was 95.38% (95% CI 87% to 99%), positive agreement was 74.32% (95% CI 63% to 84%), sensitivity was 87% and specificity was 96%. On retesting, macimorelin reproducibility was 97% (n=33). In post hoc analyses, a 5.1 ng/mL cut-off for both tests gave negative agreement 94%, positive agreement 82%, sensitivity 92% and specificity 96%. No serious adverse events were reported for macimorelin.
cards.watchOut: The study population was assembled by pre-test likelihood strata plus healthy matched controls - a spectrum that usually makes a test look better than it performs in consecutive clinic referrals. Positive agreement (74.32%) is notably weaker than negative agreement, so a positive macimorelin result at the 2.8 ng/mL cut-off is the less certain direction.
cards.source: Garcia JM et al. Macimorelin as a Diagnostic Test for Adult GH Deficiency. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2018. PMID: 29860473. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02558829, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: 2021 reanalysis: macimorelin performance was not meaningfully affected by age, BMI or sex (ROC area about 0.99), and of the cut-points tested, 5.1 ng/mL gave the best balance - specificity 96% and sensitivity 92%
cards.summary: 2021 reanalysis: macimorelin performance was not meaningfully affected by age, BMI or sex (ROC area about 0.99), and of the cut-points tested, 5.1 ng/mL gave the best balance - specificity 96% and sensitivity 92%
cards.type: Post hoc reanalysis of the phase 3 validation trial (2021) - cut-point and covariate analysis
cards.people: Post hoc analyses of the phase 3 macimorelin-versus-ITT trial data: participants aged 18-66 years with BMI under 37 kg/m2 in high (Group A), intermediate (Group B) and low (Group C) likelihood strata and matched controls (Group D); the receiver-operating-characteristic analyses used Group A (n=41) and Group D (n=29).
cards.result: Unadjusted, age-adjusted, BMI-adjusted and sex-adjusted models had ROC areas under the curve of 0.9924, 0.9924, 0.9916 and 0.9950 respectively - macimorelin performance was not meaningfully affected by age, BMI or sex. Across cut-points of 2.8, 4.0, 5.1 and 6.5 ng/mL, the 5.1 ng/mL cut-point provided maximal specificity (96%) and high sensitivity (92%) and was in good overall agreement with the ITT at the same cut-point (87%).
cards.watchOut: This is a reanalysis of the same single trial dataset as the 2018 validation report, not independent confirmation; the 5.1 ng/mL cut-off was selected post hoc from the data that are then used to praise it, which optimistically biases its apparent performance.
cards.source: Garcia JM et al. Sensitivity and specificity of the macimorelin test for diagnosis of AGHD. Endocrine connections. 2021. PMID: 33320108. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Garcia 2013 (earlier validation, against arginine+GHRH): a macimorelin cut point of 2.7 ng/mL gave sensitivity 82% and specificity 92% for adult GH deficiency
cards.summary: Garcia 2013 (earlier validation, against arginine+GHRH): a macimorelin cut point of 2.7 ng/mL gave sensitivity 82% and specificity 92% for adult GH deficiency
cards.type: Multicentre open-label diagnostic validation study (Garcia 2013) - 50 AGHD patients and 48 controls evaluated (comparator: arginine+GHRH, not the ITT)
cards.people: 50 subjects with adult GH deficiency and 48 healthy matched controls evaluated in a multicentre open-label study; the original design compared macimorelin with arginine+GHRH in 43 patients and 10 controls, and after the GHRH analogue became unavailable in the United States the study was completed by testing 10 additional patients and 38 controls with macimorelin alone.
cards.result: Peak GH after macimorelin was 2.36 +/- 5.69 ng/mL in GH-deficient patients against 17.71 +/- 19.11 ng/mL in controls (P<.0001). Receiver-operating-characteristic analysis gave an optimal macimorelin GH cut point of 2.7 ng/mL, with 82% sensitivity, 92% specificity and 13% misclassification (the record's abstract truncates at this point).
cards.watchOut: The comparator here is arginine+GHRH, not the insulin tolerance test that this shelf's question names - this card supports the test's general validity, not its ITT agreement. The mid-study loss of the comparator drug also means part of the sample has no paired comparison at all.
cards.source: Garcia JM et al. Macimorelin (AEZS-130)-stimulated growth hormone (GH) test: validation of a novel oral stimulation test for the diagnosis of adult GH deficiency. cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (diagnostic accuracy) - macimorelin agrees closely with the insulin tolerance test and is far easier to complete, but the accuracy figures come from one sponsor programme with likelihood-enriched samples
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (diagnostic accuracy) - macimorelin agrees closely with the insulin tolerance test and is far easier to complete, but the accuracy figures come from one sponsor programme with likelihood-enriched samples
cards.people: The carded evidence is the macimorelin development programme: the 2013 validation study against arginine+GHRH (50 patients, 48 controls), the 2018 phase 3 crossover validation against the insulin tolerance test (139 subjects in the efficacy analysis), and the 2021 post hoc reanalysis of that same phase 3 dataset.
cards.result: Against the ITT, macimorelin at the approved 2.8 ng/mL cut-off gives sensitivity 87% and specificity 96%; at 5.1 ng/mL, sensitivity 92% and specificity 96%. Evaluability (99% vs 82%) and reproducibility (97%) favour macimorelin, and it avoids ITT hypoglycaemia. The 2013 study's lower figures (82%/92% at 2.7 ng/mL, against a different comparator) bracket the phase 3 estimates from below. No independent, non-programme validation in consecutive referrals was found in the fetched records.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is not outcome benefit: no carded study shows that diagnosing with macimorelin rather than the ITT changes treatment or patient outcomes. Spectrum enrichment (pre-stratified likelihood groups plus healthy controls) is the standing reason this accuracy verdict stays at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Garcia JM et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2018 (PMID: 29860473, NCT02558829); Garcia JM et al. shelves.title: Prolactinoma: surgery-first versus dopamine-agonist-first (observational only, no RCT exists) - pooled cohorts find long-term remission off treatment of 67-88% after surgery against 34-52% after drug withdrawal
shelves.question: In patients with prolactinoma, does first-line transsphenoidal surgery, compared with first-line cabergoline (dopamine-agonist therapy), achieve comparable remission with better long-term treatment freedom?
shelves.mesh: Critical Pathways/standards · Dopamine Agonists/pharmacology,standards,therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Hypophysectomy/adverse effects,methods,standards · Microsurgery/adverse effects,methods,standards · Pituitary Gland/drug effects,metabolism,pathology,surgery · Pituitary Neoplasms/pathology,therapy · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Prolactin/metabolism · Prolactinoma/pathology,therapy · Remission Induction/methods · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Observational evidence only - no randomised trial of surgery-first versus drug-first exists, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. Three meta-analyses pooling non-randomised cohorts point the same way on the question that matters for this shelf - durable remission after treatment stops. The JCEM 2020 analysis (55 medical studies, 3,564 patients; 25 surgical studies, 1,836 patients) found long-term remission of 34% after dopamine-agonist withdrawal against 67% after surgery (microprolactinoma: 36% against 83%), while on-treatment biochemical control with dopamine agonists was 81% with side effects in 26%; surgery carried 0% mortality, 2% permanent diabetes insipidus and 3% cerebrospinal fluid leak. The microprolactinoma analysis (2021) adds the key nuance: while treatment continues, dopamine agonists remit more (96% vs 86% at 12 months or more), but after withdrawal surgery remits more (78% vs 44%). The 2018 analysis found long-term remission of 88% (surgery) against 52% (drugs). Selection bias runs through all of this - surgical series take smaller, non-invasive tumours - so the honest reading is: for suitably selected (especially micro-) prolactinomas, surgery-first offers comparable control and a genuinely better chance of long-term treatment freedom, unproven by randomisation.

cards.headline: JCEM 2020 meta-analysis (observational): long-term remission was 34% after dopamine-agonist withdrawal against 67% after transsphenoidal surgery; in microprolactinoma, 36% against 83%
cards.summary: JCEM 2020 meta-analysis (observational): long-term remission was 34% after dopamine-agonist withdrawal against 67% after transsphenoidal surgery; in microprolactinoma, 36% against 83%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational cohorts (2020) - 55 medical studies (3,564 patients) and 25 surgical studies (1,836 patients)
cards.people: Pooled non-randomised studies of prolactinoma patients treated with dopamine agonists (55 studies, 3,564 patients; 10 at low risk of bias) or transsphenoidal surgery (25 studies, 1,836 patients; 12 at low risk of bias), searched to July 2018. The primary outcome was disease remission after drug withdrawal or after surgery.
cards.result: Long-term disease remission after dopamine-agonist withdrawal was 34% (95% CI 26% to 46%) and 67% (95% CI 60% to 74%) after surgery. In microprolactinomas, remission after withdrawal was 36% (95% CI 21% to 52%) against 83% (95% CI 76% to 90%) after surgery. Biochemical control during dopamine-agonist treatment was 81% (95% CI 75% to 87%) with side effects in 26% (95% CI 13% to 41%). Transsphenoidal surgery resulted in 0% mortality, 2% (95% CI 0% to 5%) permanent diabetes insipidus and 3% (95% CI 2% to 5%) cerebrospinal fluid leakage (the record's abstract truncates at this point).
cards.watchOut: These are parallel pooled proportions from separate medical and surgical literatures, not head-to-head comparisons: surgeons operate on selected tumours (smaller, non-invasive, often in patients who prefer surgery), which inflates the surgical remission rate relative to unselected drug-treated cohorts.
cards.source: Zamanipoor Najafabadi AH et al. Surgery as a Viable Alternative First-Line Treatment for Prolactinoma Patients. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2020. PMID: 31665485. Registry ID: none in the record.
