cards.headline: Microprolactinoma meta-analysis 2021 (observational): dopamine agonists remit more while treatment continues (96% vs 86%), but surgery remits more after treatment stops (78% vs 44%)
cards.summary: Microprolactinoma meta-analysis 2021 (observational): dopamine agonists remit more while treatment continues (96% vs 86%), but surgery remits more after treatment stops (78% vs 44%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies in microprolactinoma (2021) - 18 studies, 661 patients
cards.people: 18 studies with 661 patients with treatment-naive microprolactinoma treated with dopamine agonists and/or surgery as initial therapy (literature to November 2020). The outcome was biochemical remission of serum prolactin to normal after treatment, and after treatment withdrawal.
cards.result: The dopamine-agonist group achieved a higher remission rate at 12 months or more of follow-up (96% vs 86%; P=0.019). After treatment withdrawal, surgery showed the higher remission rate (78% vs 44%; P=0.003). Patients with a preoperative prolactin level of 200 ng/mL or less had a higher surgical remission rate than those above 200 ng/mL (92% vs 40%; P=0.029).
cards.watchOut: Microprolactinoma only - the tumour type most favourable to surgery - and again non-randomised: the withdrawal comparison in particular compares surgical patients selected for operability with drug patients who attempted withdrawal, two differently filtered groups.
cards.source: Lu J et al. Surgery and Medical Treatment in Microprolactinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International journal of endocrinology. 2021. PMID: 34504526. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: 2018 meta-analysis (observational): long-term remission was achieved in 88% of surgically treated patients against 52% on dopamine agonists (microprolactinoma 91% vs 60%; macroprolactinoma 77% vs 43%)
cards.summary: 2018 meta-analysis (observational): long-term remission was achieved in 88% of surgically treated patients against 52% on dopamine agonists (microprolactinoma 91% vs 60%; macroprolactinoma 77% vs 43%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational cohorts (2018) - 13 publications, 809 patients
cards.people: 13 publications with 809 patients with micro- or macroprolactinoma who received primary dopamine-agonist treatment or primary surgical intervention (literature to July 2018). The clinical outcome was the long-term remission rate of prolactin in each cohort.
cards.result: In all patients, long-term remission was achieved in 88% of the surgery cohort against 52% of the dopamine-agonist cohort (P=0.001). The surgical advantage held in both size strata: microprolactinomas 91% vs 60% (P=0.002) and macroprolactinomas 77% vs 43% (P=0.003). The authors conclude that transsphenoidal surgery can be considered an alternative first-line strategy, with postoperative dopamine agonists guided by the postoperative prolactin level.
cards.watchOut: The oldest and smallest of the three pooled analyses, with the largest apparent surgical advantage - the pattern (bigger effect in the weaker synthesis) is itself a warning about selection and publication bias in the underlying surgical series.
cards.source: Ma Q et al. The Chance of Permanent Cure for Micro- and Macroprolactinomas, Medication or Surgery? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in endocrinology. 2018. PMID: 30410470. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational) - surgery-first matches drug-first for control and beats it for durable remission off treatment in pooled cohorts, but no randomised comparison exists and surgical series are selected
cards.summary: Synthesis: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational) - surgery-first matches drug-first for control and beats it for durable remission off treatment in pooled cohorts, but no randomised comparison exists and surgical series are selected
cards.people: The carded evidence is three meta-analyses of non-randomised cohorts (2018: 809 patients; 2020: 5,400 patients across separate medical and surgical literatures; 2021 microprolactinoma: 661 patients). No randomised trial of first-line surgery versus first-line cabergoline was found in the fetched records.
cards.result: On treatment, dopamine agonists control prolactin at least as well as surgery (81% biochemical control in the 2020 pooling; 96% vs 86% remission at 12 months or more in microprolactinoma). Off treatment, the direction reverses in every synthesis: long-term remission 67-88% after surgery against 34-52% after drug withdrawal, with the gap widest in microprolactinoma (83% vs 36%). Surgical harms in the pooled series were 0% mortality, 2% permanent diabetes insipidus and 3% cerebrospinal fluid leak, against a 26% side-effect rate on dopamine agonists. The treatment-freedom half of this shelf's question is supported; the 'comparable remission' half holds only while drugs continue.
cards.watchOut: Observational cap: every number here comes from cohorts in which tumour size, invasiveness, patient preference and surgeon selection decided who was operated on. A randomised trial could shrink the surgical advantage substantially; the stamp and this shelf must keep the observational label on the face.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zamanipoor Najafabadi AH et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2020 (PMID: 31665485); Lu J et al. International journal of endocrinology. 2021 (PMID: 34504526); Ma Q et al. Frontiers in endocrinology. 2018 (PMID: 30410470). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Adding aliskiren to ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy: ALTITUDE (8,561 patients) found no outcome benefit and more hyperkalaemia and hypotension - surrogate trials (AVOID, ALOFT) improved markers only
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric kidney disease (or heart failure), does adding aliskiren to ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy, compared with ACE inhibitor/ARB alone, improve cardiovascular or renal outcomes or cause net harm?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Antihypertensive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fumarates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Hyperkalemia/chemically induced · Hypokalemia · Kidney Diseases/epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Dropouts · Treatment Failure · Renin Inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit, with harm). The programme tells one coherent story in three acts. AVOID (2008; 599 patients with diabetic nephropathy) showed the surrogate promise: adding aliskiren to losartan reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by a further 20% (a relative reduction) at 6 months. ALOFT (2008; 302 heart-failure patients) showed the same pattern on natriuretic peptides: NT-proBNP fell on aliskiren while rising on placebo (P=0.0106), with no clinically important blood-pressure or biochemistry differences. Then ALTITUDE (2012; 8,561 patients with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, or both) tested outcomes - and was stopped early: the primary cardiorenal composite occurred in 18.3% on aliskiren against 17.1% on placebo (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.20; P=0.12 - the treatment made no difference), while hyperkalaemia (potassium at least 6 mmol/L, i.e. 6 mEq/L) affected 11.2% against 7.2% and reported hypotension 12.1% against 8.3% (both P<0.001). The trial's own conclusion: adding aliskiren to renin-angiotensin blockade in high-risk diabetes 'is not supported by these data and may even be harmful'. Surrogate gains did not survive contact with outcomes; the stamp is LIKELY because the outcomes trial is large, definitive in direction, and concordant with the harm pattern.

cards.headline: ALTITUDE 2012: adding aliskiren to ACE inhibitor/ARB in 8,561 high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes - primary cardiorenal endpoint 18.3% vs 17.1% (HR 1.08; P=0.12; the treatment made no difference), with more hyperkalaemia (11.2% vs 7.2%) and hypotension (12.1% vs 8.3%)
cards.summary: ALTITUDE 2012: adding aliskiren to ACE inhibitor/ARB in 8,561 high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes - primary cardiorenal endpoint 18.3% vs 17.1% (HR 1.08; P=0.12; the treatment made no difference), with more hyperkalaemia (11.2% vs 7.2%) and hypotension (12.1% vs 8.3%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled outcomes trial (ALTITUDE, NEJM 2012) - 8,561 patients, stopped prematurely
cards.people: 8,561 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, or both, randomised double-blind to aliskiren 300 mg daily or placebo as an adjunct to an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin-receptor blocker. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death or resuscitated cardiac arrest, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, unplanned heart-failure hospitalisation, end-stage renal disease, death from kidney failure, need for renal replacement, or doubling of serum creatinine. The trial was stopped prematurely after the second interim efficacy analysis; median follow-up was 32.9 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint occurred in 783 patients (18.3%) on aliskiren against 732 (17.1%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.20; P=0.12 - a relative measure; the treatment made no difference). Secondary renal endpoints were similar. Blood pressure was slightly lower on aliskiren (between-group differences 1.3 mm Hg systolic and 0.6 mm Hg diastolic) and the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio fell more (difference 14 percentage points), yet hyperkalaemia (serum potassium at least 6 mmol/L, i.e. 6 mEq/L) was significantly more frequent on aliskiren (11.2% vs 7.2%), as was reported hypotension (12.1% vs 8.3%) (both P<0.001). The authors conclude the addition of aliskiren to standard renin-angiotensin blockade in this population is not supported and may even be harmful.
cards.watchOut: The population was deliberately high-risk (diabetes plus kidney and/or cardiovascular disease) and the dose was the full 300 mg on top of maximal background blockade - the harm pattern (hyperkalaemia, hypotension) is a dual-blockade class warning, and the null result is precise enough (upper confidence limit 1.20) to exclude the benefit the surrogate trials had promised.
cards.source: Parving HH et al. Cardiorenal end points in a trial of aliskiren for type 2 diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 23121378. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00549757, from the record's databank fields. the treatment made no difference). secondary renal endpoints were similar. blood pressure was slightly lower on aliskiren (between-group differences 1.3 mm hg systolic and 0.6 mm hg diastolic) and the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio fell more (difference 14 percentage points), yet hyperkalaemia (serum potassium at least 6 mmol/l, i.e. 6 meq/l) was significantly more frequent on aliskiren (11.2% vs 7.2%), as was reported hypotension (12.1% vs 8.3%) (both p<0.001). the authors conclude the addition of aliskiren to standard renin-angiotensin blockade in this population is not supported and may even be harmful. the population was deliberately high-risk (diabetes plus kidney and/or cardiovascular disease) and the dose was the full 300 mg on top of maximal background blockade - the harm pattern (hyperkalaemia, hypotension) is a dual-blockade class warning, and the null result is precise enough (upper confidence limit 1.20) to exclude the benefit the surrogate trials had promised. parving hh et al. cardiorenal end points in a trial of aliskiren for type 2 diabetes. the new england journal of medicine. 2012. pmid: 23121378. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct00549757, from the record's databank fields. mesh: aged · amides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · angiotensin receptor antagonists/therapeutic use · angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/therapeutic use · antihypertensive agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · cardiovascular diseases/epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · diabetes mellitus, type 2/complications,drug therapy · double-blind method · drug therapy, combination · female · follow-up studies · fumarates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · humans · hyperkalemia/chemically induced · hypokalemia · kidney diseases/epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · male · middle aged · patient dropouts · treatment failure · renin inhibitors

cards.headline: AVOID 2008: aliskiren added to losartan reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by a further 20% (a relative reduction) at 6 months in 599 patients with diabetic nephropathy - a surrogate benefit that outcomes testing later failed to confirm
cards.summary: AVOID 2008: aliskiren added to losartan reduced the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by a further 20% (a relative reduction) at 6 months in 599 patients with diabetic nephropathy - a surrogate benefit that outcomes testing later failed to confirm
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (AVOID, NEJM 2008) - 599 patients
cards.people: 599 patients with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and nephropathy, randomised after a 3-month open-label run-in on losartan 100 mg daily to aliskiren (150 mg daily for 3 months, then 300 mg daily) or placebo, in addition to losartan and optimal antihypertensive therapy, for 6 months. The primary outcome was change in the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
cards.result: Treatment with aliskiren 300 mg daily reduced the mean urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio by 20% (95% CI 9% to 30%; P<0.001) compared with placebo - a relative reduction in a surrogate marker. A reduction of 50% or more occurred in 24.7% on aliskiren against 12.5% on placebo (P<0.001). End-of-study blood-pressure differences were small (systolic 2 mm Hg lower, P=0.07; diastolic 1 mm Hg lower, P=0.08). Total adverse and serious adverse events were similar between groups over this short horizon.
cards.watchOut: A 6-month albuminuria trial: albuminuria reduction is the surrogate that ALTITUDE later showed does not translate into cardiorenal outcome benefit for this drug combination. AVOID's clean short-term safety also illustrates why the harm pattern needed an 8,561-patient outcomes trial to become visible.

cards.headline: ALOFT 2008: in 302 heart-failure patients on ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker, aliskiren lowered NT-proBNP (fell 244 pg/mL vs rose 762 pg/mL on placebo; P=0.0106) over 3 months - a neurohumoral surrogate, with no outcome measurement
cards.summary: ALOFT 2008: in 302 heart-failure patients on ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker, aliskiren lowered NT-proBNP (fell 244 pg/mL vs rose 762 pg/mL on placebo; P=0.0106) over 3 months - a neurohumoral surrogate, with no outcome measurement
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ALOFT, 2008) - 302 patients with heart failure
cards.people: 302 patients with NYHA class II-IV heart failure, current or past hypertension and plasma BNP over 100 pg/mL, already treated with an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and a beta-blocker (mean age 68 years; mean ejection fraction 31%; 62% NYHA class II; 33% on an aldosterone antagonist), randomised to aliskiren 150 mg daily (156 patients) or placebo (146 patients) for 3 months. The primary efficacy outcome was the between-treatment difference in NT-proBNP.
cards.result: Plasma NT-proBNP fell by 244 +/- 2025 pg/mL on aliskiren and rose by 762 +/- 6123 pg/mL on placebo (P=0.0106). BNP and urinary (but not plasma) aldosterone were also reduced by aliskiren. Clinically important differences in blood pressure and biochemistry were not seen between groups, and the authors describe the addition as having favourable neurohumoral effects and appearing well tolerated over 3 months.
cards.watchOut: A 3-month, 302-patient biomarker study - the enormous standard deviations around the NT-proBNP changes (several times the means) show how noisy the surrogate is. ALOFT was not powered for, and does not report, clinical outcomes; read alongside ALTITUDE, it is the second act of the same surrogate-versus-outcome story.
cards.source: McMurray JJ et al. Effects of the oral direct renin inhibitor aliskiren in patients with symptomatic heart failure. Circulation. Heart failure. 2008. PMID: 19808266. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00219011, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: LIKELY (no benefit, with harm) - aliskiren added to ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy improves albuminuria and natriuretic peptides but not cardiovascular or renal outcomes, and increases hyperkalaemia and hypotension
cards.summary: Synthesis: LIKELY (no benefit, with harm) - aliskiren added to ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy improves albuminuria and natriuretic peptides but not cardiovascular or renal outcomes, and increases hyperkalaemia and hypotension
cards.people: The carded evidence is the aliskiren add-on programme: AVOID (599 patients with diabetic nephropathy, albuminuria endpoint), ALOFT (302 patients with heart failure, NT-proBNP endpoint) and ALTITUDE (8,561 high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes, hard cardiorenal outcomes, stopped early).
cards.result: Surrogates moved favourably in both small trials (albumin-to-creatinine ratio -20% relative in AVOID; NT-proBNP direction favourable in ALOFT). Outcomes did not: ALTITUDE's primary composite was 18.3% on aliskiren against 17.1% on placebo (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.20, relative - the treatment made no difference), with significantly more hyperkalaemia (11.2% vs 7.2%) and hypotension (12.1% vs 8.3%). The question's 'or cause net harm' half is therefore the operative one: no outcome benefit, a real excess of predictable adverse effects, and an early-stopped outcomes trial. Dual renin-angiotensin blockade with aliskiren should not be used for cardiorenal protection in this population.
cards.watchOut: LIKELY rests on ALTITUDE's size and precision plus the concordant harm pattern; it does not extend to aliskiren monotherapy (not this shelf's question) or to every dual-blockade combination, which have their own shelves. The surrogate trials are carded so the record shows why the strategy was once plausible - not as residual support for it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Parving HH et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2012 (PMID: 23121378, NCT00549757); Parving HH et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2008 (PMID: 18525041, NCT00097955); McMurray JJ et al. Circulation. Heart failure. 2008 (PMID: 19808266, NCT00219011). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Pioglitazone versus sulfonylureas on metformin (TOSCA.IT): cardiovascular events identical at 1.5 per 100 person-years (HR 0.96) — less hypoglycaemia, no event benefit
shelves.question: In patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or high risk, does pioglitazone, compared with sulfonylureas added to metformin, reduce cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases/drug therapy,epidemiology,etiology · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications,epidemiology · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Incidence · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Pioglitazone · Sulfonylurea Compounds/therapeutic use · Thiazolidinediones/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no difference found). TOSCA.IT randomised 3,028 people with type 2 diabetes on metformin to add-on pioglitazone or a sulfonylurea (mostly glimepiride/gliclazide) and was stopped early for futility: the primary cardiovascular composite occurred at 1.5 per 100 person-years in both groups (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.74–1.26). Pioglitazone caused far less hypoglycaemia (10% vs 34%) and no significant excess of heart failure, bladder cancer or fractures in the trial. Two smaller head-to-head imaging trials (PERISCOPE, CHICAGO) favoured pioglitazone on plaque progression — surrogates that did not convert into events. PREMISE NOTE: TOSCA.IT enrolled metformin-treated patients of whom only 11% had prior cardiovascular events, so it is a high-risk primary/secondary-prevention mix rather than a pure established-CVD cohort.

cards.headline: TOSCA.IT 2017 (the outcome trial): cardiovascular events occurred at 1.5 per 100 person-years on both pioglitazone and sulfonylureas added to metformin (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.74–1.26) — the trial was stopped early for futility
cards.summary: TOSCA.IT 2017 (the outcome trial): cardiovascular events occurred at 1.5 per 100 person-years on both pioglitazone and sulfonylureas added to metformin (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.74–1.26) — the trial was stopped early for futility
cards.people: 3,028 patients aged 50–75 years with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin monotherapy (2–3 g/day), recruited at 57 Italian diabetes clinics; 1,535 randomised to add-on pioglitazone (15–45 mg) and 1,493 to a sulfonylurea (glimepiride 48%, gliclazide 50%, glibenclamide 2%). Only 11% had a previous cardiovascular event. Open-label treatment with blinded event adjudication; median follow-up 57.3 months before the early futility stop.
cards.result: The primary composite (all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, urgent coronary revascularisation) occurred in 105 patients on pioglitazone and 108 on sulfonylureas — 1.5 per 100 person-years in both groups (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.74–1.26, P=0.79; the treatment made no difference to cardiovascular events). Hypoglycaemia was much less common on pioglitazone (148 patients [10%] versus 508 [34%], P<0.0001). Moderate weight gain (under 2 kg on average) occurred in both groups, and rates of heart failure, bladder cancer and fractures did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early on a futility analysis, and the event rate (1.5 per 100 person-years) was lower than planned — the confidence interval still includes a 26% relative benefit or harm. The sulfonylurea arm was almost entirely glimepiride and gliclazide, so the result should not be extrapolated to older sulfonylureas.
cards.source: Randomised pragmatic clinical trial | Vaccaro O et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2017. PMID: 28917544. Registry ID: NCT00700856 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as printed in the record). cards.headline: PERISCOPE 2008: pioglitazone slowed coronary atherosclerosis progression versus glimepiride on intravascular ultrasound — percent atheroma volume fell 0.16% on pioglitazone while rising 0.73% on glimepiride over 18 months
cards.summary: PERISCOPE 2008: pioglitazone slowed coronary atherosclerosis progression versus glimepiride on intravascular ultrasound — percent atheroma volume fell 0.16% on pioglitazone while rising 0.73% on glimepiride over 18 months
cards.people: 543 patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease at 97 centres in North and South America, randomised double-blind to pioglitazone (15–45 mg) or glimepiride (1–4 mg) for 18 months; repeat intravascular ultrasound was available in 360 patients. An imaging-surrogate trial, not an events trial — flagged on the face.
cards.result: Least-squares mean percent atheroma volume increased 0.73% (95% CI 0.33 to 1.12) with glimepiride and decreased 0.16% (−0.57 to 0.25) with pioglitazone (P=0.002); an imputed analysis of all randomised patients gave the same direction (P=0.02). HbA1c fell slightly more with pioglitazone (−0.55% versus −0.36% average decline). HDL cholesterol rose more and triglycerides fell with pioglitazone; hypoglycaemia was more common with glimepiride, and oedema, fractures and decreased haemoglobin more frequent with pioglitazone.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate endpoint in 360 completers: plaque-volume change over 18 months did not translate into fewer events in TOSCA.IT, so this card explains the mechanistic expectation, not the clinical answer.
cards.source: Randomised controlled trial (intravascular-ultrasound surrogate endpoint) | Nissen SE et al. JAMA. 2008. PMID: 18378631. cards.headline: CHICAGO 2006: pioglitazone also slowed carotid intima-media thickness progression versus glimepiride — mean CIMT changed −0.001 mm versus +0.012 mm over 72 weeks
cards.summary: CHICAGO 2006: pioglitazone also slowed carotid intima-media thickness progression versus glimepiride — mean CIMT changed −0.001 mm versus +0.012 mm over 72 weeks
cards.people: 462 adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 60 years, mean HbA1c 7.4%) at 28 Chicago-area sites, randomised double-blind to pioglitazone (15–45 mg/day) or glimepiride (1–4 mg/day) for 72 weeks, on varied background therapy. An imaging-surrogate trial, flagged on the face.
cards.result: Progression of mean common-carotid intima-media thickness was less with pioglitazone at every time point; at week 72 the change was −0.001 mm on pioglitazone versus +0.012 mm on glimepiride (difference −0.013 mm, 95% CI −0.024 to −0.002, P=0.02). Maximum CIMT progression was also slower with pioglitazone (0.002 versus 0.026 mm; difference −0.024 mm, P=0.008). The effect was consistent across prespecified subgroups including age, sex, blood pressure, diabetes duration, body mass index, HbA1c and statin use.
cards.watchOut: Millimetre-scale surrogate differences over 72 weeks; like PERISCOPE, this card is mechanism, not outcomes — the events answer comes from TOSCA.IT alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: on cardiovascular events, pioglitazone and sulfonylureas added to metformin are indistinguishable (TOSCA.IT, HR 0.96) — pioglitazone's advantages are slower plaque progression on imaging and far less hypoglycaemia, not fewer events
cards.summary: Synthesis: on cardiovascular events, pioglitazone and sulfonylureas added to metformin are indistinguishable (TOSCA.IT, HR 0.96) — pioglitazone's advantages are slower plaque progression on imaging and far less hypoglycaemia, not fewer events
cards.people: Synthesis of TOSCA.IT (Vaccaro 2017, n=3,028, clinical events) with the two head-to-head imaging trials PERISCOPE (n=543) and CHICAGO (n=462). Pioglitazone's other library homes cover PROactive-era and albuminuria/MASH questions; the head-to-head pioglitazone-versus-sulfonylurea comparison had no home — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session.
cards.result: TOSCA.IT is the only carded trial powered for clinical events, and it found none of the expected difference: 1.5 events per 100 person-years on each drug, hazard ratio 0.96 (0.74–1.26), stopped early for futility. The expectation of benefit came from imaging: pioglitazone slowed coronary atheroma progression (PERISCOPE) and carotid wall thickening (CHICAGO) relative to glimepiride. What did differ clinically in TOSCA.IT was hypoglycaemia — 10% of pioglitazone patients versus 34% on sulfonylureas — with no significant difference in heart failure, bladder cancer or fractures. So the choice between these add-ons rests on hypoglycaemia, weight, cost and patient factors, not on cardiovascular-event prevention.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: TOSCA.IT's early futility stop and lower-than-planned event rate leave a wide interval around the null; the synthesis does not claim the drugs are proven equal, only that no event difference was demonstrated in 3,028 patients followed a median of 57.3 months.

shelves.title: Fructosamine and glycated albumin when HbA1c is unreliable: they predict complications like HbA1c (ARIC), but in severe CKD they tracked glucose no better than HbA1c
shelves.question: In patients in whom HbA1c is unreliable (haemoglobin variants, anaemia, pregnancy, advanced CKD), do fructosamine or glycated albumin accurately reflect glycaemic control and predict complications compared with HbA1c and glucose measures?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atherosclerosis/complications,diagnosis · Cohort Studies · Diabetes Complications/diagnosis · Diabetes Mellitus/diagnosis · Diabetic Angiopathies/diagnosis · Female · Fructosamine · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Glycation End Products, Advanced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment/methods · Serum Albumin · Glycated Serum Albumin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — an evidence (test-accuracy/prognosis) shelf built on the three free ARIC reports. Prognosis: fructosamine and glycated albumin predict incident diabetes, retinopathy, CKD, cardiovascular events and death with strength comparable to HbA1c (Selvin 2014, 2015). Accuracy where it matters most: in severe/very severe CKD, correlations with fasting glucose were 0.39–0.41 for the alternative markers versus 0.48–0.52 for HbA1c (Jung 2018) — no advantage. FLAG: the dialysis slice is already homed at built shelf #2896; its PMIDs are kept out of this pack's card source lines and the free dialysis cohort was not carded, per the one-home rule (see Synthesis). No carded evidence covers haemoglobin variants or pregnancy.

cards.headline: Selvin 2014 (ARIC): fructosamine and glycated albumin above the 95th percentile carried hazard ratios of 4.96 and 6.17 for incident diabetes, predicted retinopathy and CKD (HR about 1.5) — prognostic performance close to HbA1c for kidney disease, weaker for diabetes itself
cards.summary: Selvin 2014 (ARIC): fructosamine and glycated albumin above the 95th percentile carried hazard ratios of 4.96 and 6.17 for incident diabetes, predicted retinopathy and CKD (HR about 1.5) — prognostic performance close to HbA1c for kidney disease, weaker for diabetes itself
cards.people: Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) participants measured at the 1990–92 examination: 11,348 adults without diabetes and 958 with diagnosed diabetes (types 1 and 2), followed for two decades for incident diabetes, retinopathy and chronic kidney disease. An observational prognosis cohort — no patient was managed by these markers.
cards.result: Hazard ratios for incident diabetes were 4.96 (95% CI 4.36–5.64) for fructosamine above the 95th percentile and 6.17 (5.45–6.99) for glycated albumin above the 95th percentile — relative measures; associations were attenuated but persisted after adjustment for HbA1c. Both markers were strongly associated with retinopathy (P<0.0001 for trend). Adjusted hazard ratios for incident CKD were 1.50 (1.22–1.85) for fructosamine and 1.48 (1.20–1.83) for glycated albumin. Discrimination for incident CKD was nearly identical across markers (C statistics 0.717, 0.717 and 0.726 for HbA1c), but HbA1c predicted incident diabetes better (C 0.760 versus 0.706 and 0.703). The authors conclude both markers carry prognostic value comparable to HbA1c for complications.
cards.watchOut: Prognosis in a general community cohort is not accuracy in the patients this shelf is about (haemoglobin variants, anaemia, pregnancy): ARIC shows the markers track risk like HbA1c where HbA1c works — it does not show they rescue measurement where HbA1c fails.
cards.source: Prospective cohort study (prognosis) | Selvin E et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2014. PMID: 24703046. Registry ID: none in the record (observational cohort). cards.headline: Selvin 2015 (ARIC): elevated fructosamine and glycated albumin were also associated with coronary disease, stroke, heart failure and death over two decades, with associations of similar magnitude to HbA1c — and J-shaped, with higher risk at the lowest levels too
cards.summary: Selvin 2015 (ARIC): elevated fructosamine and glycated albumin were also associated with coronary disease, stroke, heart failure and death over two decades, with associations of similar magnitude to HbA1c — and J-shaped, with higher risk at the lowest levels too
cards.people: 11,104 ARIC participants with and without diabetes, with glycated albumin and fructosamine measured on 1990–92 samples and outcomes counted over two decades of follow-up: 1,096 new coronary heart disease cases, 605 ischaemic strokes, 1,432 heart failure cases and 2,860 deaths. Observational prognosis cohort.
cards.result: Elevated baseline fructosamine and glycated albumin were significantly associated with each outcome even after adjustment for traditional cardiovascular risk factors, with especially strong associations in people with diabetes. The associations were of similar magnitude to those observed for HbA1c and, as previously seen for HbA1c, tended to be J-shaped, with risk also elevated at the lowest levels of each biomarker. The authors frame the study as establishing the long-term outcome associations a new hyperglycaemia measure needs before clinical acceptance.
cards.watchOut: 'Similar magnitude to HbA1c' is a qualitative summary in the record — no per-marker hazard ratios are printed in the fetched abstract, so none are quoted on this card. J-shaped associations mean low values are not simply 'good control' in these data.
cards.source: Prospective cohort study (prognosis) | Selvin E et al. Circulation. 2015. PMID: 26022911. Registry ID: none in the record (observational cohort). cards.headline: Jung 2018 (ARIC, by CKD status): in severe and very severe CKD, NONE of the markers tracked fasting glucose well — correlations were 0.52 for HbA1c, 0.39 for glycated albumin and 0.41 for fructosamine in severe CKD, and lower still in very severe CKD
cards.summary: Jung 2018 (ARIC, by CKD status): in severe and very severe CKD, NONE of the markers tracked fasting glucose well — correlations were 0.52 for HbA1c, 0.39 for glycated albumin and 0.41 for fructosamine in severe CKD, and lower still in very severe CKD
cards.people: Cross-sectional analysis of 1,665 ARIC participants aged 65 and older with diagnosed diabetes, comparing HbA1c, glycated albumin and fructosamine against fasting glucose across CKD categories defined by estimated GFR and urine albumin:creatinine ratio. This is the carded accuracy leg for the advanced-CKD slice of the question.
cards.result: Correlations with fasting glucose were lowest in severe CKD (HbA1c r=0.52, root mean square error 0.91; glycated albumin r=0.39, RMSE 1.89; fructosamine r=0.41, RMSE 1.87) and in very severe CKD (HbA1c r=0.48, RMSE 1.01; glycated albumin r=0.36, RMSE 2.14; fructosamine r=0.36, RMSE 2.22). Associations of glycated albumin and fructosamine with HbA1c were relatively similar across CKD categories. The authors conclude that in older adults with severe or very severe CKD, none of the three markers was highly correlated with fasting glucose, and there may be no particular advantage of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c for monitoring glycaemic control in CKD.
cards.watchOut: Fasting glucose is itself an imperfect reference for average glycaemia, and this is older adults in one cohort — but it is the only carded head-to-head accuracy comparison in advanced CKD, and it cuts against the usual rationale for switching markers.
cards.source: Cross-sectional accuracy analysis within a cohort | Jung M et al. J Diabetes. 2018. PMID: 29055090. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Synthesis: fructosamine and glycated albumin predict complications about as well as HbA1c in general populations (ARIC), and glycated albumin predicts death in dialysis — but the dialysis question is homed at shelf #2896, and in severe CKD neither marker tracked glucose better than HbA1c
cards.summary: Synthesis: fructosamine and glycated albumin predict complications about as well as HbA1c in general populations (ARIC), and glycated albumin predicts death in dialysis — but the dialysis question is homed at shelf #2896, and in severe CKD neither marker tracked glucose better than HbA1c
cards.people: Synthesis of the three free ARIC reports (Selvin 2014; Selvin 2015; Jung 2018). FLAG — ONE-HOME: the dialysis slice of this question is already homed at built shelf #2896 ('In diabetes treated with dialysis, does glycated albumin reflect glycaemic control and predict mortality better than HbA1c…', carding Freedman 2012, PMID 22723586, and the Copur 2021 meta-analysis, PMID 32862262). Those PMIDs are NOT carded here, and the free Freedman 2011 dialysis cohort (PMID 21597024) was deliberately NOT carded either, because it answers #2896's question, not this one. This pack is built on the genuinely different, broader question — accuracy and prognosis where HbA1c is unreliable — using the three ungated ARIC reports, with #2896 cross-pointed here in prose.
cards.result: What the ARIC evidence supports: fructosamine and glycated albumin are real glycaemic markers — they predict incident diabetes, retinopathy, CKD, cardiovascular outcomes and death with strength comparable to HbA1c in community populations. What it does not support is the common clinical move this shelf is asked about: in severe and very severe CKD, the setting where HbA1c is most distrusted, glycated albumin and fructosamine correlated with fasting glucose no better than HbA1c did (r 0.36–0.41 versus 0.48–0.52). For the dialysis population specifically, readers should go to shelf #2896, where glycated albumin's mortality prediction is carded. No carded study tests accuracy in haemoglobin variants or pregnancy, and none tests whether managing patients by these markers improves any outcome.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: a test-accuracy/prognosis shelf built entirely on observational cohorts — POSSIBLE is the ceiling, and the honest headline is split: prognosis, yes, comparable to HbA1c; proven superiority where HbA1c is unreliable, no — with the CKD accuracy data pointing the other way.

shelves.title: The 10 g monofilament and future foot ulcers: insensitivity roughly doubles ulcer risk (RR 1.8–2.2; pooled OR 3.18) — a moderate-risk marker, not an interval-setter
shelves.question: In people with diabetes, does loss of protective sensation on the 10 g monofilament test predict future foot ulceration and amputation well enough to guide screening intervals?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Foot/diagnosis · Humans · Predictive Value of Tests · Prognosis · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a prognosis/evidence shelf, observational throughout. Prospective cohorts agree: monofilament insensitivity predicts new ulceration with relative risks of 1.80 (Abbott 2002, 9,710 community patients) and 2.2 (Boyko 1999, 749 veterans), and the PODUS individual-patient meta-analysis (>16,000 people) gives a pooled OR of 3.184. The same evidence ranks it a moderate-risk marker below ulcer history (OR 6.589), and no carded study tests screening intervals. PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate's Perkins 2001 anchor is diagnostic accuracy against nerve conduction, not ulcer prognosis — fetched, checked, and not carded (see Synthesis).

cards.headline: Pham 2000: in a prospective multicentre study, 29% of patients developed a foot ulcer over a mean 30 months; inability to feel the 5.07 (10 g) monofilament was an independent predictor, and neuropathy score plus monofilament together reached 99% sensitivity
cards.summary: Pham 2000: in a prospective multicentre study, 29% of patients developed a foot ulcer over a mean 30 months; inability to feel the 5.07 (10 g) monofilament was an independent predictor, and neuropathy score plus monofilament together reached 99% sensitivity
cards.people: 248 patients from three large diabetic foot centres, assessed at baseline with neuropathy symptom and disability scores, vibration perception threshold, Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments, joint mobility, peak plantar pressures and vascular status, then followed every 6 months for a mean of 30 months. A high-risk clinic population — flagged on the face.
cards.result: Foot ulcers developed in 73 patients (29%), affecting 95 feet (19%). In univariate analysis, inability to feel the 5.07 Semmes-Weinstein filament carried a significant odds ratio for ulceration, and 94 of the 95 ulcerated feet (99%) had a high neuropathy disability score and/or an abnormal monofilament test, giving the highest combined odds ratio, 26.2 (95% CI 3.6–190 — a relative measure with a very wide interval). In multivariable analysis the significant factors were high disability score, vibration threshold, monofilament insensitivity and foot pressures. The disability score alone had the best sensitivity; foot pressures the best specificity.
cards.watchOut: A foot-centre cohort with a 29% ulcer incidence is not a screening population — predictive values from this card do not transfer to community diabetes care. The headline combined odds ratio has an extremely wide confidence interval.

cards.headline: Abbott 2002 (North-West Diabetes Foot Care Study): in 9,710 community patients, insensitivity to the 10 g monofilament independently predicted new ulceration (relative risk 1.80, 95% CI 1.36–2.39) over 2 years
cards.summary: Abbott 2002 (North-West Diabetes Foot Care Study): in 9,710 community patients, insensitivity to the 10 g monofilament independently predicted new ulceration (relative risk 1.80, 95% CI 1.36–2.39) over 2 years
cards.people: 9,710 people with diabetes screened in community healthcare settings across six districts of North-West England, with baseline neuropathy scores, 10 g monofilament testing, foot deformity assessment and pulse palpation; 6,613 returned the 2-year follow-up questionnaire, among whom 291 developed a new foot ulcer (2.2% average annual incidence). The community screening population this question is about.
cards.result: In Cox regression, independent predictors of new ulceration included an ulcer present at baseline (relative risk 5.32, 95% CI 3.71–7.64), past ulcer history (3.05, 2.16–4.31), abnormal neuropathy disability score (2.32, 1.61–3.35), insensitivity to the 10 g monofilament (1.80, 1.36–2.39), reduced pulses (1.80, 1.40–2.32), foot deformities (1.57, 1.22–2.02) and abnormal ankle reflexes (1.55, 1.01–2.36) — all relative measures. The authors recommend the disability score, the 10 g monofilament and pulse palpation as the screening tools for general practice.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was by postal questionnaire with about a third of the cohort not returning it, so ulcer ascertainment is incomplete; and a relative risk of 1.80 on a 2.2%-per-year baseline means most monofilament-insensitive patients still do not ulcerate in a given year.

cards.headline: Boyko 1999 (Seattle Diabetic Foot Study): foot insensitivity to the 5.07 monofilament independently predicted ulceration (relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.5–3.1) over a mean 3.7 years in 749 diabetic veterans
cards.summary: Boyko 1999 (Seattle Diabetic Foot Study): foot insensitivity to the 5.07 monofilament independently predicted ulceration (relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.5–3.1) over a mean 3.7 years in 749 diabetic veterans
cards.people: 749 diabetic veterans without foot ulcer at baseline, enrolled from a general internal medicine clinic (1,483 lower limbs assessed), with sensory and autonomic neuropathy testing and foot perfusion measures, followed for a mean of 3.7 years for full-thickness ulcers taking more than 14 days to heal. A male veteran population — flagged on the face.
cards.result: In stepwise Cox regression, foot insensitivity to the 5.07 (10 g) monofilament was independently related to ulcer risk (relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.5–3.1), alongside past amputation (2.8, 1.8–4.3), past ulcer (1.6, 1.2–2.3), insulin use (1.6), Charcot deformity (3.5), poor vision (1.9) and measures of perfusion and body weight. Diabetes duration and type, smoking and joint mobility were not independently related to ulcer risk.
cards.watchOut: Veterans, overwhelmingly male, from one clinic system; stepwise variable selection can overstate the chosen predictors. The estimate agrees with the community cohort's 1.80, which is the reassuring part.

cards.headline: Crawford 2015 (PODUS individual-patient meta-analysis): across more than 16,000 people with diabetes, inability to feel a 10 g monofilament predicted ulceration with an odds ratio of 3.184 (95% CI 2.654–3.82) — but a history of ulceration was far stronger (OR 6.589)
cards.summary: Crawford 2015 (PODUS individual-patient meta-analysis): across more than 16,000 people with diabetes, inability to feel a 10 g monofilament predicted ulceration with an odds ratio of 3.184 (95% CI 2.654–3.82) — but a history of ulceration was far stronger (OR 6.589)
cards.people: Systematic review and individual-patient-data meta-analysis of prognostic cohort studies in people with diabetes free of ulceration at entry: 16 cohort studies identified, individual data obtained for 10, covering more than 16,000 people worldwide, with one dataset held back for independent validation. The pooled evidence base for this shelf.
cards.result: In the multivariable individual-patient meta-analysis, inability to feel a 10 g monofilament predicted incident ulceration (odds ratio 3.184, 95% CI 2.654–3.82 — a relative measure), as did at least one absent pedal pulse (OR 1.968, 1.624–2.386), longer diabetes duration (OR 1.024 per year) and previous ulceration (OR 6.589, 2.488–17.45); female sex was protective (OR 0.743). The authors conclude that monofilament insensitivity or an absent pulse identifies people at moderate (intermediate) risk, while a history of ulceration or amputation alone identifies high risk, and they propose a simple clinical prediction rule built on those three items.
cards.watchOut: The pooled odds ratio (3.18) is larger than the individual community estimates (1.80–2.2) because odds ratios exaggerate relative risks when outcomes are not rare and because adjustment sets differed — the cards are deliberately not averaged. Amputation prediction is much thinner than ulcer prediction in this analysis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: loss of protective sensation on the 10 g monofilament genuinely predicts future ulceration — roughly a doubling of risk in community cohorts — well enough to place a patient in a moderate-risk stratum, but not to set screening intervals on its own
cards.summary: Synthesis: loss of protective sensation on the 10 g monofilament genuinely predicts future ulceration — roughly a doubling of risk in community cohorts — well enough to place a patient in a moderate-risk stratum, but not to set screening intervals on its own
cards.people: Synthesis of Pham 2000 (foot-centre cohort, n=248), Abbott 2002 (community cohort, n=9,710), Boyko 1999 (veteran cohort, n=749) and the PODUS individual-patient meta-analysis (Crawford 2015, >16,000 people). PREMISE CORRECTION: the slate's anchor, Perkins 2001 (PMID 11213874, fetched and checked this session), is a diagnostic-accuracy study of the monofilament against nerve-conduction studies for detecting neuropathy — not a study of future ulceration — so it is not carded as ulcer-prediction evidence. No monofilament-prognosis home exists in the library — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session (existing monofilament mentions are incidental, in leprosy, wound-closure and cooling packs).
cards.result: The prospective evidence is consistent in direction and rough size: relative risks of 1.80 (community) and 2.2 (veterans) for ulceration in monofilament-insensitive patients, with the pooled individual-patient odds ratio at 3.18. But the same evidence base ranks the monofilament below history: previous ulceration (relative risk about 3–5; pooled OR 6.59) dominates prediction, and the PODUS authors place monofilament insensitivity in the moderate-risk tier, to be combined with pulse palpation and ulcer history. On the second half of the question — screening intervals — the carded evidence is silent: no study randomises or even compares re-testing intervals, so intervals remain a guideline judgement built on risk strata, not a tested quantity. Amputation prediction is supported mainly by the same cohorts' secondary analyses and is materially weaker than ulcer prediction.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: all evidence is observational prognosis — no trial shows that acting on a monofilament result (at any interval) prevents an ulcer. The stamp reflects consistent prediction, not proven screening benefit.

shelves.title: Semaglutide and NAION: a contested observational signal — relative risks of ~2–8 in referral and registry cohorts, but absolute excesses of only ~0.02–0.05 percentage points per year in population data
shelves.question: In people prescribed semaglutide (and other GLP-1 receptor agonists), is there an increased risk of nonarteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION), and how large is the absolute excess?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Retrospective Studies · Glucagon-Like Peptides/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Optic Neuropathy, Ischemic/chemically induced,epidemiology · Aged · Incidence · Risk Factors · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm), observational only, with the absolute framing leading. The signal began with Hathaway 2024 (JAMA Ophthalmology): in a single academic centre's neuro-ophthalmology referral registry, 36-month cumulative NAION incidence was 8.9% on semaglutide vs 1.8% on non-GLP-1 drugs in type 2 diabetes (HR 4.28, 95% CI 1.62 to 11.29) and 6.7% vs 0.8% in overweight/obesity (HR 7.64, 2.21 to 26.36) — percentages that reflect a referral population already enriched for optic-nerve disease, not ordinary prescribing. Two much larger active-comparator studies found smaller relative effects and tiny absolutes: a three-database claims target-trial emulation (~482,912 matched pairs, GLP-1 RA vs SGLT2 inhibitor initiators) found HR 1.85 (1.51 to 2.27) with a rate difference of 0.29 per 1,000 person-years; the Swedish nationwide cohort found AION risks of 0.04% vs 0.02% at 1 year (RD 0.02%) and 0.12% vs 0.07% at 5 years (RD 0.05%), attenuating to RR ~1.2–1.4 and RD ~0.01–0.02% when restricted to metformin users — the authors themselves raise residual confounding by diabetes severity. Per the slate, regulators have weighed in (EMA PRAC, June 2025, classing NAION as very rare; an FDA class review in November 2026) — those reviews are context for this shelf, not carded evidence; the carded base is the three observational studies above. Causality is not established; diabetes itself is a NAION risk factor and no randomised trial can realistically be powered for an event this rare.

cards.headline: Hathaway 2024: in a neuro-ophthalmology referral registry, NAION cumulative incidence was 8.9% vs 1.8% (diabetes) and 6.7% vs 0.8% (obesity) on semaglutide vs comparators over 36 months
cards.summary: Hathaway 2024: in a neuro-ophthalmology referral registry, NAION cumulative incidence was 8.9% vs 1.8% (diabetes) and 6.7% vs 0.8% (obesity) on semaglutide vs comparators over 36 months
cards.people: Retrospective matched cohort from a centralised registry of 16,827 patients evaluated by neuro-ophthalmologists at one academic institution (Dec 2017–Nov 2023) with no NAION history: 710 with type 2 diabetes (194 prescribed semaglutide, 516 prescribed non-GLP-1 RA antidiabetic drugs) and 979 overweight/obese (361 semaglutide, 618 non-GLP-1 RA weight-loss drugs), propensity-matched on sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnoea, obesity, hyperlipidaemia and coronary disease.
cards.result: In type 2 diabetes, 17 NAION events occurred on semaglutide vs 6 on comparators; 36-month cumulative incidence 8.9% (95% CI 4.5% to 13.1%) vs 1.8% (0% to 3.5%); HR 4.28 (1.62 to 11.29; P<0.001) — a relative measure in a referral population. In overweight/obesity, 20 events vs 3; cumulative incidence 6.7% (3.6% to 9.7%) vs 0.8% (0% to 1.8%); HR 7.64 (2.21 to 26.36; P<0.001). The authors state the study shows association, and that causality requires future study.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre referral population: everyone in the denominator had been seen by neuro-ophthalmologists, so the 8.9% and 6.7% cumulative incidences cannot be applied to ordinary semaglutide users — population absolutes (cards 2–3) are two orders of magnitude smaller. Event counts are small (17–20 per cohort).
cards.source: Hathaway JT et al. Risk of Nonarteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy in Patients Prescribed Semaglutide. JAMA Ophthalmol. 2024. PMID: 38958939. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Claims target-trial emulation 2026: GLP-1 RA initiation vs SGLT2 inhibitor initiation carried HR 1.85 for presumed NAION, with a rate difference of 0.29 per 1,000 person-years
cards.summary: Claims target-trial emulation 2026: GLP-1 RA initiation vs SGLT2 inhibitor initiation carried HR 1.85 for presumed NAION, with a rate difference of 0.29 per 1,000 person-years
cards.people: New-user active-comparator cohort emulating a target trial across three insurance-claims databases (2016–2024): 482,912 propensity-matched pairs of adults with type 2 diabetes initiating a GLP-1 RA or an SGLT2 inhibitor, without prior ischaemic optic neuropathy or other optic-nerve disorders; NAION required an ischaemic optic neuropathy diagnosis code plus a same-day ophthalmologist/optometrist visit. Median on-treatment follow-up 6.7 months.
cards.result: Incident presumed NAION was more frequent on GLP-1 RAs: pooled HR 1.85 (95% CI 1.51 to 2.27) — a relative measure — with a rate difference of 0.29 (0.19 to 0.39) per 1,000 person-years, i.e. roughly 3 extra cases per 10,000 person-years. Results were consistent across subgroups and sensitivity analyses; a meta-analysis combining the semaglutide-specific estimate with previously published results gave HR 2.78 (1.39 to 5.56). The authors note the absolute increase was small.
cards.watchOut: Claims-based outcome definition ('presumed' NAION) without chart confirmation, short median follow-up (6.7 months), and observational design — confounding by diabetes severity and surveillance cannot be excluded despite matching.

cards.headline: Swedish nationwide cohort 2026: AION risk 0.04% vs 0.02% at 1 year on GLP-1 RA vs SGLT2 inhibitor (risk difference 0.02%), attenuating in metformin users
cards.summary: Swedish nationwide cohort 2026: AION risk 0.04% vs 0.02% at 1 year on GLP-1 RA vs SGLT2 inhibitor (risk difference 0.02%), attenuating in metformin users
cards.people: Nationwide register-based cohort, Sweden 2013–2024: 107,518 initiators of GLP-1 RAs vs 185,898 initiators of SGLT2 inhibitors, mostly with type 2 diabetes; outcome was anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (predominantly NAION) in the national patient register; propensity-score weighting; median follow-up 1.6 vs 1.5 years.
cards.result: AION occurred in 62 GLP-1 RA users and 64 SGLT2 inhibitor users. Risks: 0.04% vs 0.02% at 1 year (RD 0.02%, 95% CI 0.00% to 0.03%; RR 1.93, 1.00 to 3.73) and 0.12% vs 0.07% at 5 years (RD 0.05%, 0.00% to 0.10%; RR 1.69, 0.95 to 3.01) — relative risks near 2 resting on absolute differences of 2–5 extra cases per 10,000 users. Restricted to baseline metformin users, the differences attenuated substantially (1-year RD 0.01%; RR 1.40, 0.64 to 3.05; 5-year RD 0.02%; RR 1.23, 0.65 to 2.33). The authors conclude the observed increase may reflect residual confounding.
cards.watchOut: Few events (62 and 64), register diagnoses without adjudication, and limited generalisability to GLP-1 RA users without diabetes — the attenuation in the metformin-restricted analysis is the single most important caution on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent relative signal across three observational designs, a very small absolute excess in population data, and causality unresolved
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent relative signal across three observational designs, a very small absolute excess in population data, and causality unresolved
cards.people: People prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists (chiefly semaglutide): 1,689 in the referral-registry cohorts, ~965,824 matched initiators in the claims emulation, and 293,416 initiators in the Swedish registers.
cards.result: Relative estimates range from HR/RR ~1.7–1.9 in the two large active-comparator population studies to 4.28–7.64 in the small referral cohort. Absolute excesses in population data are ~0.29 per 1,000 person-years (claims) and 0.02–0.05 percentage points over 1–5 years (Sweden). One of the three studies shows substantial attenuation with a confounding-control restriction. Verdict: POSSIBLE harm, observational; the absolute risk to an individual user appears very low, and whether the association is causal remains open.
cards.watchOut: Never quote the Hathaway percentages (8.9%, 6.7%) as the risk for a typical patient — they come from a neuro-ophthalmology referral denominator. Equally, do not dismiss the signal: three designs with different biases point the same relative way.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hathaway JT et al. JAMA Ophthalmol. 2024 (PMID: 38958939); Tesfaye H et al. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2026 (PMID: 41104517); Ueda P et al. Ann Intern Med. 2026 (PMID: 42441962).

shelves.title: Adaptive thermogenesis (physiology): after a 10% weight loss, total energy expenditure falls by roughly 6–8 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day beyond the change in mass — leptin repletion reverses the adaptation, and in the extreme Biggest Loser phenotype a ~500 kcal/day adaptation was still present 6 years later
shelves.question: After weight loss, how large is adaptive thermogenesis (the fall in energy expenditure beyond that predicted by lost mass), how long does it persist, and what hormonal signals (leptin) drive it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Composition · Body Weight/physiology · Energy Intake · *Energy Metabolism · Female · Food, Formulated · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/diet therapy,metabolism · Weight Gain · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, energy-balance and hypothalamic-regulation chapters). The textbooks describe body weight as defended: lose weight and energy expenditure falls by more than the lost tissue explains, while hunger and neuroendocrine signals shift to restore the former weight — with leptin, the adipocyte signal of fat stores, as the central messenger. The carded human studies quantify that defence. In controlled inpatient weight perturbation, maintaining a weight 10% or more below usual was associated with total energy expenditure lower by 6 ± 3 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day in never-obese and 8 ± 5 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day in obese subjects, with resting and non-resting expenditure each contributing (Leibel 1995) — and the adaptation was bidirectional, expenditure rising symmetrically after 10% weight gain. The signal is leptin: in weight-reduced subjects, replacing leptin to pre-loss concentrations returned energy expenditure, skeletal muscle work efficiency, sympathetic tone and thyroid hormones to pre-weight-loss levels (Rosenbaum 2005) — the reduced state behaves as relative leptin insufficiency. Persistence is measured in years, not weeks: six years after the Biggest Loser competition, resting metabolic rate remained 704 ± 427 kcal/day below baseline and metabolic adaptation was −499 ± 207 kcal/day despite substantial regain (Fothergill 2016) — an extreme phenotype (58 kg lost in 30 weeks), but it proves the adaptation does not simply expire. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Leibel 1995: maintaining a ≥10% reduced weight lowered total energy expenditure by 6 ± 3 (never-obese) and 8 ± 5 (obese) kcal/kg fat-free mass/day — and weight gain raised it symmetrically
cards.summary: Leibel 1995: maintaining a ≥10% reduced weight lowered total energy expenditure by 6 ± 3 (never-obese) and 8 ± 5 (obese) kcal/kg fat-free mass/day — and weight gain raised it symmetrically
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (controlled inpatient weight-perturbation, Leibel/Rosenbaum/Hirsch programme)
cards.people: 18 obese subjects and 23 subjects who had never been obese (N = 41), studied as inpatients at their usual body weight and after losing 10–20% of body weight by underfeeding or gaining 10% by overfeeding, with repeated measurement of 24-hour total, resting and non-resting energy expenditure and the thermic effect of feeding.
cards.result: Maintenance of body weight at a level 10% or more below the initial weight was associated with a mean (± SD) reduction in total energy expenditure of 6 ± 3 kcal per kilogram of fat-free mass per day in the never-obese subjects (P < 0.001) and 8 ± 5 kcal per kilogram per day in the obese subjects (P < 0.001); resting and non-resting energy expenditure each decreased by 3–4 kcal per kilogram of fat-free mass per day in both groups. Maintenance at 10% above usual weight was associated with an increase in total energy expenditure of 9 ± 7 kcal per kilogram of fat-free mass per day (never-obese, P < 0.001) and 8 ± 4 kcal per kilogram per day (obese, P < 0.001). The changes were not related to the degree of adiposity or to sex — the compensation opposes maintenance of any weight different from the usual weight, in either direction.
cards.watchOut: Expenditure is expressed per kilogram of fat-free mass under formula-diet inpatient conditions: the per-kg figure is the compensatory component measured by this design, and translating it into a single kcal/day number for a given patient requires their fat-free mass — the shelf deliberately does not invent one.
cards.source: Leibel RL et al. Changes in energy expenditure resulting from altered body weight. The New England journal of medicine. 1995. PMID: 7632212. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rosenbaum 2005: restoring leptin to pre-loss levels in 10 weight-reduced subjects returned energy expenditure, muscle efficiency, sympathetic tone and thyroid hormones to pre-weight-loss values
cards.summary: Rosenbaum 2005: restoring leptin to pre-loss levels in 10 weight-reduced subjects returned energy expenditure, muscle efficiency, sympathetic tone and thyroid hormones to pre-weight-loss values
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (leptin-repletion crossover during reduced-weight maintenance, Rosenbaum programme) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 inpatient subjects (5 men, 5 women; 3 never-obese, 7 obese) studied under three conditions: maintaining usual weight on a liquid formula diet; maintaining a 10% reduced weight on the same diet; and maintaining the 10% reduced weight while receiving twice-daily subcutaneous leptin doses sufficient to restore 8 a.m. circulating leptin concentrations to pre-weight-loss levels.
cards.result: Maintenance of the reduced weight was accompanied by decreased energy expenditure due largely to increased skeletal muscle work efficiency, together with decreased sympathetic nervous system tone and decreased circulating leptin, thyroxine and triiodothyronine. During leptin administration, energy expenditure, skeletal muscle work efficiency, sympathetic nervous system tone, and circulating concentrations of thyroxine and triiodothyronine returned to pre-weight-loss levels. The authors conclude the weight-reduced state may be regarded as a condition of relative leptin insufficiency.
cards.watchOut: N = 10, printed on the face. Leptin here is a physiological probe in an inpatient experiment — this card establishes leptin as a driver of the adaptation; it is not evidence that leptin treatment maintains weight loss in clinical practice.
cards.source: Rosenbaum M et al. Low-dose leptin reverses skeletal muscle, autonomic, and neuroendocrine adaptations to maintenance of reduced weight. The Journal of clinical investigation. 2005. PMID: 16322796. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fothergill 2016: 6 years after the Biggest Loser competition, metabolic adaptation was still −499 ± 207 kcal/day, with resting metabolic rate 704 ± 427 kcal/day below baseline
cards.summary: Fothergill 2016: 6 years after the Biggest Loser competition, metabolic adaptation was still −499 ± 207 kcal/day, with resting metabolic rate 704 ± 427 kcal/day below baseline
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (6-year longitudinal cohort, extreme weight-loss phenotype)
cards.people: 14 of the 16 original 'Biggest Loser' competitors, with body composition by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and resting metabolic rate (RMR) by indirect calorimetry at baseline, at the end of the 30-week competition, and 6 years later; metabolic adaptation was defined as the residual RMR after adjusting for changes in body composition and age.
cards.result: Weight loss at the end of the competition was 58.3 ± 24.9 kg (P < 0.0001) and RMR had decreased by 610 ± 483 kcal/day (P = 0.0004). After 6 years, 41.0 ± 31.3 kg of the lost weight had been regained (P = 0.0002), yet RMR was 704 ± 427 kcal/day below baseline (P < 0.0001) and metabolic adaptation was −499 ± 207 kcal/day (P < 0.0001). Weight regain was not significantly correlated with metabolic adaptation at the competition's end (r = −0.1, P = 0.75), but subjects maintaining greater weight loss at 6 years had greater concurrent metabolic slowing (r = 0.59, P = 0.025). The authors conclude metabolic adaptation persists over time and is likely a proportional but incomplete response to contemporaneous efforts to reduce body weight.
cards.watchOut: An extreme phenotype — very rapid, very large, televised weight loss with intense exercise — in 14 people: it bounds how large and durable adaptation can be, and must not be read as the expected adaptation after ordinary clinical weight loss, which the Leibel card quantifies at conventional magnitudes.
cards.source: Fothergill E et al. Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after "The Biggest Loser" competition. Obesity (Silver Spring, Md.). 2016. PMID: 27136388. Registry ID: NCT02544009 (copied from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: the adaptation is real, bidirectional, leptin-driven, and can persist for years
cards.summary: Synthesis: the adaptation is real, bidirectional, leptin-driven, and can persist for years
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (energy-balance chapters). No new data.
cards.result: Three concordant human datasets answer the question. Size: after a 10% loss, total energy expenditure falls by about 6–8 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day beyond the new mass, resting and non-resting components contributing about equally (Leibel 1995), and the response is symmetric after weight gain — a defence of the prior weight, not a one-way ratchet. Signal: falling leptin is the messenger the brain reads — restoring leptin alone normalised expenditure, muscle efficiency, sympathetic tone and thyroid hormones in the weight-reduced state (Rosenbaum 2005). Duration: at least 6 years in the extreme phenotype, with adaptation of about −500 kcal/day still present (Fothergill 2016). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Physiology, not a treatment verdict: this shelf explains why weight-loss maintenance is biologically opposed; which interventions best overcome that opposition is answered on the obesity treatment shelves.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 7632212, 16322796, 27136388), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Ketogenesis regulation: fat supply is the throttle, the insulin-to-glucagon ratio is the gate — and residual insulin is the ceiling that keeps a fast out of ketoacidosis
shelves.question: How do the insulin-to-glucagon ratio and substrate supply regulate hepatic ketogenesis during fasting, and what sets the ceiling that normally prevents ketoacidosis?
shelves.mesh: 3-Hydroxybutyric Acid · Acetoacetates/blood · Adult · Fatty Acids, Nonesterified/blood · Female · Glucagon/blood · Heparin · Humans · Hydroxybutyrates/blood · Insulin/blood,deficiency · Ketone Bodies/biosynthesis · Male · Somatostatin · Triglycerides
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. This pack is the regulation mechanism behind the fasting time course built as pack #6255 (24–72 hours: glucose and insulin fall, fatty acids and ketones rise) — #6255 is cross-pointed, and none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. The carded human experiments agree on the architecture Guyton & Hall present from the McGarry & Foster and Cahill programmes: free-fatty-acid supply is a major determinant of ketone production even with insulin and glucagon held basal (Miles 1983, fivefold rise in production for a fivefold rise in fatty acids); glucagon augments ketogenesis only in insulin deficiency (Miles) and its suppression lowers production without changing fatty acids in insulin-deficient patients (Keller 1983); catecholamines add a direct ketogenic push (Schade & Eaton 1977). The ceiling that separates fasting ketosis from ketoacidosis is therefore not a ketone sensor but the fasting state itself: insulin falls but never vanishes, restraining lipolysis and the hepatic switch, while the brain's adaptation to ketones (Owen 1967) cuts demand. Classic small studies are carded with their Ns on the face (N = 3–6 on two cards; one record prints no N).

cards.headline: Miles 1983: with insulin and glucagon clamped at basal levels, raising free fatty acids fivefold raised ketone-body production fivefold — substrate supply alone drives ketogenesis
cards.summary: Miles 1983: with insulin and glucagon clamped at basal levels, raising free fatty acids fivefold raised ketone-body production fivefold — substrate supply alone drives ketogenesis
cards.type: Human physiological study (somatostatin pancreatic-clamp with hormone replacement and lipid infusion), J Clin Invest 1983
cards.people: Postabsorptive human volunteers studied with somatostatin infusion plus replacement insulin and glucagon to hold both hormones at basal concentrations while free fatty acids were raised with a triglyceride emulsion plus heparin; parallel arms then stopped insulin replacement or raised glucagon. The record does not print a total participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Raising plasma free fatty acids from 0.32 ± 0.06 to 1.4 ± 0.1 mmol/L (about 9 to about 40 mg/dL as oleic-acid equivalents) increased ketone-body production fivefold, from 2.2 ± 0.4 to 11.4 ± 1.2 µmol/kg/min (P < 0.001), with insulin and glucagon held basal. Stopping insulin replacement did not further increase ketone production despite a larger free-fatty-acid rise (to 1.95 ± 0.3 mmol/L, about 55 mg/dL as oleic-acid equivalents). Raising glucagon to 450–550 pg/mL did not further increase ketone production while basal insulin was maintained — but did increase it significantly when insulin replacement was stopped. The authors' reading: free-fatty-acid availability is a major determinant of ketone production in man; insulin has no direct hepatic brake demonstrable in this design, and glucagon augments ketogenesis only in the setting of insulin deficiency.
cards.watchOut: A clamp experiment in the postabsorptive state, not a fast: it isolates substrate and hormone effects over hours, so it shows what can drive ketogenesis rather than the time course of a real fast — that time course is home on pack #6255 and is not re-carded here. N not documented in the record, printed on the face.
cards.source: Miles JM et al. Effects of free fatty acid availability, glucagon excess, and insulin deficiency on ketone body production in postabsorptive man. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1983. PMID: 6134753. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Keller 1983: suppressing glucagon in insulin-withdrawn diabetic patients lowered ketone-body production by about a sixth with no change in free fatty acids — glucagon acts inside the liver
cards.summary: Keller 1983: suppressing glucagon in insulin-withdrawn diabetic patients lowered ketone-body production by about a sixth with no change in free fatty acids — glucagon acts inside the liver
cards.type: Human physiological study (ketone-body kinetics during somatostatin with and without glucagon replacement), Diabetes 1983
cards.people: Eleven C-peptide-negative (insulin-deficient) diabetic subjects studied 6 hours after interruption of a subcutaneous insulin infusion: group 1, N = 5, received somatostatin to suppress glucagon; group 2, N = 6, received somatostatin plus glucagon replacement at 2 ng/kg/min. Small classic groups, printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: During 105 minutes of glucagon suppression, ketone-body production (primed continuous infusion of labelled acetoacetate) fell from 19.5 ± 0.8 to 16.4 ± 0.4 µmol/kg/min (P < 0.01), while with glucagon replacement production was unchanged (+0.2 ± 0.4 µmol/kg/min; P < 0.01 for the contrast). Total ketone-body concentration rose from 2.2 ± 0.3 to 2.9 ± 0.2 mmol/L (about 23 to about 30 mg/dL as beta-hydroxybutyrate equivalents) during glucagon replacement but did not change during suppression. Plasma free fatty acids and glycerol did not change in either group, so the glucagon effect on ketogenesis was intrahepatic, not via fat mobilisation.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 and N = 6, in ketotic insulin-withdrawn diabetes — the extreme of insulin deficiency, not ordinary fasting; it shows glucagon is permissive for maximal ketogenesis when insulin is absent, which is exactly the combination a normal fast avoids.
cards.source: Keller U et al. Role of glucagon in enhancing ketone body production in ketotic diabetic man. Diabetes. 1983. PMID: 6132846. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Schade & Eaton 1977: norepinephrine raised ketones in diabetic man by more than its fat-mobilising effect explains — counter-regulatory hormones feed ketogenesis directly
cards.summary: Schade & Eaton 1977: norepinephrine raised ketones in diabetic man by more than its fat-mobilising effect explains — counter-regulatory hormones feed ketogenesis directly
cards.type: Human physiological study (norepinephrine infusion with heparin lipolysis control), Diabetes 1977
cards.people: Six insulin-dependent diabetic subjects infused with pathophysiological concentrations of norepinephrine (0.08 µg/kg/min), each also studied in a heparin-induced free-fatty-acid generation control experiment to match the lipolytic effect. N = 6 — a small classic study, printed plainly.
cards.result: Norepinephrine showed ketogenic activity independent of its lipolytic effect — the first demonstration of this in man, per the authors: ketones rose by more than the matched heparin free-fatty-acid control produced. Physiological elevations of norepinephrine also increased plasma glucagon concentration, which the authors read as a possible participant in the catecholamine-augmented ketogenesis.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, in insulin-dependent diabetes, and the record's abstract prints the direction and the control logic rather than a table of ketone values, so no invented concentrations are printed. This is one limb of counter-regulation, not the fasting state itself.
cards.source: Schade DS, Eaton RP. The regulation of plasma ketone body concentration by counterregulatory hormones in man. Diabetes. 1977. PMID: 908465. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Owen 1967 (the Cahill programme): after 5–6 weeks of starvation, the brain ran mainly on ketones — the adaptation that caps how fast ketones need to be made
cards.summary: Owen 1967 (the Cahill programme): after 5–6 weeks of starvation, the brain ran mainly on ketones — the adaptation that caps how fast ketones need to be made
cards.type: Human physiological study (cerebral arteriovenous balance during prolonged starvation), J Clin Invest 1967
cards.people: Three obese patients undergoing 5–6 weeks of total starvation, studied with cerebral vessel catheterisation to measure what fuel the brain extracted. N = 3 — a very small classic study, printed plainly under the physiology small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate had replaced glucose as the predominant fuel for brain metabolism, with a strikingly low cerebral respiratory quotient. Once the brain accepts ketones, whole-body glucose demand — and with it the required rate of hepatic glucose production, amino-acid release and ketogenesis — falls, which is the demand-side half of why a prolonged fast stabilises at high-but-not-runaway ketone levels.
cards.watchOut: N = 3, at 5–6 weeks — far beyond the 24–72-hour window of pack #6255; it is carded for the adaptation mechanism (brain ketone use), not as a fasting time course, and its numbers should not be extrapolated to short fasts.
cards.source: Owen OE et al. Brain metabolism during fasting. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1967. PMID: 6061736. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Synthesis: ketogenesis is set by fat supply arriving at a liver whose insulin-to-glucagon ratio has fallen — and the ceiling is insulin itself, plus a brain that learns to burn ketones
cards.summary: Synthesis: ketogenesis is set by fat supply arriving at a liver whose insulin-to-glucagon ratio has fallen — and the ceiling is insulin itself, plus a brain that learns to burn ketones
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Miles 1983; Keller 1983; Schade & Eaton 1977; Owen 1967), framed by Guyton & Hall's fat-metabolism account of the McGarry & Foster regulation model and the Cahill starvation programme as textbook framing.
cards.result: The human experiments line up with the textbook model. Substrate is the throttle: with both hormones clamped basal, a fivefold rise in free fatty acids alone raised ketone production fivefold (Miles). The insulin-to-glucagon ratio is the gate: glucagon could augment ketogenesis only when insulin was deficient (Miles), and removing glucagon in insulin-deficient patients cut production with fatty acids unchanged (Keller) — the intrahepatic switch the McGarry & Foster work localised to malonyl-CoA and carnitine palmitoyltransferase in animal liver, presented here as the textbook's account since no carded human record measures it. Counter-regulatory hormones push both limbs — more lipolysis and a direct ketogenic effect (Schade & Eaton). The ceiling in a normal fast is therefore layered: insulin never falls to zero, so lipolysis and the hepatic switch stay partly restrained and ketones plateau in the millimolar range rather than the tens of millimoles of ketoacidosis; ketones themselves feed back on lipolysis and insulin in the textbook account; and the brain's switch to ketones (Owen) cuts the glucose demand that drives the whole system. Ketoacidosis is what happens when the first layer fails — absolute insulin deficiency removes the gate while glucagon and catecholamines are high. The 24–72-hour time course of glucose, insulin, ketones and nitrogen that this regulation produces is home on pack #6255 and is deliberately not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Classic small-N physiology: two cards rest on N = 3–6 and one record prints no N; all are labelled on their faces. The malonyl-CoA/CPT-1 mechanism is animal-liver work (McGarry & Foster) and is presented only as Guyton & Hall textbook framing, never as a human evidence card.
cards.source: Synthesis of Miles JM et al., J Clin Invest 1983 (PMID: 6134753); Keller U et al., Diabetes 1983 (PMID: 6132846); Schade DS, Eaton RP, Diabetes 1977 (PMID: 908465); Owen OE et al., J Clin Invest 1967 (PMID: 6061736). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.
