shelves.title: Biphasic insulin secretion: a small ready pool fires in minutes, a reserve sustains the second phase — and the first phase is already failing before glucose rises
shelves.question: What produces the biphasic (first- and second-phase) pattern of insulin secretion, why is first-phase secretion lost early in type 2 diabetes, and how is it measured in humans?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Female · Glucose/pharmacology · Humans · Injections · Insulin/blood,physiology · Male · Pancreas/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The carded human studies carry the whole arc: Porte & Pupo's 1969 pulse experiments in man established the two-pool behaviour (a 3–5-minute acute response that a short glucose infusion depletes by 58% and a long one restores); Brunzell 1976 placed the acute response's disappearance at a fasting glucose of about 115 mg/dL across 66 subjects; Ward 1985 found relative first-phase responses already under a third of controls' in normoglycaemic women with prior gestational diabetes; and the IRAS frequently-sampled-IVGTT data (Festa 2008, n = 1,380) quantify the loss directly — about 40% in impaired glucose tolerance and up to 80% in new diabetes, far more than fasting surrogates suggest. Boron & Boulpaep / Guyton & Hall framing supplies the granule-pool mechanism (with Curry's rat-pancreas experiments named as animal framing, not carded). Small classic groups are labelled on the face (N = 8 per group on one card; one record prints no N).

cards.headline: Porte & Pupo 1969: in man, a glucose pulse releases insulin within 3–5 minutes from a small rapidly releasable pool — the human experiment behind the two-pool model
cards.summary: Porte & Pupo 1969: in man, a glucose pulse releases insulin within 3–5 minutes from a small rapidly releasable pool — the human experiment behind the two-pool model
cards.type: Human physiological study (repeated intravenous glucose pulses with insulin sampling), J Clin Invest 1969
cards.people: Normal young adult subjects given four rapid intravenous glucose injections of 5 g each, before, during and after glucose infusions of different durations. The record does not print a total participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: After the first glucose pulse, immunoreactive insulin peaked between 3 and 5 minutes and returned rapidly to baseline — the acute (first-phase) response. A short glucose infusion (300 mg/min) cut the acute response to a second pulse by 58%, but after a 20-hour infusion the acute response to a third pulse was restored to normal, and a fourth pulse after the infusion stopped produced a supernormal acute response (+200%). A simple linear glucose–insulin model cannot produce this pattern; the authors proposed a two-pool system — one pool for acute release, and a time-dependent compartment for long-term (second-phase) responses — the framework Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall still teach.
cards.watchOut: The companion biphasic experiments of Curry and colleagues were performed in the isolated perfused rat pancreas — animal work, named here as textbook framing only and not carded, in line with the physiology rule. N not documented in the record, printed on the face.
cards.source: Porte D Jr, Pupo AA. Insulin responses to glucose: evidence for a two pool system in man. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1969. PMID: 5355342. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Brunzell 1976: the acute insulin response was present below a fasting glucose of 115 mg/dL and absent above it — first-phase loss tracks the earliest rise in fasting glucose
cards.summary: Brunzell 1976: the acute insulin response was present below a fasting glucose of 115 mg/dL and absent above it — first-phase loss tracks the earliest rise in fasting glucose
cards.type: Human physiological study (intravenous glucose tolerance tests across the fasting-glucose range), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1976
cards.people: Sixty-six subjects spanning a wide range of fasting plasma glucose levels, each given an intravenous glucose tolerance test with insulin secretion and glucose disappearance measured.
cards.result: The acute insulin response to intravenous glucose was present in subjects with fasting plasma glucose below 115 mg/dL (115 mg/dL is about 6.4 mmol/L) but was absent above this level. Glucose disappearance related to the relative acute insulin response below 115 mg/dL and to the total insulin response above it; the calculated glucose disappearance rate when the acute response was zero was 1.06% per minute. The authors read 115 mg/dL as an upper limit of normal for fasting glucose and the acute response as an important determinant of glucose disappearance — first-phase secretion is therefore already gone at fasting glucose levels only modestly above today's normal range.
cards.watchOut: A cross-sectional threshold, not a longitudinal one: it shows where the acute response disappears across people, not the moment it disappears within a person. The 115 mg/dL cut-point is the study's own 1976 reading, printed as such.
cards.source: Brunzell JD et al. Relationships between fasting plasma glucose levels and insulin secretion during intravenous glucose tolerance tests. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1976. PMID: 1262429. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Ward 1985: normoglycaemic women with prior gestational diabetes already had relative first-phase responses less than a third of controls' — the defect precedes diabetes
cards.summary: Ward 1985: normoglycaemic women with prior gestational diabetes already had relative first-phase responses less than a third of controls' — the defect precedes diabetes
cards.type: Human physiological study (intravenous glucose tolerance and arginine tests in former gestational diabetes), Diabetes 1985
cards.people: Eight normoglycaemic postpartum women with recent gestational diabetes and eight controls pair-matched for age and percent of ideal body weight, studied with an intravenous glucose tolerance test and intravenous arginine at three glucose levels. Small groups, printed plainly.
cards.result: Fasting glucose only tended higher in the former-gestational-diabetes group (98 ± 3 vs 92 ± 2 mg/dL, P = 0.07; about 5.4 vs 5.1 mmol/L, about 98 vs 92 mg/dL) and basal insulin was higher (22 ± 4 vs 14 ± 2 µU/mL, P = 0.05), yet relative first-phase insulin responses to intravenous glucose were markedly lower (2,316 ± 560 vs 7,798 ± 1,036 % of basal × min, P = 0.004) and second-phase responses were also reduced (8,340 ± 946 vs 14,509 ± 2,556, P = 0.04). The insulin-sensitivity index was lower too (P = 0.001). In people at high risk of type 2 diabetes who are still normoglycaemic, the early secretory defect — first phase most of all — is already measurable.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 per group and a selected high-risk group (prior gestational diabetes), so the size of the defect should not be read onto all normoglycaemic relatives; the direction — secretion failing before glucose rises — is the finding.

cards.headline: Festa 2008 (IRAS): measured directly by frequently sampled IVGTT in 1,380 people, first-phase secretion was already about 40% lower in impaired glucose tolerance and up to 80% lower in new diabetes
cards.summary: Festa 2008 (IRAS): measured directly by frequently sampled IVGTT in 1,380 people, first-phase secretion was already about 40% lower in impaired glucose tolerance and up to 80% lower in new diabetes
cards.type: Human physiological study (frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test, multicentre cohort), Diabetes 2008
cards.people: 1,380 participants in the Insulin Resistance Atherosclerosis Study — 712 with normal glucose tolerance, 353 with impaired glucose tolerance, and 315 with newly diagnosed or diet-treated diabetes by fasting and/or 2-hour glucose — each assessed with a frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test (acute insulin response, AIR) alongside fasting surrogate markers.
cards.result: Adjusting for insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function relative to normal glucose tolerance was compromised in impaired glucose tolerance, diabetes by 2-hour glucose, diabetes by fasting glucose, and established diet-treated diabetes by 13%, 12%, 59% and 62% on HOMA-B — but by as much as 40%, 60%, 80% and 75% respectively when measured directly as first-phase AIR. Fasting surrogates (proinsulin, proinsulin-to-insulin ratio) related only modestly to AIR (r from −0.02 to −0.27), and HOMA-B markedly underestimated the size of the beta-cell defect. This is the measurement card: first-phase secretion is quantified as the acute insulin response over the first minutes of an IVGTT, and the direct measure shows a much larger early defect than fasting markers suggest.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional categories, not follow-up: the percentages compare groups at one visit. AIR is a research measurement (frequent sampling in the first 10 minutes), not a routine clinical test.
cards.source: Festa A et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: two pools explain the biphasic shape; first phase is the pool that empties first as glucose rises — and only an intravenous test measures it cleanly
cards.summary: Synthesis: two pools explain the biphasic shape; first phase is the pool that empties first as glucose rises — and only an intravenous test measures it cleanly
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Porte & Pupo 1969; Brunzell 1976; Ward 1985; Festa 2008), framed by the Boron & Boulpaep islet-physiology account (with Guyton & Hall) as textbook framing.
cards.result: The biphasic pattern is the signature of two compartments: a small, docked, rapidly releasable granule pool discharged within 3–5 minutes of a glucose rise (first phase), and a larger reserve that must be mobilised and replenished to sustain secretion (second phase) — the two-pool model Porte & Pupo inferred from human pulse experiments, with Curry's perfused-pancreas work as the animal anchor named in the textbook framing. First phase is lost early because it is the most demanding step: across 66 subjects it was present below a fasting glucose of 115 mg/dL and absent above it (Brunzell); in still-normoglycaemic women at high risk it was already under a third of control values (Ward); and measured directly in 1,380 people it was about 40% down in impaired glucose tolerance and up to 80% down in new diabetes (Festa/IRAS). Oral glucose cannot isolate it, because incretins and absorption reshape the curve — the measurement is the intravenous glucose tolerance test, ideally frequently sampled, with the acute insulin response taken over the first minutes; fasting surrogates underestimate the defect (Festa). Why the releasable pool fails first — granule docking, glucose sensing and the metabolic amplifying pathway — is presented in the Synthesis as the textbook's account, since the carded human records measure the loss rather than its molecular cause.
cards.watchOut: The human evidence measures the phenomenon and its timing, not the subcellular mechanism; one classic record prints no N and one card rests on N = 8 per group, both labelled on their faces.
cards.source: Synthesis of Porte D Jr, Pupo AA, J Clin Invest 1969 (PMID: 5355342); Brunzell JD et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1976 (PMID: 1262429); Ward WK et al., Diabetes 1985 (PMID: 3896896); Festa A et al., Diabetes 2008 (PMID: 18332099). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: The incretin effect (physiology): oral glucose evokes roughly two to three times the insulin response of matched intravenous glucose — incretin factors contribute about 73% of the insulin response in health and about 36% in type 2 diabetes
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much larger is the insulin response to oral glucose than to an isoglycaemic intravenous infusion (the incretin effect), and how much of it is lost in type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/metabolism · C-Peptide/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/metabolism · Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide/blood · Glucose/administration & dosage · Humans · Infusions, Parenteral · Insulin/blood · *Glucose Tolerance Test
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): glucose taken by mouth evokes a far larger insulin response than the same glycaemic excursion produced intravenously, because gut-derived incretin hormones (GIP and GLP-1) amplify glucose-stimulated insulin secretion — the incretin effect. The carded primary human studies quantify it three ways. Perley and Kipnis (1967) found the plasma insulin response to intravenous glucose was only 30–40% of the response to oral glucose. Nauck's isoglycaemic-infusion programme (1986) put the incretin contribution to calculated insulin secretion rates at 19.2–61.0% depending on the oral load (25–100 g), with peripheral-insulin estimates running higher because hepatic insulin extraction falls after oral glucose. The direct health-versus-diabetes comparison (Nauck 1986, Diabetologia) measured the incretin contribution to the total insulin response at 72.8% in control subjects and 36.0% in type 2 diabetic patients — about half lost — and on C-peptide responses 58.4% versus 7.6%. The mechanism split (Nauck 1993) is that GIP's insulinotropic effect is blunted in type 2 diabetes (maximum effect 54% lower) while GLP-1 [7-36 amide] retains most of its activity. The classic 1964 McIntyre intrajejunal study that first framed the effect was checked this session: its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is refused as an evidence card and named here only as the historical anchor. Every number on the cards is from a fetched record. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Perley & Kipnis 1967: the insulin response to intravenous glucose was only 30–40% of the response to oral glucose
cards.summary: Perley & Kipnis 1967: the insulin response to intravenous glucose was only 30–40% of the response to oral glucose
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oral versus intravenous glucose, insulin responses)
cards.people: Normal-weight and obese subjects, diabetic and non-diabetic, given oral and intravenous glucose in the St Louis programme; group sizes are not printed in the fetched abstract — N not documented in the record for each subgroup.
cards.result: Plasma insulin responses to intravenous glucose were only 30–40% of those seen after oral glucose, showing that an alimentary mechanism in addition to the arterial blood glucose concentration regulates insulin secretion; studies in subjects with diverted portal circulation located that mechanism in the intestinal tract. Obesity, with or without diabetes, was associated with a hypersecretory responsiveness, whereas diabetes — with or without obesity — was characterised by a marked impairment in insulin secretion. In the diabetic subjects a greater proportion of an oral load escaped initial hepatic extraction, accounting for the excessive late insulin responses during an oral glucose tolerance test.
cards.watchOut: A 1967 study using the insulin assays and non-isoglycaemic design of its era: the intravenous stimulus was not clamped to copy the oral glucose profile (that refinement came with Nauck's isoglycaemic infusions), so its 30–40% figure is the founding estimate, not the definitive quantification.
cards.source: Perley MJ, Kipnis DM. Plasma insulin responses to oral and intravenous glucose: studies in normal and diabetic sujbjects. Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1967. PMID: 6074000. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nauck 1986 (JCEM): the incretin contribution grows with the oral load — 19–61% of calculated insulin secretion, with peripheral-insulin estimates inflated by reduced hepatic extraction
cards.summary: Nauck 1986 (JCEM): the incretin contribution grows with the oral load — 19–61% of calculated insulin secretion, with peripheral-insulin estimates inflated by reduced hepatic extraction
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (isoglycaemic clamp quantification, dose-ranging oral loads)
cards.people: 6 young normal subjects given oral glucose loads of 25, 50 and 100 g and matched isoglycaemic intravenous glucose infusions; insulin secretion rates calculated from peripheral C-peptide by two-compartment kinetic analysis. N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Because the glucose profiles after all oral loads were similar, almost identical amounts of intravenous glucose (approximately 20 g) were infused in the isoglycaemic experiments. The percent contribution of incretin factors to total responses after 25, 50 and 100 g oral glucose was 85.6%, 74.9% and 93.0% when estimated from peripheral immunoreactive insulin, but significantly lower — 27.6–62.9% from C-peptide responses and 19.2–61.0% from calculated integrated insulin secretion rates. The discrepancy arises because fractional hepatic insulin extraction was significantly reduced after oral glucose (46.9–54.6%) compared with intravenous glucose (63.4–76.5%): peripheral insulin overstates secretion after oral loads.
cards.watchOut: Six subjects, and the headline percentage depends heavily on the estimator chosen (peripheral insulin versus C-peptide-derived secretion rates) — the honest range across methods and loads is roughly one fifth to three fifths of the secretion response, not a single number.
cards.source: Nauck MA et al. Incretin effects of increasing glucose loads in man calculated from venous insulin and C-peptide responses. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1986. PMID: 3522621. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nauck 1986 (Diabetologia): incretin factors contributed 72.8% of the insulin response in controls but only 36.0% in type 2 diabetes — and 7.6% versus 58.4% on C-peptide
cards.summary: Nauck 1986 (Diabetologia): incretin factors contributed 72.8% of the insulin response in controls but only 36.0% in type 2 diabetes — and 7.6% versus 58.4% on C-peptide
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (isoglycaemic comparison, type 2 diabetes versus matched controls)
cards.people: 14 patients with type 2 (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes and 8 age- and weight-matched metabolically healthy control subjects, each given a 50 g oral glucose load and an isoglycaemic intravenous glucose infusion.
cards.result: The contribution of incretin factors to total insulin responses was 72.8 ± 6.9% in control subjects and 36.0 ± 8.8% in diabetic patients (p ≤ 0.05) — about half the incretin effect lost. On connecting-peptide (C-peptide) responses the loss was starker: 58.4 ± 7.6% in controls versus 7.6 ± 14.5% in diabetic patients (p ≤ 0.05). Despite higher glucose increases, insulin and C-peptide responses after oral glucose were delayed in the diabetic patients, and the reduced hepatic insulin extraction seen in controls after oral glucose was absent in the diabetic group. Immunoreactive GIP responses did not differ between the groups — the defect lies in the response to the incretin signal, not its release.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (14 versus 8) from 1986, before modern incretin assays; the C-peptide estimate in the diabetic group (7.6 ± 14.5%) has a standard error larger than its mean, so the precise size of the loss is uncertain even though its direction and rough halving are consistent across both estimators.
cards.source: Nauck M et al. Reduced incretin effect in type 2 (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes. Diabetologia. 1986. PMID: 3514343. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nauck 1993: in type 2 diabetes the GIP limb is blunted (maximum effect 54% lower) while GLP-1 [7-36 amide] keeps most of its insulinotropic activity
cards.summary: Nauck 1993: in type 2 diabetes the GIP limb is blunted (maximum effect 54% lower) while GLP-1 [7-36 amide] keeps most of its insulinotropic activity
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (hyperglycaemic clamp with exogenous incretin infusions)
cards.people: 9 patients with type 2 diabetes (fasting plasma glucose 7.8 mmol/L [about 140 mg/dL]; HbA1c 6.3 ± 0.6%) and 9 age- and weight-matched normal subjects, studied under hyperglycaemic clamp conditions (8.75 mmol/L [about 158 mg/dL]) with infusions of synthetic human GIP, GLP-1 [7-36 amide] and placebo.
cards.result: Both incretin hormones dose-dependently augmented insulin secretion in both groups (P < 0.05). With GIP, the maximum effect in the diabetic patients was significantly lower, by 54% (P < 0.05), than in normal subjects. With GLP-1 [7-36 amide] the diabetic patients reached 71% of the increments in C-peptide seen in normal subjects, a difference that was not significant. Glucagon was lowered by the hyperglycaemic clamp in normal subjects but not in diabetic patients, and was further lowered by GLP-1 [7-36 amide] in both groups (P < 0.05) but not by GIP. The loss of the overall incretin effect in type 2 diabetes is therefore largely a loss of GIP action, with GLP-1 action substantially preserved.
cards.watchOut: Nine subjects per group with mild, well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c 6.3%) — the GIP/GLP-1 split may differ in more advanced diabetes, and the higher infusion rates produced clearly supraphysiological hormone concentrations, so the preserved GLP-1 response is partly a pharmacological-dose finding.
cards.source: Nauck MA et al. Preserved incretin activity of glucagon-like peptide 1 [7-36 amide] but not of synthetic human gastric inhibitory polypeptide in patients with type-2 diabetes mellitus. Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1993. PMID: 8423228. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the incretin effect roughly doubles-to-triples the insulin response to oral glucose in health, and about half of it is lost in type 2 diabetes — chiefly the GIP limb
cards.summary: Synthesis: the incretin effect roughly doubles-to-triples the insulin response to oral glucose in health, and about half of it is lost in type 2 diabetes — chiefly the GIP limb
cards.people: Synthesis across Perley & Kipnis 1967, Nauck 1986 (two studies) and Nauck 1993 — the primary human isoglycaemic-infusion and clamp literature.
cards.result: Three independent quantifications converge: intravenous glucose gives only 30–40% of the oral insulin response (Perley & Kipnis); the incretin contribution to secretion is load- and method-dependent at roughly 19–73% (Nauck); and the matched health-versus-diabetes comparison puts the loss at about half on insulin responses (72.8% to 36.0%) and more on C-peptide (58.4% to 7.6%). The hormone-level experiments explain the loss: GIP release is intact but its action is blunted by 54%, while GLP-1 retains most of its insulinotropic activity — the physiological basis on which GLP-1-based therapies rest.
cards.watchOut: All carded studies are small (6–14 subjects per group) and predate modern assays; the textbook's single summary percentage should be read as the middle of the measured range, not a constant of nature. The McIntyre 1964 anchor (PMID: 14149200) was refused as a card because its fetched record carries an empty abstract.
cards.source: Synthesis of Perley MJ, Kipnis DM. Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1967 (PMID: 6074000); Nauck MA et al. shelves.title: Brain fuel in prolonged fasting (physiology) — PARTIAL slice: cerebral ketone uptake is proportional to blood ketone concentration and displaces glucose at unchanged oxygen use; after 5–6 weeks of starvation ketones are the brain's predominant fuel (Owen 1967, carded on pack #6307) — roughly two-thirds of brain energy by the textbook account
shelves.question: In humans fasted for weeks, what fraction of the brain's energy comes from ketone bodies, and how was cerebral glucose-versus-ketone uptake measured?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Brain/metabolism · Carbohydrate Metabolism · Cerebrovascular Circulation · Female · Glucose/metabolism · Humans · Ketone Bodies/blood,metabolism · Male · Positron-Emission Tomography · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — PARTIAL slice, flagged prominently. Homes first: live shelf #34 already homes hepatic glucose production and its recycling fractions in fasting; pack #6255 homes the 24–72-hour whole-body fasting time course; and Owen 1967 — the anchor study for this row — is already carded on pack #6307 (hepatic ketogenesis regulation), where its cerebral finding is stated. Under the one-home rule Owen is NOT re-carded here; this shelf builds only on four free reports and cross-points the homes in prose. What the free reports establish is the measurement story the row asks for: cerebral ketone uptake rises in proportion to arterial ketone concentration and is limited by transport into the brain (Blomqvist 2002, ¹¹C-ketone PET; Mikkelsen 2015, arterio-jugular balance), and ketones displace glucose at unchanged cerebral oxygen consumption (Hasselbalch 1996, Kety–Schmidt: ketone uptake 1.11→5.60 µmol/100 g/min, glucose metabolism 25.8→17.2 µmol/100 g/min at β-hydroxybutyrate 2.16 mmol/L, ≈22 mg/dL; Svart 2018: glucose utilisation −14% at 5.5 mmol/L, ≈57 mg/dL). Owen's endpoint — after 5–6 weeks of starvation, ketones had replaced glucose as the brain's predominant fuel — and the textbook figure of roughly two-thirds (~60%) of brain energy from ketones in prolonged fasting are presented as the Guyton & Hall / Cahill account of the homed Owen study, not as numbers from this shelf's cards. Cahill's 1968 'Starvation and survival' record carries no abstract in PubMed and is therefore not carded, per the standing honesty pattern; it is carried here as programme framing only.

cards.headline: Hasselbalch 1996: with the Kety–Schmidt technique, raising blood β-hydroxybutyrate to 2.16 mmol/L (≈22 mg/dL) raised cerebral ketone uptake fivefold (1.11→5.60 µmol/100 g/min) and cut cerebral glucose metabolism from 25.8 to 17.2 — ketones displaced glucose mole-for-mole
cards.summary: Hasselbalch 1996: with the Kety–Schmidt technique, raising blood β-hydroxybutyrate to 2.16 mmol/L (≈22 mg/dL) raised cerebral ketone uptake fivefold (1.11→5.60 µmol/100 g/min) and cut cerebral glucose metabolism from 25.8 to 17.2 — ketones displaced glucose mole-for-mole
cards.type: Human physiological study (Kety–Schmidt cerebral balance + PET during ketone infusion), Am J Physiol 1996
cards.people: Healthy adult volunteers (number not documented in the record) studied with the Kety–Schmidt technique (global cerebral blood flow and arteriovenous differences) plus FDG-PET regional glucose metabolism, before and during intravenous ketone-body infusion. N not documented in the record.
cards.result: At mean blood β-hydroxybutyrate 2.16 mmol/L (≈22 mg/dL), cerebral ketone uptake rose from 1.11 to 5.60 µmol/100 g/min, counterbalanced by an equivalent fall in cerebral glucose metabolism (25.8→17.2 µmol/100 g/min), so total cerebral carbohydrate uptake and global cerebral oxygen metabolism were unchanged (144 vs 135 µmol/100 g/min). Cerebral blood flow rose 39% (51.0→70.9 mL/100 g/min). PET showed the mesencephalon oxidises ketones less than the rest of the brain. The method is the direct descendant of Owen's arteriovenous approach, applied globally and quantitatively.
cards.watchOut: Acute infusion hyperketonaemia, not weeks of fasting — it shows the brain's uptake machinery responds immediately to concentration; the fasting fraction itself comes from Owen's study, homed on pack #6307 and cross-pointed, not re-carded here. Sample size is not printed in the record.
cards.source: Hasselbalch SG et al. Changes in cerebral blood flow and carbohydrate metabolism during acute hyperketonemia. The American journal of physiology. 1996. PMID: 8967461. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Blomqvist 2002: with ¹¹C-β-hydroxybutyrate PET, cerebral ketone utilisation rose nearly in proportion to plasma ketone concentration — transport into the brain is the rate-limiting step
cards.summary: Blomqvist 2002: with ¹¹C-β-hydroxybutyrate PET, cerebral ketone utilisation rose nearly in proportion to plasma ketone concentration — transport into the brain is the rate-limiting step
cards.type: Human physiological study (¹¹C-ketone PET, nondiabetic and IDDM), Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2002
cards.people: 6 nondiabetic subjects and 6 patients with insulin-dependent diabetes, studied with positron emission tomography after bolus R-β-[1-¹¹C]hydroxybutyrate during an infusion of unlabelled β-hydroxybutyrate producing acute hyperketonaemia (0.7–1.7 µmol/mL, i.e. 0.7–1.7 mmol/L, ≈7–18 mg/dL).
cards.result: Cerebral ketone utilisation increased nearly proportionally with plasma concentration (mean 1.0 ± 0.3 µmol/mL in nondiabetic subjects, 1.3 ± 0.3 µmol/mL in IDDM). No efflux of ketones from brain was detected, and — with magnetic-resonance spectroscopy tissue data — the authors conclude transport into the brain, not intracellular metabolism, limits utilisation even in acute hyperketonaemia. No significant difference between nondiabetic and IDDM subjects.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (6 + 6) and a 10-minute uptake window after bolus tracer; the IDDM half is a patient group — the nondiabetic half carries the normal-physiology claim.
cards.source: Blomqvist G et al. Effect of acute hyperketonemia on the cerebral uptake of ketone bodies in nondiabetic subjects and IDDM patients. American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism. 2002. PMID: 12067838. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mikkelsen 2015: jugular venous sampling during β-hydroxybutyrate infusion — cerebral uptake and oxidation rose linearly with arterial concentration, with no saturation in the range tested
cards.summary: Mikkelsen 2015: jugular venous sampling during β-hydroxybutyrate infusion — cerebral uptake and oxidation rose linearly with arterial concentration, with no saturation in the range tested
cards.type: Human physiological study (arterio–jugular-venous balance + tracers during ketone infusion), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2015
cards.people: 6 healthy post-absorptive males studied basally and during three consecutive 1-hour periods of 3-, 6- and 12-fold raised β-hydroxybutyrate by infusion, with arterial, jugular and femoral venous differences combined with labelled β-hydroxybutyrate, glucose and glycerol tracers. N = 6 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Cerebral β-hydroxybutyrate uptake and subsequent oxidation were linearly related to the arterial concentration (basal 160–450 µmol/L, i.e. 0.16–0.45 mmol/L, ≈2–5 mg/dL, rising to 1.7 mmol/L, ≈18 mg/dL, at the highest infusion, where endogenous ketone appearance was completely inhibited). Systemically, even a small rise in β-hydroxybutyrate cut glucose appearance by 14 ± 2% and lipolytic rate by 37 ± 4% with insulin and glucagon unchanged; resting skeletal-muscle uptake, unlike brain, showed saturation kinetics. This is Owen's arteriovenous-difference method, organ by organ, with tracers.
cards.watchOut: N = 6, men only, post-absorptive (not prolonged-fasted); linearity is shown up to 1.7 mmol/L (≈18 mg/dL) — below the concentrations of a weeks-long fast, so extrapolation to Owen's setting is by the textbook account, not by this record.
cards.source: Mikkelsen KH et al. Systemic, cerebral and skeletal muscle ketone body and energy metabolism during acute hyper-D-β-hydroxybutyratemia in post-absorptive healthy males. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2015. PMID: 25415176. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Svart 2018: randomised PET study — infusing 3-hydroxybutyrate to 5.5 mmol/L (≈57 mg/dL) cut cerebral glucose utilisation by 14% and raised cerebral blood flow by 30%, with oxygen consumption unchanged
cards.summary: Svart 2018: randomised PET study — infusing 3-hydroxybutyrate to 5.5 mmol/L (≈57 mg/dL) cut cerebral glucose utilisation by 14% and raised cerebral blood flow by 30%, with oxygen consumption unchanged
cards.type: Human physiological study (randomised crossover PET during ketone infusion), PLoS One 2018
cards.people: 9 healthy subjects studied twice, randomised, with and without continuous 3-hydroxybutyrate infusion, with regional PET (parietal, occipital, temporal, cortical grey and frontal regions). N = 9 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: During infusion, 3-hydroxybutyrate reached 5.5 ± 0.4 mmol/L (≈57 mg/dL) — the range of a prolonged fast. Cerebral glucose utilisation fell 14% in all measured regions, oxygen consumption was unchanged, and cerebral blood flow rose 30%, so oxygen extraction fell. The authors read the pattern — same oxygen use, less glucose, more flow — as ketones substituting for glucose as oxidised fuel while delivery rises.
cards.watchOut: Glucose utilisation fell only 14% at fasting-range ketone levels in this acute study — less substitution than Owen's chronic-fasting finding, consistent with adaptation over weeks adding to the acute concentration effect; the record prints no registry ID despite the randomised design.
cards.source: Svart M et al. Regional cerebral effects of ketone body infusion with 3-hydroxybutyrate in humans: Reduced glucose uptake, unchanged oxygen consumption and increased blood flow by positron emission tomography. A randomized, controlled trial. PloS one. 2018. PMID: 29489818. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the brain takes ketones in proportion to their blood concentration — measured four ways — and after weeks of fasting that uptake makes ketones the brain's predominant fuel (Owen 1967, homed on pack #6307)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the brain takes ketones in proportion to their blood concentration — measured four ways — and after weeks of fasting that uptake makes ketones the brain's predominant fuel (Owen 1967, homed on pack #6307)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Hasselbalch 1996; Blomqvist 2002; Mikkelsen 2015; Svart 2018), framed by Guyton & Hall's account of the Cahill starvation programme as textbook framing. Owen 1967 is cross-pointed to its home on pack #6307 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Every measurement method agrees on the mechanism: cerebral ketone uptake is concentration-driven and transport-limited (Blomqvist's proportional PET uptake; Mikkelsen's linear arterio-jugular uptake), it displaces glucose uptake mole-for-mole at constant oxygen consumption (Hasselbalch: ketone uptake +4.5 µmol/100 g/min against glucose metabolism −8.6 µmol/100 g/min, the difference reflecting the different carbon content), and at fasting-range concentrations (5.5 mmol/L, ≈57 mg/dL) glucose utilisation falls measurably within hours (Svart, −14%). The chronic endpoint of that machinery is Owen's 1967 finding — after 5–6 weeks of starvation, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate had replaced glucose as the predominant fuel of the brain, measured by cerebral vessel catheterisation in three obese patients; that study is carded on pack #6307 (hepatic ketogenesis regulation), and the often-quoted figure that ketones supply roughly two-thirds (about 60%) of the brain's energy in prolonged fasting is presented as the Guyton & Hall / Cahill textbook account of Owen's data, since no card on this shelf prints that percentage. Live shelf #34 (hepatic glucose production and recycling in fasting) and pack #6255 (the 24–72-hour whole-body fasting time course) are the companion homes; this shelf is only the cerebral slice.
cards.watchOut: All four carded studies are acute-infusion experiments in fed or post-absorptive people; none repeats Owen's weeks-long fast, so the prolonged-fasting fraction rests on Owen (homed elsewhere) and the textbook account, exactly as flagged in the balance.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 8967461, 12067838, 25415176, 29489818), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. Owen 1967 is homed on pack #6307 and deliberately not re-carded. No additional source.

this shelf is only the cerebral slice. all four carded studies are acute-infusion experiments in fed or post-absorptive people; none repeats owen's weeks-long fast, so the prolonged-fasting fraction rests on owen (homed elsewhere) and the textbook account, exactly as flagged in the balance. synthesis of the cards on this shelf (pmids 8967461, 12067838, 25415176, 29489818), framed by guyton & hall textbook of medical physiology. owen 1967 is homed on pack #6307 and deliberately not re-carded. no additional source.

shelves.title: Lipolysis and fatty-acid turnover by tracers (physiology): resting glycerol appearance ~2.0 µmol/kg/min in healthy adults; fasting raises lipolysis (partly via falling glucose/insulin, with a sensitised epinephrine response); in exercise lipolysis is maximally stimulated at low intensity while plasma fatty-acid release falls as intensity rises
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the rates of lipolysis and free-fatty-acid turnover at rest, in fasting and during exercise, measured by tracers?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Epinephrine/blood · Exercise/physiology · Fasting · Fatty Acids, Nonesterified/blood · Female · Glycerol/blood · Humans · Kinetics · Lipolysis · Male · Palmitic Acid
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall): hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyses adipose triglyceride to glycerol and free fatty acids; insulin restrains it, catecholamines and fasting release it, and fatty acids not oxidised are re-esterified. The tracer literature (Wolfe and Jensen programmes) turns that account into rates: glycerol appearance — one glycerol per triglyceride split, and adipose cannot re-use glycerol — measures whole-body lipolysis, and palmitate appearance measures fatty-acid flux. At rest after an overnight fast, healthy glycerol appearance is 2.00 ± 0.16 µmol/kg/min (Klein & Wolfe 1990). Fasting to 84 hours raises lipolytic rates; restoring glucose/insulin normalises them, yet lipolysis still rises when glucose is held constant, and the epinephrine response is sensitised (Klein, Holland & Wolfe 1990). Exercise inverts the intensity intuition: peripheral lipolysis is maximally stimulated at 25% of VO₂max while plasma fatty-acid release falls at higher intensities and muscle triglyceride takes over (Romijn 1993). The Jensen ultralow-dose [U-¹³C]palmitate method reproduces radiotracer flux with a coefficient of variation of ~8–13% (Guo 1997), which is what makes these small classic numbers trustworthy as physiology.

cards.headline: Klein & Wolfe 1990: resting glycerol appearance — the whole-body lipolysis rate — was 2.00 µmol/kg/min in healthy volunteers, measured by stable-isotope glycerol and palmitate tracers
cards.summary: Klein & Wolfe 1990: resting glycerol appearance — the whole-body lipolysis rate — was 2.00 µmol/kg/min in healthy volunteers, measured by stable-isotope glycerol and palmitate tracers
cards.type: Human physiological study (stable-isotope glycerol/palmitate turnover), J Clin Invest 1990
cards.people: 10 healthy volunteers, 5 cachectic cancer-free nutritionally matched controls and 5 cachectic patients with oesophageal cancer, studied basally and during propranolol infusion with stable-isotope tracers of glycerol and fatty acids; the healthy-volunteer arm (N = 10) carries this card's normal value.
cards.result: Basal rate of glycerol appearance in healthy volunteers was 2.00 ± 0.16 µmol/kg/min — the tracer measure of whole-body lipolysis (one glycerol per triglyceride hydrolysed). Cachectic patients (2.96 ± 0.45) and matched controls (3.07 ± 0.28) were ~48% higher, a nutritional-status effect rather than a tumour effect. Triglyceride–fatty-acid cycling (re-esterification) was likewise ~50% higher in the cachectic groups, and propranolol's antilipolytic effect tracked the same pattern.
cards.watchOut: The study's purpose was cancer cachexia; the healthy value is its control arm (overnight-fasted, resting). Glycerol appearance measures lipolysis only if glycerol is not re-used by adipose tissue — the standard assumption of the method, stated in the Wolfe programme's work.
cards.source: Klein S et al. Whole-body lipolysis and triglyceride-fatty acid cycling in cachectic patients with esophageal cancer. The Journal of clinical investigation. 1990. PMID: 2243120. cards.headline: Klein, Holland & Wolfe 1990: fasting to 84 hours raised lipolytic rates — restoring glucose and insulin with an infusion pulled them back toward 12-hour values, but the heightened lipolytic response to epinephrine persisted
cards.summary: Klein, Holland & Wolfe 1990: fasting to 84 hours raised lipolytic rates — restoring glucose and insulin with an infusion pulled them back toward 12-hour values, but the heightened lipolytic response to epinephrine persisted
cards.type: Human physiological study (glycerol/palmitate tracers across an 84-hour fast), Am J Physiol 1990
cards.people: Two protocols of 5 volunteers each, studied after 12 h and after 84 h of fasting with [²H₅]glycerol and [1-¹³C]palmitate infusions, with epinephrine infusions, glucose infusions, and a protocol holding glucose at post-absorptive levels throughout the fast.
cards.result: Glucose infusion after 84 h of fasting restored glucose, insulin and lipolytic rates toward 12-hour fasting values. But when euglycaemia was maintained throughout the fast, insulin still fell and lipolytic rates still rose — the fall in glucose contributes to, but is not required for, the fasting rise in lipolysis. In both protocols the lipolytic response to epinephrine was greater after 84 h than after 12 h at similar glucose concentrations. The record's abstract reports directions and significance rather than absolute rates, so no absolute 84-hour rate is printed here.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 per protocol — classic small tracer physiology, labelled as such; the abstract gives no absolute appearance rates, and none are invented for this card.
cards.source: Klein S et al. Importance of blood glucose concentration in regulating lipolysis during fasting in humans. The American journal of physiology. 1990. PMID: 2405701. cards.headline: Romijn 1993 (Wolfe programme): during exercise, peripheral lipolysis was already maximally stimulated at 25% of VO₂max — and plasma fatty-acid release fell as intensity rose, while muscle triglyceride lipolysis only joined at higher intensities
cards.summary: Romijn 1993 (Wolfe programme): during exercise, peripheral lipolysis was already maximally stimulated at 25% of VO₂max — and plasma fatty-acid release fell as intensity rose, while muscle triglyceride lipolysis only joined at higher intensities
cards.type: Human physiological study (tracer lipolysis across exercise intensities), Am J Physiol 1993
cards.people: 5 trained subjects exercised at 25%, 65% and 85% of maximal oxygen consumption, with stable-isotope tracers and indirect calorimetry, including 2 h at 65% VO₂max and recovery from high-intensity exercise. N = 5 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: Plasma glucose uptake and muscle glycogen oxidation rose with exercise intensity, but peripheral lipolysis behaved oppositely: it was stimulated maximally at the lowest intensity (25% VO₂max) and fatty-acid release into plasma decreased with increasing intensity. Muscle triglyceride lipolysis was stimulated only at higher intensities. Over 2 h at 65% VO₂max, plasma-derived substrate oxidation rose progressively while muscle glycogen and triglyceride oxidation fell; in recovery from high-intensity exercise, lipolysis fell immediately but fatty-acid release rose — fatty acids leaving previously hydrolysed triglyceride.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 trained men-era volunteers; glycerol appearance measures whole-body lipolysis, while the muscle-triglyceride limb is inferred from the tracer/calorimetry balance, not sampled directly.
cards.source: Romijn JA et al. Regulation of endogenous fat and carbohydrate metabolism in relation to exercise intensity and duration. The American journal of physiology. 1993. PMID: 8214047. cards.headline: Guo, Nielsen & Jensen 1997: free-fatty-acid turnover can be measured with ultralow-dose [U-¹³C]palmitate — values identical to radiotracer flux, reproducible to a coefficient of variation of about 8–13%
cards.summary: Guo, Nielsen & Jensen 1997: free-fatty-acid turnover can be measured with ultralow-dose [U-¹³C]palmitate — values identical to radiotracer flux, reproducible to a coefficient of variation of about 8–13%
cards.type: Human physiological methods study (palmitate tracer flux validation), J Lipid Res 1997
cards.people: Healthy adults studied at rest and during exercise with simultaneous [U-¹³C]palmitate (0.5 nmol/kg/min at rest, 2 nmol/kg/min during exercise) and palmitate radiotracers; overnight post-absorptive flux was measured on four occasions in three individuals for reproducibility.
cards.result: Palmitate flux by the ultralow-dose stable-isotope method was virtually identical to the simultaneous radiotracer reference, and during exercise the two methods correlated at r = 0.91. Reproducibility of overnight post-absorptive flux: coefficient of variation 11–12% within a day and 8–13% between days. The method cuts the tracer dose ~100-fold versus conventional [1-¹³C]palmitate GC/MS — the Jensen programme's measurement foundation for the turnover numbers used across this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A methods card: it validates the ruler rather than printing a population flux value (the abstract gives infusion rates and reproducibility, not a mean flux), and the reproducibility series is three individuals measured repeatedly.
cards.source: Guo Z et al. Free fatty acid turnover measured using ultralow doses of [U-13C]palmitate. Journal of lipid research. 1997. PMID: 9323598. cards.headline: Synthesis: tracers put resting lipolysis at ~2 µmol/kg/min of glycerol appearance, fasting raises it (glucose/insulin-dependent in part, with a sensitised epinephrine response), and exercise stimulates it maximally at low intensity while plasma fatty-acid release paradoxically falls as intensity climbs
cards.summary: Synthesis: tracers put resting lipolysis at ~2 µmol/kg/min of glycerol appearance, fasting raises it (glucose/insulin-dependent in part, with a sensitised epinephrine response), and exercise stimulates it maximally at low intensity while plasma fatty-acid release paradoxically falls as intensity climbs
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Klein & Wolfe 1990; Klein, Holland & Wolfe 1990; Romijn 1993; Guo/Jensen 1997), framed by Guyton & Hall's fat-metabolism account as textbook framing.
cards.result: The tracer logic is uniform: glycerol appearance = lipolysis (adipose cannot re-use glycerol), palmitate appearance scaled to total fatty-acid flux, and the gap between the two is re-esterification (triglyceride–fatty-acid cycling, ~50% higher in cachexia at the same lipolysis machinery). At rest after an overnight fast the healthy rate is ~2.00 µmol/kg/min glycerol appearance. Fasting to ~84 hours raises lipolysis and fatty-acid flux; about part of that rise is the falling glucose/insulin signal (restoring them normalises rates), part is a glucose-independent sensitisation to epinephrine. Exercise redraws the map: lipolysis is maximally on at 25% of VO₂max, plasma fatty-acid release falls at high intensity (delivery, not hydrolysis, becomes limiting), and intramuscular triglyceride carries more of the load — the pattern Guyton & Hall summarise qualitatively, here with the tracer numbers attached. Absolute fasting and exercise appearance rates beyond those printed on the cards are not claimed: two of the classic records report directions and significance in their abstracts rather than absolute rates.
cards.watchOut: Classic tracer studies are small (N = 5–10 per arm) and mostly male; rates are whole-body appearance rates, not adipose-tissue blood-flow-resolved lipolysis, which the regional-balance literature measures differently.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 2243120, 2405701, 8214047, 9323598), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Paltusotine in acromegaly: IGF-1 control maintained in 83.3% versus 3.6% on placebo after switching from injections (PATHFNDR-1), and IGF-1 normalised in 55.6% versus 5.3% in uncontrolled patients (PATHFNDR-2) — the tested product is paltusotine, once-daily oral
shelves.question: In adults with acromegaly, does once-daily oral paltusotine maintain or achieve biochemical control (IGF-1) compared with placebo / prior injectable somatostatin-receptor ligands?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Acromegaly/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Receptors, Somatostatin/agonists/antagonists & inhibitors · Octreotide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Administration, Oral · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/metabolism/analysis · Peptides, Cyclic/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Ligands · Human Growth Hormone/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: The tested product is named as published: paltusotine, a once-daily oral nonpeptide selective somatostatin receptor 2 agonist (the fetched records name the drug and its class; they do not name a brand or manufacturer). Two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials from one programme point the same way. PATHFNDR-1 (N = 58), in patients already controlled (IGF-I ≤1.0× ULN) on injected octreotide or lanreotide, found that switching to paltusotine maintained IGF-I ≤1.0× ULN in 83.3% versus 3.6% on placebo over 36 weeks. PATHFNDR-2 (N = 111), in biochemically uncontrolled, medically untreated or washed-out patients, found IGF-I normalisation in 55.6% versus 5.3% on placebo at 24 weeks. The earlier phase 2 ACROBAT Edge switch study (47 enrolled; primary group N = 25) found no significant IGF-I change 13 weeks after switching from injections, with IGF-I rising significantly during a 4-week washout — consistent with the tablet holding control. Adverse events in the trials were mainly acromegaly symptoms and the gastrointestinal effects typical of somatostatin-receptor ligands. A single programme with placebo comparators and no head-to-head trial against continued injections caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Other acromegaly medical therapies are homed elsewhere (pasireotide/pegvisomant pack #5851 and live shelf #745; oral octreotide live shelf #957).

cards.headline: PATHFNDR-1 2024: after switching from injected SRLs, IGF-I control was maintained in 83.3% on paltusotine versus 3.6% on placebo
cards.summary: PATHFNDR-1 2024: after switching from injected SRLs, IGF-I control was maintained in 83.3% on paltusotine versus 3.6% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (PATHFNDR-1), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2024
cards.people: 58 adults with acromegaly whose IGF-I was ≤1.0× the upper limit of normal (ULN) on a stable dose of depot octreotide or lanreotide, switched from injections and randomised to once-daily oral paltusotine (30) or placebo (28) for 36 weeks. The primary endpoint was the proportion maintaining IGF-I ≤1.0× ULN.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: 83.3% (25/30) on paltusotine versus 3.6% (1/28) on placebo maintained IGF-I ≤1.0× ULN (odds ratio 126.53, 95% CI 13.73 to >999.99 — a relative measure with a very wide interval; P<.0001), an absolute difference of about 80 percentage points. Mean IGF-I change was +0.04 ± 0.09× ULN on paltusotine versus +0.83 ± 0.10× ULN on placebo (P<.0001); mean GH stayed <1.0 ng/mL in 87.0% (20/23) versus 27.8% (5/18); symptom-diary scores changed by −0.6 versus +4.6 (P=.02). The most common adverse events were acromegaly symptoms and gastrointestinal effects characteristic of SRLs.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is placebo after withdrawal of injections, not continued injections — the trial shows the tablet holds control that placebo loses, in patients already known to respond to SRLs; it does not compare paltusotine head-to-head with staying on injections.
cards.source: Gadelha MR et al. Acromegaly Disease Control Maintained After Switching From Injected Somatostatin Receptor Ligands to Oral Paltusotine. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2024. PMID: 38828555. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PATHFNDR-2 2026: IGF-I normalised in 55.6% on paltusotine versus 5.3% on placebo in biochemically uncontrolled acromegaly
cards.summary: PATHFNDR-2 2026: IGF-I normalised in 55.6% on paltusotine versus 5.3% on placebo in biochemically uncontrolled acromegaly
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (PATHFNDR-2), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2026
cards.people: 111 adults with biochemically uncontrolled acromegaly not on medical therapy at randomisation (stratum 1: medication-naive or off medications ≥4 months, IGF-I ≥1.3× ULN, N = 82; stratum 2: previously SRL-controlled patients after washout, N = 29), randomised to once-daily oral paltusotine (54) or placebo (57) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: IGF-I normalisation at 24 weeks — the primary endpoint — occurred in 55.6% on paltusotine versus 5.3% on placebo (odds ratio 42.81, 95% CI 8.44 to 455.82 — a relative measure with a wide interval; P<.0001), an absolute difference of about 50 percentage points, with superiority in both strata. Mean IGF-I change was −0.82 ± 0.08× ULN versus +0.09 ± 0.08× ULN (P<.0001); IGF-I fell in 92.6% of paltusotine patients within the first 4 weeks; GH <1.0 ng/mL in 57.4% versus 17.5%; symptom-diary change −2.7 versus +2.8 (P=.004). Pituitary tumour volume was stable or reduced on paltusotine. Most adverse events were acromegaly symptoms or mild, transient gastrointestinal effects.
cards.watchOut: Again a placebo comparator: in uncontrolled patients the trial shows paltusotine works against no treatment, not how it ranks against injections, pasireotide or pegvisomant; about 44% did not normalise IGF-I on paltusotine.
cards.source: Biller BMK et al. Rapid and Sustained Response of Biochemically Uncontrolled Acromegaly to Once-daily Oral Paltusotine Treatment. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2026. PMID: 41128642. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ACROBAT Edge 2023 (single-arm phase 2): IGF-I did not change significantly 13 weeks after switching from injected SRLs to paltusotine, and rose when paltusotine was stopped
cards.summary: ACROBAT Edge 2023 (single-arm phase 2): IGF-I did not change significantly 13 weeks after switching from injected SRLs to paltusotine, and rose when paltusotine was stopped
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2 switch study (ACROBAT Edge), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023
cards.people: 47 patients with acromegaly at 26 global sites switched from injected SRL-based therapy to once-daily oral paltusotine (10–40 mg/day) for 13 weeks, followed by a 4-week paltusotine washout; the primary endpoint was change in IGF-I in the group switching from octreotide LAR or lanreotide depot monotherapy (group 1, N = 25). Open-label, nonrandomised, single-arm.
cards.result: In group 1, median IGF-I change from injected-SRL baseline to week 13 was −0.03× ULN (P=.6285, not significant) and GH change −0.05 ng/mL — i.e. control was held after the switch. During the 4-week washout, IGF-I rose significantly (median +0.55× ULN, a median increase of 39%; P<.0001) and GH rose 109.1%. No patient discontinued for adverse events and there were no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and small in its primary group (N = 25): 'no significant change' after a switch is supportive, not proof of equivalence, and the washout rise mainly confirms the drug was doing the work.
cards.source: Gadelha MR et al. ACROBAT Edge: Safety and Efficacy of Switching Injected SRLs to Oral Paltusotine in Patients With Acromegaly. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2023. PMID: 36353760. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Once-weekly growth hormone in children with GHD: all three products were non-inferior to daily somatropin for height velocity — lonapegsomatropin 11.2 versus 10.3 cm/year, somapacitan 11.2 versus 11.7 cm/year, somatrogon 10.10 versus 9.78 cm/year
shelves.question: In children with growth hormone deficiency, do once-weekly growth-hormone preparations (lonapegsomatropin, somapacitan, somatrogon), compared with daily somatropin, achieve non-inferior height velocity with acceptable IGF-1 exposure?
shelves.mesh: Child · Dwarfism, Pituitary/drug therapy/metabolism/pathology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hormone Replacement Therapy · Human Growth Hormone/administration & dosage/chemistry/deficiency · Humans · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein 3/metabolism · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/metabolism · Male · Prognosis
shelves.balance: Three separate phase 3 trials, one per product, each randomised against daily somatropin for 52 weeks in treatment-naive prepubertal children with growth hormone deficiency, and all three met non-inferiority for annualised height velocity. The products are named as published: lonapegsomatropin (described in its record as TransCon hGH, a once-weekly prodrug), somapacitan (a reversible albumin-binding GH derivative), and somatrogon (a long-acting recombinant human GH). Height velocity at 52 weeks: lonapegsomatropin 11.2 versus 10.3 cm/year (non-inferior and statistically superior, P=0.009); somapacitan 11.2 versus 11.7 cm/year (non-inferiority confirmed); somatrogon 10.10 versus 9.78 cm/year (difference 0.33, 95% CI −0.24 to 0.89, against a −1.8 cm/year non-inferiority margin). IGF-1 exposure was acceptable in the trial that reports it in detail (REAL4: mean IGF-I SDS similar between groups and within the −2 to +2 range at week 52), and safety profiles matched daily GH in all three. Each product still rests on its own single pivotal trial, and adult-height outcomes are not yet in these records — the LIKELY stamp is for one-year height velocity only. Weekly somapacitan in adults is a different question, homed on pack #4794.

cards.headline: heiGHt 2021: lonapegsomatropin height velocity 11.2 versus 10.3 cm/year on daily somatropin — non-inferior and superior
cards.summary: heiGHt 2021: lonapegsomatropin height velocity 11.2 versus 10.3 cm/year on daily somatropin — non-inferior and superior
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial (heiGHt), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2021
cards.people: 161 treatment-naive, prepubertal children with growth hormone deficiency at 73 sites in 15 countries, randomised 2:1 to once-weekly lonapegsomatropin 0.24 mg hGH/kg/week or the same weekly amount of somatropin given daily, for 52 weeks. Open-label, active-controlled.
cards.result: Least-squares mean annualised height velocity at week 52 was 11.2 (SE 0.2) cm/year on lonapegsomatropin versus 10.3 (0.3) cm/year on daily somatropin (P=0.009) — the trial met non-inferiority and showed superiority. Height SDS gain was 1.10 (0.04) versus 0.96 (0.05) (P=0.01). Bone age/chronological age ratio, adverse events, tolerability and immunogenicity were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the endpoint is one-year height velocity — a surrogate for final adult height, which this trial does not report; the tested product is the TransCon prodrug formulation named in the record.
cards.source: Thornton PS et al. Weekly Lonapegsomatropin in Treatment-Naïve Children With Growth Hormone Deficiency: The Phase 3 heiGHt Trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2021. PMID: 34272849. Registry ID: NCT02781727, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: REAL4 2022: somapacitan height velocity 11.2 versus 11.7 cm/year on daily GH — non-inferior, with mean IGF-I SDS within the normal range in both groups
cards.summary: REAL4 2022: somapacitan height velocity 11.2 versus 11.7 cm/year on daily GH — non-inferior, with mean IGF-I SDS within the normal range in both groups
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial (REAL4), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2022
cards.people: 200 treatment-naive children with growth hormone deficiency at 86 sites in 20 countries, randomised 2:1 to once-weekly somapacitan 0.16 mg/kg/week or daily GH (named in the record as Norditropin, 0.034 mg/kg/day) for a 52-week main trial with a 3-year extension. Open-label, active-controlled.
cards.result: Estimated mean height velocity at week 52 was 11.2 cm/year on somapacitan and 11.7 cm/year on daily GH; non-inferiority was confirmed. Changes in height-velocity SDS, height SDS, bone age and IGF-I SDS were similar between groups, and at week 52 mean IGF-I SDS values were similar and within the normal range (−2 to +2). Injection-site reactions were reported in 5.3% on somapacitan and 5.9% on daily GH. Treatment burden fell similarly on disease measures in both groups, with a greater reduction in treatment burden on somapacitan.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a one-year primary endpoint; the point estimate slightly favours daily GH, so the claim is non-inferiority, not superiority.
cards.source: Miller BS et al. Weekly Somapacitan is Effective and Well Tolerated in Children With GH Deficiency: The Randomized Phase 3 REAL4 Trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2022. PMID: 36062966. Registry ID: NCT03811535, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Somatrogon phase 3 2022: height velocity 10.10 versus 9.78 cm/year on daily somatropin — non-inferior (difference 0.33, 95% CI −0.24 to 0.89)
cards.summary: Somatrogon phase 3 2022: height velocity 10.10 versus 9.78 cm/year on daily somatropin — non-inferior (difference 0.33, 95% CI −0.24 to 0.89)
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2022
cards.people: 228 prepubertal, treatment-naive children with growth hormone deficiency (boys aged 3–11, girls 3–10) randomised 1:1 to once-weekly somatrogon 0.66 mg/kg/week or once-daily somatropin 0.24 mg/kg/week for 12 months; 224 received at least one dose (109 somatrogon, 115 somatropin). Open-label, active-controlled.
cards.result: Annualised height velocity at month 12 was 10.10 cm/year on somatrogon and 9.78 cm/year on somatropin; the treatment difference was 0.33 cm/year (95% CI −0.24 to 0.89), whose lower bound sits above the prespecified −1.8 cm/year non-inferiority margin, demonstrating non-inferiority. Height velocity at month 6 and height SDS changes at months 6 and 12 were similar. Mild-to-moderate treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 78.9% on somatrogon and 79.1% on somatropin.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, one-year surrogate endpoint; non-inferiority margins in growth trials are wide (−1.8 cm/year), so 'non-inferior' allows a modest true deficit that the confidence interval here mostly excludes.
cards.source: Deal CL et al. Efficacy and Safety of Weekly Somatrogon vs Daily Somatropin in Children With Growth Hormone Deficiency: A Phase 3 Study. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2022. PMID: 35405011. Registry ID: NCT02968004, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Stimulated copeptin for polyuria–polydipsia: hypertonic saline testing is 95.6–96.5% accurate and beats the water deprivation test (76.6%) — arginine stimulation is easier but fell to 74.4% head-to-head
shelves.question: In adults with polyuria–polydipsia syndrome, how accurately does stimulated copeptin (hypertonic-saline-stimulated, or arginine-stimulated) distinguish AVP deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) from primary polydipsia, compared with the water deprivation test?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Arginine · Arginine Vasopressin · Diagnosis, Differential · Glycopeptides · Humans · Polydipsia · Polyuria · Saline Solution, Hypertonic · Sodium
shelves.balance: Three prospective diagnostic studies from one Swiss-led programme answer this directly, and the head-to-head trial settles the ranking. Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin (cutoff >4.9 pmol/L once plasma sodium reaches at least 150 mmol/L) made the correct diagnosis in 96.5% of 141 analysed patients in Fenske 2018, against 76.6% for the indirect water deprivation test. Arginine-stimulated copeptin looked nearly as good in its own development/validation study (pooled accuracy 93% at 3.8 pmol/L at 60 minutes; Winzeler 2019), but when both tests were done in the same 158 patients (Refardt 2023), arginine's accuracy fell to 74.4% while hypertonic saline held at 95.6% — a 21.2-percentage-point gap. So: hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin is the accurate test and has displaced the water deprivation test; arginine stimulation is simpler, safer-feeling and preferred by 72% of patients, but at the prespecified cutoff it misclassifies about one patient in four, and only extreme arginine values (3.0 pmol/L or less, or over 5.2 pmol/L) carry roughly 91% specificity. All three studies come from overlapping investigator groups and tertiary centres, which is the main reason the stamp is LIKELY rather than stronger.

cards.headline: Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin: 96.5% diagnostic accuracy versus 76.6% for the water deprivation test (N = 141 analysed)
cards.summary: Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin: 96.5% diagnostic accuracy versus 76.6% for the water deprivation test (N = 141 analysed)
cards.people: 156 patients with hypotonic polyuria recruited at 11 centres (2013–2017) who underwent both the water deprivation test and hypertonic saline infusion with plasma copeptin measured once plasma sodium reached at least 150 mmol/L; 144 completed both tests and 141 were analysed. Final diagnoses: primary polydipsia 82 (57%), central diabetes insipidus 59 (41%), nephrogenic diabetes insipidus 3 (2%).
cards.result: The hypertonic saline test (copeptin cutoff >4.9 pmol/L) gave the correct diagnosis in 136 of 141 patients (96.5%; 95% CI 92.1 to 98.6), versus 108 of 141 (76.6%; 95% CI 68.9 to 83.2) for the water deprivation test (P<0.001). For the hard distinction — primary polydipsia versus partial central diabetes insipidus — accuracy was 95.2% versus 73.3%. One serious adverse event (desmopressin-induced hyponatraemia requiring hospitalisation) occurred during the water deprivation test.
cards.watchOut: The reference diagnosis was made with copeptin results masked but incorporated the hypertonic saline test's clinical context and treatment response, which can flatter the new test; the cohort was tertiary-referral, and nephrogenic cases were almost absent (3 patients), so the 96.5% figure is about the AVP-deficiency-versus-polydipsia distinction.
cards.source: Fenske W et al. A Copeptin-Based Approach in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Insipidus. N Engl J Med. 2018. PMID: 30067922. Registry ID: NCT01940614 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Arginine-stimulated copeptin: pooled accuracy 93% at a 3.8 pmol/L cutoff in its own development and validation cohorts (98 patients)
cards.summary: Arginine-stimulated copeptin: pooled accuracy 93% at a 3.8 pmol/L cutoff in its own development and validation cohorts (98 patients)
cards.type: Prospective diagnostic accuracy study (development and validation cohorts)
cards.people: Prospective diagnostic study: development cohort of 52 patients (12 complete and 9 partial diabetes insipidus, 31 primary polydipsia) plus healthy adult and child comparator controls, and a validation cohort of 46 patients (12 complete and 7 partial diabetes insipidus, 27 primary polydipsia) plus 30 healthy adult controls, from Swiss and German centres.
cards.result: Arginine-stimulated copeptin rose substantially in primary polydipsia and healthy controls but minimally in diabetes insipidus. A cutoff of 3.8 pmol/L at 60 minutes gave a pooled diagnostic accuracy of 93% (95% CI 86–97), with sensitivity 93% and specificity 92%. Accuracy was 94% in the development cohort and 86% in the validation cohort. The test was well tolerated (median discomfort scores 3–3.5 of 10 in patients).
cards.watchOut: Accuracy was estimated against diagnoses made without a same-patient hypertonic saline comparison, and the later head-to-head trial (card 3) found substantially lower arginine accuracy in the same population — the 93% figure should not be quoted without that context.
cards.source: Winzeler B et al. Arginine-stimulated copeptin measurements in the differential diagnosis of diabetes insipidus: a prospective diagnostic study. Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31303316. Registry ID: NCT00757276 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Head-to-head in the same patients: hypertonic saline 95.6% accurate, arginine 74.4% — a 21.2-point gap (N = 158)
cards.summary: Head-to-head in the same patients: hypertonic saline 95.6% accurate, arginine 74.4% — a 21.2-point gap (N = 158)
cards.people: International noninferiority diagnostic trial: 158 adults with polydipsia and hypotonic polyuria or a known diagnosis of AVP deficiency, each undergoing hypertonic saline stimulation on one day and arginine stimulation on another; final diagnosis (AVP deficiency in 69 patients, 44%; primary polydipsia in 89, 56%) made independently by two endocrinologists.
cards.result: At the prespecified cutoffs (arginine 3.8 pmol/L at 60 minutes; hypertonic saline 4.9 pmol/L once sodium exceeded 149 mmol/L), diagnostic accuracy was 74.4% (95% CI 67.0 to 80.6) for arginine-stimulated copeptin and 95.6% (95% CI 91.1 to 97.8) for hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin (estimated difference −21.2 percentage points; 95% CI −28.7 to −14.3), so arginine was not noninferior. Adverse events were generally mild with both tests, and 72% of patients preferred the arginine test. Extreme arginine values still discriminated: 3.0 pmol/L or less identified AVP deficiency with 90.9% specificity, and over 5.2 pmol/L identified primary polydipsia with 91.4% specificity.
cards.watchOut: The reference diagnosis used the hypertonic saline test results among its inputs, which structurally favours the saline test; even so, the size of the gap and the consistency with Fenske 2018 make the ranking secure. Hypertonic saline testing requires close, rapid sodium monitoring.
cards.source: Refardt J et al. Arginine or Hypertonic Saline-Stimulated Copeptin to Diagnose AVP Deficiency. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 37966286. Registry ID: NCT03572166 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: saline-stimulated copeptin is the accurate test; arginine is the easier but weaker one
cards.summary: Synthesis: saline-stimulated copeptin is the accurate test; arginine is the easier but weaker one
cards.people: 437 patients across the three carded prospective diagnostic studies (141 + 98 + 158 analysed, with overlapping programmes).
cards.result: Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin at a 4.9 pmol/L cutoff was 96.5% and 95.6% accurate in two independent cohorts and clearly superior to the water deprivation test (76.6%). Arginine-stimulated copeptin reached 93% accuracy in its own validation setting but only 74.4% head-to-head, so it is a reasonable first test only where its result is extreme or where saline testing is impractical. PROPOSED LIKELY (test accuracy) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: All carded evidence comes from one collaborating research programme in European tertiary centres; independent external validation of the cutoffs, and performance in partial AVP deficiency specifically, remain thinner than the headline accuracies suggest.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fenske W et al. N Engl J Med. 2018 (PMID: 30067922); Winzeler B et al. Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 31303316); Refardt J et al. N Engl J Med. 2023 (PMID: 37966286). Registry IDs: NCT01940614, NCT00757276 and NCT03572166 respectively, from the records.

shelves.title: Late-night salivary cortisol for Cushing's: pooled sensitivity 95.8% and specificity 93.4% across 14,140 participants — as accurate as the dexamethasone test and urinary free cortisol, provided the assay's own cutoff is used
shelves.question: In adults being evaluated for Cushing's syndrome, how accurate is late-night salivary cortisol for diagnosis, and how does it compare with urinary free cortisol and the 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers · Clinical Laboratory Techniques · Cushing Syndrome · Humans · Hydrocortisone · ROC Curve
shelves.balance: Two meta-analyses fourteen years apart agree that late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) is as accurate as the other first-line Cushing's tests. Elamin 2008 pooled 27 studies (8,631 patients): positive likelihood ratios were 8.8 for midnight salivary cortisol, 10.6 for urinary free cortisol (UFC) and 16.4 for the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST), with negative likelihood ratios of 0.07, 0.16 and 0.06 respectively — all highly accurate in referral populations. Galm 2020, pooling 139 studies and 14,140 participants with hierarchical models, put LNSC sensitivity at 95.8% and specificity at 93.4%, essentially level with the DST (98.6%/90.6%) and UFC (94.0%/93.0%). Primary studies add the practical caveats: in Bäcklund 2023 every assay method reached an ROC area of at least 0.96, but upper reference limits for the same 23:00 sample ranged from 3.4–3.9 nmol/L by mass spectrometry to 21.6 nmol/L for one immunoassay — the number is only interpretable against the local assay's own range. In a Chinese cohort (Lin 2019), midnight salivary cortisol at a 1.7 ng/mL cutoff gave 98% sensitivity and 100% specificity and outperformed UFC (AUC 0.99 versus 0.89). Verdict: LNSC is a first-line test of accuracy comparable to DST and UFC; its weaknesses are assay-dependent cutoffs, false positives with disturbed sleep–wake cycles or sample contamination, and false negatives in mild or intermittent disease.

cards.headline: Elamin 2008 meta-analysis: salivary midnight cortisol LR+ 8.8 and LR− 0.07 — level with urinary free cortisol and the 1 mg DST (27 studies, 8,631 patients)
cards.summary: Elamin 2008 meta-analysis: salivary midnight cortisol LR+ 8.8 and LR− 0.07 — level with urinary free cortisol and the 1 mg DST (27 studies, 8,631 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analyses of 27 eligible diagnostic accuracy studies (1975–2007) in patients suspected of Cushing's syndrome; 794 of 8,631 patients (9.2%) had Cushing's syndrome — a referral-enriched sample.
cards.result: The three tests had similar accuracy: urinary free cortisol (14 studies) LR+ 10.6 (95% CI 5.5–20.5) and LR− 0.16 (0.08–0.33); midnight salivary cortisol (4 studies) LR+ 8.8 (3.5–21.8) and LR− 0.07 (0–1.2); 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (14 studies) LR+ 16.4 (9.3–28.8) and LR− 0.06 (0.03–0.14). Combined strategies performed similarly. The authors cautioned that performance in usual (non-referral) clinical practice remains unclear.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 of the 27 studies evaluated salivary cortisol, hence the very wide LR− confidence interval (0–1.2); the pooled population was enriched for severe, classic disease, which inflates accuracy for every test.
cards.source: Elamin MB et al. Accuracy of diagnostic tests for Cushing's syndrome: a systematic review and metaanalyses. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2008. PMID: 18334594. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cushing Syndrome · Dexamethasone · Humans · Hydrocortisone

cards.headline: Galm 2020 meta-analysis: late-night salivary cortisol sensitivity 95.8%, specificity 93.4% — comparable to DST and UFC (139 studies, 14,140 participants)
cards.summary: Galm 2020 meta-analysis: late-night salivary cortisol sensitivity 95.8%, specificity 93.4% — comparable to DST and UFC (139 studies, 14,140 participants)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies
cards.people: Meta-analysis using hierarchical models of 139 studies (14,140 adult participants) evaluating the overnight 1 mg DST, 2-day low-dose DST, 24-hour UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, midnight serum cortisol and dexamethasone-suppressed CRH testing for Cushing syndrome.
cards.result: Late-night salivary cortisol: sensitivity 95.8%, specificity 93.4%, LR+ 14.6 (95% CI 10.3–20.7), LR− 0.045 (0.030–0.066). Comparators: 1 mg DST sensitivity 98.6%, specificity 90.6%; UFC sensitivity 94.0%, specificity 93.0%; midnight serum cortisol sensitivity 96.1%, specificity 93.2%. Meta-regression suggested the DST is the most sensitive first-line test and UFC the least sensitive, with comparable specificity across first-line tests.
cards.watchOut: Pooled estimates average over many assays and cutoffs; a given laboratory's salivary cortisol threshold cannot be borrowed from another assay (see card 3), and mild or cyclic disease is under-represented in the underlying studies.
cards.source: Galm BP et al. Accuracy of Laboratory Tests for the Diagnosis of Cushing Syndrome. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2020. PMID: 32133504. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Assay comparison study: all six methods reached AUC ≥0.96, but the 23:00 upper reference limit ranged from 3.4 to 21.6 nmol/L by method (155 reference participants, 22 with Cushing's)
cards.summary: Assay comparison study: all six methods reached AUC ≥0.96, but the 23:00 upper reference limit ranged from 3.4 to 21.6 nmol/L by method (155 reference participants, 22 with Cushing's)
cards.people: Salivary samples at 08:00, 23:00 and 08:00 after a 1 mg DST from a reference population of 155 people and 22 patients with Cushing's syndrome, each sample measured by three LC-MS/MS methods and three immunoassays.
cards.result: Upper reference limits for 23:00 salivary cortisol were similar across LC-MS/MS methods (3.4–3.9 nmol/L) but varied widely across immunoassays: 5.8 nmol/L (Roche), 4.3 nmol/L (Salimetrics) and 21.6 nmol/L (Cisbio). Salivary cortisone limits were 13.5–16.6 nmol/L at 23:00. All methods had ROC areas under the curve of at least 0.96 for Cushing's syndrome, so accuracy was high for every method provided its own reference limit was used.
cards.watchOut: Only 22 Cushing's patients, so the AUC estimates are imprecise; the durable lesson is the sixfold spread in immunoassay reference limits — a salivary cortisol value is meaningless without the measuring assay's own cutoff.
cards.source: Bäcklund N et al. Salivary cortisol and cortisone in diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome — a comparison of six different analytical methods. Clin Chem Lab Med. 2023. PMID: 37013440.
