cards.headline: Chinese cohort: midnight salivary cortisol 98% sensitive and 100% specific at 1.7 ng/mL, AUC 0.99 versus 0.89 for urinary free cortisol (61 suspected patients, 21 controls)
cards.summary: Chinese cohort: midnight salivary cortisol 98% sensitive and 100% specific at 1.7 ng/mL, AUC 0.99 versus 0.89 for urinary free cortisol (61 suspected patients, 21 controls)
cards.people: 61 Chinese patients evaluated for suspected Cushing's syndrome (48 confirmed) plus 21 healthy volunteers; midnight salivary cortisol, midnight serum cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol were compared against the final diagnosis.
cards.result: At a cutoff of 1.7 ng/mL, midnight salivary cortisol had a sensitivity of 98% and a specificity of 100%, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.99, superior to urinary free cortisol (AUC 0.89). Mean midnight salivary cortisol was 10.18 ± 1.29 ng/mL in confirmed Cushing's versus about 0.5 ng/mL in controls.
cards.watchOut: A case-control design with healthy volunteers as part of the comparison group overstates specificity versus real clinic populations with obesity, depression or diabetes, in whom false positives concentrate.
cards.source: Lin DC et al. Midnight salivary cortisol for the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome in a Chinese population. Singapore Med J. 2019. PMID: 30488082. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: late-night salivary cortisol is a first-line test, equal in accuracy to the DST and UFC — the cutoff belongs to the assay, not the textbook
cards.summary: Synthesis: late-night salivary cortisol is a first-line test, equal in accuracy to the DST and UFC — the cutoff belongs to the assay, not the textbook
cards.people: Over 22,000 participants across the two carded meta-analyses, plus 238 participants in the two carded primary studies.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity/specificity for late-night salivary cortisol is about 96%/93% (Galm 2020), with likelihood ratios (LR+ 8.8–14.6, LR− 0.045–0.07) in the same range as the 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test and urinary free cortisol. No first-line test dominates; the choice turns on practicality (home saliva collection, repeatability for intermittent disease) and on using the local assay's validated late-night cutoff. PROPOSED LIKELY (test accuracy) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Accuracy estimates derive largely from referral populations with a high prevalence of classic disease; in low-pretest-probability screening (for example unselected diabetes or obesity), false positives will outnumber the pooled figures' implication, and guidelines still advise confirming an abnormal first test with a second, different test.

shelves.title: Low-dose versus standard-dose ACTH stimulation: two meta-analyses find the 1 µg and 250 µg tests equally accurate — both rule in secondary adrenal insufficiency, neither rules it out
shelves.question: In adults being evaluated for adrenal insufficiency, how accurate is the low-dose (1 µg) ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test compared with the standard-dose (250 µg) test, against reference standards (insulin tolerance / metyrapone testing)?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Insufficiency · Adrenocorticotropic Hormone · Adult · Humans · Predictive Value of Tests · Reproducibility of Results
shelves.balance: Two diagnostic meta-analyses, thirteen years apart, reach the same answer: the 1 µg and 250 µg cosyntropin tests perform alike. Dorin 2003 found summary ROC areas that did not differ significantly for secondary adrenal insufficiency, with sensitivities at 95% specificity of 57% (250 µg) and 61% (1 µg). Ospina 2016 pooled 30 studies (1,209 adults, 228 children) for secondary adrenal insufficiency and likewise found similar accuracy for both doses — both tests rule in reasonably (adult LR+ 9.1 high-dose, 5.9 low-dose) but neither rules out (adult LR− 0.39 high-dose, 0.19 low-dose). For primary adrenal insufficiency the high-dose test's sensitivity was 92% (5 studies, 100 patients). Primary studies show what this means at the bedside: against the insulin tolerance test, the low-dose test at a 30-minute cortisol cutoff of 550 nmol/L (about 20 µg/dL) was 97% sensitive but only 78% specific (Choi 2002, 72 patients), and in 129 pituitary patients peak cortisol on the low-dose test ran higher than on the insulin tolerance test (Simsek 2015) — cutoffs are test-specific. The practical verdict: dose choice matters far less than the cutoff and assay; a positive result on either test supports adrenal insufficiency, and a negative result on either test does not exclude secondary disease when suspicion is high — an integrated test (insulin tolerance or metyrapone) is then needed. The low-dose test also requires diluting a 250 µg ampoule, a real source of error.

cards.headline: Ospina 2016 meta-analysis: high- and low-dose ACTH tests have similar accuracy; both rule in but neither rules out secondary adrenal insufficiency (30 studies, 1,437 participants)
cards.summary: Ospina 2016 meta-analysis: high- and low-dose ACTH tests have similar accuracy; both rule in but neither rules out secondary adrenal insufficiency (30 studies, 1,437 participants)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of ACTH stimulation test accuracy: for secondary adrenal insufficiency, 30 studies enrolling 1,209 adults and 228 children; for primary adrenal insufficiency, 5 studies enrolling 100 patients.
cards.result: In adults with secondary adrenal insufficiency, likelihood ratios for a positive test were 9.1 (high-dose 250 µg) and 5.9 (low-dose 1 µg), and for a negative test 0.39 (high-dose) and 0.19 (low-dose); children's figures were in the same pattern. For primary adrenal insufficiency, only high-dose sensitivity could be estimated: 92% (95% CI 81–97%). The authors concluded both tests are adequate to rule in, but not rule out, secondary adrenal insufficiency, with low-to-moderate confidence because of bias risk, heterogeneity and imprecision.
cards.watchOut: Studies used differing cortisol cutoffs and assays and differing reference standards; pooled likelihood ratios are averages over that heterogeneity, and accuracy against modern assay-specific cutoffs may differ.

cards.summary: Dorin 2003 meta-analysis: at 95% specificity, sensitivity for secondary adrenal insufficiency was 57% (250 µg) versus 61% (1 µg) — ROC areas not significantly different
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies
cards.people: Critical review and summary ROC analysis of cosyntropin test studies (1966–2002) meeting minimum-size criteria, stratified by integrated tests of adrenal function for secondary adrenal insufficiency.
cards.result: At a specificity of 95%, summary ROC sensitivities were 97% for primary adrenal insufficiency (250 µg test), 57% for secondary adrenal insufficiency (250 µg) and 61% for secondary adrenal insufficiency (1 µg); the ROC areas for the 250 µg and 1 µg tests in secondary disease did not differ significantly (P>0.5). For the 250 µg test in secondary disease, LR+ was 11.5 (95% CI 8.7–14.2) and LR− 0.45 (0.30–0.60). Cortisol responses varied considerably among healthy people.
cards.watchOut: A 2003 evidence base using older cortisol assays; absolute cutoffs from that era (for example 550 nmol/L, about 20 µg/dL) run higher than those validated for current monoclonal immunoassays and mass spectrometry, though the dose-versus-dose comparison is assay-independent.

cards.headline: Against the insulin tolerance test, the 1 µg test at a 550 nmol/L (about 20 µg/dL) 30-minute cutoff was 97% sensitive but 78% specific (N = 72)
cards.summary: Against the insulin tolerance test, the 1 µg test at a 550 nmol/L (about 20 µg/dL) 30-minute cutoff was 97% sensitive but 78% specific (N = 72)
cards.people: Prospective study of 72 Chinese patients with suspected secondary adrenocortical insufficiency at a Hong Kong regional hospital, each undergoing the low-dose (1 µg) corticotropin stimulation test with the insulin tolerance test as the reference standard.
cards.result: The 30-minute cortisol on the low-dose test correlated most closely with the insulin tolerance test peak (r = 0.79). At the optimal cutoff of 550 nmol/L (about 20 µg/dL) or more at 30 minutes, the low-dose test had sensitivity 97%, specificity 78%, positive predictive value 81%, negative predictive value 97%, LR+ 4.4 and LR− 0.04. The test was safe and convenient.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, single-ethnicity cohort with an older cortisol assay and cutoff; the favourable LR− (0.04) is better than the pooled meta-analytic estimate (0.19) and should be read as best-case performance in expert hands.

cards.headline: In 129 pituitary patients, peak cortisol differed by test — insulin tolerance lowest, low-dose ACTH highest — so each test needs its own cutoff (N = 129)
cards.summary: In 129 pituitary patients, peak cortisol differed by test — insulin tolerance lowest, low-dose ACTH highest — so each test needs its own cutoff (N = 129)
cards.type: Primary comparative study of stimulation tests
cards.people: 129 adults (76 women, 53 men) with pituitary disorders at a Turkish university centre, each undergoing the insulin tolerance test, the low-dose ACTH stimulation test and the glucagon stimulation test; 66 patients repeated all three tests for reproducibility.
cards.result: Peak cortisol levels during the insulin tolerance test were significantly lower than during both the low-dose ACTH test and the glucagon test, and glucagon peaks were lower than low-dose ACTH peaks. All three tests had good reproducibility. The authors concluded any of the three can evaluate the HPA axis provided cutoffs are individualised for each test.
cards.watchOut: This study compares cortisol responses between tests rather than accuracy against an independent diagnosis, and it did not include the 250 µg test — it supports the cutoff-individualisation point, not a dose ranking.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the two doses are interchangeable in accuracy — what decides performance is the cutoff, the assay, and remembering that a normal result does not exclude secondary disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: the two doses are interchangeable in accuracy — what decides performance is the cutoff, the assay, and remembering that a normal result does not exclude secondary disease
cards.people: Over 1,500 participants in the carded meta-analyses' secondary-adrenal-insufficiency sets, plus 201 patients in the carded primary studies.
cards.result: Across Dorin 2003 and Ospina 2016, the 1 µg and 250 µg tests have statistically indistinguishable accuracy for secondary adrenal insufficiency; both give useful positive likelihood ratios (about 6–12) and inadequate negative likelihood ratios (about 0.2–0.45). For primary adrenal insufficiency the standard-dose test is about 92% sensitive. PROPOSED LIKELY (test accuracy) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: No carded study is a large, modern, head-to-head trial of 1 µg versus 250 µg against an integrated reference standard with a current assay; the equivalence verdict rests on two concordant meta-analyses of older, heterogeneous studies.

shelves.title: First-pass hepatic insulin extraction: about half of secreted insulin is removed before it reaches the periphery — and clearance itself is regulated
shelves.question: In humans, how much of secreted insulin is extracted by the liver on first pass, how is peripheral insulin clearance regulated (insulin resistance, secretory pattern), and how is clearance measured by C-peptide deconvolution?
shelves.mesh: Insulin · Metabolic Clearance Rate · Liver · C-Peptide · Insulin Secretion · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Human catheter and deconvolution studies agree on the shape of the answer: the splanchnic bed removed 42 ± 2% of insulin influx in the basal state and about 60% across physiological concentrations in Ferrannini's 32 catheterised subjects, falling to 29 ± 1% only at supraphysiological levels (>500 µU/mL) — extraction is large, first-pass, and saturable only far above physiology. Meier's hepatic-vein sampling in 5 healthy subjects (N = 5, printed on the face) showed the pulse pattern itself sets extraction: the liver preferentially extracts insulin pulses, so pulsatile secretion dictates systemic delivery. Clearance is regulated, not fixed: in insulin-resistant nondiabetic women the integrated insulin response was 90% higher while secretion was only 37% higher — the gap is reduced clearance (Jones 1997). Measurement rests on C-peptide: secreted equimolarly, negligibly extracted by liver, and recoverable by deconvolution — Van Cauter & Polonsky showed standard two-compartment kinetic parameters (adjusted for body surface area, sex, age) estimate secretion rates within 10–12% of individually measured ones across 200 decay curves. Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing (portal delivery, hepatic first pass, renal contribution to peripheral clearance) is named as textbook framing. One classic group is very small (N = 5) and is labelled on the face.

cards.headline: Ferrannini 1983: in 32 catheterised humans the splanchnic bed removed 42% of insulin influx basally and ~60% at physiological levels — extraction fell only at supraphysiological concentrations
cards.summary: Ferrannini 1983: in 32 catheterised humans the splanchnic bed removed 42% of insulin influx basally and ~60% at physiological levels — extraction fell only at supraphysiological concentrations
cards.type: Human physiological study (hepatic/renal vein catheterisation with clamps), Am J Physiol 1983
cards.people: Thirty-two healthy subjects with hepatic-vein or renal-vein catheters, studied in steady states of hyperinsulinaemia or hyperglycaemia achieved with the glucose–insulin clamp; arterial insulin levels of 35–1,430 µU/mL were attained with graded insulin infusions.
cards.result: In the basal state the splanchnic bed removed 42 ± 2% of the insulin influx. Splanchnic extraction stayed constant at approximately 60% across physiological insulin levels but fell to 29 ± 1% (P < 0.02) at supraphysiological concentrations (>500 µU/mL); the metabolic clearance rate of infused insulin was essentially constant within the physiological range, and hyperglycaemia (+125 mg/dL) did not alter splanchnic extraction. The kidneys extracted 25 ± 5% of arterial insulin basally, and renal insulin clearance (3.9 ± 0.4 mL/min/kg) accounted for over 80% of extrasplanchnic insulin clearance. First-pass hepatic extraction is therefore large and proportionate within physiology — the liver, not the periphery, is the dominant first site of insulin removal.
cards.watchOut: Catheter balance studies measure net splanchnic (gut + liver) extraction, labelled 'splanchnic' in the record; the purely hepatic fraction is inferred, and the record's own wording is kept here.
cards.source: Ferrannini E, Wahren J, Faber OK, Felig P, et al. Splanchnic and renal metabolism of insulin in human subjects: a dose-response study. The American Journal of Physiology. 1983. PMID: 6344651. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Meier 2005: hepatic-vein sampling in 5 healthy humans — the liver preferentially extracts insulin pulses, so the secretory pattern itself dictates systemic insulin delivery (N = 5)
cards.summary: Meier 2005: hepatic-vein sampling in 5 healthy humans — the liver preferentially extracts insulin pulses, so the secretory pattern itself dictates systemic insulin delivery (N = 5)
cards.type: Human physiological study (direct hepatic-vein sampling with deconvolution/cluster analysis), Diabetes 2005
cards.people: Five nondiabetic subjects (two men, three women; mean age 32 years, range 25–39; BMI 24.9 kg/m²), studied overnight-fasted and during a glucose infusion of 2 mg/kg/min, with simultaneous hepatic-vein and arterialised-vein sampling and direct estimation of splanchnic blood flow. Very small classic study — N = 5 printed on the face.
cards.result: Insulin and C-peptide delivery from the splanchnic bed were measured directly, and fractional insulin extraction was calculated from the difference between C-peptide and insulin delivery rates from the liver. The amplitude of insulin oscillations is approximately 100-fold higher in the portal vein than in the systemic circulation despite only a fivefold dilution — implying preferential hepatic extraction of insulin pulses. The study's conclusion: pulsatile insulin secretion dictates systemic insulin delivery by regulating hepatic insulin extraction in humans — clearance is pattern-sensitive, not a fixed fraction.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 — below the usual floor, carded as a classic direct-measurement study with the N printed on the face. The 100-fold portal-to-systemic oscillation contrast is the record's figure.
cards.source: Meier JJ, Veldhuis JD, Butler PC. Pulsatile insulin secretion dictates systemic insulin delivery by regulating hepatic insulin extraction in humans. Diabetes. 2005. PMID: 15919785. cards.headline: Van Cauter & Polonsky 1992: across 200 human C-peptide decay curves, standard kinetic parameters estimate insulin secretion rates within 10–12% of individual measurement — the basis of C-peptide deconvolution
cards.summary: Van Cauter & Polonsky 1992: across 200 human C-peptide decay curves, standard kinetic parameters estimate insulin secretion rates within 10–12% of individual measurement — the basis of C-peptide deconvolution
cards.type: Human kinetic methods study (C-peptide deconvolution validation), Diabetes 1992
cards.people: Two hundred decay curves of biosynthetic human C-peptide (after bolus intravenous injection) from normal, obese and non-insulin-dependent diabetic subjects studied in the authors' laboratory; insulin secretion rates estimated with a two-compartment model of C-peptide distribution and degradation.
cards.result: The volume of distribution and kinetic parameters of C-peptide varied by less than 30% across a population highly heterogeneous in age, sex, obesity and glucose tolerance; distribution volume correlated with body surface area (more markedly in men) and the long half-life was slightly longer in elderly subjects. With standard parameters adjusted for body surface area, sex and age, estimated mean insulin secretion rates differed by only 10–12% in each subject from those obtained with individually measured parameters. This is the measurement foundation the whole clearance literature rests on: because C-peptide is secreted equimolarly with insulin but escapes hepatic extraction, deconvolving its plasma curve recovers the secretion rate, and comparing secretion with peripheral insulin gives clearance.
cards.watchOut: A methods-validation record: its numbers are accuracy bounds for the deconvolution method (10–12%), not extraction fractions; it is carded as the measurement limb the assignment requires.
cards.source: Van Cauter E, Mestrez F, Sturis J, Polonsky KS. Estimation of insulin secretion rates from C-peptide levels. Comparison of individual and standard kinetic parameters for C-peptide clearance. Diabetes. 1992. PMID: 1551497. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jones 1997: in insulin-resistant nondiabetic women, plasma insulin responses were 90% higher but secretion only 37% higher — the difference is reduced insulin clearance
cards.summary: Jones 1997: in insulin-resistant nondiabetic women, plasma insulin responses were 90% higher but secretion only 37% higher — the difference is reduced insulin clearance
cards.type: Human physiological study (graded glucose infusion with C-peptide deconvolution), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1997
cards.people: Two groups of glucose-tolerant women chosen to represent the highest and lowest quartiles of insulin resistance in the normal population (insulin suppression test); each received graded intravenous glucose infusions (1–8 mg/kg/min), with insulin secretion rates derived by deconvolution of C-peptide using standard kinetic parameters. The record does not print the total participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Plasma glucose was only slightly higher in the insulin-resistant women, but insulin concentrations were approximately doubled. Expressed against the molar increments in plasma glucose (5 to 9 mmol/L, about 90 to 162 mg/dL), the total integrated plasma insulin response was 90% higher in the resistant group (684 ± 55 vs 360 ± 36 pmol/L per mmol/L; P < 0.001), whereas the total integrated insulin secretory rate was only 37% higher (1,494 ± 133 vs 1,093 ± 125 pmol/mmol/L/min; P < 0.05). The discrepancy demonstrates reduced insulin clearance as a regulated adaptation in insulin resistance — hyperinsulinaemia is partly a clearance phenomenon, not secretion alone.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face. Women only, selected from the extremes of the insulin-resistance distribution — the clearance difference is a between-quartile contrast, not a population average.
cards.source: Jones CN, Pei D, Staris P, Polonsky KS, et al. Alterations in the glucose-stimulated insulin secretory dose-response curve and in insulin clearance in nondiabetic insulin-resistant individuals. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1997. PMID: 9177392. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: about half of secreted insulin never leaves the liver on first pass, the pulse pattern sets the fraction, and clearance falls as insulin resistance rises
cards.summary: Synthesis: about half of secreted insulin never leaves the liver on first pass, the pulse pattern sets the fraction, and clearance falls as insulin resistance rises
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Ferrannini 1983; Meier 2005; Van Cauter & Polonsky 1992; Jones 1997), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account of portal insulin delivery as textbook framing.
cards.result: The carded human evidence supports three statements. First, first-pass extraction is large: ~42% of splanchnic insulin influx basally and ~60% across physiological concentrations, saturating only far above physiology, with the kidney clearing most of what escapes (Ferrannini, n = 32 catheterised subjects). Second, extraction is dynamic: the liver preferentially extracts pulses, so pulse mass and amplitude regulate how much insulin reaches the periphery (Meier, N = 5, direct hepatic-vein sampling). Third, clearance adapts downward in insulin resistance — a 90% higher insulin response on only 37% higher secretion (Jones). All of this is measurable in intact humans only because C-peptide deconvolution recovers secretion rates to within 10–12% using standard kinetics (Van Cauter, 200 curves). The textbook framing adds the anatomy — secretion into the portal vein, hepatic first pass, systemic delivery — as the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account; the fractions above are the fetched human records' own numbers.
cards.watchOut: Splanchnic extraction includes gut as well as liver in the catheter studies; the shelf keeps the records' wording. No animal clearance data are carded.

shelves.title: Glucose effectiveness: glucose disposes of itself at basal insulin — preserved in obesity, roughly halved in diabetes
shelves.question: In humans, what is glucose effectiveness (SG — insulin-independent glucose disposal), how is it measured with the minimal model, and how much of glucose disposal does it account for in health and type 2 diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Glucose · Glucose Tolerance Test · Insulin · Models, Biological · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Glucose effectiveness (SG) — glucose's ability, at basal insulin, to promote its own disposal and suppress its own production — is measured in humans by fitting Bergman's minimal model to a frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test (FSIGTT). Bergman's 1989 Lilly Lecture reports the core contrast: insulin sensitivity (SI) varied widely across nondiabetic groups but SG was normal in all of them, whereas in non-insulin-dependent diabetes SI was reduced 90% below normal (0.61 ± 0.16 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹ per µU/mL) AND SG alone fell with it (from 0.026 ± 0.008 to 0.014 ± 0.002 min⁻¹) — the two defects are synergistic in causing intolerance. The measurement is usable but noisy: Steil 1994 found interday coefficients of variation of ~20% for SI and ~25% for SG in 11 men studied three times. A modified minimal model extends the method to insulin-dependent diabetes (Ward 1991: SG 1.6 ± 0.5 vs 2.6 ± 0.2 × 10⁻² min⁻¹ in IDDM vs controls), and SG is itself regulated — norepinephrine raised it in NIDDM (Walters 1997). Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing (mass-action glucose uptake and hepatic glucose output suppression) is named as textbook framing. Small physiological groups (8–11) are labelled on the face.

cards.headline: Bergman 1989 (Lilly Lecture): with the minimal model, SG was normal in every nondiabetic group — but in NIDDM it fell from 0.026 to 0.014 min⁻¹ alongside a 90% fall in insulin sensitivity
cards.summary: Bergman 1989 (Lilly Lecture): with the minimal model, SG was normal in every nondiabetic group — but in NIDDM it fell from 0.026 to 0.014 min⁻¹ alongside a 90% fall in insulin sensitivity
cards.type: Human physiological programme synthesis (minimal-model FSIGTT studies), Diabetes 1989
cards.people: Human frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance tests (intravenous glucose followed by tolbutamide or insulin, with frequent sampling) analysed with the glucose minimal model, across young lean, obese nondiabetic and non-insulin-dependent diabetic subjects. The record is the programme's synthesis lecture; per-group participant numbers are not printed in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Glucose tolerance depends on insulin secretion, insulin clearance, insulin action — and on glucose per se, independent of changes in insulin, increasing glucose uptake and suppressing endogenous output: glucose effectiveness. Insulin sensitivity (SI) ranged from 7.6 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹·µU⁻¹·mL⁻¹ in young Whites to 2.3 × 10⁻⁴ in obese nondiabetic subjects, and in all nondiabetic subjects SG was normal. In NIDDM, SI was reduced 90% below normal (0.61 ± 0.16 × 10⁻⁴) and in this group alone SG was also reduced, from 0.026 ± 0.008 to 0.014 ± 0.002 min⁻¹ — defects in SI and SG are synergistic in causing glucose intolerance. SG is thus a real, separately measurable component of disposal that fails only when diabetes is present.
cards.watchOut: A lecture synthesising the programme's human studies rather than a single cohort report; the SG and SI values are the record's own. The MeSH 'Animals' tag reflects the lecture's scope — only its human minimal-model findings are carded here, and no animal data are presented as evidence.

cards.headline: Welch 1990: exogenous-insulin FSIGTTs extend minimal-model measurement to diabetic subjects — diabetic SI was 0.61 vs ~3.4–4.1 × 10⁻⁴ in normals, validating the insulin-modified test
cards.summary: Welch 1990: exogenous-insulin FSIGTTs extend minimal-model measurement to diabetic subjects — diabetic SI was 0.61 vs ~3.4–4.1 × 10⁻⁴ in normals, validating the insulin-modified test
cards.type: Human physiological methods study (insulin-modified FSIGTT, minimal model), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1990
cards.people: Normal volunteers given FSIGTTs supplemented with both tolbutamide and insulin on separate occasions, and diabetic subjects given insulin-supplemented FSIGTTs only; minimal-model analysis of insulin sensitivity in both.
cards.result: In normal subjects the tolbutamide- and insulin-modified assessments correlated strongly (r = 0.87; P < 0.001) with rank order maintained over a 3-fold range of SI, though insulin-determined SI was 16% lower (3.4 ± 0.4 vs 4.1 ± 0.4 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹ per µU/mL; P < 0.01). Diabetic subjects had markedly lower insulin sensitivity than controls (SI = 0.61 ± 0.16; P < 0.0001) — the same diabetic SI value the Bergman lecture reports alongside the reduced SG. Fasting glucose correlated inversely with both SI (r = −0.62) and acute insulin responses (r = −0.72) across subjects. The insulin-modified FSIGTT is what makes SG/SI measurement possible in people who cannot mount their own insulin response.
cards.watchOut: The record does not print the total participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record. The 16% tolbutamide-vs-insulin offset is a method difference to remember when comparing SG/SI values across studies.

cards.headline: Ward 1991: a modified minimal model in C-peptide-negative IDDM — SG was reduced (1.6 vs 2.6 × 10⁻² min⁻¹) even with supranormal insulin infused (N = 8)
cards.summary: Ward 1991: a modified minimal model in C-peptide-negative IDDM — SG was reduced (1.6 vs 2.6 × 10⁻² min⁻¹) even with supranormal insulin infused (N = 8)
cards.type: Human physiological study (modified minimal model in IDDM), Metabolism 1991
cards.people: Eight young non-obese C-peptide-negative subjects with insulin-dependent diabetes, given FSIGTTs during an exogenous insulin infusion patterned to approximate normal secretion (first-phase free insulin 62 ± 9 mU/L; second phase 34 ± 9 mU/L), with a modified minimal model estimating SI and SG. Small study — N = 8 printed on the face.
cards.result: Despite deliberately supranormal plasma free insulin, the diabetic subjects showed low-normal glucose disappearance (KG 1.3 ± 0.29 × 10⁻² min⁻¹). The modified model resolved parameters well (fractional SD < 0.5): SI was 2.5 ± 0.6 vs 8.3 ± 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹·mU⁻¹·L⁻¹ and SG was 1.6 ± 0.5 vs 2.6 ± 0.2 × 10⁻² min⁻¹ in IDDM vs controls (P < 0.05) — glucose-mediated glucose disposal itself is reduced in insulin-dependent diabetes, not merely insulin action. (Units are as printed in the record, × 10⁻² min⁻¹ for SG.)
cards.watchOut: N = 8, printed on the face. SG here depends on the infused-insulin pattern approximating physiology; the record states the achieved insulin levels so the comparison can be judged.

cards.headline: Steil 1994: minimal-model SG is repeatable enough to use but noisy — interday CV ~25% for SG and ~20% for SI in 11 men tested three times
cards.summary: Steil 1994: minimal-model SG is repeatable enough to use but noisy — interday CV ~25% for SG and ~20% for SI in 11 men tested three times
cards.type: Human physiological methods study (repeatability of FSIGTT minimal model), Diabetes 1994
cards.people: Eleven normal men each given three frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance tests over 12 days under fixed diet and limited physical activity; minimal-model analysis on both the full 30-sample and a reduced 12-sample data set.
cards.result: Insulin sensitivity from the 30-sample set averaged 0.8 ± 0.083 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹ per (pmol/L) (range 0.10–1.64) with a mean interday coefficient of variation of 20.2 ± 3.2% (range 6–44%). Glucose effectiveness was slightly less repeatable, with average interday variability of 25.1 ± 8.8%. The 12-sample set gave a near-identical mean SI (0.82 ± 0.08 × 10⁻⁴; P = 0.37 vs full set) but tended to vary more. Any single SG value therefore carries roughly a quarter-turn of measurement noise — group differences (like the near-halving in diabetes) exceed it; small individual differences may not.
cards.watchOut: Men only, N = 11. Carded as the measurement-precision limb: SG claims elsewhere on this shelf should be read against this ~25% interday variability.
cards.source: Steil GM, Murray J, Bergman RN, Buchanan TA. Repeatability of insulin sensitivity and glucose effectiveness from the minimal model. Implications for study design. Diabetes. 1994. cards.headline: Walters 1997: physiological norepinephrine raised glucose effectiveness in NIDDM (SG 0.89 → 1.63 × 10⁻² min⁻¹) while reducing overall disposal — SG is itself regulated (N = 8)
cards.summary: Walters 1997: physiological norepinephrine raised glucose effectiveness in NIDDM (SG 0.89 → 1.63 × 10⁻² min⁻¹) while reducing overall disposal — SG is itself regulated (N = 8)
cards.type: Human physiological study (randomised-order IVGTT with norepinephrine infusion), Metabolism 1997
cards.people: Eight well-controlled patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes, each given two intravenous glucose tolerance tests (after saline or norepinephrine at 25 ng/kg/min, in random order), with supplemental exogenous insulin approximating normal secretion and minimal-model estimation of SG and SI. Small study — N = 8 printed on the face.
cards.result: Norepinephrine tripled plasma norepinephrine and significantly reduced overall glucose disposal (KG 0.73 ± 0.06 vs 0.61 ± 0.06 × 10⁻² min⁻¹; P < 0.05) without reducing insulin sensitivity (2.33 ± 0.8 vs 2.62 ± 0.9 × 10⁻⁴ min⁻¹ per mU/L; not significant). Mean second-phase insulin secretion fell, but glucose effectiveness rose significantly (SG 0.89 ± 0.08 vs 1.63 ± 0.2 × 10⁻² min⁻¹; P < 0.05), with glucose effectiveness at zero insulin also increased. SG is therefore not a fixed mass-action constant — catecholamines can recruit it even as they impair disposal overall.
cards.watchOut: N = 8, printed on the face; a pharmacological-probe study. SG values are printed in the record's × 10⁻² min⁻¹ scaling and are not directly interchangeable with the × 10⁰ scaling used in the Bergman lecture card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: glucose disposes of itself — SG is a measurable, roughly halved-in-diabetes component of tolerance that only the intravenous minimal-model test can isolate
cards.summary: Synthesis: glucose disposes of itself — SG is a measurable, roughly halved-in-diabetes component of tolerance that only the intravenous minimal-model test can isolate
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human studies above (Bergman 1989; Welch 1990; Ward 1991; Steil 1994; Walters 1997), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep account of glucose uptake and hepatic output as textbook framing.
cards.result: At basal insulin, glucose itself drives a substantial share of its own disposal and suppresses hepatic glucose production — that insulin-independent component is glucose effectiveness, SG. The minimal model extracts it (with SI) from a frequently sampled IVGTT, using tolbutamide or insulin modification when endogenous secretion is inadequate (Welch: the two modifications agree, r = 0.87). The consistent human finding is selectivity: SG is preserved across lean and obese nondiabetic people while SI varies, and SG falls — from 0.026 to 0.014 min⁻¹ in the Bergman programme's NIDDM data, and to 1.6 vs 2.6 × 10⁻² min⁻¹ in Ward's IDDM study — when diabetes is present, compounding the insulin-action defect. The measure carries ~25% interday variability (Steil), and SG can be acutely raised by norepinephrine (Walters), so it is a regulated physiological variable, not a constant. Oral tests cannot isolate SG because absorption and incretins reshape the curve — the intravenous test is the measurement, per the textbook framing and the carded methods alike.
cards.watchOut: SG scalings differ between records (min⁻¹ vs × 10⁻² min⁻¹); each card keeps its record's own scaling and says so. No animal minimal-model data are carded.

shelves.title: Cortisol pulsatility: the hourly rhythm is real and changes brain responses at the same dose — the patient benefit is not yet proven
shelves.question: In humans, how is cortisol secreted in ultradian pulses across the circadian cycle, and does the pattern (pulsatile vs continuous) of glucocorticoid exposure change tissue responses at the same total dose?
shelves.mesh: Hydrocortisone · Ultradian Rhythm · Circadian Rhythm · Glucocorticoids · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. That cortisol is secreted in hourly ultradian pulses riding on the circadian wave is established human physiology (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Ganong; dynamics reviewed in the Lightman programme). Whether the pattern itself matters at equal total dose now has direct human experimental evidence — but from one research programme and small samples, hence EMERGING. In healthy men whose endogenous cortisol was suppressed and replaced at the same dose in different patterns, pulsatile vs non-pulsatile delivery changed emotional processing, recognition accuracy and attentional bias, sleep quality and working memory (Kalafatakis 2018). A 15-volunteer three-way crossover trial confirmed pattern effects on morning vigour/fatigue/concentration, diurnal mood and resting-state brain networks (Kalafatakis 2021). A validated subcutaneous pulsatile pump reproduces the physiological rhythm in volunteers (Russell 2014), and in adrenal insufficiency the 6-week PULSES crossover trial (21 analysed) found no change in its primary facial-recognition outcome but subjective fatigue/mood improvements and differential amygdala/insula processing — a null primary endpoint, printed as such. Refusal reported: the slate's named Henley et al. 2009 pulsatile-infusion anchor could not be verified as a fetched PubMed record this session and is therefore NOT carded; the shelf rests on the four fetched records below.

cards.headline: Kalafatakis & Russell 2018: the SAME cortisol dose given in different patterns changed emotional processing, sleep and working memory in healthy men — ultradian rhythmicity is necessary for normal responses
cards.summary: Kalafatakis & Russell 2018: the SAME cortisol dose given in different patterns changed emotional processing, sleep and working memory in healthy men — ultradian rhythmicity is necessary for normal responses
cards.type: Human physiological experiment (endogenous suppression with patterned cortisol replacement), Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2018
cards.people: Healthy male volunteers in whom endogenous glucocorticoid production was manipulated and cortisol restored in pulsatile vs non-pulsatile patterns at the same total dose, with emotional-face processing, recognition accuracy and attentional bias, sleep quality and working memory measured. The record does not print the participant number in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Exactly the same dose of cortisol administered in different patterns altered the neural processing underlying responses to emotional stimulation, the accuracy of recognition and attentional bias toward/away from emotional faces, the quality of sleep, and working-memory performance. The authors conclude that ultradian rhythmicity of plasma cortisol is necessary for normal emotional and cognitive responses in man — pattern is a biological variable in its own right, not a detail of delivery. (The mechanistic background the paper gives — pulses emerging from pituitary–adrenal feedforward/feedback delays, and rodent gene-expression data — is framing; the carded experiment is the human pattern comparison.)
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face; healthy men only, short-term pattern manipulation, surrogate cognitive/emotional endpoints — no clinical outcomes. The rodent work cited in the paper is not carded.
cards.source: Kalafatakis K, Russell GM, Harmer CJ, Munafo MR, et al. Ultradian rhythmicity of plasma cortisol is necessary for normal emotional and cognitive responses in man. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2018. PMID: 29632168. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kalafatakis 2021: three-way crossover in 15 volunteers — abolishing the ultradian rhythm (circadian kept) changed morning vigour, mood pattern and brain network connectivity
cards.summary: Kalafatakis 2021: three-way crossover in 15 volunteers — abolishing the ultradian rhythm (circadian kept) changed morning vigour, mood pattern and brain network connectivity
cards.type: Randomised double-blind three-way crossover physiological trial, Psychoneuroendocrinology 2021
cards.people: Fifteen healthy volunteers in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled three-way crossover trial: endogenous glucocorticoid synthesis was pharmacologically suppressed and hydrocortisone replaced in three regimes — (i) normal ultradian + circadian profile, (ii) normal circadian but ultradian rhythm abolished, (iii) a standard oral-replacement-like regime with suboptimal circadian and ultradian rhythm. Mood (ecological momentary assessment), computerised behavioural tests and resting-state functional neuroimaging were measured. Small trial — N = 15 printed on the face.
cards.result: Changing only the temporal mode of replacement changed (i) morning levels of self-perceived vigour, fatigue and concentration, (ii) the diurnal pattern of mood variation, and (iii) within-network functional connectivity of large-scale resting-state brain networks, with further effects on functional connectivity reported in the full record. Keeping the circadian wave while flattening the hourly pulses was enough to move brain and mood measures — isolating the ultradian component as the active ingredient.
cards.watchOut: N = 15, printed on the face; healthy volunteers, short exposures, imaging and mood endpoints. The abstract excerpt is truncated mid-list in the fetched record, so only the three fully stated result domains are printed here.
cards.source: Kalafatakis K, Russell GM, Ferguson SG, Grabski M, et al. Glucocorticoid ultradian rhythmicity differentially regulates mood and resting state networks in the human brain: A randomised controlled clinical trial. Psychoneuroendocrinology. 2021. cards.headline: Russell 2014: a portable subcutaneous pulsatile pump reproduced physiological circadian + ultradian cortisol rhythmicity in suppressed healthy volunteers — the delivery tool the pattern trials depend on
cards.summary: Russell 2014: a portable subcutaneous pulsatile pump reproduced physiological circadian + ultradian cortisol rhythmicity in suppressed healthy volunteers — the delivery tool the pattern trials depend on
cards.type: Human physiological validation study (pulsatile subcutaneous hydrocortisone delivery), Clin Endocrinol 2014
cards.people: Healthy volunteers under dexamethasone and metyrapone suppression of endogenous cortisol, receiving hydrocortisone by a novel portable pulsatile continuous subcutaneous delivery system, validated against physiological cortisol profiles.
cards.result: Pulsatile subcutaneous hydrocortisone more closely replicated physiological circadian and ultradian rhythmicity than conventional (smooth) replacement, which produces smooth hormone blood levels and does not replicate pulsatile secretion. The paper frames why pattern could matter at tissue level: oscillating cortisol is seen in tissues such as brain and triggers pulses of gene activation and downstream signalling, and constant vs pulsatile presentation produces different patterns of gene regulation and different neuroendocrine and behavioural responses (presented in the record as the programme's rationale). This card is the methods/delivery limb: without a pump that can actually reproduce the rhythm, the pattern question cannot be tested in patients.
cards.watchOut: A validation/feasibility record — it shows the rhythm can be reproduced, not that reproducing it improves outcomes; the outcome evidence is the Kalafatakis and PULSES cards. Participant number is not printed in the abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.source: Russell GM, Durant C, Ataya A, Papastathi C, et al. Subcutaneous pulsatile glucocorticoid replacement therapy. Clinical Endocrinology. 2014. PMID: 24735400. cards.headline: PULSES 2024: in adrenal insufficiency, 6 weeks of pulsatile pump hydrocortisone made NO difference to the primary facial-recognition outcome, with subjective fatigue/mood gains and altered amygdala/insula processing (21 analysed)
cards.summary: PULSES 2024: in adrenal insufficiency, 6 weeks of pulsatile pump hydrocortisone made NO difference to the primary facial-recognition outcome, with subjective fatigue/mood gains and altered amygdala/insula processing (21 analysed)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover feasibility trial in adrenal insufficiency, J Intern Med 2024
cards.people: Adults with primary adrenal insufficiency in a 6-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover feasibility trial (Bristol, UK; ISRCTN67193733): usual-dose hydrocortisone given either as pulsed subcutaneous pump therapy replicating circadian + ultradian rhythm, or as standard care. Twenty-two recruited, 20 completed both arms, 21 analysed; primary outcome the facial expression recognition task (FERT) at week 6.
cards.result: No change was seen in the FERT primary outcome (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). There were, however, subjective improvements in fatigue and mood, and functional MRI revealed differential neural processing to emotional cues and visual stimulation, with region-of-interest analysis identifying the left amygdala and insula — glucocorticoid-sensitive regions involved in emotional ambiguity — and a post hoc FERT analysis consistent with that response. Four serious adverse events occurred (three intercurrent illnesses, as described in the record's excerpt). The patient-population test of the pattern hypothesis is thus genuinely mixed: physiology and subjective state move, the pre-specified cognitive endpoint does not.
cards.watchOut: Feasibility-sized (21 analysed) with a null primary endpoint — carded with the null on its face. Post hoc and imaging findings are hypothesis-generating, and the shelf's EMERGING stamp reflects exactly this state of the evidence.
cards.source: Russell G, Kalafatakis K, Durant C, Marchant N, et al. Ultradian hydrocortisone replacement alters neuronal processing, emotional ambiguity, affect and fatigue in adrenal insufficiency: The PULSES trial. Journal of Internal Medicine. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: cortisol's hourly pulses are real, reproducible and biologically active in humans — but the patient-level payoff is unproven, so the pattern claim stays EMERGING
cards.summary: Synthesis: cortisol's hourly pulses are real, reproducible and biologically active in humans — but the patient-level payoff is unproven, so the pattern claim stays EMERGING
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records above (Kalafatakis 2018; Kalafatakis 2021; Russell 2014; PULSES 2024), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of pulsatile HPA secretion as textbook framing.
cards.result: Three layers are established: secretion is ultradian-pulsatile across the circadian cycle (textbook framing, and the premise every carded trial manipulates); the rhythm can be reproduced by a subcutaneous pump in suppressed volunteers (Russell 2014); and at the same total dose, pattern changes brain processing, mood dynamics, sleep and working memory in healthy men (Kalafatakis 2018, 2021 — the cleanest possible isolation of pattern from dose). The fourth layer — that restoring the pattern helps patients — is not established: the only patient trial, PULSES in adrenal insufficiency, was null on its primary cognitive endpoint with subjective and imaging signals in the other direction. Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Note on the refused anchor: the slate named Henley et al. 2009 pulsatile hydrocortisone infusion work as an anchor; no record matching it could be fetched and verified this session, so it is not carded and no Henley numbers appear on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: All positive pattern evidence comes from one programme (Bristol/Lightman group) in small samples; independent replication is the missing step. No animal pulsatility data are carded.

shelves.title: Ghrelin around meals: plasma ghrelin rises nearly twofold before a meal and falls within an hour of eating, and intravenous ghrelin increases hunger and buffet energy intake by roughly a quarter in lean volunteers and more in obese subjects
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how does ghrelin behave around meals — how high is the preprandial rise and postprandial fall, and how much does infused ghrelin increase hunger and food intake at a buffet meal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aging · Appetite/drug effects · Circadian Rhythm/physiology · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Eating/physiology · Energy Intake/drug effects · Fasting/blood · Female · Gastric Emptying/drug effects · Ghrelin · Humans · Hunger/drug effects · Insulin/blood · Leptin/blood · Male · Obesity/blood,ethnology,physiopathology · Peptide Hormones · Peptides/blood · Postprandial Period
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: ghrelin, secreted mainly by the stomach, is a hunger signal — levels rise during fasting and before meals, fall after eating, and the hormone stimulates appetite and food intake, acting reciprocally to insulin and in the opposite direction to leptin's satiety signal. The carded human studies fit that frame quantitatively: a nearly twofold preprandial rise with a fall to trough within 1 hour in 10 subjects sampled 38 times over 24 hours (Cummings 2001); a 28% rise in buffet energy intake on intravenous ghrelin in 9 volunteers, in every individual (Wren 2001); dose-dependent increases in lean and obese subjects (Druce 2005); and lower fasting levels in obesity (Tschöp 2001). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Cummings 2001: in 10 healthy subjects ghrelin rose nearly twofold before each meal and fell to trough within 1 hour after eating
cards.summary: Cummings 2001: in 10 healthy subjects ghrelin rose nearly twofold before each meal and fell to trough within 1 hour after eating
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour meal-pattern profiling) — N = 10
cards.people: 10 healthy subjects given meals on a fixed schedule, with plasma sampled 38 times over 24 hours; ghrelin, insulin and leptin measured by radioimmunoassay.
cards.result: Plasma ghrelin increased nearly twofold immediately before each meal and fell to trough levels within 1 h after eating — a pattern reciprocal to insulin. Intermeal ghrelin also showed a diurnal rhythm in phase with leptin, rising through the day to a zenith at 0100 and falling to a nadir at 0900. Pre- and post-breakfast trough values correlated strongly with the 24-h integrated area under the curve (r = 0.873 and 0.954).
cards.watchOut: Fixed-schedule meals in a study unit: the rise anticipates scheduled meals, so the record shows entrainment to meal timing as well as spontaneous hunger; it does not by itself prove ghrelin initiates the meal.
cards.source: Cummings DE et al. A preprandial rise in plasma ghrelin levels suggests a role in meal initiation in humans. Diabetes. 2001. PMID: 11473029. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wren 2001: intravenous ghrelin increased buffet energy intake by 28% in every one of 9 healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Wren 2001: intravenous ghrelin increased buffet energy intake by 28% in every one of 9 healthy volunteers
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised double-blind cross-over infusion) — N = 9 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: 9 healthy volunteers in a randomised double-blind cross-over study of intravenous ghrelin (5.0 pmol/kg/min) versus saline infusion, eating from a free-choice buffet; gastric emptying assessed by the paracetamol absorption test.
cards.result: Energy consumed at the buffet increased in every individual during ghrelin infusion (mean increase 28 ± 3.9%, P<0.001), and visual analogue appetite scores were greater on ghrelin than saline. Ghrelin had no effect on gastric emptying. The authors identified ghrelin as the first circulating hormone demonstrated to stimulate food intake in humans.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study: N=9 is printed on the face per the labelling rule for sub-10 physiology studies. The infused dose produces pharmacological, not meal-physiological, exposure; the size of the intake effect at endogenous levels is inferred, not measured here.
cards.source: Wren AM et al. Ghrelin enhances appetite and increases food intake in humans. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2001. PMID: 11739476. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Druce 2005: ghrelin infusion increased buffet intake in lean and obese subjects, most at the high dose in the obese group (+70%)
cards.summary: Druce 2005: ghrelin infusion increased buffet intake in lean and obese subjects, most at the high dose in the obese group (+70%)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (randomised double-blind infusion) — N = 24 (12 lean, 12 obese)
cards.people: 12 healthy lean subjects (mean BMI 20.5 ± 0.17 kg/m²) and 12 healthy overweight/obese subjects (mean BMI 31.9 ± 1.02 kg/m²) in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study of intravenous ghrelin at 1 and 5 pmol/kg/min.
cards.result: Low-dose ghrelin increased ad libitum buffet energy intake in the obese group only (mean increase 36.6 ± 9.4%, P<0.01). High-dose ghrelin increased intake in both groups (lean 20.1 ± 10.6%; obese 70.1 ± 15.5%; P<0.01 in both) and increased the rated palatability of food in the obese group — obese people remain sensitive to ghrelin's appetite-stimulating effect despite their lower endogenous levels.
cards.watchOut: Two dose levels and two BMI groups in 24 subjects: the subgroup percentages have wide standard errors and are presented as the record gives them, not pooled.
cards.source: Druce MR et al. Ghrelin increases food intake in obese as well as lean subjects. International journal of obesity (2005). 2005. PMID: 15917842. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tschöp 2001: fasting ghrelin was lower in obesity and negatively correlated with body fat, insulin and leptin
cards.summary: Tschöp 2001: fasting ghrelin was lower in obesity and negatively correlated with body fat, insulin and leptin
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (fasting cross-sectional measurement) — N = 30
cards.people: 15 Caucasians (31 ± 9 years, 29 ± 10% body fat) and 15 Pima Indians (33 ± 5 years, 30 ± 8% body fat), with body composition by dual X-ray absorptiometry and fasting plasma ghrelin by radioimmunoassay.
cards.result: Fasting plasma ghrelin correlated negatively with percent body fat (r = −0.45, P = 0.01), fasting insulin (r = −0.45, P = 0.01) and leptin (r = −0.38, P = 0.03). Ghrelin was lower in obese than lean Caucasians (P<0.01) and lower in Pima Indians than Caucasians (87 ± 28 vs 129 ± 34 fmol/ml, P<0.01), a difference that persisted after adjustment for fasting insulin.
cards.watchOut: Fasting, cross-sectional values only: this card sets the between-person level (lower in obesity), not the within-day meal pattern, which the Cummings and infusion cards carry.
cards.source: Tschöp M et al. Circulating ghrelin levels are decreased in human obesity. Diabetes. 2001. PMID: 11289032. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ghrelin rises before meals, falls after them, and raising it experimentally raises hunger and buffet intake — the textbook meal-initiation signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: ghrelin rises before meals, falls after them, and raising it experimentally raises hunger and buffet intake — the textbook meal-initiation signal
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (gastrointestinal/endocrine chapters). No new data.
cards.result: Endogenous ghrelin rises nearly twofold before scheduled meals and falls within an hour of eating (PMID 11473029); infused ghrelin raises buffet intake by about a fifth to a quarter in lean volunteers (PMIDs 11739476, 15917842) and by more in obese subjects at the higher dose, who remain ghrelin-sensitive despite lower fasting levels (PMIDs 15917842, 11289032). That combination — a preprandial signal, a postprandial fall, and a causal intake effect on infusion — is why the textbooks present ghrelin as a meal-initiation and hunger hormone, reciprocal to insulin and opposite in direction to leptin over the day. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: endogenous ghrelin behaviour and infused-ghrelin effects in healthy humans. Ghrelin-receptor agonist drugs for gastroparesis and the macimorelin diagnostic test are different questions, homed elsewhere (pack #2037; pack #6268).
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 11473029, 11739476, 15917842, 11289032), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: GnRH pulse-frequency decoding: at a fixed GnRH dose, slower pulses raise FSH while LH holds and faster pulses erode per-pulse responsiveness (FSH most) — shown in GnRH-deficient men and women given exogenous pulses at varied frequency, across the same range the menstrual cycle uses
shelves.question: In humans, how does GnRH pulse frequency decode at the pituitary — why do faster pulses favour LH and slower pulses favour FSH secretion, and what did the GnRH-deficient 'pituitary clamp' experiments (fixed exogenous GnRH pulses at varied frequency) show?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amenorrhea/drug therapy,physiopathology · Drug Administration Schedule · Estradiol/blood · Female · Follicle Stimulating Hormone/blood,metabolism · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Humans · Hypogonadism/blood · Luteinizing Hormone/blood,metabolism · Male · Menstrual Cycle · Periodicity · Testosterone/blood
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology). The textbook account: GnRH must arrive in pulses; the gonadotroph decodes pulse frequency, faster frequencies favouring LH and slower frequencies favouring FSH, which is how one releasing hormone differentially controls two gonadotropins across the cycle. The human evidence is the 'pituitary clamp': in GnRH-deficient people the experimenter sets the pulse train. Slowing a constant daily dose raised FSH with LH unchanged (Gross 1987); accelerating pulses reduced per-pulse responsiveness, FSH more than LH (Spratt 1987); in women, 120-minute pulses blunted the LH surge and lowered ovulation versus 60-minute pulses, without raising FSH (Filicori 1989) — a nuance against the simplest form of the slogan, printed on that card. The endogenous LH pulse interval spans ~71 to ~216 minutes across the cycle (Filicori 1986). Note on the foundation: Belchetz et al. 1978 (PMID 100883, verified by title search this session) established pulsatile-versus-continuous decoding in rhesus monkeys — animal work, so under this library's physiology rules it is NOT carded; it is named here as labelled textbook prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Gross 1987: at a constant daily LHRH dose in GnRH-deficient men, slowing the pulses from hourly to 3-hourly raised FSH from 99 to 181 ng/mL while LH stayed flat
cards.summary: Gross 1987: at a constant daily LHRH dose in GnRH-deficient men, slowing the pulses from hourly to 3-hourly raised FSH from 99 to 181 ng/mL while LH stayed flat
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (variable-frequency GnRH clamp in deficient men) — N = 7 (4 + 3; small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: Men with idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (presumed endogenous LHRH deficiency): study 1, 4 men given the same total daily LHRH at frequencies of every 1, 2 and 3 hours; study 2, 3 men given the same dose per pulse every 0.5 or every 1.5 hours.
cards.result: In study 1, as pulse frequency fell from every 1 to 2 to 3 hours, mean serum FSH rose progressively (99 ± 33 to 133 ± 34 to 181 ± 58 ng/mL, P<0.05) while serum LH did not differ between regimens (34 ± 6, 33 ± 6, 34 ± 5 ng/mL); testosterone and estradiol rose on treatment but did not differ by frequency. In study 2, FSH was 42 ± 13 ng/mL at the 0.5-hour frequency and 80 ± 19 ng/mL at 1.5 hours (P<0.05), with LH again unchanged (25 ± 5 vs 27 ± 4 ng/mL). Slower pulses selectively favour FSH.
cards.watchOut: Classic small studies: Ns of 4 and 3 are printed on the face per the labelling rule. Gonadotropins are in the assay units of the era (ng/mL); the finding carried is the direction and the LH/FSH dissociation, not a modern reference range.
cards.source: Gross KM et al. Differential control of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone secretion by luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone pulse frequency in man. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1987. PMID: 3102545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Spratt 1987: in 5 GnRH-deficient men, raising GnRH frequency from every 120 to every 15 minutes reduced responsiveness per pulse — FSH responsiveness fell more than LH
cards.summary: Spratt 1987: in 5 GnRH-deficient men, raising GnRH frequency from every 120 to every 15 minutes reduced responsiveness per pulse — FSH responsiveness fell more than LH
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (variable-frequency GnRH clamp in deficient men) — N = 5 (small N, labelled on the face)
cards.people: 5 GnRH-deficient men who had achieved normal sex-steroid levels on prior long-term GnRH replacement, studied over three 12-hour admissions as intravenous GnRH frequency was stepped from every 120 to 60, 30 and 15 minutes, at a dose previously shown to give normal-range LH and FSH in each subject.
cards.result: As frequency rose acutely, mean serum LH rose progressively but LH pulse amplitude and frequency-normalised LH (nLH) fell, while testosterone stayed constant and discrete LH pulses were not always apparent at the fastest frequencies; in two men gonadotroph responses destabilised. Mean FSH did not change, but frequency-normalised FSH (nFSH) fell progressively and fell further than nLH at each step — per-pulse FSH responsiveness is the more frequency-sensitive of the two. No further desensitisation appeared after chronic administration at 60- or 30-minute intervals.
cards.watchOut: Classic small study: N=5 is printed on the face. 'Normalised' LH/FSH (level divided by pulse frequency) is this programme's own construct for per-pulse responsiveness; it is reported as the record defines it.
cards.source: Spratt DI et al. Effects of increasing the frequency of low doses of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) on gonadotropin secretion in GnRH-deficient men. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1987. PMID: 3106396. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Filicori 1989: in women on pulsatile GnRH, 120-minute pulses blunted the midcycle LH surge and cut ovulation versus 60-minute pulses — and FSH did not rise at the slower frequency
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (variable-frequency pulsatile GnRH in deficient women) — N = 32 women, 64 cycles
cards.people: 32 women with primary hypogonadotropic amenorrhea receiving pulsatile GnRH (60–120 µg/day) at 60- or 120-minute intervals, for 64 ovulation-induction cycles in total.
cards.result: Ovulation occurred in 94% of 60-minute cycles versus 70% of 120-minute cycles (P<0.05). In ovulatory cycles, follicular estradiol did not differ, but mean LH was lower (P<0.005) and the midcycle LH surge severely blunted at the 120-minute frequency, and luteal progesterone and estradiol were lower; FSH concentrations did NOT increase at the lower frequency. Raising the daily GnRH dose to 120 µg/day reduced or abolished the frequency-associated differences.
cards.watchOut: Premise nuance, printed plainly: in these women slower pulses did not raise FSH, unlike the male clamp studies — the frequency code is clearest as 'faster pulses are required for full LH output; FSH is relatively favoured, or least lost, as frequency falls', and dose can override frequency. Ovulation induction is the clinical setting; the physiology read-out is the hormone pattern.
cards.source: Filicori M et al. Evidence for a specific role of GnRH pulse frequency in the control of the human menstrual cycle. The American journal of physiology. 1989. PMID: 2514600. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Filicori 1986: across the normal menstrual cycle the LH pulse interval shortened from 94 minutes early-follicular to 71 minutes late-follicular, then lengthened to 216 minutes by the late luteal phase
cards.summary: Filicori 1986: across the normal menstrual cycle the LH pulse interval shortened from 94 minutes early-follicular to 71 minutes late-follicular, then lengthened to 216 minutes by the late luteal phase
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (frequent-sampling across the menstrual cycle) — 51 ovulatory cycles; number of women not stated in the record
cards.people: Normal women studied through 51 ovulatory cycles, with plasma gonadotropins measured at 10-minute intervals for 20–24 hours in the early, mid- and late follicular and early, mid- and late luteal phases; LH pulses detected by two computer algorithms. (Number of women not stated in the fetched record; 51 cycles.)
cards.result: The LH interpulse interval fell during the follicular phase, from 94 ± 4 min (early) to 71 ± 4 min (late, P<0.001), then rose progressively through the luteal phase, from 103 ± 8 min (early) to 216 ± 39 min (late, P<0.001); pulse frequency also slowed during sleep in the early follicular and early luteal phases. LH pulse amplitude was highest in the early luteal phase (14.9 ± 1.7 mIU/ml) and fell by the late luteal phase (7.6 ± 1.1 mIU/ml). FSH secretion correlated with LH secretion at lags of 0–10 min in 82% of studies, consistent with a common (GnRH) drive whose frequency the cycle itself varies.
cards.watchOut: LH pulses are the observable proxy for GnRH pulses (GnRH itself is not sampled from the human portal circulation); the inference from LH frequency to GnRH frequency is the field's standard one and is labelled as such.
cards.source: Filicori M et al. Characterization of the physiological pattern of episodic gonadotropin secretion throughout the human menstrual cycle. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1986. PMID: 3084534. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the pituitary reads GnRH pulse frequency — faster pulses sustain LH output, slower pulses relatively favour FSH — and the normal cycle exploits the full range
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pituitary reads GnRH pulse frequency — faster pulses sustain LH output, slower pulses relatively favour FSH — and the normal cycle exploits the full range
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (reproductive endocrine chapters). No new data.
cards.result: In GnRH-deficient humans whose pituitary input is clamped by the experimenter, slowing a constant daily GnRH dose raised FSH while LH held (PMID 3102545), accelerating pulses eroded per-pulse responsiveness with FSH eroding most (PMID 3106396), and in women a 120-minute rhythm blunted the LH surge and reduced ovulation without raising FSH (PMID 2514600). The endogenous rhythm moves across exactly this range over the menstrual cycle, from ~71-minute intervals late-follicular to ~216 minutes late-luteal (PMID 3084534). The primate foundation experiment (Belchetz 1978) is animal work and is therefore not carded here; the human clamp studies carry the claim. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Scope: pulse-frequency decoding at the pituitary. The oestradiol trigger for the midcycle LH surge — a feedback event, not frequency decoding — is pack #6264; cross-point, do not duplicate. IVF GnRH protocols and GnRH-agonist ovarian protection are treatment shelves, not this physiology.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 3102545, 3106396, 2514600, 3084534), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology. No additional source.

shelves.title: Semaglutide 7.2 mg weekly (STEP UP): the higher dose beat both placebo and the standard 2.4 mg dose — weight change −18.7% versus −15.6% (2.4 mg) and −3.9% (placebo) without diabetes, and −13.2% versus −3.9% on placebo in type 2 diabetes — at the cost of more gastrointestinal effects and much more dysaesthesia
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, does semaglutide 7.2 mg weekly, compared with the standard 2.4 mg dose or placebo, produce greater weight loss?
mesh: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: The within-drug dose question now has two phase 3b answers that agree. In STEP UP (1,407 adults with obesity without diabetes, 72 weeks), semaglutide 7.2 mg weekly produced a mean weight change of −18.7%, versus −15.6% on the standard 2.4 mg dose (estimated difference −3.1 percentage points; P<0.0001) and −3.9% on placebo (−14.8 points; P<0.0001), with higher proportions reaching 20% and 25% weight loss than on 2.4 mg. In STEP UP T2D (512 adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes), 7.2 mg gave −13.2% versus −3.9% on placebo (−9.3 points; P<0.0001) and lowered HbA1c by a further 1.5 percentage points versus placebo. The price of the higher dose is tolerability: gastrointestinal events were more frequent (70.8% vs 61.2% on 2.4 mg and 42.8% on placebo in STEP UP; 53.1% in T2D), and dysaesthesia — an abnormal skin sensation signal specific to the high dose — occurred in 22.9% (STEP UP) and 18.9% (T2D) on 7.2 mg versus 6.0% and 4.9% on 2.4 mg and almost none on placebo. Serious adverse events were not more frequent on 7.2 mg. A small MRI substudy of STEP UP (third card, n=55 scanned) found adipose and muscle-fat losses with preserved sit-to-stand function, but is far too small to settle body-composition safety. The standard 2.4 mg record and the tirzepatide comparison are homed elsewhere (live shelf #952); this shelf claims only the dose increment. PROPOSED LIKELY for greater weight loss (Tier C: two concordant phase 3b trials).

cards.headline: STEP UP (Wharton 2025): semaglutide 7.2 mg beat both placebo and 2.4 mg — weight change −18.7% versus −15.6% (2.4 mg) and −3.9% (placebo) at 72 weeks in 1,407 adults with obesity without diabetes
cards.summary: STEP UP (Wharton 2025): semaglutide 7.2 mg beat both placebo and 2.4 mg — weight change −18.7% versus −15.6% (2.4 mg) and −3.9% (placebo) at 72 weeks in 1,407 adults with obesity without diabetes
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled phase 3b trial (STEP UP)
cards.people: 1,407 adults with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater without diabetes, at 95 sites in 11 countries, randomised 5:1:1 to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 7.2 mg (n=1,005), 2.4 mg (n=201) or placebo (n=201), all with lifestyle intervention, for 72 weeks. Mean age 47 years, 73.7% female, mean bodyweight 113.0 kg, mean BMI 39.9 kg/m2. Co-primary endpoints: percentage change in bodyweight and the proportion losing at least 5% (7.2 mg versus placebo).
cards.result: Mean weight change was −18.7% (SE 0.4) on 7.2 mg versus −15.6% (0.7) on 2.4 mg (estimated treatment difference −3.1 percentage points; 95% CI −4.7 to −1.6; P<0.0001) and −3.9% (0.6) on placebo (difference −14.8; −16.2 to −13.4; P<0.0001). Losses of at least 20% and at least 25% were significantly more likely on 7.2 mg than on 2.4 mg (odds ratios 1.8 and 2.4). Waist circumference improved versus placebo by 11.7 cm. Gastrointestinal adverse events: 70.8% on 7.2 mg versus 61.2% on 2.4 mg and 42.8% on placebo; dysaesthesia: 22.9% versus 6.0% and 0.5%. Serious adverse events: 6.8%, 10.9% and 5.5% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The 2.4 mg arm is small (n=201) relative to the 7.2 mg arm (n=1,005), so the dose-versus-dose comparison rests on fewer patients than the headline N suggests. Dysaesthesia in nearly one in four high-dose patients is a new, dose-specific tolerability signal whose mechanism and reversibility the abstract does not settle.
cards.source: Wharton S et al. Once-weekly semaglutide 7·2 mg in adults with obesity (STEP UP): a randomised, controlled, phase 3b trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2025. PMID: 40961952. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05646706, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: STEP UP T2D (Lingvay 2025): in obesity with type 2 diabetes, semaglutide 7.2 mg gave −13.2% weight change versus −3.9% on placebo and lowered HbA1c by 1.5 percentage points more than placebo at 72 weeks
cards.summary: STEP UP T2D (Lingvay 2025): in obesity with type 2 diabetes, semaglutide 7.2 mg gave −13.2% weight change versus −3.9% on placebo and lowered HbA1c by 1.5 percentage points more than placebo at 72 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, controlled phase 3b trial (STEP UP T2D)
cards.people: 512 adults with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater and type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0-10.0%), at 68 sites in eight countries, randomised 3:1:1 to once-weekly semaglutide 7.2 mg (n=307), 2.4 mg (n=103) or placebo (n=102), with lifestyle intervention, for 72 weeks. Mean age 56 years, 51.8% female, mean bodyweight 110.1 kg, mean BMI 38.6 kg/m2, mean HbA1c 8.1%. Co-primary endpoints as in STEP UP (7.2 mg versus placebo).
cards.result: Weight change was −13.2% on 7.2 mg versus −3.9% on placebo (estimated difference −9.3 percentage points; 95% CI −11.0 to −7.7; P<0.0001), with significantly more patients reaching losses of at least 5%, 10%, 15% and 20%. Waist circumference fell by 6.5 cm more than placebo and HbA1c by 1.5 percentage points more than placebo (both P<0.0001). Level 2-3 hypoglycaemia risk was low and comparable across groups. Gastrointestinal events: 53.1% on 7.2 mg, 51.5% on 2.4 mg, 25.5% on placebo; dysaesthesia: 18.9% versus 4.9% and none. Serious adverse events: 9.1%, 8.7% and 8.8%.
cards.watchOut: The confirmatory comparisons in this trial are against placebo — the abstract does not report a confirmatory 7.2 mg versus 2.4 mg weight difference, so the dose-increment claim in diabetes rests mainly on STEP UP (no diabetes) plus this trial's placebo contrast. Absolute weight loss is smaller than in the non-diabetes trial, as expected in type 2 diabetes.
cards.source: Lingvay I et al. Once-weekly semaglutide 7·2 mg in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes (STEP UP T2D): a randomised, controlled, phase 3b trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2025. PMID: 40961953. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05649137, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: STEP UP MRI substudy (Hjelmesæth 2026; prespecified secondary analysis of the same trial): in 55 scanned participants, pooled semaglutide reduced adipose volume and thigh muscle fat infiltration, with a small lean-tissue fall and preserved sit-to-stand performance
cards.summary: STEP UP MRI substudy (Hjelmesæth 2026; prespecified secondary analysis of the same trial): in 55 scanned participants, pooled semaglutide reduced adipose volume and thigh muscle fat infiltration, with a small lean-tissue fall and preserved sit-to-stand performance
cards.type: Prespecified secondary (MRI body-composition) analysis of the STEP UP trial (same trial as the first card, explicitly labelled)
cards.people: 55 of the 1,407 STEP UP participants with a valid baseline MRI scan (semaglutide 7.2 mg n=43; 2.4 mg n=6 — analysed pooled as a semaglutide group of 49; placebo n=6), assessed for changes in adipose and muscle compartment volumes, thigh muscle fat infiltration and physical function (30-second sit-to-stand) to week 72.
cards.result: Estimated treatment differences for pooled semaglutide versus placebo: adipose body tissue −11.1 L (95% CI −16.5 to −5.7; P<0.0001), visceral adipose tissue −1.5 L (P=0.04), lean body tissue −1.7 L (P=0.16, not significant), thigh skeletal muscle volume −1.1 L (P=0.07, not significant) and thigh muscle fat infiltration −0.92 percentage points (P=0.001). Sit-to-stand repetitions rose from a mean of 13 at baseline to 15 at week 72 in both pooled semaglutide and placebo groups. A sensitivity analysis of the 7.2 mg group alone versus placebo showed similar results.
cards.watchOut: Very small and unbalanced (49 vs 6 scanned patients; the two semaglutide doses pooled), so this analysis can only reassure weakly about muscle loss: the confidence intervals include meaningful lean-tissue loss, and function was a single crude test. It does not answer the sarcopenia question for the 7.2 mg dose.
cards.source: Hjelmesæth J et al. Effect of Semaglutide on Thigh Skeletal Muscle Volume, Fat Infiltration and Physical Function in People With Obesity: Secondary Analysis of STEP UP. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2026. PMID: 42764399. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05646706, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: escalating semaglutide to 7.2 mg buys about 3 percentage points more weight loss than 2.4 mg — LIKELY — with dysaesthesia as the dose-limiting signal to watch
cards.summary: Synthesis: escalating semaglutide to 7.2 mg buys about 3 percentage points more weight loss than 2.4 mg — LIKELY — with dysaesthesia as the dose-limiting signal to watch
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded on this shelf: STEP UP (n=1,407), STEP UP T2D (n=512) and the STEP UP MRI substudy (n=55, a subset of STEP UP) — a total randomised evidence base of 1,919 patients.
cards.result: Both trials show the higher dose works: −18.7% versus −3.9% (placebo) and −15.6% (2.4 mg) without diabetes, and −13.2% versus −3.9% with diabetes, where HbA1c also improved by 1.5 percentage points versus placebo. The tolerability gradient is equally consistent: more gastrointestinal events and a four- to five-fold excess of dysaesthesia over the 2.4 mg dose in both trials, without an excess of serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The comparison that matters clinically — 7.2 mg versus 2.4 mg head-to-head — is confirmatory only in STEP UP. Whether the extra ~3 percentage points of weight loss justify the dysaesthesia burden will be an individual decision, and no carded report runs beyond 72 weeks or measures what happens on stopping.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 40961952, 40961953, 42764399). No additional source.
