shelves.title: Amycretin (now zenagamtide), a GLP-1/amylin co-agonist: large early weight losses, phase 2 diabetes data — no phase 3 yet
shelves.question: In adults with obesity (and, in phase 2, type 2 diabetes), does the unimolecular GLP-1/amylin co-agonist amycretin, compared with placebo, reduce body weight?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Amycretin — renamed zenagamtide in the 2026 phase 2 reports — is a single-source investigational product of Novo Nordisk, named here under the clarification exception. Every randomised report so far favours the drug: in the subcutaneous phase 1b/2a study, weight fell 24.3% on the 60 mg maintenance dose versus 1.1% on placebo at 36 weeks, with 22.0%, 16.2% and 9.7% losses at 20 mg, 5 mg and 1.25 mg; in the two phase 2 type 2 diabetes trials (same registration, subcutaneous and oral formulations), HbA1c fell 0.9–1.7% across doses, with estimated differences versus placebo of −0.77 to −1.56 percentage points subcutaneously and −0.5 to −1.09 points orally. The cautions are structural, not directional: this is one sponsor's early-phase programme (phase 1–2 only, no phase 3), the first-in-human and phase 1b/2a cohorts are small, gastrointestinal events dominate, and the phase 1b/2a paper records a large number of withdrawals, many for reasons unrelated to adverse events — so the largest weight figures come from the cohorts most exposed to attrition. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): promising and consistent, but early-phase only.

cards.headline: Subcutaneous phase 1b/2a (Lancet 2025): −24.3% bodyweight on 60 mg vs −1.1% on placebo at 36 weeks; −22.0%, −16.2% and −9.7% at lower maintenance doses
cards.summary: Subcutaneous phase 1b/2a (Lancet 2025): −24.3% bodyweight on 60 mg vs −1.1% on placebo at 36 weeks; −22.0%, −16.2% and −9.7% at lower maintenance doses
cards.people: 125 adults aged 18–55 with overweight or obesity (BMI 27.0–39.9 kg/m²) at a single US centre, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous amycretin (n=101) or placebo (n=24) across single-ascending-dose and multiple-ascending-dose parts, with maintenance doses of 60 mg (36 weeks), 20 mg (36 weeks), 5 mg (28 weeks) and 1.25 mg (20 weeks).
cards.result: Estimated mean bodyweight change was −24.3% vs −1.1% (60 mg, week 36), −22.0% vs +1.9% (20 mg, week 36), −16.2% vs +2.3% (5 mg, week 28) and −9.7% vs +2.0% (1.25 mg, week 20), all statistically significant. Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events, mostly mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Early-phase, single-centre, small cohorts per dose. The paper states a large number of participants withdrew, with a high proportion of discontinuations for reasons unrelated to treatment-emergent adverse events — attrition this large can inflate estimated weight loss. Tested product: amycretin, Novo Nordisk (single-source investigational product, named per the clarification exception).

cards.headline: First-in-human oral phase 1 (Lancet 2025): adverse events in 62% of 144 participants, all mild or moderate, gastrointestinal predominating; no deaths
cards.summary: First-in-human oral phase 1 (Lancet 2025): adverse events in 62% of 144 participants, all mild or moderate, gastrointestinal predominating; no deaths
cards.people: 144 adults with overweight or obesity in a single-centre, double-blind phase 1 study of oral amycretin: single ascending doses (n=48), 10-day multiple ascending doses (n=36), and 12-week dose-escalation parts C/D (n=60).
cards.result: 364 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 89 of 144 participants (62%), all mild or moderate and dose-dependent in frequency; gastrointestinal events accounted for 180 of 364 events (49%). No deaths were reported. Bodyweight and fasting plasma glucose were exploratory endpoints in parts C/D; the fetched record does not report numeric weight-change results for this study, so none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: A safety/pharmacokinetic study, not an efficacy trial: do not read weight efficacy into it. Tested product: amycretin, Novo Nordisk.

cards.headline: Phase 2 in type 2 diabetes, subcutaneous zenagamtide (Lancet 2026): HbA1c −0.9% to −1.7% across 0.4–40 mg at 36 weeks; differences vs placebo −0.77 to −1.56 points
cards.summary: Phase 2 in type 2 diabetes, subcutaneous zenagamtide (Lancet 2026): HbA1c −0.9% to −1.7% across 0.4–40 mg at 36 weeks; differences vs placebo −0.77 to −1.56 points
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 trial (subcutaneous zenagamtide in type 2 diabetes)
cards.people: 262 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.0%) on metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor, at 83 sites in 11 countries, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous zenagamtide (n=225; six dose groups 0.4–40 mg) or placebo (n=37) for 36 weeks.
cards.result: Estimated HbA1c change at week 36 ranged from −0.9% at 0.4 mg (difference vs placebo −0.77 percentage points, 95% CI −1.26 to −0.28) to −1.7% at 40 mg (difference −1.56 points, 95% CI −2.05 to −1.07). cards.watchOut: The drug was renamed: amycretin is now zenagamtide — same molecule, Novo Nordisk. Placebo group is small (n=37) because of the 6:1 allocation. This report and the oral report below share one registration (NCT06542874) as two formulation limbs of one phase 2 programme — they are labelled as such and are not two independent programmes.

shelves.title: Ecnoglutide, a cAMP-biased GLP-1 agonist from China: −13.2% weight in phase 3 obesity, HbA1c non-inferior to dulaglutide
shelves.question: In adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes, does the cAMP-biased GLP-1 receptor agonist ecnoglutide, compared with placebo, reduce body weight and HbA1c?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Ecnoglutide is a single-source product of Sciwind Biosciences (Hangzhou Sciwind Biosciences), named under the clarification exception, and the entire evidence base is single-country: every trial was conducted in China. Within that limit the results are strong and concordant. In the phase 3 SLIMMER obesity trial, weight fell 9.1%, 10.9% and 13.2% at 1.2, 1.8 and 2.4 mg versus 0.1% on placebo at 40 weeks, with 77–87% achieving at least 5% loss versus 16% on placebo. In type 2 diabetes, a phase 2 placebo-controlled trial showed HbA1c reductions of 1.81–2.39% versus 0.55% on placebo, and the phase 3 EECOH-2 trial found ecnoglutide non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg (HbA1c −1.91% and −1.89% vs −1.65%); the 1.2 mg dose was statistically superior by 0.24 percentage points, a difference the trialists themselves state was not considered clinically relevant. Gastrointestinal events dominate the adverse-event profile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): real phase 3 evidence, but one programme, one country, no outcomes data.

cards.headline: SLIMMER phase 3 obesity (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025): weight −13.2% on 2.4 mg vs +0.1% on placebo at 40 weeks; ≥5% loss in 87% vs 16%
cards.summary: SLIMMER phase 3 obesity (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025): weight −13.2% on 2.4 mg vs +0.1% on placebo at 40 weeks; ≥5% loss in 87% vs 16%
cards.people: 664 Chinese adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, at 36 centres in China, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous ecnoglutide 1.2 mg (n=166), 1.8 mg (n=166) or 2.4 mg (n=167), or placebo (n=165), for 40 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean weight change was −9.1%, −10.9% and −13.2% versus +0.1% on placebo (estimated differences −9.2, −11.1 and −13.3 percentage points; all P<0.0001). At least 5% weight loss was achieved by 77%, 84% and 87% versus 16% on placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 93% on ecnoglutide versus 84% on placebo, mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events; 10 participants on ecnoglutide discontinued because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Single-country evidence (China) and a single sponsor programme (Sciwind Biosciences) — both stated on the face per standing rules. No diabetes in this trial population. Tested product: ecnoglutide, Sciwind Biosciences.

cards.headline: EECOH-2 phase 3 in type 2 diabetes (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025): HbA1c −1.91%/−1.89% vs −1.65% on dulaglutide — non-inferior; the 0.24-point superiority margin was judged not clinically relevant by the authors
cards.summary: EECOH-2 phase 3 in type 2 diabetes (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025): HbA1c −1.91%/−1.89% vs −1.65% on dulaglutide — non-inferior; the 0.24-point superiority margin was judged not clinically relevant by the authors
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (EECOH-2, type 2 diabetes, active comparator)
cards.people: 623 adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin alone, at 52 hospitals in China, randomised to once-weekly ecnoglutide 0.6 mg (n=206), 1.2 mg (n=208) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg (n=207) for 52 weeks (open-label, active-controlled); 621 in the full analysis set.
cards.result: At week 32, mean HbA1c fell 1.91% (0.6 mg) and 1.89% (1.2 mg) versus 1.65% on dulaglutide — estimated differences −0.26 (95% CI −0.39 to −0.13) and −0.24 percentage points (95% CI −0.38 to −0.11); both doses met non-inferiority and the 1.2 mg dose met statistical superiority (P=0.0002), which the authors state was not considered clinically relevant. shelves.title: Eloralintide, a selective amylin agonist: −20% bodyweight at 48 weeks in its single phase 2 trial — phase-2 only
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, does the selective amylin analogue eloralintide, compared with placebo, reduce body weight over 48 weeks?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2 only, stated plainly. Eloralintide is a single-source investigational product of Eli Lilly, named under the clarification exception. In its one phase 2 trial (n=263, 48 weeks), weight fell 9% at 1 mg and up to 20% at 9 mg and the 6–9 mg escalation, versus 0.4% on placebo — a clear dose response. Two phase 1 reports point the same way: 2.6–11.3% weight reduction over 12 weeks in a multiple-ascending-dose study (n=100), and −2.5%/−4.4% four weeks after single 4 mg/12 mg doses in a first-in-human study (human n=48). Nausea is the dominant adverse event at higher doses (up to 64% at 6 mg in phase 2), with fatigue also common; gastrointestinal events were notably infrequent in the phase 1 multiple-dose study, which used no dose escalation. There is no phase 3 trial, no diabetes population in the phase 2 (type 2 diabetes was excluded), and no outcomes data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on phase 2 evidence alone.

cards.summary: Phase 2 (Lancet 2025): weight −20% on 9 mg and 6–9 mg vs −0.4% on placebo at 48 weeks; −9% even at 1 mg
cards.people: 263 adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related comorbidity, without type 2 diabetes, at 46 US centres, randomised to once-weekly eloralintide 1 mg (n=28), 3 mg (n=24), 6 mg (n=28), 9 mg (n=54), 6–9 mg escalation (n=24) or 3–9 mg escalation (n=52), or placebo (n=53), for 48 weeks.

The commonest adverse events were nausea (11% at 1 mg rising to 64% at 6 mg; 14% on placebo) and fatigue (up to 46% in the 6–9 mg group; 12% on placebo).
cards.watchOut: Phase-2 only — the stamp says so. Type 2 diabetes was an exclusion, so nothing here speaks to diabetes populations. Tested product: eloralintide, Eli Lilly.

shelves.title: Cotadutide in diabetic kidney disease: albuminuria down ~44–50% vs placebo in one phase 2b trial — surrogate endpoint, programme not advanced
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD with albuminuria, does the GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist cotadutide, compared with placebo, reduce albuminuria?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — phase-2b only, surrogate endpoint, programme not advanced: all three qualifiers belong on the face of this shelf. In the single kidney trial (n=248, type 2 diabetes with CKD and UACR >50 mg/g), cotadutide reduced UACR dose-dependently at week 14 — by 43.9% at 300 µg and 49.9% at 600 µg versus placebo (relative reductions as reported), with effects sustained at week 26 and serious adverse events balanced across arms; a companion pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modelling report of the same trial (n=247 analysed) predicted a 45.6% relative UACR reduction versus placebo at 26 weeks for the 600 µg dose. Albuminuria is a surrogate: no eGFR-slope, kidney-failure or mortality outcome has been shown, and the programme was not advanced to a phase 3 kidney trial. The third card is glycaemic programme support from an earlier phase 2a diabetes trial, included to show the molecule's metabolic activity — it is not kidney evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on albuminuria alone.

cards.headline: Phase 2b kidney trial (Kidney Int 2024): UACR −43.9% (300 µg) and −49.9% (600 µg) vs placebo at week 14 (relative reductions), sustained at week 26
cards.summary: Phase 2b kidney trial (Kidney Int 2024): UACR −43.9% (300 µg) and −49.9% (600 µg) vs placebo at week 14 (relative reductions), sustained at week 26
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b trial (cotadutide in diabetic kidney disease)
cards.people: 248 adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD (eGFR 20 to <90 mL/min/1.73 m², UACR >50 mg/g; mean eGFR 55.3; 46.8% on SGLT2 inhibitors) randomised to standard care plus daily subcutaneous cotadutide uptitrated to 100, 300 or 600 µg, placebo (double-blind), or open-label semaglutide 1 mg weekly, for 26 weeks.
cards.result: UACR fell dose-dependently versus placebo by week 14, reaching significance at 300 µg (−43.9%, 95% CI −54.7 to −30.6) and 600 µg (−49.9%, 95% CI −59.3 to −38.4) — relative reductions as reported in the record — with effects sustained at week 26. Serious adverse events were balanced across arms, and tolerability at 600 µg was comparable to semaglutide.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate endpoint only: albuminuria change over 14–26 weeks, with no kidney-outcome data. Phase-2b only, and the programme was not advanced to phase 3 — both stated on the face per the slate flags.

cards.summary: Companion PK/PD modelling report of the same kidney trial (Br J Clin Pharmacol 2025): modelled UACR −45.6% vs placebo at 26 weeks on 600 µg (relative)
cards.type: Companion modelling report (same trial as the previous card — explicitly labelled)
cards.people: 247 participants from the phase 2b kidney trial carded above (cotadutide 100/300/600 µg, semaglutide 1 mg, or placebo) — a modelling analysis of that same trial's data, explicitly labelled here as a companion report of one trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Longitudinal exposure–response modelling found a significant relationship between cotadutide exposure and UACR, urinary albumin and body weight; model-predicted relative change versus placebo at 26 weeks on 600 µg was −45.6% for UACR (95% CI −52.4 to −38.7), −47.2% for urinary albumin and −5.3% for body weight (relative changes as reported). Baseline blood pressure and baseline urinary albumin modified the responses.
cards.watchOut: Model-predicted, not observed, outcomes — supportive of the dose–response reading of the parent trial only. Never cite this as an independent trial.

cards.headline: Phase 2a diabetes programme support (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2020): post-meal glucose AUC −21.5% vs +6.3% on placebo; weight −3.41% vs −0.08% over 49 days
cards.summary: Phase 2a diabetes programme support (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2020): post-meal glucose AUC −21.5% vs +6.3% on placebo; weight −3.41% vs −0.08% over 49 days
cards.type: Randomised phase 2a trial (glycaemic programme support — not a kidney trial)
cards.people: 65 adults with overweight/obesity and type 2 diabetes in a two-cohort, five-site randomised double-blind phase 2a study of once-daily cotadutide (50–300 µg, uptitrated) versus placebo for 49 days (46 received cotadutide, 19 placebo).

cards.watchOut: Small (n=65), 49 days, no kidney endpoints. It establishes metabolic activity of the molecule only; the kidney claim of this shelf rests entirely on the phase 2b trial above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a single phase 2b kidney trial, a labelled companion model, and glycaemic background — albuminuria yes, kidney outcomes unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single phase 2b kidney trial, a labelled companion model, and glycaemic background — albuminuria yes, kidney outcomes unknown
cards.people: Total carded evidence base on the kidney question: 248 randomised participants in one phase 2b trial (its companion modelling report covers the same 247 analysed participants and adds no new patients); 65 further participants in a glycaemic phase 2a trial.
cards.result: Cotadutide lowers albuminuria versus placebo over 14–26 weeks in diabetic kidney disease, dose-dependently. Whether that translates into slower eGFR decline or fewer kidney events is unknown, and with the programme not advanced to phase 3 it may remain unknown. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE (benefit), phase-2b and surrogate-endpoint qualifiers attached.
cards.watchOut: Do not present albuminuria reduction as kidney protection: no outcomes trial exists for this molecule.

shelves.title: Saroglitazar (Lipaglyn, India only): triglycerides −45% vs placebo and vs pioglitazone; glycaemic control comparable to pioglitazone, not better
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridaemia/diabetic dyslipidaemia, does the dual PPAR-α/γ agonist saroglitazar, compared with placebo or pioglitazone, improve triglycerides and glycaemic control?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is named per the clarification exception for products not approved or well regulated in the US: saroglitazar (Lipaglyn), Zydus — approved in India since 2013, not FDA- or EMA-approved, and every trial was conducted in India (single-country evidence, stated on the face). On triglycerides the evidence is consistent: PRESS VI showed −45.5% and −46.7% on 2 mg and 4 mg versus placebo at 12 weeks in patients uncontrolled on atorvastatin (relative changes as reported), and PRESS V showed −45% on 4 mg versus −15.5% on pioglitazone 45 mg at 24 weeks. On glycaemia the honest reading is equivalence, not superiority: in PRESS XII (n=1,155, 56 weeks), HbA1c fell 1.38% and 1.47% within the saroglitazar groups versus 1.41% on pioglitazone — the record reports within-group reductions, not a between-group advantage. No cardiovascular outcomes trial exists. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for triglyceride lowering in diabetic dyslipidaemia, on Indian evidence only.

cards.headline: PRESS VI vs placebo (Diabetes Technol Ther 2014): triglycerides −45.5% (2 mg) and −46.7% (4 mg) at 12 weeks, P<0.001 vs placebo (relative changes)
cards.summary: PRESS VI vs placebo (Diabetes Technol Ther 2014): triglycerides −45.5% (2 mg) and −46.7% (4 mg) at 12 weeks, P<0.001 vs placebo (relative changes)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (PRESS VI, vs placebo, on atorvastatin background)
cards.people: 302 adults with type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridaemia (triglycerides >200 and <500 mg/dL) not controlled on atorvastatin 10 mg, randomised to saroglitazar 2 mg (n=101), 4 mg (n=99) or placebo (n=102) for 12 weeks, in a multicentre Indian phase 3 study.
cards.result: Mean plasma triglycerides fell 45.5% on 2 mg and 46.7% on 4 mg (relative changes as reported), significantly more than placebo (P<0.001). Saroglitazar 2 mg also significantly reduced non-HDL cholesterol, VLDL cholesterol, total cholesterol and fasting plasma glucose; 4 mg additionally reduced LDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B. The drug was safe and well tolerated in this trial.
cards.watchOut: India-only evidence; short (12-week) lipid endpoint. Tested product: saroglitazar (Lipaglyn), Zydus — not FDA/EMA approved.

cards.headline: PRESS V vs pioglitazone (J Diabetes Sci Technol 2014): triglycerides −45% on saroglitazar 4 mg vs −15.5% on pioglitazone 45 mg at 24 weeks
cards.summary: PRESS V vs pioglitazone (J Diabetes Sci Technol 2014): triglycerides −45% on saroglitazar 4 mg vs −15.5% on pioglitazone 45 mg at 24 weeks
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (PRESS V, active comparator)
cards.people: 122 adults with type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridaemia (triglycerides >200 to 400 mg/dL, HbA1c >7 to 9%) at 14 Indian sites, randomised to saroglitazar 2 mg, 4 mg or pioglitazone 45 mg daily for 24 weeks; the efficacy analysis included 109 patients (37, 39 and 33 respectively).
cards.result: Triglycerides fell 26.4% on saroglitazar 2 mg (absolute change −78.2 mg/dL) and 45% on 4 mg (−115.4 mg/dL), versus 15.5% on pioglitazone (−33.3 mg/dL) — relative changes as reported, each saroglitazar reduction significant at P<0.001 as reported against baseline/comparator in the record. Saroglitazar 4 mg also reduced LDL cholesterol (5%), VLDL cholesterol (45.5%), total cholesterol (7.7%) and apolipoprotein B (10.9%). No serious adverse events were reported in the saroglitazar arms.
cards.watchOut: Efficacy analysis (n=109) is smaller than the randomised set (n=122). Active-comparator design: this card compares against pioglitazone, not placebo. India only; product Lipaglyn (Zydus), not FDA/EMA approved.

cards.headline: PRESS XII vs pioglitazone, 56 weeks (Cardiovasc Diabetol 2020): HbA1c −1.38%/−1.47% on saroglitazar vs −1.41% on pioglitazone — comparable control, not superior
cards.summary: PRESS XII vs pioglitazone, 56 weeks (Cardiovasc Diabetol 2020): HbA1c −1.38%/−1.47% on saroglitazar vs −1.41% on pioglitazone — comparable control, not superior
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (PRESS XII, 56-week, active comparator)
cards.people: 1,155 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≥7.5%) on background metformin at 39 Indian sites, randomised to saroglitazar 2 mg, saroglitazar 4 mg or pioglitazone 30 mg daily for 24 weeks, continuing in a double-blind extension to 56 weeks.
cards.result: Within-group HbA1c change at week 24 was −1.38% (saroglitazar 2 mg), −1.47% (4 mg) and −1.41% (pioglitazone), each significant against its own baseline (P<0.016); the record reports no between-group superiority for glycaemia. cards.watchOut: Read the HbA1c numbers as comparability with pioglitazone, not advantage — the fetched record supports within-group change only. India only; no cardiovascular outcomes data for this molecule.

cards.headline: Synthesis: triglyceride benefit is the reproducible finding; glycaemia matches pioglitazone; all evidence is Indian and outcomes-free
cards.summary: Synthesis: triglyceride benefit is the reproducible finding; glycaemia matches pioglitazone; all evidence is Indian and outcomes-free
cards.people: Total carded evidence base: 1,579 randomised participants across the three PRESS trials (302 + 122 + 1,155), all in India, all in Zydus's programme for saroglitazar (Lipaglyn).
cards.result: Across placebo- and pioglitazone-controlled trials, saroglitazar lowers triglycerides by roughly 45% at the 4 mg dose (relative) — the consistent, decision-relevant finding. Its glucose lowering is real but pioglitazone-like in size. There is no evidence on cardiovascular events, and the product is not approved outside India. Stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-country qualifier attached.
cards.watchOut: Availability is the practical limit: this is an India-market product (Lipaglyn, Zydus); do not present it as an option where it is not approved.

shelves.title: Once-weekly lonapegsomatropin in adults with GHD: foresiGHt — trunk percent fat −1.68% vs +0.37% on placebo (difference −2.04%), lean mass +1.60 vs −0.11 kg
shelves.question: In ADULTS with growth hormone deficiency, does once-weekly lonapegsomatropin, compared with placebo (and daily somatropin), improve body composition (trunk fat, lean mass)?
mesh: Human Growth Hormone/deficiency/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: PARTIAL row, verified before building: home pack #6477 is the PAEDIATRIC once-weekly growth-hormone question (heiGHt/REAL4 generation) and cards no adult lonapegsomatropin report; none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. The tested product is named per the clarification exception: lonapegsomatropin (Skytrofa), Ascendis Pharma — a once-weekly prodrug releasing unmodified somatropin. In the single adult phase 3 trial, foresiGHt (n = 259, 38 weeks), lonapegsomatropin reduced trunk percent fat by −1.68% versus +0.37% on placebo (least-squares difference −2.04%; P < .001) and increased total body lean mass by +1.60 kg versus −0.11 kg (difference 1.70 kg; P < .0001), with a safety profile comparable to daily somatropin. An earlier phase 2 trial (n = 37, 4 weeks) showed dose-dependent growth-hormone exposure and IGF-1 exposure similar to daily somatropin (Omnitrope) at comparable doses — pharmacology, not body-composition efficacy. A 52-week open-label extension of foresiGHt (220 enrolled) found body composition maintained or improved and injection-site reactions infrequent (5.1%), but it is uncontrolled and overlaps the phase 3 population. Adult approval in the US followed in July 2025, per the slate record. One randomised efficacy trial means the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Phase 2 in adults 2017 (n = 37, 4 weeks): weekly TransCon GH gave dose-dependent GH exposure and IGF-1 exposure similar to daily somatropin at comparable doses
cards.summary: Phase 2 in adults 2017 (n = 37, 4 weeks): weekly TransCon GH gave dose-dependent GH exposure and IGF-1 exposure similar to daily somatropin at comparable doses
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 2 trial, Endocr Connect 2017
cards.people: Multicentre, randomised, open-label, active-controlled phase 2 trial: 37 adults with growth hormone deficiency, stable on GH replacement for at least 3 months, who after a wash-out were randomised to one of three once-weekly TransCon growth hormone (lonapegsomatropin) doses (0.02, 0.04 or 0.08 mg GH/kg/week) or daily growth hormone (named in the record as Omnitrope, 0.04 mg GH/kg/week in 7 daily doses) for 4 weeks.
cards.result: TransCon GH was well tolerated; fatigue and headache were the most frequent drug-related adverse events and occurred in all groups. No lipoatrophy or nodule formation was reported, and no anti-growth-hormone-binding antibodies were detected. Growth-hormone exposure rose linearly and dose-dependently without accumulation, and maximum growth-hormone concentration and IGF-1 exposure were similar after TransCon GH or daily somatropin at comparable doses.
cards.watchOut: A 4-week pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic study in 37 already-treated adults: it shows the weekly prodrug behaves like daily GH in exposure terms; it does not measure body composition or any clinical outcome.
cards.source: Höybye C et al. A phase 2 trial of long-acting TransCon growth hormone in adult GH deficiency. Endocrine connections. 2017. PMID: 28196799. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: foresiGHt phase 3 (n = 259, 38 weeks): trunk percent fat −1.68% vs +0.37% on placebo (difference −2.04%, P < .001); lean mass +1.60 vs −0.11 kg
cards.summary: foresiGHt phase 3 (n = 259, 38 weeks): trunk percent fat −1.68% vs +0.37% on placebo (difference −2.04%, P < .001); lean mass +1.60 vs −0.11 kg
cards.type: Randomised placebo- and active-controlled phase 3 trial (foresiGHt), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2026
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial (foresiGHt, NCT04615273) at 116 centres in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific: 259 adults with growth hormone deficiency randomised 1:1:1 to once-weekly lonapegsomatropin (Skytrofa, Ascendis Pharma), once-weekly placebo (double-blind), or daily somatropin (open-label) for 38 weeks. Primary end point: change in trunk percent fat at week 38.
cards.result: Lonapegsomatropin significantly reduced trunk percent fat (−1.68% vs +0.37% on placebo; least-squares mean difference −2.04%; P < .001), increased total body lean mass (+1.60 kg vs −0.11 kg; difference 1.70 kg; P < .0001) and reduced trunk fat mass (−0.48 kg vs +0.22 kg; difference −0.70 kg; P = .0053). The safety and tolerability profile of lonapegsomatropin was comparable to somatropin.
cards.watchOut: Body composition by DXA is a surrogate for clinical outcomes in adult GHD; the daily-somatropin arm was open-label, and the placebo comparison lasts 38 weeks — long-term comparative data come only from the uncontrolled extension below.
cards.source: Biller BMK et al. Efficacy and Safety of Once-Weekly Lonapegsomatropin in Adults With Growth Hormone Deficiency: foresiGHt Trial Results. cards.headline: Open-label extension (52 weeks; 220 enrolled): body composition maintained or improved up to 90 weeks; injection-site reactions 5.1%
cards.summary: Open-label extension (52 weeks; 220 enrolled): body composition maintained or improved up to 90 weeks; injection-site reactions 5.1%
cards.type: Open-label extension of foresiGHt, Endocr Pract 2026
cards.people: Second, explicitly labelled report of the foresiGHt programme: a 52-week multicentre open-label extension enrolling 220 adults (88.7% of foresiGHt completers) who had received lonapegsomatropin, placebo or somatropin in the parent trial; all received once-weekly lonapegsomatropin in the extension. Same population as the card above — not new patients.
cards.result: After up to 90 weeks of treatment, body composition was maintained in participants continuing lonapegsomatropin and improved relative to foresiGHt baseline in those initiating or switching to it. Common adverse events across the programme were nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory infection and headache; injection-site reactions were infrequent (5.1%) and mild or moderate. A ≥10-point improvement on the Treatment-Related Impact Measure–Adult GH Deficiency total score was achieved by 43.5% of those continuing, 40.6% of those initiating and 35.8% of those switching to lonapegsomatropin.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, in trial completers who chose to continue — durability and patient-reported gains here are subject to selection and expectation effects.

shelves.title: Leptin physiology: the adiposity signal — what congenital deficiency, fasting and replacement experiments in humans show leptin does
shelves.question: In humans, what does leptin do — as shown by congenital leptin deficiency and its reversal, leptin replacement during fasting, and leptin replacement in hypothalamic amenorrhoea?
shelves.balance: Framing (textbook account, Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): leptin is secreted by adipocytes in proportion to fat mass and signals energy-store adequacy to the hypothalamus; when leptin falls, the brain reads starvation and adapts. The human experiments of nature and replacement agree with that account. In congenital leptin deficiency, replacement reversed hyperphagia, fat mass, hyperinsulinaemia and immune defects in 3 children treated for up to 4 years (PMID 12393845), and in the only 3 leptin-deficient adults identified at the time, physiological-dose replacement for 18 months took mean BMI from 51.2 to 26.9 kg/m2 and resolved type 2 diabetes and hypogonadism (PMID 15070752). During a 72-hour fast in healthy men, holding leptin at fed-state levels prevented the starvation-induced changes in the gonadal axis and partly in the thyroid axis — the fall in leptin is a necessary signal for that adaptation, while the adrenal, renin-aldosterone and growth-hormone axes changed independently of leptin in humans (PMID 12727933). In women with hypothalamic amenorrhoea, replacement restored LH pulsatility and produced ovulatory cycles in 3 of 8 women (PMID 15342807). Fenced neighbours, not re-carded here: metreleptin treatment in lipodystrophy (pack #2884), leptin as a probe in adaptive thermogenesis after weight loss (pack #6298), leptin vs insulin tracking of GH pulses (live #47) and setmelanotide in LEPR-deficiency obesity (live #1093). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the primary human studies are tiny by design (experiments of nature, N printed on every card) but concordant with each other and with the textbook account.

cards.headline: Farooqi 2002: in 3 children with congenital leptin deficiency, up to 4 years of leptin reversed appetite, fat mass, hyperinsulinaemia and T-cell defects
cards.summary: Farooqi 2002: in 3 children with congenital leptin deficiency, up to 4 years of leptin reversed appetite, fat mass, hyperinsulinaemia and T-cell defects
cards.type: Primary human study — congenital leptin deficiency, replacement (Farooqi 2002)
cards.people: 3 morbidly obese children with congenital leptin deficiency (N = 3, printed plainly — an experiment of nature, not a trial sample); daily subcutaneous recombinant human leptin for up to 4 years.
cards.result: Sustained beneficial effects on appetite, fat mass, hyperinsulinaemia and hyperlipidaemia. Plasma thyroid hormone levels rose rapidly and stayed up; gonadotropin effects facilitated appropriately timed pubertal development. Leptin deficiency had reduced circulating CD4+ T-cell numbers and impaired T-cell proliferation and cytokine release — all reversed by leptin.
cards.watchOut: N = 3 children with a single-gene defect. This shows what leptin is necessary for; it does not show that leptin treats common obesity, where leptin levels are high, not absent.
cards.source: Farooqi IS et al. Beneficial effects of leptin on obesity, T cell hyporesponsiveness, and neuroendocrine/metabolic dysfunction of human congenital leptin deficiency. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2002. PMID: 12393845. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Licinio 2004: in the only 3 leptin-deficient adults then known, 18 months of physiological-dose leptin took mean BMI from 51.2 to 26.9 kg/m2
cards.summary: Licinio 2004: in the only 3 leptin-deficient adults then known, 18 months of physiological-dose leptin took mean BMI from 51.2 to 26.9 kg/m2
cards.type: Primary human study — congenital leptin deficiency in adults, replacement (Licinio 2004)
cards.people: 3 morbidly obese homozygous leptin-deficient adults (N = 3, printed plainly); recombinant human leptin at low physiological replacement doses (0.01–0.04 mg/kg, given daily in the evening) for 18 months. Patients were hypogonadal; one also had type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: Mean BMI fell from 51.2 ± 2.5 to 26.9 ± 2.1 kg/m2 after 18 months, mainly from loss of fat mass. Leptin replacement resolved type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypogonadism, increased physical activity, and improved ingestive and non-ingestive behaviour.
cards.watchOut: N = 3, uncontrolled, in complete genetic leptin absence. The size of the weight loss describes deficiency reversal, not a drug effect available to people with intact leptin signalling.
cards.source: Licinio J et al. Phenotypic effects of leptin replacement on morbid obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism, and behavior in leptin-deficient adults. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2004. PMID: 15070752. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Welt 2004: leptin replacement in hypothalamic amenorrhoea restored LH pulsatility — 3 of 8 women had an ovulatory cycle
cards.summary: Welt 2004: leptin replacement in hypothalamic amenorrhoea restored LH pulsatility — 3 of 8 women had an ovulatory cycle
cards.type: Primary human study — controlled replacement in relative leptin deficiency (Welt 2004)
cards.people: 8 women with hypothalamic amenorrhoea due to strenuous exercise or low weight, studied for 1 month before and up to 3 months on recombinant human leptin; 6 untreated women with hypothalamic amenorrhoea served as controls (N = 8 treated, printed plainly).
cards.result: Leptin increased mean LH levels and LH pulse frequency after 2 weeks and increased maximal follicular diameter, number of dominant follicles, ovarian volume and estradiol over 3 months. Three women had an ovulatory menstrual cycle (P<0.05 against an expected spontaneous ovulation rate of 10%); two others had preovulatory follicular development and withdrawal bleeding. Free triiodothyronine, free thyroxine, IGF-1, IGF-binding protein 3 and bone-formation markers also rose; cortisol and corticotropin did not change.
cards.watchOut: Small, short and not placebo-blinded; the comparison for ovulation is an expected spontaneous rate of 10%, not a randomised control rate. It identifies leptin as a permissive signal for reproduction, not a fertility treatment.
cards.source: Welt CK et al. Recombinant human leptin in women with hypothalamic amenorrhea. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15342807. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chan 2003: holding leptin at fed levels during a 72-hour fast in men prevented the starvation response in the gonadal axis — the fall in leptin is the signal
cards.summary: Chan 2003: holding leptin at fed levels during a 72-hour fast in men prevented the starvation response in the gonadal axis — the fall in leptin is the signal
cards.type: Primary human study — randomised fasting/replacement experiment (Chan 2003)
cards.people: 6 to 8 healthy lean men (N printed as reported: six to eight) studied in a fed state and during three 72-hour fasts with placebo, low-dose, or replacement-dose recombinant methionyl human leptin designed to hold serum leptin at fed-state levels.
cards.result: Replacement-dose leptin during fasting prevented the starvation-induced changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and, in part, the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and serum IGF-1 binding capacity. In contrast, fasting-induced changes in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal, renin-aldosterone and growth hormone–IGF-1 axes, and in fuel utilisation, appeared independent of leptin in humans — a human/mouse difference the authors state explicitly.
cards.watchOut: A 72-hour fast in a handful of lean men defines the acute signal, not chronic energy balance. The leptin-independent axes are as much a part of the physiology as the leptin-dependent ones.
cards.source: Chan JL et al. The role of falling leptin levels in the neuroendocrine and metabolic adaptation to short-term starvation in healthy men. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 2003. PMID: 12727933. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: leptin is the body's fat-store adequacy signal — necessary for reproduction, thyroid tone and immune competence, and its fall is the trigger for starvation adaptation
cards.summary: Synthesis: leptin is the body's fat-store adequacy signal — necessary for reproduction, thyroid tone and immune competence, and its fall is the trigger for starvation adaptation
cards.people: Four primary human studies: congenital leptin deficiency in 3 children and 3 adults, replacement in 8 women with hypothalamic amenorrhoea, and a fasting/replacement experiment in 6–8 healthy men.
cards.result: Across all four, the same picture: absent or falling leptin produces hyperphagia, fat gain, hypogonadism, thyroid-axis suppression and immune defects, and restoring leptin reverses them; holding leptin up during a fast blocks the gonadal (and partly thyroid) starvation response. Textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall (adipose tissue, leptin and energy balance) — cited as framing, not as an evidence card. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Refusal recorded: the slate's named classic, Farooqi et al., N Engl J Med 1999 (PMID: 10486419, recombinant leptin in a child with congenital leptin deficiency), was NOT carded — its PubMed record fetched this session is abstract-empty, so its content and numbers could not be verified from the record; the verifiable Farooqi 2002 JCI report of the same deficiency programme (PMID: 12393845) is carded instead. Every N in this pack is very small because the human experiments of nature are rare; the stamp rests on concordance across independent deficiency/replacement settings, not on sample size.

shelves.title: Contraction-mediated glucose uptake: exercising muscle takes up glucose without needing insulin — a 13- to 18-fold rise in leg uptake, GLUT4 moved to the surface, AMPK alpha2 switched on
shelves.question: In humans, how does exercising skeletal muscle take up glucose independently of insulin (contraction-mediated glucose uptake), and how large is the effect?
shelves.balance: Framing (textbook account, Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology): contracting muscle disposes of glucose through a pathway that does not require insulin — which is why exercise lowers glucose even when insulin is absent or its signalling is defective. The primary human studies measure each step. Arteriovenous balance across the leg: glucose uptake by the exercising leg rose 13- to 18-fold in healthy controls and in insulin-dependent diabetic patients studied 24 hours after insulin withdrawal alike, supplying 25–28% of the leg's oxygen consumption (PMID 1133176) — uptake preserved with essentially no insulin on board. The transporter step: a single bout of cycling moved GLUT4 to the muscle plasma membrane, +71% in controls and +74% in type 2 diabetes (PMID 10331428) — the contraction pathway is intact where the insulin pathway is not. The signalling step: the alpha2 isoform of AMP-activated protein kinase was activated 3- to 4-fold by high-intensity exercise and not by low-intensity exercise, while alpha1 was not activated at either intensity (PMID 11018120). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: three independent human methods (balance, biopsy fractionation, kinase assay) converge on the textbook account. Adjacent but different questions are homed elsewhere and not re-carded: glucose effectiveness at rest (pack #6494) and the exercise cardiac-output and metaboreflex physiology shelves.

cards.headline: Wahren 1975: leg glucose uptake rose 13- to 18-fold during exercise — equally in controls and in diabetic patients 24 hours off insulin
cards.summary: Wahren 1975: leg glucose uptake rose 13- to 18-fold during exercise — equally in controls and in diabetic patients 24 hours off insulin
cards.type: Primary human study — leg balance during exercise, insulin withdrawn (Wahren 1975)
cards.people: 8 insulin-dependent diabetic patients studied 24 hours after withdrawal of insulin, and 8 healthy controls (N = 16 total, printed plainly), at rest and after 40 minutes of bicycle exercise at 55–60% of maximal capacity; leg and splanchnic exchange measured by catheter balance technique.
cards.result: Leg uptake of blood glucose rose 13- to 18-fold during exercise in both the diabetic and control groups and accounted for a similar proportion of total leg oxygen uptake in the two groups (25–28%). Splanchnic glucose output rose 3- to 4-fold above resting levels in both groups. In the insulin-withdrawn diabetic patients, exercising muscle took up glucose at the same rate as in controls — contraction-mediated uptake did not require insulin.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 per group, 1975 catheter-balance methods, and the diabetic group was hyperglycaemic and insulin-withdrawn — a deliberate physiological stress, not a treatment model. The fold-rise is from a low resting leg uptake; it is a rate measurement, not whole-body glucose disposal.
cards.source: Wahren J et al. Splanchnic and leg exchange of glucose, amino acids, and free fatty acids during exercise in diabetes mellitus. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1975. PMID: 1133176. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kennedy 1999: one bout of exercise moved GLUT4 to the muscle surface — +71% in controls and +74% in type 2 diabetes
cards.summary: Kennedy 1999: one bout of exercise moved GLUT4 to the muscle surface — +71% in controls and +74% in type 2 diabetes
cards.type: Primary human study — muscle biopsy GLUT4 translocation after acute exercise (Kennedy 1999)
cards.people: 5 subjects with type 2 diabetes (2 men, 3 women) and 5 normal controls (5 men) (N = 10 total, printed plainly); vastus lateralis biopsies at rest and after 45–60 minutes of cycle exercise at 60–70% of VO2max, with plasma membranes prepared by subcellular fractionation.
cards.result: Plasma membrane GLUT4 increased in every subject with exercise: mean +74 ± 20% above resting values in type 2 diabetes and +71 ± 18% in controls. Total GLUT4 content is normal in type 2 diabetes and insulin-stimulated translocation is defective, but exercise-stimulated translocation was preserved — direct evidence that contraction recruits GLUT4 through a route separate from insulin signalling.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 per group and a membrane-fractionation assay: the percentages are relative changes in membrane GLUT4 protein, not direct glucose-uptake rates. The study shows the transporter moves; the Wahren balance data (previous card) show the uptake itself.

cards.headline: Wojtaszewski 2000: exercise switched on the alpha2 isoform of AMPK 3- to 4-fold — only at high intensity; alpha1 stayed off
cards.summary: Wojtaszewski 2000: exercise switched on the alpha2 isoform of AMPK 3- to 4-fold — only at high intensity; alpha1 stayed off
cards.type: Primary human study — AMPK isoform activation in exercising muscle biopsies (Wojtaszewski 2000)
cards.people: Healthy human subjects (N not documented in the fetched record — printed as such) performing bicycle exercise on two occasions: low intensity (about 50% of maximal oxygen uptake for 90 minutes) or high intensity (about 75% for 60 minutes), with vastus lateralis biopsies before, immediately after, and 3 hours after exercise.
cards.result: Alpha2-AMPK was activated 3- to 4-fold immediately after high-intensity exercise and not at all after low-intensity exercise; activation had fully reversed by 3 hours of recovery. Alpha1-AMPK was not activated in either trial. The in-vitro AMP dependency of alpha2 was also greater (about 3-fold) than alpha1 (about 2-fold) — an isoform-specific, intensity-dependent energy-sensing signal in human muscle during contraction.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record fetched this session, so no N is printed beyond that statement. AMPK activation is a candidate mechanism shown alongside contraction, not proof it alone drives GLUT4 translocation; the record supports 'compatible with a role', which is how the authors word it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: contraction disposes of glucose by its own route — uptake up 13- to 18-fold without insulin, GLUT4 translocated even in type 2 diabetes, alpha2-AMPK engaged at higher intensities
cards.summary: Synthesis: contraction disposes of glucose by its own route — uptake up 13- to 18-fold without insulin, GLUT4 translocated even in type 2 diabetes, alpha2-AMPK engaged at higher intensities
cards.people: Three primary human studies: leg balance in 8 insulin-withdrawn diabetic patients and 8 controls; GLUT4 fractionation in 5 patients with type 2 diabetes and 5 controls; AMPK isoform assays in healthy subjects (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: The chain is measured at three levels in humans: whole-leg glucose uptake rises 13- to 18-fold during exercise whether or not insulin is present (PMID 1133176); the GLUT4 transporter physically moves to the cell surface, +71–74%, including in type 2 diabetes where insulin cannot do this (PMID 10331428); and the energy sensor alpha2-AMPK activates 3- to 4-fold at high exercise intensity (PMID 11018120). Textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall (exercise and muscle metabolism; insulin-independent disposal) — cited as framing, not as an evidence card. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Classic small physiology studies — Ns of 5–8 per group are the norm for catheter-balance and biopsy work and are printed on every card. The claim fenced by this pack is the acute contraction pathway; chronic training adaptations and resting glucose effectiveness are different questions homed elsewhere.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wahren J et al. The Journal of Clinical Investigation. 1975 (PMID: 1133176); Kennedy JW et al. Diabetes. 1999 (PMID: 10331428); Wojtaszewski JFP et al. The Journal of Physiology. 2000 (PMID: 11018120).

shelves.title: Muscle glycogen resynthesis after depleting exercise: fast early rates, a dose plateau near 0.7–1.5 g/kg, and a timing penalty for delayed feeding
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast is muscle glycogen resynthesised after depleting exercise — what are the biopsy-measured resynthesis rates with and without carbohydrate feeding in the first hours, how much carbohydrate maximises them, and how long does full restoration take?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence). Four biopsy programmes agree: resynthesis is fastest in the first 2 hours when carbohydrate is fed immediately (7.7 µmol/g/h, Ivy timing study, PMID 3132449, N = 12) and is cut to 2.5 by a 2-hour delay; the rate plateaus with dose — no gain doubling 1.5 to 3.0 g/kg (Ivy, PMID 3145274, N = 8) and none between 0.70 and 1.40 g/kg per feed (Blom, PMID 3316904); fructose alone is slow (3.2 versus 5.8–6.2 mmol/kg/h for glucose/sucrose); and oral versus intravenous glucose at matched glycaemia gives the same 3-hour gain (Blom, PMID 2689169, N = 5). Unfed storage is ~0.5 µmol/g/h. Full restoration over ~24 hours with adequate carbohydrate is the textbook's account — the carded records measure the first 3–6 hours.

cards.headline: Ivy 1988 (timing): feeding immediately after exercise stored glycogen at 7.7 µmol/g/h in the first 2 hours — delaying the same feed by 2 hours cut that early rate to 2.5
cards.summary: Ivy 1988 (timing): feeding immediately after exercise stored glycogen at 7.7 µmol/g/h in the first 2 hours — delaying the same feed by 2 hours cut that early rate to 2.5
cards.people: 12 male cyclists who exercised 70 minutes at 68% VO2max with six 2-minute intervals at 88%, on two occasions, receiving a 25% carbohydrate solution (2 g/kg) either immediately post-exercise or 2 hours post-exercise, with vastus lateralis biopsies at 0, 2 and 4 hours.
cards.result: Muscle glycogen immediately post-exercise did not differ between treatments. In the first 2 hours the storage rate was 7.7 µmol·g wet wt⁻¹·h⁻¹ with immediate feeding versus 2.5 with delayed feeding. In the second 2 hours the rates converged (4.3 immediate versus 4.1 delayed), but the delayed treatment's second-2-hour rate was still 45% slower than the immediate treatment's first-2-hour rate — despite significantly elevated plasma glucose and insulin in the delayed arm. Timing, not just amount, sets the early resynthesis rate.
cards.watchOut: Rates are per gram wet weight of vastus lateralis in trained male cyclists after one depletion protocol; whole-muscle and whole-body restoration times cannot be read off these 4-hour windows directly.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Ivy JL et al. Muscle glycogen synthesis after exercise: effect of time of carbohydrate ingestion. J Appl Physiol. 1988. PMID: 3132449. cards.headline: Ivy 1988 (amount): doubling carbohydrate from 1.5 to 3.0 g/kg did not speed storage — both fed rates were ~5–6 µmol/g/h against 0.5 unfed
cards.summary: Ivy 1988 (amount): doubling carbohydrate from 1.5 to 3.0 g/kg did not speed storage — both fed rates were ~5–6 µmol/g/h against 0.5 unfed
cards.people: 8 subjects who cycled for 2 hours to deplete muscle glycogen on three occasions, consuming 0, 1.5 or 3.0 g glucose/kg body weight (50% glucose polymer) immediately and 2 hours after exercise, with biopsies immediately, 2 and 4 hours post-exercise.
cards.result: Without feeding, glycogen storage ran at the basal rate of 0.5 µmol·g wet wt⁻¹·h⁻¹. Both fed treatments stored significantly faster, with no difference between 1.5 and 3.0 g/kg: first 2 hours 5.2 ± 0.9 (1.5 g/kg) versus 5.8 ± 0.7 (3.0 g/kg) µmol·g⁻¹·h⁻¹; second 2 hours 4.0 ± 0.9 versus 4.5 ± 0.6. Above a moderate dose, extra carbohydrate did not raise the early resynthesis rate — the muscle-side machinery, not substrate supply, was limiting in this window.
cards.watchOut: A separate report from the same laboratory and year as the timing study (different protocol and cohort, N = 8); doses were two large boluses, not the hourly feeding pattern of the Blom programme — compare patterns, not just totals.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Ivy JL et al. Muscle glycogen storage after different amounts of carbohydrate ingestion. J Appl Physiol. 1988. PMID: 3145274. Registry ID: none in the record (physiology study). cards.headline: Blom 1987: glycogen synthesis over 6 hours was dose-dependent up to 0.7 g/kg per feed — 2.1, 5.8 and 5.7 mmol/kg/h at low, medium and high glucose — and fructose alone was slow (3.2)
cards.summary: Blom 1987: glycogen synthesis over 6 hours was dose-dependent up to 0.7 g/kg per feed — 2.1, 5.8 and 5.7 mmol/kg/h at low, medium and high glucose — and fructose alone was slow (3.2)
cards.people: Men studied after exhaustive bicycle exercise with biopsies before, after, and every 2 hours during 6 hours of recovery: glucose 0.35 (N = 5), 0.70 (N = 5) or 1.40 (N = 5) g/kg given at 0, 2 and 4 hours; sucrose 0.70 g/kg (N = 5); fructose 0.70 g/kg (N = 7). Ns printed on the face.
cards.result: Rates of glycogen synthesis (mean ± SE) were 2.1 ± 0.5, 5.8 ± 1.0 and 5.7 ± 0.9 mmol·kg⁻¹·h⁻¹ for low, medium and high glucose — a plateau between 0.70 and 1.40 g/kg per feed, concordant with the Ivy amount study. Sucrose at 0.70 g/kg gave 6.2 ± 0.5, while fructose at the same dose gave only 3.2 ± 0.7 mmol·kg⁻¹·h⁻¹: sugar type matters, with fructose a poor direct substrate for muscle glycogen. Average plasma insulin rose with glucose dose (16, 21 and 38 µU/mL) even where the synthesis rate had already plateaued.
cards.watchOut: Small parallel groups (N = 5–7 per arm) and an abstract truncated at 250 words in the record; rates are 6-hour averages, which blend the fast early phase with the slower later phase.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study | Blom PC et al. Effect of different post-exercise sugar diets on the rate of muscle glycogen synthesis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1987. PMID: 3316904. cards.headline: Blom 1989: oral versus intravenous glucose at matched plasma glucose gave the same glycogen gain (~28 versus ~25 mmol/kg in 3 hours) despite double the insulin orally (N = 5)
cards.summary: Blom 1989: oral versus intravenous glucose at matched plasma glucose gave the same glycogen gain (~28 versus ~25 mmol/kg in 3 hours) despite double the insulin orally (N = 5)
cards.people: Five male subjects studied twice, 6–16 weeks apart, after exercise: oral glucose loads (1.4, 0.7 and 0.7 g/kg at 0, 1 and 2 hours) versus a glucose-clamp infusion titrated to reproduce the same plasma glucose pattern over a 3-hour post-exercise observation period, with muscle biopsies.
cards.result: Average plasma glucose was matched (9.2 ± 1.1 versus 9.3 ± 1.2 mmol/L, about 166 versus 167 mg/dL), but average insulin was 56 ± 12 µU/mL orally versus 26 ± 5 intravenously, and the arterio–femoral venous glucose difference was twice as large orally (1.0 ± 0.3 versus 0.5 ± 0.2 mmol/L, about 18 versus 9 mg/dL). Despite that, muscle glycogen rose by 28 ± 4 (oral) versus 25 ± 3 (intravenous) mmol/kg over 3 hours — not significantly different. Route and insulin level, at matched glycaemia, did not determine the resynthesis gain in this window.
cards.watchOut: N = 5, printed on the face; a null difference in five subjects is weak evidence of equivalence — carded for its matched-glycaemia design and its glycogen-gain figures, not as proof that insulin is irrelevant.

cards.headline: Synthesis: Muscle glycogen resynthesis after depleting exercise: fast early rates, a dose plateau near 0.7–1.5 g/kg, and a timing penalty for delayed feeding
cards.summary: Synthesis: Muscle glycogen resynthesis after depleting exercise: fast early rates, a dose plateau near 0.7–1.5 g/kg, and a timing penalty for delayed feeding
cards.people: Synthesis of Ivy 1988 (two studies), Blom 1987 and Blom 1989, framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing, not evidence cards).
cards.result: After depleting exercise, human muscle refills glycogen in a fast early phase and a slower later phase. Fed immediately, the first-2-hour rate reaches ~5–8 µmol·g wet wt⁻¹·h⁻¹ (≈ mmol·kg⁻¹·h⁻¹); unfed it is ~0.5. Three independent dose comparisons plateau: 0.70 versus 1.40 g/kg per feed (5.8 versus 5.7 mmol/kg/h) and 1.5 versus 3.0 g/kg total (5.2 versus 5.8 µmol/g/h) — beyond a moderate intake, more carbohydrate does not speed the early rate. Timing beats total: delaying the same feed by 2 hours reduced the early rate from 7.7 to 2.5 µmol/g/h. Sugar type matters (fructose 3.2, glucose 5.8, sucrose 6.2 mmol/kg/h at 0.70 g/kg), while route does not at matched glycaemia (oral versus intravenous gain 28 versus 25 mmol/kg over 3 hours, despite twofold insulin). The Bergström & Hultman needle-biopsy lineage founded this field, but no verifiable record for those 1960s reports was fetched this session, so they are named here as lineage only and are not carded; every number above comes from a carded record.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: all carded windows are 3–6 hours in young trained men; the ~24-hour full-restoration figure is the textbook's account, not a carded measurement, and rates in women, older people and untrained muscle are not established by these records.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID: 3132449; PMID: 3145274; PMID: 3316904; PMID: 2689169. Registry IDs: none in the records (physiology studies).

synthesis synthesis of ivy 1988 (two studies), blom 1987 and blom 1989, framed by guyton & hall and ganong (textbook framing, not evidence cards). after depleting exercise, human muscle refills glycogen in a fast early phase and a slower later phase. fed immediately, the first-2-hour rate reaches ~5–8 µmol·g wet wt⁻¹·h⁻¹ (≈ mmol·kg⁻¹·h⁻¹); unfed it is ~0.5. three independent dose comparisons plateau: 0.70 versus 1.40 g/kg per feed (5.8 versus 5.7 mmol/kg/h) and 1.5 versus 3.0 g/kg total (5.2 versus 5.8 µmol/g/h) — beyond a moderate intake, more carbohydrate does not speed the early rate. timing beats total: delaying the same feed by 2 hours reduced the early rate from 7.7 to 2.5 µmol/g/h. sugar type matters (fructose 3.2, glucose 5.8, sucrose 6.2 mmol/kg/h at 0.70 g/kg), while route does not at matched glycaemia (oral versus intravenous gain 28 versus 25 mmol/kg over 3 hours, despite twofold insulin). the bergström & hultman needle-biopsy lineage founded this field, but no verifiable record for those 1960s reports was fetched this session, so they are named here as lineage only and are not carded; every number above comes from a carded record. synthesis: all carded windows are 3–6 hours in young trained men; the ~24-hour full-restoration figure is the textbook's account, not a carded measurement, and rates in women, older people and untrained muscle are not established by these records. synthesis of pmid: 3132449; pmid: 3145274; pmid: 3316904; pmid: 2689169. registry ids: none in the records (physiology studies).

shelves.title: Cagrilintide monotherapy for weight management in obesity
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, does cagrilintide monotherapy, compared with placebo (and liraglutide in phase 2), reduce body weight?
shelves.balance: This shelf asks only about cagrilintide ALONE. The combination question (cagrilintide plus semaglutide, CagriSema) is homed on live shelf #1092, which cards REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2; the cagrilintide-alone arm inside REDEFINE 1 belongs to that homed report and is not re-carded here (one-home rule). PREMISE NOTE: the slate proposed that REDEFINE 1 arm as an anchor, but its PMID is already carded at #1092, so this pack is built from the remaining free monotherapy reports. On monotherapy itself: the phase 2 dose-finding trial (Lau 2021, n=706, no diabetes) found weight reductions of 6.0–10.8% across cagrilintide doses versus 3.0% on placebo at 26 weeks, with the 4.5 mg dose also beating liraglutide 3.0 mg (10.8% vs 9.0%). In type 2 diabetes, the cagrilintide-alone arm of the Frias 2023 phase 2 trial (n=30 of 92) lost 8.1% of body weight at 32 weeks, with an HbA1c fall of 0.9 percentage points — less than the combination arm in the same trial, which is #1092's subject. A 2026 pharmacokinetic report confirms single-dose cagrilintide exposure is not materially changed by renal or hepatic impairment. Gastrointestinal adverse events are the main cost (41–63% across doses versus 32% on placebo in phase 2). The dedicated phase 3 monotherapy programme (RENEW) had not reported at building, so there is no phase 3 monotherapy evidence on this shelf.

cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-finding (2021): cagrilintide alone cut body weight 6.0–10.8% versus 3.0% on placebo at 26 weeks, and the top dose beat liraglutide, n = 706
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-finding (2021): cagrilintide alone cut body weight 6.0–10.8% versus 3.0% on placebo at 26 weeks, and the top dose beat liraglutide, n = 706
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled dose-finding trial, The Lancet 2021
cards.people: 706 adults without diabetes, with BMI at least 30 kg/m², or at least 27 kg/m² with hypertension or dyslipidaemia, at 57 sites in ten countries, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous cagrilintide 0.3, 0.6, 1.2, 2.4 or 4.5 mg (100–102 per dose group), once-daily liraglutide 3.0 mg (n=99), or placebo (n=101), for 26 weeks plus 6 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: Mean percentage weight reductions (trial-product estimand) were 6.0%–10.8% across cagrilintide doses versus 3.0% on placebo (estimated treatment differences 3.0%–7.8%; p<0.001), and cagrilintide 4.5 mg beat liraglutide 3.0 mg (10.8% vs 9.0%; difference 1.8%, p=0.03). Permanent discontinuation was 10% overall and similar across groups. Gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 41%–63% on cagrilintide versus 32% on placebo, primarily nausea (20%–47% vs 18%); administration-site reactions were also more frequent.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six weeks only, in people without diabetes; participants and investigators were masked to active versus placebo but not between active treatments. This is the shelf's only dedicated monotherapy efficacy trial.
cards.source: Lau DCW, Erichsen L, Francisco AM, et al. Once-weekly cagrilintide for weight management in people with overweight and obesity: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled and active-controlled, dose-finding phase 2 trial. Lancet. 2021;398(10317):2160-2172. PMID: 34798060. Registry ID: NCT03856047. cards.headline: Phase 2 in type 2 diabetes (2023): the cagrilintide-alone arm lost 8.1% of body weight and lowered HbA1c by 0.9 points at 32 weeks, monotherapy arm n = 30
cards.summary: Phase 2 in type 2 diabetes (2023): the cagrilintide-alone arm lost 8.1% of body weight and lowered HbA1c by 0.9 points at 32 weeks, monotherapy arm n = 30
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind active-controlled trial (cagrilintide-alone arm), The Lancet 2023
cards.people: 92 adults with type 2 diabetes and BMI ≥27 kg/m² on metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor, at 17 US sites, randomised 1:1:1 to once-weekly cagrilintide-semaglutide, semaglutide alone, or cagrilintide alone (n=30), all escalated to 2.4 mg, for 32 weeks (mean age 58 years; 64% male). Only the cagrilintide-alone arm is carded here; the combination arm is homed on shelf #1092.
cards.result: In the cagrilintide-alone arm, mean body weight fell 8.1% (SE 1.23) and HbA1c fell 0.9 percentage points (SE 0.15) at week 32; fasting plasma glucose fell 1.7 mmol/L (≈31 mg/dL). For comparison within the same trial, the combination arm lost 15.6% and semaglutide alone 5.1%. Adverse events were reported by 80% of the cagrilintide-alone group, most commonly mild or moderate gastrointestinal events; no level 2 or 3 hypoglycaemia and no fatal adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The monotherapy arm is small (n=30) and the trial was designed around the combination, not around monotherapy; there was no placebo arm, so the monotherapy figures are changes from baseline, not placebo-corrected differences.
cards.source: Frias JP, Deenadayalan S, Erichsen L, et al. cards.headline: Pharmacokinetics (2026): single-dose cagrilintide exposure was not materially changed by renal or hepatic impairment, n = 65 across two studies
cards.summary: Pharmacokinetics (2026): single-dose cagrilintide exposure was not materially changed by renal or hepatic impairment, n = 65 across two studies
cards.type: Two single-dose pharmacokinetic studies in renal and hepatic impairment, Clinical Pharmacokinetics 2026
cards.people: 65 adults in two single-dose studies of cagrilintide alone: a renal-impairment study (n=33; normal function 14, mild 7, moderate 7, severe 5; single 0.6 mg dose) and a hepatic-impairment study (n=32; normal 14, mild 7, moderate 7, severe 4; single 0.9 mg dose).
cards.result: Total cagrilintide exposure (AUC) ratios versus normal function were 1.23 (90% CI 0.91–1.66), 1.18 (0.87–1.59) and 1.21 (0.87–1.68) for mild, moderate and severe renal impairment, and 0.99 (0.89–1.11), 1.01 (0.91–1.12) and 1.11 (0.96–1.30) for mild, moderate and severe hepatic impairment — no consistent pattern, leading the authors to conclude no dose adjustment is warranted for these populations. No serious treatment-emergent adverse events, withdrawals or deaths occurred in either study.
cards.watchOut: Pharmacokinetic support only: single sub-therapeutic doses, small impairment subgroups, and no weight or glycaemic efficacy data. It answers 'can the drug be given in kidney or liver impairment', not 'does monotherapy work'.
cards.source: Nielsen MJF, Becker NP, Duus HHH, et al. Renal or Hepatic Impairment Does Not Affect Pharmacokinetics, Safety, or Tolerability of Subcutaneous Cagrilintide. Clin Pharmacokinet. 2026;65(7):1087-1099. PMID: 42228334. Registry IDs: NCT04209049 and NCT05564104. cards.headline: Synthesis: monotherapy works in phase 2 — roughly 6–11% weight loss — but its phase 3 test has not reported
cards.summary: Synthesis: monotherapy works in phase 2 — roughly 6–11% weight loss — but its phase 3 test has not reported
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 2 obesity trial (706), the cagrilintide-alone arm of the phase 2 diabetes trial (30 on monotherapy) and the impairment pharmacokinetic studies (65).
cards.result: Cagrilintide alone produces dose-dependent weight loss clearly beyond placebo in the one dedicated monotherapy trial, and the small diabetes monotherapy arm is consistent with it (8.1% at 32 weeks). The effect is smaller than the same programme's combination with semaglutide, which is a different question homed on shelf #1092. With no phase 3 monotherapy report published (RENEW unreported) and the REDEFINE 1 monotherapy arm inseparable from the homed combination report, the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the combination's larger weight losses (shelf #1092) as monotherapy effects. Monotherapy durability beyond 32 weeks is untested in print.

shelves.title: Danuglipron (oral GLP-1 receptor agonist) in type 2 diabetes and obesity — a discontinued programme
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes or obesity, does the oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist danuglipron, compared with placebo, improve HbA1c and reduce body weight — and why was the programme stopped?
shelves.balance: PROGRAMME DISCONTINUED — printed on the face, as the question requires: Pfizer stopped development of danuglipron in April 2025 after a potential drug-induced liver injury case in an asymptomatic participant, and the drug will not be marketed. What the phase 2 evidence showed before that: in type 2 diabetes (n=411), twice-daily danuglipron lowered HbA1c by up to 1.16 percentage points versus placebo at 16 weeks and reduced weight at the higher doses; in obesity without diabetes (n=626 treated), weight fell 5.0–12.9% relative to placebo over 26–32 weeks. The tolerability price was high throughout the programme: in the obesity trial only 39.3% of participants completed treatment and about 38% discontinued because of adverse events (nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea predominating), and the earlier phase 2a study saw discontinuation of 27.3–72.7% across danuglipron groups versus 16.7–18.8% on placebo. So the honest balance is: genuine glycaemic and weight efficacy at phase 2, a gastrointestinal tolerability problem that dose escalation never solved, and a liver-safety signal that ended the programme. No phase 3 trial was ever run, and no cardiovascular or other outcome data exist.

cards.headline: Phase 2b in type 2 diabetes (2023): danuglipron lowered HbA1c by up to 1.16 points versus placebo at 16 weeks, n = 411
cards.summary: Phase 2b in type 2 diabetes (2023): danuglipron lowered HbA1c by up to 1.16 points versus placebo at 16 weeks, n = 411
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, JAMA Network Open 2023
cards.people: 411 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise, with or without metformin (mean age 58.6 years; 51% male), at 97 sites in 8 countries or regions, randomised to placebo or danuglipron 2.5, 10, 40, 80 or 120 mg, all taken orally twice daily with food for 16 weeks, with weekly dose escalation to reach doses of 40 mg twice daily or more. 316 participants (77%) completed treatment.
cards.result: For all danuglipron doses, HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose were significantly reduced at week 16 versus placebo: HbA1c least-squares mean difference up to −1.16 percentage points (90% CI −1.47 to −0.86) for 120 mg twice daily, and fasting glucose up to −33.24 mg/dL (90% CI −45.63 to −20.84). Body weight was significantly reduced versus placebo only at 80 mg and 120 mg twice daily (−2.04 kg and −4.17 kg least-squares mean differences). The most commonly reported adverse events were nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks only, and 23% did not complete treatment. The twice-daily with-food regimen and rapid weekly escalation are part of the tolerability story told by the later cards.
cards.source: Saxena AR, Frias JP, Brown LS, et al. Efficacy and Safety of Oral Small Molecule Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonist Danuglipron for Glycemic Control Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Phase 2b in obesity (2025): weight fell 5.0–12.9% relative to placebo — but only 39.3% completed treatment and about 38% stopped for adverse events, n = 626 treated
cards.summary: Phase 2b in obesity (2025): weight fell 5.0–12.9% relative to placebo — but only 39.3% completed treatment and about 38% stopped for adverse events, n = 626 treated
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging study, Diabetes Obesity and Metabolism 2025
cards.people: 628 adults aged 18–75 with obesity and without diabetes, randomised to danuglipron (536 treated) or placebo (90 treated) twice daily for 26 or 32 weeks, with danuglipron escalated to 40–200 mg twice daily at 1-, 2- or 4-week intervals.
cards.result: All danuglipron groups showed statistically significant weight reductions, with least-squares mean percentage decreases from baseline ranging from −5.0% (90% CI −6.8 to −3.2) to −12.9% (−16.1 to −9.5) relative to placebo. Only 39.3% of participants completed treatment; approximately 38% discontinued because of adverse events and 22% for other reasons. Nausea and vomiting were the most frequent events, gastrointestinal event rates rose with dose, and most events were mild; the authors judged the drug safe by laboratory and clinical measures, while noting discontinuation rates due to adverse events were higher than anticipated across all groups including placebo.
cards.watchOut: With roughly three in five participants not completing treatment, the weight figures describe those who could stay on the drug as much as the drug itself. This trial's tolerability failure is central context for the programme's discontinuation.
cards.source: Buckeridge C, Cobain S, Bays HE, et al. Efficacy and safety of danuglipron (PF-06882961) in adults with obesity: A randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging phase 2b study. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2025;27(9):4915-4926. PMID: 40539310. Registry ID: NCT04707313. cards.summary: Phase 2a (2023): even with slower dose escalation, discontinuation ran 27.3–72.7% on danuglipron versus 16.7–18.8% on placebo, n = 151
cards.type: Phase 2a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study, Diabetes Obesity and Metabolism 2023
cards.people: 151 randomised and treated participants: 123 adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin (mean HbA1c 8.19%) assigned to placebo or danuglipron with low (5 mg) or high (10 mg) starting doses and 1- or 2-week escalation steps to target doses of 80, 120 or 200 mg twice daily, plus 28 adults with obesity without diabetes assigned to placebo or danuglipron 200 mg twice daily, for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Discontinuation from study medication occurred in 27.3% to 72.7% of participants across danuglipron groups versus 16.7% to 18.8% on placebo, most often due to adverse events; nausea (20.0%–47.6% vs 12.5%) and vomiting (18.2%–40.9% vs 12.5%) were most common in the diabetes cohort, and gastrointestinal events tracked the target dose rather than the starting dose or escalation speed. In type 2 diabetes, HbA1c fell 1.04–1.57 percentage points on danuglipron versus 0.32 on placebo, fasting glucose fell 23.34–53.94 mg/dL versus 13.09 mg/dL, and weight fell 1.93–5.38 kg versus 0.42 kg at week 12 (generally P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: This study's purpose was to test whether gentler escalation fixed tolerability; it did not — events followed the target dose. Small per-scheme cohorts make the discontinuation range wide.
cards.source: Saxena AR, Frias JP, Gorman DN, et al. Tolerability, safety and pharmacodynamics of oral, small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist danuglipron for type 2 diabetes: A 12-week, randomized, placebo-controlled, Phase 2 study comparing different dose-escalation schemes. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2023;25(10):2805-2814. PMID: 37311722. Registry ID: NCT04617275. cards.headline: Synthesis: real phase 2 efficacy, programme-ending tolerability and liver signal — a discontinued drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: real phase 2 efficacy, programme-ending tolerability and liver signal — a discontinued drug
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: phase 2b in type 2 diabetes (411), phase 2b in obesity (626 treated) and phase 2a escalation study (151) — about 1,190 randomised participants, all phase 2.
cards.result: Danuglipron did what a GLP-1 agonist should do — HbA1c down by about a point, weight down by up to about 13% relative to placebo — but a third to two-thirds of participants could not stay on it, and Pfizer discontinued the programme in April 2025 after a potential drug-induced liver injury case in an asymptomatic participant. The stamp is POSSIBLE for the pharmacological effect; the practical answer is that this drug will not be available, and its shelf stands as the cautionary record of the first oral small-molecule GLP-1 programme to reach phase 2b.
cards.watchOut: No phase 3, no outcomes data, and no route to prescription: do not present danuglipron's phase 2 numbers alongside marketed GLP-1 therapies as if it were an available option.
cards.source: Synthesis of the three cards above (PMIDs 37213102, 40539310, 37311722). The April 2025 discontinuation and its liver-injury reason are stated on the face per the shelf's commissioning question; no additional source is carded for it.

shelves.title: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC): ~15% of the exercise oxygen cost after prolonged aerobic work, exponential in intensity, and still detectable 38 hours after heavy resistance exercise
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how large and how long is excess post-exercise oxygen consumption after aerobic and resistance exercise — what fraction is the fast (phosphagen/lactate) versus slow component, and how do intensity and duration scale the total?
shelves.mesh: Oxygen Consumption · Exercise · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for EPOC's magnitude and time course in humans, framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep (exercise metabolism and recovery). The two anchor programmes named for this row that are reviews (Gaesser & Brooks; Børsheim & Bahr) are not carded as evidence — the carded primaries carry the numbers: duration scales EPOC linearly at 70% VO₂max (12-hour EPOC 14.4% / 6.8% / 5.1% of exercise cost after 80 / 40 / 20 minutes; ~15.2% on average; N = 6); intensity scales it exponentially (1.3 L at 29%, 5.7 L at 50%, 30.1 L at 75% VO₂max for 80 minutes, lasting 0.3, 3.3 and 10.5 hours; the prolonged component requires sustained work above ~40–50% VO₂max); heavy resistance exercise leaves oxygen consumption elevated at 38 hours (N = 7); and circuit-training EPOC in the first hour is rest-interval-sensitive (10.3 vs 7.4 L) while total exercise-plus-recovery cost runs the other way. The fast-versus-slow component split is carried as the textbook's account on the Synthesis card — the primaries measure totals and time courses, not component fractions. Cross-points (prose only): the VO₂ on-kinetics and heart-rate-recovery shelves — different quantities, not duplicated.

cards.headline: Bahr 1987: at 70% of VO₂max, EPOC lasted 12 hours and scaled linearly with duration — 12-hour EPOC was 14.4%, 6.8% and 5.1% of exercise oxygen cost after 80, 40 and 20 minutes (6 men)
cards.summary: Bahr 1987: at 70% of VO₂max, EPOC lasted 12 hours and scaled linearly with duration — 12-hour EPOC was 14.4%, 6.8% and 5.1% of exercise oxygen cost after 80, 40 and 20 minutes (6 men)
cards.type: Human exercise physiology study (EPOC versus exercise duration), J Appl Physiol 1987
cards.people: Six healthy men who exercised on separate days for 80, 40 and 20 minutes at 70% of maximal oxygen consumption on a cycle ergometer, plus a no-exercise control experiment; oxygen uptake, respiratory exchange ratio and rectal temperature monitored during 24 hours of bed rest after exercise.
cards.result: An increase in oxygen uptake lasting 12 hours followed all three exercise durations, with no increase seen after 24 hours. The magnitude of 12-hour EPOC was proportional to exercise duration: 14.4 ± 1.2% after 80 minutes, 6.8 ± 1.7% after 40 minutes and 5.1 ± 1.2% after 20 minutes (percentages as printed in the record), and on average 12-hour EPOC equalled 15.2 ± 2.0% of the total exercise oxygen consumption, with no difference in that ratio between durations. The respiratory exchange ratio fell linearly with exercise duration between 2 and 24 hours (more fat oxidation after longer exercise), and recovery rectal temperature did not change. Duration, at fixed intensity, is a linear dial for EPOC.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 men, one intensity (70% VO₂max), cycle ergometry with 24-hour bed-rest measurement — the linearity is shown inside that frame.
cards.source: Bahr R, Ingnes I, Vaage O, Sejersted OM, Newsholme EA. Effect of duration of exercise on excess postexercise O2 consumption. Journal of Applied Physiology. 1987. PMID: 3558208. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). MeSH: Adult · Body Temperature · Humans · Male · Oxygen Consumption · Physical Exertion · Pulmonary Gas Exchange · Rectum · Time Factors
