cards.headline: Bahr & Sejersted 1991: intensity is an exponential dial — 80 minutes at 29%, 50% and 75% of VO₂max gave EPOC of 1.3, 5.7 and 30.1 litres, lasting 0.3, 3.3 and 10.5 hours (6 men)
cards.summary: Bahr & Sejersted 1991: intensity is an exponential dial — 80 minutes at 29%, 50% and 75% of VO₂max gave EPOC of 1.3, 5.7 and 30.1 litres, lasting 0.3, 3.3 and 10.5 hours (6 men)
cards.type: Human exercise physiology study (EPOC versus exercise intensity), Metabolism 1991
cards.people: Six healthy men who exercised on separate days for 80 minutes at 29%, 50% and 75% of maximal oxygen uptake on a cycle ergometer; oxygen uptake, respiratory exchange ratio and rectal temperature measured during 14 hours of post-exercise bed rest, against an identical no-exercise control experiment.
cards.result: Elevated oxygen uptake lasted 0.3 ± 0.1 hours after the 29% bout, 3.3 ± 0.7 hours after 50% and 10.5 ± 1.6 hours after 75%. Total EPOC was 1.3 ± 0.46 litres, 5.7 ± 1.7 litres and 30.1 ± 6.4 litres respectively — an exponential relationship between exercise intensity and total EPOC, in both the first 2 hours and the following 5 hours of recovery. The record's conclusion: prolonged exercise above roughly 40–50% of VO₂max is required to trigger the metabolic processes behind the prolonged EPOC component that extends beyond 2 hours. Below that threshold there is essentially only the fast component; above it, the slow component dominates the total.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 men, fixed 80-minute duration — intensity and duration effects come from two separate small studies and should not be multiplied together into a personal prediction.
cards.source: Bahr R, Sejersted OM. Effect of intensity of exercise on excess postexercise O2 consumption. Metabolism: Clinical and Experimental. 1991. PMID: 1861633. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Schuenke 2002: after 31 minutes of heavy resistance exercise, oxygen consumption was still elevated at 38 hours — far beyond the 16 hours previously reported (7 men)
cards.summary: Schuenke 2002: after 31 minutes of heavy resistance exercise, oxygen consumption was still elevated at 38 hours — far beyond the 16 hours previously reported (7 men)
cards.type: Human exercise physiology study (EPOC duration after resistance exercise), Eur J Appl Physiol 2002
cards.people: Seven healthy men (age 22 ± 3 years) performing a 31-minute whole-body heavy resistance protocol — four circuits of bench press, power cleans and squats, each set at the subject's predetermined ten-repetition maximum and continued to failure — with oxygen consumption measured at matched times of day from 34 hours before to 48 hours after exercise.
cards.result: Oxygen consumption was significantly elevated above same-time baseline immediately after exercise and at 14, 19 and 38 hours post-exercise (P < 0.05), and mean daily values for both post-exercise days were significantly elevated above the baseline day. The EPOC duration after heavy resistance exercise therefore extends well beyond the previously reported 16 hours — into a second day. The record reports duration and significance rather than a single total EPOC volume, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 young men, one very intense protocol taken to failure — the 38-hour tail belongs to that protocol, not to resistance exercise in general.
cards.source: Schuenke MD, Mikat RP, McBride JM. Effect of an acute period of resistance exercise on excess post-exercise oxygen consumption: implications for body mass management. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2002. PMID: 11882927. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Haltom 1999: in circuit weight training, shortening rest intervals raised 1-hour EPOC (10.3 ± 0.57 L with 20-second rests versus 7.40 ± 0.39 L with 60-second rests) — but total exercise-plus-recovery cost was higher with the longer rests (7 men)
cards.summary: Haltom 1999: in circuit weight training, shortening rest intervals raised 1-hour EPOC (10.3 ± 0.57 L with 20-second rests versus 7.40 ± 0.39 L with 60-second rests) — but total exercise-plus-recovery cost was higher with the longer rests (7 men)
cards.type: Randomised crossover human study (EPOC after circuit weight training), Med Sci Sports Exerc 1999
cards.people: Seven healthy men completing two randomised circuit weight training sessions — two circuits of eight upper- and lower-body resistive exercises, 20 repetitions at 75% of a predetermined 20-repetition maximum — differing only in rest interval (20 seconds versus 60 seconds), with 1 hour of post-exercise oxygen consumption measured.
cards.result: The 1-hour EPOC was significantly higher after the short-rest session (10.3 ± 0.57 L) than after the long-rest session (7.40 ± 0.39 L), and net caloric expenditure during the recovery hour was likewise higher (51.51 ± 2.84 versus 37.00 ± 1.97 kcal). But total gross energy expenditure (exercise plus 1-hour recovery) was significantly greater for the longer-rest protocol (277.23 versus 242.21 kcal), because more work was done during it. EPOC in isolation therefore misleads as an exercise-prescription metric: the recovery tail is real and protocol-sensitive, and the exercise cost itself is usually the larger term.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 men, 1-hour EPOC window only — it measures the fast/early component of the resistance-exercise tail that the Schuenke card shows running to 38 hours.
cards.source: Haltom RW, Kraemer RR, Sloan RA, Hebert EP, Frank K, Tryniecki JL. Circuit weight training and its effects on excess postexercise oxygen consumption. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 1999. PMID: 10589865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: EPOC is a small fast repayment plus a slow metabolic tail — minutes at low intensity, ~10 hours after hard aerobic work, and into a second day after heavy resistance exercise
cards.summary: Synthesis: EPOC is a small fast repayment plus a slow metabolic tail — minutes at low intensity, ~10 hours after hard aerobic work, and into a second day after heavy resistance exercise
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records above (the Bahr duration and intensity programmes and the two resistance-exercise studies), framed by Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep on exercise metabolism and recovery. The Gaesser & Brooks and Børsheim & Bahr programmes named as anchors for this row are review articles, not primary studies, so they are not carded as evidence here — the carded primaries carry the numbers. Cross-points, in prose only: this library's VO₂ on-kinetics and heart-rate-recovery shelves cover the exercise and immediate-recovery limbs; this shelf is the post-exercise oxygen quantity itself.
cards.result: The quantitative shape from the carded primaries: EPOC scales linearly with duration at fixed intensity (12-hour EPOC ~15% of the exercise oxygen cost on average) and exponentially with intensity (1.3 L after 80 minutes at 29% of VO₂max versus 30.1 L at 75%, with the elevated uptake lasting 0.3 versus 10.5 hours); heavy resistance exercise produces a smaller hourly rate but a tail still detectable at 38 hours; and within resistance work, rest-interval structure moves the first recovery hour materially (10.3 versus 7.4 L). The two-component account — a fast component (phosphocreatine resynthesis, lactate clearance, reloading of oxygen stores) repaid in minutes, and a slow component (elevated temperature, substrate cycling, hormonal and repair processes) lasting hours — is presented as the textbook's account (Guyton & Hall / Boron & Boulpaep framing, and the anchor reviews' organising scheme): the carded primaries measure the total and its time course, and the intensity study's threshold finding (the prolonged component requires sustained work above ~40–50% of VO₂max) is the human evidence that the slow component is a distinct, triggered process rather than a longer repayment of the same debt. In absolute terms EPOC is a modest energy quantity — tens of litres of oxygen after hard prolonged exercise, a few litres after light work — and the circuit-training card shows why it should never be quoted without the exercise cost beside it.
cards.watchOut: Every carded study is 6–7 young men; EPOC in women, older adults and trained-versus-untrained comparisons is not in the fetched records on this shelf, and feeding state (shown elsewhere to modify EPOC) was controlled differently across protocols.

shelves.title: Cortisol production rate: stable-isotope re-measurement cut the classic figure roughly in half — ~5.7 mg/m²/day (9.9 mg/day), not the accepted 12–15 mg/m²/day
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the cortisol production rate — what did the classic isotope-dilution studies measure, why did modern LC-MS/MS-era re-measurement revise the figure downward, and how does production vary with body size, sex and time of day?
shelves.mesh: Hydrocortisone · Indicator Dilution Techniques · Mass Spectrometry · Circadian Rhythm · Sex Characteristics
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the modern (stable-isotope) production figure and for the direction of the classic error, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on adrenocortical secretion. This shelf's question is the discrepancy itself. The classic radioisotope era's production estimates were high enough that replacement practice settled at 33–41 µmol/day/m² (12–15 mg/m²/day) — the figure Esteban 1991 cites as 'currently accepted' — and patients on it developed Cushingoid features and growth retardation, which prompted re-measurement. With continuous [2H3]cortisol infusion and LC-MS, 12 normal volunteers produced 27.3 ± 7.5 µmol/day — 9.9 ± 2.7 mg/day, i.e. 15.7 µmol/day/m² or 5.7 mg/m²/day: roughly half the accepted figure (Esteban 1991). Independent stable-isotope work agrees in scale: healthy children produced 4.8 ± 0.6 (boys) and 4.4 ± 0.5 (girls) mg/m²/24 h by GC-MS, with the record stating plainly that these values 'are lower than those derived by radio tracer methods, but are in agreement with previous isotopic dilution studies' (Brandon 1999). Sex matters at the modern figure: afternoon-window production estimates were 0.94 ± 0.15 mg/h in men against 0.38 ± 0.14 mg/h in women, and the difference survives body-surface correction (0.48 vs 0.22 mg/m²/h, P < 0.001; Vierhapper 1998, N = 7 + 7). Time of day matters too: Esteban found a previously unreported circadian variation in the production rate itself, with plasma cortisol tracking secretion rather than metabolism. REFUSALS: the classic series anchor — Kenny et al., 'Cortisol production rate. II. Normal infants, children, and adults' (Pediatrics 1966) — was refused because its PubMed record carries no abstract, as was the 1973 diurnal-clearance paper; no classic number is quoted from either. The classic-era figure on this shelf (12–15 mg/m²/day) is the one the Esteban record itself prints as the accepted replacement dose of its day. Cross-point: the library's cortisol-pulsatility shelf asks the secretion-pattern question — dynamics, not this daily quantity.

cards.headline: Esteban 1991: the re-measurement — 12 normal volunteers produced 27.3 ± 7.5 µmol/day (9.9 ± 2.7 mg/day; 5.7 mg/m²/day), about half the then-accepted 12–15 mg/m²/day, with a circadian rhythm in production itself
cards.summary: Esteban 1991: the re-measurement — 12 normal volunteers produced 27.3 ± 7.5 µmol/day (9.9 ± 2.7 mg/day; 5.7 mg/m²/day), about half the then-accepted 12–15 mg/m²/day, with a circadian rhythm in production itself
cards.type: Human stable-isotope dilution study (cortisol production rate by LC-MS), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1991
cards.people: Twelve normal volunteers given a continuous 31-hour infusion of stable-isotope [9,12,12-2H3]cortisol at ~5% of the anticipated production rate, with blood sampled every 20 minutes for 24 h and tracer dilution measured by thermospray liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry; the method was validated against controlled infusions in 6 patients with adrenal insufficiency, and patients with Cushing's syndrome were also studied.
cards.result: Cortisol production rate was 27.3 ± 7.5 µmol/day (9.9 ± 2.7 mg/day), or 15.7 µmol/day/m² (5.7 mg/m²/day) — against the currently accepted replacement dose the paper opens with, 33–41 µmol/day/m² (12–15 mg/m²/day), which had produced Cushingoid features and growth retardation in treated patients. A previously unreported circadian variation in the production rate was observed, and production correlated with cortisol concentration in each sampling period — secretion, not metabolism, drives the plasma rhythm. The authors' conclusion: the production rate in normal subjects may be lower than previously believed.
cards.watchOut: The classic-era comparator (12–15 mg/m²/day) is the accepted replacement dose as printed in this record — it is the era's working figure, not a re-measured classic value, and the card labels it so.
cards.source: Esteban NV, Loughlin T, Yergey AL, Zawadzki JK, et al.. Daily cortisol production rate in man determined by stable isotope dilution/mass spectrometry. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1991. PMID: 1986026. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vierhapper 1998: production is sex-specific — 0.94 ± 0.15 mg/h in healthy men versus 0.38 ± 0.14 mg/h in healthy women, and the gap survives body-surface correction (0.48 vs 0.22 mg/m²/h, P < 0.001; N = 7 + 7)
cards.summary: Vierhapper 1998: production is sex-specific — 0.94 ± 0.15 mg/h in healthy men versus 0.38 ± 0.14 mg/h in healthy women, and the gap survives body-surface correction (0.48 vs 0.22 mg/m²/h, P < 0.001; N = 7 + 7)
cards.type: Human stable-isotope dilution study (sex-specific cortisol production), Metabolism 1998
cards.people: Seven healthy men and 7 healthy women studied in the follicular phase, given a 10-hour infusion (08:00–18:00) of deuterated cortisol (116 ± 6 µg/h) with production estimated by stable-isotope dilution and GC/MS from blood pooled over the final 4 hours; 12 patients with Cushing's syndrome provided the clinical contrast. Small groups — N = 7 + 7 printed on the face.
cards.result: Estimated production rates were 0.94 ± 0.15 mg/h in men and 0.38 ± 0.14 mg/h in women; corrected for body surface area, 0.48 ± 0.09 versus 0.22 ± 0.08 mg/m²/h (P < 0.001) — so the difference is not a size artefact. Production was increased in Cushing's syndrome, though in 4 of 9 female patients it fell within the range considered normal for healthy men — the record's own demonstration that a single unsexed reference range misclassifies.
cards.watchOut: N = 7 + 7, printed on the face. The estimate is built on a daytime (08:00–18:00) infusion window — an hourly production estimate, not a directly integrated 24-hour total; do not multiply it into a daily figure.
cards.source: Vierhapper H, Nowotny P, Waldhäusl W. Sex-specific differences in cortisol production rates in humans. Metabolism: clinical and experimental. 1998. PMID: 9711994. cards.headline: Brandon 1999: the sensitive GC-MS method in healthy children gives 4.8 ± 0.6 mg/m²/24 h (boys, n = 7) and 4.4 ± 0.5 (girls, n = 4) — 'lower than those derived by radio tracer methods, but in agreement with previous isotopic dilution studies'
cards.summary: Brandon 1999: the sensitive GC-MS method in healthy children gives 4.8 ± 0.6 mg/m²/24 h (boys, n = 7) and 4.4 ± 0.5 (girls, n = 4) — 'lower than those derived by radio tracer methods, but in agreement with previous isotopic dilution studies'
cards.type: Human stable-isotope methods study (cortisol production in healthy children), Steroids 1999
cards.people: Healthy children (boys aged 10–13 years, n = 7; girls aged 7–11 years, n = 4) receiving continuous d3-cortisol infusions at 2–4% of estimated production, with 24-hour pooled serum (sampled every 30 minutes) analysed by gas chromatography–negative-ion chemical-ionisation mass spectrometry — a method 50–100-fold more sensitive than positive-ion MS, validated on standards and spiked controls (r² = 0.99). Small groups printed on the face.
cards.result: Mean 24-hour cortisol production rates were 4.8 ± 0.6 mg/m²/24 h in boys and 4.4 ± 0.5 mg/m²/24 h in girls (mean ± SEM). The record's own summary of the classic/modern question is quoted on the face: these values 'are lower than those derived by radio tracer methods, but are in agreement with previous isotopic dilution studies' — i.e. the modern methods agree with each other and disagree with the radio-tracer era, in children as in adults.
cards.watchOut: A methods paper whose human data are children (n = 7 + 4, printed on the face); carded for the independent confirmation of the downward revision, not as the adult reference value.
cards.source: Brandon DD, Isabelle LM, Samuels MH, Kendall JW, et al.. cards.headline: Synthesis: the modern cortisol production rate is ~5–6 mg/m²/day (≈10 mg/day in adults) — roughly half the radio-tracer era's working figure — and it varies with sex and time of day
cards.summary: Synthesis: the modern cortisol production rate is ~5–6 mg/m²/day (≈10 mg/day in adults) — roughly half the radio-tracer era's working figure — and it varies with sex and time of day
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human stable-isotope studies above (Esteban 1991; Vierhapper 1998; Brandon 1999), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of adrenocortical secretion as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The discrepancy the question asks about resolves in one direction: every stable-isotope/mass-spectrometry measurement fetched lands at roughly half the classic radio-tracer era's working figure — 5.7 mg/m²/day in adults (9.9 ± 2.7 mg/day), 4.4–4.8 mg/m²/24 h in children — and the records themselves attribute the gap to method (radio-tracer estimates ran high), not to biology changing. Two modifiers ride on the modern figure: sex (men produce more per m² than women in the daytime-window estimate, 0.48 vs 0.22 mg/m²/h) and time of day (production itself is circadian, and plasma levels track secretion rather than clearance). REFUSALS, stated plainly: the classic isotope-dilution series anchor, Kenny et al. 'Cortisol production rate. II' (Pediatrics 1966), and the 1973 diurnal metabolic-clearance paper were NOT carded — both PubMed records carry no abstract, so no number on this shelf rests on them; the classic era enters only through the accepted-dose figure (12–15 mg/m²/day) that the Esteban record itself prints. Cross-point: cortisol pulsatility — the pattern of secretion — is a different shelf in this library; this shelf is the daily quantity only.
cards.watchOut: Hourly (Vierhapper) and daily (Esteban, Brandon) estimates come from different sampling windows and are not arithmetically interchangeable; each card keeps its record's own window and units.

shelves.title: Aldosterone secretion rate: the classic isotope-dilution values are unverifiable in the fetched record — what survives is the method, the metabolite index, and the sodium/age/posture behaviour
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the aldosterone secretion rate, and how do posture, sodium intake and potassium loading move it — the classic isotope-dilution secretion-rate measurements and their modern successors?
shelves.mesh: Aldosterone · Secretory Rate · Renin · Sodium · Posture · Aging
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING — and the stamp itself is the honest headline of this shelf: the regulation story is textbook-settled (Guyton & Hall / Ganong: secretion rises with sodium restriction, upright posture and potassium, driven mainly through renin–angiotensin), but the classic isotope-dilution secretion-rate measurements that originally quantified it could not be verified from any record fetched this session — the two classic method anchors carry no abstracts and were refused (see Synthesis). What the verifiable record does establish: (1) method — a radioimmunoassay-based secretion-rate method agreed 'in perfect agreement' with the double-isotope dilution derivative assay it was checked against (de Man 1977); (2) an index — in cirrhosis, urinary aldosterone 18-glucuronide excretion tracked the directly measured secretion rate closely enough to serve as its index in 50 further patients, in whom the index related to plasma renin activity and plasma sodium but NOT to plasma potassium (Wilkinson 1981); (3) sodium and posture in health-adjacent data — urinary aldosterone excretion was lower in subjects over 50 than under 30 before and after sodium depletion, and upright (not recumbent) plasma aldosterone showed the same age fall, with metabolic clearance unchanged (Hegstad 1983); (4) the secretion pattern — in 9 normal men, aldosterone is released in bursts (≥60% of secretion, 80–85 min interpulse interval), and sodium restriction raises output by enlarging bursts and basal secretion (Vieweg 1992 — a plasma-concentration deconvolution study, NOT an isotope-dilution secretion rate, and labelled so wherever it appears, per this shelf's rule that the two literatures must not be conflated). The textbooks' account of the normal rate — on the order of a hundred micrograms per day on usual sodium intakes, rising severalfold when sodium is restricted — is presented as the textbook's account only; no fetched record verifies a healthy-volunteer secretion-rate value, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise. That verification gap, not disagreement, is why the stamp is EMERGING.

cards.headline: de Man 1977: the secretion rate could be measured two ways and they agreed — radioimmunoassay of the 21-monoacetate matched the double-isotope dilution derivative assay 'in perfect agreement'
cards.summary: de Man 1977: the secretion rate could be measured two ways and they agreed — radioimmunoassay of the 21-monoacetate matched the double-isotope dilution derivative assay 'in perfect agreement'
cards.type: Human methods-comparison study (aldosterone secretion-rate assays), Clin Chim Acta 1977
cards.people: A methods study (human sample size not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such): urinary pH-1-hydrolysed aldosterone was acetylated to its 21-monoacetate, purified by a single paper chromatogram and radioimmunoassayed, with the secretion rate calculated from the tritium specific activity in the eluate, and checked against the reference double-isotope assay.
cards.result: The values obtained were 'in perfect agreement' with the double-isotope assay; they did not change with extended chromatography, dilution was linear, and three different antisera gave identical values. The record also carries a methods warning: omitting the 21-monoacetate conversion and assaying hydrolysed aldosterone directly gave systematically LOWER values than the double-isotope method — an early, documented case of the measured secretion rate depending on the chemistry used to measure it.
cards.watchOut: A reliability study, not a normative-values study: it verifies that the classic quantity was measurable and cross-checked, without printing a healthy secretion-rate value this shelf can quote.
cards.source: de Man AJ, Benraad TJ. Aldosterone secretion rate: radioimmunoassay versus double isotope dilution derivative assay. Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry. 1977. PMID: 330026. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wilkinson 1981: urinary aldosterone 18-glucuronide tracked the measured secretion rate — and in 50 patients the index followed renin and plasma sodium, but not plasma potassium
cards.summary: Wilkinson 1981: urinary aldosterone 18-glucuronide tracked the measured secretion rate — and in 50 patients the index followed renin and plasma sodium, but not plasma potassium
cards.type: Human secretion-index study (ASR and its urinary metabolite in cirrhosis), Clin Endocrinol 1981
cards.people: Eight patients with cirrhosis in whom aldosterone secretion rate (ASR) and urinary 18-glucuronide excretion (U Aldo V) were both measured, then a further 50 cirrhosis patients in whom U Aldo V was used as the ASR index against plasma renin activity (PRA), plasma sodium and potassium, and cortisol excretion; plasma aldosterone was measured in 58 patients.
cards.result: U Aldo V was closely related to the directly measured ASR in the 8-patient calibration group. In the 50-patient group, U Aldo V showed statistically significant relationships to PRA and to plasma sodium concentration, but NOT to plasma potassium or to cortisol excretion (the ACTH index); plasma aldosterone likewise related to PRA and plasma sodium, and only weakly to potassium. The record's reading: control in cirrhosis runs mainly through the renin–angiotensin system, with the direction of the sodium relationship (driver or consequence of aldosterone's renal action) explicitly left uncertain. This is the potassium limb's honest answer from the verifiable record: at the secretion-index level in this population, potassium did not register — a null that belongs on the face, not a claim that potassium does not regulate aldosterone.
cards.watchOut: Cirrhosis patients, not healthy volunteers, and an index validated in only 8 subjects — carded because it is the fetched record that ties a urinary metabolite to the true secretion rate; healthy-volunteer ASR values are not claimed from it.
cards.source: Wilkinson SP, Wheeler PG, Jowett TP, Smith IK, et al.. Factors relating to aldosterone secretion rate, the excretions of aldosterone 18-glucuronide, and the plasma aldosterone concentration in cirrhosis. Clinical endocrinology. 1981. PMID: 7021011. cards.headline: Hegstad 1983: aldosterone secretion falls with age — urinary excretion was lower over 50 than under 30 before and after sodium depletion, and the upright (not recumbent) plasma level showed the same fall, with metabolic clearance unchanged
cards.summary: Hegstad 1983: aldosterone secretion falls with age — urinary excretion was lower over 50 than under 30 before and after sodium depletion, and the upright (not recumbent) plasma level showed the same fall, with metabolic clearance unchanged
cards.type: Human ageing study (urinary/plasma aldosterone, posture and sodium depletion), Am J Med 1983
cards.people: Normal subjects aged 20–59 years (number not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such), studied on unrestricted sodium intake and after sodium depletion (furosemide or a 20 mEq sodium diet), with urinary and plasma aldosterone measured recumbent and upright; 8 patients over 40 with aldosterone-producing adenoma provided the diagnostic contrast.
cards.result: Before and after sodium depletion, the mean and the upper limit of urinary aldosterone excretion were considerably lower in subjects over 50 than under 30. Recumbent plasma aldosterone on unrestricted sodium showed no age effect; upright, both before and after depletion, mean and upper-range plasma aldosterone were lower in the older group. Metabolic clearance of aldosterone was the same in younger and older subjects — so the fall is in secretion, not disposal. Clinically: 4 of 8 adenoma patients over 40 had 'normal' excretion against the unadjusted range, but all 8 were clearly elevated against the age-adjusted range.
cards.watchOut: Urinary excretion and plasma concentration are the successors to — not synonyms for — the isotope-dilution secretion rate; the unchanged clearance is what licenses the record's secretion interpretation, and the card keeps that chain visible.
cards.source: Hegstad R, Brown RD, Jiang NS, Kao P, et al.. Aging and aldosterone. The American journal of medicine. 1983. PMID: 6338717. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vieweg 1992: in 9 normal men, aldosterone is secreted in bursts every 80–85 minutes (≥60% of total secretion), and sodium restriction raises output by enlarging the bursts — a plasma-pattern study, not an isotope secretion rate
cards.summary: Vieweg 1992: in 9 normal men, aldosterone is secreted in bursts every 80–85 minutes (≥60% of total secretion), and sodium restriction raises output by enlarging the bursts — a plasma-pattern study, not an isotope secretion rate
cards.type: Human deconvolution study (renin/aldosterone secretory pattern, sodium balance), Am J Physiol 1992
cards.people: Nine normal supine men sampled every 10 minutes for 24 hours after equilibration on high- and low-sodium diets, with plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone concentration analysed by deconvolution to recover underlying secretory bursts and basal secretion. N = 9 printed on the face.
cards.result: For both renin and aldosterone, burst-like release accounted for ≥60% of total secretion and tonic release for <40%, with an 80–85-minute interpulse interval that sodium intake did not change. Sodium restriction raised plasma hormone concentrations by increasing the amount and maximal rate secreted per burst AND by raising basal (interburst) secretory rates — two regulatory processes, in the record's reading. Renin and aldosterone were coupled with a 0–20-minute aldosterone lag in both sodium states. Label, per this shelf's rule: these are secretion patterns reconstructed from plasma concentrations, the modern successor literature — not isotope-dilution secretion rates, and no µg/day figure is drawn from them.
cards.watchOut: N = 9, printed on the face. Deconvolution estimates secretion from concentrations under model assumptions; it does not measure the secretion rate by tracer dilution — the distinction this shelf exists to keep.
cards.source: Vieweg WV, Veldhuis JD, Carey RM. Temporal pattern of renin and aldosterone secretion in men: effects of sodium balance. The American journal of physiology. 1992. PMID: 1590429. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: posture, sodium and age move aldosterone output in the textbook directions — but the classic secretion-rate values themselves could not be verified, so this shelf is EMERGING
cards.summary: Synthesis: posture, sodium and age move aldosterone output in the textbook directions — but the classic secretion-rate values themselves could not be verified, so this shelf is EMERGING
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (de Man 1977; Wilkinson 1981; Hegstad 1983; Vieweg 1992), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of aldosterone regulation as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: What is solid: the secretion rate was a real, cross-validated measurement (two independent assay chemistries agreed); its urinary 18-glucuronide metabolite tracks it; sodium status is the dominant mover (restriction enlarges secretory bursts and basal output, and the secretion index follows renin and plasma sodium); upright posture is where the age-related fall in secretion declares itself, with clearance unchanged; and potassium — the third regulator in the textbook account — did NOT register against the secretion index in the one fetched record that tested it (cirrhosis, N = 50), a population-bound null that is reported, not generalised. REFUSALS, stated plainly: the classic anchors — 'Measurement of aldosterone secretion rate in man by the use of a metabolite' (Clin Sci 1961) and 'A comparison of two methods for measurement of aldosterone secretion rate in man' (Acta Endocrinol 1966) — were NOT carded: both PubMed records carry no abstract, so no classic secretion-rate value (the textbooks quote a normal rate on the order of a hundred micrograms per day, rising severalfold on low sodium — the textbook's account, labelled as such) is presented on this shelf as measured fact. The stamp is PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING because the quantity's primary healthy-volunteer measurements remain unverified in the fetched record, even though the regulatory directions are concordant across everything that could be verified.
cards.watchOut: Secretion rate, urinary metabolite excretion and plasma concentration are three different quantities; every card on this shelf names which one it reports. No animal aldosterone data are carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 330026, 7021011, 6338717, 1590429), with textbook framing as cited. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Diurnal testosterone rhythm: peak at 07:00-07:30, at least a 43% peak-to-nadir fall over 24 hours and a relative 15% by early afternoon in young men — blunting with age is real in pooled data, contested in fit older men
shelves.question: In healthy men, how large is the diurnal rhythm of serum testosterone (morning peak to afternoon/evening nadir, as a percentage), and how much does ageing blunt its amplitude?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aging/blood · Biological Availability · Circadian Rhythm · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin/analysis · Testosterone/blood · Adolescent · Aged · Circadian Rhythm/physiology · Hypogonadism/drug therapy/metabolism · Testosterone/metabolism/therapeutic use · Testosterone/blood/deficiency · Young Adult · Hypogonadism/blood · Retrospective Studies · Tandem Mass Spectrometry · Age Factors · Circadian Rhythm/drug effects · Hormone Replacement Therapy · Hypogonadism/blood/drug therapy · Testosterone Congeners/pharmacokinetics
shelves.balance: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): serum testosterone in men is secreted with a circadian rhythm — highest in the early morning, lowest in the late evening — superimposed on ultradian pulses, which is why diagnostic sampling is standardised to the morning. The fetched human records size the rhythm and disagree instructively about ageing. With 30-minute sampling over 24 hours, Diver 2003 found BOTH young (N = 10) and middle-aged (N = 8) men had a significant rhythm with a minimum fall of 43% from peak to nadir in every subject, acrophase at 07:00-07:30, and no significant difference in total-testosterone amplitude between the groups (P = 0.061) — the rhythm, in fit healthy men, is maintained into the seventh decade, though bioavailable-testosterone amplitude did differ (P = 0.031). Population modelling of hourly literature data (Gupta 2000) tells the other half: the elderly deviation from the daily mean to the maximum was 7%, less than half the young men's 16%, with modelled healthy-young peak 577 ng/dL at 06:00 and nadir 420 ng/dL at 21:42. Morning-to-afternoon sampling gives the clinic-scale number: in young men with normal testosterone (N = 11 of 21 volunteers), levels fell a relative 15% from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (423 to 358 ng/dL; Shlykova 2020), while men with low testosterone showed no rhythm (a relative 4% fall, not significant). In 506 older men with symptoms of testosterone deficiency (median age 65 — a symptomatic cohort, labelled as such, NOT healthy men), Novaes 2024 found no significant morning-afternoon mean difference at all, with the largest variations in men under 30 and a weak negative correlation between age and the morning-afternoon difference. The review framework (Pastuszak 2022) summarises the field as blunting with age and a flat profile in testosterone deficiency. This shelf therefore presents the rhythm itself as established and the size of age-blunting as genuinely unsettled between intensive-sampling studies in fit men and larger clinical cohorts. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the rhythm and its morning-peak timing; the age-blunting limb is presented as mixed on the face of the cards.

cards.headline: Every-30-minutes for 24 hours (10 young + 8 middle-aged men): both groups keep a significant rhythm with at least a 43% peak-to-nadir fall — total-testosterone amplitude does not differ significantly with age (Diver 2003)
cards.summary: Every-30-minutes for 24 hours (10 young + 8 middle-aged men): both groups keep a significant rhythm with at least a 43% peak-to-nadir fall — total-testosterone amplitude does not differ significantly with age (Diver 2003)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour intensive sampling, young vs middle-aged men)
cards.people: 10 young men and 8 middle-aged men, all healthy, sampled every 30 minutes throughout a 24-hour period for total, free and bioavailable testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin; rhythms analysed by least-squares time-series estimation (mesor, amplitude, acrophase). Small intensive-sampling study — Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: Both young and middle-aged men displayed a significant diurnal rhythm in all variables, with a minimum fall of 43% in total testosterone from peak to nadir in all subjects. For total testosterone there was no significant difference between the groups in mesor (P = 0.306), amplitude (P = 0.061) or acrophase (P = 0.972); acrophases for total, bioavailable and free testosterone fell between 07:00 and 07:30 in both groups. Bioavailable testosterone amplitude DID differ significantly (P = 0.031), and free testosterone rhythms were highly significant in both groups. The authors conclude the diurnal rhythm in indices of androgen status is maintained in fit, healthy men into the seventh decade of life.
cards.watchOut: Small Ns (10 and 8) of deliberately fit, healthy men: 'maintained into the seventh decade' describes this selected group, and the near-significant amplitude P value (0.061) means a modest blunting cannot be excluded — read against the modelling and clinical-cohort cards below.
cards.source: Diver MJ et al. Clinical endocrinology. 2003. PMID: 12780747. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Aging/blood · Biological Availability · Circadian Rhythm · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin/analysis · Testosterone/blood

cards.headline: Population modelling of hourly data (labelled analysis): the daily swing halves with age — deviation to the daily maximum 16% in young men vs 7% in the elderly; modelled young peak 577 ng/dL at 06:00, nadir 420 ng/dL at 21:42 (Gupta 2000)
cards.summary: Population modelling of hourly data (labelled analysis): the daily swing halves with age — deviation to the daily maximum 16% in young men vs 7% in the elderly; modelled young peak 577 ng/dL at 06:00, nadir 420 ng/dL at 21:42 (Gupta 2000)
cards.type: Modelling analysis of published human 24-hour testosterone data (labelled — not a primary sampling study)
cards.people: Population nonlinear mixed-effects modelling of frequently sampled (hourly) testosterone data from the published literature in young and elderly healthy volunteers, plus sparsely sampled data in young normal and hypogonadal men. Labelled modelling analysis of prior human data — not a new sampling cohort.
cards.result: A full circadian model fit the elderly data significantly better than reduced models, so the rhythm persists but shrinks: the rhythm-adjusted mean was lower in the elderly and the deviation from the mean, especially to the maximum daily value, was 7% in the elderly versus 16% in the young — less than half. In healthy young subjects the model estimated peak concentration 577 ng/dL at 06:00 and nadir 420 ng/dL at 21:42 (a relative peak-to-nadir fall of about 27% computed from those modelled values), similar to the frequently sampled young subjects. In hypogonadal men (testosterone < 300 ng/dL) no circadian rhythm was detected — a straight-line model fit best.
cards.watchOut: Model-derived, not directly sampled: the 577/420 ng/dL figures are population-model estimates pooled across literature datasets, and the young/elderly contrast is categorical — it sizes the blunting claim but cannot replace an intensive-sampling head-to-head study.
cards.source: Gupta SK et al. Journal of clinical pharmacology. 2000. PMID: 10883414. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Circadian Rhythm/physiology · Humans · Hypogonadism/drug therapy/metabolism · Male · Testosterone/metabolism/therapeutic use

cards.headline: The clinic-scale fall in young men: a relative 15% drop from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (423 to 358 ng/dL) when testosterone is normal — and no rhythm (relative 4%, NS) when it is low (Shlykova 2020)
cards.summary: The clinic-scale fall in young men: a relative 15% drop from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. (423 to 358 ng/dL) when testosterone is normal — and no rhythm (relative 4%, NS) when it is low (Shlykova 2020)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour sampling in young men by testosterone status)
cards.people: 21 male volunteers, mean age 31.7 years (range 18-49), sampled over 24 hours at 8 and 11 a.m., 2, 5 and 8 p.m. and 8 a.m. the next morning; 11 men with normal testosterone (> 300 ng/dL at 8 a.m.) and 10 with low testosterone (< 300 ng/dL), all with normal luteinising hormone. Small study — group Ns printed here on the face.
cards.result: The highest and lowest overall mean concentrations occurred at 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. respectively. In the normal group, mean testosterone fell from 423 ng/dL at 8 a.m. to 358 ng/dL at 2 p.m. — a relative decrease of 15% (P = 0.0003); calculated free testosterone fell a relative 14% (P < 0.001). In the low-testosterone group the fall was 228 to 218 ng/dL — a relative 4% (P = 0.54, not significant). Two of the 11 normal men showed no diurnal variation, and no man starting above 400 ng/dL fell below 300 ng/dL at any time point.
cards.watchOut: The 15% figure is a morning-to-early-afternoon fall, not the full peak-to-nadir swing (the 24-hour studies show at least 43%); the low-testosterone limb is a deficiency group, included because loss of rhythm is part of the physiology question, not as healthy-men data.
cards.source: Shlykova N et al. The Journal of urology. 2020. PMID: 31670607. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Circadian Rhythm/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Testosterone/blood/deficiency · Young Adult

cards.headline: In 506 older men with symptoms of deficiency (median age 65 — symptomatic cohort, not healthy men): no significant morning-afternoon difference, with the largest swings under age 30 (Novaes 2024)
cards.summary: In 506 older men with symptoms of deficiency (median age 65 — symptomatic cohort, not healthy men): no significant morning-afternoon difference, with the largest swings under age 30 (Novaes 2024)
cards.type: Primary human study (retrospective paired morning/afternoon measurements in symptomatic men)
cards.people: 506 men with symptoms of testosterone deficiency who had both early-morning and afternoon total testosterone measured (liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry) within 3 months of each other; men with prior orchiectomy, testosterone below 100 or above 1,000 ng/dL, androgen deprivation or testosterone therapy excluded. A change greater than 100 ng/dL was pre-defined as significant.
cards.result: No significant differences in mean testosterone levels by time of test were found, and age was not significantly associated with testosterone levels. There was a weak negative correlation between age and the morning-afternoon difference, with younger men showing more significant variation; the most considerable differences were in men younger than 30 years. No predictors of the magnitude of the afternoon decrease were identified. The authors note the limitations: morning and afternoon levels were not measured on the same day, the design is retrospective, and the under-30 subgroup is small.
cards.watchOut: Population warning on the face: these are symptomatic, mostly older clinic patients, not healthy volunteers — the null morning-afternoon contrast here bounds the rhythm in that population and must not be quoted as the healthy rhythm; different-day sampling also adds noise that same-day 24-hour studies avoid.
cards.source: Novaes LF et al. The journal of sexual medicine. 2024. PMID: 38481019. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Review framework (labelled synthesis): endogenous diurnal variation is well described, appears blunted as men age, and is absent — a flat profile — in testosterone deficiency (Pastuszak 2022)
cards.summary: Review framework (labelled synthesis): endogenous diurnal variation is well described, appears blunted as men age, and is absent — a flat profile — in testosterone deficiency (Pastuszak 2022)
cards.people: Literature review (searches January 2020) of diurnal variation of endogenous testosterone in healthy men and men with testosterone deficiency, written to compare therapy pharmacokinetics against the endogenous rhythm. Labelled review — not a primary study.
cards.result: The review concludes that endogenous diurnal testosterone variation is well described and appears to be blunted naturally as men age; that men with testosterone deficiency lack diurnal variation and show a flatter profile than eugonadal men; and that no single testosterone therapy exactly mimics either the young diurnal pattern or the blunted older pattern. It is carded as the field's framing summary only — every number on this shelf comes from the primary and modelling records above.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetics-motivated review with industry-linked authorship in the therapy space: its 'blunted with age' summary is the claim the intensive-sampling primary data partly contest (Diver 2003), which is why the shelf grades that limb as unsettled rather than repeating the summary as fact.
cards.source: Pastuszak AW et al. Andrology. 2022. PMID: 34510812. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a morning peak (07:00-07:30) and a peak-to-nadir fall of at least 43% across 24 hours in healthy men — a relative 15% by early afternoon — with age-blunting real in pooled data but contested in fit older men
cards.summary: Synthesis: a morning peak (07:00-07:30) and a peak-to-nadir fall of at least 43% across 24 hours in healthy men — a relative 15% by early afternoon — with age-blunting real in pooled data but contested in fit older men
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies, the modelling analysis and the review above.
cards.result: Settled: healthy men have a circadian testosterone rhythm peaking at 07:00-07:30 (Diver 2003), worth at least a 43% relative fall from peak to nadir across 24 hours in every intensively sampled subject (Diver 2003), about 27% relative between the modelled 06:00 peak (577 ng/dL) and 21:42 nadir (420 ng/dL) in young men (Gupta 2000), and a relative 15% from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. at clinic hours (423 to 358 ng/dL; Shlykova 2020) — which is why morning sampling is the diagnostic standard the textbooks (Guyton & Hall; Ganong) assume. Unsettled: how much ageing blunts it. Pooled modelling halves the swing (deviation to maximum 16% young vs 7% elderly; Gupta 2000) and a large symptomatic older cohort shows no mean morning-afternoon difference (Novaes 2024), yet fit healthy middle-aged men sampled every 30 minutes kept a full rhythm with non-significantly different total-testosterone amplitude (Diver 2003). Absent rhythm in low-testosterone states is concordant across Shlykova 2020, Gupta 2000 and the Pastuszak 2022 review. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the rhythm, its timing and its approximate size; the age-blunting limb is presented as mixed, not settled.
cards.watchOut: Percentages are relative falls from different anchors (peak-to-nadir over 24 hours vs 8 a.m.-to-2 p.m.) and are not interchangeable; assay method (mass spectrometry vs immunoassay) and sampling density move the estimates, and symptomatic-cohort data must not be relabelled as healthy-men physiology.
cards.source: Synthesis of Diver MJ et al. Clinical endocrinology. 2003 (PMID: 12780747); Gupta SK et al. Journal of clinical pharmacology. 2000 (PMID: 10883414); Shlykova N et al. The Journal of urology. 2020 (PMID: 31670607); Novaes LF et al. The journal of sexual medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38481019); Pastuszak AW et al. Andrology. 2022 (PMID: 34510812). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Insulin sensitivity by the euglycaemic clamp: the M-value, and how obesity and family history shift it
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is insulin sensitivity measured by the euglycaemic–hyperinsulinaemic clamp (glucose disposal / M-value) — its distribution in non-obese non-diabetic people, and how much do obesity, sex and family history shift it?
shelves.mesh: Glucose Clamp Technique · Insulin Resistance · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Insulin/pharmacology · Age Factors · Body Mass Index · Sex Characteristics · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, with the assembly caveat on the face: there is no single GLI-style normative clamp cohort, so the distribution is assembled here from the technique's defining paper, one large standardised database and two same-protocol comparison programmes — and M-values are protocol-bound (insulin dose and normalisation differ), never interchangeable across protocols. The defining paper (DeFronzo 1979) sets the method: insulin held at about 100 µU/ml with glucose clamped at basal, so the glucose infusion rate equals whole-body tissue glucose uptake. The EGIR database (1,146 people with normal glucose tolerance, one standardised 1 mU/min/kg clamp at 20 centres) found M fell only 0.9 µmol/min/kg per decade of age, an effect abolished by adjusting for BMI — age per se is not a significant cause of insulin resistance. At a lower insulin dose (20 µU/min/m²), non-diabetic women without a family history disposed of about 5.9–6.6 mg/min/kg fat-free mass, while a positive family history cut total disposal to 3.55; and obese non-diabetic people were as insulin resistant as type 2 diabetic patients, with hypertension adding nothing further. Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of insulin action on muscle, adipose tissue and liver, as textbook context.

cards.headline: DeFronzo 1979: the clamp defined — at insulin held near 100 µU/ml and glucose held at basal, the glucose infusion rate IS whole-body insulin sensitivity
cards.summary: DeFronzo 1979: the clamp defined — at insulin held near 100 µU/ml and glucose held at basal, the glucose infusion rate IS whole-body insulin sensitivity
cards.type: Technique-defining methods paper (the reference method for all later cards)
cards.people: Methods paper: the fetched record reports no participant cohort, so N is not documented in the record and no cohort values are claimed from it. It defines the hyperglycaemic clamp (glucose raised 125 mg/dL above basal and held there) and the euglycaemic insulin clamp in humans.
cards.result: In the euglycaemic insulin clamp, plasma insulin is acutely raised and maintained at approximately 100 µU/ml by a prime-continuous insulin infusion while plasma glucose is held constant at basal levels by a variable glucose infusion on a negative-feedback principle. Under these steady-state conditions the glucose infusion rate equals glucose uptake by all tissues in the body and is therefore the measure of tissue sensitivity to exogenous insulin (the M-value in later usage). The hyperglycaemic clamp instead reads beta-cell sensitivity: under constant hyperglycaemia the insulin response is biphasic, with an early burst in the first 6 minutes followed by a progressive rise.
cards.watchOut: A methods definition, not a normative dataset: it supplies the quantity every other card measures, and any 'normal M' must come from the cohort cards — quoted always with its insulin dose and normalisation.
cards.source: DeFronzo RA, Tobin JD, Andres R. Glucose clamp technique: a method for quantifying insulin secretion and resistance. Am J Physiol. 1979. PMID: 382871. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ferrannini 1996 (EGIR): in 1,146 people with normal glucose tolerance, M fell just 0.9 µmol/min/kg per decade — and BMI adjustment erased the age effect
cards.summary: Ferrannini 1996 (EGIR): in 1,146 people with normal glucose tolerance, M fell just 0.9 µmol/min/kg per decade — and BMI adjustment erased the age effect
cards.people: 1,146 men and women with normal glucose tolerance, aged 18–85 years, studied with a euglycaemic insulin clamp at 1 mU/min/kg at 20 European centres (European Group for the Study of Insulin Resistance database).
cards.result: Insulin action (M value) declined slightly with age, at 0.9 µmol/min/kg per decade of life (95% CI 0.4–1.3; P = 0.0002); after adjustment for BMI the relationship was no longer statistically significant, and the same held whether M was expressed per kg body weight or per kg fat-free mass, as the M:I ratio, or estimated from fasting insulin. A BMI-adjusted age decline persisted only in lean (BMI <25 kg/m²) women (1.6 µmol/min/kg per decade, 95% CI 0.6–2.5), in whom fat mass also rose with age. Insulin action was positively associated with insulin's suppression of free fatty acids. The authors conclude that in healthy Europeans, age per se is not a significant cause of insulin resistance of glucose metabolism or lipolysis.
cards.watchOut: A database of centre-recruited volunteers with normal glucose tolerance, not a population sample; the single standardised dose (1 mU/min/kg) makes its M-values internally comparable but not numerically interchangeable with the lower-dose programmes below.
cards.source: Ferrannini E et al. Insulin action and age. European Group for the Study of Insulin Resistance (EGIR). Diabetes. 1996. PMID: 8666147. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bonora 1995: women without a family history disposed of about 6 mg/min/kg fat-free mass; a positive family history cut disposal to 3.55
cards.summary: Bonora 1995: women without a family history disposed of about 6 mg/min/kg fat-free mass; a positive family history cut disposal to 3.55
cards.type: Clamp comparison studies in non-diabetic women (tracer glucose + indirect calorimetry)
cards.people: Study A: 12 Mexican-American and 12 non-Hispanic white women with normal glucose tolerance and no family history of diabetes, matched for age, body fat and fat topography. Study B: 18 normal-glucose-tolerant Mexican-American women, 9 with and 9 without a family history of diabetes, similarly matched. Insulin sensitivity by euglycaemic clamp at 20 µU/min/m² with tritiated glucose and indirect calorimetry.
cards.result: In study A (4-hour clamp), total glucose utilisation was 6.32 ± 0.64 mg/min/kg fat-free mass in Mexican-Americans versus 6.62 ± 0.81 in non-Hispanic whites (oxidative 3.54 ± 0.24 vs 3.51 ± 0.19; non-oxidative 2.78 ± 0.48 vs 3.11 ± 0.75), with similar suppression of hepatic glucose production (0.33 ± 0.13 vs 0.35 ± 0.13) — no ethnic difference without a family history. In study B (2-hour clamp), women with a positive family history had markedly lower total disposal (3.55 ± 0.39 vs 5.93 ± 0.59 mg/min/kg fat-free mass; P < 0.001), oxidative disposal (3.31 ± 0.25 vs 4.32 ± 0.17; P < 0.01) and non-oxidative disposal (0.24 ± 0.28 vs 1.61 ± 0.49; P < 0.01), with similar hepatic suppression.
cards.watchOut: Small matched groups of women only (n = 9–12 per group, printed plainly) at a low insulin dose, and the two studies used different clamp durations (4 h vs 2 h): the family-history contrast is large and internally controlled, but the absolute values belong to this protocol.
cards.source: Bonora E et al. Insulin sensitivity is not impaired in Mexican-American women without a family history of diabetes. Diabetes Care. 1995. PMID: 7555509. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bonora 1993: obese non-diabetic people were as insulin resistant as type 2 diabetic patients — and hypertension added nothing
cards.summary: Bonora 1993: obese non-diabetic people were as insulin resistant as type 2 diabetic patients — and hypertension added nothing
cards.type: Clamp comparison study across obesity, diabetes and hypertension strata
cards.people: 11 normal non-diabetic control subjects, 20 obese non-diabetic subjects (10 hypertensive, 10 normotensive) and 26 type 2 diabetic subjects (13 hypertensive, 13 normotensive), the obese and diabetic groups matched for sex, age, race, BMI and fat distribution; glucose metabolism by euglycaemic insulin clamp (20 mU/min/m²) with 3-[3H]glucose and indirect calorimetry.
cards.result: Glucose disposal rates (total, oxidative and non-oxidative) were similar in obese subjects with and without hypertension, and both obese groups were markedly insulin resistant compared with controls. Type 2 diabetic subjects were equally insulin resistant whether normotensive or hypertensive, and the severity of insulin resistance was nearly identical in the obese and diabetic groups. Insulin's suppression of hepatic glucose output, lipolysis and lipid oxidation was blunted in diabetic subjects, and its antilipolytic action was impaired in obese subjects. The authors conclude hypertension does not confer greater insulin resistance than obesity and type 2 diabetes already carry. The record reports these contrasts qualitatively, without printing the groups' numeric disposal rates in its abstract, so none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Modest strata (controls N = 11, printed plainly) and a single low insulin dose: the study ranks groups against each other under one protocol and cannot supply a population distribution.
cards.source: Bonora E et al. In vivo glucose metabolism in obese and type II diabetic subjects with or without hypertension. Diabetes. 1993. PMID: 8482434. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no single normative clamp cohort exists — the distribution is assembled, protocol-bound, and shifted most by adiposity and family history
cards.summary: Synthesis: no single normative clamp cohort exists — the distribution is assembled, protocol-bound, and shifted most by adiposity and family history
cards.people: The technique-defining paper, one 1,146-person standardised multicentre database, and two same-laboratory low-dose clamp programmes (42 non-diabetic women in matched comparisons; 57 subjects across control/obese/diabetic strata). Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of insulin action in muscle, adipose tissue and liver, as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-points: hepatic glucose production and insulin:glucagon regulation are shelved separately; this shelf is peripheral glucose disposal only.
cards.result: Assembled honestly, the picture is: at a standardised 1 mU/min/kg clamp, insulin action in normal-glucose-tolerant adults declines only trivially with age and the decline is explained by adiposity (BMI adjustment abolishes it); at 20 µU/min/m², non-diabetic women without a family history dispose of roughly 6 mg/min/kg fat-free mass, a positive family history cuts disposal by about 40% relative (3.55 vs 5.93 mg/min/kg fat-free mass in absolute terms), and obesity alone produces insulin resistance as severe as that of type 2 diabetes, with hypertension adding no further defect. Sex enters chiefly through body composition in the large database. Any quoted 'normal M' must carry its insulin dose, duration and normalisation with it.
cards.watchOut: This pack was built under the row's floor-risk condition and meets it only in the assembled sense stated on the face: three comparable-protocol cohorts (the EGIR standardised database and the two 20-unit-dose Bonora programmes) plus the defining methods paper — not a single reference cohort. Cross-protocol numeric pooling would be invalid and is not done. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session.

shelves.title: The cortisol awakening response: free cortisol rises by about 50% within 30 minutes of awakening in roughly three-quarters of healthy adults, is moderately heritable and stable within a person, and is valid only under strict awakening-referenced sampling
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what is the cortisol awakening response — the rise in cortisol over the first 30–45 minutes after awakening: its typical size, its dependence on awakening time, light and sleep, and its day-to-day within-person variability under the expert-consensus measurement protocol?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Arousal · Child · Circadian Rhythm · Female · Genotype · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Hypothalamo-Hypophyseal System · Male · Middle Aged · Pituitary-Adrenal System · Stress, Psychological · Twins, Dizygotic · Twins, Monozygotic · Wakefulness
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (HPA-axis circadian regulation; textbook framing, not evidence), with the measurement protocol framed by the Stalder expert-consensus guidelines for cortisol awakening response assessment (2016, updated 2022) — named here and on the Synthesis card as protocol framing, not as evidence cards, per this stream's rule. Three primary healthy-cohort studies are carded: the four-study normative dataset of Wüst and colleagues (N=509 combined), their twin study (52 monozygotic and 52 dizygotic pairs sampled on two days), and the Federenko awakening-time experiment (24 shift-working nurses and 31 students, N=55). They agree the response is real and sizable — a mean free-cortisol increase of about 50% (a relative rise) within the first 30 minutes, present in about 75% of healthy adults — and moderately stable within a person (correlations up to r=0.63). One honest tension is kept on the face: the normative dataset found no considerable effect of awakening time across ordinary morning ranges, while the experiment spanning shifts and evening naps found awakening time matters and that waking per se is insufficient — the consensus position, reflected here, is that sampling must be strictly referenced to the moment of awakening, with objective verification, because timing non-adherence is the dominant threat to validity.

cards.headline: Wüst 2000 (normative dataset, N=509): free cortisol rose by a mean of about 50% within 30 minutes of awakening, about 75% of adults were responders, and within-person stability reached r=0.63
cards.summary: Wüst 2000 (normative dataset, N=509): free cortisol rose by a mean of about 50% within 30 minutes of awakening, about 75% of adults were responders, and within-person stability reached r=0.63
cards.people: Four separate studies combined, totalling 509 healthy adult subjects, with salivary free cortisol sampled with strict reference to the time of awakening (samples at awakening and over the following hour, including 30, 45 and 60 minutes in the programme's standard protocol).
cards.result: A mean cortisol increase of about 50% (a relative rise from the awakening value) occurred within the first 30 minutes after awakening, and the rise was consistent, with responder rates of about 75%. Intraindividual stability over time was remarkably high, with correlations up to r=0.63 for the area under the response curve. Women showed a virtually identical increase to men but a significantly delayed subsequent decrease. The authors report that neither age, oral contraceptive use, habitual smoking, time of awakening (within the ranges studied), sleep duration nor alarm-clock use had a considerable impact on free cortisol levels after awakening — the normative reference against which the awakening-time experiment below must be read.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record carries no MeSH this session (fallback printed above), and the 50% figure is a mean relative rise — absolute salivary concentrations vary widely between people and assays, which is why the consensus protocol quantifies the response within-person rather than against a universal concentration cut-off.

cards.headline: Wüst 2000 (twin study, 208 twins): heritability of the awakening response was h²=0.40 for the mean increase and h²=0.48 for the area under the curve — a genetic signal specific to the awakening response, absent from the daytime profile
cards.summary: Wüst 2000 (twin study, 208 twins): heritability of the awakening response was h²=0.40 for the mean increase and h²=0.48 for the area under the curve — a genetic signal specific to the awakening response, absent from the daytime profile
cards.people: 52 monozygotic and 52 dizygotic twin pairs (208 individuals), sampled on two consecutive days at 0, 30, 45 and 60 minutes after awakening, plus a short daytime profile (0800, 1100, 1500 and 2000 h), with questionnaires on chronic stress, self-esteem and self-efficacy.
cards.result: Heritability estimates were h²=0.40 for the mean increase after awakening and h²=0.48 for the area under the response curve, indicating a significant genetic influence on cortisol levels after awakening — while no genetic influence was observed on the short daytime profile, marking the awakening response as a separately regulated quantity rather than a slice of the general diurnal curve. Several aspects of perceived chronic stress ('worries', 'social stress', 'lack of social recognition') were significantly associated with the awakening response, and the authors report the response as consistently enhanced under chronic stress conditions.
cards.watchOut: Twin-model heritability from one sample of 104 pairs — the estimates describe variance partitioning in that population, not a fixed biological constant, and the stress associations are observational, not causal.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (twin study) | Wüst S, Federenko I, Hellhammer DH, Kirschbaum C. Genetic factors, perceived chronic stress, and the free cortisol response to awakening. Psychoneuroendocrinology. 2000. PMID: 10938450. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Federenko 2004: awakening time does matter at wide ranges — the response was most pronounced after early-shift waking (04:00–05:30) and cortisol fell after an evening nap, so waking per se is insufficient to trigger the response
cards.summary: Federenko 2004: awakening time does matter at wide ranges — the response was most pronounced after early-shift waking (04:00–05:30) and cortisol fell after an evening nap, so waking per se is insufficient to trigger the response
cards.people: 55 women: 24 shift-working nurses studied on the first and second days of early (awakening 04:00–05:30), late (06:00–09:00) and night shifts (awakening 11:00–14:00), and 31 female students on a regular sleep–wake cycle studied after a short nap on two consecutive weekdays (awakening 18:45–20:30); saliva at 0, 30, 45 and 60 minutes after awakening in all conditions.
cards.result: Mean cortisol increased significantly after awakening under all three shift conditions (p<0.01) but decreased in the student nap sample (p<0.05). Within the shift conditions, responses after early-shift waking were more pronounced than after late-shift (p<0.01) and night-shift (p<0.05) waking. The authors conclude that across a large range of awakening times an impact of awakening time on the response can be observed, and that waking up per se is insufficient for adrenocortical stimulation — the response is tied to morning awakening in the circadian cycle, not to any arousal from sleep.
cards.watchOut: Women only, and the extreme awakening times come from shift work and laboratory naps — the study bounds the ordinary-morning null finding of the normative dataset rather than overturning it; light exposure and sleep architecture were not isolated as separate factors in this design.
cards.source: Primary human physiology study (controlled awakening-time experiment) | Federenko I, Wüst S, Hellhammer DH, Dechoux R et al. Free cortisol awakening responses are influenced by awakening time. Psychoneuroendocrinology. 2004. PMID: 14604599. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a roughly 50% relative rise in the first 30 minutes, in about three-quarters of healthy adults, moderately heritable and stable within a person — and measurable only under the consensus awakening-referenced protocol
cards.summary: Synthesis: a roughly 50% relative rise in the first 30 minutes, in about three-quarters of healthy adults, moderately heritable and stable within a person — and measurable only under the consensus awakening-referenced protocol
cards.people: Synthesis of Wüst 2000 normative dataset (N=509), Wüst 2000 twin study (208 twins) and Federenko 2004 (N=55), framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong (textbook framing) and by the Stalder expert-consensus guidelines for cortisol awakening response assessment (2016, updated 2022) as protocol framing — none of these is an evidence card.
cards.result: The carded healthy-human data define the cortisol awakening response as a distinct, protocol-bound quantity. Size: a mean free-cortisol increase of about 50% (relative to the awakening value) within the first 30 minutes after awakening, shown by about 75% of healthy adults, with women matching men's rise but declining more slowly. Stability and origins: within-person stability is substantial (correlations up to r=0.63 for the area under the curve), and twin modelling attributes a moderate share of between-person variance to genetic factors (h²=0.40–0.48) — an influence specific to the awakening response and absent from the daytime profile, supporting the textbook picture of a separately regulated awakening signal superimposed on the circadian rhythm. Dependence on context: across ordinary morning awakening times the normative dataset found no considerable effect of awakening time, sleep duration or alarm use, but across shift-work and nap ranges awakening time clearly matters and an evening awakening produces no rise at all — waking per se is insufficient. The consensus guidelines (Stalder 2016; evaluated and updated 2022) turn these facts into method: samples must be taken at awakening and at timed intervals over the first 30–45 minutes with objective verification of awakening and sampling times, because self-reported timing errors are common and, as the 2022 evaluation found, methodological compliance improved little after the original guidelines — which is why this shelf treats protocol adherence, not any single concentration, as the core content. Cross-points, in prose only: the cortisol pulsatility and cortisol production-rate shelves elsewhere in this library ask different cortisol questions and are not duplicated here.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: all three carded studies come from one research programme (the Trier group) — the normative values are concordant within that programme and codified by international consensus guidelines, but independent large normative replications under objective timing verification remain the field's stated gap.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wüst S et al. Noise Health. 2000 (PMID: 12689474); Wüst S et al. Psychoneuroendocrinology. 2000 (PMID: 10938450); Federenko I et al. Psychoneuroendocrinology. 2004 (PMID: 14604599). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: LH pulsatility in healthy men: ~19.5 pulses per 24 h (every ~74 min) at intensive sampling, amplitudes 1–28 mIU/mL — basal secretion preserved with ageing, stimulated bioactive reserve attenuated
shelves.question: In healthy men, what is the pulsatile pattern of luteinising hormone secretion — pulse frequency and amplitude over 24 hours, the sleep-related changes of puberty/young adulthood, and how pulse frequency, amplitude and bioactivity change with ageing?
shelves.mesh: Luteinizing Hormone · Pulsatile Flow · Circadian Rhythm · Aging · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for pulse frequency and amplitude in healthy young men and for the ageing pattern, framed by Ganong / Guyton & Hall on pulsatile gonadotropin secretion as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. Intensive 5-minute sampling over 24 hours gives a stable estimate in men of about 19.5 pulses per 24 hours — a periodicity near 74 minutes — with very wide normal ranges: interpulse intervals from 10 to 330 minutes (median 60) and pulse amplitudes from 1 to 28 mIU/mL (median 4.1) (Veldhuis 1986, N = 8 men). Two mathematically independent peak-detection methods (Cluster and Detect) agree on that frequency in the same sampling series, so the number is not an artefact of one algorithm (Veldhuis 1988) — but that second report reanalyses the same eight men's series and is carded as methods cross-validation, not as an independent cohort. Ageing: basal bioactive LH concentrations and spontaneous pulse properties are preserved in healthy older men, yet the pituitary reserve is attenuated — responses to exogenous GnRH pulses and to antiestrogen (tamoxifen) release are reduced or absent (Urban 1988). The textbooks describe sleep-entrained augmentation of LH pulses at puberty; the fetched records on this shelf sampled across 24 hours but do not report a sleep-stage breakdown in their abstracts, so that sleep/puberty detail is presented here as the textbook's account, not as carded data. Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's GnRH pulse-frequency decoding shelf asks how the pituitary responds to imposed pulses, and the testosterone diurnal-rhythm shelf asks about the downstream circadian signal; this shelf asks the endogenous pulse statistics themselves.

cards.headline: Veldhuis 1986: at intensive 5-minute sampling, healthy men show 19.5 ± 1.9 LH pulses per 24 h (periodicity 73.8 ± 6.5 min), with interpulse intervals of 10–330 min and amplitudes of 1–28 mIU/mL — N = 8 men
cards.summary: Veldhuis 1986: at intensive 5-minute sampling, healthy men show 19.5 ± 1.9 LH pulses per 24 h (periodicity 73.8 ± 6.5 min), with interpulse intervals of 10–330 min and amplitudes of 1–28 mIU/mL — N = 8 men
cards.type: Human intensive-sampling physiology study (5-minute LH sampling over 24 h), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1986
cards.people: Eight normal men and eight normal women in the early follicular phase, sampled at 5-minute intervals for 24 hours; constituent 5-, 10-, 15- and 20-minute series and 6-, 12- and 24-hour durations were analysed with a technique minimising false-positive immunoassay peaks. The male data are the carded limb for this shelf's question; N = 8 men printed on the face.
cards.result: Stable pulse-frequency estimates at intensive sampling: 19.5 ± 1.9 (± SEM) pulses/24 h in men (periodicity 73.8 ± 6.5 min/pulse) and 20.6 ± 3.6 in women. Capturing 90% of pulses would require sampling every 3.1 minutes in men. Counting error fell with duration — in men, 49%, 35% and 24% of the observed frequency for 6-, 12- and 24-hour sessions — and was 30–50% higher at conventional 20-minute than at 5-minute sampling. Measured interpulse intervals in men ranged 10–330 min (median 60 min; 131 pulses) and absolute amplitudes 1–28 mIU/mL (median 4.1 mIU/mL).
cards.watchOut: N = 8 men, printed on the face — a classic small intensive-sampling study. Pulse counts depend on sampling intensity and duration by the record's own analysis; sparser clinical sampling will undercount.

cards.headline: Veldhuis 1988: Cluster and Detect — two independent algorithms — give statistically indistinguishable LH pulse frequencies on the same 24-hour series in 8 healthy young men
cards.summary: Veldhuis 1988: Cluster and Detect — two independent algorithms — give statistically indistinguishable LH pulse frequencies on the same 24-hour series in 8 healthy young men
cards.type: Human methods cross-validation study (LH peak detection in healthy men), J Androl 1988
cards.people: Eight healthy young men with serum LH measured in blood withdrawn at 5-minute intervals for 24 hours; the same comprehensive time series was analysed by two independently formulated statistical peak-detection methods (Cluster and Detect), each at alpha 0.01 and 0.05, and on constituent 10- to 45-minute sampling series. N = 8 printed on the face.
cards.result: Computer estimates of physiological LH pulse frequency by the two algorithms were statistically indistinguishable at both alpha levels, and the methods stayed concordant across the original 5-minute series and its 10-, 15-, 20-, 30- and 45-minute constituent series. The cross-validation delineates the spectrum of spontaneous LH pulse properties within and between men under basal conditions — the frequency estimate is method-robust, not algorithm-specific.
cards.watchOut: This is a reanalysis of an intensive-sampling series of the same size and design as the 1986 study's male limb — carded as methods validation, NOT as a second independent cohort; the shelf does not count it twice as population evidence.

cards.headline: Urban 1988: basal bioactive LH and spontaneous pulse properties are preserved in healthy ageing men, but pituitary reserve is attenuated — GnRH and tamoxifen responses reduced or absent
cards.summary: Urban 1988: basal bioactive LH and spontaneous pulse properties are preserved in healthy ageing men, but pituitary reserve is attenuated — GnRH and tamoxifen responses reduced or absent
cards.type: Human ageing physiology study (bioactive LH secretion and reserve), J Clin Invest 1988
cards.people: Healthy young and older men (group sizes not documented in the record's abstract — printed as such) probed with the rat interstitial-cell testosterone in-vitro bioassay of LH bioactivity under three conditions: basal pulsatile secretion, exogenous GnRH stimulation (10 micrograms IV pulses), and tamoxifen (nonsteroidal antiestrogen) release of estrogen negative feedback, over 12-hour sampling.
cards.result: Mean basal plasma bioactive LH concentrations, bioactive:immunoactive (B:I) ratios and spontaneous LH pulse properties (frequency, amplitude, duration, within-peak B:I enhancement) did not differ with age, though some older men showed irregular bioactive bursts followed by transiently low B:I ratios. By contrast, augmentation of bioactive LH secretion and B:I ratios by pulsed exogenous GnRH was significantly reduced or absent in older men, and tamoxifen raised 12-hour mean bioactive LH, B:I ratios and peak amplitudes significantly less in older than in young men — an impaired secretory reserve for biologically active LH despite preserved basal secretion.
cards.watchOut: Group sizes are not stated in the fetched record's abstract and are printed as not documented rather than guessed. Bioassay-era measurements: bioactive LH is a different quantity from immunoactive LH pulse counts on the other cards.

cards.headline: Synthesis: LH pulses about every 74 minutes in healthy young men (≈19–20 per 24 h) with very wide normal ranges; basal secretion is preserved with ageing while stimulated bioactive reserve falls
cards.summary: Synthesis: LH pulses about every 74 minutes in healthy young men (≈19–20 per 24 h) with very wide normal ranges; basal secretion is preserved with ageing while stimulated bioactive reserve falls
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human studies above (Veldhuis 1986; Veldhuis 1988; Urban 1988), framed by the Ganong / Guyton & Hall account of pulsatile gonadotropin secretion as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The settled core: endogenous LH secretion in healthy young men is pulsatile at roughly 19.5 pulses per 24 hours when sampled intensively, and two independent detection algorithms agree on that frequency; the normal ranges around it are wide (interpulse 10–330 min; amplitude 1–28 mIU/mL), so a single sparse sample cannot characterise the signal. With healthy ageing the basal pattern and bioactive concentrations hold, but the reserve does not — GnRH- and tamoxifen-evoked bioactive release is attenuated. The sleep-entrained pubertal augmentation described in the textbooks is NOT quantified by any carded record here and is carried as textbook framing only. No refusals on this shelf: all three slated anchors had abstract-present records whose numbers verified. No animal data are carded; animal GnRH-pulse mechanism appears only in the textbook framing.
cards.watchOut: Two of the three cards rest on the same intensive-sampling programme (one a methods reanalysis); the independent population base is small and is labelled as such on each face.
