shelves.title: Lobeglitazone in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c down about 0.6–1.0 points — non-inferior to pioglitazone and sitagliptin on metformin, and better than placebo added to dual therapy (single-region TZD evidence)
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (with or without additional oral agents), does the thiazolidinedione lobeglitazone, compared with placebo, sitagliptin or pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Metformin · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Thiazolidinediones · Glycated Hemoglobin · Drug Therapy, Combination · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Adult · Pyrimidines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Lobeglitazone, a thiazolidinedione approved in South Korea and India and not FDA/EMA-approved (flagged on the face; a single-source Chong Kun Dang product, named for clarification), lowers HbA1c consistently across designs: non-inferior to pioglitazone 15 mg in SENSITIZE INDIA (328 patients; HbA1c −1.01 points) and to sitagliptin as a metformin add-on (247 patients; −0.79% versus −0.86%), and superior to placebo when added to metformin + sitagliptin (231 patients; −1.00% versus +0.02%) and to empagliflozin + metformin in two replicate trials reported in one publication (−0.71% and −0.62% versus placebo). Both cautions are printed on the face: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists, and the thiazolidinedione class safety history (fluid retention, weight gain, fracture) is cross-pointed in the synthesis rather than re-carded — the short trials here showed broadly comparable adverse events, which does not settle class risks.

cards.headline: SENSITIZE INDIA phase 3 (Joshi 2024): 328 patients — lobeglitazone added to metformin lowered HbA1c by 1.01 points and was non-inferior to pioglitazone 15 mg
cards.summary: SENSITIZE INDIA phase 3 (Joshi 2024): 328 patients — lobeglitazone added to metformin lowered HbA1c by 1.01 points and was non-inferior to pioglitazone 15 mg
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, multicentre trial versus pioglitazone (active comparator), 16 weeks
cards.people: 328 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.5–10.5%) on a stable metformin dose in India, randomised equally to lobeglitazone sulfate 0.5 mg once daily or pioglitazone 15 mg, each added to metformin.
cards.result: HbA1c fell significantly in the lobeglitazone group (least-squares mean change −1.01; p<0.0001); the least-squares mean difference versus pioglitazone was 0.05 (95% CI −0.18 to 0.27), meeting non-inferiority (reported p=0.0013). Fasting and postprandial glucose also fell significantly. Treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator non-inferiority trial against a low pioglitazone dose (15 mg), with no placebo arm — it shows lobeglitazone works about as well as pioglitazone 15 mg as a metformin add-on, not its absolute placebo-adjusted effect in this population.
cards.source: Joshi S et al. Randomized, Double-blind, Phase III Trial of Lobeglitazone Add-on to Metformin in Type 2 Diabetes (SENSITIZE INDIA). The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 2024. PMID: 38736072. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Versus sitagliptin on metformin (Kim 2020): 247 patients — HbA1c −0.79% on lobeglitazone versus −0.86% on sitagliptin at 24 weeks, non-inferior, with a larger fall in metabolic-syndrome components
cards.summary: Versus sitagliptin on metformin (Kim 2020): 247 patients — HbA1c −0.79% on lobeglitazone versus −0.86% on sitagliptin at 24 weeks, non-inferior, with a larger fall in metabolic-syndrome components
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial versus sitagliptin (active comparator), 24 weeks
cards.people: 247 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin, with two or more other metabolic-syndrome components, randomised to lobeglitazone 0.5 mg (n=121) or sitagliptin 100 mg (n=126) as add-on therapy for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change was −0.79% on lobeglitazone and −0.86% on sitagliptin; the between-group difference of 0.08% (95% CI −0.14% to 0.30%) showed non-inferiority. The proportion of patients having two or more other metabolic-syndrome components fell more on lobeglitazone than sitagliptin (−11.9% versus −4.8%; P<0.0174), lipid changes favoured lobeglitazone, and the safety profile was similar to sitagliptin.
cards.watchOut: Again an active-comparator non-inferiority design — glycaemic equivalence to sitagliptin, in a population selected for metabolic-syndrome features; class-typical thiazolidinedione effects (weight, fluid) need the longer and placebo-controlled reports for context.

cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 weeks plus 28-week open-label phase
cards.people: 231 Korean patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.0%) inadequately controlled on metformin (at least 1000 mg/day) plus sitagliptin 100 mg/day, randomised to lobeglitazone 0.5 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks; all patients then received lobeglitazone in a 28-week open-label phase.
cards.result: At week 24, HbA1c change was −1.00% on lobeglitazone versus +0.02% on placebo (adjusted between-group difference −1.03%; p<0.0001). cards.watchOut: A placebo-controlled add-on in triple-therapy candidates — the cleanest absolute effect estimate on this shelf, in a single-country (Korean) population over 24 weeks.

cards.headline: Add-on to empagliflozin + metformin (Seo 2026): two replicate trials reported in one publication — HbA1c −0.71% and −0.62% versus placebo at week 24 (one report, both trials labelled)
cards.summary: Add-on to empagliflozin + metformin (Seo 2026): two replicate trials reported in one publication — HbA1c −0.71% and −0.62% versus placebo at week 24 (one report, both trials labelled)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials — Study 1 and Study 2 reported together in a single publication (counted as one report)
cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (at least 1000 mg/day) plus empagliflozin 10 mg/day (Study 1) or 25 mg/day (Study 2), randomised to lobeglitazone 0.5 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks, followed by a 28-week open-label extension (the record's abstract does not state the total number randomised).
cards.result: At week 24, HbA1c change was significantly greater on lobeglitazone than placebo in both trials: −0.71% (95% CI −0.88 to −0.55; p<0.001) in Study 1 and −0.62% (95% CI −0.79 to −0.45; p<0.001) in Study 2. The proportion reaching HbA1c below 7% was 48.7% versus 13.4% (Study 1) and 44.4% versus 13.0% (Study 2) (both p<0.001). Adverse-event incidence differed numerically between groups without statistical significance.
cards.watchOut: Two replicate trials in one publication count as one report on this shelf, as labelled; the empagliflozin background means the population and the fluid-retention context differ from the metformin-only add-on trials above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent HbA1c lowering of about 0.6–1.0 points across comparators and backgrounds — a single-region thiazolidinedione with a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial; POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent HbA1c lowering of about 0.6–1.0 points across comparators and backgrounds — a single-region thiazolidinedione with a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial; POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SENSITIZE INDIA (328 patients, versus pioglitazone), the sitagliptin comparison (247 patients), the placebo-controlled metformin + sitagliptin add-on trial (231 patients), and the empagliflozin + metformin publication reporting two replicate placebo-controlled trials.
cards.result: Every randomised comparison shows lobeglitazone lowering HbA1c: non-inferior to pioglitazone 15 mg and to sitagliptin as metformin add-ons, and about 0.6–1.0 percentage points better than placebo when added to dual therapy. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout, all evidence is from South Korea and India (where lobeglitazone — a single-source Chong Kun Dang product, named for clarification — is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved), and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. The thiazolidinedione class safety history (fluid retention, weight gain, fracture) is cross-pointed here rather than re-carded: within these 16–24-week trials, adverse events were broadly comparable with comparators, which does not settle class risks.
cards.watchOut: Weight gain and oedema are dose- and background-dependent class effects (the programme's dose-finding work found more weight gain at 0.5 mg than 0.25 mg); patients with heart failure are the population in which this class is used most cautiously, and no carded trial enrolled them deliberately.
cards.source: Synthesis of Joshi S et al. The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 2024. PMID: 38736072; Kim SG et al. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. synthesis synthesis of the cards above: sensitize india (328 patients, versus pioglitazone), the sitagliptin comparison (247 patients), the placebo-controlled metformin + sitagliptin add-on trial (231 patients), and the empagliflozin + metformin publication reporting two replicate placebo-controlled trials. every randomised comparison shows lobeglitazone lowering hba1c: non-inferior to pioglitazone 15 mg and to sitagliptin as metformin add-ons, and about 0.6–1.0 percentage points better than placebo when added to dual therapy. hba1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout, all evidence is from south korea and india (where lobeglitazone — a single-source chong kun dang product, named for clarification — is approved; it is not fda/ema-approved), and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. the thiazolidinedione class safety history (fluid retention, weight gain, fracture) is cross-pointed here rather than re-carded: within these 16–24-week trials, adverse events were broadly comparable with comparators, which does not settle class risks. weight gain and oedema are dose- and background-dependent class effects (the programme's dose-finding work found more weight gain at 0.5 mg than 0.25 mg); patients with heart failure are the population in which this class is used most cautiously, and no carded trial enrolled them deliberately. synthesis of joshi s et al. the journal of the association of physicians of india. 2024. pmid: 38736072; kim sg et al. diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. pmid: 32406573; hong eg et al. diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2025. pmid: 40726438; seo dh et al. diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2026. pmid: 41236870. registry ids as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Crisugabalin in diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain: beat placebo from week 1 in a 596-patient phase 2/3 trial and pregabalin in a small inadequate-responder trial; dizziness in 27% over a year
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, does the alpha-2-delta ligand crisugabalin (HSK16149), versus placebo or pregabalin, reduce average daily pain scores, and how durable and tolerable is it over a year?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetic Neuropathies · Middle Aged · Male · Pregabalin · Female · Treatment Outcome · Analgesics · Pain Measurement · Aged · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid · Neuralgia · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. In the phase 2/3 adaptive trial (596 patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain), crisugabalin 40 and 80 mg/day reduced average daily pain scores versus placebo from week 1 through week 13, while pregabalin 300 mg/day separated only from week 6 (the report gives significance, not absolute point differences). In a separate small phase 2 trial (93 patients whose pain was inadequately controlled on pregabalin), crisugabalin 40 mg/day beat pregabalin 300 mg/day on Short-Form McGill pain change at 4 weeks (least-squares mean difference −7.2). Over a 52-week single-arm extension of the phase 2/3 trial (301 patients, no comparator), treatment-related adverse events occurred in 38.9% — dizziness 27.2%, somnolence 8.3%, peripheral oedema 3.0%. The whole programme is China-generated: crisugabalin (HSK16149) is approved in China and is not FDA- or EMA-approved. A separate phase 3 trial of crisugabalin in postherpetic neuralgia (JAMA Dermatology 2024) asks a different diagnosis question and is cross-pointed here only — it is not evidence for the diabetic-pain question.

cards.headline: Phase 2/3 adaptive trial (Pan 2025, report of HSK16149-201/301): crisugabalin 40 and 80 mg/day beat placebo on average daily pain score from week 1 through week 13; pregabalin separated only from week 6
cards.summary: Phase 2/3 adaptive trial (Pan 2025, report of HSK16149-201/301): crisugabalin 40 and 80 mg/day beat placebo on average daily pain score from week 1 through week 13; pregabalin separated only from week 6
cards.type: Phase 2/3 adaptive randomised, double-blind trial report (rapid-onset analysis of the trial's data), 13 weeks
cards.people: 596 adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain in China, in four groups: crisugabalin 40 mg/day, crisugabalin 80 mg/day, placebo, and pregabalin 300 mg/day, treated for 13 weeks.
cards.result: Both crisugabalin groups showed statistically significant reductions in average daily pain score versus placebo starting at week 1 and continuing through week 13 (P<0.05); the pregabalin group separated from placebo only from week 6. Numeric rating scale and daily sleep interference scores improved in both crisugabalin groups, significantly from as early as day 2. The report describes crisugabalin as well tolerated, with a low incidence of serious adverse events and no significant increase in dropout rates. The abstract reports the significance pattern without the absolute point differences in pain score, so no effect size is printed here.
cards.watchOut: This is an analysis report of the single phase 2/3 trial, not a second trial; the trial was conducted in China, where crisugabalin is approved — it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. Absolute pain-score differences are not stated in the record's abstract and are not estimated here.

cards.summary: Phase 2 active-controlled trial (Li 2026): in pregabalin inadequate responders, crisugabalin 40 mg/day reduced SF-MPQ pain more than pregabalin 300 mg/day over 4 weeks (least-squares mean difference −7.2)
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised controlled trial, active-controlled, 4 weeks
cards.people: 93 adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain inadequately controlled on prior pregabalin, randomised 1:1 to crisugabalin 40 mg/day (47 patients) or pregabalin 300 mg/day (46 patients) for 4 weeks; the efficacy analysis included 90 patients.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference in change in Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire pain score at 4 weeks was −7.2 points (95% CI −12.4 to −2.0; P=0.007) favouring crisugabalin. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 29.5% (13/44) on crisugabalin and 47.8% (22/46) on pregabalin.
cards.watchOut: A small (n=93), short (4-week) trial in a selected population — people who had already responded inadequately to pregabalin — so it does not estimate crisugabalin's effect in pregabalin-naive patients. China-conducted; crisugabalin is not FDA- or EMA-approved.

cards.headline: 52-week single-arm extension (Guo 2026): patients from the phase 2/3 trial continued on crisugabalin 80 mg/day — treatment-related adverse events 38.9%, dizziness 27.2%, pain scores lower than baseline at week 52 (no comparator)
cards.summary: 52-week single-arm extension (Guo 2026): patients from the phase 2/3 trial continued on crisugabalin 80 mg/day — treatment-related adverse events 38.9%, dizziness 27.2%, pain scores lower than baseline at week 52 (no comparator)
cards.type: Single-arm open-label 52-week safety/efficacy extension of the phase 2/3 trial (same programme, labelled as such)
cards.people: 301 patients who had been in the crisugabalin or placebo groups of the phase 2/3 trial and were invited to receive crisugabalin 80 mg/day for a further 52 weeks (mean age 59.7 years; 58.1% men).
cards.result: Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 38.9% (117/301): dizziness 27.2%, somnolence 8.3%, peripheral oedema 3.0%; grade 3 or higher treatment-related events in 1.7%. Dose reduction for adverse events in 13.6%; interruption and discontinuation each in 1.0%. At week 52 the Short-Form McGill pain rating index was −2.5 points and the visual analogue pain score −23.4 points versus the extension baseline (both P<0.0001, within-group comparisons with no control group).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator — the pain-score falls cannot be separated from natural history, regression to the mean, or expectancy, and this report is the same trial programme as the first card, not independent evidence. Dizziness in about one in four patients is the dominant tolerability cost of a year at 80 mg/day.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a China-generated programme — one placebo-controlled phase 2/3 trial positive from week 1, one small pregabalin-controlled trial in pregabalin inadequate responders, and a single-arm year of tolerability data dominated by dizziness
cards.summary: Synthesis: a China-generated programme — one placebo-controlled phase 2/3 trial positive from week 1, one small pregabalin-controlled trial in pregabalin inadequate responders, and a single-arm year of tolerability data dominated by dizziness
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the programme, crisugabalin reduced diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain versus placebo over 13 weeks in the phase 2/3 trial, beat pregabalin 300 mg/day over 4 weeks in the small trial of pregabalin inadequate responders, and was continued for 52 weeks in 301 patients with treatment-related adverse events in 38.9% (dizziness 27.2%, somnolence 8.3%). There is no trial outside China, no FDA or EMA approval, and no long-term controlled comparison, so class harms of alpha-2-delta ligands (dizziness, somnolence, weight gain, misuse potential) cannot be assumed milder than pregabalin's beyond the short head-to-head data carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: IGF-I reference intervals by age and sex: adolescent peak, steady adult fall — and intervals that belong to their assay
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are serum IGF-I reference intervals by age and sex — the standardised centile curves — and how much do the six common immunoassays disagree on the same samples?
shelves.mesh: Insulin-Like Growth Factor I/analysis · Reference Values · Age Factors · Sex Characteristics · Immunoassay/standards
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 75 (growth hormone / somatomedins) and Ganong, and resting on large standardised reference programmes: 1,685 healthy Japanese subjects give LMS centile curves peaking in mid-adolescence (median 310 ng/mL in boys at 14 years, 349 ng/mL in girls at 13) and falling to about 124/103 ng/mL by age 70; 14,970 healthy subjects across 11 cohorts anchor the IDS iSYS intervals across the lifespan; and the six-assay comparison in 911 French adults shows why the assay must be named beside every interval — lower reference limits were similar across kits but upper limits varied markedly, with pairwise concordance only moderate to good (weighted kappa 0.38–0.70). The age/sex shape is settled; the numbers are assay property, not biology alone.

cards.headline: Isojima 2012: standardised LMS centile curves in 1,685 healthy Japanese subjects — median IGF-I peaks at 310 ng/mL (boys, age 14) and 349 ng/mL (girls, age 13), falling to 124 and 103 ng/mL by age 70
cards.summary: Isojima 2012: standardised LMS centile curves in 1,685 healthy Japanese subjects — median IGF-I peaks at 310 ng/mL (boys, age 14) and 349 ng/mL (girls, age 13), falling to 124 and 103 ng/mL by age 70
cards.type: Human reference-interval study (LMS centiles, Japanese population), Endocr J 2012
cards.people: 1,685 healthy Japanese subjects (845 males, 840 females) aged 0–83 years, excluding diseases that could affect IGF-I and obese or extremely thin adults; IGF-I measured by commercially available immunoradiometric assays, with reference intervals calculated by the LMS method.
cards.result: Median IGF-I reached 310 ng/mL in males at age 14 years and 349 ng/mL in females at age 13 years, falling to 124 ng/mL and 103 ng/mL respectively by age 70 years. For context, mean pretreatment IGF-I SD scores in severe growth-hormone deficiency were −2.1 ± 1.6 (Foundation for Growth Science database) and −4.9 ± 2.5 (adult GHD clinical studies) against these references — the utility the authors claim for screening.
cards.watchOut: One population and one assay family: the centiles are the Japanese immunoradiometric-assay intervals, and the six-assay card below shows why they cannot simply be read off a different kit's scale.

cards.headline: Chanson 2016: six immunoassays on the same 911 healthy French adults gave similar lower reference limits but markedly different upper limits — concordance only moderate to good (kappa 0.38–0.70)
cards.summary: Chanson 2016: six immunoassays on the same 911 healthy French adults gave similar lower reference limits but markedly different upper limits — concordance only moderate to good (kappa 0.38–0.70)
cards.type: Human assay-comparison reference study (six immunoassays), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016
cards.people: 911 healthy adults (18–90 years) from a cross-sectional multicentre cohort drawn as a large random sample of the French general adult population; IGF-I measured with six immunoassays (iSYS, LIAISON XL, IMMULITE, IGFI RIACT, Mediagnost ELISA and Mediagnost RIA, named as published), with 2.5th–97.5th percentile reference ranges by age group and sex and a formula for SD-score calculation.
cards.result: Although the lower limits of the six assays' reference intervals were similar, the upper limits varied markedly. Pairwise concordances for raw values and SD scores were moderate to good (0.38–0.70, weighted kappa for categorised SD scores). The authors' conclusion is the shelf's core teaching point: reference intervals obtained in the same healthy population differ notably by kit, so agreement between methods is only moderate to good.
cards.watchOut: The disagreement is largest exactly where clinical decisions bite — the upper limit used to judge excess — so a value near an upper limit can change category purely by changing kit; the record does not print each kit's full interval table in its abstract, and none is invented here.
cards.source: Chanson P et al. Reference Values for IGF-I Serum Concentrations: Comparison of Six Immunoassays. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2016. PMID: 27167056. cards.headline: Friedrich 2014: 14,970 healthy subjects across 11 cohorts (US, Canada, Europe) give lifespan age- and sex-specific intervals on the IDS iSYS assays — the IGF-I/IGFBP-3 ratio peaks at about age 15, earlier and higher in females
cards.summary: Friedrich 2014: 14,970 healthy subjects across 11 cohorts (US, Canada, Europe) give lifespan age- and sex-specific intervals on the IDS iSYS assays — the IGF-I/IGFBP-3 ratio peaks at about age 15, earlier and higher in females
cards.type: Human multicentre reference-interval study (IDS iSYS, lifespan), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014
cards.people: 14,970 healthy subjects covering all ages from birth to senescence, from 11 cohorts in the United States, Canada and Europe, in a multicentre study measuring IGFBP-3 and the molar IGF-I to IGFBP-3 ratio with the newly developed IDS iSYS IGF-I and IGFBP-3 automated chemiluminescence assays (named as published).
cards.result: Both IGFBP-3 concentration and the IGF-I to IGFBP-3 ratio are mainly determined by age: IGFBP-3 rises until age 22 with a plateau at 15–25 years, while the ratio's peak occurs already around age 15 years (driven by the high peripubertal IGF-I peak), slightly earlier and higher in females. Beyond age 60, IGFBP-3 remains higher in females whereas IGF-I and the ratio remain significantly higher in males.
cards.watchOut: The paper's named analytes are IGFBP-3 and the ratio; its IGF-I values are the iSYS assay's, and its abstract reports the ratio's age pattern rather than a full IGF-I centile table — it is carded as the third, largest reference population and for the sex-divergence after 60, not for stand-alone IGF-I centiles.

cards.headline: Synthesis: IGF-I peaks in mid-adolescence and falls steadily across adult life — and every interval belongs to its assay
cards.summary: Synthesis: IGF-I peaks in mid-adolescence and falls steadily across adult life — and every interval belongs to its assay
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (1,685 Japanese subjects with LMS centiles; 911 French adults measured on six assays; 14,970 subjects across 11 international cohorts on one automated platform), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 75 and Ganong on growth hormone and the somatomedins.
cards.result: The physiology is concordant: IGF-I rises through childhood, peaks in mid-adolescence (median 310–349 ng/mL at 13–14 years in the Japanese curves), then declines across adult life to roughly a third of peak by age 70 (124 ng/mL in men, 103 ng/mL in women on those curves), with sex differences that persist and partly reverse after 60. The measurement lesson is equally concordant: six kits on identical samples agree on lower limits but diverge markedly on upper limits (kappa 0.38–0.70), so an IGF-I result is only interpretable against the reference interval of the assay that produced it.
cards.watchOut: No carded record here quantifies nutritional or illness effects on IGF-I in healthy people, and none of the abstracts prints a complete centile table — the shelf teaches the shape, the peak and the assay rule, and points to each paper's own tables for clinical centiles.

shelves.title: CGM profiles without diabetes: mean ~100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), 96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L), and excursions are normal
shelves.question: In healthy humans without diabetes, what do continuous glucose monitoring profiles look like — mean glucose, time above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L), glycaemic variability and the 'glucotype' patterns — by age, BMI and time of day?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring/methods · Reference Values · Circadian Rhythm · Healthy Volunteers
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 79 (insulin, glucagon and glucose regulation), and resting on concordant current-generation sensor data: in 153 healthy non-diabetic people aged 7–80, mean glucose was 98–99 mg/dL (5.4–5.5 mmol/L), rising to 104 mg/dL (5.8 mmol/L) over age 60, with a median 96% of time between 70 and 140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L) and a within-person coefficient of variation of 17 ± 3%; 39 healthy children aged 1–6 read almost identically (mean 103 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L), median 96% in range). Two qualifications are part of the physiology, not footnotes: people normoglycaemic by standard measures still spend time in prediabetic and diabetic sensor ranges (the glucotype finding), and in the 12-week ADAG monitoring 93% of non-diabetic participants exceeded 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) at some point. All CGM homes in diabetes ask a different (management) question; this shelf is the non-diabetic norm only.

cards.headline: Shah 2019: 153 healthy non-diabetic people aged 7–80 on a Dexcom G6 — mean glucose 98–99 mg/dL (5.4–5.5 mmol/L), median 96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L)
cards.summary: Shah 2019: 153 healthy non-diabetic people aged 7–80 on a Dexcom G6 — mean glucose 98–99 mg/dL (5.4–5.5 mmol/L), median 96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L)
cards.type: Human multicentre prospective CGM normative study, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2019
cards.people: 153 non-pregnant, healthy, non-diabetic children and adults (age 7–80 years) with non-obese BMI at 12 centres in the T1D Exchange Clinic Network, each wearing a blinded Dexcom G6 CGM (named as published) with once-daily calibration for up to 10 days, in a multicentre prospective study.
cards.result: Mean average glucose was 98 to 99 mg/dL (5.4 to 5.5 mmol/L) for all age groups except those over 60 years, in whom it was 104 mg/dL (5.8 mmol/L). Median time between 70 and 140 mg/dL (3.9 to 7.8 mmol/L) was 96% (interquartile range 93–98). Mean within-individual coefficient of variation was 17 ± 3%. Median time above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) was 2.1% (30 min/day) and median time below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) was 1.1% (15 min/day).
cards.watchOut: Up to 10 days of blinded sensor wear in non-obese volunteers: sensor values are interstitial, not blood, values, and a different sensor generation will not reproduce these figures exactly — the device is named on the face for that reason.
cards.source: Shah VN et al. Continuous Glucose Monitoring Profiles in Healthy Nondiabetic Participants: A Multicenter Prospective Study. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2019. PMID: 31127824. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hall 2018: 'glucotypes' — people normoglycaemic by standard measures still spent 15% of time in prediabetic and 2% in diabetic sensor ranges (N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Hall 2018: 'glucotypes' — people normoglycaemic by standard measures still spent 15% of time in prediabetic and 2% in diabetic sensor ranges (N not documented in the record)
cards.type: Human CGM phenotyping study (glucotypes), PLoS Biol 2018
cards.people: Participants phenotyped with continuous glucose monitoring, standardised nutrient challenges, and measures of insulin resistance and secretion, grouped by an analytical framework into patterns of glycaemic response ('glucotypes'). The record's abstract does not state the participant number — N not documented in the record, printed here as required rather than supplied from memory.
cards.result: Even individuals considered normoglycaemic by standard measures exhibited high glucose variability on CGM, with glucose levels reaching prediabetic ranges 15% of the time and diabetic ranges 2% of the time. Glycaemic responses to identical meals varied widely between individuals and reflected variable underlying physiology (insulin resistance and secretion), which the authors use to argue that glucose dysregulation is more prevalent and heterogeneous than single-time-point measures suggest.
cards.watchOut: The cohort mixes glucose-regulation categories by design — it is a dysregulation-pattern study, not a healthy-normative cohort — so its 15%/2% figures describe what CGM reveals inside 'normoglycaemic' classifications, and must not be read as the healthy population's time-above-range (that is the Shah card's 2.1% median above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L)).
cards.source: Hall H et al. Glucotypes reveal new patterns of glucose dysregulation. PLoS Biology. 2018. PMID: 30040822. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: DuBose 2022: healthy children aged 1–6 years (n = 39) on a Dexcom G6 Pro — mean glucose 103 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L), median 96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L)
cards.summary: DuBose 2022: healthy children aged 1–6 years (n = 39) on a Dexcom G6 Pro — mean glucose 103 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L), median 96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L)
cards.type: Human prospective CGM normative study (young children), J Endocr Soc 2022
cards.people: 39 healthy, non-diabetic children aged 1–6 years with normal BMI in an institutional prospective observational study, each wearing a blinded Dexcom G6 Pro CGM (named as published) for approximately 10 days.
cards.result: Mean average glucose was 103 mg/dL (5.7 mmol/L). Median time between 70 and 140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L) was 96% (interquartile range 92–97%), mean within-individual coefficient of variation was 17 ± 3%, median time above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) was 3.4% (49 min/day), and median time below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) was 0.4% (6 min/day) — essentially the adult pattern of the Shah card, in toddlers and pre-schoolers.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine children at one institution, from the same research network as the Shah study — a distinct age cohort, not an independent replication in a different population; very young children's sensor wear and calibration differ from adults'.
cards.source: DuBose SN et al. Continuous Glucose Monitoring Profiles in Healthy, Nondiabetic Young Children. Journal of the Endocrine Society. 2022. PMID: 35506147. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Borg 2010 (ADAG): over 12 weeks of monitoring, 93% of 80 people without diabetes exceeded 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) — median 26 min/day above it — and 9% reached diabetic-range values above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
cards.summary: Borg 2010 (ADAG): over 12 weeks of monitoring, 93% of 80 people without diabetes exceeded 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) — median 26 min/day above it — and 9% reached diabetic-range values above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
cards.people: 80 participants without diabetes in the A1C-Derived Average Glucose (ADAG) study, selected on a very low baseline fasting plasma glucose with normal HbA1c, completing an intensive glucose monitoring period of 12 weeks, with time above plasma-glucose thresholds, postprandial indices and variability derived from the monitoring.
cards.result: 93% of participants reached glucose concentrations above the impaired-glucose-tolerance threshold of 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) and spent a median of 26 min/day above this level during continuous monitoring. Eight individuals (10%) spent more than 2 hours in the IGT range — they had higher HbA1c, fasting glucose, age and BMI — and seven participants (9%) reached concentrations above 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL). Brief excursions into 'prediabetic' ranges are therefore part of monitored non-diabetic life, not proof of disease.
cards.watchOut: An older monitoring era and a cohort deliberately selected for very low fasting glucose — if anything that selection biases excursions downward, yet excursions were near-universal; the 12-week window also captures far more excursions than a 10-day sensor wear, so its percentages are not directly comparable with the Shah/DuBose medians.
cards.source: Borg R et al. Real-life glycaemic profiles in non-diabetic individuals with low fasting glucose and normal HbA1c: the A1C-Derived Average Glucose (ADAG) study. Diabetologia. 2010. cards.headline: Synthesis: without diabetes, glucose sits at a mean of about 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) with ~96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L) — and brief excursions above range are normal
cards.summary: Synthesis: without diabetes, glucose sits at a mean of about 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) with ~96% of time at 70–140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L) — and brief excursions above range are normal
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human records (153 people aged 7–80 and 39 children aged 1–6 on current-generation Dexcom sensors; the glucotype phenotyping cohort, N not documented in its record; and 80 ADAG participants monitored for 12 weeks), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 79 on insulin, glucagon and glucose regulation.
cards.result: The concordant norm: mean sensor glucose 98–104 mg/dL (5.4–5.8 mmol/L) across the lifespan (slightly higher over 60), a median 96% of time between 70 and 140 mg/dL (3.9–7.8 mmol/L), within-person variability (CV) of about 17%, and only minutes per day below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). The equally concordant qualification: excursions are universal — a median 2.1% of time above 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) over 10 days, and over 12 weeks 93% of non-diabetic people exceed 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) and 9% exceed 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL). 'Normal' CGM is therefore a distribution with tails, and the glucotype work shows the tails' patterns differ by underlying physiology even when standard measures call everyone normoglycaemic.
cards.watchOut: Sensor generation moves values: the two Dexcom G6 cohorts anchor the current-generation norm, the ADAG limb is an earlier monitoring era, and no carded record here stratifies the healthy norm by BMI category beyond the non-obese/normal-BMI inclusion of the Dexcom cohorts.

shelves.title: DHEA-S across adult life: peak in the early 20s, then a steady fall to about a fifth of peak after 70
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) concentrations across adult life — the peak in the third decade and the rate of decline ('adrenopause') by sex — in cross-sectional population samples?
shelves.mesh: Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate/blood · Age Factors · Sex Factors · Aging/blood · Reference Values
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 78 (adrenocortical hormones) and Ganong on adrenal androgens, and resting on the classic cross-sectional programme: in 981 men and 481 women aged 11–89, DHEA-S peaked at age 20–24 years in men (log mean 3,470 ng/mL) and 15–19 years in women (log mean 2,470 ng/mL), then declined steadily to log means of 670 ng/mL (men) and 450 ng/mL (women) after age 70 — the 'adrenopause' pattern — with a second healthy cohort (n = 216) and the population-based Massachusetts Male Aging Study (1,709 men enrolled) both confirming a significant decline with age, the MMAS longitudinally within the same men. This is a measurement shelf only: it carries no supplementation claim of any kind (DHEA replacement in adrenal insufficiency is a separate treatment shelf, live #1750, and none of its record is carded here).

cards.headline: Orentreich 1984: in 981 men and 481 women aged 11–89, DHEA-S peaked at 20–24 years in men (log mean 3,470 ng/mL) and 15–19 years in women (2,470 ng/mL), falling to 670 and 450 ng/mL after age 70
cards.summary: Orentreich 1984: in 981 men and 481 women aged 11–89, DHEA-S peaked at 20–24 years in men (log mean 3,470 ng/mL) and 15–19 years in women (2,470 ng/mL), falling to 670 and 450 ng/mL after age 70
cards.type: Human cross-sectional population study (classic DHEA-S age programme), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1984
cards.people: 981 men and 481 women aged 11–89 years in a cross-sectional study, with serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate measured and analysed by 5-year age groupings after logarithmic transformation (the data were asymmetrically distributed); a supplementary longitudinal study followed weekly specimens from 4 normal men aged 36–59 years — N = 4, printed on the face.
cards.result: DHEA-S peaked at age 20–24 years in men (logarithmic mean 3,470 ng/mL) and at age 15–19 years in women (log mean 2,470 ng/mL). Mean values then declined steadily in both sexes (log mean at over 70 years: 670 ng/mL in men, 450 ng/mL in women) and were significantly higher in men than women at ages 20–69 years. In the 4-man longitudinal substudy, individual variability averaged a coefficient of variation of 19%, with no monthly, seasonal or annual rhythmicity; sera stored frozen 10–15 years gave results indistinguishable from fresh specimens. The paper presents a table of normal ranges for adult men and women as a clinical reference.
cards.watchOut: 1984 radioimmunoassay values in ng/mL, reported as logarithmic means because the distribution is skewed — they anchor the shape and the peak ages, and a modern assay's reference range will differ in absolute terms; the longitudinal rhythmicity limb rests on 4 men and is printed as such.
cards.source: Orentreich N et al. Age changes and sex differences in serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentrations throughout adulthood. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1984. PMID: 6235241. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Chiu 1999: in 216 healthy adults aged 20–95, DHEA-S declined with age (P < 0.0001) and was lower in women than men
cards.summary: Chiu 1999: in 216 healthy adults aged 20–95, DHEA-S declined with age (P < 0.0001) and was lower in women than men
cards.type: Human cross-sectional healthy-adult study, Age Ageing 1999
cards.people: 216 healthy adults aged 20–95 years in a cross-sectional study measuring serum L-carnitine and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, analysed by age and sex.
cards.result: Serum DHEA-S levels declined with age (P < 0.0001), while total carnitine increased; total and free carnitine and DHEA-S levels were all lower in women than in men (P < 0.0001). The study confirms, in an independent healthy sample spanning 20–95 years, the two Orentreich patterns — steady age decline and a persistent sex gap — though its abstract reports significance and direction rather than age-band concentrations, and no age-band values are invented here.
cards.watchOut: The paper's framing hypothesis (carnitine availability and energy metabolism) is the authors' interpretation, not a finding of this shelf; the card is used only for the DHEA-S age and sex patterns, which are the measured quantities.
cards.source: Chiu KM et al. Correlation of serum L-carnitine and dehydro-epiandrosterone sulphate levels with age and sex in healthy adults. Age and Ageing. 1999. PMID: 10350421. cards.headline: Feldman 2002 (Massachusetts Male Aging Study): in a population-based random sample of 1,709 men aged 40–70, DHEA-S showed significant longitudinal declines within the same men over 7–10 years
cards.summary: Feldman 2002 (Massachusetts Male Aging Study): in a population-based random sample of 1,709 men aged 40–70, DHEA-S showed significant longitudinal declines within the same men over 7–10 years
cards.type: Human population-based longitudinal cohort (MMAS), J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2002
cards.people: 1,709 men aged 40–70 years enrolled in 1987–1989 in the Massachusetts Male Aging Study, a large population-based random-sample cohort, of whom 1,156 were followed up 7–10 years afterward; cross-sectional age trends at each wave and longitudinal trends within subjects were estimated simultaneously by repeated-measures analysis for testosterone and related hormones including dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate.
cards.result: Dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, cortisol and estrone showed significant longitudinal declines within subjects, whereas dihydrotestosterone, pituitary gonadotropins and prolactin rose longitudinally. Apparent good health (absence of chronic illness, prescription medication, obesity or excessive drinking) added 10–15% to the level of several androgens. The DHEA-S decline is therefore not only a cross-sectional contrast between different men of different ages — it happens within the same men over time.
cards.watchOut: Men only, aged 40–70 at baseline, and the record's abstract does not give a DHEA-S percentage decline — none is printed; the quantified per-year declines in this paper belong to testosterone fractions, a different analyte, and are not transferred to DHEA-S here.
cards.source: Feldman HA et al. Age trends in the level of serum testosterone and other hormones in middle-aged men: longitudinal results from the Massachusetts male aging study. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2002. PMID: 11836290. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: DHEA-S peaks in the early 20s (earlier in women), then falls steadily for life — by over 70, levels are about a fifth of peak — with men higher than women through midlife
cards.summary: Synthesis: DHEA-S peaks in the early 20s (earlier in women), then falls steadily for life — by over 70, levels are about a fifth of peak — with men higher than women through midlife
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (the 1984 cross-sectional programme of 981 men and 481 women; the 216 healthy adults aged 20–95; and the 1,709-man population cohort followed longitudinally), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 78 and Ganong on adrenal androgen physiology.
cards.result: All three agree: DHEA-S is the adrenal androgen that peaks young — at 15–19 years in women and 20–24 years in men in the classic data — and then declines steadily and significantly with age in both sexes, cross-sectionally and within the same individuals, reaching log means of 670 ng/mL (men) and 450 ng/mL (women) after age 70 against peaks of 3,470 and 2,470 ng/mL. Men run higher than women from age 20 to 69. There is no monthly, seasonal or annual rhythm in the (very small, N = 4) longitudinal substudy, and within-person variability is about 19%. This shelf describes concentrations only; it makes no claim that replacing DHEA-S does anything — that treatment question lives on other shelves.
cards.watchOut: Absolute concentrations are assay-era values (1984 radioimmunoassay, log means); modern laboratories must use their own age- and sex-banded ranges. The 'about a fifth of peak' summary is arithmetic on the Orentreich log means (670/3,470 in men; 450/2,470 in women), printed as a description of that dataset, not as a universal ratio.
cards.source: Synthesis of Orentreich N et al. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1984 (PMID: 6235241); Chiu KM et al. Age and Ageing. 1999 (PMID: 10350421); Feldman HA et al. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2002 (PMID: 11836290), all carded above, with Guyton & Hall / Ganong textbook framing. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Chiglitazar in type 2 diabetes: three phase 3 trials lowered HbA1c (placebo-adjusted −0.87% to −1.05%; noninferior to sitagliptin; added benefit on metformin) — surrogate endpoint, China only
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the PPAR pan-agonist (α/γ/δ) chiglitazar, compared with placebo, sitagliptin, or added to metformin, improve glycaemic control (CMAP / CMAS / RECAM programme)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors · Hypoglycemic Agents · Carbazoles · Propionates
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control, on three consistent phase 3 trials — with two limits printed on the face: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout, and the evidence is single-region (China; chiglitazar is approved there and not FDA/EMA-approved), with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial. CMAP (n=535): placebo-adjusted HbA1c reductions of −0.87% (32 mg) and −1.05% (48 mg) at 24 weeks. CMAS (n=739): chiglitazar was noninferior to sitagliptin 100 mg (HbA1c −1.40% and −1.47% vs −1.39%). RECAM (n=533): added to metformin, HbA1c fell −0.91% and −1.14% versus −0.49% on placebo. The recurring harms are the glitazar-pattern ones seen in the trials: slight weight gain and mild oedema. Chiglitazar is a single-source product (Chipscreen) — named here under the clarification exception. The wider glitazone/glitazar class history is cross-pointed, not re-carded.

cards.headline: CMAP phase 3 RCT (Ji 2021): chiglitazar beat placebo on HbA1c at 24 weeks — placebo-adjusted reductions of −0.87% (32 mg) and −1.05% (48 mg)
cards.summary: CMAP phase 3 RCT (Ji 2021): chiglitazar beat placebo on HbA1c at 24 weeks — placebo-adjusted reductions of −0.87% (32 mg) and −1.05% (48 mg)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (CMAP), chiglitazar 32 mg or 48 mg vs placebo, monotherapy
cards.people: 535 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by strict diet and exercise alone were randomised to chiglitazar 32 mg (n=167), chiglitazar 48 mg (n=166) or placebo (n=202) once daily for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Both chiglitazar doses produced significant HbA1c reductions; the placebo-adjusted estimated treatment differences at week 24 were −0.87% (95% CI −1.10 to −0.65; P<0.0001) for 32 mg and −1.05% (95% CI −1.29 to −0.81; P<0.0001) for 48 mg. Glycaemic control, insulin sensitivity and triglyceride measures also improved. Overall adverse-event frequency and discontinuation for adverse events were similar across groups; low incidences of mild oedema and body-weight gain were reported in the chiglitazar groups.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week HbA1c (surrogate) trial in patients on lifestyle therapy only, conducted in China; it says nothing about cardiovascular or other long-term outcomes.
cards.source: Ji L et al. Efficacy and safety of chiglitazar, a novel peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor pan-agonist, in patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial (CMAP). Science Bulletin. 2021. PMID: 36654286. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CMAS phase 3 RCT (Jia 2021): chiglitazar was NONINFERIOR to sitagliptin 100 mg — HbA1c −1.40% (32 mg) and −1.47% (48 mg) vs −1.39% on sitagliptin at 24 weeks
cards.summary: CMAS phase 3 RCT (Jia 2021): chiglitazar was NONINFERIOR to sitagliptin 100 mg — HbA1c −1.40% (32 mg) and −1.47% (48 mg) vs −1.39% on sitagliptin at 24 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind active-comparator noninferiority trial (CMAS), chiglitazar vs sitagliptin, monotherapy
cards.people: 739 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled despite strict diet and exercise were randomised 1:1:1 to chiglitazar 32 mg (n=245), chiglitazar 48 mg (n=246) or sitagliptin 100 mg (n=248) once daily for 24 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by −1.40%, −1.47% and −1.39% respectively; both chiglitazar doses were noninferior to sitagliptin, with mean differences of −0.04% (95% CI −0.22 to 0.15) for 32 mg and −0.08% (95% CI −0.27 to 0.10) for 48 mg. Compared with sitagliptin, chiglitazar gave greater reductions in fasting and 2-hour postprandial plasma glucose and in fasting insulin. Overall adverse-event rates were similar; a small increase in mild oedema in the 48 mg group and slight weight gain in both chiglitazar groups were reported.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority to sitagliptin is a 'no worse than' result against a modest-potency comparator, on a surrogate endpoint over 24 weeks — not evidence of superiority or of outcome benefit.
cards.source: Jia W et al. Chiglitazar monotherapy with sitagliptin as an active comparator in patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized, double-blind, phase 3 trial (CMAS). Science Bulletin. 2021. PMID: 36654287. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: RECAM phase 3 RCT (Gao 2025): chiglitazar added to metformin lowered HbA1c more than placebo — −0.91% (32 mg) and −1.14% (48 mg) vs −0.49% at 24 weeks
cards.summary: RECAM phase 3 RCT (Gao 2025): chiglitazar added to metformin lowered HbA1c more than placebo — −0.91% (32 mg) and −1.14% (48 mg) vs −0.49% at 24 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (RECAM), chiglitazar added to metformin
cards.people: 533 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by metformin were randomised 1:1:1 to chiglitazar 32 mg (n=178), chiglitazar 48 mg (n=177) or placebo (n=178), each added to metformin for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c changes were −0.91% (95% CI −1.03 to −0.79), −1.14% (95% CI −1.26 to −1.02) and −0.49% (95% CI −0.62 to −0.36); both chiglitazar doses beat placebo (both P<0.001) and 48 mg beat 32 mg (P=0.008). Fasting and 2-hour postprandial glucose improved, triglyceride and free fatty acid levels fell and HDL cholesterol rose. Adverse-event incidence was comparable across groups, with a slight increase in weight gain and mild oedema on chiglitazar.
cards.watchOut: Again a 24-week surrogate-endpoint trial in Chinese patients; the placebo group also improved on metformin (−0.49%), so the added drug effect is the between-group difference, roughly −0.4 to −0.65 percentage points.
cards.source: Gao L et al. Efficacy and safety of chiglitazar add-on to metformin in type 2 diabetes mellitus (RECAM study). Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2025. PMID: 40842343. Registry ID: NCT04807348. cards.headline: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials (n=535, 739 and 533) consistently show chiglitazar lowers HbA1c — versus placebo, noninferior to sitagliptin, and added to metformin — with slight weight gain and mild oedema, and no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials (n=535, 739 and 533) consistently show chiglitazar lowers HbA1c — versus placebo, noninferior to sitagliptin, and added to metformin — with slight weight gain and mild oedema, and no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Chiglitazar 32 mg and 48 mg lowered HbA1c in every setting tested: placebo-adjusted −0.87% and −1.05% as monotherapy (CMAP), noninferior to sitagliptin as monotherapy (CMAS), and −0.91% and −1.14% versus −0.49% on placebo when added to metformin (RECAM). All three trials are 24-week, Chinese, surrogate-endpoint studies; there is no cardiovascular-outcomes or other hard-outcome trial, and the drug is not FDA/EMA-approved. The benefit claim is therefore confined to glycaemic and lipid measures over 24 weeks.

shelves.title: Avexitide for post-bariatric hypoglycaemia: small phase 2 reports only (n=18, 16 completers, n=19) — glucose nadir rose a relative 21–26% vs placebo in PREVENT; no phase 3 evidence
shelves.question: In adults with post-bariatric (post-surgical) hypoglycaemia, does the GLP-1-receptor antagonist avexitide (exendin 9-39), compared with placebo, raise glucose nadir and reduce hypoglycaemic events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bariatric Surgery · Blood Glucose · Cross-Over Studies · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Male · Middle Aged · Peptide Fragments · Postoperative Complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — based on a very small total evidence base (n=18, 16 completers and n=19 across three short phase 2 reports; every N is printed on the face). Avexitide, a GLP-1-receptor antagonist, consistently raised glucose nadir and reduced hypoglycaemic events over treatment periods of 3 to 28 days: in the placebo-controlled crossover PREVENT trial (n=18 women) the glucose nadir rose by a relative 21% (30 mg twice daily) and 26% (60 mg once daily) versus placebo; in the phase 2b study (16 completers, broader post-surgical population) diurnal Level 2 events fell by a relative 47.7% and 59.0% versus a baseline run-in — not versus placebo. Two of the three reports enrolled women only. There is no approved therapy for post-bariatric hypoglycaemia and no phase 3 results are carded — all phase 3 claims are fenced. Avexitide is a single-source investigational product, named under the clarification exception.

cards.headline: PREVENT phase 2 crossover RCT (Craig 2021) — SMALL N=18, printed on the face: avexitide raised the glucose nadir by a relative 21% (30 mg twice daily) and 26% (60 mg once daily) versus placebo in post-bariatric hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: PREVENT phase 2 crossover RCT (Craig 2021) — SMALL N=18, printed on the face: avexitide raised the glucose nadir by a relative 21% (30 mg twice daily) and 26% (60 mg once daily) versus placebo in post-bariatric hypoglycaemia
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial (PREVENT) — SMALL N=18, women only
cards.people: 18 female patients with post-bariatric hypoglycaemia in a multicentre phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled crossover study (PREVENT): placebo for 14 days, then avexitide 30 mg twice daily and 60 mg once daily, each for 14 days in random order. Outcomes were glucose nadir and insulin peak on mixed-meal tolerance testing, plus hypoglycaemic events by self-monitoring, electronic diary and blinded continuous glucose monitoring.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, avexitide 30 mg twice daily and 60 mg once daily raised the glucose nadir by a relative 21% (P=0.001) and 26% (P=0.0002) and lowered the insulin peak by a relative 23% (P=0.029) and 21% (P=0.042), corresponding to 50% and 75% fewer participants requiring rescue during mixed-meal testing. Rates of Level 1 to 3 hypoglycaemia (self-monitored glucose <70 mg/dL, <54 mg/dL, and severe events requiring assistance) fell significantly, continuous monitoring showed less hypoglycaemia without clinically relevant hyperglycaemia, and avexitide was well tolerated with no increase in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: SMALL N=18, women only, and only 14 days per treatment period: the only placebo-controlled report in the programme, and far too small and short to establish durable event reduction or safety.
cards.source: Craig CM et al. PREVENT: A Randomized, Placebo-controlled Crossover Trial of Avexitide for Treatment of Postbariatric Hypoglycemia. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 2021. PMID: 33616643. Registry ID: NCT03373435. cards.headline: Phase 2b study (Craig 2026) — SMALL N: 16 participants completed: avexitide 45 mg twice daily and 90 mg once daily reduced diurnal Level 2 hypoglycaemia events by a relative 47.7% and 59.0% versus a baseline run-in (not versus placebo)
cards.summary: Phase 2b study (Craig 2026) — SMALL N: 16 participants completed: avexitide 45 mg twice daily and 90 mg once daily reduced diurnal Level 2 hypoglycaemia events by a relative 47.7% and 59.0% versus a baseline run-in (not versus placebo)
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised-order crossover study versus baseline run-in (no placebo arm) — SMALL N: 16 completers
cards.people: Adults with clinically important hypoglycaemia following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, total gastrectomy or Nissen fundoplication; 16 participants completed the study. After a 14-day baseline run-in, each participant received subcutaneous avexitide 45 mg twice daily and 90 mg once daily for 14 days each in random order. The primary endpoint was the rate of diurnal Level 2 events (<54 mg/dL by continuous glucose monitoring, 8 am to 10 pm). The enrolled N is not stated in the record; 16 completed.
cards.result: Compared with baseline, avexitide 45 mg twice daily and 90 mg once daily significantly reduced diurnal Level 2 events by continuous monitoring (relative reductions of 47.7% and 59.0%, both P≤0.0001), Level 2 events by self-monitoring (relative −56.8%, P=0.0027; −53.3%, P=0.0043), Level 3 (severe) events (relative −67.5% and −66.1%, both P=0.0003) and percent time below 54 mg/dL (relative −45%, P=0.0007; −64%, P<0.0001). Improvements were consistent across surgical subtypes; the 90 mg once-daily regimen also improved quality-of-life scores. There were no serious adverse events and no discontinuations for adverse events.
cards.watchOut: SMALL N and no placebo: comparisons are against each participant's own 14-day baseline, so regression to the mean and period effects are uncontrolled; the population is also broader than post-bariatric hypoglycaemia alone (gastrectomy and fundoplication included).
cards.source: Craig C et al. Efficacy and safety of avexitide for treatment of hypoglycemia following bariatric and other upper gastrointestinal surgeries: a phase 2b study. Metabolism: Clinical and Experimental. 2026. PMID: 42744082. Registry ID: NCT04652479. cards.headline: Repeat-dosing phase 2 study (Tan 2020) — SMALL N=19, women only: liquid avexitide 30 mg twice daily raised the glucose nadir by a relative 47% and cut peak insulin by a relative 67% over 3 days of dosing
cards.summary: Repeat-dosing phase 2 study (Tan 2020) — SMALL N=19, women only: liquid avexitide 30 mg twice daily raised the glucose nadir by a relative 47% and cut peak insulin by a relative 67% over 3 days of dosing
cards.type: Phase 2 multiple-ascending-dose study, sequential (non-randomised) dose assignment — SMALL N=19, women only, 3 days of dosing
cards.people: 19 women with post-bariatric hypoglycaemia at a single centre (Stanford University): 14 were sequentially assigned to one of four ascending twice-daily dose levels of lyophilised avexitide for 3 days, and 5 further participants received a liquid formulation at a fixed 30 mg twice daily for 3 days, with oral glucose tolerance testing at baseline and on day 3.
cards.result: Lyophilised avexitide reduced symptomatic hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia at all dose levels, with dose-dependent improvements in glucose nadir, insulin peak and symptom score; at doses of 20 mg twice daily or more no glycaemic rescue (given at glucose <2.8 mmol/L (≈50 mg/dL)) was required. On liquid avexitide 30 mg twice daily no participant required rescue, with a relative 47% increase in glucose nadir, a relative 67% reduction in peak insulin and a relative 47% reduction in overall symptom score. Both formulations were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: SMALL N=19, women only, sequential rather than randomised dose assignment, and only 3 days of treatment: a pharmacology and dose-finding report, not evidence of sustained clinical benefit.
cards.source: Tan M et al. Safety, efficacy and pharmacokinetics of repeat subcutaneous dosing of avexitide (exendin 9-39) for treatment of post-bariatric hypoglycaemia. cards.headline: Synthesis: three small, short phase 2 reports (n=18, 16 completers, n=19) all point the same way — avexitide raises glucose nadir and reduces hypoglycaemic events — but no report is large, long, or phase 3
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small, short phase 2 reports (n=18, 16 completers, n=19) all point the same way — avexitide raises glucose nadir and reduces hypoglycaemic events — but no report is large, long, or phase 3
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The placebo-controlled PREVENT crossover (n=18) showed relative glucose-nadir increases of 21–26% versus placebo; the phase 2b study (16 completers) showed relative reductions of about half in Level 2 and two-thirds in Level 3 events versus baseline; the ascending-dose study (n=19) showed dose-dependent nadir and insulin effects over 3 days. The direction is consistent and mechanistically coherent for a GLP-1-receptor antagonist, but the total evidence base is 53 participants at most across three reports, treatment lasted at most 28 days, and two reports enrolled women only. Acute-rescue hypoglycaemia treatments (for example the dasiglucagon shelf) answer a different question and are cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: TSH reference intervals by assay and inclusion rule: upper limits of 3.70 (antibody-excluded, Hong Kong), 4.07 (NACB validation, N = 1,512) and 4.45 mIU/L (Brazil) — the number that defines subclinical hypothyroidism is selection-dependent
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for TSH and the thyroid hormones — the 2.5th-97.5th percentile ranges in antibody-negative, iodine-sufficient adults — and how much do the inclusion rules (antibody exclusion, ultrasound screening), assay platform, age and population iodine status shift the upper TSH limit that defines subclinical hypothyroidism?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, thyroid hormone chapters; Ganong, thyroid physiology. Four primary datasets, each carded WITH ITS ASSAY PLATFORM AND INCLUSION RULES, as this measurement demands: 3,123 iodine-adequate Lanzhou adults on Abbott Architect (sex-specific intervals; manufacturer's values do not transfer; numbers not printed in the record), 272 Brazilian adults by electrochemiluminescence (TSH 0.56-4.45 mIU/L; ultrasound screening inessential), Hong Kong Chinese adults after explicit antibody exclusion (TSH 0.68-3.70 mIU/L, the shelf's lowest upper limit; FT4 sex-specific), and the 1,512-person NACB validation study (0.58-4.07 mIU/L in antibody-free adults; TPO antibodies raise TSH, TgAb alone does not). Pregnancy intervals are explicitly NOT this row. Cross-points (IGF-I, DHEA-S shelves) are prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Largest dataset (3,123 healthy adults, Lanzhou; Abbott Architect): locally established TSH and thyroid-hormone intervals differ from the manufacturer's — sex-specific values required (Lu 2023)
cards.summary: Largest dataset (3,123 healthy adults, Lanzhou; Abbott Architect): locally established TSH and thyroid-hormone intervals differ from the manufacturer's — sex-specific values required (Lu 2023)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (thyroid hormone reference intervals, Abbott Architect platform)
cards.people: 3,123 individuals (1,680 men, 1,443 women) perceived as healthy in Lanzhou, an iodine-adequate subplateau city in northwest China; TSH, total T3, total T4, free hormones and thyroid antibodies (ATG, ATPO) measured on the Abbott Architect analyser; 95% reference intervals estimated as the 2.5th-97.5th percentiles.
cards.result: TSH, total T3, ATG antibody and ATPO antibody levels correlated significantly with sex (P < 0.05): TSH, ATG and ATPO were significantly lower in men than women, while total T3 was significantly higher in men. TSH, total T4 and ATPO correlated significantly with age (P < 0.05), and TSH, total T3 and total T4 differed across age groups. The established reference intervals for TSH, ATG and ATPO differed between sexes (P < 0.05), and the locally established intervals were inconsistent with the manufacturer-provided values — the authors conclude validated sex-specific values are required for diagnosing thyroid disease. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval values themselves, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: The biggest cohort on this shelf is also the least numerically auditable from its record: it establishes that manufacturer intervals do not transfer to this population, while the transferable numbers come from the smaller cards below — platform (Abbott Architect) and population (iodine-adequate Lanzhou) are part of the finding.
cards.source: Lu Y et al. Thyroid Hormone Reference Intervals among Healthy Individuals In Lanzhou, China. Endocrinology and metabolism (Seoul, Korea). 2023. PMID: 37312257. cards.headline: Brazilian electrochemiluminescence interval (272 healthy adults, ages 18-50): TSH 0.56-4.45 mIU/L — upper limit matching the manufacturer's 4.20, lower limit double its 0.27; ultrasound screening did not change selection (Gurgel 2020)
cards.summary: Brazilian electrochemiluminescence interval (272 healthy adults, ages 18-50): TSH 0.56-4.45 mIU/L — upper limit matching the manufacturer's 4.20, lower limit double its 0.27; ultrasound screening did not change selection (Gurgel 2020)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (TSH reference interval, electrochemiluminescence assay, ultrasound-selection limb)
cards.people: 272 adults aged 18-50 years with normal thyroid function in Fortaleza, Brazil, cross-sectional; three nested groups — all participants (n = 272), those undergoing thyroid ultrasonography (TUS, n = 170), and the final reference individuals (n = 124). TSH, FT4, total T3, TgAb and TPOAb by electrochemiluminescence assay; the reference interval taken as the 2.5th-97.5th percentiles.
cards.result: Mean TSH was 1.74 (SD 0.96) mIU/L, and the TSH reference interval was 0.56-4.45 mIU/L. TSH concentrations did not differ between men and women, nor between the nested groups — thyroid ultrasonography did not appear essential for selecting the reference group. Against the assay manufacturer's interval, the upper limit was comparable (4.45 vs 4.20 mIU/L) but the lower limit was not (0.56 vs 0.27 mIU/L) — a difference the authors note could misdiagnose euthyroid patients as subclinical hyperthyroidism if the manufacturer's lower limit is used.
cards.watchOut: The final reference group is n = 124 of the 272 recruited — percentile tails from ~124 people are statistically fragile, and the interval is this assay's, in this population.
cards.source: Gurgel MHC et al. Establishment of reference interval for thyroid-stimulating hormone using electrochemiluminescence assay in a healthy adult population from Fortaleza, Brazil. Archives of endocrinology and metabolism. 2020. PMID: 32725064. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Antibody-exclusion interval in Hong Kong Chinese adults (212 sampled): after excluding thyroid-antibody-positive subjects, TSH 0.68-3.70 mIU/L — and including them changed the intervals only minimally (Chan 2011)
cards.summary: Antibody-exclusion interval in Hong Kong Chinese adults (212 sampled): after excluding thyroid-antibody-positive subjects, TSH 0.68-3.70 mIU/L — and including them changed the intervals only minimally (Chan 2011)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (TSH/FT4 reference intervals after antibody exclusion)
cards.people: Apparently healthy, drug-free local adult Chinese recruited by health questionnaire; serum TSH, free T4 (FT4), thyroglobulin antibody and thyroid peroxidase antibody measured in 212 subjects — 51 seropositive for thyroglobulin antibody, 31 for thyroid peroxidase antibody, 27 for both. After excluding seropositive subjects, TSH was log-transformed and reference limits defined as mean ± 1.96 SD; FT4 limits as the 2.5th-97.5th percentiles.
cards.result: The antibody-negative reference intervals were: TSH 0.68-3.70 mIU/L; FT4 13.5-21.3 pmol/L (≈1.05-1.65 ng/dL) in males and 12.6-19.7 pmol/L (≈0.98-1.53 ng/dL) in females. Including the antibody-positive subjects only minimally changed the reference intervals of these hormones — the authors caution that the importance of excluding antibody-positive subjects from the reference population should not be overemphasised, and propose percentile-equivalent action limits rather than one absolute TSH cut-off.
cards.watchOut: The upper TSH limit here (3.70 mIU/L) is the lowest on this shelf — a full 0.75 mIU/L below the Brazilian upper limit — in the very study that applied the antibody-exclusion rule most explicitly; method (mean ± 1.96 SD of log-TSH vs percentiles) also differs between cards.
cards.source: Chan AO et al. The reference interval of thyroid-stimulating hormone in Hong Kong Chinese. Journal of clinical pathology. 2011. PMID: 21422036. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The NACB-guideline validation study (1,512 adults, ages 17-66; AutoDELFIA): in antibody-free adults TSH shows no age or sex effect, and the common interval is 0.58-4.07 mIU/L — higher than NACB guidelines expected (Jensen 2004)
cards.summary: The NACB-guideline validation study (1,512 adults, ages 17-66; AutoDELFIA): in antibody-free adults TSH shows no age or sex effect, and the common interval is 0.58-4.07 mIU/L — higher than NACB guidelines expected (Jensen 2004)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (TSH reference interval, NACB-guideline validation, antibody effects)
cards.people: 1,512 individuals aged 17-66 years; 250 had at least one thyroid antibody, 121 were taking medications other than oestrogens and occasional analgesics, and 105 reported a family history of thyroid disease. Serum TSH, thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOab) and thyroglobulin antibodies (Tgab) by AutoDELFIA; TSH-receptor antibodies by radioreceptor assay (Brahms).
cards.result: For individuals without thyroid antibodies and other risk factors, no effect of age or gender on serum TSH was seen. Medication had no influence, nor did Tgab alone; TPOab alone or combined with Tgab was associated with increased serum TSH. Subgroup and combined distributions were log-Gaussian, with the central 95% within the 95% CI in rankit plots. A common reference interval for serum TSH of 0.58-4.07 mIU/L was established for all adults aged 17-66 — much higher, the authors note, than expected from the NACB guidelines. (The record prints the unit as 'mlU/l'; it is rendered here as mIU/L.)
cards.watchOut: The antibody limb is the finding: TPO antibodies shift TSH upward within the 'healthy' population, which is why antibody-negative selection lowers upper limits on other cards — an interval is partly a decision about who counts as healthy.
cards.source: Jensen E et al. Establishment of a serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) reference interval in healthy adults. The importance of environmental factors, including thyroid antibodies. Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 2004. PMID: 15327019. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: across four populations and three assay families, antibody-aware TSH intervals cluster at a lower limit of 0.56-0.68 mIU/L and an upper limit of 3.70-4.45 mIU/L — the upper limit, which defines subclinical hypothyroidism, is the assay- and selection-dependent number
cards.summary: Synthesis: across four populations and three assay families, antibody-aware TSH intervals cluster at a lower limit of 0.56-0.68 mIU/L and an upper limit of 3.70-4.45 mIU/L — the upper limit, which defines subclinical hypothyroidism, is the assay- and selection-dependent number
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (thyroid hormone chapters) and Ganong (thyroid physiology). The four datasets: the largest (3,123 adults, Abbott Architect, iodine-adequate Lanzhou) establishes sex differences and that manufacturer intervals do not transfer, without printing its numbers in the record (Lu 2023); the Brazilian electrochemiluminescence study gives 0.56-4.45 mIU/L and shows ultrasound screening is not essential to reference selection (Gurgel 2020, reference n = 124); the Hong Kong study, after explicit antibody exclusion, gives the shelf's lowest upper limit, 0.68-3.70 mIU/L, with sex-specific FT4 intervals — yet finds including antibody-positive subjects changes intervals only minimally (Chan 2011); and the 1,512-person NACB validation study gives 0.58-4.07 mIU/L for antibody-free adults aged 17-66, with TPO antibodies (not TgAb alone) raising TSH (Jensen 2004). Pregnancy intervals are a separate limb and are NOT this shelf. Cross-points in prose only: the built IGF-I and DHEA-S reference shelves — the same assay-dependence teaching on different axes. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the interval structure; the upper-limit spread (3.70-4.45) is printed, not averaged away.
cards.watchOut: Name the assay platform and the inclusion rules beside every TSH interval: 'normal TSH' from an antibody-screened Hong Kong cohort and from a manufacturer's package insert are different claims, and the difference sits exactly at the subclinical-hypothyroidism boundary.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Without diabetes, HbA1c centres near 5.0% and skews right with age — a small black–white gradient (~0.2%) survives adjustment for glucose itself
shelves.question: In people without diabetes, what does the HbA1c distribution look like — mean, spread and the fraction above 5.7% and 6.5% — by age, sex and race/ethnicity in population surveys, and how much of the between-group difference survives adjustment for glucose itself?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 79 (insulin, glucagon and glucose regulation). HbA1c is a single-analyte distribution question — the companion to the continuous-glucose profiles shelf — and the population surveys agree on its shape: unimodal and right-skewed, centred near 5.0% in young people, shifting higher and more skewed with age (Menke 2014, NHANES A1C N = 16,209, a whole-population sample that includes people with diabetes — flagged on its card). In people not treated for diabetes, US youth mean HbA1c was 4.99% (SD 0.50), with a small but persistent race/ethnicity gradient that survives adjustment (non-Hispanic black 5.17% vs white 4.93% unadjusted; Saaddine 2002, N = 7,968). Brazilian cohorts without diabetes show the same skin-colour gradient at ages 18 and 30 (Buffarini 2016), and Korean nationwide data give dual-unit means — 5.42% (35.7 mmol/mol) at ages 10–19 and 5.32% (34.7 mmol/mol) at 20–29 (Seo 2018, N = 6,418). This is a measurement shelf only: it carries no diagnostic-threshold recommendations, which live on the diabetes shelves, and anaemia and haemoglobin-variant distortion of HbA1c belongs on the face. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: NHANES 2005–2010 (A1C N = 16,209): the HbA1c distribution is unimodal and right-skewed, shifting higher and more skewed with age, and shifted higher in non-Hispanic black than white adults — a whole-population sample including people with diabetes (Menke 2014)
cards.summary: NHANES 2005–2010 (A1C N = 16,209): the HbA1c distribution is unimodal and right-skewed, shifting higher and more skewed with age, and shifted higher in non-Hispanic black than white adults — a whole-population sample including people with diabetes (Menke 2014)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population distribution of HbA1c and glucose markers, NHANES)
cards.people: Nationally representative US adults in NHANES 2005–2010, including people with and without diabetes: A1C measured in 16,209 participants (fasting glucose N = 7,250; 2-hour glucose N = 5,851); distributions smoothed by kernel density estimation and compared by age, race-ethnicity and sex with cumulative logistic regression.
cards.result: All three marker distributions were generally unimodal and right-skewed. Every distribution was shifted higher and more right-skewed in older age groups (P < .001 for each marker). Compared with non-Hispanic whites, the A1C distribution was shifted higher for non-Hispanic blacks (P < .001), whereas the fasting glucose distribution was shifted higher for Mexican-Americans (P = .01) — that is, the A1C group difference is not simply the glucose group difference. Fasting glucose was shifted higher for men (P < .001) and 2-hour glucose higher for women (P = .01). The authors provide a graphic reference against diabetes cut-points; the fetched record reports distribution shifts and shape, not numeric fractions above 5.7% or 6.5%, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Premise flag, printed deliberately: this sample INCLUDES people with diabetes, so its upper tail is a whole-population tail, not a without-diabetes tail — the without-diabetes anchors are the Saaddine and Buffarini cards. HbA1c is also distorted by anaemia and haemoglobin variants, which no distribution in this shelf adjusts away.
cards.source: Menke A et al. Hemoglobin A1c, fasting plasma glucose, and 2-hour plasma glucose distributions in U.S. population subgroups: NHANES 2005-2010. Annals of epidemiology. 2014. PMID: 24246264. Registry ID: none in the record.
