cards.headline: NHANES III youth not treated for diabetes (N = 7,968, ages 5–24): mean HbA1c 4.99% (SD 0.50) — non-Hispanic black 5.17%, Mexican-American 5.05%, white 4.93%, and the gradient survives adjustment (Saaddine 2002)
cards.summary: NHANES III youth not treated for diabetes (N = 7,968, ages 5–24): mean HbA1c 4.99% (SD 0.50) — non-Hispanic black 5.17%, Mexican-American 5.05%, white 4.93%, and the gradient survives adjustment (Saaddine 2002)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (HbA1c distribution in US children and young adults not treated for diabetes)
cards.people: 7,968 participants aged 5–24 years in the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (1988–1994) who had not been treated for diabetes; distributions compared by age, sex, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, parental diabetes history, overweight and serum glucose, with multiple linear regression.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c was 4.99% (SD 0.50). Unadjusted means were 4.93% in non-Hispanic whites, 5.05% in Mexican-Americans and 5.17% in non-Hispanic blacks — very small absolute differences, present within every age group, in both sexes, and in overweight and non-overweight subjects. After adjustment for confounders, HbA1c remained higher in non-Hispanic blacks (5.15%) and Mexican-Americans (5.01%) than in non-Hispanic whites (4.93%), i.e. the between-group difference is not completely explained by demographic and health-related variables, including glucose. Values are reported in % as the record gives them; the record gives no mmol/mol equivalents.
cards.watchOut: A 1988–1994 survey with the assay of its era: the shape and the group gradient are the durable findings; absolute means should not be transplanted onto a modern assay without that caveat. 'Not treated for diabetes' is the record's own population definition — undiagnosed diabetes is not excluded by it.
cards.source: Saaddine JB et al. Distribution of HbA(1c) levels for children and young adults in the U.S.: Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Diabetes care. 2002. PMID: 12145229. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pelotas birth cohorts without diabetes: mean HbA1c 5.10% (SD 0.43) at age 30 and 4.89% (SD 0.50) at age 18 — higher in black/brown than white skin colour in both cohorts (Buffarini 2016)
cards.summary: Pelotas birth cohorts without diabetes: mean HbA1c 5.10% (SD 0.43) at age 30 and 4.89% (SD 0.50) at age 18 — higher in black/brown than white skin colour in both cohorts (Buffarini 2016)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (HbA1c distribution in adolescents and adults without diabetes, Brazil)
cards.people: Adults aged 30 years (1982 cohort) and adolescents aged 18 years (1993 cohort) in the Pelotas, Brazil birth cohorts, without diabetes mellitus; HbA1c described against early-life and contemporary characteristics collected prospectively since birth.
cards.result: The HbA1c distribution was approximately normal in both cohorts, with mean (SD) 5.10% (0.43) in the 1982 cohort and 4.89% (0.50) in the 1993 cohort. Mean levels were significantly higher in individuals self-reporting black/brown skin colour than in those self-reporting white, in both cohorts — the same direction as the US surveys. Parental history of diabetes was associated with higher mean HbA1c in adults; stunting at 1 year was inversely related in adolescents; no other early-life or contemporary factor was associated in either cohort. The authors call for work on genomic ancestry as a possible basis for the skin-colour gradient. Values in % as the record gives them.
cards.watchOut: Two single-age cohort slices (18 and 30 years), not an age span: the 0.21% gap between cohorts mixes age with cohort and assay timing, and should be read as two anchored means, not an ageing rate.
cards.source: Buffarini R et al. Distribution of Glycated Haemoglobin According to Early-Life and Contemporary Characteristics in Adolescents and Adults without Diabetes: The 1982 and 1993 Pelotas Birth Cohorts. PloS one. 2016. PMID: 27626274. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Korean nationwide youth and young adults (N = 6,418, ages 10–29): HbA1c 5.42% (35.7 mmol/mol) at 10–19 years and 5.32% (34.7 mmol/mol) at 20–29, higher in males, peaking at 10–14 years (Seo 2018)
cards.summary: Korean nationwide youth and young adults (N = 6,418, ages 10–29): HbA1c 5.42% (35.7 mmol/mol) at 10–19 years and 5.32% (34.7 mmol/mol) at 20–29, higher in males, peaking at 10–14 years (Seo 2018)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (nationwide HbA1c distribution in Korean youth and young adults)
cards.people: 6,418 participants aged 10–29 years (3,140 male) from the Korea Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011–2015; HbA1c percentiles calculated and values compared by age, sex and associated factors. The record describes a nationwide population sample; a diabetes exclusion is not stated in the fetched record and is not assumed here.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c was 5.42 ± 0.01% (35.7 ± 0.1 mmol/mol) in youths (10–19 years) and 5.32 ± 0.01% (34.7 ± 0.1 mmol/mol) in young adults (20–29 years) (P < 0.001) — the record's own dual-unit reporting. Males had significantly higher HbA1c than females (P < 0.001). In 5-year age bands HbA1c was highest at 10–14 years and lowest at 20–24 years, and after adjustment youth and male values remained significantly higher. This is the shelf's youngest-age anchor and its only record reporting % and mmol/mol side by side.
cards.watchOut: Population sample without a stated diabetes exclusion in the record, and a pubertal-age peak (10–14 years) that should not be read as a without-diabetes reference interval for adults — it anchors the young end of the distribution only.
cards.source: Seo JY et al. Distribution of glycated haemoglobin and its determinants in Korean youth and young adults: a nationwide population-based study. Scientific reports. 2018. PMID: 29386645. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: without diabetes, HbA1c centres near 5.0% with a right skew that grows with age — and a small black–white gradient (~0.2%) that adjustment for glucose and demographics does not erase
cards.summary: Synthesis: without diabetes, HbA1c centres near 5.0% with a right skew that grows with age — and a small black–white gradient (~0.2%) that adjustment for glucose and demographics does not erase
cards.people: Synthesis of the four population datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall, ch. 79. Across four population programmes the picture is consistent: the distribution is unimodal and right-skewed, shifting higher and more skewed with age (Menke 2014); means without diabetes sit near 4.99% (SD 0.50) in US youth not treated for diabetes (Saaddine 2002), 4.89% at 18 and 5.10% at 30 in Brazil (Buffarini 2016), and 5.32–5.42% (34.7–35.7 mmol/mol) in Korean 10–29-year-olds (Seo 2018). The race/ethnicity gradient is small in absolute terms (~0.2% black vs white in the US data) but appears on three continents and survives adjustment, including for glucose itself in the NHANES III analysis — so a single population mean conceals a real, unexplained group shift. What the fetched records do NOT give is a verified numeric fraction above 5.7% or 6.5% in people without diabetes: Menke plots the distributions against the cut-points graphically, and no card here invents those fractions. Anaemia and haemoglobin variants distort HbA1c independently of glucose and belong on the face of any use of these distributions. This shelf makes no diagnostic-threshold recommendation; thresholds live on the diabetes shelves. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert the older surveys' % means into mmol/mol by formula and present them as reported values: only the Korean record reports both units, and the cards keep each record in its own units.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Lorcaserin for obesity — WITHDRAWN 2020 over a cancer imbalance in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61: it did produce weight loss (BLOOM/BLOSSOM) and passed cardiovascular non-inferiority, with no cardiovascular benefit
shelves.question: In adults with overweight or obesity (with or without type 2 diabetes), does the serotonin 2C agonist lorcaserin, compared with placebo plus lifestyle intervention, produce weight loss — and what was its cardiovascular-safety profile (BLOOM / BLOSSOM / CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Obesity Agents · Behavior Therapy · Benzazepines · Blood Pressure · Cardiovascular Diseases · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Valve Diseases · Humans · Insulin · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity · Overweight · Risk Factors · Serotonin 5-HT2 Receptor Agonists · Serotonin Receptor Agonists · Waist Circumference · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on weight loss — for a WITHDRAWN product. Lorcaserin (Belviq) was withdrawn from the US market in 2020 after CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 showed a numerical excess of cancers; that history leads this shelf, the cancer data are presented as the trial programme reported them (an imbalance in a safety trial not powered for cancer), and the drug cannot be prescribed. On efficacy the record is consistent: BLOOM and BLOSSOM showed about 47% versus 20–25% of patients losing at least 5% of body weight at 1 year (absolute differences about 22–27 percentage points), with mean losses around 5.8 kg / 5.8% versus 2.2 kg / 2.8% on placebo plus lifestyle intervention. CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 (12,000 high-risk patients) met cardiovascular non-inferiority (major cardiovascular events 2.0% versus 2.1% per year; hazard ratio 0.99) but no cardiovascular superiority (hazard ratio 0.97) — cardiovascular outcomes were a safety question, not an efficacy benefit, and relative measures above are labelled relative with the absolute rates beside them.

cards.headline: BLOOM RCT (Smith 2010): lorcaserin produced weight loss of 5.8 kg versus 2.2 kg on placebo at 1 year; 47.5% versus 20.3% lost at least 5% of body weight
cards.summary: BLOOM RCT (Smith 2010): lorcaserin produced weight loss of 5.8 kg versus 2.2 kg on placebo at 1 year; 47.5% versus 20.3% lost at least 5% of body weight
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (BLOOM), lorcaserin vs placebo plus lifestyle counselling
cards.people: 3182 obese or overweight adults (mean body-mass index 36.2) randomised to lorcaserin 10 mg or placebo twice daily for 52 weeks, all with diet and exercise counselling; at week 52 the placebo group continued placebo and the lorcaserin group was re-randomised to lorcaserin or placebo for year 2 (1553 patients continued).
cards.result: At 1 year, 47.5% of the lorcaserin group and 20.3% of the placebo group had lost 5% or more of body weight (P<0.001) — an absolute difference of 27.2 percentage points — corresponding to average losses of 5.8 ± 0.2 kg versus 2.2 ± 0.1 kg (P<0.001). Among year-1 lorcaserin patients who had lost at least 5%, the loss was maintained at year 2 in 67.9% of those who continued lorcaserin versus 50.3% of those switched to placebo (P<0.001). Cardiac valvulopathy rates (2472 evaluated at 1 year, 1127 at 2 years) were not increased. Headache, dizziness and nausea were the commonest adverse events; serious adverse-event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: Attrition was high — only 55.4% (lorcaserin) and 45.1% (placebo) remained at week 52 — so the 1-year weight figures rest on a completer-leaning analysis; and the drug was later withdrawn over a cancer imbalance in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 (see balance and the CAMELLIA card).
cards.source: Smith SR et al. Multicenter, placebo-controlled trial of lorcaserin for weight management. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20647200. Registry ID: NCT00395135. cards.headline: BLOSSOM RCT (Fidler 2011): lorcaserin 10 mg twice daily produced least-squares mean weight loss of 5.8% versus 2.8% on placebo at 1 year; 47.2% versus 25.0% lost at least 5%
cards.summary: BLOSSOM RCT (Fidler 2011): lorcaserin 10 mg twice daily produced least-squares mean weight loss of 5.8% versus 2.8% on placebo at 1 year; 47.2% versus 25.0% lost at least 5%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (BLOSSOM), lorcaserin twice daily / once daily vs placebo plus lifestyle programme
cards.people: 4008 patients aged 18–65 (body-mass index 30–45, or 27–29.9 with an obesity-related comorbidity) at 97 US centres, randomised 2:1:2 to lorcaserin 10 mg twice daily, lorcaserin 10 mg once daily, or placebo for 1 year, all with diet and exercise counselling; serial echocardiograms monitored heart valves.
cards.result: At least 5% weight loss was achieved by 47.2% (twice daily) and 40.2% (once daily) versus 25.0% on placebo (P<0.001 versus twice daily) — an absolute difference of 22.2 percentage points for the twice-daily dose. Least-squares mean weight loss was 5.8% (95% CI 5.5% to 6.2%) twice daily, 4.7% once daily and 2.8% on placebo (least-squares mean difference 3.0% for twice daily). At least 10% loss: 22.6% and 17.4% versus 9.7%. FDA-defined echocardiographic valvulopathy occurred in 2.0% on placebo and 2.0% on lorcaserin 10 mg twice daily. Headache, nausea and dizziness were the commonest lorcaserin-related events.
cards.watchOut: A weight-loss efficacy trial: its cardiovascular measures are risk-factor changes, not outcomes, and echocardiographic valvulopathy surveillance over 1 year cannot exclude longer-term valve or other harms — the withdrawal history (cancer imbalance in the later safety trial) leads this shelf's balance.
cards.source: Fidler MC et al. A one-year randomized trial of lorcaserin for weight loss in obese and overweight adults: the BLOSSOM trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2011. PMID: 21795446. Registry ID: NCT00603902. cards.headline: CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 RCT (Bohula 2018): lorcaserin was non-inferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events (2.0% versus 2.1% per year; hazard ratio 0.99) but not superior on the extended cardiovascular outcome (hazard ratio 0.97)
cards.summary: CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 RCT (Bohula 2018): lorcaserin was non-inferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events (2.0% versus 2.1% per year; hazard ratio 0.99) but not superior on the extended cardiovascular outcome (hazard ratio 0.97)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind cardiovascular-safety (non-inferiority) trial (CAMELLIA-TIMI 61), lorcaserin vs placebo
cards.people: 12,000 overweight or obese patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors randomised to lorcaserin 10 mg twice daily or placebo, followed for a median 3.3 years; the primary safety outcome (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) was tested against a non-inferiority boundary of 1.4, then the extended cardiovascular efficacy outcome for superiority.
cards.result: At 1 year, at least 5% weight loss had occurred in 1986 of 5135 patients (38.7%) on lorcaserin versus 883 of 5083 (17.4%) on placebo (odds ratio 3.01, 95% CI 2.74 to 3.30; P<0.001) — an absolute difference of 21.3 percentage points. The primary safety outcome rate was 2.0% per year on lorcaserin versus 2.1% per year on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.14; P<0.001 for non-inferiority); the extended major cardiovascular outcome was 4.1% versus 4.2% per year (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.07; P=0.55) — no cardiovascular benefit. Serious hypoglycaemia was more frequent with lorcaserin (13 versus 4 patients, P=0.04). This was a safety (non-inferiority) trial, not powered for cancer: the numerical cancer excess that later prompted withdrawal is not quantified in this report's abstract and is stated on this shelf's face from the withdrawal history, neither minimised nor overstated.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority for cardiovascular events is not evidence of cardiovascular benefit (the superiority test was negative), and the trial was not designed or powered to assess cancer — do not read its cardiovascular reassurance as an all-clear on the harm that led to withdrawal.
cards.source: Bohula EA et al. Cardiovascular Safety of Lorcaserin in Overweight or Obese Patients. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 30145941. Registry ID: NCT02019264. cards.headline: Synthesis: lorcaserin produced modest, consistent weight loss and passed its cardiovascular-safety test — and was withdrawn in 2020 after a numerical excess of cancers in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61
cards.summary: Synthesis: lorcaserin produced modest, consistent weight loss and passed its cardiovascular-safety test — and was withdrawn in 2020 after a numerical excess of cancers in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: WITHDRAWN PRODUCT: lorcaserin (Belviq) was withdrawn from the US market in 2020 after CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 showed a numerical excess of cancers — that history leads this shelf; the drug cannot be prescribed. On efficacy, two 1-year placebo-controlled trials (BLOOM, 3182 patients; BLOSSOM, 4008 patients) consistently showed modest weight loss: about 47% versus 20–25% achieving at least 5% loss (absolute differences of about 22–27 percentage points), mean losses of about 5.8 kg / 5.8% versus 2.2 kg / 2.8%. On cardiovascular safety, CAMELLIA-TIMI 61 (12,000 high-risk patients) met non-inferiority for major cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.99) but showed no cardiovascular benefit (extended outcome hazard ratio 0.97). Weight loss was the efficacy outcome throughout; the cardiovascular trial was a safety question, not an efficacy benefit, and it was not powered for the cancer outcome on which withdrawal turned.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.question: In adults with overweight or obesity (including patients with dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, or metabolic risk factors), does the cannabinoid-1 receptor blocker rimonabant, compared with placebo plus diet, reduce weight and improve cardiometabolic risk factors (RIO programme)?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on weight and surrogate risk factors — for a WITHDRAWN product. Rimonabant (Acomplia) was suspended/withdrawn in 2008 over psychiatric harm (depression and suicidality) and was never FDA-approved; that history leads this shelf and the drug cannot be prescribed. On efficacy, the four RIO trials (Europe, Lipids, North America, Diabetes) consistently showed rimonabant 20 mg plus diet producing 1-year weight loss of about −5.3 to −6.7 kg versus −1.4 to −1.8 kg on placebo, with better waist, HDL-cholesterol and triglyceride changes — all surrogate cardiometabolic endpoints, with relative percentage changes labelled relative and printed beside absolute weight/waist changes on the cards. There is no outcomes evidence: the cardiovascular-outcomes trial (CRESCENDO) was terminated early and is fenced off from any efficacy claim.

cards.headline: RIO-Europe RCT (Van Gaal 2005): rimonabant 20 mg produced 1-year weight loss of −6.6 kg versus −1.8 kg on placebo, with greater improvements in waist, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and insulin resistance
cards.summary: RIO-Europe RCT (Van Gaal 2005): rimonabant 20 mg produced 1-year weight loss of −6.6 kg versus −1.8 kg on placebo, with greater improvements in waist, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and insulin resistance
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (RIO-Europe), rimonabant 5 mg / 20 mg vs placebo plus hypocaloric diet
cards.people: Overweight or obese patients (body-mass index ≥30, or >27 with treated or untreated dyslipidaemia, hypertension, or both) randomised double-blind to placebo, rimonabant 5 mg or rimonabant 20 mg once daily for 1 year, all on a mild hypocaloric diet (600 kcal/day deficit); the total randomised number is not stated in the fetched abstract.
cards.result: Weight loss at 1 year was −3.4 kg (SD 5.7) on rimonabant 5 mg (P=0.002 versus placebo), −6.6 kg (SD 7.2) on 20 mg (P<0.001) and −1.8 kg (SD 6.4) on placebo — an absolute difference of 4.8 kg for the 20 mg dose. Significantly more patients on rimonabant 20 mg achieved weight loss of 5% or more and of 10% or more (both P<0.001), and 20 mg produced significantly greater improvements than placebo in waist circumference, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, insulin resistance and metabolic-syndrome prevalence; the 5 mg effects were of less clinical significance. Side effects were described as generally mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: A 1-year surrogate-endpoint trial (weight and risk factors, not cardiovascular events) from a programme whose drug was later withdrawn over psychiatric harm — the mild-and-transient tolerability description here must be read against that withdrawal history, which leads this shelf.
cards.source: Van Gaal LF et al. Effects of the cannabinoid-1 receptor blocker rimonabant on weight reduction and cardiovascular risk factors in overweight patients: 1-year experience from the RIO-Europe study. Lancet (London, England). 2005. PMID: 15836887. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: RIO-Lipids RCT (Després 2005): rimonabant 20 mg produced weight loss of −6.7 kg (repeated-measures) versus placebo, HDL cholesterol +10.0% and triglycerides −13.0% in patients with untreated dyslipidaemia; triglycerides at entry were >1.69 mmol/L (approx. 150 mg/dL)
cards.summary: RIO-Lipids RCT (Després 2005): rimonabant 20 mg produced weight loss of −6.7 kg (repeated-measures) versus placebo, HDL cholesterol +10.0% and triglycerides −13.0% in patients with untreated dyslipidaemia; triglycerides at entry were >1.69 mmol/L (approx. 150 mg/dL)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (RIO-Lipids), rimonabant 5 mg / 20 mg vs placebo plus hypocaloric diet, in dyslipidaemia
cards.people: 1036 overweight or obese patients (body-mass index 27–40) with untreated dyslipidaemia (triglycerides >1.69 to 7.90 mmol/L (approx. 150 to 700 mg/dL), or a cholesterol-to-HDL ratio >4.5 in women and >5 in men) randomised double-blind to placebo, rimonabant 5 mg or rimonabant 20 mg daily for 12 months plus a hypocaloric diet; completion rates were 62.6% (placebo), 60.3% (5 mg) and 63.9% (20 mg).
cards.result: Versus placebo, rimonabant 20 mg gave mean weight loss of −6.7 ± 0.5 kg by repeated measures (−5.4 ± 0.4 kg by last-observation-carried-forward), waist reduction of −5.8 ± 0.5 cm (−4.7 ± 0.5 cm LOCF), an HDL-cholesterol increase of +10.0 ± 1.6% (+8.1 ± 1.5% LOCF) and a triglyceride reduction of −13.0 ± 3.5% (−12.4 ± 3.2% LOCF) (all P<0.001); these percentage changes are relative changes in surrogate measures, printed beside the absolute weight and waist changes. Plasma adiponectin rose 57.7% (relative change). The most frequent adverse events causing discontinuation were depression, anxiety and nausea.
cards.watchOut: About 37% of patients did not complete the study, so estimates lean on imputation (both analyses are shown). Depression and anxiety already appear here as leading causes of discontinuation — the psychiatric harm that later ended the programme.
cards.source: Després JP et al. Effects of rimonabant on metabolic risk factors in overweight patients with dyslipidemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 16291982. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: RIO-North America RCT (Pi-Sunyer 2006): rimonabant 20 mg produced 1-year weight change of −6.3 kg versus −1.6 kg on placebo in 3045 patients; patients switched to placebo in year 2 regained weight
cards.summary: RIO-North America RCT (Pi-Sunyer 2006): rimonabant 20 mg produced 1-year weight change of −6.3 kg versus −1.6 kg on placebo in 3045 patients; patients switched to placebo in year 2 regained weight
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 2-year trial (RIO-North America), rimonabant 5 mg / 20 mg vs placebo plus diet
cards.people: 3045 obese (body-mass index ≥30) or overweight (≥27 with hypertension or dyslipidaemia) adults at 64 US and 8 Canadian centres, randomised after a 4-week placebo-plus-diet run-in to placebo, rimonabant 5 mg/day or rimonabant 20 mg/day for 1 year; rimonabant patients were then re-randomised to continue the same dose or switch to placebo for year 2. Year-1 completion was about 51–55% per group.
cards.result: At year 1, rimonabant 20 mg versus placebo gave greater mean reductions in weight (−6.3 [SEM 0.2] kg versus −1.6 [0.2] kg; P<0.001 — an absolute difference of 4.7 kg) and waist circumference (−6.1 versus −2.5 cm; P<0.001), a triglyceride percentage change of −5.3% versus +7.9% (P<0.001) and an HDL-cholesterol percentage change of +12.6% versus +5.4% (P<0.001) — the lipid figures are relative percentage changes, printed beside the absolute weight and waist changes. Patients switched from rimonabant 20 mg to placebo in year 2 regained weight; those who continued maintained the loss and the risk-factor changes. The commonest drug-related adverse event was nausea (11.2% on 20 mg versus 5.8% on placebo).
cards.watchOut: Very high dropout (roughly half of each group by year 1) limits certainty, and the year-2 design shows the effect depends on continuing a drug that was later withdrawn — there is no usable long-term strategy here.
cards.source: Pi-Sunyer FX et al. Effect of rimonabant, a cannabinoid-1 receptor blocker, on weight and cardiometabolic risk factors in overweight or obese patients: RIO-North America: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2006. PMID: 16478899. Registry ID: NCT00029861. cards.headline: RIO-Diabetes RCT (Scheen 2006): rimonabant 20 mg produced 1-year weight loss of −5.3 kg versus −1.4 kg on placebo in 1047 patients with type 2 diabetes, and improved HbA1c and cardiometabolic risk factors
cards.summary: RIO-Diabetes RCT (Scheen 2006): rimonabant 20 mg produced 1-year weight loss of −5.3 kg versus −1.4 kg on placebo in 1047 patients with type 2 diabetes, and improved HbA1c and cardiometabolic risk factors
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (RIO-Diabetes), rimonabant 5 mg / 20 mg vs placebo plus diet, in type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 1047 overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes (body-mass index 27–40; HbA1c 6.5–10.0%, mean 7.3%) inadequately controlled on metformin or sulfonylurea monotherapy, randomised to placebo (348), rimonabant 5 mg/day (360) or rimonabant 20 mg/day (339) for 1 year, all with a mild hypocaloric diet and activity advice; 692 completed 1 year.
cards.result: Weight loss at 1 year was −1.4 kg (SD 3.6) on placebo, −2.3 kg (SD 4.2) on rimonabant 5 mg (P=0.01 versus placebo) and −5.3 kg (SD 5.2) on 20 mg (P<0.0001) — an absolute difference of 3.9 kg for the 20 mg dose. The report states rimonabant 20 mg also improved HbA1c and a number of cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors (the fetched abstract does not give the HbA1c figure, so none is printed here). Discontinuation-causing adverse events were slightly more frequent on rimonabant 20 mg, mainly depressed mood disorders, nausea and dizziness.
cards.watchOut: Depressed mood disorders were among the leading causes of discontinuation even in this 1-year trial — the psychiatric signal that ended the programme is visible inside the efficacy record, not separate from it.
cards.source: Scheen AJ et al. Efficacy and tolerability of rimonabant in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomised controlled study. Lancet (London, England). 2006. PMID: 17098084. Registry ID: NCT00029848. shelves.title: Prolactin reference intervals are per-platform: Elecsys monomeric 3.4–18.5 ng/mL (women) / 2.7–13.1 (men), VITROS total 94–500 mIU/L in women, and macroprolactin explained 22.9% of raised totals
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for total and for monomeric (post-PEG-precipitation) prolactin — by sex and assay platform — and in what fraction of apparently raised prolactin results is macroprolactin the explanation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Case-Control Studies · Chemical Precipitation · Confidence Intervals · Diagnosis, Differential · Female · Humans · Hyperprolactinemia/diagnosis · Immunoassay/methods,standards · Male · Middle Aged · Polyethylene Glycols/chemistry · Prolactin/blood,immunology,isolation & purification,standards · Prolactinoma/diagnosis · Reagent Kits, Diagnostic · Reference Values · Young Adult · Aged, 80 and over · China/epidemiology · Cross-Sectional Studies · Diagnostic Techniques, Endocrine/standards · Hyperprolactinemia/blood,diagnosis,epidemiology · Prolactin/analysis,blood · Child · Prolactin · Biological Assay · Healthy Volunteers
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, pituitary hormone chapters, and Ganong, endocrine physiology — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Three platform-bound datasets: a six-platform study (healthy donors: 96 women, 127 men) that derived parametric total and monomeric (post-PEG) sex-specific intervals for six immunoassays and validated them against gel filtration chromatography — its fetched record does not print the numeric intervals, and this shelf claims none from it, but it establishes that PEG-precipitation macroprolactin screening is required on current automated assays and that misclassification counts differ by platform (Cobas fewest, Architect/Kryptor most among the macroprolactinaemic sera tested); a Chinese Elecsys study that DOES print monomeric intervals (women 3.4–18.5 ng/mL; men 2.7–13.1 ng/mL, from 120 healthy donors of each sex) and found macroprolactinaemia in 261 of 1,140 (22.9%) patients with raised total prolactin; and a Russian VITROS ECi 3600 study (879 healthy subjects) printing total prolactin intervals of 66–436 mIU/L in men and 94–500 mIU/L in women, systematically above the manufacturer's expected values. The fraction of raised results due to macroprolactin is therefore assay- and population-dependent — about a quarter in the one large screened series carded. Pregnancy intervals are NOT this row. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the intervals are platform-specific by the evidence's own showing, and only one carded dataset prints monomeric numeric limits. Hyperprolactinaemia treatment is homed at live shelves #2070/#2071, cross-pointed, not re-carded.

cards.headline: Six-platform study (Overgaard 2017): parametric total and monomeric sex-specific prolactin intervals derived for six immunoassays (96 healthy women, 127 healthy men) — PEG macroprolactin screening required; misclassification differed by platform (Cobas fewest, Architect/Kryptor most)
cards.summary: Six-platform study (Overgaard 2017): parametric total and monomeric sex-specific prolactin intervals derived for six immunoassays (96 healthy women, 127 healthy men) — PEG macroprolactin screening required; misclassification differed by platform (Cobas fewest, Architect/Kryptor most)
cards.type: Primary human physiology / methods study (total and monomeric prolactin reference intervals across six platforms)
cards.people: Healthy donor sera (female n=96, male n=127) used to determine parametric total and monomeric (post-polyethylene-glycol-precipitation) gender-specific reference intervals for six automated immunoassay methods; validation sera from 27 hyperprolactinaemic and macroprolactinaemic patients whose monomeric and macro forms were characterised by gel filtration chromatography.
cards.result: The study derived 2.5th–97.5th percentile total and monomeric intervals for all six platforms; the fetched record does not print the numeric intervals, and this card claims none. On validation, the monomeric reference-interval method showed more discordant classifications (mean 2.8, 95% CI 1.2 to 4.4) than the post-PEG recovery cut-off method (mean 1.8, 95% CI 0.8 to 2.8), a non-significant difference (p=0.089). Among macroprolactinaemic sera, the Cobas assay showed the lowest and the Architect/Kryptor assays the highest number of misclassifications. The authors concluded current automated prolactin assays require PEG-precipitation macroprolactin screening to separate true from false elevation.
cards.watchOut: The intervals exist per platform in the full report but are not printed in the fetched record: do not quote a numeric prolactin range from this card — the numeric cards are the Elecsys and VITROS cards below, each bound to its platform.
cards.source: Overgaard M et al. Serum prolactin revisited: parametric reference intervals and cross platform evaluation of polyethylene glycol precipitation-based methods for discrimination between hyperprolactinemia and macroprolactinemia. Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine. 2017. PMID: 28236625. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Elecsys monomeric intervals (Hu 2021): post-PEG monomeric prolactin 3.4–18.5 ng/mL in women and 2.7–13.1 ng/mL in men (120 healthy donors each); macroprolactinaemia explained 261 of 1,140 (22.9%) raised total prolactin results in Chinese patients
cards.summary: Elecsys monomeric intervals (Hu 2021): post-PEG monomeric prolactin 3.4–18.5 ng/mL in women and 2.7–13.1 ng/mL in men (120 healthy donors each); macroprolactinaemia explained 261 of 1,140 (22.9%) raised total prolactin results in Chinese patients
cards.type: Primary human physiology / methods study (monomeric prolactin reference intervals, Elecsys platform; macroprolactinaemia frequency in raised results)
cards.people: Post-PEG monomeric prolactin reference intervals for the Elecsys immunoassay (Roche Diagnostics) established from healthy female (n=120) and male (n=120) donors and validated against 20 gel-filtration-confirmed macroprolactinaemic sera; then 1,140 Chinese patients with high total prolactin were screened by PEG precipitation.
cards.result: Monomeric reference intervals were 3.4–18.5 ng/mL in females and 2.7–13.1 ng/mL in males. Among the 1,140 hyperprolactinaemic patients, macroprolactinaemia accounted for 261 (22.9%) and true hyperprolactinaemia for 879 (77.1%). Menstrual disturbance was the commonest feature in both groups; galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and visual disturbance were significantly more frequent in true hyperprolactinaemia (P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: The 22.9% macroprolactin fraction is a property of this assay, this PEG protocol and this referred patient population — it is not a universal constant, and the intervals apply to post-PEG monomeric prolactin on Elecsys, not to total prolactin on any platform.
cards.source: Hu Y et al. Establishment of reference intervals of monomeric prolactin to identify macroprolactinemia in Chinese patients with increased total prolactin. BMC endocrine disorders. 2021. cards.headline: VITROS total prolactin intervals (Kolesnikova 2023): 879 healthy subjects — adult men 66–436 mIU/L and women 94–500 mIU/L on the VITROS ECi 3600, systematically higher at both limits than the manufacturer's expected values
cards.summary: VITROS total prolactin intervals (Kolesnikova 2023): 879 healthy subjects — adult men 66–436 mIU/L and women 94–500 mIU/L on the VITROS ECi 3600, systematically higher at both limits than the manufacturer's expected values
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (total prolactin reference intervals by age group, VITROS ECi 3600 platform)
cards.people: Monocentric study of 879 serum samples from apparently healthy subjects (women, men and children of different age groups) at a Russian endocrinology centre; prolactin measured on the VITROS ECi 3600 automatic chemiluminescence analyser (Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics); locally derived reference values compared with the manufacturer's expected levels for the same system. Adult values are carded here; the child values in the same report are outside this row's adult question.
cards.result: For adult men the reference interval was 66–436 mIU/L and for adult women 94–500 mIU/L. Against the manufacturer's expected values for the VITROS ECi 3600, both sexes showed a systematic shift upward in the lower and upper limits — the paper's point is that method-specific, population-specific intervals are needed because manufacturer ranges and clinical pictures diverge. The authors also note prolactin's within-person variability and its transient rises with stress and exertion as interpretation hazards.
cards.watchOut: Units and analyte differ from the Elecsys card: these are TOTAL prolactin in mIU/L on VITROS (including any macroprolactin present), not post-PEG monomeric values in ng/mL — the two cards must never be converted into one another or averaged.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prolactin has no platform-free reference interval — monomeric (post-PEG) limits on Elecsys are 3.4–18.5 ng/mL (women) and 2.7–13.1 ng/mL (men), total limits on VITROS run 94–500 mIU/L in women, and about a quarter of raised totals in the large screened series were macroprolactin, not true elevation
cards.summary: Synthesis: prolactin has no platform-free reference interval — monomeric (post-PEG) limits on Elecsys are 3.4–18.5 ng/mL (women) and 2.7–13.1 ng/mL (men), total limits on VITROS run 94–500 mIU/L in women, and about a quarter of raised totals in the large screened series were macroprolactin, not true elevation
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above (six-platform donor study, 223 healthy donors plus 27 validation sera; Elecsys study, 240 healthy donors and 1,140 patients screened; VITROS study, 879 healthy subjects).
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (pituitary hormones) and Ganong (endocrine physiology) — framing brief; the primary interval literature carries the shelf. The three datasets converge on method, not numbers: every interval is bound to its platform and to whether macroprolactin has been precipitated out; PEG screening is required to interpret a raised total (Overgaard 2017); where numbers are printed they are platform-labelled (Elecsys monomeric, Hu 2021; VITROS total, Kolesnikova 2023); and macroprolactinaemia explained 22.9% of raised totals in the one large screened series. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: cross-platform disagreement is the evidence's own central finding, and only one carded dataset prints monomeric numeric limits, so no single interval can yet be stated as settled physiology.
cards.watchOut: A raised total prolactin is a screening result, not a diagnosis: without PEG precipitation (or an equivalent macroprolactin screen) roughly a quarter of such results in the carded series need no treatment pathway at all — treatment questions live at live shelves #2070/#2071.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Steroid panel by LC-MS/MS: intervals are sex-, age- and time-of-day-banded (2,458 healthy subjects); immunoassays agreed with mass spectrometry only patchily — cortisol on Elecsys E170 the exception
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are the reference intervals for serum cortisol and the wider steroid panel when measured by LC-MS/MS — by sex, age and time of day — and how do mass-spectrometry intervals differ from the immunoassay intervals laboratories have historically printed?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Age Factors · Cross-Sectional Studies · Healthy Volunteers · Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry/methods · Reference Values · Sex Factors · Steroids/blood,metabolism · Tandem Mass Spectrometry/standards · Androstenedione/blood · Chromatography, Liquid/methods,standards · Hydrocortisone/blood · Immunoassay/methods · Indicator Dilution Techniques · Mass Spectrometry/methods,standards · Progesterone/blood · Sensitivity and Specificity · Steroids/blood · Testosterone/blood
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, adrenocortical hormone chapters, and Ganong, adrenal physiology. Cross-points: pack #6498 (cortisol pulsatility / circadian pattern — a secretion-pattern question) and pack #7084 (cortisol awakening response — a dynamic-response question); neither gives laboratory reference intervals for a timed serum sample, which is this shelf's slice, and neither is re-carded. Three mass-spectrometry datasets: a lifespan LC-MS/MS panel study (2,458 healthy subjects aged 0–77 years, 16 steroid metabolites, cortisol and cortisone quantifiable in at least 90% of samples, with sex- and age-specific intervals modelled across minipuberty, puberty, adulthood and the menopausal transition); an isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS adult study (416 healthy adults) that established adult intervals and showed only the Elecsys E170 cortisol immunoassay agreed with mass spectrometry among the four immunoassays compared, with the other comparisons (testosterone in females, low progesterone, androstenedione, DHEA, 17-hydroxyprogesterone) in poor agreement; and a diurnal study (120 healthy women, 62 healthy men, paired AM/PM samples) showing cortisone, cortisol, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and DHEA all differ significantly by time of day in both sexes. Sampling time is therefore part of the interval — a morning and an afternoon cortisol are different measurements, carded per time band — and immunoassay cross-reactivity is the reason this row exists. The fetched records establish and model the intervals but do not print the numeric cortisol limits in their abstracts, so this shelf prints no invented µg/dL or nmol/L limits (the US-units pairing — µg/dL with nmol/L, ×27.59 — is stated for when local MS intervals are read). Pregnancy and oral-contraceptive limbs are separate limbs, not this row. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the method conclusion (mass spectrometry over immunoassay; time-banded intervals) is consistent across all three datasets, but the numeric limits themselves are not yet in the fetched record to state as settled.

cards.headline: Lifespan LC-MS/MS panel (Frederiksen 2024): 16 steroid metabolites quantified simultaneously in 2,458 healthy subjects aged 0–77 years — sex- and age-specific reference intervals established for cortisol and 11 other steroids quantifiable in ≥90% of samples
cards.summary: Lifespan LC-MS/MS panel (Frederiksen 2024): 16 steroid metabolites quantified simultaneously in 2,458 healthy subjects aged 0–77 years — sex- and age-specific reference intervals established for cortisol and 11 other steroids quantifiable in ≥90% of samples
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (LC-MS/MS steroid panel reference intervals, healthy subjects across the lifespan)
cards.people: Cross-sectional cohorts of healthy infants, children, adolescents and adults aged 0.17 months to 77 years (n=2,458); serum analysed by a newly developed isotope-diluted LC-MS/MS method quantifying 16 steroid metabolites simultaneously; sex- and age-specific reference intervals modelled across the lifespan. Adult intervals are this shelf's focus; the paediatric bands in the same report are outside the row's core.
cards.result: Progesterone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, androstenedione, testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, 11-deoxycorticosterone, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, cortisol and cortisone were quantifiable in at least 90% of samples; estrone sulfate, aldosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone in 77%, 75% and 60%; 21-deoxycortisol was detectable in only 2.5% of healthy samples. Sex- and age-dependent fluctuations were observed in minipuberty, puberty and adulthood including the menopausal transition, enabling valid reference intervals from birth to late adult life for both sexes. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval limits, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: An interval set spanning 0–77 years must be read in its age band: the adult cortisol band cannot be extracted from the lifespan headline, and 21-deoxycortisol's 2.5% detectability in health is itself the reference fact for that analyte.
cards.source: Frederiksen H et al. Sex- and age-specific reference intervals of 16 steroid metabolites quantified simultaneously by LC-MS/MS in sera from 2458 healthy subjects aged 0 to 77 years. Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry. 2024. PMID: 38977173. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Adult ID-LC-MS/MS intervals and immunoassay comparison (Fanelli 2011): 416 healthy adults — of four immunoassays compared, only Elecsys E170 cortisol (and male testosterone, progesterone above 1 ng/mL) agreed with mass spectrometry; the rest showed poor agreement
cards.summary: Adult ID-LC-MS/MS intervals and immunoassay comparison (Fanelli 2011): 416 healthy adults — of four immunoassays compared, only Elecsys E170 cortisol (and male testosterone, progesterone above 1 ng/mL) agreed with mass spectrometry; the rest showed poor agreement
cards.type: Primary human physiology / methods study (ID-LC-MS/MS steroid reference intervals in healthy adults; immunoassay comparison)
cards.people: 416 healthy adult subjects in whom reference intervals for a nine-steroid serum panel (cortisol, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, deoxycorticosterone, testosterone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, dehydroepiandrosterone and progesterone) were established by a validated isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS method (0.9 ml serum, C18 extraction, two-dimensional LC, 21-minute run); results compared with the routine immunoassays used in the authors' laboratory.
cards.result: Of the four immunoassays compared with ID-LC-MS/MS, only Elecsys E170 results for cortisol, testosterone in males and progesterone above 1 ng/ml agreed with mass spectrometry. Elecsys E170 for testosterone in females and progesterone below 1 ng/ml, Immulite 2000 for androstenedione, DSL-9000 for DHEA and the 17-hydroxyprogesterone Bridge assay showed poor agreement. Adult reference intervals and age- and fertility-related steroid fluctuations were established by the MS method; the fetched record does not print the numeric limits, and this card claims none. The authors conclude the MS method is reliable and sensitive and exposes the limits of routine immunoassays at low concentrations.
cards.watchOut: Agreement for cortisol on one immunoassay platform does not rehabilitate immunoassays for the rest of the panel — the disagreement is analyte- and concentration-specific, worst exactly where concentrations are low (female testosterone, low progesterone).
cards.source: Fanelli F et al. Serum steroid profiling by isotopic dilution-liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry: comparison with current immunoassays and reference intervals in healthy adults. Steroids. 2011. PMID: 21112348. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diurnal variation study (Parikh 2018): paired AM/PM samples in 120 healthy women and 62 healthy men — cortisol, cortisone, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and DHEA all differed significantly by time of day in both sexes; progesterone did not
cards.summary: Diurnal variation study (Parikh 2018): paired AM/PM samples in 120 healthy women and 62 healthy men — cortisol, cortisone, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and DHEA all differed significantly by time of day in both sexes; progesterone did not
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (diurnal variation and time-dependent steroid reference intervals by LC-MS/MS)
cards.people: 120 healthy females and 62 healthy males recruited from several centres; nine steroid markers measured in AM and PM couplets by isotope-dilution HPLC-tandem mass spectrometry using 0.1 mL of serum; time-dependent reference intervals derived. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Diurnal values differed significantly in both females and males for cortisone, cortisol, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone and dehydroepiandrosterone. Testosterone showed significant diurnal variance only in males. Progesterone showed no significant AM–PM difference in either sex and may serve as an internal control. The authors emphasise standardisation of collection times and time-appropriate reference intervals when diagnosing endocrine disorders. The fetched record reports which steroids vary, not the numeric AM and PM limits, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: An untimed cortisol is an uninterpretable cortisol: this card is why every interval on this shelf must be read with its sampling-time band, and why a single all-day reference range for cortisol is a category error.
cards.source: Parikh TP et al. Diurnal variation of steroid hormones and their reference intervals using mass spectrometric analysis. Endocrine connections. 2018. PMID: 30400040. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

primary human physiology study (diurnal variation and time-dependent steroid reference intervals by lc-ms/ms) 120 healthy females and 62 healthy males recruited from several centres; nine steroid markers measured in am and pm couplets by isotope-dilution hplc-tandem mass spectrometry using 0.1 ml of serum; time-dependent reference intervals derived. this record carries no mesh terms (see source line). diurnal values differed significantly in both females and males for cortisone, cortisol, corticosterone, 11-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone and dehydroepiandrosterone. testosterone showed significant diurnal variance only in males. progesterone showed no significant am–pm difference in either sex and may serve as an internal control. the authors emphasise standardisation of collection times and time-appropriate reference intervals when diagnosing endocrine disorders. the fetched record reports which steroids vary, not the numeric am and pm limits, and this card claims none. an untimed cortisol is an uninterpretable cortisol: this card is why every interval on this shelf must be read with its sampling-time band, and why a single all-day reference range for cortisol is a category error. parikh tp et al. diurnal variation of steroid hormones and their reference intervals using mass spectrometric analysis. endocrine connections. 2018. pmid: 30400040. registry id: none in the record. mesh: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: by LC-MS/MS the steroid panel has sex-, age- and time-of-day-specific intervals; immunoassays agree with mass spectrometry only patchily (cortisol on one platform was the exception, not the rule) — and the numeric MS limits live in the full reports, not in any fetched abstract on this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: by LC-MS/MS the steroid panel has sex-, age- and time-of-day-specific intervals; immunoassays agree with mass spectrometry only patchily (cortisol on one platform was the exception, not the rule) — and the numeric MS limits live in the full reports, not in any fetched abstract on this shelf
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above (2,458 healthy subjects across the lifespan; 416 healthy adults; 182 healthy adults with paired AM/PM samples).
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (adrenocortical hormones) and Ganong (adrenal physiology). The three datasets agree on the structure: a single LC-MS/MS run can quantify the whole panel in health (Frederiksen 2024); adult intervals established by isotope-dilution MS expose immunoassay cross-reactivity as the historical intervals' main flaw, with agreement the exception (Fanelli 2011); and most of the panel, cortisol included, moves significantly between morning and afternoon in both sexes, so intervals must be time-banded (Parikh 2018). Cortisol pulsatility (#6498) and the cortisol awakening response (#7084) are the dynamic-pattern cross-points. Where local MS intervals are read, cortisol is reported in µg/dL with nmol/L equivalents (µg/dL × 27.59 = nmol/L) per the US-units rule. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the method and time-banding conclusions are consistent and large-based, but no numeric cortisol limit is printed in any fetched record carded here, so the shelf states the structure and declines to invent the numbers.
cards.watchOut: Refusal, stated plainly: several steroid records with empty or number-free abstracts were not used to supply numeric limits, and no interval on this shelf should be quoted as a µg/dL or nmol/L range — the quotable content is the method hierarchy, the partitioning (sex × age × time of day) and the detectability facts on the cards.

shelves.title: WITHDRAWN — Sibutramine for obesity: dose-related weight loss and better maintenance (STORM), but SCOUT showed more nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke in high-risk patients (11.4% vs 10.0%) and it was withdrawn in 2010
shelves.question: In adults with overweight or obesity (including patients at high cardiovascular risk), does the serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor sibutramine, compared with placebo plus lifestyle intervention, produce and maintain weight loss — and what was its cardiovascular-outcomes profile (SCOUT)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Appetite Depressants · Blood Pressure · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cyclobutanes · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction · Obesity · Overweight · Stroke
shelves.balance: WITHDRAWN — that status leads this shelf. Sibutramine (Meridia/Reductil) was withdrawn in 2010 after SCOUT, and LIKELY (harm) is the governing stamp for the high-risk population SCOUT studied. The efficacy side is real: Bray 1999 (1,047 randomised, 24 weeks) showed dose-related weight loss (completers: 6.1% of body weight at 10 mg, 7.4% at 15 mg, vs 1.2% on placebo), and STORM showed sibutramine maintained weight loss better than placebo after an initial loss (43% vs 16% of completers kept at least 80% of the loss at 2 years). The outcomes side overrides it in high-risk patients: SCOUT (9,804 randomised, age ≥55 with cardiovascular disease and/or type 2 diabetes, mean treatment 3.4 years) found the primary cardiovascular outcome in 11.4% on sibutramine vs 10.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.16 — a relative measure; the absolute difference was 1.4 percentage points), driven by nonfatal myocardial infarction (4.1% vs 3.2%; HR 1.28, relative) and nonfatal stroke (2.6% vs 1.9%; HR 1.36, relative), with no increase in cardiovascular or all-cause death. Populations differ and are printed exactly: the weight-loss trials were in lower-risk obesity; SCOUT's harm was in high-risk patients and must not be generalised beyond that population without saying so. A labelled SCOUT secondary analysis (weight loss itself associated with lower subsequent risk) is carded as programme support, not as an independent trial.

cards.headline: SCOUT primary (James 2010): sibutramine increased the primary cardiovascular outcome in high-risk patients (11.4% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio 1.16, a relative measure) — nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke, not death
cards.summary: SCOUT primary (James 2010): sibutramine increased the primary cardiovascular outcome in high-risk patients (11.4% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio 1.16, a relative measure) — nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke, not death
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled cardiovascular-outcomes trial (SCOUT), sibutramine plus weight management vs placebo plus weight management, after a sibutramine lead-in
cards.people: 10,744 overweight or obese subjects aged 55 or older with preexisting cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, or both, all receiving sibutramine plus a weight-management programme in a 6-week single-blind lead-in; 9,804 then underwent double-blind randomisation to sibutramine (n=4,906) or placebo (n=4,898). Mean treatment duration 3.4 years. The primary endpoint was time to first nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, resuscitation after cardiac arrest, or cardiovascular death.
cards.result: Mean weight loss in the lead-in was 2.6 kg; after randomisation the sibutramine group achieved and maintained a further mean reduction of 1.7 kg. Blood pressure fell in both groups, less on sibutramine (mean difference 1.2/1.4 mm Hg). The primary outcome occurred in 11.4% (sibutramine) vs 10.0% (placebo): hazard ratio 1.16 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.31; P=0.02) — a relative measure, an absolute difference of 1.4 percentage points. Nonfatal myocardial infarction: 4.1% vs 3.2% (HR 1.28, relative; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.57; P=0.02). Nonfatal stroke: 2.6% vs 1.9% (HR 1.36, relative; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.77; P=0.03). Rates of cardiovascular death and death from any cause were not increased.
cards.watchOut: A high-risk population by design (age ≥55 with cardiovascular disease and/or diabetes) — the harm result belongs to that population and is not a measurement of risk in the lower-risk patients of the weight-loss trials; every participant also received sibutramine in the lead-in, so the randomised comparison is continuation versus withdrawal to placebo.
cards.source: James WPT et al. Effect of sibutramine on cardiovascular outcomes in overweight and obese subjects. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20818901. Registry ID: NCT00234832. cards.headline: STORM (James 2000): after an initial sibutramine-assisted loss, continuing sibutramine maintained at least 80% of the loss in 43% of completers vs 16% on placebo at 2 years
cards.summary: STORM (James 2000): after an initial sibutramine-assisted loss, continuing sibutramine maintained at least 80% of the loss in 43% of completers vs 16% on placebo at 2 years
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled weight-maintenance trial (STORM), continuing sibutramine vs placebo after a sibutramine weight-loss phase
cards.people: 605 obese patients (body-mass index 30–45 kg/m²) at 8 European centres entered a 6-month weight-loss phase on sibutramine 10 mg/day with an individualised 600 kcal/day deficit diet; the 467 (77%) who lost more than 5% were randomised to sibutramine 10 mg/day (n=352, increasable to 20 mg) or placebo (n=115) for a further 18 months. The primary outcome was maintaining at least 80% of the weight lost by month 6, at year 2.
cards.result: Dropout was high: 148 (42%) on sibutramine and 58 (50%) on placebo left the trial. Among completers, 89 of 204 (43%) on sibutramine maintained at least 80% of their original weight loss, versus 9 of 57 (16%) on placebo (odds ratio 4.64, a relative odds measure; P<0.001). Triglyceride, VLDL cholesterol, insulin, C-peptide and uric acid improvements from the loss phase were sustained on sibutramine but not placebo; HDL cholesterol rose 20.7% vs 11.7% (P<0.001). Twenty patients (3%) were withdrawn because of blood-pressure increases; on sibutramine, systolic pressure changed +0.1 mm Hg, diastolic +2.3 mm Hg and pulse +4.1 beats/min from baseline to 2 years.
cards.watchOut: Only initial responders were randomised (467 of 605), and the headline 43% vs 16% is among completers after 42–50% dropout — it describes maintenance in patients who already lost weight on the drug, not weight loss in an unselected population.
cards.source: James WPT et al. Effect of sibutramine on weight maintenance after weight loss: a randomised trial. STORM Study Group. Sibutramine Trial of Obesity Reduction and Maintenance. Lancet (London, England). 2000. PMID: 11191537. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dose-ranging RCT (Bray 1999): sibutramine produced dose-related weight loss over 24 weeks — completers lost 6.1% of body weight at 10 mg and 7.4% at 15 mg vs 1.2% on placebo
cards.summary: Dose-ranging RCT (Bray 1999): sibutramine produced dose-related weight loss over 24 weeks — completers lost 6.1% of body weight at 10 mg and 7.4% at 15 mg vs 1.2% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, sibutramine 1–30 mg daily for 24 weeks in uncomplicated obesity
cards.people: 1,047 patients with obesity randomised at 7 clinical centres to 24 weeks of sibutramine 1, 5, 10, 15, 20 or 30 mg or placebo once daily, with a standardised diet, activity and lifestyle programme after a 2-week placebo run-in; 683 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Weight loss was dose-related and statistically significant versus placebo (P<0.05) at every time point for doses from 5 mg to 30 mg. Percent weight loss from baseline at week 24 among completers: placebo 1.2%; 1 mg 2.7%; 5 mg 3.9%; 10 mg 6.1%; 15 mg 7.4%; 20 mg 8.8%; 30 mg 9.4%. Weight loss at week 4 predicted weight loss at week 24. HDL cholesterol rose and triglycerides, total and LDL cholesterol and uric acid fell with weight loss. Small mean increases in blood pressure and pulse rate occurred on sibutramine, with considerable individual variability; the most frequent adverse events were dry mouth, anorexia and insomnia.
cards.watchOut: Completer percentages after substantial dropout (683 of 1,047 finished), over only 24 weeks, in uncomplicated obesity — a lower-risk population than SCOUT's, and the doses above 15 mg exceed the dose later marketed.
cards.source: Bray GA et al. Sibutramine produces dose-related weight loss. Obesity research. 1999. PMID: 10102256. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme secondary analysis — SCOUT weight-loss analysis (Caterson 2012): within SCOUT, greater maintained weight loss was associated with lower subsequent cardiovascular risk in the whole population — a secondary analysis of the SCOUT card above, NOT an independent trial
cards.summary: Programme secondary analysis — SCOUT weight-loss analysis (Caterson 2012): within SCOUT, greater maintained weight loss was associated with lower subsequent cardiovascular risk in the whole population — a secondary analysis of the SCOUT card above, NOT an independent trial
cards.type: Secondary analysis of the SCOUT randomised trial (same programme as the James 2010 card above — labelled programme support, not independent comparative evidence)
cards.people: The SCOUT population (10,744 enrolled; 9,804 randomised — 4,906 sibutramine, 4,898 placebo, as in the primary report), examining the relationship between weight loss during the lead-in and through month 12 and subsequent primary outcome events and cardiovascular mortality over the 5-year assessment.
cards.result: Mean weight change during the lead-in (on sibutramine) was −2.54 kg; post-randomisation mean total weight change to month 12 was −4.18 kg (sibutramine) and −1.87 kg (placebo). In the total population, greater weight loss during the lead-in or through month 12 was progressively associated with lower risk of primary outcome events and cardiovascular mortality; the authors concluded that a modest weight loss of approximately 3 kg in the lead-in appeared to offset the increased event rate seen in the randomised sibutramine group, and that moderate weight loss (3–10 kg) was associated with fewer cardiovascular deaths across cardiovascular-disease severity strata.
cards.watchOut: Post-randomisation, observational-within-trial analysis: patients who lose more weight differ from those who do not in many ways, so this association does not cancel SCOUT's randomised harm result and is carded only to complete the programme record.
cards.source: Caterson ID et al. Maintained intentional weight loss reduces cardiovascular outcomes: results from the Sibutramine Cardiovascular OUTcomes (SCOUT) trial. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2012. PMID: 22192338. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: sibutramine worked for weight loss and maintenance — and was withdrawn in 2010 because SCOUT showed more nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke in high-risk patients; the withdrawn status governs this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: sibutramine worked for weight loss and maintenance — and was withdrawn in 2010 because SCOUT showed more nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke in high-risk patients; the withdrawn status governs this shelf
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (SCOUT, n=9,804 randomised; STORM, n=467 randomised; Bray 1999, n=1,047; plus the labelled SCOUT secondary analysis).
cards.result: The efficacy record is consistent: dose-related weight loss over 24 weeks (Bray) and better maintenance of an achieved loss over 2 years (STORM). The outcomes record is decisive the other way in the population SCOUT studied: a primary cardiovascular outcome rate of 11.4% vs 10.0% (hazard ratio 1.16, relative), from nonfatal myocardial infarction (4.1% vs 3.2%) and nonfatal stroke (2.6% vs 1.9%), without increased mortality. Sibutramine was withdrawn in 2010 on that result. The two halves belong to different populations — lower-risk obesity for efficacy, high-risk older patients for harm — and this shelf prints both exactly rather than merging them. The SCOUT secondary analysis associating weight loss itself with lower subsequent risk is programme support and does not reverse the randomised comparison.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: WITHDRAWN 1997 — that status leads this shelf. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn worldwide in 1997 after the valvular-heart-disease and pulmonary-hypertension signals; nothing in the modest efficacy record below rehabilitates them as obesity treatment. The efficacy base is old (1989–1998) and short: ISIS (822 patients, dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily — 30 mg/day — plus diet vs placebo; the report carded is the 6-month interim of a planned 1-year trial, published in a French-language journal and carded here from its English abstract, as printed on its card) found about twice as many dexfenfluramine patients achieved an important weight loss, with greater cumulative loss, but its abstract prints no kilogram figure and none is claimed here. The active-comparator trials quantify the size of effect: dexfenfluramine lost 3.2 kg in 12 weeks against sibutramine's 4.5 kg (Hanotin 1998), and 6.9 kg in 15 weeks against an ephedrine/caffeine combination's 8.3 kg (Breum 1994); a small combination trial (n=33, printed on its card) found adding dexfenfluramine to fluoxetine lost more than fluoxetine alone. These obesity doses (15 mg twice daily) were far higher than the low-dose fenfluramine used for Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes at live shelf #992 — a different population and question, cross-pointed in the synthesis and never merged or re-carded here.

cards.headline: ISIS 6-month interim report (Guy-Grand 1989): dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily plus diet — about twice as many patients achieved an important weight loss as on placebo (822 patients; French-language journal, carded from its English abstract)
cards.summary: ISIS 6-month interim report (Guy-Grand 1989): dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily plus diet — about twice as many patients achieved an important weight loss as on placebo (822 patients; French-language journal, carded from its English abstract)
cards.type: International multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ISIS), dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily plus diet — 6-month interim report of a planned 1-year trial; journal article in French with an English abstract (language printed here as the row directs; carded from the English abstract)
cards.people: 822 obese patients in an international multicentre randomised double-blind trial of dexfenfluramine combined with diet versus placebo, planned for one year; this report presents the intermediate 6-month results (dexfenfluramine n=404, placebo n=418), analysed by intention to treat. Dexfenfluramine dose: 15 mg twice daily (30 mg/day).
cards.result: Significant differences favoured dexfenfluramine: the drug-withdrawal rate was lower (mainly because more placebo patients were dissatisfied with their weight loss); about twice as many treated patients achieved an important loss of weight in terms of percentage of initial weight or overweight; and cumulative weight loss was greater. Transient side-effects — fatigue, diarrhoea, dry mouth, polyuria and drowsiness — were more frequent on dexfenfluramine. The report's abstract prints no kilogram weight-loss figure, so none is given here.
cards.watchOut: An interim report whose abstract gives directions and proportions, not kilogram amounts — any precise ISIS weight-loss figure would have to come from the full text, and none is printed on this shelf; the trial also predates the 1997 withdrawal by eight years, so it contains no valvulopathy surveillance of the kind the withdrawal later required.
cards.source: Guy-Grand B et al. [International study of the effect of dexfenfluramine in obesity (ISIS): 6 months' results]. La Revue de medecine interne. 1989. PMID: 2669089. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Active-comparator RCT (Hanotin 1998): dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily lost 3.2 kg in 12 weeks, less than sibutramine 10 mg daily (4.5 kg)
cards.summary: Active-comparator RCT (Hanotin 1998): dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily lost 3.2 kg in 12 weeks, less than sibutramine 10 mg daily (4.5 kg)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-comparator trial, dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily vs sibutramine 10 mg daily for 12 weeks (no placebo arm)
cards.people: 226 healthy outpatients aged 18 to 65 with body-mass index ≥27 kg/m², in a 12-week randomised double-blind parallel-group study of sibutramine 10 mg once daily (n=112) versus dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily (n=112; endpoint analysis numbers as reported).
cards.result: Mean absolute weight loss at endpoint was 4.5 ± 0.4 kg on sibutramine and 3.2 ± 0.3 kg on dexfenfluramine; among completers, 4.7 ± 0.4 kg (n=101) and 3.6 ± 0.3 kg (n=94) respectively. Under the conventional null hypothesis of equality (a secondary analysis), weight loss on sibutramine was significantly greater (P<0.05). Adverse-event profiles were similar (77% of patients reported events; withdrawals for adverse events: 6 on sibutramine, 11 on dexfenfluramine). Pulse rate rose on sibutramine (+3.6 bpm) and fell on dexfenfluramine (−0.9 bpm).
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm and only 12 weeks: it sizes dexfenfluramine against another (also later-withdrawn) appetite suppressant, not against no treatment, and it was published in 1998 — after the 1997 withdrawal — from a trial conducted in the pre-withdrawal era.
cards.source: Hanotin C et al. A comparison of sibutramine and dexfenfluramine in the treatment of obesity. Obesity research. 1998. PMID: 9688105. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Active-comparator RCT (Breum 1994): dexfenfluramine lost 6.9 kg in 15 weeks in general practice, similar to an ephedrine/caffeine combination (8.3 kg)
cards.summary: Active-comparator RCT (Breum 1994): dexfenfluramine lost 6.9 kg in 15 weeks in general practice, similar to an ephedrine/caffeine combination (8.3 kg)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-comparator trial in general practice, dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily vs ephedrine/caffeine for 15 weeks (no placebo arm)
cards.people: 103 patients with 20–80% overweight in a 15-week double-blind multicentre general-practice trial, randomised to dexfenfluramine 15 mg twice daily (n=53) or ephedrine 20 mg / caffeine 200 mg three times daily (n=50), both with a 5 MJ/day diet; 43 dexfenfluramine and 38 ephedrine/caffeine patients completed.
cards.result: After 15 weeks, completers on dexfenfluramine had lost 6.9 ± 4.3 kg and those on ephedrine/caffeine 8.3 ± 5.2 kg (P=0.12). In the subgroup with body-mass index ≥30 kg/m² (n=59), losses were 7.0 ± 4.2 kg (dexfenfluramine, n=29) and 9.0 ± 5.3 kg (ephedrine/caffeine, n=30; P<0.05). Blood pressure fell similarly on both. Side-effects were reported by 23 patients (43%) on dexfenfluramine and 27 (54%) on ephedrine/caffeine; central-nervous-system effects predominated on ephedrine/caffeine and gastrointestinal symptoms on dexfenfluramine, and effects in both groups declined markedly during the first month.
cards.watchOut: Completer analysis (81 of 103 finished) against an active comparator, not placebo; the abstract was truncated at 250 words in the record, so later-trial detail is limited to what is printed here.
cards.source: Breum L et al. Comparison of an ephedrine/caffeine combination and dexfenfluramine in the treatment of obesity. A double-blind multi-centre trial in general practice. International journal of obesity and related metabolic disorders : journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity. 1994. PMID: 8148931. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Small combination RCT (Pedrinola 1996): adding dexfenfluramine 15 mg at night to fluoxetine lost 13.4 kg vs 6.2 kg on fluoxetine alone over 8 months — a combination read in 33 patients, not dexfenfluramine-alone evidence
cards.summary: Small combination RCT (Pedrinola 1996): adding dexfenfluramine 15 mg at night to fluoxetine lost 13.4 kg vs 6.2 kg on fluoxetine alone over 8 months — a combination read in 33 patients, not dexfenfluramine-alone evidence
cards.type: Small randomised double-blind combination trial (n=33), fluoxetine plus dexfenfluramine vs fluoxetine plus placebo
cards.people: 33 patients with obesity randomly assigned, double-blind, to fluoxetine 40 mg plus placebo (n=13) or fluoxetine 40 mg plus dexfenfluramine 15 mg at night (n=20), followed for 8 months. The small N (33) is printed here on the face of the card, as this shelf's labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Both groups lost significant weight by 8 months: fluoxetine alone 6.2 ± 2.8 kg (mean ± SEM) and the combination 13.4 ± 6.3 kg (P<0.05), with the between-group difference in body-mass index reaching significance after 4 months and in weight after 6 months. HDL cholesterol rose and serum cholesterol and triglycerides fell in both groups. Side-effects were relatively minor, with no altered vital signs or abnormal laboratory values observed. The authors themselves note the study's small size does not permit broad generalisation.
cards.watchOut: A combination add-on question in only 33 patients with very wide variability (±6.3 kg SEM in the combination arm): it cannot be read as dexfenfluramine-alone efficacy and is carded as the programme's fourth, weakest report — labelled, never load-bearing.
cards.source: Pedrinola F et al. The addition of dexfenfluramine to fluoxetine in the treatment of obesity: a randomized clinical trial. Obesity research. 1996. PMID: 8946439. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: dexfenfluramine at obesity doses (15 mg twice daily) produced modest short-term weight loss in 1989–1998 trials — and both drugs were withdrawn worldwide in 1997 for valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension; that withdrawal, not the efficacy, governs this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: dexfenfluramine at obesity doses (15 mg twice daily) produced modest short-term weight loss in 1989–1998 trials — and both drugs were withdrawn worldwide in 1997 for valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension; that withdrawal, not the efficacy, governs this shelf
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (ISIS, n=822; Hanotin 1998, n=226; Breum 1994, n=103; Pedrinola 1996, n=33).
cards.result: The placebo-controlled evidence (ISIS, 6-month interim) shows dexfenfluramine plus diet beat placebo on the proportion achieving important weight loss, without a kilogram figure in its report; the active-comparator trials size the effect at roughly 3–7 kg over 12–15 weeks, no better than the comparators of their day. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn worldwide in 1997 after the valvular-heart-disease and pulmonary-hypertension signals — the harm that defines these drugs historically is not measured in these short efficacy trials and is stated here from the withdrawal record, not from the carded reports. Dose discipline: the obesity dose carded here (15 mg twice daily) is far above the low-dose fenfluramine used in epilepsy; that separate question — Dravet and Lennox–Gastaut syndromes, with its own cardiac monitoring — is homed at live shelf #992 and is cross-pointed only, never re-carded or merged with this shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
