shelves.title: WITHDRAWN 2000 — Troglitazone in type 2 diabetes: real insulin-sensitising, glucose-lowering efficacy (approximately 20% lower glucose at 400–600 mg), withdrawn for hepatocellular injury including liver-failure deaths
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the thiazolidinedione troglitazone, compared with placebo (alone or added to sulfonylurea therapy), improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Blood Glucose · C-Peptide · Chromans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucose · Glucose Clamp Technique · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Insulin Resistance · Liver · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Regression Analysis · Thiazoles · Thiazolidinediones · Troglitazone
shelves.balance: WITHDRAWN — that status leads this shelf. Troglitazone (Rezulin) was withdrawn in 2000 for idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury, including liver-failure deaths; the glycaemic efficacy below is historical and does not rehabilitate the drug. Maggs 1998 (randomised placebo-controlled monotherapy, 93 patients, 6 months): troglitazone 400 mg and 600 mg lowered fasting and postprandial glucose by approximately 20% (as reported) and increased insulin-stimulated glucose disposal by approximately 45%, in clamp studies. Ghazzi 1997 (Troglitazone Study Group, 154 patients, 48 weeks vs glyburide): no increase in left ventricular mass, with long-term HbA1c and C-peptide improvement (its abstract prints no HbA1c figures, so none are claimed here). Fonseca 2000 — OPEN-LABEL extension studies, labelled as such: at a fixed 600 mg dose, HbA1c changes from baseline were −0.4% (monotherapy), −1.8% (with sulfonylurea) and −1.0% (with insulin), in patients who had completed the parent double-blind studies (758 completed the extensions). FENCE, printed here so it cannot be missed: the Diabetes Prevention Program troglitazone report is a diabetes-ONSET question in prediabetes; it is NOT carded on this treatment shelf, and any diabetes-onset wording for it says 'delay', never 'prevent'.

cards.headline: Monotherapy RCT (Maggs 1998): troglitazone 400–600 mg lowered fasting and postprandial glucose by approximately 20% over 6 months and raised insulin-stimulated glucose disposal by approximately 45%
cards.summary: Monotherapy RCT (Maggs 1998): troglitazone 400–600 mg lowered fasting and postprandial glucose by approximately 20% over 6 months and raised insulin-stimulated glucose disposal by approximately 45%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled monotherapy trial with clamp and meal-test metabolic endpoints, troglitazone 100–600 mg for 6 months
cards.people: 93 patients (mean age 52 years) with type 2 diabetes (mean fasting plasma glucose 11.2 mmol/L [≈202 mg/dL]) treated with diet alone or after discontinuing oral antidiabetic therapy, at 6 US general clinical research centres; randomly assigned to troglitazone 100, 200, 400 or 600 mg daily or placebo for 6 months, with meal-tolerance tests and hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamps before and after treatment.
cards.result: Troglitazone 400 mg and 600 mg decreased both fasting (P<0.001) and postprandial (P=0.016) plasma glucose by approximately 20% (percent change as reported). All four doses decreased fasting (P=0.012) and postprandial (P<0.001) triglycerides; 600 mg decreased fasting free fatty acids (P=0.018). Plasma insulin fell in the 200, 400 and 600 mg groups (P<0.001). Basal hepatic glucose production was suppressed at 600 mg versus placebo (P=0.02), and glucose disposal rate rose by approximately 45% above pretreatment levels at 400 and 600 mg (P=0.003). Troglitazone therapy was the strongest predictor of glucose decrease in stepwise regression; higher baseline fasting C-peptide predicted a greater effect.
cards.watchOut: A mechanistic metabolic trial (n=93 across five arms): its endpoints are glucose levels and clamp physiology, not HbA1c outcomes or clinical events, and its percent changes are printed as the report states them, not converted into absolute glucose falls the abstract does not give.
cards.source: Maggs DG et al. Metabolic effects of troglitazone monotherapy in type 2 diabetes mellitus. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1998. PMID: 9454525. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Troglitazone Study Group RCT (Ghazzi 1997): troglitazone 800 mg over 48 weeks produced no increase in left ventricular mass versus glyburide, with long-term HbA1c improvement (no HbA1c figures printed in the report's abstract)
cards.summary: Troglitazone Study Group RCT (Ghazzi 1997): troglitazone 800 mg over 48 weeks produced no increase in left ventricular mass versus glyburide, with long-term HbA1c improvement (no HbA1c figures printed in the report's abstract)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial, troglitazone 800 mg vs glyburide for 48 weeks, with echocardiographic cardiac endpoints and glycaemic measures
cards.people: 154 patients with NIDDM (type 2 diabetes) randomised to troglitazone 800 mg once daily or glyburide titrated to glycaemic control (up to 20 mg twice daily or once daily), for 48 weeks in a multicentre study designed primarily to test whether troglitazone causes the cardiac mass increase reported in animals with this drug class; echocardiograms were read by a blinded central interpreter.
cards.result: Left ventricular mass index on troglitazone was not statistically or clinically different from baseline at 24 or 48 weeks. Stroke volume index and cardiac index increased significantly and diastolic pressure and estimated peripheral resistance decreased significantly on troglitazone. Glycaemic benefits were observed as long-term improvement in HbA1c and C-peptide (the abstract reports the direction, not the amounts, and no amounts are claimed here). Triglycerides were significantly lower and HDL significantly higher at weeks 24 and 48 on troglitazone.
cards.watchOut: A cardiac-safety-designed trial at a high dose (800 mg, above the later marketed range): its glycaemic content is qualitative in the record, and its reassurance about cardiac mass says nothing about the hepatic injury that withdrew the drug three years later.
cards.source: Ghazzi MN et al. Cardiac and glycemic benefits of troglitazone treatment in NIDDM. The Troglitazone Study Group. Diabetes. 1997. PMID: 9032099. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Open-label extension studies (Fonseca 2000) — labelled open-label: at 600 mg, HbA1c fell 0.4% on monotherapy, 1.8% added to sulfonylurea and 1.0% added to insulin, in patients completing the parent double-blind studies
cards.summary: Open-label extension studies (Fonseca 2000) — labelled open-label: at 600 mg, HbA1c fell 0.4% on monotherapy, 1.8% added to sulfonylurea and 1.0% added to insulin, in patients completing the parent double-blind studies
cards.type: Open-label extension studies of three parent double-blind trials (labelled open-label — uncontrolled long-term follow-on, not randomised evidence)
cards.people: Patients who completed one of three double-blind studies (6-month troglitazone monotherapy; 52-week troglitazone plus micronised glyburide; 6-month troglitazone plus insulin) entered open-label extensions of those studies, with dose titration to a maximum of 600 mg (except in the insulin combination). 758 patients completed the extensions, with total exposure of 16,264 patient-months.
cards.result: For patients on a fixed 600 mg dose, mean changes from baseline to the end of the open-label phase: fasting serum glucose −57 mg/dL and HbA1c −0.4% (monotherapy); −49 mg/dL and −1.8% (sulfonylurea combination); −31 mg/dL and −1.0% (insulin combination). Across the combined cohort, the proportion achieving HbA1c ≤8% was 54%, versus 19% at baseline. Mean triglycerides fell 18% (a relative percent change, as reported) among fixed-600 mg patients. Troglitazone was reported as well tolerated in these extensions, with minimal adverse events over the exposure recorded.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, completer-only follow-on data: patients who tolerated and stayed on troglitazone are exactly those who remain, so these HbA1c figures overstate what an unselected population would achieve; the extensions' 'well tolerated' framing also predates and does not answer the hepatotoxicity that withdrew the drug in 2000.
cards.source: Fonseca V et al. Long-term effects of troglitazone: open-label extension studies in type 2 diabetic patients. Diabetes care. 2000. PMID: 10868865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: troglitazone genuinely improved insulin sensitivity and glycaemic control — and was withdrawn in 2000 for hepatocellular injury including liver-failure deaths; the withdrawn status, and the fenced diabetes-onset report, govern this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: troglitazone genuinely improved insulin sensitivity and glycaemic control — and was withdrawn in 2000 for hepatocellular injury including liver-failure deaths; the withdrawn status, and the fenced diabetes-onset report, govern this shelf
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (Maggs 1998, n=93; Ghazzi 1997, n=154; Fonseca 2000, open-label extensions, 758 completers).
cards.result: The randomised record shows a real insulin-sensitising effect: approximately 20% lower fasting and postprandial glucose and approximately 45% higher glucose disposal at 400–600 mg over 6 months (Maggs), no cardiac-mass increase with glycaemic improvement over 48 weeks (Ghazzi), and sustained HbA1c reductions in open-label extension — largest as an add-on to sulfonylurea (−1.8% at 600 mg), in completers only. None of that changes the governing fact: troglitazone (Rezulin) was withdrawn in 2000 for idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury including liver-failure deaths, a harm these glycaemic trials were not designed or powered to detect. Fence, restated: the Diabetes Prevention Program troglitazone report asks a diabetes-onset question in prediabetes, is not carded here or anywhere on this shelf, and any wording about it must say it delayed — never 'prevented' — diabetes onset.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Aleglitazar in type 2 diabetes — DISCONTINUED programme: SYNCHRONY lowered HbA1c dose-dependently, but AleCardio showed no cardiovascular benefit (HR 0.96) with more renal dysfunction and GI haemorrhage, and was terminated early
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (including patients stabilised after an acute coronary syndrome), does the dual PPAR-α/γ agonist aleglitazar, compared with placebo on standard therapy, improve glycaemic control and reduce cardiovascular events (SYNCHRONY / AleCardio programme)?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Cardiovascular Diseases · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Oxazoles · PPAR alpha · PPAR gamma · Pioglitazone · Safety · Single-Blind Method · Thiazolidinediones · Thiophenes · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT, on a discontinued programme — that history leads this face. This is a programme-level shelf holding two questions, as the commissioning row directs: glycaemia (SYNCHRONY) and post-ACS cardiovascular outcomes (AleCardio). Glycaemia: SYNCHRONY (phase II, 332 randomised, 16 weeks) showed dose-dependent HbA1c lowering versus placebo, from −0.36% at 50 µg to −1.35% at 600 µg, with dose-dependent oedema, haemodilution and weight gain. Outcomes: AleCardio (phase 3, 7,226 patients with type 2 diabetes after an acute coronary syndrome) was TERMINATED EARLY for futility plus safety signals, and showed no cardiovascular benefit — primary endpoint 9.5% on aleglitazar vs 10.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.96, a relative measure; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11; P=.57) — with more renal dysfunction (7.4% vs 2.7%), more gastrointestinal haemorrhage (2.4% vs 1.7%) and numerically more heart failure (3.4% vs 2.8%). Programme support carded and labelled: a renal study at the supratherapeutic 600 µg dose (measured GFR fell 16.9%, reversible on stopping) and an AleCardio exposure–response secondary analysis (not an independent trial). Distinct-trial count is 3 (SYNCHRONY, AleCardio, the renal study) with 4 cardable reports; the two AleCardio reports are one trial reported twice and are labelled as such. Aleglitazar was never marketed.

cards.headline: SYNCHRONY phase II dose-ranging RCT (Henry 2009): aleglitazar lowered HbA1c dose-dependently versus placebo, from −0.36% at 50 µg to −1.35% at 600 µg over 16 weeks
cards.summary: SYNCHRONY phase II dose-ranging RCT (Henry 2009): aleglitazar lowered HbA1c dose-dependently versus placebo, from −0.36% at 50 µg to −1.35% at 600 µg over 16 weeks
cards.type: Phase II randomised double-blind dose-ranging study (SYNCHRONY), aleglitazar 50–600 µg vs placebo, with open-label pioglitazone reference arm
cards.people: 332 patients with type 2 diabetes (drug-naive or pre-treated with up to two oral agents) at 47 sites in 7 countries, randomised after a single-blind placebo run-in to aleglitazar 50, 150, 300 or 600 µg once daily or matching placebo (n=55 per group), or to open-label pioglitazone 45 mg (n=57) as a reference, for 16 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in HbA1c; the efficacy analysis excluded 6 patients without an evaluable post-baseline HbA1c.
cards.result: Aleglitazar reduced HbA1c versus placebo dose-dependently: −0.36% (95% CI 0.00 to −0.70; P=0.048) at 50 µg to −1.35% (95% CI −0.99 to −1.70; P<0.0001) at 600 µg, with the time trend suggesting the maximum effect had not yet been reached at 16 weeks. Oedema, haemodilution and weight gain occurred dose-dependently; at doses below 300 µg no patient had congestive heart failure, oedema frequency was similar to placebo (1 case at 50 µg, 2 at 150 µg, 3 on placebo, 4 on pioglitazone), and weight gain was less than on pioglitazone (0.52 kg at 150 µg vs 1.06 kg).
cards.watchOut: Short (16 weeks), surrogate (HbA1c) endpoint, and the doses showing the largest HbA1c falls (300–600 µg) are above the 150 µg dose later taken into the outcomes trial — the glycaemic promise and the dose the programme could actually use are not the same thing.
cards.source: Henry RR et al. Effect of the dual peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha/gamma agonist aleglitazar on risk of cardiovascular disease in patients with type 2 diabetes (SYNCHRONY): a phase II, randomised, dose-ranging study. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19515415. Registry ID: NCT00388518. cards.headline: AleCardio phase 3 primary (Lincoff 2014): aleglitazar did NOT reduce cardiovascular outcomes after acute coronary syndrome (9.5% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio 0.96, a relative measure) — the trial was terminated early for futility and safety signals
cards.summary: AleCardio phase 3 primary (Lincoff 2014): aleglitazar did NOT reduce cardiovascular outcomes after acute coronary syndrome (9.5% vs 10.0%; hazard ratio 0.96, a relative measure) — the trial was terminated early for futility and safety signals
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled cardiovascular-outcomes trial (AleCardio), aleglitazar 150 µg after acute coronary syndrome — terminated early
cards.people: 7,226 patients with type 2 diabetes hospitalised for an acute coronary syndrome (myocardial infarction or unstable angina) at 720 hospitals in 26 countries (enrolled February 2010–May 2012), randomised 1:1 to aleglitazar 150 µg or placebo daily on standard therapy; treatment was planned for at least 2.5 years and 950 adjudicated primary events.
cards.result: The trial was terminated on July 2, 2013, after a median follow-up of 104 weeks, on the data and safety monitoring board's recommendation for futility at an unplanned interim analysis and increased rates of safety endpoints; 3.1% of patients were lost to follow-up and 3.2% withdrew consent. The primary endpoint (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke) occurred in 344 patients (9.5%) on aleglitazar and 360 (10.0%) on placebo: hazard ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.11; P=.57) — a relative measure whose interval includes no effect. Serious adverse events were increased: heart failure 3.4% vs 2.8% (P=.14), gastrointestinal haemorrhage 2.4% vs 1.7% (P=.03), and renal dysfunction 7.4% vs 2.7% (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: Early termination for futility means the null is a stopped-early null: the confidence interval (0.83 to 1.11) excludes a large benefit but not a small one; the safety increases, especially renal dysfunction, are the firmer findings and ended the programme.
cards.source: Lincoff AM et al. Effect of aleglitazar on cardiovascular outcomes after acute coronary syndrome in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: the AleCardio randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 24682069. Registry ID: NCT01042769. cards.headline: Renal study — SESTA R (Herz 2011): supratherapeutic aleglitazar 600 µg/day reduced measured GFR by 16.9% over 26 weeks versus 4.6% on pioglitazone, reversibly on stopping
cards.summary: Renal study — SESTA R (Herz 2011): supratherapeutic aleglitazar 600 µg/day reduced measured GFR by 16.9% over 26 weeks versus 4.6% on pioglitazone, reversibly on stopping
cards.type: Randomised double-blind renal-function study (SESTA R), supratherapeutic aleglitazar 600 µg vs pioglitazone 45 mg for 26 weeks — programme support for the renal-harm side
cards.people: 174 patients with type 2 diabetes and normal to mildly impaired renal function (estimated GFR 60–120 mL/min/1.73 m²) in a 26-week randomised double-blind multicentre study of aleglitazar 600 µg/day versus pioglitazone 45 mg/day; 118 patients had evaluable measured-GFR (mGFR) measurements (baseline mean mGFR 97.6 ± 17.5 on aleglitazar, 101.9 ± 21.6 on pioglitazone).
cards.result: Mean percent change in mGFR was −16.9% (90% CI −22.0 to −11.5) on aleglitazar and −4.6% (90% CI −10.15 to 1.35) on pioglitazone — a mean treatment difference of −13.0% (−19.0 to −6.5). The fall was consistent with a 19% fall in MDRD estimated GFR, plateaued after 4 weeks without further progression on treatment, and returned to pretreatment levels within the 4–8-week follow-up after withdrawal, suggesting reversible haemodynamic change. Dose-dependent PPAR class effects (peripheral oedema, weight gain, congestive heart failure) were also seen at this supratherapeutic dose.
cards.watchOut: A supratherapeutic-dose study (600 µg, four times the AleCardio dose) in 174 patients with only 118 evaluable for the primary measure: it characterises the renal effect's mechanism and reversibility, and must not be quoted as the renal risk at the 150 µg therapeutic dose — AleCardio's 7.4% vs 2.7% renal dysfunction is that figure.
cards.source: Herz M et al. Effects of high dose aleglitazar on renal function in patients with type 2 diabetes. International journal of cardiology. 2011. PMID: 20837369. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme secondary analysis — AleCardio exposure–response (Koomen 2020): clopidogrel co-treatment raised aleglitazar exposure and modified its HbA1c, haemoglobin, creatinine and adiponectin effects — an analysis OF the AleCardio card above, NOT an independent trial
cards.summary: Programme secondary analysis — AleCardio exposure–response (Koomen 2020): clopidogrel co-treatment raised aleglitazar exposure and modified its HbA1c, haemoglobin, creatinine and adiponectin effects — an analysis OF the AleCardio card above, NOT an independent trial
cards.type: Exposure–response secondary analysis of the AleCardio trial (same trial as the Lincoff 2014 card above — labelled programme lineage, not independent evidence)
cards.people: The AleCardio population (7,226 patients randomised to aleglitazar 150 µg or placebo on standard care), with a population pharmacokinetic substudy identifying covariates of aleglitazar exposure, whose effects on surrogate and clinical outcomes were then assessed in the full population.
cards.result: Concomitant clopidogrel influenced aleglitazar's apparent clearance: mean predicted area under the concentration-time curve was 174.7 ng·h/mL (SD ±112.9) in patients using clopidogrel versus 142.2 ng·h/mL (SD ±92.6) in those not using it. Clopidogrel use modified aleglitazar's effect versus placebo on HbA1c, haemoglobin, serum creatinine and adiponectin (P for interaction 0.007, 0.002, <0.001 and <0.001 respectively): clopidogrel users had additional HbA1c lowering at the expense of additional haemoglobin decrease and creatinine and adiponectin increases. The authors attribute this to clopidogrel's moderate CYP2C8 inhibition, aleglitazar being metabolised by CYP2C8.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetic interaction analysis of a terminated trial: it explains part of the variability in aleglitazar's effects and adds no efficacy evidence; counting it as a second outcomes trial would double-count AleCardio.
cards.source: Koomen JV et al. Exposure and response analysis of aleglitazar on cardiovascular risk markers and safety outcomes: An analysis of the AleCardio trial. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. PMID: 31468659. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: aleglitazar lowered HbA1c dose-dependently in phase II, then failed its outcomes test — AleCardio showed no cardiovascular benefit and more renal dysfunction and gastrointestinal haemorrhage, and the programme was discontinued
cards.summary: Synthesis: aleglitazar lowered HbA1c dose-dependently in phase II, then failed its outcomes test — AleCardio showed no cardiovascular benefit and more renal dysfunction and gastrointestinal haemorrhage, and the programme was discontinued
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (SYNCHRONY, n=332; AleCardio, n=7,226, plus its labelled exposure–response analysis; SESTA R renal study, n=174). Distinct trials: 3; cardable reports: 4.
cards.result: The programme's two questions have opposite answers. On glycaemia, SYNCHRONY showed a clear dose–response (HbA1c −0.36% to −1.35% versus placebo over 16 weeks), albeit largest at doses above the 150 µg taken forward. On outcomes, AleCardio — the only outcomes trial — was stopped early for futility and safety, with a primary-endpoint hazard ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.11, relative) and absolute rates of 9.5% vs 10.0%, alongside more renal dysfunction (7.4% vs 2.7%) and gastrointestinal haemorrhage (2.4% vs 1.7%). The renal study shows the kidney effect is a reversible haemodynamic fall in GFR at supratherapeutic dose, and the exposure–response analysis shows clopidogrel raised aleglitazar exposure — neither changes the outcomes answer. Aleglitazar was never marketed; this shelf is the record of a discontinued dual-PPAR programme.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Evogliptin in type 2 diabetes (single-region evidence — South Korea/India, not FDA/EMA-approved): non-inferior to sitagliptin and linagliptin on HbA1c, and superior to placebo added to dapagliflozin plus metformin; no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (or on metformin-based combinations), does the DPP-4 inhibitor evogliptin, compared with sitagliptin or placebo, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dipeptidyl-Peptidase IV Inhibitors · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Linagliptin · Piperazines · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control, on four randomised trials — with two framings printed on the face: this is SINGLE-REGION evidence (South Korea and India; evogliptin is approved there, not FDA/EMA-approved), and HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint with no cardiovascular-outcomes trial for this agent (class outcomes evidence lives on the sitagliptin/linagliptin shelves and is not re-carded here). Three trials are active-comparator non-inferiority studies: EVERGREEN (207 patients, vs linagliptin — the comparator is linagliptin, printed exactly) found HbA1c −0.85% vs −0.75% (difference −0.10%, 95% CI −0.32 to 0.11, within the 0.4% margin); Hong 2017 (222 patients, added to metformin, vs sitagliptin) found −0.59% vs −0.65% (difference 0.06%, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.22, within the 0.35% margin); EVOLUTION INDIA (184 patients, added to metformin, vs sitagliptin) likewise met non-inferiority at 12 weeks. The fourth is placebo-controlled superiority: added to dapagliflozin plus metformin (283 patients), evogliptin beat placebo by a least-squares mean HbA1c difference of −0.65% at week 24 and −0.55% at week 52. Adverse events and hypoglycaemia were comparable to comparators across the trials.

cards.headline: EVERGREEN (Kim 2020): evogliptin 5 mg was non-inferior to linagliptin 5 mg on HbA1c at 12 weeks (−0.85% vs −0.75%; difference −0.10%) — the comparator is linagliptin
cards.summary: EVERGREEN (Kim 2020): evogliptin 5 mg was non-inferior to linagliptin 5 mg on HbA1c at 12 weeks (−0.85% vs −0.75%; difference −0.10%) — the comparator is linagliptin
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind active-controlled trial with open-label extension (EVERGREEN), evogliptin vs linagliptin for 12 weeks
cards.people: 207 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%–10.0%) randomised 1:1 to evogliptin 5 mg (n=102) or linagliptin 5 mg (n=105) daily for a 12-week double-blind phase, followed by a 12-week open-label extension in which both groups received evogliptin (evogliptin/evogliptin n=95; linagliptin/evogliptin n=92). The primary endpoint was change in HbA1c at week 12; glycaemic variability (mean amplitude of glycaemic excursion, by continuous glucose monitoring) was the secondary endpoint.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change at week 12 was −0.85% on evogliptin and −0.75% on linagliptin: between-group difference −0.10% (95% CI −0.32 to 0.11), meeting non-inferiority against a 0.4% margin. Mean amplitude of glycaemic excursion fell significantly from baseline in both groups (−24.6 mg/dL evogliptin; −16.7 mg/dL linagliptin) without a significant between-group difference. At week 24 the evogliptin/evogliptin group had an HbA1c reduction of −0.94%, with 80.2% below 7.0%. Adverse events were comparable between groups over 24 weeks, with no serious adverse events attributed to evogliptin.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to another DPP-4 inhibitor shows evogliptin works like its class, not that it beats placebo in this trial; the 24-week figures come from an open-label extension in which the comparator group had also switched to evogliptin.
cards.source: Kim G et al. Efficacy and safety of evogliptin treatment in patients with type 2 diabetes: A multicentre, active-controlled, randomized, double-blind study with open-label extension (the EVERGREEN study). Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2020. PMID: 32319168. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Add-on-to-metformin RCT (Hong 2017): evogliptin 5 mg added to metformin was non-inferior to sitagliptin 100 mg on HbA1c at 24 weeks (−0.59% vs −0.65%; difference 0.06%)
cards.summary: Add-on-to-metformin RCT (Hong 2017): evogliptin 5 mg added to metformin was non-inferior to sitagliptin 100 mg on HbA1c at 24 weeks (−0.59% vs −0.65%; difference 0.06%)
cards.type: Phase III multicentre randomised double-blind double-dummy active-controlled trial with open-label extension, evogliptin vs sitagliptin added to metformin (South Korea)
cards.people: 222 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.5%–11%) inadequately controlled on stable metformin (≥1,000 mg/day), randomised 1:1 to add-on evogliptin 5 mg (n=112) or sitagliptin 100 mg (n=110) once daily for a 24-week double-blind double-dummy phase, with a 52-week open-label extension. Non-inferiority required the upper limit of the 95% CI for the HbA1c difference to be below 0.35%.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c changes were −0.59% (evogliptin) and −0.65% (sitagliptin); the between-group difference was 0.06% (95% CI −0.10 to 0.22), demonstrating non-inferiority. After 52 weeks of treatment the evogliptin reduction persisted (−0.44% ± 0.65%, P<.0001, within-group). Both treatments were well tolerated with comparable adverse events; hypoglycaemic events, mostly mild, occurred in 0.9% on evogliptin and 2.8% on sitagliptin over 24 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority design against sitagliptin, an established agent: it places evogliptin within the class effect and cannot show superiority; the 52-week persistence figure is an uncontrolled within-group extension result.
cards.source: Hong SM et al. Efficacy and safety of adding evogliptin versus sitagliptin for metformin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes: A 24-week randomized, controlled trial with open label extension. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2017. PMID: 28058750. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: EVOLUTION INDIA (Ajmani 2019): evogliptin added to metformin was non-inferior to sitagliptin on HbA1c at 12 weeks in Indian patients (adjusted difference −0.022%)
cards.summary: EVOLUTION INDIA (Ajmani 2019): evogliptin added to metformin was non-inferior to sitagliptin on HbA1c at 12 weeks in Indian patients (adjusted difference −0.022%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial, evogliptin vs sitagliptin added to metformin (India)
cards.people: 184 Indian patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7% to <10%) on stable metformin monotherapy (≥1 g/day for at least 8 weeks), randomised to add-on evogliptin 5 mg or sitagliptin 100 mg for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in HbA1c at 12 weeks, with a non-inferiority margin of 0.35%.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c reductions at 12 weeks were −0.37 (SD 1.06) on evogliptin and −0.32 (SD 1.14) on sitagliptin; the adjusted mean difference was −0.022 (95% CI −0.374 to 0.330; P=0.901), demonstrating non-inferiority. Fasting and postprandial glucose reductions and body-weight changes were similar between groups at 12 and 24 weeks; the proportions reaching HbA1c <7.0% were 26.7% (evogliptin) and 20% (sitagliptin). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 52 patients (25% evogliptin, 31.5% sitagliptin) and were generally mild.
cards.watchOut: The absolute HbA1c falls here (−0.37% and −0.32%) are smaller than in the Korean add-on trial and the confidence interval (−0.374 to 0.330) only just fits inside the 0.35% margin — non-inferiority is met, but narrowly and on a 12-week primary endpoint.
cards.source: Ajmani AK et al. Efficacy and safety of evogliptin versus sitagliptin as an add-on therapy in Indian patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus inadequately controlled with metformin: A 24-week randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority, EVOLUTION INDIA study. Diabetes research and clinical practice. 2019. PMID: 31526825. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Placebo-controlled add-on RCT (Moon 2023): evogliptin added to dapagliflozin plus metformin beat placebo on HbA1c by 0.65% at week 24 and 0.55% at week 52
cards.summary: Placebo-controlled add-on RCT (Moon 2023): evogliptin added to dapagliflozin plus metformin beat placebo on HbA1c by 0.65% at week 24 and 0.55% at week 52
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial with extension, evogliptin added to dapagliflozin plus metformin
cards.people: 283 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%–10.5%) inadequately controlled on dapagliflozin 10 mg plus metformin (≥1,000 mg), randomised 1:1 to add-on evogliptin 5 mg or placebo in a 24-week double-blind phase 3 trial with a 28-week extension (52 weeks total). The primary endpoint was the HbA1c difference from baseline at week 24.
cards.result: Evogliptin was superior to placebo: least-squares mean HbA1c differences of −0.65% at week 24 and −0.55% at week 52 (95% CI −0.79 to −0.51 and −0.71 to −0.39; P<0.0001 for both). At week 52, 32.14% on evogliptin versus 8.51% on placebo had HbA1c <7% (odds ratio 5.62, a relative odds measure; P<0.0001). Fasting and mean daily glucose fell significantly and a beta-cell function index improved (least-squares mean difference 9.04; 95% CI 1.86 to 16.21; P=0.0138). Adverse events were similar between groups and no serious adverse drug reactions were reported on evogliptin.
cards.watchOut: This is a triple-therapy add-on read: the effect belongs to evogliptin added to an SGLT2-inhibitor/metformin background, not to evogliptin alone, and the endpoint remains the HbA1c surrogate over 52 weeks.
cards.source: Moon JS et al. Efficacy and Safety of Evogliptin Add-on Therapy to Dapagliflozin/Metformin Combinations in Patients with Poorly Controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A 24-Week Multicenter Randomized Placebo-Controlled Parallel-Design Phase-3 Trial with a 28-Week Extension. Diabetes & metabolism journal. 2023. PMID: 37750183. Registry ID: NCT04170998. cards.headline: Synthesis: evogliptin lowers HbA1c like its class — non-inferior to sitagliptin and linagliptin in three trials and superior to placebo as a third agent — on single-region, surrogate-endpoint evidence with no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: evogliptin lowers HbA1c like its class — non-inferior to sitagliptin and linagliptin in three trials and superior to placebo as a third agent — on single-region, surrogate-endpoint evidence with no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (EVERGREEN, n=207; Hong 2017, n=222; EVOLUTION INDIA, n=184; Moon 2023, n=283).
cards.result: Four randomised trials point the same way: evogliptin 5 mg is non-inferior to sitagliptin (twice, added to metformin) and to linagliptin on HbA1c, and — the shelf's one placebo-controlled superiority result — beats placebo by 0.65% at 24 weeks when added to dapagliflozin plus metformin. Tolerability matched the comparators, with low hypoglycaemia rates. The limits are structural: all four trials are South Korean or Indian (evogliptin is not FDA/EMA-approved), follow-up is 12–52 weeks, and the endpoint is HbA1c, a surrogate; no cardiovascular-outcomes trial of evogliptin exists, and the DPP-4 class outcomes evidence is homed on the sitagliptin and linagliptin shelves, cross-pointed here and not re-carded.

shelves.title: Gemigliptin in type 2 diabetes (renal impairment included): HbA1c −0.66 points vs placebo on dapagliflozin + metformin; no difference vs linagliptin in renal impairment; BALANCE is a combination read
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (including patients with renal impairment and patients on metformin-based combinations), does the DPP-4 inhibitor gemigliptin, compared with sitagliptin, linagliptin or placebo, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Metformin · Hypoglycemic Agents · Glycated Hemoglobin · Blood Glucose · Piperidones · Pyrimidines · Benzhydryl Compounds · Glucosides
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a single-region (South Korea) base with a surrogate endpoint. Gemigliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in South Korea and some other markets, not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent. The one clean placebo-controlled read is SOLUTION: added to dapagliflozin plus metformin, gemigliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.66 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (315 randomised). In renal impairment, the GUARD extension found no significant difference between continued gemigliptin and a switch to linagliptin at 52 weeks (HbA1c reductions 1.00 vs 0.65 points from baseline; between-group P=0.148). BALANCE is carded third and is labelled throughout as a fixed-dose COMBINATION read (gemigliptin/rosuvastatin) — it is not gemigliptin-alone evidence. Adverse-event rates were similar across arms in all three reports.

cards.headline: SOLUTION (Lee 2023): gemigliptin added to dapagliflozin + metformin lowered HbA1c by 0.66 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (least-squares mean difference −0.66%, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.52)
cards.summary: SOLUTION (Lee 2023): gemigliptin added to dapagliflozin + metformin lowered HbA1c by 0.66 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (least-squares mean difference −0.66%, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.52)
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SOLUTION), gemigliptin add-on to dapagliflozin + metformin vs placebo, 24 weeks plus 28-week switch extension
cards.people: 315 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin and dapagliflozin were randomised to gemigliptin 50 mg (n=159) or placebo (n=156) for 24 weeks in this Korean phase III study; after week 24 the placebo group switched to gemigliptin and all patients continued to week 52.
cards.result: At week 24 the least-squares mean difference in HbA1c change was −0.66% (standard error 0.07; 95% CI −0.80% to −0.52%), showing superior HbA1c reduction with gemigliptin. After the placebo group switched to gemigliptin, its HbA1c fell significantly, while the original gemigliptin group's reduction was maintained to week 52. Treatment-emergent adverse events to week 24 occurred in 27.67% (gemigliptin) versus 29.22% (placebo), with no new safety findings, including for hypoglycaemia, after week 24.
cards.watchOut: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; the trial tests gemigliptin as a third agent on top of dapagliflozin plus metformin, not as monotherapy, and the post-week-24 period has no placebo control because the placebo arm switched to gemigliptin.
cards.source: Lee BW et al. Efficacy of Gemigliptin Add-on to Dapagliflozin and Metformin in Type 2 Diabetes Patients: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study (SOLUTION). cards.headline: GUARD extension (Han 2018): in type 2 diabetes with renal impairment, 52 weeks of gemigliptin versus a switch to linagliptin — HbA1c fell in both groups with no significant between-group difference (P=0.148)
cards.summary: GUARD extension (Han 2018): in type 2 diabetes with renal impairment, 52 weeks of gemigliptin versus a switch to linagliptin — HbA1c fell in both groups with no significant between-group difference (P=0.148)
cards.type: 40-week extension of a randomised double-blind study (GUARD), continued gemigliptin vs placebo-to-linagliptin switch, in renal impairment
cards.people: Extension of a randomised study in type 2 diabetes with moderate or severe renal impairment (HbA1c 7% to 11%, eGFR 15 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2): the main 12-week study randomised 66 patients to gemigliptin 50 mg and 66 to placebo; in the 40-week extension, 50 patients continued gemigliptin and 52 patients switched from placebo to linagliptin (102 consented to the extension, 79 completed).
cards.result: At week 52, adjusted mean HbA1c was 1.00% ± 0.21% lower than baseline in the gemigliptin group and 0.65% ± 0.22% lower in the placebo/linagliptin group (P<.001 and P=.003 versus baseline respectively), with no significant difference between groups (P=.148). Fasting glucose, fructosamine and glycated albumin trends were similar; eGFR fell significantly from baseline in both groups with no between-group difference, urinary albumin excretion changed little, and overall adverse-event rates, including hypoglycaemia risk, were similar.
cards.watchOut: An extension report, not a fresh randomisation: only 102 of the original 132 patients entered it and 79 completed, and after week 12 there is no placebo arm — the comparison is gemigliptin against linagliptin, another DPP-4 inhibitor, so it cannot show whether either drug beats no treatment in renal impairment.
cards.source: Han SY et al. Comparative efficacy and safety of gemigliptin versus linagliptin in type 2 diabetes patients with renal impairment: A 40-week extension of the GUARD randomized study. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2018. PMID: 28719008. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BALANCE (Bae 2019) — COMBINATION trial, labelled as such: fixed-dose gemigliptin/rosuvastatin lowered both HbA1c and LDL cholesterol; this is a combination read, not gemigliptin-alone evidence
cards.summary: BALANCE (Bae 2019) — COMBINATION trial, labelled as such: fixed-dose gemigliptin/rosuvastatin lowered both HbA1c and LDL cholesterol; this is a combination read, not gemigliptin-alone evidence
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (BALANCE) of a fixed-dose gemigliptin/rosuvastatin COMBINATION versus each monotherapy — combination evidence, labelled as such
cards.people: 290 patients with type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia at 33 Korean hospitals were randomised 1:1:1 to fixed-dose gemigliptin 50 mg/rosuvastatin 20 mg, gemigliptin 50 mg alone, or rosuvastatin 20 mg alone (rosuvastatin up-titrated from 5 to 20 mg/day) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: At 24 weeks the combination group showed an HbA1c reduction of −0.81% (least-squares mean; P<0.0001 vs the rosuvastatin-alone group) and an LDL-cholesterol percentage reduction of −51.9% (P<0.0001 vs the gemigliptin-alone group). HbA1c fell significantly in both gemigliptin-containing groups, but the reduction was significantly greater with gemigliptin alone than with the combination despite the same gemigliptin dose; the LDL-cholesterol decrease over time was similar in the combination and rosuvastatin-alone groups. Adverse events did not differ significantly among groups.
cards.watchOut: COMBINATION trial: the headline read pairs a glucose drug with a statin, so neither the HbA1c nor the LDL result can be credited to gemigliptin alone; it is carded, labelled as a combination read, only because the commissioning row directs it, and the gemigliptin-alone arm paradoxically lowered HbA1c more than the combination arm.
cards.source: Bae JC et al. Efficacy and safety of fixed-dose combination therapy with gemigliptin (50 mg) and rosuvastatin compared with monotherapy in patients with type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia (BALANCE): A multicentre, randomized, double-blind, controlled, phase 3 trial. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2019. PMID: 30084112. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Teneligliptin in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c 0.71–0.94 points lower than placebo across four East Asian phase 3 trials, alone and added to metformin
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (drug-naïve, on metformin, or on metformin-based combinations), does the DPP-4 inhibitor teneligliptin, compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dipeptidyl-Peptidase IV Inhibitors · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazoles · Thiazolidines
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit for glycaemic control only, on a single-region (East Asian) base with a surrogate endpoint. Teneligliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in Japan, India, Korea and China, not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent. Four randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials agree: teneligliptin 20 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.71 to 0.94 points more than placebo over 16–24 weeks, as monotherapy in Chinese and Korean patients and added to metformin in Chinese and Korean patients. Fasting glucose fell in parallel, and adverse-event and hypoglycaemia rates were similar to placebo in every report.

cards.headline: Phase 3 monotherapy, China (Ji 2021): teneligliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (least-squares mean difference −0.80%, P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Phase 3 monotherapy, China (Ji 2021): teneligliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (least-squares mean difference −0.80%, P<0.0001)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, teneligliptin monotherapy vs placebo, 24 weeks
cards.people: 254 Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise (HbA1c 7.0% to <10.0%, fasting glucose <270 mg/dL) at 42 sites were randomised 1:1 to teneligliptin 20 mg (n=127) or placebo (n=127) once daily for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.95% with teneligliptin versus −0.14% with placebo (difference −0.80%, P<0.0001). Fasting blood glucose changed by −21.9 mg/dL versus −1.4 mg/dL (difference −20.5 mg/dL, P<0.0001). Adverse-event and adverse-drug-reaction rates, including hypoglycaemia, were similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and the population is single-region (China); no outcomes trial exists for teneligliptin.

cards.headline: Phase 3 add-on to metformin, China (Ji 2021): teneligliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.71 points more than placebo at 24 weeks, and 41.7% versus 16.1% reached HbA1c <7.0%

cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, teneligliptin added to metformin vs placebo added to metformin, 24 weeks
cards.people: Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on stable metformin (≥1000 mg/day; HbA1c 7.0% to <10.0%, fasting plasma glucose <270 mg/dL) were randomised to teneligliptin 20 mg once daily or placebo added to metformin for 24 weeks (per-arm numbers not stated in the fetched record).
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change was −0.72% (standard error 0.07) with teneligliptin versus −0.01% (0.07) with placebo — a between-group difference of −0.71% ± 0.11% (P<.0001); the fasting plasma glucose difference was −16.5 ± 4.7 mg/dL (P=.0005). At week 24, 41.7% on teneligliptin versus 16.1% on placebo achieved HbA1c <7.0% (P<.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 58.9% (teneligliptin) versus 68.3% (placebo); the most common were upper respiratory tract infection, hyperuricaemia and hyperlipidaemia.
cards.watchOut: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; single-region (China) population, and the fetched record does not state the per-arm randomised numbers.

cards.people: 142 Korean patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise were randomised 2:1 to teneligliptin 20 mg (n=99) or placebo (n=43) for 24 weeks in this multicentre phase III study.
cards.result: At week 24 the between-group differences in change favoured teneligliptin: HbA1c −0.94% (least-squares mean 95% CI −1.22 to −0.65) and fasting plasma glucose −1.21 mmol/l (≈ −21.8 mg/dL; 95% CI −1.72 to −0.70 mmol/l, ≈ −31.0 to −12.6 mg/dL), all P<0.001. cards.headline: Synthesis: four placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in China and Korea consistently show teneligliptin 20 mg lowers HbA1c by 0.71–0.94 points more than placebo over 16–24 weeks, alone or added to metformin, with placebo-like adverse-event rates
cards.summary: Synthesis: four placebo-controlled phase 3 trials in China and Korea consistently show teneligliptin 20 mg lowers HbA1c by 0.71–0.94 points more than placebo over 16–24 weeks, alone or added to metformin, with placebo-like adverse-event rates
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The direction and size of the HbA1c effect are consistent across monotherapy (China −0.80, Korea −0.94 points versus placebo) and metformin add-on settings (China −0.71, Korea −0.78 points), with parallel fasting-glucose reductions and no excess hypoglycaemia or adverse events. All evidence is East Asian, HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint, follow-up is at most 24 weeks, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for teneligliptin, which is not FDA/EMA-approved.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Anagliptin in type 2 diabetes: HbA1c −0.80 points vs placebo on metformin + empagliflozin; REASON is open-label with an LDL endpoint (−4.5 mg/dL vs sitagliptin)
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the DPP-4 inhibitor anagliptin, compared with sitagliptin or placebo (alone, with metformin, or added to metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor), improve glycaemic control and glycaemic variability?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cholesterol, LDL · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines · Sitagliptin Phosphate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a single-region (Japan/Korea) base with surrogate endpoints. Anagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor approved in Japan, not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent. The REASON trial is OPEN-LABEL with an LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint — labelled as such on its card and here: anagliptin lowered LDL cholesterol by 4.5 mg/dL more than sitagliptin over 52 weeks, with HbA1c non-inferior (a secondary endpoint). A small double-blind trial found the twice-daily anagliptin regimen improved glycaemic variability (MAGE, post-dinner time in range) more than once-daily sitagliptin, with no HbA1c difference. The strongest glycaemic read is the 2026 phase 3 trial: added to metformin plus empagliflozin, anagliptin lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points more than placebo at 24 weeks.

cards.headline: REASON (Morimoto 2019) — OPEN-LABEL trial with an LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint: anagliptin lowered LDL-C by 4.5 mg/dL more than sitagliptin at 52 weeks (estimated difference −4.5 mg/dL, P=0.01 for superiority); its HbA1c data are secondary
cards.summary: REASON (Morimoto 2019) — OPEN-LABEL trial with an LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint: anagliptin lowered LDL-C by 4.5 mg/dL more than sitagliptin at 52 weeks (estimated difference −4.5 mg/dL, P=0.01 for superiority); its HbA1c data are secondary
cards.type: 52-week OPEN-LABEL randomised trial (REASON), anagliptin vs sitagliptin, LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint (glycaemic data secondary) — design and endpoint labelled as directed
cards.people: 353 eligible participants (of 380 enrolled) with type 2 diabetes, atherosclerotic vascular lesions and a statin prescription were randomised at 17 Japanese centres to anagliptin or sitagliptin for 52 weeks; mean age 68 years, 61% men, baseline median LDL cholesterol 108 mg/dL and HbA1c 6.9%.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol changed by −3.7 mg/dL with anagliptin versus +2.1 mg/dL with sitagliptin (estimated treatment difference −4.5 mg/dL, P=0.01 for superiority on the primary endpoint). HbA1c — a secondary endpoint — changed by +0.02% with anagliptin versus +0.12% with sitagliptin (P<0.0001 for non-inferiority).
cards.watchOut: OPEN-LABEL with an LDL-cholesterol primary endpoint: the absolute LDL difference is small (−4.5 mg/dL against a baseline median of 108 mg/dL), participants were already statin-treated with near-target HbA1c (median 6.9%), and the glycaemic comparison is a secondary non-inferiority read, not a test of glucose lowering.

cards.headline: Glycaemic variability RCT (Lee 2023): anagliptin 100 mg twice daily reduced MAGE more than sitagliptin 100 mg once daily (−30.4 vs −9.5 mg/dL) and raised post-dinner time in range more, with no difference in HbA1c change
cards.summary: Glycaemic variability RCT (Lee 2023): anagliptin 100 mg twice daily reduced MAGE more than sitagliptin 100 mg once daily (−30.4 vs −9.5 mg/dL) and raised post-dinner time in range more, with no difference in HbA1c change
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled trial, anagliptin twice daily vs sitagliptin once daily (both on metformin), glycaemic-variability endpoints, 12 weeks
cards.people: 89 patients with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin alone (HbA1c >6.5% and <8.5%) were randomised 1:1 to anagliptin 100 mg twice daily or sitagliptin 100 mg once daily for 12 weeks, with continuous glucose monitoring before and after treatment.
cards.result: The decrease in mean amplitude of glycaemic excursion (MAGE) was significantly greater with anagliptin twice daily than sitagliptin once daily (P<.05): −30.4 ± 25.6 mg/dL (P<.001 within group) versus −9.5 ± 38.0 mg/dL (P=.215). Post-dinner time in range rose by 33.0% ± 22.0% versus 14.6% ± 28.2% (between-group P=.009). Changes in HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: A regimen comparison (twice-daily anagliptin against once-daily sitagliptin), not anagliptin against placebo: the variability advantage may reflect dosing frequency, the trial is small (n=89) and short (12 weeks), and HbA1c did not differ.

cards.headline: Phase 3 add-on trial (Moon 2026): anagliptin added to metformin + empagliflozin 25 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (difference −0.80%, 95% CI −0.95 to −0.64)
cards.summary: Phase 3 add-on trial (Moon 2026): anagliptin added to metformin + empagliflozin 25 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.80 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (difference −0.80%, 95% CI −0.95 to −0.64)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, anagliptin added to metformin + empagliflozin vs placebo, 24 weeks plus 28-week open-label extension
cards.people: 200 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (≥1000 mg/day) plus empagliflozin 25 mg/day (HbA1c 7.0–11.0%; baseline HbA1c 7.76%) were randomised 1:1 to anagliptin 100 mg twice daily or placebo for 24 weeks, followed by a 28-week open-label extension; 197 were analysed.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.83% with anagliptin versus −0.03% with placebo (difference −0.80%; 95% CI −0.95 to −0.64; P<0.0001). HOMA-β changed by +10.45 versus −6.02 (between-group difference 16.46, P=0.0003). Adverse events were similar between groups, with no severe hypoglycaemia or deaths.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled read is the 24-week period only (the extension is open-label); HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and this is a triple-therapy intensification setting, not monotherapy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: anagliptin's clean glycaemic evidence is one placebo-controlled add-on trial (−0.80 HbA1c points on metformin + empagliflozin); REASON is open-label with an LDL primary endpoint and a small absolute difference, and the variability trial compares dosing regimens, not drug against placebo

cards.result: Anagliptin lowered HbA1c versus placebo when added to metformin plus empagliflozin (Moon 2026), was non-inferior to sitagliptin for HbA1c while lowering LDL cholesterol slightly more in the open-label REASON trial (primary endpoint LDL cholesterol, difference −4.5 mg/dL), and its twice-daily regimen improved continuous-glucose-monitoring variability measures more than once-daily sitagliptin without an HbA1c difference. All evidence is Japanese/Korean, endpoints are surrogates, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for anagliptin, which is not FDA/EMA-approved.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits — in particular REASON's open-label design and LDL primary endpoint; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Harmonised testosterone interval: 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L) in non-obese men 19–39 — the interval slice pack #7072 (diurnal rhythm) does not give
shelves.question: In healthy men, what is the reference interval for serum total testosterone measured by harmonised / standardised assays — the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range in non-obese young men and its decline across adult age bands — and how much do assay calibration and population (obesity exclusion, ancestry) move the lower limit used to define hypogonadism?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the harmonised interval. PARTIAL shelf: pack #7072 homes the DIURNAL RHYTHM of testosterone (morning peak to afternoon nadir) — a rhythm is not an interval, and #7072 gives no 2.5th–97.5th percentile reference range. This shelf cards ONLY the reference-interval slice and cross-points #7072 in prose for sampling time; the rhythm is not re-carded. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, male reproductive hormone chapters, and Ganong, gonadal physiology (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary reference-range literature). The harmonised range: in healthy non-obese men aged 19–39, cross-calibrated to the CDC reference method across four US/European cohorts (9,054 men), the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles are 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L), median 531 ng/dL (18.4 nmol/L) (Travison 2017). Age moves the whole distribution down: 27,687 Korean men aged ≥40 averaged 4.8 ± 1.8 ng/mL (480 ng/dL (16.7 nmol/L)), declining ≈0.021 ng/mL per year (2.1 ng/dL/year (0.07 nmol/L/year)), with biochemical hypogonadism (<2.5 ng/mL = 250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L)) rising from 5.5% at 40–49 to 11.6% at ≥70 (Kim 2026). Symptom-anchored thresholds in Han Chinese men cluster higher than the harmonised lower limit (≈12.55–14.35 nmol/L (362–414 ng/dL) for individual sexual symptoms; Liu 2016) — a threshold-for-symptoms is a different kind of number from a population percentile, and the two are never merged here. Morning sampling underlies the harmonised range; for the size of the morning-to-evening fall see pack #7072.

cards.headline: Harmonised reference range (4 cohorts, 9,054 men; assays cross-calibrated to the CDC reference method): in healthy non-obese men aged 19–39 the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles are 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L), median 531 ng/dL (18.4 nmol/L) (Travison 2017)
cards.summary: Harmonised reference range (4 cohorts, 9,054 men; assays cross-calibrated to the CDC reference method): in healthy non-obese men aged 19–39 the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles are 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L), median 531 ng/dL (18.4 nmol/L) (Travison 2017)
cards.type: Primary physiology / reference-range study (harmonised multi-cohort, CDC reference method)
cards.people: 9,054 community-dwelling men in four US and European cohort studies (Framingham Heart Study; European Male Aging Study; Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study; Male Sibling Study of Osteoporosis). Testosterone in 100 participants per cohort was measured by the CDC reference method; Passing-Bablok normalising equations converted cohort assays to harmonised values, from which age-specific reference ranges were derived.
cards.result: Harmonisation reduced intercohort variation between measurements in men of similar ages. In healthy non-obese men aged 19–39, the harmonised 2.5th, 5th, 50th, 95th and 97.5th percentile values were 264, 303, 531, 852 and 916 ng/dL (9.2, 10.5, 18.4, 29.6 and 31.8 nmol/L) respectively. Age-specific harmonised concentrations in non-obese men were similar across cohorts and greater than in all men. The authors conclude a substantial proportion of intercohort variation in testosterone levels is due to assay differences, and that harmonised ranges can be applied to assays calibrated to a reference method and calibrator.
cards.watchOut: The 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L) range belongs to NON-OBESE men aged 19–39 on harmonised assays: applying its lower limit to older or obese men, or to an uncalibrated local assay, re-creates exactly the assay variation this study removed.
cards.source: Travison TG et al. Harmonized Reference Ranges for Circulating Testosterone Levels in Men of Four Cohort Studies in the United States and Europe. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2017. PMID: 28324103. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nationwide Korean data (27,687 men aged ≥40, morning samples): mean testosterone 4.8 ± 1.8 ng/mL (480 ng/dL (16.7 nmol/L)), falling ≈0.021 ng/mL per year (P < 0.001); biochemical hypogonadism (<250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L)) rose from 5.5% at 40–49 to 11.6% at ≥70 years (Kim 2026)
cards.summary: Nationwide Korean data (27,687 men aged ≥40, morning samples): mean testosterone 4.8 ± 1.8 ng/mL (480 ng/dL (16.7 nmol/L)), falling ≈0.021 ng/mL per year (P < 0.001); biochemical hypogonadism (<250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L)) rose from 5.5% at 40–49 to 11.6% at ≥70 years (Kim 2026)
cards.type: Primary physiology / population distribution study (Korean nationwide health-examination cohort)
cards.people: 27,687 men aged ≥40 who underwent routine health examinations at 20 hospitals across South Korea (2015–2024); men on testosterone therapy or androgen-affecting medication, or with orchiectomy, chemotherapy or testicular radiation, were excluded. Morning serum testosterone by chemiluminescent immunoassay; biochemical hypogonadism defined as total testosterone <2.5 ng/mL (250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L)). This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Mean testosterone was 4.8 ± 1.8 ng/mL (480 ng/dL (16.7 nmol/L)), with a significant linear decline of approximately 0.021 ng/mL per year (2.1 ng/dL/year (0.07 nmol/L/year); P < 0.001). Biochemical hypogonadism prevalence rose from 5.5% (ages 40–49) to 11.6% (≥70 years). In multivariable analysis, higher BMI, fasting glucose and triglycerides were independently associated with lower testosterone; PSA, HDL and LDL were not significant.
cards.watchOut: A health-examination cohort aged ≥40 on a single immunoassay platform, not a harmonised-assay reference sample: its 250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L) hypogonadism cut-off is a study definition, and its absolute levels are not interchangeable with the CDC-harmonised range on the card above.
cards.source: Kim TH et al. Age-Related Testosterone Decline and Metabolic Determinants in 27,687 Korean Men Aged ≥40 Years: A Nationwide Population-Based Study. The world journal of men's health. 2026. PMID: 42220225. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Han Chinese community sample (944 men aged 40–79): sexual-symptom thresholds for total testosterone were ≈12.55 nmol/L (362 ng/dL) for sexual activity and morning erections and 14.35 nmol/L (414 ng/dL) for libido; late-onset hypogonadism prevalence 9.1% on combined symptom + level criteria (Liu 2016)
cards.summary: Han Chinese community sample (944 men aged 40–79): sexual-symptom thresholds for total testosterone were ≈12.55 nmol/L (362 ng/dL) for sexual activity and morning erections and 14.35 nmol/L (414 ng/dL) for libido; late-onset hypogonadism prevalence 9.1% on combined symptom + level criteria (Liu 2016)
cards.type: Supporting limb: symptom-threshold study (community sample of Han Chinese men)
cards.people: 944 Han Chinese men aged 40–79 randomly selected from nine urban communities; total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin measured, calculated free testosterone derived, and the Aging Male Symptoms questionnaire administered. Three sexual symptoms (decreased ability/frequency of sexual activity, decreased morning erections, decreased libido) were confirmed as related to total and free testosterone.
cards.result: Total-testosterone thresholds were approximately 12.55 nmol/L (362 ng/dL) for decreased ability/frequency to perform sex, 12.55 nmol/L (362 ng/dL) for decreased frequency of morning erections, and 14.35 nmol/L (414 ng/dL) for decreased sexual desire; calculated free-testosterone thresholds were 281.14, 264.90 and 287.21 pmol/L respectively. Total testosterone <13.21 nmol/L (381 ng/dL) (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.0–1.9; P = 0.037) or calculated free testosterone <268.89 pmol/L (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1–20, as printed; P = 0.020) was associated with having all three symptoms. Prevalence of late-onset hypogonadism under the combined criteria was 9.1%.
cards.watchOut: These are thresholds at which symptoms become more common, not population percentiles — they sit above the harmonised 2.5th percentile by design, and the odds ratios are relative measures with confidence intervals that include near-null values; free-testosterone values depend on the calculation method and are carded as published only.
cards.source: Liu ZY et al. Identification of late-onset hypogonadism in middle-aged and elderly men from a community of China. Asian journal of andrology. 2016. PMID: 26354142. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the harmonised interval for non-obese young men is 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L); the distribution then slides down with age and metabolic load, while symptom-based thresholds sit well above the percentile lower limit — three different kinds of number, kept separate
cards.summary: Synthesis: the harmonised interval for non-obese young men is 264–916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L); the distribution then slides down with age and metabolic load, while symptom-based thresholds sit well above the percentile lower limit — three different kinds of number, kept separate
cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (male reproductive hormones) and Ganong (gonadal physiology) — framing brief. Travison 2017 supplies the interval itself, on CDC-harmonised assays; Kim 2026 (n=27,687) sizes the adult decline (≈2.1 ng/dL/year (0.07 nmol/L/year) after 40) and the rising prevalence below 250 ng/dL (8.7 nmol/L); Liu 2016 shows why a symptom threshold (≈362–414 ng/dL (12.55–14.35 nmol/L)) cannot be substituted for the 2.5th percentile (264 ng/dL (9.2 nmol/L)). Sampling time is part of the measurement — morning sampling underlies these data; the diurnal rhythm itself is homed at pack #7072 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the harmonised interval slice carded here.
cards.watchOut: If pack #7072 is ever widened from the diurnal rhythm to all testosterone measurement physiology, this shelf collapses into it; until then the interval and the rhythm are separate homes by design.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Trelagliptin (once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor, Japan): non-inferior to daily alogliptin, and HbA1c −0.72% vs placebo in severe renal impairment and −0.63% added to insulin — surrogate endpoints only
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (including patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease, and patients inadequately controlled on insulin), does the once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor trelagliptin, compared with daily alogliptin or placebo, improve glycaemic control?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Single-region evidence — every trial is Japanese, and trelagliptin is approved in Japan as a once-weekly agent, not FDA/EMA-approved; that flag leads this shelf. On the surrogate endpoint HbA1c, three randomised trials are consistent: trelagliptin 100 mg weekly was non-inferior to alogliptin 25 mg daily over 24 weeks (HbA1c change −0.33% vs −0.45%; difference 0.11%, 95% CI −0.054 to 0.281, against a 0.4% margin; Inagaki 2015); trelagliptin 25 mg beat placebo in severe renal impairment / end-stage renal disease (−0.71% vs +0.01%; difference −0.72%, P < 0.0001; Kaku 2020); and trelagliptin 100 mg added to insulin beat placebo (least-squares mean difference −0.63%, P < 0.0001) with no severe hypoglycaemia (Kaku 2018). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and NO cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists for this agent — both facts are printed here, not buried. The stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher, because the base is one region, one development programme and surrogate outcomes only.

cards.headline: Phase 3 non-inferiority trial (243 analysed): trelagliptin 100 mg once weekly matched alogliptin 25 mg daily — HbA1c −0.33% vs −0.45%, difference 0.11% (95% CI −0.054 to 0.281) against a 0.4% margin (Inagaki 2015)
cards.summary: Phase 3 non-inferiority trial (243 analysed): trelagliptin 100 mg once weekly matched alogliptin 25 mg daily — HbA1c −0.33% vs −0.45%, difference 0.11% (95% CI −0.054 to 0.281) against a 0.4% margin (Inagaki 2015)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (trelagliptin weekly vs alogliptin daily vs placebo)
cards.people: 357 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise were enrolled at 26 sites in Japan; 243 were analysed (101 trelagliptin 100 mg weekly, 92 alogliptin 25 mg daily, 50 placebo) in a 24-week double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled design.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change was −0.33% (SE 0.059) on trelagliptin and −0.45% (SE 0.061) on alogliptin; the difference (trelagliptin minus alogliptin) was 0.11% (95% CI −0.054 to 0.281), inside the 0.4% non-inferiority margin. Both active groups reduced HbA1c significantly versus placebo (P < 0.0001). Adverse-event frequency was similar between groups; no hypoglycaemia was reported with trelagliptin.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to another DPP-4 inhibitor on a surrogate endpoint over 24 weeks, in one country's population: it shows the weekly agent is not worse than the daily one by more than 0.4% HbA1c — nothing about outcomes.

cards.headline: Phase 3 trial in severe renal impairment / ESRD (107 randomised): trelagliptin 25 mg lowered HbA1c −0.71% vs +0.01% on placebo at 12 weeks (difference −0.72%, P < 0.0001) (Kaku 2020)
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial in severe renal impairment / ESRD (107 randomised): trelagliptin 25 mg lowered HbA1c −0.71% vs +0.01% on placebo at 12 weeks (difference −0.72%, P < 0.0001) (Kaku 2020)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (trelagliptin 25 mg vs placebo, severe renal impairment / ESRD)
cards.people: 107 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes and severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min) or end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis, on diet/exercise with or without one antidiabetic drug: 55 randomised to trelagliptin 25 mg (A/A) and 52 to placebo (P/A) for a 12-week double-blind phase, followed by 40 weeks of open-label trelagliptin for all.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at the end of the double-blind phase was −0.71% (95% CI −0.885 to −0.542) on trelagliptin and +0.01% (95% CI −0.170 to 0.183) on placebo — difference −0.72% (95% CI −0.966 to −0.473; P < 0.0001). The placebo group caught up once switched to trelagliptin, and levels stayed comparable to week 52. Treatment-emergent adverse events in the double-blind phase: 72.7% (A/A) vs 61.5% (P/A), mostly mild-to-moderate; serious events 7.3% vs 3.8%.
cards.watchOut: The renal dose tested is 25 mg weekly, a quarter of the standard dose — do not read this card as evidence for 100 mg in renal impairment; the double-blind phase is only 12 weeks and the population is small and high-risk at baseline.

cards.headline: Phase IV add-on-to-insulin trial (240 randomised): trelagliptin 100 mg with insulin lowered HbA1c by a least-squares mean difference of −0.63% vs placebo (P < 0.0001), with no severe hypoglycaemia (Kaku 2018)
cards.summary: Phase IV add-on-to-insulin trial (240 randomised): trelagliptin 100 mg with insulin lowered HbA1c by a least-squares mean difference of −0.63% vs placebo (P < 0.0001), with no severe hypoglycaemia (Kaku 2018)
cards.type: Phase IV randomised double-blind trial (trelagliptin add-on to insulin vs placebo)
cards.people: 240 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 7.5–10.0% on 8–40 units of insulin per day, randomised to insulin plus trelagliptin 100 mg weekly (n=116) or insulin plus placebo (n=124) for a 12-week double-blind phase, then 40 weeks of open-label trelagliptin for all.
cards.result: HbA1c fell significantly more on trelagliptin than placebo at the end of the double-blind phase (least-squares mean difference −0.63%, 95% CI −0.83 to −0.44; P < 0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events: 44.0% on trelagliptin vs 47.6% on placebo. No patient experienced severe hypoglycaemia during trelagliptin treatment, and long-term treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week double-blind surrogate-endpoint phase: 'no severe hypoglycaemia' over 12 weeks in 116 exposed patients does not exclude uncommon hypoglycaemia risk on insulin combinations in wider use.
cards.source: Kaku K et al. Efficacy and safety of trelagliptin in combination with insulin therapy in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes: Results from a randomized, Phase IV study. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2018. PMID: 29862617. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: once-weekly trelagliptin lowers HbA1c as a daily DPP-4 inhibitor does, and beats placebo in renal impairment and on insulin — a consistent surrogate-endpoint record from one Japanese programme, with no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: once-weekly trelagliptin lowers HbA1c as a daily DPP-4 inhibitor does, and beats placebo in renal impairment and on insulin — a consistent surrogate-endpoint record from one Japanese programme, with no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three randomised trials, three settings, one direction: non-inferior to alogliptin in diet/exercise-controlled patients (−0.33% vs −0.45%), superior to placebo in severe renal impairment/ESRD (−0.72% difference) and as add-on to insulin (−0.63% difference). No trial measured cardiovascular or other clinical outcomes, all participants were Japanese, and the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real, replicated glycaemic efficacy on a surrogate endpoint, from a single-region programme with no outcomes evidence.
cards.watchOut: Weekly dosing is the intervention's point (adherence convenience); none of these trials measured whether weekly dosing actually improves adherence or outcomes versus a daily agent in practice.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Mitiglinide in type 2 diabetes: matched nateglinide in two trials and lowered HbA1c −0.45%/−0.67% added to pioglitazone — Japan/China evidence, surrogate endpoints only
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the rapid-acting insulin secretagogue mitiglinide, compared with nateglinide or added to pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control (fasting and postprandial glucose, HbA1c)?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Single-region evidence (Japan/China; mitiglinide is not FDA/EMA-approved) — that flag leads this shelf. The meglitinide class home is pack #2886, whose question names repaglinide and nateglinide only; mitiglinide is not carded there and this agent question is unasked there — #2886 is cross-pointed in prose, its studies are not re-carded here. Three randomised trials: mitiglinide 10–20 mg three times daily was non-inferior in effect to nateglinide 120 mg three times daily over 20 weeks (HbA1c −0.77% vs −0.71%; Gao 2009, n=291); in newly diagnosed patients the HbA1c fall was numerically larger on mitiglinide (−1.11% vs −0.76%) but not statistically significant (P = 0.06), with hypoglycaemic episodes in 2.8% on nateglinide and none on mitiglinide (Li 2012, n=225); and added to pioglitazone, mitiglinide 5 mg and 10 mg lowered HbA1c −0.45% and −0.67% vs −0.02% on pioglitazone alone (both P < 0.001; Kaku 2009, n=381). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists — printed here. Mitiglinide/voglibose fixed-dose-combination reports are a combination question and are NOT carded on this shelf.

cards.headline: Multicentre non-inferiority trial in China (n=291): mitiglinide 10–20 mg three times daily matched nateglinide 120 mg three times daily — HbA1c at week 20 −0.77% vs −0.71% (Gao 2009)
cards.summary: Multicentre non-inferiority trial in China (n=291): mitiglinide 10–20 mg three times daily matched nateglinide 120 mg three times daily — HbA1c at week 20 −0.77% vs −0.71% (Gao 2009)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (mitiglinide vs nateglinide)
cards.people: 291 Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise; mitiglinide started at 10 mg three times daily for 12 weeks, increasable to 20 mg three times daily thereafter, versus nateglinide 120 mg three times daily, for 20 weeks, double-blind.
cards.result: HbA1c change at week 12 was −0.53 ± 1.08% on mitiglinide and −0.58 ± 1.04% on nateglinide, deepening by week 20 to −0.77 ± 1.06% and −0.71 ± 1.12% versus baseline. The intergroup difference was 0.05% (95% CI −0.19 to 0.30) at week 12 and 0.06% (95% CI −0.31 to 0.19, as printed) at week 20. Similar changes were seen in patients with baseline HbA1c <8.0% and in those aged ≥60. Adverse events: 54.5% on mitiglinide vs 57.9% on nateglinide. The authors conclude mitiglinide provided similar blood glucose control to nateglinide.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence to nateglinide — itself a modest-efficacy agent — on HbA1c: 'as good as nateglinide' is the whole claim, and the week-20 confidence interval is reproduced as printed in the record.
cards.source: Gao X et al. Multicentre, double-blind, randomized study of mitiglinide compared with nateglinide in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients in China. The Journal of international medical research. 2009. PMID: 19589264. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Newly diagnosed patients (n=225): HbA1c fell −1.11% on mitiglinide vs −0.76% on nateglinide — a numerical, NOT statistically significant, difference (P = 0.06); hypoglycaemic episodes in 2.8% on nateglinide and none on mitiglinide (Li 2012)
cards.summary: Newly diagnosed patients (n=225): HbA1c fell −1.11% on mitiglinide vs −0.76% on nateglinide — a numerical, NOT statistically significant, difference (P = 0.06); hypoglycaemic episodes in 2.8% on nateglinide and none on mitiglinide (Li 2012)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (mitiglinide vs nateglinide, newly diagnosed)
cards.people: 225 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 7–10% after 3 months of diet and exercise, randomised to mitiglinide (n=111, 5–20 mg per meal) or nateglinide (n=114, 60–120 mg per meal) for 16 weeks, double-blind.
cards.result: Baseline HbA1c was 8.2% and 8.3% in the two groups. At study end the HbA1c reduction was slightly greater on mitiglinide (−1.11%) than nateglinide (−0.76%) but not statistically significant (P = 0.06). Final fasting and postprandial glucose were comparable. Hypoglycaemic episodes occurred in 2.8% of nateglinide-treated subjects and none on mitiglinide. The authors conclude the two agents had similar effects on fasting glucose, postprandial glucose and HbA1c.
cards.watchOut: The headline numerical gap (−1.11% vs −0.76%) is a non-significant difference (P = 0.06) and must never be quoted as mitiglinide superiority; zero hypoglycaemia in 111 patients over 16 weeks does not exclude the class risk.
cards.source: Li L et al. Efficacy and safety of mitiglinide versus nateglinide in newly diagnose patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a randomized double blind trial. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2012. PMID: 21895920. Registry ID: none in the record.
