cards.headline: Add-on to pioglitazone (381 randomised): mitiglinide 5 mg and 10 mg three times daily lowered HbA1c −0.45% and −0.67% vs −0.02% on pioglitazone alone (both P < 0.001) (Kaku 2009)
cards.summary: Add-on to pioglitazone (381 randomised): mitiglinide 5 mg and 10 mg three times daily lowered HbA1c −0.45% and −0.67% vs −0.02% on pioglitazone alone (both P < 0.001) (Kaku 2009)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (mitiglinide add-on to pioglitazone vs pioglitazone alone)
cards.people: 381 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on pioglitazone 15–30 mg/day (after a 4-week diet-plus-pioglitazone run-in), randomised to additional mitiglinide 5 mg or 10 mg three times daily or placebo three times daily for 16 weeks, double-blind.
cards.result: HbA1c change (mean ± SD) was −0.02 ± 0.60% on pioglitazone alone and −0.45 ± 0.77% and −0.67 ± 0.59% in the mitiglinide 5 mg and 10 mg combination groups (both P < 0.001 vs pioglitazone alone). Significantly more patients achieved HbA1c targets in the combination groups (P < 0.001), and fasting and postprandial glucose improved significantly. No increase in adverse events was noted with the combination; hypoglycaemic events were infrequent and similar across groups, and weight gain and oedema presented no clinical problem.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is continuing a failing monotherapy, so the −0.45%/−0.67% figures measure add-on effect against no change, not against any active alternative add-on agent.
cards.source: Kaku K et al. Addition of mitiglinide to pioglitazone monotherapy improves overall glycemic control in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized double blind trial. Endocrine journal. 2009. PMID: 19352048. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: mitiglinide matches nateglinide head-to-head in two trials and adds a real HbA1c effect on top of pioglitazone — a coherent surrogate-endpoint record for a single-region secretagogue with no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: mitiglinide matches nateglinide head-to-head in two trials and adds a real HbA1c effect on top of pioglitazone — a coherent surrogate-endpoint record for a single-region secretagogue with no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Two head-to-head trials (n=291 and n=225) find mitiglinide and nateglinide glycaemically similar — the second trial's numerical mitiglinide advantage was not significant (P = 0.06) and is not claimed. The pioglitazone add-on trial (n=381) shows a dose-ordered placebo-controlled effect (−0.45% at 5 mg, −0.67% at 10 mg). The class question (repaglinide/nateglinide) is homed at pack #2886, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) — replicated HbA1c efficacy on a surrogate endpoint, single-region (Japan/China), not FDA/EMA-approved, no outcomes evidence.

This shelf cards only the glycaemic programme: exactly 2 publications reporting 4 distinct phase 3 trials (AMPLITUDE-M, -D, -L, -S) — the report count is stated exactly, per the row's flag. AMPLITUDE-M (monotherapy vs placebo): least-squares mean HbA1c reductions superior to placebo at every dose at week 30 (−0.5%, −0.8%, −1.0% at 2, 4, 6 mg). AMPLITUDE-D: non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg (treatment differences −0.03% at 4 mg, −0.08% at 6 mg). AMPLITUDE-L and -S: numerically greater HbA1c and weight reductions than placebo at all doses. Two facts lead the face alongside the efficacy: all three trials in the 2023 report were TERMINATED EARLY BY THE SPONSOR FOR FUNDING REASONS, not safety or efficacy; and efpeglenatide was NEVER MARKETED (development discontinued). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; hypoglycaemia level 2 (<54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)) was reported in few participants; gastrointestinal events were the most frequent adverse events, consistent with the GLP-1 class.

cards.headline: AMPLITUDE-M phase 3 monotherapy trial: once-weekly efpeglenatide beat placebo at every dose at week 30 — HbA1c least-squares mean reductions −0.5% (2 mg), −0.8% (4 mg) and −1.0% (6 mg) vs placebo (Frias 2022)
cards.summary: AMPLITUDE-M phase 3 monotherapy trial: once-weekly efpeglenatide beat placebo at every dose at week 30 — HbA1c least-squares mean reductions −0.5% (2 mg), −0.8% (4 mg) and −1.0% (6 mg) vs placebo (Frias 2022)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (AMPLITUDE-M: efpeglenatide monotherapy vs placebo)
cards.people: Adults with type 2 diabetes suboptimally controlled with diet and exercise alone, randomised to once-weekly efpeglenatide 2, 4 or 6 mg or placebo for up to 56 weeks in a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial; baseline HbA1c 8.1%. The fetched record does not print the randomised N, and this card claims none.
cards.result: At week 30, HbA1c fell from 8.1% at baseline to 6.9%, 6.6% and 6.4% on efpeglenatide 2, 4 and 6 mg respectively. Least-squares mean reductions were statistically superior to placebo for each dose (2 mg, −0.5% (95% CI −0.9 to −0.2; P = 0.0054); 4 mg, −0.8% (−1.2 to −0.5; P < 0.0001); 6 mg, −1.0% (−1.4 to −0.7; P < 0.0001)). A greater proportion on efpeglenatide achieved HbA1c <7% versus placebo (P < 0.0001 for all doses), and body weight and fasting plasma glucose fell significantly at 4 and 6 mg (P < 0.05). Gastrointestinal adverse events were most common, generally transient and mild/moderate; few patients reported hypoglycaemia.
cards.watchOut: The primary comparison is at week 30 of a planned 56-week trial in diet/exercise-only patients — the easiest population in the programme; effect sizes here are the programme's ceiling, not its average.
cards.source: Frias JP et al. Efficacy and Safety of Once-Weekly Efpeglenatide Monotherapy Versus Placebo in Type 2 Diabetes: The AMPLITUDE-M Randomized Controlled Trial. Diabetes care. 2022. PMID: 35671039. Registry ID: NCT03353350. cards.headline: AMPLITUDE-D: efpeglenatide added to metformin was non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg for HbA1c reduction to week 56 — treatment differences −0.03% (4 mg) and −0.08% (6 mg), with ≈3 kg weight loss in all groups (Aroda 2023, trial 1 of 3 in this report)
cards.summary: AMPLITUDE-D: efpeglenatide added to metformin was non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg for HbA1c reduction to week 56 — treatment differences −0.03% (4 mg) and −0.08% (6 mg), with ≈3 kg weight loss in all groups (Aroda 2023, trial 1 of 3 in this report)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (AMPLITUDE-D: efpeglenatide vs dulaglutide, add-on to metformin) — one of three trials in this publication
cards.people: People with type 2 diabetes suboptimally controlled on metformin, in a phase 3 multicentre randomised trial of once-weekly efpeglenatide 4 or 6 mg versus dulaglutide 1.5 mg. This trial was terminated early by the sponsor because of funding rather than safety or efficacy concerns (see the synthesis card). The fetched record does not print the randomised N, and this card claims none.
cards.result: Non-inferiority of efpeglenatide to dulaglutide 1.5 mg was shown for HbA1c reduction from baseline to week 56: least-squares mean treatment difference −0.03% (95% CI −0.20 to 0.14) at 4 mg and −0.08% (−0.25 to 0.09) at 6 mg. Body-weight reductions (approximately 3 kg) to week 56 were similar across all treatment groups. ADA level 2 hypoglycaemia (<54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)) was reported in ≤1% of participants. Gastrointestinal adverse events were most frequent, consistent with other GLP-1 receptor agonists.
cards.watchOut: One publication reports three trials; this card is the AMPLITUDE-D slice only and must not be counted as a separate publication from the AMPLITUDE-L/-S card below — the programme's report count is 2 publications / 4 trials, stated on the face.

cards.headline: AMPLITUDE-L and AMPLITUDE-S: efpeglenatide beat placebo numerically on HbA1c and weight at all doses — added to basal insulin ± oral agents (L) and to metformin ± sulphonylurea (S) (Aroda 2023, trials 2 and 3 in this report)
cards.summary: AMPLITUDE-L and AMPLITUDE-S: efpeglenatide beat placebo numerically on HbA1c and weight at all doses — added to basal insulin ± oral agents (L) and to metformin ± sulphonylurea (S) (Aroda 2023, trials 2 and 3 in this report)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trials (AMPLITUDE-L and AMPLITUDE-S: efpeglenatide vs placebo) — two of three trials in this publication
cards.people: People with type 2 diabetes suboptimally controlled on basal insulin with or without oral glucose-lowering drugs (AMPLITUDE-L) or on metformin with or without a sulphonylurea (AMPLITUDE-S), in two phase 3 multicentre randomised trials of once-weekly efpeglenatide versus placebo. Both trials were terminated early by the sponsor because of funding rather than safety or efficacy concerns. The fetched record does not print the randomised Ns, and this card claims none.
cards.result: In both trials, numerically greater reductions in HbA1c and body weight were observed at all efpeglenatide doses than on placebo — reported as numerical, not tested-superiority, differences in the fetched record, and carded as such. ADA level 2 hypoglycaemia (<54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)) was reported in few participants (AMPLITUDE-L ≤10%; AMPLITUDE-S ≤4%). The adverse-event profile was consistent with other GLP-1 receptor agonists, gastrointestinal events most frequent.
cards.watchOut: 'Numerically greater' is the record's own wording: with both trials terminated early for funding, the placebo comparisons in L and S are descriptive in the fetched record and are not upgraded to proven superiority on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a complete-looking glycaemic programme from 2 publications / 4 trials — superior to placebo as monotherapy, non-inferior to dulaglutide, numerically ahead of placebo on insulin and oral backgrounds — for a drug that was never marketed
cards.summary: Synthesis: a complete-looking glycaemic programme from 2 publications / 4 trials — superior to placebo as monotherapy, non-inferior to dulaglutide, numerically ahead of placebo on insulin and oral backgrounds — for a drug that was never marketed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: AMPLITUDE-M gives the clean placebo-controlled monotherapy result (−0.5% to −1.0% vs placebo by dose); AMPLITUDE-D gives non-inferiority to an established weekly GLP-1 agent; AMPLITUDE-L and -S extend the direction of effect to insulin-treated and oral-agent backgrounds. Against that: the three 2023 trials were terminated early by the sponsor for funding (not safety or efficacy), efpeglenatide was never marketed and its development was discontinued, and HbA1c is a surrogate — the cardiovascular/renal outcomes evidence (AMPLITUDE-O) is homed at live #72 and is cross-pointed only, never re-carded here. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for glycaemic efficacy within this programme, on exactly the 2-publication / 4-trial base stated.
cards.watchOut: A discontinued programme's trials answer the efficacy question they asked, but no prescriber can act on them: this shelf is an evidence record, not a treatment recommendation.

shelves.title: Mazindol in obesity: a split 1970s base — significant 1 lb/week loss in the four-centre trial, no advantage over placebo in the therapist-comparison trial
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, does the non-amphetaminic anorectic mazindol, compared with placebo (with or without behavioural modification), produce weight loss?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Body Weight · Clinical Trials as Topic · Humans · Indoles · Mazindol · Middle Aged · Obesity · Placebos · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a 1970s trial base that splits. The four-centre six-week trial (245 assigned) found mazindol without behavioural modification and behavioural modification alone each produced a statistically significant mean weight loss of 1 lb/patient/week, with the combination greater still; a crossover/long-term evaluation found weight loss greater on mazindol than in controls and maintained for longer. Against that, the double-blind therapist-comparison trial (60 patients) found weight loss averaged 1.1 lb/week overall with NO advantage of either mazindol preparation over placebo — a null drug result inside the base, printed as such. Two further typed-RCT reports (PMIDs 322112 and 1097046) have empty PubMed abstracts and were refused as anchors this session. Mazindol's marketing status differs by country and it is not FDA-approved for obesity in the US.

cards.headline: Four-centre trial (Walker 1977): mazindol alone and behavioural modification alone each produced significant mean weight loss of 1 lb/patient/week over six weeks; the combination produced more
cards.summary: Four-centre trial (Walker 1977): mazindol alone and behavioural modification alone each produced significant mean weight loss of 1 lb/patient/week over six weeks; the combination produced more
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial, mazindol vs placebo, with and without behavioural modification
cards.people: 245 obese patients assigned randomly in four centres to two mazindol groups and one placebo group; 98 patients receiving mazindol and 40 receiving placebo completed the protocol. In one centre behavioural modification was also employed; in the other centres no additional weight-loss measures were used. Six-week double-blind placebo-controlled study.
cards.result: The placebo group did not lose weight without behavioural modification and had a higher drop-out rate than the mazindol group, attributed to dissatisfaction with failure to lose weight. Mazindol therapy without behavioural modification and behavioural modification alone both resulted in a statistically significant mean weight loss of 1 pound/patient/week, and mazindol plus behavioural modification resulted in a greater mean weight loss — by 1/2 pound/patient/week — than behavioural modification alone. No significant clinical or laboratory abnormalities occurred from mazindol therapy.
cards.watchOut: A 1977 six-week trial reporting weight loss in pounds per week; only 138 of the 245 assigned patients completed the protocol, and one centre differed from the others by adding behavioural modification.
cards.source: Walker BR et al. A multicentre study comparing mazindol and placebo in obese patients. The Journal of international medical research. 1977. PMID: 326596. cards.headline: Crossover and long-term evaluation (Enzi 1976): weight loss was greater on the anorectic than in controls and was maintained for longer periods, in simple and refractory obesity
cards.summary: Crossover and long-term evaluation (Enzi 1976): weight loss was greater on the anorectic than in controls and was maintained for longer periods, in simple and refractory obesity
cards.type: Short-term crossover trial and long-term evaluation, mazindol vs control, in simple and refractory obesity
cards.people: Patients with simple obesity and with refractory obesity, evaluated in a short-term crossover trial and in a long-term clinical trial (the abstract prints no N and no numeric effect, and none is claimed on this card).
cards.result: In the short-term crossover trial, effectiveness and tolerance were more evident when the anorexiant was given in a late phase of treatment. The association of an anorexiant drug with a hypocaloric diet was effective in so-called refractory obesity. In the long-term evaluation, weight loss was greater and remained so for longer periods in patients receiving the anorexiant than in controls, related to better maintenance of a restricted calorie regimen. Mazindol did not affect the improvement of glucose tolerance and insulin secretion which follows weight reduction.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative 1976 report: its abstract prints no sample size and no numeric weight-loss effect, so this card supports direction only and carries no numbers; it is not the load-bearing anchor of this shelf.

cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, two mazindol preparations vs placebo, nested in a physician vs nonphysician therapist comparison
cards.people: 60 obese patients assigned in groups of 12 to five therapists (physician and nonphysician); the patients of each therapist were then randomly assigned in groups of four to placebo or one of two preparations of mazindol. Randomised double-blind trial; 93% of patients completed the nine weeks of treatment.
cards.result: Weight loss averaged 1.1 lb per week and there was NO advantage to pharmacological agents over placebo; the investigators could not find a significant effect of either form of mazindol compared with placebo. There were significant differences between therapists, and weight loss by patients assigned to physicians was no better than for those assigned to nonphysician personnel.
cards.watchOut: The null result of this shelf: in this trial any weight loss tracked the therapist, not the drug. It is carded in full, not buried, and it is why this shelf's stamp is SPLIT rather than a benefit stamp.

cards.result: Refusals, stated on the face: two further typed-randomised-trial reports of mazindol in obesity — PMID 322112 (Maclay 1977) and PMID 1097046 (Smith 1975) — have EMPTY PubMed abstracts, verified this session; under this library's abstract discipline they cannot anchor and are refused, and the refusal is recorded here rather than the reports being silently dropped. The 2022 mazindol-plus-metformin report (PMID 35770520) is a combination question (mazindol vs mazindol + metformin, no placebo arm) and is programme support only, never an anchor here. The carded base is therefore exactly three abstracted reports from the 1970s, with short durations and pound-per-week reporting: Walker 1977 (significant weight loss on mazindol), Enzi 1976 (qualitative, greater and longer-maintained loss) and Atkinson 1977 (null versus placebo). Mazindol's marketing status differs by country and it is not FDA-approved for obesity in the US.

shelves.title: Diethylpropion (amfepramone) in obesity: about 10% body-weight loss vs about 3% on placebo at 6 months, sustained in three placebo-controlled trials
shelves.question: In adults with obesity, does the sympathomimetic anorectic diethylpropion (amfepramone), compared with placebo plus diet, produce and maintain weight loss over six to twelve months?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Appetite Depressants · Body Weight · Diet, Reducing · Diethylpropion · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Obesity · Placebos · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on weight loss, on three placebo-controlled trials of the same drug under its two names (diethylpropion = amfepramone — one drug, one home). At 6 months: −9.8% of initial body weight vs −3.2% on placebo (69 adults, P < 0.0001) and −7.7 kg vs −1.1 kg (156 Mexican patients); at 52 weeks in the five-drug comparative trial: −10.0 kg vs −3.1 kg on placebo (P < 0.001), with at least 5% weight loss in 71.4% vs 33.3%. No differences in blood pressure, pulse, ECG or psychiatric evaluation in the long-term trial; dry mouth and insomnia were the most frequent adverse events, with constipation, anxiety and irritability signals in the comparative trial. Diethylpropion is a sympathomimetic anorectic with short-term-use regulatory status. One further long-term report (PMID 4589633) has an empty PubMed abstract and was refused as an anchor this session.

cards.headline: Long-term RCT (Cercato 2009): diethylpropion lost 9.8% of initial body weight at 6 months vs 3.2% on placebo (P < 0.0001), sustained to 12 months, with no cardiovascular or psychiatric safety differences
cards.summary: Long-term RCT (Cercato 2009): diethylpropion lost 9.8% of initial body weight at 6 months vs 3.2% on placebo (P < 0.0001), sustained to 12 months, with no cardiovascular or psychiatric safety differences
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, diethylpropion 50 mg twice daily vs placebo for 6 months, with a 6-month open-label extension
cards.people: 69 obese healthy adults on a hypocaloric diet, randomised after a 2-week screening period to diethylpropion 50 mg twice daily (n=37) or placebo (n=32) for 6 months; all participants then received diethylpropion in an open-label extension for a further 6 months.
cards.result: After 6 months the diethylpropion group lost an average of 9.8% (SD 6.9%) of initial body weight vs 3.2% (3.7%) in the placebo group (P < 0.0001). From baseline to month 12, mean weight loss on diethylpropion was 10.6% (8.3%); participants switched from placebo to diethylpropion after 6 months lost an average of 7.0% (7.7%), and the between-group difference at month 12 was not significant (P = 0.07). No differences in blood pressure, pulse rate, ECG or psychiatric evaluation were observed. Dry mouth and insomnia were the most frequent adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled phase is 6 months and 69 patients; the 12-month figures come from an open-label extension in which the placebo group had switched to diethylpropion, so the month-12 comparison is no longer a randomised contrast.
cards.source: Cercato C et al. A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study of the long-term efficacy and safety of diethylpropion in the treatment of obese subjects. International journal of obesity (2005). 2009. PMID: 19564877. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase III RCT (Soto-Molina 2015): amfepramone 75 mg lost 7.7 kg at 6 months vs 1.1 kg on placebo; at least 5% weight loss in 64 vs 8 patients
cards.summary: Phase III RCT (Soto-Molina 2015): amfepramone 75 mg lost 7.7 kg at 6 months vs 1.1 kg on placebo; at least 5% weight loss in 64 vs 8 patients
cards.type: Phase III double-blinded randomised controlled trial, amfepramone (diethylpropion) 75 mg daily vs placebo for 6 months
cards.people: 156 obese adult Mexican volunteers with body mass index greater than 30 kg/m2 and less than 45 kg/m2, resistant to diet and exercise, randomised to amfepramone 75 mg daily or placebo for 6 months. Double-blinded randomised controlled trial.
cards.result: Amfepramone produced greater weight loss than placebo at 3 months (−4.9 kg vs −0.7 kg) and at 6 months (−7.7 kg vs −1.1 kg). At 6 months, 64 patients on amfepramone achieved at least 5% weight loss and 34 achieved at least 10%, compared with 8 and 0 patients on placebo. Amfepramone also significantly improved body mass index and waist circumference, with only favourable tendencies in metabolic and blood-pressure parameters. Amfepramone produced only mild adverse events, more numerous than placebo only at 3 months, dry mouth being the main adverse event.
cards.watchOut: A single-region (Mexican) trial population, as printed; amfepramone and diethylpropion are the same drug — this is a second trial of the shelf's agent, not a different agent.
cards.source: Soto-Molina H et al. Six-month efficacy and safety of amfepramone in obese Mexican patients: a double-blinded, randomized, controlled trial. cards.headline: Five-drug comparative RCT (Suplicy 2014): diethylpropion lost 10.0 kg over 52 weeks vs 3.1 kg on placebo (P < 0.001); at least 5% weight loss in 71.4% vs 33.3%
cards.summary: Five-drug comparative RCT (Suplicy 2014): diethylpropion lost 10.0 kg over 52 weeks vs 3.1 kg on placebo (P < 0.001); at least 5% weight loss in 71.4% vs 33.3%
cards.type: Prospective randomised placebo-controlled comparative study of five centrally acting drugs over 52 weeks — diethylpropion arm only carded here
cards.people: 174 obese premenopausal women at a single academic institution, randomised to diethylpropion 75 mg (n=28), fenproporex 25 mg (n=29), mazindol 2 mg (n=29), sibutramine 15 mg (n=30), fluoxetine 20 mg (n=29) or placebo (n=29) daily over 52 weeks, with diet and physical activity encouraged. Only the diethylpropion-vs-placebo contrast is carded here.
cards.result: Weight loss was greater than placebo (−3.1 kg) with diethylpropion (−10.0 kg; P < 0.001). Twenty of 28 women (71.4%; P < 0.001) on diethylpropion lost at least 5% of initial weight, compared with 10 (33.3%) on placebo. Each medically treated group experienced more adverse events than placebo (P < 0.001); compared with placebo, constipation was more prevalent with diethylpropion, anxiety was more prevalent with diethylpropion (P = 0.01), and irritability occurred more frequently with diethylpropion.
cards.watchOut: The trial's other arms belong to their own questions — fenproporex, mazindol, fluoxetine and sibutramine are cross-pointed only and are NOT re-carded here (mazindol is homed on its own shelf; sibutramine on its own). Women only, single institution.
cards.source: Suplicy H et al. A comparative study of five centrally acting drugs on the pharmacological treatment of obesity. International journal of obesity (2005). 2014. PMID: 24287940. shelves.title: Quinagolide vs bromocriptine in hyperprolactinaemia: prolactin normalised at least as often and tolerability was better in a small 1990–1991 base (total N under 90; one n=7 phase sub-floor, not counted)
shelves.question: In women with hyperprolactinaemia, does the non-ergot dopamine agonist quinagolide (CV 205-502), compared with bromocriptine, normalise prolactin, restore menstrual bleeding and relieve galactorrhoea — and is it better tolerated?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aminoquinolines · Bromocriptine · Dopamine Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hyperprolactinemia · Iodine Radioisotopes · Menstruation · Middle Aged · Prolactin · Radioimmunoassay · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a small, old (1990–1991) trial base whose total randomised N across the three anchors is under 90. Prolactin normalised in 8 of 11 women on quinagolide vs 2 of 9 on bromocriptine by 8 weeks in the first trial (P < 0.002), and in 81% vs 70% in the second (47 patients); the third found the two drugs equally effective over six months. Tolerability favoured quinagolide in two trials — adverse reactions milder and less persistent, with four bromocriptine patients but no quinagolide patients discontinuing for adverse reactions in the first trial — and did not differ in the third. The third anchor's acute crossover phase (n=7) is below the ~10-human floor, is labelled sub-floor on its card, and is never load-bearing; only its randomised long-term phase (n=12) is counted. Prolactin normalisation is a biochemical endpoint; tumour-shrinkage outcomes are not in this base. Quinagolide was never FDA-approved — a European-market agent whose licences have since been withdrawn or discontinued in several markets. The cabergoline-vs-bromocriptine home is cross-pointed only.

cards.headline: Double-blind comparison (Homburg 1990): 8 of 11 women on quinagolide achieved normal prolactin by 8 weeks vs 2 of 9 on bromocriptine (P < 0.002); four bromocriptine patients, but no quinagolide patients, discontinued for adverse reactions
cards.summary: Double-blind comparison (Homburg 1990): 8 of 11 women on quinagolide achieved normal prolactin by 8 weeks vs 2 of 9 on bromocriptine (P < 0.002); four bromocriptine patients, but no quinagolide patients, discontinued for adverse reactions
cards.type: Double-blind randomised comparison, quinagolide (CV 205-502) vs bromocriptine over 6 months
cards.people: 22 hyperprolactinaemic women randomly allocated to bromocriptine or the non-ergot long-acting dopamine agonist CV 205-502 (quinagolide), in a double-blind study over 6 months: quinagolide 0.075 mg once daily vs bromocriptine 5 mg daily in divided doses.
cards.result: With once-daily quinagolide 0.075 mg, eight of 11 women achieved normal prolactin concentrations after 8 weeks of treatment compared with two of nine receiving bromocriptine (P < 0.002). With doses of 0.075–0.15 mg quinagolide, 10 of 11 women achieved normal prolactin at 24 weeks, compared with three of the remaining seven women on bromocriptine 5–10 mg. Four patients in the bromocriptine group, but none in the quinagolide group, discontinued because of adverse reactions; adverse reactions on the new drug were milder and more transient. Regular menstrual bleeding was restored and galactorrhoea relieved in the majority of patients, with marginally greater efficacy with quinagolide.
cards.watchOut: Only 22 women, and the bromocriptine arm shrank by discontinuation (9 evaluated at 8 weeks, 7 remaining at 24 weeks) — the 24-week contrast is against a depleted comparator group.
cards.source: Homburg R et al. A double-blind study comparing a new non-ergot, long-acting dopamine agonist, CV 205-502, with bromocriptine in women with hyperprolactinaemia. cards.headline: Randomised double-blind comparison (van der Heijden 1991): prolactin normalised in 81% on quinagolide vs 70% on bromocriptine over 24 weeks, with no difference in menstrual restoration or galactorrhoea resolution and milder adverse reactions on quinagolide
cards.summary: Randomised double-blind comparison (van der Heijden 1991): prolactin normalised in 81% on quinagolide vs 70% on bromocriptine over 24 weeks, with no difference in menstrual restoration or galactorrhoea resolution and milder adverse reactions on quinagolide
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind comparison, quinagolide (CV 205-502) vs bromocriptine over 24 weeks
cards.people: 47 hyperprolactinaemic patients with serum prolactin persistently above 1500 mU/L, treated with CV 205-502 (quinagolide) or bromocriptine in a prospective randomised double-blind fashion over 24 weeks; two women were excluded for poor compliance in the first month, leaving 45 patients for evaluation.
cards.result: Prolactin normalised within the study period in 81% of patients in the quinagolide group and 70% in the bromocriptine group, generally within 8 to 12 weeks. There were no differences between the two drugs regarding restoration of the menstrual cycle or disappearance of galactorrhoea. Both drugs caused adverse reactions, especially at initiation, but those on quinagolide were less severe and persistent; tolerability was judged very good or good by 90% of women on quinagolide vs 75% on bromocriptine.
cards.watchOut: The largest anchor of a small base (47 patients); the normalisation difference (81% vs 70%) is printed without a significance claim in the abstract, and none is made here.
cards.source: van der Heijden PF et al. CV 205-502, a new dopamine agonist, versus bromocriptine in the treatment of hyperprolactinaemia. cards.headline: Acute and long-term comparison (Verhelst 1991): the randomised long-term phase (n=12) found quinagolide and once-daily bromocriptine equally effective over six months — the acute phase (n=7) is SUB-FLOOR (N < 10), labelled, and never load-bearing
cards.summary: Acute and long-term comparison (Verhelst 1991): the randomised long-term phase (n=12) found quinagolide and once-daily bromocriptine equally effective over six months — the acute phase (n=7) is SUB-FLOOR (N < 10), labelled, and never load-bearing
cards.type: Double-blind study in two phases: acute single-dose crossover phase (n=7, SUB-FLOOR, never load-bearing) and randomised long-term phase (n=12, counted)
cards.people: Two phases, both Ns printed on the face. Acute phase: 7 hyperprolactinaemic patients — SUB-FLOOR (N = 7, below the ~10-human floor), labelled and never load-bearing — compared over 24 hours after a single oral dose of quinagolide 0.05 mg vs bromocriptine 2.5 mg. Long-term phase: 12 hyperprolactinaemic patients randomised to once-daily bromocriptine or quinagolide in incremental doses for six months; only this randomised long-term phase is counted as evidence on this shelf.
cards.result: Acute phase (n=7, sub-floor — not counted): compared with placebo, both bromocriptine and quinagolide showed potent prolactin-inhibiting and growth-hormone-releasing effects, comparable at 24 hours, with no significant changes in TSH, LH, FSH or cortisol. Long-term phase (n=12, counted): both drugs were equally effective, with no differences in adverse reactions or prolactin levels during repeated diurnal sampling. The authors concluded the two drugs are therapeutically equivalent in long-term use when each is given once daily.
cards.watchOut: Read the two phases separately: the n=7 acute phase is below the floor and carries no weight on this shelf; the counted long-term phase is itself only 12 patients and found equivalence, not superiority — it tempers, rather than supports, any benefit claim.
cards.source: Verhelst JA et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small 1990–1991 base (total randomised N under 90) — quinagolide normalised prolactin at least as often as bromocriptine and was better tolerated in two of three trials; the third anchor's n=7 acute phase is sub-floor and was never counted
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small 1990–1991 base (total randomised N under 90) — quinagolide normalised prolactin at least as often as bromocriptine and was better tolerated in two of three trials; the third anchor's n=7 acute phase is sub-floor and was never counted
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the three anchors: normalisation favoured quinagolide numerically in the 22-woman trial (8/11 vs 2/9 at 8 weeks, P < 0.002) and in the 47-patient trial (81% vs 70%), while the 12-patient randomised long-term phase of the third report found the drugs equally effective. Tolerability favoured quinagolide in the first two trials and did not differ in the third. The third report's acute crossover phase enrolled 7 patients — below the ~10-human floor, labelled sub-floor on its card, and never load-bearing; only its long-term phase (n=12) is counted, giving a total randomised base under 90 patients. Prolactin normalisation is a biochemical endpoint; no tumour-shrinkage outcomes are in this base. Quinagolide was never FDA-approved and has since been withdrawn or discontinued in several European markets. The cabergoline-vs-bromocriptine prolactinoma home (pack #5852 / live #2070) is a different agent question and is cross-pointed only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Bexagliflozin in type 2 diabetes (6 randomised reports): HbA1c -0.37% in stage 3a/3b CKD, -0.79% placebo-adjusted as monotherapy, non-inferior to sitagliptin, glimepiride and dapagliflozin — no outcomes trial, never marketed at scale
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (as monotherapy, added to metformin, or with stage 3a/3b chronic kidney disease), does the SGLT2 inhibitor bexagliflozin 20 mg, compared with placebo, sitagliptin, glimepiride or dapagliflozin, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Pyrans/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/complications,drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit for glycaemic control, on exactly 6 randomised reports, printed as the row directs. Against placebo: HbA1c lowered by 0.37% in stage 3a/3b CKD (312 analysed), placebo-adjusted change -0.79% at week 24 in the 96-week monotherapy trial (288 randomised), and a difference of -0.53% added to metformin (317 randomised). Against active comparators, bexagliflozin was non-inferior each time: versus sitagliptin on metformin (HbA1c -0.74% vs -0.82%; 386 participants), versus glimepiride on metformin at week 60 (426 randomised; odds ratio 0.12 for severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia — a relative measure, with fewer events on bexagliflozin), and versus dapagliflozin on metformin in Chinese patients (-1.08% vs -1.10%, difference 0.03% against a 0.4% margin; 406 randomised). Status flags, on the face: bexagliflozin is FDA-approved in the US (2023) but was never marketed at scale, and there is NO cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial — the CKD report's endpoint is glycaemic (HbA1c in stage 3a/3b CKD), not kidney progression. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only).

cards.headline: CKD stage 3a/3b trial (Allegretti 2019): bexagliflozin lowered HbA1c by 0.37% versus placebo at 24 weeks (0.31% in stage 3a, 0.43% in stage 3b), with a 20.1% relative reduction in albuminuria geometric mean ratio
cards.summary: CKD stage 3a/3b trial (Allegretti 2019): bexagliflozin lowered HbA1c by 0.37% versus placebo at 24 weeks (0.31% in stage 3a, 0.43% in stage 3b), with a 20.1% relative reduction in albuminuria geometric mean ratio
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (bexagliflozin in T2D with stage 3a/3b CKD)
cards.people: 312 patients analysed across 54 sites in 4 countries, with type 2 diabetes, stage 3a or 3b chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2), HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5%, on oral hypoglycaemic agents; randomised to bexagliflozin 20 mg daily or placebo for 24 weeks in a phase 3 double-blind trial sponsored by Theracos Sub, LLC, as published.
cards.result: Bexagliflozin lowered HbA1c by 0.37% (95% CI 0.20% to 0.54%; P<0.001) compared with placebo; reductions were 0.31% in stage 3a (P=0.007) and 0.43% in stage 3b (P=0.002). It also decreased body weight by 1.61 kg (P<0.001), systolic blood pressure by 3.8 mmHg (P=0.02), fasting plasma glucose by 0.76 mmol/L (about 14 mg/dL; P=0.003) and albuminuria (geometric mean ratio reduction of 20.1% relative; P=0.03). Urinary tract infection and genital mycotic infections were more common on bexagliflozin; otherwise adverse-event frequencies were comparable. The trial was not designed to evaluate long-term kidney or cardiovascular outcomes, as its authors state.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is glycaemic — HbA1c in patients who happen to have stage 3a/3b CKD — not kidney progression; do not read this card as a renal-outcomes result. Industry-sponsored (Theracos Sub, LLC, as published).
cards.source: Allegretti AS et al. Safety and Effectiveness of Bexagliflozin in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Stage 3a/3b CKD. American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation. 2019. PMID: 31101403. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 96-week monotherapy trial (Halvorsen 2019): placebo-adjusted HbA1c change -0.79% at week 24; serious adverse events 2.8% on bexagliflozin vs 8.5% on placebo
cards.summary: 96-week monotherapy trial (Halvorsen 2019): placebo-adjusted HbA1c change -0.79% at week 24; serious adverse events 2.8% on bexagliflozin vs 8.5% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled monotherapy trial, 96 weeks (the record's own conclusion calls this programme report a phase 2 trial — labelled as published)
cards.people: 288 adults with type 2 diabetes from the USA, Colombia and Mexico, randomised 1:1 to bexagliflozin 20 mg or placebo as monotherapy for 96 weeks; the primary endpoint was placebo-adjusted HbA1c change at week 24, with dosing continued a further 72 weeks for safety and durability.
cards.result: The placebo-adjusted change in HbA1c at week 24 was -0.79% (95% CI -1.06 to -0.53; P<0.0001). The unadjusted change through week 96 was -0.55% ± 1.184% on bexagliflozin versus +0.53% ± 1.215% on placebo (P<0.0001). Significant decreases in body mass, systolic and diastolic blood pressure were attributed to bexagliflozin. Serious adverse events were less frequent on bexagliflozin (2.8%) than placebo (8.5%), and urinary tract infections occurred less frequently in the active arm (14.5%) than the placebo arm (20.6%) in this trial.
cards.watchOut: Labelled as published: the record's conclusion describes this 96-week report as a phase 2 trial even though the programme is a phase 3 development programme — the phase label is the record's own. The week-96 comparison is an unadjusted change against a placebo arm few trials would maintain for two years; the week-24 placebo-adjusted figure (-0.79%) is the load-bearing number.
cards.source: Halvorsen YC et al. A 96-week, multinational, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of bexagliflozin as a monotherapy for adults with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2019. PMID: 31297965. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Versus sitagliptin on metformin (Halvorsen 2019): HbA1c -0.74% on bexagliflozin vs -0.82% on sitagliptin at 24 weeks — non-inferiority established, with larger fasting glucose and weight falls on bexagliflozin
cards.summary: Versus sitagliptin on metformin (Halvorsen 2019): HbA1c -0.74% on bexagliflozin vs -0.82% on sitagliptin at 24 weeks — non-inferiority established, with larger fasting glucose and weight falls on bexagliflozin
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-controlled non-inferiority trial (bexagliflozin vs sitagliptin, both on metformin)
cards.people: 386 participants with type 2 diabetes randomised to bexagliflozin 20 mg or sitagliptin 100 mg, each added to their existing metformin dose, for 24 weeks; the primary endpoint was non-inferiority of bexagliflozin to sitagliptin for HbA1c change.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change was -0.74% (95% CI -0.86% to -0.62%) on bexagliflozin and -0.82% (95% CI -0.93% to -0.71%) on sitagliptin, establishing non-inferiority. Changes in fasting plasma glucose, body mass and systolic blood pressure were -1.82 mmol/L (about -33 mg/dL), -3.35 kg and -4.23 mmHg on bexagliflozin versus -1.45 mmol/L (about -26 mg/dL), -0.81 kg and -1.90 mmHg on sitagliptin — significant for fasting glucose and body mass as published. Adverse events affected 47.1% (bexagliflozin) and 56.0% (sitagliptin); serious adverse events 3.7% and 2.1%.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority result against an active comparator — it shows bexagliflozin is not worse than sitagliptin by the prespecified margin, not that either beat placebo in this trial; the placebo-controlled estimates are the other cards.
cards.source: Halvorsen YD et al. cards.headline: Add-on to metformin versus placebo (Halvorsen 2023): HbA1c difference -0.53% at 24 weeks (317 randomised); placebo-adjusted weight -2.51 kg and systolic pressure -7.07 mmHg
cards.summary: Add-on to metformin versus placebo (Halvorsen 2023): HbA1c difference -0.53% at 24 weeks (317 randomised); placebo-adjusted weight -2.51 kg and systolic pressure -7.07 mmHg
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (bexagliflozin added to metformin)
cards.people: 317 participants randomised to bexagliflozin 20 mg or placebo, each added to metformin, for 24 weeks; primary endpoint HbA1c change at week 24. A separate open-label arm enrolled participants with HbA1c above 10.5% and was analysed separately (not part of the randomised comparison).
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change was -1.09% (95% CI -1.24% to -0.94%) on bexagliflozin and -0.56% (-0.71% to -0.41%) on placebo — a difference of -0.53% (-0.74% to -0.32%; P<0.0001); excluding observations after rescue medication, the difference was -0.70%. The open-label high-HbA1c group's change was -2.82%, reported separately as published. Placebo-adjusted changes were -7.07 mmHg for systolic blood pressure, -1.35 mmol/L (about -24 mg/dL) for fasting plasma glucose and -2.51 kg for body mass (all P<0.0001). Adverse events affected 42.4% (bexagliflozin) and 47.2% (placebo), with fewer serious adverse events on bexagliflozin.
cards.watchOut: The -2.82% open-label figure comes from an uncontrolled arm of patients starting above 10.5% HbA1c — regression to the mean is built into it; it is printed, labelled open-label, and is not part of the randomised evidence.

cards.headline: Versus glimepiride on metformin (Halvorsen 2023): HbA1c non-inferior at week 60 (difference -0.05%), weight -4.31 kg and systolic pressure -6.53 mmHg in bexagliflozin's favour, and an odds ratio of 0.12 (relative measure) for severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Versus glimepiride on metformin (Halvorsen 2023): HbA1c non-inferior at week 60 (difference -0.05%), weight -4.31 kg and systolic pressure -6.53 mmHg in bexagliflozin's favour, and an odds ratio of 0.12 (relative measure) for severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-controlled non-inferiority trial (bexagliflozin vs glimepiride, both on metformin)
cards.people: 426 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5%), randomised to bexagliflozin 20 mg or optimally titrated glimepiride as adjuncts to metformin, in a 96-week double-blind trial; the primary endpoint was the intergroup HbA1c difference at week 60.
cards.result: The intergroup HbA1c difference (bexagliflozin minus glimepiride) at week 60 was -0.05% (95% CI -0.21 to 0.11), establishing non-inferiority by the prespecified 0.35% margin. Prespecified tests gave a body-mass difference of -4.31 kg (95% CI -5.10 to -3.52; P<0.0001), a systolic pressure difference of -6.53 mmHg (95% CI -10.56 to -2.51; P=0.0008), and an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.28; P<0.0001) for severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia — a relative measure; the fetched record does not print the absolute event rates, so none are claimed. At follow-up, the mean eGFR difference between arms was 6.05 mL/min/1.73 m2 (95% CI 3.24 to 8.87) in bexagliflozin's favour.
cards.watchOut: The hypoglycaemia odds ratio of 0.12 is a relative measure with no absolute rates in the fetched record — it must not be restated as an absolute risk reduction. The eGFR difference is a follow-up-visit laboratory difference, not a kidney-outcomes result.

cards.headline: Head-to-head versus dapagliflozin on metformin in Chinese patients (Xie 2024): HbA1c -1.08% vs -1.10% at 24 weeks, difference 0.03% against a 0.4% non-inferiority margin — nearly identical effects and safety
cards.summary: Head-to-head versus dapagliflozin on metformin in Chinese patients (Xie 2024): HbA1c -1.08% vs -1.10% at 24 weeks, difference 0.03% against a 0.4% non-inferiority margin — nearly identical effects and safety
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind active-controlled non-inferiority trial (bexagliflozin vs dapagliflozin, both on metformin)
cards.people: 406 Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by metformin, randomised to bexagliflozin 20 mg or dapagliflozin 10 mg, each added to metformin, for 24 weeks in a multicentre phase 3 double-blind active-controlled trial; primary endpoint non-inferiority for HbA1c change.
cards.result: Model-adjusted mean HbA1c change was -1.08% on bexagliflozin and -1.10% on dapagliflozin; the intergroup difference of 0.03% (95% CI -0.14% to 0.19%) was below the prespecified 0.4% margin, confirming non-inferiority. Changes in fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour postprandial glucose, body weight and systolic pressure were -1.95 mmol/L (about -35 mg/dL), -3.24 mmol/L (about -58 mg/dL), -2.52 kg and -6.4 mmHg on bexagliflozin versus -1.87 mmol/L (about -34 mg/dL), -3.07 mmol/L (about -55 mg/dL), -2.22 kg and -6.3 mmHg on dapagliflozin. Adverse events: 62.6% vs 65.0%; serious adverse events 4.4% vs 3.5%.
cards.watchOut: The record describes this as the first direct randomised comparison of two SGLT2 inhibitors; non-inferiority to dapagliflozin for HbA1c does not transfer dapagliflozin's outcomes-trial results to bexagliflozin — bexagliflozin has no outcomes trial of its own.
cards.source: Xie L et al. Efficacy and safety of bexagliflozin compared with dapagliflozin as an adjunct to metformin in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A 24-week, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: six randomised reports agree — bexagliflozin 20 mg lowers HbA1c by about 0.4-0.8% against placebo across monotherapy, metformin add-on and stage 3a/3b CKD populations, and is non-inferior to sitagliptin, glimepiride and dapagliflozin, with weight and blood-pressure falls and (versus glimepiride) far fewer hypoglycaemic events on a relative measure
cards.summary: Synthesis: six randomised reports agree — bexagliflozin 20 mg lowers HbA1c by about 0.4-0.8% against placebo across monotherapy, metformin add-on and stage 3a/3b CKD populations, and is non-inferior to sitagliptin, glimepiride and dapagliflozin, with weight and blood-pressure falls and (versus glimepiride) far fewer hypoglycaemic events on a relative measure
cards.people: All six reports carded on this shelf (312 + 288 + 386 + 317 + 426 + 406 randomised or analysed participants across the six reports).
cards.result: Placebo-controlled HbA1c effects: -0.37% in stage 3a/3b CKD, -0.79% placebo-adjusted at week 24 as monotherapy, and -0.53% added to metformin. Active-controlled results are non-inferiority throughout: versus sitagliptin (-0.74% vs -0.82%), versus glimepiride at week 60 (difference -0.05%, with an odds ratio of 0.12 — a relative measure — for severe or documented symptomatic hypoglycaemia), and versus dapagliflozin (difference 0.03% against a 0.4% margin). Weight (about -2.5 to -4.3 kg in the comparative figures) and systolic pressure fall consistently. Status, printed plainly: FDA-approved in the US in 2023 but never marketed at scale; no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists, and the CKD report is a glycaemic-endpoint trial. The SGLT2 class-level shelves ask class questions and do not card this agent; this shelf is its only home.
cards.watchOut: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout this shelf; non-inferiority margins and the open-label arm are labelled per card, and this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Henagliflozin in type 2 diabetes — SINGLE-REGION (China) evidence: placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91%/-0.94% as monotherapy and -0.76%/-0.80% on metformin in two phase 3 trials; 7-day open-label CSII trial raised time in range to 79.85% vs 74.06%
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor henagliflozin, compared with placebo (as monotherapy or added to metformin) or added to continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion in severe hyperglycaemia, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Bridged Bicyclo Compounds, Heterocyclic · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Glycated Hemoglobin/analysis · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Metformin/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Insulin Infusion Systems
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit for glycaemic control — SINGLE-REGION EVIDENCE (China; approved there, not FDA/EMA-approved), flagged here and on the title as the row directs. The chronic-efficacy claim rests on two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials: monotherapy (468 randomised — placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91% at 5 mg and -0.94% at 10 mg, both P<0.001) and add-on to metformin (483 randomised — least-squares mean differences versus placebo -0.76% at 5 mg and -0.80% at 10 mg, all P<0.0001). The third report is a different, narrower question printed exactly: a 7-day, open-label, phase IV trial in 210 adults diagnosed within the past 2 years with severe hyperglycaemia, in which adding henagliflozin to continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion raised time in range to 79.85% versus 74.06% on infusion alone (P=0.005). The retagliptin + henagliflozin combination trial is a combination question, not counted here and cross-pointed only. HbA1c and time-in-range are surrogate endpoints; no outcomes trial exists — both printed. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control, single-region China evidence).

cards.headline: Phase 3 monotherapy (Lu 2021): placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91% at 5 mg and -0.94% at 10 mg at 24 weeks (468 randomised), with weight -1.3 and -1.5 kg and systolic pressure -5.1 and -4.4 mmHg versus placebo
cards.summary: Phase 3 monotherapy (Lu 2021): placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91% at 5 mg and -0.94% at 10 mg at 24 weeks (468 randomised), with weight -1.3 and -1.5 kg and systolic pressure -5.1 and -4.4 mmHg versus placebo
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (henagliflozin monotherapy, China)
cards.people: 468 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on diet and exercise (HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5%), randomised 1:1:1 to once-daily placebo, henagliflozin 5 mg or henagliflozin 10 mg in a multicentre Chinese phase 3 trial: a 24-week double-blind placebo-controlled period followed by a 28-week extension in which placebo patients switched to henagliflozin.
cards.result: At week 24, placebo-adjusted least-squares mean HbA1c changes were -0.91% (95% CI -1.11% to -0.72%; P<0.001) at 5 mg and -0.94% (-1.13% to -0.75%; P<0.001) at 10 mg. Placebo-adjusted changes were -1.3 kg (95% CI -1.8 to -0.9) and -1.5 kg (-2.0 to -1.1) in body weight, and -5.1 mmHg (-7.2 to -3.0) and -4.4 mmHg (-6.5 to -2.3) in systolic blood pressure (all P<0.05). Improvements were sustained over the additional 28 weeks. Adverse events occurred in 81.0% (placebo), 78.9% (5 mg) and 78.9% (10 mg); no diabetic ketoacidosis or major hypoglycaemia episodes occurred.
cards.watchOut: Single-region evidence (China) — flagged on the face. The 28-week extension is not placebo-controlled (placebo patients switched to active drug), so durability beyond week 24 is an open follow-on, not a randomised comparison.

Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2021. PMID: 33417292. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Phase 3 add-on to metformin (Weng 2021): least-squares mean HbA1c differences versus placebo -0.76% at 5 mg and -0.80% at 10 mg at 24 weeks (483 randomised: 161 placebo, 162 at 5 mg, 160 at 10 mg)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (henagliflozin added to metformin, China)
cards.people: 483 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with metformin (HbA1c 7.0% to 10.5%), randomised to once-daily placebo (n=161), henagliflozin 5 mg (n=162) or henagliflozin 10 mg (n=160) in a multicentre Chinese phase 3 trial: 24 weeks double-blind placebo-controlled, then a 28-week extension with placebo patients switched to henagliflozin.
cards.result: At week 24, least-squares mean HbA1c changes versus placebo were -0.76% at 5 mg and -0.80% at 10 mg (all P<0.0001). Both doses also lowered fasting and 2-hour postprandial glucose, body weight and blood pressure versus placebo, and increased the proportions achieving HbA1c below 7.0%; trends were sustained over the additional 28 weeks. Slightly higher proportions of ketosis and urine ketone bodies were seen on henagliflozin than placebo at week 24; no diabetic ketoacidosis or severe hypoglycaemia was reported.
cards.watchOut: Single-region evidence (China) — flagged on the face. The ketosis / urine-ketone signal is the card's harm note: proportions were 'slightly higher' on drug as published, with no absolute rates printed in the fetched record, so none are claimed.

cards.headline: Phase IV CSII add-on in severe hyperglycaemia (Huang 2026): 7-day open-label trial in 210 recently diagnosed adults — time in range 79.85% on henagliflozin + insulin infusion vs 74.06% on infusion alone (P=0.005)
cards.summary: Phase IV CSII add-on in severe hyperglycaemia (Huang 2026): 7-day open-label trial in 210 recently diagnosed adults — time in range 79.85% on henagliflozin + insulin infusion vs 74.06% on infusion alone (P=0.005)
cards.type: Phase IV randomised open-label trial (henagliflozin added to CSII in severe hyperglycaemia, China)
cards.people: 210 adults with type 2 diabetes diagnosed within the past 2 years, with severe hyperglycaemia, randomised 1:1 to henagliflozin plus continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) or CSII alone in a multicentre, randomised, open-label, parallel-group study over 7 days; the primary endpoint was time in range (glucose 3.9-10.0 mmol/L, about 70-180 mg/dL).
cards.result: Time in range was significantly greater with henagliflozin + CSII than CSII alone (79.85% vs 74.06%; P=0.005), and the time to achieve the target (time in range above 70%) was shorter. Time above range, insulin dosage, mean glucose and glucose management indicator were significantly lower in the combination group; time below range, mean amplitude of glycaemic excursions, coefficient of variation and mean of daily differences did not differ significantly. Adverse events — urinary tract infection, diabetic ketoacidosis and hypoglycaemic events — did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Printed exactly as the row directs: 7 days, open-label, in adults diagnosed within the past 2 years presenting with severe hyperglycaemia — a short inpatient-style intensification question, not chronic therapy; it supports nothing about long-term glycaemic control, which rests on the two phase 3 cards.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two Chinese phase 3 trials establish henagliflozin's chronic glycaemic effect (placebo-adjusted HbA1c about -0.8 to -0.9% at 5-10 mg, as monotherapy and on metformin); a 7-day open-label CSII trial adds a narrow severe-hyperglycaemia result — all single-region (China) evidence, with no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: two Chinese phase 3 trials establish henagliflozin's chronic glycaemic effect (placebo-adjusted HbA1c about -0.8 to -0.9% at 5-10 mg, as monotherapy and on metformin); a 7-day open-label CSII trial adds a narrow severe-hyperglycaemia result — all single-region (China) evidence, with no outcomes trial
cards.people: All three reports carded on this shelf (468 + 483 + 210 randomised participants).
cards.result: Monotherapy: placebo-adjusted HbA1c -0.91% (5 mg) and -0.94% (10 mg) at 24 weeks. Added to metformin: -0.76% and -0.80% versus placebo at 24 weeks, with weight and blood-pressure falls in both trials and a ketosis / urine-ketone signal on drug. Added to insulin infusion in severe hyperglycaemia over 7 days: time in range 79.85% vs 74.06% (P=0.005) with lower insulin doses. Single-region flag, printed plainly: all evidence is from China, where the agent is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved. The retagliptin + henagliflozin combination trial is a combination question and is cross-pointed only — it is not counted in this shelf's base and is not carded here. No cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists.
cards.watchOut: HbA1c and time-in-range are surrogate endpoints throughout; the extension phases of the phase 3 trials are not placebo-controlled, as printed per card, and this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Enavogliflozin in type 2 diabetes (3 Korean phase 3 trials): HbA1c −0.99% vs placebo as monotherapy, non-inferior to dapagliflozin on metformin — single-region (Korea) evidence, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In Korean adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor enavogliflozin 0.3 mg, compared with placebo or dapagliflozin (as monotherapy or added to metformin, with or without gemigliptin), improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Blood Glucose · Body Weight · Cholesterol · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Glycated Hemoglobin · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Lipids · Republic of Korea/epidemiology · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on single-region (Korea) evidence. Three Korean phase 3 randomised trials of enavogliflozin 0.3 mg: as monotherapy it lowered HbA1c by 0.99% more than placebo at 24 weeks, with 71% versus 24% reaching HbA1c <7.0%; added to metformin it was non-inferior to dapagliflozin (HbA1c change −0.80% vs −0.75%, difference −0.04% against a 0.35% margin); and added to metformin plus gemigliptin it matched dapagliflozin (−0.92% vs −0.86%). SINGLE-REGION FLAG: all evidence is Korean; enavogliflozin is approved in Korea and is not FDA/EMA-approved. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists for this agent. The placebo-controlled efficacy claim rests on the monotherapy trial; the other two anchors are active-comparator non-inferiority trials.

cards.headline: Phase 3 monotherapy RCT (Kwak 2023): enavogliflozin 0.3 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.99% more than placebo at 24 weeks in Korean patients; 71% vs 24% reached HbA1c <7.0%

cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, enavogliflozin monotherapy vs placebo
cards.people: 167 Korean people with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on diet and exercise (HbA1c 7.0%–10.0%), randomised at 23 hospitals to enavogliflozin 0.3 mg (n=83) or placebo (n=84) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: The placebo-adjusted mean change in HbA1c at week 24 was −0.99% (95% CI −1.24% to −0.74%). HbA1c <7.0% was achieved by 71% on enavogliflozin versus 24% on placebo (P<0.0001). Placebo-adjusted changes in fasting plasma glucose (−40.1 mg/dL) and body weight (−2.5 kg) were also statistically significant (P<0.0001). No significant increase in treatment-related adverse events was observed for enavogliflozin.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (Korea) evidence; HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists for enavogliflozin. This is the programme's only placebo-controlled anchor — the other two cards are non-inferiority trials against dapagliflozin.

cards.headline: Phase 3 add-on-to-metformin RCT (Han 2023): enavogliflozin non-inferior to dapagliflozin — HbA1c change −0.80% vs −0.75% at 24 weeks (difference −0.04%, non-inferiority margin 0.35%)
cards.summary: Phase 3 add-on-to-metformin RCT (Han 2023): enavogliflozin non-inferior to dapagliflozin — HbA1c change −0.80% vs −0.75% at 24 weeks (difference −0.04%, non-inferiority margin 0.35%)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind randomised non-inferiority trial, enavogliflozin vs dapagliflozin, both added to metformin
cards.people: 200 Korean patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin, randomised to enavogliflozin 0.3 mg/day (n=101) or dapagliflozin 10 mg/day (n=99), both added to metformin, for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Adjusted mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.80% on enavogliflozin and −0.75% on dapagliflozin (difference −0.04%; 95% CI −0.21% to 0.12%), meeting the prespecified 0.35% non-inferiority margin. HbA1c <7.0% was achieved by 61% and 62% respectively. Body-weight changes were comparable (−3.77 kg vs −3.58 kg), and both drugs were safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority design against an active comparator: it shows enavogliflozin matches dapagliflozin on the surrogate HbA1c endpoint, not that either beats placebo in this population. Single-region (Korea) evidence.

cards.headline: ENHANCE-D RCT (Kim 2023): enavogliflozin added to metformin plus gemigliptin matched dapagliflozin — HbA1c change −0.92% vs −0.86% at 24 weeks (between-group difference −0.06%)
cards.summary: ENHANCE-D RCT (Kim 2023): enavogliflozin added to metformin plus gemigliptin matched dapagliflozin — HbA1c change −0.92% vs −0.86% at 24 weeks (between-group difference −0.06%)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised active-comparator trial (ENHANCE-D), enavogliflozin vs dapagliflozin added to metformin plus gemigliptin
cards.people: 270 Korean patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (≥1000 mg/day) plus gemigliptin 50 mg/day, randomised to enavogliflozin 0.3 mg/day (n=134) or dapagliflozin 10 mg/day (n=136) added to that background therapy for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Both treatments significantly reduced HbA1c at week 24 (−0.92% enavogliflozin, −0.86% dapagliflozin; between-group difference −0.06%, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.06). Fasting plasma glucose changes also did not differ (between-group difference −3.49 mg/dL, 95% CI −8.08 to 1.10). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 21.64% on enavogliflozin versus 23.53% on dapagliflozin.
cards.watchOut: Active-comparator design on a two-drug background (metformin plus the DPP-4 inhibitor gemigliptin): there is no placebo arm, so this card supports equivalence to dapagliflozin, not absolute efficacy. Single-region (Korea) evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three Korean phase 3 trials — one placebo-controlled win (−0.99% HbA1c) and two non-inferiority matches against dapagliflozin; single-region evidence, surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: three Korean phase 3 trials — one placebo-controlled win (−0.99% HbA1c) and two non-inferiority matches against dapagliflozin; single-region evidence, surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (167 + 200 + 270 randomised patients, all in Korea, all 24 weeks).
cards.result: Enavogliflozin 0.3 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.99% more than placebo as monotherapy, and was non-inferior / equivalent to dapagliflozin 10 mg when added to metformin (−0.80% vs −0.75%) or to metformin plus gemigliptin (−0.92% vs −0.86%). A pooled renal-function analysis of the two dapagliflozin-comparator trials is a derivative of cards 2–3 and is not carded; a 52-week extension report of the monotherapy trial is programme support only and is not carded. No cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists for this agent, and all evidence is from Korea, where the drug is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout, and the non-inferiority cards must not be read as placebo-controlled efficacy.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Remogliflozin etabonate in type 2 diabetes: non-inferior to dapagliflozin at 24 weeks (−0.72%/−0.77% vs −0.58% HbA1c), with 12-week dose-ranging placebo data — limited-region programme, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor remogliflozin etabonate, compared with placebo, pioglitazone or dapagliflozin, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucosides/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Prodrugs/administration & dosage/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2/metabolism · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on a single-/limited-region programme. In the 24-week Indian phase 3 trial, remogliflozin etabonate 100 mg and 250 mg twice daily were non-inferior to dapagliflozin on metformin (HbA1c change −0.72% and −0.77% vs −0.58%). Two earlier 12-week dose-ranging trials in drug-naïve / treatment-naïve patients showed significant dose-response HbA1c effects versus placebo (reductions versus placebo of 0.64% to 1.07% across twice-daily doses in one). SINGLE-/LIMITED-REGION FLAG: the phase 3 was conducted in India and the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved. Two of the three anchors are 12-week dose-ranging trials, so the durable-efficacy claim rests mainly on the single 24-week non-inferiority trial. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: Phase 3 active-controlled RCT (Dharmalingam 2020): remogliflozin etabonate 100 mg and 250 mg twice daily non-inferior to dapagliflozin on metformin — HbA1c change −0.72% and −0.77% vs −0.58% at 24 weeks
cards.summary: Phase 3 active-controlled RCT (Dharmalingam 2020): remogliflozin etabonate 100 mg and 250 mg twice daily non-inferior to dapagliflozin on metformin — HbA1c change −0.72% and −0.77% vs −0.58% at 24 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind double-dummy active-controlled trial, remogliflozin etabonate vs dapagliflozin, both added to metformin
cards.people: 612 patients in India with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin ≥1500 mg/day (HbA1c ≥7% to ≤10%), randomised to remogliflozin etabonate 100 mg twice daily (n=225), remogliflozin etabonate 250 mg twice daily (n=241) or dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily (n=146), all on metformin, for 24 weeks; 167, 175 and 103 patients respectively completed the study.
cards.result: Mean (±SE) HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.72 ± 0.09% (100 mg), −0.77 ± 0.09% (250 mg) and −0.58 ± 0.12% (dapagliflozin). The differences versus dapagliflozin were −0.14% (90% CI −0.38 to 0.10) and −0.19% (90% CI −0.42 to 0.05), meeting non-inferiority (P<0.001; margin 0.35). No significant differences were found in fasting or postprandial glucose or body weight versus dapagliflozin. Treatment-emergent adverse events were comparable (32.6%, 34.4% and 29.5%), mostly mild to moderate, with no severe adverse events reported.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against an active comparator in a single-region (India) population; completion was incomplete (445 of 612 randomised patients completed). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Dharmalingam M et al. Efficacy and Safety of Remogliflozin Etabonate, a New Sodium Glucose Co-Transporter-2 Inhibitor, in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A 24-Week, Randomized, Double-Blind, Active-Controlled Trial. Drugs. 2020. PMID: 32162274. Registry ID: CTRI/2017/07/009121. cards.headline: 12-week once-daily dose-ranging RCT (Sykes 2015): a statistically significant dose-response trend for HbA1c change (P<0.047) — the abstract prints no per-dose HbA1c values and none are claimed here
cards.summary: 12-week once-daily dose-ranging RCT (Sykes 2015): a statistically significant dose-response trend for HbA1c change (P<0.047) — the abstract prints no per-dose HbA1c values and none are claimed here
cards.type: 12-week double-blind randomised placebo- and active-controlled dose-ranging trial, once-daily remogliflozin etabonate vs placebo or pioglitazone
cards.people: 252 newly diagnosed, drug-naïve people with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0% to ≤9.5%), randomised to remogliflozin etabonate once daily (100, 250, 500 or 1000 mg, or 250 mg twice daily), placebo, or pioglitazone 30 mg once daily for 12 weeks.
cards.result: A statistically significant trend in the dose-response relationship for change in HbA1c at week 12 was observed (P<0.047). Remogliflozin etabonate was generally well tolerated and no effects on LDL cholesterol were observed. The fetched abstract reports no per-dose HbA1c effect sizes, so this card supports a dose-response signal only, not a quantified placebo-adjusted effect.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week dose-ranging trial — short, and its abstract gives no per-dose numbers. It is programme support for a dose-response, not durable-efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Sykes AP et al. Randomized efficacy and safety trial of once-daily remogliflozin etabonate for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2015. PMID: 25238025. cards.headline: 12-week twice-daily dose-ranging RCT (Sykes 2015): HbA1c reductions versus placebo ranging from 0.64% to 1.07% across twice-daily doses (all P<0.001), with a decreasing dose response
cards.summary: 12-week twice-daily dose-ranging RCT (Sykes 2015): HbA1c reductions versus placebo ranging from 0.64% to 1.07% across twice-daily doses (all P<0.001), with a decreasing dose response
cards.type: 12-week double-blind randomised active- and placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, twice-daily remogliflozin etabonate vs placebo or pioglitazone
cards.people: 336 treatment-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%–9.5%), randomised to remogliflozin etabonate twice daily (50, 100, 250, 500 or 1000 mg), matching placebo, or pioglitazone 30 mg once daily for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Remogliflozin etabonate produced a decreasing dose response in HbA1c at week 12 (P<0.001), with reductions in HbA1c versus placebo ranging from 0.64% to 1.07% (P<0.001). Statistically significant reductions in body weight versus placebo were also observed, and twice-daily remogliflozin was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week dose-ranging trial across five doses — it establishes short-term placebo-controlled activity, not durability; the doses tested far exceed the 100–250 mg twice-daily doses carried into phase 3.
cards.source: Sykes AP et al. Randomized trial showing efficacy and safety of twice-daily remogliflozin etabonate for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2015. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (612 + 252 + 336 randomised patients).
cards.result: Remogliflozin etabonate lowered HbA1c versus placebo in two 12-week dose-ranging trials (0.64% to 1.07% versus placebo across twice-daily doses; a significant once-daily dose-response trend) and was non-inferior to dapagliflozin over 24 weeks on metformin (−0.72% and −0.77% vs −0.58%). A report of remogliflozin in type 1 diabetes is a different population and is not carded here. The agent was developed in India, is not FDA/EMA-approved, and has no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial; HbA1c is a surrogate throughout.

shelves.title: Tofogliflozin in type 2 diabetes (Japanese programme): HbA1c −0.80% to −1.02% vs −0.03% on placebo as monotherapy; insulin add-on data open-label after week 16 — single-region (Japan) evidence
shelves.question: In Japanese adults with type 2 diabetes, does the SGLT2 inhibitor tofogliflozin, compared with placebo (as monotherapy, dose-ranging, or added to insulin), improve glycaemic control and body weight?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Asian People/ethnology · Benzhydryl Compounds/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/drug therapy/ethnology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucosides/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Ketosis/chemically induced/diagnosis · Male · Middle Aged · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2/metabolism · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on single-region (Japan) evidence. In the combined phase 2/3 Japanese monotherapy study, tofogliflozin 10, 20 and 40 mg lowered HbA1c by −0.797%, −1.017% and −0.870% at 24 weeks versus −0.028% on placebo (all P<0.0001). A multinational 12-week dose-finding trial showed dose-dependent placebo-subtracted reductions up to 0.56% at 40 mg. Added to insulin (J-STEP/INS), HbA1c fell by 0.76% over 52 weeks in the continuous-tofogliflozin group, but the randomised placebo-controlled phase of that study lasted only 16 weeks and the 52-week figures come from its open-label extension. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: the programme is Japanese (the dose-finding trial multinational); tofogliflozin is approved in Japan and is not FDA/EMA-approved. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: Combined phase 2/3 monotherapy RCT (Kaku 2014): tofogliflozin lowered HbA1c by −0.797% (10 mg), −1.017% (20 mg) and −0.870% (40 mg) at 24 weeks versus −0.028% on placebo (all P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Combined phase 2/3 monotherapy RCT (Kaku 2014): tofogliflozin lowered HbA1c by −0.797% (10 mg), −1.017% (20 mg) and −0.870% (40 mg) at 24 weeks versus −0.028% on placebo (all P<0.0001)
cards.type: Combined phase 2/3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled monotherapy trial, tofogliflozin vs placebo
cards.people: 230 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on diet/exercise, randomised at 33 centres to placebo (n=56) or tofogliflozin 10, 20 or 40 mg once daily (n=58 each) for 24 weeks; 229 patients were in the full analysis set.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.028% (95% CI −0.192 to 0.137) on placebo, compared with −0.797% (10 mg), −1.017% (20 mg) and −0.870% (40 mg) on tofogliflozin (P<0.0001 for the differences versus placebo for all doses). Fasting and 2-hour postprandial glucose and body weight also fell prominently versus placebo. The main adverse events were hyperketonaemia, ketonuria and pollakiuria; the incidence of hypoglycaemia was low and most adverse events were mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: A combined phase 2/3 report, labelled as such. Single-region (Japan) evidence; HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Kaku K et al. Efficacy and safety of monotherapy with the novel sodium/glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor tofogliflozin in Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a combined Phase 2 and 3 randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group comparative study. cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on diet and exercise alone, or diet/exercise plus stable metformin, randomised to tofogliflozin 2.5, 5, 10, 20 or 40 mg or placebo for 12 weeks (the fetched abstract does not print the total number randomised, and none is claimed here).
cards.result: Statistically significant dose-dependent HbA1c reductions were shown at all doses except 2.5 mg, with a maximum placebo-subtracted reduction of 0.56% at 40 mg, alongside increased urinary glucose excretion. Dose-dependent reductions in fasting plasma glucose and body weight were observed. No deaths or treatment-related serious adverse events were reported; adverse-event incidence was 37.9% on placebo versus 35.9%–46.3% across tofogliflozin groups.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week dose-finding trial — it supports the dose-response, while the durable placebo-controlled claim rests on the 24-week combined phase 2/3 card. The participant total is not printed in the fetched abstract.

cards.headline: J-STEP/INS phase 4 add-on-to-insulin study (Terauchi 2018): HbA1c change to week 52 of −0.76% in the continuous-tofogliflozin group — but the placebo-controlled phase lasted only 16 weeks, with a 36-week open-label extension
cards.summary: J-STEP/INS phase 4 add-on-to-insulin study (Terauchi 2018): HbA1c change to week 52 of −0.76% in the continuous-tofogliflozin group — but the placebo-controlled phase lasted only 16 weeks, with a 36-week open-label extension
cards.type: Phase 4 multicentre randomised study (J-STEP/INS): 16-week double-blind placebo-controlled phase plus 36-week open-label extension, tofogliflozin added to insulin
cards.people: 210 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.5%–10.5%) on insulin (alone, or basal insulin plus a DPP-4 inhibitor) received treatment per randomisation: a 16-week double-blind placebo-controlled phase followed by a 36-week open-label extension in which all patients received tofogliflozin (the 'tofo-tofo' group took tofogliflozin for 52 weeks; the 'pla-tofo' group for 36 weeks).
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change from baseline to week 52 was −0.76% ± 0.077 in the tofo-tofo group and −0.73% ± 0.102 in the pla-tofo group; body weight changed by −1.52 kg and −2.13 kg respectively. Hypoglycaemia was the most common treatment-emergent adverse event (42.9% in the tofo-tofo group and 29.4% in the pla-tofo group, both groups receiving tofogliflozin for most of the study). Genital infection, urinary tract infection, excessive urination and volume-depletion events were also reported in the tofo-tofo group (2.1%, 2.1%, 7.1% and 10.0%).
cards.watchOut: The 52-week changes are from the open-label extension and must never be presented as placebo-controlled results — the randomised comparison lasts 16 weeks, and the fetched abstract prints no week-16 placebo-adjusted HbA1c figure. Hypoglycaemia rates reflect insulin background therapy.
cards.source: Terauchi Y et al.
