cards.result: Tofogliflozin lowered HbA1c versus placebo in the combined phase 2/3 monotherapy study (−0.797% to −1.017% across 10–40 mg vs −0.028% on placebo at 24 weeks) and dose-dependently in the 12-week dose-finding trial (maximum placebo-subtracted 0.56% at 40 mg). Added to insulin, HbA1c fell 0.76% over 52 weeks of continuous tofogliflozin, but that figure comes from a design whose placebo-controlled phase was 16 weeks followed by open-label treatment. Tofogliflozin is approved in Japan and is not FDA/EMA-approved; HbA1c is a surrogate and no cardiovascular- or renal-outcomes trial exists.

shelves.title: Ipragliflozin in type 2 diabetes (3 randomised trials in 3 publications): HbA1c −0.46% on metformin, −0.3% at 12 weeks in Russia, −0.77% on sitagliptin vs placebo — limited-region evidence, no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin or sitagliptin, does the SGLT2 inhibitor ipragliflozin 50 mg, compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control and body weight?
shelves.mesh: Asian People · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects · Female · Glucosides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Metformin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Thiophenes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only, on single-/limited-region evidence (Japan / East Asia / Russia). Report count stated exactly: 3 publications reporting 3 randomised trials (171 + 165 + 143 randomised patients) plus one open-label safety cohort (n=77). Added to metformin in Korea/Taiwan, ipragliflozin 50 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.46% more than placebo at 24 weeks; in Russian patients the placebo-adjusted difference was a more modest −0.3% at week 12 (P=0.048); added to sitagliptin in Japan, the difference was −0.77% at 24 weeks. Ipragliflozin is approved in Japan and is not FDA/EMA-approved. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and no outcomes trial exists. Pooled safety / blood-pressure / subgroup analyses of this programme are derivatives and are not carded.

cards.headline: Phase 3 add-on-to-metformin RCT (Lu 2016): ipragliflozin 50 mg lowered HbA1c by −0.94% vs −0.47% on placebo (between-group difference −0.46%, P<0.001) at 24 weeks in Korea and Taiwan
cards.summary: Phase 3 add-on-to-metformin RCT (Lu 2016): ipragliflozin 50 mg lowered HbA1c by −0.94% vs −0.47% on placebo (between-group difference −0.46%, P<0.001) at 24 weeks in Korea and Taiwan
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, ipragliflozin added to metformin vs placebo
cards.people: 171 Asian patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin, randomised at 18 sites in Korea and 12 in Taiwan to ipragliflozin 50 mg (n=87) or placebo (n=83) for 24 weeks while continuing metformin.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c change was −0.94% (SD 0.75) on ipragliflozin versus −0.47% (SD 0.81) on placebo (between-group difference −0.46%, P<0.001). Fasting plasma glucose and body-weight changes were also significantly greater on ipragliflozin (between-group differences −14.1 mg/dL and −1.24 kg, both P<0.001). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (9.2% vs 12.0%) and urinary tract infection (6.9% vs 2.4%).
cards.watchOut: Single-/limited-region evidence (Korea/Taiwan). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists for ipragliflozin.

cards.headline: Add-on-to-metformin RCT in Russian patients (Shestakova 2018): placebo-adjusted HbA1c difference −0.3% at week 12 (P=0.048) and body-weight difference −1.34 kg (P<0.001), followed by an open-label uptitration phase
cards.summary: Add-on-to-metformin RCT in Russian patients (Shestakova 2018): placebo-adjusted HbA1c difference −0.3% at week 12 (P=0.048) and body-weight difference −1.34 kg (P<0.001), followed by an open-label uptitration phase
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (12-week controlled phase) with open-label uptitration, ipragliflozin added to metformin
cards.people: 165 Russian patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin, randomised 2:1 to ipragliflozin 50 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks at 14 centres; patients with HbA1c ≥7.0% at week 12 received additional open-label ipragliflozin from week 12 to 24 (uptitration to 100 mg/day).
cards.result: At week 12 — the placebo-controlled comparison — HbA1c and body weight favoured ipragliflozin (adjusted mean difference to placebo −0.3%, P=0.048, and −1.34 kg, P<0.001). Uptitration to 100 mg/day produced a further mean weight change of −0.65 kg from week 12 (P=0.004) and an additional 9 of 69 patients (13%) reaching HbA1c <7.0% at week 24. Adverse-event incidence was similar between groups and between the 50 mg/day (23.7%) and 100 mg/day (24.6%) periods.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled phase is 12 weeks and the HbA1c effect is the smallest and least precise of this shelf (−0.3%, P=0.048); week-24 figures after open-label uptitration are not placebo-controlled.

cards.headline: Add-on-to-sitagliptin report (Kaku 2021) — ONE publication reporting TWO trials: randomised Trial 843 (143 patients) gave a least-squares mean HbA1c difference of −0.77% versus placebo at week 24 (P<0.001); open-label Trial 849 (n=77) was a 52-week safety cohort
cards.summary: Add-on-to-sitagliptin report (Kaku 2021) — ONE publication reporting TWO trials: randomised Trial 843 (143 patients) gave a least-squares mean HbA1c difference of −0.77% versus placebo at week 24 (P<0.001); open-label Trial 849 (n=77) was a 52-week safety cohort
cards.type: One publication reporting two trials: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Trial 843) and an open-label 52-week safety trial (Trial 849), ipragliflozin added to sitagliptin
cards.people: Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%–10.0%) on sitagliptin 50 mg once daily. Trial 843: randomised 1:1 to ipragliflozin 50 mg once daily (n=73) or placebo (n=70) for 24 weeks. Trial 849: open-label ipragliflozin 50 mg once daily added for 52 weeks (n=77), with safety/tolerability as the primary objective.
cards.result: In Trial 843, adding ipragliflozin gave a significantly greater HbA1c reduction than placebo at week 24 (least-squares mean difference −0.77%, 95% CI −0.98 to −0.57; P<0.001); adverse-event incidences overall and for prespecified events of interest were similar between groups. In Trial 849, adverse events with incidence ≥5% included nasopharyngitis, pollakiuria, back pain, thirst, constipation, influenza and arthralgia; drug-related events in ≥2 patients were pollakiuria, thirst and constipation.
cards.watchOut: Count this publication exactly as the row states: one randomised trial plus one open-label safety cohort — Trial 849 carries no efficacy comparison and must not be counted as a second randomised trial.

cards.summary: Phase 3 monotherapy RCT (Seino 2014): luseogliflozin 2.5 mg lowered HbA1c by −0.63% vs +0.13% on placebo (between-group difference −0.75%, P<0.001) over 24 weeks in Japanese patients
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled monotherapy trial, luseogliflozin vs placebo
cards.people: 158 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.9%–10.5%), randomised to luseogliflozin 2.5 mg (n=79) or placebo (n=79) once daily for 24 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell by −0.63% on luseogliflozin versus +0.13% on placebo (between-group difference −0.75%, P<0.001). Fasting and postprandial glucose, body weight and abdominal circumference were also significantly reduced versus placebo (all P<0.05). Adverse-event incidence did not differ significantly (59.5% luseogliflozin vs 57.0% placebo), no adverse event led to discontinuation, and no severe adverse event was reported; the authors note the short duration and small sample size as limitations.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (Japan) evidence and a modest sample (158 patients); HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.

cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, luseogliflozin added to metformin vs placebo
cards.people: 328 Caucasian patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on a stable metformin regimen (HbA1c ≥7% to ≤10%), randomised to luseogliflozin 2.5 mg (n=80), 5.0 mg (n=86) or 10.0 mg (n=79) or placebo (n=83) for 12 weeks; mean age 58.5 years, 64.6% women, mean HbA1c 8.54%.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c reductions were −0.98%, −1.09% and −1.18% on luseogliflozin 2.5, 5 and 10 mg versus −0.73% on placebo; compared with placebo, HbA1c was significantly lower by 0.25% (P=0.045), 0.36% (P=0.006) and 0.45% (P=0.001) respectively. cards.watchOut: A 12-week trial, and the placebo group itself fell 0.73% — the placebo-subtracted effects (0.25%–0.45%) are the smallest on this shelf. This is the one non-Japanese anchor; the doses tested (up to 10 mg) exceed the 2.5 mg dose of the Japanese monotherapy trial.

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for glycaemic control only — the glycaemic slice of the VERTIS programme. VERTIS MET: placebo-adjusted HbA1c changes of −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.9% (15 mg) at 26 weeks on metformin (both P<0.001). VERTIS SITA2: −0.7% and −0.8% added to metformin plus sitagliptin (both P<0.001), maintained to 52 weeks. VERTIS SU: ertugliflozin 15 mg was non-inferior to glimepiride on metformin at 52 weeks (HbA1c change −0.6% vs −0.7%), with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia and more genital mycotic infections than glimepiride. Ertugliflozin is a globally approved agent (FDA/EMA) — NOT single-region. This shelf asks the glycaemic question only: the VERTIS CV cardiovascular-outcomes trial builds separately at shelf #7512 and is cross-pointed here, never carded on this shelf. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint in all three anchors.

cards.headline: VERTIS MET RCT (Rosenstock 2018): ertugliflozin added to metformin gave placebo-adjusted HbA1c changes of −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.9% (15 mg) at week 26 (both P<0.001)
cards.summary: VERTIS MET RCT (Rosenstock 2018): ertugliflozin added to metformin gave placebo-adjusted HbA1c changes of −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.9% (15 mg) at week 26 (both P<0.001)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (VERTIS MET), ertugliflozin added to metformin vs placebo
cards.people: 621 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin monotherapy (≥1500 mg/day; HbA1c 7.0%–10.5%), randomised 1:1:1 to placebo or ertugliflozin 5 or 15 mg/day for 26 weeks (with an ongoing 78-week extension).
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted least-squares mean HbA1c change from a baseline of 8.1% was −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.9% (15 mg) (both P<0.001), to final means of 7.3% and 7.2%; the odds of HbA1c <7.0% were significantly greater on ertugliflozin. Fasting glucose, body weight and blood pressure were significantly reduced versus placebo. Genital mycotic infections were more frequent on ertugliflozin (women: 0.9% placebo vs 5.5% and 6.3%; men: 0% vs 3.1% and 3.2%), as were urinary tract infections and symptomatic hypoglycaemia; hypovolaemia events were similar, and there was no adverse impact on bone mineral density at week 26.
cards.watchOut: Glycaemic (surrogate) endpoint at 26 weeks; the extension phase is not part of this card's comparison.

cards.headline: VERTIS SITA2 RCT (Dagogo-Jack 2018): ertugliflozin added to metformin plus sitagliptin gave placebo-adjusted HbA1c changes of −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.8% (15 mg) at week 26 (both P<0.001), maintained to week 52
cards.summary: VERTIS SITA2 RCT (Dagogo-Jack 2018): ertugliflozin added to metformin plus sitagliptin gave placebo-adjusted HbA1c changes of −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.8% (15 mg) at week 26 (both P<0.001), maintained to week 52
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (VERTIS SITA2), ertugliflozin added to metformin plus sitagliptin vs placebo
cards.people: 464 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin ≥1500 mg/day plus sitagliptin 100 mg/day (HbA1c 7.0%–10.5%; mean baseline HbA1c 8.0%), randomised to ertugliflozin 5 mg, ertugliflozin 15 mg or placebo once daily; treatment continued to week 52.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted least-squares mean HbA1c changes at week 26 were −0.7% (5 mg) and −0.8% (15 mg) (both P<0.001); HbA1c <7.0% was reached by 17.0% on placebo versus 32.1% (5 mg) and 39.9% (15 mg). Fasting glucose, body weight and systolic blood pressure fell significantly versus placebo, and the glycaemic, weight and blood-pressure effects were maintained through week 52. Genital mycotic infections were more frequent on ertugliflozin (3.7%–14.1% vs 0%–1.9% on placebo through week 52); urinary tract infection, symptomatic hypoglycaemia and hypovolaemia incidences were not meaningfully different.
cards.watchOut: Glycaemic (surrogate) endpoint; the population was already on two background agents, so this is a third-line add-on comparison.

cards.headline: VERTIS SU RCT (Hollander 2018): ertugliflozin 15 mg non-inferior to glimepiride on metformin at week 52 — HbA1c change −0.6% vs −0.7% (difference 0.1%, meeting the 0.3% non-inferiority criterion), with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia and more genital mycotic infections
cards.summary: VERTIS SU RCT (Hollander 2018): ertugliflozin 15 mg non-inferior to glimepiride on metformin at week 52 — HbA1c change −0.6% vs −0.7% (difference 0.1%, meeting the 0.3% non-inferiority criterion), with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia and more genital mycotic infections
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised non-inferiority trial (VERTIS SU), ertugliflozin vs glimepiride, both added to metformin
cards.people: 1,326 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin ≥1500 mg/day (HbA1c ≥7.0% and ≤9.0%; mean baseline 7.8%), randomised 1:1:1 to ertugliflozin 15 mg, ertugliflozin 5 mg or glimepiride (titrated from 1 mg; mean/median dose 3.0 mg/day) once daily for 52 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 52 was −0.6% (15 mg), −0.6% (5 mg) and −0.7% (glimepiride); the between-group difference for ertugliflozin 15 mg versus glimepiride was 0.1% (95% CI −0.0 to 0.2), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (upper bound <0.3%). Greater body-weight and systolic blood-pressure reductions were observed with ertugliflozin than glimepiride. Overall adverse-event incidence was similar; symptomatic hypoglycaemia was less frequent and genital mycotic infection more frequent with ertugliflozin than glimepiride; urinary tract infection and hypovolaemia incidences were not meaningfully different.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority comparison against an active sulfonylurea, not a placebo-controlled win; only the 15 mg dose was formally tested against the non-inferiority criterion. The record for this report carries no MeSH terms (see source line).

cards.headline: Synthesis: the VERTIS glycaemic programme is consistently positive on HbA1c (two placebo-controlled trials, one non-inferiority match against glimepiride) — this shelf is the glycaemic slice only; the VERTIS CV outcomes trial is homed separately at shelf #7512
cards.summary: Synthesis: the VERTIS glycaemic programme is consistently positive on HbA1c (two placebo-controlled trials, one non-inferiority match against glimepiride) — this shelf is the glycaemic slice only; the VERTIS CV outcomes trial is homed separately at shelf #7512
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (621 + 464 + 1,326 randomised patients).
cards.result: Ertugliflozin 5 and 15 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.7%–0.9% versus placebo added to metformin, and by 0.7%–0.8% added to metformin plus sitagliptin, and ertugliflozin 15 mg was non-inferior to glimepiride over 52 weeks, with less symptomatic hypoglycaemia, more genital mycotic infections, and greater weight and systolic blood-pressure reductions than glimepiride. The VERTIS FACTORIAL co-administration trial (ertugliflozin with sitagliptin started together) is a combination question and is programme support only, not carded here. The cardiovascular-outcomes question for this agent (VERTIS CV) is NOT asked on this shelf: it builds separately at shelf #7512 — see that shelf for the outcomes verdict; the two shelves cross-point and the outcomes trial is not duplicated here (one-home rule).
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint in all three anchors, and no outcomes conclusion should be drawn from this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Metanephrine reference intervals by LC-MS/MS: supine normetanephrine upper limit rises to 1.05 nmol/L over age 60 (age adjustment lifts specificity 88.3% to 96.0%); seated samples need seated limits (specificity 94.6% vs 83.5%)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrine (and urinary free metanephrines) measured by LC-MS/MS — by sampling posture (supine vs seated), age and sex — and how much do posture and the age adjustment for normetanephrine move the upper limits used to exclude phaeochromocytoma?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenal Gland Neoplasms/blood,complications,diagnosis · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Case-Control Studies · Child · Child, Preschool · False Positive Reactions · Female · Humans · Hypertension/blood,complications,diagnosis · Male · Metanephrine/blood · Middle Aged · Normetanephrine/blood · Pheochromocytoma/blood,complications,diagnosis · Reference Values · Sensitivity and Specificity · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, adrenal medulla / catecholamine chapters — framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Three independent reference populations, carded PER SAMPLING POSTURE because posture is part of the measurement and supine and seated intervals are different numbers, never merged. Supine (Eisenhofer 2013; 1,226 subjects sampled supine, including 575 normotensive and hypertensive adults and 535 patients in whom phaeochromocytoma was ruled out): the upper cut-off for plasma normetanephrine rises with age, from 0.47 nmol/L in children to 1.05 nmol/L in subjects over 60 — the age adjustment for normetanephrine is this shelf's core content — and an age-adjusted curvilinear model plus a higher metanephrine cut-off (0.45 vs 0.32 nmol/L) raised diagnostic specificity from 88.3% to 96.0% with minimal sensitivity loss (93.9% to 93.6%). Seated (Lin 2023; reference population 736 people aged 14–92 — the record includes adolescents from age 14 and the adult bands are the carded content): seated intervals applied to seated samples gave the same 100% sensitivity and better specificity (94.6% vs 83.5%) than applying published age-adjusted supine intervals, and halved-to-a-third the borderline band (5.3% vs 15.7% of suspected patients fell between the upper limit and twice it). Plasma and urine by LC-MS/MS (Eisenhofer 2019; 590 hypertensive and normotensive reference subjects, intervals optimised against 2,056 patients tested for phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma): age is the dominant consideration for plasma normetanephrine and sex the most practical basis for urinary metabolite intervals. CKD-specific intervals are a patient-population limb and are not a dataset here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Seated reference intervals by LC-MS/MS (Lin 2023, reference population 736 people aged 14–92): applying seated intervals to seated samples kept sensitivity at 100% and improved specificity to 94.6% vs 83.5% for (misapplied) supine intervals; the borderline band shrank from 15.7% to 5.3%
cards.summary: Seated reference intervals by LC-MS/MS (Lin 2023, reference population 736 people aged 14–92): applying seated intervals to seated samples kept sensitivity at 100% and improved specificity to 94.6% vs 83.5% for (misapplied) supine intervals; the borderline band shrank from 15.7% to 5.3%
cards.type: Primary reference-interval dataset (plasma metanephrines, SEATED sampling, LC-MS/MS)
cards.people: A reference population of 736 people aged 14–92 years (the record includes adolescents from age 14; the adult bands are this shelf's content) whose seated plasma metanephrines were measured by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), with a validation population of 1,068 patients aged 8–87 years tested for pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma.
cards.result: There was no correlation between seated plasma metanephrines and age (P>0.05), values differed by sex (P<0.0001) and differed among the various disease groups (P<0.05). The upper reference limit established in the seated position had the same sensitivity (100%) and better specificity (94.6% vs 83.5%) than the published age-adjusted supine reference intervals, and the proportion of suspected patients with values in the borderline range between the upper limit and twice the upper limit was lower with seated intervals (5.3% vs 15.7%). The authors conclude that using the corresponding seated intervals for seated samples reduces unnecessary re-examination of patients with slightly elevated metanephrines, and that seated sampling is an acceptable, more convenient and more economical practice than supine sampling. The fetched record does not print the numeric seated limits, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Posture is the measurement: these intervals validate seated sampling judged against seated limits. The study's comparative point is precisely that judging a seated sample against supine limits manufactures false positives and borderline re-tests — the two postures' intervals must never be interchanged.
cards.source: Lin Y et al. Establishment of reference intervals for plasma metanephrines in seated position measured by LC-MS/MS and assessment of diagnostic performance in pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. Annals of clinical biochemistry. 2023. PMID: 36653315. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Supine reference intervals with the age adjustment for normetanephrine (Eisenhofer 2013, 1,226 subjects sampled supine): the normetanephrine upper cut-off rises from 0.47 nmol/L in children to 1.05 nmol/L over age 60; age-adjusted cut-offs plus a metanephrine cut-off of 0.45 (vs 0.32) nmol/L raised specificity from 88.3% to 96.0% at minimal sensitivity cost
cards.summary: Supine reference intervals with the age adjustment for normetanephrine (Eisenhofer 2013, 1,226 subjects sampled supine): the normetanephrine upper cut-off rises from 0.47 nmol/L in children to 1.05 nmol/L over age 60; age-adjusted cut-offs plus a metanephrine cut-off of 0.45 (vs 0.32) nmol/L raised specificity from 88.3% to 96.0% at minimal sensitivity cost
cards.type: Primary reference-interval dataset (plasma free metanephrines, SUPINE sampling, with age-adjusted normetanephrine cut-offs)
cards.people: 1,226 subjects aged 5–84 years from whom blood was collected in the supine position — including 116 children, 575 normotensive and hypertensive adults and 535 patients in whom phaeochromocytoma was ruled out — with the optimised cut-offs validated in a separate group of 3,888 patients tested for phaeochromocytoma, including 558 with confirmed disease. The adult supine values are this shelf's content; the paediatric end of the age curve is reported only as the lower anchor of the age adjustment.
cards.result: Plasma metanephrine, but not normetanephrine, was higher in men than in women (P<0.001), though reference intervals did not differ by sex. Age showed a positive relationship with plasma normetanephrine (P<0.0001) and a weaker one with metanephrine (P=0.021). Upper cut-offs for normetanephrine increased from 0.47 nmol/L in children to 1.05 nmol/L in subjects over 60 years. A curvilinear age-adjusted model for normetanephrine, together with a higher cut-off for metanephrine (0.45 vs 0.32 nmol/L), produced a substantial gain in diagnostic specificity (from 88.3% to 96.0%) with minimal loss of sensitivity (from 93.9% to 93.6%).
cards.watchOut: A single fixed normetanephrine cut-off is the error this dataset exists to correct: applying a young-adult upper limit (near 0.47 nmol/L) to a patient over 60 — whose reference limit is 1.05 nmol/L — manufactures false positives. Supine sampling throughout: these limits do not govern seated samples (see the Lin card).
cards.source: Eisenhofer G et al. Reference intervals for plasma free metanephrines with an age adjustment for normetanephrine for optimized laboratory testing of phaeochromocytoma. Annals of clinical biochemistry. 2013. PMID: 23065528. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Plasma and urinary intervals by LC-MS/MS (Eisenhofer 2019, 590 reference subjects; optimisation against 2,056 tested patients): age is the key consideration for plasma normetanephrine, sex the practical basis for urinary metabolite intervals; urinary free and deconjugated fractions are separately referenced
cards.summary: Plasma and urinary intervals by LC-MS/MS (Eisenhofer 2019, 590 reference subjects; optimisation against 2,056 tested patients): age is the key consideration for plasma normetanephrine, sex the practical basis for urinary metabolite intervals; urinary free and deconjugated fractions are separately referenced
cards.type: Primary reference-interval dataset (plasma free, urinary free and urinary deconjugated metanephrines and methoxytyramine, LC-MS/MS)
cards.people: 590 hypertensive and normotensive reference subjects in whom plasma free, urinary free and urinary acid-hydrolysed deconjugated normetanephrine, metanephrine and methoxytyramine were measured by LC-MS/MS; reference intervals were optimised using data from 2,056 patients tested for pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma.
cards.result: Multivariate analyses correcting for age and body surface area indicated higher plasma and urinary metanephrine in males than females, with sex differences in urinary normetanephrine and free methoxytyramine that largely reflected body-size variation. Age was positively associated with plasma metabolites but negatively related to urinary free metanephrine and methoxytyramine. Plasma and urinary normetanephrine were higher in hypertensives than normotensives, though the differences were small. Optimisation indicated that age was the most important consideration for plasma normetanephrine and sex the most practical basis for urinary metabolites; the study establishes sex-specific reference intervals for the urinary metabolites. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval limits, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Three different specimen/fraction combinations (plasma free, urinary free, urinary deconjugated) each carry their own intervals in this study — a urinary free value judged against a deconjugated (total) interval, or vice versa, repeats the posture error in a second form. Numeric limits must be taken from the full text for the exact fraction assayed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: metanephrine reference intervals are posture-, age- and specimen-specific — supine normetanephrine's upper limit more than doubles across adult life (to 1.05 nmol/L over 60), seated samples need seated limits, and urinary intervals are sex-specific
cards.summary: Synthesis: metanephrine reference intervals are posture-, age- and specimen-specific — supine normetanephrine's upper limit more than doubles across adult life (to 1.05 nmol/L over 60), seated samples need seated limits, and urinary intervals are sex-specific
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (adrenal medulla and catecholamines; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature). The three datasets divide the measurement by its decisive variables. Posture: seated intervals applied to seated samples held sensitivity at 100% and raised specificity to 94.6% versus 83.5% for supine intervals misapplied to them, with the borderline band shrinking from 15.7% to 5.3% (Lin 2023). Age: under supine sampling the normetanephrine upper cut-off climbs from 0.47 nmol/L in children to 1.05 nmol/L over age 60, and age adjustment plus a 0.45 nmol/L metanephrine cut-off lifted specificity from 88.3% to 96.0% (Eisenhofer 2013). Specimen and sex: plasma normetanephrine is age-driven, urinary metabolites are best referenced sex-specifically, and free and deconjugated urinary fractions are distinct measurements (Eisenhofer 2019). PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: three independent reference populations converge on the same structure — the interval is a function of posture, age and specimen, not a single number.
cards.watchOut: The three classic errors this shelf exists to prevent: a seated sample judged by supine limits, an older patient's normetanephrine judged by a young fixed cut-off, and a urinary free value judged by a deconjugated interval.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: TSH distribution and reference intervals: reference mean ≈1.40 mIU/L (NHANES III), but upper limits of 3.60 (South Germany), 7.06 (screened Koreans) and 8.86 mIU/L (Chinese ≥65, vs 6.57 under 65)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the population distribution and reference interval for serum thyrotropin (TSH) — median, spread and 97.5th percentile by age, sex, ancestry and iodine status — how much does the upper limit rise in older adults, and how far do antibody-negative 'reference population' limits sit below whole-population limits?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Black or African American/statistics & numerical data · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Autoantibodies/analysis · Demography · Female · Humans · Iodide Peroxidase/immunology · Iodine/urine · Male · Mexican Americans/statistics & numerical data · Middle Aged · Nutrition Surveys · Thyroglobulin/immunology · Thyrotropin/blood · Thyroxine/blood · White People/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, thyroid hormone chapters — framing brief; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature, and says so. This is a DISTRIBUTION row, not a treatment-threshold row: subclinical-hypothyroidism therapy lives on its own shelves. Four independent populations, carded with the reference-population DEFINITION beside every interval, because the definition (antibody-negative, ultrasound-screened, or disease-free by history) moves the upper limit more than the assay does — and iodine status differs by population (US / Korean / German / Chinese) as content, not caveat. NHANES III (17,353 US participants aged ≥12; antibody-negative reference population 13,344): geometric mean TSH 1.40 mIU/L in the reference population, rising with age, and lower in Black participants (1.18) than White (1.45) or Mexican American (1.37) participants. An ultrasonography- and antibody-screened Korean health-check population (19,465) produced a WIDER interval, 0.73–7.06 mIU/L — positive antibodies or abnormal ultrasound widened the central 95% interval, and smokers' values shifted lower. South German KORA F4 (3,080 examined; 710 thyroid-healthy after exclusions) gave 0.52–3.60 mIU/L with a median of 1.49 and no significant age or sex influence. A 10-city Chinese survey (15,008) shows the age effect the other datasets flatten: the older-adult (≥65) interval was 0.75–8.86 mIU/L (median 2.58) versus 0.76–6.57 (median 2.38) in younger adults, and applying the age-specific range cut the labelled prevalence of subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults from 19.87% to 3.3%. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: NHANES III (Hollowell 2002, 17,353 US participants aged ≥12; reference population 13,344): geometric mean TSH 1.40 mIU/L in the antibody-negative reference population, rising with age; lower in Black (1.18) than White (1.45) or Mexican American (1.37) participants
cards.summary: NHANES III (Hollowell 2002, 17,353 US participants aged ≥12; reference population 13,344): geometric mean TSH 1.40 mIU/L in the antibody-negative reference population, rising with age; lower in Black (1.18) than White (1.45) or Mexican American (1.37) participants
cards.type: Primary population dataset (national survey; TSH distribution in disease-free and antibody-negative reference populations, US)
cards.people: 17,353 people aged ≥12 years representing the geographic and ethnic distribution of the US population (NHANES III, 1988–1994), with serum TSH, total T4, antithyroperoxidase (TPOAb) and antithyroglobulin (TgAb) antibodies measured. The disease-free population (no reported thyroid disease, goitre or thyroid medication) numbered 16,533; the reference population of 13,344 was selected from it by additionally excluding pregnancy, androgen/oestrogen use, thyroid antibodies, and biochemical hypo- or hyperthyroidism.
cards.result: In the disease-free population, mean serum TSH was 1.50 mIU/L (95% CI 1.46 to 1.54), higher in females than males, and higher in White non-Hispanic participants (1.57, 95% CI 1.52 to 1.62) than in Black non-Hispanic (1.18, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.21; P<0.001) or Mexican American participants (1.43, 95% CI 1.40 to 1.46; P<0.001). In the reference population, geometric mean TSH was 1.40 ± 0.02 mIU/L and increased with age, and was significantly lower in Black participants (1.18 ± 0.02) than in White (1.45 ± 0.02) or Mexican American (1.37 ± 0.02) participants. TPOAb were positive in 11.3% and TgAb in 10.4% of the population, more prevalent in women, increasing with age, and less prevalent in Black participants (TPOAb 4.5% vs 12.3% in White participants). Hypothyroidism was found in 4.6% of the US population (0.3% clinical, 4.3% subclinical) and hyperthyroidism in 1.3%.
cards.watchOut: Two populations, two answers: the disease-free mean (1.50 mIU/L) and the antibody-negative reference-population geometric mean (1.40 mIU/L) are different quantities, and the ancestry differences are distribution facts of this US survey — they describe the sampled population's TSH and antibody prevalence, not individual-level diagnostic rules.
cards.source: Hollowell JG et al. Serum TSH, T(4), and thyroid antibodies in the United States population (1988 to 1994): National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III). The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2002. PMID: 11836274. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ultrasound- and antibody-screened Korean population (Kim 2015, 19,465 health-check participants): TSH reference interval 0.73–7.06 mIU/L — wider than Western intervals; positive antibodies or abnormal ultrasound widened the central 95% interval, and smokers' TSH shifted lower
cards.summary: Ultrasound- and antibody-screened Korean population (Kim 2015, 19,465 health-check participants): TSH reference interval 0.73–7.06 mIU/L — wider than Western intervals; positive antibodies or abnormal ultrasound widened the central 95% interval, and smokers' TSH shifted lower
cards.type: Primary population dataset (TSH reference interval in an ultrasonography-screened Korean health-check population)
cards.people: 19,465 subjects recruited at routine health check-ups in Korea; subjects with overt thyroid disease, a prior history of thyroid disease or a family history of thyroid cancer were excluded. The reference population was defined by National Academy of Clinical Biochemistry criteria, ultrasound findings and smoking status, with sex and age considered in the distribution analysis.
cards.result: In the presence of positive anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies or abnormal ultrasound findings, the central 95-percentile interval of serum TSH widened; the distribution shifted toward lower values in current smokers. The reference interval obtained in the normal Korean reference population was 0.73 to 7.06 mIU/L. Serum TSH was higher in females than in males in all groups, and there were no age-dependent shifts. The authors conclude the Korean interval is higher than those of other countries and that the upper and lower limits previously defined by Western studies should be raised for Korean populations.
cards.watchOut: The widest interval on this shelf (upper limit 7.06 mIU/L) comes from the most aggressively screened population — the opposite of the naive expectation that screening narrows intervals — because screening here defines who counts as reference-normal in a high-TSH population. It is a Korean health-check population's interval, not a universal upper limit, and it found no age shift, against the Chinese dataset below.
cards.source: Kim M et al. Reference interval for thyrotropin in a ultrasonography screened Korean population. The Korean journal of internal medicine. 2015. PMID: 25995664. cards.headline: KORA F4, South Germany (Burkhardt 2014, 3,080 examined; 710 thyroid-healthy after exclusions): TSH reference range 0.52–3.60 mIU/L, median 1.49, on Siemens Vista analysers; no significant influence of age or sex; urinary iodine excretion median 118.6 µg/g creatinine
cards.summary: KORA F4, South Germany (Burkhardt 2014, 3,080 examined; 710 thyroid-healthy after exclusions): TSH reference range 0.52–3.60 mIU/L, median 1.49, on Siemens Vista analysers; no significant influence of age or sex; urinary iodine excretion median 118.6 µg/g creatinine
cards.type: Primary population dataset (TSH reference range in a population-based South German cohort, thyroid-healthy subset)
cards.people: 3,080 individuals aged 32–81 years from the population-based KORA F4 study (Cooperative Health Research in the Region of Augsburg, South Germany), examined for thyroid history, sonography and clinical chemistry; after excluding individuals with known as well as previously unknown thyroid disorders revealed by the study, 710 thyroid-healthy individuals remained for the TSH, fT3 and fT4 reference ranges.
cards.result: For thyroid-healthy men and women the TSH reference range was 0.52–3.60 mIU/L on Siemens Vista analysers, with a median of 1.49 mIU/L. No statistically significant influence of age or sex was found. Median urinary iodine excretion in the healthy population was 118.6 µg/g creatinine, above the recommended target of 100 µg/g. The authors note the South German reference value is higher than that assessed in the Northeast-German SHIP study 10 years earlier, and that population-based and apparatus-specific examinations are necessary to define a TSH reference value.
cards.watchOut: The narrowest interval on this shelf rests on the smallest reference subset (710 of 3,080 after exclusions) and is explicitly apparatus-specific (Siemens Vista) and region-specific — the same country's northeast study a decade earlier gave a lower value, which the authors attribute to iodine supply and laboratory equipment differences.
cards.source: Burkhardt K et al. [TSH-reference range of adults: results from the population-based study KORA F4]. Deutsche medizinische Wochenschrift (1946). 2014. PMID: 24496892. cards.headline: Age-specific ranges in 10 Chinese cities (Zhai 2018, 15,008 adults): the ≥65 reference range was 0.75–8.86 mIU/L (median 2.58) vs 0.76–6.57 (median 2.38) under 65 — and using the age-specific range cut labelled subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults from 19.87% to 3.3%
cards.summary: Age-specific ranges in 10 Chinese cities (Zhai 2018, 15,008 adults): the ≥65 reference range was 0.75–8.86 mIU/L (median 2.58) vs 0.76–6.57 (median 2.38) under 65 — and using the age-specific range cut labelled subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults from 19.87% to 3.3%
cards.type: Primary population dataset (age-specific TSH reference ranges, cross-sectional survey in 10 Chinese cities)
cards.people: 15,008 randomly selected adults in 10 cities in China (2010–2011) who completed urinary iodine measurement, serum TSH, TPOAb and TgAb titres, thyroid ultrasonography and questionnaires; the age-specific reference range was formulated according to National Academy of Clinical Biochemistry guidelines, and disease prevalence in older adults (≥65 years) was computed under both the general-population and the age-specific ranges.
cards.result: Both the median and the upper limit of serum TSH were higher in older adults than in younger adults (2.58 [0.75–8.86] mIU/L vs 2.38 [0.76–6.57] mIU/L; P<0.001). Using the general-population range, the prevalence of subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults was 19.87%; using the age-specific range it was 3.3% — while overt hypothyroidism changed little (1.6% vs 2.09%). Positive TPOAb was associated with subclinical hypothyroidism in older adults under both ranges. The authors conclude the TSH rise with age may represent a normal compensatory phenomenon in older adults and recommend age-specific reference ranges to prevent misdiagnosis and mistreatment.
cards.watchOut: The prevalence swing (19.87% to 3.3%) is a labelling consequence of the reference range chosen, not a change in anyone's thyroid: it shows how much of 'subclinical hypothyroidism' in older adults is manufactured by applying a young population's upper limit. Whether the age-related rise is benign compensation is the authors' interpretation, printed as such — this distribution shelf takes no position on treatment thresholds.

cards.headline: Synthesis: TSH distributions are population-, definition- and age-bound — reference means cluster near 1.4–1.5 mIU/L, but upper limits run from 3.60 (South Germany) to 7.06 (screened Koreans) to 8.86 mIU/L in Chinese adults ≥65, so the 'normal TSH' question has no population-free answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: TSH distributions are population-, definition- and age-bound — reference means cluster near 1.4–1.5 mIU/L, but upper limits run from 3.60 (South Germany) to 7.06 (screened Koreans) to 8.86 mIU/L in Chinese adults ≥65, so the 'normal TSH' question has no population-free answer
cards.people: Synthesis of the four primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (thyroid hormones; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population-survey literature). The centres agree: NHANES III's antibody-negative reference geometric mean is 1.40 mIU/L (Hollowell 2002) and KORA F4's thyroid-healthy median is 1.49 mIU/L (Burkhardt 2014). The tails do not agree, and the disagreements are the content: the upper reference limit is 3.60 mIU/L in South Germany, 7.06 mIU/L in an ultrasound-screened Korean population (Kim 2015), and 8.86 mIU/L in Chinese adults aged ≥65 versus 6.57 under 65 (Zhai 2018). NHANES III adds the ancestry structure (reference geometric means 1.18 Black, 1.37 Mexican American, 1.45 White participants) and the definitional lesson — its disease-free and antibody-negative reference populations give different means from the same blood samples. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the distribution and its dependence on reference-population definition, age, ancestry and iodine status are demonstrated across four large independent populations totalling over 55,000 participants.
cards.watchOut: Never quote a TSH upper limit without its population and its reference-population definition; and never convert this distribution shelf into a treatment threshold — whether to treat a given TSH is decided on the subclinical-hypothyroidism shelves, not here.

shelves.title: VERTIS CV (one trial, four reports): ertugliflozin NONINFERIOR for MACE (11.9% vs 11.9%), not superior — with prespecified heart-failure (HR 0.70 for first hospitalisation) and exploratory kidney signals in the same trial
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, does ertugliflozin, compared with placebo, reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, heart-failure hospitalisation and kidney progression (the VERTIS CV outcomes trial and its prespecified companion reports)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Atherosclerosis/complications,drug therapy · Bridged Bicyclo Compounds, Heterocyclic/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology,mortality · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications,drug therapy · Diabetic Nephropathies/complications · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos/therapeutic use · Sodium-Glucose Transporter 2 Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, confined to heart-failure and kidney signals) — and the headline must be read exactly as the trial printed it: VERTIS CV is a NONINFERIORITY result, not an outcomes win. Report count stated exactly: this shelf cards four reports of the SINGLE VERTIS CV trial (primary, prespecified heart-failure, prespecified kidney, prespecified eGFR-slope) plus one further secondary analysis in older adults, labelled programme support — one programme, not five trials. In 8,246 randomised patients with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease followed a mean of 3.5 years, major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 11.9% on ertugliflozin and 11.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.97, 95.6% CI 0.85 to 1.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority against the 1.3 margin), and the first key secondary composite — cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation — did NOT reach superiority (8.1% vs 9.1%; hazard ratio 0.88, 95.8% CI 0.75 to 1.03; P=0.11). The favourable signals live in the prespecified companion reports and are printed as such: first heart-failure hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.90) with total heart-failure events rate ratio 0.70; the exploratory kidney composite (sustained 40% eGFR reduction, dialysis/transplant or renal death) at 6.0 vs 9.0 events per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88), while the trial's own secondary kidney composite gave hazard ratio 0.81 (95.8% CI 0.63 to 1.04); and a placebo-adjusted chronic eGFR-slope difference of 1.19 mL/min/1.73 m² per year over weeks 6–156. Amputations were numerically more frequent on ertugliflozin (2.0% on 5 mg, 2.1% on 15 mg, vs 1.6% on placebo). The glycaemic question for this drug (the VERTIS MET / SITA2 / SU programme) is a different question, homed at pack #7468; it is cross-pointed here in prose and none of its studies is carded on this shelf (one-home rule).

cards.headline: VERTIS CV primary report (Cannon 2020, n=8,246, mean follow-up 3.5 years): ertugliflozin was NONINFERIOR to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events — 11.9% vs 11.9%, hazard ratio 0.97 (95.6% CI 0.85 to 1.11) — and the cardiovascular-death/heart-failure-hospitalisation composite did not reach superiority (P=0.11)
cards.summary: VERTIS CV primary report (Cannon 2020, n=8,246, mean follow-up 3.5 years): ertugliflozin was NONINFERIOR to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events — 11.9% vs 11.9%, hazard ratio 0.97 (95.6% CI 0.85 to 1.11) — and the cardiovascular-death/heart-failure-hospitalisation composite did not reach superiority (P=0.11)
cards.type: Primary report of the VERTIS CV multicentre double-blind cardiovascular outcomes trial (ertugliflozin 5/15 mg pooled vs placebo) — ONE trial; all other cards on this shelf are reports of this same trial
cards.people: 8,246 patients with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, randomised in a multicentre double-blind trial to ertugliflozin 5 mg, ertugliflozin 15 mg or placebo once daily (the two dose groups pooled for analysis; 8,238 received at least one dose) and followed for a mean of 3.5 years. The primary objective was noninferiority for major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke) against a margin of 1.3 on the upper boundary of the 95.6% confidence interval.
cards.result: A major adverse cardiovascular event occurred in 653 of 5,493 patients (11.9%) in the ertugliflozin group and 327 of 2,745 (11.9%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.97, 95.6% CI 0.85 to 1.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority). Death from cardiovascular causes or hospitalisation for heart failure occurred in 444 of 5,499 (8.1%) versus 250 of 2,747 (9.1%) (hazard ratio 0.88, 95.8% CI 0.75 to 1.03; P=0.11 for superiority — not significant). The hazard ratio for cardiovascular death was 0.92 (95.8% CI 0.77 to 1.11), and for death from renal causes, renal replacement therapy or doubling of serum creatinine 0.81 (95.8% CI 0.63 to 1.04) — hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute rates. Amputations were performed in 54 patients (2.0%) on the 5 mg dose and 57 (2.1%) on the 15 mg dose, versus 45 (1.6%) on placebo. The trial was funded by Merck Sharp & Dohme and Pfizer.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is the finding: identical absolute MACE rates (11.9% vs 11.9%) and a non-significant first key secondary composite mean this trial must never be presented as showing cardiovascular-event reduction. The favourable heart-failure and kidney numbers on the cards below are prespecified secondary/exploratory analyses of this same trial, not independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Prespecified heart-failure analysis of VERTIS CV (Cosentino 2020 — same trial, labelled): first heart-failure hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.90, P=0.006) and total heart-failure events rate ratio 0.70, while first HHF/cardiovascular death remained non-significant (0.88, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.03)
cards.summary: Prespecified heart-failure analysis of VERTIS CV (Cosentino 2020 — same trial, labelled): first heart-failure hospitalisation hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.90, P=0.006) and total heart-failure events rate ratio 0.70, while first HHF/cardiovascular death remained non-significant (0.88, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.03)
cards.type: Prespecified secondary (heart-failure) analysis of the VERTIS CV trial — a report OF the trial carded above, not a separate trial
cards.people: The VERTIS CV population (8,246 randomised; 5,499 ertugliflozin pooled doses, 2,747 placebo), of whom 1,958 (23.7%) had a history of heart failure and 5,006 (60.7%) had a pretrial ejection fraction available, including 959 with ejection fraction ≤45%. Prespecified secondary analyses compared pooled ertugliflozin versus placebo on time to first heart-failure hospitalisation (HHF) and the composite of HHF/cardiovascular death, with Andersen-Gill modelling for total (first plus recurrent) events.
cards.result: Ertugliflozin did not significantly reduce first HHF/cardiovascular death (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.03) but reduced first HHF (hazard ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.90; P=0.006). A history of heart failure did not modify the first-HHF effect (with HF: 0.63, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.90; without HF: 0.79, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.15; P for interaction = 0.40), though the reduction tended to be greater with ejection fraction ≤45% (0.48, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.76) than >45% (0.86, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.29), and was greater in patients with baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m², albuminuria or diuretic use (each P for interaction <0.05). Ertugliflozin also reduced total HHF events (rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.87) and total HHF/cardiovascular death (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.96) — hazard and rate ratios are relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Labelled companion report of the same single trial: the HHF reduction sits inside a trial whose primary outcome was neutral and whose HHF/cardiovascular-death composite was non-significant in both the primary report and this analysis — the HHF signal is real within its prespecified analysis but carries no independent replication on this shelf.

cards.headline: Prespecified kidney analysis of VERTIS CV (Cherney 2021 — same trial, labelled): the EXPLORATORY composite (sustained 40% eGFR reduction, dialysis/transplant or renal death) occurred at 6.0 vs 9.0 events per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88); UACR was 16.2% relatively lower at 60 months
cards.summary: Prespecified kidney analysis of VERTIS CV (Cherney 2021 — same trial, labelled): the EXPLORATORY composite (sustained 40% eGFR reduction, dialysis/transplant or renal death) occurred at 6.0 vs 9.0 events per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88); UACR was 16.2% relatively lower at 60 months
cards.type: Prespecified kidney analysis of the VERTIS CV trial — a report OF the trial carded above, not a separate trial
cards.people: The VERTIS CV population (8,246 randomised, mean follow-up 3.5 years; ertugliflozin 5 mg and 15 mg pooled versus placebo, added to existing treatment). This analysis evaluated the trial's kidney composite (doubling of serum creatinine, renal dialysis/transplant or renal death — reported in the primary paper), a prespecified EXPLORATORY composite substituting sustained 40% eGFR decrease for doubling of creatinine, and the time course of urinary albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR) and eGFR.
cards.result: The exploratory kidney composite occurred at a lower event rate on ertugliflozin than placebo (6.0 vs 9.0 events per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88), against the trial's own secondary kidney composite hazard ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.63 to 1.04) reported in the primary paper. At 60 months, placebo-corrected changes from baseline were −16.2% (95% CI −23.9 to −7.6) for UACR — a relative percentage change — and +2.6 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI 1.5 to 3.6) for eGFR. Ertugliflozin was associated with a consistent decrease in UACR and attenuation of eGFR decline across subgroups, with a suggested larger effect in the macroalbuminuria and KDIGO high/very-high-risk subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The significant composite is the EXPLORATORY one (40% eGFR decline); the trial's prespecified secondary kidney composite (doubling of creatinine) was not significant (0.81, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.04). Printing the 0.66 without that distinction would overstate the kidney claim, so both are printed on this card.

cards.headline: Prespecified eGFR-slope analysis of VERTIS CV (Cherney 2021, CJASN — same trial, labelled): after an early dip, the chronic slope over weeks 6–156 favoured ertugliflozin by 1.19 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI 0.95 to 1.42)
cards.summary: Prespecified eGFR-slope analysis of VERTIS CV (Cherney 2021, CJASN — same trial, labelled): after an early dip, the chronic slope over weeks 6–156 favoured ertugliflozin by 1.19 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (95% CI 0.95 to 1.42)
cards.type: Prespecified eGFR-slope analysis of the VERTIS CV trial — a report OF the trial carded above, not a separate trial
cards.people: The VERTIS CV population (ertugliflozin pooled doses n=5,499 versus placebo n=2,747), with eGFR slopes estimated by random-coefficient models over separate periods (weeks 0–6; weeks 6–52) and as total and chronic slopes to weeks 104, 156, 208 and 260, overall and by baseline kidney status.
cards.result: Over weeks 0–6 the least-squares mean eGFR slope was more negative on ertugliflozin than placebo (−0.54 vs −0.07 mL/min/1.73 m² per week; difference −0.47, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.36) — the expected early dip. Over weeks 6–52 the slopes were +1.62 versus −0.12 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (difference 1.74, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.45), and over weeks 6–156 (the chronic slope) −0.32 versus −1.51 mL/min/1.73 m² per year, a placebo-adjusted difference of 1.19 (95% CI 0.95 to 1.42). Over weeks 0–156 the placebo-adjusted difference was 1.06 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.27). Findings were consistent by baseline kidney status, and the authors note the placebo-adjusted slope exceeded the ≥0.75 mL/min/1.73 m² per year preservation proposed as a surrogate for kidney-disease progression.
cards.watchOut: Slope is a surrogate: a 1.19 mL/min/1.73 m² per year slower modelled decline supports the kidney-composite signal but is not itself a dialysis or renal-death result, and the early 6-week dip (−0.47 per week difference) must be read with the chronic slope, not mistaken for harm or hidden from it.

cards.headline: Programme support — older-adults secondary analysis of VERTIS CV (Pratley 2023 — same trial, labelled programme support, not a fifth anchor): effects on cardiorenal outcomes and safety were generally similar in participants ≥65 and ≥75 years as in the overall cohort
cards.summary: Programme support — older-adults secondary analysis of VERTIS CV (Pratley 2023 — same trial, labelled programme support, not a fifth anchor): effects on cardiorenal outcomes and safety were generally similar in participants ≥65 and ≥75 years as in the overall cohort
cards.type: Programme support: secondary age-subgroup analysis of the VERTIS CV trial — a report OF the trial carded above, not an independent trial and not a fifth anchor
cards.people: The VERTIS CV population analysed by baseline age (prespecified ≥65 vs <65 years; post hoc ≥75 vs <75): of 8,238 participants who received at least one dose, 4,145 (50.3%) were aged ≥65 and 903 (11.0%) were ≥75; 70.0% were male and 87.8% White. Older subgroups had lower mean eGFR, longer diabetes duration and more cardiovascular outcomes.
cards.result: Similar to the overall cohort, ertugliflozin did not increase the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation, cardiovascular death alone, or the kidney composite outcome (doubling of creatinine, dialysis/transplantation or kidney death) in the older subgroups, and reduced heart-failure hospitalisation and the exploratory kidney composite (40% sustained eGFR decrease) in those subgroups (P for interaction >0.05 for the outcomes assessed). A slower eGFR decline and a smaller UACR increase over time were observed in all age subgroups on ertugliflozin versus placebo, and safety outcomes across age subgroups were consistent with the known profile of ertugliflozin.
cards.watchOut: Programme support only, as commissioned: a subgroup consistency analysis (one cut prespecified, the ≥75 cut post hoc) — it shows the trial's pattern was not confined to younger patients, and adds no new comparative evidence beyond the four reports above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, four reports plus labelled programme support — ertugliflozin met noninferiority for MACE (11.9% vs 11.9%) without superiority on the cardiovascular-death/heart-failure composite, with prespecified heart-failure-hospitalisation and exploratory kidney signals inside the same trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, four reports plus labelled programme support — ertugliflozin met noninferiority for MACE (11.9% vs 11.9%) without superiority on the cardiovascular-death/heart-failure composite, with prespecified heart-failure-hospitalisation and exploratory kidney signals inside the same trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf — every one a report of the single VERTIS CV trial (NCT01986881).
cards.result: VERTIS CV (8,246 randomised, mean 3.5 years) established that ertugliflozin is noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.97, 95.6% CI 0.85 to 1.11) — a safety/noninferiority conclusion, not event reduction: the absolute rates were identical and the first key secondary composite missed superiority (P=0.11). Within the same trial, prespecified analyses found fewer first heart-failure hospitalisations (hazard ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.90), a lower rate of the exploratory kidney composite (6.0 vs 9.0 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.66) beside a non-significant prespecified kidney composite (0.81), and a slower chronic eGFR decline by 1.19 mL/min/1.73 m² per year; the older-adults analysis (programme support) found the same pattern at ≥65 and ≥75 years. Amputations were numerically higher on ertugliflozin (2.0–2.1% vs 1.6%). The drug's glycaemic efficacy programme is a separate question at pack #7468 and is cross-pointed, not carded, here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Counting reminder: four reports and one programme-support analysis of ONE trial — never cite this shelf as five studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Efsubaglutide alfa in type 2 diabetes (China-only programme): HbA1c −1.26%/−1.68% vs placebo in SUPER 1 and −1.06% in SUPER 2 at 24 weeks — no outcomes trial
shelves.question: In Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes (drug-naïve on lifestyle alone, or inadequately controlled on metformin), does the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist efsubaglutide alfa, compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Hypoglycemic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Aged · Glycated Hemoglobin · Adult · Blood Glucose · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only), on single-region evidence: every trial was conducted in China and efsubaglutide alfa is not FDA/EMA-approved — that flag is on the face of this shelf. Two seamless phase IIb/III placebo-controlled programmes agree: SUPER 1 (drug-naïve, phase III stage 297 randomised) cut HbA1c by 1.73% on 1 mg and 2.15% on 3 mg at week 24 (estimated treatment differences versus placebo −1.26% and −1.68%), and SUPER 2 (added to metformin) cut HbA1c by 1.80% on 3 mg versus 0.74% on placebo (difference −1.06%, P<0.001). A third, small (59-patient), open-label, 12-week dosing-interval trial found 3 mg every two weeks comparable to 1 mg weekly — it has no placebo arm and is not load-bearing for efficacy. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. Gastrointestinal adverse events (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, decreased appetite) were the most common, mostly mild to moderate.

cards.headline: SUPER 1 (Zhu 2026): efsubaglutide alfa in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes — HbA1c fell 1.73% on 1 mg and 2.15% on 3 mg at week 24 (treatment differences vs placebo −1.26% and −1.68%)
cards.summary: SUPER 1 (Zhu 2026): efsubaglutide alfa in drug-naïve type 2 diabetes — HbA1c fell 1.73% on 1 mg and 2.15% on 3 mg at week 24 (treatment differences vs placebo −1.26% and −1.68%)
cards.type: Two-stage seamless phase IIb/III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SUPER 1), efsubaglutide alfa weekly vs placebo, drug-naïve type 2 diabetes
cards.people: Adults in China newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes inadequately managed by diet and exercise. Two-stage seamless phase IIb/III trial: phase IIb stage 140 randomised (1, 2 or 3 mg weekly or placebo, 12 weeks); phase III stage 297 randomised to efsubaglutide alfa 1 mg (n=118), 3 mg (n=117) or placebo (n=62) once weekly.
cards.result: At week 24 in the phase III stage, HbA1c reductions were −1.73% (1 mg) and −2.15% (3 mg); estimated treatment differences versus placebo were −1.26% (95% CI −1.68 to −0.84 in percentage terms; printed as −13.71 mmol/mol, 95% CI −17.39 to −10.06) for 1 mg and −1.68% (−18.36 mmol/mol, 95% CI −22.08 to −14.64) for 3 mg. HbA1c below 7.0% was achieved by 56% (1 mg) and 68% (3 mg). Fasting plasma glucose fell by 2.04 mmol/L (≈37 mg/dL) on 1 mg and 2.49 mmol/L (≈45 mg/dL) on 3 mg. Body weight fell 0.97% on 1 mg and 3.14% on 3 mg. Gastrointestinal symptoms — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and decreased appetite — were the most common adverse events, mostly mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Seamless IIb/III design: the phase IIb stage was dose-finding and the phase III doses were chosen by interim analysis — the placebo-controlled efficacy claim rests on the phase III stage printed here. Single-region (China) evidence; HbA1c is a surrogate and no outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: SUPER 2 (Jia 2026): efsubaglutide alfa added to metformin — HbA1c fell 1.80% on 3 mg versus 0.74% on placebo at week 24 (difference −1.06%, P<0.001)
cards.summary: SUPER 2 (Jia 2026): efsubaglutide alfa added to metformin — HbA1c fell 1.80% on 3 mg versus 0.74% on placebo at week 24 (difference −1.06%, P<0.001)
cards.type: Two-stage adaptive phase 2b/3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SUPER 2), efsubaglutide alfa added to metformin vs placebo
cards.people: Adults in China with type 2 diabetes on metformin. Two-stage adaptive phase 2b/3 trial: phase 2b randomised participants to efsubaglutide 1 mg, 3 mg or placebo for 12 weeks; in phase 3, new participants were randomised 1:1 to efsubaglutide 3 mg or placebo for 24 weeks, followed by a 28-week open-label extension. The fetched abstract does not print the phase 3 randomised N, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: At week 24 in phase 3, HbA1c decreased by 1.80% with efsubaglutide 3 mg versus 0.74% with placebo (estimated treatment difference −1.06%; P<0.001). In phase 2b at week 12, HbA1c decreased by 1.10% with 1 mg and 1.43% with 3 mg (both P<0.0001). Adverse events were predominantly mild to moderate gastrointestinal events. The report also describes β-cell functional responses, as its title states.
cards.watchOut: The phase 3 randomised N is not printed in the fetched abstract and is not claimed on this card. Seamless adaptive design with a dose selected after phase 2b; single-region (China) evidence; surrogate endpoint only.

cards.type: Randomised open-label multicentre dosing-interval trial, efsubaglutide alfa 3 mg every two weeks vs 1 mg weekly (no placebo arm)
cards.people: 59 adults in China with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with lifestyle intervention, randomised 1:1 to efsubaglutide alfa 3 mg every two weeks or 1 mg weekly for 12 weeks after a 1-week 1 mg run-in, in a multicentre open-label trial.
cards.result: HbA1c decreased by −1.45% on the every-two-week regimen and −1.53% on weekly dosing; least-squares mean difference 0.09% (95% CI −0.32 to 0.50). Time in range 3.9–10.0 mmol/L (70–180 mg/dL) rose to 77.2% (every two weeks) versus 75.1% (weekly). HbA1c below 7.0% at week 13 was achieved by 55.2% versus 65.5%. Gastrointestinal adverse events predominated and were mostly mild to moderate; no hypoglycaemia or cardiovascular events occurred.
cards.watchOut: 59 patients, 12 weeks, open-label, no placebo arm: this card answers a dosing-interval question only and carries none of the shelf's placebo-controlled efficacy weight, which rests on SUPER 1 and SUPER 2.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two seamless phase IIb/III placebo-controlled programmes (SUPER 1 drug-naïve; SUPER 2 on metformin) both show ~1–1.7% placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions at 24 weeks — single-region (China) evidence, surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: two seamless phase IIb/III placebo-controlled programmes (SUPER 1 drug-naïve; SUPER 2 on metformin) both show ~1–1.7% placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions at 24 weeks — single-region (China) evidence, surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Efsubaglutide alfa once weekly lowered HbA1c versus placebo in both placebo-controlled programmes: SUPER 1 treatment differences −1.26% (1 mg) and −1.68% (3 mg) at week 24, and SUPER 2 a difference of −1.06% (3 mg added to metformin). The 59-patient open-label dosing-interval trial suggests 3 mg every two weeks performs comparably to 1 mg weekly over 12 weeks, but it has no placebo arm. All evidence is from China, the agent is not FDA/EMA-approved, HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint, and no cardiovascular-outcomes trial exists. The LIGHT 1 obesity trial and the diabetes-remission secondary analysis of the SUPER programme ask different questions and are not carded here (one-home rule).
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Pegloxenatide in type 2 diabetes (China-only programme): HbA1c −1.02%/−1.34% vs −0.17% on placebo as monotherapy and −1.16%/−1.14% vs +0.35% added to metformin — no outcomes trial reported
shelves.question: In Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes, does the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist polyethylene glycol loxenatide (pegloxenatide, PEX168), compared with placebo (as monotherapy or added to metformin) or insulin glargine, improve glycaemic control?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · China · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Peptides · Polyethylene Glycols · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit — glycaemic control only), on single-region evidence: every trial was conducted in China, where pegloxenatide is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved — that flag is on the face of this shelf. Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials agree: monotherapy (361 randomised) cut HbA1c by −1.02% on 100 µg and −1.34% on 200 µg versus −0.17% on placebo at week 24, and added to metformin the least-squares mean changes were −1.16% and −1.14% versus +0.35% on placebo. A third card — a 78-patient, open-label, single-centre CGM trial versus insulin glargine — found more time in range on pegloxenatide; it is not load-bearing for durable efficacy. HbA1c and time in range are surrogate endpoints, and the BALANCE-3 cardiovascular-outcomes trial is a protocol only: no outcomes trial has reported.

cards.headline: Phase 3a monotherapy trial (Shuai 2021): pegloxenatide cut HbA1c by −1.02% (100 µg) and −1.34% (200 µg) versus −0.17% on placebo at week 24
cards.summary: Phase 3a monotherapy trial (Shuai 2021): pegloxenatide cut HbA1c by −1.02% (100 µg) and −1.34% (200 µg) versus −0.17% on placebo at week 24
cards.type: Phase 3a multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, pegloxenatide monotherapy vs placebo
cards.people: 361 patients in China with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycaemic control (HbA1c 7.0%–10.5%), randomised 1:1:1 to weekly subcutaneous placebo, pegloxenatide (PEX168) 100 µg or 200 µg for 24 weeks, followed by a 28-week extension.
cards.result: HbA1c least-squares mean change at week 24 was −1.02% (100 µg) and −1.34% (200 µg) versus −0.17% on placebo (superiority P<0.0001 for both doses). HbA1c below 7% was achieved by 34.7% and 46.6% versus 15.7% on placebo. Nausea occurred in 5.6% (100 µg) and 10.0% (200 µg) versus 0% on placebo, and vomiting in 2.4% and 8.3% versus 0%. Six patients (1.6%) discontinued because of adverse events; antidrug antibodies developed in 1.2%.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (China) evidence; 24-week surrogate endpoint (HbA1c); no outcomes trial has reported — the BALANCE-3 outcomes trial is a protocol only.
cards.source: Shuai Y et al. Efficacy and safety of polyethylene glycol loxenatide monotherapy in type 2 diabetes patients: A multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3a clinical trial. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2021. PMID: 32965075. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase 3b add-on trial (Gao 2020): pegloxenatide added to metformin — HbA1c changes −1.16% and −1.14% versus +0.35% on placebo at week 24 (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Phase 3b add-on trial (Gao 2020): pegloxenatide added to metformin — HbA1c changes −1.16% and −1.14% versus +0.35% on placebo at week 24 (P<0.001)
cards.type: Phase 3b multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, pegloxenatide added to metformin vs placebo added to metformin
cards.people: Chinese patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%–10.5%) on metformin at 44 sites, randomised 1:1:1 to metformin plus placebo, pegloxenatide 100 µg or pegloxenatide 200 µg weekly for a 24-week core period followed by a 28-week extension. The fetched abstract does not print the randomised N, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −1.16% (100 µg) and −1.14% (200 µg) versus +0.35% on placebo (P<0.001 for superiority for both). HbA1c below 7.0% was achieved by 37.4% and 40.6% versus 16.8% on placebo (both P<0.001). Gastrointestinal reactions were mild; hypoglycaemia and weight-gain risks did not increase; anti-pegloxenatide antibodies were noted in under 2% of patients; no treatment-emergent serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The randomised N is not printed in the fetched abstract and is not claimed on this card. Single-region (China) evidence; surrogate endpoint only.

cards.headline: CGM trial versus insulin glargine (Zhang 2023): time in range 3.9–10.0 mmol/L (70–180 mg/dL) was 13.4 percentage points greater on pegloxenatide — a 78-patient open-label single-centre trial
cards.summary: CGM trial versus insulin glargine (Zhang 2023): time in range 3.9–10.0 mmol/L (70–180 mg/dL) was 13.4 percentage points greater on pegloxenatide — a 78-patient open-label single-centre trial
cards.type: Randomised open-label single-centre parallel-group trial, pegloxenatide vs insulin glargine on metformin, CGM-measured
cards.people: 78 patients (39 per group) aged 45 years or older with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%–11.0%) treated with metformin for at least 3 months, at a single centre in Shantou, China, randomised to pegloxenatide or insulin glargine for 24 weeks in an open-label parallel-group trial; glycaemia was measured by continuous glucose monitoring.
cards.result: Over weeks 22–24, time in range 3.9–10.0 mmol/L (70–180 mg/dL) was greater on pegloxenatide (estimated treatment difference 13.4%, 95% CI 6.8 to 20.0; P<0.001), as was tight time in range 3.9–7.8 mmol/L (70–140 mg/dL) (difference 15.6%, 95% CI 8.9 to 22.4). Mean glucose was lower on pegloxenatide by −1.2 mmol/L (≈−22 mg/dL; 95% CI −1.9 to −0.5). Time below range was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: 78 patients, open-label, single centre, CGM surrogate endpoints over 24 weeks: this card does not carry the shelf's durable-efficacy claim, which rests on the two phase 3 trials above.
cards.source: Zhang S et al. Efficacy of polyethylene glycol loxenatide versus insulin glargine on glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes: a randomized, open-label, parallel-group trial. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2023. PMID: 37214446. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Taspoglutide in type 2 diabetes (DISCONTINUED, never marketed): HbA1c beat placebo, exenatide and sitagliptin in T-emerge — abandoned for nausea, injection-site and allergic reactions
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin-based therapy, does the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist taspoglutide, compared with placebo, exenatide or sitagliptin, improve glycaemic control (the T-emerge programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Delayed-Action Preparations · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Metformin · Middle Aged · Peptides · Pioglitazone · Placebos · Thiazolidinediones · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: DISCONTINUED AGENT — this flag leads. Taspoglutide's development was halted in 2010 and it was never marketed; this shelf is a historical programme record. The glycaemic efficacy was real: across the T-emerge programme, once-weekly taspoglutide lowered HbA1c more than placebo (T-emerge 3: −1.35%/−1.40% versus −0.45%), more than twice-daily exenatide (T-emerge 2: −1.24%/−1.31% versus −0.98%) and more than sitagliptin (T-emerge 4: −1.23%/−1.30% versus −0.89%). The tolerability was the failure: nausea in 35–59% across trials, vomiting in up to 37%, injection-site reactions in 24% versus 5% on placebo, systemic allergic reactions, anti-taspoglutide antibodies in 46–49%, and high discontinuation — the gastrointestinal intolerance and hypersensitivity that ended the programme are printed on every card. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: T-emerge 3 (Henry 2012): taspoglutide added to metformin + pioglitazone — HbA1c −1.35%/−1.40% versus −0.45% on placebo; nausea 35%/44% and injection-site reactions 24%/24%
cards.summary: T-emerge 3 (Henry 2012): taspoglutide added to metformin + pioglitazone — HbA1c −1.35%/−1.40% versus −0.45% on placebo; nausea 35%/44% and injection-site reactions 24%/24%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (T-emerge 3), taspoglutide added to metformin + pioglitazone vs placebo
cards.people: 326 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with metformin plus pioglitazone, randomised to once-weekly subcutaneous taspoglutide 10 mg, taspoglutide 20 mg (10 mg for the first 4 weeks) or placebo for 24 weeks, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: HbA1c least-squares mean change at week 24 was −1.35% (10 mg) and −1.40% (20 mg) versus −0.45% on placebo (P<0.0001). HbA1c of 7% or less was reached by 69.8% and 76.1% versus 35.1%. Fasting plasma glucose fell by −1.87 mmol/L (−34 mg/dL) and −2.12 mmol/L (−38 mg/dL) versus −0.57 mmol/L (−10 mg/dL). Weight changed by −0.64 kg and −1.04 kg versus +0.59 kg on placebo. The most frequent adverse events on 10 mg, 20 mg and placebo were nausea (35%, 44%, 10%), vomiting (21%, 24%, 2%) and injection-site reactions (24%, 24%, 5%).
cards.watchOut: Discontinued agent (development halted in 2010; never marketed): efficacy here is historical. The nausea, vomiting and injection-site reaction rates on this card are the tolerability record that ended the programme.
cards.source: Henry RR et al. Efficacy and safety of taspoglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with metformin plus pioglitazone over 24 weeks: T-Emerge 3 trial. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2012. PMID: 22539590. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: T-emerge 2 (Rosenstock 2013): taspoglutide beat twice-daily exenatide on HbA1c (−1.24%/−1.31% vs −0.98%) — with nausea in 53%/59% versus 35% and antibodies in 49%
cards.summary: T-emerge 2 (Rosenstock 2013): taspoglutide beat twice-daily exenatide on HbA1c (−1.24%/−1.31% vs −0.98%) — with nausea in 53%/59% versus 35% and antibodies in 49%
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised trial (T-emerge 2), taspoglutide weekly vs exenatide twice daily
cards.people: 1,189 overweight adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin with or without a thiazolidinedione, randomised to taspoglutide 10 mg weekly (n=399), taspoglutide 20 mg weekly (n=398) or exenatide 10 µg twice daily (n=392) in an open-label multicentre trial; primary endpoint HbA1c change at 24 weeks.
cards.result: Mean baseline HbA1c was 8.1%. HbA1c fell by −1.24% (taspoglutide 10 mg; difference versus exenatide −0.26, 95% CI −0.37 to −0.15) and −1.31% (20 mg; difference −0.33, 95% CI −0.44 to −0.22) versus −0.98% on exenatide (both P<0.0001), and effects were maintained at 52 weeks. Weight fell −1.6 kg, −2.3 kg and −2.3 kg respectively. Nausea occurred in 53%, 59% and 35%, and vomiting in 33%, 37% and 16%. Allergic and injection-site reactions were more common with taspoglutide, discontinuations were greater, and anti-taspoglutide antibodies were detected in 49% of patients. The authors' own conclusion names 'unacceptable levels of nausea/vomiting, injection-site reactions, and systemic allergic reactions'.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design. The trial's title — 'The fate of taspoglutide' — reflects that the programme had already been halted for tolerability when this report appeared; read the efficacy and the adverse-event rates together.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. The fate of taspoglutide, a weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist, versus twice-daily exenatide for type 2 diabetes: the T-emerge 2 trial. Diabetes care. 2013. PMID: 23139373. Registry ID: NCT00717457.
