cards.headline: T-emerge 4 (Bergenstal 2012): taspoglutide beat sitagliptin on HbA1c (−1.23%/−1.30% vs −0.89%; placebo −0.10%) — and its adverse events 'led to the discontinuation of dosing'
cards.summary: T-emerge 4 (Bergenstal 2012): taspoglutide beat sitagliptin on HbA1c (−1.23%/−1.30% vs −0.89%; placebo −0.10%) — and its adverse events 'led to the discontinuation of dosing'
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy trial (T-emerge 4), taspoglutide vs sitagliptin or placebo, added to metformin
cards.people: 666 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (baseline HbA1c 7.96%), randomised to taspoglutide 10 mg weekly (n=190), taspoglutide 20 mg weekly (n=198), sitagliptin 100 mg daily (n=185) or placebo (n=93) for 24 weeks, in a double-blind double-dummy trial with extension periods.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c reductions at week 24 were −1.23% (taspoglutide 10 mg) and −1.30% (20 mg) versus −0.89% on sitagliptin and −0.10% on placebo; treatment differences versus sitagliptin were −0.34 (95% CI −0.49 to −0.19) and −0.41 (95% CI −0.56 to −0.26). Weight loss was −1.8 kg and −2.6 kg versus −0.9 kg (sitagliptin) and −0.5 kg (placebo). No severe hypoglycaemia occurred on any active treatment. Gastrointestinal adverse events and allergic and injection-site reactions were higher on taspoglutide, causing higher discontinuation rates; anti-taspoglutide antibodies were confirmed in 46% of patients. The abstract concludes that the safety profile 'led to the discontinuation of dosing'.
cards.watchOut: Discontinued agent: this trial's own abstract records that its safety profile led to discontinuation of dosing. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists.
cards.source: Bergenstal RM et al. Efficacy and safety of taspoglutide versus sitagliptin for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T-emerge 4 trial). cards.headline: Synthesis: a discontinued programme — taspoglutide lowered HbA1c more than placebo, exenatide and sitagliptin across T-emerge 3, 2 and 4, and was abandoned for gastrointestinal intolerance and hypersensitivity, not for lack of efficacy
cards.summary: Synthesis: a discontinued programme — taspoglutide lowered HbA1c more than placebo, exenatide and sitagliptin across T-emerge 3, 2 and 4, and was abandoned for gastrointestinal intolerance and hypersensitivity, not for lack of efficacy
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the three carded T-emerge trials (326, 1,189 and 666 randomised), once-weekly taspoglutide consistently produced larger HbA1c reductions than its comparators at 24 weeks. The same record shows why the agent does not exist in practice: nausea in 35–59%, vomiting in 21–37%, injection-site reactions in 24% versus 5% on placebo, systemic allergic reactions, antibodies in 46–49% and high discontinuation. Development was halted in 2010 and taspoglutide was never marketed. This shelf is a historical-programme record in the same discipline as the library's other discontinued-agent shelves; nothing on it is a treatment option today.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Muraglitazar in type 2 diabetes (NEVER MARKETED): JAMA 2005 CV-safety relative risk 2.23 (1.47% vs 0.67%) ended the programme despite real HbA1c efficacy
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the dual PPARα/γ agonist muraglitazar, compared with placebo, pioglitazone or glimepiride, improve glycaemic control and lipids — and what did the cardiovascular safety record show?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Fasting · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Glycine · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin · Male · Middle Aged · Oxazoles · Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors
shelves.balance: NEVER-MARKETED AGENT — the harm record leads. Muraglitazar, a dual PPARα/γ agonist, was abandoned after the 2005 JAMA cardiovascular safety meta-analysis of its phase 2/3 programme (3,725 patients): death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke occurred in 35 of 2,374 (1.47%) on muraglitazar versus 9 of 1,351 (0.67%) on placebo/pioglitazone controls — relative risk 2.23 (95% CI 1.07 to 4.66; P=0.03), a relative measure with the absolute rates printed beside it; the wider composite including transient ischaemic attack and heart failure gave a relative risk of 2.62 (2.11% versus 0.81%). This was despite an 8:1 FDA advisory vote recommending approval. The glycaemic efficacy underneath was real (monotherapy HbA1c −1.05%/−1.23% versus −0.32% on placebo; better HbA1c and lipid changes than pioglitazone 30 mg added to metformin), and the trials themselves showed more oedema, weight gain and heart failure on muraglitazar. The meta-analysis rests on sponsor trial documents released for the advisory meeting, not on a dedicated outcomes trial. HbA1c and lipids are surrogate endpoints.

cards.headline: Cardiovascular safety meta-analysis (Nissen 2005, JAMA): death, MI or stroke in 1.47% on muraglitazar versus 0.67% on controls — relative risk 2.23 (95% CI 1.07 to 4.66)
cards.summary: Cardiovascular safety meta-analysis (Nissen 2005, JAMA): death, MI or stroke in 1.47% on muraglitazar versus 0.67% on controls — relative risk 2.23 (95% CI 1.07 to 4.66)
cards.type: Cardiovascular safety meta-analysis of the phase 2/3 randomised programme (sponsor documents released for the FDA advisory meeting)
cards.people: 3,725 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7%–10%) across the prospective randomised double-blind phase 2 and 3 trials of muraglitazar (2,374 on muraglitazar; 1,351 on placebo or pioglitazone controls), as monotherapy or combined with metformin or glyburide, in trials of 24 to 104 weeks. The source material was sponsor trial documents released under public disclosure laws for the September 9, 2005 FDA advisory committee meeting, which had voted 8:1 to recommend approval.
cards.result: The primary composite of death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke occurred in 35 of 2,374 (1.47%) on muraglitazar versus 9 of 1,351 (0.67%) on controls — relative risk 2.23 (95% CI 1.07 to 4.66; P=0.03), a relative measure; the absolute difference was 0.80 percentage points. The wider composite adding transient ischaemic attack and congestive heart failure occurred in 50 of 2,374 (2.11%) versus 11 of 1,351 (0.81%) — relative risk 2.62 (95% CI 1.36 to 5.05; P=0.004). Adjudicated congestive heart failure occurred in 13 of 2,374 (0.55%) versus 1 of 1,351 (0.07%) — relative risk 7.43 (95% CI 0.97 to 56.8; P=0.053). The authors concluded the agent should not be approved on laboratory endpoints until safety was documented in a dedicated cardiovascular events trial.
cards.watchOut: Not a dedicated outcomes trial: the analysis pools sponsor phase 2/3 documents released for an advisory meeting, event counts are small (35 versus 9 for the primary composite), and the relative risks must be read with the absolute rates printed on this card. Muraglitazar was never marketed.
cards.source: Nissen SE et al. Effect of muraglitazar on death and major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 16239637. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Monotherapy trial (Buse 2005): muraglitazar cut HbA1c by −1.05% (2.5 mg) and −1.23% (5 mg) versus −0.32% on placebo at 24 weeks in drug-naïve patients
cards.summary: Monotherapy trial (Buse 2005): muraglitazar cut HbA1c by −1.05% (2.5 mg) and −1.23% (5 mg) versus −0.32% on placebo at 24 weeks in drug-naïve patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled 24-week monotherapy trial, muraglitazar vs placebo, drug-naïve type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 340 patients (179 men, 161 women) aged 18–70 with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise participated in the double-blind phase, randomised to muraglitazar 2.5 mg, muraglitazar 5 mg or placebo for 24 weeks; a parallel open-label cohort of 109 patients with higher HbA1c received muraglitazar 5 mg.
cards.result: Mean baseline HbA1c was 7.9%–8.0%. At week 24, HbA1c fell by −1.05% (2.5 mg) and −1.23% (5 mg) versus −0.32% on placebo (P<0.001). HbA1c below 7.0% was achieved by 58%, 72% and 30% respectively. Triglycerides fell by −18% and −27% relative, and HDL cholesterol rose by 10% and 16% relative (relative changes as printed). Oedema-related adverse events occurred in 8%–11% of patients in all groups; mean weight change was +1.1 kg (2.5 mg) and +2.1 kg (5 mg) versus −0.8 kg on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate endpoints over 24 weeks in a never-marketed agent: this efficacy card must be read under the cardiovascular safety record on the first card of this shelf, which is why that card leads.

cards.headline: Pioglitazone-comparative trial (Kendall 2006): muraglitazar 5 mg on metformin reached HbA1c 6.98% versus 7.28% on pioglitazone 30 mg — with more oedema, weight gain, heart failure and deaths on muraglitazar
cards.summary: Pioglitazone-comparative trial (Kendall 2006): muraglitazar 5 mg on metformin reached HbA1c 6.98% versus 7.28% on pioglitazone 30 mg — with more oedema, weight gain, heart failure and deaths on muraglitazar
cards.type: Double-blind randomised pioglitazone-comparative trial, muraglitazar vs pioglitazone, both added to metformin
cards.people: 1,159 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin, randomised double-blind to muraglitazar 5 mg or pioglitazone 30 mg once daily, both added to open-label metformin, for 24 weeks with a further 26-week double-blind continuation.
cards.result: At week 24, mean HbA1c was 6.98% on muraglitazar (−1.14% from baseline) versus 7.28% on pioglitazone (−0.85%; P<0.0001). At week 12, triglycerides changed by −28% versus −14% relative and HDL cholesterol by +19% versus +14% relative (relative changes as printed; P<0.0001 for both comparisons). Oedema at week 24 occurred in 9.2% versus 7.2%. By week 50, heart failure had been reported in seven patients (five on muraglitazar, two on pioglitazone), and seven deaths had occurred — six in the muraglitazar group (three sudden deaths, two cerebrovascular accidents, one pancreatic cancer) and one in the pioglitazone group (perforated duodenal ulcer). The authors note the pioglitazone dose was submaximal (30 mg).
cards.watchOut: The comparator was pioglitazone 30 mg, described by the authors as a submaximal dose — the HbA1c and lipid advantages are against that dose, not against pioglitazone 45 mg. The death and heart-failure counts in this single trial are small and are part of the wider programme record carded first on this shelf.

cards.headline: Glimepiride-comparative trial (Rubin 2008): muraglitazar 5 mg plus metformin was superior for HbA1c at 52 weeks — with oedema, weight gain and heart failure more evident and a mortality imbalance favouring glimepiride

cards.type: Double-blind randomised active-control trial, muraglitazar vs glimepiride, both with metformin, 52 weeks
cards.people: 1,805 patients with type 2 diabetes who, after open-label metformin monotherapy, received randomised double-blind therapy with muraglitazar 2.5 mg, muraglitazar 5 mg or glimepiride 1 mg for 52 weeks.
cards.result: At week 52, the HbA1c reduction with muraglitazar 5 mg plus metformin was superior (P<0.0001) and with 2.5 mg non-inferior to glimepiride; the fetched abstract prints no numeric HbA1c change and none is claimed here. At week 12, muraglitazar significantly decreased triglycerides and increased HDL cholesterol (both P<0.0001). Oedema, weight gain and heart failure were more evident with muraglitazar. Cardiovascular events were similar among groups (about 2%), but there was an imbalance of total mortality in favour of glimepiride.
cards.watchOut: The fetched abstract prints superiority/non-inferiority conclusions without the numeric HbA1c changes, so no effect size is claimed on this card. The mortality imbalance is reported as the abstract reports it, without counts.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a never-marketed agent whose glycaemic and lipid efficacy was real and whose cardiovascular safety record ended it — the JAMA 2005 relative risk of 2.23 for death, MI or stroke (1.47% vs 0.67% absolute) leads this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: a never-marketed agent whose glycaemic and lipid efficacy was real and whose cardiovascular safety record ended it — the JAMA 2005 relative risk of 2.23 for death, MI or stroke (1.47% vs 0.67% absolute) leads this shelf
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Muraglitazar lowered HbA1c versus placebo (−1.23% on 5 mg versus −0.32%), beat pioglitazone 30 mg on HbA1c and lipids when added to metformin, and was superior (5 mg) or non-inferior (2.5 mg) to glimepiride at 52 weeks. Against that, the pooled phase 2/3 safety analysis found death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke in 1.47% on muraglitazar versus 0.67% on controls (relative risk 2.23, a relative measure), the individual trials showed more oedema, weight gain and heart failure, and one trial showed a mortality imbalance favouring glimepiride. The agent was abandoned after the 2005 analysis and never marketed, despite an 8:1 FDA advisory vote for approval. Its class siblings troglitazone and aleglitazar are homed on their own shelves and are not re-carded here (one-home rule).
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Tesaglitazar in type 2 diabetes (DISCONTINUED; GALLANT programme): HbA1c matched pioglitazone and beat placebo in four 24-week trials — dose-dependent creatinine rises ended development
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (as add-on to sulfonylurea, metformin or insulin, or versus pioglitazone), does the dual PPARα/γ agonist tesaglitazar improve glycaemic control and lipids (the GALLANT programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alkanesulfonates · Blood Glucose · Cholesterol, HDL · Cholesterol, LDL · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylpropionates · Pioglitazone · Thiazolidinediones · Time Factors
shelves.balance: DISCONTINUED AGENT — this flag leads. Tesaglitazar, a dual PPARα/γ agonist, was discontinued during development over a renal signal that runs through every carded report: dose-dependent increases in serum creatinine (and decreases in haemoglobin) that no comparator produced. The GALLANT programme's four 24-week trials — published as a single journal-issue programme set — show consistent surrogate efficacy: tesaglitazar 1 mg was non-inferior to pioglitazone 45 mg for HbA1c, and placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions were −0.93%/−1.3% added to sulfonylurea, significant versus placebo added to metformin, and −0.66% added to insulin, with triglyceride, HDL-C and non-HDL-C improvements throughout. All four reports are 24-week surrogate-endpoint trials (HbA1c, lipids); no outcomes trial exists, and the creatinine signal must stay on the face, not in a footnote.

cards.headline: GALLANT head-to-head (Bays 2007): tesaglitazar 1 mg was non-inferior to pioglitazone 45 mg for HbA1c (difference −0.056) — but only tesaglitazar raised serum creatinine
cards.summary: GALLANT head-to-head (Bays 2007): tesaglitazar 1 mg was non-inferior to pioglitazone 45 mg for HbA1c (difference −0.056) — but only tesaglitazar raised serum creatinine
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (GALLANT programme), tesaglitazar vs pioglitazone, 24 weeks
cards.people: 1,707 patients with type 2 diabetes, randomised double-blind for 24 weeks to tesaglitazar 0.5 mg or 1 mg or pioglitazone 15 mg, 30 mg or 45 mg.
cards.result: Tesaglitazar 1 mg was non-inferior to pioglitazone 45 mg for change in HbA1c at 24 weeks (difference −0.056, 95% CI −0.161 to 0.049; P<0.001 for the non-inferiority hypothesis). Tesaglitazar 1 mg improved triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol versus all pioglitazone doses (P<0.001) and lowered LDL cholesterol in most comparisons. Both agents increased body weight and peripheral oedema dose-dependently, but only tesaglitazar increased serum creatinine.
cards.watchOut: Discontinued agent: the creatinine rise on this card is the signal that ended development, and it recurs in every other carded GALLANT report. Surrogate endpoints only; no outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: GALLANT add-on to sulfonylurea (Wilding 2007): placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions of −0.93% (0.5 mg) and −1.3% (1 mg) — with dose-dependent creatinine rises and haemoglobin falls
cards.summary: GALLANT add-on to sulfonylurea (Wilding 2007): placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions of −0.93% (0.5 mg) and −1.3% (1 mg) — with dose-dependent creatinine rises and haemoglobin falls
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (GALLANT programme), tesaglitazar added to sulfonylurea vs placebo
cards.people: 568 patients with type 2 diabetes poorly controlled on sulfonylurea therapy titrated to the highest tolerated dose, randomised double-blind to tesaglitazar 0.5 mg, tesaglitazar 1 mg or placebo as add-on treatment for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Placebo-corrected HbA1c reductions at week 24 were −0.93% (0.5 mg; 95% CI −1.09 to −0.77) and −1.3% (1 mg; 95% CI −1.46 to −1.14), both P<0.0001. Insulin, fasting plasma glucose and triglycerides fell significantly, and HDL cholesterol rose significantly. Tesaglitazar was associated with dose-dependent increases in serum creatinine and decreases in haemoglobin. The abstract itself records that tesaglitazar 'has now been discontinued from clinical development'.
cards.watchOut: Discontinued agent; 24-week surrogate endpoints. The creatinine and haemoglobin changes are dose-dependent and are part of the answer, not a side note.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the GALLANT programme — four 24-week trials published as one journal-issue set — shows consistent HbA1c and lipid efficacy and a consistent dose-dependent creatinine signal; tesaglitazar was discontinued and no outcomes trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: the GALLANT programme — four 24-week trials published as one journal-issue set — shows consistent HbA1c and lipid efficacy and a consistent dose-dependent creatinine signal; tesaglitazar was discontinued and no outcomes trial exists

cards.result: Tesaglitazar matched pioglitazone 45 mg on HbA1c head-to-head, and lowered HbA1c versus placebo when added to sulfonylurea (−0.93%/−1.3% placebo-corrected), metformin (significant, numeric change not printed in the fetched abstract) and insulin (−0.66% on 0.5 mg), with lipid improvements throughout. Every report also shows the renal signal: dose-dependent serum creatinine increases (with haemoglobin decreases on the sulfonylurea trial) seen with tesaglitazar and not with pioglitazone. Development was discontinued; the agent was never marketed. All evidence is 24-week surrogate-endpoint evidence. Its class siblings troglitazone and aleglitazar are homed on their own shelves and are not re-carded here (one-home rule).

shelves.title: Avosentan in diabetic nephropathy (FLOOR-RISK — 2 reports, 1 trial): ASCEND stopped early for cardiovascular harm; heart-failure HR 2.76; no progression benefit detected
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and overt diabetic nephropathy on ACE-inhibitor / ARB therapy, does the endothelin-receptor antagonist avosentan, compared with placebo, slow kidney progression?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Body Weight · Diabetic Nephropathies · Disease Progression · Endothelins · Female · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Heart Failure · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Kidney Failure, Chronic · Male · Middle Aged · Proteinuria · Pyridines · Pyrimidines · Treatment Outcome · Water-Electrolyte Imbalance
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — FLOOR-RISK: for the kidney-progression question this shelf rests on exactly 2 reports, both from the single ASCEND trial, and that count is on the face. ASCEND (1,392 randomised) was terminated prematurely after a median follow-up of only 4 months because of an excess of cardiovascular events on avosentan; no difference in the primary composite of doubling of serum creatinine, ESRD or death was detected in that truncated follow-up. The albuminuria reduction (median albumin-to-creatinine-ratio reductions of 44.3% and 49.3% relative on 25 mg and 50 mg versus 9.7% on placebo — relative changes) never translated into a detectable progression benefit, and it must not be read as kidney protection. The post-hoc ASCEND analysis quantifies the harm: avosentan increased congestive heart failure risk versus placebo (hazard ratio 2.76, 95% CI 1.68 to 4.54), with fluid overload and heart failure dominating the excess discontinuations (19.6% and 18.2% versus 11.5%). A fourth card — the programme's earlier 12-week dose-ranging albuminuria trial (286 patients) — is labelled programme support only: it tested a surrogate over 12 weeks, is not a progression report, and is not counted in the 2-report progression base. Avosentan was never marketed.

cards.headline: ASCEND (Mann 2010): the sole progression trial — TERMINATED EARLY after a median of 4 months for excess cardiovascular events; no difference in doubling of creatinine, ESRD or death
cards.summary: ASCEND (Mann 2010): the sole progression trial — TERMINATED EARLY after a median of 4 months for excess cardiovascular events; no difference in doubling of creatinine, ESRD or death
cards.type: Multicentre multinational double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ASCEND), avosentan vs placebo on ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy — terminated prematurely
cards.people: 1,392 participants with type 2 diabetes and overt diabetic nephropathy, randomised to oral avosentan 25 mg, avosentan 50 mg or placebo, in addition to continued ACE-inhibitor and/or ARB therapy, in a multicentre multinational double-blind placebo-controlled trial. The composite primary outcome was time to doubling of serum creatinine, ESRD or death.
cards.result: The trial was terminated prematurely after a median follow-up of 4 months (maximum 16 months) because of an excess of cardiovascular events with avosentan. No difference in the frequency of the primary outcome between groups was detected. Median albumin-to-creatinine-ratio reductions were 44.3% (25 mg) and 49.3% (50 mg) relative versus 9.7% on placebo (relative changes as printed). Adverse events led to discontinuation significantly more often on avosentan (19.6% and 18.2% versus 11.5%), dominated by fluid overload and congestive heart failure. Death occurred in 21 patients (4.6%) on 25 mg, 17 (3.6%) on 50 mg and 12 (2.6%) on placebo (P=0.225 and P=0.194 versus placebo). The authors concluded avosentan reduces albuminuria but induces significant fluid overload and congestive heart failure.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base: this is the only progression trial that exists for avosentan, and its follow-up was truncated at a median of 4 months by its own harm — 'no difference detected' in the primary outcome is a statement about a stopped trial, not evidence of no effect, and the albuminuria result is a surrogate that never translated into a progression benefit.
cards.source: Mann JF et al. Avosentan for overt diabetic nephropathy. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2010. PMID: 20167702. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ASCEND post-hoc heart-failure analysis (Hoekman 2014): avosentan increased congestive heart failure risk — hazard ratio 2.76 (95% CI 1.68 to 4.54); early weight gain was the warning signal
cards.summary: ASCEND post-hoc heart-failure analysis (Hoekman 2014): avosentan increased congestive heart failure risk — hazard ratio 2.76 (95% CI 1.68 to 4.54); early weight gain was the warning signal
cards.type: Post-hoc predictor analysis of the ASCEND randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same ASCEND trial population (N=1,392 participants with diabetes and nephropathy) — a post-hoc analysis of which baseline characteristics predicted congestive heart failure (CHF) during avosentan treatment, and whether early post-randomisation changes in body weight and haemoglobin signalled fluid retention. This is a second report OF the ASCEND trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Relative to placebo, avosentan increased CHF risk (hazard ratio 2.76, 95% CI 1.68 to 4.54). Patients allocated to avosentan had a median body-weight increase of 0.6 kg and a median haemoglobin decrease of 1.4 g/dL at the first post-randomisation measurement; the avosentan-related weight increase was associated with CHF development (P for interaction = 0.04), whereas the haemoglobin decrease was not (P for interaction = 0.64). The authors conclude close body-weight monitoring could provide an early signal of CHF in future endothelin-antagonist trials.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc analysis of the single ASCEND trial: it quantifies and explains the harm that stopped the trial; it is not independent confirmatory evidence, and the shelf's progression base remains exactly 2 reports / 1 trial.
cards.source: Hoekman J et al. Predictors of congestive heart failure after treatment with an endothelin receptor antagonist. Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN. 2014. PMID: 24408122. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme support — dose-ranging albuminuria trial (Wenzel 2009): avosentan cut urinary albumin excretion over 12 weeks, with peripheral oedema in 12% — a surrogate-endpoint trial, NOT a progression report and not counted in this shelf's 2-report base
cards.summary: Programme support — dose-ranging albuminuria trial (Wenzel 2009): avosentan cut urinary albumin excretion over 12 weeks, with peripheral oedema in 12% — a surrogate-endpoint trial, NOT a progression report and not counted in this shelf's 2-report base
cards.type: Programme report: randomised double-blind dose-ranging trial of urinary albumin excretion over 12 weeks (programme support only — not a kidney-progression report)
cards.people: 286 patients with diabetic nephropathy and macroalbuminuria, randomised double-blind to avosentan (SPP301) 5, 10, 25 or 50 mg or placebo for 12 weeks, in addition to standard ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy.
cards.result: Relative to baseline, all avosentan dosages decreased mean relative urinary albumin excretion rate (−16.3% to −29.9% relative) compared with placebo (+35.5%); median relative changes were −28.7% to −44.8% versus +12.1% on placebo (relative changes as printed). Creatinine clearance and blood pressure were unchanged at 12 weeks. The main adverse event was peripheral oedema (12%), mainly at dosages of 25 mg or more; 21 patients (7.3%) withdrew because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Labelled programme support, on the discipline of the library's programme-report cards: a 12-week albumin-excretion surrogate trial. It does not test kidney progression, does not add a trial to the progression base (which remains exactly 2 reports from the single ASCEND trial), and its oedema signal foreshadows the fluid overload that stopped ASCEND.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: For the question whether avosentan slows kidney progression, the entire base is the ASCEND trial and its post-hoc heart-failure analysis — 2 reports, 1 trial. ASCEND was terminated prematurely for an excess of cardiovascular events; within its truncated follow-up no difference in doubling of creatinine, ESRD or death was detected, while albumin-to-creatinine ratio fell by 44.3–49.3% relative on avosentan versus 9.7% on placebo — a surrogate result that must not be presented as kidney protection. The harm is quantified: heart failure hazard ratio 2.76, discontinuation for adverse events 19.6%/18.2% versus 11.5%, dominated by fluid overload. The 2009 dose-ranging albuminuria trial is carded as programme support only and is not counted in the progression base. Avosentan was never marketed. The atrasentan diabetic-kidney-disease question (SONAR) is homed on its own shelf and is not re-carded here (one-home rule).

shelves.title: Beinaglutide for weight (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports, China only): −6.0% vs −2.4% vs placebo at 16 weeks; thrice-daily dosing; no randomised diabetes anchor
shelves.question: In Chinese adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, does the thrice-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist beinaglutide, compared with placebo or metformin, reduce body weight?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Overweight · Obesity · Weight Loss · Double-Blind Method · China · Peptide Fragments · Glucagon-Like Peptide 1
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: the randomised report count is exactly 2, and that count is on the face. Both randomised trials are short (16 and 12 weeks), both are from China (where beinaglutide is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved — single-region flag), and both enrolled NON-diabetic people with overweight or obesity: the phase 3 trial (427 randomised) found mean weight change of −6.0% on beinaglutide 0.2 mg thrice daily versus −2.4% on placebo (difference −3.6%), and the metformin comparison (78 randomised, 64 completed) found 9.5% versus 5.1% weight loss. The type 2 diabetes weight claim has NO randomised anchor in this base — the diabetes reports are single-arm, are carded here as one labelled programme-support card only, and are explicitly not counted. Thrice-daily dosing is itself part of the answer: every other GLP-1 shelf in this library concerns an agent dosed daily or less often. Nausea was frequent (49.3% versus 7.1% on placebo) and adverse-event discontinuation was 5.9% versus 0.7%.

cards.headline: Phase 3 weight-management trial (Chen 2024): beinaglutide 0.2 mg thrice daily — weight −6.0% versus −2.4% on placebo at 16 weeks (difference −3.6%); nausea 49.3% versus 7.1%
cards.summary: Phase 3 weight-management trial (Chen 2024): beinaglutide 0.2 mg thrice daily — weight −6.0% versus −2.4% on placebo at 16 weeks (difference −3.6%); nausea 49.3% versus 7.1%
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, beinaglutide thrice daily vs placebo, adjunct to lifestyle intervention
cards.people: 427 Chinese adults without diabetes, with body mass index 28 kg/m² or higher (obesity) or 24–27.9 kg/m² (overweight) with weight-related complications, randomised 2:1 to beinaglutide 0.2 mg subcutaneously thrice daily (n=282) or placebo (n=138 analysed) for 16 weeks, as an adjunct to lifestyle intervention, in a multicentre double-blind trial.
cards.result: Mean body weight change at week 16 was −6.0% on beinaglutide versus −2.4% on placebo (mixed-model difference −3.6%, 95% CI −4.6 to −2.6; P<0.0001). A weight reduction of 5% or more was achieved by 58.2% versus 25.4% (odds ratio 4.4 — a relative measure) and of 10% or more by 21.3% versus 5.1% (odds ratio 5.5 — a relative measure). Waist circumference fell by an additional −1.81 cm on beinaglutide. Nausea, transient and mild to moderate, occurred in 49.3% versus 7.1%; discontinuation because of adverse events was 5.9% versus 0.7%. No pancreatitis or increased resting heart rate was observed.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — one of exactly 2 randomised reports. Sixteen weeks only, non-diabetic population, single-region (China) evidence, and a thrice-daily injection regimen; the odds ratios on this card are relative measures and the absolute proportions are printed beside them.

cards.headline: Randomised comparison versus metformin (Gao 2022): weight loss 9.5% (9.1 kg) on beinaglutide versus 5.1% (4.5 kg) on metformin over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Randomised comparison versus metformin (Gao 2022): weight loss 9.5% (9.1 kg) on beinaglutide versus 5.1% (4.5 kg) on metformin over 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised comparison, beinaglutide vs metformin for weight loss in non-diabetic overweight/obesity, 12 weeks
cards.people: 78 non-diabetic patients with overweight or obesity, randomised to beinaglutide or metformin for 12 weeks; 64 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Patients on beinaglutide lost more body weight than those on metformin: 9.5% (9.1 kg) versus 5.1% (4.5 kg), a difference of approximately 4.5 kg (95% CI 2.2 to 6.9; P<0.01). Weight loss of 5% or more was achieved by 90.6% versus 46.9%, and of 10% or more by 40.6% versus 12.5%. The weight loss on beinaglutide resulted mainly from loss of fat mass, and beinaglutide also decreased serum insulin levels and ameliorated insulin resistance, as the report states.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — the second of exactly 2 randomised reports. Only 64 of 78 randomised patients completed; the comparator is metformin (itself weight-reducing), not placebo; 12 weeks, single-region (China) evidence, non-diabetic population.

cards.type: Programme report: single-arm before-and-after study in type 2 diabetes (programme support only — not randomised, not counted)
cards.people: 36 adult Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes and body mass index of 24 kg/m² or higher, treated with beinaglutide for three months in a single-arm before-and-after study measuring weight, glucose, fat areas and inflammatory biomarkers. There was no control group.
cards.result: After three months, the report states that body weight, body mass index, fasting and postprandial glucose, HbA1c and visceral and subcutaneous fat areas changed significantly, and that serpin E1, leptin, C-reactive protein and tumour necrosis factor-α decreased significantly; the fetched abstract prints no numeric weight change and none is claimed here. Without a comparator, none of this can be attributed to beinaglutide rather than to time, co-treatment or regression to the mean.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, 36 patients, no comparator: carded, labelled as programme support, only because it is the programme's only diabetes-population weight report — it is never load-bearing, and the shelf's randomised count stays exactly 2. A second single-arm report (107 patients, visceral fat in type 2 diabetes) is likewise not counted and not carded.
cards.source: Wang G et al. Effect of beinaglutide treatment on weight loss in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and overweight/obesity. Archives of endocrinology and metabolism. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports, both short, both in non-diabetic Chinese adults: −6.0% vs −2.4% against placebo at 16 weeks and 9.5% vs 5.1% against metformin at 12 weeks; the diabetes weight claim has no randomised anchor, and dosing is thrice daily
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports, both short, both in non-diabetic Chinese adults: −6.0% vs −2.4% against placebo at 16 weeks and 9.5% vs 5.1% against metformin at 12 weeks; the diabetes weight claim has no randomised anchor, and dosing is thrice daily
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Beinaglutide 0.2 mg thrice daily reduced weight versus placebo (−6.0% versus −2.4%; difference −3.6%) over 16 weeks and versus metformin (9.5% versus 5.1% loss) over 12 weeks, in the only two randomised reports that exist for this question. Both enrolled non-diabetic people with overweight or obesity in China, where the agent is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved. The programme's diabetes reports are single-arm and are not counted — so for patients with type 2 diabetes, the population in which the agent originated, there is no randomised weight evidence on this shelf. Nausea affected about half of treated patients in the phase 3 trial. No longer-term or maintenance trial is carded, because none is in this base.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes (treated with diet and exercise alone, or inadequately controlled on metformin), does once-daily oral orforglipron, compared with placebo or dapagliflozin, improve glycaemic control — the uncarded ACHIEVE-1 and ACHIEVE-2 slice of the phase 3 diabetes programme, beside live shelf #1091?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, stated on the face. FENCE POSITION, printed deliberately: live shelf #1091 (orforglipron phase 2 and the ATTAIN-1 obesity trial) fences the ACHIEVE phase 3 diabetes programme in its synthesis BY NAME, naming ACHIEVE-3 (against oral semaglutide), ACHIEVE-5 (added to insulin glargine) and the cardiovascular-safety trial ACHIEVE-4 — those three trials are fenced and gated and are NEVER carded here. ACHIEVE-1 and ACHIEVE-2 were never named in that fence, never carded and are gate-free; the slate-16 assembly adjudication (adjudication 2, common-questions-slate16) rows this uncarded ACHIEVE-1/-2 slice deliberately as a PARTIAL + FLOOR-RISK pack, so the developer can pull it at verdict if he reads the fence more broadly. On that 2-report base: ACHIEVE-1 (559 randomised, diet-and-exercise only) — HbA1c change at week 40 of −1.24, −1.47 and −1.48 percentage points on orforglipron 3, 12 and 36 mg vs −0.41 on placebo (differences −0.83, −1.06, −1.07, all P < 0.001). ACHIEVE-2 (962 randomised on metformin) — HbA1c change −1.23%, −1.50% and −1.56% vs −0.81% on dapagliflozin (differences −0.42%, −0.70%, −0.75%, all P < 0.0001, meeting and exceeding the 0.3% non-inferiority margin), at a gastrointestinal price: GI events in 46–54% on orforglipron vs 12% on dapagliflozin and discontinuation in 15–20% vs 6%. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint, and NO outcomes claim is made: the cardiovascular-safety trial (ACHIEVE-4) is fenced and gated and forms no part of this pack.

cards.headline: ACHIEVE-1 (Rosenstock 2025): orforglipron lowered HbA1c by −1.24 to −1.48 percentage points vs −0.41 on placebo at week 40 in early, diet-and-exercise-treated type 2 diabetes (559 randomised) — differences −0.83, −1.06 and −1.07, all P < 0.001
cards.summary: ACHIEVE-1 (Rosenstock 2025): orforglipron lowered HbA1c by −1.24 to −1.48 percentage points vs −0.41 on placebo at week 40 in early, diet-and-exercise-treated type 2 diabetes (559 randomised) — differences −0.83, −1.06 and −1.07, all P < 0.001
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (ACHIEVE-1), orforglipron vs placebo, diet-and-exercise-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 559 participants with type 2 diabetes treated only with diet and exercise, HbA1c 7.0–9.5% and BMI at least 23.0, randomised 1:1:1:1 to orforglipron 3, 12 or 36 mg or placebo once daily for 40 weeks (phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled); mean baseline HbA1c 8.0%.
cards.result: At week 40 the estimated mean HbA1c change was −1.24 percentage points (3 mg), −1.47 (12 mg), −1.48 (36 mg) and −0.41 (placebo); all three doses were superior to placebo (estimated differences −0.83, 95% CI −1.10 to −0.56; −1.06, 95% CI −1.33 to −0.79; and −1.07, 95% CI −1.33 to −0.81; P < 0.001 for all). Mean HbA1c at week 40 was 6.5 to 6.7% on orforglipron. Body weight fell by 4.5%, 5.8% and 7.6% across the doses vs 1.7% on placebo. The most common adverse events were mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events, mostly during dose escalation; no severe hypoglycaemia was reported; permanent discontinuation for adverse events occurred in 4.4 to 7.8% on orforglipron vs 1.4% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: An early-diabetes, diet-and-exercise-only population with a 40-week surrogate (HbA1c) endpoint: it does not answer glycaemic control on background metformin (that is ACHIEVE-2, carded next) and makes no cardiovascular-outcomes claim.
cards.source: Rosenstock J et al. Orforglipron, an Oral Small-Molecule GLP-1 Receptor Agonist, in Early Type 2 Diabetes. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40544435. Registry ID: NCT05971940. cards.headline: ACHIEVE-2 (Welch 2026): orforglipron beat dapagliflozin on metformin — HbA1c −1.23%, −1.50% and −1.56% vs −0.81% at week 40 (differences −0.42%, −0.70%, −0.75%, all P < 0.0001) — but GI events ran 46–54% vs 12% and discontinuation 15–20% vs 6% (962 randomised)
cards.summary: ACHIEVE-2 (Welch 2026): orforglipron beat dapagliflozin on metformin — HbA1c −1.23%, −1.50% and −1.56% vs −0.81% at week 40 (differences −0.42%, −0.70%, −0.75%, all P < 0.0001) — but GI events ran 46–54% vs 12% and discontinuation 15–20% vs 6% (962 randomised)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label (dose-blinded) non-inferiority randomised trial (ACHIEVE-2), orforglipron vs dapagliflozin on metformin
cards.people: 962 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (at least 1,500 mg/day), HbA1c 7.0–10.5% (53–91 mmol/mol), BMI at least 23.0 kg/m², randomised 1:1:1:1 at 73 sites in six countries to orforglipron 3, 12 or 36 mg once daily or dapagliflozin 10 mg, for 40 weeks (phase 3, open-label with orforglipron dose-blinded); mean age 56.1 years, mean HbA1c 8.14%, mean diabetes duration 8.0 years, 49% women.
cards.result: All orforglipron doses were non-inferior to dapagliflozin for HbA1c change at week 40 against the 0.3% non-inferiority margin, and the estimated differences favoured orforglipron: HbA1c change −1.23% (3 mg), −1.50% (12 mg) and −1.56% (36 mg) vs −0.81% on dapagliflozin (treatment-regimen estimand; differences −0.42%, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.23; −0.70%, 95% CI −0.90 to −0.49; −0.75%, 95% CI −0.96 to −0.55; all P < 0.0001). Gastrointestinal events occurred in 47%, 46% and 54% on the orforglipron doses vs 12% on dapagliflozin, and study-intervention discontinuation in 15%, 18% and 20% vs 6%. No severe hypoglycaemia was reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label against an active comparator with a surrogate endpoint: the glycaemic advantage over dapagliflozin is real on these numbers, but one in five participants on the top dose discontinued the study intervention, mostly against a 12% gastrointestinal-event rate on the comparator — tolerability, not efficacy, is this trial's open question.
cards.source: Welch M et al. Orforglipron compared with dapagliflozin in adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycaemic control with metformin (ACHIEVE-2): a multicentre, randomised, non-inferiority, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2026. PMID: 42259339. Registry ID: NCT06192108. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: ACHIEVE-1 (559 randomised) and ACHIEVE-2 (962 randomised) only.
cards.result: On a deliberately rowed two-report base, once-daily oral orforglipron improved glycaemic control in both settings tested: against placebo in early diet-and-exercise-treated diabetes (HbA1c differences −0.83 to −1.07 percentage points at week 40; ACHIEVE-1) and against dapagliflozin on metformin (differences −0.42 to −0.75 percentage points, non-inferiority met and exceeded; ACHIEVE-2). Tolerability is the counterweight: gastrointestinal events in 46–54% vs 12% on dapagliflozin and discontinuation in 15–20% vs 6% in ACHIEVE-2 (4.4–7.8% vs 1.4% against placebo in ACHIEVE-1), with no severe hypoglycaemia in either trial. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; the cardiovascular-safety trial ACHIEVE-4 is fenced at live #1091 and gated, and makes no part of this pack — no cardiovascular-outcomes claim is made or implied.
cards.watchOut: A two-report FLOOR-RISK base: quote these HbA1c figures only with the trial, dose and comparator attached, and never as an outcomes result.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: PARTIAL — and the withdrawn-agent flag leads: albiglutide was withdrawn from the market (2018, a commercial decision), and live shelf #72 already prints 'a drug no longer sold' for its cardiovascular card. This pack cards the glycaemic HARMONY slice that #72 does not: #72 cards Harmony Outcomes (cardiovascular) only, cross-pointed here and never re-carded. The glycaemic record is mixed by comparator. Against placebo added to pioglitazone ± metformin (HARMONY 1, 310 randomised), albiglutide won clearly: HbA1c difference −0.8 percentage points at week 52, with hyperglycaemia rescue in 24.4% vs 47.7%. Against sitagliptin in renal impairment it won modestly (−0.83% vs −0.52% at week 26, P = 0.0003). But the head-to-head anchor FAILED its test: in HARMONY 7, albiglutide was NOT non-inferior to once-daily liraglutide (HbA1c −0.78% vs −0.99%; difference 0.21%, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.34; non-inferiority P = 0.0846 against the 0.3% margin) — HARMONY 7 must not be presented as equivalence. A 3-year pooled report of five HARMONY trials (3,132 randomised) supports durability, labelled as programme support. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; the cardiovascular-outcomes result lives at #72.

cards.headline: HARMONY 7 (Pratley 2014): albiglutide FAILED non-inferiority against liraglutide — HbA1c −0.78% vs −0.99% at week 32 (difference 0.21%, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.34; non-inferiority P = 0.0846); injection-site reactions 12.9% vs 5.4%, GI events 35.9% vs 49.0% (841 enrolled)
cards.summary: HARMONY 7 (Pratley 2014): albiglutide FAILED non-inferiority against liraglutide — HbA1c −0.78% vs −0.99% at week 32 (difference 0.21%, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.34; non-inferiority P = 0.0846); injection-site reactions 12.9% vs 5.4%, GI events 35.9% vs 49.0% (841 enrolled)
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label non-inferiority randomised trial (HARMONY 7), albiglutide vs liraglutide
cards.people: 841 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral drugs (BMI 20–45 kg/m²), randomised at 162 sites in eight countries to albiglutide 30 mg once weekly titrated to 50 mg (422 allocated) or liraglutide 0.6 mg once daily titrated to 1.8 mg (419 allocated), for 32 weeks (open-label phase 3 non-inferiority study); the primary analysis included 402 vs 403 participants.
cards.result: Model-adjusted HbA1c change at week 32 was −0.78% (95% CI −0.87 to −0.69) on albiglutide vs −0.99% (−1.08 to −0.90) on liraglutide; the treatment difference was 0.21% (95% CI 0.08 to 0.34), and non-inferiority against the 0.3% margin was NOT met (non-inferiority P = 0.0846). Injection-site reactions were more frequent with albiglutide (12.9% vs 5.4%; P = 0.0002), while gastrointestinal events were less frequent (35.9% vs 49.0%; P = 0.00013). The authors' conclusion is plain: once-daily liraglutide produced greater HbA1c reductions than once-weekly albiglutide.
cards.watchOut: A failed non-inferiority test, carded as one: the confidence interval (0.08 to 0.34) crosses the 0.3% margin, so albiglutide cannot be described as equivalent or non-inferior to liraglutide on glycaemia — and the trial was open-label.
cards.source: Pratley RE et al. Once-weekly albiglutide versus once-daily liraglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on oral drugs (HARMONY 7): a randomised, open-label, multicentre, non-inferiority phase 3 study. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2014. PMID: 24703047. Registry ID: NCT01128894. cards.headline: HARMONY 1 (Reusch 2014): added to pioglitazone ± metformin, albiglutide beat placebo by −0.8 percentage points of HbA1c at week 52 (310 randomised); fasting glucose −1.3 mmol/L (≈ −23 mg/dL) vs +0.4 mmol/L (≈ +7 mg/dL); rescue 24.4% vs 47.7%
cards.summary: HARMONY 1 (Reusch 2014): added to pioglitazone ± metformin, albiglutide beat placebo by −0.8 percentage points of HbA1c at week 52 (310 randomised); fasting glucose −1.3 mmol/L (≈ −23 mg/dL) vs +0.4 mmol/L (≈ +7 mg/dL); rescue 24.4% vs 47.7%
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (HARMONY 1), albiglutide added to pioglitazone ± metformin
cards.people: 310 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on pioglitazone (with or without metformin), randomised to additional albiglutide 30 mg once weekly (155) or matching placebo (155) in a 3-year double-blind placebo-controlled study; the primary endpoint was HbA1c change at week 52.
cards.result: Model-adjusted HbA1c change at week 52 differed by −0.8 percentage points in albiglutide's favour (95% CI −1.0 to −0.6; P < 0.0001). Fasting plasma glucose changed by −1.3 mmol/L (≈ −23 mg/dL) on albiglutide vs +0.4 mmol/L (≈ +7 mg/dL) on placebo (P < 0.0001). Hyperglycaemia rescue up to week 52 was needed by 24.4% on albiglutide vs 47.7% on placebo (P < 0.0001). Albiglutide had no impact on weight; severe hypoglycaemia was rare (n = 2); gastrointestinal event rates at 52 weeks were similar (31.3% vs 29.8%).
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparison on a pioglitazone background — a background therapy now little used — so the −0.8-point margin answers the add-on question for that regimen, not albiglutide's standing against active modern comparators (see HARMONY 7).
cards.source: Reusch J et al. Efficacy and safety of once-weekly glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist albiglutide (HARMONY 1 trial): 52-week primary endpoint results from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus not controlled on pioglitazone, with or without metformin. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2014. PMID: 25155146. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Renal-impairment trial (Leiter 2014): albiglutide beat sitagliptin in renally impaired type 2 diabetes — HbA1c −0.83% vs −0.52% at week 26 (P = 0.0003), across eGFR categories down to 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² (52-week phase 3 study)
cards.summary: Renal-impairment trial (Leiter 2014): albiglutide beat sitagliptin in renally impaired type 2 diabetes — HbA1c −0.83% vs −0.52% at week 26 (P = 0.0003), across eGFR categories down to 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² (52-week phase 3 study)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised trial in renal impairment, albiglutide vs sitagliptin
cards.people: Adults with type 2 diabetes and renal impairment (eGFR categories: mild ≥60 to ≤89, moderate ≥30 to ≤59, severe ≥15 to ≤29 mL/min/1.73 m²) inadequately controlled on diet/exercise and/or oral agents, randomised to once-weekly albiglutide or daily sitagliptin for 52 weeks (phase 3, double-blind, multicentre); overall mean age 63.3 years, BMI 30.4 kg/m², HbA1c 8.2% (66 mmol/mol), diabetes duration 11.2 years. The fetched record prints no randomised N, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: HbA1c change at week 26 (the primary endpoint) was −0.83% on albiglutide vs −0.52% on sitagliptin (P = 0.0003), with decreases in HbA1c, fasting glucose and weight maintained through week 52 and a significantly longer time to hyperglycaemia rescue on albiglutide (P = 0.0017). Gastrointestinal events were modestly more frequent with albiglutide (overall 31.7% vs 25.2%; diarrhoea 10.0% vs 6.5%; nausea 4.8% vs 3.3%; vomiting 1.6% vs 1.2%), and most adverse events were mild or moderate in both groups.
cards.watchOut: No randomised N is printed in the fetched record, so none is claimed; the margin over sitagliptin (0.31 percentage points) is modest, and sitagliptin dosing in renal impairment is itself eGFR-adjusted — the comparison is of two renally usable regimens, not of maximal doses.
cards.source: Leiter LA et al. Efficacy and safety of the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist albiglutide versus sitagliptin in patients with type 2 diabetes and renal impairment: a randomized phase III study. Diabetes care. 2014. PMID: 25048383. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme support — 3-year pooled HARMONY report (Home 2017): across five 3-year HARMONY trials (3,132 randomised), 55–71% on albiglutide remained rescue-free vs 35–51% on placebo, with rescue-free HbA1c reductions of −0.52% to −0.98% at 3 years (a pooled programme report, not a new trial)
cards.summary: Programme support — 3-year pooled HARMONY report (Home 2017): across five 3-year HARMONY trials (3,132 randomised), 55–71% on albiglutide remained rescue-free vs 35–51% on placebo, with rescue-free HbA1c reductions of −0.52% to −0.98% at 3 years (a pooled programme report, not a new trial)
cards.type: Programme report: pooled 3-year analysis of five HARMONY phase 3 trials (same programme as the cards above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 3,132 participants randomised to albiglutide or comparator across five of the eight HARMONY phase 3 trials that ran a preplanned 3 years (comparators included placebo, glimepiride, insulin glargine, sitagliptin and pioglitazone), with protocol-defined rescue medication for uncontrolled hyperglycaemia.
cards.result: A greater proportion on albiglutide remained rescue-free (55–71%) than on placebo (35–51%; P < 0.001 to P = 0.002); the rescue-free proportion did not differ from glimepiride or insulin glargine, was higher than with sitagliptin (P = 0.013) and lower than with pioglitazone (P = 0.045). At 3 years, rescue-free participants on albiglutide had HbA1c reductions of −0.52% to −0.98%, and albiglutide was associated with modest weight reductions against the weight gain seen with pioglitazone, glimepiride and insulin glargine.
cards.watchOut: A pooled programme report across unlike comparators: it supports durability of the glycaemic effect, and its rescue-free analyses condition on staying on therapy — it is not a fourth head-to-head result and must not be counted as one.
cards.source: Home PD et al. Three-year data from 5 HARMONY phase 3 clinical trials of albiglutide in type 2 diabetes mellitus: Long-term efficacy with or without rescue therapy. Diabetes research and clinical practice. 2017. PMID: 28683300. Registry ID: NCT00849017; NCT00849056; NCT00838903; NCT00838916; NCT00839527. cards.headline: Synthesis: albiglutide lowered HbA1c against placebo (−0.8 points, HARMONY 1) and sitagliptin in renal impairment (−0.83% vs −0.52%), with 3-year durability in the pooled programme — but it failed non-inferiority against liraglutide (HARMONY 7), and the drug was withdrawn in 2018; its cardiovascular win lives at live #72
cards.summary: Synthesis: albiglutide lowered HbA1c against placebo (−0.8 points, HARMONY 1) and sitagliptin in renal impairment (−0.83% vs −0.52%), with 3-year durability in the pooled programme — but it failed non-inferiority against liraglutide (HARMONY 7), and the drug was withdrawn in 2018; its cardiovascular win lives at live #72
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The glycaemic HARMONY slice is comparator-dependent: a clear win over placebo on a pioglitazone background (HARMONY 1), a modest win over sitagliptin in renal impairment (Leiter 2014), durable control over 3 years in the pooled five-trial programme report (Home 2017) — and a failed non-inferiority test against once-daily liraglutide, the programme's only GLP-1 head-to-head (HARMONY 7: difference 0.21%, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.34; non-inferiority P = 0.0846). Albiglutide was withdrawn from the market in 2018 as a commercial decision; this shelf is therefore a record of what the drug did glycaemically, not a treatment recommendation. Its cardiovascular-outcomes result (Harmony Outcomes) is homed at live shelf #72 and is cross-pointed, never re-carded (one-home rule).

shelves.title: Omarigliptin: weekly DPP-4 inhibition matched daily sitagliptin (HbA1c −0.47% vs −0.43%); CV safety study neutral (HR 1.00) but terminated early — Japan-only, never US-marketed
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor omarigliptin, compared with placebo, sitagliptin or usual therapy, improve glycaemic control — and what did its cardiovascular safety study show?

shelves.balance: Single-region approval on the face: omarigliptin, a once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor, is approved in Japan and was NEVER marketed in the US — the fetched safety-study record states the sponsor made a business decision not to submit a US marketing application and terminated the cardiovascular safety study early; both facts are printed here, not footnoted. Glycaemically it behaved like its daily class sibling: non-inferior to sitagliptin 100 mg daily on metformin at week 24 (HbA1c −0.47% weekly vs −0.43% daily; difference −0.03%, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.08, meeting the 0.3% criterion; 642 randomised), and modestly better than placebo as monotherapy (−0.49% vs −0.10%; difference −0.39%, P < 0.001; 329 randomised). The cardiovascular safety study (4,202 randomised with established cardiovascular disease) found MACE in 5.45% on omarigliptin vs 5.43% on placebo (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.29) over a median follow-up of about 96 weeks — but it was TERMINATED EARLY, so that neutral estimate rests on truncated follow-up and is printed with that caveat. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: Head-to-head vs sitagliptin (Goldenberg 2017): once-weekly omarigliptin was non-inferior to once-daily sitagliptin on metformin — HbA1c −0.47% vs −0.43% at week 24 (difference −0.03%, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.08; 642 randomised)
cards.summary: Head-to-head vs sitagliptin (Goldenberg 2017): once-weekly omarigliptin was non-inferior to once-daily sitagliptin on metformin — HbA1c −0.47% vs −0.43% at week 24 (difference −0.03%, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.08; 642 randomised)
cards.type: Double-blind non-inferiority randomised trial, omarigliptin once weekly vs sitagliptin once daily on metformin
cards.people: 642 adults with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (at least 1,500 mg/day; HbA1c 6.5–9.0%), randomised double-blind to omarigliptin 25 mg once weekly (322) or sitagliptin 100 mg once daily (320) for 24 weeks; mean baseline HbA1c 7.5% in both groups.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.47% on omarigliptin and −0.43% on sitagliptin, a between-group difference of −0.03% (95% CI −0.15 to 0.08), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (upper bound below 0.3%). Fasting plasma glucose change and the proportions reaching HbA1c below 7.0% or 6.5% were similar between groups, as were adverse events; symptomatic hypoglycaemia was infrequent and similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to a modest-effect comparator at a low baseline HbA1c (7.5%): the trial shows weekly dosing matches daily sitagliptin, not that either produces large glycaemic reductions.
cards.source: Goldenberg R et al. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2017. PMID: 28093853. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Monotherapy trial (Home 2018): omarigliptin lowered HbA1c by −0.49% vs −0.10% on placebo at week 24 (difference −0.39%, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.19, P < 0.001; 329 randomised), with no symptomatic hypoglycaemia on omarigliptin over 54 weeks
cards.summary: Monotherapy trial (Home 2018): omarigliptin lowered HbA1c by −0.49% vs −0.10% on placebo at week 24 (difference −0.39%, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.19, P < 0.001; 329 randomised), with no symptomatic hypoglycaemia on omarigliptin over 54 weeks
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised monotherapy trial (24 weeks plus 30-week extension), omarigliptin vs placebo
cards.people: 329 people with type 2 diabetes not on glucose-lowering medication (or washed off monotherapy / low-dose dual therapy), randomised double-blind to omarigliptin 25 mg once weekly (165) or matching placebo (164) for 24 weeks, followed by a 30-week extension in which metformin was added to the placebo group and metformin placebo to the omarigliptin group; mean baseline HbA1c 8.0–8.1%.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.49% (95% CI −0.73 to −0.24) on omarigliptin vs −0.10% (−0.34 to 0.14) on placebo — a difference of −0.39% (95% CI −0.59 to −0.19; P < 0.001). Protocol deviations in metformin use by 38 of 252 evaluable participants probably attenuated the result; after censoring those participants the difference was −0.53% (95% CI −0.75 to −0.32). Adverse-event rates were similar over 24 and 54 weeks; over 54 weeks there were no symptomatic hypoglycaemia events on omarigliptin and 5 on placebo, and most omarigliptin participants remained rescue-free with a persistent HbA1c reduction.
cards.watchOut: A modest absolute effect (−0.39 percentage points) typical of the DPP-4 class, in a washed-off / treatment-naive population; the extension phase's metformin cross-addition means only the 24-week limb is a clean placebo comparison.
cards.source: Home P et al. cards.headline: Cardiovascular safety study, TERMINATED EARLY (Gantz 2017): MACE 5.45% on omarigliptin vs 5.43% on placebo (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.29) in 4,202 patients with established cardiovascular disease, over a median follow-up of ~96 weeks; heart-failure hospitalisation HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.35 to 1.05)
cards.summary: Cardiovascular safety study, TERMINATED EARLY (Gantz 2017): MACE 5.45% on omarigliptin vs 5.43% on placebo (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.29) in 4,202 patients with established cardiovascular disease, over a median follow-up of ~96 weeks; heart-failure hospitalisation HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.35 to 1.05)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled cardiovascular safety study (early-terminated), omarigliptin vs placebo
cards.people: 4,202 patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, randomised double-blind to omarigliptin 25 mg once weekly (2,092) or matching placebo (2,100) added to existing diabetes therapy; median follow-up approximately 96 weeks (range 1.1 to 178.6 weeks). The study was terminated early after the sponsor's business decision not to submit a US marketing application (see watchOut).
cards.result: The primary MACE outcome (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke) occurred in 114 of 2,092 patients (5.45%; 2.96 per 100 patient-years) on omarigliptin and 114 of 2,100 (5.43%; 2.97 per 100 patient-years) on placebo — hazard ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.29), a relative measure printed beside the absolute rates. Hospitalisation for heart failure occurred in 20 (0.96%) vs 33 (1.57%) patients (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.05). At 142 weeks the least-squares mean HbA1c difference favoured omarigliptin by −0.3% (95% CI −0.46 to −0.14). Adverse events, serious adverse events and discontinuations were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: TERMINATED EARLY: the fetched record states a business decision was made not to submit a marketing application for omarigliptin in the United States and the CV safety study was terminated — so the neutral MACE estimate (HR 1.00) rests on truncated follow-up (~96 weeks median) and a wide confidence interval (0.77 to 1.29) that does not exclude clinically important harm or benefit. Omarigliptin is approved in Japan only and was never marketed in the US.
cards.source: Gantz I et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled study of the cardiovascular safety of the once-weekly DPP-4 inhibitor omarigliptin in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Cardiovascular diabetology. 2017. PMID: 28893244. Registry ID: NCT01703208. cards.headline: Synthesis: omarigliptin matched daily sitagliptin glycaemically (−0.47% vs −0.43%), beat placebo modestly (−0.39 points), and showed a neutral but truncated cardiovascular safety estimate (MACE HR 1.00 on ~96 weeks) — a Japan-only, never-US-marketed weekly DPP-4 inhibitor

cards.result: The three reports tell one coherent, bounded story: once-weekly omarigliptin gives sitagliptin-like glycaemic control (Goldenberg 2017, non-inferiority met on metformin) and a small placebo-adjusted HbA1c reduction as monotherapy (Home 2018, −0.39 percentage points), and its early-terminated cardiovascular safety study found no MACE signal on the follow-up it achieved (Gantz 2017: 5.45% vs 5.43%; HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.29; median ~96 weeks). The programme's further Japanese reports (add-on to insulin, haemodialysis and combination add-on studies) are programme support only and are not carded. The shelf's limits are structural: a surrogate glycaemic endpoint, a truncated safety study, and an agent approved in Japan that was never submitted for US marketing.

shelves.title: Renin and aldosterone reference intervals: six healthy-population datasets — intervals belong to their assay (RIA reads aldosterone 59% higher than LC-MS/MS), sex and age; healthy ratio limits 14.2–25.5
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for plasma renin (activity and direct concentration) and plasma aldosterone concentration — the central 95% ranges by age, sex, assay method (radioimmunoassay, chemiluminescence immunoassay, LC-MS/MS) and population — how far do method-specific intervals sit from one another, what sampling influences (including posture) are recognised, and what upper limit for the aldosterone-to-renin ratio follows from healthy-population distributions rather than from hypertensive referral cohorts?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aldosterone/blood,standards · Cohort Studies · Diagnostic Techniques, Endocrine/standards · Female · Germany · Health · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Population · Reference Values · Renin/blood,standards · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, adrenal / renin–angiotensin–aldosterone sections, and Boron & Boulpaep, adrenal gland chapter — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Six independent healthy-population datasets (1,347 German population-based subjects; 328 Chinese Han chemiluminescence subjects; 282 Belgian LC-MS/MS volunteers, aldosterone limb only; 170 Hong Kong normotensive volunteers; 309 northern Chinese Han volunteers; 5,200 rigorously screened Yunnan individuals) agree on the structure: intervals are specific to assay, sex and age band, renin activity and direct renin concentration are different measurements with different intervals, and healthy-population aldosterone-to-renin ratio upper limits (14.2–25.5 by sex and age) sit clearly below hypertensive-referral cut-offs. The single most important number is a bias: radioimmunoassay reads plasma aldosterone on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS. Intervals are never merged across methods on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Population-based intervals, north-east Germany (Hannemann 2010; SHIP-1): upper aldosterone-to-renin ratio limits of 14.2 and 20.3 (younger) and 22.4 and 25.5 (older) in men and women — clearly below referral-cohort cut-offs
cards.summary: Population-based intervals, north-east Germany (Hannemann 2010; SHIP-1): upper aldosterone-to-renin ratio limits of 14.2 and 20.3 (younger) and 22.4 and 25.5 (older) in men and women — clearly below referral-cohort cut-offs
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset 1 of 6 (population-based reference intervals, radioimmunometric assay, Germany)
cards.people: Reference population of 1,347 healthy subjects selected from 3,300 participants in the first follow-up of the population-based Study of Health in Pomerania (SHIP-1), north-east Germany; plasma aldosterone and renin concentration measured by radioimmunometric procedures. Reference intervals are the central 95% range (2.5th to 97.5th percentiles), presented by sex and age band (25–54 and 55–74 years). The fetched record does not print the numeric aldosterone or renin interval limits themselves, so none are claimed for those analytes on this card.
cards.result: The upper reference limit for the aldosterone-to-renin ratio was 14.2 in younger men and 20.3 in younger women, and 22.4 in older men and 25.5 in older women — clearly lower than previously reported values from hypertensive patients in primary care or hypertension referral centres. Time of blood sampling had no influence on the ratio, while beta blockers and agents acting on the renin–angiotensin system were associated with higher and lower ratios respectively; aldosterone and renin were also associated with sex, age and estrogen intake.
cards.watchOut: Radioimmunometric-era intervals from one German region: the ratio limits are this assay's and this population's, and the medication associations mean a 'healthy-population' interval still shifts with common antihypertensive drugs.
cards.source: Hannemann A et al. Reference intervals for aldosterone, renin, and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio in the population-based Study of Health in Pomerania (SHIP-1). Hormone and metabolic research = Hormon- und Stoffwechselforschung = Hormones et metabolisme. 2010. PMID: 20157876. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chinese Han chemiluminescence intervals (Deng 2018): men — aldosterone 76–722 pmol/L (about 2.7–26.0 ng/dL), direct renin 3.3–92.7 mIU/L; women — aldosterone 85–1,010 pmol/L (about 3.1–36.4 ng/dL), renin 3.7–99.8 mIU/L
cards.summary: Chinese Han chemiluminescence intervals (Deng 2018): men — aldosterone 76–722 pmol/L (about 2.7–26.0 ng/dL), direct renin 3.3–92.7 mIU/L; women — aldosterone 85–1,010 pmol/L (about 3.1–36.4 ng/dL), renin 3.7–99.8 mIU/L
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset 2 of 6 (chemiluminescence reference intervals, Chinese Han population)
cards.people: 328 healthy Chinese Han individuals, with plasma aldosterone and direct renin concentration measured on a fully automated chemiluminescence analyser (DiaSorin LIAISON XL); within-laboratory imprecision was 5.6–6.7% for aldosterone and 3.0–3.3% for renin, and the limits of quantitation were 72.2 pmol/L and 1.27 mIU/L respectively.
cards.result: Central 95% reference intervals for men: aldosterone 76–722 pmol/L (about 2.7–26.0 ng/dL in US units), direct renin 3.3–92.7 mIU/L, aldosterone-to-renin ratio 2.2–46.0 pmol/mIU. For women: aldosterone 85–1,010 pmol/L (about 3.1–36.4 ng/dL), renin 3.7–99.8 mIU/L, ratio 3.6–68.4 pmol/mIU. Upper ratio limits for younger and older men were lower than for women, and the authors recommend sex- and age-specific intervals. The chemiluminescence ratio and the radioimmunoassay (activity-based) ratio showed almost perfect agreement for primary-aldosteronism screening in their comparison set (kappa 0.815).
cards.watchOut: Direct renin concentration (mIU/L) is not plasma renin activity — intervals for the two renin measures are not interchangeable, and this dataset's ratio units (pmol/mIU) differ from activity-based ratios elsewhere on this shelf.
cards.source: Deng L et al. Analytical validation and investigation on reference intervals of aldosterone and renin in Chinese Han population by using fully automated chemiluminescence immunoassays. cards.headline: Belgian LC-MS/MS aldosterone intervals (Le Goff 2018 — aldosterone limb only): women 0.07–0.73 nmol/L (about 2.5–26.3 ng/dL), men 0.04–0.41 nmol/L (about 1.4–14.8 ng/dL) — and radioimmunoassay read on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS in plasma
cards.summary: Belgian LC-MS/MS aldosterone intervals (Le Goff 2018 — aldosterone limb only): women 0.07–0.73 nmol/L (about 2.5–26.3 ng/dL), men 0.04–0.41 nmol/L (about 1.4–14.8 ng/dL) — and radioimmunoassay read on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS in plasma
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset 3 of 6 (LC-MS/MS plasma and urine aldosterone intervals, Belgium — aldosterone limb only, no renin interval)
cards.people: 282 healthy Belgian Caucasian volunteers (114 men, mean age 35 years; 168 women, mean age 42 years) for the plasma reference-interval study, with a subset of 139 providing 24-hour urine collections; a laboratory-developed LC-MS/MS method was validated against the existing radioimmunoassay (RIA), with 68 plasma and 23 urine samples in the method comparison. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: The proposed LC-MS/MS reference interval for plasma aldosterone is 0.07–0.73 nmol/L in women (about 2.5–26.3 ng/dL in US units) and 0.04–0.41 nmol/L in men (about 1.4–14.8 ng/dL); the urinary aldosterone reference interval was below 60.94 nmol/day, with no sex difference. Regression comparison showed RIA results on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS in plasma and 11% higher in urine — the assay bias is itself a card-level finding: an RIA-era interval cannot be applied to an LC-MS/MS result.
cards.watchOut: An aldosterone-only limb: this dataset contributes no renin interval, and its volunteers were younger (means 35 and 42 years) than several other datasets on this shelf.
cards.source: Le Goff CM et al. Migration from RIA to LC-MS/MS for aldosterone determination: Implications for clinical practice and determination of plasma and urine reference range intervals in a cohort of healthy Belgian subjects. cards.headline: Hong Kong LC-MS/MS intervals (Cheng 2022): age-specific renin-activity and aldosterone intervals from 170 normotensive volunteers — a renin-activity difference below versus above age 45, and no sex difference
cards.summary: Hong Kong LC-MS/MS intervals (Cheng 2022): age-specific renin-activity and aldosterone intervals from 170 normotensive volunteers — a renin-activity difference below versus above age 45, and no sex difference
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset 4 of 6 (LC-MS/MS normotensive reference intervals, Hong Kong — renin activity, not direct renin concentration)
cards.people: 170 normotensive healthy volunteers recruited to establish the normotensive reference intervals for plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone concentration by LC-MS/MS in a Hong Kong teaching-hospital laboratory. A further 362 essential-hypertensive patients were also analysed in the same report; that hypertensive limb is NOT a healthy-population dataset and is not counted among this shelf's six. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval limits, so none are claimed here.
cards.result: There was no sex-specific difference in renin activity or aldosterone for normotensive (or hypertensive) reference subjects. Differences in both analytes were noted between normotensive subjects aged below 45 and their older counterparts, so age-specific central 95% reference intervals were established accordingly; in the hypertensive group the age difference held for renin activity but not aldosterone.
cards.watchOut: Renin ACTIVITY intervals (this card) and direct renin CONCENTRATION intervals (the chemiluminescence and Pomerania cards) measure different things and their limits must never be interchanged; the absence of a sex difference here, against sex partitioning in other datasets, is itself part of the cross-population picture.

cards.headline: Northern Chinese Han LC-MS/MS intervals (Yin 2023): intervals for renin activity, aldosterone, angiotensin II and 24-hour urinary aldosterone in 309 healthy volunteers — aldosterone partitioned by sex, angiotensin II by region, urinary aldosterone by urine potassium
cards.summary: Northern Chinese Han LC-MS/MS intervals (Yin 2023): intervals for renin activity, aldosterone, angiotensin II and 24-hour urinary aldosterone in 309 healthy volunteers — aldosterone partitioned by sex, angiotensin II by region, urinary aldosterone by urine potassium
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset 5 of 6 (LC-MS/MS multi-analyte reference intervals, northern Chinese Han population)
cards.people: 309 healthy volunteers recruited in three northern-Chinese cities, with plasma renin activity, aldosterone and angiotensin II and 24-hour urinary aldosterone all measured by a laboratory-developed LC-MS/MS method whose performance was verified in the report. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval limits, so none are claimed here.
cards.result: Variance-component analysis showed the aldosterone interval must be partitioned by sex (standard deviation ratio 0.466), the angiotensin II interval by region (0.407), and the 24-hour urinary aldosterone interval by urine potassium (0.579); reference intervals were then determined by the nonparametric percentile method for each analyte. The partitioning structure — which factor splits which analyte — is this dataset's cardable product.
cards.watchOut: Three cities pooled with a region partition for one analyte only: a single 'northern Chinese' interval hides the region effect the authors themselves found for angiotensin II.
cards.source: Yin Y et al. Reference intervals for LC-MS /MS measurements of plasma renin activity, aldosterone, angiotensin II, and 24-hour urinary aldosterone in Northern Chinese Han population. cards.headline: Yunnan intervals (Zhang 2025): 5,200 rigorously screened healthy individuals — renin concentration lower in women and falling with age; aldosterone higher in men, lowest at 18–24 years and peaking at 25–64
cards.summary: Yunnan intervals (Zhang 2025): 5,200 rigorously screened healthy individuals — renin concentration lower in women and falling with age; aldosterone higher in men, lowest at 18–24 years and peaking at 25–64
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset 6 of 6 (age- and sex-specific renin and aldosterone intervals, Yunnan, China)
cards.people: Cross-sectional survey in Yunnan Province, China (multi-stage stratified sampling across four districts/counties, urban and rural): 9,129 ostensibly healthy individuals formed the initial sample, and after exclusions (pregnancy, lactation, contraceptive use, hypertension, hypokalaemia, renal insufficiency, obesity and diagnosed disease) 5,200 individuals were successfully included for age- and sex-specific reference intervals for plasma renin concentration and plasma aldosterone concentration. The fetched record does not print the numeric interval limits, so none are claimed here. The report's background lists body posture among the factors known to influence renin and aldosterone measurement.
cards.result: Renin and aldosterone levels differed significantly across sex and age groups: plasma renin concentration was significantly lower in women than men and decreased with age, while plasma aldosterone concentration was significantly higher in men than women, lowest in the 18–24 age group and peaking in the 25–64 age group. Age- and sex-specific reference intervals were established within the redefined groups — the largest single dataset on this shelf, and the one whose screening rigour (5,200 retained from 9,129) defines what 'healthy' means for its intervals.
cards.watchOut: The strict exclusions (including obesity and any hypertension) make this a super-healthy reference population; its intervals will sit differently from a general-population sample such as SHIP-1's, and the two sampling frames must not be averaged.
cards.source: Zhang C et al. Age- and sex-specific reference intervals for renin and aldosterone in healthy individuals in Yunnan Province, China. Journal of human hypertension. 2025. PMID: 40670656.
