cards.headline: Synthesis: six independent healthy-population datasets agree that renin and aldosterone reference intervals are assay-, sex- and age-specific and must never be merged across methods — radioimmunoassay reads aldosterone on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS in plasma, and healthy-population aldosterone-to-renin ratio limits sit well below hypertensive-referral cut-offs
cards.summary: Synthesis: six independent healthy-population datasets agree that renin and aldosterone reference intervals are assay-, sex- and age-specific and must never be merged across methods — radioimmunoassay reads aldosterone on average 59% higher than LC-MS/MS in plasma, and healthy-population aldosterone-to-renin ratio limits sit well below hypertensive-referral cut-offs
cards.people: Synthesis of the six primary datasets carded above (1,347; 328; 282; 170; 309; and 5,200 healthy subjects).
cards.result: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall (adrenal / renin–angiotensin–aldosterone sections) and Boron & Boulpaep (adrenal gland chapter) — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Across six populations and four measurement approaches (radioimmunometric, chemiluminescence, and LC-MS/MS for both renin activity and direct renin concentration), the consistent findings are structural: intervals partition by sex (chemiluminescence aldosterone 76–722 pmol/L, about 2.7–26.0 ng/dL, in men versus 85–1,010 pmol/L, about 3.1–36.4 ng/dL, in women; LC-MS/MS aldosterone 0.04–0.41 nmol/L in Belgian men versus 0.07–0.73 nmol/L in women) and by age (a renin-activity split at 45 years in Hong Kong; renin falling with age in Yunnan's 5,200), and they belong to their assay — RIA reads 59% higher than LC-MS/MS in plasma. Healthy-population upper limits for the aldosterone-to-renin ratio (14.2–25.5 by sex and age in SHIP-1) sit clearly below referral-cohort cut-offs. No dataset carded here prints a posture-partitioned interval in its fetched record, so posture is carried as a recognised influence on sampling (named in the Yunnan report's background), not as a carded interval. Aldosterone secretion rate by isotope dilution (pack #6964) and the ratio's diagnostic accuracy in primary-aldosteronism screening (pack #6062) are different measurements and questions — cross-points only, never re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Never apply one method's interval to another method's result, and never interchange renin activity with direct renin concentration; several datasets' numeric limits are not printed in their fetched records and are claimed nowhere on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: Discontinued agent — this flag leads. Rivoglitazone was never marketed despite a phase 3 that met superiority against pioglitazone at the higher dose. Its glycaemic record is consistent (HbA1c −0.7% on 1.5 mg in the phase 3; placebo-subtracted falls of −0.55% to −1.10% dose-dependently in the dose-ranging trial; significant falls versus placebo in a 12-week Chinese trial), but HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint, no outcomes trial exists, the dose-ranging trial lost more than half its participants early, and the class harms — peripheral oedema (5.2–6.2% drug-related in the phase 3 versus 0.7% on placebo) and weight gain — are printed on the face. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control only.

cards.headline: Phase 3 monotherapy trial (Chou 2012): HbA1c fell −0.7% on rivoglitazone 1.5 mg vs −0.6% on pioglitazone 45 mg — statistically superior (P = 0.0339); drug-related peripheral oedema 5.2–6.2% on rivoglitazone vs 0.7% on placebo
cards.summary: Phase 3 monotherapy trial (Chou 2012): HbA1c fell −0.7% on rivoglitazone 1.5 mg vs −0.6% on pioglitazone 45 mg — statistically superior (P = 0.0339); drug-related peripheral oedema 5.2–6.2% on rivoglitazone vs 0.7% on placebo
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo- and pioglitazone-controlled monotherapy trial, rivoglitazone in type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 1,912 treated subjects with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c >7.0% and ≤8.5%, treatment-naïve or on a non-thiazolidinedione monotherapy, randomised after washout and placebo run-in to placebo (137), rivoglitazone 1.0 mg (274), rivoglitazone 1.5 mg (750) or pioglitazone 45 mg (751) daily for 26 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c changes from baseline were −0.7% on rivoglitazone 1.5 mg, −0.4% on rivoglitazone 1.0 mg and −0.6% on pioglitazone: rivoglitazone 1.5 mg was statistically superior to pioglitazone (P = 0.0339) and 1.0 mg was non-inferior. Rivoglitazone also significantly reduced fasting plasma glucose (P < 0.0001) and improved insulin-sensitivity estimates, HDL cholesterol and other metabolic and inflammatory biomarkers. The most common drug-related adverse events were peripheral oedema (5.2–6.2% across active arms versus 0.7% on placebo), increased weight (1.6–3.1% versus 0%) and pitting oedema (1.3–2.2% versus 0%), with overall treatment-emergent event rates similar to pioglitazone.
cards.watchOut: Superiority on a surrogate (HbA1c) by 0.1 percentage points over pioglitazone, in a drug that was never marketed: the result answers the glycaemic question, not whether any patient outcome is improved, and the oedema/weight class signature is present in the same abstract.
cards.source: Chou HS et al. A 26-week, placebo- and pioglitazone-controlled monotherapy study of rivoglitazone in subjects with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2012. PMID: 22686944. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dose-ranging trial (Truitt 2010): placebo-subtracted HbA1c −0.55%, −0.99% and −1.10% on rivoglitazone 1, 2 and 3 mg vs −0.59% on pioglitazone — but early discontinuations exceeded 50%
cards.summary: Dose-ranging trial (Truitt 2010): placebo-subtracted HbA1c −0.55%, −0.99% and −1.10% on rivoglitazone 1, 2 and 3 mg vs −0.59% on pioglitazone — but early discontinuations exceeded 50%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind dose-ranging trial, rivoglitazone vs pioglitazone and placebo in type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 441 randomised adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≥7.0% and <10.5%), treatment-naïve or switched from prior therapy, in a 26-week randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo- and pioglitazone 45 mg-controlled dose-ranging study of rivoglitazone 1, 2 or 3 mg daily.
cards.result: Placebo-subtracted HbA1c changes at week 26 were −0.55% (P = 0.0034), −0.99% (P < 0.0001) and −1.10% (P < 0.0001) on rivoglitazone 1, 2 and 3 mg, and −0.59% (P = 0.0016) on pioglitazone. The incidence of early discontinuations was over 50%, mostly lack of efficacy (highest on placebo) or adverse experiences (highest on rivoglitazone 3 mg). The commonest drug-related adverse events on rivoglitazone were peripheral oedema and weight gain, increasing with dose and higher at 2 and 3 mg than on pioglitazone or rivoglitazone 1 mg.
cards.watchOut: More than half of participants discontinued early and the analysis is last-observation-carried-forward: the dose–response gradient is real but rests on a heavily depleted trial, a limit the authors themselves state.
cards.source: Truitt KE et al. A 26-week, placebo- and pioglitazone-controlled, dose-ranging study of rivoglitazone, a novel thiazolidinedione for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Current medical research and opinion. 2010. PMID: 20370378. Registry ID: NCT00143520. cards.headline: Chinese trial (Kong 2011): HbA1c −0.11%, −0.22% and −0.17% on rivoglitazone 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mg vs −0.06% on pioglitazone 30 mg and +0.61% on placebo over 12 weeks (all active arms P < 0.05 vs placebo); oedema 7.7% on rivoglitazone vs 16.2% on pioglitazone
cards.summary: Chinese trial (Kong 2011): HbA1c −0.11%, −0.22% and −0.17% on rivoglitazone 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mg vs −0.06% on pioglitazone 30 mg and +0.61% on placebo over 12 weeks (all active arms P < 0.05 vs placebo); oedema 7.7% on rivoglitazone vs 16.2% on pioglitazone
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo- and pioglitazone-controlled trial, rivoglitazone in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 174 randomised Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes (of 287 enrolled; HbA1c ≥6.5% to <10%), treatment-naïve or on a single oral agent, in a 12-week double-blind randomised trial of rivoglitazone 0.5, 1.0 or 1.5 mg, pioglitazone 30 mg or placebo daily. Single-region (China) trial — flagged here on the face.
cards.result: HbA1c changes were −0.11%, −0.22% and −0.17% on the three rivoglitazone doses, −0.06% on pioglitazone and +0.61% on placebo; all active arms differed significantly from placebo (all P < 0.05). HDL cholesterol rose and triglycerides fell versus placebo at the 1 and 1.5 mg doses respectively (P < 0.05). Drug-related oedema was reported in 7.7% across the rivoglitazone groups, 16.2% on pioglitazone and 3.0% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Single-region, 12-week, small per-arm numbers with modest absolute HbA1c falls against a rising placebo arm: supportive of the phase 3 glycaemic claim, not independent proof of it, and the pioglitazone dose here (30 mg) is lower than in the phase 3 (45 mg).

Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2011. PMID: 21492364. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a glitazone that won its phase 3 comparison and was still abandoned — glycaemic efficacy yes, outcomes unknown, class harms present
cards.summary: Synthesis: a glitazone that won its phase 3 comparison and was still abandoned — glycaemic efficacy yes, outcomes unknown, class harms present
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (phase 3 n=1,912 treated; dose-ranging n=441 randomised; Chinese trial n=174 randomised).
cards.result: Rivoglitazone lowers HbA1c versus placebo in every trial carded, and at 1.5 mg was statistically superior to pioglitazone 45 mg in the 1,912-patient phase 3 (−0.7% versus −0.6%). The costs visible in its own abstracts are the thiazolidinedione class costs — peripheral oedema in 5.2–6.2% drug-related versus 0.7% on placebo, and dose-related weight gain — and the dose-ranging trial's >50% early discontinuation rate limits its weight. HbA1c is a surrogate; no cardiovascular or microvascular outcomes trial exists, and the drug was never marketed. The stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control only.
cards.watchOut: Never present the pioglitazone superiority as a reason the drug should have been used: the margin was 0.1 HbA1c percentage points on a surrogate, the sponsor still did not market it, and no outcomes data exist for this molecule.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity (with or without chronic kidney disease), does the GLP-1/glucagon co-agonist cotadutide, compared with placebo or liraglutide, improve glycaemic control and body weight (the glycaemic programme slice)?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL slice only — this flag leads. The kidney question stays homed at pack #6665 under the one-home rule, and #6665's own glycaemic support card (the phase 2a JCEM trial, PMID 31608926) is homed there and is cross-pointed here, never re-carded; this shelf cards only the three glycaemic-programme reports that are carded nowhere else. On that slice: the 54-week phase 2b trial (834 randomised) found cotadutide significantly decreased HbA1c and body weight versus placebo at weeks 14 and 54 (all P < 0.001; the record prints no HbA1c point estimates and none are claimed), with nausea in 35% and vomiting in 17%; the 32-day CKD phase 2a trial (41 randomised) cut mixed-meal glucose AUC by 26.71% relative and weight by 3.41 kg; the mechanistic phase 2a trial's primary endpoints were hepatic glycogen — a surrogate of a surrogate. All anchors are phase 2, two are very short (32 days; 28/35 days), the programme was not advanced to phase 3 on the glycaemic question, and no outcomes trial exists. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: 54-week phase 2b trial (Nahra 2021): cotadutide significantly decreased HbA1c and body weight vs placebo at weeks 14 and 54 (all P < 0.001) in 834 randomised adults; weight loss at 300 µg exceeded liraglutide 1.8 mg; nausea 35%, vomiting 17%
cards.summary: 54-week phase 2b trial (Nahra 2021): cotadutide significantly decreased HbA1c and body weight vs placebo at weeks 14 and 54 (all P < 0.001) in 834 randomised adults; weight loss at 300 µg exceeded liraglutide 1.8 mg; nausea 35%, vomiting 17%
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b trial (54 weeks), cotadutide vs placebo and open-label liraglutide in overweight/obesity with type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 834 adults with BMI 25 kg/m² or over and type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin (HbA1c 7.0–10.5% [53–91 mmol/mol]), randomised to double-blind cotadutide 100 µg (100), 200 µg (256) or 300 µg (256), placebo (110) or open-label liraglutide 1.8 mg (110), all subcutaneous, with the randomised interventions continued to week 54; co-primary endpoints were changes in HbA1c and body weight at week 14.
cards.result: Cotadutide significantly decreased HbA1c and body weight at weeks 14 and 54 versus placebo (all P < 0.001) — the fetched record prints no HbA1c or weight point estimates, and none are claimed on this card. Weight loss with cotadutide 200 µg was similar to liraglutide 1.8 mg and greater with cotadutide 300 µg than with liraglutide. The most common adverse events on cotadutide were nausea (35%) and vomiting (17%), decreasing over time.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2b with significance statements but no point estimates in the record: the size of the HbA1c and weight effects cannot be quoted from this shelf, and the liraglutide arm was open-label. The trial's hepatic-parameter findings belong to the liver question and are not carded here.
cards.source: Nahra R et al. Effects of Cotadutide on Metabolic and Hepatic Parameters in Adults With Overweight or Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes: A 54-Week Randomized Phase 2b Study. Diabetes care. 2021. PMID: 34016612. Registry ID: NCT03235050. cards.headline: Phase 2a trial in T2D with CKD (Parker 2022): mixed-meal glucose AUC −26.71% relative vs +3.68% on placebo (P < 0.001) and weight −3.41 kg vs −0.13 kg over 32 days in 41 randomised patients
cards.summary: Phase 2a trial in T2D with CKD (Parker 2022): mixed-meal glucose AUC −26.71% relative vs +3.68% on placebo (P < 0.001) and weight −3.41 kg vs −0.13 kg over 32 days in 41 randomised patients
cards.type: Randomised phase 2a trial (32 days), cotadutide vs placebo in type 2 diabetes with CKD
cards.people: 41 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m², BMI 25–45 kg/m², HbA1c 6.5–10.5% [48–91 mmol/mol]) on insulin and/or oral therapy, randomised 1:1 to once-daily subcutaneous cotadutide 50–300 µg (21) or placebo (20) for 32 days; the primary endpoint was mixed-meal-tolerance-test glucose AUC.
cards.result: Cotadutide significantly reduced mixed-meal glucose AUC versus placebo (−26.71% versus +3.68%; P < 0.001 — relative changes as published), increased time in target glucose range on continuous monitoring (+14.79% versus −21.23%; P = 0.001) and reduced body weight (−3.41 kg versus −0.13 kg; P < 0.001). In the subgroup with baseline micro- or macroalbuminuria (n = 18), urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio fell 51% relative at day 32 versus placebo (P = 0.0504) — a kidney signal cross-pointed here only; the kidney question itself is homed at pack #6665 and is not re-carded. Mean eGFR change did not differ significantly. Mild/moderate adverse events occurred in 71.4% on cotadutide versus 35.0% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two days and 41 patients: a pharmacodynamic glycaemic demonstration, not durability or outcomes evidence — and its albuminuria subgroup (n = 18, P = 0.0504) is a cross-point to the kidney shelf #6665, never a second kidney card.

cards.headline: Mechanistic phase 2a trial (Parker 2023, Nature Metabolism): cotadutide produced greater reductions in hepatic glycogen (primary endpoints, days 28/35) and hepatic fat than placebo and liraglutide — attributed to glucagon-receptor engagement
cards.summary: Mechanistic phase 2a trial (Parker 2023, Nature Metabolism): cotadutide produced greater reductions in hepatic glycogen (primary endpoints, days 28/35) and hepatic fat than placebo and liraglutide — attributed to glucagon-receptor engagement
cards.type: Randomised phase 2a mechanistic trial (two-part), cotadutide vs placebo and liraglutide — hepatic glycogen endpoints
cards.people: Men and women with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes in a two-part randomised phase 2a trial of cotadutide versus placebo and liraglutide; primary endpoints were change in postprandial hepatic glycogen at day 28 (part A) and fasting hepatic glycogen at day 35 (part B). The fetched record prints no randomised N, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: The trial met its primary endpoints: cotadutide promoted greater reductions in liver glycogen and in hepatic fat than placebo and liraglutide, which the authors attribute to glucagon-receptor engagement — evidence that the molecule's glucagon limb is pharmacologically active in the human liver, supporting the glycaemic findings of the other cards. Safety and tolerability were comparable to previous cotadutide reports. The record prints no effect sizes for the glycogen endpoints, and none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Mechanistic by design: hepatic glycogen is a surrogate of a surrogate for glycaemic control, the treatment periods were 28 and 35 days, and no N is printed in the record — this card explains mechanism and must never carry the shelf's efficacy claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the uncarded glycaemic slice is three phase 2 reports — a large 54-week trial, a 32-day CKD trial and a mechanistic study — beside the kidney shelf #6665, whose own glycaemic card is not re-carded here
cards.summary: Synthesis: the uncarded glycaemic slice is three phase 2 reports — a large 54-week trial, a 32-day CKD trial and a mechanistic study — beside the kidney shelf #6665, whose own glycaemic card is not re-carded here
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (phase 2b n=834; CKD phase 2a n=41; mechanistic phase 2a, N not printed in its record). Cross-point, not carded: the phase 2a glycaemic trial homed inside pack #6665 (PMID 31608926).
cards.result: Cotadutide improves glycaemic control and body weight versus placebo in type 2 diabetes across its phase 2 programme: significant HbA1c and weight reductions sustained to 54 weeks in the 834-patient phase 2b trial, a 26.71% relative fall in mixed-meal glucose AUC and 3.41 kg greater weight loss over 32 days in CKD, and a hepatic-glycogen mechanism consistent with glucagon-receptor engagement. The costs are gastrointestinal (nausea 35%, vomiting 17% in the phase 2b). Everything here is phase 2, the programme was not advanced to phase 3 on the glycaemic question, and no outcomes trial exists. The kidney question — including this programme's albuminuria trial — remains homed at pack #6665 under the one-home rule. The stamp is POSSIBLE (benefit) for glycaemic control and weight only.
cards.watchOut: One-home rule: PMID 31608926 is cross-pointed, never re-carded, and nothing on this shelf answers the kidney question — for albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease, use pack #6665.

shelves.title: Fasiglifam (GPR40) for T2D: HbA1c fell −0.65% to −0.93% vs placebo — and liver injury (ALT ≥3× ULN 2.1% vs 0.5%) terminated the programme and its outcomes trial; never marketed
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the GPR40 (free fatty acid receptor 1) agonist fasiglifam (TAK-875), compared with placebo or added to sitagliptin, improve glycaemic control — and what liver injury ended its development?

shelves.balance: LIKELY harm-led, discontinued agent — the termination leads. Fasiglifam (TAK-875), a GPR40 agonist, lowered HbA1c consistently (global phase 3: −0.65% and −0.93% vs −0.17% on placebo; Japanese phase 3: −0.57% and −0.83% vs +0.16%; added to sitagliptin: a further −0.45% to −0.61%) — and was never marketed, because its own trials documented drug-induced liver injury: ALT >3× ULN in 3.6% and 2.8% versus none on placebo in the global phase 3, and in the cardiovascular-outcomes trial — terminated at 3,207 of 5,000 planned participants for liver safety — ALT or AST ≥3× ULN in 2.1% versus 0.5% and ≥10× ULN in 0.31% versus 0.06%. That terminated trial's HR 1.05 rests on 40 events and is uninformative about cardiovascular safety. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout; one anchor is a single-region (Japan) trial, flagged on its card.

cards.headline: Global phase 3 monotherapy trial (421 people, 24 weeks): HbA1c −0.65% (25 mg) and −0.93% (50 mg) vs −0.17% on placebo — and ALT elevations >3× ULN only on fasiglifam (3.6% and 2.8%, none on placebo), which contributed to terminating the programme
cards.summary: Global phase 3 monotherapy trial (421 people, 24 weeks): HbA1c −0.65% (25 mg) and −0.93% (50 mg) vs −0.17% on placebo — and ALT elevations >3× ULN only on fasiglifam (3.6% and 2.8%, none on placebo), which contributed to terminating the programme
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (global monotherapy, 421 randomised)
cards.people: 421 people with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0–10.5%, mean baseline 8.05%; mean age 53.5 years; mean body-mass index 32.3 kg/m²) who had received only diet and exercise for ≥12 weeks, randomised to fasiglifam 25 mg, fasiglifam 50 mg or placebo for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was −0.65% on fasiglifam 25 mg, −0.93% on 50 mg and −0.17% on placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 53.3% (25 mg), 48.2% (50 mg) and 39.9% (placebo); 3 participants in each group had a serious adverse event. Nine participants had ALT elevations >3× the upper limit of normal: 5 (3.6%) on fasiglifam 25 mg, 4 (2.8%) on 50 mg and none on placebo. The abstract states these ALT elevations contributed to the decision to terminate the fasiglifam programme after completion of this study.
cards.watchOut: HARM ON THE FACE: the liver signal is in this trial's own abstract, not a later discovery — no efficacy figure from this card may be quoted without the ALT figures beside it. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Marcinak J et al. Fasiglifam for glycaemic control in people with type 2 diabetes: A phase III, placebo-controlled study. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2017. PMID: 28493502. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Japanese phase 3 trial (192 randomised, 24 weeks) — SINGLE-REGION trial, flagged: HbA1c +0.16% on placebo, −0.57% on 25 mg and −0.83% on 50 mg (both P < 0.0001); hypoglycaemia in 1 patient; global liver-safety concerns terminated development after this trial
cards.summary: Japanese phase 3 trial (192 randomised, 24 weeks) — SINGLE-REGION trial, flagged: HbA1c +0.16% on placebo, −0.57% on 25 mg and −0.83% on 50 mg (both P < 0.0001); hypoglycaemia in 1 patient; global liver-safety concerns terminated development after this trial
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Japan, single-region, 192 randomised)
cards.people: 192 Japanese patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise, randomised to fasiglifam 25 mg (n = 63), fasiglifam 50 mg (n = 62) or placebo (n = 67) once daily for 24 weeks in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 study.
cards.result: Least-squares mean HbA1c change at week 24 was +0.16% on placebo, −0.57% on fasiglifam 25 mg and −0.83% on 50 mg (both P < 0.0001 vs placebo). The proportion reaching HbA1c <6.9% at week 24 was 30.2% (25 mg) and 54.8% (50 mg) versus 13.8% on placebo (both P < 0.05). Fasiglifam reduced fasting plasma glucose from week 2; hypoglycaemia was reported in 1 patient (fasiglifam 50 mg), and there were no clinically meaningful body-weight changes. The abstract records that concerns about liver safety from the overall global programme arose in a recent review and clinical development was terminated after this trial was completed.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (Japan) trial — flagged on the face, per the row: its efficacy replicates the global trial's, but it is not independent evidence about liver safety, whose signal came from the global programme.

cards.headline: Sitagliptin-combination phase 2 trial (368 patients, 12 weeks): fasiglifam + sitagliptin beat sitagliptin alone on HbA1c by −0.45% (25 mg) and −0.61% (50 mg), with fasting glucose an extra −1.1 mmol/L (approx. −20 mg/dL) lower; liver enzymes >3× ULN in 4 patients across the fasiglifam arms
cards.summary: Sitagliptin-combination phase 2 trial (368 patients, 12 weeks): fasiglifam + sitagliptin beat sitagliptin alone on HbA1c by −0.45% (25 mg) and −0.61% (50 mg), with fasting glucose an extra −1.1 mmol/L (approx. −20 mg/dL) lower; liver enzymes >3× ULN in 4 patients across the fasiglifam arms
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind trial (fasiglifam ± sitagliptin combination, 368 patients)
cards.people: 368 patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with diet/exercise (with or without metformin), randomised for 12 weeks to placebo, sitagliptin 100 mg, fasiglifam 25 or 50 mg, or sitagliptin 100 mg plus fasiglifam 25 or 50 mg, in a randomised double-blind phase 2 study.
cards.result: The combination regimens produced significantly greater HbA1c reductions than sitagliptin alone (treatment differences −0.45% for 25 mg and −0.61% for 50 mg; both P < 0.01) and than the respective fasiglifam monotherapy doses (−0.43% and −0.48%; both P < 0.01), and significantly greater fasting plasma glucose reductions than sitagliptin (−1.1 mmol/L (approx. −20 mg/dL) for both combination regimens; P < 0.01). Hypoglycaemia rates were low (≤3.3%) and similar across treatments. Liver enzymes >3× the upper limit of normal occurred in 4 patients (fasiglifam 25 mg, n = 1; fasiglifam 50 mg, n = 2; fasiglifam/sitagliptin 50/100 mg, n = 1).
cards.watchOut: A 12-week phase 2 glycaemic (surrogate) trial: the combination advantage is real on HbA1c but short and surrogate, and the liver-enzyme cases appear here too — the harm is programme-wide, not confined to monotherapy.
cards.source: Peng XV et al. Diabetes, obesity & metabolism. 2017. PMID: 28239939. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Terminated cardiovascular-outcomes safety trial (3,207 enrolled of 5,000 planned): stopped for liver safety — ALT or AST ≥3× ULN in 2.1% vs 0.5% and ≥10× ULN in 0.31% vs 0.06% (both P < 0.001); the CV composite occurred in 2.5% in each arm (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.63) on only 40 events
cards.summary: Terminated cardiovascular-outcomes safety trial (3,207 enrolled of 5,000 planned): stopped for liver safety — ALT or AST ≥3× ULN in 2.1% vs 0.5% and ≥10× ULN in 0.31% vs 0.06% (both P < 0.001); the CV composite occurred in 2.5% in each arm (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.63) on only 40 events
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised cardiovascular-outcomes safety trial — TERMINATED early for liver safety (3,207 of 5,000 planned)
cards.people: A phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial intended to randomise 5,000 participants with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk to fasiglifam or placebo, designed to rule out an upper noninferiority bound above 1.3 for the hazard ratio for the major adverse cardiovascular composite (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, hospitalisation for unstable angina). It enrolled 3,207 participants and was terminated because of liver safety concerns. Registry ID: NCT01609582.
cards.result: Increased liver enzyme elevations were observed on fasiglifam: ALT or AST ≥3× the upper limit of normal in 2.1% versus 0.5% on placebo (P < 0.001), and ≥10× ULN in 0.31% versus 0.06% (P < 0.001). A primary cardiovascular composite outcome occurred in 40 participants — 2.5% in each arm at 12 months — with hazard ratio 1.05 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.63); a hazard ratio is a relative measure. The authors conclude development was terminated due to concerns of drug-induced liver injury, and that performance of the FDA-mandated cardiovascular outcomes trial supported terminating the programme.
cards.watchOut: NOT a completed outcomes trial: it stopped at 3,207 of 5,000 planned participants with only 40 composite events, so its HR 1.05 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.63) is uninformative about cardiovascular safety and must never be presented as cardiovascular reassurance. Its informative result is the liver injury that stopped it.
cards.source: Menon V et al. Fasiglifam-Induced Liver Injury in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: Results of a Randomized Controlled Cardiovascular Outcomes Safety Trial. Diabetes care. 2018. PMID: 30459247. Registry ID: NCT01609582. cards.headline: Synthesis: 4 reports — glycaemic efficacy was real and consistent (−0.57% to −0.93% HbA1c vs placebo; −0.45% to −0.61% added to sitagliptin), and the programme was terminated for drug-induced liver injury documented inside its own phase 3 and outcomes-trial abstracts; fasiglifam was never marketed
cards.summary: Synthesis: 4 reports — glycaemic efficacy was real and consistent (−0.57% to −0.93% HbA1c vs placebo; −0.45% to −0.61% added to sitagliptin), and the programme was terminated for drug-induced liver injury documented inside its own phase 3 and outcomes-trial abstracts; fasiglifam was never marketed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the four reports carded: the global phase 3 monotherapy trial (421 people) gave HbA1c −0.65% and −0.93% versus −0.17% on placebo, with ALT >3× ULN in 3.6% and 2.8% on fasiglifam and none on placebo; the Japanese phase 3 trial (192 randomised, single-region) replicated the glycaemic effect (−0.57% and −0.83% vs +0.16%); the phase 2 sitagliptin-combination trial (368 patients) added −0.45% to −0.61% HbA1c over sitagliptin alone with liver enzymes >3× ULN in 4 fasiglifam-arm patients; and the cardiovascular-outcomes safety trial was terminated at 3,207 of 5,000 planned participants because of liver safety, with ALT or AST ≥3× ULN in 2.1% versus 0.5% and ≥10× ULN in 0.31% versus 0.06%. The harm leads: this is a discontinued, never-marketed agent whose own trial abstracts document the drug-induced liver injury that ended it. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint throughout, and the terminated outcomes trial's HR 1.05 on 40 events says nothing about cardiovascular safety.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. The liver-safety programme reviews of this same trial experience are programme support only and are not carded or counted.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Insulin peglispro (IMAGINE): HbA1c wins over glargine in type 1 and type 2 diabetes — against increased liver fat, triglycerides and liver enzymes; discontinued, never marketed
shelves.question: In adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, does the hepato-preferential basal insulin peglispro (LY2605541), compared with insulin glargine, improve glycaemic control — and what did it do to liver fat, triglycerides and liver enzymes (the IMAGINE programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin Glargine · Insulin Lispro · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a discontinued, never-marketed hepato-preferential basal insulin whose glycaemic wins came with a hepatic price, printed beside every win. Across the IMAGINE programme peglispro beat insulin glargine on HbA1c in type 2 diabetes (IMAGINE 2 difference −0.29%; IMAGINE 5 difference −0.52% at 26 weeks) and in type 1 diabetes (IMAGINE 1 difference −0.37%), with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms in all three trials. Against that, triglycerides and aminotransferases were higher on peglispro in every trial, MRI liver fat content rose on peglispro versus glargine in IMAGINE 5 and failed to fall as it did on glargine in IMAGINE 2, injection-site reactions were more frequent, and in type 1 diabetes total hypoglycaemia was 29% higher in relative terms with more severe hypoglycaemia. Development stopped after phase 3; there is no outcomes trial. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: IMAGINE 2 (Davies 2016): peglispro beat glargine on HbA1c in insulin-naïve type 2 diabetes (difference −0.29%) — but triglycerides and liver enzymes were higher and liver fat did not fall
cards.summary: IMAGINE 2 (Davies 2016): peglispro beat glargine on HbA1c in insulin-naïve type 2 diabetes (difference −0.29%) — but triglycerides and liver enzymes were higher and liver fat did not fall
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial (IMAGINE 2), peglispro vs glargine in insulin-naïve type 2 diabetes
cards.people: Insulin-naïve adults with type 2 diabetes on pre-study oral antihyperglycaemic medications, randomised double-blind to basal insulin peglispro or insulin glargine; primary assessment at 52 weeks (study ran 52 or 78 weeks). The fetched abstract prints no randomised N, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: Peglispro was non-inferior and then superior on HbA1c: least-squares mean difference −0.29% (95% CI −0.40 to −0.19), with a lower nocturnal hypoglycaemia rate (relative rate 0.74, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.91; P = .005 — a relative measure) and more patients achieving HbA1c <7.0% (odds ratio 1.97, 95% CI 1.57 to 2.47). Total hypoglycaemia did not improve. At 52 weeks the peglispro group had higher triglycerides (1.9 vs 1.7 mmol/L (≈ 168 vs 151 mg/dL)), alanine aminotransferase (34 vs 27 IU/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (27 vs 24 IU/L). MRI liver fat content was unchanged on peglispro but decreased 3.1% on glargine (difference 2.6%, 95% CI 0.9 to 4.2; P = 0.002). Injection-site reactions: 3.5% vs 0.6% (P < .001).
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints no randomised N. The glycaemic win and the hepatic signal are in the same abstract and must travel together: liver fat content fell on glargine and did not fall on peglispro.
cards.source: Davies MJ et al. Basal insulin peglispro versus insulin glargine in insulin-naïve type 2 diabetes: IMAGINE 2 randomized trial. Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2016. PMID: 27349219. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: IMAGINE 5 (Buse 2016): in basal-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, peglispro lowered HbA1c more than glargine (−0.82% vs −0.29% at 26 weeks) — and liver fat content increased on peglispro
cards.summary: IMAGINE 5 (Buse 2016): in basal-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, peglispro lowered HbA1c more than glargine (−0.82% vs −0.29% at 26 weeks) — and liver fat content increased on peglispro
cards.type: Open-label treat-to-target randomised trial (IMAGINE 5), peglispro vs glargine in basal-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 466 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≤9%) previously treated with basal insulin alone or with three or fewer oral agents, randomised open-label treat-to-target to peglispro (n = 307) or glargine (n = 159) for 52 weeks; mean baseline HbA1c 7.42%.
cards.result: At 26 weeks HbA1c fell −0.82% on peglispro vs −0.29% on glargine (least-squares mean difference −0.52%, 95% CI −0.67 to −0.38; P < 0.001), maintained at 52 weeks; more peglispro patients achieved HbA1c <7% (P < 0.001). The nocturnal hypoglycaemia rate was 60% lower in relative terms on peglispro, and total hypoglycaemia rates were lower at 52 weeks (P = 0.03). But triglycerides and aminotransferases were higher with peglispro (P < 0.05), and liver fat content, assessed in a 162-patient subset, increased from baseline with peglispro versus glargine (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treat-to-target design, and the liver-fat result comes from a 162-patient MRI subset of the 466 randomised — the direction is consistent with IMAGINE 2, but the subset is not the whole trial.
cards.source: Buse JB et al. Randomized Clinical Trial Comparing Basal Insulin Peglispro and Insulin Glargine in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes Previously Treated With Basal Insulin: IMAGINE 5. Diabetes Care. 2016. PMID: 26577417. Registry ID: NCT01582451. cards.headline: IMAGINE 1 (Garg 2016): in type 1 diabetes peglispro lowered HbA1c (7.06% vs 7.43%) with 36% less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms — but 29% more total hypoglycaemia and more severe hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: IMAGINE 1 (Garg 2016): in type 1 diabetes peglispro lowered HbA1c (7.06% vs 7.43%) with 36% less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms — but 29% more total hypoglycaemia and more severe hypoglycaemia
cards.type: Open-label randomised trial (IMAGINE 1), peglispro vs glargine plus prandial lispro in type 1 diabetes
cards.people: 455 adults with type 1 diabetes randomised (295 peglispro vs 160 glargine) to bedtime peglispro or glargine, both with prandial insulin lispro, for 78 weeks with the primary endpoint at 26 weeks, across nine countries.
cards.result: At 26 weeks mean HbA1c was 7.06% on peglispro vs 7.43% on glargine (difference −0.37%, 95% CI −0.50 to −0.23; P < .001); 44.9% vs 27.5% achieved HbA1c <7% (P < .001). Peglispro patients lost weight and had 36% less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms, but 29% more total hypoglycaemia in relative terms and more severe hypoglycaemia. Alanine aminotransferase increased on peglispro, with more patients having elevations ≥3× the upper limit of normal; serum triglycerides rose from baseline, and injection-site reactions were more frequent.
cards.watchOut: In type 1 diabetes the hypoglycaemia trade runs both ways — less nocturnal, more total and more severe — and must not be summarised as a hypoglycaemia win. The hepatic signal (aminotransferases, triglycerides) appears here too.

cards.headline: Synthesis: peglispro consistently beat glargine on HbA1c with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia — and consistently raised triglycerides, liver enzymes and liver fat; the programme was discontinued and never marketed
cards.summary: Synthesis: peglispro consistently beat glargine on HbA1c with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia — and consistently raised triglycerides, liver enzymes and liver fat; the programme was discontinued and never marketed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: IMAGINE 2 (insulin-naïve type 2 diabetes), IMAGINE 5 (466 randomised, basal-insulin-treated type 2 diabetes) and IMAGINE 1 (455 randomised, type 1 diabetes).
cards.result: HbA1c differences favouring peglispro: −0.29% (IMAGINE 2), −0.52% at 26 weeks (IMAGINE 5) and −0.37% (IMAGINE 1), each with less nocturnal hypoglycaemia in relative terms. The other side of the ledger is equally consistent: higher triglycerides and aminotransferases in all three trials, MRI liver fat content increased versus glargine in IMAGINE 5 and not reduced in IMAGINE 2, more injection-site reactions, and in type 1 diabetes 29% more total hypoglycaemia in relative terms with more severe hypoglycaemia. No cardiovascular or other outcomes trial exists. SPLIT: real glycaemic benefit against a real hepatic and (in type 1 diabetes) hypoglycaemia harm signal, in an agent that was never marketed.

shelves.title: Pramlintide in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes: modest HbA1c benefit with weight loss across two 52-week trials (the type 2 slice; type 1 homed at #1779)
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin, does adjunctive pramlintide (the amylin analogue), compared with placebo, improve glycaemic control and body weight (the type-2-diabetes slice)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Amyloid · Blood Glucose · Body Weight · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Incidence · Insulin · Islet Amyloid Polypeptide · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the type 2 diabetes slice only (the type 1 programme is homed at pack #1779 and is not re-carded). Four reports but only TWO distinct trials: two 52-week randomised trials in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes (656 and 538 randomised) plus two pooled post-hoc analyses of those same trials, carded and labelled as programme reports. Effects are modest and consistent: on the higher doses HbA1c fell about 0.6–0.7% from baseline at 52 weeks, significantly more than placebo (placebo-corrected ≈ −0.4 to −0.6% in the pooled analyses), with weight loss instead of insulin-associated gain (−1.4 kg vs +0.7 kg at week 52 in one trial; placebo-corrected −1.8 to −2.0 kg in the pooled analyses) and no overall increase in severe hypoglycaemia. Nausea is the signature harm. The trials predate modern background therapy (insulin ± sulfonylurea/metformin era, baseline HbA1c ≈ 9%). HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; no outcomes trial exists.

cards.headline: Hollander 2003 (52-week RCT): pramlintide 120 µg twice daily lowered HbA1c (−0.62% at week 52) with weight loss (−1.4 kg vs +0.7 kg) and no overall increase in severe hypoglycaemia
cards.summary: Hollander 2003 (52-week RCT): pramlintide 120 µg twice daily lowered HbA1c (−0.62% at week 52) with weight loss (−1.4 kg vs +0.7 kg) and no overall increase in severe hypoglycaemia
cards.type: 52-week double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, adjunctive pramlintide (three dose regimens) in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 656 patients with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin (alone or with sulfonylureas and/or metformin), mean age 57 years, mean BMI 34.0 kg/m², baseline HbA1c 9.1 ± 1.2%, randomised double-blind to preprandial pramlintide 60 µg three times daily, 90 or 120 µg twice daily, or placebo for 52 weeks.
cards.result: On pramlintide 120 µg twice daily, HbA1c fell −0.68% at week 26 and −0.62% at week 52 from baseline, significantly more than placebo (P < 0.05). The proportion reaching HbA1c <8% was about twofold greater on pramlintide 120 µg twice daily than placebo (46% vs 28%, P < 0.05). Weight changed −1.4 kg on pramlintide vs +0.7 kg on placebo at week 52 (P < 0.05), without an overall increase in the severe hypoglycaemia event rate. The commonest adverse event was transient, mild-to-moderate nausea.
cards.watchOut: Baseline HbA1c was 9.1% on insulin-era background therapy (sulfonylureas/metformin) — the absolute falls here start from much poorer control than a modern clinic population, and the headline dose (120 µg twice daily) is one of three regimens tested.
cards.source: Hollander PA et al. Pramlintide as an adjunct to insulin therapy improves long-term glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes: a 1-year randomized controlled trial. Diabetes Care. 2003. PMID: 12610038. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ratner 2002 (52-week dose-ranging RCT): pramlintide 150 µg three times daily lowered HbA1c 0.6% at week 52 (P = 0.0068 vs placebo), with weight reduction in all dose groups
cards.summary: Ratner 2002 (52-week dose-ranging RCT): pramlintide 150 µg three times daily lowered HbA1c 0.6% at week 52 (P = 0.0068 vs placebo), with weight reduction in all dose groups
cards.type: 52-week double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging randomised trial, adjunctive pramlintide in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes
cards.people: 538 insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes randomised double-blind to pramlintide 30, 75 or 150 µg three times daily with major meals, or placebo, for 52 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c fell 0.9% and 1.0% from baseline at week 13 on the 75 and 150 µg doses (P = 0.0004 and P = 0.0002 vs placebo), and 0.6% at week 52 on 150 µg (P = 0.0068 vs placebo). The glycaemic improvement came without increases in insulin use or severe hypoglycaemia, with significant weight reduction in all dose groups versus placebo (P < 0.05). A combined HbA1c-and-weight reduction at week 52 was achieved by 48% on pramlintide 150 µg vs 16% on placebo. Nausea was the commonest adverse event, mild to moderate and dissipating early.
cards.watchOut: Three-times-daily mealtime injections on top of insulin — the burden is part of the intervention and these efficacy records do not measure real-world persistence. Week-13 effects were larger than the week-52 effect, which is the durable number.
cards.source: Ratner RE et al. Adjunctive therapy with the amylin analogue pramlintide leads to a combined improvement in glycemic and weight control in insulin-treated subjects with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes Technology & Therapeutics. 2002. PMID: 12017421. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme report — pooled near-target analysis (Hollander 2003): in the 166 patients entering with HbA1c 7.0–8.5%, pramlintide beat placebo by −0.43% HbA1c and −2.0 kg at week 26 (a pooled analysis of the two trials above, not an independent trial)
cards.summary: Programme report — pooled near-target analysis (Hollander 2003): in the 166 patients entering with HbA1c 7.0–8.5%, pramlintide beat placebo by −0.43% HbA1c and −2.0 kg at week 26 (a pooled analysis of the two trials above, not an independent trial)
cards.type: Programme report: pooled post-hoc analysis of the two 52-week trials carded above (same trials — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 166 patients from the two 52-week trials carded above whose entry HbA1c was 7.0–8.5% (86 on pramlintide 120 µg twice daily + insulin, baseline HbA1c 8.0%, weight 92.5 kg; 80 on placebo + insulin, baseline HbA1c 8.0%, weight 87.3 kg), in a pooled post-hoc analysis.
cards.result: At week 26, pramlintide reduced HbA1c by −0.43% and weight by −2.0 kg relative to placebo (both P < 0.001, placebo-corrected differences). Severe hypoglycaemia rates were 0.13 events per patient-year on pramlintide vs 0.19 on placebo — no increase in the near-target subset.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc subset of the same two trials: it answers whether the effect persists nearer target, not whether a third trial agrees. Counted as a programme report, never as independent evidence.
cards.source: Hollander P et al. Addition of pramlintide to insulin therapy lowers HbA1c in conjunction with weight loss in patients with type 2 diabetes approaching glycaemic targets. cards.headline: Programme report — pooled weight analysis (Hollander 2004): in 498 overweight/obese participants from the same two trials, placebo-corrected changes at week 26 were −0.41% HbA1c and −1.8 kg weight (not an independent trial)
cards.summary: Programme report — pooled weight analysis (Hollander 2004): in 498 overweight/obese participants from the same two trials, placebo-corrected changes at week 26 were −0.41% HbA1c and −1.8 kg weight (not an independent trial)
cards.type: Programme report: pooled post-hoc weight analysis of the two 52-week trials carded above (same trials — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 498 overweight or obese participants (BMI >25 kg/m²) from the two 52-week trials carded above: 254 on pramlintide 120 µg twice daily (baseline HbA1c 9.2%, weight 96.1 kg) and 244 on placebo (baseline HbA1c 9.4%, weight 95.0 kg), in a pooled post-hoc analysis.
cards.result: At week 26, placebo-corrected reductions were −0.41% for HbA1c and −1.8 kg for weight (both P < 0.0001). A ≥5% weight loss occurred in 9% on pramlintide vs 3% on placebo (P = 0.0005). The largest placebo-corrected weight reductions were in patients with BMI >40 kg/m² (−3.2 kg) and in those also taking metformin (−2.5 kg), both P < 0.001.
cards.watchOut: Same patients as the two trial cards: the ≥5% weight-loss figure (9% vs 3%) also shows most patients did not lose that much. Pooled post-hoc analyses support, and cannot extend, the two trials.
cards.source: Hollander P et al. Effect of pramlintide on weight in overweight and obese insulin-treated type 2 diabetes patients. Obesity Research. 2004. PMID: 15090634. shelves.title: Benfluorex (withdrawn): valvular regurgitation 27% vs 11% in its own REGULATE trial (OR 2.97, relative) leads — HbA1c fell ~1% vs placebo
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does the anorectic/insulin-sensitising agent benfluorex (Mediator), compared with placebo, metformin, sulfonylurea alone or pioglitazone, improve glycaemic control — and what valvular harm did its own randomised echocardiography trial show?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the withdrawal harm leads the balance. Benfluorex, a fenfluramine derivative marketed in France for decades, was withdrawn in 2009 over valvular heart disease, and its own randomised echocardiography trial (REGULATE, 846 randomised vs pioglitazone) documented emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% on benfluorex vs 11% on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.63 — a relative measure; absolutes 27% vs 11%), while glycaemic non-inferiority was not confirmed. The glycaemic effects were real but surrogate-only: HbA1c −1.01% vs placebo as sulfonylurea add-on and −0.86% endpoint difference vs placebo as monotherapy (+0.28% vs metformin). No card on this shelf presents the glycaemic wins without the valvular harm.

cards.headline: REGULATE echocardiography trial (Derumeaux 2012): emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% on benfluorex vs 11% on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.63 — a relative measure; absolutes 27% vs 11%) — and glycaemic non-inferiority was NOT confirmed (P = 0.19)
cards.summary: REGULATE echocardiography trial (Derumeaux 2012): emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% on benfluorex vs 11% on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.63 — a relative measure; absolutes 27% vs 11%) — and glycaemic non-inferiority was NOT confirmed (P = 0.19)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial vs pioglitazone with blinded echocardiography (REGULATE), 1 year
cards.people: 846 patients with type 2 diabetes uncontrolled on sulfonylurea randomised (423 vs 423) to benfluorex 150–450 mg/day or pioglitazone 30–45 mg/day for 1 year in a double-blind non-inferiority trial with blinded echocardiographic safety assessment; 615 patients (310 vs 305) had assessable paired echocardiography.
cards.result: HbA1c fell to 7.77% on benfluorex vs 7.45% on pioglitazone; the last HbA1c was significantly lower on pioglitazone (P < 0.001) and non-inferiority of benfluorex was not confirmed (P = 0.19). Emergent valvular regurgitation (new or worsened by ≥1 grade) occurred in 82 patients (27%) on benfluorex vs 33 (11%) on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.63) — an odds ratio is a relative measure; the absolute rates are 27% vs 11%. Emergent morphological valvular abnormalities occurred in 8 vs 4 patients (OR 1.99, 95% CI 0.59 to 6.69). Regurgitations were mainly grade 1; there was no moderate or severe regurgitation. At baseline, 51% already had at least one morphological and 84% at least one functional valvular abnormality. The authors conclude the results provide evidence for the valvular toxicity of benfluorex.
cards.watchOut: This card leads the shelf by design: it is the randomised, blinded-echocardiography documentation of the harm that withdrew the drug. Most emergent regurgitation was grade 1, printed as published — the signal is incidence of new/worsened regurgitation, not severe valve disease within the trial year.
cards.source: Derumeaux G et al. Echocardiographic evidence for valvular toxicity of benfluorex: a double-blind randomised trial in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. PloS one. 2012. PMID: 22723853. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Add-on to sulfonylurea (Moulin 2006): HbA1c fell from 8.34% to 7.52% on benfluorex vs a rise to 8.52% on placebo — adjusted difference −1.01% (95% CI −1.26 to −0.76, P < 0.001); target HbA1c ≤7% in 34% vs 12%
cards.summary: Add-on to sulfonylurea (Moulin 2006): HbA1c fell from 8.34% to 7.52% on benfluorex vs a rise to 8.52% on placebo — adjusted difference −1.01% (95% CI −1.26 to −0.76, P < 0.001); target HbA1c ≤7% in 34% vs 12%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, benfluorex add-on to sulfonylurea, 18 weeks
cards.people: 325 patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7–10%) on maximal sulfonylurea with a contraindication to, or poor tolerance of, metformin, randomised double-blind to benfluorex 450 mg/day (n = 165) or placebo (n = 160) for 18 weeks.
cards.result: HbA1c decreased on benfluorex from 8.34% to 7.52% (P < 0.001) and tended to increase on placebo from 8.33% to 8.52%, a mean adjusted between-group difference of −1.01% (95% CI −1.26 to −0.76; P < 0.001). The target HbA1c (≤7%) was achieved by 34% on benfluorex vs 12% on placebo. Fasting plasma glucose differed by −1.65 mmol/L (≈ −30 mg/dL) in favour of benfluorex (P < 0.001), and insulin resistance (HOMA) also favoured benfluorex. Overall tolerance was similar, though serious adverse events were more frequent in the benfluorex group without evidence of a causal relationship, as published.
cards.watchOut: A real glycaemic effect on a surrogate endpoint (HbA1c) over 18 weeks, in patients who could not take metformin — it does not offset the valvular harm carded above, and no outcomes (event) endpoint was measured.
cards.source: Moulin P et al. Efficacy of benfluorex in combination with sulfonylurea in type 2 diabetic patients: an 18-week, randomized, double-blind study. Diabetes care. 2006. PMID: 16505498. cards.headline: Monotherapy vs placebo and metformin (Del Prato 2003): HbA1c fell 0.60% on benfluorex vs a 0.50% rise on placebo (endpoint difference −0.86%, P < 0.001); vs metformin the difference was +0.28% (90% CI 0.07 to 0.48), meeting the trial's non-inferiority test (P = 0.037)
cards.summary: Monotherapy vs placebo and metformin (Del Prato 2003): HbA1c fell 0.60% on benfluorex vs a 0.50% rise on placebo (endpoint difference −0.86%, P < 0.001); vs metformin the difference was +0.28% (90% CI 0.07 to 0.48), meeting the trial's non-inferiority test (P = 0.037)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, benfluorex vs placebo and vs metformin, 6 months
cards.people: 722 diet-failed patients with type 2 diabetes randomised after a 2-month strict-diet run-in to placebo (n = 144), benfluorex 150–450 mg/day (n = 294) or metformin 850–2550 mg/day (n = 284), double-blind for 6 months after a 5-week dose-finding phase; baseline HbA1c 7.4% (placebo), 7.7% (benfluorex) and 7.8% (metformin).
cards.result: At end of treatment HbA1c had decreased by 0.60% on benfluorex and increased by 0.50% on placebo (intention-to-treat), a mean endpoint difference of −0.86% (SE 0.17%; P < 0.001). The endpoint difference vs metformin was +0.28% (SE 0.12%; 90% CI 0.07 to 0.48), and the non-inferiority test (equivalence limit 0.5%) was significant at P = 0.037 — the authors describe benfluorex as of relatively lower potency than metformin. Baseline fasting glucose was 9.7 mmol/L (≈ 175 mg/dL) on placebo, 10.0 mmol/L (≈ 180 mg/dL) on benfluorex and 10.2 mmol/L (≈ 184 mg/dL) on metformin. Emergent adverse events were reported by 39% on benfluorex, 38% on placebo and 43% on metformin.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to metformin was declared against a generous 0.5% margin while the point estimate favoured metformin (+0.28%) — read the margin, not just the P value; again HbA1c is a surrogate, and valvular outcomes were not assessed in this trial.
cards.source: Del Prato S et al. Six-month efficacy of benfluorex vs. placebo or metformin in diet-failed type 2 diabetic patients. Acta diabetologica. 2003. PMID: 12682825. cards.headline: Insulin-treated obese patients (Leutenegger 1998): daily insulin dose fell 8.7 IU on benfluorex vs 2.7 IU on placebo (P = 0.032) and HbA1c fell −0.73% vs +0.01% over 3 months — on a background of higher baseline insulin dose and HbA1c in the benfluorex arm
cards.summary: Insulin-treated obese patients (Leutenegger 1998): daily insulin dose fell 8.7 IU on benfluorex vs 2.7 IU on placebo (P = 0.032) and HbA1c fell −0.73% vs +0.01% over 3 months — on a background of higher baseline insulin dose and HbA1c in the benfluorex arm
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in insulin-treated obese type 2 diabetes, 3 months
cards.people: 76 obese insulin-requiring patients with type 2 diabetes (benfluorex n = 37, placebo n = 39) on insulin ≥0.5 IU/kg and a low-calorie diet, double-blind for 3 months after a 1-month run-in. At inclusion the benfluorex arm had higher daily insulin dose (59.9 vs 50.4 IU; P = 0.012) and higher HbA1c (7.72% vs 6.96%; P = 0.025) — a baseline imbalance printed here as the abstract prints it.
cards.result: The decrease in daily insulin dose was greater on benfluorex (8.7 ± 10.1 vs 2.7 ± 8.1 IU; P = 0.032), HbA1c fell −0.73% on benfluorex (P = 0.026) vs +0.01% on placebo, and body weight fell more on benfluorex (1.77 vs 0.21 kg; P = 0.013). Fasting blood glucose tended to fall more on benfluorex (−1.43 mmol/L (≈ −26 mg/dL) vs +0.42 mmol/L (≈ +8 mg/dL)). Adverse events were reported in 11 benfluorex vs 5 placebo patients (not significant).
cards.watchOut: The smallest and oldest trial (N = 76), with a baseline imbalance favouring more room to improve in the benfluorex arm — supportive only; the shelf's glycaemic estimate rests on the two larger placebo-controlled trials above.
cards.source: Leutenegger M et al. Added benfluorex in obese insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes. Diabetes & metabolism. 1998. PMID: 9534010. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the harm leads — benfluorex lowered HbA1c by ~0.9–1.0% vs placebo, but its own randomised echocardiography trial found emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% vs 11% (OR 2.97, relative), and the drug was withdrawn in 2009 over valvular heart disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: the harm leads — benfluorex lowered HbA1c by ~0.9–1.0% vs placebo, but its own randomised echocardiography trial found emergent valvular regurgitation in 27% vs 11% (OR 2.97, relative), and the drug was withdrawn in 2009 over valvular heart disease
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Benfluorex — a fenfluramine derivative marketed in France for decades as an appetite suppressant / diabetes adjunct — was withdrawn in 2009 over valvular heart disease, and REGULATE (846 randomised, blinded echocardiography) is the trial-level documentation of that harm: emergent regurgitation 27% vs 11% on pioglitazone (OR 2.97, 95% CI 1.91 to 4.63, a relative measure), with glycaemic non-inferiority not confirmed (HbA1c 7.77% vs 7.45%). The glycaemic wins were real but surrogate-only: −1.01% HbA1c vs placebo as sulfonylurea add-on (325 randomised, 18 weeks), −0.86% endpoint difference vs placebo as monotherapy with a +0.28% difference vs metformin (722 randomised, 6 months), and insulin-dose sparing in 76 insulin-treated obese patients. HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint and the trials predate modern background therapy. This shelf exists so the library records both halves of the benfluorex record — efficacy and the valvular harm that ended it — with the harm first.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: no glycaemic figure on this shelf may be quoted without the REGULATE regurgitation result (27% vs 11%) beside it.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Anakinra in type 2 diabetes (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70): HbA1c −0.46 points at 13 weeks in the sole Larsen trial; secretion gain not maintained after withdrawal
shelves.question: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra, compared with placebo, improve glycaemia and beta-cell function? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70 (the Larsen trial and its withdrawal follow-up).
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose · Body Mass Index · C-Reactive Protein · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gene Expression Regulation · Glucose Tolerance Test · Glucose Transporter Type 4 · Glycated Hemoglobin · Heat-Shock Proteins · Humans · Insulin Resistance · Insulin-Secreting Cells · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein · Interleukin-6 · Male · Middle Aged · Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Gamma Coactivator 1-alpha · RNA, Messenger · Receptors, Interleukin-1 · Recombinant Proteins · Transcription Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70, printed on the face. The entire base is the single Larsen trial: 70 patients randomised (34 anakinra 100 mg/day, 36 placebo) for 13 weeks, in which glycated haemoglobin was 0.46 percentage points lower on anakinra (P = 0.03), C-peptide secretion was enhanced (P = 0.05), the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio fell (P = 0.005), and interleukin-6 (P < 0.001) and C-reactive protein (P = 0.002) fell, with no difference in insulin resistance, body-mass index or adipokines and no drug-related serious adverse events. The second report is a follow-up OF THE SAME TRIAL, not an independent trial: 39 weeks after treatment withdrawal, the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio and the inflammatory-marker reductions were maintained, but stimulated C-peptide was NOT maintained except in a genetically defined low-baseline-IL-1Ra subgroup. A mechanistic muscle gene-expression substudy of the same trial is carded labelled as a programme report and is not counted. The HbA1c effect is modest, the trial predates modern background therapy, and no second trial of anakinra for glycaemia in type 2 diabetes has ever published. The canakinumab shelves (live #2020; pack #2021) are a different agent and question and are not re-carded.

cards.headline: Larsen RCT (2007): the shelf's only trial — in 70 patients, anakinra lowered glycated haemoglobin by 0.46 percentage points versus placebo over 13 weeks (P = 0.03) and improved beta-cell secretory measures
cards.summary: Larsen RCT (2007): the shelf's only trial — in 70 patients, anakinra lowered glycated haemoglobin by 0.46 percentage points versus placebo over 13 weeks (P = 0.03) and improved beta-cell secretory measures
cards.type: Randomised double-blind parallel-group trial (the Larsen trial), anakinra vs placebo — the only trial on this shelf
cards.people: 70 patients with type 2 diabetes randomised double-blind (34 to anakinra 100 mg subcutaneously once daily, 36 to placebo) for 13 weeks; all underwent oral glucose-tolerance testing with intravenous glucose, glucagon and arginine challenges at baseline and 13 weeks, and 35 underwent hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp studies.
cards.result: At 13 weeks the glycated haemoglobin level was 0.46 percentage point lower in the anakinra group than in the placebo group (P = 0.03). C-peptide secretion was enhanced (P = 0.05), the ratio of proinsulin to insulin fell (P = 0.005), and interleukin-6 (P < 0.001) and C-reactive protein (P = 0.002) levels fell. Insulin resistance, insulin-regulated gene expression in skeletal muscle, serum adipokine levels and body-mass index were similar between groups. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia was not observed and there were no apparent drug-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: One 70-patient, 13-week trial from 2007 is the entire randomised base: a modest 0.46-point HbA1c difference on the background therapy of its era, with no replication in the nearly two decades since.
cards.source: Larsen CM et al. Interleukin-1-receptor antagonist in type 2 diabetes mellitus. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17429083. Registry ID: NCT00303394. cards.summary: Withdrawal follow-up (Larsen 2009): a follow-up report of the same trial, not an independent trial — 39 weeks after stopping anakinra, the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio and inflammatory-marker gains persisted, but the C-peptide secretion gain did NOT
cards.type: Programme report: double-blind withdrawal follow-up of the Larsen randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 67 of the 70 patients from the Larsen trial who completed 13 weeks of anakinra or placebo, followed double-blind for 39 weeks after treatment withdrawal; participants had HbA1c over 7.5% and BMI over 27 kg/m² at trial entry.
cards.result: Thirty-nine weeks after anakinra withdrawal, the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio remained improved versus placebo (by −0.07, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.02, P = 0.011), and reductions in C-reactive protein (−3.2 mg/L, P = 0.014) and interleukin-6 (−1.4 ng/L, P = 0.036) were maintained to the end of the study. Stimulated C-peptide, however, was not maintained — except in a subgroup characterised by genetically determined low baseline interleukin-1-receptor-antagonist levels, who kept the improvement gained during treatment.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of the same 70-patient trial adds durability information only; it is not confirmation by a second study, and its own headline is mixed — the beta-cell secretion gain did not persist off treatment outside a genetically defined subgroup.
cards.source: Larsen CM et al. Sustained effects of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist treatment in type 2 diabetes. Diabetes care. 2009. PMID: 19542207. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme report — muscle gene expression (Berchtold 2009): a mechanistic substudy of the Larsen trial, labelled as such — anakinra did not significantly alter skeletal-muscle gene expression (microarray limb n = 5, below the reference floor and printed as such)

cards.type: Programme report: mechanistic muscle-biopsy substudy of the Larsen trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence, not counted)
cards.people: Patients from the Larsen trial: muscle biopsies (vastus lateralis) from 5 obese patients (BMI over 27 kg/m²) before and after 13 weeks of anakinra for microarray profiling, with candidate-gene quantification by qRT-PCR in 12 placebo-treated and 11 anakinra-treated patients.
cards.result: No significantly altered gene-expression levels could be demonstrated after false-discovery-rate correction; concordance among the four analysis algorithms was low, protein-network analysis revealed no altered networks or pathways, and none of the candidate genes (including COL1A1, CDKN1C, HSP70, HLA-A, IL-1 and IL-6) was significantly altered by qRT-PCR. The authors conclude that interleukin-1-receptor antagonism did not significantly affect skeletal-muscle gene expression in this limited, selected sample.
cards.watchOut: The microarray limb rests on 5 patients — below the library's reference floor (N < 10), printed on the face of this card, and never load-bearing; this card is carded only to complete the one-trial programme record and carries no glycaemic-efficacy weight.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70: a single 13-week trial showed a modest HbA1c benefit (−0.46 points) with improved beta-cell and inflammatory measures; off treatment, the secretion gain did not persist
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 reports, 1 trial, N = 70: a single 13-week trial showed a modest HbA1c benefit (−0.46 points) with improved beta-cell and inflammatory measures; off treatment, the secretion gain did not persist
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Anakinra 100 mg/day for 13 weeks lowered glycated haemoglobin by 0.46 percentage points versus placebo (P = 0.03), enhanced C-peptide secretion, reduced the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio and lowered interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein, without drug-related serious adverse events. Thirty-nine weeks after withdrawal, the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio and inflammatory-marker reductions remained, but stimulated C-peptide did not (outside a genetically defined subgroup), and a mechanistic substudy found no significant skeletal-muscle gene-expression effect. No second trial of anakinra for glycaemia in type 2 diabetes exists: this is a landmark proof-of-concept trial for inflammation-targeted diabetes therapy, and its evidence base is exactly one trial.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Lacosamide for painful diabetic neuropathy: SPLIT — two of three phase 3 trials met their primary at 400 mg/day (responder 58% vs 46% in one), the third missed it, and 23–40% stopped the effective doses for adverse events
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does oral lacosamide (200–600 mg/day), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?
shelves.mesh: Acetamides/administration & dosage · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics/administration & dosage · Comorbidity · Diabetic Neuropathies/drug therapy,epidemiology · Dopamine Uptake Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology · Female · Fibromyalgia/diagnosis,drug therapy,epidemiology · Humans · Incidence · Lacosamide · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement/drug effects · Placebo Effect · Treatment Outcome · United States/epidemiology · Acetamides/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diabetic Neuropathies/drug therapy,physiopathology · Pain/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Statistics, Nonparametric · Time Factors · Diabetic Neuropathies/drug therapy
shelves.balance: PARTIAL slice only — the home, pack #2351, was read in full: it is the adjunctive-epilepsy shelf (partial-onset seizures; Ben-Menachem 2007 and Chung 2010) and contains zero mention of diabetes or neuropathy, so the epilepsy question stays homed there under the one-home rule and only this diabetic-neuropathy slice is carded here. This is a failed programme with SPLIT primaries, and the split leads: of three 18-week phase 3 trials, the fixed-dose trial met its primary at 400 mg/day (responders with ≥2-point or 30% pain reduction 58% vs 46% on placebo — a 12-percentage-point contrast) and the flexible-titration trial met it at exactly P = 0.05, while the slow/standard-titration trial did NOT meet its primary (400 mg/day P = 0.12; 600 mg/day P = 0.18). The 200 mg/day dose never separated significantly, and 600 mg/day was significant only in observed cases in one trial. The dose that works is also the dose at which nearly a quarter of patients stopped for adverse events (23% at 400 mg/day and 40% at 600 mg/day vs 9% on placebo; dizziness, nausea, tremor). Pain scores are symptom surrogates. Lacosamide was never approved for diabetic neuropathic pain. The three trials are not pooled into a single clean win on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Fixed-dose phase 3 trial (Wymer 2009): the 400 mg/day group MET the primary endpoint (Likert pain change over the last 4 weeks of maintenance); responders 58% on 400 mg/day vs 46% on placebo; 200 mg/day not significant on any measure, and 600 mg/day significant only in observed cases, not intention-to-treat
cards.summary: Fixed-dose phase 3 trial (Wymer 2009): the 400 mg/day group MET the primary endpoint (Likert pain change over the last 4 weeks of maintenance); responders 58% on 400 mg/day vs 46% on placebo; 200 mg/day not significant on any measure, and 600 mg/day significant only in observed cases, not intention-to-treat
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled fixed-dose randomised trial, lacosamide vs placebo in painful diabetic neuropathy
cards.people: Adults with painful diabetic neuropathy in a multicentre double-blind trial: 2-week run-in, 6-week titration, 12-week maintenance, randomised to placebo or fixed-dose lacosamide 200, 400 or 600 mg/day with no back-titration. The abstract prints no randomised N, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: The lacosamide 400 mg/day group showed statistically significant improvement in Likert pain score over placebo on the primary measure. At end of treatment, 58% of the 400 mg/day group achieved at least a 2-point or 30% reduction in Likert pain score, compared with 46% on placebo. The 200 mg/day group separated numerically but was not significant for any primary or secondary measure; the 600 mg/day group was significant in observed cases but not in the intention-to-treat population, probably because of a high premature-withdrawal rate for adverse events during titration. Discontinuation for adverse events: 8% (200 mg), 23% (400 mg) and 40% (600 mg) vs 9% on placebo. The most common adverse events were dizziness, nausea, tremor, headache and fatigue; somnolence, cognitive/behavioural effects, weight change and oedema were notably low. The authors judged 400 mg/day the optimal balance of efficacy and side effects.
cards.watchOut: The responder contrast at the best dose is 12 percentage points (58% vs 46%), and the 400 mg/day dose that met the primary is the dose at which 23% stopped for adverse events — efficacy and tolerability cannot be quoted separately.
cards.source: Wymer JP et al. Efficacy and safety of lacosamide in diabetic neuropathic pain: an 18-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial of fixed-dose regimens. The Clinical journal of pain. 2009. PMID: 19454870. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Flexible-titration phase 3 trial (Shaibani 2009): endpoint pain reduction reached significance at 400 mg/day at exactly P = 0.05, and over the whole treatment period at 400 mg/day (P = 0.02) and 600 mg/day (P = 0.03)
cards.summary: Flexible-titration phase 3 trial (Shaibani 2009): endpoint pain reduction reached significance at 400 mg/day at exactly P = 0.05, and over the whole treatment period at 400 mg/day (P = 0.02) and 600 mg/day (P = 0.03)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (flexible titration), lacosamide vs placebo in painful diabetic neuropathy
cards.people: Patients with painful diabetic neuropathy in an 18-week double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of oral lacosamide 200, 400 and 600 mg/day, with 400 mg/day the primary target dose to be confirmed; the primary endpoint was change in pain score over the last 4 weeks of the 12-week maintenance period. The abstract prints no randomised N, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: Endpoint reductions in mean pain score were higher with all lacosamide doses, reaching significance at 400 mg/day (P = 0.05). Over the whole treatment period (titration plus maintenance), pain relief was significantly greater than placebo at 400 mg/day (P = 0.02) and 600 mg/day (P = 0.03), with an early-onset effect during titration. Non-parametric and mixed-model analyses gave similar results. Patient's Global Impression of Change, responder rates and pain-free days provided additional support. Adverse events included dizziness, nausea and headache; cognitive and behavioural adverse events were low.
cards.watchOut: A primary met at exactly P = 0.05 is a borderline met, and it prints as such; this trial's whole-period and titration-period significances are secondary time windows, not a second primary.
cards.source: Shaibani A et al. Lacosamide in painful diabetic neuropathy: an 18-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial. The journal of pain. 2009. PMID: 19409861. cards.headline: Slow/standard-titration trial (Ziegler 2010): the primary endpoint was NOT met — last-4-weeks Numeric Pain Rating Scale change, 400 mg/day P = 0.12 and 600 mg/day P = 0.18 vs placebo — although titration, maintenance and whole-period analyses were significant (P = 0.005–0.03)
cards.summary: Slow/standard-titration trial (Ziegler 2010): the primary endpoint was NOT met — last-4-weeks Numeric Pain Rating Scale change, 400 mg/day P = 0.12 and 600 mg/day P = 0.18 vs placebo — although titration, maintenance and whole-period analyses were significant (P = 0.005–0.03)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (slow vs standard titration), lacosamide vs placebo in painful diabetic polyneuropathy — primary endpoint not met
cards.people: Diabetic patients with at least moderate neuropathic pain, randomised to placebo or lacosamide 400 mg/day (slow or standard titration) or 600 mg/day, over 6-week titration and 12-week maintenance periods. The abstract prints no randomised N, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: For the primary endpoint, pain reduction was numerically but not statistically greater with lacosamide than placebo (400 mg/day P = 0.12; 600 mg/day P = 0.18). Both doses were significantly more effective than placebo over the titration (P = 0.03 and P = 0.006), maintenance (P = 0.01 and P = 0.005) and entire treatment periods (P = 0.03 and P = 0.02). Safety profiles were similar between titration schemes. The authors state the primary criterion was not met possibly because of an increased placebo response over the last 4 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The miss is the card's headline, not a footnote: significant secondary time-window analyses do not convert a missed primary into a met one, and the late-placebo-response explanation is the authors' attribution, printed as such.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: PARTIAL slice vs pack #2351 (the adjunctive-epilepsy home, read in full — it asks the seizure question and mentions neither diabetes nor neuropathy). Three phase 3 trials of lacosamide in painful diabetic neuropathy, primaries SPLIT: the fixed-dose trial met its primary at 400 mg/day with a 58% vs 46% responder contrast (Wymer 2009); the flexible-titration trial met it at exactly P = 0.05 (Shaibani 2009); the slow/standard-titration trial missed it at both doses (P = 0.12 and P = 0.18) despite significant secondary windows (Ziegler 2010). No trial prints its randomised N in its abstract, and none is claimed here. The Cochrane review of lacosamide for neuropathic pain is programme support only and is not counted in this base. SPLIT: a real but borderline and dose-toxic pain signal — 23% adverse-event discontinuation at 400 mg/day and 40% at 600 mg/day vs 9% on placebo — in a programme never approved for this indication.
cards.watchOut: Do not pool the three trials into a single win, and do not carry the epilepsy shelf's LIKELY stamp across: the same drug at the same dose has a different, split record in diabetic neuropathic pain.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Ranirestat for diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy: conduction-only benefit — sub-1 m/s nerve-conduction differences across 1,906 randomised patients, with clinical scores (mTCNS) and sensory testing null in every trial
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor ranirestat (AS-3201), compared with placebo, slow nerve-conduction deterioration or improve symptoms and signs?
