shelves.balance: Electrophysiology-only benefit — the flag leads. Across three placebo-controlled trials totalling 1,906 randomised patients, ranirestat's consistent finding is a sub-1 m/s nerve-conduction difference: the dose-ranging trial's summed SENSORY conduction primary did not differ significantly (change 2.0 m/s placebo vs 3.2–3.8 m/s ranirestat), with summed motor conduction improved at 20 mg/day; the global 24-month trial missed its own prespecified clinically-meaningful goal (peroneal motor NCV changes +0.49 placebo vs +0.95 and +0.90 m/s, not significant; the +0.44 m/s combined-dose figure is POST-HOC, labelled as such wherever used); and the Japanese phase 3 trial found a +0.52 m/s tibial motor difference (P = 0.021). Against that, the modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score and quantitative sensory testing did NOT differ in any trial — no benefit on symptoms, signs or quality of life anywhere. Nerve conduction velocity is a surrogate endpoint. Ranirestat was never marketed. Every conduction number on this shelf prints beside the clinical-score nulls. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE — for nerve-conduction velocity only.

cards.headline: Dose-ranging trial (Bril 2009): summed SENSORY nerve conduction velocity — the primary reading — did NOT differ significantly (change 2.0 m/s placebo vs 3.2–3.8 m/s ranirestat); summed motor NCV improved at 20 mg/day, but the modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score and quantitative sensory testing did not differ among groups at any point
cards.summary: Dose-ranging trial (Bril 2009): summed SENSORY nerve conduction velocity — the primary reading — did NOT differ significantly (change 2.0 m/s placebo vs 3.2–3.8 m/s ranirestat); summed motor NCV improved at 20 mg/day, but the modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score and quantitative sensory testing did not differ among groups at any point
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging randomised trial, ranirestat 10/20/40 mg/day vs placebo for 52 weeks
cards.people: 549 patients with diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy randomised to placebo or ranirestat 10, 20 or 40 mg/day for 52 weeks in a multicentre double-blind study; efficacy by nerve conduction studies, the modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score (mTCNS) and quantitative sensory tests (QST).
cards.result: At week 52 the summed sensory (bilateral sural plus proximal median sensory) NCV did not show significant changes from baseline (2.0 m/s for placebo compared with 3.2–3.8 m/s for ranirestat). Significant improvement in summed motor (peroneal, tibial and median) NCV was observed with 20 and 40 mg/day at week 12 and at weeks 24 and 36, and in peroneal motor NCV at weeks 36 and 52, for the 20 mg/day group (P ≤ 0.05 as published). The mTCNS and QST results did not differ among the groups during the study. Ranirestat was well tolerated, with no pertinent differences in drug-related adverse events or laboratory, vital-sign or ECG effects.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own summary is the honest one: an effect on motor nerve function, with the sensory primary not significant and no clinical-score or sensory-testing benefit — a surrogate-only result.
cards.source: Bril V et al. Ranirestat for the management of diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Diabetes care. 2009. PMID: 19366965. Registry ID: NCT00101426. cards.headline: Global phase 2/3 trial (Polydefkis 2015): the prespecified goal was NOT achieved — 24-month peroneal motor NCV changes +0.49 (placebo), +0.95 and +0.90 m/s, not significant against the ≥1.2 m/s goal; the +0.44 m/s combined-dose difference (P = 0.0237) is POST-HOC; no secondary or exploratory endpoint differed
cards.summary: Global phase 2/3 trial (Polydefkis 2015): the prespecified goal was NOT achieved — 24-month peroneal motor NCV changes +0.49 (placebo), +0.95 and +0.90 m/s, not significant against the ≥1.2 m/s goal; the +0.44 m/s combined-dose difference (P = 0.0237) is POST-HOC; no secondary or exploratory endpoint differed
cards.type: Global double-blind phase 2/3 randomised trial, ranirestat 40/80 mg/day vs placebo for 24 months — primary goal not achieved
cards.people: 800 patients (265 placebo / 264 ranirestat 40 mg/day / 271 ranirestat 80 mg/day) aged 18–75 with stable type 1 or 2 diabetes and mild-to-moderate diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy, treated for 24 months in a global double-blind trial; 633 completed. Primary endpoint: change in peroneal motor NCV, with a prespecified goal of ≥1.2 m/s improvement vs placebo.
cards.result: The peroneal motor NCV difference from placebo was significant at 6, 12 and 18 months in both ranirestat groups but was under 1.2 m/s; at 24 months mean improvement from baseline was +0.49, +0.95 and +0.90 m/s for placebo, 40 mg and 80 mg respectively (not significant). The treatment difference reached significance only when the ranirestat groups were combined in a post-hoc analysis (+0.44 m/s; P = 0.0237) — labelled post-hoc wherever it is used. There was no effect of ranirestat on safety assessments, secondary or exploratory endpoints vs placebo. The authors note the placebo group did not worsen, underscoring the difficulty of polyneuropathy trials in well-controlled diabetes.
cards.watchOut: The largest and longest trial is the weakest result: it missed its own definition of a meaningful conduction effect, and its only significant 24-month figure is post-hoc. Never quote the +0.44 m/s figure without the post-hoc label.
cards.source: Polydefkis M et al. Safety and efficacy of ranirestat in patients with mild-to-moderate diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Journal of the peripheral nervous system : JPNS. 2015. PMID: 26313450. Registry ID: NCT00927914. cards.headline: Japanese phase 3 trial (Sekiguchi 2019): tibial motor NCV differed by +0.52 m/s (P = 0.021) in ranirestat's favour, with concordant small gains in median motor and sensory nerves — but the co-primary modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score showed NO significant difference
cards.summary: Japanese phase 3 trial (Sekiguchi 2019): tibial motor NCV differed by +0.52 m/s (P = 0.021) in ranirestat's favour, with concordant small gains in median motor and sensory nerves — but the co-primary modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score showed NO significant difference
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (Japan), ranirestat 40 mg/day vs placebo for 52 weeks
cards.people: 557 patients with diabetic polyneuropathy randomised to ranirestat 40 mg/day or placebo for 52 weeks in a multicentre, placebo-controlled, double-blind parallel-group phase 3 study in Japan. Co-primary endpoints: change in tibial motor nerve conduction velocity and total modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score.
cards.result: There was a significant increase in tibial motor NCV in the ranirestat group compared with placebo; the between-group difference in change at last observation was 0.52 m/s (P = 0.021). Increases in NCV were also found in the median motor nerves, proximal median sensory nerves and distal median sensory nerves. No significant differences in modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score or safety parameters were found between the groups. The authors conclude ranirestat was well tolerated and improved NCV, with no detectable benefit over placebo on symptoms and signs during the 52 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A statistically significant +0.52 m/s conduction difference is about half the 1.2 m/s the programme itself prespecified as meaningful in its global trial — significance is not the same as clinical importance, and the co-primary clinical score was null.
cards.source: Sekiguchi K et al. Aldose reductase inhibitor ranirestat significantly improves nerve conduction velocity in diabetic polyneuropathy: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study in Japan. Journal of diabetes investigation. 2019. PMID: 29975462. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: Three placebo-controlled trials, 1,906 randomised patients (549 + 800 + 557), one pattern: ranirestat moves nerve conduction by less than 1 m/s and moves nothing a patient can feel. The dose-ranging trial's sensory primary was not significant while motor conduction improved at 20 mg/day (Bril 2009); the 24-month global trial missed its prespecified ≥1.2 m/s goal (+0.49 vs +0.95 / +0.90 m/s, not significant; +0.44 m/s only post-hoc) with no secondary or exploratory endpoint differing (Polydefkis 2015); the Japanese phase 3 trial found +0.52 m/s on tibial motor conduction (P = 0.021) with its co-primary clinical score null (Sekiguchi 2019). The 2022 meta-analysis of this programme is support only and is not counted. POSSIBLE — for nerve-conduction velocity only; there is no demonstrated benefit on symptoms, signs or quality of life in any trial, and the agent was never marketed.
cards.watchOut: Conduction velocity is a surrogate: a shelf that quoted the conduction gains without the three clinical-score nulls would misstate this programme. Its class sibling epalrestat (shelf #7699) rests on a weaker, open-label base and is not interchangeable evidence.

shelves.title: Acetyl-L-carnitine for diabetic neuropathy: SPLIT — the two anchor papers DISAGREE on conduction (De Grandis 2002: significant gains, sural +7 vs +1.0 m/s; Sima 2005, 1,257 patients: conduction did NOT improve), with biopsy regeneration and vibration gains and pain better in one of two large trials
shelves.question: In adults with chronic diabetic neuropathy, does acetyl-L-carnitine (500–1,000 mg three times daily), compared with placebo, improve pain, nerve fibre regeneration and vibration perception?

shelves.balance: Three trials reported in two papers — labelled as such — and the anchor papers are DISCORDANT on conduction, which is printed on the face, not smoothed over. The 2002 De Grandis trial (333 enrolled; 294 with impaired electrophysiology at baseline) reports significant nerve conduction velocity and amplitude gains vs placebo over 1 year (sensory sural +7 vs +1.0 m/s) and a 39% within-group fall in visual-analogue pain vs 8% on placebo. The much larger 2005 Sima analysis of two 52-week trials (1,257 intention-to-treat patients) reports the opposite on electrophysiology — conduction velocities and amplitudes did NOT improve — with its positive findings on sural nerve fibre numbers and regenerating clusters (biopsy morphometry, a surrogate), vibration perception (improved in both studies) and pain (significant in one of the two studies, and in the combined 1,000 mg three-times-daily cohort). Per the standing naming rule: the trials tested pharmaceutical-grade acetyl-L-carnitine (levacecarnine) at 1.5–3 g/day; current supplement products may differ in content and effect. Cross-point: in chemotherapy-induced neuropathy this agent WORSENED neuropathy (pack #2809) — a different population, stated here so the diabetic result is not read as a general neuropathy claim. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.

cards.headline: De Grandis 2002 long-term trial: among 294 patients with impaired electrophysiology at baseline, nerve conduction velocity and amplitude improved significantly vs placebo (P < 0.01) — sensory sural +7 vs +1.0 m/s at 12 months — and visual-analogue pain fell 39% from baseline on treatment vs 8% on placebo
cards.summary: De Grandis 2002 long-term trial: among 294 patients with impaired electrophysiology at baseline, nerve conduction velocity and amplitude improved significantly vs placebo (P < 0.01) — sensory sural +7 vs +1.0 m/s at 12 months — and visual-analogue pain fell 39% from baseline on treatment vs 8% on placebo
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (1 year), acetyl-L-carnitine vs placebo in diabetic neuropathy
cards.people: 333 patients meeting clinical and/or neurophysiological criteria for diabetic neuropathy, enrolled across 20 centres in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group study. Acetyl-L-carnitine (levacecarnine) was given intramuscularly 1,000 mg/day for 10 days, then orally 2,000 mg/day for the remaining 355 days (1 year in total).
cards.result: Among the 294 patients with impaired electrophysiological parameters at baseline, the treated group showed statistically significant improvement in mean NCV and amplitude vs placebo (P < 0.01). The greatest NCV changes at 12 months were in the sensory sural nerve (+7 m/s treated vs +1.0 m/s placebo), sensory ulnar nerve (+2.9 vs +0.1 m/s) and motor peroneal nerve (+2.7 vs −0.2 m/s); the greatest amplitude change was in the motor peroneal nerve (+2.2 vs +0.1 mV). After 12 months, mean visual-analogue pain scores were reduced from baseline by 39% in treated patients vs 8% in placebo recipients — within-group percentage falls as published, printed as such. Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: This is the SMALLER and older of the two anchor papers, and its conduction result is directly contradicted by the larger 2005 analysis carded next — neither paper may be quoted without the other. The 39% pain figure is a within-group fall from baseline, not a 39% advantage over placebo.
cards.source: De Grandis D et al. Acetyl-L-carnitine (levacecarnine) in the treatment of diabetic neuropathy. A long-term, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Drugs in R&D. 2002. PMID: 12455197. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sima 2005 — analysis of TWO 52-week trials in one paper (labelled): sural nerve fibre numbers and regenerating fibre clusters improved significantly and vibration perception improved in both studies — but nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes did NOT improve
cards.summary: Sima 2005 — analysis of TWO 52-week trials in one paper (labelled): sural nerve fibre numbers and regenerating fibre clusters improved significantly and vibration perception improved in both studies — but nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes did NOT improve
cards.type: Analysis of two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials reported in one paper (labelled as such) — structural, vibration and conduction outcomes
cards.people: Frozen databases from two 52-week randomised placebo-controlled trials of acetyl-L-carnitine 500 or 1,000 mg three times daily in chronic diabetic neuropathy, evaluated separately and combined; 1,257 intention-to-treat patients (93% of those enrolled). Endpoints: sural nerve morphometry, nerve conduction velocities, vibration perception thresholds, clinical symptom scores and a visual-analogue scale for the most bothersome symptom.
cards.result: Data showed significant improvements in sural nerve fibre numbers and regenerating nerve fibre clusters. Nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes did NOT improve — the direct discordance with De Grandis 2002, printed here on the face. Vibration perception improved in both studies. The regeneration findings rest on sural nerve biopsy morphometry, a surrogate endpoint.
cards.watchOut: One paper, two trials: this card and the next are two outcome slices of the SAME paper and must never be counted as separate reports. The conduction null in 1,257 patients outweighs, on size alone, the positive conduction result in the 294-patient electrophysiology subset of the 2002 trial.
cards.source: Sima AA et al. Acetyl-L-carnitine improves pain, nerve regeneration, and vibratory perception in patients with chronic diabetic neuropathy: an analysis of two randomized placebo-controlled trials. Diabetes care. 2005. PMID: 15616239. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three trials in two papers. De Grandis 2002 (333 enrolled) found significant conduction and amplitude gains and a 39% vs 8% within-group pain fall; Sima 2005 (two trials, 1,257 intention-to-treat patients) found NO conduction or amplitude improvement, with significant sural fibre regeneration on biopsy, vibration perception improved in both trials, and pain significantly better in one trial and in the combined 1,000 mg three-times-daily cohort. The discordance between the anchor papers on conduction is the shelf's central fact. The 1995 report located for this question (PMID 7744218) was fetched this session and its abstract is EMPTY, so it is refused as an anchor and counted only as support; the acetyl-L-carnitine + methylcobalamin combination trial is a different question and is not counted. SPLIT. Cross-points, not carded here: chemotherapy-induced neuropathy, where this agent worsened neuropathy (pack #2809), and hepatic encephalopathy (pack #6877). The trials tested pharmaceutical-grade levacecarnine at 1.5–3 g/day; current supplement products may differ in content and effect.
cards.watchOut: Never present the 2002 conduction gains without the 2005 conduction null from a base four times larger, and never present the biopsy regeneration finding as a patient-felt benefit — it is a morphometric surrogate.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Benfotiamine for diabetic polyneuropathy: SPLIT by duration — a 40-patient 3-week pilot and a 6-week trial (primary significant only per-protocol) are positive-short, while the only 12-month trial (BOND, structural primary) is null across essentially every measure
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic polyneuropathy, does benfotiamine (a lipid-soluble thiamine prodrug), compared with placebo, improve neuropathy symptoms — and what did the 12-month trial with a structural primary endpoint find?

shelves.balance: The short-small-positive / long-rigorous-null arc leads. BEDIP is a 40-inpatient, 3-week pilot whose Katzenwadel neuropathy score improved significantly (P = 0.0287), driven by pain. BENDIP is a 6-week phase 3 trial (165 randomised; 133 intention-to-treat) whose primary Neuropathy Symptom Score was significant only in the PER-PROTOCOL population (P = 0.033) and just above significance intention-to-treat (P = 0.055), with the Total Symptom Score not differing. BOND — the only 12-month trial, with a structural primary endpoint (corneal nerve fibre length) — found NO difference on its primary and essentially no difference on any secondary morphometric, neurophysiological, clinical or quality-of-life measure, with only the Neuropathy Symptom Score tending to improve (P = 0.098), even though thiamine analyte levels rose as expected (all P ≤ 0.003). Symptom scores are subjective endpoints, and the positive trials last 3 and 6 weeks. A fourth located report (PMID 33069584) has an EMPTY abstract in its PubMed record and is refused as an anchor — support-only at most, stated on the Synthesis card. Benfotiamine is a supplement: no tested brand is named in any anchor abstract, stated plainly on this shelf, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.

cards.headline: BEDIP pilot (Haupt 2005): 40 inpatients over 3 WEEKS — the Katzenwadel neuropathy score improved significantly (P = 0.0287), driven by pain (P = 0.0414); vibration perception did not change
cards.summary: BEDIP pilot (Haupt 2005): 40 inpatients over 3 WEEKS — the Katzenwadel neuropathy score improved significantly (P = 0.0287), driven by pain (P = 0.0414); vibration perception did not change
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled double-blind pilot study (BEDIP), benfotiamine 400 mg/day vs placebo for 3 weeks
cards.people: 40 inpatients (20 benfotiamine, 20 placebo) with type 1 or 2 diabetes and polyneuropathy of no longer than 2 years' duration, at two centres. Benfotiamine was given as two 50 mg tablets four times daily (400 mg/day) for 3 weeks in a randomised placebo-controlled double-blind pilot study. Outcomes: the neuropathy score of Katzenwadel et al., vibration perception threshold, and physician and patient global assessments.
cards.result: A statistically significant improvement in the neuropathy score was observed in the active-drug group vs placebo (P = 0.0287). The most pronounced effect was a decrease in pain (P = 0.0414). There was no statistically significant change in the tuning-fork (vibration) test. More benfotiamine patients than placebo patients considered their condition improved (P = 0.052). No side effects attributable to benfotiamine were observed, and the between-group differences could not be attributed to metabolic change — HbA1c and blood-sugar profiles did not alter significantly.
cards.watchOut: A pilot by its own name: 40 inpatients and 3 weeks of a subjective symptom score cannot carry a chronic-disease claim, and its objective limb (vibration) was null even here.
cards.source: Haupt E et al. Benfotiamine in the treatment of diabetic polyneuropathy--a three-week randomized, controlled pilot study (BEDIP study). International journal of clinical pharmacology and therapeutics. 2005. PMID: 15726875. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BENDIP phase 3 (Stracke 2008): 6 weeks — the primary Neuropathy Symptom Score differed significantly in the PER-PROTOCOL population (P = 0.033) but was just above significance intention-to-treat (P = 0.055); the Total Symptom Score did not differ
cards.summary: BENDIP phase 3 (Stracke 2008): 6 weeks — the primary Neuropathy Symptom Score differed significantly in the PER-PROTOCOL population (P = 0.033) but was just above significance intention-to-treat (P = 0.055); the Total Symptom Score did not differ
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (BENDIP), benfotiamine 600/300 mg/day vs placebo for 6 weeks
cards.people: 165 patients with symmetrical distal diabetic polyneuropathy randomised to benfotiamine 600 mg/day, benfotiamine 300 mg/day or placebo (181 screened); 133 patients were analysed intention-to-treat and 124 per-protocol (600 mg: 47/43; 300 mg: 45/42; placebo: 41/39 as published for the ITT/PP sets). Treatment lasted 6 weeks after a wash-out phase.
cards.result: After 6 weeks the primary outcome, the Neuropathy Symptom Score, differed significantly between the treatment groups in the per-protocol population (P = 0.033); in the intention-to-treat population the improvement was slightly above significance (P = 0.055). The Total Symptom Score showed no significant differences after 6 weeks. Improvement was more pronounced at the higher dose and increased with treatment duration; within the Total Symptom Score the best results were for the symptom 'pain'. Treatment was well tolerated in all groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on the analysis population: per-protocol positive, intention-to-treat not significant. Any quotation of BENDIP that omits the ITT P = 0.055 misstates the trial.
cards.source: Stracke H et al. Benfotiamine in diabetic polyneuropathy (BENDIP): results of a randomised, double blind, placebo-controlled clinical study. Experimental and clinical endocrinology & diabetes : official journal, German Society of Endocrinology [and] German Diabetes Association. 2008. PMID: 18473286. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BOND trial (Ziegler 2026): 12 MONTHS, structural primary — change in corneal nerve fibre length did NOT differ between benfotiamine and placebo, and neither did essentially any secondary morphometric, neurophysiological, clinical or quality-of-life measure; only the Neuropathy Symptom Score tended to improve (P = 0.098)
cards.summary: BOND trial (Ziegler 2026): 12 MONTHS, structural primary — change in corneal nerve fibre length did NOT differ between benfotiamine and placebo, and neither did essentially any secondary morphometric, neurophysiological, clinical or quality-of-life measure; only the Neuropathy Symptom Score tended to improve (P = 0.098)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (BOND), benfotiamine 300 mg twice daily vs placebo for 12 months — primary endpoint null
cards.people: 57 participants with type 2 diabetes and mild-to-moderate symptomatic diabetic sensorimotor polyneuropathy, randomised 1:1 in a monocentric double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial to benfotiamine 300 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months. Primary endpoint: change in corneal nerve fibre length by corneal confocal microscopy. Secondaries spanned three further corneal parameters, skin biopsy (four parameters), nerve conduction (13 measures), quantitative sensory testing, autonomic and sudomotor testing, 15 clinical scores and 13 quality-of-life / depression instruments, plus six thiamine analytes.
cards.result: Changes from baseline to 12 months in corneal nerve fibre length did not differ between the groups. The corresponding changes in the secondary morphometric, functional and clinical neuropathic outcomes and in quality of life were also similar in the two groups. Only the Neuropathy Symptom Score tended to improve after benfotiamine (P = 0.098 vs placebo). Benfotiamine increased the concentrations of all six thiamine analytes studied (all P ≤ 0.003 vs placebo) — exposure was achieved; effect was not. Safety showed no relevant between-group differences in adverse-event rates.
cards.watchOut: The longest, broadest-measured trial is the null one, and its pharmacokinetic limb closes the usual escape route: blood thiamine analytes rose on treatment, so the null is not explained by non-exposure. BOND is small (57 randomised), which bounds how final its null can be — printed here, not hidden.
cards.source: Ziegler D et al. Effects of benfotiamine treatment over 12 months on morphometric, neurophysiological and clinical measures in type 2 diabetes patients with symptomatic polyneuropathy: a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial (BOND study). BMJ open diabetes research & care. 2026. PMID: 41571333. Registry ID: DRKS00014832. cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three abstract-verified reports. BEDIP (40 inpatients, 3 weeks) and BENDIP (165 randomised, 6 weeks; primary significant per-protocol only) are positive on short symptom scores; BOND (57 randomised, 12 months, structural primary) is null across essentially every measure despite proven thiamine exposure. REFUSAL, stated as required: a fourth located report of a 12-month benfotiamine trial (PMID 33069584) was fetched this session and its PubMed abstract is EMPTY, so no number in it can be verified — it is refused as an anchor and held as support-only at most; this shelf rests on the three reports above. The diabetic-NEPHROPATHY slice of benfotiamine is a different question with its own single null trial and is not pooled here. SPLIT — split by trial duration and rigour, with the long trial null. No tested brand is named in any anchor abstract, and current supplement products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: Do not average the three trials into a modest positive: the pattern is duration-dependent (weeks positive, a year null), which is itself the answer to the question this shelf asks.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK — the exact base is printed here and on every card: 3 reports, 1 trial, N = 603 randomised (594 analysed in the primary report), the ADCT trial at 112 Japanese facilities. THE DESIGN IS THE CAVEAT: ADCT was open-label and randomised patients to epalrestat 150 mg/day or to NO TREATMENT — there is no placebo and no blinding. Over 3 years epalrestat prevented the deterioration in median motor nerve conduction velocity, minimum F-wave latency and vibration perception threshold seen in controls (between-group difference in median motor NCV change 1.6 m/s, P < 0.001); numbness, sensory abnormality and cramping improved significantly, while cardiovascular autonomic measures did not reach significance. The stratified report's efficacy odds ratio was approximately 2:1 overall and approximately 4:1 in the HbA1c ≤7.0% subgroup — odds ratios are relative measures, labelled as such. The primary endpoint is a nerve-conduction surrogate, the symptom benefits are secondary and unblinded, and the effect is concentrated in well-controlled patients without advanced retinopathy. Epalrestat is marketed only in parts of Asia (Japan, India, China) — a single-region programme. Its class sibling ranirestat (shelf #7696) has the stronger, placebo-controlled base. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: ADCT primary report (Hotta 2006) — report 1 of 3 of the ONE ADCT trial: open-label, NO placebo; epalrestat prevented the deterioration in median motor NCV, minimum F-wave latency and vibration perception seen in untreated controls over 3 years (between-group difference in median motor NCV change 1.6 m/s, P < 0.001)
cards.summary: ADCT primary report (Hotta 2006) — report 1 of 3 of the ONE ADCT trial: open-label, NO placebo; epalrestat prevented the deterioration in median motor NCV, minimum F-wave latency and vibration perception seen in untreated controls over 3 years (between-group difference in median motor NCV change 1.6 m/s, P < 0.001)
cards.type: Report 1 of 3 of the single ADCT trial — open-label randomised trial, epalrestat vs no-treatment control (no placebo), 3 years
cards.people: Patients with diabetic neuropathy, median motor nerve conduction velocity ≥40 m/s and HbA1c ≤9%, enrolled in an open-label multicentre study and randomised to epalrestat 150 mg/day or a control (no-treatment) group. After excluding withdrawals, 289 (epalrestat) and 305 (control) patients were analysed — 594 of the trial's 603 randomised. Primary endpoint: change from baseline in median motor NCV at 3 years.
cards.result: Over 3 years, epalrestat prevented the deterioration of median motor NCV, minimum F-wave latency and vibration perception threshold seen in the control group; the between-group difference in change in median motor NCV was 1.6 m/s (P < 0.001). Cardiovascular autonomic nerve function variables favoured epalrestat but did not reach statistical significance. Numbness of limbs, sensory abnormality and cramping improved significantly with epalrestat vs control. Effects on median motor NCV were most evident in subjects with better glycaemic control and no or mild microangiopathy. Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK design caveat, on the face: open-label with an untreated control means symptom outcomes are unblinded and expectancy-prone, and the primary endpoint is a conduction surrogate. This one trial is the entire evidence base for this shelf.
cards.source: Hotta N et al. Long-term clinical effects of epalrestat, an aldose reductase inhibitor, on diabetic peripheral neuropathy: the 3-year, multicenter, comparative Aldose Reductase Inhibitor-Diabetes Complications Trial. Diabetes care. 2006. PMID: 16801576. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ADCT second report (Matsuoka 2007) — report 2 of 3 of the SAME trial (not a second trial): 603 randomised at 112 facilities; median motor conduction at 3 years 52.1 vs 52.0 m/s from baselines of 52.0 vs 53.3 m/s, between-group change difference P < 0.0001, benefit concentrated in patients without advanced retinopathy
cards.summary: ADCT second report (Matsuoka 2007) — report 2 of 3 of the SAME trial (not a second trial): 603 randomised at 112 facilities; median motor conduction at 3 years 52.1 vs 52.0 m/s from baselines of 52.0 vs 53.3 m/s, between-group change difference P < 0.0001, benefit concentrated in patients without advanced retinopathy
cards.type: Report 2 of 3 of the single ADCT trial — prospective randomised open-label study of motor conduction velocity over 3 years (same cohort as the primary report)
cards.people: The same ADCT cohort as the previous card: 603 diabetic patients with median motor conduction velocity >40 m/s and HbA1c <9% randomly allocated at 112 facilities to epalrestat (50 mg three times daily, 150 mg/day; n = 289, age 61 ± 9.8 years) or control (n = 305, age 61 ± 9.1 years), with conduction velocity measured yearly for 3 years — the analysed groups sum to 594 of the 603 randomised, as published.
cards.result: Median motor conduction velocity (mean ± SD) at baseline, 1 year and 3 years was 52.0 ± 4.5, 52.2 ± 4.9 and 52.1 ± 4.6 m/s in the epalrestat group and 53.3 ± 4.4, 52.4 ± 4.2 and 52.0 ± 4.6 m/s in controls; after 3 years the difference from baseline differed significantly between groups (P < 0.0001). Among subjects with HbA1c <7.0%, controls showed marked deterioration while the epalrestat group showed no significant deterioration (P < 0.001). In subjects with background retinopathy or no retinopathy the epalrestat group's deterioration rate was significantly less than controls' (P < 0.0001), with no between-group difference in pre-proliferative or proliferative retinopathy. No remarkable side effects serious enough to discontinue the study were observed.
cards.watchOut: The near-identical 3-year absolute velocities (52.1 vs 52.0 m/s) show what the 'prevention of deterioration' claim is made of: the groups started 1.3 m/s apart and converged — a change-score result in an unblinded trial, printed with its baselines so the reader can see it.
cards.source: Matsuoka K et al. A long-term effect of epalrestat on motor conduction velocity of diabetic patients: ARI-Diabetes Complications Trial (ADCT). Diabetes research and clinical practice. 2007. PMID: 17599629. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ADCT stratified analysis (Hotta 2008) — report 3 of 3 of the SAME trial: efficacy odds ratio approximately 2:1 vs control overall and approximately 4:1 in the HbA1c ≤7.0% subgroup (odds ratios — relative measures, labelled as such)
cards.summary: ADCT stratified analysis (Hotta 2008) — report 3 of 3 of the SAME trial: efficacy odds ratio approximately 2:1 vs control overall and approximately 4:1 in the HbA1c ≤7.0% subgroup (odds ratios — relative measures, labelled as such)
cards.type: Report 3 of 3 of the single ADCT trial — stratified / logistic-regression analysis of the same cohort (same trial, not new patients)
cards.people: Stratified and multiple logistic regression analyses of the ADCT trial's longitudinal data over 3 years, in the subset with HbA1c and symptom data analysed here: epalrestat n = 231, control n = 273 (a subset of the trial's 603 randomised — not additional patients). Patients had diabetic peripheral neuropathy, median motor NCV ≥40 m/s and HbA1c ≤9.0%.
cards.result: Stratified subgroup analyses showed significantly better efficacy of epalrestat in patients with good glycaemic control and less severe diabetic complications. In the control group, no improvement in nerve function was seen regardless of symptomatic benefit; in the epalrestat group, nerve function deteriorated less or improved in patients whose symptoms improved. The odds ratio of the efficacy of epalrestat vs control was approximately 2:1 overall, and approximately 4:1 in patients with HbA1c ≤7.0% — odds ratios are relative measures and are printed as such, with no absolute response rates in the fetched record to set beside them. The authors conclude epalrestat will provide clinically significant prevention and treatment benefit if used in appropriate patients.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup odds ratios from one unblinded trial are hypothesis-shaping, not confirmatory: the 4:1 figure selects the subgroup (HbA1c ≤7.0%) in which the already-open-label effect was largest, and no absolute rates accompany it in the record.
cards.source: Hotta N et al. Stratified analyses for selecting appropriate target patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy for long-term treatment with an aldose reductase inhibitor, epalrestat. Diabetic medicine : a journal of the British Diabetic Association. 2008. PMID: 18644069. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: FLOOR-RISK, stated in full: this shelf's entire base is 3 reports of 1 trial — ADCT, 603 randomised at 112 Japanese facilities, open-label, epalrestat 150 mg/day vs NO treatment, no placebo, 3 years. The primary report (594 analysed) found prevention of median motor conduction deterioration (change difference 1.6 m/s, P < 0.001) with significant gains in numbness, sensory abnormality and cramping and non-significant autonomic results (Hotta 2006); the second report gives the yearly conduction values and the retinopathy concentration of the effect (Matsuoka 2007); the stratified analysis gives relative efficacy odds of about 2:1 overall and 4:1 at HbA1c ≤7.0% (Hotta 2008). The Chinese epalrestat + alpha-lipoic-acid combination trials are a different (combination) question and are not counted. MAYBE (weak evidence): ADCT is the largest and longest aldose-reductase trial in diabetic neuropathy and epalrestat is the class's only marketed member, which is why this row was kept at FLOOR-RISK — not because the base is strong.
cards.watchOut: One open-label trial reported three times is one trial's worth of evidence however it is carded; for a placebo-controlled read on this drug class, see ranirestat (shelf #7696), whose clinical scores were null throughout.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Nitisinone for alkaptonuria: homogentisic acid fell 99.7% relative to control, but clinical benefit is modest — a slower severity-score rise over 4 years, and the NIH trial's primary clinical outcome missed
shelves.question: In adults with alkaptonuria, does nitisinone (10 mg daily), compared with no treatment, reduce homogentisic acid excretion and slow clinical disease progression (the SONIA programme and the NIH trial)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alkaptonuria · Cyclohexanones · Drug Administration Schedule · Enzyme Inhibitors · Female · Homogentisic Acid · Humans · Internationality · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Nitrobenzoates · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the biochemical/clinical split on the face. Nitisinone's effect on homogentisic acid is near-total (SONIA 2: 99.7% relative reduction vs no treatment at 12 months; SONIA 1: clear dose-response to 0.15 mmol at 8 mg). The clinical benefit is much more modest: SONIA 2 found a significantly smaller increase in the cAKUSSI severity score over 48 months (adjusted difference −8.6 points, P=0.023), while the separate NIH randomised trial's selected primary outcome did not demonstrate significant clinical benefit and its supportive SF-36 / 6-minute-walk findings are a post-hoc per-protocol analysis. Neither SONIA trial had a placebo arm (no-treatment controls, effectively unblinded), and tyrosinaemia occurred at every dose.

cards.headline: SONIA 1 dose-response RCT (Ranganath 2016): 24-hour urinary homogentisic acid fell dose-dependently — adjusted geometric mean 31.53 mmol with no treatment down to 0.15 mmol at 8 mg daily; 98.8% relative reduction vs baseline at the top dose; tyrosine rose at every dose
cards.summary: SONIA 1 dose-response RCT (Ranganath 2016): 24-hour urinary homogentisic acid fell dose-dependently — adjusted geometric mean 31.53 mmol with no treatment down to 0.15 mmol at 8 mg daily; 98.8% relative reduction vs baseline at the top dose; tyrosine rose at every dose
cards.type: Randomised open-label no-treatment-controlled dose-response trial (SONIA 1), nitisinone 1–8 mg daily vs no treatment, 4 weeks
cards.people: 40 patients with alkaptonuria randomised into five groups of 8 — no treatment, or nitisinone 1, 2, 4 or 8 mg once daily — for 4 weeks, in an international multicentre open-label study.
cards.result: At 4 weeks the adjusted geometric mean 24-hour urinary homogentisic acid excretion was 31.53 mmol (no treatment), 3.26 mmol (1 mg), 1.44 mmol (2 mg), 0.57 mmol (4 mg) and 0.15 mmol (8 mg) — a clear dose-response. At 8 mg this was a mean reduction of 98.8% relative to baseline. Tyrosine levels increased at all doses, with a less clear dose-response. No serious adverse events were reported over the 4 weeks and the authors reported no safety concerns despite the tyrosinaemia.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 weeks, 8 patients per group, and a urinary metabolite endpoint: SONIA 1 establishes the dose-response for homogentisic-acid lowering, not clinical benefit. The raised tyrosine (tyrosinaemia) is an on-mechanism effect seen at every dose.
cards.source: Ranganath LR et al. Suitability Of Nitisinone In Alkaptonuria 1 (SONIA 1): an international, multicentre, randomised, open-label, no-treatment controlled, parallel-group, dose-response study to investigate the effect of once daily nitisinone on 24-h urinary homogentisic acid excretion in patients with alkaptonuria after 4 weeks of treatment. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2016. PMID: 25475116. Registry ID: NCT01828463. cards.headline: SONIA 2 RCT (Ranganath 2020): nitisinone 10 mg daily lowered urinary homogentisic acid by 99.7% relative to no treatment at 12 months, and the clinical severity score rose significantly less over 4 years (adjusted difference −8.6 points, P=0.023)
cards.summary: SONIA 2 RCT (Ranganath 2020): nitisinone 10 mg daily lowered urinary homogentisic acid by 99.7% relative to no treatment at 12 months, and the clinical severity score rose significantly less over 4 years (adjusted difference −8.6 points, P=0.023)
cards.type: Phase 3-style 4-year randomised open-label evaluator-blind no-treatment-controlled trial (SONIA 2), nitisinone 10 mg daily vs no treatment
cards.people: 138 patients aged 25 or older with confirmed alkaptonuria and clinical disease manifestations, randomised 69 to nitisinone 10 mg daily and 69 to no treatment for 4 years at three sites in the UK, France and Slovakia; 55 on nitisinone and 53 controls completed. Open-label with evaluator blinding — urine colour changes prevented patient masking.
cards.result: Urinary homogentisic acid at 12 months was decreased by 99.7% relative to control (adjusted geometric mean ratio 0.003, 95% CI 0.003 to 0.004, P<0.0001). At 48 months the increase in the clinical Alkaptonuria Severity Score Index (cAKUSSI) from baseline was significantly smaller on nitisinone (adjusted mean difference −8.6 points, 95% CI −16.0 to −1.2, P=0.023). Adverse events occurred in 59 of 69 patients (86%) on nitisinone and 57 of 69 (83%) on no treatment (400 vs 284 events); no treatment-related deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm and effectively unblinded patients (urine darkening/colour change reveals allocation). The biochemical effect is near-total; the clinical effect is a difference in the slope of a composite severity score over 4 years — no fracture, valve-surgery or mortality outcome has been randomised.
cards.source: Ranganath LR et al. Efficacy and safety of once-daily nitisinone for patients with alkaptonuria (SONIA 2): an international, multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2020. PMID: 32822600. Registry ID: NCT01916382. phase 3-style 4-year randomised open-label evaluator-blind no-treatment-controlled trial (sonia 2), nitisinone 10 mg daily vs no treatment 138 patients aged 25 or older with confirmed alkaptonuria and clinical disease manifestations, randomised 69 to nitisinone 10 mg daily and 69 to no treatment for 4 years at three sites in the uk, france and slovakia; 55 on nitisinone and 53 controls completed. open-label with evaluator blinding — urine colour changes prevented patient masking. urinary homogentisic acid at 12 months was decreased by 99.7% relative to control (adjusted geometric mean ratio 0.003, 95% ci 0.003 to 0.004, p<0.0001). at 48 months the increase in the clinical alkaptonuria severity score index (cakussi) from baseline was significantly smaller on nitisinone (adjusted mean difference −8.6 points, 95% ci −16.0 to −1.2, p=0.023). adverse events occurred in 59 of 69 patients (86%) on nitisinone and 57 of 69 (83%) on no treatment (400 vs 284 events); no treatment-related deaths occurred. no placebo arm and effectively unblinded patients (urine darkening/colour change reveals allocation). the biochemical effect is near-total; the clinical effect is a difference in the slope of a composite severity score over 4 years — no fracture, valve-surgery or mortality outcome has been randomised. ranganath lr et al. efficacy and safety of once-daily nitisinone for patients with alkaptonuria (sonia 2): an international, multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. the lancet. diabetes & endocrinology. 2020. pmid: 32822600. registry id: nct01916382. mesh: adult · aged · alkaptonuria · cyclohexanones · drug administration schedule · enzyme inhibitors · female · homogentisic acid · humans · internationality · longitudinal studies · male · middle aged · nitrobenzoates · single-blind method · treatment outcome

cards.type: Programme report: post-hoc per-protocol analysis of patient-reported outcomes from a separate 3-year randomised nitisinone trial (NIH programme) — labelled as a report of that trial, not an independent trial
cards.people: Patients with alkaptonuria enrolled in a separate 3-year randomised trial of nitisinone (NIH programme); this report is a post-hoc per-protocol analysis of patient-reported outcomes and a functional assessment from that trial. The abstract does not state the analysed number, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: The report states plainly that the parent randomised trial confirmed the biochemical efficacy and tolerability of nitisinone but its selected primary outcome did not demonstrate significant clinical benefit. In this post-hoc per-protocol analysis, nitisinone-treated patients showed significant improvements in complementary domains of the 36-Item Short-Form Survey (SF-36) and in the 6-minute walk test, which the authors interpret as suggesting improved quality of life and function.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and per-protocol: the affirmative readings come from an analysis chosen after the parent trial's primary clinical outcome missed. It must never be read as overturning that primary result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two SONIA trials plus one labelled NIH-trial report — homogentisic-acid lowering is near-total and undisputed (99.7% relative reduction at 12 months in SONIA 2), while clinical benefit is modest: a significantly smaller rise in a composite severity score over 4 years, a missed primary clinical outcome in the NIH trial, and post-hoc patient-reported gains

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: SONIA 1 (40 randomised), SONIA 2 (138 randomised) and the NIH trial's patient-reported-outcomes report.
cards.result: The contrast is the answer. Biochemically, nitisinone 10 mg daily almost abolishes homogentisic acid excretion. Clinically, the evidence is a −8.6-point difference in cAKUSSI progression over 4 years in an open-label, no-treatment-controlled trial, set against a separate randomised trial whose selected primary outcome showed no significant clinical benefit and whose supportive patient-reported findings are post-hoc. Tyrosinaemia occurred at every dose in SONIA 1 and is part of the tested record. No trial randomised a fracture, valve or mortality endpoint.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Sorbinil for diabetic neuropathy: a largely negative founding programme — null in the 497-patient trial, positive only in the smallest (N = 15) trial
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor sorbinil, compared with placebo, improve neuropathic pain, nerve conduction or clinical neuropathy measures?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — the nulls lead. This is the aldose reductase class's founding programme, and sorbinil was never marketed. The 497-patient trial found no evidence that early clinical signs and symptoms of diabetic neuropathy were altered; the 22-patient and 31-patient trials were null on nerve function and on every clinical and neurophysiological measure respectively. The only positive signals are in the smallest trial (N = 15, with a 4-patient idiosyncratic reaction) and in one peroneal-nerve velocity distribution — a surrogate — in the largest. A hypersensitivity reaction recurs across the programme.

cards.headline: Painful-neuropathy crossover trial (Young 1983): in 15 patients only pain, tendon reflex scores and sural sensory potential amplitude improved significantly on sorbinil, clinical sensory examination scores deteriorated — and 4 patients had an idiosyncratic reaction that recovered on stopping the drug
cards.summary: Painful-neuropathy crossover trial (Young 1983): in 15 patients only pain, tendon reflex scores and sural sensory potential amplitude improved significantly on sorbinil, clinical sensory examination scores deteriorated — and 4 patients had an idiosyncratic reaction that recovered on stopping the drug
cards.people: 15 patients (age 35–68 years) with chronic painful diabetic neuropathy in a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial of sorbinil, an aldose reductase inhibitor. This is the smallest trial in the programme; N = 15 is above the ~10-human reference floor but small, and its N is printed on the face of this card.
cards.result: Among the many measurements, only pain, tendon reflex scores and sural sensory potential amplitude improved significantly during sorbinil administration, while scores of clinical sensory examination deteriorated. Four patients experienced an idiosyncratic reaction that rapidly recovered on discontinuing the drug. The authors suggest sorbinil may have an effect on symptomatic diabetic neuropathy.
cards.watchOut: The programme's only clearly positive symptomatic signal sits in its smallest trial (N = 15), alongside a 4-patient idiosyncratic-reaction signal — never present this trial without both facts.
cards.source: Young RJ et al. A controlled trial of sorbinil, an aldose reductase inhibitor, in chronic painful diabetic neuropathy. Diabetes. 1983. PMID: 6225686. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Asymptomatic-neuropathy crossover trial (Martyn 1987): sorbinil 125 mg/day showed very significant aldose reductase inhibition in erythrocyte sorbitol but NO improvement in either peripheral or autonomic nerve function in 22 patients
cards.summary: Asymptomatic-neuropathy crossover trial (Martyn 1987): sorbinil 125 mg/day showed very significant aldose reductase inhibition in erythrocyte sorbitol but NO improvement in either peripheral or autonomic nerve function in 22 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, two 6-month periods (N = 22)
cards.people: 22 diabetic patients with subclinical (asymptomatic) abnormalities of nerve function; placebo-controlled double-blind crossover, each treatment period 6 months, sorbinil 125 mg daily.
cards.result: Measurement of erythrocyte sorbitol concentrations demonstrated very significant inhibition of aldose reductase activity with sorbinil treatment, but no concomitant improvement in either peripheral or autonomic nerve function was observed. Peripheral function was assessed electrophysiologically and by quantitative sensory testing; autonomic function by five cardiovascular reflexes and mean heart rate from 24-hour ECG.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacodynamic success and a clinical null in the same trial: target engagement (erythrocyte sorbitol) must never be printed as evidence of nerve benefit.
cards.source: Martyn CN et al. Six-month treatment with sorbinil in asymptomatic diabetic neuropathy. Failure to improve abnormal nerve function. Diabetes. 1987. PMID: 3111914. cards.headline: One-year trial (O'Hare 1988): NO beneficial effect of sorbinil 250 mg/day on symptoms, clinical manifestations or any neurophysiological measurement in 31 randomised patients over 12 months; neuropathic ulceration developed in 4 on sorbinil vs 1 on placebo
cards.summary: One-year trial (O'Hare 1988): NO beneficial effect of sorbinil 250 mg/day on symptoms, clinical manifestations or any neurophysiological measurement in 31 randomised patients over 12 months; neuropathic ulceration developed in 4 on sorbinil vs 1 on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 12 months (N = 31 randomised)
cards.people: 31 patients randomised (21 sorbinil 250 mg/day / 10 placebo) after a 2-month placebo run-in, studied for a further 12 months with neurophysiological measurements at 3-month intervals, clinical examination and extensive self-assessment of symptoms.
cards.result: There were no changes in symptoms by self-assessment scores and no beneficial effect on either the clinical manifestation or the neurophysiological measurements. Two subjects on sorbinil developed a hypersensitivity reaction and were withdrawn. No patient entered with neuropathic ulcers, but ulceration developed in 4 patients during sorbinil treatment and in 1 on placebo. Metabolic control and neuropathy severity did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: A complete null over a full year, with the hypersensitivity signal recurring (2 withdrawals) and more ulceration on sorbinil (4 vs 1) — small counts, printed as counts, not as a proven harm.
cards.source: O'Hare JP et al. Aldose reductase inhibition in diabetic neuropathy: clinical and neurophysiological studies of one year's treatment with sorbinil. Diabetic medicine : a journal of the British Diabetic Association. 1988. PMID: 2974776. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sorbinil Retinopathy Trial neuropathy results (1993): in 497 randomised patients nearly 30% in BOTH groups worsened on clinical polyneuropathy measures with very little difference between groups; the authors conclude there was no evidence early clinical signs and symptoms of diabetic neuropathy were altered by sorbinil
cards.summary: Sorbinil Retinopathy Trial neuropathy results (1993): in 497 randomised patients nearly 30% in BOTH groups worsened on clinical polyneuropathy measures with very little difference between groups; the authors conclude there was no evidence early clinical signs and symptoms of diabetic neuropathy were altered by sorbinil
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial — neuropathy results of the Sorbinil Retinopathy Trial (N = 497 randomised; nerve conduction in 192)
cards.people: 497 patients randomised, aged 18–56 years with insulin-dependent diabetes of 1–15 years' duration, sorbinil vs placebo; nerve conduction was studied in 192 patients. This is the programme's large trial and its clinical measures lead this shelf.
cards.result: Nearly 30% of patients in both groups showed worsening of clinical measures of distal symmetric polyneuropathy at maximum follow-up, with very little difference between groups. For median motor, median sensory and peroneal nerves there were no benefits in maximum amplitudes; velocity changes for median motor and sensory nerves were not significantly different. Only for the peroneal nerve, at 30 months and maximum follow-up, did the distribution of velocity change favour sorbinil (overall improvement on sorbinil, decline on placebo; difference in distributions statistically significant). Overall, the authors found no evidence that early clinical signs and symptoms of diabetic neuropathy were altered by sorbinil. Nerve conduction is a surrogate endpoint wherever it moves.
cards.watchOut: The single favourable finding is a distribution of peroneal-nerve velocity change — a surrogate — inside an otherwise null 497-patient trial; it must never be printed as a clinical neuropathy benefit.
cards.source: Sorbinil Retinopathy Trial Research Group et al. The sorbinil retinopathy trial: neuropathy results. Sorbinil Retinopathy Trial Research Group. Neurology. 1993. PMID: 8170559. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a largely negative founding programme — the nulls lead: no nerve-function improvement in 22 asymptomatic patients, no benefit on any measure over 12 months in 31 patients, and no alteration of clinical neuropathy in 497 randomised patients; the only positive signals are in the smallest trial (N = 15) and in one peroneal velocity distribution
cards.summary: Synthesis: a largely negative founding programme — the nulls lead: no nerve-function improvement in 22 asymptomatic patients, no benefit on any measure over 12 months in 31 patients, and no alteration of clinical neuropathy in 497 randomised patients; the only positive signals are in the smallest trial (N = 15) and in one peroneal velocity distribution
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Four trials of the aldose reductase inhibitor sorbinil, never marketed, are carded: the 15-patient painful-neuropathy crossover (only pain, tendon reflex scores and sural sensory potential amplitude improved significantly; sensory examination scores deteriorated; 4 idiosyncratic reactions), the 22-patient asymptomatic crossover (very significant aldose reductase inhibition, no improvement in peripheral or autonomic nerve function), the 31-patient one-year trial (no beneficial effect on symptoms, clinical manifestations or any neurophysiological measurement; 2 hypersensitivity withdrawals; ulceration in 4 on sorbinil vs 1 on placebo) and the 497-patient Sorbinil Retinopathy Trial neuropathy results (nearly 30% worsened in both groups; no amplitude benefit; only the peroneal velocity-change distribution favoured sorbinil). A hypersensitivity / idiosyncratic reaction recurs across the programme. The class's later electrophysiology findings for other aldose reductase inhibitors are different agents' evidence and are not sorbinil evidence.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: sorbinil was never marketed, and no card on this shelf presents target engagement or a single nerve-conduction distribution as clinical benefit.

synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. four trials of the aldose reductase inhibitor sorbinil, never marketed, are carded: the 15-patient painful-neuropathy crossover (only pain, tendon reflex scores and sural sensory potential amplitude improved significantly; sensory examination scores deteriorated; 4 idiosyncratic reactions), the 22-patient asymptomatic crossover (very significant aldose reductase inhibition, no improvement in peripheral or autonomic nerve function), the 31-patient one-year trial (no beneficial effect on symptoms, clinical manifestations or any neurophysiological measurement; 2 hypersensitivity withdrawals; ulceration in 4 on sorbinil vs 1 on placebo) and the 497-patient sorbinil retinopathy trial neuropathy results (nearly 30% worsened in both groups; no amplitude benefit; only the peroneal velocity-change distribution favoured sorbinil). a hypersensitivity / idiosyncratic reaction recurs across the programme. the class's later electrophysiology findings for other aldose reductase inhibitors are different agents' evidence and are not sorbinil evidence. see the individual cards: sorbinil was never marketed, and no card on this shelf presents target engagement or a single nerve-conduction distribution as clinical benefit. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: SPLIT — a split, small, old base, and the split leads. The largest trial (216 patients) is positive only at its top dose (675 mg/day) and only on nighttime pain and sleep; the second-largest (95 patients) is null on its global measure with positive exploratory subgroups; the third (29 patients) is frankly underpowered and null; only the 16-completer crossover is clearly positive on symptoms. All treatment periods are 3 weeks where stated. Mexiletine is a cardiac antiarrhythmic: one patient was hospitalised for palpitations, and the trial authors' own restriction — patients without heart disease, unresponsive or intolerant to standard therapy — prints on the face.

cards.headline: Mexiletine Study Group trial (Oskarsson 1997): in 216 insulin-treated patients, a significant reduction in sleep disturbances and nighttime pain was observed at the highest dosage (675 mg/day) vs the other groups over 3 weeks
cards.summary: Mexiletine Study Group trial (Oskarsson 1997): in 216 insulin-treated patients, a significant reduction in sleep disturbances and nighttime pain was observed at the highest dosage (675 mg/day) vs the other groups over 3 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, three dosages, 3 weeks (N = 216)
cards.people: 216 insulin-treated diabetes patients with painful diabetic neuropathy randomised to three mexiletine dosages or placebo for 3 weeks; pain/discomfort scored daily on a visual analogue scale in daytime and nighttime, sleep disturbances recorded, plasma levels and 24-hour ECG mapping assessed.
cards.result: A significant reduction in sleep disturbances and pain during nighttime was observed in the group taking the highest dosage (675 mg/day) compared with the other groups. No significant correlation was found between plasma concentration and therapeutic effect or adverse events. No serious adverse events were seen, and 24-hour ECG mapping did not disclose onset of significant arrhythmias in any patient.
cards.watchOut: Positive only at the top dose and only on nighttime pain and sleep, over 3 weeks, in an ECG-screened population — no wording may imply a safety record beyond 3-week exposures with ECG screening; mexiletine is a cardiac antiarrhythmic.
cards.source: Oskarsson P et al. Efficacy and safety of mexiletine in the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy. The Mexiletine Study Group. Diabetes care. 1997. PMID: 9314641. cards.headline: Three-dosage trial (Stracke 1992): in 95 patients the global visual-analogue assessment showed NO difference vs placebo and the total McGill evaluation fell just below significance — exploratory sensory and miscellaneous subclasses and complaint-type subgroups (stabbing or burning pain, heat sensations, formication) favoured mexiletine
cards.summary: Three-dosage trial (Stracke 1992): in 95 patients the global visual-analogue assessment showed NO difference vs placebo and the total McGill evaluation fell just below significance — exploratory sensory and miscellaneous subclasses and complaint-type subgroups (stabbing or burning pain, heat sensations, formication) favoured mexiletine
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, three dosages (N = 95)
cards.people: 95 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy treated in three mexiletine dosages; pain measured by visual analogue scale and McGill verbal rating scale.
cards.result: A global assessment of the visual analogue scale showed no differences between mexiletine and placebo, and the total evaluation (PRIT) of the McGill scale fell just below the level of significance. More specific exploratory evaluations of McGill subclasses gave differences favouring mexiletine in sensory and miscellaneous items, and subgroups formed by complaint type showed advantages with both scales — in particular stabbing or burning pain, heat sensations or formication. The authors suggest a medium regimen of 450 mg/day as appropriate, and report no cardiovascular side effects at the medium dose range.
cards.watchOut: Null on its global measure: every favourable finding here is exploratory (subclasses and post-hoc complaint subgroups) and must be printed as exploratory, never as the trial's result.
cards.source: Stracke H et al. Mexiletine in the treatment of diabetic neuropathy. Diabetes care. 1992. PMID: 1468285. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Small double-blind trial (Wright 1997): in 29 patients the symptom-score difference was NOT statistically significant and the visual-analogue difference was 16.5 mm (95% CI −7.1 to 40.2, P = 0.16) — the authors state the study was underpowered and that mexiletine should be reserved for patients unresponsive or intolerant to standard therapy and without heart disease
cards.summary: Small double-blind trial (Wright 1997): in 29 patients the symptom-score difference was NOT statistically significant and the visual-analogue difference was 16.5 mm (95% CI −7.1 to 40.2, P = 0.16) — the authors state the study was underpowered and that mexiletine should be reserved for patients unresponsive or intolerant to standard therapy and without heart disease
cards.type: Prospective double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 3 weeks (N = 29 randomised)
cards.people: 29 patients randomised to mexiletine 600 mg/day or matching placebo for 3 weeks; a four-item symptom score (pain, dysesthesias, paresthesias, nightly exacerbations) and a 100-mm visual analogue scale, with independent patient and investigator global assessments.
cards.result: The difference between median changes in symptom scores (mexiletine 5.5, placebo 2) was not statistically significant; global assessments did not differ (P = 0.19); the mean visual-analogue difference was 16.5 mm (95% CI −7.1 to 40.2 mm, P = 0.16). The authors state inadequate statistical power (1−β = 0.40) may have resulted from small sample size, small effect magnitude or variability. Adverse effects were more common on mexiletine (not statistically significant), and one mexiletine patient was hospitalised for palpitations. The authors conclude mexiletine should be reserved for patients unresponsive or intolerant to standard therapy, without evidence of heart disease, and with burning heat, formication or stabbing pain sensations.
cards.watchOut: Frankly underpowered and null — and it carries the programme's clearest safety flag (a palpitation hospitalisation) plus the trial authors' own 'no heart disease' restriction, both printed on the face of this shelf.
cards.source: Wright JM et al. Mexiletine in the symptomatic treatment of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. The Annals of pharmacotherapy. 1997. PMID: 8997461. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Crossover trial (Dejgard 1988): in 16 completers the five-item clinical symptom scale improved significantly during the mexiletine phase and pain fell on mexiletine but not placebo; no effect on reflexes, vibration threshold or autonomic measures
cards.summary: Crossover trial (Dejgard 1988): in 16 completers the five-item clinical symptom scale improved significantly during the mexiletine phase and pain fell on mexiletine but not placebo; no effect on reflexes, vibration threshold or autonomic measures
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover trial (19 entered, 16 completed)
cards.people: 19 patients entered and 16 completed a randomised double-blind crossover of oral mexiletine 10 mg/kg/day for chronic painful diabetic neuropathy; median age of the 16 completers 50 years (range 30–64).
cards.result: Assessment with a five-item clinical symptom scale showed significant improvement during the mexiletine phase compared with the placebo phase, and pain was reduced during mexiletine but not during placebo on a visual analogue rating scale. Mexiletine had no effect on tendon reflexes, vibration threshold levels, beat-to-beat variation in heart rate during deep breathing, or postural blood pressure response. Mild side-effects were seen in 3 of the 16 patients during mexiletine treatment.
cards.watchOut: The smallest and oldest trial is the most clearly positive on symptoms — the inverse of the usual pattern, and a reason the base as a whole is split rather than positive; symptom scales only, no objective nerve measure moved.
cards.source: Dejgard A et al. Mexiletine for treatment of chronic painful diabetic neuropathy. Lancet (London, England). 1988. PMID: 2891940. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: Four placebo-controlled trials of oral mexiletine (a class IB antiarrhythmic / oral local-anaesthetic analogue) in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy are carded, and they do not agree: Mexiletine Study Group (216 patients, 3 weeks — significant reduction in sleep disturbances and nighttime pain at 675 mg/day only; no serious adverse events; no significant arrhythmias on 24-hour ECG), Stracke (95 patients — global visual-analogue assessment no difference, total McGill just below significance, exploratory subclasses and complaint subgroups favouring mexiletine), Wright (29 patients, 3 weeks — not significant on symptom score or visual analogue scale, 16.5 mm, 95% CI −7.1 to 40.2, P = 0.16; authors state underpowered, 1−β = 0.40) and Dejgard (16 completers, crossover — symptom scale significantly improved, pain fell on mexiletine but not placebo, no objective measure moved). One mexiletine patient was hospitalised for palpitations (Wright), and the trial authors' restriction — reserve for patients unresponsive or intolerant to standard therapy and without heart disease — is part of this shelf's finding, not a footnote.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: mexiletine is a cardiac antiarrhythmic, every exposure here is short (3 weeks in the two trials that state a period), and no safety claim beyond ECG-screened short exposures is supported.

shelves.question: In adults with symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the protein kinase C-β inhibitor ruboxistaurin (32–64 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve vibration perception, neuropathy symptoms and quality of life?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, symptoms in subgroups only) — PARTIAL slice only, and a null primary leads. This shelf cards only the neuropathy outcomes of the ruboxistaurin programme; the eye programme is home on pack #7656 (read in full), and ruboxistaurin was never marketed for any indication (regulatory history on #7656, cross-pointed). The one adequately sized trial (205 randomised, 1 year) showed no treatment difference on its primary endpoint, vibration detection threshold, in the full population; benefits appear only in the baseline-symptomatic subgroup (NTSS-6, 64 mg/day, P = 0.015), a post-hoc less-severe subgroup, a 40-patient single-site skin-blood-flow trial, and a small two-agent quality-of-life study.

cards.headline: Phase 2 one-year trial (Vinik 2005): in 205 randomised patients the PRIMARY endpoint, change in vibration detection threshold, showed NO treatment difference overall — among the 83 with clinically significant symptoms at baseline, NTSS-6 fell significantly more on 64 mg/day (P = 0.015) but not 32 mg/day, and in a post-hoc less-severe subgroup (n = 50) both doses improved VDT

cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group trial, 1 year (N = 205 randomised) — primary endpoint missed
cards.people: 205 patients randomised (66 ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day / 71 at 64 mg/day / 68 placebo) with symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy identified by abnormal vibration detection threshold (VDT) verified by examination and electrophysiology, treated for 1 year. PARTIAL slice: this shelf cards only the neuropathy outcomes of the ruboxistaurin programme; the retinopathy / macular-edema programme is home on pack #7656, read in full before building, and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here.
cards.result: No treatment differences were observed for change in VDT, the primary endpoint. Among the 83 patients with clinically significant symptoms at baseline (NTSS-6 total score > 6), the NTSS-6 total score fell significantly more on 64 mg/day (P = 0.015) but not on 32 mg/day (P = NS) vs placebo at 12 months. In a post-hoc subgroup with clinically significant symptoms and less severe DPN (n = 50), NTSS-6 fell significantly more on 64 mg/day (P = 0.006) and VDT improved significantly on both 32 mg/day (P = 0.012) and 64 mg/day (P = 0.026) vs placebo. Ruboxistaurin appeared well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A null primary with subgroup benefits — the null leads: every positive finding on this card sits in a symptomatic subgroup or a post-hoc less-severe subgroup, and must never be printed as the trial's overall result.

cards.headline: Skin-microvascular trial (Casellini 2007): in 40 patients, endothelium-dependent skin blood flow rose +78.2% (percent change, P < 0.03) and C-fibre-mediated flow +56.4% (percent change, P < 0.03) on ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day, and the between-group NTSS-6 change favoured ruboxistaurin (−66.0% vs −13.1%, percent changes, P < 0.03)
cards.summary: Skin-microvascular trial (Casellini 2007): in 40 patients, endothelium-dependent skin blood flow rose +78.2% (percent change, P < 0.03) and C-fibre-mediated flow +56.4% (percent change, P < 0.03) on ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day, and the between-group NTSS-6 change favoured ruboxistaurin (−66.0% vs −13.1%, percent changes, P < 0.03)
cards.type: Randomised double-masked placebo-controlled single-site trial, 6 months (N = 40)
cards.people: 40 patients (20 ruboxistaurin 32 mg/day / 20 placebo) with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and diabetic peripheral neuropathy, in a randomised double-masked single-site 6-month study of skin microvascular blood flow (SkBF) and other neuropathy measures.
cards.result: Endothelium-dependent (+78.2%, percent change, P < 0.03) and C fibre-mediated (+56.4%, percent change, P < 0.03) skin blood flow at the distal calf increased from baseline to endpoint on ruboxistaurin. Between-group differences in baseline-to-endpoint change favoured ruboxistaurin for NTSS-6 total score (ruboxistaurin −66.0% vs placebo −13.1%, percent changes, P < 0.03) and the Norfolk QOL-DN symptom subscore (−41.2% vs −4.0%, percent changes, P = 0.041); within the ruboxistaurin group the Norfolk total score also improved (−41.0, P = 0.04, as printed). No significant ruboxistaurin effects were demonstrated for the remaining efficacy measures. All percent figures on this card are percent changes, printed with their P values, not absolute point differences.
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient single-site mechanistic trial: skin blood flow is a microvascular surrogate, and the symptom and quality-of-life differences are percent changes on small denominators — supportive, never a substitute for the 205-patient trial's null primary above.

cards.headline: Quality-of-life trial report (Boyd 2011): total QOL-DN scores improved in both active groups but not placebo, and NTSS-6 improved significantly within the ruboxistaurin group (4.38 → 1.49, P < 0.001) — in a three-arm study shared with topiramate, whose objective-measure gains are NOT ruboxistaurin's
cards.summary: Quality-of-life trial report (Boyd 2011): total QOL-DN scores improved in both active groups but not placebo, and NTSS-6 improved significantly within the ruboxistaurin group (4.38 → 1.49, P < 0.001) — in a three-arm study shared with topiramate, whose objective-measure gains are NOT ruboxistaurin's
cards.type: Prospective placebo-controlled trial report of two agents (ruboxistaurin and topiramate) — ruboxistaurin arm only carded (n = 18 as printed)
cards.people: 60 patients with diabetic neuropathy described as allocated in a prospective placebo-controlled trial of two agents — ruboxistaurin (n = 18), topiramate (n = 18) or placebo (n = 18), as printed in the record — with Norfolk QOL-DN and objective nerve-function measures at entry and end of study. Labelled on its face as a two-agent report: only the ruboxistaurin-arm figures are carded here.
cards.result: Total quality-of-life scores improved significantly in both active groups (ruboxistaurin −9.56 ± 4.13; topiramate −12.22 ± 2.76) but not placebo (−5.56 ± 3.49). NTSS-6 changes were significant for both treatments: ruboxistaurin 4.38 (0.75) to 1.49 (0.38), P < 0.001. The report states ruboxistaurin produced significant improvement in large-fibre measures while topiramate produced significant changes in small-fibre measures, and that the neurological, sensory, motor, impairment and total-neuropathy-score gains detailed in the report belong mainly to the topiramate arm — they are not credited to ruboxistaurin on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A small three-arm quality-of-life study shared with another drug: within-group symptom improvement on n = 18 is the weakest design on this shelf, and importing the topiramate arm's objective gains into a ruboxistaurin claim would be an error this card exists to prevent.
cards.source: Boyd A et al. Quality of life and objective measures of diabetic neuropathy in a prospective placebo-controlled trial of ruboxistaurin and topiramate. Journal of diabetes science and technology. 2011. PMID: 21722587. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: This shelf homes only the diabetic-peripheral-neuropathy slice of the ruboxistaurin programme, per the diagnosis-first rule: the retinopathy / macular-edema slice is home on pack #7656 (read in full before building), where the programme's regulatory history — ruboxistaurin was never marketed for any indication — is printed; that history is cross-pointed here, not repeated as this shelf's finding. Carded here: Vinik 2005 (205 randomised, 1 year — primary VDT endpoint no treatment difference overall; NTSS-6 benefit at 64 mg/day, P = 0.015, only among the 83 with NTSS-6 > 6 at baseline; post-hoc less-severe subgroup n = 50 positive on VDT and NTSS-6), Casellini 2007 (40 patients, 6 months — skin blood flow percent changes +78.2% and +56.4%, between-group NTSS-6 percent changes −66.0% vs −13.1%) and Boyd 2011 (ruboxistaurin arm n = 18 of a two-agent quality-of-life study — total QOL-DN and NTSS-6 improved within the ruboxistaurin group; the objective-measure gains in that report belong mainly to topiramate). The programme's albuminuria / eGFR report in DPN patients and its 2013 systematic review are support only, not carded and not counted here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards and pack #7656: never marketed, a missed primary endpoint, and subgroup-only benefits — no wording on this shelf may present ruboxistaurin as an established neuropathy treatment.

shelves.title: Tolrestat for diabetic neuropathy: a surrogate-led 1990s programme — conduction, reflex and vibration gains and a paraesthetic-symptom signal across five reports, inside a class whose Cochrane synthesis was null overall (SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05)
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic peripheral (sensorimotor and autonomic) neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor tolrestat (200 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve neuropathic symptoms, nerve conduction or autonomic function?
