shelves.balance: A surrogate-heavy 1990s programme — the surrogates lead. Five reports of tolrestat 200 mg/day (analysis sets from 45 to 372 patients, plus a labelled single-centre report with no centre N in its abstract) show improvement or non-deterioration on nerve conduction velocities, cardiovascular reflex tests and vibration thresholds, a withdrawal trial in which stopping long-term tolrestat led to deterioration, and one symptom signal confined to paraesthetic symptoms — painful symptoms improved equally on placebo in the largest trial. The class-level Cochrane synthesis of 32 aldose reductase inhibitor trials found no overall significant difference in neurological function (standardised mean difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05), with a tolrestat subgroup favouring treatment; that null class context is part of this shelf's balance, and the concordant-responder analysis (28% vs 5%) is not a patient-important outcome. The withdrawal trial randomised patients after a mean 4.2 years of open treatment, enriching for tolerators and responders.

cards.headline: Multicentre symptomatic-neuropathy trial (Boulton 1990): tolrestat 200 mg/day improved paraesthetic symptoms at 1 year (p = 0.04) and tibial and peroneal motor conduction velocities at 52 weeks, while painful symptoms improved on both tolrestat and placebo; sustained concordant improvement in 28% on tolrestat vs 5% on placebo (p = 0.001)
cards.summary: Multicentre symptomatic-neuropathy trial (Boulton 1990): tolrestat 200 mg/day improved paraesthetic symptoms at 1 year (p = 0.04) and tibial and peroneal motor conduction velocities at 52 weeks, while painful symptoms improved on both tolrestat and placebo; sustained concordant improvement in 28% on tolrestat vs 5% on placebo (p = 0.001)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial, tolrestat in symptomatic diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy (52 weeks)
cards.people: Patients with chronic symptomatic diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy in a randomised placebo-controlled 52-week multicentre trial of four tolrestat doses; the abstract confines further analyses to the 200 mg group (n = 112) vs placebo (n = 107) — the total randomised across all four dose groups is not printed in the abstract and is not claimed here.
cards.result: Only the highest dose (200 mg once daily) showed subjective and objective benefit. Paraesthetic symptoms improved at one year (p = 0.04); painful symptoms improved on both placebo and active therapy. Tibial and peroneal motor nerve conduction velocities improved significantly at 52 weeks, and concordant improvement in both conduction velocities and paraesthetic scores was significantly better on tolrestat at 24, 42 and 52 weeks, with long-term (sustained) benefit in 28% vs 5% (p = 0.001).
cards.watchOut: The concordant-responder figure (28% vs 5%) is a composite of two surrogate/symptom-score measures, not a patient-important outcome, and the only symptom signal is paraesthetic — painful symptoms improved equally on placebo. Analyses are confined to the 200 mg subgroup of a four-dose trial.
cards.source: Boulton et al. A multicentre trial of the aldose-reductase inhibitor, tolrestat, in patients with symptomatic diabetic neuropathy. Diabetologia. 1990. PMID: 2119323. cards.headline: Mild-neuropathy trial (Giugliano 1993, N = 45): tolrestat 200 mg/day improved autonomic reflex measures over 52 weeks — postural hypotension fell 5.9 mm Hg (95% CI 1.6 to 8.7), deep-breathing heart-rate ratio rose 0.026 and the 30:15 ratio rose 0.032 — while placebo results mostly deteriorated
cards.summary: Mild-neuropathy trial (Giugliano 1993, N = 45): tolrestat 200 mg/day improved autonomic reflex measures over 52 weeks — postural hypotension fell 5.9 mm Hg (95% CI 1.6 to 8.7), deep-breathing heart-rate ratio rose 0.026 and the 30:15 ratio rose 0.032 — while placebo results mostly deteriorated
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, tolrestat in mild diabetic autonomic and peripheral neuropathy (52 weeks)
cards.people: 45 patients with diabetes and asymptomatic autonomic neuropathy (at least one pathological cardiovascular reflex test), randomised after a 4-week single-blind placebo run-in to tolrestat 200 mg/day (n = 25) or placebo (n = 20) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: At 12 months, postural hypotension decreased by 5.9 mm Hg (95% CI 1.6 to 8.7), the expiration/inspiration heart-rate ratio increased by 0.026 (95% CI 0.015 to 0.036) and the 30:15 ratio increased by 0.032 (95% CI 0.027 to 0.052) on tolrestat; in the placebo group all test results except postural hypotension deteriorated. Vibration perception threshold improved on tolrestat and tended to worsen on placebo. No important side effects were detected in either group.
cards.watchOut: 45 patients and surrogate reflex-testing endpoints only — no symptom or clinical-event outcome. Small single-centre-era trial; its precision does not carry the shelf.
cards.source: Giugliano et al. Tolrestat for mild diabetic neuropathy. A 52-week, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1993. PMID: 8416161. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, tolrestat in mild diabetic autonomic and peripheral neuropathy (52 weeks) 45 patients with diabetes and asymptomatic autonomic neuropathy (at least one pathological cardiovascular reflex test), randomised after a 4-week single-blind placebo run-in to tolrestat 200 mg/day (n = 25) or placebo (n = 20) for 52 weeks. at 12 months, postural hypotension decreased by 5.9 mm hg (95% ci 1.6 to 8.7), the expiration/inspiration heart-rate ratio increased by 0.026 (95% ci 0.015 to 0.036) and the 30:15 ratio increased by 0.032 (95% ci 0.027 to 0.052) on tolrestat; in the placebo group all test results except postural hypotension deteriorated. vibration perception threshold improved on tolrestat and tended to worsen on placebo. no important side effects were detected in either group. 45 patients and surrogate reflex-testing endpoints only — no symptom or clinical-event outcome. small single-centre-era trial; its precision does not carry the shelf. giugliano et al. tolrestat for mild diabetic neuropathy. a 52-week, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. annals of internal medicine. 1993. pmid: 8416161. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aldehyde reductase/antagonists & inhibitors · autonomic nervous system diseases/drug therapy,etiology · blood pressure/drug effects · cardiovascular system/innervation · diabetes mellitus, type 2/complications · diabetic neuropathies/drug therapy · double-blind method · female · follow-up studies · heart rate/drug effects · humans · male · middle aged · naphthalenes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · peripheral nerves/drug effects · reflex/drug effects · sensation/drug effects · single-blind method

cards.headline: Subclinical-neuropathy trial (Giugliano 1995, N = 57): tolrestat 200 mg/day normalised the squatting vagal test in 25 patients vs 6 on placebo (P = 0.02) over 52 weeks, and vibration threshold improved by 6 ± 3 V on tolrestat while deteriorating by 3 ± 1.8 V on placebo (both P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Subclinical-neuropathy trial (Giugliano 1995, N = 57): tolrestat 200 mg/day normalised the squatting vagal test in 25 patients vs 6 on placebo (P = 0.02) over 52 weeks, and vibration threshold improved by 6 ± 3 V on tolrestat while deteriorating by 3 ± 1.8 V on placebo (both P < 0.001)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, tolrestat in subclinical (early autonomic) diabetic neuropathy (52 weeks)
cards.people: 57 patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes and early autonomic involvement (only one pathological squatting test) in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel 52-week study of tolrestat 200 mg/day vs placebo; the abstract does not print the per-group split and none is claimed here.
cards.result: At 12 months nerve function improved on tolrestat and deteriorated on placebo: the squatting vagal test normalised in 25 patients on tolrestat vs 6 on placebo (P = 0.02), and vibration perception threshold improved by 6 ± 3 V on tolrestat (P < 0.001) while deteriorating by 3 ± 1.8 V on placebo (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: This is a trial of early nerve-function changes in established diabetes, not a diabetes-onset trial; its outcomes are reflex tests and vibration threshold (surrogates), and 'normalisation' of a single reflex test is not a clinical event prevented.
cards.source: Giugliano et al. Tolrestat in the primary prevention of diabetic neuropathy. Diabetes care. 1995. PMID: 7497865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Withdrawal trial (Santiago 1993, N = 372 randomised after a mean 4.2 years of tolrestat): patients switched to placebo deteriorated significantly in motor nerve conduction velocity while those maintained on tolrestat did not (p < 0.05), with treatment differences favouring tolrestat for toe sensation and pain (p < 0.05)
cards.summary: Withdrawal trial (Santiago 1993, N = 372 randomised after a mean 4.2 years of tolrestat): patients switched to placebo deteriorated significantly in motor nerve conduction velocity while those maintained on tolrestat did not (p < 0.05), with treatment differences favouring tolrestat for toe sensation and pain (p < 0.05)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind withdrawal trial, tolrestat continuation vs discontinuation after long-term treatment (52 weeks)
cards.people: 372 patients who had taken tolrestat continuously for a mean 4.2 years, randomised double-blind to continued tolrestat or placebo for 52 weeks; patients who perceived worsening after 3 months could switch once to the alternate group while maintaining the blind (28 switched tolrestat→placebo; 36 switched placebo→tolrestat).
cards.result: Patients assigned to placebo deteriorated significantly in motor nerve conduction velocity while those maintained on tolrestat did not (p < 0.05); the 28 who switched from tolrestat to placebo deteriorated and the 36 who switched from placebo to tolrestat improved (p < 0.05). Treatment differences favouring tolrestat were observed for toe sensation and pain (p < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: Randomisation after 4.2 years of open treatment enriches for tolerators and responders, and the permitted one-way switch makes this a withdrawal-effect estimate, not an all-comer treatment effect. Endpoints remain conduction velocity and sensation measures.
cards.source: Santiago et al. Withdrawal of the aldose reductase inhibitor tolrestat in patients with diabetic neuropathy: effect on nerve function. The Tolrestat Study Group. cards.headline: Single-centre European-trial report (van Gerven 1992, labelled as such): conduction velocity and vibration threshold deteriorated on placebo over 6 months and did not deteriorate on tolrestat, and the placebo group's deterioration stopped when tolrestat was given open-label
cards.summary: Single-centre European-trial report (van Gerven 1992, labelled as such): conduction velocity and vibration threshold deteriorated on placebo over 6 months and did not deteriorate on tolrestat, and the placebo group's deterioration stopped when tolrestat was given open-label
cards.type: Single-centre report of a larger European trial (labelled) — double-blind phase then open-label phase, tolrestat in diabetic sensory polyneuropathy
cards.people: Patients with confirmed diabetic sensory polyneuropathy at a single centre of a larger European trial — a 6-month double-blind placebo-controlled phase followed by a 6-month open-label phase in which most patients received tolrestat. The abstract does not print the single-centre N, and none is claimed here (N not documented in the abstract).
cards.result: After the double-blind phase, motor and sensory nerve conduction velocity had deteriorated significantly in the placebo group but not on tolrestat, and vibration threshold likewise deteriorated on placebo only. During open-label tolrestat, conduction velocity and vibration threshold improved, and the deterioration in patients initially on placebo stopped.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre slice of a larger trial, reported qualitatively in its abstract with no centre N and no effect sizes — supporting evidence only, never load-bearing, and not a fifth independent trial population separate from the European programme it belongs to.

cards.headline: Class context (Cochrane synthesis, Chalk 2007 — programme support, not counted in this shelf's trial base): across 32 aldose reductase inhibitor trials there was no overall significant difference in neurological function (standardised mean difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05), although a four-trial tolrestat subgroup favoured treatment
cards.summary: Class context (Cochrane synthesis, Chalk 2007 — programme support, not counted in this shelf's trial base): across 32 aldose reductase inhibitor trials there was no overall significant difference in neurological function (standardised mean difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05), although a four-trial tolrestat subgroup favoured treatment
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of aldose reductase inhibitors in diabetic polyneuropathy — programme/class support only, not counted as a tolrestat trial
cards.people: 32 randomised controlled trials of aldose reductase inhibitors vs control lasting at least 6 months in diabetic polyneuropathy; meta-analysis data were available for 13 studies (879 treated participants and 909 controls).
cards.result: No overall significant difference in change in neurological function between aldose reductase inhibitor and control groups (SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05); one subgroup analysis (four tolrestat trials) favoured treatment. A dichotomised symptom analysis suggested benefit while continuous-scale symptom trials contradicted it; there was no overall benefit on nerve conduction parameters or foot ulceration, and quality of life was assessed in no trial.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis is the class-level counterweight and must stay on the face: the tolrestat trials carded above sit inside a class whose pooled neurological-function result is null. It is support context, not a sixth tolrestat report.
cards.source: Chalk et al. Aldose reductase inhibitors for the treatment of diabetic polyneuropathy. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2007. PMID: 17943821. cards.headline: Synthesis: tolrestat 200 mg/day shows modest, surrogate-led signals across five reports — paraesthetic (not painful) symptom improvement and conduction/reflex gains in small 1990s trials, deterioration on withdrawal after long-term use — inside a class whose Cochrane synthesis is null overall, so the stamp stays POSSIBLE and surrogate-qualified
cards.summary: Synthesis: tolrestat 200 mg/day shows modest, surrogate-led signals across five reports — paraesthetic (not painful) symptom improvement and conduction/reflex gains in small 1990s trials, deterioration on withdrawal after long-term use — inside a class whose Cochrane synthesis is null overall, so the stamp stays POSSIBLE and surrogate-qualified
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the multicentre symptomatic trial (200 mg analysis set n = 112 vs placebo n = 107), the mild-neuropathy trial (N = 45), the subclinical-neuropathy trial (N = 57), the withdrawal trial (N = 372) and the labelled single-centre European report (centre N not documented in its abstract), plus the Cochrane class synthesis as support only. Class siblings are homed separately: sorbinil (pack #7724), ranirestat and epalrestat (wave-53 assignments), ponalrestat (pack #7760) and fidarestat (pack #7766).
cards.result: Every positive endpoint in the trial base is nerve conduction, cardiovascular reflex testing or vibration threshold; the one symptom signal in the largest analysis is confined to paraesthetic symptoms, with painful symptoms improving equally on placebo. The class Cochrane result (SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.56 to 0.05) is printed on this shelf's face so the tolrestat subgroup signal is never read as a class effect.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Tolrestat was a 1990s programme and is not a current treatment recommendation.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Ponalrestat for diabetic neuropathy: a uniformly negative programme — four randomised trials totalling 423 patients found no significant benefit on symptoms, conduction or autonomic measures
shelves.question: In adults with chronic symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor ponalrestat (600 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve symptoms, nerve conduction or autonomic function?

shelves.balance: A uniformly negative programme — the nulls lead, in full. Four randomised placebo-controlled reports of ponalrestat 600 mg/day totalling 423 patients (259 over 18 months; 50 and 60 over one year; 54 over 24 weeks at 300/600 mg) found no significant benefit on any prespecified symptom, conduction, vibration, thermal or autonomic measure. The single positive signal is one autonomic subgroup in the largest trial (patients with an abnormal 30:15 ratio on ponalrestat did not deteriorate on that test while placebo patients did; n = 84). Ponalrestat was never marketed. This shelf records the aldose reductase class's negative pole beside tolrestat (pack #7759) and sorbinil; no benefit is claimed.

cards.headline: UK/Scandinavian Ponalrestat Trial (Sundkvist 1992, N = 259, 18 months): NO beneficial effect of ponalrestat 600 mg/day on vibration perception thresholds, nerve conduction velocities or nerve action potential amplitudes; the placebo group did not deteriorate, so prevention of deterioration was not tested
cards.summary: UK/Scandinavian Ponalrestat Trial (Sundkvist 1992, N = 259, 18 months): NO beneficial effect of ponalrestat 600 mg/day on vibration perception thresholds, nerve conduction velocities or nerve action potential amplitudes; the placebo group did not deteriorate, so prevention of deterioration was not tested
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (UK/Scandinavian Ponalrestat Trial), ponalrestat in diabetic peripheral neuropathy (18 months)
cards.people: 259 patients with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy (abnormal vibration perception threshold and abnormal peroneal motor conduction velocity) in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of ponalrestat 600 mg daily for 18 months.
cards.result: Overall, no beneficial effect of ponalrestat was detected on vibration perception thresholds, nerve conduction velocities or nerve action potential amplitudes. In the subgroup with an abnormal 30:15 heart-rate ratio (n = 84), patients on ponalrestat did not deteriorate on that autonomic test while those on placebo did — the single positive signal in this shelf's base.
cards.watchOut: The one autonomic subgroup finding (n = 84) does not offset the null primary picture, and because placebo patients did not deteriorate, this trial cannot support any claim that ponalrestat prevents progression.

cards.summary: One-year single-centre trial (Krentz 1992, N = 50): NO significant differences between ponalrestat 600 mg/day and placebo in motor or sensory conduction velocities, vibration thresholds, symptom scores or autonomic tests at 52 weeks; ponalrestat was clinically well tolerated
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled single-centre trial, ponalrestat in chronic symptomatic diabetic neuropathy (52 weeks)
cards.people: 50 patients with chronic symptomatic distal symmetrical diabetic neuropathy in a 52-week randomised double-blind parallel-group placebo-controlled single-centre study (peroneal motor conduction velocity of at least 30 m/s required).
cards.result: At 52 weeks there were no significant differences between ponalrestat and placebo in motor (ulnar, median, peroneal) or sensory (ulnar, radial) nerve conduction velocities, vibration perception thresholds, adjectival symptom scores or autonomic function tests. Ponalrestat had no significant effect on glycaemic control.
cards.watchOut: A complete null across every prespecified measure. The authors note the neuropathy may have been too advanced and the neurophysiological techniques poorly reproducible — context for the null, not a positive finding.

cards.people: 60 patients with symptomatic diabetic neuropathy randomised 2:1 to ponalrestat 600 mg once daily or placebo over 12 months after a 4-week placebo run-in; 46 completed (30 ponalrestat, 16 placebo).
cards.result: No significant differences between groups could be demonstrated during the study across motor and sensory conduction, thermal and vibration thresholds, heart-rate variation, E/I ratio, pupillary measures and symptom scores; the only signals were 6-month trends (P = 0.06). cards.people: 54 patients (median age 56 years) with chronic symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, randomly allocated to placebo or ponalrestat 300 or 600 mg for 24 weeks; patients with very abnormal vibration or thermal thresholds were excluded.

cards.watchOut: The shortest and smallest trial in the base, with the most abnormal patients excluded — still null at both doses.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ponalrestat 600 mg/day is a uniformly negative programme — four randomised reports totalling 423 patients found no significant benefit on any prespecified symptom or electrophysiological measure, and the nulls lead this shelf in full

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the UK/Scandinavian trial (N = 259), the single-centre trial (N = 50), the Ziegler trial (60 randomised) and the dose trial (N = 54) — 423 randomised patients in total. Class siblings are homed separately: tolrestat (pack #7759), sorbinil (pack #7724), ranirestat and epalrestat (wave-53 assignments) and fidarestat (pack #7766).
cards.result: The single positive signal in the entire base is one autonomic subgroup in the largest trial (non-deterioration of the 30:15 ratio, n = 84). Nothing in this base supports a benefit claim, and no wording on this shelf softens four nulls into 'mixed' evidence. Ponalrestat was never marketed; the shelf exists so the aldose reductase record carries the class's negative pole beside tolrestat and sorbinil.

shelves.title: Oxcarbazepine for painful diabetic neuropathy: a split base — the small titrated trial was positive (pain −24.3 vs −14.7), while the two larger trials missed their primary endpoints at every dose
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does oxcarbazepine (600–1,800 mg/day), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?

shelves.balance: A split base — the split leads. Three 16-week placebo-controlled trials totalling 634 patients disagree on their primary endpoints: the smallest (N = 146), which titrated oxcarbazepine 300→1,800 mg/day to effect, was positive (visual-analogue pain −24.3 vs −14.7, p = 0.01; >50% reduction 35.2% vs 18.4%); the fixed-dose 1,200 mg/day trial (N = 141) found no significant difference; and the dose-ranging trial (N = 347) found no difference at 600, 1,200 or 1,800 mg/day on its primary endpoint, with significant differences only in a secondary whole-phase analysis at the two higher doses. Any benefit appears dose-dependent at 1,200–1,800 mg/day, doses at which the carbamazepine family's tolerability burden matters; the fetched abstracts report adverse events as mostly mild-to-moderate and titration-phase, and nothing here supports a cleaner record than 16-week trials show.

cards.headline: Titrated-dose trial (Dogra 2005, N = 146): oxcarbazepine titrated 300→1,800 mg/day reduced average visual-analogue pain by −24.3 vs −14.7 units on placebo (p = 0.01) over 16 weeks; >50% pain reduction in 35.2% vs 18.4% (p = 0.0156; number needed to treat 6.0)
cards.summary: Titrated-dose trial (Dogra 2005, N = 146): oxcarbazepine titrated 300→1,800 mg/day reduced average visual-analogue pain by −24.3 vs −14.7 units on placebo (p = 0.01) over 16 weeks; >50% pain reduction in 35.2% vs 18.4% (p = 0.0156; number needed to treat 6.0)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial, titrated oxcarbazepine in painful diabetic neuropathy (16 weeks)
cards.people: 146 patients with a 6-month to 5-year history of diabetic neuropathic pain (visual-analogue score ≥50 units), randomised to oxcarbazepine titrated from 300 mg/day to a maximum 1,800 mg/day (n = 69) or placebo (n = 77) for 16 weeks.
cards.result: Average visual-analogue pain fell −24.3 on oxcarbazepine vs −14.7 on placebo (p = 0.01), with separation as early as week 2. A >50% pain reduction occurred in 35.2% vs 18.4% (p = 0.0156; NNT 6.0), and the global therapeutic-effect rating improved in 48% vs 22% (p = 0.0025). Most adverse events were mild to moderate and transient.
cards.watchOut: The only one of this shelf's three trials that is positive on its primary endpoint — and the smallest. Titration to effect means the achieved doses vary; the result does not identify a fixed effective dose.

cards.people: 141 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy randomised to oxcarbazepine 1,200 mg/day (n = 71) or placebo (n = 70) in a multicentre double-blind 16-week study.
cards.result: The primary efficacy variable — change in mean visual-analogue score from baseline to the last study week — was similar between the oxcarbazepine and placebo groups, with no statistically significant difference. cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre dose-ranging trial, oxcarbazepine in painful diabetic neuropathy (16 weeks)
cards.people: 347 patients with diabetic neuropathy randomised to oxcarbazepine 600 mg/day (n = 83), 1,200 mg/day (n = 87), 1,800 mg/day (n = 88) or placebo (n = 89) in a multicentre double-blind 16-week study.
cards.result: No oxcarbazepine group differed from placebo on the primary endpoint. The 1,200 and 1,800 mg/day groups showed non-significant trends on that endpoint (P = 0.101, P = 0.096) and statistically significant differences on overall mean weekly visual-analogue scores across the whole treatment phase (P = 0.038 and P = 0.005).
cards.watchOut: The positive findings sit in a secondary whole-phase analysis after a null primary endpoint — they are hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory. Any benefit signal is confined to 1,200–1,800 mg/day, where the carbamazepine-family tolerability burden (dizziness, somnolence, hyponatraemia risk) matters; the fetched abstracts report adverse events as mostly mild-to-moderate and titration-phase.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a split base — the split leads. Only the smallest trial (titrated to effect, N = 146) is positive on its primary endpoint; the two larger trials (N = 141 and N = 347) both missed theirs, so oxcarbazepine's DPN evidence is SPLIT with the dose-ranging signal confined to secondary analyses at 1,200–1,800 mg/day

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the titrated-dose trial (N = 146), the fixed-dose 1,200 mg/day trial (N = 141) and the dose-ranging trial (N = 347) — 634 randomised patients in total, all 16-week trials. A 30-patient open-label study located at mining is support only and is not counted. Oxcarbazepine's trigeminal-neuralgia and antiseizure-in-pregnancy shelves are different questions (cross-point only).
cards.result: Primary-endpoint results: positive (titrated, p = 0.01), null (fixed 1,200 mg/day), null at all three doses (dose-ranging), with the dose-ranging trial's significant findings limited to a secondary whole-phase analysis at 1,200 and 1,800 mg/day. No wording on this shelf presents the secondary analysis as a primary win.

shelves.title: Lamotrigine for painful diabetic neuropathy: inconsistent at scale — a strongly positive 59-patient trial, then a 720-patient replicate programme positive in one study only at 400 mg
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does lamotrigine (200–400 mg/day), compared with placebo or amitriptyline, reduce neuropathic pain?

shelves.balance: Inconsistent at scale — the inconsistency leads. The 59-patient placebo trial was strongly positive (pain 6.4→4.2 vs 6.5→5.3, p < 0.001), but the adequately powered replicate programme — two studies of 360 patients each in a single report — found a lamotrigine 400 mg effect on the week-19 primary endpoint in Study 2 only (−2.7 vs −1.6, p ≤ 0.05), not replicated in Study 1, with 200 and 300 mg null in both studies; the authors themselves conclude lamotrigine was inconsistently effective. A 53-patient crossover against amitriptyline found no significant difference between treatments. Rash recurs in both the replicate programme (adverse events 71–82% on lamotrigine vs 63–70% on placebo; headache and rash commonest) and the crossover (rash in 7%), and lamotrigine's slow titration requirement applies. The crossover's preferred dose (25 mg twice daily) is far below the placebo-tested doses and the two findings are not merged into a dose claim here.

cards.headline: Small placebo trial (Eisenberg 2001, N = 59): lamotrigine titrated 25→400 mg/day reduced daily numerical pain scores from 6.4 to 4.2 vs 6.5 to 5.3 on placebo over 6 weeks (p < 0.001 at doses of 200, 300 and 400 mg); McGill, disability and depression scores were unchanged in both groups
cards.summary: Small placebo trial (Eisenberg 2001, N = 59): lamotrigine titrated 25→400 mg/day reduced daily numerical pain scores from 6.4 to 4.2 vs 6.5 to 5.3 on placebo over 6 weeks (p < 0.001 at doses of 200, 300 and 400 mg); McGill, disability and depression scores were unchanged in both groups
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, lamotrigine vs placebo in painful diabetic neuropathy (6 weeks)
cards.people: 59 patients with diabetic neuropathy pain randomised to lamotrigine (titrated 25→400 mg/day; 29 assigned, 24 completed) or placebo (30 assigned, 22 completed) for 6 weeks.
cards.result: Daily numerical pain scores fell from 6.4 to 4.2 on lamotrigine vs 6.5 to 5.3 on placebo (p < 0.001 for lamotrigine doses of 200, 300 and 400 mg). McGill Pain Questionnaire, Pain Disability Index and Beck Depression Inventory scores were unchanged in both groups; the global assessment favoured lamotrigine and the adverse-event profile was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A strongly positive result in 59 patients over 6 weeks — the small-study end of this shelf's base. It did not survive replication at scale (next two cards), and the pattern must be read whole.

cards.headline: Replicate programme, Study 1 (Vinik 2007 — one of two replicate studies in a single report, labelled as such): lamotrigine 400 mg/day did NOT beat placebo on the primary endpoint (mean pain-intensity reduction at week 19), and 200 and 300 mg did not differ from placebo either

cards.type: Replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study 1 of 2 (single report, labelled slice), lamotrigine in painful diabetic neuropathy (19 weeks)
cards.people: 360 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy in Study 1 of two replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled studies, randomised to lamotrigine 200, 300 or 400 mg daily or placebo over 19 weeks (7-week escalation, 12-week fixed-dose maintenance).
cards.result: The Study 2 finding (next card) was not replicated in Study 1: no lamotrigine dose separated from placebo on the week-19 primary endpoint in Study 1. Across both studies, adverse events occurred in 71–82% on lamotrigine vs 63–70% on placebo, the most common being headache and rash.
cards.watchOut: Study 1 and Study 2 are two studies in ONE publication (PMID 17161535) — they are carded as labelled slices of that report so the non-replication is visible, and the report counts once in this shelf's base of three reports.

cards.summary: Replicate programme, Study 2 (Vinik 2007 — second study in the same single report, labelled as such): lamotrigine 400 mg/day beat placebo on the primary endpoint in Study 2 only (observed pain scores −2.7 vs −1.6, p ≤ 0.05); the authors conclude lamotrigine was inconsistently effective
cards.type: Replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study 2 of 2 (single report, labelled slice), lamotrigine in painful diabetic neuropathy (19 weeks)
cards.people: 360 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy in Study 2 of the same replicate programme, randomised to lamotrigine 200, 300 or 400 mg daily or placebo over 19 weeks.
cards.result: Mean pain-intensity reduction at week 19 was greater on lamotrigine 400 mg than placebo in Study 2 (observed scores −2.7 vs −1.6 on a 0–10 scale, p ≤ 0.05). Lamotrigine 200 and 300 mg did not differ from placebo at week 19 in either study, and 300/400 mg were only occasionally more effective on secondary endpoints.
cards.watchOut: One positive study of two at one dose (400 mg) is inconsistency, not confirmation. Rash recurs as an adverse event in this programme and must stay on the face, with the slow titration lamotrigine requires.

cards.headline: Active-comparator crossover trial (Jose 2007, N = 53): good pain relief in 41% on lamotrigine vs 28% on amitriptyline by patient global assessment, with NO significant difference between treatments on global assessments, McGill or Likert scales; of 44 adverse events, 33 (75%) were on amitriptyline and 11 (25%) on lamotrigine, including rash in 3 patients (7%)
cards.summary: Active-comparator crossover trial (Jose 2007, N = 53): good pain relief in 41% on lamotrigine vs 28% on amitriptyline by patient global assessment, with NO significant difference between treatments on global assessments, McGill or Likert scales; of 44 adverse events, 33 (75%) were on amitriptyline and 11 (25%) on lamotrigine, including rash in 3 patients (7%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover active-comparator trial, lamotrigine vs amitriptyline in painful diabetic neuropathy
cards.people: 53 patients with chronic painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy in a randomised double-blind crossover trial of lamotrigine (25–100 mg twice daily) vs amitriptyline (10–50 mg at night), each dose level for 2 weeks with optional titration, separated by a 2-week placebo washout.
cards.result: Good, moderate and mild relief were reported in 41%, 13% and 15% on lamotrigine vs 28%, 11% and 33% on amitriptyline by patient global assessment, with no significant difference between treatments on patient/physician global assessments, McGill questionnaire or Likert scale; both treatments improved pain from 2 weeks. Adverse events: 33 of 44 on amitriptyline (sedation commonest, 43% of patients) vs 11 on lamotrigine, including rash in 3 patients (7%) and creatinine elevations in 4 (9%). The preferred lamotrigine dose was 25 mg twice daily.
cards.watchOut: No placebo group, so this trial cannot estimate lamotrigine's effect size — and its preferred dose (25 mg twice daily) is far below the 200–400 mg doses tested against placebo, so the two findings must not be merged into a dose claim.
cards.source: Jose et al. Randomized double-blind study comparing the efficacy and safety of lamotrigine and amitriptyline in painful diabetic neuropathy. shelves.title: Tramadol for painful diabetic neuropathy: pain reduced over 42–66 days in two placebo-controlled trials (444 patients) — an opioid-class agent on short double-blind evidence, with only an open extension beyond that
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does tramadol (alone or as the fixed tramadol/acetaminophen combination), compared with placebo, reduce neuropathic pain?

shelves.balance: An opioid-class agent on short double-blind evidence — the class flag leads. Two placebo-controlled trials totalling 444 patients show tramadol reduces diabetic neuropathic pain over 42 days (monotherapy, average 210 mg/day, p < 0.001 on mean pain intensity) and 66 days (tramadol/acetaminophen combination, pain −2.71 vs −1.83, p = 0.001); an open extension of the monotherapy trial's completers shows maintenance to 6 months without a control group. The combination trial had no tramadol-alone or acetaminophen-alone arm, so it cannot isolate tramadol's contribution. Tramadol's dependence, hyponatraemia and falls record is homed at pack #5874 and is cross-pointed here; 6-week efficacy is not a long-term benefit–harm balance.

cards.headline: Monotherapy trial (Harati 1998, N = 131, 42 days): tramadol at an average 210 mg/day was significantly more effective than placebo on mean pain intensity (p < 0.001), with better physical (p = 0.02) and social functioning (p = 0.04) ratings and no significant treatment effect on sleep
cards.summary: Monotherapy trial (Harati 1998, N = 131, 42 days): tramadol at an average 210 mg/day was significantly more effective than placebo on mean pain intensity (p < 0.001), with better physical (p = 0.02) and social functioning (p = 0.04) ratings and no significant treatment effect on sleep
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial, tramadol monotherapy in painful diabetic neuropathy (42 days)
cards.people: 131 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy (65 tramadol / 66 placebo) in a multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group trial with a 42-day double-blind phase after analgesic washout; tramadol given in divided doses four times daily.
cards.result: Tramadol was significantly more effective than placebo on mean pain intensity (p < 0.001) and on physical (p = 0.02) and social functioning (p = 0.04) ratings; no statistically significant treatment effect on sleep was identified. The most frequent adverse events were nausea, constipation, headache and somnolence.
cards.watchOut: 42 days of double-blind evidence for an opioid-class agent. This trial cannot speak to long-term benefit–harm, dependence or falls — those are the subject of the homed harm shelf (pack #5874), cross-pointed on this shelf's face.

cards.headline: Combination trial (Freeman 2007, N = 313, 66 days): tramadol 37.5 mg / acetaminophen 325 mg tablets reduced average daily pain by −2.71 vs −1.83 on placebo (p = 0.001), with greater improvement in sleep interference and global impression; nausea in 11.9% vs 3.3%
cards.summary: Combination trial (Freeman 2007, N = 313, 66 days): tramadol 37.5 mg / acetaminophen 325 mg tablets reduced average daily pain by −2.71 vs −1.83 on placebo (p = 0.001), with greater improvement in sleep interference and global impression; nausea in 11.9% vs 3.3%
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial, tramadol/acetaminophen combination in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (66 days)
cards.people: 313 adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy of the lower extremities (160 combination / 153 placebo), randomised to tramadol/acetaminophen 37.5/325 mg tablets (1–2 tablets four times daily) or placebo for 66 days; the trial is registered as NCT00210847.
cards.result: Average daily pain fell −2.71 on the combination vs −1.83 on placebo (p = 0.001), with significantly greater improvement on pain intensity, sleep interference, global impression and several quality-of-life and mood measures. Nausea occurred in 11.9% vs 3.3%; adverse events led to early discontinuation in 8.1% vs 6.5%.
cards.watchOut: The design had no tramadol-alone or acetaminophen-alone control group (the authors state this limitation), so this trial cannot isolate tramadol's contribution — the combination result must never be printed as a tramadol monotherapy effect.

randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial, tramadol/acetaminophen combination in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (66 days) 313 adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy of the lower extremities (160 combination / 153 placebo), randomised to tramadol/acetaminophen 37.5/325 mg tablets (1–2 tablets four times daily) or placebo for 66 days; the trial is registered as nct00210847. average daily pain fell −2.71 on the combination vs −1.83 on placebo (p = 0.001), with significantly greater improvement on pain intensity, sleep interference, global impression and several quality-of-life and mood measures. nausea occurred in 11.9% vs 3.3%; adverse events led to early discontinuation in 8.1% vs 6.5%. the design had no tramadol-alone or acetaminophen-alone control group (the authors state this limitation), so this trial cannot isolate tramadol's contribution — the combination result must never be printed as a tramadol monotherapy effect. freeman et al. randomized study of tramadol/acetaminophen versus placebo in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy. current medical research and opinion. 2007. pmid: 17257476. registry id: nct00210847. mesh: acetaminophen/therapeutic use · adult · aged · analgesics, non-narcotic/therapeutic use · analgesics, opioid/therapeutic use · analysis of variance · diabetic neuropathies/drug therapy,psychology · double-blind method · drug combinations · female · humans · male · middle aged · mood disorders/psychology · pain measurement · placebos · proportional hazards models · quality of life · sleep/drug effects · tablets · tramadol/therapeutic use · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Open-extension report (Harati 2000 — an open-label extension of the monotherapy trial, labelled as such): 117 patients entered up to 6 months of open tramadol 50–400 mg/day; former-placebo patients' pain intensity converged to the former-tramadol level by day 90 (both 1.4 on a 0–4 scale) and was maintained; 13 patients discontinued for adverse events

cards.type: Open-label extension report of the monotherapy trial (labelled), tramadol in painful diabetic neuropathy (up to 6 months)
cards.people: 117 patients (56 former tramadol / 61 former placebo) who completed the 42-day double-blind monotherapy trial and entered an open extension of up to 6 months on tramadol 50–400 mg/day.
cards.result: On day 1 of the extension, former-placebo patients had higher pain intensity (2.2 ± 1.02 vs 1.4 ± 0.93, P < 0.001); by day 90 both groups had mean pain intensity of 1.4, maintained to day 180, with similar pain-relief scores from day 30. Four patients discontinued for ineffective relief and 13 for adverse events; the most common adverse events were constipation, nausea and headache.
cards.watchOut: An open extension of completers of a 6-week trial — no control group, survivor-selected, and not a third trial. It shows maintenance in patients who stayed on treatment, nothing more.

shelves.title: Tapentadol ER for painful diabetic neuropathy: maintenance of relief in enriched responders in both phase 3 randomised-withdrawal trials (differences −1.3 and −0.95 points; pooled −1.14) — not an all-comer effect
shelves.question: In adults with chronic painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does tapentadol extended release (100–250 mg twice daily), compared with placebo in an enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal design, maintain pain relief?

shelves.balance: An enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal base — the design flag leads. The corrected base is three reports: both individual phase 3 trials (395 and 318 patients randomised after open-label titration) plus their pooled analysis of the same patients. In both trials, patients who had already responded to open-label tapentadol ER (100–250 mg twice daily) and were then randomised to continue it worsened less than patients withdrawn to placebo (least-squares mean differences −1.3 and −0.95 points; pooled −1.14, 95% CI −1.435 to −0.838). These are maintenance effects in responders, not all-comer treatment effects, and the placebo worsening is withdrawal in responders. Tapentadol is an opioid: nausea in 21.1% and vomiting in 12.7% during maintenance in trial 2, and treatment-emergent adverse events in 74.7% vs 56.0% in the pooled maintenance data; its other homed question (vs oxycodone in low back pain) is pack #5723.

cards.headline: Phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trial 1 (Schwartz 2011, NCT00455520): of 588 titration entrants, the 395 with ≥1-point pain reduction were randomised; the least-squares mean difference in pain change to week 12 was −1.3 (95% CI −1.70 to −0.92; p < 0.001) favouring continued tapentadol ER over withdrawal to placebo
cards.summary: Phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trial 1 (Schwartz 2011, NCT00455520): of 588 titration entrants, the 395 with ≥1-point pain reduction were randomised; the least-squares mean difference in pain change to week 12 was −1.3 (95% CI −1.70 to −0.92; p < 0.001) favouring continued tapentadol ER over withdrawal to placebo
cards.type: Phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trial, tapentadol ER in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (NCT00455520)
cards.people: 588 patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (≥3 months of analgesic use, dissatisfaction with current treatment, pain ≥5/10) entered a 3-week open-label titration to optimal-dose tapentadol ER 100–250 mg twice daily; the 395 with ≥1-point pain reduction were randomised 1:1 to placebo or their fixed optimal dose for 12 weeks.
cards.result: The least-squares mean difference in change in average pain intensity from randomisation to week 12 was −1.3 (95% CI −1.70 to −0.92; p < 0.001) favouring tapentadol ER. During titration 60.5% (356/588) achieved ≥30% pain improvement; of those randomised to tapentadol ER, 53.6% (105/196) maintained ≥30% improvement from pre-titration to week 12. The most common double-blind treatment-emergent adverse events on tapentadol ER included nausea, anxiety, diarrhoea and dizziness.
cards.watchOut: Enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal design: only open-label responders were randomised, so −1.3 measures maintenance of effect in responders — never an all-comer treatment effect. The placebo group's worsening is withdrawal of a drug that had already helped those patients, and unblinding through side-effect changes is a stated limitation.
cards.source: Schwartz et al. Safety and efficacy of tapentadol ER in patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy: results of a randomized-withdrawal, placebo-controlled trial. Current medical research and opinion. 2011. PMID: 21162697. Registry ID: NCT00455520. cards.headline: Phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trial 2 (Vinik 2014): 358 patients completed titration and 318 were randomised (152 placebo / 166 tapentadol ER); pain change during maintenance was +1.30 on placebo vs +0.28 on tapentadol ER (least-squares mean difference −0.95, 95% CI −1.42 to −0.49; P < 0.001), with nausea in 21.1% and vomiting in 12.7% on tapentadol ER
cards.summary: Phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trial 2 (Vinik 2014): 358 patients completed titration and 318 were randomised (152 placebo / 166 tapentadol ER); pain change during maintenance was +1.30 on placebo vs +0.28 on tapentadol ER (least-squares mean difference −0.95, 95% CI −1.42 to −0.49; P < 0.001), with nausea in 21.1% and vomiting in 12.7% on tapentadol ER
cards.type: Phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trial (replicate), tapentadol ER in chronic painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy
cards.people: Adults with moderate to severe diabetic peripheral neuropathy pain, titrated to tapentadol ER 100–250 mg twice daily over 3 weeks open-label; those with ≥1-point pain reduction were randomised to placebo or their optimal tapentadol ER dose for a 12-week double-blind fixed-dose maintenance phase. This report's own record carries no registry ID (the trial is NCT01041859 as named in the pooled report, card 3).
cards.result: Mean pain intensity fell from 7.33 at titration start to 4.16 at week 3 open-label. During double-blind maintenance, pain changed by +1.30 on placebo vs +0.28 on tapentadol ER (least-squares mean difference −0.95, 95% CI −1.42 to −0.49; P < 0.001). Treatment-emergent adverse events ≥10% on tapentadol ER during maintenance were nausea (21.1%) and vomiting (12.7%).
cards.watchOut: Same enriched design as trial 1: a maintenance effect in responders only. The −0.95 difference is the gap between slight worsening on continued treatment (+0.28) and larger worsening on withdrawal (+1.30) — it must never be printed as pain relief versus untreated patients.
cards.source: Vinik et al. cards.headline: Pooled analysis (Schwartz 2015 — a pooled analysis of the two trials above, labelled as such; randomised n = 343 placebo / 360 tapentadol ER): pain change to week 12 of maintenance +1.28 vs +0.08 (least-squares mean difference −1.14, 95% CI −1.435 to −0.838; P < 0.001); treatment-emergent adverse events in 74.7% on tapentadol ER vs 56.0% on placebo during maintenance
cards.summary: Pooled analysis (Schwartz 2015 — a pooled analysis of the two trials above, labelled as such; randomised n = 343 placebo / 360 tapentadol ER): pain change to week 12 of maintenance +1.28 vs +0.08 (least-squares mean difference −1.14, 95% CI −1.435 to −0.838; P < 0.001); treatment-emergent adverse events in 74.7% on tapentadol ER vs 56.0% on placebo during maintenance
cards.type: Pooled analysis of the two phase 3 trials above (labelled) — not an independent report, tapentadol ER in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy
cards.people: Pooled data from the two similarly designed enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trials above (NCT00455520 and NCT01041859) — the same patients as cards 1 and 2, not additional patients.
cards.result: Mean pain change from baseline to week 12 of maintenance was +1.28 (SD 2.41) on placebo vs +0.08 (SD 1.87) on tapentadol ER (least-squares mean difference −1.14, 95% CI −1.435 to −0.838; P < 0.001), with consistent efficacy across age, sex, race, opioid-experience and pain-intensity subgroups and several quality-of-life subscales favouring tapentadol ER. Treatment-emergent adverse events during maintenance occurred in 74.7% on tapentadol ER vs 56.0% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of cards 1 and 2: it adds precision and subgroup detail, not a third trial. The corrected base for this shelf is exactly three reports — both individual phase 3 reports plus this pooled analysis — and the pooled N (703 randomised) must never be added to the individual trials' Ns.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the corrected base is three reports — both individual phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trials plus their pooled analysis — and they consistently show tapentadol ER maintains pain relief in patients who already responded to it (differences −0.95 to −1.3 points), which is a maintenance claim in responders, not efficacy in all-comers
cards.summary: Synthesis: the corrected base is three reports — both individual phase 3 enriched-enrollment randomised-withdrawal trials plus their pooled analysis — and they consistently show tapentadol ER maintains pain relief in patients who already responded to it (differences −0.95 to −1.3 points), which is a maintenance claim in responders, not efficacy in all-comers
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: phase 3 trial 1 (588 titration entrants, 395 randomised, NCT00455520), phase 3 trial 2 (358 titration completers, 318 randomised) and their pooled analysis (703 randomised across the two trials — the same patients, counted once). Tapentadol's other homed question is tapentadol vs oxycodone in chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component (pack #5723) — a different population, cross-point only.
cards.result: Both trials used enriched enrollment: only patients with ≥1-point improvement during open-label titration were randomised, and the placebo arm is withdrawal in responders. Tapentadol is an opioid (mu-agonist / noradrenaline-reuptake inhibitor): nausea (21.1%) and vomiting (12.7%) in trial 2's maintenance phase and the class dependence record belong on this shelf's face, cross-pointed to pack #5723.

shelves.title: Methylcobalamin for diabetic neuropathy: exactly one placebo-controlled trial (N = 90, B12-low metformin users) — the rest of the base is dose, route and combination comparisons without placebo, with monotherapy the weakest arm head-to-head
shelves.question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (largely with low vitamin B12 status), does oral methylcobalamin (vitamin B12), compared with placebo, a different B12 dose or route, or combination therapy, improve neuropathy symptoms, signs or nerve function?

shelves.balance: Exactly one placebo-controlled trial — the composition leads. The base is four reports plus a supporting synthesis, but the placebo contrast rests on a single 90-patient, 1-year trial in metformin-treated patients selected for B12 < 400 pmol/L, which was positive across neurophysiological, sudomotor, pain and quality-of-life measures. The other three reports have no placebo group: a dose comparison (1,000 vs 2,000 µg/day, both arms improved, no between-dose difference, likewise B12-low patients only), an open-label comparison in which methylcobalamin alone was by far the weakest arm (pain fall 0.58 vs ~4 points for the pregabalin and duloxetine combinations), and a route comparison on a corneal-microscopy surrogate (32 completers). The supporting meta-analysis found mecobalamin alone not effective on pain or symptom outcomes across a mostly high-risk-of-bias literature. Nothing in this base estimates an effect in B12-replete diabetic neuropathy, and no wording here generalises beyond B12-low populations.

cards.headline: The base's ONLY placebo-controlled trial (Didangelos 2021, N = 90, 1 year): oral methylcobalamin 1,000 µg/day improved vibration threshold, questionnaire score, quality of life, pain score, sural conduction velocity, sural amplitude and sudomotor conductance (p from 0.014 to < 0.0001), while several measures deteriorated significantly on placebo
cards.summary: The base's ONLY placebo-controlled trial (Didangelos 2021, N = 90, 1 year): oral methylcobalamin 1,000 µg/day improved vibration threshold, questionnaire score, quality of life, pain score, sural conduction velocity, sural amplitude and sudomotor conductance (p from 0.014 to < 0.0001), while several measures deteriorated significantly on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial — the single placebo-controlled report in this base, oral methylcobalamin in diabetic neuropathy with B12 < 400 pmol/L (1 year)
cards.people: 90 patients with type 2 diabetes on metformin for ≥4 years, with peripheral and autonomic neuropathy and vitamin B12 < 400 pmol/L, randomised to oral methylcobalamin 1,000 µg/day (n = 44) or placebo (n = 46) for 1 year in a double-blind trial.
cards.result: B12 rose from 232.0 ± 71.8 to 776.7 ± 242.3 pmol/L on treatment. Vibration perception threshold, neuropathy questionnaire score, quality of life, pain score, sural conduction velocity, sural amplitude and foot sudomotor conductance all improved significantly on B12, while cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests and the examination score improved non-significantly; on placebo, the autonomic resultant, questionnaire score, sural velocity and amplitude, and pain score deteriorated significantly.
cards.watchOut: This one 90-patient trial carries the entire placebo contrast for the shelf, in a selected population: metformin-treated patients with B12 < 400 pmol/L. Nothing in it estimates an effect in B12-replete diabetic neuropathy, and it must never be presented as one of several placebo-controlled trials.
cards.source: Didangelos et al. Vitamin B12 Supplementation in Diabetic Neuropathy: A 1-Year, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Nutrients. 2021. PMID: 33513879. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dose-comparison trial (Mansour 2026 — a randomised dose-comparison trial with NO placebo group, labelled as such): in 35 randomised patients (32 completed) with B12 < 200 pg/mL, pain scores fell on both 1,000 µg/day (7.00 ± 2.03 → 5.60 ± 2.19, P = 0.016) and 2,000 µg/day (6.18 ± 2.40 → 4.42 ± 2.50, P = 0.007), with no significant between-group difference in neuropathic outcomes and a greater B12 rise at 2,000 µg (P = 0.049)
cards.summary: Dose-comparison trial (Mansour 2026 — a randomised dose-comparison trial with NO placebo group, labelled as such): in 35 randomised patients (32 completed) with B12 < 200 pg/mL, pain scores fell on both 1,000 µg/day (7.00 ± 2.03 → 5.60 ± 2.19, P = 0.016) and 2,000 µg/day (6.18 ± 2.40 → 4.42 ± 2.50, P = 0.007), with no significant between-group difference in neuropathic outcomes and a greater B12 rise at 2,000 µg (P = 0.049)
cards.type: Randomised dose-comparison trial with no placebo group (labelled), oral methylcobalamin 1,000 vs 2,000 µg/day in diabetic neuropathy with B12 < 200 pg/mL (16 weeks)
cards.people: 35 adults with type 2 diabetes, diabetic peripheral neuropathy and low serum B12 (< 200 pg/mL), randomised 1:1 to oral vitamin B12 (methylcobalamin) 1,000 or 2,000 µg/day for 16 weeks; 32 completed. Registered as IRCT20210925052566N3.
cards.result: Serum B12 rose significantly in both groups, more at 2,000 µg (P = 0.049). Pain (numerical rating scale) and examination (MNSIE) scores improved significantly in both groups with no significant difference between doses; the disability score (NDS) was unchanged in both. The 1,000 µg group improved HbA1c significantly; the 2,000 µg group showed a significant decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate.
cards.watchOut: Without a placebo group, within-group falls in pain scores cannot be attributed to B12 — regression to the mean and natural history are unconstrained. This trial compares doses; it is not efficacy evidence against no treatment, and it likewise enrolled only B12-low patients.
cards.source: Mansour et al. cards.headline: Open-label comparative trial (Sharma 2021, N = 100, 12 weeks): methylcobalamin ALONE was by far the weakest arm — visual-analogue pain fall 0.58 ± 0.14, against 3.82 ± 0.05 for methylcobalamin + pregabalin and 4.17 ± 0.48 for methylcobalamin + duloxetine; vibration-perception responder proportions 11.6% (alone) vs 37.9% / 41.4% (combinations)
cards.summary: Open-label comparative trial (Sharma 2021, N = 100, 12 weeks): methylcobalamin ALONE was by far the weakest arm — visual-analogue pain fall 0.58 ± 0.14, against 3.82 ± 0.05 for methylcobalamin + pregabalin and 4.17 ± 0.48 for methylcobalamin + duloxetine; vibration-perception responder proportions 11.6% (alone) vs 37.9% / 41.4% (combinations)
cards.type: Prospective randomised open-label comparative trial, methylcobalamin alone vs methylcobalamin combinations in painful diabetic neuropathy (12 weeks)
cards.people: 100 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy in a prospective randomised open-label three-group trial: methylcobalamin alone, methylcobalamin + pregabalin, or methylcobalamin + duloxetine, assessed over 12 weeks.
cards.result: The fall in visual-analogue pain was 0.58 ± 0.14 on methylcobalamin alone vs 3.82 ± 0.05 (with pregabalin) and 4.17 ± 0.48 (with duloxetine). Increases in vibration perception were 11.6% (alone) vs 37.9% / 41.4% (combinations); pressure and thermal sensitivity showed the same ordering. Adverse effects occurred in 0% (alone), 6.9% and 10.3% (combinations).
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo group: the combination arms' larger falls cannot be separated from pregabalin/duloxetine effects and expectation. The load-bearing reading is the monotherapy arm's small fall (0.58 points) — the weakest result in this shelf's base for methylcobalamin itself.

cards.headline: Route-comparison trial (Zhang 2021 — a randomised route-comparison trial with NO placebo group, labelled as such; NCT04372316): intramuscular mecobalamin improved corneal inferior-whorl length (21.64 ± 3.00 vs 17.64 ± 4.83 mm/mm² baseline, P < 0.01) while oral tablets did not; 15 (injection) and 17 (oral) patients completed 8 weeks, with no adverse events in either group
cards.summary: Route-comparison trial (Zhang 2021 — a randomised route-comparison trial with NO placebo group, labelled as such; NCT04372316): intramuscular mecobalamin improved corneal inferior-whorl length (21.64 ± 3.00 vs 17.64 ± 4.83 mm/mm² baseline, P < 0.01) while oral tablets did not; 15 (injection) and 17 (oral) patients completed 8 weeks, with no adverse events in either group
cards.type: Randomised route-comparison trial with no placebo group (labelled), intramuscular vs oral mecobalamin in diabetic peripheral neuropathy (8 weeks; NCT04372316)
cards.people: Patients with mild-to-moderate diabetic peripheral neuropathy randomised to mecobalamin intramuscular injection (0.5 mg/day three times weekly) or oral tablets (1.5 mg/day) for 8 weeks; 15 injection and 17 oral patients completed, assessed by corneal confocal microscopy.
cards.result: Corneal inferior-whorl length improved significantly on injection but not on tablets; corneal nerve fibre length, branch density and autonomic symptom score likewise improved on injection only. No adverse events occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Corneal confocal microscopy is a surrogate endpoint, the completer N is 32, and there is no placebo group — this trial compares routes, not treatment vs no treatment. It cannot support an efficacy claim for either route against untreated neuropathy.
cards.source: Zhang et al. Using corneal confocal microscopy to compare Mecobalamin intramuscular injections vs oral tablets in treating diabetic peripheral neuropathy: a RCT. Scientific reports. 2021. PMID: 34282267. Registry ID: NCT04372316. cards.headline: Programme support (Sawangjit 2020 systematic review / meta-analysis — support only, not counted): across 15 mecobalamin RCTs (1,707 patients with diabetic or herpetic neuropathy), mecobalamin alone was NOT effective on pain score or neuropathic symptom outcomes, combination treatment was effective on conduction outcomes, and 11 of 15 included studies were rated high risk of bias

cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of mecobalamin RCTs — programme support only, not counted in this shelf's base
cards.people: 15 randomised trials of mecobalamin in peripheral neuropathy (diabetic peripheral neuropathy and herpetic neuropathy), 1,707 patients, searched to December 2019; 73% of included studies were rated high risk of bias, 20% some concerns and 7% low risk.
cards.result: Mecobalamin alone (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.33) and in combination (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.21 to 1.45) exceeded active control on a composite 'clinical therapeutic efficacy' outcome — relative measures against active comparators, not placebo. Only combination treatment was effective on nerve conduction outcomes; neither alone nor in combination was effective on pain score or neuropathic symptom outcomes. No serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis of a mostly high-risk-of-bias literature, pooling diabetic and herpetic neuropathy and active-control comparisons — it does not add a placebo-controlled trial to this shelf, and its null pain/symptom result for mecobalamin alone is part of this shelf's balance.

cards.headline: Synthesis: exactly ONE placebo-controlled trial exists in this base — the composition leads. A single 90-patient trial in B12-low metformin users was positive across neurophysiological and symptom measures; the remaining reports are a dose comparison and a route comparison (both without placebo) and an open-label comparison in which methylcobalamin alone was the weakest arm, so the base is MAYBE (weak evidence) and applies to B12-low populations only

A single 90-patient trial in B12-low metformin users was positive across neurophysiological and symptom measures; the remaining reports are a dose comparison and a route comparison (both without placebo) and an open-label comparison in which methylcobalamin alone was the weakest arm, so the base is MAYBE (weak evidence) and applies to B12-low populations only
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the placebo-controlled trial (N = 90), the dose-comparison trial (35 randomised, no placebo), the open-label comparative trial (N = 100, no placebo) and the route-comparison trial (32 completers, no placebo), plus the Sawangjit synthesis as support only. Methylcobalamin's other homed question is ultra-high-dose intramuscular methylcobalamin in ALS (pack #6741) — a different disease and dose, cross-point only; the factorial acetyl-L-carnitine ± methylcobalamin trial sits as support in pack #7697 and is not counted here.
cards.result: Composition, printed plainly: 1 placebo-controlled trial; 3 non-placebo comparisons; 1 supporting synthesis whose pain/symptom result for mecobalamin alone was null. The dose and placebo trials both enrolled only B12-low patients (< 200 pg/mL and < 400 pmol/L respectively), so nothing here estimates an effect in B12-replete diabetic neuropathy. shelves.question: In adults with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does the aldose reductase inhibitor fidarestat (1 mg/day), compared with placebo, improve nerve conduction or subjective symptoms over 52 weeks?

shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK: the entire clinical base is exactly 1 report — the count leads. One 52-week multicentre placebo-controlled trial (Hotta 2001, 279 patients, fidarestat 1 mg/day) found five of eight electrophysiological measures improved from baseline on fidarestat (two of eight significantly better than placebo at study end: median F-wave conduction velocity and minimal latency), a subjective-symptom battery uniformly significant vs placebo, and an adverse-event profile not differing significantly from placebo. This shelf cards that single report as four labelled slices (design, electrophysiology, symptoms, tolerability/context) to meet the format without inflating the count: the report count is 1. One unreplicated trial from a single-region programme, for a drug never marketed, rowed deliberately under slate 21's explicit invitation to complete the aldose reductase class shelf — it contracts back to the audit record if the developer declines.

shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does venlafaxine (75–225 mg/day), compared with placebo, imipramine or pregabalin/carbamazepine, reduce neuropathic pain?

shelves.balance: Composition first: of the 3 reports carded, only ONE is a placebo-controlled trial in diabetic neuropathy — Rowbotham 2004 (N = 244, 6 weeks), where pain fell 50% on venlafaxine extended-release 150–225 mg/day vs 27% on placebo (P < 0.001; NNT 4.5 for 50% pain reduction), while 75 mg was near-placebo (32% vs 27%). The second DPN report (Razazian 2014, N = 257) has no placebo group and ranked venlafaxine last of three active drugs (pregabalin more efficacious; no significant superiority between carbamazepine and venlafaxine). The third report (Sindrup 2003) is a mixed-aetiology polyneuropathy crossover — not diabetes-specific — in which venlafaxine matched imipramine. Seven patients on venlafaxine in the placebo-controlled trial had clinically important ECG changes. Cross-points only: venlafaxine's hot-flush shelf (#1788) and the homed DPN agents (duloxetine pathway #3522, capsaicin 8% patch #2697, mirogabalin #2031) ask different questions and share no anchors with this shelf.

cards.headline: Rowbotham 2004 — the base's ONLY placebo-controlled DPN trial: pain fell 50% on venlafaxine 150–225 mg vs 27% on placebo at 6 weeks (P < 0.001); the 75 mg dose was near-placebo (32%)
cards.summary: Rowbotham 2004 — the base's ONLY placebo-controlled DPN trial: pain fell 50% on venlafaxine 150–225 mg vs 27% on placebo at 6 weeks (P < 0.001); the 75 mg dose was near-placebo (32%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in painful diabetic neuropathy (Rowbotham 2004) — report 1 of 3, and the base's only placebo-controlled DPN trial
cards.people: 244 adult outpatients with metabolically stable type 1 or type 2 diabetes and painful diabetic neuropathy, in a multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of venlafaxine extended-release 75 mg/day, 150–225 mg/day or placebo for 6 weeks. Baseline pain intensity 68.7 mm (moderately severe).
cards.result: Percentage reduction in visual-analogue pain intensity at week 6 was 27% on placebo, 32% on 75 mg and 50% on 150–225 mg (P < 0.001 vs placebo). The number needed to treat for 50% pain-intensity reduction at 150–225 mg was 4.5. Nausea and somnolence were the most common treatment-emergent adverse events, and seven patients on venlafaxine had clinically important ECG changes during treatment.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is confined to the 150–225 mg dose: 75 mg (32%) barely separated from placebo (27%). Six weeks is the longest double-blind DPN exposure in this base, and the seven clinically important ECG changes belong beside any efficacy claim.
cards.source: Rowbotham MC et al. Venlafaxine extended release in the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Pain. 2004. PMID: 15288411. cards.headline: Razazian 2014 — DPN trial with NO placebo group: venlafaxine ranked last of three active drugs; pregabalin was more efficacious, with no significant superiority between carbamazepine and venlafaxine
cards.summary: Razazian 2014 — DPN trial with NO placebo group: venlafaxine ranked last of three active drugs; pregabalin was more efficacious, with no significant superiority between carbamazepine and venlafaxine
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-comparator trial in painful diabetic neuropathy, no placebo group (Razazian 2014) — report 2 of 3
cards.people: 257 patients with clinically definite painful diabetic neuropathy randomised at a single centre in Iran (Dec 2012–Dec 2013) to carbamazepine, venlafaxine or pregabalin in a double-blind parallel-group trial. There was no placebo group.
cards.result: Mean visual-analogue scores fell from 74.5 to 46.6 on venlafaxine, 74.5 to 39.6 on carbamazepine and 82.3 to 33.4 on pregabalin. Pregabalin was more efficacious than both other drugs; no significant superiority was shown between carbamazepine and venlafaxine. Sleep, mood and work-interference scores improved in all groups.
cards.watchOut: Without a placebo group this trial cannot show that venlafaxine beats no treatment — only how it ranked against two active drugs, where it finished last. Within-group falls from baseline are not efficacy evidence.

cards.people: 40 patients with painful polyneuropathy of mixed aetiology (not diabetes-specific) assigned to a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled three-way crossover of venlafaxine 225 mg/day, imipramine 150 mg/day and placebo, each for 4 weeks; 29 completed all three periods. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: 3 reports carded: exactly 1 placebo-controlled trial in diabetic neuropathy (Rowbotham 2004, N = 244, 6 weeks), 1 DPN active-comparator trial with no placebo group (Razazian 2014, N = 257), and 1 mixed-aetiology polyneuropathy crossover (Sindrup 2003, 40 assigned, 29 completers).
cards.result: The diabetes-specific placebo contrast rests on a single 6-week trial, and within it on the 150–225 mg dose alone (50% vs 27% pain reduction; NNT 4.5); the 75 mg dose was near-placebo. The active-comparator trial ranked venlafaxine last of three drugs, and the crossover supports a class-consistent analgesic effect in polyneuropathy generally, not in diabetes specifically. Seven clinically important ECG changes occurred on venlafaxine in the placebo-controlled trial. No report in this base exceeds 6 weeks of double-blind DPN exposure.
cards.watchOut: Never summarise this base as three placebo-controlled DPN trials — that composition error is exactly what this shelf exists to avoid. The Cochrane venlafaxine-for-neuropathic-pain review is programme support only and is not counted as a report here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Sodium valproate for painful diabetic neuropathy — one programme, three reports: pain scores improved in both placebo-controlled trials, nerve conduction never did, and there is no independent replication
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, does sodium valproate, compared with placebo (alone or in a factorial combination with glyceryl trinitrate spray), reduce neuropathic pain?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/complications/physiopathology · Diabetic Neuropathies/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Double-Blind Method · Electrophysiology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Neurons/drug effects/physiology · Neurons, Afferent/drug effects/physiology · Pain/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Pain Measurement · Time Factors · Valproic Acid/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Diabetic Neuropathies/drug therapy/physiopathology · GABA Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Neural Conduction/drug effects · Pain Measurement/methods · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Aspartate Aminotransferases/blood · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/physiopathology · GABA Agents/therapeutic use · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Nitroglycerin/therapeutic use · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Patient Selection · Placebos · Valproic Acid/therapeutic use · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Provenance first: all 3 reports come from one research group in one country, enrol 43–83 patients each and run 1–3 months — there is no independent replication anywhere in this base. Both placebo-controlled trials (Kochar 2002, 52 analysed, 1 month; Kochar 2004, 43 randomised, 3 months) found significant improvement on subjective pain scores (P < 0.05; p < 0.001) with electrophysiological changes not significant in either. The factorial trial (Agrawal 2009, 83 randomised) gave numbers needed to treat of 7 for valproate, 5 for glyceryl trinitrate spray and 4 for the combination. One patient in each of the first two trials stopped treatment for raised transaminases; valproate's teratogenicity and weight-gain record (homed in the epilepsy/pregnancy shelves) is cross-pointed on the face.

cards.people: Patients with type 2 diabetes and painful neuropathy in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial: 60 screened, 52 analysed over 1 month. Pain was scored with the short-form McGill questionnaire; motor and sensory conduction, amplitude and H-reflex were measured.
cards.result: Pain score improved significantly on sodium valproate compared with placebo at 1 month (P < 0.05). Changes in electrophysiological data were not significant. One patient developed raised AST/ALT after 15 days of treatment and stopped.
cards.watchOut: A 1-month trial of 52 analysed patients from the same group as reports 2 and 3 — there is no independent replication of this finding anywhere in the base. The significant finding is a subjective pain score; nerve conduction was null.

shelves.title: Desipramine for painful diabetic neuropathy — a very-small-N crossover base: 3 reports from 1990–92 totalling 96 assigned patients, none a parallel-group trial
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, does desipramine, compared with active placebo, clomipramine, amitriptyline or fluoxetine, reduce neuropathic pain?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Benztropine/therapeutic use · Depression/complications · Desipramine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Diabetic Neuropathies/complications/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Emotions/drug effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Clomipramine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Desipramine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Diabetic Neuropathies/drug therapy · Drug Evaluation · Phenotype · Sparteine/metabolism · Aged, 80 and over · Amitriptyline/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Desipramine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Fluoxetine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Infant, Newborn · Pain/drug therapy
shelves.balance: The counts lead: 3 reports, all 2–6-week crossovers from 1990–92, totalling 96 assigned patients (20 vs active placebo; 19 completers in a three-way crossover; 57 assigned across two studies, of whom 38 form the desipramine comparison) — no parallel-group trial exists in this base. The direction is consistent: 11 of 20 patients reported at least moderate relief on desipramine vs 2 on active placebo (Max 1991); both desipramine and clomipramine beat placebo in the three-way crossover, with three withdrawals for side effects on each drug (Sindrup 1990); and moderate-or-greater relief was 61% on desipramine vs 74% on amitriptyline, 48% on fluoxetine and 41% on placebo, with desipramine and amitriptyline both superior to placebo and not significantly different from each other (Max 1992). The row exists because desipramine is the least anticholinergic/sedating first-generation tricyclic and its founding trials were never agent-checked — not because the base is strong.

cards.headline: Max 1991 — active-placebo crossover, 20 patients: pain relief on desipramine was significant in weeks 5–6; 11 patients reported at least moderate relief on desipramine vs 2 on placebo
cards.summary: Max 1991 — active-placebo crossover, 20 patients: pain relief on desipramine was significant in weeks 5–6; 11 patients reported at least moderate relief on desipramine vs 2 on placebo
cards.type: Double-blind crossover trial vs active placebo, N = 20 (Max 1991) — report 1 of 3 in a very-small-N crossover base
cards.people: 20 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy in a double-blind crossover trial of 6 weeks of desipramine (mean dose 201 mg/day) vs active placebo.
cards.result: Pain relief with desipramine was statistically significant in weeks 5 and 6. Eleven patients reported at least moderate relief on desipramine, compared with 2 on placebo. Relief tended to be greater in depressed patients but was also observed in patients who did not show an antidepressant effect.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, one crossover, 1991. The comparator was an active placebo, which strengthens blinding but does not enlarge the base. This report can support a signal, never a settled effect size.
cards.source: Max MB et al. Efficacy of desipramine in painful diabetic neuropathy: a placebo-controlled trial. Pain. 1991. PMID: 1861872. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sindrup 1990 — three-way crossover, 19 completers: both clomipramine and desipramine significantly reduced neuropathy symptoms vs placebo; three patients withdrew due to side effects on each drug
cards.summary: Sindrup 1990 — three-way crossover, 19 completers: both clomipramine and desipramine significantly reduced neuropathy symptoms vs placebo; three patients withdrew due to side effects on each drug
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled three-way crossover, 19 completers (Sindrup 1990) — report 2 of 3 in a very-small-N crossover base
cards.people: 19 patients completed a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled crossover (2 + 2 + 2 weeks) of clomipramine, desipramine and placebo, with doses adjusted by sparteine phenotype (extensive metabolisers: clomipramine 75 mg/day, desipramine 200 mg/day).
cards.result: Both clomipramine and desipramine significantly reduced the symptoms of neuropathy on observer and self ratings compared with placebo; clomipramine tended to be more efficacious. Side-effect ratings did not differ between the drugs, and three patients withdrew due to side effects on each drug.
cards.watchOut: Two-week treatment periods in 19 completers, from 1990. Three withdrawals for side effects on each drug, in a base this small, is a substantial tolerability signal and belongs beside the efficacy reading.
cards.source: Sindrup SH et al. Clomipramine vs desipramine vs placebo in the treatment of diabetic neuropathy symptoms. A double-blind cross-over study. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 1990. PMID: 2271367. Registry ID: none in the record.
