cards.headline: Max 1992 — head-to-head crossover programme, 57 assigned in total: moderate-or-greater relief in 61% on desipramine (38 patients) vs 74% on amitriptyline, 48% on fluoxetine and 41% on placebo
cards.summary: Max 1992 — head-to-head crossover programme, 57 assigned in total: moderate-or-greater relief in 61% on desipramine (38 patients) vs 74% on amitriptyline, 48% on fluoxetine and 41% on placebo
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind crossover studies with cross-study first-period comparison, 57 assigned (Max 1992) — report 3 of 3 in a very-small-N crossover base
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind crossover studies in painful diabetic neuropathy: amitriptyline vs desipramine in 38 patients, and fluoxetine vs placebo in 46 patients; 57 patients were assigned in total, permitting cross-study comparison of first-treatment periods. Mean daily doses after titration: amitriptyline 105 mg, desipramine 111 mg, fluoxetine 40 mg.
cards.result: Moderate-or-greater relief occurred in 74% on amitriptyline, 61% on desipramine, 48% on fluoxetine and 41% on placebo. Both amitriptyline and desipramine were superior to placebo; the amitriptyline–desipramine difference was not significant, and fluoxetine did not differ significantly from placebo overall.
cards.watchOut: The desipramine figure (61%) comes from the 38-patient study, not from 57 desipramine patients — the 57 is the combined assignment across both studies. Desipramine's apparent parity with amitriptyline is a non-significant difference in a small crossover, not demonstrated equivalence.
cards.source: Max MB et al. Effects of desipramine, amitriptyline, and fluoxetine on pain in diabetic neuropathy. New England Journal of Medicine. 1992. PMID: 1560801. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: 3 crossover reports from 1990–92 totalling 96 assigned patients (20 + 19 completers + 57 assigned); the largest desipramine arm is 38 patients. No report is a parallel-group trial, and no period exceeds 6 weeks.
cards.result: All three reports point the same way — desipramine relieved pain more than placebo/active placebo and about as much as amitriptyline — but every estimate rests on very small crossover samples from 1990–92. Tricyclic harms are on the face: three withdrawals for side effects on each drug in the three-way crossover, and the class's cardiac and anticholinergic record is cross-pointed to the older-adults initiation shelf (#5724). Desipramine's interest is as the least anticholinergic/sedating first-generation tricyclic — a tolerability rationale, not a stronger evidence base.
cards.watchOut: Small-N labelling applies to this whole shelf: do not quote any percentage from these reports without its denominator beside it. Amitriptyline's homed questions (#3522 pathway comparison, #5724 initiation in older adults) ask different questions and share no anchors with this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Capsaicin 0.075% cream/lotion for painful diabetic neuropathy (PARTIAL slice beside the 8%-patch home #2697) — a split base: 1991–92 positives, a null 2019 placebo-controlled trial, and a 300-patient trial with no placebo group
shelves.question: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does low-concentration capsaicin cream/lotion (0.075%), compared with vehicle/placebo or an active topical comparator, reduce neuropathic pain?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL slice, stated plainly: pack #2697 asks only the clinic-applied capsaicin 8% patch question in painful DPN (read in full at build); this shelf asks the self-applied 0.075% cream/lotion question, which #2697 does not ask, and borrows none of the patch's evidence. The base is 4 reports — PMID 1737537 is a same-subjects sensory companion of the 22-subject trial, never a fifth report. The split leads: the two positive vehicle-controlled reports are from 1991–92 (22 refractory subjects; and one whose abstract documents no N — N not documented), the only modern placebo-controlled report (2019 crossover, 42 enrolled) was null on every pain measure, and the largest report (300 patients, vs turpentine oil) had no placebo group and showed no between-group difference (p = 0.399).

cards.headline: Tandan 1992 — vehicle-controlled trial, 22 subjects refractory to conventional therapy: capsaicin 0.075% cream beat vehicle on physician's global evaluation (P = 0.038); mean pain intensity fell 16% vs 4.1%
cards.summary: Tandan 1992 — vehicle-controlled trial, 22 subjects refractory to conventional therapy: capsaicin 0.075% cream beat vehicle on physician's global evaluation (P = 0.038); mean pain intensity fell 16% vs 4.1%
cards.type: Vehicle-controlled trial of capsaicin 0.075% cream (Tandan 1992) — report 1 of 4 in this slice
cards.people: 22 randomly assigned subjects with chronic severe painful diabetic neuropathy unresponsive or intolerant to conventional therapy, in an 8-week controlled study of capsaicin 0.075% cream vs vehicle applied four times daily. This is report 1 of the 4 reports in this slice's base.
cards.result: Capsaicin was more beneficial than vehicle on physician's global evaluation (P = 0.038) and categorical pain severity (P = 0.057). Mean pain-intensity decrease was 16% on capsaicin vs 4.1% on vehicle, and mean pain relief 44.6% vs 23.2%. In open-label follow-up, approximately 50% reported improved pain control or were cured. Application-site burning decreased in magnitude and duration over time.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two subjects, all refractory to or intolerant of conventional therapy — an enriched population whose results do not transfer to unselected painful DPN. The categorical pain-severity reading (P = 0.057) did not reach significance.
cards.source: Tandan R et al. Topical capsaicin in painful diabetic neuropathy. Controlled study with long-term follow-up. Diabetes Care. 1992. PMID: 1737545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tandan 1992 sensory-function companion — LABELLED COMPANION of the trial above, the SAME 22 subjects, NOT a fifth report: no significant warm or vibration threshold change after 8 weeks
cards.summary: Tandan 1992 sensory-function companion — LABELLED COMPANION of the trial above, the SAME 22 subjects, NOT a fifth report: no significant warm or vibration threshold change after 8 weeks
cards.type: Sensory-function companion of Tandan 1992 — same 22 subjects, labelled companion slice, NOT an independent report
cards.people: The same 22 subjects as the therapeutic trial carded above, examined for thermal and vibration thresholds after 8 weeks of capsaicin 0.075% cream or vehicle, with a smaller open-label extension to 32 weeks. This card is a labelled slice of report 1's subjects and is never counted as an independent report.
cards.result: There was no significant change in warm and vibration thresholds; the cold threshold was significantly reduced by capsaicin and vehicle creams to an equal degree. In the open-label phase there was no significant effect on sensory thresholds after up to 32 weeks. The authors state the small number of subjects does not justify an inferential statement on safety.
cards.watchOut: Counting this paper as a second trial overstates the base by one — the base of this slice is 4 reports, not 5. Its safety reassurance is explicitly limited by its own authors to hypothesis level.
cards.source: Tandan R et al. Topical capsaicin in painful diabetic neuropathy. Effect on sensory function. Diabetes Care. 1992. PMID: 1737537. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Scheffler 1991 — vehicle-controlled trial with N not documented in its abstract: 90% of capsaicin-treated patients improved over 8 weeks

cards.headline: Kulkantrakorn 2019 — the only modern placebo-controlled report, and it is NULL on every measure: no significant improvement with capsaicin 0.075% lotion in intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses
cards.summary: Kulkantrakorn 2019 — the only modern placebo-controlled report, and it is NULL on every measure: no significant improvement with capsaicin 0.075% lotion in intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses
cards.type: Randomised double-blind crossover placebo-controlled trial (Kulkantrakorn 2019) — report 3 of 4 in this slice, and its only modern placebo-controlled report
cards.people: 42 subjects with painful diabetic neuropathy enrolled in a randomised double-blind crossover placebo-controlled trial of capsaicin 0.075% lotion vs placebo, each for 8 weeks with a 4-week washout; 27 completed at least one 8-week period.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analysis showed no significant improvement in pain control with capsaicin lotion compared with placebo on any pain measure, and the proportions achieving 30% or 50% pain relief did not differ; per-protocol analyses were consistent. Capsaicin lotion was well tolerated but local skin reactions were common.
cards.watchOut: This 2019 null must always be printed beside the 1991–92 positives. A crossover in which only 27 of 42 enrollees completed even one period also carries attrition risk, but its direction — no separation on any measure — is the opposite of the older trials'.
cards.source: Kulkantrakorn K et al. 0.075% capsaicin lotion for the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy: A randomized, double-blind, crossover, placebo-controlled trial. Journal of Clinical Neuroscience. 2019. PMID: 30472337. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Musharraf 2017 — largest report (300 patients) but NO placebo or vehicle group: capsaicin was indistinguishable from turpentine oil (between-group p = 0.399)
cards.summary: Musharraf 2017 — largest report (300 patients) but NO placebo or vehicle group: capsaicin was indistinguishable from turpentine oil (between-group p = 0.399)
cards.type: Randomised active-comparator trial with no placebo/vehicle group (Musharraf 2017) — report 4 of 4 in this slice
cards.people: 300 patients already taking one oral drug for painful diabetic neuropathy, randomised to topical capsaicin or topical turpentine oil for 3 months. There was no placebo or vehicle group.
cards.result: Visual-analogue scores fell in both groups (7.91 to 5.10 on capsaicin; 7.83 to 5.20 on turpentine oil), with no significant between-group difference (p = 0.399); efficacy was recorded in 53% on capsaicin and 47% on turpentine oil.
cards.watchOut: Within-group falls on an unblinded-feeling topical comparator cannot separate drug effect from natural history, background oral therapy and expectation. This report's size (300) must not be allowed to outweigh its missing control group.
cards.source: Musharraf MU et al. Comparison of topical capsaicin and topical turpentine Oil for treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy. Journal of Ayub Medical College Abbottabad. 2017. cards.people: 4 reports in this slice (plus 1 labelled same-subjects companion, never counted): 2 vehicle-controlled trials from 1991–92 (22 subjects; N not documented), 1 modern placebo-controlled crossover that was null on every measure (42 enrolled, 27 completing a period), and 1 active-comparator trial of 300 patients with no placebo group. The clinic-applied capsaicin 8% patch is a different formulation and dose, homed at pack #2697, and none of its evidence is borrowed here.
cards.result: The split is the answer: two small, old, refractory-population vehicle-controlled trials favoured the cream, the only modern placebo-controlled trial found nothing, and the largest trial could not distinguish capsaicin from turpentine oil. The sensory companion found no threshold harm in the same 22 subjects, with the authors' own small-N caveat. The tested concentration (0.075%) is named as the publications give it, under the clarification exception — clarification, not promotion.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this slice with pack #2697 (8% patch) or pack #2565 (cream formulations in postherpetic neuralgia, a different condition) — cross-points only, no shared anchors.
